project_name: TURKEY - International Organization for Migration
Columbia - Action against Hunger
Provision of Shelter and NFI assistance to vulnerable populations affected by conflict and displacement in Syria
project_objective:
The purpose of the Shelter and NFI intervention is to provide life-saving and life-sustaining shelter and NFI support and contribute towards the resilience and cohesion of communities and households by improving housing and related community/public infrastructure in Syria.  NRC will respond to the diverse problems and needs faced by vulnerable populations throughout Syria through the delivery of a multi-faceted Shelter response. The different components of NRC’s Shelter project are intended to contribute to HRP Shelter & NFI Sector Objectives 1 and 2. 
NRC will deliver this project through a combination of direct, partner-led and hybrid modalities. Partner names have not been included in this submission for reasons of confidentiality
Geographic areas will be targeted based on the severity and scale of needs, inter-agency coordination at hub-level, and access. NRC will provide assistance to vulnerable conflict and displacement-affected populations, including IDPs, refugees, members of host communities, IDP and refugee returnees, and non-displaced households suffering the effects of the conflict. All interventions will seek to prioritize the most vulnerable households. Where appropriate, multi-sectoral vulnerability scoring techniques will be used that integrate vulnerability indicators
In line with the NRC Syria Country Strategy, the Shelter programme will include emergency, transitional and recovery response options. These options are not intended to be “standalone” and may be delivered in conjunction with one another. The proportion of emergency, transitional and recovery related outputs will vary between different parts of Syria, depending on context, needs, access and implementation modality in those locations. Shelter and WASH activities will be delivered as a fully-integrated joint programme where relevant. The implementing modality (direct, partner-led or hybrid) will be defined by the Area Office based on access constraints and NRC/partner capacity.
The Shelter programme will contribute to NRC’s:
-	Emergency response through the provision of one-off support as part of an integrated, multi-sector response in accordance with the Emergency Preparedness and Response Plans (EPRPs).  Comprises of three Result Areas: Temporary Shelter(with an overall target of 1600 assistance reaching 9600 ind), Household Assets (which includes shelter NFI kits of Blankets, mats, Jerry cans, plastic sheets and kitchen set, the overall target = 7,352 kits reaching 38,360 individuals) and Support to Education in Emergencies.
-	Provision of medium-term shelter support at household and settlement-level to populations living in and out-of-camps.  Comprises of three Result Areas: Community Infrastructure and Services in Camps, Temporary Shelter and Support to Education Pathways. 
-	Provision of longer-term assistance at household and settlement-level in urban and peri-urban out-of-camp areas.  Comprises of two Result Areas: I-WISH (i.e. Housing Rehabilitation) targeting 976 Households reaching 4,880 ind), and school rehabilitation (see NRC’s Education project submission). 
All “permanent” Shelter activities require a full HLP Due Diligence process to verify ownership and usage rights to a reasonable level of certainty.

project_name: Provision of Effective and Sustainable Health and Nutrition services for conflict affected population in West Darfur ,West Kordofan and South Kordofan State
project_objective:
The intervention aims to link to the strategic objectives of the HRP 2017-2019 by providing assistance during or in the aftermath of any disaster, provide displaced populations and host communities with basic services and improve the nutrition of vulnerable residents in the targeted areas. The main focus is on providing basic health and nutrition services for both IDP and host communities in the program areas and providing a response in case of emergencies in the target area if they occurring program implementation.
In each location the activities will focus on improving the health and nutritional status of the beneficiaries.  The activities will continue to support the nutritional activities at the chosen locations based on on CMAM approaches, using well trained nutrition staff. This will include the screening and treatment of children under five for acute malnutrition as well pregnant and lactating mothers in the host and IDP communities.
The program will provide SAM and MAM treatment services through fixed and outreach centres using OTP and SFP programs respectively. There will also be the provision of systemic treatment of antibiotic and vitamin supplementation to all the children who need it. For prevention and to raise awareness routine nutritional education and IYCF counselling will be provided during clinic days.

For health facilities will be provided with basic  preventive and curative services  to treat common ailments .This provision of basic health services will include immunization for all children, referral of complicated cases and provision of reproductive care.

Concern will ensure protection for its beneficiaries by providing ensuring that all the staff, partners engaged in the
Delivery of services sign Concern participants Protection policy (PPP) and strictly implemented. 

A key component of this project is the training of the health workforce and each cadre of staff will be provided with relevant on the job training as well as any other additional trainings which will be beneficial to their role. Care will also be taken to ensure that none of the activities implemented negatively affect the environment. This means the project will use ensure proper disposal of waste products from the service delivery such as empty therapeutic and supplementary sachets will be returned to the services delivery points for proper disposal.
As part of improving sustainability, the project will collaborate with WHO and the NMSF for the procurement of medicine and medical supplies. This will shorten the delivery time frame as well as use local structures to facilitate delivery

project_name: Comprehensive Nutrition project to address under-nutrition among vulnerable populations living in the Registered , Makeshift camp and  in Ukhia & Teknaf.
project_objective:
Needs: 
According to the latest (October 2018) Inter Sector Coordination Group (ISCG), as of 04 September 2018, there are approximately 921,000 Rohingya Refuges (215,796 families) in Cox Bazar. Out of these, 631,000 refugees are in Kutupalong and Balukhali Expansion Sites, 275,000 refugees in other camps and 15,000 refugees in Host Communities. This constitute one of the biggest refugee crises in the world at present. The majority of the population are women and children (52% are women and girls, 55% are children under 18).
  
Despite the response, An Integrated Nutrition Assessment (SMART) conducted in Kutupalong makeshift and Nayapara registered camp from 28 April to 28 May 2018, indicates the prevalence of acute malnutrition among all children 6-59 months of age is considered serious, if not emergency, according to WHO emergency threshold (12% & 13.5% respectively) . The survey conducted in makeshift settlements indicates that nearly half of children suffered from anemia (Hb<11.0g/dL), represents a severe public health problem according to WHO threshold (40%).
Data from a two-week recall of diarrhea, acute respiratory infection, and fever are concerning indicating a high disease burden among children under five. The prevalence of Diarrhea has reduced from 41.3% in November 2017 to 20.9% in May 2018 in make shift settlements while similar decline recorded in Nayapara RC from 34.3% to 23.9%.  According to May 2018 SMART survey result the prevalence of Acute respiratory tract infection is 20.1% (Round 1-57.7%) and 21.5% (round 1-50.3%) in Makeshifts and Nayapara RC respectively.  The same survey finding indicates that, the rate of fever without cough has increased from 25.2% to 40% in Makeshifts and from 16.9% to 40.5% in Nayapara within the six-month gap between the two surveys.
In July and August 2018, SLEAC assessment (quantitative and qualitative) was conducted by the Nutrition Sector in SAM (OTPs) and MAM services (TSFPs). A total of 10,742 cases were screened from five zones within the refugees camp. Results indicate that, despite considerable efforts, 27.7% (95% CI: 22.5-32.9%) of SAM cases were covered by OTP services and
34.1% (95% CI: 31.9-36.4%) of MAM cases were covered by TSFP services
There is a need to maintain the existing services, while continuing to explore scaling up SAM treatment through implementation of IYCF integrated Stabilization Centers (SC) and Outpatient Therapeutic Programme (OTP) programmes to address the needs of Rohingya refugee population. In addition, it is crucial to monitor the nutrition status and situation of the new refugee population for programming and adaptive response. Therefore, nutritional assessments will be conducted to determine the nutritional status of children and woman and compare it with Round 2 SMART survey result and plan for further assessments in the coming year to monitor the situation and respond accordingly. 
Activities or outputs: 
1. Screening, identification,  refferal of children and PLW with acute malnutrition
2. Management of SAM & MAM 
3. Inpatient Management of SAM with complicated cases
4. Prevention based program (IYCF)
5. Community Mobilization(Male Forum, Female Forum, Model Mother, Mother led MUAC, School Nutrition Program, IFA/MNP distribution)

project_name: Treatment and prevention of moderate acute malnutrition in South Sudan
project_objective: South Sudan continues to present a complex humanitarian and food and nutritional security situation, characterized by national and localized conflicts, displacements and a deteriorating economic climate. An estimated 1.5 million children under five years, and pregnant & lactating women are acutely malnourished. Similarly, 4.4 million people (43% of the population) are estimated to be facing crisis, emergency or catastrophe (IPC Phases 3, 4 and 5) acute food insecurity (IPC, 2018). The proportion of ad hoc localized nutrition surveys reporting global acute malnutrition (GAM) levels above the World Health Organization (WHO) emergency threshold of 15 percent was 57% among the 37 SMART surveys conducted between January and September 2018. About 76% of the SMART surveys conducted during the same period and locations in 2017 and 2018 reported GAM prevalence above the emergency threshold (≥15%). The persistent high malnutrition levels are attributed to high levels of food insecurity, displacements, conflict and poor infrastructure which hamper availability and access to basic health and nutrition services, low harvests, dysfunctional markets, poor infant young child feeding (IYCF) practices and high morbidity. The project will ensure that populations affected by conflict and displacement have access to emergency nutrition services in order to prevent morbidity and mortality due to acute malnutrition. WFP will continue to work with cooperating partners to support an emergency nutrition response through blanket supplementary feeding (BSFP) and treatment services for moderate acute malnutrition targeting children aged 6-59 months, pregnant & lactating women, and people living with HIV/TB across South Sudan. BSFP and targeted supplementary feeding programme (TSFP) services are provided both to IDPs and host populations. WFP also conducts direct delivery of life-saving nutrition services in hard-to-reach areas under the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM). The project implementation will use an integrated approach through synergies with activities supported by other clusters (health, FSL, WASH).

project_name: Supporting Recovery Of Economic Sector and Economic Stability in Ar-Raee and Azaz in Northern Syria
project_objective:
The project aims to recover and expand the economic situation of the returnees, Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) and host community business owners in the Aleppo governorate of Northern Syria, specifically targeting Ar-Ra'ee and Azaz sub-districts as hot spots for high number of returnees and IDPs. 
These early recovery efforts will be achieved by, firstly, conducting a needs assessment on understanding the factors of production (Labor, Capital, Input and Technology) for Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) which will lead to development of customized business development plans for local SMEs; and secondly, by providing a combination of business development services in the form of consultancy and seed grants based on the needs of the local businesses to revive and enhance the production capacities of local businesses in the targeted locations.
The overall aim of this intervention is to improve the local population’s access to the labour market by stabilizing and/or expanding local businesses in order to generate further jobs. In order to enhance social cohesion and reduce competition for resources, the project will target 360 businesses, supporting 30% IDPs and 70% host community enterprises, including 54 female business owners.
The factors of production needs assessment will be conducted in the form of a base and end-line multi-sectorial assessments on the local economy in the targeted locations, defining the gaps in factors of production as well assessing the causes of these gaps, their effect on the production capacity of local SMEs in the selected locations.
Upon completion of the needs assessment, WATAN will conduct a concentrated assessment among potential beneficiaries (business owners) to understand the operational status and size, their business production rates, financial situation, potential absorption and growth capacity. Assessed businesses will be filtered through a prioritization system according to their operational status, estimated capital size, number of employees and their market share. Integrating a tailored response model into early recovery efforts will ensure the restoration of productivity and expansion of economic activity at the local level. 
Upon acceptance into the programme, WATAN will be responsible for providing business development services through a combination of consultancy and seed grants. 
The support package can contribute towards the purchase of assets including consumable raw materials, initial premise rental payments, water and fuel infrastructure, electricity generation, repair of equipment and productive assets, the rehabilitation of work premises, and staffing costs. Business consultancy will continue to be offered after delivery of the support package, with WATAN coordinating referrals among IDPs and the host community to job opportunities that have been generated as a result of the project.

project_name: Critical Support to Revitalize of Essential Agricultural Production to Ensure Household Food Security and Livelihoods in the crisis affected Tribal Districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, Pakistan.
project_objective:
Natural and anthropogenic disasters take a variety of forms, but all of them can severely affect people’s lives and livelihoods through loss of assets. The very diverse geopolitical, terrain and climatic conditions of Pakistan make it susceptible to various forms of disasters. North-western part of the county is facing humanitarian crisis since last few decades. More specifically, the Newly Merged District of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (formerly known FATA) remained the most impoverished and marginalized part of the country and have experienced their worst period of anthropogenic disasters and instability in the last two decades. Almost half of FATA’s population (approx. 550,000 families) was displaced to other part of the country due to insurgency and counter-insurgency. In response to FATA Sustainable Return and Rehabilitation Strategy (SRRS), The government, with the help of humanitarian partners, have facilitated the displaced families to return to their home. The economic background of the returned household are quite weak. Displacement coupled with fragile economy, pervasive poverty and unemployment has rendered many families’ food insecure and susceptible to future shocks. The families that have returned have extremely limited capital to repair or rebuild homes, to re-establish livelihoods, or to restore critical community infrastructure. More than 97% population of tribal districts reside in the rural area which relies agriculture as the mainstay of their subsistence and livelihood. Local food production in tribal districts is far from adequate to meet the needs of the population.  The returned families have extremely limited capacity to re-establish their livelihoods. Their productive agriculture lands were left barren for many years. Large numbers of livestock were either lost or sold at lower prices, their shelters were destroyed and a substantial amount in the form of wheat straw, maize stock and fodder seeds has been damaged. 
Support is agriculture sector is time critical to ensure foods security and livestock-based livelihood of the affected families. If these families are not supported timely, severe food insecurity and nutrition challenges will emerge, especially for the more vulnerable and impoverished communities. The failure to respond immediately can also serve as a trigger for returning families to adopt negative coping strategies.
 The proposed activities will target approximately 458113 Individuals to resume their agriculture-based subsistence and to revitalize their agriculture-based livelihood in district newly merged districts

To improve the well-being of out of camp displaced, returnee and host community populations by ensuring access to well managed WASH services, well maintained WASH infrastructure at health and education facilities, and improved community level wastewater and solid waste management.
project_objective:
ACF’s WASH project for 2019 is in line with  the WASH cluster strategy 2019 for the HRP, aiming at improving and sustain the quality of the WASH services to the targeted population groups. The main objective of the project is to improve the well-being of out of camp displaced, returnee and host community populations by ensuring access to well managed WASH services, well maintained WASH infrastructure at health and education facilities, and improved community level wastewater and solid waste management. ACF will also work to support and build the capacities of local NGO’s. Within the 2019 HRP there is a drive to keep an emergency response capacity, but to focus more on sustaining and/or improving WASH services of all kinds when possible after immediate needs have been served.  During 2019 ACF aims to keep a focus on out-of-camp restoring basic WASH services for highly vulnerable population in areas of return, displacement, high risk and in other shocks areas s (cluster objective 2 and 3), and developing the linkage of recovery activities to support a more durable, sustainable and cost effective public service (cluster objectives 4). This will be achieved by capitalizing on ACF’s ongoing presence in Ninewa and Dohuk, and focusing on the added value of technically sound and well documented interventions, and by developing linkages with other core sectors such as MHPSS and livelihoods. During 2019, ACF will strengthen its current WASH intervention at schools and health facilities level, mainstreaming gender for the provided services.   ACF WASH intervention will target Ninewa, Dohuk, Anbar and Salah Al-Adin. Currently ACF has presence in the governorates of Ninewa and Dohuk and in 2019 new areas of intervention have been considered including Anbar and Salah Al-Adin, where needs are high.    
The intervention in 2019 is expected to target 123,000 individual of population in needs among Returnees, Host Community and IDPs in the mentioned governorates. According to IOM DTM as of 31 October 2018, the total number of returnees was at 4,113,660 across 1,568 locations of return. 1,866,594 IDPs remain in displacement. Ninewa (1,591,734 returnees) remains the highest governorate witnessing returns in October, followed by Anbar (1,283,292) and Salah al-Din (575,736). About 50% of IDPs report lack of basic services, including water and waste removal, as a reason they are not returning to their homes, and 20% or more of communities in the targeted areas report significant water access issues.

project_name: Provision of cash for food and In-kind food assistance to Vulnerable Palestine Refugees in Syria
project_objective:
The project envisages the distribution of cash assistance for food as well as in-kind food distribution for vulnerable Palestine Refugees. Food assistance is a critical component of UNRWA’s emergency response in Syria, as food insecurity continues to negatively impact the Palestine refugees who have become increasingly dependent on UNRWA to meet their minimum needs. UNRWA provides two types of food assistance to up to 418,000 Palestine Refugees: 1) in kind food baskets and 2) cash assistance for food. The interventions were designed to be complementary in addressing the food insecurity of Palestine refugees. 

UNRWA estimates that 418,000 out of 445,000 Palestine refugees in Syria will continue to require humanitarian assistance in 2019. However, UNRWA will be working towards a targeted approach of assistance that prioritizes the most vulnerable Palestine refugees.  A vulnerability assessment was conducted in 2018 to identify the most vulnerable Palestine refugees, who will be prioritized for assistance.  

In this sense, UNRWA is planning to adopt a two-tier approach for humanitarian food assistance in 2019. The focus will be on four main groups that can be identified through UNRWA’s registration system. These categories are: families headed by a person older than 60 years; families headed by a person with disability, and people with disabilities; female-headed families; and orphans. UNRWA estimates that 126,000 Palestine Refugees fall under the identified categories and will accordingly provide them with cash for food assistance amounting to USD 17.5 per person per month, and in-kind food assistance.  Meanwhile, UNRWA will provide the remaining 292,000 Palestine Refugees in need of assistance with cash for food equivalent to USD 8.75 per person per month to mitigate food insecurity among them and prevent them from falling into further poverty.

project_name: Provision of quality education services for children and adolescents in Northern Syria.
project_objective:
The context of Syria dramatically changed during 2018 leading to more displacement towards Northeast Syria (NES) and Northwest Syria (NWS), to either camps or within host communities in cities. Save the Children (SC) works to address the educational needs of children through different projects, locations and approaches. Evaluations were carried out for the latest education projects funded by the Norwegian Ministry of Foreign Affairs (NMFA) and the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC - in NWS only) in 2018 and these learnings, alongside current programming, were explicitly used in the design of this Action.

Children’s educational and protection needs are increasingly complex and must be addressed with flexible education service models with the eventual goal of reintegrating children into formal schools. Assessments conducted at enrolment ensure students are provided with the appropriate level and type of education services and self/home learning measures are used for children who are forced to keep moving with no access to traditional education services. Trainings for teachers and facilitators are offered in order to ensure quality learning outcomes and monthly participation activities are conducted with parents, teachers and members of the wider community. Research shows multiple benefits to classroom based SEL in education in emergencies, including a stronger preparedness for learning and increased concentration and sense of control. SEL is widely regarded as both a preventative and curative intervention for children. Through this project, SC will use its new Social Emotional Learning Foundations (SEL-F) programme. In addition, a comprehensive capacity building plan will be developed to ensure Child Protection (CP) is mainstreamed in Education services and that minimum standards are maintained.

The areas for implementation in NWS were selected based on numbers of out-of-school children and the capacity of the hosting communities to accommodate them within existing schools. Vulnerability criteria also priorities newly displaced children, unaccompanied and separated children (UASC) and children with disabilities. The protection severity rating of the locations selected is five out of six on average and it has been identified that the number of people in need for protection services is 313,772 in the targeted areas. In NES, SC’s Education team has worked in six camps - Newroz, Roj, Alhole, Ein Issa, Areesha and Mabrooka. These camps include very different groups of populations such as Iraqi refugees including Arabs and Yezedians, Syrian IDPs and foreign families).

SC recognizes the need for having a gender balanced recruitment and training strategy to ensure that dialogue with communities, implementation of activities, and coordination with stakeholders take the needs of both genders into consideration. An estimated 50%+ of the targeted children are girls, but girls will still be explicitly targeted and prioritized for inclusion. An equal number of female and male beneficiaries will be targeted by resourcing a gender balanced number of facilitators. SC teams identify barriers to participation and inclusion and implement measures to mitigate these, for example by separating parent/community group meetings, where cultural norms dictate to facilitate female participation; or by ensuring males are also recipients of our key messaging on education as they are usually the gatekeeper in household level decisions. In addition, diversity must be considered very carefully, especially regarding religion, ethnicity or nationality. The contents of education activities must be neutral and suitable for all children in the learning space.

This action is in line with SC Whole of Syria strategic plan. In NWS SC is co-leading the Education Cluster together with UNICEF and in NES SC established and has led the Education Working Group (EWG) for the education sector coordination since 2017.

project_objective: UNRWA will provide food assistance to Palestine refugee families surveyed through the Agency specific poverty based targeting system, identified as living on less than $3.87 per person per day. project_name: Facilitating early recovery & livelihoods through access to sustainable income generation opportunities, rehabilitation of community Infrastructures and restoration of governance in North East Nigeria
project_objective:
The crisis in north-east Nigeria has severely affected access to basic and social services and livelihoods, including trading and tannery activities. There are currently an estimated 5.5 million people in urgent need of early recovery and livelihoods assistance in 2019. Considerable efforts by the Nigerian Government, humanitarian and development actors have yet to close the huge remaining gaps in humanitarian and recovery needs. For many households, the conflict and subsequent displacement has led to a loss of housing, livelihoods, productive assets, and access to markets. About 86 per cent of households spend more than they earn, and 30 per cent are economically inactive.

According to a Household Survey conducted by the UN Development Programme (UNDP) to assess changes in livelihoods and economic recovery, 7 out of 10 people in the states of Yobe, Borno, Adamawa and Gombe were living below the World Bank extreme-poverty line of less than $1.90 a day, and economic opportunities were severely limited. The situation has only worsened since then. For the past three years, fields have gone unplanted and once-vibrant market places are near empty, with prices of goods skyrocketing to almost 150 per cent higher than in 2016. Insecurity has affected access to basic services, farmlands, markets, and other sources of livelihoods leading to high unemployment rates and low economic participation. The main coping strategies adopted by households include child labor, begging, debt contraction, and reduction in the number of meals per day and sale of assets.

In addition, the current conflict has worsened the pre-existing issues of exclusion and, in some cases, ruptured the bonds and relationships between and within groups and communities. Intra-communal structures and processes that traditionally regulated violence and resolved conflicts weakened. There are signs of social fragmentation as tensions based on ethno-religious, social and other divisions including between IDPs and host communities, are emerging. Borno State has the highest number of IDPs (1.4 million). 
This project seeks to contribute to the recovery and resilience-building of conflict-affected populations through a series of community support interventions. As people continue return to places of origin, there is an urgent and significant need to restore infrastructure, promote early recovery of economic means of livelihood, and facilitate a robust resilience building process. The proposed livelihood activities aim at strengthening the existing IOM emergency livelihood response. Livelihood Programme interventions will include Cash for Work (CFW), and promotion of livelihoods skills acquisition. Vocational skills training will be organized as per labor market assessments to create human capital, as necessary for the early recovery phase, with a special focus on youth. Each targeted beneficiary will also receive business start-up capital to establish small scale business. CFW and skilled labor schemes will support activities such as comprehensive neighborhood upgrades and light community infrastructure rehabilitation. 
Cash based interventions are planned for the project, for accessible areas where this is modality is feasible.  These will aim to empower affected populations, promote peaceful co-existence and benefit local economies.
While immediate early recovery needs must be addressed, enhanced coordination and complementarity between humanitarian, stabilization and development partners, through a people-centered approach, is also essential. The provision of technical and logistical support to community peace, and security committees’ operations as well as building the capacity of law enforcement bodies, including traditional/religious leaders, to prevent and respond to GBV incidents in compliance with human rights standards and through a survivor-centered approach, would be part of this endeavor. Additionally, IOM plans to guarantee the participation of women and men as equals to ensure that the special needs of each group are taken into consideration. The design of activities and services will address specific needs of each gender and age group, and specifically address women and girls specific needs, especially in terms of protection and access concerns. All activities related to this project will equally benefit women and men, girls and boys and will be delivered on a sustainable and equitable basis. In regard to assessments, monitoring and evaluation of gender specific needs and the impact of activities, IOM will engage with community structures on the ground in these locations during missions and set-up communication channels with them where possible. All activities will be centered on adherence to Do No Harm principles.

project_name: Gender-Based Violence Prevention and Response in North East Nigeria
project_objective:
Since the beginning of 2015, the North-East of Nigeria has witnessed an increase in violence perpetrated by the Non-State Armed Groups (NSAG), causing a major humanitarian crisis. The intensification of attacks has resulted in prolonged insecurity, exacerbating the plight of vulnerable civilians and triggering waves of forced displacement as well as violations of human rights resulting into forms of Gender-Based Violence (GBV). More 1.9 million individuals have been displaced due to the conflict and displacement continues to be a significant factor in 2018, with the highest number of displacements and returns taking place in Adamawa, Borno, and Yobe States (IOM Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) Round 23). Under this project, activities will focus on Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) and stand-alone protection interventions through MHPSS teams and resource centers/safe spaces, capacity building for humanitarian actors and GBV risk mitigation. . IOM’s MHPSS Mobile Teams and safe spaces will implement GBV prevention and response services in camp and camp-like settings. The proposed project aims to strengthen the existing protection and MHPSS response in the North-East, through the following areas of intervention:
i.	In response to cases of GBV in camp and camp-like settings, IOM’s MHPSS Mobile Teams will provide the following array of services: survivors of GBV will be provided with Psychological First Aid (PFA) (Level 1 and 3 of IASC MHPSS Intervention Pyramid) to attend to acute needs of the individual and support long-term interventions by linking them to specialized services (legal, medical, mental health); targeted survivors of GBV will be provided with structured psychosocial counselling, either as a stand-alone service or to complement other specialized services (Level 3 of IASC MHPSS Intervention Pyramid); Survivors of GBV will be referred to specialized services for case management and dedicated follow-up as appropriate (Level 4 of IASC MHPSS Intervention Pyramid); Families of GBV survivors will be provided structured psychosocial counselling and family support sessions (Level 3 of IASC MHPSS Intervention Pyramid). IOM will ensure that safety, confidentiality, respect and non-discrimination principles are adhered to, to protect the rights and dignity of survivors and promote resilience. IOM will also maintain and ensure a survivor-centered approach through making sure that the survivor’s informed consent is obtained before any action is taken.. Referral of survivors in need of other specialized services will be conducted as to benefit from comparative advantages across the agencies. Services part of the standard and discrete service package will be delivered by the support of IOM MHPSS safe spaces. The IOM MHPSS Safe Spaces act as resource centres to the community and support the carrying out of IOM’s MHPSS activities, recreational activities, livelihood activities, lay counselling and focus group discussions. 

ii.	To mitigate the risk of GBV in camp and camp-like settings IOM Mobile Teams will conduct sensitization and awareness campaigns in the targeted camp and camp-like settings (Level 1 and 2 of IASC MHPSS Intervention Pyramid). Campaigns will be tailored to the contextual needs of the community, and take in to account age and gender categories as well as socio-cultural, ethnic and religious aspects. This will help increase coverage and reach across population subgroups. Moreover, campaigns will be designed in participation with the community with equal representation regardless of gender, sex and identified vulnerabilities. 

iii.	To build the capacities of humanitarian actors in North East Nigeria by mainstreaming protection principals in programming and GBV risk mitigation.  . This will be carried out with the overall objective to improve the health, security, privacy and dignity of conflict-affected populations in displacement settings and in areas of return. With the objective and the centrality of protection in mind, IOM will seek to target humanitarian actors who deliver services in both displacement sites and areas of return.

project_name: Protecting and Promoting Mental Health and Psychosocial wellbeing of conflict affected population in North East Nigeria (Protection and MHPSS)
project_objective:
Since the beginning of 2015, the north-east of Nigeria has witnessed an increase in violence perpetrated by Non-State Armed Groups (NSAG), causing a major humanitarian crisis. The intensification of attacks has resulted in prolonged insecurity, exacerbating the plight of vulnerable civilians and triggering waves of forced displacement as well as violation of the human rights resulting into forms of Gender Based Violence (GBV). More than 1.9 million individuals have been displaced due to the conflict and displacement continues to be a significant factor in 2018, with the highest number of displacements and returns taking place in Adamawa, Borno, and Yobe State ((IOM Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) Round 23). Despite the fact that some displaced individuals have started to return home after relative security has been restored and more areas are now accessible to humanitarian actors, the situation on the ground remains dire and several remain in inaccessible areas. Through this twelve-month project under the HRP, IOM will contribute to protecting and promoting the mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) wellbeing of conflict affected people in Borno, Yobe and Adamawa states, by: a) supporting existing MHPSS mobile teams (direct MHPSS and protection service provision to affected population through MHPSS teams and safe spaces/resource centers); b) carrying out capacity building initiatives for protection and MHPSS service providers working with affected populations (IDPs and hosting communities) and supporting national institutions’ capacities; and c) Mainstreaming MHPSS, protection including Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA), counter-trafficking (CT) and GBV risk mitigation into humanitarian response sector activities. 

The project aims to protect and promote conflict affected populations’ mental health and psychosocial wellbeing. In particular, and in line with Nigeria’s Protection Sector’s objectives, the project will ensure the provision of targeted protection services through the provision of tailored MHPSS services. In addition, the project will contribute to the mainstreaming of protection and MHPSS approach through other sectors. With the overall aim of helping ensure programming in North-East Nigeria adheres to the diversity of protection needs of the affected population during the implementation of services, IOM will strengthen the capacity of humanitarian workers to mainstream protection principles in their programming. This will be carried out with the overall objective to improve the health, security/safety, privacy and dignity of conflict-affected populations in displacement settings and in areas of return. With the objective and the centrality of protection in mind, IOM will seek to target humanitarian actors who deliver services in both displacement sites and areas of return. Services in camp and camp-like settings and areas of return act in accord, whereas the improved resilience is essential to adapt to new situations and challenges associated with transition i.e. transitioning from a situation of displacement to re/integration in areas of return. Promotion of protection sensitive programming in camp and camp-like settings should seek to enhance the sustainability and impact of initiatives in areas of return, while they together promote coherent service provision and the sustainability of transition-oriented objectives. IOM’s capacity building activities will include training relevant stakeholders, partners and institutions involved in the field of mental health and psychosocial support. IOM will work closely with the national institutions, through its role as co-chair the MHPSS working group; working with the Borno state Ministry of Health as chair of the working group.

project_name: Projet d’Amélioration de la Sécurité Nutritionnelle dans le cercle de Tombouctou 2018 – 2020 (PASEN)
LEBANON - Terre des Hommes International
Réponse intégrée aux besoins urgents des populations vulnérables dans les zones affectées par les pics d'insécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle au Nord et au Sud du Mali (GAO et KAYES)
project_objective:
Cette proposition de projet contribue à l'OS1 et à l'OS2 du Cluster SA, ainsi qu'à l'OS transversal du Cluster SA (renforcement de capacités). Elle se situe dans les axes stratégiques prioritaires du plan de réponse humanitaire du Cluster Sécurité Alimentaire, à savoir :
1)	Le renforcement des moyens d’existence des ménages pauvres et de la capacité des acteurs nationaux et communautés locales
2)	Le soutien intégré aux populations vulnérables à l’insécurité alimentaire et à la malnutrition
3)	La réponse d’urgence aux besoins alimentaires de base (soudure) 
L’objectif spécifique de ce projet est d’améliorer la couverture des besoins alimentaires et non-alimentaires des ménages et renforcer les moyens d’existence des populations très affectées par les crises liées au climat et au conflit dans la région de Gao et répondre aux besoins nutritionnels essentiels pour les enfants de moins de 5 ans et les Femmes Enceintes et Femmes Allaitantes (FEFA) dans la Région de Kayes. 
Concernant les activités de sécurité alimentaire et moyen d'existence, les résultats attendus sont les suivants:
Résultat 1: Les besoins alimentaires et non alimentaires essentiels des ménages en insécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle sévère (IANS) sont couverts à travers une intervention coordonnée et intégrée,
Résultat 2: Les capacités de préparation, d’adaptation et de protection et renforcement des moyens d'existence des ménages très vulnérables à l’IAN sont renforcée face aux chocs agro climatiques et sécuritaires
Résultat 3: Les capacités des acteurs nationaux de coordination des réponses d'urgence et de résilience et des populations affectées sont renforcées
Résultat 4 : La gouvernance en matière de sécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle est renforcée
Les activités qui concourent à l'atteinte de ces résultats sont entre autres: L'assistance alimentaire et non alimentaire pendant la période de soudure et dans le cadre du RRM, l'appui aux activités agricoles et d’élevages, le CFW pour l'amélioration des revenus des ménages et la réhabilitation des moyens d'existence, le renforcement des capacités des acteurs et des communautés, l'appui à l'amélioration de la gouvernance des ressources naturelles, le plaidoyer. 
Ce projet appuiera 7580 ménages, soit 45480 personnes.

project_name: Assistance en protection pour les populations affectées par les conflits et les déplacements au nord et au centre du Mali
project_objective:
Ce projet vise à répondre en urgence aux problèmes de protection affectant les populations victimes au nord et au centre du Mali à travers des évaluations rapides de protection, des recommandations concrètes sur la réponse à apporter le cas échéant, et des réponses et/ou référencements rapides des problématiques identifiées. Ce projet s’appuiera sur le procédé RRM (Rapid Response Mechanism) déjà existant, et déploiera une équipé additionnelle, dédiée en protection, lors des alertes RRM, afin de conduire une évaluation des besoins en protection, et dans les 72 heures, émettre un rapport de synthèse des risques de protection, une analyse sensible au conflit et des réponses suggérées qui sera soumis et présenté dans les divers forums de coordination (notamment cluster protection régional et national). 
Ce projet permettra d’identifier les problèmes de protection à traiter immédiatement, soit en interne, soit avec des parties prenantes, dans le but d’avoir un impact immédiat pour la survie ou le maintien de la vie et de la dignité des populations touchées. 
Le projet fournira également des orientations aux acteurs humanitaires non liés à la protection sur la manière de fournir une assistance dans un contexte particulier et d’une manière compatible avec les principes humanitaires et de protection. Il fournira des informations critiques en vue d’actions éventuelles de plaidoyer et de surveillance continue, et enfin, assurera un suivi des problématiques identifiées et de l’implémentation des réponses appropriées.

project_name: NFI Coordination and Collective Shelters activities: strengthening Haiti’s local capacities, resilience and emergency preparedness
project_objective:
Due to its position over major tectonic faults, and being situated within the ""Hurricane Alley"", Haiti is exposed to extreme weather conditions and frequent natural disasters. Between 2004 and 2018, there has been two (2) earthquakes, twelve (12) notable hurricanes, four (4) tropical storms as well as major floodings. Most recently, on October 6th 2018, a 5.9 magnitude earthquake struck 20 km north of Port-de-Paix (North-West department). This earthquake was the strongest to hit Haiti since the devastating earthquake that struck the country on January 12th2010.
IOM, in its collaboration with DPC in disaster risk management and preparedness, was able to identify many lessons learnt and unresolved issues which are likely to worsen the effect of the upcoming tropical cyclone on the Haitian Population if not improved. Building upon solid results achieved in the previous interventions and based upon IOM’s lessons learned, as well as the key strategic priorities of the DPC 2018 Contingency Plan, IOM’s proposed Action aims to strengthen the capacities of the   disaster preparedness and response DPC  local authorities through a multifaceted intervention. 
IOM co-leads the Shelter and NFI Working Group (WG) with the Unité de construction de logements et bâtiments publics (UCLBP) and with the DPC, the Ministry of Social Affairs, the Ministry of Interior, the Entreprise Publique de Promotion de Logements Sociaux (EPPLS) and local authorities in the targeted areas.  As such, the proposed activities are designed in line with the Government’s response strategy and build upon IOM’s on-going activities in the North West, North and Artibonite Departments, Nippes and Grand’Anse . Since the 2018 Hurricane season, a platform to manage the NFI response in case of emergency is available. 
The overall objective of this project is to ensure emergency preparedness and response capacity of government authorities and communities through the availability of rapid NFI response, and to reinforce capacity of people managing collective shelters.   

Government of Haiti, Directorate of Civil Protection (DPC) ;
National System for Disaster Risk Management (SNGRD) ; 
Emergency Operation Centers, Departmental and Local (COUD, COUL) ; 15.000 vulnerable, disaster-affected families

project_name: Improving short-term and long-term food availability and livelihoods access in Western Equatoria, Western Bahr el Ghazal, Jonglei, Warrap, Upper Nile and Lakes states through investment in food production assets, and utilization and strengthening of local capacities
project_objective:
Through this project, ACTED will aim to provide food assistance to 45,000 HH (270,000 beneficiaries).

ACTED will provide immediate food assistance to insecure individuals (25,000 HH/ 150,000 beneficiaries) in Greater Equatoria, Western Bahr el Ghazal, Jonglei, Warrap, Upper Nile and Lakes states, while working with communities to invest in long term food security interventions. To provide immediate food assistance, ACTED plans to make unconditional cash transfers, conditional cash transfers, and restricted cash vouchers. Conditional cash transfers through Cash for Assets programs will not only improve purchasing power of beneficiaries, but will also contribute to creation, construction and rehabilitation of key livelihood assets such as water catchments and dykes to manage floods, community access roads to improve movement and access (particularly for producers to markets), and shallow wells to improve access to water. Restricted cash will focus on purchase of livelihood inputs and assets such as seeds and tools to enable beneficiaries invest on their lands thereby increasing amount of land planted, and addressing the challenge of seeds scarcity.

Long-term investment and capacity building on agricultural production, modern farming techniques and productive assets will also be achieved through resilience programming, targeting 20,000 HH (120,000 beneficiaries). ACTED will adopt the APFS model to facilitate learning and encourage transfer of knowledge and skills in modern farming techniques, encourage community engagement through participatory risk assessments, toward participatory planning and joint ownership of resources. Such an investment will be pegged on utilization of local capacities and knowledge, which will then be reinforced through interactive sessions toward realizing improved livelihoods, reduced gender inequality, inclusive economic and social growth, and overall transformation of communities. In addition, ACTED will also support agricultural production through seeds and tools distributions, seed multiplication farms, vegetable gardening, post-harvest management training and construction of post-harvest structures such as granaries and drying slabs. Moreover, ACTED will support pastoralists and livestock activities through training and support to community animal health workers (CAHWs) and awareness and vaccination campaigns.

Livelihood changes have been felt across the country due to constant displacement, economic downturn, pests and diseases especially the FAW, lack of quality seeds, failed or delayed rains, and poor post-harvest management. ACTED aims to alleviate extreme hunger through immediate lifesaving assistance and interventions to build on community resilience through models that address underlying causes of food insecurity, inequality, and promote transformative change in the face of man-made and natural disasters. This is in line with the FSL cluster integration model and response strategy where ACTED will focus on building sustainable livelihoods through inclusive programming.

project_name: Support to Emergency Response and Humanitarian Assistance of South Sudanese Refugees in Sudan (Darfur & South Kordofan)
project_objective:
For many years now, Sudan has been under a protracted crisis driven by conflict, natural disasters, poor governance and insecurity. As a result a considerable proportion of the population in Darfur, South Kordofan and Blue Nile were displaced.  The total number of people in need of humanitarian assistance in Sudan is estimated at 4.8 million including 2.3 million IDPs in conflict affected areas . In addition to that, an estimated 795,353 (421,537F, 373,816M) South Sudanese refugees live in Sudan; 46,430 (24,608F, 21,822M) of them live in South Kordofan, 51,847 (27,479F, 24,368 M) in South Darfur and 169,043 (89593F, 79,450M) in White Nile states. In 2017, about 192,404 (101,974F, 90,430 M) South Sudanese refuges crossed the border to Sudan; 60,429 (32,027F, 28,402M), 33,581(17,798F, 15,783M) and 26,810 (14,209F, 12,601M) of them arrived in White Nile, South Darfur and South Kordofan states respectively .

With reports of an upsurge in armed conflict and emergency levels of food insecurity in areas of South Sudan near the Sudan border, the influx of refugees will likely increase in the coming months. An estimated 64% live in out-of-camp settings, either collectively or dispersed, and an estimated 65% of them are children. As humanitarian actors have concentrated their limited efforts to refugee camps, very little attention has been given to those refugees who live scattered amongst host communities, making use of their limited resources that have been stretched already even before the arrival of refugees. The increasing refugee influx coupled with the ongoing conflict in Sudan has created a significant pressure on the already stretched infrastructure and basic services in different affected regions such as Darfur, South and North Kordofan and Blue Nile states. South Sudanese refugees particularly live in dire situation. They suffer from malnutrition, lack access to clean water, and health services. According to WFP 2017 report 78% of South Sudanese refugees surveyed in Darfur are food insecure. 

In two years, the project aims to strengthen community structures to improve basic services in WASH, Health and DRR thereby contributing towards improvement in resilience of the communities.

project_name: Supporting safe and protected communities in north Syria
project_objective:
In 2019, Mercy Corps aims to strengthen our protection interventions to support of the overall protection cluster objectives towards the provision of quality and integrated protection services with a focus on community-based approaches. In 2018, Mercy Corps supported community based child protection programming in North Syria. In 2019, Mercy Corps will deepen the commitment to protection programming, to projects that support youth and livelihoods, social cohesion partners in NES and integrating Mercy Corps projects to support vulnerable persons Mercy Corps has a three pillar approach to our protection response:
a) Continuing child protection programming in Syria with partners, with a focus on youth/adolescents and livelihoods where possible across northern Syria.
b) Providing cash assistance to vulnerable individuals and households, in coordination with protection actors in NES.
c) Embedding protection mainstreaming across all our activities, including strengthening data collection and referral systems.

The protection response supported by Mercy Corps is in line with the protection needs overview (including child protection) and protection severity ranking, with partners operating in locations ranked severity 5/6 in the HNO severity scale and in coordination with the child protection AoR. Partners are encouraged to coordinate their operational planning and response closely with their respective AoR.

project_name: Inter-agency NGO coordination mechanisms for the Syria response are enhanced
project_objective:
Syria International NGO Regional Forum (SIRF): In light of the increasingly regional nature of the Syrian Crisis, and the humanitarian and political effects on neighboring countries, a regionally focused forum was assembled in April 2013 to give voice to INGOs conducting humanitarian responses in the region and to facilitate their collective engagement. SIRF exists to serve the needs of its members and advocate on behalf of populations affected by the Syrian Crisis, articulated around 4 core functions: coordination, representation, advocacy and information management.

NES INGO Forum: The NES INGO Forum is the lead coordination body for NGOs working cross border from Iraq in Syria, as endorsed by the WoS Strategic Steering Group. The NES Forum objective is to ensure a principled, appropriate, accountable, and effective NGO humanitarian response in NES. The forum has made significant strides in ensuring a cohesive coordination structure and that NES response actors are well-represented. In the absence of formal UN leadership structures for cross border NGOs, the NES Forum will continue to take an expanded role in coordinating with the UN hub in Qamishli, the WoS Inter-Sector Group and OCHA Regional Office.
The NES INGO Forum continues to lead needs identification, strategic planning and response monitoring around the humanitarian response in NES. The NES Forum also enables humanitarian space for NGOs through leading on negotiations with local authorities around NGO access and protection concerns, and direct engagement with the UN in Qamishli. Additionally, the Forum seeks to enhance communication and information-sharing across hubs through management of inter-sector data flow through 4Ws and response matrices.

Humanitarian Access Team: The HAT plays a critical role in the transmission of granular reporting and analysis to the wider humanitarian community, taking a WoS learning approach. The HAT maintains an online map-based web platform with critical humanitarian and conflict-related data that is published on www.humanitarianaccessteam.org:
- Humanitarian Analysis: market locations, service provision, community assessments with stakeholder analysis, and access impediments.
- Conflict Analysis: key conflict incidents and trends, zones of control, military infrastructure and proximity to relevant programmatic areas, control of and access to road networks, local armed actor developments, and risk by sub-district.
- Thematic reports and situation reports improve strategic understanding of the conflict.
The HAT currently shares reports and access to the HAT web platform with approximately 1,000 users from 300 humanitarian actors, donors and policy makers. With local partners, the HAT shares various reports and are exploring ways to give access to the platform while maintaining security. As such, the HAT fills a critical gap in the coordination architecture by contributing to a better-understanding of social, political, economic, and conflict dynamics as they pertain to humanitarian needs and access.

project_name: Strengthen socio-economic well-being and adaptive capacities of people and communities in North Syria
project_objective:
The program’s overall objective is to strengthen resilience of communities in Northeast Syria. Mercy Corps emphasizes an integrated approach that builds households’ economic well-being as well as communities that are cohesive, inclusive and equitable. 
Mercy Corps’ Making Markets Work in Crisis approach will drive interventions to increase economic opportunities. Through this approach, Mercy Corps will target market support to key value chains, market actors, producers and local institutions. The specific implementation approach will vary according to the different contexts in Syria, taking into account market robustness, and the constraints. While some of the activities can include simple financial support to key businesses, such as micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) or smart subsidies using vouchers, other activities go deeper, analysing market systems and then providing support that enables both market actors and consumers to cope and recover through the local economy. These interventions may include better access to informal financial services and quality agricultural input supplies. For example, linking traders to bigger suppliers and providing them with better market information or short-run subsidies can reduce their operating risks. This improves traders’ ability to access key goods and sell these goods at affordable prices. Through this program Mercy Corps will address: 1) limited access to economic opportunities and financial services; and 2) the weak and insufficient, but slowly growing, body of private agricultural input suppliers in Syria.
Strengthening cohesive communities is vital to supporting the stability that is finally emerging in NES, and reinforcing post-conflict economic recovery. The combination of improving inter-communal relationships and reducing resource-based tensions will serve to prevent the escalation of some economic-based disputes into violence – for example between host and IDP communities over livelihood opportunities or social service provision – and reduce the ability of political actors to manipulate ethno-religious divisions and mobilise violence. To this end, and in close collaboration with local and neighborhood councils, Mercy Corps will implement community service projects to support local economic development and address resource-based tensions.

project_name: Conflict-affected households in North Syria benefit from food and livelihoods assistance.
project_objective:
Mercy Corps (MC) will respond to priority needs with life-saving and life-sustaining food and livelihoods assistance across the governorates of Al-Hasakeh, Aleppo, Ar-Raqqa, Deir-ez-Zor and Idleb. 

One-off multi-purpose cash transfers
Where money transfer agents are available and functional markets are accessible, one-off MPCT will be provided allowing HHs to determine and prioritise their most immediate needs. MPCT will be based on the survival minimum expenditure basket (SMEB) rates of each location, which includes food assistance. MCs Women Cash Pilot in Dar’a highlighted that when women in female-headed HHs are provided with cash, they retain the spending power within the HH and according to our findings (see Annex 10) were able to more effectively determine how to use the cash to meet the priority needs, as opposed to when cash was provided to male-headed HHs, or men within the HH. 
In-kind food
Where cash and vouchers are not feasible, MC will distribute Ready to Eat food rations for newly displaced HHs or a food basket for HHs with access to cooking facilities.
Repeat assistance to food insecure and underserved communities
Primarily targeting out of camp populations, MC will focus on vulnerable populations, such as IDPs, returnees and people of concern with repeat assistance. This will typically be provided for 3 months through MPCT, voucher or food assistance. This action will consider all HHs as potential beneficiaries and will target the most vulnerable regardless of their status. Where repeat cash or in-kind food is a viable and effective form of assistance for IDP camps, this option will be explored; with particular attention to potential protection concerns and pull factors.
Livelihoods 
MC provides vulnerable households with temporary income through CFW and contributes to the restoration of productive assets through promoting adapted techniques for food production at household level and distributing agricultural inputs.

project_name: LEBANON - Sonbola Group for Education and Development
JORDAN - Norwegian Refugee Council
EGYPT - United Nations Children's Fund
JORDAN - CARE International
Increase access to equitable quality essential health services for IDPs and vulnerable population  in South Sudan  through provision of immunization core pipeline and use of Rapid Response Mechanism
project_objective:
In line with UNICEF’s Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) and Core Commitments for Children, UNICEF will continue to provide for South Sudan’s humanitarian affected populations, especially children under 5 years and pregnant and lactating women and girls, with equal access to quality preventive and curative health services, and respond to diseases outbreaks. To achieve this, UNICEF adopts a two-pronged programme approach by which static and mobile mechanisms are put in place to support humanitarian delivery in a complementary manner. Integrated Rapid Response Mechanisms (IRRM) activities enable UNICEF, through direct implementation, to provide high impact and immediate lifesaving emergency responses. 

This project aims to increase access to quality equitable essential primary health care interventions through IRRM and provide a core pipeline to increase access to quality equitable immunization services by vulnerable populations living in host communities and internally displaced persons (IDPs) living in POCs, formal IDP camps or host communities in conflict affected areas in South Sudan.
The activities to be implemented are:
•	Procurement and distribution of emergency vaccines.
•	Procurement, distribution and maintenance of cold chain equipment
•	Technical support for improved vaccine and cold chain management
•	Training of front line partners of vaccine and cold chain management
•	 Conduct 36 RRM missions (3 per month) in the project duration will include: 

The expected beneficiaries of the immunization core pipeline activities are  150,000  IDP children aged 6 months-years (78000 females and 72000 males). These children will benefit from emergency measles vaccines and cold chain equipment to be procured.

The expected beneficiaries of the IRRM mission are estimated 30,000 individuals (16,600 female and 13,400 male). These will include children aged 6 months-15years who will be reached with immunization services and curative consultations and pregnant women who are expected to benefit from ANC services, tetanus toxoid vaccination, curative consultations and the provision of long lasting insecticide treated nets (LLITN).

project_name: Giving childhood a second chance in North East Nigeria

This will be achieved by providing responsive case management services and cross-sectoral specialized services, building resilience by providing community based mental health and psychosocial support, reintegration of children who have suffered grave child rights violations including survivors of GBV and strengthening of community based mechanisms to prevent and respond to child protection incidences. Continued advocacy and programming on the situation of grave child rights violations in northeast Nigeria will be supported with focus on the engagement of duty-bearers, children and community members. 
UNICEF will provide financial and technical support to assess the capacity gaps within the Child Protection Sub-Sector and to implement prioritized capacity development actions to strengthen institutional, technical and coordination capacities for delivery of child protection services.

project_name: Enhancing the protection environment for crisis affected populations in NW Syria through provision of integrated protection services, including case management and legal support on CSD and HLP
project_objective:
IOM will continue to provide and further expand its provision of integrated protection services to conflict-affected populations across NW Syria in dedicated community centres. Services include:
•	Specialised child protection and gender-based violence (GBV) case management
•	Psycho-social support (PSS)
•	Protection monitoring (on-site and mobile teams)
•	Legal support (civil status documentation and housing, land and property)
•	Community mobilization and outreach

Overall, IOM will directly support 50,000 beneficiaries (10000 men, 17500 women, 12500 girls and 10000 boys) across NW Syria through the provision of integrated protection services including legal support, community-based and individually targeted protection interventions. Project locations are Al-Bab, Darkoush, Ariha, Maaret Elkhwan (IOM Planned Camp) and Afrin. The purpose of these interventions is to mitigate and reduce protection risks and vulnerabilities for crisis-affected populations, with a focus on CP and GBV case management and providing access to legal information and support with regards to civil status documentation and HLP. Specifically, activities comprise of:

•	Provision of integrated protection activities in Darkoush community center which provides a space where men, women, boys and girls can gain access to specialized protection services, including GBV and CP case management, obtain specialized information/legal support on Civil Status Documentation (CSD)/Housing Land and Property (HLP), and receive information on services available in the wider area. The project, running from Sept 2018 - June 2019, will assist an overall 6,000 beneficiaries. 

•	Provision of protection services in Al-Bab, Aleppo Governorate, to ensure that a greater number of Syrians have access to information and protection services in their community. Services provided include GBV and CP case management, information/legal support on Civil Status Documentation (CSD)/Housing Land and Property (HLP), and community outreach on services available in the area. The project started in September 2018 and will end in December 2019 and assist an overall of 15,000 individuals.

•	Provision of integrated protection services at IOM’s Planned Camp in Maaret ElKhwan to provide the full range of integrated protection services; namely PSS, CP and GBV case management, legal support and protection monitoring through in-site and mobile teams. These services will also be offered at Maarzaf community centre in Ariha. Both projects will run from March 2019 to December 2019 and assist 7,500 beneficiaries respectively.

•	Provision of child protection services in two centres in Ariha and Taftanaz. Full CP case management, PFA and PSS will be provided, with a focus on children with special needs. Parenting session will be provided to both men and women to mainstream child protection concepts and contribute to reducing the risks of child abuse. Throughout 2019, the project will assist an overall of 14,000 beneficiaries.

In addition, HLP Due Diligence support across XB Clusters is ongoing and will be continued throughout 2019, including through the formulation of sector-specific guidance on how to minimize the risks of contributing to HLP grievances and appropriate trainings of humanitarian workers. This work will be closely aligned with the XB HLP Technical Working Group.  In addition, IOM will conduct assessments on key HLP issues around early returns, risks and challenges in accessing HLP documentation in NW Syria and existing formal and alternative/complementary HLP dispute resolution mechanisms to identify best practices and recommendations for HLP programming, and development of key messages on HLP. The findings of these assessments will inform IOM’s ongoing Due Diligence activities as well as legal capacity-building for humanitarian workers and first line responders on HLP core concepts, providing much-needed sensitization of front line responders in HLP issues.
