project_name: IM support for the CCCM Cluster and Partners (REACH Initiative)
Provision of emergency shelter and NFI assistance for conflict affected populations in Iraq
project_objective:
In 2019, ACTED plans to continue to respond to the emergency shelter and SNFI needs of vulnerable households affected by conflict across Iraq. ACTED will target IDPs living in formal camps and informal sites, returnees, and host communities. Intention surveys indicate that the majority of IDPs do not intend to return to their area of origin. Almost 500,000 IDPs continue to live in camps. Critical SNFI service provision gaps have been identified in camps, including the need to upgrade AFAD tents in identified camps in Dohuk and Kirkuk. Under this project, ACTED thus plans to replace up to 6,600 AFAD tents in identified camps in Dohuk and in Kirkuk.

ACTED aims to provide highly vulnerable returnees with assistance packages at their place of return. As the recent conflict in Iraq has left numerous shelters damaged, ACTED furthermore plans to support at least 300 individual shelter rehabilitation for returnee households through cash and /or conditional voucher assistance Finally, as discussed with the SNFI Cluster, ACTED plans to provide up to 1,500 Sealing Off Kits and 1,500 NFIs to meet emergency needs in out of camp settings. ACTED’s geographical coverage will include the Kirkuk, Diyala, and Ninewa governorates.

project_name: Camp Coordination and Camp Management for the Basateen Al Sheoukh IDP Camp and the establishment of a CRC
project_objective:
CAOFISR will continue its coordination and management of Basateen Al Sheoukh IDP Camp in order for the camp residents to receive the timely distribution of aid and shelter, while mitigating risks and hazards within the camp. Due to the expressed need from the families, in addition to the CCCM activities, CAOFISR will be focusing on resilience based activities that will assist families with returning home. 

This project's objective is ""This project is aimed at supplying the camp population with life saving support through CCCM activities, while simultaneously providing them with vocational trainings that will assist their return home."" The main objective is to allow for CAOFSIR, as the CCCM actor, to empower the camp population to begin functioning independently, identify needs that can also assist that process, and coordinate the assistance. Current mechanisms will be updated and reinforced to ensure the sharing of information is efficient, and that the government takes a larger role with managing the population in need.""

Protection is the main concern for CCCM, and through all activities, the mitigation of risks and hazards are done through the program activities. The activities are aimed to support the camp population by maintaining the database of the camp population, identifying needs within the camp, referring individuals to the correct authorities, mitigating risks and hazards, supplying individuals with financial aid through CFW activities, providing trainings and awareness session on GBV and gender equality and establishing government structures. The goal of this project is to create a plan forward for the families in the camp so that they become less dependent on aid and the responsibility of their livelihood shifts from the CCCM partner, to themselves. 

Since there has been a large expressed intention for the current camp families to remain in Shirqart, CAOFISR will have a team of individuals that are dedicated to analyzing the current market, and developing vocational and business trainings for camp residents to assist their departure from the camp. These activities will include: 
-conducting market research in Shirqat, surveys... etc. 
-vocational and business trainings, targeting 600-800 men and women
-linking them with possible job opportunities
-CFW activities
-assistance with legal documents
-advocating to the government about their needs
-social cohesion projects  (art show and football tournament)

project_name: Critical humanitarian assistance for the most vulnerable populations to receive access to adequate shelter and basic services in displacement and returning locations
project_objective:
The Danish Refugee Council (DRC) in Iraq proposes a 12-month intervention in line with the HRP strategic priorities to support families and communities affected by the 2014 conflict. The proposed program will be part of a DRC multisector response to support those who return to reintegrate into their communities but face a host of challenges, including ongoing violence and loss of homes and livelihoods; as well as displaced households who wish to return but are unable to do so for a variety of reasons and face escalating protection risks; and finally, host communities who have been impacted by the conflict, including through destruction of infrastructure, lack of available services, and population influx. The program aims to continue providing services to most vulnerable communities, based on both sector-specific and integrated needs assessments, and builds on DRC’s achievements implementing Protection, WASH, Shelter, and Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM) activities under previous grant awards in 2015-2018. The program will be implemented in both camp and non-camp settings.
The multi-sectoral program will be strengthened through further integration of proposed activities, including through beneficiary selection modalities, referrals, and assessments, using an “area-based” approach where possible. In line with this approach, DRC expects a large proportion of the individuals targeted by this project to benefit from multiple DRC services. The program also incorporates increased attention to training of local authorities, civil society, community leaders and other duty bearers to identify and meet the needs of populations of concern through technical support.
To implement the Shelter/NFI components DRC intends to incorporate a greater focus on market-based approaches to the delivery of assistance to support the economic recovery of the targeted communities. This will depend on the beneficiary specific needs and individual context, not often are women volunteers for construction related labour at such special provisions will be made in this case. DRC will also continue to implement a strong protection focused programme to insure the prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse, consideration for those with specific needs due to disability, access constraints and gender as well as integrated HLP support as part of the multi-sectoral objectives of the program. Household activities will be tailored to the needs of those benefiting, with particular attention to better access for those with disabilities.

project_name: Critical camp management and coordination for highly vulnerable populations in camps and areas of return in Anbar, Ninewa and Salah al-Din
project_objective: Displaced people living in camps will require continued service provision this year. Many will remain unable to return to their AoO due to safety concerns, lack of access to basic services, destroyed or contested property, contamination, lack of livelihood opportunities and potential retribution in AoO. Perceived affiliation and retribution through violence, destruction of housing, inability to return, detention and disappearance are significant emerging threats, as those under suspicion face increased risk of rights violations, exploitation and violence, which is tantamount to collective punishment and in contravention of IHL. These risks will likely be compounded in 2019, as funding reduces for services in camps in favor of supporting return movements, and challenges persist in maintaining the humanitarian and civilian character of the camps. In parallel, while the GoI and the JCMC have begun a process of joint planning for consolidation with the humanitarian community through GRCs, threats of closure continue at a field and camp level, demonstrating little consideration for process, guidelines and coordination and resulting in secondary displacement. In areas of return, there is a severe need for support and coordination of services for formerly displaced families.

project_name: Critical humanitarian assistance for conflict affected populations to receive access to safe, sufficient water and sanitation services
project_objective:
The Danish Refugee Council (DRC) in Iraq proposes a 12-month intervention, in line with the HRP strategic priorities, to support families and communities affected by the 2014 conflict. The proposed program will be part of a DRC multisector response to support those who return to reintegrate into their communities with inadequate community infrastructure, lack of available services, and population influx and to continue providing services to most vulnerable communities in their location of displacement and their host communities. Activities will be based on both sector-specific and integrated needs assessments, and build on DRC’s achievements implementing Protection, WASH, Shelter, and Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM) activities under previous grant awards in 2015-2018. The program will be implemented in both camp and non-camp settings. Where possible activities will be validated and confirmed by inclusive community committees as part of local development plans.
The multi-sectoral program will be strengthened through further integration of proposed activities, including through beneficiary selection modalities, referrals, and assessments, using an “area-based” approach where possible. In line with this approach, DRC expects a large proportion of the individuals targeted by this project to benefit from multiple DRC services. The program also incorporates increased attention to training of local authorities, civil society, community leaders and other duty bearers to meet the needs of populations of concern as an exit strategy.
DRC intends to incorporate a greater focus on market-based approaches to the delivery of WASH assistance to support the economic recovery of the targeted communities. This is through engaging with local vendors and implementing elements of work through cash for work where possible. DRC will continue to implement a strong protection focused programme to ensure the prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse, consideration for those with specific needs due to disability, access constraints and gender as well as integrated HLP support for household assistance as part of the multi-sectoral objectives of the program. Household activities will be tailored to the needs of those benefiting, with particular attention to better access for those with disabilities, the elderly and the chronically sick.

project_name: Delivery of mine action activities in Ninewa, Kirkuk and Salah al Din
project_objective:
As the humanitarian crisis in Iraq has entered a new phase and hundreds of thousands of displaced people are willing to return to their communities, major efforts are undertaken to clear return areas of explosive hazards and rubble and restore vital infrastructure and socio-economic facilities. At the same time there is increased pressure on kick starting local economies and encouraging education, livelihoods and economic opportunities, so that the returnees can access credit, gain incomes and provide for their families, therefore being self-sustaining.

In line with the 2019 Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) and the Protection Cluster (PC) strategic objectives and based on the Mine Action Sub-Cluster (MASC) strategic interventions, activities and geographical focus, this project seeks to deliver much needed mine action programming to some of the most affected communities in Ninewa, Kirkuk and Salah al-Din in the post-conﬂict phase.

More speciﬁcally the project will seek to address HRP SO1 “increase access to basic services for the most vulnerable conﬂict-affected people and ensure responsible transition to durable solutions for those with prolonged humanitarian needs” and PC O1 “provide specialized protection assistance, and community-based support, to vulnerable conﬂict- affected individuals, thereby enabling them to secure their rights, access humanitarian assistance and public services, and overcome barriers to achievement of durable solutions.”

With more camps planning to close in 2019, survey and clearance activities in areas of origin and return and risk education activities in both camp and out of camp settings as well as informal settlements remain at the core of the humanitarian response.

By implementing non-technical (NTS) and technical survey (TS), manual and mechanical clearance as well as risk education (RE) and community liaison (CL) activities, DDG ‘ efforts will encourage future returns of population as well as help relieve the pressure put on communities that host large numbers of IDPs. By facilitating humanitarian access as well as allowing some of the most vulnerable people to access
 
services and vital infrastructure, DDG will facilitate socio-economic development and contribute to the transition towards durable solutions in the post-conﬂict environment across some of the most affected areas in Iraq. DDG will also continue to support the efforts made by the Government of Iraq and subsequently the Directorate of Mine Action (DMA), in achieving their priorities with regards to the mine action response while mitigating the threats posed by explosive hazards.

project_name: Support to rural rehabilitation and transition of agriculture, livelihoods and food production towards recovery
project_objective: The project directly addresses the revitalization of livelihood options for smallholder farmers through rehabilitation and replacement of rural agriculture assets and equipment. This rehabilitation of infrastructure and provision of machinery will provide the means to rebuild livelihoods of the rural families improving access to food and income for their families as well as for rural young/ poor through cash-interventions.  Altogether, this would help the families involved in accessing better diets while also increasing their cash income.

project_name: Improve protection and service delivery for conflict-affected population through CCCM
project_objective: In 2019, NRC’s Camp Management Team seeks to implement programming to ensure holistic, evidence-based and community-driven support to displacement-affected populations, thereby empowering and positioning them towards durable solutions. NRC will achieve this by increasing access to information, humanitarian assistance and government services for displacement-affected populations in out-of-camp areas of return. Community engagement and community governance will be enhanced, in a move towards durable solutions for displacement-affected populations, and NRC will also maintain access to assistance and protection in formal settlements through direct camp management or camp management support. In 2019, NRC aims to continue to inform policy and decision-making towards dignified and durable solutions to ending displacement.

project_name: Delivery of community-based services and referrals to promote well-being and enhance protection among IDPs, returnees and other at risk populations of concern in Iraq
project_objective: The proposed project will expand IMC’s contributions to the Protection Cluster’s efforts to provide GBV prevention and response to the areas where conflict–affected Iraqis, especially girls and women, are most vulnerable.

project_name: Displacement Management in Formal and Informal Settlements in Iraq and Support to National Actors for Preparedness and Response
project_objective:
The humanitarian crisis triggered by the appearance of the so-called Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant (ISIL) in 2014, and the subsequent military operations by the Iraqi government, forced the displacement of over 5 million persons within the territory of Iraq. Since then, IOM has been an active member of the humanitarian community in supporting the Government of Iraq in responding to the crisis within, among others, the shelter, non-food items and camp coordination and camp management sectors.
In 2019 IOM aims at building the capacity of national actors for preparedness and response to crises while, at the same time, providing direct assistance through, among others, camp coordination and camp management programme activities facilitating the coordination of provision of services to affected populations through:

•	Camp Management Operations
•	Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM) Cluster Coordination Support
•	Area-Based Approach through Community Resource Centres (CRCs)
•	Capacity Building of National Actors

Through each of these interventions, IOM seeks to ensure meaningful participation of local actors and camp residents to strengthen their ability to manage (formal and informal) displacement sites without direct support from IOM or other international actors. 

IOM developed its CCCM response for 2019 based on the analysis of the current displacement and return trends, as well as the plans of Iraqi authorities regarding camp consolidation and camp closure. Furthermore, IOM has taken into consideration the intentions expressed by Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) in and out of camps in reference to their plans for return, local integration or in some cases extended displacement in camps or camp-like settings.

project_name: Provision of healthcare services to crisis-affected populations in Iraq
project_objective:
Guided by health needs assessments and requests from the Ministry of Health (MoH) to fill gaps in service provision, IOM is currently providing comprehensive primary healthcare (PHC) services across Iraq in coordination with the Health Cluster, along with referrals to specialized secondary and tertiary health services. 

IOM has been requested by Departments of Health (DoH) to continue to support and provide lifesaving primary health services including reproductive health and emergency services, referral and health facility support, and provide mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) to conflict-affected and liberated areas across Iraq to support returnees and host communities and continue camp-based clinic responses for internally displaced persons (IDPs). IOM will support the MoH DoH through building their capacity for preparedness and response, and offering services. In line with Health Cluster objectives 1, 2 and 3 this project thus aims to increase the well-being of IDPs and highly vulnerable people and their communities. It responds to the critical health needs resulting from the extreme conflict during 2014-2018, that resulted in millions of people experiencing distressful events, disruption of social networks, loss of property and harsh living conditions. 

IOM’s support includes PHC in camp clinics, non-emergency referrals from camps to secondary/tertiary health facilities inside cities, and health facility support/capacity building training sessions. Services will be offered to two main vulnerable categories of people:
-	Displaced people in camps, temporary, formal and informal settlements: offered primary healthcare consultations, obstetrics gynecology (OB-GYN) and pediatric consultation through static clinics in camps; and non-emergency referral will be offered. MHPSS services will be offered though static community centers, and referrals supported when specialized services are not available in camp.
-	Returnees and vulnerable host communities: supported by enabling primary healthcare clinics (PHCCs) and hospitals in the areas of return to support free services to affected population, through minor revitalization and operational costs. PHCCs will also be supported to integrate MHPSS services though trained staff and revitalized MHPSS units.

project_name: Education in emergency and child protection integrated intervention in support of children affected by conflict in Iraq
project_objective:
INTERSOS’ strategy for 2019 is to strengthen and scale-up the education interventions in the areas where it is present with other sectors, i.e. Protection and Health. For what concern the education sector this geographically translates into Ninewa governorate (Tel Afar, Mosul IDP camps), Kirkuk (Hawiga and Kirkuk), KRI and Salah ad-Din governorate.
Drawing from lessons learned and best practices, the education interventions will continue to go hand-in-hand with child protection, while reinforcing the child protection component through the expertise gained in general protection case management. Following the change in the Iraqi context and the new challenges posed by the current stage of the crisis, INTERSOS will focus on supporting the formal schools in the retaken areas and only intervening with its own structured Temporary Learning Spaces (TLSs) or in the community centers (CC) when no other option is available to children. Support to formal schools does not mean a disengagement from non-formal education (NFE) services, but in fact it entails an additional effort to improve the interaction and the complementary between NFE and the formal system in coordination with other NGOs and with the government. In non- camp setting the school becomes the central space to restore the well-being of the child. The engagement of the community in all the stages of the process enhances the creation of child friendly protective environments along with promoting social cohesion and ownership of the beneficiaries. 
The proposed intervention ensures that the targeted conflict-affected children and adolescent returnees in the retaken areas and IDPs living in/outside camps are guaranteed access to quality education, by supporting the rehabilitation of schools, capacity building to teachers and PTAs members, provision of equipment and material, delivery of NFE activities, PSS and child protection mainstreaming through awareness raising in the communities. In the retaken areas the action targets returnees and vulnerable children supporting the quality of formal education and promoting the enrolment of out of schools’ children through outreaching and individual paths of re-enrolment basing on individual needs’ assessed. The innovative element, core of the integrated action, is the establishment of a school based CP system, where teachers become focal points for case management internal referral. A community based approach is followed throughout the all action ensuring the participation of teachers, parents, community representatives and children in the design of the activities and in the implementation phase. In the camp setting the intervention targets school-aged children with a focus on extremely vulnerable girls and boys. Thanks to the cooperation with the Directorate of Education, the children with more difficulties in catching up with the curriculum will be referred to the TLS or CC and will be supported in their learning process. In the camp where formal school is not an option, the TLS will be the only way to provide access to education and avoid to widen the gap of education of a whole generation of children. Thanks to a holistic approach, these children will receive also emotional and psychological support during recreational and PSS activities

project_name: Strengthening the protection environment for conflict affected populations in Iraq and KR-I
project_objective:
The proposed intervention aims at strengthening the protection environment for all conflict affected populations ( IDPs, returnees and host communities) Ninewa, Salah al Din, Erbil and Kirkuk Governorates. This initiative will provide comprehensive and holistic protection assistance packages to targeted individuals in order to mitigate protection risks as well as to foster self-resilience of affected individuals, with tailored assistance for highly vulnerable cases. Protection assistance includes protection monitoring aimed at identifying and referring vulnerable persons in need of case management or other services and collecting data on protection issues/incidents and trends to inform evidence based advocacy; legal assistance (awareness, counseling, administrative and court representation) services including civil documentation, HLP (only counseling and awareness) and family law for GBV survivors and children at risk; full case management services for Persons with Specific Needs, CP and GBV survivors. For vulnerable persons under case management, a package of internal specialized services such as psychological individual counseling, legal assistance, emergency cash assistance for high risk cases, sexual and reproductive health and structured PSS will be provided as needed; structured PSS targeting children and adults (particularly women and PWSN); awareness sessions on various protection topics and risks faced by the community including legal topics, sexual and reproductive health, general protection topics, availability of services; sensitization of the community for prevention of child labor and child marriage.
Intervention will target girls, boys, men and women among displaced and returnees communities in urban and camps targeted locations of Ninewa, Erbil, Salah al Din and Kirkuk Governorates with a mix of mobile and static interventions.

project_name: Harmonized Multi-Purpose Cash Assistance for the Most Vulnerable Conflict-Affected Households in Iraq
project_objective:
Markets in Iraq are functioning and accessible, and vulnerable households have a variety of critical basic needs. CCI PDM surveys show 79% of vulnerable households that receive cash transfers reduced their usage of negative coping strategies. Meanwhile, 99% of beneficiaries prefer cash to in-kind assistance. Accordingly the CCI will utilize MPCA as an appropriate, relevant and preferred humanitarian response modality to meet the critical basic needs of vulnerable households in conflict-affected out-of-camp communities across Iraq in 2019 and contribute to the CWG objectives:
 
Obj.1: Provide MPCA to extremely vulnerable households affected by armed conflict and to vulnerable households affected by a shock generating humanitarian needs that cannot be covered by existing national services, and;
Obj.2: Facilitate vulnerable households access complementary and critical humanitarian and national services including non-contributory social protection programs
 
Although needs may change and the CCI will pivot accordingly, priority areas of intervention for this program currently include the following: Mosul, Tel Afar, Tilkaif, Baaj, and Sinjar in Ninewa; Ana, Al Qaim and Ru’ua in West Anbar; Heet, Fallujah, Khaladiya, and Ramadi in East Anbar; Shirqat, Tikrit, Touz, Balad, and Baiji in Salah al-Din; Kirkuk, Daquq, and Hawija in Kirkuk governorate; and Khanaqin and Ba’quba in Diyala. However, with operational presence across 11 governorates (including Baghdad, Erbil, Najaf, Dohuk and Sulaymaniyah) the CCI has access to all CWG priority areas of intervention if required and in coordination with other CWG actors. 
CCI partners will aim to reach 60,000 vulnerable households (360,000 individuals) with MPCA in accordance with CWG guidelines.  In addition, CCI partners will also utilize established mechanisms to facilitate access to free in-house legal assistance and support to access barriers to Iraq’s SSN and other services. The CCI anticipates that at least 8,000 households will require support to obtain ID and/or support to register with the PDS, MoDM, or MoLSA (as feasible). CCI partners will also refer 5,000 households into other critical humanitarian services they have on offer including CfW, tailored protection support, shelter assistance, MHPSS, etc. Moreover, the consortium structure provides value and opportunity as follows:   	
The inter-agency CCI governance structure is already established and coordination is mandated by the MoU. The CCI coordination mechanism is proven to work, and provides an important cross-sector forum to coordinate and harmonize tools. Shared ways of working are established, partners trust each other, compromise, pivot and work together to promote a more effective overall response. 
The shared database enables rapid and efficient two-way data sharing, and prevents duplications with CCI and non-CCI partners (five DSAs are already established with ACTED, TDH, CARE, Tearfund, and PIN, while a DSA is under development with ICRC and Reach Iraq).  An automatic referral mechanism is established and automated which ensures consistent access to services on offer at different CCI partners. The CCI provides free in-house legal counsel and support to obtain legal documentation and, if required, register with the SSN. Moreover, CCI partners refer households into other CCI and bilateral programming including tailored protection, shelter, CfW services etc.
With 50 offices across 11 governorates, CCI partners have expansive infrastructure to promote reach and access for comprehensive, and coordinated, community-based programming at scale.
All CCI partners are engaged in the national and subnational CWGs, report on ActivityInfo and 4Ws, and actively participate in the CWG-led JPMI, the JRAMs, as well as the TVTF and MMTF, and the CWG-MoLSA SPF.  The CCI’s common fund enables partners to rapidly respond to unanticipated shock and needs and promotes preparedness.

project_name: Crisis affected children and youth rights to education are upheld, to continually access quality and relevant learning in a safe, inclusive and protected environment.
project_objective: NRC's overall objective is that Iraqi children and youth affected by conflict and displacement are able to achieve improved protection and socio-economic prospects vital for achieving durable solutions. Education interventions will target displaced (in and out of camps), returnee, remainee and host community children and youth, including persons with disabilities. NRC seeks to improve access to and strengthen basic formal education and non-formal education and address the three-year learning gaps many children face. Children will be supported to perform at grade level within the formal school system, passing national examinations and completing the academic cycle, enabling them to access further education. Youth are able to access existing or even create new livelihood opportunities, contribute to community initiatives and generation of household income and are more acknowledged as valued members of their communities.

project_name: Emergency Child Protection Support to Boys and Girls Affected by Violence and Conflict in Iraq
project_objective:
The humanitarian crisis in Iraq is entering a new phase. Combat operations against the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) have ended and hundreds of thousands of displaced people are returning to their homes and communities. In 2019, Save the Children (SC) will continue to provide Child Protection (CP) assistance to the most vulnerable communities, targeting conflict-affected boys and girls and their families across Ninewa, Dohuk, Salah Al-Din, Diyala, and Kirkuk. 
To respond to the needs of youth and boys and girls, structured psycho-social support (PSS), such as child resilience and youth resilience programs, will be provided through existing child protection spaces, community centres and schools. Case management will be provided to children at risk, with a specific focus on unaccompanied and separated children, child victims of neglect and abuse, child-headed households, children with disabilities and out of school children. Child Protection Committees (CPC) and other community-based structures will continue to be supported and equipped with necessary skills including basic child protection, identification and safe referrals, gender equality and inclusion, community mobilization and awareness raising, to increase communities’ resilience and capacity to respond to child protection needs. SC will continue to work and coordinate closely with the Ministry of Displacement and Migration (MoDM) Ministry of Youth and Sports (MoYS), Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs (MoLSA), Ministry of Education (MoE), and other relevant government stakeholders.

project_name: Emergency Education to Boys and Girls Affected by Violence and Conflict in Iraq
project_objective: The humanitarian crisis in Iraq is entering a new phase. Combat operations against the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) have ended and hundreds of thousands of displaced people are returning to their homes and communities. Yet the impact of conflict and displacement in Iraq on education has been stark. All affected children have witnessed violence and suffered disruption to their learning. Educational facilities have been destroyed and a shortage of teachers – who have suffered underpayment and lack of investment in their development – has meant that quality education has suffered. The Education Cluster estimates that a total of 2.6 million children will require assistance to access education in 2019. Through the proposed project, Save the Children (SC) will continue to provide Education assistance to the most vulnerable communities, targeting conflict-affected boys and girls and their families across Ninewa, Dohuk, Salah Al-Din, Diyala, and Kirkuk in 2019.

project_name: Provision of WaSH services and facility upgrades in Mosul, Muhalabiya and Nimrud Camp
project_objective:
The Solidarités International (SI) proposal aims to continue critical water infrastructure works in the Old City of Mosul, and to extend into two areas of high need which have been under-supported in the last few years - the Muhalabiya area of Mosul district and Nimrud Camp. The team have been working closely with key authorities such as the Departments of Water and Sanitation (DoW and DoS) for Mosul, the Director of Muhalabiya and the WaSH Cluster who are coordinating the efforts of WaSH actors. The proposed programme covers a comprehensive WaSH programme, tailored to the specific needs in the three different areas. 

In the Muhalabiya sub-district SI proposes to improve the water quality at the household level, which threatens health of the population and for which we are already seeing some water-related illnesses being reported. In line with the allocation strategy, SI will support water quality improvement with the training of community hygiene promoters to promote safe water handling and disease prevention, including cholera prevention. SI will also ensure the provision of water through water trucking in the southern areas of Muhalabiya sub-district for households in acute need where there is no water network connection, and explore options for a sustainable solution for this district, to be proposed in the first allocation of 2019. Additional support for the improvement of the water treatment facilities is planned to complement this activity, in conjunction with local authorities and other NGOs which work with the water station. 

SI is proposing to upgrade and maintain the WaSH facilities at Nimrud Camp; improving drainage, sanitation facilities and implementing longer-term solutions for the camp. SI will also provide water trucking to the population, while exploring options to rehabilitate storage solutions and extend water networks to the site. Community-led hygiene promotion activities are being proposed, to include promoting safe water handling and improved water quality through water treatment. Assessments are underway for the planning of activities, which will also consider gender and protection risks of camp settings, and where possible SI will upgrade facilities to make a safer environment for women, boys and girls.

project_name: Multi-purpose Cash Assistance for conflict-affected households in Iraq
project_objective: This project is to provide cash assistance for conflict-affected returnee, remainee and IDP households. Cash enables households to appropriately and effectively meet their emergency needs, including rent, food, utilities and others.

project_name: Support for returnees and IDPs in Salah Al Din and Ninewa governorates to access services through community structures and coordination mechanisms
project_objective: Tdh project will respond to the needs of internally displaced person (IDPs) living in informal sites and collective centers in Salah al Din through conducting Camp Coordination and Camp Management activities. These include creation and capacity building of the community structures, regular needs assessment, referrals to service providers as well as coordination among humanitarian actors. Returnee and IDP population living in Tal Afar District (Ninewa) will be supported by operating a Community Resource Centre (CRC). The CRC will serve as information hub for the community by collecting data on available services and employment opportunities. Furthermore the CRC community structures will allow the beneficiaries to monitor their needs in a participatory manner and submit them to humanitarian actors through CRC coordination structure.

project_name: Child protection assistance to highly affected communities (IDPs and returnees) in Anbar, Ninewa, Salah Al Din and Kirkuk governorates
project_objective:
In 2019 Tdh will continue to assist highly affected IDPs and returnee communities in hard to reach areas and areas of displacement. Tdh will provide specialised protection support to children and their communities to improve access to services, promote community-supported child protection dynamics and increase mainstreaming and understanding of CP concerns among services providers. In line with Tdh capacity and expertise in the Country, Tdh is pursuing an integrated CP and Education approach. 

Tdh action in 2019 aligns with the HRP Strategic Objective  1 and 2, and with Cluster Strategic Objectives 1 and 2. 

Under HRP CO 1, the proposed activities within the CP response are pronged over the following streams of intervention: 

-Culturally appropriate case management services for children at protection risk. It will includes, when relevant, assistance in accessing legal documentation and specialised MHPSS support. Dedicated secured programme will targets the needs of children in contact with the law in detention and for reunification and reintegration to their communities. 

-Structured and sustained psychosocial support to reduce risk to children’s wellbeing and enhance resilience skills among children. Activities will be organised to be culturally appropriate in line with a gender equality and age lens, but also to be inclusive for children living with disabilities, marginalised children, vulnerable children at protection risk. 

-Adolescents-group’s led projects  as a mean to boost peer-to-peer dynamics, sense of self-efficacy and ownership, participation and connectedness. Adolescents girls and boys out of school, exposed to child labor and early marriage protection risks will be prioritized. 

-CP system strengthening. Tdh response drawn from an ecological model on Child protection and it aims at strengthening multiple layers of responsibility. The action is pronged over a set of activities focusing on enhancing ownership on CP by communities and governmental staff. Some key activities will be carried out under this specific objectives, among them: awareness raising on CP concerns to promote children and communities’ capacity to protect themselves, identify, prevent, mitigate and respond to child protection concerns. Training of governmental staff on selected CP concerns, including MoLSA staff and Education staff (with a specific focus on CM Teachers focal points for safe identification and referral of cases eligible for a CM support). Parenting skills and parents groups. Capacity building of front-lines social workers. 
 
 Under HRP CO2 Tdh will continue to focus on capacity building of CP and non CP actors on CP mainstreaming. In hard to reach areas the action is particularly important to enhance the capacity of limited actors to coordinate with Tdh staff and enhance the scope of the direct assistance of Tdh response. 

Tdh programming in CP is strongly oriented to mainstream child safeguarding and protection from sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA) within the response, as per Tdh’s relevant global policies. 
Tdh programming is framed by a Quality and Accountability Framework, which is informed by the Core Humanitarian Standards and actively seek to establish relevant strategies to link relief, rehabilitation and development.

project_name: Child Protection and Education integrated approach in Iraq (Federal Iraq and KRI)
project_objective:
The proposed intervention is complying with HRP 2019 Strategic Objectives for Iraq, and more specifically Strategic Objective 1 “Post-conflict transition towards durable solutions” and Strategic Objective 2 “Strengthening the Centrality of Protection”. It also complies with the Protection Cluster Objective 1 and 2, the Child Protection Sub-Cluster’s operational framework and the Education Cluster Objective 1 and 2.

Based on TGH extensive experience in Child Protection / Education integrated approach in rural, urban and camp settings, the project aims at providing timely, culturally appropriate and gender sensitive child protection and education services to conflict affected children and their families, while strengthening community based mechanisms of risks prevention and response. As such, both immediate responses and long term solutions will be implemented, notably by strengthening systems and service delivery, and building capacities. TGH proposes to focus on Ninewa, Salah Al-Din, Erbil, Dohuk and Suleymaniah Governorates, and notably in rural and urban area, through a mix of static and mobile modalities depending on the context. This two-fold, flexible approach will allow TGH to maximize its population coverage, including in underserved areas, and deploy its teams shortly based on needs and gaps.

Notably, and thanks to teams composed of Child protection, Education and Youth Empowerment staff, the intervention will tackle various risks that affects’ children’s development, resilience and well-being, and provide a comprehensive response. The intervention will be implemented in close coordination with TGH legal partner Justice Center in Ninewa and SAD to ensure children’s access to their rights.

It will directly target children, adolescents but also their parents, and to a larger extent their community. Educational, vocational and psychosocial activities adapted to age, gender and specific needs will be provided by taking into each group’s specificities at all stages of the intervention. TGH will develop activities in schools and learning spaces (such as PSS, trainings of teachers and social workers, awareness events, support and linkage between members CPCs and PTAs). Integration of Child Protection and Education component will also imply smooth mutual referrals between activities based on children’s needs, thanks to mix teams of staff (composed of teachers, case workers, PSS facilitators and Community and Youth Empowerment counsellors). In parallel, the mobile approach in villages will allow to reach families and children that do not access services. 

TGH has been implementing child protection activities in Erbil, Ninewa, Dohuk and Suleymaniyah Governorates since 2013. TGH therefore has experience in urban, peri urban and rural settings, as well as in IDP camps (Khazer M1, Salamiyah 1 and 2, and Nimrud camps) where TGH is Child protection focal point (and previously in Nargaziliah where TGH was the Education focal point). In Erbil governorate, TGH has been providing Child protection and education services from 2013 until August 2017 in several localities around Erbil. In Bashiqa sub-district in 2017-2018 and in Mosul until now, TGH has implemented non formal education, child protection and youth empowerment activities (including vocational trainings). Finally TGH is supporting MoLSA/DoSA in all Governorates of Kurdistan to strengthen their capacity in Child protection and notably case management (2017-2018).

Therefore, the proposed intervention, based on TGH expertise, is fully in line with the 2019 Humanitarian Strategy for Iraq.

project_name: GBV assistance in the Nineva Governorate
project_objective:
The project will support the provision of comprehensive GBV services, including case management and Psycho-social support for GBV survivors, for IDPs in and out of camps, returnees and vulnerable host communities in Ninewa (with a specific focus on West Mosul). Mitigation of GBV risk and prevention of further violence will also be included through a community approach involving extensively men and boys. 
The capacity of GBV service providers will be strengthened in order to ensure that the access to GBV service provision is safe, confidential and timely.
The project will support static women’s centers inside PHCs in Ninewa Governorate, where GBV-related services and activities will be offered. The spaces are already operative since 2017 and will continue to be supported, while the new spaces will be equipped to ensure safety and confidentiality and comfortable provision of case management and PSS activities. Basic child-friendly spaces inside the centers will be in place in order to facilitate the participation of women with children.

project_name: Supporting Enhanced Access to Essential Vaccination, Nutrition, and Neonatal Health Care Services to Vulnerable U5 Children and Women affected by emergencies.
project_objective:
The project will support improvements in health and nutrition outcomes for new-borns, children under 5, and their mothers in eight governorates (Anbar, Baghdad, Dahuk, Erbil, Kirkuk, Ninewa, Salah al Din and Sulaymaniyah). 

Activities will include routine immunization targeting children under 5 in internally displaced people (IDP) camps and in returnee areas (including Mosul City); promoting optimal Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) practices, with special attention to early initiation of breastfeeding and feeding counselling for new mothers; management of malnourished children including screening, treatment and referral; neonatal and maternal health will be supported via a programme of home visits in IDP camps.

Complementary support to systems strengthening will take the form of provision of health and nutrition supplies including cold chain supplies/equipment, nutritional supplementation, and anthropometric equipment, as well as training of medical and paramedical staff on maternal, neonatal, and child health and nutrition (MNHCN) services. Behaviour change will be encourage through targeted social mobilization interventions (‘Communication for Development’ or C4D) that aim to increase uptake of vaccination services and improve knowledge, attitudes and practices in relation to infant and young child health outcomes.

To enable a smooth exist strategy, UNICEF has been focusing since 2017 on enhancing the capacity of different level medical and paramedical staff to provide quality health care services. Also, supported the overstretched health facilities (due to high influx of IDPs and returnees) with basic rehabilitation and replenishment of supplies and equipment (cold chain supplies, anthropometric equipment, incubators, etc). Furthermore, UNICEF re-constructed the vaccines store in Anbar, Salaheldeen and Ninevah. On the other hand, UNICEF has supported the DOHs to do evidence generation (nutrition survey and assessments and barrier analysis studies on IYCF and vaccination services, cold chain inventory assessment).

project_name: Enhance response to women reproductive health needs among IDP, host community and vulnerable returnees in Iraq
project_objective:
UNFPA aims to continue providing IDPs, host communities and returnees with quality reproductive health services at all levels – primary and referral.
The demand for reproductive health services still in high demand due to the existing IDP camps as well as returns to the areas of origin, where basic social services are yet to be fully functional. Given this situation, lack of services including health is one of the top three concerns of both IDPs and returnees in Anbar (60% among returnees and 41% among IDPs), while it is the top concern among returnees in Kirkuk (100% among returnees), and Ninewa (72% among returnees and 51% among IDPs), and 81% among Salah al-din returnees. Preliminary findings from reproductive health service mapping reveal that while many partners have started to provide reproductive health services, such as, antenatal care, family planning and sexually-transmitted infections syndromic treatment, none of the partners provide support to emergency obstetric and newborn care (EmONC), both basic or comprehensive.
Through implementation of this project  UNFPA plans to intervene in selected governorates and districts  on the basis of numbers of IDPs, residents and  returnees in the governorates of Ninewa, Salah al-din, Kirkuk, Anbar, Diyala, Duhok, Erbil and Sulaymaniyah. UNFPA will ensure uninterrupted RH services in all 52 IDP cams, four delivery rooms in IDP camps, six delivery rooms in hosting communities and six maternity hospitals in selected governorates. UNFPA during the implementation of the project will provide support to the service providers, procure and distribute RH kits and essential medical equipment to strengthen the technical capacity of health faculties. Through the implementation of this project, UNFPA will conduct series of training for service providers to strengthen their technical capacity.

project_name: Emergency Telecommunications Cluster (ETC)
project_objective: Recognising that humanitarian response in Iraq is shifting focus from emergency frontline assistance to addressing recovery, resilience and development-peace nexus activities, the Emergency Telecoms Cluster (ETC) has planned to phase out of Iraq by 30 March 2019.  Therefore, during Q1 of 2019, the ETC will close internet connectivity services in 18 camps in As Salamiyah, Haj Ali  and Hassan Sham as there is availability of services from local providers that humanitarian actors can contract directly.  The ETC will also complete outstanding projects for which commitments have been made to the humanitarian community and handover support and maintenance of the security communications network to either United Nations Department of Safety and Security (UNDSS) or lead agency to be agreed by Iraq ICT Working Group.

project_name: Ensuring essential health care services for the existing IDPs in the camps, returnees and host communities in the hard to reach locations  and initiating transition
project_objective:
The project will aim to provide essential health care services for the IDPs in the camps and returnees in the remote locations where the routine health care services have not been established yet. In addition to that, the project will emphasize the transition and integration of humanitarian health care services into the national health system.  
The response strategy will include providing the following services to the target population
1. Provide comprehensive primary health care services including improved physical and mental health screening facilities 
2. Continue and improve referral health services with standard physical and mental health services
3. Transpose the Early warning and response network of communicable diseases and initiate integration of early warning system into the routine disease surveillance system 
4. Conduct assessments, surveys and case studies to enhance information management, evaluate the quality of services and plan for evidence-based interventions through an integrated health care service.

project_name: Critical support to ensure food security and agriculture-based subsistence livelihoods of drought affected population in Balochistan and Sindh
project_objective: Critical support to ensure food security and agriculture-based subsistence livelihoods of drought affected population in Balochistan and Sindh provinces of Pakistan

project_name: Provision of primary health care and emergency services to Iraqi refugees, IDPs and local communities in North East Syria
project_objective:
This project aims to target a variety of direct and indirect beneficiaries across all North East Syria.
First of all, refugees and IDPs will be mainly targeted in Al Hol camp. Displaced people are to be considered as the most vulnerable of all, and ensuring continued access to health care is crucial for their wellbeing, with special regard to children, women and elderly. 
Women and girls will be specifically targeted through the reproductive health programs that UPP is already implementing: all the health facilities included in this project proposal (PHCs in Al Hol and Shaddadi), are equipped with delivery rooms, while specialized staff such as gynecologists and midwives are available to provide assistance to patients in need 24/7. 
Children will be assisted too, as pediatricians will be also available in the clinics for consultations. 
Emergency and trauma cases, including people wounded by mines, Improvised Explosive Device (IEDs) and other remnants of war, will also receive medical assistance: emergency rooms for trauma stabilization are attached to each PHC, while ambulances are available 24/7 to refer patients to better equipped health facilities in Hassakeh.
People with disabilities (PWDs) will be targeted too, mainly through the distribution of assistive devices both project locations, besides the regular consultations provided by the doctors and the medications dispensed at the pharmacies. Their families should be considered as indirect beneficiaries, as they will also be relieved by this kind of specific care. 
Where possible, people with chronic diseases will also be assisted. In Al Hol camp, a broad spectrum program for the distribution of medications for such diseases has been already put in place, with the support of the Committee of Health in Hassakeh. A similar assistance will be provided in other project locations as well, at least for the most common illnesses, such as diabetes, hypertension, etc.. 
People with complex medical conditions will also be taken care of, and referred to better equipped facilities for secondary and tertiary care, in order to receive more specialized services, such as c-sections, surgery, x-ray, etc.; if required, they will be evacuated to Damascus or Iraq.
Women, men, children, and elderly will also be targeted by health and hygiene promotion campaigns in both camps and urban settings, as well by other awareness raising-related activities: teams made up of community health workers and outreach volunteers will be available in each project location in order to sensitize beneficiaries on a range of important topics, including mine risk, fire hazards, insect bites, etc., mainly through face-to-face interaction with patients, outreach visits and thematic sessions. Camp residents and local communities will benefit from this crucial activity directly and indirectly, especially in terms of public health.
Although mental health and Sexual Gender Based Violence (SGBV) are not specifically part of this project, patients and survivors will also benefit from a basic kind of assistance, as UPP and  are already coordinating with other NGOs and service providers in order to refer such cases to psychiatrists and case management actors.

project_name: Strengthening resilience and protection of vulnerable internally displaced and host community children, youth and their families in Syria through ensuring a protective environment that is conducive to their healthy development, psychosocial wellbeing and positive coping.
project_objective:
After over seven years of violence, the Syria remains one of the most dangerous area for children. The CP needs across Syria are immense, far outweighing the available provision of necessary services. Conflict affected girls, boys and their families are facing appalling protection, neglect and deprivation risks on a daily basis, exacerbated by conflict‑related stress, exclusion or separation from their families. 

This project aims to provide life-saving assistance and to promote a protective environment for conflict-affected children and their families, while strengthening their resilience and protection. SC will be establishing and supporting community-based child protection programming, provide specialised child protection services and CP capacity building initiatives.  

In terms of community-based child protection, SCI will establish/support 78 CP Committees and Networks in NE and NW Syria through trainings, regular meetings and action planning to identify, prevent and respond to CP issues at the community level. SC will also provide child protection and PSS activities through child and adolescent friendly spaces, targeting 10,998 children and adolescent boys and girls, and will run child and adolescent clubs which children can engage in child-led activities/initiatives. Outreach will ensure that vulnerable and excluded children, including children with disabilities, are able to participate in activities. In order to strengthen children’s protective environment within the family, SC will engage 2,050 parents and caregivers in parenting groups and mother toddler groups, with priority given to vulnerable caregivers, such as child mothers. At the community level, awareness raising campaigns will be conducted with 50,000 girls, boys, women and men on key topics identified by CPCs, child clubs, and community members, including violence against children, the prevention of separation and mine risk awareness. Child protection situation monitoring will also be conducted across SC operational sites, as well as rapid assessments in new locations based on influxes and changes in the population. CP monitoring teams will also conduct mine risk education awareness, and refer locations where explosive hazards have been identified to mine clearance agencies.
 
Through case management, trained CW's will support 3,570 vulnerable and at-risk children, including unaccompanied and separated children, cases of child marriage and child mothers, child labour, and children experiencing violence, abuse, exploitation and neglect, including child survivors of sexual violence. Appropriate alternative care will also be provided/supported for UASC, with a focus on community-based and family-based care. Capacity building will also be undertaken with case management teams, relevant authorities and foster parents to strengthen the quality of alternative care. SC will also maintain a children’s emergency fund to respond to needs which cannot be met by other service providers for vulnerable and at-risk children, based on children’s case plans.  
 
SC will also work to strengthen human resource capacity both internally and at the NES and NWS levels through capacity assessments, capacity building plan development, training roll-out and through coaching and supervision support. Training will target 1000 women and men, including SC staff, CP actors, relevant ministries and authorities, and non-child protection actors.  

SC coordinates with a range of other actors in the implementation of CP activities, particularly for case management referrals. For example, depending upon the issues identified, external referrals will be made to local stakeholders for alternative care and SC also coordinates with actors such as (but not limited to) KRC (Kurdish Red Crescent), MSF, IRC and PHC's when referrals to medical services are required. SC will also continue to maintain active participation in sub-cluster meetings and other relevant coordination forums.

project_objective: In the Far North region, the Boko Haram insurgency in Nigeria has displaced 100,504 Nigerian refugees in Cameroon as of October 2018, and 98,590 of them live in the Far North region (UNHCR, October 2018). Boko Haram attacks have also resulted in 227,581 internally displaced persons (IDPs) (UNHCR, October 2018), who are struggling to survive in strenuous conditions in villages or small towns in the area. The region is predominantly arid and regularly hit by drought and seasonal floods. Access to basic services is also more limited than in other regions of the country. The arrival of IDPs in food-insecure areas has severely affected host communities as well. This has put enormous pressure on already scarce community resources and the local economy by reducing farm productivity and access to land and food markets. Boko Haram attacks have disrupted the economic, agricultural, and pastoral activities in the Far North region, causing a depletion of livelihoods and household assets. As a consequence, the existing chronic vulnerability and structural food insecurity have been aggravated. Therefore, WFP will target total 40,000 local population to engage in community asset creation activities for the early recovery from March to August 2019. Early recovery activities will use food assistance for assets (FFA) to mitigate community stresses so those who engage in this activity will be equal participants, decision-makers and beneficiaries in food(25,000 beneficiaries) and cash-based support(15,000 beneficiaries) to promote early recovery of local communities from the crisis and shocks.

project_name: Enhancing access to safe water and basic sanitation and hygiene services for vulnerable conflict-affected populations in Northwest Syria
project_objective:
Building on the expertise and operational capacity of ACTED staff and its partner Ihsan Relief and Development (Ihsan) in Syria, the intervention will provide targeted and effective WASH support to those most vulnerable across the country. To ensure that needs are met comprehensively, ACTED and its partners will provide WASH assistance both in and out-of-camp in Northwest Syria. The action will focus on restoring cost-efficient, sustained and safe access to quality water to populations. Temporary sources of safe water will be installed where no alternatives to water trucking exist and under performing water and sanitation infrastructure will be rehabilitated. Rehabilitated assets will be handed over to local actors to increase community resilience. Community sensitization on hygiene practices and water usage will be mainstreamed to heighten the impact of the intervention.

Under the WASH sector, ACTED will build on its expertise conducting multi-faceted WASH programming and will combine elements of emergency response while establishing durable solutions. In Syria, ACTED's WASH approach is based on three layers of intervention. First, immediate interventions aim to meet the emergency needs of those most vulnerable through the distribution of WASH NFIs and the establishment of emergency water treatment units and distribution points. Key WASH-related awareness raising is mainstreamed throughout the approach. A second layer of interventions focuses on improving access to sustainable safe water sources through existing infrastructure. The initial emergency response is thus paired with the rehabilitation of WASH assets such as canals, water stations, and boreholes. Additionally, ACTED provides technical and operational support to the authorities managing the rehabilitated sites. A third layer focuses on ensuring the handover of rehabilitated assets to, and establishment of cost-recovery and water safety plans with, local stakeholders to ensure the sustainability of the self-managed infrastructure.
This intervention will focus on emergency response and sustainable resilience, so as to provide the most adapted and cost-efficient assistance to those most in need. Synergies will be drawn between activities and with other ongoing ACTED interventions. 

ACTED and Ihsan will deliver an integrated package of WASH assistance in Northwest Syria. Water quantity and quality will be improved to SPHERE standards, with a focus on ensuring durable and cost-efficient access to safe water. A particular effort will be put on offering sustainable alternatives to water trucking where no other sources of safe water are available. In turn, it will allow actors currently conducting water trucking to redirect emergency assistance to other areas. Mainstreamed community sensitization on water conservation, usage, and hygiene will contribute to decreasing Water Born Diseases (WBD) concerns. An effective exit strategy will be ensured by working closely with local stakeholders, building their capacity to operate and maintain rehabilitated infrastructure.

project_name: Lifesaving health assistance to returnees in tribal districts and IDPs still displaced in selected districts of KP
project_objective:
Return of the TDPs in tribal districts is 98% completed. As of November 2018, over 1,303,530 people have returned to their place of origin. A small number around 100,000 people are still in displacement which will likely be returned by end of the year 2019. Most of the returning population are settling in the newly merged districts of Khyber, Orakzai, Kurram, North Waziristan and South Waziristan in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. Access to health services by the returning TDPs and the host population is poor. Findings from vulnerability assessment revealed that only 30% of the population in the target districts have access to essential life-saving health interventions . The average distance traveled by the population in these districts to the nearest health facility is 5.1 Km. According to WHO HeRAMS assessment, more than 31% of health infrastructures have been damaged as a result of civil unrest. Many of the displaced health staff, especially the female health worker, have not returned to duty. Nearly 50% medical officers are not available. Only 10% of the responders in these districts have ever been visited by LHW. Availability of essential lifesaving health care services is very low such as Routine immunization services at the primary healthcare level on average is 47%. For management of sick child, the application of integrated management of neonatal and childhood illnesses (IMNCI) protocol is very low at the primary healthcare level and stands at 23% only. Availability of nutrition screening services is also low at 25%. Availability of basic EmONC is 23% at PHC level. Availability of ANC services was 29% hence only 11.4% of the pregnant women visit the health facility 4 times during pregnancy. That aside the disease surveillance activities were very weak in most of the health facilities visited, and outbreaks of Measles, Cutaneous Leishmaniasis, Dengue Fever, Diphtheria and Pertussis were reported. The Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) rate in tribal districts is 19.5% and the Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) rate is 4.4%. This GAM is above the 15% emergency threshold. In the last two year the districts registered disease outbreaks of Measles, Cutaneous Leishmaniasis, Dengue Fever, Diphtheria and Pertussis. These outbreaks were notified late.
Access to safe water and sanitation is also poor with 45% of the population in return areas relying on unsafe drinking water. 36% of returnees have no toilets and practice open defecation. The presence of water-borne diseases is high with 33% household-reported diarrhoeal cases in tribal districts. 16% of the responders reported that they have ever suffered from mental illness. 
We propose to rehabilitate damaged health facilities, revitalize non-functional health facilities, strengthen service delivery particularly for the vulnerable groups such as women, children <5 years, adolescent boys and girls, elderly and the disabled by existing primary health care facilities, and establish community health services. In addition, we will strengthen disease surveillance and response to mitigate and control communicable diseases outbreaks which carries high morbidity and mortality at both community and facility level. 
We expect that through this project, we will ensure improved access by the 1,303,530 returning population and the 200,000 IDPs & host populations to essential life-saving health interventions.

project_name: Safeguarding women and girls in drought affected areas in Pakistan
project_objective: Some 3 million people in Sindh Province of Pakistan are directly affected by the drought. There is a severe shortage of water and poor access to sanitation. The current severe acute malnutrition level in Tharparkar is 22.7% which is above the emergency threshold of 15% (National Nutrition Survey 2018, unpublished). Access to health facilities is extremely poor due to long distances (avg. 19.8 km), the high cost of transport to the health facility, poor road infrastructure and a lack of transport facilities. This is further compounded by the poor socioeconomic situation of the population. There is an acute shortages of lifesaving medicines at health facilities and a general lack of essential medical equipment. In Balochistan, an estimated 2 million people have been affected by the ongoing drought. Some 670,000 children under 5 years and 370,000 pregnant and lactating women are in dire need of health services (PDMA, 2018). The average distance to reach heath facilities is 30kms. The per capita OPD utilization in 2018 is 0.4 which is far below the acceptable range of 1 to 1.2, implies that only 40 per cent of the population access health care services (DIHS, 2018). Some 73 per cent of cases who attend OPD are suffering from communicable disease. There is a high suicide rate among women attributed to the acute drought crisis (NDMA, October-November 2018). The two provinces are also reporting outbreaks of dengue, and more than 3,700 confirmed cases have been reported in 2018 in Sindh alone. In addition, there are ongoing outbreaks of crimean congo hemorrhagic fever (CCHF), chikungunya, leishmaniasis and malaria. Killa Abdulla district has documented some 5000 cases of leishmaniasis in 2018. The prevalence of acute respiratory infection (ARI) is 46 per cent. The proportion of fully immunized children at 24 months is just 29 per cent, which is evident from the measles outbreaks of 2017 and 2018, where 29 and 36 documented measles outbreaks were reported with death tolls of 77 and 44 respectively. Cases of water-borne disease are also on the increase as indicated in OPD records which states that over 20 per cent of the patients suffer from diarrhea. These figures are an underestimation since they are health facility-based and represent only the 40 per cent of the population who seek health services at the health facility.
