Supporting household  resilience of  Lake Chad Basin communities affected by the Boko Haram insurgency in Cameroon through the development of low input integrated systems of agriculture, and aquaculture.
project_objective:
Les divisions Logone et Chari, en particulier la région autour du lac Tchad, souffrent des effets de l'assèchement du lac Tchad. La situation est aggravée par un climat imprévisible qui caractérise toutes les zones arides (alternance d'inondations et de sécheresses) et par un accès limité aux services sociaux de base. Cela perturbe les moyens de subsistance de la population, en particulier ceux des districts de Blangoua, Darak et Hile-Halifa, qui dépendent principalement d'activités liées à la pêche, à l'élevage et à l'agriculture. La population de la division Logone et Chari est estimée à 486 997 personnes et 176 976 personnes (28 997 ménages) sont vulnérables (personnes déplacées, rapatriées et réfugiés hors du camp), ce qui représente 36% de la population. La majorité des personnes déplacées se trouvent dans les districts de Makary (49 341 personnes), Kousseri (20 009 personnes), Fotokol (15 837 personnes), Logone-birni (12 398 personnes) et Blangoua (7 467 personnes). Les mineurs représentent environ 65% de la population et la taille moyenne des ménages est de 7,7 personnes. Pour inverser la tendance actuelle, des actions positives significatives devront être menées en créant des opportunités de travail dans le but principal d'améliorer les conditions de vie des populations locales d'abord et de celles du bassin.  Afin d’obtenir des résultats durables, des activités spécifiques seront menées afin de consolider et de protéger les acquis des interventions passées. En outre, la réponse sera diversifiée, l’accent sera mis sur la réhabilitation et la promotion des moyens de subsistance dans l’agriculture, l’élevage et la pêche. L’objectif de ce projet est de soutenir la résilience des communautés du bassin du lac Tchad touchées par l'insurrection de Boko Haram au Cameroun par le développement de systèmes à faibles intrants,  Systèmes intégrés pour les activités de l'agriculture, de l'élevage et de l'aquaculture. Spécifiquement il sera question : d'améliorer l'accès des agro-pasteurs vulnérables à la terre, aux actifs et aux intrants pour augmenter et diversifier leur production d'améliorer l'accès des pisciculteurs aux masses d'eau et aux intrants nécessaires à la protection; de renforcer les capacités des ménages vulnérables défavorisés, en particulier des ménages dirigés par une femme, afin de maintenir leurs moyens de subsistance et leur sécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle;
la remise en état des terres du lac se fera à l'aide de pelles mécaniques associées au travail manuel de la population locale. C’est une action aux résultats multiples qui vise en même temps à résoudre le problème épineux du dragage du lac Tchad (dont la quantité de gisements reste le défi le plus important à relever). Le choix de l'utilisation de la main-d'œuvre locale pour le développement de ses périmètres labourables est motivé pour des raisons sociales et économiques. En effet, plus la population sera impliquée dans la phase de mise en œuvre, plus il sera facile d'assurer la durabilité de cette initiative. Les remblais formés sont constitués de terres cultivées draguées. Ces terres sont essentiellement constituées de bons sols, enrichis en déchets végétaux, lessivés par les pluies dans les régions moyennes. Les tallus ainsi déplacés seront mis à la disposition des familles vulnérables identifiées par les autorités traditionnelles et administratives locales. La construction des remblais et des étangs à poissons se fera par le biais d'activités à forte intensité de main-d'œuvre ""travail contre salaire"". Cette activité aura un impact rapide sur les moyens de subsistance vulnérables.  la population totale des bénéficiaires est estimée à 9450 personnes dont 7 personnes en moyenne par ménage) 7700 personnes parmi les PDI vulnérables, les rapatriés, les agro-pasteurs et la communauté d'accueil. le projet a une durée de 2 ans et sera mise en oeuvre avec l'appui d'un partenaire technique et des services deconcentrés du MINEPIA et du MINADER.

project_name: Columbia - Pan American Development Foundation
Strengthening humanitarian coordination and advocacy in Iraq
project_objective:
Despite the end of large scale military operations in December 2017, humanitarian needs persist in the country. Some 6.5 million people are in need of some type of humanitarian assistance. Of these, the humanitarian community will target 1.75 million people through the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) for 2019. This includes one million people displaced in 125 camps and out-of-camp locations (concentrated in Baghdad, Dahuk, Diyala, Erbil, Kirkuk, Najaf, Ninewa, Salah al-Din, Sulaymaniyah), half a million returnees who are in locations with high and very high severity of conditions (concentrated in Anbar, Baghdad, Diyala, Erbil, Kirkuk, Ninewa and Salah al-Din governorates) and most vulnerable residents living in communities hosting a large number of IDPs. 

OCHA presence is important to foster responsible transition of the response from humanitarian relief operations towards recovery, stabilization and development solutions. OCHA will support this evolution by coordinating effective and principled humanitarian action, advocating for the rights of people in need, promoting preparedness and contingency planning and facilitating sustainable solutions for displaced people.  OCHA will continue to provide advocacy and strategic guidance to the Humanitarian Coordinator (HC) and the Humanitarian Country Team (HCT) and work with the Inter-Cluster Coordination Group (ICCG) to advance leadership protection priorities. These include protecting women and children with perceived affiliation, enhancing assistance to gender-based violence assistance (GBV), working to prevent sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA) and intensifying accountability to affected populations (AAP). 

OCHA also plays a crucial role in facilitating coordination and cooperation among all relevant stakeholders who work to serve Iraq’s most vulnerable people. The 2019 Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) and HRP corroborate the need to maintain a sizeable humanitarian footprint during the coming year. There are currently 13 clusters/sectors operating in Iraq, of which only three indicated their intention to scale down their operations in 2019 as a result of declining needs – Emergency Telecommunications, Logistics and Rapid Response Mechanism. According to data reported by partners to the Iraq Humanitarian Dashboard, nearly 170 organizations - 85 national non-governmental organizations, 74 international NGOs and eight UN entities have been operating in 420 locations spanning across 107 districts out of 109 districts in 2018. OCHA needs to maintain a presence in the country throughout 2019 to be able to provide humanitarian coordination and information management support to as well as to facilitate engagement with a wide range of counterparts, including national, regional and local authorities, military actors and development actors.

project_name: Renforcement de la coordination et du plaidoyer humanitaire au Tchad
project_objective: Le projet vise à renforcer la mobilisation et la coordination  de la réponse humanitaire au Tchad afin de sauver des vies et protéger les personnes affectées par les crises, notamment celles affectées par la crise du lac Tchad. Une coordination humanitaire efficace et performante permet aux acteurs humanitaires de mieux identifier et répondre aux priorités humanitaires. OCHA jouera un rôle clé dans la création d'espaces d'échange et d'analyse d'informations, pour mieux guider les actions humanitaires, répondre aux besoins les plus aigus et être mieux préparé face aux urgences soudaines. Le projet permettra également d’assurer conjointement avec la communauté humanitaire le plaidoyer en faveur du respect des principes humanitaires, de la protection des civils, de l'accès humanitaire et pour la mobilisation et l'allocation efficace de ressources humanitaires. OCHA continuera de jouer  également un rôle moteur dans le renforcement du lien entre les acteurs humanitaires et de développement et la transformation de la réponse humanitaire, en lien avec les engagements pris au Sommet mondial de l'action humanitaire de 2016 et ceci à travers la nouvelle façon de travailler (NWOW).OCHA continue de mettre en oeuvre sa mission à travers ses fonctions clés (Coordination, Gestion de l' information et plaidoyer). Un accent a été mis sur l' opérationalisation de la nouvelle façon de travailler, la mise en oeuvre des plans d' action de la redevabilité envers les populations affectées (AAP) et la PSEA, la préparation aux urgences et le plaidoyer pour plus de visibilités et de mobilisation de ressources pour les différentes crises au Tchad (Bassin du Lac Tchad, insécurité alimentaire et malnutrition, épidémie sanitaires). De même, OCHA à travers sa participation dans le groupe de travail sur le CASH, continu de faire le plaidoyer pour renforcer l' utilisation du CASH pour la réponse humanitaire dans tous les secteurs et du Cash à usage multiple (Multipurpose CASH)

project_name: Humanitarian Coordination Assistance for the Syria Response Plan
project_objective:
The 2019 Syria Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) provides an overarching framework for humanitarian response efforts by humanitarian actors based in Syria and from neighboring countries (Turkey and Iraq) responding inside Syria. Leveraging these capacities and efforts under a single strategic framework, the plan aims to increase the effectiveness of the response by improving the identification of needs and gaps, reducing overlap and duplication, and monitoring of changes. 

The United Nations Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator for Syria leads and coordinates humanitarian action inside Syria. His work is complemented by the Regional and Deputy Regional Humanitarian Coordinators for the Syria Crisis and Humanitarian Coordinators in neighboring countries.

OCHA, in line with its global mandate, supports the humanitarian leadership in ensuring the effective coordination of the response inside Syria. To do so, OCHA maintains country offices both inside Syria, Turkey, and a Regional Office based in Amman. OCHA requires sustained levels of funding to be able to maintain and further strengthen the effective coordination of humanitarian responses from these various offices. The funding requirements reflect the needs of OCHA's three offices involved in the Syria response.

project_name: Enhancing the protective environment for individuals and communities affected by conflict and displacement in South Sudan.
project_objective:
Given the ongoing protection crisis in South Sudan, DRC will continue to work with populations affected by conflict and displacement to enhance the protective environment of individuals and communities, and identify, prevent and address protection risks. The main objectives of the project, aligned with the Protection Cluster Humanitarian Response Plan objectives, are: 
-	Provide immediate lifesaving assistance to address priority protection needs for the most vulnerable populations in hard-to-reach areas
-	Prevent, mitigate and respond to protection risks through enhanced preparedness and resilience
-	Enable durable solutions for IDPs and other affected populations
The project is designed to alleviate suffering of the most vulnerable individuals, and ensure safety and well-being of conflict-affected communities are prioritised and achieved. The project will focus on three main components: 
-	Protection analysis and advocacy: DRC will focus on protection data collection and analysis, for the purpose of ensuring an in-depth understanding of the protection environment, allowing for appropriate prevention and response activities. In parallel, DRC will ensure protection concerns are captured in protection information products, such as assessment reports, monitoring reports, and protection snapshots, allowing for appropriate and relevant advocacy with the clusters, humanitarian partners, and other main stakeholders. DRC protection programming will ensure evidence-based interventions, at the individual and community levels, ensuring appropriate and principled action is taken to prevent and respond to protection risks. 
-	Protection risk prevention: DRC will continue to work closely with communities, particularly existing community structures, and vulnerable groups and individuals, to identify protection risks, coping strategies, community and individual intentions, and resilience among the affected population, to ensure preparedness and resilience of communities and at risk individuals are enhanced. DRC will work with community-based protection networks, facilitate focus group discussions, awareness raising, trainings on human rights and protection mainstreaming, and establish community-driven action plans, aiming to prevent and mitigate identified protection risks. 
-	Protection response: DRC provides tailored protection responses to individuals at risk and communities affected by violence and displacement. The responses include protection monitoring, individual protection assistance (IPA), through case management, and mobile responses, identification and support to vulnerable individuals at risk, psychosocial support, service mapping and referrals, community based protection networks, and other necessary interventions based on needs in various locations, such as housing land and property (HLP) and legal aid. 
DRC’s approach in South Sudan is both through static presence (mainly in Upper Nile and Unity States) and mobile teams, who rove throughout the country based on new shocks and movements of populations. In Unity State, DRC forms part of a group of agencies implementing the “Beyond Bentiu Response” strategy, which aims at assessing locations beyond the Bentiu POC, and providing services to hard-to-reach communities in different counties. DRC adopts an integrated approach, linking general protection with sexual and gender based violence (SGBV) prevention and response, food security and livelihood (FSL), shelter and non-food items (SNFIs) and camp coordination and camp management (CCCM). DRC will continue to engage with other humanitarian partners and the relevant clusters to coordination and ensure aid effectiveness, as well as focus on mainstreaming protection throughout its programming. DRC will put ample focus on the centrality of protection, ensuring safety and dignity of persons of communities affected by displacement are prioritised and a do-no-harm approach is mainstreamed during all aspects of the project cycle.

project_name: WASH Response Interventions in drought affected districts of Zimbabwe
project_objective: Zimbabwe is at risk of multiple hydro-meteorological hazards namely drought, flooding and diarrhea diseases epidemics (Cholera and Typhoid). The projection of the El Niño phenomenon will negatively affect the provision of safe water thereby increasing the risk of WASH related diseases among the vulnerable communities. Currently, the country is experiencing a cholera outbreak in Harare and 17 other districts. As of 07 December 2018, the country recorded a cumulative 10,550 (10,269 suspected and 281 confirmed) cases and 59 deaths with a case fatality rate of 0.56%. The WASH Response to the eminent El Niño phenomenon and risk of cholera will be guided by three (3) strategic objectives – (i) Restore access to sufficient water of appropriate quality and quantity to fulfil basic needs, (ii) Increase awareness of safe hygiene and sanitation practices, with a focus on participatory health and hygiene education (PHHE) and water conservation and (iii) Provide access to critical WASH related Non-food items (NFIs), with a focus on the most vulnerable families in the targeted areas. The response is specifically targeted at WASH needs arising from and aggravated by the current cholera and eminent drought

project_name: Child Protection  for children affected by El Nino induced drought humanitarian situation
project_objective:
The humanitarian intervention aims to ensure that girls and boys, especially the most vulnerable and those affected by humanitarian situations, are protected from all forms of violence, exploitation, abuse and harmful practices. The persistent drought and economic shocks have increased the vulnerability of children, adolescents and women to protection risks and may be exacerbated by the probable El Niño. This proposal is targeting 100,000 people, primarily children and their caregivers, adolescents especially girls including adolescent mothers, community, child protection structures as well as other humanitarian sectors responding to the effects of drought in 15 districts targeted by the child protection sub-sector. In cases of drought girls are the most affected as they suffer from family separation, child labour and child marriage. Children adopt negative coping mechanisms such as migration and this heighten increase exposure to sexual violence, exploitation and other forms of abuse. Furthermore, family tension escalate children and particularly women suffer from domestic violence. 

The implementation scale and scope of humanitarian intervention is to strengthen CPiE coordination, capacity building of Child Protection sub-sector community based mechanisms, integrate CPiE prevention and response in other intervention sectors, strengthen the resilience of children and adolescent and provide quality comprehensive child protection case management services. 

The objective is ensure that girls and boys rights to protection from violence, abuse and exploitation are sustained and promoted in humanitarian situations. Vulnerable children and those engaged in risky coping mechanisms are reached with child and social protection support to keep them safe. 

The priority intervention is support the availability and accessibility of quality comprehensive and vulnerability sensitive child protection services for all children with special needs including separated children, children with disabilities, children in contact with the law children with HIV and child survivors of violence. This is building on the National Case Management Systems which is operational in all districts. There is an existing community workforce of 10,500 Community Childcare Workers (CCWs) who have limited understanding of CPiE whose capacity requires to be strengthened. 

The expected output from this support is improved coordination of the child protection sub-sector response, strengthened capacity of child protection actors who are responsive to the needs of children and adolescents. The following target group will benefit children without appropriate care including separated and unaccompanied children, children at risk of violence, children at risk of exposure to child labour, pregnant adolescents and young mothers in need of psycho social support.

project_name: Early Identification and Provision of Life -Saving Treatment for children with Acute Malnutrition in ELi-Nino affected Districts
project_objective:
The Zimbabwe Vulnerability Assessment Committee (ZimVAC) assessment report of June 2018 reported a deterioration in the food security situation during the peak hunger period (January to March 2019). According to the report, over 1.1 million people are at risk of being food insecure during the peak hunger period.  Adding to that, the Integrated Phase Classification (IPC) which was conducted in May 2018 projected that over 2.4 million people will be food insecure during the peak hunger period and at least 1.7 million people are projected to be in IPC Phase 4 (Emergency). The country is likely to experience an increase in numbers of children with acute malnutrition resulting from food insecurity, compromised child care and feeding practices due to negative coping mechanisms. The drought situation could be further exacerbated by the recent cholera outbreak and on-going poor macro-economic situation affecting access to basic food commodities. 
It is anticipated that 72,228 children could be affected by acute malnutrition (25,280 SAM and 46,948 MAM) in all 63 districts in the country between January and June 2019. In addition, 360,000 young children (0 to 23 months), 905,933 children aged 6 to 59 months and 575,384 pregnant and lactating women with elevated nutrition needs  in the selected 24 districts are likely to be immediately affected by the prevailing and up-coming food insecurity including through the looming El-Nino drought (90% likelihood according to the most recent SARCOF analysis). 
The UNICEF response in the affected districts will aim at: 1.	Supporting  active screening for early identification and referral of children with acute malnutrition through community based health workers and community volunteers. 2. Capacity building for facility based health workers on treatment, management and reporting of children with acute malnutrition. 3. Procurement, pre-positioning and distribution of life-saving nutrition commodities (F75, F100, RUTF and anthropometric materials to all affected districts. 4.  Provision of community level support for IYCF-e to parents and caregivers of children below the age of two years through the establishment of mothers support/care groups for Maternal, Infant and Young Child Feeding. 5. Provision of micro-nutrients (vitamin A for children aged 6 to 59 months; multiple micro-nutrient powders for children aged 6 to 23 months; iron and folate for pregnant women; and provision of zinc in diarrhoea management. 6. Provide effective coordination for the Nutrition Sector response and strengthen government coordination structures at provincial, district and sub-district levels. 

From July 2019 to April 2020:
""1. To provide leadership for a coordinated nutrition response to women and children affected by the drought.
2. To protect the nutrition status of vulnerable children under the age of five years (includes children with disabilities and those affected by HIV; pregnant and lactating women from deterioration due to the impact of the drought.
3. To provide life-saving nutrition treatment to all children affected by acute malnutrition.
4. To provide community level Infant and Young Child Feeding in Emergencies (IYCF-e) support to parents and caregivers of children below the age of two years in collaboration with the HIV programme.
5. To improve decision making and effective nutrition response through strengthened data collection, reporting and information systems using the rapid-pro platform.

project_name: Mitigating against the health impact of shortages of essential medicines at health facilities.
project_objective:
Zimbabwe is experiencing an acute on chronic shortage of medicines and medical sundries due to unavailability of foreign currency. The level of medicines in both the public and private sector is a serious cause of concern, characterised by stock-outs of certain commodities and less than 2 weeks cover for others. Availability of medicines is at overall 26% against a target of 60%; Vital is 30% against a target of 100% and Essential is 24% against a target of 80%. Availability of medical sundries is 22% against a set target of 80%.
JUSTIFICATION 
There is an acute shortage of essential medicine, diagnostics, supplies and consumables at all levels of the health system, making access to health care out- of- reach for most of the poor and vulnerable population. The current stock levels indicate less than two weeks cover for essential medicines. Although financial support has been received from various donors in the form of the Health Development Fund, Global Fund, the US government through its various implementing partners, the support has been directed at primary health services as well as programmes for specific conditions like malaria, HIV, TB, Family and Child Health.
The shortage of medicines affects the poor in the country who cannot afford alternative care from private providers and leads to poor utilisation of services in general and increased preventable deaths, some of which may not be reported to the health service. It is noteworthy that the above prevailing condition exacerbates the vulnerability of communities especially in the rural settings where communities cannot access foreign currency that is demanded by most pharmacies. The cost of health services provided by the private sector is not regulated and could be prohibitive for vulnerable populations. The private not-for-profit is also faced with economic constraints which impacts negatively on their ability to import adequate medicines and supplies.
THE REQUEST 
This appeal requests for support to provide medicines and medical supplies to cover 9, 170 000 million vulnerable population to mitigate against preventable illnesses, disabilities and deaths. The medicines and medical supplies  will cover the essential  requirements of 1 568 primary health care facilities in 80 districts  for  a period of 6 months.  
Prioritisation 
The prioritisation took into consideration the vulnerability and proportion of the population to be reached. In this regard, consideration was made for rural residence where 67% of the population live largely served by primary health care facilities.

This project will strive to expand access and improve retention for boys and girls by providing quality and equitable education to ensure that the children do not lose out on their right to education. This will be done through continuous mobilization of community to enroll their children in school, promoting safe learning environment through construction and rehabilitation of classrooms and Temporary Learning Spaces, provision of safe drinking water, supplementary school feeding, teaching/learning and recreational materials, trainings as well as paying incentives for their teachers since the parents can afford to pay the fees of their children. The massive displacement of children in the new locations means additional pressure on the already overstretched facilities like, classrooms, teaching learning materials and hygiene and sanitation facilities.

The project will be implemented in the Districts of Baidoa, Kismayo, Beletweyne, Boroma, Zeyla, Lughaya, Burao, Odwayne, Aynabo, Lasanod, Hudun, Erigavo, El-Afwayn, Gardho, Rako, Bocame, Badhan, Galkacio, Galdagob, Dangorayo and Garowe districts. . The project will directly target 18,300 (50% girls) children ) of different ages from communities most affected by the effects of conflicts, drought, floods, tropical storms, and returnees from Kenya  with the most needed, life- saving interventions like supplementary feeding, hygiene and sanitation facilities. The project will be school-based, targeting 60 schools hosting children most affected by the drought.  All this is aimed at ensuring that IDPs, returnees and host community children, both boys and girls are enrolled and retained at school, and are protected.

Save the Children will also provide incentives to some teachers in the targeted schools, especially to those who are not benefiting from incentives from the Ministry of Education or any other agency including communities. With the massive influx of new children to their schools, it means additional responsibilities on the shoulders of these teachers, and the incentives will motivate them.

project_name: Access to quality education to all children in Syria
project_objective:
UNICEF aims to advance equitable access to quality learning for the most disadvantaged
children, adolescents and youth in Syria. UNICEF’s priority areas are as follows:
a) Scaling up equitable access to education
b) Enhancing the quality of education services
c) Strengthening education systems
With over 2m children out of school, UNICEF will focus on both increasing access to the
hardest to reach especially the displaced, those across lines of control in the midst of the
ongoing crisis and ensuring safe learning environments for those returning to newly
accessible areas and at risk dropping out. Within this framework UNICEF will continue to
advocate for greater humanitarian access and seek to reach the most marginalized
children. Priority vulnerable groups will entail those who are displaced and out of school
and who are in the communities that host them. Geographical priority will be given to
areas with high severity, including newly accessible, militarily encircled, besieged and hard

Gaziantep hubs in a Whole of Syria approach.
As these vulnerable groups face multiple barriers to schooling, it is critical to strengthen a
knowledge/evidence base and address their barriers in a cross sectorial way. UNICEF will
increase synergies with Social/Child Protection, Adolescent Development and
Participation (ADAP), Communication for Development (C4D), and Water, Sanitation and
Hygiene (WASH).
UNICEF will respond to immediate humanitarian needs as investments for the future. It
will strengthen partnership with authorities, NGOs, communities and schools in view of
resilience building and early recovery. Furthermore, UNICEF will coordinate with other UN
agencies to leverage resources in jointly selected communities and schools. UNICEF leads
the education sector coordination in all the WoS hubs including the sub hubs of Aleppo,

project_name: Improving livelihoods opportunities for vulnerable households in Northwest Syria and livelihoods-based infrastructure
project_objective:
The activities under Sector Objective 1 aim to give access to livelihood opportunities to vulnerable households (HHs), while at the same time improving local infrastructure relevant for Agriculture and, more broadly, the livelihoods sector. Activities include the provision of short-term labour opportunities to skilled and unskilled workers, supporting 214 HHs, small business opportunities for 50 HHs and support to small-medium enterprises for 10 HHs. These activities are complementary to the Agricultural- and Livestock-based activities included in the submission for the FSA sector. As this project continues in 2020, it is expected that 30 HH will be supported in 2019 and 30 HHs in 2020. The budget included in section 5 is only for 2019.

Temporary labour opportunities will involve the completion of essential works, both those prioritised by the local council and benefitting the wider community in the target locations, particularly in relation to agricultural infrastructure (e.g. seed storage, agricultural roads, livestock water points, etc.) as well as providing increased income to the households participating in the Action. It is anticipated that with the reinvigoration of agro-pastoralist livelihoods there will be continued demand for agricultural labour beyond the project. In addition, supporting small-scale income generating activities, and small/medium businesses and market actors to re-start or expand their activities will contribute to business development, generate income and enable them to sustain their operations, contributing to the functioning of the local market. Capacity building and training of local stakeholders in improved and sustainable agricultural practices as well as the involvement of local councils and extension workers throughout project activities will ensure that knowledge and capacity gained will remain within the community with a view to building sustainability at household and community level.

The project will involve both IDPs and host communities, selected based on selection criteria. Eligibility criteria includes the ability to work; however, a key project selection criterion is considerations to increase the inclusion of women and people with unique needs. As actors are facing challenges in identifying projects that can be implemented through CfW and are at the same time beneficial for the community and culturally appropriate for women, SC has raised the concern for discussion within the Cash-Based Response TWG with the objective of obtaining lessons learnt from the international community to achieve higher women’s participation. Vulnerability criteria will prioritize households with pregnant and lactating women and children under 2, who are most at-risk for malnutrition, and will likely include female-headed households, households will high dependency ratios, households with a person with a disability as appropriate.

project_name: Safer and resilient communities in central Mali
project_objective:
In Central Mali, intercommunal conflicts and tensions continue to lead to population displacements. According to DCA’s Rapid Response Mechanism, 5445 IDPs have been registered in April 2018 in Koro Circle/District of Mopti region, due to intercommunal clashes between the Dogons (farmers) and Fulani (pastoralists) groups. In the same month, in Djenne Circle/District of Mopti, 3700 IDPs have been registered.  There are predispositions to confrontations related to the economy, history and behavior of the army. The quasi-disappearance of State control over the area is being maximally exploited by violent extremist groups to fuel these intercommunal conflicts. Therefore, social cohesion is of a great need for these populations. 
In addition to the above, the food security situation has continuously deteriorated since 2016. The frequency of shocks and aggravating factors (climatic, environmental, economic, security) accentuates the deterioration of livelihoods for poor and very poor households and increases significantly their level of vulnerability, while greatly reducing their resilience. There are few favorable signals to hope that this trend will reverse in 2019. Poor and very poor households need assistance to face the lean season and in long term perspective to improve their resilience to ever recurring shocks. 
Finally, the operational capacity of local CSOs for delivering actions to reinforce social cohesion remains a great challenge as many are characterized by institutional and organizational weaknesses.
Targets groups of the projects are underserved and insecurity affected communities, IDPs and returnees, Women headed of households, very poor farmers and pastoralists, CSOs.

project_name: Enabling safe and sustainable returns through the provision of Risk Education, Survey and Clearance
project_objective: There is still extensive explosive hazard contamination across Iraq that poses dangers to vulnerable individuals, inhibits the safe return of displaced persons and impedes the provision of humanitarian assistance to vulnerable populations. The objective of the project is to address the needs of the most vulnerable conflict-affected people and enable safe and sustainable returns through the provision of Risk Education, Survey and Clearance. The project will focus its activities in Ninewa governorate, and will target the most vulnerable people in the project area. The majority of the project budget will be allocated for costly but life-saving survey and clearance activities in Mosul, Telafar, Tilkaif and Sinjar, with parallel awareness raising and risk education activities.

project_name: Addressing basic needs of households acutely affected by armed conflict
project_objective:
The objective of this project is to provide humanitarian assistance, and enhance the resiliencies of vulnerable IDPs, returnees and host communities in hard to reach parts of Syria. Given the incredible complexity of the situation in Aleppo and Ar Raqqa governorates, which may vary from one district to another, different modalities will be employed to provide an integrated yet tailored response. 
Overall, 2000 households (12,000 individuals) will be targeted by Shelter and NFI activities.
Sector Objective 1: Provide life-saving and life-sustaining shelter and NFI support.
Sector outcome indicator: Targeted crisis-affected households, including those in HTR locations, have their core and essential non-food item needs met.
Activity: 1.1 Provision of core and essential NFIs (e.g. mattress/mat, plastic sheet, blankets, jerry can, kitchen set, solar lamps, including cash/voucher for these items). Regular NFI distributions will ensure that the basic needs of displaced and/or vulnerable households are met, while supporting their dignity.
Sector outcome indicator: Targeted people are protected from seasonally harsh conditions.
Activity: 1.2 Provision of seasonal and supplementary NFIs and shelter assistance.
In addition to the distribution of core and essential items, the project will provide winterization assistance to households living in sub-standard shelter, i.e. living in camps, informal settlements or damaged/unfinished buildings.
Sector Objective 2: Contribute towards the resilience and cohesion of communities and households by improving housing and related community/public infrastructure.
Sector Outcome Indicator:  Increase in adequate housing stock available to targeted households and communities.
Activity 2.1 Support to sustainably repair or rehabilitate housing and related community/public infrastructure and facilities provided to owners/tenants/host families (can include: materials, cash, voucher, cash-for-work, labour, etc.).
Shelter Rehabilitation activities will be implemented through the provision of Cash for Shelter grants, which will be accompanied by regular technical support from the project Shelter and Infrastructure Team.

project_name: Provision of emergency reproductive, maternal, new born and child health services including disease prevention and strengthening national and regional emergency preparedness and response capacities
project_objective:
This project will strive to preserve the gains made in 2018 and will deliver lifesaving emergency health services including maternal, neonatal and child health and contribute to disease prevention and strengthening national and regional emergency preparedness and response capacities in the three zones of Somalia for an estimated 974,000 out of 3 million crisis affected population in need of healthcare. Through deployment of trained health workers including midwives and community health workers in facilities and mobile teams, primary health care services including treatment of common childhood illnesses, as well as emergency obstetric and neonatal care for pregnant and lactating women will be provided.
The proposed action complements UNICEF's core interventions in Somalia and the intervention focuses on an integrated, multi-sectoral response to drought, displacement and conflict, providing life-saving services. To maximize impact, this project will provide evidence-based curative, promotional and preventive services and will enable complementarity with nutrition including priorities such as deworming, breastfeeding, complementary feeding, vitamin deficiencies, & micronutrient supplementation. In collaboration with Health Cluster, UNICEF will support the appropriate management of children with SAM and cholera co-morbidity admitted in AWD/Cholera treatment centres. Scaling up the WASH component as part of an integrated and coordinated response, will focus on disease outbreaks, especially cholera. Thus, the integrated action focuses on increasing response in areas of highest need and lowest levels of predictable access in Somalia. 

UNICEF supported health facilities will be equipped with essential medicines and equipment and trained staff will provide quality services. Emphasis will be laid on Maternal and Child Health, including Basic Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care and Expanded Programme on Immunization to IDPs and most vulnerable communities and attention will be paid on application of treatment guidelines as per the Essential Package of Health Services and Primary Health Care. Support to outreach immunization for hard-to-reach areas will be promoted to ensure equity and reaching a wider catchment. UNICEF will deliver comprehensive reproductive health care to women of reproductive age, men and adolescent boys among the target beneficiaries and promote health seeking behaviour including adoption of preventive practices through campaigns, health and hygiene education sessions for men and ado. UNICEF will also integrate surveillance and emergency preparedness ensuring adequate stocks for epidemic outbreaks of AWD/Cholera and measles are prepositioned. The project will also contribute to strengthening early warning disease surveillance through weekly submission of Communicable and Disease Surveillance reports from all the functional supported health facilities. Referral system for patients seeking secondary healthcare services will be strengthened. The project will also refer GBV victims to health facilities for comprehensive care and psychosocial support.

project_name: Integrated life saving and preventive nutrition interventions and strengthened nutrition information system in South Sudan.
project_objective: The findings of county level nutrition assessments conducted in 2018 reveal that 68 per cent of the 32 SMART surveys had global acute malnutrition (GAM) prevalence above the emergency threshold of 15 per cent. This signals a critical nutrition situation in South Sudan in 2019 which will require scale up in nutrition intervention by UNICEF and implementing partners. The purpose of this nutrition project is to support preventive and lifesaving nutrition interventions through treatment of children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM), provision of maternal infant and young child nutrition (MIYCN), capacity building and robust information systems in all the ten states of South Sudan including use of integrated rapid response mechanism (IRRM) modality to deliver nutrition services in the hardest to reach locations. UNICEF will also work closely with other sectors to deliver integrated nutrition sensitive interventions through an array of cross-sectoral linkages with education, health, water and sanitation, child protection interventions to contribute to reduction in stunting and acute malnutrition. In response to the humanitarian needs in South Sudan, UNICEF together with implementing partners plan to reach 984,701 pregnant women and caregivers of children below the age of 24 months and 220,680 children with SAM. The total cost of delivering UNICEF front line project is estimated to be USD 33,283,200 for a duration of twelve months.

project_name: Protection of conflict-affected girls, boys and women exposed to child protection risks and gender based violence in South Sudan
project_objective: The UNICEF Child Protection programme provides support to the most vulnerable, conflict-affected girls, boys and women in South Sudan who are exposed to child protection risks and gender based violence. The programme includes providing case management and family tracing and reunification services, psychosocial support, reintegration interventions for children associated with armed forces and groups (CAAFAG), mine risk education (MRE) monitoring of grave child rights violations through the monitoring and reporting mechanism (MRM), gender based violence interventions, and critical, frontline emergency services, through integrated rapid response mechanisms (IRRMs). Within the programme budget $19.4m is needed for CPiE, $7.5m for GBV and $1.6m for MRE.

project_name: Provision of urgently needed lifesaving Health and Nutrition interventions for vulnerable women, boys and girls in Gaza
project_objective:
The project objective is to respond to the Health and nutrition cluster objective to ensure the availability,
accessibility, acceptability and quality of essential lifesaving health services to the most vulnerable communities in Gaza including through health
system strengthening, preparedness and community resilience building
This project aims to provide urgent response to immediate health needs by ensuring access to health and nutrition services for the most vulnerable
patients (pregnant, lactating women, neonates and children under age of five; boys and girls) through the provision of medical supplies, targeted outreach postnatal home visiting services and solarization of 2 Neonatal Intensive Care Units (NICUs).
The project will respond to the key components of the Health and Nutrition cluster emergency response, namely
procurement of essential medical supplies to increase the availability of drugs, disposables, and medical equipment to ensure accurate diagnostics and treatment for the high risk pregnant and lactating women including victims of or at risk of GBV, newborns and children under age of
five (boys and girls) across the 5 governorates in Gaza Strip. Furthermore, access to the quality newborn and child health and nutrition care
will be improved through solairzation of 2 NICUs (European Gaza and NPH), further enhancement of health workers’(doctors and nurses; females and males) capacity on lifesaving health and nutrition interventions, including essential newborn care, Infant and Young Child Feeding in Emergency (IYCF-E) and provision of early intervention services to children with delays and disabilities and strengthening community’s preparedness, response and resilience, especially during crises. After the completion of joint UNICEF, Save the Children and WFP ongoing Nutrition needs assessment in Gaza, interventions will be informed and response will be amplified to decrease risks of acute malnutrition among young children, pregnant and lactating women.
The total number of women and children that will benefit from the HRP funding will be 60,695 across the 5 Gaza governorates
over a twelve-month period. It is estimated that 25,000 high-risk women and caregivers and 35,595 children under age of five (18,153 boys and 17,442 girls) and 100 health professionals(doctors and nurses;  female 60 percent and 40 percent males)  will benefit from urgently
needed lifesaving health and nutrition interventions.

project_name: Restoring livelihoods of crisis affected population in Syria through light rehabilitation of the critical irrigation infrastructure at community level.
project_objective:
The United Nations (UN) estimates number of crisis-affected population in need of humanitarian assistance in Syria at 11.7 million people(49.8% male and 50.2% female) out of which 4.7 million and 5 million live in areas of major severity of needs (inter-sector severity 3) and acute severity of need (inter-sector severity 4-6) respectively. The above include 6.2 million protracted Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs); 1.4 million returnees; 324,000 IDPs in hard to reach areas, 1.6 million-population movement and the rest overburdened host communities in addition to 480,000 Palestine refugees.  67% of the 11.7 million people in need of humanitarian assistance are accessible from within Syria according to Syria Response Access Dynamic December report (OCHA, 2018).  Overall, 9 million of people are estimated to be food insecure and at risk of food insecurity by Food Security Sector. 

In this context, FAO has designed a project to assist 75,000 vulnerable crisis affected food insecure farming households (equivalent to 450,000 people) in Syria. About 15% of the targeted households will be selected from those who receive food support to help them shift from depending on food support to producing their own food and secure their lives. The objective of the proposed action is to protect and re-establish  livelihoods of vulnerable crisis affected farmers and internally displaced populations through restoration of critical irrigation infrastructures to increase household food production and security. The expected outputs of the projects are:-

Output 1: Critical small-scale irrigation infrastructures in the targeted governorates are assessed and light rehabilitation undertaken. 

Output 2. Capacity of technical staff and relevant stakeholder’s strengthened 
A training programme on enhancing irrigation management, water use efficiency in small-scale irrigation, agricultural land management will be based on FAO standards and approaches.  Stakeholders and farmers will join this training. 

This project is expected to contribute to increase access to irrigation water for crisis-affected farmers and their families in the targeted areas through light rehabilitation of critical small scale irrigation infrastructures. Cultivation and other agricultural practices including livestock and pastures production will consequently benefit from the water supply plans as an emergency response to crisis. The proposed intervention will strengthen household food production capacities and knowledge; and address immediate food and nutrition security. It will also increase availability of food within the country.  This may in turn promote flourishing of agricultural based livelihoods in the rural community, which would contribute to social cohesion, peace and stability.  The project seeks to utilize intensive labor in order to reach the maximum possible community participation and inject cash into the local community.

project_name: UNICEF Refugee Multi-Sectoral
project_objective:
Under Sudan’s MYHS 2017-2019 and HRP 2019, UNICEF will endeavour to support the most vulnerable and marginalized particularly, women and children. UNICEF positions itself to work in the deprived communities with the highest level of vulnerability aiming to address the underlying immediate and long-term causes. Based on the comparative advantage of UNICEF’s programming and hands-on experience of 60 years in Sudan, it is evident that a meaningful impact and results only be attained by adopting inter-sectoral approaches given they are fully integrated. 
UNICEF aims to deliver an integrated package for children by adopting a “whole child” approach wherein, the UNICEF led sectors would work together by identifying the geographic convergence, improving programmatic complementarity under a common result framework thus, realizing rights of the most vulnerable children in the areas of health, education, WASH and protection. This will allow UNICEF to enhance sustainability within the projects and build resilience of the affected population and thus, bridging the humanitarian and development. 
UNICEF in partnership with UNHCR has developed a modus operandi for refugee response both for in-camps and out-of-camp population. UNICEF is ensuring the delivery of an integrated maternal child health and nutrition package along with WASH, education and child protection in camps. Provision of out-of-camp services has been mainstreamed with the service delivery for host communities. In the spirit of partnership and the new way of working, UNICEF submits an intersectoral proposal – a progressive step in the direction of achieving integration.

project_name: Provision of Cash assistance for NFI and in kind non-food items (NFIs) to vulnerable Palestine Refugees in Syria
project_objective:
UNRWA estimates that 418,000 out of 445,000 Palestine refugees in Syria will continue to require humanitarian assistance in 2019. However, UNRWA will be working towards targeting its assistance towards the most vulnerable Palestine refugees.  A vulnerability assessment was conducted in 2018 to ensure delivery of humanitarian assistance towards the most vulnerable.  

The project includes two main components which are cash assistance for NFI and distribution  of in-kind NFIs. Under the cash component, UNRWA is planning to adopt a two-tier approach for humanitarian NFIs assistance in 2019.  The focus will be on four main groups that can be identified through UNRWA’s registration system. These categories are: families headed by a person older than 60 years; families headed by a person with disability, and people with disabilities; families headed by a female; and orphans.  UNRWA estimates that 126,000 Palestine Refugees fall under the identified categories and will accordingly provide them with cash assistance for NFIs amounting to USD 10.5 per person per month. Meanwhile, UNRWA will provide the remaining 292,000 Palestine Refugees in need of assistance with cash assistance for NFIs equivalent to USD 5.25 per person per month to help them meet their basic needs.  

Under the in-kind NFIs distribution, UNRWA in 2019 will focus its response on areas where access is restricted, acute emergency setting, and according to the needs in newly accessible areas.  In addition, UNRWA will stop large scale distributions undertaken since 2012 to all IDPs and will focus on creating a contingency stock for 5000 families in need, including all main NFIs distributed by UNRWA namely blankets, mattresses, tarpaulin, clothes, kitchen sets, jerry cans, baby kits, cleaning sets etc.

project_name: Emergency support to food insecure small scale herders affected by the crisis to protect their livestock assets.
project_objective:
The United Nations (UN) estimates number of crisis-affected population in need of humanitarian assistance in Syria at 11.7 million people (49.8% male and 50.2% female) out of which 4.7 million and 5 million live in areas of major severity of needs (inter-sector severity 3) and acute  need (inter-sector severity 4-6) respectively(HNO, 2019). The above include 6.2 million protracted Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs); 1.4 million returnees; 324,000 IDPs in hard to reach areas, 1.6 million-population movements and the rest overburdened host communities. In addition, 480,000 Palestine refugees are considered part of the people in need.   67% of the 11.7 million people in need of humanitarian assistance are accessible from within Syria according to Syria Response Access Dynamic December (OCHA, 2018).  Overall, 9 million of people are estimated to be food insecure and at risk of food insecurity by Food Security Sector. In this context, FAO has designed a project to assist 90,000 small-scale herders' households (equivalent to 540,000 people) in Syria. The objective of the proposed action is to improve food security and strengthen resilience of 90,000 vulnerable herders' households through restocking, provision of animal feed and capacity building. The project expected outputs are:
Output 1. Production assets for 15,000 vulnerable crisis affected breeders is restored through re-stocking. This output aims at restocking through provision of small ruminants (2 female ewes/sheep per households in line with sector recommendations) for 15,000 vulnerable households for purposes of asset restoration 
Output 2. Livestock productivity for 55,000 vulnerable crisis affected breeders is maintained. 
The output aims at improving availability of feeds for purposes of assets protection of 55,000 vulnerable households (400 kg of the feed per households in line with sector recommendations).
Output 3: Improved skills and livestock management capacity of 90,000 households.
It is expected that the introduction of agriculture based livelihood protection support in current protracted nearly eight years of crisis will be able to increase local availability of food, self-reliance and improve food and nutrition security of the Syrian people, especially the most vulnerable ones.

project_name: Provision of Small livelihood Assets for vulnerable Host Communities and Returnees in Ninewa Governorate
project_objective: According to EL cluster, there are 158,103 in need in Telafar, which is known to be the top areas in need in Iraq in multiple sectors with EL flagged as most severe. Based on MCNA assessment, 36% IDPs are in need of EL assistance.  The needs of returnees and non-displaced population (Host Communities) are comparable to those of IDPs in most aspects, with 39% of Host Communities (HC) in need of EL assistance. The EL need gap is affecting other sectorial outcomes, like education, protection and health. At least half of the expenditure ratio is spent on food items for over 50% of the Telafar population, whereas negative difference between income and expenditure on basic needs significantly contribute in increased debt ratio among. In response to this humanitarian crises, and aligned with EL Objective 1 “Provide immediate access to income to support highly vulnerable displaced persons living in camps, temporary, formal and informal settlements in order to assist and facilitate safe returns and strengthen resilience”, WV proposes to reach 500 households small livelihood Assets replacement interventions, which protection and gender perspective will be mainstreamed throughout the project, with vulnerable groups (e.g. women) representatives involved in key decision making through intensive capacity building for vulnerable community groups who are less familiar with business for Asset Transfer.

project_name: Providing multisectoral life-saving humanitarian assistance to the most vulnerable people living in IDP sites in Northwest Syria
Addressing the water, sanitation and hygiene needs of vulnerable conflict-affected populations in Iraq
project_objective:
ACTED will provide comprehensive WASH assistance to highly vulnerable populations residing in camp (Salamiyah 1 and 2 camp) and out of camp (Ba’aj, Sinjar, Telafar, Mosul) in Ninewa Governorate, in Iraq. The proposed interventions will target a total of 7930 IDPs As Salamiyah 1 and 20035 IDPs in As Salamiyah 2 camp, aiming at facilitating safe access to emergency water and sanitation services and hygiene practices. ACTED plans to provide emergency water supply through water trucking and/or the establishment, rehabilitation and maintenance of water networks, as well as sanitation support through maintenance and upgrading of sanitation facilities and services, including waste management and desludging. 
Hygiene promotion activities will address a range of essential topics, including but not limited to: hand-washing, safe use of water, safe defecation practices, water conversation, waste management, and basic health to promote a healthy environment and prevention of disease outbreaks. 
ACTED furthermore plans to target an estimated 40,000 IDP’s, returnees and host community members in Ba’aj, Sinjar, Telafar and Mosul district with WASH interventions aiming at improving access to WASH services and hygiene practices, in addition to rehabilitating and maintaining community WASH infrastructures. 
In order to support a timely response in case of evolving WASH needs, ACTED further plans to establish contingency sanitation mobile capacities, focusing on providing as hoc sanitation support to WASH partners in IDP camps in Ninewa and Dohuk governorate
Additionally, with the establishment of a Sludge Treatment Plant in Dohuk governorate ACTED plans to mitigate the negative impacts of poor human waste disposal practices in the governorate.

project_name: Provide Full WASH Package for IDPs in Haj Ali camp
project_objective: We plan to implement Water, sanitation and hygiene activities for IDPs in Haj Ali camp in south of Mosul. the activities will include monitoring the provision of water, organizing the water distribution, water quality, operating and maintenance of Sanitation facilities and daily cleaning for it, desludging, conduct hygiene promotions sessions and distribute of hygiene kits there. the activities will be for twelve months with total amount about (500,000) USD.

project_name: Maintaining WASH services in the non- camps areas (Serving IDPs and Returnees) in Al Anbar Governorate (Ana, Rawa, Heet, Qaim, Bzabiz, Amriat Al Fallujah, Al Khalidiyah)""
project_objective:
Maintain and manage the WASH services for schools, health care centers and non-camp areas for IDPs and Returnees in Al Anbar (Bzabiz, Amriat Al Fallujah, HTC, Al Khalidiyah, Heet, Ana, Rawa and Al Qaim).
 SSORD will make sure to coordinate the efforts with other partners intervening in order to make use of the resources available and not to duplicate the services.

project_name: Restore water and sanitation services for vulnerable returnees
project_objective:
Since west Mosul (Ninewa Governorate) was recaptured from ISIL in July of 2017 and Al-Shirqat (Salah ad Din Governorate )  in September 2016, displaced families have begun to return to their areas of origin to rebuild their livelihoods and communities. Unfortunately due to the massive destruction left behind after the conflict, many do not have the resources needed to safely return in a dignified manner. This project focuses on improving the  WASH conditions of vulnerable returnees and host communities in  West Mosul  and  Center East Shirqat. 
COOPI will work on the rehabilitation of WASH facilities (in schools), network and WTP, providing water supplies, cash for work for the rehabilitation in order to restore basic water and sanitation services. This intervention will facilitate takeover of care and maintenance of water and sanitation facilities by local authorities. Special attention will be paid to identify the barriers and the areas with severe shortages of drinking water. Incorporation of the research with local information provided by various stakeholders and a need assessment will identify the most reasonable, cost-effective, and practical solutions. To maximise the effects of the intervention COOPI will also organise a distributions of vouchers for NFI in order to encourage and sustain good hygiene practices but also to boost both the supply and demand side of local markets.Special attention will be paid to no discrimination, balancing the number of toilets in schools by GENDER and adding innovative (portable prefab toilets) toilets for students with disabilities. To tackle the issue of water quality in public places of interest, COOPI will pilot cost-effective, innovative and durable solutions to ensure water safety at school level. Beneficiaries will be involved directly in the quality monitoring so as to facilitate the phasing-out of the assistance and foster the long-term overall sustainability of the intervention.

project_name: Provision of restored WaSH assistance to vulnerable populations in Sinjar District and Mosul City
project_objective:
The proposed action’s main objective is to restore basic water and sanitation services to vulnerable IDPs, returnees and host communities in old Mosul city, Sinjar city, Sinuni city and surrounding villages, as well as to promote good hygiene practices among targeted beneficiaries. Ninawa governorate ranks the highest in severity of living conditions of return for livelihoods, basic services and social cohesion, with hotspots concentrating in Sinjar district and Mosul City.
The Water, Sanitation and Health Directorates are overstretched and under-resourced. They struggle to cover the urgent critical needs and are not in capacity to mitigate a sudden deterioration of the epidemiological situation is case of waterborne diseases outbreaks. French Red Cross (FRC) and IRCS (Iraqi Red Crescent Society)’s experience in the area and analysis of the situation led designing this project that aims to fill part of the gaps of the basic WaSH services and ensures a safe hygiene environment.
For water supply service, the FRC/IRCS propose to rehabilitate damaged boreholes in Sinjar District, secondary water network in Old Mosul and support vulnerable households to connect to the network. The action will extend the current support to the municipalities in maintaining solid waste collection service, complemented by waste collection support in the communities. Hygiene promotion campaigns focusing on personal hygiene, safe water storage and waste management will be rolled out for all beneficiaries with a strong focus on menstrual hygiene management. School WaSH infrastructures will be rehabilitated and complemented by a participative hygiene training for school aged children using the CHAST (Children Hygiene and Sanitation Training) approach adapted to Iraqi context.

project_name: RI Emergency Health, and WASH Response in Anbar, Salahaldin and Kirkuk Governorates
project_objective:
Following liberation from the Islamic State at the end of 2017, Iraq entered a transition period from emergency humanitarian relief to emergency recovery. Despite this transition, there are areas still possessing significant humanitarian needs in the fields of WASH and health. 

There is an immediate health risk caused by inadequate access to safe water, poor sanitary conditions in camp and out of camp settings, and bad hygiene practices. Affected communities have insufficient access to safe water and sanitation, inadequate supply of safe drinking water, lack of functioning latrines, and limited availability of basic hygiene items. The general situation presents a significant risk of waterborne and diarrheal diseases, with an increased risk of infections such as cholera arising in areas where local authorities do not have the capacity to cover the needs, and where only a limited number of humanitarian actors are currently operating. In particular, the lack of WASH infrastructure in schools is a huge challenge as the current situation prevents children from returning to education, or exposes those who do return to the risk of communicable diseases.

Primary healthcare provision remains insufficient in several areas which continue to be overwhelmed and in critical need of support, particularly for children, pregnant women and neonates. There is a lack of medical qualified staff, inadequate medical supplies and pharmaceuticals, a lack of referral pathways for critical and severe patients, and lack of secondary healthcare services. Communities suffering these conditions, do not have any established Primary Healthcare Centers (PHCs), and continue to rely on the provision of healthcare through Mobile Medical Teams (MMTs).

 
Considering the needs, Relief International (RI) aims at addressing the three areas of concern through an integrated program approach. It will build upon its current WASH, and health interventions to continue providing emergency lifesaving health assistance to the most vulnerable and underserved populations in the areas of Anbar, Kirkuk and Salahaldin governorates. For WASH, RI will focus on the provision of safe drinking water and sanitation facilities, and the promotion of hygiene, specifically in schools and health facilities; the overall intervention will target 133,000 beneficiaries. In terms of Health, RI will continue its intervention with Static Primary Healthcare Centers in camp settings; the overall intervention will target 470,583 beneficiaries. 

In terms of targeted population, both male and female, IDPs, returnees and host communities, will be targeted. The intervention will be tailored considering that each gender group requires a specific response; therefore, specific attention will be posed to the needs of women and children to design a more effective response. The description of the activities related to each program will be developed in the following dedicated section.

project_name: Restoring basic WASH infrastructure and local capacity for service provision and providing WASH emergency services in Ninewa, Anbar, Salah Al Din and Kirkuk governorates
project_objective: Project aims at restoring basic water and sanitation services and supporting good hygiene practices for highly vulnerable populations in areas of return and facilitate takeover of care and maintenance of water and sanitation facilities by local authorities in  Ninewa,  Salah Al Din, Anbar and  Kirkuk governorates. The restoration and rehabilitation of damaged WASH infrastructure in conflict-affected areas of the four governorates will contribute to WASH cluster objective  number 2 to support highly vulnerable displaced families who are willing to return to their homes but are unable to do so without sufficient access to basic WASH services. Access to a clean and easily available water supply is one of the most important aspects of daily life, and to support those who seek to return Tdh will focus specifically on rehabilitation of WTP/pumping station/boreholes, water networks, school  and , health center WASH facilities, improve solid waste management in the school, health centers and in the communities, and  roll out hygiene promotion in close cooperation with DoWs, DoEs, DoHs, mayors. Furthermore the project will support water and waste management at household level with the local communities. The response will also seek to maintain a WASH emergency response capacity an contribute to cluster objective number 3 by pre-positioning WASH NFI kits in high risk areas.

project_name: Enhancing Accountability for Gender Based Violence with Humanitarian Nutrition Organizations
project_objective:
Gender based violence (GBV) is a pervasive, protection and human rights issue that is often exacerbated in emergency contexts. As stated at the IASC guidelines for integrating Gender Based Violence Interventions in Humanitarian Action, while the existence of GBV may be undocumented in any given emergency, research has shown that incidences of GBV are underreported and occur regardless of the presence or absence of evidence. While humanitarian actors acknowledge the importance of systematic prevention, mitigation and response to GBV, there are still many gaps in our system that prevent this from happening. 

As a leading INGO in the fight against hunger, AAH will contribute to addressing these main barriers by targeting global and national humanitarian nutrition coordination mechanisms. AAH is a member of the Global Nutrition Cluster, and is also an active member of national nutrition coordination mechanisms across 45 countries, reaching a total of 14.9 million direct beneficiaries from 2010 to 2015. AAH is thus a legitimate and powerful actor that can make an impact within its level of influence by addressing some of the gaps identified in outcome number 2 of the GBV Call to Action. 

More specifically, this project aims to establish a solid foundation to strengthen GBV coordination mechanisms within the nutrition cluster and national nutrition coordination mechanisms by strengthening accountability and providing effective leadership through example. Thus, the project will contribute to Indicator 2a of the call to action  “85% of global level GBV Area of Responsibility members satisfied with leadership, performance, and accountability of the global humanitarian GBV coordination mechanism by 2020”. 
 
This project will also proactively promote effective local leadership of and robust engagement in assessment, planning, implementation and monitoring of GBV and gender equality interventions; one of the key actions identified at outcome 2 of the GBV call to action. In order to do so, 3 countries of operation will be targeted within the AAH international network, one in East Africa, one in West Africa and one in Asia.  The criteria used to select pilot countries will include composition of beneficiaries (50% of beneficiaries being refugees), vulnerability of affected population, access to beneficiaries and the interest of the country office and nutrition organizations nationally in hosting the pilot experience.

project_name: Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan
project_objective:
The current security and humanitarian situation in South Sudan affected 299,123 refugees in South Sudan as of October 2018. The majority of them originated from Sudan (277,183) followed by DRC (15,683), Ethiopia (4,163) and CAR (1,999). They reside in 21 camps and urban locations in Upper Nile, Unity, Western Equatoria, Central Equatoria, and Jonglei regions. South Sudan maintains an open-door policy for refugees and grants those arriving from Sudan, DRC, and CAR prima facie refugee status. There are additionally 2,454 asylum-seekers from Ethiopia, Eritrea, Somalia, Burundi and other countries waiting for determination on their individual refugee claims.  Daily border crossing continues with 17,317 new arrivals registered in 2018 (as of October 2018) from Blue Nile and South Kordofan States of Sudan. 

Refugees reside in conflict-affected regions where security remains precarious with fragile relations with host communities. The continuous economic decline, weak rule of law, limited development support and lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as the conditions in the refugees’ areas of origin mean that refugees will continue to rely on lifesaving humanitarian assistance and on social cohesion with and acceptance by the host community for protection.
Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will benefit from various forms of protection interventions from UNHCR and its partners, including individual registration and documentation. Specific protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identified at-risk groups. While food, water, health and education services are available for all refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with specific protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as verification exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the efficiency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of refugees in need of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban setting will also continue to benefit from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services. 

UNHCR and partners will continue delivery of protection and multi-sectoral assistance to refugees. UNHCR and partners will continue programs ensuring refugees’ access to healthcare services, education, WASH, livelihoods, food and NFI distribution. Access to reproductive health and HIV services will be ensured through complete ANC coverage, health facility deliveries and skilled health workers, as well as comprehensive HIV/AIDS programmes allowing refugees to have access to ant-retroviral treatments (ART) through ART centers in all camps and the two referral hospitals. 
Initiatives to strengthen SGBV prevention and response mechanisms and child protection will be further promoted. While facilitating traditional justice mechanisms, such as conflict resolution committees and joint customary courts, UNHCR will support re-establishment of statutory courts in refugee sites.

project_name: Food support to Refugees at Tongogara Refugee Camp
project_objective:
WFP Zimbabwe, in partnership with UNHCR and jointly-selected partner Terre Des Hommes (TDH), is currently supporting more than 13,000 refugees in Tongogara Refugee Camp (TRC) with monthly food assistance. The refugees are mainly from DRC (72.3%), Mozambique (13.7%), Burundi (6.04%) and Rwanda (5%), with others from the Horn of Africa including Somalia, Ethiopia and South Sudan. TRC the only refugee camp in Zimbabwe, located in Chipangayi, Chipinge District in Manicaland Province, about 500 kilometres South East of the capital, Harare and approximately 80km west of Chipinge town. The camp was established in 1981 to cater for an influx of refugees from Mozambique during its civil war. The number of refugees residing at TRC has consistently increased, with a sharp rise from 5,000 in 2015 to the current 13,000. The population is expected to grow further in 2019, considering the rising tensions in DRC.
The camp measures approximately 800ha, with a possible maximum of 1,000ha available for current use and planning requirements, according to Government of Zimbabwe (GOZ).The camp is in natural region 5, characterized by temperatures that in mid-summer can average more than 40 degrees Celsius, with mean annual rainfall of less than 450mm/year and of a sporadic nature that is not suitable for growing the staple maize crop. The camp experiences cycles of floods and droughts and can go through an entire season without rain; the nearby Save River becomes an important water resource for agricultural-based livelihoods.
The GOZ and UNHCR manage the camp, and work with other partners to ensure basic needs and protection of rights of concerned population. In line with the global agreement, WFP is the main partner managing and providing food assistance for refugees at the camp since 2015; accordingly, it has built up substantial capacity to run the programme in collaboration with partners. The refugees are fully reliant on WFP’s food assistance for survival.
WFP provides monthly food assistance of the resident refugees, through cash-based transfers, sufficient to meet 100 percent of the daily energy requirements of an adult person. Chronically ill people also receive a top-up of Super Cereal through camp health facilities, enabling them to consume up to 2,380 kcal per day. The new arrivals at the camp receive an in-kind transfer for the first three months to cover the gap between their arrival at the camp and the completion of their registration, after which they are entitled to the regular cash-based assistance. 
WFP has been implementing cash transfers at the camp since 2016. The cash-based assistance has empowered the persons of concern to buy food commodities of their choice furthering their dignity and opportunity to access food, increasing diversity of food consumption and stimulating local markets. It has also empowered some of them towards pursuing other livelihoods options.
The refugee population is continuously increasing by an average of 150 persons every four weeks. This is in addition to the already existing 450 caseload of people seeking asylum. Following this trend, Zimbabwe is likely to experience a wave of new asylum seekers, with the numbers reaching 20,000 by December 2019. WFP immediately requires US$1,765,248.00, to provide the much-needed food assistance to the refugees for approximately six months, from January to June 2019. 
WFP proposes to respond through its CSP Activity 1.2 Support to Refugees, to ensure that the food-insecure refugees in TRC are enabled to meet their basic food and nutrition requirements. Support to refugees contributes to SDG target 2.1 (ending hunger and ensuring access to food) as well as SDG target 2.2 (ending all forms of malnutrition). This contribution will assist WFP to pursue the objective to improve food access to vulnerable refugees through the provision of cash-based transfers and in-kind commodities.
