project_name: Ameliorer l'accès à l’eau potable, l’assainissement et l’hygiène pour les personnes déplacées dans les communautés d'accueil et les sites de deplaces dans  les départements du Logone et Chari et Mayo Sava
project_objective:
La crise humanitaire qui sévit dans le bassin du Lac Tchad, les exactions de Boko Haram et les opérations militaires qui en résultent ont dévasté certaines localités de la région de l’Extrême Nord, notamment dans le département du Mayo Sava, Mayo Tsanaga et Logone et Chari. Selon le DTM 15/OIM de Septembre 2018 on dénombre 244,347  Personnes déplacées internes, 100,925 retournés, 41,763 réfugiés hors camp affectées par la crise, dont 65% sont âgées de moins de 18 ans. Les départements les plus touchés sont le département du Mayo Sava avec une cible de 102,202 personnes et le département du Logone et Chari avec une cible de 178 949 personnes, tous composé de 63% de PDI, 26% de retournes et de 11% de refugies hors camps. 
L’International Rescue Committee (IRC), fort de son expertise et de sa présence dans la zone se propose d’améliorer les conditions de vie de ces ménages touchés par la crise dans les Départements du Mayo-Sava et du Logone-et-Chari. Pour ce faire, la réponse proposée vise à améliorer l’accès à l’eau, l’hygiène et l’assainissement pour une cible de 45,000 personnes déplacées vulnérables. Les activités proposées pour atteindre cet objectif consisteront en la construction des nouveaux points (forages et borne fontaines), des réhabilitations des points d’eau, la construction des latrines d’urgence et douches d’urgences pour les populations déplaces se trouvant dans des camps, des latrines familiales et des fosses a ordures ; accompagnées de sensibilisations à l’hygiène. Par ailleurs, des dotations en kits WASH/NFI, des kits de gestion des déchets et des kits de maintenance et gestion d’hygiène au tour des points d’eau seront effectuées. Elle aura également pour objectif d’améliorer les conditions de vie des bénéficiaires ciblés. La stratégie d’intervention vise à rendre la dignité et l’autonomie des bénéficiaires par des méthodologies d’intervention basées sur l’implication des communautés pour augmenter durablement leur capacité de résilience.

project_name: Provision of essential Child health care and nutrition services in Libya
project_objective: UNICEF in close coordination with Ministry of Health, National Center for Diseases Control, WHO, UNFPA, IOM and UNHCR  will provide essential and lifesaving health and nutrition services with focus on vulnerable children and their families in undeserved and remote areas of the country and in the detention centers. The target population include children under five children especially newborns,  Pregnant and Lactating women. Due to protracted emergency in Libya most of the population has limited access to functioning public services and utilities exposing vulnerable groups such as mothers, newborns and children to preventable and curable disease. The health care delivery network and infrastructure in most of the districts is unable to provide needed health services to the population due to major service gaps and inaccessibility.  According to SARA 2017 report the average general service readiness based on amenities, equipment, and medicine is 69 percent in hospitals and 37 percent in PHC centers leaving 31 percent of the health facilities without essential health services. The same report identified lack of essential medicines and supplies in health facilities across Libya with high risk of communicable diseases (polio, measles and others). The immunization supply chain system has dramatically suffered from the conflict and severe shortage of vaccines have been reported at the national level. In July 2018, The Ministry of Health declared a measles outbreak as a result of the increasing number of cases reaching a total of 702 (Report October 2018) with two deaths already reported.  The national health authorities could not mobilize local resources to carry out an outbreak response due to the political fragmentation, ongoing conflict, insecurity, and weaken health system. UNICEF and WHO are supporting National Centre for Diseases Control/ministry of health to undertake a nationwide measles outbreak response immunization. In addition, the highly mobile population, as well as Libya being a transit country for a large number of migrants from the African continent, the risks for a broader outbreak for number of vaccine preventable and communicable diseases are high. This long and large-scale measles outbreak with 40 percent of suspected children without vaccination reflects very low routine immunization coverage. More than 50% of the under five children die within the first 28 days of life, most of these deaths are prevented through provision of Integrated Management of Newborn and Childhood Illnesses. In the given situation there is urgent need for strengthening health system for proving preventive and curative lifesaving and essential services to most vulnerable population in the country including all Detentions centers. This project is expected to contribute significantly in prevention of maternal, neonatal and child morbidity and mortality.

project_name: Emergency Mental Health, Psychosocial and Rehabilitation support to the most vulnerable populations in South Sudan
project_objective:
This project addresses the urgent need for functional and physical rehabilitation and psychosocial support in South Sudan through a flexible response. Humanity & Inclusion understands that the needs in areas affected by the protracted crisis are alarming, but it also acknowledges that there are still unmet needs in protracted situations, which may grow more acute as the situation protracts. This project will, therefore, be a flexible intervention model to address these needs through both a static and mobile response. To that end the project is designed to target Jonglei, Unity, Central Equatoria, Eastern Equatoria, Western Equatoria, and Western Bahrel Ghazal in its interventions. HI already has a static presence (2016-2019) in the 3 Equatoria, frequent mobile missions in Unity and recent (2016) static presence in Jonglei. 

The action targets the most vulnerable persons at risk of exclusion (including people with disabilities, people with injuries and chronic diseases, people experiencing psychosocial distress or mental health troubles, children, older persons), who are often invisible to mainstream relief organizations due to the specificity of their needs. By identifying specific vulnerabilities and providing targeted assistance to these vulnerable individuals through the deployment of a team of specialists providing rehabilitation and psychosocial support to the conflict-affected locations, the action will reduce vulnerability and will mitigate the impact of the conflict. It will do this by facilitating access to lifesaving services, improving functional capacities and independence, strengthening positive coping mechanisms, rebuilding social ties, promoting wellbeing, reducing the chances of psychological distress, and eventually improving the dignity of the targeted beneficiaries.

This project will contribute to the South Sudan HRP 2019 and the specific Health Cluster objectives through providing rehabilitation services to 13802 women, men, boys, and girls with disabilities and by providing mental health and psychosocial support to 20705 people in need of such services, including staff of humanitarian agencies who have gone through traumatizing incidences while on duty. Through identifying and assessing persons with disabilities for rehabilitation and mobility devices and services, this project will contribute to the Health Cluster objective 1, indicator 3 (and HRP objective 1) by ensuring that all persons, regardless of mobility challenges can reach lifesaving services as well as OPD services. Once assessed, persons in need of rehabilitation will have a treatment plan created for them and then implemented to include basic therapeutic activities, physio therapy, and occupational therapy. Caregivers will also be attended to as they are supported to care for their relation with a disability through basic disability education, device maintenance, and mental health care. 

This project will also contribute to the Health Cluster objective 4, indicators 1 and 2 (and HRP objective 3) through providing access to mental health and psychosocial services to strengthen the resilience of communities and by training health care workers on providing MHPSS services to persons with disabilities, on basic MHPSS and PFA, and training them on how to work with survivors of SGBV. Though the mental health of all persons will be focused on in this project, a special consideration will be given to the mental health of persons with disabilities and their caregivers. This will happen through referrals to the PSS team by the rehabilitation team of those with disabilities who are provided with rehab services and in need of PSS services.Those in need of individual and family counseling will also receive that support. Additionally women SGBV survivors will receive special counseling sessions in safe houses and safe spaces and there will be collaboration with protection partners on mapping SGBV services and referrals.

project_name: Southern Cone - United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees

Providing Durable water  solutions by increasing access to emergency and sustained water, sanitation facilities and hygiene promotion for displaced vulnerable women, girls, boys and men in IDP settlements and host communities targeting beneficiaries in South Central and Somali land
project_objective:
The proposed project will provide durable solutions to chronic and recurrent water problems by providing adequate safe water, sanitation facilities and hygiene education targeting 66,000 beneficiaries (32,340 male and 33,660 female) - without double counting. 60,000 beneficiaries will be reached through water supply services. Specifically, 24,000 beneficiaries will benefit through water provision (18,000 in Mogadishu and 6,000 in Lower Shabelle), 21,000 will benefit through construction of mega rain water catchment pan in Bardhere, 13,800 will be reached through construction of water treatment unit in Bardhere, and 1,200 will be reached through construction of  3 berkerds in Somaliland. 
On sanitation, 21,000 beneficiaries will be reached through constriction of 700 latrines (250 Bardhere, 150 Mogadishu, 200 Baidoa and 100 Lower Shabelle). 15,000 beneficiaries will be discounted from the total since the same beneficiaries will benefit from water facilities. On hygiene promotion, 7000 AWD kits (2,500 in Bardhere, 1,500 in Mogadishu, 2000 in Baidoa and 1000 kits in Lower Shabelle) will be distributed to reach 42,000 beneficiaries. Each kit will comprise 200 sachets of aqua tabs, 2 jerry cans and 12 pieces of soap each weighing 200g to give 2400g.  All hygiene promotion beneficiaries will be discounted from the total to avoid double counting.
In Gedo region,  Bardhere, the water treatment unit is aimed at improving the water  quantity and quality will comprise the intake unit, flocculation chamber, sedimentation chamber, chlorination unit, elevated tower and distribution system. The intake unit will comprise a suction pump fitted with a flexible pipe with a floater extending to the river. Water will be delivered to the flocculation unit where aluminium sulphate is added and mixed .Water will then flow to the sedimentation unit which allows settling of large flocs. Water then flows to the chlorination unit where chlorination occurs before it is pumped to a 50 cubic elevated tower through a 2km pipe before distribution occurs through four the water kiosks constructed within the IDP camp. Water will also be pumped to existing elevated RC tank 12meters high  with a capacity of 130 cubic and distributed through and existing water distribution system to serve host communities. ; On sanitation concern plans to construct 250 latrines in the IDP camps. The latrines will be fitted with hand washing facilities aimed at promoting handwashing after use of the latrines and at critical times for AWD/Cholera prevention.  In Belet Xawa, Concern will construct a mega water pan with an improved sand filtration system. The water pan will be lined with a geotextile material to prevent seepage. The Mega Water pan will have a holding capacity of 26,965,000 liters capacity and expected to have water in all the seasons. The water pan will be fenced and provided with a drawing point and fitted with water pump. Animal troughs will also be provided for use. On hygiene, the project propose hygiene education through trained Community Health Promoters. The project will recruit and train hygiene promoters to disseminate hygiene messages during house to house visit;  mass hygiene promotion awareness using radio messaging, hygiene messages on bill-boards located in strategic locations; distribution of hygiene kits will be made to the most vulnerable members of the community; promotion of house hold water treatment through distribution of water purification tablets for rural communities
In Banadir and Bay (lower Shabelle) region, concern will provide water to 24000 IDPs through pipelines. Water will be supplied through existing pipelines and where possible extension of pipelines will be made to ensure beneficiaries get water within a minimum distance of 500 meters. Private water companies owning boreholes near the IDP locations will provide water. All the water points will be metered and payment will be made based on the actual amount of water consumed by the beneficiaries.
In Somaliland, 3 berkerds will be constructed to reach 1200 beneficiaries. The berkerds will be constructed in strategic locations to ensure maximum volume is captured during the rains. The water harvested will be utilized during the dry season.
In order to ensure sustainability of water facilities, Concern will  work with the community and local authorities to identify and train a private company managing water in Bardhere. The Private Company in Bardhere and management committee in Belet Xawa & Somaliland will be trained on management, operation and maintenance of the water supply system. The trained teams will then be issued with operation and maintenance tools for water treatment unit in Bardhere and water pan in Belet Xawa and equipment. The committee and private company will be then continue the operations after the end of the project. This will be done in close collaboration with the local authorities and leaders, the ministry of water and other stakeholders.
To ensure environmental sustainability for the water infrastructure, the operators will be trained on sludge management. Water treatment unit will be designed to have score pipes that will flush accumulated sludge from the system to a soak away pit to ensure there is no environmental pollution. Further, water point locations will be identified based on sanitary survey and absence of source contamination within 30 meters radius. 
In order to ensure the infrastructure will continue to deliver water in cases of flooding, the water treatment unit and water points will be sited on a higher ground free from flooding. Beneficiaries will access water at water points delivered through pipeline to avoid any cases of contamination. The Mega water pan will have a raised draw off well, fitted with a hand pump and linked to the Mega water pan through pipe. project_name: (GBV) Providing life-saving GBV prevention and response activities to conflict-affected women and girls
project_objective:
Five years after the outbreak of internal conflict in South Sudan nearly 4.5 million people have been forced out of their homes in search of safety, nearly 2 million of them internally. While the intensity of conflict may have reduced and clashes contained to certain regions, the humanitarian situation continues to be critical with impacts spilling through 2019. Gender-Based Violence (GBV), including sexual violence, is widespread in South Sudan. Even in displacement settings, threats and risks of GBV against women and girls, particularly rape and child marriages and forced marriage persist. During intercommunal fights and cattle raids, women are abducted and raped, just as during the armed conflict. Some of the key drivers of GBV are gender inequality, on-going conflict, inter-communal fighting, fragile community support systems and weak protection mechanisms, including limited availability and accessibility to basic social services, particularly for women and girls

Survivors of GBV need to access lifesaving psychosocial case management services to meet their complex and multiple needs. The reduced access to essential and lifesaving reproductive health services, and the lack of basic items which respond to the hygiene and reproductive health needs of women and girls, make living very difficult for displaced women and girls to maintain acceptable hygiene standards. Displaced women and girls need basic items in order to interact comfortably in public and maintain their personal hygiene, particularly menstrual hygiene. Without access to culturally appropriate clothing and hygiene items, the mobility of women and girls is restricted and their health might be compromised. Furthermore, without certain items women may be unable to seek basic social services, including humanitarian aid, which may increase their vulnerability to GBV
With the recent, signing of the peace agreement, there is a growing recognition to seize further recovery and development opportunities, where they exist, and to strengthen synergies between these efforts and the ongoing humanitarian response.  UNFPA will work towards strengthening the current model of safe spaces into robust fully sustained multi purposes centers for women and girls with a strong focus on adolescent girls. The centers will provide both prevention and response services scaling up basic skills training, income generation activities, basic literacy classes. WGFS offers opportunities to other actors and services to coordinate and co-locate programming through WGFS to ensure a harmonized and integrated approach to GBV prevention and response and women’s empowerment more broadly. Opportunities for partnerships include with child friendly spaces (CFSs), youth centers, -school clubs, sports centers, health services, nutrition centers, livelihoods and economic empowerment projects. Strong referral networks and pathways are crucial in a WGFS. However, the principle of ‘integrated support systems’ could take coordination further, so that links are made between actors who can collaborate in terms of activities and resources (e.g. space).

project_name: Increasing coverage and access to quality Sexual and Reproductive Health Services and Information for conflict affected population in South Sudan
project_objective:
It is estimated that 3,571,191 million people in South Sudan will be in need of humanitarian healthcare services by the end of 2018 and most likely the whole of 2019. The main health related humanitarian needs in the country include; access to basic primary, secondary healthcare and specialised care such as reproductive health, GBV services and others; access to comprehensive obstetrical care surgical care and case referral; and access to essential medicines and medical supplies. 

The situation of reproductive health and especially the availability of commodities and supplies remains one of the major challenges of increasing access to services. Antenatal visits and skilled delivery remain a major challenge with only 17% of pregnant women attending four visits and a chronic shortage of Basic emergency obstetrics and neonatal services. The unmet need for family planning remains high at 24%. 

Through this project, UNFPA will directly target 180,000  of the estimated 892,798 women of reproductive age, including pregnant women affected by the crisis.  Using pre-crisis birth rates, there will be a projected number of 107,136 births, among which 16,068 will require Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care (EMONC) services of which 5,352 will need a caesarean section, without which death is likely. Lactating women also require special support to ensure safe infant feeding practices and family planning

The main purpose of the project is to provide lifesaving emergency healthcare services to vulnerable populations by increasing and expanding coverage and access to essential quality Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare services. The main interventions to achieve the project purpose include among others: 
•	Health education to women, men, families and community to increase awareness on benefits of safe sex, family planning, ANC, PNC and delivery in health facility by skilled birth attendants;
•	Procuring, prepositioning, and distribution of a whole range of RH kits for delivery of RH services at the community, and health facilities;
•	Procuring other RH equipments for EmONC (delivery beds, examination couches, lighting, and others.
•	Training service providers on essential lifesaving service areas like rational use of RH kits, MISP, CMR, PAC and other lifesaving interventions 
•	Procuring materials for IEC materials. 
•	Conducting quarterly joint assessments and monitoring of services including support supervision missions to the field to ensure proper warehousing, usage of supplies and quality delivery of SRH services.
•	Supporting the 24/7 referral system of complicated obstetric cases
•	Establishing a functional CEmONC Centre in Mingkaman

The activities of the project will ensure that pregnant women have access to ante natal, peri natal and post natal care, including for services for complicated pregnancy and delivery, benefit from basic and comprehensive emergency obstetric care.  Lactating women will be assisted to benefit from health education and promotion information related to exclusive breastfeeding and supplementary feeding.  Men and boys will also be targeted in community awareness sessions and as referal agents for maternal and newborn care services.

project_name: Access to life saving shelter and NFI services to IDPs and returnees across South Sudan
project_objective:
As Shelter and NFI (S-NFI) Cluster Lead Agency (CLA), IOM is requesting USD 10,945,779 to respond to the lifesaving humanitarian needs faced by an estimated 7.1 million displaced persons across South Sudan. With the requested funding, IOM will reach up to 220,816 individuals considered extremely vulnerable (defined as those in acute and moderate need according to the Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) methodology) and whose capacity to anticipate, cope with and recover from conflict stresses have been eroded. These most vulnerable individuals in the targeted communities include newly displaced persons, IDPs in protracted displacement in POCs and collective centres, IDPs living with host communities, returnees, and members of host communities who have lost their income, shelter, assets and food sources. Proposed activities are in line with HRP strategic objectives, as well as the S-NFI Cluster objectives and key activities.  The outputs of the proposed IOM S-NFI project are as follows:

Output 1:  Provide effective and quality Cluster coordination to better respond to Shelter and essential NFI needs and enhance resilience of most vulnerable displaced population in South Sudan. (HRP SO 1, SO2 & SO3; S- NFI Cluster Objectives 1, 2, & 3.
Output 2: Improve access to life saving shelter and life sustaining non-food items and enhance resilience of most vulnerable population through area-based and settlement programming. (HRP SO1, SO2 & SO3; S- NFI Cluster Objectives 1, 2, & 3.

The S-NFI Cluster will further enhance national and sub-national level coordination between government and partners to improve access to IDPs and returnees, as well as continue to advocate at all forums and levels for adequate funding to meet the S-NFI needs of affected people. 

In its efforts to effectively mainstream protection sensitive responses, address gender based violence, and ensure accountability to affected populations (AAP) in 2018, the Cluster has successfully rolled out new tools to mainstream Protection, GBV, AAP and GBV, which will be fully employed to enhance the overall quality of S-NFI response. The S-NFI Cluster will continue to encourage partners to build on the success of CBI programming implemented in the last two years and maintain the target of at least 30% of the target caseload being assisted through Cash Based Interventions (CBI). The Shelter-NFI Cluster will continue to invest and explore effective avenues to strengthen the capacity of both established and new partners in 2019.

As the S-NFI leading agency, IOM will respond to 22% of the Cluster target caseload for 2019 and provide shelter, NFI and settlement support to a total of 220,816 individuals in 2019, with the aim of increasing the resilience of the target population when addressing their S-NFI needs. In line with the Cluster objective to improve integrated responses, IOM has piloted a Settlement project in Wau, and intends to replicate the model to other areas, including Rubkona, Yambio and Renk. IOM will reach a total of 80,000 people (61% of the Cluster’s total settlement target) based on evidence generated from the project, and ensure alignment with the Global Shelter Cluster strategy. For settlement programming, IOM aims to reach 8,000 HHs in Wau and the rest of the beneficiaries in Yambio, Renk, Rubkona. IOM will continue to expand its CBI and plans to reach 40% of its target caseload through CBI approach. IOM will ensure that the needs of men, women, boys and girls are taken into account throughout the project cycle.

IOM will further improve its program quality by strengthening its MEAL capacities, data analysis and evidence to inform planning, coordination, and decision-making.

Through the provision of site care and maintenance, community engagement, strengthened communication with communities, site planning and support in technical advice, IOM will further contribute to the capacity of the humanitarian responses and provide timely and targeted humanitarian assistance. In line with cluster target objectives, IOM intends to target 668,543 persons in need across the geographical area of operations, namely Central Equatoria, Unity, Western Bahr el Gazal, Jonglei and Upper Nile states. Centrality of protection remains at the core of Camp Management programming, observing conflict sensitivity and considering the specific needs of women, men, girls and boys in project planning and execution.

With the cluster advice and coordination, IOM will ensure Camp Management reaches out to populations in need out of the PoC sites with mobile and remote responses. This will further contribute to continuous efforts to avoid concentration of services in the PoC sites and ensure hard to reach populations have access to life saving support.

In promotion of resilience and support to efforts to decongest PoC sites, IOM will continue to offer information management and data sharing with partners and communities. Through partnerships with specialized agencies, camp management will explore means to facilitate and contribute to multisector efforts to meet the needs of target populations across the country.

project_name: Provision of emergency WASH assistance for affected populations in South Sudan
project_objective:
This project intends to provide timely equitable access to safe, water, sanitation and hygiene for IDPs/ host communities and returnees. The project will build on existing WASH services and support rapid response mechanisms, which provide lifesaving WASH services to conflict-affected populations in hard-to-access areas. 

IOM will provide integrated WASH services in Bentiu, Malakal and Wau PoC sites and collective sites, targeting 274,119 beneficiaries. IOM will ensure that WASH activities are maintained at a good standard and able to scale up in the case of population influxes. Activities will include: operation and maintenance of water treatment and supply systems; care and maintenance of sanitation facilities; and solid and liquid waste management. IOM will sustain and improve the promotion of hygiene and public health, focusing on community ownership methods, including menstrual hygiene management for displaced women and adolescent girls. IOM plans to expand WASH services through the construction and/or improvement of key infrastructure and hygiene promotion to assist IPDs outside of PoC sites and host communities. 

IOM’s WASH Emergency Preparedness and Response (EPnR) teams will expand access to WASH services to underserved and vulnerable populations in remote and hard-to-reach locations lacking access to basic services, as identified in coordination with WASH Cluster coordination mechanisms, targeting 274,119 beneficiaries. IOM will ensure provision of safe water through borehole rehabilitation, manual drilling of boreholes, rehabilitation of surface water treatment systems, distribution water treatment supplies and water trucking. IOM will ensure the sustainability of water supply through the formation and training of water management committees and the provision of spare parts for ongoing care and maintenance of boreholes. IOM will additionally promote good hygiene and sanitation practices through hygiene promotion activities and distribution of basic household hygiene items.

The project will additionally contribute to mitigating WASH-related GBV. Gender equality and prevention of GBV will be mainstreamed in all WASH activities such as building women’s leadership to manage water resources and participatory risk-reduction activities. IOM will facilitate the construction/ rehabilitation and maintenance of water and sanitation facilities will adhere to the GBV WASH facilities check list developed by the GBV Sub-cluster and supported by the WASH Cluster. IOM will ensure the active participation of the population in all components, in order to create or reinforce technical skills of community members and to promote actions to dignify the population. All WASH projects incorporate cross-sectoral linkages with health and nutrition to create integrate interventions and scale-up impact.

project_name: Addressing acute food insecurity in rural areas of Somalia
project_objective:
This profile responds to the distinct needs and vulnerabilities of food insecure rural populations in Somalia. Within the 2019 HRP, over 1 million rural Somalis are prioritized for food security assistance in the aftermath of severe drought in 2016-17 and the more recent impacts of flooding, cyclones and conflict in 2018. FAO's contribution to assisting the rural population in need centres on: (i) addressing immediate food needs, while (ii) restoring livelihoods, and (iii) protecting food and income sources against likely shocks in 2019. Outside of the HRP, it is critical that acutely food insecure rural households in IPC 2 that are not targeted within the 2019 HRP receive urgent assistance through resilience programmes or other response planning mechanisms. 

FAO will target 72 700 rural households (436 200 people) directly with cash and/or livelihood support programmes, prioritizing the most vulnerable in IPC Phases 2-4. In addition, large animal health campaigns and preparedness efforts will indirectly serve around 2.7 million people across Somalia. The main purpose of the assistance is to assure immediate access to food, while protecting and restoring rural people’s own food production and income within the shortest lapse of time.  All proposed cash interventions are linked to productive livelihood activities. All livelihood activities tailor to the needs and vulnerabilities of distinct livelihood zones.  

Cash+. FAO’s Cash+ programme will deliver 3-months’ of unconditional cash transfers (UCTs) plus emergency livelihood packages to re-engage farmers, agropastoralists, pastoralists and fishers in productive livelihoods, with the aim to stabilize households' own access to food and income in 4-9 months. 

Cash-for-work. Rural households will engage in 24 weeks of paid work to rehabilitate community-based infrastructures that support the restoration of rural livelihoods (e.g. water catchments and small irrigation canals), or in other productive works such as the control of prosopis. Highly vulnerable families unable to work will receive UCTs (e.g. pregnant women, elderly, ill or disabled people).

Emergency livestock support. FAO will support pastoral communities to protect their remaining livestock and related food sources through a nationwide animal health campaign and fodder production. The animal health interventions include vaccination of 14.5 million goats against Contagious Caprine Pleuropneumonia (CCPP), treatment of 3.5 million livestock against common illness and disease.  

Preparedness. Emergency preparedness interventions are planned to reduce the risk – or possible impacts – of likely climate shocks and food chain threats in 2019, with a particular focus on localized flooding and outbreaks of livestock/crop pests and diseases. Mitigation measures include the repair of broken river embankments, crop pest and disease awareness campaigns and control measures, vector-borne disease control in riverine areas and the pre-positioning of strategic stocks of veterinary vaccines and equipment, plus related trainings (in line with the Global Eradication Strategy of Peste des Petits Ruminants - PPR).

project_name: Improving flood and drought risk management in Somalia through FAO early warning information.
project_objective: The repeated impact of climatic extremes, such as floods and droughts, has had profound direct and indirect effects on Somalia’s economy. Floods and droughts are among the most dangerous and costly of natural disasters. The project objective is to reduce flood and drought impacts through the use of FAO’s early warning information and foster a better understanding of the Juba and Shabelle river basins in Somalia through detailed river surveys that will see durable and sustainable measures to reduce frequent occurrence of floods. The project will aim to scale up the use of modernized early warning systems and climate information to save lives and enhance livelihoods in vulnerable communities through expansion of hydro-meteorological monitoring network that will generate data which will be used in turn in the production of early warning information for early action. To sustain this, FAO will strengthen institutional and indigenous capacities for use of Early Warning Systems (EWS) and Climate Information (CI) in preparedness for response to climate related disasters. The project will also undertake river survey and morphological study for sustainable flood risk management of the Juba and Shabelle river basins. The study results will be used to build institutional and indigenous capacities to mitigate flood risks along the two rivers.

project_name: Ensuring safe and timely access to Gender-Based Violence (GBV) services among the conflict affected populations in Libya
project_objective:
This project aims at strengthening safe and timely access to Gender-Based Violence (GBV) services among the conflict affected populations as well as migrants and refugees throughout Libya in order to promote their healing, safety and well-being.
Recognizing that women and girls are disproportionately affected by GBV, the target population of this project is mostly female, with a specific focus on adolescent and young girls, and elderly. This project will work to ensure that vulnerable minorities have access to services, namely the Tawergha community, and refugees and migrants (in communities and detention centers). Persons with disabilities will be prioritized across the targeted populations to ensure that all services are accessible to them. Men and boys are also subjected to GBV in Libya, especially conflict-related sexual violence. Anecdotal evidence reports ruthless stories of men – especially vulnerable minorities and Tawerghans – coerced into raping other men and women in an attempt to cover up a perfect crime of political revenge that will leave an unhealable scar on a generation of Libyans, refugees and migrants. Men and boys will thus be targeted by the services in an attempt to help them overcome the profound wounds and involve them in the fight against gender-based violence.

In total, this project is expected to reach 100,000 direct beneficiaries. It is worth noting that some of these beneficiaries will have access to more than one service, like dignity kits procured by UNFPA and distributed by local INGOS. Additionally, UNFPA is operating in collaboration with several implementing partners as explained further, and is looking at scaling up the interventions in an effort to cover the existing gaps and as provider of last resort.

Static and outreach activities will be started in women's centers, one in each of the locations of Al Kufra and Murzuq, based on the findings of the protection sector on severity. Additionally, current activities carried out by UNFPA and implementing partners in Tripoli (3 centers with CESVI, Al Safa and Al Bayan), Benghazi (1 center with PSS Team and Amazonet), Sebha (1 center with Women's Union) and Misrata ( 1 center with IRC) will be sustained. The project will be carried out in synergy with other sectors. 
Close coordination with IOM and UNHCR is envisaged, in particular, for the implementation of the GBV prevention and response services in selected detention centers as well as in the to be established Gathering and Departure Facility once operational under UNHCR management. These activities will specifically aim at strengthening the detection of GBV survivors and migrant women at risk of sexual exploitation and abuse, providing GBV and Sexual and Reproductive Health (SRH) services and improving the referral systems for cases of survivors among migrants, refugees and vulnerable Libyans. Using innovative approaches, UNFPA will target migrant and refugee women and people-at-risk with messages raising awareness on their basic rights and informing on the availability of SRH and GBV response services, while engaging young community leaders to be agents of behavioral change in host communities and reduce the stigma on displaced people, particularly women and GBV survivors. Outreach activities carried out by volunteers from the Scouts and Y-Peer network will ensure a participatory approach for boys, girls, adolescents and adults (In 2017 and 2018, UNFPA conducted several focus group discussions and consultations with youth and adults). Given the sensitivity of GBV in conflict in a conservative society and the nature of the activities to be carried out, the need for highly specialized human resources is anticipated.
The approach to GBV case management requires the provision of a multi-sectoral package of services, therefore case managers will be providing psychosocial support and referring survivors to other services such as Clinical Management of Rape (CMR). SRH services will also be provided by UNFPA teams in static and mobile service delivery points, and in collaboration with PUI in some locations. Specialized mental health care will be offered by other organizations such as IMC. UNFPA is also scaling up the capacity of specialized nurses to provide PSS support and mental health services in Tripoli, Misrata and Benghazi. Access to legal and judicial support remains a challenge for GBV survivors in Libya. Efforts will be put on advocacy for the availability of these services. Local and INGO partners in each area will help in designing and implementing the activities in a way to ensure community participation and access to areas which are hard to reach, namely El Safa, El Bayan, PSS Team, Women Union, The Scouts, Libyan Red Crescent, Amazonet, Cesvi, and IRC.

In addition UNFPA seeks to strengthen the overall coordination of GBV in order to upscale GBV prevention, response and risk mitigation in Libya. Currently, UNFPA has deployed a GBV sub-sector coordinator. Key achievements so far include; completion of a GBV service mapping and gap analysis; finalization of the GBV referral pathway for Tripoli; and completion of the Interagency GBV action plan. The sub-sector is currently working on the interagency GBV prevention and response in standards operating procedures. The process of establishing functional GBV working groups in different Mantikas has been initiated. UNFPA envisages that in 2019, at least 3 GBV working groups will be functional inside Libya. The roll out of the Gender Based Violence Information Management System (GBVIMS) has also been initiated under the leadership of UNFPA. It is envisaged that the process will be achieved and an information sharing protocol will be developed in the last quarter of 2019 to ensure interagency data sharing.

project_name: Ensuring access to quality life saving GBV response and prevention services for Rohingya refugees and their host communities
project_objective: The project ensures lifesaving services delivered through 20 WFS, including case management, clinical management of rape, family planning, STI prevention and response, psychosocial support and access to services through functional referral pathways, with continuous service evaluation through Client Satisfaction surveys.  It ensures Advocacy and engagement with communities, including men and boys for GBV prevention and response. It also Ensure GBV mainstreaming in all 20 UNFPA-supported Health Facilities, including direct GBV service linkage, outreach and information dissemination about available services for women and girls, and safe and ethical referrals of GBV survivors by health staff. 10 UNFPA-supported Women Led Community Centres (WLCC), providing life-skills training, psychosocial support and a community mobilization intervention for the prevention of GBV, through the engagement of men and boys and empowerment of women and girls, with an ongoing process of consultation with participants to assess and improve WLCC classes and services. It Continue training GBV service providers on GBV case management and psychosocial support services, and ensure specialized MHPSS mentoring and supervision for case management service provision. Train health personnel on GBV guiding principles and referral pathways.  Promote sustainability by working with local IPs and community volunteers to build their capacity for GBV prevention, response and referrals.  Engage in capacity development opportunities for national governmental institutions.  Include specific information on do no harm that is tailored to training types.

project_name: Integrated Comprehensive Primary Healthcare Services for Rohingya Refugees and Affected Host Communities
project_objective:
This project aims to address the health needs of Rohingya refugees and host community and will be implementing following activities reaching 405,068 patients. 

5 Comprehensive Primary Health Care Centers providing 24/7 health services 
● 9 Health Posts providing services during day time and 30 community health outlets providing referral and basic health services
● In addition, 30 community health outlet will provide basic health services ( counseling, referral, and , ORS)
The facilities will provide primary health care service according to the essential primary health care services packages (ESP)with  special focus on  sexual reproductive health, maternal, neonatal, child health, and adolescent health, non-communicable diseases and Mental health psychosocial services in addition to the regular and routine  services such as Outpatient departments, Inpatient departments, Child health, EPI, Nutrition, non-communicable diseases, Referral services, Information Management, Waste management and infection control.
5 Primary health care center and 9 Health posts are functional to a more durable, permanent and sustainable structures operational. 
● 1,200,000 Medical Consultation provided in a year desegregated by sex, age provided to Rohingya (60 % are female and 40% males)
● 3,600 deliveries safely conducted by skilled birth attendant
● 36,000 family planning services provided
● 14 health facilities have at least one staff trained on Mental Health Gap Action Program
● 14 health facilities have at least one staff trained on clinical management of rape.
● 14 health facilities providing care ( screening, diagnosing, labs, treatment) of non communicable diseases such as diabetes, hypertension, and heart diseases. 
● 14 health facilities providing a comprehensive mixture of family planning methods at  least four short methods(pills, injectable, condom) and one Long Acting Method (Implant, IUD). 
● 300  Community health worker and volunteers trained (75 % are female)
● 2000 group awareness session conducted focusing especially on women, reaching 36,000 participants (60% of the participants are women).
● 5 Ambulances functional and available 24/7
● All health professionals (Doc,Para,MW,HW) will be trained on Basic First Aid and Public Health in Emergencies.

project_name: Transition to Sustainable WASH for Rohingya Refugees and Host Communities in Cox's Bazar District
project_objective: The project aims to provide sustainable WASH facilities and services for affected populations in Cox Bazar, designed, implemented and managed in collaboration with communities. It's purpose is to support a transition from emergency WASH to more sustainable systems, foster community ownership and engagement with these systems and services and foster social cohesion through joint management and increased service provision for both Rohingya and host communities.

project_name: Strengthening essential healthcare services, prevention and control of outbreaks, risk communications and coordination of health sector
project_objective:
The overall goal of the WHO emergency response strategy is to reduce morbidity and mortality among the Rohingya population and host community in Cox’s Bazar. The specific objectives of the project are to:
1. Improve equitable access to and utilization of quality lifesaving and comprehensive primary and secondary health services for crisis-affected populations with special focus on sexual reproductive, maternal, neonatal, child and adolescent health; mental health and psychosocial support; and  non-communicable diseases.  
2. Encourage healthy living; improve health seeking behavior and utilization of essential service package among refugees and host populations through community engagement, with special attention to gender considerations and vulnerable groups.
3. Strengthen health sector coordination and information management with a focus on rational and accountable health service delivery systems, including monitoring of minimum standards and the quality of the services provided.
The project targets the entire 1,242,441 Rohingya and host population in need in Cox's Bazar. 
WHO supports the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Bangladesh, the Civil Surgeon’s Office, Cox’s Bazar, Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commissioner’s Office (RRRC), and works in conjunction with sector partners, in particular those in the health, WASH, protection and nutrition sectors. This project will focus on health systems strengthening as a part of transition from emergency response to sustained development. A sustained development strategy will be developed and implemented to deliver health services and strengthen the health system to the benefit of the refugees as well as the host community. The underlying principles will be to support national health systems to deliver an effective response, increased direct investment in public and local institutions, and meaningful and measurable capacity development. This will include strengthening all building blocks of national health systems as relevant to the Cox’s bazar set up, namely liaise with national government on the governance and leadership through Civil Surgeon’s office and DGHS coordination cell; availability of health workforce, vaccines and essential technology, health information, financing of health sector, service delivery based on minimum services package, amongst others for both the Rohingyas and the host community. 
WHO will continue to support government institutions to establish more sustainable emergency preparedness and response capacities to ensure continuity of emergency services during the monsoon and cyclone seasons. WHO has a separate DRR/contingency plan to respond to crisis caused by natural disasters or disease outbreak.
Following the risk communication strategy, WHO will undertake studies to gather community perceptions and beliefs that affect the health and health seeking behavior of the community with due consideration to the gender, social cohesion, and accountability to affected population. WHO will develop appropriate risk communication materials and reference documents on priority areas. The needs of different population sub-groups and their feedback on interventions will be taken into consideration while formulating activities targeted at improving healthcare services.
WHO will continue to co-lead and coordinate the health sector, monitor the health needs of the target population and quality of healthcare services and ensure equity in distribution of the services. WHO will focus on strengthening information management systems and coordination structure at all levels, closely collaborating with other sectors such as WASH, nutrition and protection and CWC working group to address emerging health crisis and ensure the best possible health outcomes for the refugee and host populations.

project_name: “We're all going to school, we're all going to learn ""
project_objective: UNICEF will re-establishing access to educational services for 152,000 school-aged children and play-based activities for 30,400 3-5-year-old children in the most affected areas of Manica, Sofala, Tete and Zambézia; and 15,000 school-aged children and played-based for 2,500 3-5 years old in the most affected areas of Cabo Delgado and Nampula provinces. UNICEF will provide schools with teaching and learning materials, including school- in-a-box, chalkboards, learner kits and ECD kits. The ECD kits target pre-school population in the catchment areas and Child Friendly Spaces (CFS) in partnership with the child protection section. In these locations, they will benefit from play-based activities, bringing a sense of normalcy.

project_name: Emergency Health HIV Response to IDAI cyclone and flooding
project_objective:

project_objective:

project_name: Provide Life saving Emergency Health Response to IDAI cyclone affected population until end of May 2020
project_objective: 1. Strengthen and sustain the capacity of the provincial,  district, health facility and community to promptly detect, confirm and promptly respond to disease outbreaks. 2. Ensure continuity of basic life saving health services in the affected districts, resetlement areas, hard to reach areas and insecure areas feeling critical gaps that can not be addressed by the recovery program in the short term. 3. Strengthen the coordination and leadership in the health sector; 3. Procure and preposition essential medicines and medical and laboratroty supplies such as Interagency Emergency Health Kit (IEHK), Interagency Diarrhoeal Disease Kits (IDDK; revised Cholera Kit (RCK), Reproductive Health Kit (RHK), Non-communicable diseases kit (NCDK) SAM kits etc.

project_name: Urgent nutritional support for U5s and PLW affected by cyclone IDAI and floods
project_objective: Immediate humanitarian assistance: (1) screening and treatment of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) for children under 5, (2) immediate nutritional support for PLW with acute malnutrition and/or HIV, (3) information and counselling support on infant and young child feeding (IYCF) for pregnant/lactating women (PLW), and (4) essential micronutrient interventions for children under 5 (vitamin A, MNPs, and deworming)

project_name: WASH emergency response for people affected by cyclone Idai in Mozambique II
project_objective:
UNICEF will target affected households in Zambezia, Manica, Nampula, and Sofala Provinces to restore access to WASH services and facilities through a holistic package of interventions that include the following activities:
• Effective WASH sector coordination for emergency response
• Restoration of water supply services from centralized systems focusing on small town systems in partnership with FIPAG, AIAS, DNAAS, and private systems
• Water supply to resettlement areas 
• Distribution of point-of-use water treatment materials / products, including training and monitoring on proper use at household level.
• Rehabilitation and disinfection of existing water points affected by cyclone / flooding and re-establishment / support for water committees.
• Construction of new water sources for most vulnerable communities / resettlement areas.
• Solid waste management (including collection, removal, disposal and drainage) in resettlement camps.
• Promotion activities for self-construction of household latrines and garbage pits in long-term resettlement and returning areas.
• Dissemination of WASH related messages through mass communication media.
• Community and household level hygiene promotion activities in resettlement areas, affected communities, and related institutions.
• Procurement and distribution of WASH related non-food items, with focus on most vulnerable families / households.

project_name: Emergency life-saving primary healthcare for crisis-affected and vulnerable populations including internally displaced persons (IDPs), migrants, and host communities in Somaliland, Puntland, and South-Central Somalia
project_objective: In the 2019 HRP project for health, IOM will increase access and utilization of primary healthcare services among the most vulnerable and crisis-affected populations in the country. IOM will operate 27 static health facilities with integrated community outreach, as well as 4 mobile medical teams; many of the facilities are in areas that are hard-to-reach, remote, conflict-affected and isolated, lack other health actors, and where the population does not have access to basic life-saving health services. IOM will provide comprehensive primary healthcare services, continuously build the capacity of health workers to ensure quality of services, and preposition medicines and medical supplies in regional hubs to ensure continuous supply to all of IOM’s health facilities, as well as to the region at large in the event of a sudden emergency. IOM will upgrade health posts to provide basic emergency obstetric and newborn care (BEMONC) services, particularly in regions where there is no other facility for safe deliveries. To mitigate against recurrent and expected shocks and the effects of continued conflict, IOM will conduct mass vaccination at the entry points to IDP sites, thus increasing immunization coverage and reducing outbreaks of communicable diseases. IOM will utilize health education in communities to effect behavior change in health and hygiene practices that contribute to high excess morbidity and mortality, and to increase demand and utilization of preventative services such as antenatal care, facility delivery, and immunization. IOM will address gaps in mental health care and psychosocial support (MHPSS) through mainstreaming and integration of MHPSS into primary healthcare, coupled with community-level approaches. The project will benefit 511,500 individuals, including 309,313 children under 18 years. The project will be part of IOM’s integrated emergency response program which includes shelter and NFIs, camp coordination and management, WASH, and displacement tracking and monitoring.

project_name: Food security requirements for Concern Worldwide
project_objective: CW plans to contribute to lasting improvement in food and nutrition security through technical support and capacity building. Activities include the promotion of conservation agriculture, rice intensification systems, rehabilitation of solar greenhouses, household kitchen gardening support, fixed irrigation systems, provision of threshing and food processing equipment. The programme also promotes resilience building through introduction of climate smart agriculture models to overcome the impacts of Climate Change and disasters.

project_name: Prévention, prise en charge et stimulation psychosociale intégrée de la malnutrition aigüe sévère dans les Districts Sanitaires de Bankass, Djenné (Région de Mopti) et Tominian (Région de Ségou)
project_objective:
Ce projet, faisant suite à la première phase de l'intervention de COOPI financée par UNICEF dans la région de Mopti, assure : a) la continuité des interventions en cours dans les districts sanitaire de Bankass et Djenné, tout en renforçant la prévention de la malnutrition et orientant les structures sanitaires vers une intégration; b) l'autonomisation en voie d'une pérennité de toutes les activités du projet <Prévention et prise en charge de la malnutrition aigüe sévère chez les enfants de moins de 5 ans dans les Districts Sanitaire de Bankass , Djenné et Tominian / Mali >.
Conformément à la norme de PCIMA, ce projet vise à offrir un paquet minimum de qualité, en renforçant l’accès et le maintien des plus vulnérables à travers un soutien aux accompagnants d’enfants MAS et le déploiement des intrants dans les CSCOM.   Les enfants MAS et leurs accompagnants bénéficieront de kit wash, de la stimulation psycho cognitive et de la sensibilisation sur les pratiques familiales essentielles. L’initiative PB Mère sera mise en œuvre. L’augmentation de la prévalence de la malnutrition aigüe serait prévenue à travers la sensibilisation des communautés sur les pratiques familiales essentielles incluant EHA et ANJE communautaire à travers les GSAN et  les Relais Communautaires.
 Un appui au système sanitaire dans la PEC gratuite des enfants malnutris, à travers la formation au personnel, l’appui financier aux ASACO et aux CSREF sera effectif.   
Renforcement des capacités des trois  points focaux nutrition des 3 Districts Sanitaire en collecte et analyse des données, élaboration du plan de distribution et techniques de supervision. Renforcement des capacités des ASACO en gestion administrative et financière.

Le projet vise à intégrer l’approche innovante de la stimulation psychosociale dans la réponse nutritionnelle. Les enfants malnutris présentant souvent de l’apathie et de l’insensibilité ne reçoivent pas la stimulation et les réponses parentales nécessaires pour le cerveau pour développer toute sa capacité. De plus, par conséquent, le soignant peut réduire la quantité de la stimulation qui met en péril le développement social, émotionnel, physique et cognitif de l’enfant. Dans le cadre de l’intégration, l’approche de COOPI se base sur deux axes :
A)	Mener des activités de formation aux acteurs et aux relais communautaires des centres nutritionnels dans les domaines tels que 1) la santé mentale infantile et le support psychosocial dans la programmation nutritionnelle, 2) santé mentale maternelle et 3) premiers secours psychologique. 
B)	Mise en place des activités de sensibilisation et des clubs des soignants pour promouvoir l’inclusion de la stimulation psychosociale dans les unités nutritionnelles

project_name: Integrated primary health care and referral services, including the prevention, detection and control of public health hazards in 11 States of Sudan
project_objective:
WHO 2019 Emergency program aligns and respond to its main functions and commitments for humanitarian response. Through the well-established 12 central and field offices will continue to ensure jointly with MOH the coordination and leadership of the humanitarian response of international and national stakeholders. Technical and operational support will be provided by the WHO to strengthen the SMOHs coordination and emergency response teams up to community level. The collection, centralization, analysis and dissemination of essential health data dis-aggregated by sex and age-groups will be maintained and strengthen by WHO field teams jointly with all partners. Sectorial and inter agency assessments will complement the information for evidence-based needs and gap identification, prioritization, planning, task distribution and monitoring of life-saving humanitarian actions. WHO technical and cluster coordination team will ensure that the standard health cluster tools, such as EWARS, HERAM, 4Ws, Risk and vulnerability mapping, HNO, HRP, epidemiological briefings, bulletin are timely and regularly updated and utilized by health partners. The focus of WHO and partners will be the district and community level structures contributing and aligned with the national health strategies, adherence to national and international standards for an equitable, and quality emergency health services. 
The projects significantly contributes to increase the access to, and the quality of emergency health services for the most vulnerable, IDPs, Returnees, and host communities in 69 localities (11 states) as prioritized by the 2019 HNO exercise through; procurement and distribution of free of charge medicines to support the NGOs and SMOH deal with humanitarian case load at all levels, while ensuring a rapidly revolving pipeline for addressing acute events in 2019. Rapid Response Kits adapted to the protracted crisis in Sudan address specific needs of children (boys and, girls), women in general and women of reproductive age, men and elderly. In addition medicines for case-management and lab regent for confirmation during outbreaks, and PEP for rape management. Training of health workers directly related to humanitarian action(Universal Precautions, case management, IMCI, EnNOC, RRT, surveillance/EWARS), small repair and rehab of damaged HFs; operational costs for scaling up the humanitarian health services as necessary, and bridging for short periods funding shortages in essential areas (rapid surge of health partners), and community mobilization and healthy behavior. An integrated approach that facilitates the access to services of all age groups, male and female with their specific health needs and adapted to the local cultural customs, including advocacy and synergic linkages with ongoing recovery-development interventions (GBV, FGM, Protection, FSL, WASH, Nutrition, NFI, and Education)
Optimal capacity for early notification, investigation, confirmation and immediate response to public health threats (outbreaks) is another priority of WHO emergency preparedness and response significantly contributing to the health security of targeted groups and beyond through; technical, and operational support for EWARS, alert investigation and response operations by the RRTs, response vaccination campaigns and strengthening the routine immunization, reagents and medicines to fill in the gaps during eventual outbreaks. Well established linkages with the development initiatives such as IHR, Cross Border collaboration, event-based community surveillance, and real time EWARs are complementary and aim to a stronger preparedness and quick recovery. The target for the project is 2,44 million vulnerable communities – IDPs, Returnees, Host Communities  in 11 states and 69 localities. The activities related to outbreak control are not restricted only to the 69 targeted localities, but wherever the needs arise.

project_name: Provision of Logistics Cluster Common Services in Support of the Humanitarian Community responding to Cyclone Idai in Mozambique
project_objective:

project_name: Provision of psychosocial support; activation of protection mechanisms to prevent and respond to violence, exploitation, abuse and neglect against children; and support access to birth registration.
project_objective:
1) Mobilize affected communities around the protection and wellbeing of all children and provide access to affected girls and boys of various ages, including children with disabilities, with psychosocial support, opportunities to play and acquire contextually relevant skills.
2) Provide child protection case management services to child survivors of violence, exploitation, abuse and neglect, including specialised support for children with disabilities.

4) Strengthen capacities of service providers, including social welfare, police and justice sector actors, to re-establish prevention, referral and response services.
5) Identify entry points for birth registration and issuance of identification documents for children who have either never been registered or have lost birth registration documentation to facilitate access to essential services.

project_name: Améliorer notre réponse collective à une crise complexe à  travers une coordination efficace, souple et fondée sur les principes humanitaires
project_objective:
L’objectif du projet est de renforcer la coordination de la réponse humanitaire au Cameroun afin de sauver des vies, de protéger les plus vulnérables et d’améliorer la résilience des populations. Avec l’aggravation de la crise dans les régions du Nord-Ouest et du Sud-Ouest courant 2018, le pays est désormais confronté à trois crises humanitaires complexes qui affectent 8 des 10 régions du Cameroun. L’impact de ces trois crises sur les conditions de vie des populations affectées est renforcé par des vulnérabilités structurelles préexistantes qui entravent leur relèvement.

La complexité et l’étendue de ces crises requièrent donc plus que jamais une coordination efficace, adaptée aux différents terrains d’intervention et fondée sur les principes humanitaires. Le projet de coordination d’OCHA Cameroun permettra ainsi d’atteindre une réponse humanitaire mieux financée, plus stratégique et qui centralise les droits humains et la protection des personnes. Il permettra aussi d’atteindre une meilleure complémentarité entre les actions d’urgence et les programmes de développement, afin de combattre ensemble les besoins humanitaires et leurs causes sous-jacentes.

A cette fin, OCHA fournira les services essentiels de diffusion de produits d'information clés, de coordination du Cycle de Programmation Humanitaire et de facilitation d'évaluations des besoins multisectorielles conjointes. Sa présence à Yaoundé, Maroua, Buea, Bamenda et Kousseri lui permettra d'apporter un appui décisif aux mécanismes de coordination et de favoriser la cohérence entre les enjeux opérationnels terrain et les instances décisionnelles stratégiques. Cette position clé lui permet aussi d'avancer les considérations primordiales de Centralité de la Protection et Protection transversale, de Protection contre l'Exploitation et les Abus Sexuels (PEAS) et de nexus humanitaire développement.  Depuis ses sous-bureaux de l'Extrême-Nord et du Sud-Ouest, OCHA favorisera enfin la mise à l'échelle de la réponse dans ces régions, notamment à travers la gestion des responsabilités CMCoord et d'accès humanitaire, ainsi que le renforcement des capacités des répondants locaux.

project_name: UNICEF ZIMBAWE WASH CYCLONE IDAI RESPONSE
project_objective: Women, men and children affected by Cyclone IDAI disaster have restored access to safe water, appropriate sanitation and hygiene practices to reduce incidence of diarrheal diseases.
