project_objective: To provide timely and essential logistic services and access to hard to reach areas impacted by Cyclone IDAI.

project_name: Integrated lifesaving Sexual and Reproductive Health including maternal health and Gender Based Violence related response services to the most vulnerable populations in Sudan
project_objective: Sexual and Reproductive Health (SRH) is a human right and, like all other human rights, applies to refugees, internally displaced persons, and others living in humanitarian settings. To realize this right, affected populations (Women, men, young boys and girls) must have access to comprehensive SRH information and services so they are free to make informed choices about their health and well-being. The Minimum Initial Services Package - MISP - for Sexual and Reproductive Health care will be delivered by UNFPA and partners as essential elements to reduce the risk of maternal/ neonatal mortality and morbidity among the affected population. The planned interventions will prioritize the ensuring of timely access to Antenatal and postnatal care, women nutritional services, Emergency Obstetric care and save delivery. In addition to support of the referral system, capacity building of healthcare providers on Sexual Reproductive health, availability and accessibility of Family Planning services, HIV and STIs prevention and response program, Clinical management of SGBV survivor’s, and demand creation through awareness raising and educational  activities.  The coordination of SRH programs in humanitarian is also prioritized at national and states level. The UNFPA project will consider the needs for youth and adolescent (boys & girls) through the Youth Peer program aiming to build the capacity of Y Peers to design and deliver high-quality peer-to-peer education on issues affecting young people in humanitarian, including adolescent youth Reproductive health and gender-based violence, empowerment skills and partnership between youth and adults. Maternal morbidity and disability such as Obstetric fistula in fragile states will be given an especial attention by UNFPA. The SRH service package will be operationalized through the procurement of Emergency Reproductive Health Kits, micro-nutrients, medical equipment and supplies. UNFPA will coordinate closely with WHO, UNICEF, (I)NGOs and Ministries of Health during the program implementation period. In addition Gender and protection mainstreaming will be considered as critical cross cutting programs.  The natural impact on environment with mitigation and enhancement procedures is considered by UNFPA.

project_name: Providing Comprehensive Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) Assistance to Affected Populations in Darfur, Kordofan States and East Sudan
project_objective: This project aims to provide humanitarian WASH assistance to 113,788 beneficiaries (37,550 women, 28,448 men, 23,895 girls, 23,895 boys - 12% of whom are estimated to be either elderly or disabled) to mitigate the suffering of populations affected by natural or man made disasters and reflects all 3 outcomes of the Multi Year Humanitarian Response Plan strategy. Under Outcome 1 IOM will provide life saving assistance to people newly displaced by conflict or natural disasters in an effort to recreate pre emergency conditions using early recovery approaches to improve the overall access to WASH services, connecting the need for short term emergency interventions with long term solutions and applying development principles by working directly with local communities to facilitate ownership and accountability. The objective is to not only focus on WASH emergency interventions but gradually contribute to socio economic inclusion of forcibly displaced populations and returnees by directly increasing access to basic services for the displaced and host communities and indirectly increasing employment opportunities. Under Outcome 2 IOM seeks to improve and sustain access to safe water in target communities especially in Durdeb, Abyei, North Darfur and South Darfur as these communities primarily rely on agriculture and livestock, therefore water is critical to their livelihoods. Under Outcome 3 improving and sustaining access to safe water and sanitation facilities and hygiene messages will address malnutrition related risks and increase community resilience to disease outbreaks. IOM will consider emergency water provision, access to proper sanitation facilities and hygiene campaigns; coupled with the establishment and rehabilitation of water points. This will include environmental impact mitigation such as the provision of solar technology to power water points and monitoring ground water to moderate depletion levels. Exit strategies will be developed to alleviate aid dependency in protracted emergencies by strengthening self-reliance and facilitating community solutions in a more holistic approach.

project_name: Support to Internally Displaced Persons in South Sudan through Provision of Protection Assistance and Targeted Support to Persons with Specific Needs and to Promote Resilience and Durable Solutions to Internally Displaced Persons in South Sudan
project_objective:
UNHCR as protection lead agency will maintain both static and mobile field presence response in the greatest areas of concern in 2019 being Central and Southern Unity, Central and Eastern Jonglei, parts of Upper Nile, Western Bar-al-Ghazel (in particular Wau county) and in Yei as well as UNHCR priority locations in EES, WES, Northern Bar-al-Ghazel, Lakes and Warrap states. The project will cover IDPs, returnees and host communities. Interventions will be based on rapid needs assessments to prioritise interventions. Throughout the program consultations with affected populations will be carried out taking into account age, gender and diversity approach. In 2018, UNHCR focused on prioritised activities in general protection, child protection and GBV. Field missions were undertaken to hard-to-reach areas for life-saving activities and protection assessments. Protection Monitoring was strengthened as were activities aimed at promoting solutions including surveys, FGDs and population profiling. In 2019 UNHCR and partners will continue to build on the protection gains achieved to further strengthen a rights-based protection response for the populations, in particular those most vulnerable through: timely life-saving activities in remote or hard-to-reach areas, with a focus in expanding outreach to 190 identified priority locations both in POCs and outside POCs; developing the capacity of affected communities to cope, recover and contribute to durable solutions paying attention to specific needs of  the youth;  and mainstreaming protection across other clusters. To this effect, UNHCR will maintain its mobile outreach team to ensure a strong presence in integrated missions, rapid assessments and RRM intervention. There will also be need for continued coordination of activities at national and state levels to implement protection and assistance activities.
The recent revitalised peace process has created optimism for new opportunities for the protection and durable solutions for persons of concern in 2019. These developments, combined with noticeable slow reduction in related conflict as well as spontaneous returns of IDPs and refugees from neighbouring countries highlights the need to focus on solution-oriented programming in 2019. In order to improve quality of responses and support implementation of durable solutions objective of the Protection Cluster and HCT, UNHCR will engage in protection profiling through its protection teams and Joint IDP profiling Service (JIPS) for a collaborative profiling exercise. 
The changing context in view of the peace agreement will require increased capacity for UNHCR and its partners to carry out protection activities if access for humanitarians improves. Protection activities in support for durable solutions such as HLP, community empowerment, income generating activities for protective outcomes, quick impact projects, peacebuilding and peaceful co-existence initiatives and youth related activities will be enhanced. Multi-purpose cash-based initiatives to support durable solutions will be implemented based on needs assessment and protection risk analysis. To maximise impact UNHCR will seek to explore possibilities to target the required assistance to the most vulnerable categories of the affected populations and to join efforts with other clusters ensuring centrality of protection in humanitarian intervention and seek linkages with development actors for complementarity with other frameworks to promote resilience and solutions. UNHCR will support accession to Kampala Convention and its operationalisation supporting the government in finalising of the national legislation on internal displacement and related legal reforms such as in HLP and land resource issues supporting access to resources by women and vulnerable populations and to promote national responsibility to prevent, protect and resolve internal displacement

project_name: Targeted Support to Persons with Specific Needs with lifesaving Non-food Items and Emergency Shelter Support to Internally Displaced Persons in South Sudan
project_objective:
Based on the current security situation in South Sudan, multiple displacement of Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) is likely to continue. IDPs are expected to continue living in with host communities, facing the direst living conditions without an alternative coping mechanism with host families. Families are often displaced without substantial household items. Also, given the long rainy season, the limited scope to earn a livelihood, the lack of access to markets and the often-protracted nature of displacement, need for provision of basic and domestic items remain a priority. Therefore, stock needs to be replenished on a regular basis so that UNHCR can respond quickly to the identified vulnerable persons as part of the protection responses. Through the provision of core relief items, UNHCR’s material assistance will continue to be targeted and protection focused, aiming that the most vulnerable displaced households are not left without basic material support and specific needs of woman and girl are catered for. 

While UNHCR aims to reach some 42,000 households, corresponding to some 30% of the overall target population, as priority, UNHCR plans to assist the most vulnerable 128,430 individuals with selected core relief items, covering only 13% of the comprehensive target population in spite of life-saving nature of the material assistance and their relevance for protection interventions. In the context of further budget reductions, delivery of assistance will continue to be based on a targeted approach of supporting the most vulnerable PSNs identified during protection assessment and protection monitoring process. The items to be distributed will be selective, taking into account the most urgent protection needs of persons of concern that can be addressed via provision of NFIs, availability of other actors, logistical and security constraints / feasibility. Resources allowing, UNHCR also plans to provide dignity kits (sanitary cloths, soap, and underwear) and solar lanterns to some 2,000 households as complementarity to CRIs and targeted protection activities especially for women and girls. 

Due to the fluid and unpredictable nature of the IDP and security situation in South Sudan, the type of shelter support required varies as IDPs are moving from one place to another. Despite the efforts by humanitarian agencies, shelter needs of IDPs outside of POC sites remain a challenge. Returning IDPs and refugee returnees often face the additional challenge of finding their former housing damaged, destroyed and/or occupied by other households. The need for decent shelter in areas of potential return are critical to realizing UNHCR’s solutions oriented IDP strategy. UNHCR will assess the HLP and conflict sensitive issues in at least three location. UNHCR shelter strategy is mainly on protection response to support the most vulnerable IDP and returnee families to reduce the protection risks and associated vulnerabilities. Training and capacity building of partner staff, in collaboration with the community, will greatly contribute to the successful identification and assistance to 286,500 PSNs in 2019. In some locations, shelter support will focus on reconstruction of damaged housing, while other locations will focus on transitional shelter and on emergency shelter. Resources and security conditions allowing, UNHCR will continue to provide support to the persons of concern in terms of rehabilitating the local infrastructures such health facilities and learning shelters to enable access to basic services like medication and education. 

UNHCR will assess the HLP situation in at least three location.

UNHCR will remain an active member of the ES/NFI Cluster, particularly at the field level, and will maintain its cooperation  with the Cluster actors to advocate for protection mainstreaming and enhanced vulnerability assessment, and optimize the available resources and focus and timely respond to the most critical needs of vulnerable IDPs among other affected populations.

From earlier years’ experience, UNHCR has realized that UNHCR and its partners are playing complementary role where UNHCR has strong ability to response quicker and where UNHCR and partners are static in ten key locations in South Sudan. UHNCR will follow the agreed SOP between S/NFI cluster and UNHCR for the emergency assistance of S/NFI.

For HRP Plan only 49% of total UNHCR Plan in South Sudan is included.

project_name: Strengthened Camp Management and Camp Coordination to displaced population in South Sudan
project_objective:
UNHCR response planned for 2019 is aligned with the CCCM Cluster Strategic Objectives 1, 2, 3 and 4. The project aims to ensure the provision of timely, well-coordinated and integrated humanitarian interventions for improving the well-being of displaced populations, their resilience and participation in decision-making processes. In this regard, UNHCR aims to strengthen coordination, advocacy and capacity building of key actors to ensure quality services are delivered in an equal and needs-based manner, considering the views of the community (SO1 &4 ). Further, the project covers continuous and prioritized support to new arrivals, returnees ,existing IDPs in displaced sites  with specific needs and the most vulnerable, ensuring response and prevention takes into account peculiarities relevant to each group, integrating protection mainstreaming in all CCCM activities (SO 2 and 4). A key component of the project is also focused on strengthening community mobilization, community ownership and self-management structures, with support to community-based structures to enhance participation in planning, decisions and response, with further empowerment of communities, particularly vulnerable groups to share their views in improving service delivery, management structures, site planning and communication channels vis a vis their needs, identified risks and priorities (SO 3).

To facilitate sustained response and need-based intervention, UNHCR also intends to rehabilitate, renovate and install communication equipment at the Bentiu Humanitarian Hub in order to ease partners operations related to Beyond Bentiu Response plan as it is anticipated that some of the humanitarian actors may opt to live outside the UNMISS Bentiu compound to be closer to the affected population for improved service delivery.

The project will also aim to provide timely assistance and necessary support to returnees from the neighbouring countries following the signed revitalized peace agreement in Khartoum on the 12th September 2018 and the subsequent peace celebration on the 31st Oct, 2018 in Juba by all the warring parties and other key actors. UNCHR intends to establish way stations in strategic locations along the border of South Sudan and its East African neighbours so as receive and facilitate the return of South Sudanese to their homeland and areas of their choice.

project_name: Ecuador - CARE
Treatment and Prevention of Malnutrition in Children Under 5 and Pregnant and Lactating Women & Girls in Sudan
project_objective:
The main objectives of this project are:

1. To ensure the provision of quality, lifesaving nutrition services for acutely malnourished children (boys and girls 6 - 59 months of age) and pregnant and lactating women (PLW) among highly vulnerable communities   
2. Improve equitable access to integrated program interventions for the prevention of under nutrition among affected communities

The project targets children aged 6–59 months and Pregnant and Lactating Women and Girls with specialized nutritious foods and social and behaviour change messages aimed at the prevention and treatment of acute malnutrition across selected states and localities in Sudan. 

A comprehensive package of food and non-food based interventions are provided taking into account nutritional vulnerabilities. 

The proposed response from WFP is in line with the Nutrition Sector Strategy and with the Multi-Year Humanitarian Response Strategy of Sudan. Through this project, WFP will be responding to the nutritional needs of targeted beneficiaries under Outcome 1, 2 and 3. 
 
With a particular focus on Do No Harm and Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) principles, WFP Sudan strives to enhance protection mainstreaming through the following priority areas: 1) Training and capacity building of key WFP and Cooperating Partners (CP); 2) protection risk analysis focused on safety, dignity and integrity of beneficiaries; 3) integration of protection indicators into program tools, notably Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E) tools; 4) design, implementation and adjustment of programs in line with identified protection concerns particularly for those disabled and with special needs; and 5) strengthened partnerships and coordination on protection issues.

project_name: Strengthening humanitarian coordination, advocacy and quality of humanitarian assistance
project_objective: (i) expanding humanitarian access to deliver life-saving assistance and protection in Diffa, Tillabery and Tahoua a complex operating environment where the security situation remains volatile; (ii) Better coordination of the response in other parts of the country during peaks of malnutrition, food insecurity, epidemics and  flooding to update needs and highlight gaps; (iii) establishing an efficient humanitarian coordination mechanism in Diffa, Tillabery and Thoua (iv) optimizing the cooperation with the Government of Niger and development actors trough the operationalization of the humanitarian / development nexus, capitalizing on the willingness of government of Niger  to take the lead on humanitarian issues while considering how to further support them in terms of capacity building; (v) ensuring adequate funding for humanitarian activities in all humanitarian sectors, including by working closely with donors towards more support and funding tools to national  responders, and the scaling up of cash-based programming; (VI) conduct discussions for a possible revision of the coordination mechanisms after the 3 years strategy and support national NGOs to be better organized in view of their representation  in the HCT .

project_name: Improved protection and psychosocial well-being through increased access to preventive and response protection services for girls and boys affected by drought in Somalia
project_objective: The project will benefit 59,015 boys, girls, women and men from IDP camps, returnee and host communities across Somalia through various child protection interventions. Key interventions will include strengthening community based child protection structures to prevent, respond and refer cases of violence against children , providing case management support and referral services to children with protection concerns including SGBV, providing FTR services  to UASC, and preventing of physical and humiliating punishment by rolling out  the parenting without violence program. Efforts will be made to ensure equal participation of minority groups like excluded clans, less participating groups like men, female, and people with disability.

project_name: Strengthening the food security coordination system in the West Bank and Gaza
project_objective:
-Strengthening coordination and prioritization of humanitarian interventions, and facilitating linkages with developmental programmes.
-Supporting the gathering, production and sharing of information required for effective planning and coordination for food security.
-Improving cooperation with line ministries and institutions in charge of coordination at the central and decentralised levels in order to progressively absorb FSS coordination functions.

The budget presented in this project sheet represents the calendar year requirements for Jan – Dec 2019, covering the specific activities planned during this period only. For the following periods of the multi-year planning, specific yearly budgets will cover each year of operations. The requirements and contributions will be reported in FTS accordingly.

project_name: Provision of life-saving health services to vulnerable children in 69 targeted localities in Sudan.
project_objective:
Through this project, UNICEF aims to support the humanitarian actors in providing quality, cost-effective health interventions to 1,208,781 under fifteen years of age children (boys and girls) in humanitarian settings. It is proposed to support provision of an integrated primary health care package (immunization, IMCI, ANC, skilled birth attendance, postnatal and new born care and prevention of mother to child transmission of HIV/AIDS) through
fixed, mobile and outreach services in addition to supporting provision of community based health interventions (integrated community case management for children under five for instance). UNICEF is also going to support procurement and distribution of the essential health supplies (measles and polio vaccines, IMCI kits, MW Kits, ORS, and Zinc supplements) and commodities to cover the needs of the most vulnerable children and
women in the emergency affected areas in addition to the supplies needed for emergency response to the natural disasters and epidemics (LLITNs and AWD kits). UNICEF will also support the implementing partners in building the capacity of the front-line health care providers to ensure provision of high quality child health services. Furthermore, community engagement and health promotion will be supported to strengthen community’s resilience, enhance utilization of the existing health services and promote for
healthy practices.

project_name: Saving Lives in Gaza
project_objective:
The Health and Nutrition Cluster partners estimated the number of people in need of humanitarian health/nutrition interventions across the oPt to be 1.2 million, of whom almost 900,000 are in Gaza (HNO, 2019).  The enormous rise in casualties is overwhelming Gaza’s fragile health sector, already buffeted by the 11-year blockade, the deepening intra-Palestinian political divide, an energy crisis, inconsistent payment of medical personnel, and shortages in medicines and disposables. 

As a result, a significant proportion of population in Gaza risks having limited or no access to essential life-saving health interventions. The Health and Nutrition Cluster partners estimated that the most vulnerable include those non-trauma patients who would require life-saving interventions in emergency departments of Gaza’s public hospitals, patients with non-communicable diseases, people with disabilities and elderly. Boys and girls under the age of five and pregnant/lactating women are particularly vulnerable.

The project aims to ensure access to essential life-saving health services of the most vulnerable affected population in Gaza through provision of essential drugs and medical supplies as well as providing priority health facilities with alternative energy sources. A total of 550,000 men and women in the Gaza Strip will be targeted by provision of life-saving medicines and access to interventions in emergency departments.

project_name: Integrated emergency healthcare support to vulnerable Palestine refugees
project_objective:
The current socioeconomic conditions compounded by the blockade, energy crisis, salary cuts for PA
employees, high unemployment and volatile security situation in Gaza are undermining its health sector.
This has led to high and increasing rates of health problems among the population who have no
alternative means to access healthcare under the prevailing humanitarian conditions. Meanwhile, the
Agency's ability to respond to emergency health needs in Gaza is greatly constrained by the tight
funding situation compromising its ability to respond as needed.
On top of an already on the verge of collapsing public health sector, the ongoing humanitarian crisis
that started on 30 March 2018 has resulted, so far, in an important number of casualties that can hardly
be absorbed. The needs for both urgent treatment and emergency preparedness of the health sector in
Gaza are therefore extremely important.
In light of these conditions, and within UNRWA strategic outcome of 'Refugees' health is protected and
disease burden is reduced' this proposed intervention aims, under the emergency health umbrella, to
support the provision of critical healthcare for (mainly) Palestine refugees in Gaza Strip through (1)
Providing lifesaving and urgent medicines and supplies to refugees, (2) Supporting health interventions
received outside UNRWA facilities, and (3) Supporting rehabilitative care for needed patients (4).

project_name: Supporting Gaza Health system in providing life-saving reproductive health services, and strengthening community’s preparedness and resilience to the protracted crisis.
project_objective:
This project is aligned to HNO 2018-2020 Cluster Strategic Objectives 1 & 2. It also contributes to strategic objectives 1 and 2 of the Every Newborn Action Plan “ENAP” 2017-2020, developed and adopted as a joint collaboration among major UN agencies, WHO, UNCEF and UNFPA in addition to other active stakeholders i.e. MAP-UK. 

The recent developments in Gaza and deteriorating situation following aid cuts, massive casualties due to ""Great March of Return"", have further exacerbated the humanitarian needs, and reduced access to essential life-saving maternal health services. UNFPA aims to save women’s lives and ensure that, despite the toll on the health system, women and girls have access to essential maternal and Reproductive Health (RH) services and information. This will be achieved through filling gaps in reproductive health including maternal health services, mitigating the impact of massive trauma casualties on essential maternal care and RH service provision and preventing excess mortality and morbidity through;
-	Ensuring a continuum of care and provision of life sustaining RH services, counselling and information including strengthening community preparedness. 
-	Provision of essential life-saving maternal health equipment and supplies
-	Implementation of MISP and training on emergency obstetric care, safe birth etc.
-	Actively engaging communities, supporting coping mechanism, sensitization, awareness raising and outreach.
-	Support linking and informing communities to available service with special focus to marginalized communities and groups including disabled, elderly etc. 

While this project is meant to address immediate response to urgent and critical needs of Gazan’s women’s, and young girls, especially those in marginalized areas, it will also support men and other vulnerable adolescents and strengthen the preparedness and resilience of both the community and the health system for absorbing shocks, saving lives and recovering from crises.

project_name: Ecuador - United Nations Children's Fund

Improved living conditions, promotion of rights and physical safety to promote dignity and protection of vulnerable displacement affected populations of the South West and North West Regions of Cameroon.
project_objective: The project aims to provide people affected by displacement in the South West and North West Regions with improved living condition and physical safety to promote dignity and protection of vulnerable displacement affected population. The project will target IDPs and vulnerable host communities in the two regions. Special attention will be paid to women as they appear to be more affected by the conflict and more vulnerable as well. During a recent survey conducted by NRC in the Fako division, 30% of the surveyed displaced community members attested to be living in plank/wooden houses called ‘karabout’ which are poorly constructed with sometimes 8-15 persons leaving in a room exposing women and girls to protection risks. These overcrowded households with poorly constructed shelters are prone to cold (during low temperatures), mosquitoes and water leaks which most times leads to children falling sick with malaria. There is need to provide them with improved shelter material for physical protection but also against diseases.

project_name: Children affected by Cyclone Idai can access timely and quality prevention and response interventions to child protection concerns
project_objective:
1: Children and adolescents’ psychosocial wellbeing is improved through resilience programming and children aged 3-18 have access to structured psychosocial activities.
2: Children and families can access timely and quality case management support for child protection concerns appropriate to the best interests of the child that meet the Minimum Standards for Child Protection in Humanitarian Action, including SGBV, alternative care, and FTR services.

4: Research on post-resettlement coping strategies (200 participants)
5: Cash grants

project_name: Columbia - United Nations Children's Fund
Peru - United Nations Children's Fund
Nutrition requirements for WFP
project_objective: WFP aims to reduce hunger and prevent undernutrition. The assistance will consist of locally produced fortified cereals and biscuits, with a special focus on children’s institutions, under-five children and pregnant and lactating women. TB patients and their families will also be targeted with nutritious food due to the strong correlation between TB and undernutrition. WFP will maintain operational and technical support to the eleven local food processing facilities to ensure production of high-quality blended foods. WFP will continue discussions with the Government and in-country partners on food fortification. Assistance to beneficiaries will be continued on a regular basis to ensure populations most in need have adequate access to nutrition interventions.

project_name: Emergency Food Assistance and Livelihoods for Refugees Across Sudan
project_objective: The overall intervention aims to support populations affected by disasters in target areas to meet their basic food needs during and after crises. Food-insecure people affected by long-term conflict and/or displacement are able to meet their basic food needs and increase their self-reliance throughout the year.

project_name: Promoting Rights and Supporting Protection Needs in BAY states.
project_objective:
The proposed intervention builds on IRC’s previous and ongoing protection programming in Borno, Yobe and Adamawa states. The intervention will target both IDPs, returnees and host community members through a well-coordinated approach that will foster access to specialized services to prevent and mitigate the harmful effects of violence on women, children and men. This will be achieved through a focus on prevention of harm by seeking to ensure that women, men, boys and girls are safe in their wider communities and receive support when they experience harm and response actions that ensure women, men, boys and girls are protected from the consequences of harm. IRC will provide or facilitate access to safe and dignified specialized services that can help women, men, boys and girls to survive, heal and recover when they experience harm.  This will be done by ensuring that:
•	Community members have information about laws, their rights and availability of services: Through protection monitoring activities, the IRC will identify and monitor protection trends/risks in order to improve contextual understanding for purposes of ensuring responsive services throughout the action; protection reporting will also be shared with relevant humanitarian actors to support improved humanitarian response and coordination, as well as evidence-driven advocacy. Monitoring teams will also actively share information on rights and service access with households and community focal points to improve access to services; cases in need of response services that are identified during protection monitoring will be supported through a safe referral process, if informed consent to do so is received. Protection monitoring will be conducted through, weekly safety audits with women and girls at the transit center, camps and surrounding communities, gender/age/ability segregated FGDs, site observation and household/community level key informant interviews.
•	Community members take individual and collective action: Through community-based protection (CBP), guided by IRC’s new guidance for CBP that sets out a 5-step chronological process to maximise impact and promote sustainability, IRC will involve IDPs and returnees in the prioritization, planning and implementation of activities. This will be primarily achieved by engaging Protection action groups and other community based structures working with other sectors in IRC. To promote a specialized focus on protection risks facing individual segments of the IDP and returnee population, new or existing community groups will each have specific objectives while at the same time working together across groups to ensure holistic and mutually reinforcing actions to advance the protection of IDPs and returnees.
•	Services and structures are safe and reduce opportunities for harm: This action will ensure that protection is mainstreamed across all sectors throughout the project period by promoting four key elements of protection mainstreaming: meaningful access to assistance and services; prioritizing safety, dignity and doing no harm; accountability and participation and empowerment of beneficiaries. IRC’s Protection Mainstreaming Monitoring and Evaluation System and global protection cluster resources will guide the projects’ protection mainstreaming interventions. Foundational capacity building activities for project staff are continuously conducted to strengthen and promote a shared understanding of protection mainstreaming, including child safe guarding principles, integrating GBV in humanitarian assistance; and prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse.  IRC draws from its client responsiveness approach which fosters the effective functioning of feedback and complaints. The approach details systematic and deliberate processes to regularly listen to and collect diverse perspectives of populations of concern, use their feedback to inform programing decisions and explain to clients what actions have been taken in response to their feedback.
Twice a year the IRC conducts protection mainstreaming beneficiary assessments for feedback on the integration safety and dignity, meaningful access, participation and empowerment of target populations into project design and implementation. IRC sensitizes the community on IRC’s accountability for quality services and on the ways they can provide confidential feedback. The IRC Child Protection team  works together with other IRC sectors to provide trainings/information on the IRC Child Safeguarding Policy during trainings for their volunteers community structures members and awareness raising sessions for community members,  protection mainstreaming is also achieved through the development of protection mainstreaming action plans which are be monitored and adjusted throughout the project. Joint monthly community dialogues are held by protection teams with Bulamas, community structures, community/opinion leaders and community members to discuss uptake of project services, key challenges, gaps including issues on protection, GBV and child protection identified. The forum is also used to provide feedback and discuss ways to mitigate risks and threats. Decisions are communicated back to the beneficiaries through community leaders, social support groups and during one on one or group sensitization sessions. 

•	Relevant stakeholders follow rules and laws to protect civilians: IRC will strengthen the knowledge, skills, capacity and accountability of duty bearers in both government institutions (e.g. SEMA, NEMA) and at the community level (e.g. religious and traditional leaders). This will be achieved through technical and material support; monitoring duty bearers’ actions and through pursuing an evidence based advocacy strategy targeting duty bearers at all levels, including where appropriate, at the national level and regional levels. Knowledge and skills will be enhanced through trainings to ensure duty bearers access information and know about protective rules and laws pertinent to the prevailing context in the North East. This will focus on protection principles; housing, land and property (HLP) rights and responsibilities; protection mainstreaming and legislative frameworks governing IDPs such as guiding principles on internal displacement and dignified returns, the Kampala Convention on IDPs, humanitarian law, human rights, the Nigerian constitution and state laws of interest.
•	Women, girls, boys and men have their urgent protection needs met: IRC protection team will strengthen referrals for specialized services for women, children and other vulnerable individuals or groups, to ensure they receive timely, appropriate and adequate services for their healing and recovery. Internal referrals will be provided for beneficiaries, including those identified through protection monitoring, by community groups, or through self-reporting to IRC’s information centers or IRC staff. Externally, IRC will also participate in updating and disseminating referral pathways developed by the protection subsector working groups (Child protection, General Protection and Gender Based Violence) and ensure that people with specific identified protection needs are referred to relevant organization for specialized services. IRC will also support access to civil documentation (in partnership with National Population Commission (NPC), National Identity Management Commission (NIMC)) and legal services (including legal counselling and case management services) and provide targeted individual assistance to address immediate needs of victims or survivors of violence (including urgent medical support. TIA which can be in form of cash or in-kind is provided to enable most vulnerable individuals in a situation where no other alternative response, assistance or support exists to meet their most urgent protection needs with dignity and reduce their vulnerability and exposure to risks and promote meaningful access for the most vulnerable. It aims to build on rather than replace existing support mechanisms, meet immediate/most urgent needs and prioritize the most vulnerable.

project_name: Child Protection for UASC,Adolescents and their Caregivers in BAY States
project_objective:
The IRC Child Protection (CP) intervention will focus on Unaccompanied and Separated Children (UASC), adolescents and their caregivers by providing them case management services and linking them to specialized services that will cater for their peculiar and immediate needs arising from the effect of the conflict. This will include Health, Nutrition, Gender Based Violence (GBV) services and support from other IRC sectors while the CP team offers specialized case management services to the categories of children mentioned and their caregivers. The IRC tool kits for Socio-Emotional Learning (SEL) and the parenting skills, with 24 weeks sessions each of lessons, games and activities will be used to provide the support they require. These tool kits aim at providing children and their caregivers social and emotional support which will in turn help them become resilient and take control of their lives that have been shattered by the conflict. The intervention will also provide them with the opportunity to develop positive coping strategies through acquisition of skills that will empower them economically thereby providing them with proper means of survival. Also the intervention will provide trainings for IRC staff, volunteers and partners on the Child Protection Minimum Standards (CPMS) and the Organization's Child Safe Guarding Policy (CSP) and Anti Sexual Harassment Policy (ASHP). This is as a preventive measure aimed at protecting beneficiaries from sexual exploitation and abuse. 
The IRC will continue to be a part of the Child Protection sub Working Group (CPsWG) and contribute to achieving the overall set objectives of the CPsWG while it supports the building the capacity of local partners.

project_name: Strengthening women and girls' safety and recovery in BAY
project_objective:
Gender based violence remains a serious challenge within northeast Nigeria, causing more psychological imbalance for armed conflict-affected IDPs as well as returnees, especially women and girls. Displacement and continued movement of IDPs creates major protection concerns women and girls which has increased gender-based violence and access services remain a serious gap especially in hard to reach Local Governmental Areas. According to Humanitarian Response Plan, 2018, an estimated 2.4 million people have been identified to be in need of gender-based violence prevention and response across Adamawa, Borno, and Yobe states. Women and girls are often targeted while performing basic tasks such as travelling to water points, collecting firewood to cook food and going to communal latrines. They are often exposed to SEA, forced into prostitution, early marriages, and survival sex in exchange for food, their movement is restricted and basic needs are deprived. Women and girls are abducted by armed groups, are often raped and forcibly married and may be used in person borne improvised explosive device (PBIED) attacks. These women and girls, along with their children born as a result of rape, are often feared by communities and ostracized from society because they are suspected to be sympathizers of armed opposition groups. Upon their return, they require access to a full range of services to meet multiple immediate and reintegration needs as well as those of their children. Despite the consequences, families are still forcibly marrying daughters as young as 12 years old to men or members of armed opposition groups, citing poverty as the main reason. Between August 2017 and April 2018, the IRC provided case management services for over 400 gender based violence survivors in Adamawa, Borno and Yobe, indicating the high need for continued support.
 An April 2018 assessment from OCHA shows that violence against women and girls is the most widely reported protection issue (24% of all key informants). From the October 2017 OCHA assessment in Yobe, child marriage was reported to affect over a third of households in each population group in eight LGAs throughout the state, including Gujba. Additionally, according to the Nigeria HRP 2018, sexual violence, including rape, is a defining characteristic of the ongoing conflict, with 6 out of 10 women in the northeast having experienced one or more forms of GBV. Women and girls are at particular risk within the current environment, with many reports of survival sex in exchange for food, money, and freedom of movement (into and out of IDP sites). This exposes the population to increasing incidences of sexually transmitted infections including HIV, unwanted pregnancies, and obstetric fistula caused by sexual violence, leading to overall poor sexual and reproductive health outcomes. The crisis has significantly affected the dignity of women and children. This further entrenches pre-existing gender disparities. In the Global Gender Gap Index, Nigeria ranks 118th out of 144 countries.

project_name: Life-saving food assistance and livelihoods support in North-East Nigeria.
project_objective:
WFP will provide unconditional food-assistance to the most food-insecure, crisis-affected populations. 
Life-saving general food assistance (in-kind food and cash-based transfers) will be delivered to IDPs, returnees and host populations in North-East Nigeria (Borno, Yobe and Adamawa States). 
Early recovery and resilience to shocks will be promoted through asset creation and preservation, increased livelihoods opportunities, and enhanced agricultural value chains. 
Joint multi-sectoral assessments and Emergency Food Security Analysis will be conducted regularly to monitor the nutrition, food security, and markets situation in crisis-affected states. 
A gender-transformative approach that reflects the needs of women, men, girls and boys will be adopted. WFP will mainstream protection throughout its work, supported by a solid understanding of the operational context and protection analysis. Training and capacity building of staff and partners in protection and humanitarian principles will include on-the-job coaching. WFP will ensure that affected populations (women and men) will be consulted throughout the programme cycle; beneficiary feedback mechanisms will be tailored to their preferred means of communication. Beneficiaries will continue to be empowered with knowledge on their food assistance entitlements and their rights, including WFP’s zero tolerance policy on Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA). Protection against Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) will be embedded in M&E tools, complaint feedback mechanisms and training of partners and staff. 

WFP will focus on concrete operational solutions to avoid situations in which people assisted by WFP could be exposed to SEA. Along these lines WFP will enhance its support to income generation activities targeted to women, expand their engagement in the production and use of fuel efficient stoves, deploy women as beneficiary registrars, monitors and security personnel. The referral system and monitoring system will be reviewed to maximize user friendliness and access by assisted populations as well as operational adjustments for problem solving. Particular attention will be given to supervise the retailers and operators in the distribution of cash based transfers. WFP will support milling activities for the grain commodities it provides and will implement effective solutions for the provision of condiments and cash. Deep field presence through the hubs and proximity to affected populations will be enhanced for these purposes. Three experienced international and six Nigerian protection officers will be deployed. Reporting will be done on a monthly basis through standard WFP reporting and meetings. Regular oversight and evaluations will be conducted.

WFP will continue the collection of key information on beneficiaries and assistance provided as part of its M&E activities. Monthly monitoring will include distribution and activity site management; beneficiary and entitlement verification; and ensuring adequate protection and gender measures. Lessons will be regularly drawn from monthly process and biannual outcome monitoring and reporting, and periodic reviews and evaluation to inform strategic and operational decisions.

WFP will further consolidate partnerships to enhance national and state-level emergency preparedness and response systems, including in food security and nutrition assessment and monitoring, early warning, protection, gender analysis, targeting and registration processes, safety nets, cash-based transfer capacities and supply chain. 

Where security and access to land allows, increasing livelihood activities will complement food assistance to support access to productive assets, income generating activities and self-reliance in the long-term. Assistance will be coordinated with government distributions, to ensure food assistance is complementary and fills gaps. Through an integrated approach to analyzing and addressing food and nutrition security, integrated, multi-sectoral interventions will be encouraged, for example through collaborations with the Nutrition, Health, WASH and Protection Sectors, among others. WFP will also continue to proactively engage with a wide range of federal and state actors, including the Ministries of Agriculture and Rural Development, Health, Budget and National Planning, Finance, the National Social Investment Office (NSIO), Women Affairs and Social Development, PCNI as well as other federal and state institutions. Furthermore, WFP and the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) will continue to strengthen cooperation between the two agencies. WFP will continue to partner with a number of local and international NGOs and will work with civil society organizations to continue strengthening the capacities of national actors.

The project addresses the underlying causes of the protracted crisis by further integrating humanitarian and development assistance and improving disaster risk reduction in alignment with WFP’s dual mandate and the international policy debate on bridging and operationalizing the humanitarian-development nexus, thus using a development lens in its humanitarian responses, and aligning early recovery and development interventions accordingly.

project_name: Nutrition prevention and treatment activities in North-East Nigeria and support to multi-sectoral approach.
project_objective:
WFP response will support a preventative nutrition approach that delivers both nutrition specific and nutrition sensitive interventions to prevent and manage malnutrition amongst the most vulnerable populations with a focus on children under five years and women of reproductive age, and emphasizing the critical 1,000 Days ‘window of opportunity’.

WFP’s prevention activities, through blanket supplementary feeding (BSFP), and treatment of moderate acute malnutrition (MAM) through TSFP will be integrated and aligned with WFP’s food assistance, including social behavior change communication (SBCC) activities. 

WFP will also collaborate with federal and state-level institutions, partners and communities to deliver a multi-sectoral preventative package that targets children 6-23 months, PLW and mothers/caregivers with fortified complementary foods and cash transfers through nutrition-sensitive and specific activities integrated with health, education, WASH, food security and livelihood responses.

Joint multi-sectoral assessments and Emergency Food Security Analysis will be conducted regularly to monitor the nutrition, food security, and markets situation in crisis-affected states. WFP will mainstream protection throughout its work, supported by a solid understanding of the operational context and protection analysis. A gender-transformative approach that reflects the needs of women, men, girls and boys will be adopted and affected populations (women and men) will be consulted throughout the programme cycle.

In the formal schools, we will establish a tutoring program to provide children at risk of drop-out with needed additional academic support. project_name: Provision of Quality Lifesaving Nutrition Intervention to conflict affected communities in Borno and Yobe State
project_objective:
The ongoing conflict has also further affected the health system with only 30 per cent of health facilities remaining functional in Borno State, where malaria is endemic and cholera and other diseases affect the population regularly and are often life-threatening 

The last Nutrition surveillance was conducted between the month of May and June 2018 has highlighted a downwards deterioration in GAM rates between round 4 to round 5, from 6.0 (4.0- 8.9 95% CI) to 8.8 (6.4-13.8 95% CI) in East Borno (Bama, Dikwa, Gwoza, Kala/Balge and Dikwa LGAs) and from 6.9 (4.8-10.0 95% CI) to 10.7 (7.4-15.2 95% CI) in Northern Borno (Mobbar, Kukawa and Nganzai LGAs). This may be attributed to the high influx of new arrivals in the last few months and the high malnutrition rates among newly arrived children as they have been deprived of humanitarian assistance for several years

Recent SMART nutrition surveys conducted by both SCI (in Kaga, Jere, Konduga and Magumeri LGAs) and UNICEF (in Bama LGA) in August 2018 indicated poor prevailing nutrition situation with GAM rates estimated at 15.7% (12.2-20.0 95% CI) and 7.8 % (37.5% per cent in reception sites among newly arrived children). While the nutrition situation in Yobe State which higher GAM rates in nothern domains . The observed high level of GAM among newly arrived children from hard to reach areas has also been seen through the periodic MUAC assessment conducted systematically by the nutrition sector partner.

The Nutrition sector projection for 2019 has identified about 2.248M people in need of some sort of nutrition assistance across Borno and Yobe state and the majority of them are IDPs, Returnees and communities living in hard to reach areas.

project_name: Integrated SRH and GBV Service Delivery for Rohingya Refugees in Cox’s Bazar (2018-19)
project_objective: The ISCG identified GBV support services as a critical need, highlighting safety and security concerns for women and girls, as the sites are overcrowded without proper planning, lighting, privacy, availability of dignity and hygiene materials for basic dignity, safety and mobility. According to the November 2017 ACAPS report, an estimated 448,000 people are in need of GBV support with widespread reports of the use of sexual violence against women and girls while in transit. Women and girls are at risk of trafficking, domestic violence, assault, or other abuse. As of 12 November, over 2,000 GBV cases have been reported. While the exact number of women experiencing sexual violence is not known, it is believed to be high as women and girls have indicated being limited in their movement due to a lack of culturally appropriate clothing, a fear of harassment, and a fear of getting lost. Given the widespread reports on the use of sexual violence in the conflict, ongoing risk of GBV in the target sites and the lack of available services, there is a critical need for GBV prevention and response services for survivors. Rohingyas have conservative social and cultural norms, creating additional barriers on women’s empowerment. Women experience barriers to freedom and access to, and control over resources, with girls’ access and mobility restricted once they reach puberty. Women’s mobility is also restricted by the observance of purdah - the covering of themselves and removing themselves from public space, is limiting their ability to access aid or GBV services - a problem compounded by the stigma faced by GBV survivors and the limited information to which women have access. Lack of sufficient lighting at night in the camps exposes women to risks of attack, and limited consideration of gender sensitive services (e.g. gender segregated WASH facilities; shelters with lockable doors etc.) put women at further risk. Seventy seven percent of women and girls located in the 28 identified settlement sites across Cox’s Bazar District reported feeling unsafe. The lack of space for community structures also limits the ability of humanitarian actors to provide protection services, including community centres, child-friendly spaces (CFS) and safe spaces for women and girls.

project_name: Projet de prise en charge de la malnutrition aigue moderée dans la bande sahélienne
project_objective:
La malnutrition aiguë demeure un problème de santé publique majeur au Tchad avec une prévalence de malnutrition aigüe globale (MAG) estimée à 13,5%, très proche du seuil critique fixé par l’OMS et, avec une prévalence de la malnutrition aiguë sévère (MAS) estimée à 4,0%. On note de fortes disparités régionales avec douze (15) régions sur les vingt-trois (23) que compte le pays, ayant une prévalence de la MAG dépassant le seuil critique de 15% fixé par l’OMS et ou MAS au dela des seuils d'urgence.
Le traitement de la malnutrition aiguë s’inscrit dans le cadre global de la prise en charge intégrée de la malnutrition aiguë qui comporte d’autre composantes telles que la mobilisation communautaire pour l’identification et le suivi des cas de malnutrition et la prise en charge de la malnutrition aiguë sévère en ambulatoire et en hospitalisation. Le programme de traitement de la malnutrition aiguë modérée poursuit cinq objectifs: i) permettre la récupération nutritionnelle des personnes atteintes de malnutrition aiguë modérée au sein de groupes cibles spécifiques; ii) éviter que les personnes atteintes de malnutrition aiguë modérée ne passent au stade de la malnutrition aiguë sévère; iii) prévenir la mortalité liée à la malnutrition; iv) assurer une prise en charge à l'issue du traitement de la malnutrition aiguë sévère afin d'éviter les rechutes; v) prévenir la détérioration de l'état nutritionnel des mères et l'insuffisance pondérale à la naissance qui en résulte.Le traitement de la malnutrition aiguë modérée s'inscrit dans le cadre plus large de la prise en charge communautaire de la malnutrition aiguë, qui constitue la forme d'intervention préconisée face à la malnutrition aiguë. Les programmes de supplémentation alimentaire ciblée sont généralement mis en place dans les pays, provinces ou districts où la prévalence de la malnutrition aiguë globale est supérieure ou égale à 10 pour cent chez les enfants âgés de 6 à 59 mois, ou comprise entre 5 pour cent et 9 pour cent en présence de facteurs aggravants. La durée moyenne d’assistance des bénéficiaires dans le programme est de 90 jours pour les enfants et de 180 jours pour les femmes enceintes et allaitantes en référence au protocole national de prise en charge de la malnutrition aiguë.

project_objective: UNHCR leads two Sectors – Emergency Shelter and Non-Food Items (ES/NFI) and Protection, in addition to partaking in coordination in the RRR Sector both at the National and Sub National Level. UNHCR interventions target all five Darfur States, South, West and North Kordofan states, in addition to Blue Nile State for IDP (new and protracted) – an estimated 430,000 individuals and 300,000 individuals’ returnees. UNHCR will improve the protection of IDPs and returnees through durable solutions profiling, strengthened monitoring, provision of community-based protection initiatives to enhance resilience, shelters/NFI and capacity of partners at the national and state level. UNHCR will target all new IDPs with protection and ES/NFI, and provide assistance to protracted IDPs and returnees based on needs assessment and verification. UNHCR will engage and lead needs assessments and verification of beneficiaries of ES/NFI to ensure priority assistance is given to people with specific needs (PSNs) and women (targeting an estimated 60%) in coordination with government counterparts (Ministry of Social Welfare, Humanitarian Aid Commissioner and Voluntary Return and Reintegration Commission), and partners.  Thematic issues such as disaster risk reduction for fire and flood affected households, using environmental friendly shelter solutions, and engage with local communities to ensure their participation.
