Under two outputs, the intervention will ensure that rural families can meet their immediate food needs while protecting and restoring their own food production (through Cash+ interventions) and prevent further losses of their essential livestock through the delivery of critical supplies.

project_name: Provision of access to essential health services to the most vulnerable (Enhanced Maternal, Emergency Obstetrical and New Born Care)
project_objective:
The project objective is to respond to the Health and nutrition cluster objective to ensure the availability, accessibility, acceptability and quality of essential lifesaving health services to the most vulnerable communities in West bank including through health system strengthening, preparedness and community resilience building

This project aims to improve the quality and accessibility of Hebron residents to essential and lifesaving health care services. 
The project will include both responsive and remedial interventions to meet the needs of children, especially neonates, and pregnant and lactating mothers. 
It will address critical gaps in the health sector response for women and children in West Bank, especially in Hebron (H2 and Area C) communities, including the need for the maternal and child health, and neonate services.

In addition, the proposed activities are aligned with the UN strategy for Hebron, and responds to the latest multi-sectoral needs assessment conducted by OCHA, and the neonate services assessment recently completed by WHO. The project will address the gaps through the provision of critically needed equipment, medical consumables, and drugs.  The project will also address the needs to ambulatory services, through conducting basic life support training to front line health professionals and community members, to enhance the skills and competencies to respond to immediate life-threatening incidents, this will include neonate resuscitation training, and infant and young child feeding in emergencies training. 

The total number of women, children, and men that will benefit from the HRP funding will be 40,000 across the H2 area and two localities in Area C in Hebron district over a twelve-month period. It is estimated that at least 14,750 high-risk pregnant and lactating women and 10,000 children under age of five (5,000 boys and 5,000  girls) will benefit from urgently needed lifesaving health and nutrition interventions.  300 female front line health care providers, and community members, and 200 male front line providers and community members will receive lifesaving training interventions and preparedness training. Some 14,750 men will receive primary health care services as part of the minimal package services

project_name: Protection and prevention services to the most vulnerable children (boys and girls) in the West Bank, and documentation of protection incidents in Israel/ State of Palestine
project_objective:
This project is in line and contributes to the Protection Cluster objective that calls for putting in place protection response mechanisms to prevent and mitigate the effects of occupation and conflict-related violence. It will ensure the most vulnerable children (boys & girls aged 7-17 years old) exposed to conflict related violence are reached with protection and prevention services in the West Bank. 

This project aims for boys and girls to be equally safe, protected, and secure from violence, exploitation and grave violations. It will provide support to caregivers (mothers, fathers, teachers) and children to access protection services including structured mental health and psycho social support in the worst affected areas in the West Bank. Capacities of legal counselling and representation providers will be built, and legal aid for children will be strengthened.  This will be achieved through identifying possible areas of interventions, prioritization of location with highest gap of service provision, capacity building of staff and volunteers, supporting interventions based on existing partnerships or centers and strengthening of coordination and information mechanisms. 

The project will also support incident monitoring, data analysis and reporting on grave violations trends related to child protection concerns in Israel/State of Palestine (both Gaza and the WB) to provide evidence and inform advocacy. Data collection and monitoring will be enhanced through documentation of testimonies of children in military detention.

project_name: Safe access to learning in the West Bank and East Jerusalem
project_objective:
Children in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, face severe and chronic protection challenges getting to and from school every day. They cross Israeli military check points and go through closed military zones where they can experience harassment and even violence.  On their daily commute, they pass by Israeli settlements which can also be a source of abuse, harassment and violence.
The project will contribute to the 2019 HRP education objective 2 of improving safe access to quality learning environment in vulnerable areas by providing protection in accessing education to primary and secondary students (ages 6-17), 6700 (2700girls and 4000 boys) and 200 teaches (100 female and 100 male) in H2, South Hebron Hills, Bethlehem, South Nablus, East Jerusalem and other selected areas in need in the North of West Bank. Children and teachers facing obstacles to schools or children exposed to risks of harassment on their way to schools will be accompanied by international volunteers. 
This intervention has been developed in consultation with the affected communities who express increased demand for it and will also be coordinated with the Protection Cluster. Several assessments, including recently completed Hebron H2 household survey conducted by OCHA in August 2018 have shown that parents are likely to send their children to school when they are accompanied on their way to and from school. 
The lack of safe access to education has significant and negative consequences for children’s schooling and results in a decrease of school hours, an increased drop out rate of children, discouraging teaching staff and the displacement or separation of families as they seek solutions in getting their children in schools elsewhere. In the most severe cases, these negative factors effect children’s overall well being. In coordination with and building on the ongoing evaluation of the protective presence by the Protection Cluster UNICEF will conduct an evidence-based study to evaluate the current protective presence approach and its effectiveness as it relates to the education access and retention. The study will  suggest alternative modalities that would mitigate the risks of relying on the international NGO partner in case of access constraints. Communities, parents, students and teachers will be included in the study through focus groups and surveys. UNICEF team is also responsible for monitoring of the implementation to ensure quality and course-correct if needed and achievement of all planned objectives.

project_name: Emergency WASH interventions for unconnected vulnerable communities in Area C
project_objective:
The project activities and objectives are aligned with the Country and Cluster objectives. Cluster Objective 1: Fulfilment of fundamental human right to water by ensuring equitable, sufficient and sustainable access to basic quality WASH services, available when needed in accordance with safety and dignity of the unserved, underserved and most vulnerable Palestinians under occupation in Gaza and the West Bank. The project aims to ensure access to basic WASH services and avoid displacement of water-scarce communities in the West Bank and Strengthen their WASH preparedness and response capacity. The construction and rehabilitation of water networks and transmission pipeline will reduce water leakages and improve the water pressure, thereby increasing the quantity of water delivered to households which will improve their access to safe and clean water.
The project will target the most vulnerable communities in Area C with humanitarian interventions aimed at alleviating the challenging living conditions of the target population. These vulnerable communities suffer from limited access to water services due to the Israeli restrictions on construction and development in the area. The proposed interventions will target unserved and underserved communities with essential WASH services, that will also protect the most vulnerable families under threat of forcible transfer.
The main targeted areas of the project are the farming and herding families who depend on livestock and agricultural activities to maintain their livelihoods. The most urgent need for these communities is the lack of access to safe water, at the required quality, availability, and affordability at the household level. Families have developed coping mechanisms to respond to the limited access to water - mainly through rainwater harvesting and the collection in cisterns to deal with the water shortages they are suffering from. This has also forced families to reduce their water consumption to less than 30 l/c/d and to reduce their expenditure on basic needs like health and education to cover high water costs.
The intervention will also target unconnected households in Area C communities to increase their capacity to treat and safely store water at the household level and to increase the quality of water consumed. This will be ensured through the installation of water filters; hygiene practices will also be promoted and improved through awareness sessions especially for those practicing open defecation. 
•	The project will target 8,991 people (2,043 women, 2,151 men, 2,285 girls, 2,405 boys, 52 elderly women, and 55 elderly men) in the humanitarian situation have improved/increased access to drinking water of at least 30 l/c/d of high-quality water for a period of 3 months.
•	1,460 students (748 girls, 712 boys) have improved/increased their access to drinking water of at least 5 l/c/d of high-quality water for a period of 3 months.
•	1,153 people (262 women, 276 men, 293 girls, 308 boys, 7 elderly women, 7 elderly men) in the humanitarian situation have improved their access to drinking water through safe drinking water through HHs connections.

project_name: Humanitarian assistance in shelter and NFI to armed crisis affected population in the regions of Tahoua and Tillabéry, Niger
project_objective: IOM aims at ensuring the continuity of shelter and Non-Food Items (NFIs) provision for the population affected by armed crisis in Niger in the regions of Tahoua and Tillabéry. The population targeted by this assistance is comprised of Refugees, IDPs, Returnees and host communities. IOM’s case load for 2019 is 12,000 households (84,000 individuals) with a varied package from emergency shelters for newly displaced households to transitional shelters for more stable households in line with increasing their resilience and improving their living conditions through safe and dignified housing.

project_name: Renforcement de la résilience des  personnes déplacées internes, retournées et communautés hôtes dans les régions de Tahoua et Tillabery.
project_objective: Ce projet cible 60000 personnes des régions de Tahoua et Tillaberi affectées par la crise relative aux mouvements de populations à travers un paquet d'intervention EHA (eau en urgence, eau durable incluant le forage profond de Assagueygueye, l'assainissement à travers l'ATPC en situation d'urgence) et la mise à disposition d'intrants aux acteurs RRM pour les nouveaux déplacés dans les régions de Tahoua et Tillabery

project_name: Projet d'assistance en securite alimentaire, sante et nutrition en faveur des refugies de Tahoua et Tillabery.
project_objective:
Au Niger, le Programme alimentaire mondial (PAM) déroule, sous le leadership du Gouvernement, un programme novateur, visant à soutenir les populations rurales, pour la satisfaction de leurs besoins alimentaires et nutritionnels. Ce programme est fortement focalisé sur l’adoption, par les communautés rurales, de techniques agricoles simples leur permettant de s’adapter à l’impact du changement climatique et d’accroître leur production agricole. La récupération, la redistribution et le développement des terres jadis inexploitables, la mobilisation de l’eau (surcreusement et faucardage des mares, construction de bassins d’eau et de réseaux d’irrigation, etc.) et le développement de l’élevage sont quelques activités qui permettent d’atteindre cet objectif.
La malnutrition au Niger doit être traitée – bien que quelque peu offensive et discutable sur la forme, a certes permis une intense mobilisation de moyens, mais elle a grandement compliqué la gestion d’une crise qui avait de nombreuses autres dimensions que la malnutrition infantile.
Le présent projet a pour objectif d’améliorer la sécurité alimentaire des populations dans les zones à risques de conflit. L’objectif étant de promouvoir l’engagement des femmes dans la gestion de la sécurité alimentaire à travers les activités génératrices de revenus. A traves ce projet, 23 700 personnes bénéficieront de l’assistance alimentaire, un total de 17,000 personnes pourront vivre à travers le cash for work, et finalement un total de 100 associations de femmes avec des activités génératrices de revenus effectives et opérationnelles. 
Dans le cadre de la nutrition, les activités seront focalisées sur l’octroi de la ration alimentaire des enfants de 6 à 23 mois et leur suivi. L’utilisation des vouchers pour la prise en charge nutritionnelle pour les maliens.

project_name: Prévention, préparation et réponse sanitaire aux principales maladies à potentiel épidémique au Niger
project_objective:
Contribuer à la prévention, à la préparation et à la réponse sanitaire rapide aux flambées  des principales maladies à potentiel épidémique (méningite, choléra, rougeole, fièvre de la vallée du Rift, hépatite E) au Niger
Activités et Outputs
Renforcer la surveillance épidémiologique y compris le recyclage du personnel de santé, home et femme, en Surveillance Intégré des Maladies et Riposte (SMIR) et la production des 50 Bulletins de rétro information hebdomadaire et la mise en œuvre du Règlement Sanitaire International (RSI 2005)
•	Renforcer la surveillance transfrontalière  et au niveau des 44 postes frontières pour les  épidémies courantes (cholera, méningite, , Lassa, ...), dans le cadre du Règlement Sanitaire International (RSI 2005) 
•	Organiser des campagnes de vaccination de riposte contre la rougeole et contre les autres épidémies de l’enfance évitables par la vaccination
•	Assurer la formation du personnel de santé, hommes et femmes, à la gestion des risques sanitaires courants y compris la prise en charge correcte des cas de choléra
•	Appuyer la prévention et la prise en charge du paludisme en cas de pics épidémiques, pour les enfants de moins de cinq ans et les femmes enceintes, dans les districts sanitaires affectés par l’approvisionnement en Moustiquaires Imprégnées d'Insecticide à Longue Durée d'Action (MIILDA), en combinaisons thérapeutiques à base d'artémisinine (CTA), en  tests de diagnostic rapide (TDR) ainsi que par la mise en œuvre des stratégies de chimio prévention du paludisme saisonnier (CPS) chez les enfants et du traitement préventif intermittent (TPI) chez les femmes enceintes
•	Appuyer la mise à jour du Plan national d’élimination du choléra au Niger.
•	Assurer le pré positionnement des Kits inter agences contre les maladies diarrhéiques (IDDK),en Kits interangences (IEHK), des Kits de santé reproductive  et autres médicaments essentiels/équipements médicaux de base, dans les districts sanitaires affectés par les crises
•	Renforcer des capacités de laboratoire la confirmation des maladies à potentiel épidémiques, y compris les fièvres hémorragiques virales.
•	Assurer les campagnes de riposte vaccinale lors des flambées de maladies évitables par la vaccination.

project_name: IRAQ - World Food Programme
Site Maintenance Engineering and Disaster Resilience Project
project_objective: Improvement of accessibility through engineering works on critical infrastructure, combined with risk mitigation through slope protection, terracing, perimeter fencing, constructing dams, clearing drainage canals etc.

project_name: Unconditional food assistance to food-insecure households affected by shocks
project_objective:
In line with the Government’s effort to improve emergency preparedness and response, WFP keeps a contingency food stock to respond rapidly in case of hurricane or other shocks. Most recently, the stock was essential to the swift and rapid response to initial needs during the hurricane Matthew emergency. The stocks are stored on WFP premises and, after a shock occurs, are distributed by its cooperating partners in close collaboration with the Government and in particular with Civil Protection Agency (DPC) agents in the affected communes. 
WFP will seek to purchase its emergency food assistance locally or nationally in order to support agricultural production and promote sustainable food systems. project_name: JORDAN - Plan International
Enhance immediate food security and rebuilding of vulnerable livelihood in Jonglei, Upper Nile Western Bahr el Ghazal and Lake states
project_objective:
Oxfam’s immediate objectives are to save lives, meet the immediate food needs and protect the livelihoods of the most vulnerable groups of women, men, boys and girls in the targeted counties. 
Extreme food insecurity persists throughout South Sudan and increased humanitarian assistance is needed to prevent the loss of lives and their livelihoods. An estimated 1.7 million people remain internally displaced in South Sudan, many of whom have been displaced more than once. Another 2.5 million people have fled South Sudan to neighbouring countries since December 2013. 
A collapse in national economy, reduced crop production and dependence on imports seriously deteriorate people’s ability towards food security round the year, putting millions of lives at risk. An estimates 6.1 million people are at risk of severe food insecurity during last lean season according to Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) report of September 2018.

Most of the targeted counties in Jonglei are at critical stages regarding food insecurity like Uror (IPC phase 3!), Nyirol (IPC phase 3!), Pibor (IPC phase 4) and Twic East (IPC phase 4) during January – March 2018. On the other hand, Malakal under Upper Nile state is a bit instable in terms of population movement from PoC to Malakal town. The population movement is also a critical state in Wau under Western Bahr el Ghazal. Moreover; there is a potential risk of catastrophe in Pibor (20% population which is 20,000 people) and Wau (0.2% that means 1000 people) from January -March 2019. 
The driving forces are a below average rainfall, constrains of humanitarian assistance delivery and high possibility of continued armed conflict, and upcoming dry season from January -March 2019 it is highly likely of increased people being classified under IPC 4. Additionally, there has been infestation of crops by fall army worm across the entire region, which will contribute to low yields for the harvest this year. Households are facing significant constraints to meeting their basic food needs. Prices remain extremely high and with limited income, most households are unable to purchase sufficient food from markets. Conflict has also prevented many households from engaging in typical livelihood activities, such as farming, lowering food available through own production. Households throughout the state are facing food consumption gaps. Levels of malnutrition are expected to decline in dry (January – March) and lean season (July -August) and remain at ‘Critical’ (GAM(WHZ)>15%) levels in many counties.

Oxfam has been working in Jonglei, Upper Nile, Western Bahr el Ghazal and Lake states for long time. A total of 55,000 people will be targeted through different means of Food Security & Livelihood interventions in Jonglei ( Uror, Nyirol, akobo, Pibor and Twic East), Upper Nile ( Malakal) ,and Western Bahr el Ghazal (Wau) and Lake states ( Cuiebet). The affected population are IDPs, returnees and host communities.

Based on the analysis of relevant assessment reports the basic interventions are General Food Distribution (GFD), Conditional food distribution through Food for Asset, unconditional and conditional Cash Transfer Initiatives, Seeds and tools provision either direct distribution or voucher programming, capacity building initiatives to improve livelihoods, increasing agricultural production linking with market to ensure food and nutrition security.

project_name: LEBANON - Concern Worldwide

Improved food security and dietary diversity to vulnerable and conflict affected populations in Aweil West and Aweil North, Northern Bahr el Ghazal, Juba PoC, Central Equatoria and Guit, Unity, South Sudan 2019
project_objective:
Since 2013, on-going conflict has resulted in 2.48 million refugees fleeing and 1.84 million internally displaced with around 203,000 residing in PoCs (OCHA, Sep 2018). Conflict has impacted on food security, and based on the IPC analysis, by March 2019 it is anticipated that 49% of the population will be at Crisis or Emergency Levels of food insecurity. High rates of morbidity along with poor health, nutrition and hygiene practices, as well has high levels of food insecurity have resulted in high malnutrition rates. Although NBeG is relatively calm, it has suffered indirect impacts of conflict as well as erratic rainfall affecting staple crop performance with 54.6% of the population in NBeG were under Crisis, Emergency and Humanitarian Catastrophe (IPC, Sep 2018). Households in Juba PoC lack the means for income generation and are dependent on food aid to meet food needs. In Unity, lack of access to nutritious foods places households in Bentiu PoC and outside the PoC at severe risk of malnutrition as well as poor nutrition practices. Despite the re-vitalised peace agreement in August 2018, persistent insecurity in many locations means high levels of returns are unlikely from Juba PoC.
While this project will not directly focus on the FSL cluster objective 1, Concern aims to partner with WFP to ensure food access in Juba PoC through GFDs; and in Aweil West (another partner provides GFDs in Aweil North) during the lean period from July-September. This project will contribute to the FSL cluster objective 2 to increase food production and improve dietary diversity. In Aweil West and Aweil North, extremely vulnerable households whose main livelihood is agriculture will be supported with emergency seed provision to improve food production. Seeds will be provided through voucher fairs where beneficiaries will have more choice in selecting seeds according to their preference. Concern will use Community Agricultural Extension Workers and lead farmers through a training of trainer approach on climate smart agriculture and biopesticide production as well as post-harvest handling. Beneficiaries will be formed into groups for block farming to pool resources and share risks. Dry season agricultural support will focus on vegetable gardens with households with members in OTP/TSFP to improve access to nutritious foods. In Juba PoC, Bentiu PoC and Guit, linked with the Nutrition programme, Concern will support MtMSGs to engage in sack farming in PoCs and kitchen gardens outside of PoCs for improving consumption of nutritious foods. 
The project will contribute to the FSL Cluster objective 3 though targeted life sustaining cash assistance to strengthen households and community coping capacities by building productive assets and reduce reliance on food aid through conditional cash transfers. With hazards associated with erratic climate in Aweil West and Aweil North such as prolonged dry periods and flooding, Concern will support vulnerable communities with CFA. Communities will prioritise assets such as shallow wells, feeder road and dykes, which will be constructed by vulnerable beneficiaries who will then receive cash transfers to meet emergency needs during the lean period. 
The relatively stable situation in NBeG allows for linking with Concern’s longer-term integrated programmes focused on resilience-building such focusing on more training on climate smart agricultural techniques; addressing the high rate or morbidity through improving water and sanitation infrastructure and hygiene practices; increasing iCCM for early detection and prevention of common illnesses; and improving health and nutrition behaviours. In NBeG, beneficiaries of this programme will also feed into these resilience programmes. In Unity, beneficiaries of vegetable production inputs will also be targeted by WASH and MICYN interventions and Juba PoC Concern will coordinate with WASH partners to ensure Concern’s beneficiaries are targeted.

project_name: Strenghtening access to primary health care services in camps and physical rehabilitation services for conflict affected vulnerable communities in Iraq
project_objective:
The project aims at ensuring the continuity of quality health care services for most vulnerable people in
KRI,  Ninewa Governorates and northern - central governorates of Iraq through the provision of comprehensive curative quality health services for Iraqi IDPs hosted in Ashti and Arbat camps and the provision of rehabilitation and social reintegration services for amputee patients referred from all the governorates of KRI and Iraq to the EMERGENCY Rehabilitation Center in Sulaymaniyah. The first component of the project focuses on the provision of essential packages of health services to IDPs (2822 men, 3304 women, 3391 boys and 3691 girls) depending on humanitarian aid, in close coordination with the stakeholders working in the area. Comprehensive health care services include the provision of free health care (curative and preventive) and referral system for emergency and elective cases. The second component focuses on the provision of medical support and rehabilitation services to people (3797 men, 763 women, 1199 boys and 241 girls) who have been heavy injured in most conflict affected areas, where Mines and IEDs are still causing several victims even after the end of fighting.
This component will be implemented in close collaboration with the functional Rehabilitation Centers of the Iraqi governorates, as well as with the local authorities (MoH and  DoHs). The project strategy covers the gaps of the local capacity to respond adequately to the humanitarian crisis and combines short terms activities (provision of services) with long term ones (training on the job and capacity building of local staff) in order to ensure the sustainability of the action, in the sight of a successful hand-over to the local authorities. An accurate needs assessment, as well as a long experience in the country, has permitted to identify the health needs of the beneficiaries and to define the activities in order to cover the specific necessities of every category of beneficiaries: women, girls, men and boys, elderly and disabled people.
A handover plan will be written in collaboration with Sulaymaniyah DoH in order to ensure a smooth exit strategy as well as the continuation of the activities. Monthly meetings will be organized in order to define the handover steps and to increase the involvement of DOH in the management of Ashti PHCC.

project_name: Food Security Programme in Idleb and Aleppo Governorates
project_objective:
The FSL I Programme started on 1 January 2018 and has been reported under the HRP 2018. The project end date has been extended until 31 March 2019.  This submission is for the period of 01 January – 31 March 2019.

The FSL I programme aims to contribute to increased food security for vulnerable displaced and host community households in Idleb and Aleppo Governorates. 
FSL I comprises of two components: Household Food Security and Bakery Support. 

The Household Food Security component targets an average of 250,000 food-insecure individuals per month with in-kind food assistance (food kits) and cash modality (food restricted vouchers). 

The Bakery Support component provides an approximate 600,000 individuals living in supported bakeries’ catchment area with bread at a reduced and stabilised price. This is achieved through subsiding up to 50% input (flour and yeast) of bread production thus supporting local bakeries to produce a stable quantity of bread that meets local needs. This support is conditioned upon the selling of this bread in the local markets at a reduced and stabilised price agreed with and monitored by NGO X’s Cash and Markets, and Monitoring Teams. 


This project is implemented in partnership with several other INGOs whose names have been concealed for security reasons. One INGO (whose name has been provided via email to the FSL Cluster Coordination Team) will submit their planned activities under this project separately based on a prior agreement between the two agencies. The two agencies have coordinated carefully the programme targets and figures to avoid duplication.

project_name: Stabilizing the livelihoods of conflict affected returnees, internally displaced persons and the host communities in the Equatorias, Jonglei, Unity, Greater Bahr el Ghazal and Greater Upper Nile through integrated emergency and static Food Security and Livelihood response.
project_objective:
This project aims to meet the immediate, medium and long-term food security needs of the target communities in Eastern Equatoria, Western Bahr el Ghazal, Unity, Jonglei and Central Equatoria states that were affected by armed conflict, insecurities, climate change and displacement. This will be achieved by:
a)	Access to cereal seed kits: To ensure the target communities recover from hunger cereal seed kits and tools accompanied by agricultural extension activities, focusing on good agronomic practices including season of planting, seedbed preparation, planting and spacing, weed management, irrigation, integrated pest and production management, harvesting and post-harvest management. This intervention will be delivered using lead farmers and farmer field school approaches with demonstration plots.
b)	Access to vegetable kits: In areas with access sufficient water for vegetable growing, beneficiaries will be provided with vegetable kits containing a variety of vegetable seeds followed by extension training on good agronomic practices including seed and nursery bed preparation, seed planting and spacing, irrigation, integrated pest and production management, harvesting and post-harvesting management.
C) Access to fishing kits: Intervening at the household level to meet the emergency food security needs through provision of fishing NFIs. Fishing has a potential to immediately address the food security needs of the targeted vulnerable households through provision of fishing equipment to enable the people to immediately harvest fish from the rivers and swamps in the areas.
d) Improving the capacity of farmer field schools: lead farmers and extension workers will be trained as trainers for community farmers. The lead farmers and extension workers will then facilitate discussions and demonstration on good agronomic practices for the vegetable and cereal crops producer groups.
e) Setting up irrigation system: Vegetable farmers will be provided with treadle pumps, watering cans at household levels while drip irrigation systems will be established at farmer field school gardens or demonstration plots. Drip irrigation systems together with community training on their adequate and sustainable use will enhance the copying mechanism during the dry season.
f) School feeding program: Food for education and school feeding programme will be considered in the project areas where PAH carries food security and livelihood activities with seeds distribution and vegetable and cereal crops production.
i) Conditional General food distribution: Conditional general food distribution programming/project is already being developed and submitted awaiting approval. This will target the most vulnerable food insecure population with limited access to markets and having poor road network. 
j) Cash Programming is based on initial market and community assessments, considering cash vouchers or cash for work. Food for asset/cash will be conducted in the areas where there is need and local markets are able to support the project targeting establishment of community structures and facilities like schools and infrastructures like community road projects and communal farms establishment.
k) Integration: For more holistic approach, PAH will integrate interventions with sectors of WASH, nutrition, education, protection and S/NFI through combined hygiene and nutrition promotion in addition to screening and referral to nutrition partners. Education and health will be integrated through training of school hygiene clubs and school gardening and awareness at the schools, nutrition and health centers. PAH will work with nutrition and health partners like Johanniter in Wau, RMF in Boma while the PAH ERT will integrate the WASH, S/NFI and FSL as in the projects in Magwi, Boma, Koch and Jur River counties since 2017. Protection will be mainstreamed across all sectors and additional protection team will be supporting the community where PAH implements FSL and other sectors.

project_name: Creation and rehabilitation of household/Group-based and communal-level productive assets through Food Assistance for Assets (FFA); and  enhanced human capital through Food Assistance for Training (FFT).
project_objective:
WFP Syria’s interim Country Strategy Plan (iCSP) 2019-20 envision an increase in livelihood programming to support almost 2 million beneficiaries. The project activities provide an overarching chapeau under which a range of interventions will serve to strengthen livelihoods at household/ group-based and community-level. The project will support food insecure and vulnerable households with two activity pillars via Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) and Food Assistance for Training (FFT). 
1.	Food Assistance for Assets (FFA)
FFA aims to restore and rebuild livelihoods of vulnerable Syrian households and communities through household-level productive assets, income generation activities and rehabilitation of communal infrastructure to enhance agricultural production. 
The project is planning to support the targeted households through two types of interventions a) provision of household, group and community-based productive assets; and b) rehabilitation of communal agrarian infrastructure; 

Pillar 1a: Household and Group-Based Productive Assets: 
Provision of agricultural inputs and technical assistance to households in rural areas to improve and diversify household food consumption and provide income generating opportunities. 
Pillar 1b – Rehabilitation of Communal Agrarian Infrastructure 
The project aims to rehabilitate and fix irrigation and other agricultural infrastructure in the rural areas. Its’s critical to encourage smallholder famers to return to cultivation, improve agricultural productivity, and revitalize local markets. 

2.	Human Capital Development/Vocational Skills Training via FFT
FFT aims to enhance human capital and skills development, with a focus on urban women and youth. Active labour market support activities will provide participants with technical and vocational skills training (VST) based on local labour market needs and post-training support to enter the labour market or establish small businesses. 

Additionally WFP will provide cross-cutting livelihood support via Retail Sector Rehabilitation (Pillar 3) and Support to Social Transfers/Financial Inclusion (Pillar 4).Pillar 3 focuses on food systems, strengthening local economic recovery and basic service provision, with the aim of stimulating economic employment opportunities for vulnerable communities and providing WFP an opportunity to encourage and/or facilitate the employment of members from vulnerable, food insecure households. Where WFP support is targeted at businesses related to food production and sales, WFP support will directly increase community access to, and consumption of, food commodities, thereby enhancing local food security. Pillar 4 represents a new approach to livelihood activities for WFP. Financial inclusion for unbanked households has been identified by WFP as a key enabler of improved livelihoods, including by contributing to food insecurity and poverty reduction. WFP has defined financial inclusion as ensuring that individuals understand, and have access to, affordable financial services and products. A cross cutting issue, financial inclusion is an enabler and accelerator of food security, nutrition, and development.

project_objective:
This project will encompass the deployment of an integrated mine action response across accessible areas in Syria.  

Dense, widespread contamination across Syria – both conventional and improvised – is preventing the safe return of displaced populations, increasing risks to physical safety, restricting access for humanitarian actors and disrupting early recovery efforts where hostilities have ceased. The prevalent use of improvised landmines and booby traps by ISIS has further escalated the threat to Syrian populations. Increased access to areas formerly under ISIS control, together with largescale Internally Displaced People (IDP) movements, has led to a significant increase in civilian casualties from improvised devices and Explosive Ordnance (EO), highlighting the threat posed by contamination.  Items are commonly found in civilian homes, community infrastructure and agricultural areas. Across Syria, information on contamination is limited due to restricted mine action activities, however it is expected that following years of war and multiple military offensives the contamination from conventional as well as improvised devices is high. Contamination is likely to be found across all areas including agricultural land, residential areas and urban settings. 

This project will aim to deploy an integrated mine action approach for WoS where access is permissible.  The project will include manual and mechanical clearance operations, where operations will have a humanitarian focus to remove and destroy explosive items that present a risk to life and limb or is blocking access to community structures.  All tasks will be prioritized internally against determined indictors to determine those with the highest humanitarian impact.  National teams will be trained and deployed with International oversight to ensure activities are conducted safely and to International mine action standards.  The project will also deploy Community liaison (CL) teams to deliver Risk Education (RE) sessions in order to promote safe behaviours, train community focal points to deliver safety messages to wider communities and provide RE to humanitarian workers.  The CL teams and the manual clearance teams will also conduct Non-Technical and Technical Survey respectively to help provide a more detailed picture of the contamination profile to guide a safer humanitarian response and future clearance efforts.

The proposed Action aims to reach the most vulnerable IDPs, returnees and host communities in the crisis-affected areas. Target locations have been proposed according to severity of humanitarian needs and number of population in need. They may be altered depending on the evolution of the context on the ground, access and people's movement.
The Action aims to create an access to multi-purpose cash grants to improve food security and coping strategy.
The Action is informed by rapid assessments, observation visits, Oxfam's ongoing work, consultations with Syrian and international NGOs, and reliable secondary data, including the Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) 2018. The action is designed to meet specific life-saving needs around emergency food security (EFS).
Oxfam plans to provide multipurpose cash grants to the most vulnerable HHs in the targeted crsis-affected locations. This plan forms the second phase of piloting cash by Oxfam in Syria. In July 2018 Oxfam completed a pilot cash distribution to families living in Herjelleh IDP site in Rural Damascus. Oxfam will perform thorough market assessments in order to make sure that cash modality is appropriate and to avoid any increase in the inflation in the local markets, in addition Oxfam will monitor price fluctuation in the local markets. Oxfam will perform thorough vulnerability analysis in order to agree on the vulnerability characteristics and select the most vulnerable HHs accordingly. 
Oxfam will transfer cash through local licensed Financial Service Providers FSPs after running all the required vetting and checking processes.

project_name: Water Provision in Idleb Governorate
project_objective:
NGO X has been supporting the operation of four Water Units serving the conflict-affected population of Idleb Governorate since 2014.  An estimated 560,000 individuals rely on the water pumped by 50 water station within the four units for their households’ drinking and hygiene needs. The programme will continue to provide inputs and technical expertise to allow for the continuation of services while strengthening the financial and management capacity of local stakeholders to manage the utility and continue on a path towards sustainability.  In addition, NGO X will provide emergency assistance to recently displaced households to allow them to meet their basic hygiene needs.

In September 2018 NGO X managed to get an emergency fund to support additional 15 water stations that provide water to approximately 210,000 individuals in Idleb governorate. As a result, currently, NGO X is supporting 65 water stations by providing water to approximately 770,000 individuals in Idleb governorate, both projects are going to end by 31 March 2019 and it is expected that NGO X is going to receive fund to run the essential project which provide water to 560,000 individuals and NGO X will work to find a fund to continue the emergency project.  

Prior to the conflict in Syria, the water and sanitation resources in Syria were under pressure from population growth and urbanization.  Syrian water resources faced significant managerial challenges and had been prioritized by the Syrian government for modernization.  Water utilities were heavily subsidized and as of 2006 were only covering 55% of their operational costs and were unable to accumulate funds for investment.   The sector was further challenged by its complex management structure with different Ministries and sectors having overlapping responsibilities and functions.  The protracted conflict has worsened the situation.  Unreliable electricity, damaged water infrastructure, the influx of IDPs, threats from militant groups inside Idleb, and households with few financial resources are all challenges facing the water sector. 

The NGO X programme’s desired outcome is that community water systems are efficiently and effectively managed and the community is informed, invested and supportive of local institutions and has sustained access to safe drinking water and hygienic conditions.’  

Key activities include:
•	Providing inputs (fuel, oil, HTH, salaries) to enable the stations to pump water for over 101 villages. 
•	Intense organisational capacity building to ensure water units and stations have the financial, administrative and management skills necessary to manage the stations in a transparent manner that prioritises accountability to customers, the community and donors.  
•	Stations develop realistic and achievable cost recovery targets based on financial analysis and communicate the approach to communities. 
•	Continue using the modality of ‘Infrastructure Stability’ fund that water stations can apply to for upgrading or investing in their stations and water networks.  Maintains resources to enable emergency repairs conducted by NGO X. 
•	Supporting recent arrivals into Idleb with hygiene kits and hygiene promotion.

project_name: Integrated response to end gender based violence against vulnerable women and adolescent girls in Eastern Ukraine
project_objective:
The project will target vulnerable and affected populations population in the regions of eastern Ukraine most affected by the armed conflict (Donetsk, Luhansk, Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia and Kharkiv regions) where UNFPA has already built the key elements of a response mechanism as part of its humanitarian interventions. It will place an increasing emphasis on strengthening community resilience, with particular attention to supporting most vulnerable population. 
Differentiated approaches to programming will continue to be applied in 2019 considering the prevailing humanitarian situation and its evolution: 
•	The primary focus for humanitarian response will remain to be on the communities along the contact line (Donetsk and Luhansk regions). 
•	Critical needs of the most vulnerable IDPs and host communities members will be prioritized in other three conflict affected eastern regions (Kharkiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia) with a more gradual transition toward longer term solutions for response to GBV. 
•	As humanitarian access to the NGCA for protection activities remains restricted, the project will seek alternative opportunities for partnerships with local actors; will reach out to those in need through remote solutions such as national and regional hotlines and social media; and will use existing access points such as healthcare facilities for delivering aid. 
UNFPA supported models of service delivery will eventually build trust to those services among survivors and trigger their willingness to report their cases and seek help. Engagement of non-state actors (local NGO’s, FBO’s, CBO’s) to act as service providers and/or actors on GBV prevention at the local community level, working with affected population of those communities, their opinion leaders, ATO veterans and their family members will strengthen the prevention pillar of the overall GBV response mechanism and strategy and diversify sources of support to those at risk of GBV. 
NGOs and community groups representing the voices of IDPs and survivors of GBV will be directly involved into the project work through inclusion in its governing structures and working groups, elaborating policy and guideline documents at the national and regional levels as well as through involvement in project monitoring activities. 
Finally, targeted communication and advocacy campaign will eventually support change of attitudes towards GBV, eliminate stereotypes among community members, particularly young people and lead to less tolerance towards GBV in the affected communities . Awareness raising sessions and events will continue to be conducted with communities where PSS MTs operate, as well as with staff of difference service providers to promote responsive behavior and active participation in monitoring the GBV situation in their communities and providing/referring those in need to respective services.   
A monitoring and evaluation plan, defined through previous interventions to manage the process of assessing and reporting progress against project targets, are used to ensure quality of project results. This plan describes the whole M&E system, including indicators, tools, breakdown of responsibilities and communication channels within the project implementers and beneficiaries and between them. Monitoring visits will be conducted by UNFPA M&E team to follow up on the outcome and impact of project activities. Additionally evaluation of PSS mobile team model will be conducted in order to analyses and verify its  functionality and impact, measure the achievements and flaws, draw out lessons learned, and most importantly to develop evidence-based practical recommendations for further institutionalization and development of the model integrating it into the existing system of PSS services provision in conflict effected regions. The process will engage all PSS project stakeholders at the local communities levels, local service providers, GBV response referral networks, PSS MT members, PSS service clients, local communities where MTs operate, possibly local media. While all stakeholders are important sources of information for the evaluation, the direct beneficiaries – GBV survivors will be put in the center of attention. 
A feedback mechanism from project beneficiaries (GBV survivors, local service providers and partners, local authorities responsible for GBV response and coordination) will be operating, including through regular GBV WGs and GBV SC meetings, National Toll Free Hot Line on prevention of violence to make sure that the opinions of target vulnerable population are heard and taken into consideration. Complaints and suggestions related to the implementation of project activities will be timely responded to. 
In order to achieve maximum complementarity and potentiate the results, the project will seek to coordinate, and to the extent possible work jointly, with other complementary projects and initiatives in the area of gender equality and GBV (OSCE, Council of Europe, EUAM, UN agencies, etc.) or those working to rehabilitate and develop local social infrastructure and institutional capacity (such as GIZ, UNDP, UNHCR, UNICEF)

project_name: PROTECTING AND EMPOWERING WOMEN AND GIRLS AFFECTED BY CONFLICT IN FAR NORTH OF CAMEROON
project_objective:
The project focuses on the urgent needs of women and girls affected by Boko Haram crisis in Far North region,particularly in the areas of protection and livelihood. Overall goal of the initiative is to ensure that women and girls lead, participate in, and are empowered by and benefit from humanitarian response and recovery efforts by meeting specific needs of women and girls as well as mainstreaming gender in humanitarian actions. It also contributes to the prevention and mitigation of violent extremism, addressing some of the key drivers of radicalization such as limited economic opportunities. It builds on the success of UN Women’s humanitarian work since 2014 in response to the refugee crisis from Central African Republic (CAR) in the East and the Boko Haram crisis in the Far North, much of which was supported by the Government of Japan (GoJ). These consecutive initiatives have improved the lives of thousands of women and girls by providing an integrated service package at women cohesion spaces created in the refugee camps. 
	
This project consists of four outcome areas:  
•	Outcome 1: Women and girls in affected areas have increased protection against gender-based violence (GBV)
•	Outcome 2: Women and girls have new sources of income and economic opportunities
•	Outcome 3: Women’s leadership and engagement is increased  in community mobilization, social cohesion and decision making 
•	Outcome 4: Gender analysis and assessments are reflected in multi-sectoral humanitarian crisis response planning and programming 
The project is in line with the Cameroon Humanitarian Response Plan 2019

project_name: NIGER INTERIM COUNTRY STRATEGIC PLAN
project_objective:
'An average of 5.6 million people in Niger are unable to fully meet their food and nutrition needs because of insufficient food availability associated with inadequate production, security constraints, demographic growth and other factors. Of these, about 2.65 million are affected year-on-year. The global acute malnutrition rate of 15.3 percent and the stunting rate of 45.2 percent exceed the World Health Organization’s threshold for a “critical” nutrition situation. In addition.
Conflict in neighbouring countries is also resulting in increasing threats at the borders with Mali, Libya, and Nigeria,  and negatively impacts Niger’s security, economy, migration, humanitarian needs and long-term development. 
The country ranks 187th out of 188 in the 2017 Human Development Index, with a poverty rate of 44.1 percent. Widespread poverty, demographic pressure, economic shocks combined with persistent gender inequalities,  limited national budgets for food security, and constraints on national capacities significantly exacerbate food insecurity. All these factors impede development and adequate government response.

project_name: Provision of MHPSS Specialized services in Albab and Afrin Areas
project_objective:
The proposed project will contribute to alleviate the impact of the Syrian crisis on the most affected people, local communities and IDPs, in Aleppo/Al Bab and Afrin areas. The most important needs identified related to Mental Health & Psychosocial Support, MHPSS will be addressed by two axes: Acute Mental Health Inpatients Unit in Al Bab area in addition to Fixed MHGAP Unit in Afrin Area. The most affected people will benefit from specialized MHPSS services - which are not available effectively in the area to respond to the high needs of those people by establishing an Acute Mental Health Inpatients Unit in Al Bab area in addition to a Fixed MHGAP Unit in Afrin area. The main goal of the project is to provide specialized mental health services qualified to address more severe mental health disorders alongside with Psychological First Aid, PFA and referral of more severe and serious cases. 
The Acute MH Inpatient Unit: will provide an acute inpatient service for more urgent presentations of severe mental health disorders, like schizophrenia (acute psychotic episodes), bipolar disorder (manic episode), severe depression, suicidal risk, severe substance misuse disorder and severe behavioral disorder related to mental health problems which cannot be managed in the community.
In addition, providing a multidisciplinary mental health service in the community (outpatient psychiatric units, psychiatric supervision, follow up and case management, individual, couple and group psychotherapy and tele-mental health supervision), and receiving referrals of more severe and complicated psychiatric cases from other agencies and health providers.
The Fixed MH Unit: will provide assessment and diagnosis of cases; women, men, children and adolescences presenting mental health disorder’s signs and symptoms according to the mental health disorders which are addressed in the MHGAP program (Depression, epilepsy, Psychosis…. Etc.) in addition to the provision of proper interventions including specific kinds of psychotropic medications.
In addition, in both clinics, there will be a team of 2 PSWs who will provide the intake assessment for cases in the outpatient clinic and refer the cases in need to the MHGAP doctors in addition to psychoeducation and awareness sessions for beneficiaries, families and caregivers. 
Also, in both areas, group sessions and individual consultations with follow up mechanisms will be provided by the psychosocial workers (PSWs) supervised by the MHGAP doctors. In the projects, IDPs camps, schools and home visits will be targeted by a team of outreach PSWs who in turn will provide PSS activities for children and adolescences and awareness sessions for families on protection and MH concerns.  
Objectives of the Project:
•	Cases with severe and acute MH disorders will receive specialized MH interventions. 
•	Cases with different ages presenting signs and symptoms of mental health disorders will receive interventions based on MHGAP program.
•	Beneficiaries have better awareness and knowledge on mental health and protection concerns.
•	Children improved coping skills dealing with the stressful circumstances with better.  
•	Beneficiaries with different ages have access to other services provided by other humanitarian actors in the area. 
•	The project staff of PSWs have better knowledge and skills of protection minimum standards and stress management and detecting signs and symptoms of mental health disorders alongside with PSS principles and activities.

project_name: Psychosocial support, care and protection from violence, exploitation and abuse for displaced children affected by the anglophone crisis in Cameroon.
project_objective:
With the on-going crisis, access to essential services has been severely curtailed due to insecurity, large-scale displacement, destruction or closure of health facilities and schools, withdrawal of implementing partners, and relocation of health, education, and social workers. An estimated 246,000 children have been displaced inside the South West, 105,000 in the North West, and around 86,000 displaced to neighboring West and Littoral regions (Interagency Needs Assessment Oct 9, 2018).  So far, most people are displaced in the bush in hard to reach areas. Pressing needs of IDPs in the bush/hard to reach areas include child protection needs among others as reported in various assessment missions including those conducted by UNICEF between November 2017-August 2018 but also in a multisectoral assessment conducted in March 2018 and various assessments conducted by CSO and INGOs. 
As of today, the provision of humanitarian aid is mainly ensured by local NGOs at a very small scale. These NGOs are not familiar with humanitarian interventions and principles but possess knowledge of the area and can negotiate access and acceptance. UNICEF has established partnerships with non governmental partners already present in the 2 regions to increase acceptance by all stakeholders. UNICEF began implementing emergency response activities in August 2018 with a focus on IDPs in hard to reach areas, both in government controlled or not areas.     
In order to protect children from violence, abuse and neglect, as a priority and main intervention, UNICEF will work on the offer of services and provide psychosocial support to 135,367 children including 69,548 girls affected by the conflict in 133 child friendly spaces or youth clubs in urban, peri-urban and hard to reach areas.
As a direct corollary, an estimated 3,764 unaccompanied and separated children (UASC) is foreseen to be identified during the implementation of the project with an estimated number of 1,910 girls. All the 3,764 children will benefit from alternative care arrangements, support and individual follow up while due to the difficult access and insecurity UNICEF plans to reunify a minimum of 740 unaccompanied or separated children with their family.
UNICEF will complement its support to children activities, work on the demand side with awareness raising and prevention activities at community-level. Concretely, UNICEF with its implementing partners will run sensitization campaigns with the aim to reach out to 122,143 persons with specific attention to parents to pass on messages on child protection in emergencies, trauma early warning signs for children, effects of family separation, GBV and other types of violence children are at risk of at the community level so that parents and community members can play an active role in child protection in emergencies.
UNICEF and its partners will also provide support to an estimated 961 unregistered, displaced children being particularly vulnerable to various forms of discrimination and abuse because of the lack of birth certificates.
Taking into account the implementation environment and the need for capacity building of implementing partners, UNICEF will build and strengthen the capacity of humanitarian actors on child protection mainstreaming throughout all sectors/clusters, but also enhance their knowledge and technicalities in child protection in emergencies through the organization a total of 5 workshops in different locations (Boyo, Mezam, Fako, Manyu and Mémé) targeting a minimum of 403 field staff responding to the crisis and its child protection component. UNICEF as lead of the Child Protection Area of Responsibility will continue to lead the child protection in emergency sub-cluster in Buea with an antenna in Bamenda, in order to consolidate the coordination and ensure alignment and complementarity of interventions in the field of child protection.

project_name: Multi-sector project in WASH; FSL; NFI-IES; EDUCATION, RRR to ensure life-saving and sustainable responses to IDPs, returnees, and vulnerable residents in West and Central Darfur
project_objective:
In 2019, continuous return dynamics from Chad and IDPs camp to villages in Darfur are likely to be observed. In parallel to this “normalization” process, localized and violent clashes are likely to occur particularly in Jebel Marra, causing massive displacements. The action aims at responding to both dynamics by providing emergency responses and durable solutions to be implemented in protracted contexts to develop access to basic services and build capacities of communities on facilities management while including a timely and appropriate response to new emergencies.
Based on this current situation, an integrated approach is required in order to address the most basic humanitarian needs to ensure an access to WASH, Food security and livelihoods, NFI/Shelters and Education services that will allow the beneficiaries to maintain or regain minimal dignity and mitigate the health, environmental and the other displacement/return related risks. Chronic deficiency of basic services is aggravated by the increased pressure on natural resources induced by new arrivals and the increase in prices of items of first necessity due to the current economic crisis. Return dynamic is expected to continue and to potentially increase in Central and West Darfur while new population displacements are expected considering the formal restart of the tripartite agreement for Sudanese refugees repatriation and also the persistence of a relatively stable security context .  
The combination of protracted and urgent needs in Darfur calls for the humanitarian-development nexus, a core element of the project is therefore the development of sustainable approaches to support the process of returns started in 2016. As the security context has significantly improved in 2018 in most of the areas of CD and WD, longer-term solutions are needed to find viable exit strategies. Involvement of communities in the design of the action as well as in the management of facilities is a precondition for durability and a progressive phase out of humanitarian actors.
TGH therefore proposes an integrated project in line with following sectors:
- WASH: through the proposed project TGH will ensure both a timely emergency and sustainable WASH response to reduce mortality and morbidity and prevent disease to vulnerable, conflict or natural disaster affected communities of CD&WD.
- FSL: The project will aim at building livelihood opportunities, improving economic self-reliance, reducing food insecurity and vulnerability. The ongoing economic crisis is leading to the deterioration of livelihood opportunities for vulnerable HH in a WD&CD. The project will therefore aim at mitigating the economic issues related to the reduction of the HHs’ sources of income.   
- NFI/IES: By enhancing the access to NFIs and shelters for vulnerable people, TGH will improve living conditions of new returnees, IDPs and conflict/natural disaster affected population in WD&CD.
- Education: In response to the lack of educational infrastructures and services TGH will support schools with hard (rehabilitation, furniture etc.) and soft (trainings; enrolment campaign, school gardening, school clubs, etc.) components. The empowerment of educations actors to mainstream conflict sensitivity and peacebuilding into education services will be increased as well (WD&CD).
- RRR sector: TGH will align its project with the durable solutions approach developed in 4 villages namely Aboujaradil, Marari, Salaley, Sorey (around 34,115 individuals) in order to support the self-sustainability and self-resilience of IDPs, returnees and host communities, in coordination with DSWG&RRR strategy. The intervention will be in line with TGH current RRR project implemented in Aboujaradil, Magan, Beltebei, Garaia since 2017 and up to 2019, and will be integrated in the action plan of each villages as developed last 2 years.
TGH will coordinate with other stakeholders on the ground in order to ensure the quality and efficiency of the reponse.

project_name: Projet d’assistance nutritionnelle aux enfants agés de 6 à 23 mois et aux femmes enceintes et allaitantes vivant dans les ménages plus vulnérables pendant la période de soudure au Sahel
project_objective:
La malnutrition aiguë demeure un problème de santé publique majeur au Tchad avec une prévalence de malnutrition aigüe globale (MAG) estimée à 13,5%, très proche du seuil critique fixé par l’OMS et, avec une prévalence de la malnutrition aiguë sévère (MAS) estimée à 4,0%. On note de fortes disparités régionales avec douze (12) régions sur les vingt-trois (23) que compte le pays, ayant une prévalence de la MAG dépassant le seuil critique de 15% de MAG et ou 2% de MAS  fixé par l’OMS au dela des seuils d'urgence. La situation nutritionnelle etant en grande partie liée à l'insécurité alimentaire, la provision de suppléments nutritionnels spécialisés assoicés à la promotions des pratiques familiales essentielles en matière de santé et nutritiondurant la période de soudure est une réponse efficace pour prévenir la malnutrition chez les groupes vulnérables que sont les enfants de moin s de deux ans et les femmes enceintes et allaitantes. En outre le dépistage et la référence des cas de malnutrition intégrés à cette activité, permettra d'articuler le programme de prévention au programme de traitement de la mlanutrition aiguë. Les effets de cette intervention sur le statut nutritionnnel des bénéficaires et la diversification alimentaire seront mesurés à travers des enquêtes PDM qui seront réalisées tout le ong de la mise en oeuvre. 

Le PAM propose une projet dont le but est d'atténuer les effets de la période de soudure chez prés de 100000 enfants âgés de 6 à 23 mois et 50000 femmes enceintes et allaitantes vivant dans les régions de la bande sahélienne du Tchad affectées par l'insécurité alimentaire.

project_name: Human rights in humanitarian action – deployment of monitors to Luhansk and Donetsk regions
project_objective:
As per the Centrality of Protection in Humanitarian Action statement by the IASC Principals of 17 December 2013 protection in a humanitarian setting entails upholding human rights and respect for international humanitarian law (IHL). 

1  The project “Human rights in humanitarian action” seeks to increase the presence of the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine in the conflict affected areas, both in the areas controlled by armed groups and areas controlled by the Government of Ukraine, and to establish a stable and continuous monitoring mission with geographical coverage throughout the Donetsk and Luhansk regions, including the ability to cover the grey zones.

2  An important aspect is to ensure that analysis stemming out of the human rights monitoring is utilized by key humanitarian actors, and thus contribute to shape their humanitarian response to the protection needs of the conflict affected population. A human rights approach including gender analysis to the humanitarian response is vital where the population is suffering due to lack of protection and failure of accountability mechanisms. 

3  The project also aims at providing direct support to victims and their families, and strengthening the protection of the conflict affected population as the physical presence of human rights monitors in conflict affected areas may deter further human rights violations and serve in itself as a protection mechanism. By engaging directly with victims and witnesses of human rights violations, this will allow to refer victims to life saving humanitarian services, promote an environment that is conducive to the promotion and respect for human rights and contribute to protect the humanitarian space. HRMMU will also place a specific focus on accountability for the affected population, as its monitoring and reporting work will culminate in documentation of the information that would lay a foundation for future accountability through international mechanisms, and as an early collection of accounts that may bolster transitional justice and reconciliation efforts. In addition, HRMMU will help to create conditions for increased accountability for human rights violations.

project_name: WHO Emergency health response to consequences of the conflict in Ukraine – 2019
project_objective: The health needs remain high after five years of conflict in Ukraine. The protracted nature of the hostilities continues to affect the health status and well-being of the population and further burdens the most vulnerable populations such as the women, children, and elderly. Currently, 5.2 million people are directly affected in eastern Ukraine, with around 1.3 million people within 20-km of the “contact line” in need of life-saving and essential health services. The conflict has isolated rural government controlled areas (GCA) health facilities from major health centers located in urban areas in non-government controlled areas (NGCA) due to insecurity, increased distances, travel times and impeded access to referral hospitals and pharmacies, including restrictions caused by landmine and explosive remnants of war (ERW) contamination. National health care system has limited capacities to address the health care needs of vulnerable populations in the areas close to the contact line. Mobile health care services are not well developed, and most of health care has been provided in cities or rayon centres, leaving remoted places without adequate health care coverage. Access to health care services in GCA and NGCA is impeded due to: 1.	Conflict induced insecurity and limited access to health care facilities; 2.	Lack of access to primary, secondary and tertiary health care services particularly affecting vulnerable populations such as women, children and elderly facing limited access to preventative, curative and maternal health care; 3.	Lack of qualified medical staff and brain drain; 4.	Lack of training of medical staff (physicians and nurses). 5.	Lack of sustainable capacity building for health care workers; 6. Lack of access to standardized medical protocols; 7.	Lack of essential medicines, medical supplies, laboratories and equipment; 8.	Stretched health care financing resulting in increased out-of-pocket contributions in an economically disadvantaged context; 9.	Disrupted health information system. The population remains at high risk of acute, communicable, non-communicable and water-borne diseases as well as trauma and landmines. Advanced medical equipment such as endoscopic, laparoscopic and radio-logical and other diagnostic tools are insufficient which affects health outcomes. Humanitarian organizations face difficulties when collecting data to promote evidence-based decision-making and in providing medicines, medical supplies, medical equipment as well as training to health care workers. project_name: Support vulnerable households in Northeastern Syria to meet their emergency basic needs.
project_objective:
The IRC’s theory of change related to people meeting basic needs outcomes posits that the primary reason that vulnerable households employ negative coping strategies is in order to ensure adequate access to income or goods and services to meet their and their families’ survival needs. If people have sufficient purchasing power to buy basic necessities according to households’ diverse, self-identified needs, and local markets are functional and accessible, then people will be able to meet their basic needs and avoid negative coping strategies that may be damaging, unsafe, exploitative and/or undermine future income earning potential. Through  Multi-Purpose Cash Assistance (MPCA), households are empowered to address their unique and self-identified immediate basic needs that they deem to be essential to their survival.  

The IRC will continue to provide unconditional MPCA to the most vulnerable households in Northeast Syria, including recent returnees, newly displaced and protracted IDP households as well as to highly vulnerable host community members. The justification for targeting both host and IDP communities is to avoid creating tensions by only supporting one group, and out of a recognition that host communities in Northeast Syria are often equally, if not occasionally more, vulnerable than IDPs, ensuring a needs-based rather than status-based approach to assistance.

project_name: Provision of child protection services to the vulnerable children of South Sudan
project_objective:
Tdh has been implementing child protection activities in South Sudan since 2014. Tdh has demonstrated adaptability and creativity in its CP programming, implementing in some areas where there are no other CP actors. As one of the principal CP actors in South Sudan, Tdh is noted for its commitment to effective coordination and communication within the sector. Tdh is an active member of the Case Management Task Force in Juba. Tdh has the tools, guidelines and policies in place that ensure we are able to implement and monitor quality programming. Tdh has embraced a holistic approach to programming whereby integrated, multi-sectoral programs aim to improve outcomes for children and contribute to improving the broader child protection outcomes, including a focus on improving children’s sense of security and self-confidence through physical, social and educational program activities. Tdh’s integrated approach links CP interventions with its FSL, WASH and education interventions. 
CP/FSL integration is a priority for Tdh to improve the child wellbeing, as caregiver/household economic vulnerabilities can lead to direct and indirect negative protection coping strategies and CP risks. Improving household food security and access to livelihoods, alongside school feeding and school gardens, has previously proven to help children to stay in school and decrease school dropout due to emergency shocks and negative coping strategies to survival including early marriage, child labour and exploitation. 
Similarly, WASH/CP integration will be achieved by increasing sustainable use of protection sensitive WASH services such as water supply and latrines, alongside comprehensive hygiene promotion and ensuring appropriate, sustainable WASH in schools, with the aim of ultimately leading towards improved child protection outcomes: children are able to live and learn in a clean and safe environment. Child friendly areas and schools can be assisted to meet minimum standards of WASH facilities, separated by gender and have adequate hand washing facilities installed. Additionally, WASH promotion in communities can decrease rates of open defecation especially prevalent among children, by promoting community solutions for increased access to child friendly latrines, where small children do not use adult latrines for fear of injury. GBV risks can also be reduced by increasing safe access to WASH for female community members.

The Tdh CP approach will prioritize rigor in assessments and ensuring that programs are directly addressing the specific needs of the targeted beneficiaries. In addition to implementing direct child protection activities, including case management and psychosocial support for specific vulnerabilities among children, particularly UASC and CAAFAG, Tdh will also ensure mainstreaming activities, including training other actors on CP concepts. 
In Juba an inter-agency CP assessment on street children has been discussed but is still pending, and Tdh could consider spearheading this assessment, to explore the uncovered needs with respect to juvenile justice, street children and the worst forms of child labour. Tdh aims to reduce the protection vulnerabilities among children and youth in the IDP and host communities. For the year to come, Tdh sees great opportunities for this multi-sectoral, integrated approach to CP as a means to expand our geographic presence in South Sudan, to respond where priorities emerge.

project_name: Projet d’amélioration de l’accès des ménages vulnérables à des moyens d’existence sécurisés et durables
project_objective:
Depuis 2013, la crise politique en RCA a engendré la fuite massive d'une partie de sa population vers le Cameroun. Mi 2018, le HCR estimait le nombre de réfugiés centrafricains au Cameroun à presque 265 000, dont près de 70% dans la région de l'Est (UNHCR, août 2018). Dans cette région, et plus spécifiquement dans le département du Lom et Djerem, les communes de Garoua Boulaï et Bétaré Oya ont été tout particulièrement affectées par cet afflux. La pression démographique sur les villages de l’axe relient Garoua Boulaï à Ndokayo a vocation à durer : la situation politique en RCA demeure instable et on observe des arrivées régulières de nouveaux réfugiés sur la zone. 
Après une phase d’urgence de près de 5 ans marquée par des interventions humanitaires, il est aujourd’hui nécessaire d’établir un nexus entre aide humanitaire et appui au développement. Cette transition consiste à renforcer un environnement favorable à l'inclusion économique des réfugiés. L’objectif visé est non seulement de renforcer les capacités de résilience dans les milieux d’installation, mais également de parvenir à une réduction significative de la demande en assistance. Pour cela, il est nécessaire de développer et sécuriser les moyens d'existence des populations hôtes et réfugiées. 

Afin d’atteindre cet objectif, la réponse de SI combinera 3 axes: 1) un appui ponctuel en cash inconditionnel afin de soutenir les ménages bénéficiaires, le temps de développer 2) les productions agricoles et 3) la structuration et l’opérationnalisation des activités économiques de ces ménages pour leur permettre de dégager des revenus et ainsi couvrir durablement leurs besoins de base. Afin de contribuer à la stabilité des activités développées, SI favorisera l'autonomisation des bénéficiaires et de la cohésion sociale dans la zone d'intervention.

project_name: Increase access to protection and quality education opportunities for adolescents and children in TelAfar district

project_name: School meals for vulnerable children
project_objective: Crisis affected children attending school receive timely and adequate school meals that meet their food requirements.WFP will support the Ministry of Education, regional and local school authorities, schools and communities with technical assistance and provide school meals to encourage school attendance. In its inter actions with its partners it will advocate multi sector, multi actor education strategies that include school meals and nutrition.
