project_name: Emergency Food Security and Livelihoods Response Project in Somalia
project_objective: The proposed Emergency Food Security and Livelihood Response Program seeks to to help save lives, alleviate suffering through protection against hunger, malnutrition & destitution and maintain the dignity of those affected by conflict, floods and draught by providing an appropriate, timely and effective food security response. The project will improve access and availability of food, protect and restore livelihoods assets for a total of 15 000 food insecure households in areas hosting IDPs, returnees. Mercy Corps targets areas that were highly affected by the ongoing drought in Galmudug, Gedo, the Shabelles, Lower Juba and Baidoa that have experienced acute drought conditions as well as areas of displacements (IDP camps) in Baidoa, Kismayu, Mogadishu (Afgooye Corridor) and Galkacyo/Cadado/ Abudwak. The project will also target new regions with emerging needs including Wooqoyi Galbeed & Toghdeer in Somaliland. The objectives of the project will be achieved through provision of unconditional cash transfers to vulnerable households and those at particular risk of exclusion from accessing livelihoods. This will increase their access to food, alleviate hunger and strengthen purchasing power for essential household items and services. This activity will target at least 60% female headed household beneficiaries, women are economically vulnerable in Somalia. The project will also support Cash for Work activities to generate sufficient income for targeted vulnerable households. This activity targets the rehabilitation of communal assets/ basic services linkage facilities such as roads, irrigation canals and will target between 50 60% female participants taking into consideration gender roles. Moreover, the project will provide support to crop production through enabling access to inputs and training of farmers on good agricultural practices. In collaboration with FAO, the project will support livestock through training and strengthening the capacity of CAHWs and also ensuring availability of fodder.

project_name: Provision of lifesaving integrated nutrition and health essential services to children under 5 and PLW in Bari, Sool, Sanag, Lower Juba regions of Somalia.
project_objective:
Malnutrition is one of the most persistent humanitarian challenges in Somalia despite concerted efforts to address it. Acute malnutrition in children between 6-59 months is a direct outcome indicator of recent changes in nutritional status which could be attributed to changes in food security, WASH and health situations among others. The significant deterioration of malnutrition situation seen among the IDPs can be attributed to high morbidity (disease incidence e.g. AWD, measles …etc), low humanitarian support, poor child feeding and caring practices. Similarly, partners on the ground generally felt that food insecurity, limited health service availability, like poor EPI coverage, and increased morbidity, poor health seeking behaviour, and difficulty of accessing clean water supply are driving factors for the current situation.CARE is currently implementing integrated nutrition, health and wash services in parts of Bari, Sanaag, Sool and Lower Juba regions across three states (Puntland, Somaliland, Jubaland). We are targeting IDPs in Bosaso and Kismayo as well as rural pastoralists from livelihoods of Northern Inland Pastoral (Sool and Sanaag regions) that are considered by FSNAU as malnutrition hotspots requiring urgent lifesaving nutrition and health interventions. The most recent FSNAU post GU assessment found critical level of Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) of 15.5% in most of Sanag and Sool regions; 17.1% GAM in Bosaso IDPs and a serious nutrition situation with GAM of 14.4%   Kismayo IDP. Whats most worrying is the critical high level of SAM found in these regions that are ranging from 2-3.3%. 

High HH food insecurity is most likely to further exacerbate the malnutrition rate into 2019.  Childhood morbidity in Bari, Lower Juba, Sool and Sanaag is also high ad ranges between 14.3% to 29.1% and this predisposes children to malnutrition through a cycle of repeated episodes of illnesses leading to rapid weight loss. According to most recent IYCF KAP study conducted by CARE in 5 districts of Sanaag, and Sool regions in September 2018 found sub-optimal IYCF practices, including low rate of exclusive breastfeeding (69%), poor dietary diversity (4.6%) and generally low IYCF awareness. Only 56.8% of children continued to breastfed to one year and 69.8% of the children had the minimum meal frequency (2-3 meals a day). This predisposes children to reduced immunity to diseases and faltering growth. In addition, inappropriate and poor feeding practices, poor hygiene and unsafe water exacerbate malnutrition. The rate of continuation of breastfeeding up to 2 years is also very low at 28%. The extremely poor dietary diversity leads to micronutrient deficiencies.  Most families were unable to purchase and consume a balanced diet due to their low purchasing power. In addition, the rate of bottle feeding was 46.8% which is very high and carries an increased cost burden of buying formula milk or cow milk as a substitute to breastfeeding children under 6 months of age making these households prone to food shocks when food prices rise.

Therefore there is a huge need to scale up IYCF-E services to improve practices, prevent further deterioration and reduce child deaths. The drought has also had negative impacts on the consumption of milk in children, pregnant and lactating women (PLW) especially in pastoralist HH contributing to increased malnutrition. PLW are facing multiple challenges that hinders optimal child care practices.They are engaged in petty jobs to earn a living restricting exclusive breastfeeding and the same time trek for a long distance to fetch water. This is coupled with low income levels resulting in poor dietary diversification. This compromises IYCF, including exclusive breastfeeding for children less than 6 months. Malnutrition in mothers, especially those who are pregnant or breastfeeding, can set up a cycle of deprivation that increases the likelihood of low birth weight, child mortality, serious disease, poor classroom performance and low work productivity. This is because women and children are particularly vulnerable to malnutrition due to their physiological needs for both growth and they extra needs during pregnancy and lactation. In Somalia women and girls are often marginalised and excluded from employment and education opportunities, this makes women and girls very vulnerable to fall into the traps of poverty. Vulnerable women, especially those in female-headed households, frequently have limited access to nutrition information and the resources they need to improve food security, such as income, land, equipment, financial services and training. They also require 2.5% more dietary iron than men, and women need more protein than usual when pregnant and lactating. In many societies including Somalia men and boys are given priority when meals are served. This can contribute to under nutrition in women and girls and due to the apparent vulnerability of PLWs and children aged 6-59 months will be targeted.

HEALTH 
The fragility in Somalia in the past two and a half decades has resulted in the collapse of the health sector and a subsequent focus on emergency response interventions to recurrent crises characterized by high levels of population displacement, widespread vulnerability, insufficient and weak health service delivery. Somalis’ overall health status is poor due to multiple factors including fragmented service delivery; poor community participation, low behavior change; inadequate funding and human resource allocation; and inadequate health systems strengthening. The U5MR is 137 per 1,000 live births with one in seven Somali children dying before they reach their fifth birthday-unacceptably high rates despite them declining.  The leading causes of under-five mortality are acute respiratory illnesses such as pneumonia (24%), diarrhea (19%), neonatal disorders (17%), and measles (12%) . Immunization coverage rates remain low in Somalia, with an estimated under 50% coverage for measles and DPT3 in 2014. 

Somalia has one of the highest maternal mortality rates due to limited antenatal care (ANC) being only accessible to a quarter of women and only 1/3 of births attended by skilled medical personal.  Despite the implementation of the Essential Package of Health Services (EPHS), use of health services in Somalia remains very low. Over a Somali woman’s lifetime, she will face a 1-in-18 chance of dying from causes related to pregnancy or childbirth. The maternal mortality ratio (MMR) in Somalia is 732 per 100,000 live births; among the world’s highest. Somalia is ranked as the worst place in the world to be a mother in Save the Children’s 2016 State of the World’s Mothers report. Although the MMR is down from 1210 in 1990.  The average fertility rate is 6.6 children per woman with unmet need for birth spacing.  Access to maternal health services is low with 44 and 38% of births in Somaliland and Puntland being attended by skilled birth attendants.  Only 25% of women receive professional ANC with only 6% attending more than the recommended 4 visits. 

Across all sub-sectors, Sool and Sanaag regions continue to be highlighted as key gap regions by the Health Cluster as well as in CARE’s rapid assessment in February, 2018 in which there was poor access to basic health services, with low coverage of HFs and services, inadequate health partner coverage and limited MOH capacity  Morbidity in the regions is high, especially with respiratory illness and diarrheal diseases. The community indicates the greatest need is improved access to health services, especially basic MCH services, as the rural areas have few health posts with vast distances between HFs and overall limited service availability. A rapid needs assessment conducted in March 2018 by American Refugee Committee indicated that over 50% of all assessed HFs in Sool and Sanaag lacked basic infrastructure, essential supplies, and human resource incentives support .  Furthermore, none of the MCHs surveyed had readily available, equipped ambulances resulting in delayed access to comprehensive emergency obstetric care.

Therefore in light of all of  the increasing humanitarian situation forcasted in 2019 the situation calls for sustained humanitarian interventions in the form of integrated nutrition, wash, health services and in order to prevent further deterioration in the nutrition and health situation. CARE will implement an integrated package of health, nutrition and wash curative and preventative services targeting children aged 6-59 months and pregnant and lactating women. The intervention will provide access to basic health, wash and nutrition services through both mobile and fixed health facilities. Protection will be mainstreamed by considering separate waiting areas for males and females, providing PSEA sensitisation training to health care professional working in the health facilities, having a proportionate number of female and male health staff; employing health staff with skills and experiences working with children. We will also consult with the community at the design, response and monitoring stages of the projects to understand better how power dynamics in the community can affect the patient’s response and attitude towards seeking nutrition and health services. 

As we are targeting children under 5 and pregnant and lactating mothers for nutrition and health services, we will conduct community meeting sessions with caretakers of children under 5, fathers and PLW separately to gauge get an understanding of the nutritional status of girls and boys, women and men, including older people and those with chronic illness and how they seek help for nutrition problems. We will do this by: 
•	The targeting of the project’s intervention is informed by an analysis of how girls, boys, women and men are distinctly affected by under nutrition, malnutrition and micronutrient deficiency diseases
•	The design of nutrition services is determined through consultation of men and women, including pregnant and lactating adolescent girls, in order to ensure equitable access and
•	Special arrangements are in place to ensure that those with limited access to services, due to mobility issues, to risks of violence or to domestic and care work, receive assistance

project_name: Emergency WASH Response for Somaliland and Puntland
project_objective: Oxfam is currently working in Somaliland and Puntland implementing essential lifesaving activities for drought affected people in Sool and Sanag and cyclone affected people in Awdal region of Somaliland and Nugaal region of Puntland. In 2019, Oxfam will continue working in these areas and deliver life saving water supply, by constructing new systems, rehabilitating existing water sources and improving quality of water sources; sanitation support through constructing emergency latrines for high concentration IDP camps, and hygiene awareness campaigns including on menstrual hygiene management. Oxfam will target the most vulnerable communities and IDPs in Oxfam interventions areas. To effectively respond to severe water scarcity in Sool and Sanaag, Oxfam will move from water trucking to Cash for Water (CfW) modality. The lessons learnt from previous WaSH response has led to Oxfam successfully piloting Cash for Water in place of water trucking, which is often costly and complex to manage. Previous CfW pilots show that locally established Water Committees can bargain better with water vendors, negotiating lower prices than Oxfam ever could. On average a barrel of water costs between 3$ - 5$. When purchasing water in bulk-a full 8m3 water truck-the price per barrel drops by an average of 25% to 30%. Water vendors without the guarantee of selling a full truckload, refuse to deliver. Thus, to ensure uninterrupted and safe access to water for the most vulnerable households, the Water Committees in each target community will be provided with Telesom Zaad accounts (mobile money transfer modality) restricted to the purchase of water from pre-selected water trucking companies. Oxfam will facilitate drafting of MoUs between the two parties, and between the Committees and Oxfam. The Committees will be responsible to purchase and distribute the water and keep a register listing all recipients. They will be supported by Oxfam staff members and by Community Health Volunteers in providing water to the most marginalized beneficiaries, distribution and vendor engagement. Each family (6 members/HH) will receive the minimum daily requirement of 7,5l./person/day, with an entitlement of 40l. of water a day (or the weekly equivalent). To ensure adequate water storage facilities at community and household levels, Oxfam will provide 10m3 water storage tanks for temporary bulk water storage, and each targeted household will receive 2 jerry-cans. It is imperceptive to note that periodic random water quality tests will be held through out the project life cycle.

project_name: Increased life-saving and sustainable access to water, sanitation and hygiene for Displacement Affected Communities in Somalia targeting women, men, boys and girls
project_objective:
DRC proposes to undertake a life-saving and sustainable assistance to Disaster and Conflict Affected Communities (DACs) through provision of emergency and sustainable WASH interventions (water, sanitation and hygiene). Areas that are mostly affected by droughts, famine and floods will be targeted in the emergency interventions, some of the key areas to be targeted include the following Mogadishu, Baidoa, Baletweyne and mudug regions. proposed key activities to be implemented include water trucking through water voucher, construction of emergency latrines and other related WASH activities. DRC defines DACs as people who are internally displaced and are affected by drought and other factors  and returnees  seeking for reintegration. Therefore, DRC targets IDPs, returnees, refugees and host communities. DRC understands that the primary displacements in Somalia is as a result of natural disasters and mana-made conflict. However, secondary displacements are now a common reality due to either military offensive or forced evictions by government. These displacements are the key driver of humanitarian WASH needs in Somalia. IDPs are currently residing in urban and peri-urban informal crowded settlements, with insufficient access to WASH services that raise protection and health concerns. Therefore, DRC will ensure that, where IDPs settle they get immediate assistance of life-saving interventions. These will include water trucking where there is no safe water source, emergency latrine, sanitation ,  hygiene kits and rapid hygiene promotion. On the other hand, DRC targets Host Communities - to ensure peaceful coexistence between the local population and target groups and also because many of them are equally vulnerable and in need of humanitarian assistance. Returnees are also targeted with durable solutions in which case DRC will focus on governance and overall management of water and sanitation facilities. In this case, DRC will ensure there is a robust market system in place for continued service provision. For the case of water, DRC will encourage existing water source owners – both private and government, to extend water services to the settlements of DACs. For the case of sanitation, DRC will encourage a market-based approach – looking at creating demand for latrine construction and building capacity of the supply side to ensure enterprise-creation and therefore sustainable services beyond the project period



DRC has developed standard designs for water and sanitation facilities with detailed description scope of work. DRC also has a team of engineers and WASH staff across areas of operation. This provides a good basis for strong monitoring of project quality. The quality of program delivery will be monitored intermittently by the different staff frequently including the Area Managers of the respective areas, wash technical manager, National wash coordinator, Field Officers and dedicated M&E staff, the above mentioned team will develop master plan to guide the implementation, a pre-KAP survey will be initiated with the project to inform the current water, sanitation, and hygiene behaviors.  Prior to any implementation DRC will organize project familiarization meeting with all stakeholders, and bilaterally with project beneficiaries to discuss project objectives, implementation strategies, scope, DRC feedback and complaint system, beneficiary selection criteria, beneficiary entitlement and roles.
 Furthermore, DRC wash technical team will assess the needs technically with close consultation of local authority, community elders and concerned cluster, together will develop outstanding Designs and BOQ for the needs, which includes but not limited to construction/rehabilitation of strategic water sources, sanitation facilities and hygiene promotion activities then procurement process will start to get eligible contractor who filled the selection criteria  under continuous monitoring and supervision of dedicated wash team, after work completed as per technical designs/specification ,the village water committee will sign off on progress and completion of the project, witnessed (co-signed) by Village Chairman and local authority. 
Furthermore, DRC will organize two joint monitoring visits with key stakeholders including Federal government, Local Authority, OCHA, other cluster members and independent monitoring agency to assess the project progress and beneficiary satisfaction on the project activities. The joint team will be provided all project documents and telephone contacts for community members benefiting from the project (especially numbers of the most vulnerable), such as CHPs, water management committee members, vendors, contractors and authorities and those that did not benefit from the project. As well they will be provided all direct beneficiaries contact details to allow them independent monitoring and easier contact. In addition, DRC will facilitate any Independent third monitoring required by OCHA and WASH Cluster. 
In principle, all DRC staff are obliged to collect the telephone contact information of all beneficiaries as per DRC compliance policies, the same will be applied for this project. DRC to address the concerns of the beneficiaries has set up a comprehensive complain/feedback platform free of charge, where all beneficiaries can raise their concerns/complaints confidentially. 
The reporting arrangements will be done in accordance with grant agreement, additionally DRC is committed to update the 4W matrix on monthly basis. Any other information’s requested by the donor and cluster will be provided on timely manner. 
DRC will ensure that activities implemented with an approach of building back better (BBB), where the infrastructure rehabilitation or construction are done in such a manner that they have in inbuilt disaster risk reduction (DRR).

project_name: Prevention and Response to Rights violations in conflict affected regions, focusing on survivors of GBV and Unaccompanied/ Separated boys and girls in Banaadir, Lower Shebelle and Gedo Region.
project_objective: Based on the analysis of the conflict situation in Banaadir, Lower Shebelle, and Gedo region, NoFYL intends to scale up its protection programme to contribute towards enhancing protection, increasing safety and promoting dignity of conflict-affected women, men, girls and boys, in target regions. These areas are currently concerned by prolonged drought, displacement and voluntary return movements and, with the intensification of the military operations around AS control areas especially in Lower Shebelle and Gedo regions, it is expected that a high number of newly displaced people and/or newly accessible people will be imminently in need of critical assistance. The aim being protection against and prevention of GBV and child rights violations and effective protection service delivery in humanitarian crisis. This will also be ensured through building up community structures and protection capacity. This will improve the prevention of protection risks, response and access to protective services for IDPs and other civilians affected by conflict, violence, human rights violations or disaster.

project_name: Food Access and Livelihood Asset Protection in Somalia (Gedo , Awdal, Maroodijeex  and Bay regions) (FALAP)
project_objective:
Poor rains and extended drought compounded with internal conflict over multiple seasons have had a major impact on rural livelihoods and food security in Somalia, pushing the country to the brink of famine, just a few years after the crisis of 2011 that claimed the lives of over quarter of a million people. As the result, most pastoral and agro pastoral lost 70% of the livestock herd which are the sources of income and food for the households. The project addresses the crises facing more than 4.6 million vulnerable households in Somalia. 
The Action aims to prevent further depletion of assets, short term support, promotion of income generation activities and livestock related interventions to stem food insecurity and livelihoods to mitigate costlier interventions in the future. Th Action is therefore designed in line with the needs and priorities identified by  the food security cluster to prevent further deterioration of food security and livelihoods of  vulnerable households and thus  directly contributes to the HRP food security cluster objectives which are: 
Objective 1: To improve immediate access to food, priority activities include unconditional transfers (e.g. food assistance and cash), conditional transfers (e.g. cash-for-work for small-scale infrastructure repairs).Approximately 1.6 million people facing severe levels of food insecurity (IPC Phases 3, 4 and 5) will be supported under this objective.
Objective 2: To protect and restore livelihoods related to food and income sources. Priority activities include provision of: (i) seasonally appropriate agricultural inputs (e.g. certified quality seed, farm tools, training, land preparation and irrigation support); (ii) emergency livestock assistance (e.g. supportive treatment, vaccination, feed, fodder production); (iii) livelihood diversification (e.g. fishing, backyard poultry and vocational programmes); (v) improved post-harvest practices; and (vi) response to
Objective 3: To support resilience of vulnerable populations against shocks. This objective will contribute to protecting and conserving natural resources on whose lives and livelihoods depend, such as water, soil, land and forest resources.
VSF Germany  is proposing an integrated humanitarian response for food security and livelihoods intervention response to address immediate food access for households in IPC3&4 through unconditional cash transfer, protect and restore livelihoods through animal health services, fisheries input and conditional cash transfer(Cfw) as well as livelihood recovery; livestock herd restoring (restocking ) and capacity building through training of  CAHWs . The Action targets 1000hh in IPC 3&4(including IDPs) with cash transfer for immediate food access; 1720hh in IPC2 with livelihood support; Restocking(150hh)-for livelihood recovery; Animal health services(1500hh)-for livelihood protection; Fisheries input-50hh  and training-for capacity building(20CAHWS) and   with income opportunities through Cash for work(Cfw) -1200hh.The Action targets Maroodjeex and ,Awdal reigns(Somaliland) and Gedo and Bay regions( Southern Somalia)

project_name: Enhance the resilience and food security of vulnerable farmers in Jerusalem through land rehabilitation.
project_objective: To enhance the resilience of 125 vulnerable families (600 capita); including 167 female, 173 male, 260 children, 298 adult , 42 elderly and 81 refugees through improving the food security of vulnerable farmers through land rehabilitation 6 locations located  in Jerusalem governorate on area C . The proposed project addressed directly to the cluster strategic objective of the 2019 humanitarian response plan (part of 2108-2020 HRP).  Where “the resilience , food security and the productive capacity of vulnerable households are restored/enhanced livelihoods . The planned interventions are directly response to the need of improving the access for basic services by vulnerable Palestinians, which is in this project is food (rehabilitation of 500 dunums of lands at household level. The project was developed in a participatory approach at community levels (October 2017 and updated assessment April 2018 coordinated by the food security thematic group, and lastly during october 2018 by PARC staff), and coordination and consultation with key stakeholders at institutional level (working NGOs and related govemental ministries). The  targeted areas are characterized as a very remote areas with weak services As it is mention on the Strategic objectives, Palestinians are vulnerable to rights violations, especially in relation to their livelihood, with which they struggle due to the prolonged crisis of the OPT. One of the main concerns of the Palestinian population is the impact of protection threats and violations on livelihoods, due to the fact that these communities rely heavily on agriculture and livestock as their main source of income. The inability to access land due to lack of access and resources means that the infrastructure to facilitate the crop is deteriorated or non existent, thus causing many lands to be rehabilitated in order to be re cultivated

project_name: Humanitarian Support to Protect Education from Attacks in West Bank, including East Jerusalem- phase IV
project_objective: The proposed project is in line with the EIEWG education 2019 framework objectives 1 and 2 and the protection objective related to legal aid in West Bank. The project aims to provide protection of vulnerable children affected by conflict and other situations of violence, particularly those at risk of denied access to educational services and individual and mass forcible transfer in the West Bank. The project will target 69 most vulnerable Ministry of Education and Higher Education (MoEHE) schools supporting children access to a protective and enabling educational experience and will be four-fold: 1) provision of psycho-educational support through training of teachers on how to manage a classroom with children who have gone through stressful and traumatic events, how to better support under-achievers and training of counsellors to support students with chronic nightmares that severely affect their school functioning thought the NRC flagship ‘Better Learning Program’ (BLP); 2) provision of emergency school kits to support crisis-disaster risk reduction in tandem with capacity building; 3) delivery of legal information sessions through awareness raising of students, school staff and parents about legal rights and protection as well as response to incidents/violations through documentation, including response and referral mechanism to document interferences/impediments to the delivery of education in schools, and strengthen the legal response of the ‘Alert Mechanism’; and 4) advocacy pursuing enhanced protection from violations of the right to education.

project_name: Address basic health and rehabilitation needs of the most vulnerable persons with injuries, persons with disabilities, and elderly in emergency and post-emergency situations
project_objective:
The proposed action will provide basic life support to persons with injuries, persons with disabilities and elderly health, rehabilitation and psychological needs through combination of designed activities. 
The proposed action follows multidisciplinary and holistic approaches to better respond to most affected populations who suffer from lack of or/and difficulties to access to services.  The project will build collaboration with 5 local service providers and organizations through partnerships. It will cover the Gaza Strip and Area C of four governorates of West Bank. The project will support the deployment of outreach and center-based teams to assist the vulnerable beneficiaries through the development of admission and exclusion criteria. These criteria will be based on the socioeconomic conditions and through coordination with local referral bodies to enhance trauma pathways and improve networking among action’s stakeholders. The project will also work on building capacity of partners and other stakeholders.

project_name: Building Farmers' Resilience and Enhancing the Productivity of Agriculture Based Livelihoods for Vulnerable Populations in South Hebron
project_objective:
The intervention aims to support vulnerable agriculture-based livelihoods, mainlyin Area C,  to provide more sustainable access to food while working with farmers from these families to build their resilience, and coping mechanism and enhance the productivity of agricultural and herding assets for vulnerable communities in the south Hebron Governorate, namely; the governorate of Yatta. In parallel, the intervention aims to strengthen ability of acutely vulnerable Palestinian households, particularly female headed households, across fourteen targeted areas to cope with protracted threats and shocks. 
The intervention will achieve this through a multi- pronged approach to supporting the steadfastness, protection and resilience of vulnerable families livelihoods mainly through: (i) creation of project support committees to ensure transparency, accountability and engagement in the monitoring of the project and selection of beneficiaries. Particularly the PSC will report on violence incidents and advise for timely and effective implementation ensuring “Do no harm” principles. (ii) Contribute to restoring and enhancing the productive capacity of vulnerable and affected HH by protecting and promoting their livelihood and assets through rehabilitation of agricultural lands through cash transfer modalities including cash for work. (iii) rehabilitation and provision of basic assets, and increasing access to resources through rehabilitation of agricultural roads , rehabilitation of water storage  and livestock shelters. Moreover, the intervention will prioritize identification of and response to gender-based vulnerabilities in order to support the eroded coping capacities of female- headed households in particular.  
The range of interventions outlined in activities and outputs below reflect specific community needs and align with two HRP Country Strategic Objectives. Beyond expanding access to basic resources for which the occupying power and other authorities have failed to adequately assume responsibility (CSO2), the project emboldens highly vulnerable Palestinian communities to cope with shocks including demolitions carried out by Israeli forces and damages to land caused by settler violence, (CSO3). Targeted communities are located in a highly contested zone, where communities live between multiple settlements, settlers’ cultivated agriculture land, and Israeli-controlled nature reserves.  

Uncultivated land is a major attraction to settlers’ activities, which in many cases lead to confrontations with local communities over land and water resources. Developing and maintaining access to food-productive assets is of paramount importance to these communities. Availability of agriculture roads leading to farm lands means secure access to highly-needed food and water resources. Rehabilitation of farm lands and animal shelters provides communities with higher levels of resilience and allow them to withstand attacks by Israeli forces and settlers. The intervention further contributes the FSS cluster key objectives (FSSO2) & (FSSO3) through by improving access to, and the productive potential of various resources, and by improving productivity of farmers agricultural lands and water sources, rehabilitation of agricultural roads and rehabilitation of livestock sheds.

project_name: Integrated Protection Approach to address WASH and GBV Concerns of Vulnerable Groups in Wadi Al Salqa Area
project_objective:
The project aims at improving equitable, affordable and sustainable access to safe and sufficient WASH services during emergencies and shocks in accordance with dignity of the underserved and most vulnerable communities of Wadi Al Salqa in the Gaza Strip. The project targets the most vulnerable communities of Wadi Al Salqa Area with particular focus on hardship cases, female headed households, GBV survivors, and people with Disabilities. The objective of this action is consistent with the assigned objectives of the WASH Cluster 2019 HRP, objective 1: “Ensure equitable, affordable and sustainable access to safe and sufficient WASH services in accordance with dignity of the. unserved, underserved and most vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation in Gaza and the West Bank""; and objective 2: “Strengthen WASH preparedness and response capacity to the unserved, underserved and most vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation in Gaza and the West Bank, to reduce threats and to cope with emergencies and shocks”. The main activities include (1) installing renewable energy / solar systems for public desalination plants, (2) provide spare parts for public desalination plants, (3) maintenance of in-house WASH facilities (age, gender, and culturally sensitive WASH facilities (including toilets, kitchen and bathing facilities), (4) Maintenance/replacement of cesspits, (5) distribution of storage tanks for domestic and drinking water, (6) distribution of jerrycans, (7) Building the Emergency Planning and Response capacity of Wadi Al Salqa Municipality to be responsive for the flooding emergency situations, and (8) Hygiene promotion activities and distribution of sanitary supplies and hygiene materials

In addition, the project responses to detected GBV concerns in the conflict affected area of Wadi Al Salqa. The project targets WASH beneficiaries who showed GBV related concerns. This includes mainly the cases of GBV survivors who already had been identified with poor access to WASH services through the conducted assessment, besides other cases who will be supported under WASH component and show GBV concerns. This action is consistent with the assigned objectives of the Protection Cluster 2019 HRP, objective 2:” Protection response mechanisms are in place to prevent and mitigate the effects of the occupation and conflict related violence”. The main activities include (1) provide case management and referral services; (2) distribution of dignity kits; and (3) awareness raising on GBV. The intervention will include to study more in-depth the relation between GBV and poor access to equitable and adequate WASH services.

project_name: Emergency shelter support for the most vulnerable households in the Jordan Valley.
project_objective:
The aim of this project is to respond to emergency shelter needs of vulnerable households, mainly in Area C of the Jordan Valley, with provision of timely and adequate shelter and NFI solutions through a comprehensive integrated approach that supports building resilience, reinforcing protection, and supporting the steadfastness of the most poor and vulnerable households at risk of displacement or exposed to harsh weather and protection concerns. 

The intervention will addresses immediate needs, as well as the underlying conditions that give rise to those needs through a multi- pronged approach that includes; (i) Establishment of community based protection committees and provision of tailored capacity building to empower affected people to cope with sudden and protracted shocks and stresses, increase accountability, information dissemination and transparency specifically to report protection concerns, disseminate DRP practices with the inclusion of training on SPHERE standards and monitoring of intervention. (ii-a) provision of durable climate protection shelter materials and technical rehabilitation support and oversight to the most vulnerable households whom are exposed to harsh weather or protection concerns or at risk of displacement. (ii-b) Prioritized Shelter rehabilitation with full technical support and oversight for Persons with disabilities and widowed, separated or abandoned female headed households through MA’ANs local technical team. (iii)  Stockpiling and prepositioning of adequate shelter/NFIs stocks, and protective shelter material for HHs under risk of displacement and/ or at risk of exposure to natural or manmade hazards or settler violence and increase the capacity to respond to natural and manmade hazards in a timely, efficient and effective manner.

The intervention is built on MA’AN and ACTEDs Community Protection and emergency response approaches, & previous shelter rehabilitation experience in the area, placing emphasis on the themes of (1) Engagement at the community level with a focus on community ownership and responsiveness (2) Community Driven Resilience focusing on Protection mechanisms for vulnerable groups in communities.  To ensure effectiveness of intervention, targeted communities and neighborhoods have been coordinated with the shelter cluster, other partner organizations and actors working in the area to avoid overlap of assistance and ensure best reach in emergencies. MA'AN has prior experience and good understanding about the current legal situation for the construction in Area C and employs strategies in employing a low profile including: Rehabilitating structures from the inside of shacks and tents, Carrying out work at night, Staggering assistance over a prolonged period of time, coordinating with households and key communities members to stay updated with IOF activity in the area. Moreover, As the communities are subject to ongoing threats, and harassment, Project Management will also supervise the promotion and public announcement of the project among the inhabitants of the targeted communities to ensure an update of priority households in the database at the project start. Women in these communities will play an integral part in the selection of beneficiaries as part of the established CBPC , other members include village council heads and representatives, Mokhtar ( village head), and community members. Project Management unit will ensure that CBPCs and selected households are well informed about their rights, obligations and potential risks involved regarding housing, land and property issues and provide their consent to all proposed project activities.

The intervention contributes the Country Strategic Objective 2 “The basic needs of vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation are met through the provision of essential services, in accordance with the rights of protected persons under IHL.” For beneficiaries for whom a full upgrade is not possible, the action will provide emergency winterization and transitional support, this contributing to the Country Strategic Objective 3 “the ability of vulnerable Palestinians to cope with the protracted crisis, including environmental threats, is supported, while solutions to violations and other root causes of threats and shocks are pursued”.

The Intervention  design endorses all of the Shelter Cluster recommendations, in particular by providing a tailored combination of modalities to maximize impact on beneficiaries while fostering ownership and resilience through a demanding community based self implementation approach. Through its upgrade component, the action will contribute to the Shelter Cluster objective 1 “Support to displaced populations to mitigate immediate harm and ensure adequate and safe temporary shelter solutions.” Likewise, the transitional assistance / winterization component will contribute the Shelter cluster objective 2 “Support to vulnerable households exposed to harsh weather and protection concerns.”

project_name: Meeting the Protection Needs of Vulnerable Children Victims of Child Labour in the Gaza Strip
project_objective:
In a context- like Gaza's one- characterized by prolonged strain and economic isolation, vulnerable families have resorted to different negative coping mechanisms to deal with the high level of poverty and vulnerabilities. Child labour, withdrawal from schools, and engaging children in risky occupations were amongst the commonly used distress mechanisms to alleviate poverty (Overseas Development Institute, 2014; Tdh, 2018). Recently OCHA (Oct 2018), has identified providing mental health and psychosocial support to children who could resort to negative coping mechanism or could be the victims of harmful practices, including children drooping out of schools and children involved in child labour as a key humanitarian response. This project is a response to such needs. The project aims to eliminate child labour in the Gaza Strip, particularly in Gaza North and Khanyounis governorates through provision of child protection services, psychosocial services, educational reintegration, family support and increased community mobilization toward the issue of child Labour and dropout of schools. This project focuses on the right of the child to be protected from economic exploitation and from performing any work that is likely to be hazardous or to interfere with his or her education, or to be harmful to health or physical, mental, spiritual, moral or social development. The project will target 8584 beneficiaries, including 400 working and or dropped out of school children (300 boys and 100 girls, as child labour is more common among boys). The proposed activities will include responsive, remedial, and environment-building child protection activities. The responsive activities will include (1). Provision of psychological first aid to the identified cases of working and or dropped out of school children, with particular focus on children victims of worst forms of child labour, (2). Provision of child protection services to the identified cases of working and or dropped out of school children, including individual counseling sessions. 
Focusing on providing activities that aim to prevent further harm, remedial activities will include (1) provision of child protection case management, including provision of remedial classes, provision of individual and group counseling sessions, joint child-parent interaction activities, life skills, integration into schools and vocational training centers, referral to specialized mental health services. (2) Provision of economic support to 40 families of working children. Finally, environment- Building activities will include conducting training sessions to 8000 community members, all are caregivers, on the importance of eliminating child labour (4000 men and 4000 women), a total of 250 sessions will be conducted. The project team will provide services to the identified cases through the two child protection centers, in Beit Lahyia and Khanyounis. Under this Action, Tdh and its partner organizations will utilize the Child Protection Web-based Case Management System and the referral pathways that have been developed jointly by Tdh and UNICEF in 2017, in partnership with the Ministry of Social Development. A high level of coordination with relevant ministries and relevant clusters, including protection and education. Finally, Tdh will report its intervention to Protection cluster, Child Protection Working Group, and FSS.

project_name: Responding to the protection needs of the most vulnerable Palestine refugees in Gaza (GBV, child labour and Great March of Return)
project_objective:
Poverty, the consequences of past hostilities that continue to be felt, displacement, political instability, weak protection systems, sub-standard housing and overcrowding continue to increase vulnerabilities, especially for women, children and persons with disabilities. In addition, since March 2018, Gaza is facing an ongoing humanitarian crisis during where more than 21,000 have been injured - including 4,250 children (OCHA figures, 4 October 2018), posing serious concerns in terms of civilian protection and access to emergency health. 
Through its programmes and services, UNRWA will mitigate the impact of the erosion of coping mechanisms and increasing poverty, which heightens protection risks for the most vulnerable. Thematically, specific Agency efforts will focus on Gender Based Violence (GBV), child labour and the aftermaths of the 
 ongoing Great March' mass demonstrations.
Operationally, UNRWA will seek to strengthen inter-programme coordination and cooperation, referral systems, protection mainstreaming, and internal capacity. The training of front-line staff will continue, focusing on basic protection principles, referral systems and GBV (response, mitigation and prevention) in emergency situations. UNRWA will also raise awareness on the protracted and current humanitarian crisis in Gaza and its protection implications for Palestine refugees through inter-agency coordination and direct contact with external interlocutors. In particular, the Agency will take advantage of visits by foreign delegations to Gaza, providing up-to-date information on the humanitarian and protection environment and advocating for refugee rights.

project_name: Decreasing Premature Deaths from Chronic Diseases
project_objective:

project_name: Integrated CCCM and SNFI Response to vulnerable and conflict affected IDPs in Borno State
project_objective:
The proposed nine-month project aims to provide an integrated response to urgent needs faced by IDPs in Borno State through the provision of emergency CCCM, Shelter and NFI assistance in formal and informal camp settlements. In order to contribute to a comprehensive humanitarian response, ACTED proposes to build on its experience and current presence on the ground in priority areas, to provide CCCM assistance in Mafa and Dikwa IDP sites, through dedicated static CCCM Teams, in order to facilitate site improvements, strengthen partner coordination, and improve information sharing and management structures. To strengthen the rapid response capacity of the Shelter and NFI sector to address onsets of IDP influxes, ACTED proposes to establish a pipeline of emergency shelter and non-food item assistance kits, available to Shelter and NFI Sector Partners for distribution. 
In light of the volume of IDPs living in formal camps and informal settlements in Borno State, and the continuous increase in new arrivals, the CCCM set-up in the State is insufficient to meet the large-scale needs, with limited funding and too few active sector partners – ACTED is one of only two active INGO partners in the CCCM sector. As a result, living standards in camps do not meet SPHERE standards, and there is a lack of coordination between implementing partners at the camp level, resulting in unaddressed critical assistance gaps. To address this, the proposed project aims to support and strengthen existing CCCM activities in Dikwa and Mafa, set up by IOM, by establishing static CCCM Teams, in order to strengthen reception systems, camp coordination, information sharing, and camp management mechanisms to facilitate a comprehensive humanitarian response. CCCM Teams will work with existing camp management structures to strengthen coordination of intervention systems, and will promote sustainability by supporting camp committees to gain relevant skills and tools required for community-led intervention activities. The static CCCM Teams and associated assistance is expected to benefit a total of 27,626 beneficiaries in Dikwa, and 25,243 in Mafa.

Secondly, the project aims to establish a pipeline of Bama type emergency shelters, ESKs and NFIs in strategically located warehouses in Monguno, in order to facilitate rapid response time for SNFI Sector partners operating within these LGAs and the surrounding areas. Stockpiled NFIs and emergency shelters will be made available to sector partners for distribution in order to facilitate significant reduction in sector response time, and enabling immediate emergency response to new arrivals. Thus, the proposed activity will act in conjunction with the wider CCCM and SNFI Sector. The goods procured under this project would enable direct emergency shelter and NFI assistance to 10,000 households, projected to benefit 50,000 beneficiaries.

project_name: Providing safe, inclusive, equitable and quality education to vulnerable boys and girls in Sudan
project_objective: The action will provide safe, inclusive and equitable quality basic education to conflict affected and vulnerable boys and girls. It will reach beneficiaries comprising of girls, boys, teachers, and Parents-Teachers Association (PTA) members and community leaders. The project will strengthen community participation and ownership of children's education ensuring protection, resilience and improved learning outcomes. Save the Children (SC) will prioritize emotional and psycho-social protection, physical protection (Safe Schools), teaching and learning (Literacy Boost in Emergencies - LBiE) parents and community participation (Improving Learning Environments Together -ILET) and school leadership and management. To achieve this, SC will work with education community structures including PTAs, case workers, local leaders and relevant local authorities. Priority will be on bringing back to school out of school boys and girls who have not been attending school due to a variable amount of reasons. SC will work with relevant authorities and schools to raise awareness on the Safe Schools Declaration. The purpose of the program is to enhance the ability of the most deprived children of vulnerable groups to gain access to quality basic education to lead to socially and economically productive lives, and to strengthen their resilience and that of their communities. Subsequently, this, the action will contribute to creating better living conditions, enhancing social cohesion, and reducing the risk of these populations being pushed into negative coping mechanisms, which include forced displacement. The project is using the model Save the Children's integrated approach that links education to other sectors: WASH, Health Protection and Food Security &Livelihood.

EGYPT - World Food Programme
TURKEY - World Food Programme

Integrated Response to improve WASH and health conditions of conflict-affected populations along the contact line in Eastern Ukraine
project_objective:
The project intends to provide an integrated response to better alleviate critical health and WASH needs of populations affected by the conflict in Eastern Ukraine. Life-saving health assistance and essential WASH services will be provided on EECPs. Population’s access to quality healthcare will be improved through the following:
-	Decrease of associated costs (voucher for free access to drugs/medicines, voucher for transportation)
-	Improve quality of care by provision of essential medical supplies 
-	Develop health staff education/skills through supportive supervision, capacity building (including MHPSS) 
-	Improvement of WASH-in-Health conditions in HFs
Morbidity/hygiene risks linked to poor water supply systems will also be decreased through repairs/rehabilitation of water supply networks.

The project intends to multiply the effects of this combined WASH and Health intervention by increasing the geographical consistency between all its components and trying to link the different activities together in similar locations, based on the needs. All project sites will be in the 0-5km zone, where needs are critical, but actual referral pathways will be taken into consideration when selecting SHCs to implement the voucher programs, as patients go to SHCs located outside of the 0-5km zone for essential, emergency healthcare services.  

Lastly, the project seeks to both answer emergency needs (by supporting essential services at EECPs, primary healthcare package in health facilities and by restoring access to water supply) and look at middle/long term solutions to ensure communities and stakeholders have sufficient capacities to cope with the effects of the conflict (capacity building of health staff including when it comes to the health reform, MHPSS needs taken into consideration, WASH-in-Health, etc…). Though the proposed activities only cover 2019, their design will be constantly assessed during implementation to make sure they answer the needs adequately. Depending on the needs and the context development, PUI is willing to continue this approach in 2020, in line with the Ukraine HRP (with readjustment of the activities if necessary), in order to allow sufficient time to alleviate the consequences of the protracted conflict and allow communities to build their own resilience mechanisms.  
In NGCA, PUI will work with Donbass Development Center, a local NGO that has been partnering with PUI for more than 3 years. DDC has excellent knowledge of the difficulties in the targeted areas and solid capacities to implement the e-voucher program. Besides, this will facilitate the acceptation of the project by the de-facto authorities, who are reluctant to let INGOs operate directly.

project_name: Improved protection of children and women from displacement affected communities through community based protection and systems strengthening
project_objective:
The objective of the project is to enhance the protective environment for displacement affected communities esp. women and children through response and remedial action, as well as environment building. Special focus will be put on support for GBV and child rights violation survivors through case management and case referral using a survivor-centered approach. 6000 GBV survivors and 1000 children will benefit from case management and FTR. 2000 most vulnerable families, that were worst affected by unlawful eviction will receive cash support to reestablish their shelters, making sure this does not trigger an artificial inflation of 'self-evictions'.
To strengthen resilience, existing community structures will be strengthened through capacity building to strengthen community - based protection - 1200 representatives will be trained and follow up support to community protection activities will be provided. DRC will also conduct protection mainstreaming trainings for non-protection actors - NGO field staff, local authorities.  3000 boys and girls will benefit from Child Friendly Spaces which will be also an entry point to share information about other available protection-focused services. 
DRC will engage in advocacy for HLP rights and prevention of forced evictions and will facilitate discussions on title deeds and rental agreements between land owners, government and displaced communities.
Lastly, DRC will work with other PC partners on  set up and update of referral pathways and will lead the roll out of the Protection Monitoring System to support regular monitoring of protection risks and rights abuses for evidence based advocacy and adaptive response management.

project_name: Provision of life saving assistance to the conflict affected vulnerable people through comprehensive CMAM service and community based infant and young child nutrition in north east Nigeria
project_objective:
The project will be implemented in the north east Nigeria,  BAY state. Plan International Nigeria has a field office in Maiduguri, which will provide technical and administration support, and will be responsible for the implementation of the project. The project will focus on two main areas with its response i) Treatment and prevention of acute malnutrition through comprehnsive Community based Managament of Acute Malnutrition (CMAM) approach, Infant and Young Child Feeding in Emergency (IYCF-E) and Micro Nutrient Powder (MNP); ii) promoting behavioral changes with a focus on sanitation and hygiene. 
In the targted LGA, the health and nutrition support consist of primary health care, general hospital and Maternal and Child Health (MCH) clinics. The project will focus on providing life saving support for vunerable children and PLW by providing treatment  of uncomplicated Sever Acute Malnutrition (SAM)  in decenteralized Mobile outreach actvities Out Patient Therapeutic Program (OTP), treatment of complicated SAM in Stabilization center (SC), community Mobilization/out reach (community sensitation, active case finding and follow up of admited SAM cases). The house to house sensitization and screening of children will be conducted by Community Nutrition Volunteers (CNV), and referred to the nearest Mobile Outreach OTP community if needed. The beneficiaries identified by the CNVs in each communities will include children under five as well as pregnanat and lactating women. The CMAM officer/health workers within the Mobile Outreach OTP sites will support children identified as malnourished with RUTF and medecine as per the CMAM protocol. The CMAM officers will furthermore monitor the screening activities, including delivering  IYCF message as per Plan International's messaging, based on national established manuals. The treatment of uncomplicated SAM  for children under five will be done by CMAM officers at Mobile Outreach OTP sites, while for the complicated SAM children age under five will be supported SC officers (Nurse), SC coordinator ( Doctor) and Nutrition assistant.  On top of this in each SAM treatment sites the psycho social support counselling will be provided by trained CMAM/ SC officer, health workers and psycho social support officer. Furthermore this project will organize  basic CMAM and IYCF training for government health and nutrition wrokers and plan International nutrition staff to strength the capacity of governemt in treatment of acute malnutrition and  prevention of  under nutrition in the local government area. As part of the emergency nutrition support, therapeutic food support will be provided to caregivers of children with complicated SAM receiving treament at  SC at general hospital. 

For IYCF project plan international will established a Care Group using care group model, focusing on pregnant women, and mothers of children under two years (the ‘first 1,000 days’). Each care group will be composed of 12 volunteer Lead Mothers who will be trained on gender integrated Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF). The target group for IYCF activities will include lactating mothers with children less than 24 months and pregnant/non-pregnant women of reproductive age aimed to improve child caring and IYCF practices. 
The purpose of the project is Improved nutritional status of vulnerable groups, particularly acutely malnourished girls and boys under 5 years of age and pregnant and lactating women (PLW). The target group for this project is children under five year and pregnant and lactating women.

project_name: Food security and livelihoods opportunities for vulnerable households in Aleppo and Rural Damascus
project_objective:
Due to the past 8 years of conflict vulnerable households often struggle to make ends meet. As husbands are either involved in conflict activities, fled the country or have passed away, women are left at home caring for their children. This project is especially targeting food insecure women-headed households or generally vulnerable households from among returnee populations with a 3-months food assistance intervention in Aleppo and Rural Damascus. Beneficiaries are selected from among households that were identified through community-based protection interventions or through civil society organisations in both locations, and intend to support the households with much-needed assistance to overcome food insecurity.
DAI intends to assist 2,498 of IDPs/returnees and 4,427 of host communities with a 3-months food provision. Close operational coordination with SARC ensures that benefiting households remain eligible to be supported by SARC's provisions before or after this project has been implemented.

project_name: Basic Health, Nutrition, and Food Security and Livelihood Assistance to IDPs and Host Communities in North Darfur
project_objective:
The main purpose of this project is to improve the access and utilization of quality primary health services, and to improve the nutritional and FSL status of IDPs and the most vulnerable households in North Darfur. 
The health program mainly provides the minimum package of essential health services including consultation of communicable, reproductive health services (ANC, Deliveries, and referrals), EPI vaccination, and referrals to secondary units, minor trauma care, pharmacy services, and health education. The nutrition program mainly targets children six-to-59 months and pregnant and lactating women (PLWs). The program delivers preventive and curative services which include screening, referral, admission and treatment of SAM children in OTP; and MAM children and PLWs in TSFP. OTPs form the basis of the CMAM approach aimed at addressing and treating cases of severe malnutrition without complications. SAM patients will be rehabilitated using RUTF “Plumpy Nut” along with medical treatment. MAM patients will also receive supplemental feeding in the form of pre-mixed dry rations consisting of highly improved fortified Super Cereal Plus food. A key intervention in nutrition also include IYCF interventions, which includes food demonstration, promotion of vegetable gardening, and breastfeeding counseling to mothers. 
The FSL component is a preventive and complementary component to the nutrition intervention through increased access to nutrition food and household incomes. RI will support households to access quality animal health services, which improves the household dairy consumption to reduce malnutrition,  particularly among the most vulnerable groups ( <5 children and PLWs). It also improves the households’ resilience through alternative livelihood options during times of shocks.
