project_name: REGIONAL - United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East
Renforcement de la coordination (cluster national et coordination des ONG), du système rapide d’évaluation et de réponses pour la protection des populations affectées par le conflit
project_objective:
Ce projet vise à répondre en urgence aux risques de protection affectant les populations victimes du conflit dans la région de Mopti à travers des Évaluations Rapides de Protection (ERP), des référencements des problématiques identifiées et enfin à travers des interventions dédiées. Ce projet viendra renforcer les secteurs d’assistance actuels du RRM (Rapid Response Mechanism), en déployant, lors des alertes RRM, une équipe additionnelle dédiée en protection. L’objectif est à la fois de fournir des informations rapides aux acteurs de protection concernant la situation de crise évaluée, de faciliter le référencement auprès des acteurs en capacité de prise en charge, mais également d’analyser comment mieux protéger les communautés et au cas par cas, selon les priorités de pouvoir apporter des réponses adaptées, localisées et suffisamment flexibles pour répondre aux besoins spécifiques des communautés affectées par une crise.
Le projet fournira également des recommandations aux acteurs humanitaires non liés à la protection sur la manière d'apporter une assistance en accord avec les principes humanitaires et de protection, grâce à une analyse sensible au conflit et des informations critiques en vue d’actions éventuelles de plaidoyer. NRC propose également de continuer à soutenir le cluster protection en tant que co-facilitateur, avec une stratégie qui vise à améliorer la gestion de l'information, aussi bien que la coordination interne et externe. Ce sont 6.300 bénéficiaires ciblés par cette action.
Individus : 
- 300 individus : les bénéficiaires directs sont les 100 points focaux et membres des comités de veille et de crise du projet RRM, ainsi que les membres de 20 organisations (Agences des Nations Unies, ONGs internationales, ONGs locales, CBOs, Membres des clusters...) partenaires du projet, qui bénéficieront des formations en protection et de la remontée des données des rapports d’évaluations. 
- 6000 individus : Les bénéficiaires directs seront les femmes, filles, garçons et hommes ayant bénéficié d’activités de NRC, que ce soit de sensibilisations, référencements externes ou réponses de protection. Ils seront les bénéficiaires cibles des actions recommandées, jugées prioritaires dans les rapports d’évaluation et selon des critères de validation priorisant les besoins les plus vitaux et les plus urgents.

project_name: OHCHR strengthening protection and enhancing the integration of international human rights and humanitarian law in the humanitarian response to the Syria crisis
project_objective:
The OHCHR proposal aims at strengthening the protection of rights under IHL/IHRL across the humanitarian response to the Syria crisis, including by contributing to the 2019 HRP Strategic Objective to ensure human rights protection is central and upfront in the response to support analysis and mitigation of protection risks, promote accountability of duty bearers, ensure a victim-centered response and enhance protection mainstreaming by all sectors. This including by ensuring that the needs of particularly vulnerable groups, such as women and girls, youth, elderly people, people with disabilities are adequately addressed. 

A central element of the project is to support a consistent, effective and robust implementation of the SSG protection strategy adopted in 2017 and advise the humanitarian leadership at Syria and WOS level on advocacy firmly grounded on IHL and IHRL through direct substantive technical support in the three hubs.

project_name: Management and monitoring of emergency response, and enhancing safety and security
project_objective:
Management coordination is essential to enable UNRWA to deliver a timely and effective humanitarian assistance. The project consists of three main components: ‎management and monitoring of humanitarian response, safety and security, and repair and maintenance of UNRWA premises in the new accessible areas. One of ‎UNRWA’s main priorities in 2019 is to resume its service in the new accessible areas to better respond to the needs of Palestine Refugees and ensure capacity in place ‎to provide the service particularly in light of the spontaneous returns of IDPs and Refugees to camps and gathering areas. In order to ensure effective delivery of ‎service as well as support of operations in the logistic and administrative fields, deployment of local and international staff based in the target locations is a must. ‎

Considering the scale of the humanitarian needs, UNRWA will continue to require dedicated technical staff to manage, support and monitor multi-sectorial activities as ‎well as emergency operations in Syria. International dedicated experts (e.g. humanitarian officers, monitoring and evaluation specialists, donor relations officers) will ‎continue to be deployed at the central office to increase programme quality and neutrality. Adequate staffing is essential for UNRWA to implement its operations, ‎especially with regard to direct implementation, as well as to ensure an efficient coordination with all stakeholders and to enhance advocacy on behalf of Palestine ‎refugees.‎

UNRWA has made significant investments in the security and safety of its staff, assets and facilities security procedures. UNRWA requires funding to maintain as well ‎as strengthen the existing facilities.  The main investments in this regard will be, procurement of communication devices such as VHF radios, maintenance of vehicles, ‎purchase of personal protection equipment, and uniforms for security staff. UNRWA will also continue to conduct safety and security as well as fire safety trainings for ‎staff in Syria. Additionally, UNRWA will continue installing surveillance systems in the main office and do the necessary security repairs to ensure that UNRWA assets ‎and premises are safeguarded. These investments are mandatory as they constitute a prerequisite for UNRWA to continue operating in Syria, especially in high risk ‎areas, and delivering vital assistance to affected Palestine refugees 
Needs assessment carried out by UNRWA through 2018, particularly in new accessible areas, indicated that most of UNRWA facilities were either partially or fully ‎damaged. UNRWA developed area specific implementation plans based on the assessment mission reports.  UNRWA facilities have been extensively damaged in the ‎past 7 years due to the effects of the crisis, making it more difficult for Palestine refugees to receive humanitarian assistance, access basic services, and enjoy a ‎measure of protection. Repair and maintenance of UNRWA facilities in the newly accessible areas will remain critical in 2019 to contribute to the provision of ‎humanitarian assistance, protective environments and access to basic services for 445,000 affected Palestine refugees.‎
‎ ‎

project_name: Protection services and interventions for Palestine refugees in Syria
project_objective:
In 2019, UNRWA will continue to provide critical protection assistance to Palestine refugees, including to those who are displaced and those returning to their habitual residence in Syria. The Agency will seek to improve the protection of Palestine refugees in Syria through various interventions. Mainstreaming protection within UNRWA services will remain a priority. Corresponding to needs, protection trainings, including on disability inclusion, GBV, PSEA, addressing violence against children, will continue to be delivered to a wide range of staff and volunteers. In addition, UNRWA will continue to build the capacity of programmes to strengthen case management and referral processes for high-risk protection cases, including unaccompanied/separated Palestine refugee children, persons with disabilities, older persons and those affected by violence, GBV, abuse and neglect. Dedicated programmatic responses will be implemented through regular service-delivery and stand-alone initiatives to support the needs of vulnerable populations including to address psychosocial distress. Areas most affected by conflict-related violence as well as displaced and returning populations will be prioritized. Legal support services will continue to be offered to women experiencing GBV through assistance to obtain civil documentation and referrals to external partners. Mine risk awareness campaigns will continue throughout the country targeting students and other community members, with a specific focus on areas of spontaneous returns.  

Protection monitoring, reporting and advocacy will continue to be prioritised through the participation of UNRWA in global protection mechanisms and the international human rights system (IHRS), and through interaction with relevant stakeholders, including with the protection sector of the Humanitarian Country Team (HCT) in Syria. In parallel, UNRWA will focus specifically on monitoring the return of Palestine refugees displaced within and outside Syria.

project_name: Sustained and improved provision of WASH services and support to practice good hygiene in targeted IDP camps in Anbar
project_objective:
In response to the severe WASH gaps identified in the IDP camps in Anbar, IOM proposes to sustain and improve the provision of WASH services, construct and/or rehabilitate the most urgent WASH-related infrastructure while integrating activities aimed at improving hygiene practices in camps managed by, or with the camp management support of IOM.

The main objective of the present action is to continue to operate, improve, upgrade and sustain quality and standards of water and sanitation services, and provide an enabling environment for good hygiene practices in protracted displacement (in camps).

project_name: Mitigate identified protection risks, reduce vulnerabilities and enhance the protection of displaced persons, returnees and conflict affected host communities in Syria through integrated, community based protection activities to prevent and respond to rights violations.
project_objective:
The project aims to assist IDPs, returnees and crisis-affected communities by fostering an improved protection environment through the provision of community-based protection services. Protection interventions include 1) legal counselling and assistance 2) protection monitoring, referrals and information sharing on services 3)  social protection and support on PSS; GBV prevention and response programmes 4) child protection; 5) case management; 6) provision of in kind assistance covering basic needs and programmes of elderly and persons with disabilities; 7) non-formal education support for children at risk; 8) social protection through small-scale vocational skills training and socio-economic support specifically directed to the most vulnerable individuals, ; 9) campaigns and awareness  session including on mine risk education for communities targeting women, men, boys and girls and; 10) capacity building of first responders working in communities, volunteers, partners and government counterparts to provide better protection services. Legal aid interventions will facilitate access to civil/HLP documentation for IDPs and returnees and provide support in legal matters related to GBV, CP and other protection issues. Support to community initiatives will also be implemented engaging communities to address their own protection concerns. Intervention in the context of refugee returnees will focus on, legal aid, coordination with government counterparts and stakeholders, information management and return tracking systems and sub – district profiling to better inform return programming and interventions. In addition, the project will support coordinated protection interventions with UNHCR Syria continuing to lead Protection Sector.
Accountability to affected population in the project will be realized through participatory engagement of communities and outreach programmes conducted through community volunteers’ network. Over 2844 outreach volunteers and 112 CC were mobilized in 2018 and this project will build on this approach, to ensure a continuous link with communities, including to receive feedback on project programmes.

Through the project intervention approximately 3.35 million IDPs, returnees and crises affected individuals in host communities (70.5%, 15.5% and 14% respectively) will be reached in government and non-government controlled areas redressing their protection concerns. In addition 4,140 humanitarian workers and local authority staff will be trained and 624 communities assessed. 30% of the project beneficiaries are girls, 25% are boys, 26% are women, and 15% are men and 2% elderly women and 2% elderly men.

project_name: Contribute to the health and wellbeing of IDPs and other conflict-affected persons in Iraq, through integrated health  interventions
project_objective:
The purpose of the proposed intervention is to respond to continuing health needs in camp and non-camp locations, challenged with protection concerns. IMC will provide an integrated package of services spanning primary health including basic reproductive health, mental health and psychosocial support, community health and incorporating appropriate GBV prevention and response activities. Services provided under the proposed intervention will address specific needs of women, men, girls, and boys, including older persons and persons with disabilities. The proposed program will add on training and capacity-building support across sectors especially to existing government sectoral facilities to ensure appropriate and standardized service provision. All phases of the intervention will rely on close coordination and consultation with affected populations, as well as key stakeholders, including national and sub-national clusters, Directorates of Health, and relevant line ministries. The target beneficiaries will mainly be IDPs, host and returnee populations in areas of priority that continue to experience inadequate basic services, overwhelming existing resources and are yet to experience relatively stable security.
IMC continues to participate within the health cluster as well as conduct bilateral discussions with respective DOH’s to monitor ongoing interventions as part of its exit strategy. Eventual hand-over to IMC’s local counterparts is the exit strategy, thus the continuing dialogue with the relevant stakeholders. The project builds upon the capacities among the staff who have previously participated in IMC’s trainings and programming as well as those affiliated with government agencies such as the DoH.

project_name: Ensuring Safe Quality Education for Children affected by natural Disasters in Haiti
project_objective: The purpose of this project is to ensure safe quality education to 30, 000 children affected by natural disasters in Haiti including  4, 000 children deported from the Dominican Republic .  To reach this goal different interventions will be carried out during the implementation phase of this project:  establishment of Temporary Learning Spaces or light rehabilitation for the schools  that have been damaged or totally destroyed by the earthquake of October 6th, 2018  or by Hurricane Matthew  on October 5th,   2016; distribution of school kits  and school material, psycho-social support  support to children and teachers affected by those natural disasters, direct cash transfers to the most vulnerable families, capacity building of the Ministry of Education in Disaster Risk Reduction and Management.

project_name: Protection Response for most Vulnerable Groups in Iraq
project_objective:
Oxfam Protection response adapts the community-based Protection approach targeting IDPs, returnees and vulnerable host communities across, Anbar, Salah Al-din, Ninwa, Diyala and Kirkuk. Oxfam’s 2019 Protection project will aim to target up to 13,664 beneficiaries. The Programme will consist of Mobile Protection unit that will jointly work with Oxfam Country Humanitarian (CHT) team to conduct community-level Protection assessments. This will be in-line with the Protection Cluster Strategy 2/2 ‘to strengthen data collection and impact monitoring to enable strategic programming and evidence-based advocacy to address identified protection needs and risks, and to ensure the Protection of civilians.’ In addition, five Protection teams will be stationed in the areas of intervention to strengthen access to humanitarian assistance and public services through service mapping and dissemination of information during awareness raising activities. Oxfam will work with Local Partners and community-based Protection structures to strengthen their capacity to identify, mitigate and respond to Protection risks responding to their community and individual Protection needs. 
In order to inform referrals, individuals identified through this intervention who require specialised assistance will be referred to relevant organisations, emergency cash will be provided to facilitate access to specialised services.  
Under this response up to 300 staff of Local NGOs and government offices, in particular Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs (MoLSA) and governorate authorities will be targeted.

project_name: Protection and assistance to South Sudanese refugees
project_objective:
The response is aligned with the 2019-2020 Regional Refugee Response Plan (RRRP) for the South Sudan situation, with multi-sectoral objectives, namely: 
1.	Providing protection and basic services assistance for new arrivals;
2.	Addressing ongoing and unmet protection and basic services needs among the existing refugee caseload and improving service provision to meet sectoral standards; and
3.	Contributing towards building self-reliance among refugees and host communities and sustainability of interventions across the response.
The response seeks to ensure that international standards of protection are met, upheld and applied. This includes a focus on improving Sudan’s protection environment and support for expansion of civil, social and economic rights of South Sudanese refugees to maximize self-reliance. This also includes prevention of- and response to SGBV; child protection; access to registration and documentation; provision of humanitarian assistance, including scale-up of health, nutrition and WASH services; access to education; prevention of statelessness; and enhanced resilience for refugees and host communities. 

The strategy also aligns with the inter-agency response plan for an estimated 58,000 South Sudanese refugees in Khartoum’s ‘open areas’ settlements who continue to live in dire humanitarian conditions, despite renewed access for partners granted by the Government of Sudan in December 2017. Urgent needs persist across all sectors. The response aims to build on community resilience to advance protection-oriented solutions that address key vulnerabilities, bolster self-reliance and support the wellbeing and dignity of refugees who wish to remain in Khartoum.  

The 2019 response also emphasizes efforts for improved resilience, including: support for livelihoods and promotion of economic inclusion; integrating refugees into national and local systems of service provision; increased focus on sustainable energy and environment; and moving towards more durable infrastructure and sustainability of interventions. Inter-agency partners will work to strengthen community and individual endurance in order to mitigate the need for ongoing blanket assistance. This is especially relevant for Sudan, given the protracted situation that many South Sudanese refugees and their host communities are now facing in a context of chronic under funding.

project_name: Support education of returnees and IDPs
project_objective:
Integrate returnee children into the school system in order to prevent the continuation of NGO-managed parallel systems.  
Provision of schools grants to the returnees, IDPs and host community children of school-going age.

project_objective: The project will address humanitarian needs and improve the protection of basic rights of displacement affected populations and other vulnerable groups

project_name: Teacher capacity building and access to quality education opportunities for crisis-affected Rohingya and host community youth
project_objective: NRC will target 2150 youth ages 15-24 with lifelong learning opportunities, including life skills and vocational training. NRC will also provide Education Sector-wide capacity building opportunities to 150 Master Trainers and 3695 learning facilitators from across all implementing partners. Please note that only youth are contained in NRC's overall target beneficiary number, per Sector request.

project_name: Support to Strengthening Protection, Inclusion and Empowernment of Refugee and Host Communities, Women, Men, Girls and Boys
project_objective:
The project aims to address access to civil, identity and other documentation, basic services, and housing, land and property issues faced by both refugees and host communities through information dissemination, counselling and legal assistance. 
In order to prioritize safety and dignity of refugees over other considerations, ICLA will conduct protection risk assessments (Do no Harm), adopt conflict and context sensitive approach to dealing with beneficiaries, ensure informed beneficiary consent and acting on instructions of beneficiaries, securing confidentiality and data protection. In addition, ICLA will use additional protection technical expertise to supplement its interventions; coordinate with specialised protection actors to assist with conducting protection risk assessment of ICLA beneficiaries, carry out combined ICLA/protection campaign around protection issues; in collaboration with gender / child protection actors, conduct joint legal and protection research around a particular protection issue or risk in order to inform programming or recruit staff with expert protection skills in NRC. For example, although the Bangladesh legal framework might enshrine certain rights and entitlements that NRC would ideally like to pursue for refugees, NRC will not do so, if the process of accessing justice were assessed as likely to do harm to the claimants.

NRC’s Protection Policy, Gender Policy, Code of Conduct and Child Safeguarding Policy and guidance notes and tools including Core Competency Quality Assessment tools and the Protection Resource Pack all contribute to reinforcing and providing guidance on how to action the protection policy. NRC’s Code of Conduct holds staff, partners and associates (e.g. contractors) accountable, while projecting a common set of standards to the beneficiaries being served. PSEA prevention and response training is part of the induction for all staff. 

ICLA will support multi-sectoral, sustainable, and integrated programming with the NRC Camp Management (CM) and Education programmes and with other humanitarian actors, which will allow people to preserve or increase their resources and opportunities, thus making them more resilient, and more likely to find durable solutions. ICLA will conduct needs assessments, service mapping and where relevant, refer to other NRC core competencies or other partners providing specific services. 
NRC will actively and regularly participate in the PWG and its Sub-sectors and relevant Task-teams and collaborate with SMS and CwC on awareness raising, sensitisation and information dissemination activities to ensure that refugees have meaningful access to information and feedback mechanisms. In addition, ICLA will work to include training on basic CDR principles and skills in the package of training to be provided on/to Camp Community Governance structure, for NRC SMS sites at a minimum and, if possible, sector-wide. ICLA will conduct joint planning and harmonize interventions on developing CDR skills with PWG and Education through life-skills programme. Moreover, ICLA will ensure to prioritise advocacy activities aimed at removing barriers to access protection and assistance as jointly identified by all PWG.
NRC ICLA aspires to have a local partner to ensure sustainability of the programme once ICLA exit the country. Assessment is currently ongoing to identify possible partner(s). The partnership modality could be one of sub-granting or of no-cost cooperation based on skills-sharing. 
NRC ICLA will support SMS, CwC and PWG in the assessment, dissemination of information and implement referral pathways in order to ensure coordinated prevention and response to seasonal emergency.

project_name: Provision of air-transport service to support access for humanitarian organisations
project_objective: UNHAS will aim to maintain an air-transport service to all humanitarian organisations operating across Libya, with a focus on main hubs such as Tripoli, Misratah, Sebha and Benghazi, based on operational bottlenecks, humanitarian access and presence, in order to facilitate movements and projects implementation within the country.

project_name: Security Support to Humanitarian Response in 2019 for NE Nigeria
project_objective: This project is to provide reliable security coverage for the scaled up UN and partner presence and operations in newly accessible areas of North East Nigeria to the UN agencies working in this area. It is absolutely vital and relevant as majority of agencies have significantly expanded their existing programmes and staff presence in terms of capacity and geographical location. The existing capacity of UNDSS is not sufficient to meet the additional security burden this will place on the existing UNDSS organisation in NE Nigeria.

project_name: Emergency child protection prevention and response for the internally displaced persons and most vulnerable host communities in Lakes, Jonglei, Eastern and Central Equatoria States.
project_objective: The project will provide life-saving child protection prevention and response services through provision of Comprehensive case management services and referrals for children with critical protection concerns; Psychosocial Support (PSS) activities; Child protection awareness raisings or campaigns and Strengthening of community-based child protection mechanisms to prevent and respond to child protection concerns targeting 35,617 most vulnerable individuals (12,657 girls,10,783 boys, 6,777 women and 5,400 men). The project will be implemented Plan’s existing field locations of Eastern Equatoria (Kapoeta East and Torit); Lakes (Rumbek Centre, Wulu, Yirol East, Awerial); Central Equatoria (Lainya and Yei) and in Jonglei (Pibor). The project will target IDPs as well as host communities. Plan International will coordinate closely with the Child Protection Sub-Cluster and UNICEF in implementing this project. Further, in the different field locations, Plan will work closely with other child protection partners (Save the Children, DRDA, TDH, GREDO and Caritas Torit) to avoid overlapping and duplication of efforts. For instance, will work in different payams or bomas from other CP actors in the target locations. Plan will also coordinate with CP partners through referrals of CP cases.

project_name: Rapid Response Mechanisme - Reponse d'urgence en Multisectoral Assessments (MSA) et Biens Non Alimentaires (NFI) dans les régions de Tahoua et de Tillaberi
project_objective: Le projet consiste à garder une veille humanitaire dans les zones d'urgences, mener des évaluations multisectorielles, réaliser le ciblage et des distributions en NFI et en abris. Les interventions réalisées seront ensuite monitorées pour une amélioration de la qualité et une capitalisation des leçons apprises. La protection meanstrorming et la redevabilité sont intégrées dans le projet.

project_name: Renforcement de l'accès aux services de soins de santé de base pour les enfants et les femmes en situation de vulnérabilité de Diffa
project_objective:
Le projet vise à maintenir l'accès aux services de santé, en particulier pour les enfants et les femmes, par le biais de stratégies préventives et curatives fixes, mobiles, communautaiires et de sensibilisation. L’UNICEF appuiera la disponibilité de médicaments essentiels et de fournitures médicales par le biais des services d’achat, ainsi que la disponibilité et les performances du personnel de santé grâce au renforcement des capacités.

project_objective: Prevention and treatment of severe acute malnutrition in Niger

project_name: Emergency Health and Protection Response for Vulnerable, Crisis Affected Persons in Libya
project_objective:
The project aims to address the widening gap between the number of people with specific needs and the deteriorating health care services in Libya after years of conflict and economic crisis. In order to avoid a likely decline in the physical and mental health state of the most vulnerable people, HI’s intervention seeks to respond to the most urgent needs identified at individual level, while at the same time improving the quality of and access to local-level services. 
The project will target people with physical and functional limitations suffering from psychological distress due to injuries/ disabilities within the conflict affected population, IDP settings and areas of return. After years of conflict in Libya, it is expecting that conflict-affected and injured persons may have now developed severe physical and functional complications as consequences of a lack of physiotherapy at hospital level during the early stages of the recovery (often linked to the lack of trained medical staff on early rehabilitation but also due to the lack of access to rehabilitation services).

project_name: Improve Food Security to vulnerable people across Syria
project_objective:
Food insecurity is affecting an estimated 6.5 million Syrians and an additional 2.5 million people are at risk of food insecurity.  The number of negative Coping strategies adopted by the population are increasing – including reducing quality of food consumed and number of daily meals; more extreme coping strategies include taking sending children to work, early marriage of girls and transactional sex.  
The project adheres to the Sector Objective 1 by implementing two activities:  (1) Newly affected people who have immediate food needs for 1 week will receive a minimum of 2100 kcal per person per day of ready to eat food in the form of Ready to Eat Rations (target of 3,500 households); (2) The most food insecure IDPs and returnees will receive a minimum of 1,600 Kcal per person per day as a monthly food ration for the family (target of 3,500 households).  The amount of humanitarian food assistance provided will adhere to sector recommendations.  Activities will also be implemented aligned with the Sector Objective 2 aim to reduce host communities’ dependence on food aid.  Distribution of emergency seeds (vegetable, wheat and barley; cultivated in home-gardens, greenhouses or open fields), tools and water delivery inputs, together with technical capacity building will be implemented to improve the household food security status.   The distributed vegetable seeds can be cultivated in three growing seasons (late summer, winter and spring) to allow households to have access to year-round harvested vegetables.  The seed wheat will allow harvesting of wheat to produce flour; and the harvested seed barley to be used as a fodder resource for livestock farmers.  The activities implemented under this objective include:  (1) Distribution of agricultural inputs, such as seeds, fertiliser, pesticide and equipment, and related training (target of 3,500 households); (2) Support to asset building and asset protection (small livestock and animal feed distribution) including winterisation activities, and related training (target of 3,500 households); and (3) Emergency livestock treatment and training for veterinary services (including community animal health worker) (target 100 para-vets).  The Action adheres to the sector defined indicators.  
Protection issues will be addressed in all activities through identification of the risk – for example, relating to beneficiary selection, inclusion of women in selection processes, feedback mechanisms, distribution processes, potential tension between male and female beneficiaries, and diversion of aid.  Mitigation measures have been given for each identified risk – with particular focus on inclusion of women at all stages of the humanitarian action.   Gender receives particular attention with inclusion of women at the project design (needs analysis), design of the humanitarian assistance, participation and monitoring phases.

project_name: Rohingya  Crisis:  Enhancing  Food  Security,  Self  Reliance  and Livelihoods  in the camps and host community
project_objective: The proposed HELVETAS response seeks to address the above listed priority needs through four inter-linked project components. Project components  focus on the needs of Rohingya refugees in the camps, while the last phase of the project is being put in place to sustainably improve agriculture-based livelihoods and productivity in affected host communities.

project_name: Health requirements for UNICEF
project_objective: UNICEF is supporting the Ministry of Public Health in the field of maternal, new-born and child health through capacity building of health facilities staff and provision of supplies. This includes the provision of emergency maternal and neonatal care equipment, essential medicines and oral rehydration solution, as well as basic vaccines. In addition, UNICEF will provide technical assistance in adapting the policies, guidelines and protocols related to maternal and child health, prioritizing the integrated approach specially for the detection and treatment of childhood TB. UNICEF has an emergency preparedness plan as well as emergency stockpiles to allow for timely interventions following a disaster.

project_name: Nutrition requirements for UNICEF
project_objective: UNICEF will maintain high coverage of nutrition programmes aiming to reach at least 1.6 million children (6-59 months) with Vitamin A supplementation, and screening and referral for treatment for all under-five children identified with SAM and MAM with concurrent illnesses in all provinces. UNICEF plans to reduce the gap in micronutrient supplementation, as well as scale up community IYCF counselling services, with special attention on complementary feeding. UNICEF also targets 500,000 children (6-23 months) with multi-micronutrient powder supplements (MNP- Sprinkles) for home fortification of their complementary foods and 240,000 pregnant and lactating women with multi-micronutrient tablets (MNT). UNICEF will continue strengthening technical knowledge and skills of health care providers on IYCF counselling and treatment of acute malnutrition.

project_name: WASH requirements for UNICEF
project_objective: In collaboration with the Ministry of City Management, UNICEF will provide access to safe drinking water through gravity-fed water supply systems. The programmes focus on nationwide promotion of hygiene and sanitation to reduce diarrhoea, particularly in those communities with higher rates of SAM/MAM children underserved by functional piped water. They will provide WASH supplies, including emergency WASH kits and continue advocacy programmes.

project_name: Enhancing and improving the protection of population affected by the crisis through community-based and individually targeted protection interventions
project_objective:
The proposed interventions are centrally located within all of the 2019 protection GBV, and CP cluster objectives. For 2019, WVI will build on existing protection, child protection, GBV responses that are already in place Ezaz. Projects will directly target IDPs, host community, and returnees at a household, collective centres, informal settlements, collective centres and camps in A'zaz under the following objectives: 
Objective 1: The protection of population affected by the crisis is improved through community-based and individually targeted protection interventions and through advocacy with duty bearers. WVI provide quality and integrated protection services with a focus on community-based approaches, including awareness raising, psychosocial assistance, targeted support to persons with specific protection needs and other community initiatives through community centers and outreach mechanisms.

Under Objective 3: Survivors have access to quality specialized GBV services and measures are in place to prevent and reduce risks of GBV. The intervention focuses on providing GBV specialized services to survivors including case management and PSS support, provide activities empowering women and adolescent’s girls and GBV prevention and mitigation activities. 

Under Objective 4: Increased and more equitable access for boys and girls to quality child protection interventions in targeted locations in line with the Child Protection Minimum Standards in Humanitarian Action. The child protection teams will provide psychosocial and recreational support through structured and age appropriate group and individual activities, including recreational, skill building, and basic learning activities. These activities will also provide children with a protective and conducive environment to play, socialize, learn, express themselves and receive tailored support as they and their caregivers rebuild their lives. The child protection team will also provide psychosocial support services and activities that will reach children, youth and caregivers thereby strengthening the continuum of care for vulnerable children both inside and outside of the home. The parenting skills training will be based on a WVI parenting curriculum.

project_name: Emergency Basic Education Support project for IDPs and emergency affected populations in hard to reach areas in Togdheer, Nugaal, Bay and Bakool Regions
project_objective:
The project has been designed to analyze emergency dynamics, and forecast future events in order to support and implement agile mechanisms to respond to the evolving education needs in Somalia. Through this project WV will ensure that 10,800 (4580 female) emergencies and crisis affected children from primary schools are supported for various emergency education interventions. The overarching goal is to provide the boys and girls with access to quality education in emergencies interventions.  Firstly, leveraging on education supplies from GiK, WV has prepositioned education school supplies including furniture at strategic points/districts for ease of dispatch in the event of an emergency occurring. Further, in line with the WV ongoing global campaign on ending violence against children, the project will continue to undertake advocacy campaigns to increase girls’ enrolment and participation since they are adversely affected by school drop outs compared to their male counterparts.  Support with purchase for uniforms, and learning materials, particularly targeting IDP settlements, where school access is marginally lower will be enhanced. 
WV will also ensure teachers providing education in emergencies services have complied with the Code of Conduct and ensure minimal disruption of teaching and learning by providing emergency incentives. The teachers in collaboration with the respective ministries of education will ensure learning outcomes assessments are conducted periodically to ensure quality services are being offered to the children. This will be achieved through continuous in-service training of teachers during emergencies. Teachers will also be equipped with basic skills for identification of children who are being abused or violated and facilitated to offer psycho social first aid and referral of cases that need expert attention to health facilities.   In addition, to ensure that the school environment is safe and protective, the project will ensure child to child club activities are encourage to increase children’s ability to protect themselves e.g. child-led DRR activities. Accountability mechanisms will be rolled out by the project to ensure each school has a robust feedback and complaints mechanism. project_name: Securing of basic needs of people affected by conflict in Ukraine with in-kind aid, 2019-2020 (funded by German Federal Foreign Office)
project_objective:
Overall context of crises in Ukraine:
The human toll of the armed conflict in eastern Ukraine is critical, with 4.4 million people affected by the crisis, of whom 3.4 million require humanitarian assistance and protection. The shelling of urban areas and civilian infrastructure means that 60 per cent of 200,000 people living along the 457-kilometre ‘contact line’ in the Government-controlled area (GCA) are affected by shelling regularly, and almost 40 per cent are affected every day. There is just under a million individual crossings of the ‘contact line’ each month, which is rapidly becoming one of the most mine contaminated stretches of land in the world. Food insecurity has doubled since 2016, with 1.2 million people food insecure, and there are escalating cases of multi-drug resistant TB, HIV and even polio. HIV prevalence among pregnant women in conflict-affected oblasts is significantly higher than the national average. These impacts are aggravated by Ukraine’s extremely harsh winter, severe restrictions on humanitarian access and limited livelihood opportunities for those affected by the crisis. As hopes of a political solution have waned, so have people’s savings and their ability to cope. Four years into the crisis, millions of people, including 1.6 million internally displaced persons (IDPs), half of whom are the elderly, are being forced to make impossible choices between food, medicine, shelter, heating or their children’s education. The unique demographics of the crisis in Ukraine is that the elderly make up almost 30 per cent of people in need. Those who are most vulnerable are increasingly resorting to risky means to cope, including survival sex, trafficking and alcoholism. Today, the dire humanitarian crisis in eastern Ukraine is protracted and complex, whilst the response is severely underfunded and largely forgotten by the international community.
(HNO2019)

Basic needs of affected population are not secured

Core cause 1	
Lack of access of beneficiaries to needed goods

Access to necessary goods  is ensured. Beneficiaries have appropriate conditions to keep goods.

project_name: Distribution of Food Baskets in Northern Syria
project_objective:
The project was designed based on SADAD's needs assessment in 2018, in coordination with (OCHA).
This project will target 7 Sub-districts in the Idleb and Aleppo which are classified among the areas most of the need according to the Food Security Sector Report. The percentage of IDPs in the targeted areas reached 64.12% of the total population.
SADAD aims to improve the food security of people suffering from food insecurity and provide life-saving humanitarian assistance to the most vulnerable displaced families, focusing on areas with high needs.

The baskets will be transferred to the targeted areas in Aleppo and Idlib after identifying the spots of IDPs especially in open-lands, collective centers and informal settlement in the targeted locations on a daily basis according to the distribution plan and under the supervision of the Field Project Manager, the Monitoring and Evaluation team, the Logistics Team, and the Security and Safety team and then deliver it to the beneficiaries.
SADD's team will cooperate and coordinate with the local councils in accordance with the needs assessment conducted previously by preparing lists of beneficiaries that will be approved by the local councils according to predefined selection criteria:
- Displaced families (a key priority for choice, especially for newly displaced families)
- Family income must be less than $ 50 per month.
- The breadwinner is a woman whose husband is lost, injured or disabled.
- Poor families that have (elderly or young children under 15 years or widowed women).
The Monitoring and Evaluation team in collaboration with the field team will verify the names of the beneficiaries who will be provided with cards containing (the village code and beneficiary code) certified by the organization before starting the distribution.
Field Distribution Teams will begin the distribution process according to the beneficiary name lists and under the supervision of the distribution supervisors within a pre-defined comprehensive distribution plan for the targeted villages.

Ce projet de protection des enfants affectés par le conflit au Mali contribuera aux efforts de construction d’un environnement protecteur de l’enfant au Mali a travers les actions de prévention des violations des droits des enfants et par l’appui a la démobilisation, prise en charge et la réinsertion communautaire des enfants sortis des groupes armés.

Ce projet tiendra compte de la dimension du genre en accordant une attention particulière aux besoins spécifiques des garçons et des filles, tels que des sections et des locaux séparés pour les filles et les garçons dans les centres de transit et d’orientation, des kits spécifiques pour les filles tenant compte de leurs besoins en matière d’hygiène et des activités de groupe de discussion mixtes et séparées pour permettre aux garçons et aux filles de s’exprimer librement et donner les perceptions qu’ils trouvent les uns contre les autres. Toutes les activités de sensibilisation et de la mobilisation communautaire cibleront les hommes et les femmes. 2 staffs des urgences de L'UNICEF incluant le spécialiste MRM et celui de la protection de l’enfant en urgence/CPiE assureront le suivi de la mise en œuvre des activités du projet. Ils veilleront à ce que tous les partenaires de mise en œuvre prennent en compte le genre dans toutes les activités. 
Les groupes spécifiques et vulnérables notamment les handicaps et personnes a mobilité réduite ainsi que les viellards seront pris en compte dans les activités. Les membres de la communauté composés des groupes d’hommes, femmes, enfants et jeunes garcons et filles seront impliqués dans les évaluations a mi-parcours et finales des activités. Un mécanisme de gestion de plainte sera mis en place pour recueillir les opinions des communautés sur le déroulement des activités du projet et pemettront d’ajuster en consequence l’intervention.

project_name: Emergency nutrition for children under 5 years, PLW for target districts affected by drought induced food insecurity
project_objective:
The number of malnourished CU5 and PLW is expected to continue increasing due mainly to El Nino induced drought and macro-economic challenges that hinder access to balanced diets. This is compounded by inadequate knowledge among mothers and caregivers of appropriate and healthy diets, especially in the first 1,000 days of life and poor IYCF practices. In addition, 21.2% of children have Vit A deficiency while 62% of women of child bearing age are iron. These aspects necessitate the need for supplementary feeding and micronutrient supplementation. Furthermore, there are capacity gaps within MOHCC staff and community health workers to deliver high impact nutrition services to community members, which necessitate the need for training and mentorship on IYCF-E, IMAM and provision of job aides. There are also reporting and coordination gaps which leads to duplication, wastage of resources, slow responses to needy people

To address these needs, the project interventions will include strengthening active screening to ensure early identification of malnourished children and referral through community health workers and family led MUAC screening, complemented by increasing availability and access to therapeutic (RUTF) and complementary foods. Facilitate micro-nutrient supplementation to children 6-59 months and pregnant and lactating women; he project will facilitate distribution of micronutrient supplements for children, pregnant and lactating mothers (MNPs, VAS, Iron and Folate Supplements). In addition, strengthen Care Groups and PD Hearth implementation to rehabilitate underweight children, enhancing sustainable nutrition practices through home visits and counselling sessions by VHWs/Care Group Lead mothers and continued promotion of preparation of nutrition dense foods through Positive Deviance Hearth model. Strengthen capacity of MOHCC staff and Community Health workers on IYCF-E through capacity building trainings, mentorship and provision of job aides. Reporting and quality will be enhanced through supporting monthly review and reporting meetings.

Objective from July 2019 to April 2020:

project_name: Wash assistance for displaced families and vulnerable children and adolescents in schools in the North East and South of Syria.
project_objective: The main objective of the proposed project is to protect the health of vulnerable and war affected people the south and north east of Syria by providing WASH assistance to vulnerable IDPs, returnees, host communities and school aged children in areas with high rates of displacement and large-scale destruction. The consequences of the conflict have been particularly severe and have converted many parts of the governorates into hard-to-reach areas, where people suffer from extreme needs, due to the enormous destruction, the lack of public services and the inability to access local markets. To support displaced families and also focus on war affected children, the project will contribute to increase their access to sufficient quantities of portable water for people’s and student’s daily consumption, to ensure their access to safe and dignified sanitation facilities, disseminate hygiene knowledge and create a clean environment. Therefore, the intervention will include the provision of water through water trucking and the rehabilitation of water and sewage network, the rehabilitation of existing WASH-facilities in schools, hygiene awareness trainings for girls and boys in schools and garbage collection. Those measures will serve to cover the daily water consumption, improve sanitation habits and reduce the risk of waterborne and other diseases.

project_name: Emergency and resilience–oriented shelter assistance to IDPs, returnees and affected population
project_objective:
UNHCR is a lead agency coordinating the shelter responses and implementing shelter programme from inside Syria, as well as from Gaziantep (Turkey).  UNHCR shelter project is designed to ensure the affected populations and returnees shelter needs are met and to continue the support of IDPs and returnees returning to their houses. 
Particular specific and vulnerable groups including female-headed households, youth, and persons with disabilities, elderly persons at risk and large-size families will be particularly considered within the response. 

The shelter program will further distinguish between shelter needs of short-term and long-term solutions. Therefore, in 2019, the shelter assistance will continue to provide an emergency response through life-saving, life-sustaining quick impact solutions, such as rehabilitation of collective shelters, upgrading of private collective structures, distribution and installation of shelter kits and tents along with provision of technical assistance. Equally, the shelter program will enhance sustainable, recovery-oriented shelter solutions through support to IDPs returning and returnees to their original homes, contribute to rehabilitation of buildings in newly accessible areas, and support urbanization projects in various stages of completion. UNHCR’ shelter response will also contribute to public infrastructure rehabilitation to ensure sustainable community development. The shelter program will be aligned with the Syrian Humanitarian Response Plan as well as the Shelter Sector Strategy and coordinated with the different stakeholders and partners such as MoLAE and national/international NGOs.

UNHCR’s shelter programme aims to address shelter needs of 26,000 vulnerable households/130,500 individuals through basic house repairs and to improve the shelter conditions of 20,000 households/110,000 individuals by providing 20,000 emergency shelters kits.  As well as providing emergency shelter to 100,000 individual /20,000 households through tents distribution, camp construction, collective shelter and unfinished buildings, to provide safe and proper access to shelter for affected population in returnee areas.  UNHCR will support the returnee communities by removing 250,000 cubic meter of debris that will support 500,000 individuals/100,000 households and install 21,000 solar street light column with device in 30 neighbourhoods to support 750,000 individuals /150,000 returnee families and host community. To ensure our program will be implemented with adequate project management and technical skills 225 engineers from local government will be trained over the course of the project.

Objective 1:   Provide life-saving and life-sustaining shelter 
Objective 2:   Contribute towards the resilience and cohesion of communities and households by improving housing and related community/public infrastructure

The project is in line with objective 3 of the health chapter of Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP). It is also in line with strategic objective 1 of the same document.

Vulnerable groups including migrants, returnees, displaced families and poor host communities will remain the direct beneficiaries of the project as it will detect, respond to and contain outbreaks at an early stage.

project_name: Increase access to safe and sustainable water for conflict affected population in Idleb and Aleppo
project_objective:
Leveraging our organization's existing presence in the targeted areas, excellent contextual understanding and over three years operational experience delivering WASH program activities in northern Syria, the proposed action will directly support implementation of the 2019 Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) through addressing the critical WASH needs of IDP and host communities, and establishing community-based mechanisms to safeguard ongoing water provision through cost recovery. We planned programme of activities under the WASH sector will increase and safeguard access to safe and adequate water for approximately 126,071 conflict-affected people. Areas have been selected based on People in Need (PIN) and Severity of Need as presented in the draft Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) for 2019, in addition to our understanding of targeted systems, well-established operations and high levels of acceptance in targeted areas. 

Targeted water stations are in urgent need of essential rehabilitation and support to maintain operations, essential for safe water provision to highly vulnerable populations in areas with high severity of need. The proposed action will deliver an evidence-based program of assistance to targeted water units to immediately increase access to safe water, while also safeguarding WASH service provision beyond the implementation period through working in coordination with Local Councils and water units to establish cost recovery mechanisms. 

Targeted water systems arebelow: 

Andan water station (Haritan sub-district, Aleppo) and Mseibin water station (Ariha sub-district, Idleb). Fully funded by the Turkey Humanitarian Fund (THF) from 01 January - 06 February 2019, reaching 31,239 direct beneficiaries, inclusive of approximately 10,121 IDPs in addition to a host population of 21,118 people.
Al Mastumeh water station, Ariha, Idleb: Total 99,157 beneficiaries, of which 16,408 IDP  and 82,749 host (funding not secured)
Haritan water station, Haritan sub-district, Aleppo:  Total 12,756 beneficiaries, of which 2,000 IDP and 10,756 host (funding not secured)
Bsarton water station, Daret Azza sub-district, Aleppo: Total 7,098 beneficiaries of which 4,538 IDP and 2,380 host (funding not secured)
Jandairis water station, Jandaris sub-district, Aleppo: Total 7,060 beneficiaries, the majority of whom are returnees with an estimated 405 IDP (funding not secured)

Planned activities will build on our WASH expertise gained over three years, specifically Al Mastumah water station from December 2015 through April 2018.  As referenced in the needs assessment below, in April 2018 (when our last project supporting the Al Mastumah water station finished) the number of Waterborne Disease (WBD) cases in our area of operation was only 1 - as reported by EWARN. In August 2018, four months after our assistance to the station ceased, this number raised to 221 cases. By October 2018, an additional 134 cases were reported. These numbers emphasize the urgent, proven need for improved water treatment in the area. From 2015 through 2018, we developed excellent working relationships with the Idleb Water Directorate in addition to a highly nuanced technical understanding of the Al Mastumah water system, which will directly benefit planned activities proposed for 2019. 

More recently, we have expanded a successful model of station support to increase access to safe water for catchment populations of Andan and Mseibin water stations in Haritan and Ariha sub-districts respectively. This has included successfully establishing Cost Recovery Mechanisms to safeguard access to affordable, safe water after grant completion. Building on this experience, we will work with the four new stations targeted during 2019 to also establish Cost Recovery Mechanisms which are informed by and responsive to the needs of conflict affected populations in the station catchment areas.

project_name: Learning for a Brighter Tomorrow: Quality Formal and Informal Education for Children and Youth in Northern Syria
project_objective:
From 01 January through 31 December 2019 and in partnership with Lead Partner INGO, we will continue our currently running EuropeAid-funded Education programme under which we currently supports four schools in the Ariha sub-district of Idleb governorate, assisting 1,515 students, 97 teachers/school staff (including 4 psychosocial (PSS) facilitators) over the course of this grant. 

We are proposing to support an additional six schools for a total of ten schools under a formal education component of this programme in addition to 16 Self Learning Program (SLP) temporary learning spaces in four camps under a non-formal education component, expanding it educational activities into the HNO 2019’s highly prioritized geographic areas of Saraqab and Darkosh sub-districts of Ariha, Idleb (in addition to the current coverage of Ariha sub-district); Madiq Castle in Hama and Afrin, Jandairis, Haritan and Zarbah in rural Aleppo. 

Structured around our holistic model for education during times of crisis and recovery, the proposed program has three primary objectives: (1) to improve academic teaching and learning; (2) to promote student wellbeing and protection; and (3) to strengthen educational access and resources. Comprising both formal and non-formal education components, the program will reach a total of 5920 children (3163 males, 2757 females) — of which 35 percent are adolescents and youth — as well as 291 teachers / school staff (166  males and 125 females) and 640 caretakers (256 males  and 384 females). 

Under the formal education component - via the ten schools - we aim to reach a total of 4000 children (2196 males, 1804 females) as well as 209 teachers (119 males and 90 female) and 400 caretakers (150 males and 250 females), noting that all students who receive formal education under this project will also have access to the non-formal education component. Under the non-formal education component - 16 Self-Learning Program (SLP) temporary learning spaces in 4 camps, we aim to prepare 1920 out-of-school children (967 male, 953 female) for integration into formal primary schools after one year of study, including 16 teachers (8 males and 8 females).  Note: expansion on both components’ activities can be found under the Implementation of Activities section of this proposal.

Academic teaching and learning is coupled with program components focused on student safety and wellbeing. School personnel receive training in child protection and psychosocial care, and all students participate in weekly, age-appropriate PSS sessions led by dedicated facilitators. These activities aim to promote positive social-emotional development among children, and include a youth Life Skills curriculum for older students. Further, each school has a Protection Facilitator who is responsible for monitoring protection mainstreaming measures, such as a case management and referral system for students requiring external support.  School personnel are also trained on emergency preparedness and response, and develop plans to deal with threats like attacks on or near schools. 

In light of economic barriers that require some students to work rather than attend school, the proposed intervention also includes a supplemental livelihoods pilot component. This pilot will target the most vulnerable children and families who rely on child labor as an economic coping mechanism by offering conditional cash-vouchers or food baskets to offset the financial losses incurred when transitioning children from work to school.

project_name: Cellule d'urgence nationale en appui à la réponse cholera médicalisée dans les  départements à risque
project_objective:
Plusieurs rencontres  ont eu lieu avec l’OMS/OPS, l’UNICEF et les coordonnateurs des maladies infectieuses  afin de préciser les préoccupations des différents acteurs relatives aux capacités limitées des Directions sanitaires départementales pour contenir les flambées cholériques.  La difficulté  pour les DDS de gérer adéquatement les réponses institutionnelles (ressources humaines insuffisantes notamment) dans un contexte de désengagement de plusieurs partenaires est ressortie comme prioritaire 

Le présent projet propose une intervention en appui aux quatre (4) Directions sanitaires départementales où le risque de flambées est toujours existant et d’autre part, appuyer les autorités sanitaires des autres départements en cas de flambées majeurs. 

L’intervention  s’articule autour de l’amélioration de deux déterminants majeurs concernant le choléra soit : 
- Capacités accrues de gestion des flambées du choléra par les autorités sanitaires dans 4 départements d’Haïti.  
- Accès renforcés des services de prise en charge de qualité en cas de flambées, dans les différents départements ciblés d’Haïti 
Elle cible 4100 bénéficiaires directs soit 342 cas/mois selon l’incidence de 2017-2018 (1,927 femmes, 2,173 hommes / 47 % de femmes et 53% d’hommes) avec prise en charge médicale ainsi que  les familles et voisins qui vivent dans l’entourage des bénéficiaires (10 familles) 209,100 bénéficiaires indirects (98,277 femmes, 110,823 hommes) qui eux bénéficieront en parallèle de la prise en charge au niveau communautaire réalisée par les équipes EMIRA et WASH supportées par d’autres partenaires. Les bénéficiaires directes se répartissent majoritairement sur les 4 départements du pays de l’Ouest, de l’Artibonite et du Nord-Ouest où il y a des foyers persistants du vibrio cholera.  

Approche et méthodologie

Une Cellule d’urgence constituée de points focaux départementaux soit 3 pour les 4 départements à haut risque de flambées, accompagnée d’un superviseur Wash aura comme mandat d’une part, le renforcement des DDS dans leur capacité à gérer des flambées et d’autre part de renforcer les services de prise en charge de qualité en cas de flambée en coordination avec les DDS et les CMI, les EMIRA et les acteurs WASH. En cas de flambée majeure dans les départements non ciblé, la cellule d’urgence pourra appuyer les DDS et les CMI desdits départements dans la mise en place de pools d’urgence afin de faciliter la réponse médicalisée en cas de flambée.

Dans les 4 départements ciblés, la cellule d’urgence renforcera la capacité des DDS à gérer les flambées selon le protocole de contingence du MSPP  (coordination des acteurs et dimensionnement), et appuiera les services de prise en charge par le déploiement de pools d’urgence composés de personnels soignants et d'hygiénistes qui ont été formés, conformément à la Stratégie du MSPP qui est de renforcer la réponse médicalisée actuellement trop faible dans les différents hôpitaux et centres de santé du pays. Ces pools d’urgence sont donc déjà disponibles pour intervenir en renfort au personnel des structures de santé, et si la situation l'exige, contribuer à l'ouverture de structures temporaires. Cela permet, lors des flambées, d'améliorer considérablement l'accès et la prise en charge  des patientes et patients. Un pré-positionnement de matériel, en accord avec les CMI et si possible avec la Direction de la Protection Civile (DPC), doit être envisagé dans lesdits  départements où il existe toujours des flambées pour les zones éloignées
Les pools d’urgences seront déployés en moins de 48 heures en coordination avec les autorités sanitaires lors des flambées et en cas d’insuffisance de prestataires réguliers dans les structures des  départements précités. Leur déploiement devra être coordonné avec celui des EMIRA et les acteurs en WASH  qui ont le mandat de sensibiliser et de travailler avec les communautés sur les mesures de prévention et d’hygiène, et référencement vers les CTDA. .

project_name: Strengthening the trauma system in Gaza
project_objective:
Since the mass demonstrations began, the cumulative number of people killed and injured by the response of Israeli forces to the mass demonstrations, keeps growing on a weekly basis. This takes place within the context of an already under-resourced and collapsing health system, suddenly exposed to an overwhelming number of trauma patients suffering from tear gas exposure, gunshot wounds and explosions. Yet, the Gaza trauma system is based on a “scoop and run” pre-hospital policy, the tertiary hospitals are overloaded and there is very limited post-operative and rehabilitation capacity. Furthermore, the trauma services in Gaza have been supported by multiple players deploying international and national emergency medical teams in an ad-hoc and fragmented way. 

In response, the World Health Organization (WHO) aims to support the Ministry of Health by continuing to strengthen the Trauma System at its weakest points. 

In addition to the work already being developed, WHO will work in partnership with the MoH to address priority gaps in the trauma pathway:
1 – Establish an EMT Coordination Cell (EMT-CC) within the MoH. This coordination cell will ensure that all deployed EMTs meet a minimum standard and are coordinated and directed to the appropriate health facilities. The EMT-CC will play a fundamental role in the emergency response to the current crisis.
2 – Ensure a procurement and supply process for trauma equipment and emergency consumables 
3 – Develop information tools that better capture and demonstrate the actual caseload and system constrains.
4 – Coordinate the implementation and development of a unified limb reconstruction unit in Gaza

project_name: Appui à la prise en charge médico-nutritionnelle des enfants de moins de 5 ans, des femmes enceintes et femmes allaitantes dans les districts de Ngouri, Isseirom et Liwa (Région du Lac).
project_objective:
ALIMA et son partenaire Alerte Santé auront pour objectif de contribuer à la réduction de la mortalité des enfants de moins de 5 ans dans les districts de Ngouri, Isseirom et de Liwa à travers l'amélioration des statuts sanitaires et nutritionnels de 31 061 enfants de moins de 5 ans et femmes enceintes et allaitantes(8 177 hommes et 22 344 femmes)  à travers les activités de prise en charge, de sensibilisation à la malnutrition aigüe sévère et le renforcement des capacités de 52 professionnels de santé dans les zones d’intervention dont 15 hommes et 37 femmes.  
Des campagnes de dépistages de masse couplés au formation PB mères seront intégrés dans le projet afin d’assurer une prise en charge précoce et préventive. 
A Ngouri et Isseirom, 30 centres de santé seront appuyés pour la prise en charge médico-nutritionnelle des moins de 5 ans. Les activités curatives et préventives de la stratégie 1000 jours débutées en 2017, seront poursuivies dans les 6 centres de santé initialement ciblés.
A Liwa, L'action vise à contribuer à la réduction de la morbidité et de la mortalité chez les populations déplacées et autochtones difficilement accessible du district sanitaire à travers la mise en place des cliniques mobiles dans les sites déplacés et la prise en charge médico-nutritionnelle des enfants de moins de 5 ans souffrant de MAS. lLes Sites de déplacés ciblés sont situés au dela de 10-15km d'un centre de santé afin d'améliorer l'accès aux soins des populations déplacés. Les besoins dans le domaine de santé nutrition restent importants dans certains sites de déplacés du district sanitaire de Liwa et 2 centres de santé (Goum et Kaiga Kindjiria),  qui ne reçoivent pas d'appui des acteurs humanitaires et 8 sites des déplacés. Les autorités sanitaires (MCD et délégué régionale) ont demandé officiellement à ALIMA/AS d'appuyer le centre de santé de Goum et Kaiga Kindjria dans lesquels se trouve une population importante des déplacés et autochtones vulnérables. L'UNT sera également appuyé pour la mise en place d'un service de soins intensif pour la prise en charge des cas MAS compliqués et pédiatriques.
Tel que l'énonce la Charte ALIMA ""le patient d'abord"", le bénéficiaire est au centre de tout dispositif d'intervention de l'organisation. L'ONG médicale entend donc exécuter son mandat de manière responsable en tenant en compte des spécificités ou non des populations qu'elle assiste et vis-à-vis desquelles elle sera redevable tout au long du cycle de projet. 
Les populations affectées sont considérées comme des ""partenaires"" et intégrées dans la programmation humanitaire, notamment dans l'identification des besoins, la conceptualisation, la mise en œuvre de la réponse, le suivi et l'évaluation de fin de cycle. 
-	Organiser 2 enquêtes de satisfactions des bénéficiaires 
-	Incorporer systématiquement la notion de redevabilité dans sa programmation ; 
-	Assurer la transparence à travers le partage d'informations avec la population affectée ; 
-	Mettre en place un mécanisme de collecte et gestion des plaintes.

project_objective:
The project of ""Comprehensive Protection Response through provision of psychosocial, mental health, case management and transitional shelter assistance for Female Headed of households (neglected women, wives of mental health patients, addicts and women with cancer), GBV survivor’s victim of violence in the Gaza strip"" aims to contribute to mitigate the impact of conflict on the psychosocial, mental health and wellbeing of affected women, men, boys and girls in the Gaza Strip. The main outcomes of the project are: 1) provision of GBV & mental health services for women affected by conflict in Gaza. 2) build the capacities and awareness of duty bearers (a) Men and Women in the community and family of neglected women (b) community leaders and service providers through raising their awareness on GBV, and Women legal rights. The outputs are: 1.1) Mental health services provided for GBV survivors. 1.2) Case management for GBV including transitional sheltering and economic empowerment. 2.1) Improved the copying mechanisms and resilience for the families of targeted women in the Gaza strip. 2.2) The capacities of service providers build on Hawa elzahra and case management.
 Aisha will work to achieve these outcomes through various activities starting from coordination with main stakeholder to outreach the affected women, and networking with partner CBOs receive GBV survivors to host the project activities. Then, providing structured psycho-therapy and specialized mental health, integrated security, and empowerment training activities for Female Headed of households (neglected women, wives of mental health patients, addicts), GBV survivor’s victim of violence, and detect the severely affected person in need for advanced psychological, mental health service to Aisha mobile clinics. 
On other hand, Aisha and the protection cluster partner will apply the principle of do no harm in all activities especially during the period of providing transitional shelter assistance for six months where it will provide these services as transitional phase until the targeted women will be able to manage their own issues which will be through the case management services that provided to them. As well as, AISHA and the protection cluster partner will adopt the inclusion in this project through targeting different groups of women, harmonize the sessions for targets groups and WWDs.
Moreover, AISHA will apply the previously developed manual Hawwa Zahra(attached), developed according to IASC guidelines, that was revised and mainstreamed among the protection cluster and it sub- working group member. In addition, in 2017 Aisha established Aisha community center for mental health, substance abuse, and GBV that was license from the Ministry of Interior and the Ministry of Health. With UNFPA support Aisha developed the protocol of Aisha community center including 5 parts, management of common mental health disorders, case management for GBV, Case management for substance abuse, and 32 of related NGOs and INGOs and ministries staff trained on this protocol for 20 days. The clinic starts working officially in February 2018 with full time staff (psychiatrist, 2 psychologists, nurse, and others) where during this project, cases in need for specialized mental health services, medication and case management will be referred internally to Aisha Community Center. Also, AISHA has already a referral mechanism in which all referrals and needed information are followed up and traced. It is worth mentioning that AISHA is already a part of the SOPs' manual managed by UNICEF and includes all referral pathways.
It is worth mention that AISHA with the protection cluster partner designed the project in partner with the community through conducting focus groups and data base and will engage them in the whole project cycle through conducting regular follow up for the project implementation, complaint system, field visits, interviews and focus groups, in order to assess the needs of the beneficiaries.

management activities, and transitional shelter assistance by provision of rental fees to most vulnerable families in close coordination with shelter cluster

project_name: Child Protection Prevention and Response Services for Boys and Girls Affected by Conflict in Iraq
project_objective:
Boys and girls in post -conflict Iraq are affected by severe psychological distress, risk of arrest and detention due to perceived affiliation to extremist groups, denial of access to birth registration and civil documentation, social threats and stigma against boys and girls born of rape by extremist group. At the same time, sextual violence and exploitation, child marriage, child labour and children joining armed forces due to economic reasons are observed in post conflict Iraq. 

This project aims to intervene on child protection issues and risk outlined above by providing child protection prevention and response services such as community based, structured psychosocial support activities, case management, legal assistance and support to obtain civil documentation, legal representation and release and reintegration for children in detention, family tracing and reunification of separated and unaccompanied children including children of foreign nationalities, advocacy with key government ministries to find solution for barriers affecting to provide service for critical child protection issues. This project targets boys and girls in IDPs (in camp and out of camp), returnees and host communities who have been most affected by conflict.

project_name: Strengthening Gender Based Violence (GBV) Prevention and Multi-sectoral Response Services for Survivors of GBV and Conflict-affected Women and Children in Iraq.
project_objective:
Women and girls have been disproportionately impacted by the Gender Based Violence (GBV) during the conflict in Iraq. Pervasive GBV abuses, including systematic and targeted rape, abductions, sexual slavery, mutilation, executions, torture and forced marriage have been documented as a deliberate tactic by the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant (ISIL). In displacement settings as well as areas of return, threats and risks of GBV against women and girls persist, particularly sexual violence, intimate partner violence, family violence, sexual exploitation, harassment and early and forced marriage. Many women and girls may struggle with fears for their personal safety, as possible targets of violence. Cases of sexual violence being used by some militias and armed actors as a reprisal for actual or perceived ties with ISIL have been documented by human rights watch groups. Even before the conflict, GBV was widespread in Iraq and fears of harassment and stigmatization, including honour killing, remain major barriers to seeking services and justice for GBV survivors. Exposure to such violence and chronic stressors may often inflict on survivors’ psychosocial well-being and mental health.
The objectives of the proposed project are GBV prevention at community level and multi-sectoral support services for women and children affected by violence and conflict. The project will support the delivery of an integrated package of risk mitigation and prevention of GBV activities, at the community level, and specialized services to survivors in the areas with severe needs. The aim of community-based GBV prevention interventions is to provide immediate support to women and children at risk, mitigate risks of GBV, and shift social norms that underpin GBV by promoting gender equality and behavioural change and working with community-based structures. The project will also strengthen service provision with a strong focus on improving care for child survivors and the most complex cases and the quality of specialized services such as case management and PSS. Complementing the specialized services and PSS, recreational activities supported by the project will help women and children cope with the psychological aftermath of conflict and violence and strengthen their resilience skills, with a strong focus on adolescent girl-focused interventions to empower girls and increase girls’ access to services.
To ensure that quality case management services are available to survivors in some of the worst conflict-affected areas of Iraq, the project will also address capacity strengthening of the critical sectors (PSS, health, legal, security) to provide quality services to survivors of GBV, and will increase access to support and services through women and girls’ centers and targeted GBV legal assistance. This project targets women, girls and boys in IDPs (in and out of camp), returnees and host communities.

project_name: Protecting Vulnerable Iraqi Children from Harsh Winter Elements
