project_name: Urban area-based early recovery and livelihood program for restoration of community services in Daraa, Deir-Ezzor, Homs, Rural Damascus and Aleppo
project_objective:
Rationale:
8 years of conflict in Syria has not only led to destruction and reduced functionality of infrastructure, but also affected socio-economic patterns, and diminished Syria’s population’s ability to sustain living standards, to benefit from decent and gainful livelihood opportunities and to access essential services. Consequently, protraction of this situation has led to a further strain on social cohesion and community security, stressing the Social Capital of Syrian communities.
Needs assessments through various sources indicate that currently more than 8.6 million Syrians are in acute need of Early Recovery and Livelihood support.
Based on the humanitarian needs analysis done by the ERL sector, needs have been categorized under the three interrelated components: infrastructure and basic services; livelihood and community security.
Through the area-based approach, UN-Habitat aims to provide sustainable housing, restoration of essential infrastructure and access to services to displaced-, host- and returnee- populations in selected neighborhoods in Daraa, Deir-Ezzor, Homs, Rural Damascus and Aleppo. In practice, the approach consists in rehabilitation and reinforcement of repairable buildings and infrastructure, restoration of basic services and promotion of livelihood activities in damage-affected neighborhoods, selected through ‘Neighborhood Action Plans”, developed through the municipality-led MTOS (Municipal Technical Office Support) program. The holistic notion to serve entire conflict-affected, vulnerable communities through a comprehensive package of housing, essential infrastructure and related services, as well as early recovery and livelihood under the objective to revive neighborhoods, is a t the core of this project.

Objectives:
This area-based livelihood project, derived from experience gained in previous pilot projects and evaluation of similar interventions, aims to: 
•	Restore essential infrastructure and services, promote the rehabilitation of living space, key factors in reviving affected neighborhoods and contributing to improve stability in areas,
•	Provide productive assets in addition to shops rehabilitation in neighborhoods, to contribute in reviving local economies and to support residents and returnees to rebuild their life,
•	Enhance security in communities through provision of street lighting, 
•	Involve the community members and main stakeholders in identifying community-based needs, planning of suitable response options and implementation of activities, thus to promote neighborhood ownership
•	Enhance municipalities capacity to assess, plan and implement adequate programs to respond to communities’ most urgent needs, thus to reinforce local coping capacity.

Project components:
The project targets 250,000 vulnerable returnees, IDPs and Host families in Daraa, Deir-Ezzor, Homs, Rural Damascus and Aleppo. Planned and implemented through neighbourhood action plans developed through MTOS (Municipal Technical Office Support) programs, its main components comprise
•	Procurement and installation of solar street lighting systems,
•	Public – space-, sidewalks- and road- rehabilitation, implemented to the best possible extent through local workforce, especially unemployed youth; also, to make places available to promote social cohesion between  IDPs/refugees/ returnees and host communities.
•	Rehabilitation of market areas and shops, including support for productive assets and employment of local workforce, 

•	Capacitating municipal staff to improve service delivery at the municipality- and neighbourhood- level through training workshops and provision of technical equipment to support the technical services, improve the data collection, analysis, planning and monitoring. 
All activities will be carried out in consideration of environmental- and aspects of protection of cultural heritage

project_name: Improve living conditions for returnees and host residents in Daraa, Deir-Ezzor, Homs, Rural Damascus and Aleppo through an urban area-based approach to improve infrastructure and basic services
project_objective:
Rationale:
Based on WASH assessments, estimated 15.6 million people in Syria require WASH assistance, 6.2 million of whom are considered in acute need, in particular displaced people in camps or informal settlements, host communities and returnees. Already prior the crisis, only 65 per cent of the population had access to 42 built-up sewage treatment plants; this number has significantly decreased due to the fact that. many of these facilities are no longer operational due to damage, non-availability of critical supplies, and inefficient management, altogether leading to significant community health risks. Garbage collection services are primarily provided by municipalities/local authorities in most parts of the country and usually provide a basic level of service. However, due to the lack of comprehensive disposal strategies and operational challenges, additional efforts are needed in specific rural and urban communities to strengthen and upgrade the quality and regularity of solid waste management. 

Objectives:
Based on above, UN-HABITAT is proposing an area-based approach aimed to assist communities in selected areas / neighborhoods through rehabilitation of essential infrastructure and basic services, prioritized on the basis of needs and vulnerabilities. Overall, the project aims to ensure 
•	Sufficient provision of safe water, 
•	Increased water quality assurance, through support to water system-rehabilitation, operation and maintenance, in addition to 
•	Rehabilitation of the sewage systems, including distribution - discharge networks and repair of waste water treatment plants. 
The project plans to reach 2,558,250 beneficiaries (direct and indirect) in five governorates (Aleppo 1,6 M beneficiaries, Homs 630,000 beneficiaries, Deir-ez-Zor 152,250 beneficiaries, Rural Damascus 55,000 beneficiaries, and Daraa 176,000 beneficiaries).

UN-HABITAT has significantly increased its targets in 2019 compared to previous years through continuing to support existing water systems in an effort to stabilize and reduce their decline, and to ensure provision of safe water through public water supply networks. Wherever possible comprehensive approach will be promoted to fully restore safe water supply at the sufficient level. Critical activities include basic rehabilitation of infrastructure for life-saving and/or resilience-oriented purposes, in addition to prevent the discharge of raw sewage and contamination of water bodies and soil. In light of very limited wastewater treatment capacities across the country alternative sanitation solutions will be considered. Additionally, capacity building for staff and operation and maintenance of wastewater infrastructure and solid waste (municipal and medical waste) management systems will be supported along with provision of required materials and technology to reduce overall public health risks and environmental pollution caused by the degradation of those systems.  

Project Components:
In each location, the project consists of Four main components as follows:
1.	Repair, rehabilitation, augmentation of water systems;
2.	Support to sewage and solid waste management systems;
3.	Distribution of essential WASH NFIs and Hygiene promotion
4.	Capacity building: (training, orientations, learning visits/exposure etc.).

project_name: Improving access to housing, basic infrastructure and cadastral services for displaced, hosts and returnees through an urban area-based approach in Daraa, Deir-Ezzor, Homs, Rural Damascus and Aleppo
project_objective:
Rationale:
The rationale of this area-based project is derived from experience gained from previous pilots and shelter projects, as well as evaluation of Shelter Sector interventions’ challenges and impact during the last years, concluding that
•	Targeting individual housing units scattered across cities, reduces the desired impact of emergency response to enhance stability and social cohesion in areas,
•	Restoration of services and infrastructure is a key factor in reviving the affected neighborhoods and improving stability,
•	Community (and municipality) involvement in project identification and planning processes is a prominent element in emergency assistance, as it serves to mitigate possible tensions arising from perceived or real discrimination in selection processes. It is however essential to manage expectations of beneficiary populations, thus to boost positive impact of outcomes of delivered assistance,

Objectives:
Through the area-based approach, UN-Habitat aims to contribute in securing safe access for returnees to their destroyed homes by restoration of essential infrastructure and access to cadastral services to displaced-, host- and returnee- populations in selected neighborhoods in Daraa, Deir-Ezzor, Homs, Rural Damascus and Aleppo. The holistic notion to serve entire conflict-affected, vulnerable communities through a comprehensive package of essential infrastructure and related services, under the objective to revive neighborhoods, is at the core of this project.


Project Components:
 Based on the municipalities’ neighborhood action plans, developed through the municipality-led MTOS program (Municipal Technical Office Support) the project will cover the 
•	Connection of residential buildings to water- and sewage mains,
•	Light rehabilitation of roads in the residential areas including sidewalk, street lighting, and repair the damaged Asphalt layers.
•	Support to local cadastral departments to restore its functions and to provide services in regards of ownership and tenure documentation to all citizens.

project_name: Increase the access of people with disabilities and war injuries  to protection services through multi-sector approach , Reduce the impact of ERWs and providing schools based protection services
project_objective:
The project will continue to contribute to reducing stigma and to promoting dignity of the survivors by harnessing a concept of ‘capabilities’ opposed to ‘disabilities’ among the survivors, their families and community members. Also, will contribute in increasing the war survivors’ access to services through multidisciplinary approach and enhanced referral system. 
This project  will also  address acute vulnerability of newly arrived IDPs and the most neglected and least served groups in hosting communities through multi-sectoral approach. Linking up with other existing life-saving interventions (health, nutrition, survivor assistance) of Hand in Hand for Aid and Development , the project will demonstrate high complementarity to serve the urgent needs and long-term supports of the IDPs and communities in northern Syria.  In absence of protection institutions and social and family protection networks and structures, the project will introduce alternative social protection to the most vulnerable families through one-off material supports (assistive devices, modiﬁed bedding, communication devices, transportation) which enable to address diversiﬁed needs of individual households to prevent the vulnerable households to be engaged in negative coping mechanism. In addition, the mobile outreach unit can serve as a point of detection/referral any suspected cases of gender based violence. Through in-house health referral mechanism as well as collaboration with other GBV actors, survivors of GBV will have access to service in a timely manner.  
Additionally, due to lack of understandings on disability mainstreamed interventions across humanitarian assistance providers in northern Syria, persons and children with impairments and injuries may live inaccessible or dangerous environments and may face discrimination, marginalization and exclusion. The project will address this challenge
this project also aim to protect the civilians in Idleb, Aleppo governorates form the risks of Mines and ERWs (Explosive Remnants of War) through: conducting Risk Education session, build other NGOs capacities, conducting CIS. in addition to provide comprehensive protection service through school-based approach that will increase the access to protection service in schools and increasing the people with disabilities access to the schools

project_name: Provision of Food Security and Livelihoods Support for Conflict Affected populations in North Darfur and South Kordofan
project_objective:
The proposed activities under this action will address access to food sources which will impact on both food insecurity and thus dietary uptake. The FSL approach adopted by GOAL recognizes that food security cannot be treated as a basic need, separate from wider livelihoods considerations. Households may go hungry in order to preserve seed, tools, animals or other assets. GOAL plans to provide emergency FSL support to conflict-affected households, including IDPs, returnees, and vulnerable host households, in three localities in South Kordofan: Reif el Shargi (1230 households), Rashad (900 households), and Talodi (290 households). FSL activities will be integrated with Health, Nutrition, and WASH interventions in the same localities implemented by GOAL and/or partners (including the IMC SHF Consortium in Reif el Shargi), and closely coordinated through the FSL sector and directly with other partners to ensure complementary approaches with no overlapping locations of intervention. GOAL's FSL intervention will focus on agriculture and livestock activities, including seed and tool voucher fairs for agricultural inputs for both cereal and winter-season (vegetable) crops; goat restocking activities providing local female and improved-species male goats to increase assets, improve milk consumption, and small income; and in some cases support women to start VSLA groups to better manage imporved inocmes. In Talodi, GOAL will also pilot support for beekeeping, a common activity in the locality but damaged by conflict and economic crisis; the pilot aims to restore this as a viable economic activity for vulnerable households.
In North Darfur, GOAL will target 18,263 direct beneficiaries comprising of IDPs, rural underserved communities, nomadic pastoralists and host communities experiencing protracted crisis. Activities will complement the ongoing Health and Nutrition as well as WASH interventions, holistically addressing the ongoing critical situation in Kutum and Al Waha localities. Improving access to food sources and food availability will be provided by increasing access to locally adaptable improved crop seeds and varieties through the implementation of seed voucher and fairs as an alternative seed distribution approach (seed fairs have been acknowledged as one of the best mechanisms to assist farmers in emergency and early recovery situations, such as currently in North Darfur). Besides, vegetable seeds for micro gardens will be distributed to vulnerable households attending nutrition supplementary feedings programmes. In Darfur, it is noted that for many households livestock plays an important role in promoting food security by diversifying food sources and providing a potential source of cash income. The importance of small ruminants in improving food security among women and children is especially great. Therefore, GOAL proposes to distribute small ruminants (goats) as well as chickens to target communities. GOAL will also work with vulnerable and disempowered women to provide training, support and mobilisation in livelihoods diversification and income generation through implementation of Village Saving and Loan Association (VSLAs). GOAL will also continue to support Nursery sites located in strategic locations that were established in 2018.

project_name: Addressing underlying causes of malnutrition through food systems and food-based approaches
project_objective:
FAO will contribute to Nutrition Cluster efforts to reduce malnutrition prevalence among children, women and their households by integrating nutrition-sensitive approaches across its food security and livelihood responses within the Food Security Cluster. 

More specifically, FAO will integrate tailored nutrition awareness materials into livelihood programmes targeting farmers, agropastorists, pastoralists and fishers to improve dietary diversity and encourage the production and consumption of fresh and nutrient rich foods (targeting at least 50 000 households). Education campaigns will be led by empowered village-level nutrition champions, who will disseminate acquired knowledge and work with their communities to improve dietary diversity. 

In addition, FAO will complement Nutrition Cluster food and nutrition education in rural communities, including through training and demonstrations on food hygiene, food preparation, food storage, food preservation and small-scale homestead processing tailored to women and with a focus on nutrient retention. Knowledge, Attitude and Practice (KAP) analysis of fish, milk and meat products will be conducted through a nutrition lens in five key locations to develop and fine-tune nutrition sensitive programming. In addition, context-specific materials and campaigns will be developed for food waste and food loss prevention, reduction and management in both rural and urban areas. 50 small school gardens will be established, where children (age 10+) learn about the food path, including the provision of vegetable gardening kits, micro irrigation systems and teachers’ notes.  FAO will continue efforts to promote fish consumption through at least 20 tastings, cooking demos and nutrition education campaigns. 

Gender will be mainstreamed in all activities (e.g. each village will have 1 female and 1 male nutrition champion). Also, due attention will be paid to women’s engagement in project activities are not a burden or take time away from other caretaking and other key roles.

This profile links to FAO resilience activities (including as part of the FAO/WFP/UNICEF Joint Resilience Acton 2018-2022) which ultimately aims to improve household food security and nutrition through integrated approaches.

project_name: Prevention, Response, and Outreach to Empower Conflict Related Sexual Violence (CRSV) Trauma Survivors in Iraq (""PROTECTS""/ IRAQ)
project_objective:
NCA is an active member of the Mosul, Duhok, and the Iraq (national) MHPSS working groups, and regularly co-ordinates with other MHPSS providers to provide care to those who need it the most. The beneficiaries that NCA serves are vulnerable women, girls, boys, and men that have been impacted by trauma and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)   as a result of conflict. Based upon the findings generated from NCA’s three years of experience providing GBV services in Iraq; collaborative discussions with local government, local and international NGOs, UN organizations, and other stakeholders; and other independent research, NCA proposes the following program in Iraq for 2019-2020 to address the country’s most dire needs as it strives to recover from the deeps wounds left by ISIS and other inter-group conflict: 

The overall goal of the proposed project is to empower conflict-affected women, girls, boys, and men to overcome the traumatic impact of GBV and displacement. To achieve this, NCA will continue to offer holistic wrap-around GBV and MHPSS services to internally displaced persons (IDPs), returnees and host communities in conflict-impacted areas of Ninawa and Dohuk. With this project, NCA also proposes to expand its ongoing activities into conflict-impacted areas of Ninawa plains. 

The target beneficiaries will continue to include women, girls, boys and men; families; and other vulnerable people in camps, non-camps and return areas in Ninawa. Key activities will include provision of high quality, culturally appropriate multi-sectoral support to GBV and CRSV survivors. Services will include wrap-around case management, community-based mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), peer support groups, livelihood and economic assistance, and life skills courses. In line with rights-based aid, NCA is planning to include cash-for-protection as a component of its case management services. This will enable women, girls, boys, and men survivors of GBV and CRSV who have been subjected to trafficking, sexual slavery, and rape to depend on themselves; it will also enhance their resiliency, reduce vulnerability, and mitigate the risk of ongoing GBV. 

Through MHPSS and GBV specific capacity-building activities with local partners, the Department of Health (DOH) of Ninawa and Dohuk, and other parties, NCA will seek to reduce the incidence of ongoing GBV by teaching boys and men more effective anger management skills. Finally, through carefully designed inclusive, participatory activities, NCA will seek to improve social cohesion so that communities can stabilize and effectively work together to eliminate GBV. The need for this project is based on the fact that the local authorities and its departments are currently unable to deliver the response that is so critically needed to assist the large number of traumatized women, girls, boys, and men overcome the debilitating effects of the complex traumatization that they experienced during the reign of ISIS.
