project_name: Ensuring provision for sexual and reproductive health and GBV support to Rohingya refugee and host communities in Bangladesh
project_objective:
Context and background/history
On 25 August 2017, violence erupted in Rakhine State, Myanmar, triggering a massive and swift refugee influx into Bangladesh. Many of the refugees who arrived required critical medical treatment for physical injuries including gunshot wounds and burns, they also needed preventive treatment to mitigate against communicable diseases, antenatal care, emergency obstetric care services, reproductive health and GBV case management including clinical management of rape. 
Needs Assessment 
CARE conducted a Rapid Gender Analysis 19-23 September 2017 noted the community’s history of poor family planning practices, recognizing that most married women had between three and seven children. It also identified the social stigma attached to menstruation management. Adolescents in the camps especially those without one or more parents are now even more vulnerable to sexual harassment, forced or child marriage,  trafficking and other forms of gender-based violence including rape. Many married women were already pregnant but have never received any reproductive health support. In the upheaval, countless women were raped as they fled their homes and tried to cross the border. 

Strategic orientations/goals

To provide SRH and GBV services along with PHC services through outreach doorstep activities and static health facilities across the people living in the camps including the host community with special focused on women girls and children. 

Description of activities and implementation Modalities:
Based on the context/background and the needs CARE recognized the need for static health care clinics in November 2017, and in December opened 4 clinics to provide SRH and basic health services in Camp 12, Camp 13 and Camp 14. In opening the facilities, they recognize the gender divide in patients and therefore instituted an outreach system, which enlisted healthcare practitioners and volunteers to visit shelters to actively seek out women and offer them support. Therefore, CARE seeks to utilize these resources to continue funding the clinics and strengthen their activities. In this phase of the project, we will also further incorporate GBV support and SRH education. 

Beneficiaries of the project 

There are approximately 50,000 who will be targeted. This represents 11,500 women, 9,500 men, 14,500 girls, and boys. Among these there are 2,000 pregnant and 3500 lactating women.

project_name: Sustainable WASH for Women, Men, Girls and Boys in Camps and Host Communities
project_objective:
On 25 August 2017, violence erupted in Rakhine State, Myanmar, triggering a massive refugee influx into Bangladesh, 728,000 refugees have since arrived, bringing the total refugee population to 921,000.  Over the past year, humanitarian actors have sought to meet the basic and emergent needs of the refugee community, yet given the critical needs and lack of funding response activities have focused on short term solutions, leaving households still highly vulnerable as they dwell in weak shelters, lack sufficient clean water, relevant health services, and the prevalence of gender based violence (GBV) increases. The monsoon season lasting from May through September led to a deterioration of conditions, over 50,00 people were affected by landslides, windstorms, fires, waterlogging and flooding. There were 6,000 refugees that were displaced.  There were substantial number of latrines that were damaged or required decommissioning, and also number of tube wells were damaged or found contaminated and GBV and protection risks increased.  Weakened infrastructure further hampered mobility and access to services which disproportionately impacted the 75% of the refugee population that are women and children decreasing their ability to access required health and gender-based violence services. 

Following the monsoon season, a year into this response, only 39% of the Join Response Plan for 2018 has been funded. Funding is particularly low for health (28%), WASH (27%) and protection and GBV (37%) programming.  The lack of funding for these sectors have direct implications on the safety, security, wellbeing and health of women and children. The current Joint Reponses Plan for 2018 has identified the remaining gaps in maternal health, family planning, GBV response and prevention support, safe spaces for women and girls, clean water, sufficient latrines and effective hygiene promotion in order to minimize contamination and disease outbreaks. It also recognized that weak gender mainstreaming and referral mechanisms between health, GBV and WASH are undermining the efficacy and efficiency of available services.  Based on the inter sector coordination groups strategies this project seeks to increase access for women and girls to life-saving reproductive health services, provide trauma and GBV response and prevention support, and enhance WASH infrastructure and hygiene awareness. By offering a integrated multi-sectoral project we seek to enhance links between services to leverage available resources for greater impact.CARE has operated in Bangladesh since 1949 and has established its expertise in GBV, WASH, health, and SRH. CARE’s thematic, technical and local experience enabled CARE to be a first responder within this crisis, beginning programming in September 2017. Over the past year, CARE has implemented over 30 programs. Based on assessed gaps, CARE’s programming has been centralized in camps 12, 13, 14, 15, 16 and 1 W. This project will seek to build on our efforts, the relationships established with the community and the momentum achieved to respond to the persistent needs in camps 12, 14, 15, and 16.By continuing our work on WASH, we can compound our efforts and achieve more substantial and substantive gains.

CARE Bangladesh places women and girls at the centre of its work. CARE aims to create an enabling environment that supports women and girls’ empowerment and leadership in humanitarian decision-making CARE`s response will aim to address specific needs of women and girls, and also men and boys throughout all stages of the WASH project activities by applying principles of the five gender minimum commitments in our programming. This assertion is based on recent 'Rapid Gender Assessment' that CARE conducted.

project_name: Building women and adolescent girls' resilience through GBV prevention and response (with ASRH components)
project_objective: This project aims to build women and girls' resilience through GBV prevention and response. Specifically, it aims to establish safe spaces with GBV response services, support self-reliance skills, and strengthen social networks within and between host and refugee communities. The SSWG models will vary depending on the needs and opportunities within targeted operating areas in camps 1E, 1W 14, 15, 16 and host community Palong Khali. SSWG response services will include structured psychosocial support services and case management services coupled with GBV targeted community engagement with women, men, girls and boys for GBV prevention and mitigation. To enhance self-reliance skills and opportunities of women and girls, relevant, appropriate and adapted trainings and recreational activities will be conducted. Intervention design will be based on on-going feedback and consultation with women and girls, men and boys, as well as project learnings to date. To support solidarity and trust building within and among host and refugee communities to further build a protective environment, selected areas of host and refugee will be linked to each other.  It will integrate adolescent sexual and reproductive health (ASRH) in the safe spaces through key services as per SSWG model (family planning and maternal health services, information and education on SRH and GBV, young mothers’ clubs).  The project will be complimented with on-going projects in host communities’ safe spaces and CARE’s on-going programs (Shelter, Site Management, WASH and Host community program) through GBV mainstreaming and integration, with other sectors in the areas of operation.

project_name: Integrated GBV, Shelter and WASH to promote protection, safety and dignity of vulnerable households in Camps 13 and 16
project_objective:
OBJECTIVE: Ensure 7,000 vulnerable affected households (31,500 individuals) have appropriate access to durable shelter and household items that provide increased safety, security, privacy, dignity, comfort and resilience to shocks.
The overall aim of this multi-sectoral project is to support vulnerable households and individuals (especially women and girls, children, persons with disabilities, and the elderly) to have access to safe and dignified shelter, settlement living conditions and communal WASH infrastructure, with access to basic items that meet household needs and provide safety and dignity. The overall objective of the Shelter-NFI component is ensure vulnerable affected households have appropriate access to shelter and household items that provide increased safety, security, privacy, dignity, comfort and resilience to shocks (such as high winds/storms), while meeting immediate and longer-term specific needs. 
Throughout 2018 and in early 2019 (through already-secured funding), CARE Bangladesh will meet the needs of around 700 households (approximately 3,200 individuals) in Camp 16, through the construction of Mid-Term Shelters and Transitional Shelters, coordinated through CARE's role as Site Management Agency and in complementarity with Gender/GBV teams and WASH activities. This leaves around 4,000 households (18,000 individuals) in Camp 16 without access to improved shelter, many of whom continue to live in precarious site conditions at risk of health issues, fire and other safety risks, most notably for women and girls for whom GBV continues to be a real threat. This project aims to strengthen the integration of CARE's response, tying together settlement-level activities in shelter, WASH, site management and site development, while increasingly targeting towards self-identified needs in line with vulnerability, with a particular focus on the specific needs of women and girls to prevent gender-based violence. Furthermore, as CARE's presence expands (likely to include Camp 13 in 2019), additional households in need are likely to be identified (Camp 13 has a total population of around 9,900 households/43,000 individuals).

project_name: Infrastructure support project for Myanmar refugees and host communities living in Camps 13 and 16
project_objective:
The Site Development activities proposed in this project complement the camp coordination and camp management activities CARE is already undertaking, which are funded by IOM in the camp(s) of operation (Camp 16, and potentially Camp 13), extending the impact of the small-scale site infrastructure works as well as ongoing shelter programming funded by other donors. The activities proposed under this project will build on and further address the priorities self-identified by communities in specific infrastructure and sites. It will be supported by complementary activities in WASH, Shelter, NFI and GBV to ensure that a holistic approach to address needs and support individuals and groups with specific needs, particularly those at risk. This includes women and girls (particularly adolescent girls), the elderly and persons with disabilities. As a core focus of CARE's mandate is supporting women and girls, the design and implementation of site development activities will be supported by CARE's Gender, GBV and Protection teams which are engaged early on to help facilitate community mapping of risks (e.g. through safety audits), engagement and participation, and the identification of priorities and feasible options for infrastructural work. This cross-disciplinary Site Management and Site Development team also coordinates other activities such as information provision, complaints handling, follow up with vulnerable individuals/families, and supporting subsidiary activities (such as temporary or permanent relocation) to ensure that a supportive, dignified and respectful process is maintained throughout. As part of the IOM-funded Site Management activities in the camp(s) of operation, CARE will strengthen/establish contextualised common and community-based Complaints, Feedback and Response mechanisms (CFRM). These will identify and integrate existing partner and community accountability mechanisms to streamline feedback collection, and strengthen the referral mechanisms to ensure timely responses to complaints. 
ACTIVITIES: 
1. CAMP OPERATION
- Conduct community risk assessments and safety audits with a gender focus, updating current fire safety plans through findings
- Develop and disseminate a fire safety plans, taking into account the specific needs, capacities and vulnerabilities of different groups (e.g. persons with disability, elderly, young children, pregnant and lactating mothers, and female headed households) 
- Establish a risk reduction action plan for each block and sub-block establishing action plans and procuring contingency supplies, taking into account the abovementioned vulnerabilities.
- Facilitate relocation and decongestion activities undertaking requisite site enhancement and infrastructural development activities, through a participatory and protection-led approach.
2. IMPROVED LIVING CONDITIONS IN THE CAMP
- Participate in a community-led integrated (multi-sectoral) site plan and site improvement plan at the macro level (camp) as well as micro level (block)
- Contribute to the development of a community approved Camp Strategy and support community to implement it providing required tools and resources.
- Install and maintain required infrastructure, protection and safety equipment including bridges, stairs, pathways, fire points, drains, handrails and accessibility features, and stabilize high risk slopes. 
- Offer training and local labour employment for community members to undertake site enhancement and planning activities, including for females wherever feasible (e.g. through community outreach, facilitation, engagement, information sharing, and monitoring of activities). 
3. SUSTAINABLE APPROACHES: SLOPE STABILISATION
- Conduct reforestation and environmental rehabilitation activities, promoting social forestry and slope mitigation through planting trees, grass plants and other relevant vegetation.

project_name: Restoring disrupted livelihoods for Palestine refugees in Syria
project_objective:
In 2019, UNRWA will maintain its Technical and Vocational Education Training (TVET) long term and short term courses in Damascus, Dera’a, Homs and Aleppo depending on the availability of funds. As demand for TVET services grows, the Agency will continue its efforts to better link students with the job market and increase employability rates of graduates. Reconstruction/rehabilitation-focused courses, such as electricity, plumbing or masonry, will continue to be an area of focus. 

Despite significant challenges, the microfinance programme continues to provide a growing number of loans to Syrians and Palestine refugees within Syria. In 2019, the microfinance team will continue to provide inclusive financial services to Palestine refugees and Syrians requiring additional capital through the direct disbursement of loans to meet the growing demand for financial products. The majority of the loans requested are consumer loans, which enable a household to cover unforeseen expenditures, such as the purchase of assets. Entrepreneur loans are less in demand, reflecting the ongoing constraints of the socioeconomic context in Syria. 

In 2019, UNRWA will aim to resume microfinance activities in areas of spontaneous return such as Sbeineh, Qabr Essit and Khan Eshieh camps through the provision of consumer loans, business loans or youth and women focused loans. Special microfinance products focusing on the most vulnerable members of the community such as women and youth will continue to be developed by UNRWA and will be further promoted in order to stimulate livelihood activities in recovering areas. 

Finally, and in response to the evolving needs of the Palestine refugees in Syria, UNRWA is exploring the feasibility of conducting small scale cash-for-work initiatives in 2019  . Work opportunities would be provided to support the provision of current UNRWA services (health, and education), or to support the restoration of Agency services in newly accessible areas.

project_name: Improving water access for unconnected communities and most vulnerable groups in the West Bank
project_objective: Ensure equitable access to WASH essential services, in safety and dignity, to the most vulnerable women, men, girls and boys located in unconnected communities, thus contributing to the achievement of WASH cluster objective no.1. The project addresses immediate needs as well as the underlying drivers of those needs, in line with the water master plan for Area C developed by GVC and AAH, in cooperation with PWA, as well as the PWA National Water Sector Strategic Plan and Action Plan (2017-22). The intervention encompasses: - A responsive measure, comprehensive of water access massive interventions (pipeline, filling point, HHs connection) and storage water intervention (rain water harvesting cisterns); - A remedial measure, through the provision of sanitation facilities The initiative allows to reduce and more effectively address the core vulnerabilities of people in need increasing water access for unconnected communities in area C and guarantee a safe level of sanitation for the most vulnerable groups in the West Bank. The initiative will connect 6 communities (3,980 people) in Area C with safe water domestic connections. 3 communities (425 people) will increase their storage capacity through construction of rainwater harvesting cisterns while 4 (445 people) will see improved their level of sanitation and hygiene. The action aims to support gender and age -sensitive relief provision and gender and age-responsive protection as a means to meeting specific vulnerable groups’ material and safety needs, ensure gender and age responsive assistance and equitable access to humanitarian goods and services, prevent/mitigate potential negative effects of the action on different gender/age groups and ensure adequate participation. The action aims at responding to the differentiated vulnerabilities of all community members, considering the needs of every age, gender, and level of ability. Analyses and strategies utilized throughout the project take special consideration of the vulnerability and needs of women, children, people with disabilities and the elderly. Needs analyses, activities, outcomes, and indicators consider the diverse needs of each community member and vulnerable groups. All the interventions will trigger a positive effect on the reduction of vulnerability and the increase of resilience of the community members, especially the most vulnerable groups as boys, girls, women and men. The action has been endorsed by PWA and in line with the PWA Strategic Plan (2017-22) –, and is in compliance with the water Master Plan for Area C. These activities are in line and part of the 2017-22 PWA Strategy Plan, and the priorities set for 2019 by the Joint Service Councils, West Bank Water Department and PWA. The action is in line with the Sustainable Development Goals, specifically contributing with “Goal 6: Ensure access to water and sanitation for all”.

project_name: Strengthen WASH and Shelter preparedness and response capacity for the most vulnerable families in the North Gaza Governorate
project_objective:
The proposed action is fully in line with 2019 WASH Cluster Objectives 1 and 3. The action also contributes to the Shelter Cluster Objective 2.
The action aims to work at two levels: 
-	Community level through life saving emergency WASH response interventions and preparedness to the most vulnerable communities through improvement their drainage water systems, domestic water quality monitoring and reducing hazards for private/public hygiene. This will also enhance service provider’ preparedness capacity and support communities’ resilience building in face of protracted threats and chronic vulnerability and especially in terms of Health and WASH.
-	Household level through rehabilitation and/or upgrading of shelters, HH wastewater connection and hygiene promotion, which will reduce the exposure of targeted beneficiaries to both man-made and natural disasters, weather conditions and risk of water borne diseases and health problems, by enabling them to live meeting adequate standards. 
Lack/poor drainage water infrastructure place thousands of families at a risk of displacement and destruction of their properties. This problem has even worst consequences when stormwater mixes with garbage and/or HH cesspits, polluting the surrounding environment and enhancing the existence and spread of insects/rodents causing serious illnesses. Sicknesses of HHs’ members imply an extra burden for women as family’s caregivers, as per their traditionally imposed role.
Providing adequate shelter will contribute to reduce and mitigate the effects, vulnerabilities and risks associated with living in access restricted area (ARA), especially women, children, elderly and people with disabilities (PwDs). Shelter rehabilitation and upgrading activities, will allow to advance in the fulfillment of the objectives of empowering communities, in terms of coping capacities and protection response mechanisms, enhancing their capacities to respond to protracted crisis and reinforcing the local capacities as mitigation and preparedness to environmental and man- made hazards.
The project will address the needs of acutely vulnerable HHs living in substandard overcrowded housing units, improving the accessibility to adequate and safe shelter through providing increased thermal comfort, protection from the effects of extreme climate during the summer and winter, and promoting safety, privacy, and hygiene. Particularly, the project will provide comprehensive upgrades and repairs alleviating its immediate effects, promote an adequate standard of living and create a safer environment to cope with environmental threats. 
The proposed intervention will target the North Gaza Governorate, specifically Bet Lahia, Bet Hanoun, Jabalia, Jabalia Camp al Umm Al Nasser, directly benefiting 1,544 HHs, meaning a total of 9,293 individuals (2,459 girls, 2,569 boys, 2,112 women and 2,153 men) and 377,125 people in an indirect way.  As mentioned above, in the target areas there is an urgent need of strengthen WASH and Shelter preparedness and response capacities to emergencies at both HH level and community level (service providers).This action is in line with the PWA Storm water management policy and is considered as high and urgent priority by CMWU, ensures access to essential services strengthening the population to cope with protracted threats, and is seen as an emergency time critical response, which is not currently addressed by CMWU and PWA intervention due to funding constraints.
The project includes the following activities based on the protection egg model:
Responsive (50% of the budget):  Connection of households to the municipal wastewater system; Enhancing of operation of 16 municipal water wells
Remedial (38% of the budget): Repairing/upgrading of HHs main structures facilities (WASH and Shelter);  Hygiene and environmental health awareness campaign and distribution of hygiene kits
Environmental building (12% of the budget): Provision of protective clothes and tools; Cleaning and dislodging of 15 wastewater pumping stations and wastewater networks. The shelter component aims at responding to their needs in terms of shelter and protection, and indirectly WASH and Health, and it complies with the minimum SPHERE standards for adequate housing, Shelter Cluster, minimum agreed standards, gender, and adequate access to housing by people with disabilities.  The beneficiaries of this action are selected among the most vulnerable households in terms of socioeconomic and protection related vulnerabilities which are connected to inadequate shelter. The shelter rehabilitation will target 100 HHs through different techniques,  to improve the shelter conditions, including protection from natural hazards and climate, and to ensure privacy and safety, to contribute to self- recovery, to reduce the risk of GBV and other protection-related risk. The assessment carried out during the proposal elaboration, highlighted the following issues: presence of old shelters in urgent need of rehabilitation, including severe electrical damage, persistent dampness, and leaking and caving roofing, and many other critical needs; incapacity of the shelters to guarantee proper summer insulation and proper hygiene conditions; need for installation of doors and windows to prevent the entrance of animals,   need for privacy (especially for women who suffer from lack of privacy in their rooms and in the WASH facilities inside their homes and for boys and girls to facilitate their homework); unhealthy and unhygienic WASH conditions due to old sewage systems in their shelters. The assessments shows that the inability of the community to improve structures is due mainly to economic deprivation. The action contributes to the Shelter Cluster Objective 2 and will be implemented in coordination with stakeholders involved in the WASH & shelter sectors, including the PWA, CMWU and MoSD. Women CBOs- local implementing partners, will be responsible for HH field surveys and soft activities such as distribution of NFI, awareness sessions etc. The average cost for rehabilitation  is estimated at 2,700 USD  and winterization   300 USD  per household

project_name: Reinforce the capacities of protection from natural, man-made hazards and conflict escalations of acutely vulnerable Palestinian households
project_objective:
This is an urgent emergency response to reinforce the capacities, resilience and protection of vulnerable Palestinian communities in Area C of the West Bank from natural and manmade hazards. 
The action includes the rehabilitation and upgrading of shelters and provision of capacity building and training, which will reduce the exposure of targeted beneficiaries to both man-made and natural disasters, weather conditions and risk of water borne diseases and health problems, by enabling them to live with adequate standards, and improve their preparedness (remedial and environmental building action)

The action aims at preventing, reducing, mitigating the threats against persons and communities and support resilience building in face of protracted threats and chronic vulnerability while responding  to their needs in terms of shelter and protection, and indirectly WASH and Health.
 Providing adequate shelter and protective assets will contribute to reduce and mitigate the effects, vulnerabilities and risks associated with the coercive environment in Area C, especially women, children, elderly and PWDs. Shelter rehabilitation and upgrading activities, coupled with the implementation of the community participation methodology will allow to advance in the fulfilment of the objectives of empowering communities, in terms of coping capacities, ownership and expertise, and protection response mechanisms, enhancing their resilience and capacities to respond to protracted crisis and mitigation and preparedness to environmental and man- made hazards.

The action, which is fully in line with the 2019 HRP Strategic Objective 2 and 3, complies with the minimum SPHERE standards for adequate housing, Shelter Cluster minimum agreed standards, gender, and adequate access to housing by people with disabilities. This integrated approach endeavors to ensure that communities are sufficiently protected and equipped with both tangible and intangible assets, in order to remain in their current location of choice, and thus prevent their forcible transfer. 

The beneficiaries of this action are among the most vulnerable households in terms of socio-economic and protection related vulnerabilities which are connected to the physical and political-related characteristics of Area C communities, including H2 Hebron.  Residents of these communities are highly affected by setter and ISF violence, lack of access to basic services, inadequate shelter, and movement restrictions among many other hindrances.
Specifically, the action will target 30 communities (8 in Hebron -including 3 in H2-Tal Al Rumeideh, Haret al Salaymeh, Wadi Al Hussien);  2 in Bethlehem; 1 in Jenin; 3 in Jericho; 1 in Ramallah; 15 in Tubas) and 1326 beneficiaries  (666 adults – 334 women and 332 men, 68 elders-36 women and 33 men, 359 adolescents- 164 girls and 196 boys, 234 children-110 girls and 124 boys). GVC is present in 24 of these communities since 2015 as focal point in the WBPC and MAAN has been actively working in the rest of the communities in shelter rehabilitation over the years. 
The shelter rehabilitation will target 150 HH through different techniques (rehabilitation of concrete shelters with composite roof, rehabilitation of concrete shelter with asphalted roof with internal renovation works; provision of PVC plastic cover). In addition, GVC and MAAN will conduct capacity building to the community members on self- implemented house renovation and techniques to improve the shelter conditions, including protection from natural hazards and climate, and to ensure privacy and safety. GVC and MAAN will support the targeted communities who suffer from inadequate and overcrowded shelters, with activities and sessions to contribute to self- recovery, to reduce the risk of GBV and other protection-related risk, and to sensitize the communities about privacy inside shelters, WASH facilities hygiene and privacy, PWD minimum living standards. 
 
These high-priority interventions will be implemented in partnership by GVC and MAAN (already partners since 2015), in coordination with the Palestinian Authority-related bodies. The action is part of a multi-year action which aims at covering the total assessed needs (462 shelters in need of rehabilitation) in 3 years’ time.  The partnership will capitalize on GVC’s and MAAN presence and experience in shelter rehabilitation as well as outreach capacity to the communities. . The action foresees the self-rehabilitation of shelters, implemented using a community implementation approach which relies on the active participation of the community to reduce protection risks and improve coping mechanisms. The action responds to communities’ needs and looks beyond the mere material needs to the broader issues of personal safety and dignity
The action aims to support gender and age-sensitive relief provision and gender and age-responsive protection as a means to meeting  specific material and safety needs, ensure gender and age responsive assistance and equitable access to humanitarian goods and services, prevent and mitigate potential negative effects of the Action on different gender and age groups and ensure adequate participation. The action aims at responding to the differentiated vulnerabilities of all community members, considering the needs of every age, gender, and level of ability. In this regard, analyses and strategies utilized throughout the project take special consideration of the vulnerability and needs of women, children, people with disabilities and the elderly. Based on a   protection-centred approach to humanitarian responses  it aims at meeting the humanitarian and protection needs of communities at risk of FT. The action is  guided by protection principles and considers safety and dignity, meaningful access, accountability as well as participation and empowerment. It aims to reduce the beneficiaries’ exposure to forced displacement by mitigating the effects of the above-mentioned factors and to restore more dignified living conditions

project_name: Soutien aux femmes et filles réfugiées, victimes et survivantes des violences basées sur le Genre et des violences sexistes au Camp de Minawao dans la région de l’Extrême-Nord du Cameroun
Psychosocial and Child Protection for Children and Families affected by Conflict-Related Violence in Area C, H2, and East Jerusalem
project_objective:
This project targets Palestinian children directly and indirectly exposed to violence and abuse related to the Israeli Occupation, including settler violence, unsafe school environments, home and school demolitions, and detention and/or arrests. War Child Holland (WCH) and its partner will be targeting acutely affected children and families living in Area C (Jordan Valley and Tubas), East Jerusalem (communities outside the West Bank Barrier), and Hebron H2. 

This project aims to strengthen the resilience of children, caregivers, schools, and communities in the face of chronic exposure to conflict-related violence by: (1) providing community-based child protection, psychosocial and mental health services to children and their families, (2) supporting parents, school staff, and community-based organizations with psychosocial interventions and capacity building to better take care of and respond to the needs of children in distress, (3) case management and referrals to specialized mental health, social, and educational services, including vocational and remedial education, and (4) addressing IHL and IHRL violations through advocacy initiatives targeting all duty bearers and based on documentation of grave violations. 

The outputs are designed to meet HRP 2018-2020 strategic objectives 1: “The rights of Palestinians living under occupation….are protected, respected and promoted in accordance with IHL and IHRL”; and 2: “providing support to meet the basic needs of the vulnerable population, particularly children”, and the Protection Cluster’s Objective 2 “Protection response mechanisms are in place and mitigate the effects of the occupation and conflict related violence.""

This project aims to strengthen the social safety net around children who have been exposed to conflict-related violence including killings, arrest and detention, injury, and home demolitions. Through the project, children will have access to psychosocial and mental health interventions provided by CBOs supported by WCH, as well as specialized services through case management and referrals. Children acutely affected by conflict-related violence will participate in inclusive structured recreational psychosocial support (PSS) workshops (‘TeamUp”) in and after school. TeamUp was co-developed by War Child, UNICEF and Save the Children in the Netherlands and is now used in multiple conflict-affected contexts. The group sessions are delivered on a drop-in basis, making the activity more inclusive for those children whose circumstances prevent them from regularly attending more structured interventions. Within the sessions, children and adolescents play, learn, make friends and have fun in a safe and protective setting. The activities are designed to allow emergency affected children to explore socioemotional themes in a safe and non-confrontational environment, themes including anger, fear, stress and tension, conflict, respect, bullying, assertiveness, and friendship. The modular, activity-based design of the program allows facilitators to tailor each session to the perceived needs of the particular children attending, including age, space available, physical and sensory abilities. TeamUp also acts as an entry point for children who are experiencing distress or child protection risks to be identified and referred. Children in need of more structured PSS and preventive mental health support will be referred to WCH’s most widely implemented PSS program – the DEALs - to help children and young people at high risk of occupation related violence to develop positive and alternative coping strategies, and engage in regular activities in a safe and protective environment. The DEALs  intervention  aims  to  increase  children’s  wellbeing and resilience  by  strengthening  their  social relationships; helping them cope effectively with stress and difficult emotions; and to increase their  confidence  and  sense  of  efficacy, and has specific curricula for different age groups as well as a dedicated add-on program for adolescent girls. 
 
Facilitators of the PSS activities will be trained in identification and referral of more severely affected children, who will have access to case management from War Child’s case workers. WCH’s caseworkers will have regular presence in the targeted communities, attend the Child Protection Network’s (CPN) monthly meetings in targeted governorates, and will be responsible for implementing community-based child protection activities and case management. In addition to providing timely and ongoing individualized support to the child and family, WCH’s case workers in each location will identify and refer children struggling with child protection and clinical mental health issues to specialized services, in line with the national referral pathway, including the Child Protection Network. Children and families in need of specialized mental health and/or legal services will have access to (EU-funded) individual, group and family counseling and therapy provided by WCH partners Treatment and Rehabilitation Center (TRC), and Palestinian Counseling Center (PCC), and DCIP, under its EIHDR project operating in the targeted locations of this project. Children and their families may also be referred to external mental health and other service providers, (e.g., the Ministry of Health and Palestinian Red Crescent Society), as required. There will also be a particular focus on supporting and enabling young people to re-engage with education (formal, non-formal or vocational) after conflict-related disruptions such as detention, home arrest, and injury through coordination with and referrals to protection and education cluster partners, ensuring that children receive multidisciplinary and holistic support. To ensure efficiency, timeliness, standardized vulnerability and prioritization criteria, and that minimum standards are met, a technical committee made up of WCH, CPN focal persons, and relevant service providers will be formed under this project to routinely monitor and review the referral process, including forms used, information management, feedback on the services provided and address any challenges faced in the referral process and mechanism.

To address the MHPSS needs of caregivers – who are also in need of safe, supportive places to share their worries and challenges, get support, and learn techniques for stress management - parents and school staff will be offered WCH’s caregiver wellbeing interventions designed to help caregivers manage their own stress in order to better support children, and reduce harsh parenting practices. The caregiver support intervention is research informed, and designed based on the identification of common elements of evidence-based stress management programs. It is delivered within communities by community members and para-professionals trained and supervised by War Child. The caregiver support intervention was successfully piloted in Gaza and is now undergoing randomized controlled trial in Lebanon.  Referrals for specialized legal and mental health services will also be provided to caregivers, as well as support to those in need of family counseling through WCH’s already established referral network.

Capitalizing on their cohesive network of sources including local media, health workers, CBOs, and community leaders and members throughout the West Bank, partner field workers will closely monitor, document, and rapidly report grave violations against children, including child killings and injuries; settler violence; and recruitment.  Strengthened monitoring and reporting of grave violations will yield thematic reports and advocacy initiatives to address protection violations and call for greater accountability on IHL and IHRL by duty bearers.

project_name: Emergency Food Security Response for internally displaced population affected by the crisis in the Far North region of Cameroon
project_objective:
The project aims to provide immediate food assistance to save lives and reduce suffering of households unable to access food that meets basic food and nutritional requirements. The project will be implemented in the 3 most affected departments (Logone et Chari, Mayo Sava and Mayo Tsanaga) targeting 3,100 individuals (40% male and 60% female) including IDPs (50%), returnees (30%) and vulnerable host communities (20%). NRC will pay attention to youth and women affected by displacement. Participation of all beneficiary groups will be key in ensuring ownership of the project.
To achieve the above objectives, NRC will strengthen the resilience and economic security of vulnerable households through the following activities:

1. Provision of cash/voucher to most vulnerable people to meet food needs 
Despite security concerns in Far-North, local markets are functional and accessible by both women and men, although these markets are not yet operating at the same level as before the crises. Cash approach will help ensure that households have unrestricted access to nutritious foods and additional income that would protect their remaining livelihoods assets as well as ensuring that the agricultural inputs, livestock or IGA start-up kits will not be sold and that they will be used as intended. This food assistance will also allow vulnerable individuals to build their resilience helping households not to further deplete their productive assets and avoid further use of negative coping strategies. 

2. Reestablishment of agricultural activities
NRC will negotiate with the local communities and where needed secure access to land for targeted IDPs and returnees. Once the access to land secured, NRC will provide small ruminants, seeds, inputs (agricultural tools, fertilizers, etc.) and trainings. This will improve agricultural production and provide better access to nutrient-rich food. NRC will also promote gardening, which provides households with a source of food or income during the lean season. 

3. Provision of improved stoves 
NRC will also distribute food handling kits that will allow target households to prepare food in a more effective and environment-friendly way. Improved stoves will save households money on firewood and help curb deforestation. For better community acceptance, those stoves will be made locally. They will have a more efficient use of charcoal, thus reducing the quantity needed and reduce the expenses of households for it. 

4.Provision of awareness raising on food hygiene, food diversity, food storage and food preparation  
All emergency activities will be also integrated by sessions to raise the awareness of the targeted populations on food hygiene and diversity, food preparation, and food storage. Through these trainings, beneficiaries are expected to acquire the knowledge and best practices they need to better use the food and improve the results on their nutritional status.

project_name: Assistance multisectorielle sur les îles de retour
project_objective:
Selon les estimations du HNO 2018, 51 000 personnes sont actuellement ""déplacés retournés"" dans les îles de la cuvette sud du Lac Tchad, dont 40 000 dans les îles du Sud de Bol et 11 000 dans les îles autour de Kangalom). L'étude conduite par REACH en mars-avril 2018 a contribué à mettre en évidence les dynamiques de mouvements pendulaires de ces ménages affectées par la crise de déplacement, lié à la nécessité d'obtenir une assistance humanitaire au cours du processus de réinstallation.

Dans ce contexte, ACTED souhaite appuyer cette réinstallation en intervenant directement sur les îles à travers une réponse aux besoins multi sectoriels de ces populations. Cette intervention serait conduite en coordination avec les partenaires humanitaires intervenants sur les sites dans les terres, afin d'assurer la transition progressive de l'assistance humanitaire vers les zones de retours et de prévenir les incitations contraires.

Dans le cadre de cette appui, ACTED:

- Appuierait la construction ou la réhabilitation de logements semi-durables pour 30 600 personnes, ainsi que par la fourniture d'articles ménagers essentiels pour ces ménages affectés.

- Contribuerait à la réduction de l'insécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle, et au renforcement des moyens d'existence de 30 600 personnes par un appui aux activités agropastorales à travers une modalité ""cash +"", combinant intrants en nature et dotation en espèces. Ces distributions seraient accompagnés de formations spécifiques, ainsi que d'un suivi des équipes techniques d'ACTED.

- Soutiendrait le développement d'Activités Génératrices de revenus pour 4680 femmes vulnérables sur les îles de retour. Ces femmes seraient appuyés par des formations sur la création et la gestion d'AGR (dont marketing), et appuyés par des transferts monétaires pour le lancement ou le renforcement de leurs activités. 

- Améliorerait la situation de protection dans la zone par le soutien à la mise en place de comités mixtes de protection sur les violences sexuelles et basées sur le genre et de protection de l'enfance. Ces comités seraient formés et intégré au processus de référencement auprès des acteurs clés de la protection et de la santé dans la zone.

- En lien avec Impact Initiatives, déploierait l'initiative REACH afin de contribuer à informer l'intervention humanitaire par une évaluation de la situation des abris dans l'ensemble de la région du Lac.

project_objective:

teachers will be trained on (child-centred and protective pedagogy, active learning, life-skills, psychosocial support and referral mechanisms, Education in Emergencies (EiE) and national/INEE minimum standards (MS)) in addition to provision teachers and education personnel (90 females and 210 males) with monthly incentives to attract the skilled teachers and improve the learning outcomes, PTA meetings to make sure a good level of coordination and engagement with parents which is also part of our accountability mechanism to make sure feedback from parents is taken and address,

project_name: Improving the nutritional status of vulnerable or conflict affected communities through integrated lifesaving emergency nutrition services for acute malnutrition in Melut and Ulang Counties; Upper Nile State (UNS).
project_objective:
GOAL’s primary purpose for 2019 is to deliver quality life-saving management of acute malnutrition for the most vulnerable and at-risk girls and boys 6-59 months and PLWs in Melut and Ulang Counties, Greater Upper Nile. Protracted conflict and displacements in South Sudan have contributed to insufficient crop production, worsening levels of food insecurity and malnutrition throughout the country, with most areas in at least IPC 3 ""Crisis"" phase of food insecurity. Communities in Melut and Ulang are particularly vulnerable to malnutrition; the counties were classified as IPC 3 “crisis” (Melut) and 4 “emergency” (Ulang) phase of food insecurity as of September 2018, and although Melut is expected to improve to IPC2 during the last quarter of 2018, both counties are anticipated to deteriorate to IPC3 (Melut) and IPC4 (Ulang) at the start of 2019. Recent analysis indicates GAM rates of 21.7% (Melut, WVI SMART Survey March 2018) and 20.1% (Ulang, UNKEA SMART Survey March 2018), which are above the emergency threshold rates for treatment of malnutrition. To respond to these needs, GOAL will implement management of acute malnutrition in Melut and Ulang. Further, GOAL will provide MIYCN counselling services to prevent under-nutrition for most vulnerable and at-risk. GOAL will conduct enhanced nutrition situation monitoring, analysis and utilization of early warning information for timely coordinated response decision making.  GOAL will also support at-risk communities to sustain their capacity to cope with significant shocks, while reinforcing protection, promoting access to basic health services, and integrating FSL and hygiene activities for the displaced and other vulnerable people. 
GOAL proposes to provide nutrition services through a network of 21 TSFP sites in Melut (9 sites) and Ulang (12 sites) Counties, where GOAL has been operational since 2014 and 2007 respectively; in Melut, these services will be integrated with GOAL’s primary health services through 2 clinics and 1 mobile outreach to provide a comprehensive package of care. GOAL will strengthen linkages between partners implementing management for severe acute malnutrition (SAM), referring identified SAM cases to OTP for treatment and receiving beneficiaries discharged from OTP into TSFP for continuum of care. GOAL will enhance integration across sectors to provide comprehensive services for beneficiaries. GOAL will focus on integration of food security and livelihoods (FSL) into nutrition services by linking TSFP beneficiaries to ongoing FSL programming to address drivers of poor health and nutrition in the community. GOAL will also incorporate integration of WASH, aiming for clean water supply, safe and hygienic latrines and waste disposal facilities and handwashing stations at the nutrition centres, using WASH FIT (Water and Sanitation for Health Facility Improvement Tool). GOAL’s programming will focus on enhanced integration of protection into project activities to safeguard beneficiaries. GOAL health facilities in Melut are equipped to respond to and manage any cases of gender-based violence (GBV) presenting at the facilities; GOAL will also strengthen the referral mechanism to InterHealth, the Protection partner in Melut, and ARC, the Protection partner in Ulang. Further, GOAL will promote community utilization of its FCRM as a means for beneficiaries to voice feedback, questions, or concerns about programming, or to raise protection issues; GOAL will continue raising awareness of the mechanism to ensure beneficiaries are informed of the methods available to them in providing feedback to implementing partners.

project_name: Provision of lifesaving assistance to IDPs, returnees and host community in Ninewa and Salah al-Din governorates
project_objective:
The main objective of the project is to tackle the consequences of 3 years of conflict and protracted displacement on the population of Ninewa and Salah Al Din Governorates. The intervention will contribute to reduce morbidity and mortality rates of the most vulnerable populations in Iraq by supporting the re-establishment and the strengthening of primary health care, reproductive health  services in the targeted areas. Specifically, through this intervention, 70,665 vulnerable women, girls, boys and men in west Ninewa and SAD districts will have improved access to quality life-saving health services, including reproductive health. The package of services provided includes: Provision of primary health care services to children, adults and elderly patients; Integrated management of childhood illness (IMCI)  (0-4 years), including support to vaccinations; Sexual reproductive health, including ANC/PNC, and gynaecological consultations; detection/screening and treatment/referral of acute malnutrition among children; establishment of 24hX7 emergency rooms where needed, support of community level healthcare awareness and referral activities;; in addition to the logistical and managerial support to PHCCs, where needed.

As people slowly continue to return to their areas of origin, healthcare services, and especially specialised ones such as RH and MHPSS, are either completely absent or not able to keep up with the increasing number of people in need. This is likely to cause severe discrepancies between the demand for services and the public offer, which can badly worsen the precarious situation of both returnees and people who did not leave the areas. Through providing support to Primary Health Care Centres (PHCCs), the impact of the project will expand to serve people of larger communities, who will access the centres for both the diverse and quality services, including drugs, and for the fact the such services are for free (outside governmental hours).

Along with the quantitative aspect of the project, INTERSOS will be focusing on the quality of services provided. This will be realised through the provision of regular training and on-the-job coaching to medical and paramedical staff in the PHCCs, as well as through the administrative and managerial support which aims as well at making the centres eﬃcient and effective.

Finally, the project will benefit from the long-standing dialogue and cooperation INTERSOS has established with local DOH and Health Sector offices in the targeted areas. Such cooperation is going to remain at the core of INTERSOS intervention as a pillar to ensure effectiveness, efficiency and sustainability. 
INTERSOS exit strategy at the end of the program will be based on two factors pursued and developed during through the year: technically and materially equipping the supported PHCCs, and constantly liaising and cooperation with relevant DOH offices. On the one hand, INTERSOS, through the provision of material support, i.e. medical equipment and supplies, drugs and equipment, and technical capacity building to both medical and non-medical staff, i.e. on-the-job coaching, trainings and technical supervision, strengthen the sustainability of the project both terms of continuation of services and in term of keeping high standards. On the other hand, coordination with relevant DOH offices aims not only at easing the implementation phase of the project, but as well at ensuring proper hand-over of the activities to governmental institutions in order to continue the work and keep up with the quantity and quality of services provided.

The program will be moving in two directions: maintaining the support to the existent PHCCs when governmental authorities will not be able, or are not willing, to keep up with the same amount and level of services; moving to new areas, mainly remote and hard-to-reach areas with new intervention in support of new health structures.

project_name: Emergency Control of Leishmaniasis Amongst Conflict Affected Communities in Northern Syria.
project_objective:
The MENTOR Initiative is a non-profit international NGO that specializes in reducing deaths and suffering caused by vector-borne and neglected tropical disease. MENTOR has been leading the international response to the leishmaniasis epidemic in Syria since 2013, has a proven track record of working effectively with local authorities and achieving direct access to the homes of millions of people in conflict affected areas each year to achieve its disease control aims. MENTOR is highly respected throughout its area of operations in northern Syria and works in close collaboration with the WHO, national authorities and other health agencies to address the epidemic across the region. 
MENTOR - supported by WHO Gaziantep - has come to recognize that to bring the leishmaniasis epidemic under control, that it along with the overall HA community must intensify efforts in hopes of truly impacting the spread of this disease. MENTOR has developed a goal of local controlled elimination to tackle this epidemic with a goal of 10% incident case reduction each year over the next 3-5 years. Building on efforts to date this plan can be actioned with OFDA support through 2019. 
This will include the provision of medical support to one hundred twenty nine (129) medical points serving a catchment area of over 3 million people and assuring access for all in need; while conducting targeted prevention campaigns to protect 1,159,347 of the most vulnerable people from the disease vector (sandfly) that is responsible for disease transmission. 
The statistical records accumulated by MENTOR demonstrate that MENTOR’s activities have had a significant controlling effect on the level and intensity of the leishmaniasis epidemic (see Section 2.a.1 ‘Needs Assessments Communicable Disease’ pages 7-9). The program will continue to use an established and extensive network of contacts and trained personnel, using disease control and treatment protocols that the organisation has already honed, and that adhere strictly to WHO guidelines

project_name: LEBANON - PCPM - Polish Center for International Aid
Emergency Housing Rehabilitation for Women Headed Households and Vulnerable Families in Area C
project_objective:
The overall objective of the project over 2 years is to respond to the immediate shelter needs of vulnerable populations in Area C communities surrounding area A and B of the West Bank. This response will be through self-help approach for the most vulnerable families to provide shelter repairs and transitional shelter solutions close to existing homes, in order to: 1) Promote self-reliance, maintain, and support most vulnerable families who live with the effect of violence, coercion, and deprivation with shelter related solutions. 2) Enhancing the protection and reducing the likelihood of displacement or forced eviction. 3) Contributing in solving the problem of overcrowding houses by creating new spaces through rearrangement to ensure privacy and dignity 4) Reduce the cost of living by adopting green approach. 5) Extend the life span of existing shelters; in sight of the nullity of the issuance of building permits in Area C. Thus, complying with the second HRP strategic objectives “SO2: The basic needs of vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation are met through the provision of essential services”. And complying with the shelter cluster strategic objectives “Vulnerable households exposed to harsh weather and protection concerns are supported to meet basic needs and enhance their coping capacity” and “Capacity to respond to natural or manmade hazards in a timely, efficient and effective manner is increased”.
This project comply with PHC’s Rehabilitation Program objectives, aiming at contributing of elimination some poverty effects on vulnerable women HH’s, improving the quality of the proper housing stock, reducing land designation for housing and infrastructure by restoring the existing housing stock and improving the social, economic, and health conditions for the beneficiaries. 
The project will provide urgent housing rehabilitation to 196 FHH or vulnerable families in Area C of the West Bank whose shelter is unfit for weather conditions, overcrowded, and/or unsafe. In the first year, PHC will commence to respond to 50 vulnerable families located in Area C of the West Bank as described hereafter.

project_name: Provision of Emergency WASH Services for Vulnerable IDPs in Banadir, Middle and Lower Shabelle Regions
project_objective:
This project is part of scale up of emergency WASH activities in Banadir, Lower and Middle Shabelle regions of Somalia. Over 126,400 beneficiaries’ disaster displaced IDP population are targeted in Afgoye corridor, Arbiska, Lafole, Balcad and Jowhar district. At the moment, IDPs and urban poor and rural community are among the most vulnerable groups in the society. Since the capacity of the local community to address their needs is very weak it is clear that the increasing number of IDPs and urban poor in crisis requires an urgent comprehensive action to support the target populations.
The project responds to urgent humanitarian needs including: (1) Deliver life-saving WASH assistance to reduce acute needs among the most vulnerable settlements and communities (2) 2 - Reduce risk of violence against women, children and vulnerable groups when accessing WASH services, and (3) Provide or restore sustainable access to safe water and adequate sanitation services in targeted communities and institutions.
In Banaadir, population influx has put pressure on existing WASH services. There is a risk of disease outbreak in the new IDP settlements due to poor sanitary conditions, rampant open defecation, poor hygiene practices, and lack of safe water supply. The project will provide emergency water supply to IDPs through in kind water provision and or pipeline extensions. Project will provide hygiene kits, hygiene promotion and construct community latrines. In Middle and Lower Shabelle the project will target riverine farming communities where AWD/cholera outbreak is common, and the community have high incidence rates of malnutrition in Somalia. Emergency water trucking will provide temporary safe water supply while sustainable exit strategies are put in place. Open defecation is widespread, and CLTS will be implemented in the early recovery phase of the project. Project will support WASH services and infection control measures at cholera treatment centres, case tracing and follow-up WASH actions in affected communities. Development of water supply infrastructure will be undertaken as part of exit strategy. Community institutions such as schools and health units should be used as entry point for behavioural change in hygiene practice. All activities will be delivered using a stronger protection lens and where feasible and adequate. Many components of the project will involve close collaboration with government and local communities including sensitivities surrounding latrine construction, land tenure and latrine de-sludging work.

project_name: Emergency Medical Assistance to Host and displaced populations in Borno State
project_objective:
This project aims to improve access to free comprehensive Primary Health Care (PHC) services including Nutrition, Mental Health and GBV services for conflict affected populations in Borno State, Nigeria in Maiduguri / Jere LGA (local government areas), and in Damboa LGA.

Médecins du Monde (MdM) has been active in Nigeria since August 2016 in the fields of primary healthcare (PHC), nutrition, gender-based violence (GBV) and mental health and psychosocial services (MHPSS). MdM aims to respond to the emergency situation caused by the violent armed conflict in the North-eastern part of Nigeria. 

Three different modalities of intervention will be implemented to follow the dynamic of IDPs movements in Borno State. Those 3 modalities of intervention will be closely monitored in order to timely adapt to changes: 

•	“MdM run” fixes clinics in IDP settlements and informal camps;
•	Revitalization & strengthening of Primary Health Care services in MoH facilities; 
•	An Emergency Preparedness & Response Plan (EPREP). 

This project proposal will enable a scale up of MdM’s capacity in the field to ultimately reinforce its emergency healthcare intervention as a way to respond to the immediate needs of the target population while strengthening the capacity of local organizations and MOH in the locations which are of safe access for humanitarian teams. This support is aims to improve the access to health services through different modalities (MDM clinics, support to MOH HF when possible, EPREP) and reinforcing MOH capacity to deliver free PHC services to host and IDPs communities. In addition, Primary Health Care structures will be continually assessed, and support will be adapted according to identified gaps in terms of rehabilitation, provision of medical equipment and drugs, and staff capacity building. Primary Health Care structures will be targeted according to the influx of IDPs in its catchment area and take into account the dynamic movement of IDPs population. 

MdM aims to provide a rapid response to the immediate needs of IDPs population in new spontaneous settlements accessible or during outbreaks in Borno State. Activities of the emergency response team will be coordinated with other stakeholders’ active in the state, through continued coordination mechanisms at local level and throughout MdM’s involvement within the relevant Clusters. In terms of operational approach, MdM will consider first direct support to MOH and SEMA, wherever HF is still available or functional, in reinforcing care management capacities and quality of care. Should this be the case, MdM will set-up a temporary clinic to cover the essential and most urgent healthcare needs in the targeted area.

project_name: EGYPT - Plan International
Shelter/NFI emergency response to vulnerable households affected by natural disasters in Gaza Strip
project_objective:
The project overall objective is to ensure that most vulnerable households exposed to impacts of natural disasters (harsh weather and flooding) are supported to meet their basic needs and enhance their coping capacity by providing a timely, efficient, and effective response with emergency shelter support and NFIs (Shelter/NFI Cluster Objective 2). Providing essential shelter support meets basic needs of vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation (Strategic Objective 2) and strengthens their capacity to cope with the protracted crisis (Strategic Objective 3).
As part of its emergency response for the 2018/2019 winter season, NRC will support already identified 480 most vulnerable households exposed to harsh winter climate (flooding, storms) by providing winter emergency repair & winter NFI support. Winter emergency repairs include basic sealing off for roof, external door and walls, and windows to ensure that affected households are protected from harsh weather (modality: conditional cash). Winter NFIs include sealing off-kit, bedding-kit, and winter clothing sets for boys and girls of climate-affected households (modality: in-kind/voucher/cash).

project_name: Evidence-based planning and programming for humanitarian actors in Syria
project_objective:
REACH aims to facilitate evidence-based planning and programming for humanitarian actors in Syria by providing information management and coordination support to at least 200 humanitarian organisations REACH will be leading on the implementation of project activities. More specifically, this will be done through the following activities:

•	Monthly Market Monitoring assessments
•	In-depth Market Assessments
•	Camps & Sites Profiling and Camp Infrastructure Mapping
•	Urban Damage Assessments
•	Rapid Assessments and Situation Overviews
•	Support to Clusters and Coordinated Data Collection Exercises 
•	Monthly Humanitarian Situation Overviews in Syria (HSOS)
•	Thematic assessments/Trends Analyses
•	Information management to the Northeast Syria Response activities
•	IDP Situation Monitoring in Northeast Syria

REACH has designed this intervention on the basis of needs identified in the field and successful experiences in implementing similar activities in south and northern Syria over the past five years. The activities proposed herein aim to address the challenges humanitarian organisations face in accessing information and data to effectively identify gaps, plan and implement a humanitarian response. 

This project is already fully funded, but may require additional top-ups later in the year.

IMPACT is a leading Geneva based think-and-do-tank, created in Switzerland in 2010 on the initiative of ACTED and firstly operationalised in 2012. While autonomous organizations, IMPACT and ACTED operate together thanks to a formalised global partnership. Together, IMPACT, ACTED and UNOSAT set up the REACH program in order to promote and facilitate the development of information products that enhance the humanitarian community’s decision making and planning capacity. IMPACT is the lead-organization in REACH and hosts the REACH global team in its Geneva HQ. As sister organizations, IMPACT and ACTED coordinate on field implementation. In all field operations of the REACH program, ACTED provides operational support (security management, office space, cars, national HR recruitment, etc.), while IMPACT provides strategic and programmatic oversight through its global team and is in charge of the validation and dissemination of reports, and external relations.

project_name: WASH 2019 Ukraine relief in Eastern Ukraine
project_objective:
The project aims to cover the distinct needs of women, girls, boys and men people living in the close to the conflict line settlements in drinking water (target: 18 000),  wastewater disposal systems (target: 2500); solid waste disposal services in accordance with sanitary norms and rules (target: 2500). The aim will be achieved using different intervention strategies, addressing the results of the assessments in each location (drilling new wells, repairing existing water sources, upgrading of existing equipment). The main objectives:
●	To improve access to drinking water using assessment based interventions (drilling of new wells for water, repair, modernization of existing or currently closed wells).
●	To reduce the risk of spread of infectious diseases through the installation of the wastewater disposal systems.
●	To reduce the epidemic risks through the organization of solid waste disposal processes. 
●	To implement behavior interventions aimed on changing attitude of local population to the usage of water and waste management.

project_name: Camp Management Assistance to Displaced Persons in South Sudan
project_objective:
The displacement context in South Sudan remains fluid. The country continues to experience conflict and natural disaster-driven displacements in communities in both urban and hard-to-reach areas. PoCs and collective sites continue to host IDPs in a protracted displacement situation across the country. Concurrent with this are spontaneous returns and relocations of IDPs and refugees, the latter of which can end up finding themselves in a new displacement situation once back in South Sudan.

IOM will target 568,623 of the 800,000 beneficiaries targeted by the Cluster. IOM will focus on providing camp coordination and camp management under the following areas:

I.	Static Operations (PoCs and Collective Centers): As CM agency in Bentiu and Wau, and care and maintenance focal point in Malakal, IOM will continue to improve the living conditions and meet the basic needs of affected populations in these sites. 

Output 1: IDPs living in PoCs and CCs have improved and dignified living conditions in support of a conducive environment for durable solutions and with meaningful community engagement. 

II.	Deploy mobile teams to new and unreached displacement sites as prioritized by the Cluster.

Output 2: Deployment of sustainable mobile responses to unmanaged sites to ensure coordination and community ownership in camp-like settings or spontaneous settlements.

II.	Co-Lead the Camp Coordination and Camp Management Cluster

Output 3: Fully functional, staffed, and well-managed CCCM Cluster supports partner agencies in accountable CCCM responses and systems

project_name: Renforcer la résilience de la communauté du lac Tchad face au changement climatique et assurer l'intégration socio-économique de la population touchée par la crise
project_objective:
Le projet a pour objectif de contribuer à la relance économique dans la région du Lac Tchad afin d’assurer une meilleure intégration des réfugiés, retournés et déplacés ainsi qu’une cohabitation pacifique de ces populations avec les communautés hôtes. 
Pour cela le projet va créer des opportunités d’emploi et favoriser la cohésion sociale à travers des actions visant l’autonomisation et l’intégration socioéconomique des réfugiés, retournés, déplacés et communautés hôtes du Lac. Pour faire face aux problématiques, la stratégie de réponse aura pour objectif de construire la résilience en en en identifiant et réduisant les risques et catastrophe, en renforçant la protection des communautés et les dynamiques économiques locales afin d’éviter ainsi la décapitalisation de la zone de sa force productive et sociale. Il s’agira aussi de mettre à la disposition des jeunes, femmes et hommes des dotations de fonds pour leur offrir des opportunités d’emploi et de revenus plus décents. Enfin, des actions d’amélioration rapide de la gouvernance locale seront mises en place en vue d’améliorer la cohésion sociale en matière de résilience.  
Le premier résultat visé par le projet est l’amélioration des conditions alimentaires et nutritionnelles des retournés, réfugiés, déplacés et communautés hôtes. Pour cela les bénéficiaires seront appuyés en matière de production agro pastorale (formation, distribution des kits agricoles, foires aux petits ruminants), les filières porteuses de la zone seront identifiées puis appuyées, des séances de promotion des bonnes pratiques d’hygiène seront organisées en lien avec les activités de nutrition et enfin des jardins scolaires seront développés afin de transmettre les bonnes pratiques à adopter dès le plus jeune âge (R1).
Dans un second temps, les femmes et les jeunes (filles et garçons) seront appuyés afin de leur permettre d’accéder à une meilleure intégration dans le tissu économique de la zone du projet, favorisant ainsi leur autonomisation. Afin d’atteindre ce résultat des activités a haute intensité de mains d’œuvre seront développées en collaboration avec les autorités locales et les autres projets qui seront mis en place par CARE et ses partenaires. 100 groupements AVEC seront mis en place et appuyés grâce à des activités d’alphabétisation notamment. Le projet renforcera également les groupements AVEC mis en œuvre par des projets précédant grâce à des séances de recyclage.
Le projet appuiera également au renforcement des capacités des communautés cibles en matière d’adaptation et de réduction des risques de catastrophe et au renforcement de la cohabitation pacifique. 
Pour cela des études d’Analyse de la Vulnérabilité des communautés face à aux variabilités climatiques seront menées dans les trois départements d’intervention du projet, les capacités de mitigation des populations seront également renforcées grâce à l’organisation d’ateliers de Planning de Scenarii Participatifs. De même, des magasins de stockage seront construits afin de permettre aux bénéficiaires de conserver leurs récoltes, des conventions locales de gestion des ressources seront élaborées et des séances de promotion de protection de l’environnement seront mises en œuvre par les équipes.

project_name: Integrated Emergency WASH, Food Security and Education Services for IDPs and vulnerable host communities in Blue Nile
project_objective:
This proposed project aims to sustain, expand the provision of improved WASH, food security and livelihood, and Education services to conflict affected IDPs, returnees and vulnerable host communities in the localities (Al Kurmuk, Damazine, Rosaries and Geissan) in Blue Nile state. The project will address the WASH, FSL and Education needs of 25000 persons.
 This project will enhance and sustain access to improved drinking water and basic safe sanitation through drilling and installation of new HPs, rehabilitation of nonfunctional HPs, training of HP mechanics and provision of hand pump maintenance tool sets. WASH activities will reduce overcrowding at host community water sources that are partially utilized by IDPs – i.e. the intervention will contribute to improved social cohesion between the IDPs and host communities. Aiming at enhancing access to safe basic sanitation facilities for the IDPs, especially those will be affected by AWD, the project interventions will include construction of school latrines; building the capacity of communities through training of WASH committees on water resources management; establishment and support of sanitation clubs; conduct of sanitation awareness campaigns; provision of hand washing facilities; training on CHAST approaches; and water quality monitoring and testing. Hygiene promoters training will be key part of the project activities to facilitate safe knowledge and practices transfers to lead beneficiaries towards sustainable behavior change and adoption of good hygiene practices. To preserve the natural environment, the project contains solid waste management, vector control, and environmental friendly technologies will be adopted.   In FSL sector the project will provide varied interventions to support livelihoods of vulnerable displaced and host communities that have suffered widespread conflict and violence. The proposed project will achieve this through provision of emergency agricultural inputs and services which include distribution of food crops and vegetable seeds, tools and extension service; provide emergency livelihoods training and start up kits, free animal vaccination as part of emergency livestock inputs and veterinary services that will be provided to the IDPs, formation and support of women farmer associations, and natural resources conservation and management. 
In Education sector, the project will focus on the construction and rehabilitation of both girls and boys government schools, aiming at creating a child and education friendly environment with maximum enrollment and minimum drop outs. Quality of education will be enhanced through teacher trainings and provision of reaching aids e.g. quality furniture for teachers and schools, learning and recreation kits and improved water and sanitation services.
