project_name: prevention of undernutrition in children aged 6-23 months, pregnant and lactating women and girls in vulnerable areas of the North West and South West region
project_objective:
The consequences of the various humanitarian crises in Cameroon are aggravating factors for the deterioration of the already fragile nutritional status of affected populations. Indeed, the prevalence of stunting in children under 5 is above the WHO serious threshold of 30% in all regions affected by humanitarian crises and rates of acute malnutrition do not show significant changes for several years and remain on the poor thresholds. Children under the age of 5 with acute malnutrition are more likely to die than their healthy peers. 
Pregnant and lactating women are also particularly affected because they have limited access to adequate quality and quantity of food in a context of limited access to basic social services. Added to this are the close links between the nutritional status of mother and child during the first 1,000 days of life (from conception to the age of two). In a context of massive displacement of people (internally displaced persons or refugees), women and young children are particularly exposed to poor living conditions and the accumulation of trauma that can affect practices feeding infants and young children, in particular the ability of mothers to ensure optimal breastfeeding, further weakening the nutritional status of the already most vulnerable populations
The level of acute malnutrition in the North West and South West regions are not well known as access constraints has hampered the realization of a formal nutrition survey.  Nutrition indicators has been integrated into emergency food security assessment (EFSA) conducted in October 2019 and revealed a proxy Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) rates of 5.1% and 7.4% for the NW and SW regions respectively. Furthermore and prior to the crisis, the 2 regions were facing high levels of stunting and poor Infant and young Children feeding indicators with stunting prevalence of 36% and 28% in NW and SW respectively (MICS 2014), exclusive breast-feeding rates of 42.5% and 58.3% in NW and SW region respectively. Furthermore, the proportion of children who meet their minimum acceptable diet remains extremely low at less than 30% per cent.   
The nutrition situation is likely to deteriorate in the coming months since acute malnutrition in children aged 6-59 months is a direct outcome indicator of recent changes in the nutritional status which could be attributed to changes in food security, health and WASH situations among others considering that the displacements started in October/November 2017. 
WFP’s programme focuses on preventing malnutrition amongst the most vulnerable populations through strengthening supplementary feeding with focus on the first 100days of life. The programme targets all children aged 6-23 months and pregnant and lactating women and girls in food insecure household. The programme activities include:
1.Screening for malnutrition and referral of severe cases for treatment, Social and behavioral change communication in favor of appropriate  infant and young child feeding practices and other Family practices, distribution of specialized nutritious food to children aged 6-23months and Pregnant and lactating women and girls(PLWGs) and promotion of the use of the blanket feeding platform for provision of complementary services including immunization, micro-nutrient supplementation, deworming, malaria and other childhood illnesses prevention, family planning etc
WFP in 2020 intends to target about 40,000 beneficiaries across all 6 regions ( North west,24150 and South west15,400 with the package of malnutrition prevention activities

project_name: Renforcement de la surveillance épidémiologique pour la prévention du choléra et des autres épidémies dans la région du Nord Cameroun
project_objective:
La région du Nord Cameroun est affectée par une épidémie de choléra depuis le 18 mai 2018. Cette épidémie a déjà fait 1209 cas avec 62 décès. Cette épidémie s’est étendue dans la région de l’Extrême-Nord (350 cas avec 16 décès) puis au Tchad. Le principal facteur engendrant l’épidémie est un faible accès à l’eau potable ainsi qu’aux dispositifs d’assainissement. Bien plus, une analyse des données de l’épidémie a montré que 50% des décès ont eu lieu en communauté et de même, que les décès hospitaliers sont survenus dans les 2h ayant suivi l’admission dans une formation sanitaire. Ceci dénote une détection et une arrivée tardive des cas dans les formations sanitaires ainsi qu’une insuffisance de sensibilisation des populations sur la conduite à tenir lors de l’apparition des premiers symptômes.
Afin de sauver des vies en détectant précocement les épidémies et en menant des actions de riposte à temps il est indispensable, dans la région du Nord, de renforcer la surveillance à base communautaire. Ce projet se propose d’une part de renforcer les capacités des relais communautaires et à les motiver pour la détection et au référencement précoce ainsi que pour la sensibilisation des populations, et suivre l’action des relais communautaires d’autre part. 
Les bénéficiaires directs de l’assistance sont évalués à 33 511 personnes dont 17090 femmes et 14 744 enfants de moins de 16 ans qui sont les plus affectés en situation d’épidémie.

project_name: Improving Access to Timely and Equitable Health care to the affected populations of the North and South West regions of Cameroon
project_objective:
The North West and South West regions of Cameroon are affected by a complex humanitarian crisis that is hindering access to essential protection, education and health services for an important part of the population. In most of affected areas, health services are not available or even of poor quality. The present project aims to reduce excess morbidity and mortality of internal displaced population (IDP) in the North West and South West regions of Cameroon affected by the humanitarian crisis by providing an integrated quality health assistance. The project will target 345,105 IDPs, 249,222 members of host communities (51% of this target are women, 16% are children under 5, and 11% are people over 60 years old). The areas of intervention are Fako, Meme, Manyu, Ndian and Kupe - Muanenguba divisions in the South-West, Mezam, Momo, Bui, Ngo-ketunjia and Boyo in the North-West region, Mungo and Wouri in the Littoral region and in the West region, Menoua, Mifi, Ndé and Noun divisions. The project will emphasize on timely access to equitable health care for men and women (taking into consideration the distance to the closest health facilities for women, children under 5 and people above 60) and quality of interventions (assistance by skilled attendant, referral of cases).
Given that a huge portion of the affected population has been displaced, most the assistance will be provided through mobile clinics to attain populations in their new settlements. An emphasis will be laid on community-based health interventions to strengthen the EWARS in the box project already implemented to get information on potential disease outbreaks as well as cases requiring assistance such as pregnant women. A special attention will be given to person with disabilities to ameliorate their access to health services and care.

project_name: Sustaining resilience of children affected by conflict in North-east Nigeria
project_objective:
The UNICEF Child Protection project, in line with the Minimum Standards for Child Protection and Gender-Based Violence in Humanitarian Actions, will focus on strengthening access to quality preventive and responsive services that address the needs, rights and dignity of children and their caregivers’ in the conflict affected states of Adamawa, Borno and Yobe. This project will ensure that child protection in emergencies response prioritizes the most vulnerable and at-risk children and their families.  
The project is designed with the understanding that investment in the well-being of conflict-affected children and women in North-east Nigeria through coordinated response is instrumental in protecting their rights and contributes to the achievement of SDG 16, in particular targeting 16.2. 
Building on previous experiences and lessons learned, this project aims to prevent violence against children and women. The project will empower affected communities to break the culture of silence and bring about significant change in social norms through awareness raising. In addition, project actions will help strengthen the social service workforce to improve the quality and coordination of response. UNICEF will specifically target children affected by or at-risk of abuse, exploitation, neglect and violence against children. The general community, community leaders, families, parents and caregivers will also be targeted.   
Results will be achieved by providing integrated child protection case management services for children affected by conflict including unaccompanied and separated children and delivering quality socio-economic reintegration services to children formerly associated with armed groups as well as other vulnerable children and their families. 
Conflict-affected children will have access to community-based mental health and psychosocial support services (MHPSS) including and structured recreational activities and adolescents’ life skills education. The project will also contribute to strengthening capacity of service delivery to GBV survivors. Child survivors of GBV will in addition have access to comprehensive minimum life-saving GBV services including health, psychosocial and safety services.

project_name: Prevention of  morbidity and mortality among women and children in the drought affected districts
project_objective: This project aims to prevent morbidity and mortality among women and children in the priority districts affected by drought. Procurement of essential medicines, commodities and supplies is an important aspect of the response activities by UNICEF. This will enable a targeted 3,042,251 people to have access to  health services ensuring there are no stock outs of essential medicines in all health facilities. To reduce the under five mortality rate, UNICEF will conduct capacity building trainings on case management and proper referrals of childhood illnesses among Health Workers and Community Health Workers and procure and preposition vaccines for routine immunizations and the Solar Direct Drive(SDD) Refrigerators within these districts. In addition UNICEF, will conduct activities to reduce the proportion of children born without assistance of a skilled health personnel. These include, conducting capacity building for Basic Emergency Obstretric and newborn care (BEmONC) and Emergency Triage and Treatment (ETAT) to health care workers as well as training CHWs on proper  referrals to health facilities for safe delivery among pregnant women. In addition UNICEF, will support and compliment the Ministry of Health and Child Care with real time data collection from the health facilities using a Rapid Pro System

project_name: Emergency nutrition response to save life and protect nutritional status of the most vulnerable rural and urban populations affected by drought and economic crisis in all 56 rural and 2 urban districts of Zimbabwe.
project_objective: This project considers the vulnerabilities of rural and urban populations as a result of multiple hazards, mainly drought, floods and disease outbreaks worsened by the on-going economic crisis. The primary attention is given to children under five years at risk of dying due to acute malnutrition, providing life-saving nutrition treatment to 36,038 children, and protecting the nutritional status of 606,349 children under five years and pregnant and lactating from deteriorating. UNICEF will therefore target all 56 districts, included 25 districts with a high intensity nutrition intervention package, across all the country’s 8 provinces and urban centres of Harare, Bulawayo and Chitungwiza. The High Intensity package will include all the emergency response activities from intensive community level screening, including campaigns, acute malnutrition treatment, IYCF, Micronutrient supplementation as well as cluster coordination at sub-national level.

project_name: Zimbabwe WASH Humanitarian Response
project_objective:
The economic crisis in Zimbabwe is affecting household economies, with disproportionate impacts on the poorest and most vulnerable, who resort to harmful coping mechanisms. This crisis combined with climate shocks (extreme rainfall and prolonged drought) and epidemics (cholera and endemic typhoid) continues to deepen the humanitarian situation in Zimbabwe. Tropical Cyclone Idai affected the population in the Provinces of Manicaland, Masvingo and Mashonaland East, who continue to require humanitarian assistance, mainly the internally displaced persons in temporary camps or living with host families. Continuing drought conditions is impacting nearly 5.5 million people (including ~2.6 million children) in rural Zimbabwe who are in urgent need of humanitarian assistance and protection especially during the critical period January to March 2020 as food and water security are threatened. A total of 2.2 million people in urban areas are cereal insecure, and about 1.5 million households are living below the Food Poverty Line and are unable to meet their basic needs. 

In rural areas, of the 55,593 water sources tracked by the rural water information management system (RWIMS), only 30% are with water, functional and protected.  According to ZIMVAC 2019 report, sixteen percent (16%) of households have to travel more than 1km to fetch water from the nearest primary water source and 32% over 500m. This means access to safe water and practice of good sanitation and hygiene is compromised increasing the risk of diarrheal diseases

Women and girls face a heightened risk of protection concerns and loss of education due to socio-economic roles, including supporting vulnerable family members and migrating to cities. In Zimbabwe, it is the role of the female members to ensure that the family is fed and that there is sufficient water for the family. In times of scarcity, women and girls travel long distances to fetch water and may be predisposed to dangers of wild animals or rape. Nationally about 83.4% of women bear the responsibility of fetching water for the household.  Furthermore, time taken to fetch water may compromise the children’s participation in school. 
In urban areas electricity and chemical supply challenges have led to a significant decrease in piped water supply leading populations to higher reliance on unsafe sources and increased vulnerability for girls and women. Water production for Harare had reduced by half in September 2019, compared to the same period last year. This has increased reliance on alternative water sources, many of which are unprotected and pose a risk to diarrheal diseases. Diarrheal diseases have been increasing in Harare (September - November) with significant concerns in cholera hotspot suburbs. Thus, the risk of water-borne disease outbreaks is high.

 Based on the above triggers, UNICEF will carry out the following interventions to achieve the three Sector Objectives:
•	Rehabilitation/upgrading/ construction of strategic water points with a focus of maximizing use of perennial water sources to cover needs of institutions (schools, health centres) and vulnerable communities
•	Improving safe hygiene and sanitation practices, with a focus on participatory health and hygiene education in institutions (health facilities, schools) and communities with high malnutrition rates. This will include training of Environmental Health Technicians (EHTs), Village Health Workers (VHWs) and Community Health Workers (CHWs) supporting community-based counselling of caregivers on infant and young child feeding practices on critical lifesaving WASH messages / hygiene practices. May also entail provision of temporary latrines/ mobile toilets where appropriate
•	Distribution of WASH hygiene kits targeting care givers of severe and moderate acute malnourished children
•	Strengthening coordination and surveillance mechanisms at national and sub-national levels

project_name: Strengthening GBV risk mitigation and multi-sectoral survivor-centered GBV response for hard to reach women and girls in 26 most vulnerable districts
project_objective:
The vulnerability of women and girls to GBV is heightened in the Zimbabwean multi-hazard humanitarian crisis, where violence and discrimination directly related to the emergency crisis exacerbates pre-existing, persistent gender and social inequalities, as well as traditional harmful socio-cultural practices. Women and girls are disproportionately affected by the protection consequences of the climate change and economic hardship related challenges. As a result of these multiple factors, more than 1,255,000 women and girls will face increased risks of exposure to GBV in 2020. 
GBV vulnerability assessments conducted between August and November 2019 reported that drought is contributing to modify daily routine patterns (e.g. water fetching and firewood collecting) which forces women and girls to walk long distance and spend long hours away from home, generating tension on the homestead, and leading to increased IPV. In the eastern provinces, where Apostolic faith sectarianism is predominant, girls are increasingly exposed to early marriage, in an attempt to appeal spirits responsible for the drought and economic hardship. Bordering towns also represent hotspots for GBV, as women and girls are exposed to trafficking and illegal migration, while female headed households become the most frequent target for SEA. IDPs in the eastern provinces continue to face increased GBV risks as they continue to be hosted at temporary camps with limited GBV risk mitigation measures. Women and girls with disabilities are also among the most vulnerable to GBV risks, as three times more prone to sexual gender-based violence, compared with others. 
The protracted drought, compounded by the economic crisis, contributes to constraining the capacity of survivors to sustain transport fees to reach services. The gradually decreasing availability of basic health services further contributes to the pre-existing critically low access to Clinical management of sexual violence. From January to October 2019, 7.971 cases of Sexual violence were reported to health facilities (Data source: HMIS), with only 27.8% of total cases reporting within 72h. When available, GBV multi-sectoral services remain fragmented, and mostly available at provincial and district level, often resulting out of reach for those living in most remote areas. The proliferation of traditional healing systems deriving from the health system constraints, also results in an increased GBV risk (sex for treatment fee).
In order to respond to the heightened GBV concerns, UNFPA with support from international and local NGOs will scale up GBV mitigation and response interventions targeting a total of 323,040 individuals in 26 districts among the most vulnerable to GBV and SEA. The proposed interventions aim at: 
1)	Enhancing effectiveness of community-based GBV risk mitigation mechanisms; 
2)	Strengthening the availability and accessibility of life saving multi-sectoral survivor-centered GBV services for GBV survivors in the most hard to reach areas 
3)	Improving the capacity of GBV specialized and non-specialized humanitarian actors to integrate GBV and PSEA interventions across programs, to avoid unintended GBV consequences and ensure DO-NO Harm.

project_name: PROJECT REVISED - Provision of life-saving curative nutrition services for crisis-affected displaced populations and their host communities in Somalia
project_objective: IOM's 2020 HRP nutrition project will contribute to the reduction of emergency levels of acute malnutrition through an integrated approach for management for Severely Acute Malnutrition (SAM) in children under 5 years. Outpatient Therapeutic Programme (OTP) services for SAM treatment will be integrated into all of IOM’s static and mobile primary healthcare facilities across Somalia. In addition to reduction of SAM cases, the project will improve family and community capacity to promote appropriate infant and young child feeding (IYCF) practices, as well as provide micro-nutrient supplementation and link to immunization services particularly measles vaccination. The project will ensure effective referral mechanisms to and from other nutritional services. The project will target 86,000 children (43,860 girls and 42,140 boys) aged 6-59 months living in IDP settlements and their host communities. A further 12,500 pregnant and lactating mothers will benefit from learning and adopting proper IYCF practices, with continued counseling and follow-up. The project is aligned with protection mainstreaming to ensure safety and dignity for affected populations without causing harm; there will be meaningful access, accountability and participation of beneficiaries in the delivery of nutrition services. The project will be a part of an IOM integrated emergency response program consisting of nutrition, health, WASH, CCCM, shelter, NFI, and protection activities.

project_name: Maternal and Child Nutrition Emergency Response in South Sudan.
project_objective:
According to the recent Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) analysis, 6.35 million people (54 per cent of the population) are classified in Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse acute food insecurity, among whom an estimated 1.7 million people are facing Emergency (IPC Phase 4) acute food insecurity and 10,000 people are in Catastrophe (IPC phase 5) in August. In the period of September to December 2019, seasonal harvests become available with an estimated 4.54 million people (39 per cent of the population) likely to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse acute food insecurity. Projection of January to April 2020, the food security situation will deteriorate and an estimated 5.5 million people (47 per cent of the total population) are likely to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse acute food insecurity. Moreover, the overall nutrition situation during the lean season of 2019 is worse compared to same period in 2018. The prevalence of acute malnutrition has increased significantly from 13.3 per cent in 2018 to 16.2 per cent in 2019 which is above the 15 per cent emergency threshold. 

UNICEF and implementing partners will support preventive and lifesaving nutrition interventions through provision of maternal, infant and young child nutrition (MIYCN), treatment of children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM), capacity building and robust information systems nationwide. UNICEF will respond in collaboration with sister UN agencies and NGOs to avert a life-threatening nutrition situation in South Sudan in 2020 using a multisectoral approach with health, WASH, Food Security and Livelihood (FSL), Education and Child Protection interventions. These cross-sectoral linkages will result in optimum synergetic effect to contribute not only in reduction of acute malnutrition but also chronic malnutrition – stunting and micronutrient deficiencies.

Given the current nutrition situation and in response to humanitarian needs in South Sudan, UNICEF and nutrition implementing partners have projected to reach 1,098,241 pregnant women and caregivers of children below the age of 24 months and 268,045 children with SAM. The estimated total cost of delivering the UNICEF nutrition project is estimated USD 57,484,671 for the year 2020.

project_name: PROJECT REVISED-WHO Health Emergency Preparedness and Response in Somalia
project_objective:
In alignment with HRP Strategic Objective #1: Physical and mental well-being”, herewith is a summary of WHO interventions:

Intervention A: Support Emergency Preparedness and Response Capacities of the Somali Health Sector: The project will contribute to strengthening the health system’s ability to withstand and cope with recurrent shocks and disasters. Its purpose is to build preparedness and response capacities of health authorities at all levels, as well as health cluster partners who provide services to Somali communities. In this respect, this intervention will seek to: (i) finalize national action plan for health hazards; (ii) training of senior level managers from health authorities on public health risk assessment and development of contingency plans; (iii) train 100 health workers from health cluster partners on public health risk assessment and development contingency plans; (iv) provide epidemic prone disease case management training to health workers from selected health facilities; and (v) support establishment and functionality of health emergency units at federal and state levels. 

Intervention B: Expand the Early Warning Alert and Response Network (EWARN) for Epidemic-Prone Diseases in Somalia: Somalia is prone to epidemic disease outbreaks due to protracted conflict which has led to a total breakdown of health systems and displacement. People in IDP (internally displaced persons) camps have limited access to safe water and proper sanitation, which predisposes them to disease outbreaks, especially cholera, measles and malaria. Early detection and notification of epidemic disease alerts which are supported by real time responses can lead to a reduction in morbidity and mortality. To this end, this intervention will (i) strengthen existing EWARN reporting facilities; and (ii) expand the number of reporting facilities which report through the EWARN system.

Intervention C: Health Emergency and Resilience Building in Somalia: In line with the objectives of the “Somalia Recovery and Resilience Framework”, this project aims to respond to immediate, lifesaving needs of vulnerable communities in Somalia, as well as strengthen resilience in health across the country by: (i) responding to immediate, lifesaving needs of vulnerable communities; (ii) strengthening health resilience through health education and promotion at community level; (iii) preventing and responding to outbreak-prone diseases, including vaccine-preventable disease outbreaks; and (iv) enhancing the capacity of local health workers to be equipped with the skills and knowledge necessary for providing relevant health services.

Intervention D: Improving Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) care for conflict affected persons in Somalia: MHPSS services are largely non-existent in Somalia. Moreover, in a health system where formal institutions are ill-equipped to deal with such problems, affected individuals often resort to harmful coping strategies, (e.g. self-medication, substance abuse), which worsen mental health and the psychosocial effects, and reinforce existing stigmas around mental illness. In alignment with the Inter-Agency Standing Committee on Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in Emergency Settings, this intervention will seek to ensure that: (i) health professionals and community health workers in conflict-affected communities gain professional-level capacity to deliver MHPSS services (including youth-centered and gender-sensitive services); (ii) persons with mental illness and psychosocial issues in conflict-vulnerable communities are provided with socially inclusive MHPSS services through community-based psychosocial support approaches and health service delivery; and (iii) community awareness on mental health/substance abuse, stigmatization, harmful behaviors and negative coping mechanisms that drive conflict is increased, thereby empowering communities to effect positive change through peer sensitization/education.

project_name: Improving access of vulnerable population to life saving non communicable diseases prevention and treatment services in conflict affected districts of Libya.
project_objective: The primary goal of this project is to reduce avoidable morbidity, mortality and disability as a result of NCDs complications and mental health disorders through supporting existing health facilities. The project establishes an improved access of vulnerable people including migrants, displaced families, returnees and people with special needs to quality health service that will include treatment of NCDs. In this project, WHO will strengthen the capacities of the health facilities with the provision of basic and supplementary medical equipment for the treatment of NCDs. In addition to strengthening MoH capacity on managing NCDs during emergencies as well as pre and post emergencies.

project_name: Provision of front-line services to ensure girls and boys aged 3 - 18 (40 percent girls) in humanitarian situations have improved access to safe and protective education services in South Sudan
project_objective:
The project is planned to support education services of IDPs, returnees and host community children in South Sudan. The main goal of the project is to ensure girls and boys aged 3-18 years (40 percent girls), adolescents/ youth affected by conflict have improved access to safe and protective education services. Train teachers (male and female) and PTA/SMC members (male and female) for improved capacity and quality of education. The project will also ensure community engagement  through social mobilization and sensitization to support enrollment and school environment as well as contribute to the Education Cluster objectives.

Since the outbreak of the second conflict in July 2016 , South Sudan has been confronted with many challenges. These include large population displacements, skyrocketing hyperinflation, protracted civil conflict and severe food insecurity that made the country volatile. The humanitarian crisis, displacement, protracted conflict emergency, poverty, and livelihood insecurity are the main drivers leading to interruption of education (HRP 2020 Education Cluster Narrative).  The already fragile education system drastically deteriorated at both the systemic and service delivery levels. It is characterized by high numbers of out-of-school children and adolescents /youth, particularly those affected by conflict and other emergencies estimated to be 2.2 million (UNESCO 2018, Global Initiative on Out-of-school children: South Sudan Country Study). 

Through this project of frontline services, children (boys and girls), particularly the most vulnerable and those affected by conflict will have increased access to quality education services in safe and protective environments.

project_name: Psychosocial Support, care and protection from violence, exploitation and abuse for children affected by the North-West and South-West crisis in Cameroon
project_objective:
Since the crisis escalation in late 2017 the North-West and South-West regions have experienced a drastic deterioration of living conditions, putting children and women at high risk of various forms of abuses, exploitation and violence. Access to essential services has been severely curtailed due to insecurity, large-scale displacement, destruction or closure of health facilities and schools, withdrawal of implementing partners, and relocation of health, education, and social workers.
Girls and boys are the primary victims of the current anglophone crisis. This translates into serious violations of their fundamental rights and constant insecurity, causing both visible and invisible trauma in the short and long-term, separation from their families and limited access to basic social services such as education, for the past three years. Being direct or indirect witnesses of violence linked to the conflict, their wellbeing, both physical and psychological, is fundamentally at stake.

An estimated 279,545 children are currently displaced in the North-West and South-West region (Multi-Sectoral Needs Assessment (MSNA), September 2019). This is in addition to the estimated 120,113 children from the NWSW displaced in the neighbouring Littoral and West regions (October 2019 MultiSector Rapid Assessment (MIRA), OCHA). 

In order to protect children from violence, abuse and exploitation, as a priority and main intervention, UNICEF will work on the offer of services and provide psychosocial support to 79,431 children including 40,510 girls affected by the conflict through Psychosocial Support Units, youth clubs and Psychosocial First Aid in urban, peri-urban and hard to reach areas. Psychosocial support will be provided to caregivers as well to the extent possible and when necessary so that they are better equipped to protect their children. 
As a direct corollary, an estimated 1,630 unaccompanied and separated children (UASC) are foreseen to be identified during the implementation of the project with an estimated number of 831 girls. All the 1,630 children will benefit from alternative care arrangements, support and individual follow-up while due to the difficult access and insecurity UNICEF plans to reunify a minimum of 163 unaccompanied or separated children with their family.
UNICEF will complement its support to children activities, work on the demand side with awareness raising and prevention activities at community-level. Concretely, UNICEF with its implementing partners will run sensitization campaigns with the aim to reach out to 158,863 persons with specific attention to parents to pass on messages on child protection in emergencies, trauma early warning signs for children, effects of family separation, GBV and other types of violence children are at risk of at the community level so that parents and community members can play an active role in child protection in emergencies.
UNICEF and its partners will also provide support to an estimated 2,418 conflict-children who do not have a birth certificate, as they are particularly vulnerable to various forms of discrimination and abuse because of the lack of birth certificates.
UNICEF as lead of the Child Protection Area of Responsibility will continue to lead the child protection in emergency sub-cluster in Buea with an antenna in Bamenda, in order to consolidate the coordination and ensure alignment and complementarity of interventions in the field of child protection.
