project_name: Prevention and Response to Child Protection violations in communities affected by humanitarian situation induced by multi-hazards  in Zimbabwe
project_objective:
Child Protection Sector estimates that 1,206,804  girls, boys, adolescents and women will be in need of  protection services as a result of humanitarian hazards affecting Zimbabwe.

UNICEF in partnership with several Civil Society Organisations, child protection networks, networks for specially vulnerable children, government departments including Department of Social Welfare, Judicial Service Commission, Victim Friendly Unit, Legal Aid Directorate will require additional resources to  target more than  422,000  in 35 priority districts in the  country.  The multi-hazards include possible floods, hails storms and mudslides, diarrheal disease outbreaks, prevailing food insecurity induced by drought and hyperinflation on basic food commodities.  UNICEF – as cluster lead has made an situation analysis with regards to  child protection risks and   caseloads. Data from the Victim Friendly System indicates more than 20% increase in cases that have gone through the system compared to the same period in 2018.  A 24% increase in reported child abuse cases and a 20% increase in reported child sexual abuse for 2019. According to the Legal Aid Directorate of Zimbabwe, quarter 3 of 2019 saw the highest caseload of children in contact with the law needing legal aid. Most cases reflect the increasing number of children in street situations trying to survive by committing petty crime. The country’s Civil Court also recorded a 50% increase in claims for child maintenance support submitted to court system, mostly by single mothers. Child placements in residential care has increased by 31%.

project_name: Increasing Access to Emergency Obstetric Care and other Maternal Health Services to Pregnant Women at High Risk of Developing Obstetric Complications in 16 Most Drought-Affected Districts of Zimbabwe
project_objective:
Zimbabwe is among countries worst affected by drought in Eastern and Southern Africa. According to inter-sectoral needs assessment undertaken in 2019 from October November, 465,000 women are in need of maternal health services in the 16 most drought-affected districts in Zimbabwe. Identified districts are Bulawayo Urban, Chitungwiza, Harare Urban, Buhera, Chipinge Rural, Makoni, Mutare Rural Mutare Urban, Mazowe, Goromonzi, Hurungwe, Zvimba, Chiredzi Rural, Gokwe North, Gokwe South and Gweru. The affected districts have higher needs for maternal health services compared to other drought affected districts. 

Pregnancy is a critical period during which maternal nutrition has a major effect on a mother’s and baby’s health. Lack of adequate nutrition of good quality and quantity during pregnancy have adverse impacts on both the mother and her foetus. Maternal malnutrition increases the risk of gestational anaemia, hypertension, miscarriages and foetal deaths, pre-term delivery and maternal mortality. For newborn, it can cause low birth weight, foetal intrauterine growth retardation that may have long-term consequences on newborn development and quality of life. The deteriorating economic environment has led to industrial action by health service providers (nurses and doctors) leading to a serious human resource crisis in many parts of the country, thus constraining access to health care services, especially maternity services. This is further aggravated by the aging and malfunctioning health care equipment in most health facilities. The prevailing drought coupled with the deteriorating economic environment is likely to lead to constrained household income. The limited resources available will result in relegation of SRH from the household priorities; diverting resources towards maternity and health care needs such as transportation, consultation fees and medicines to other immediate and more pressing needs such as food. This limits access to health care services and the much needed ante-natal and post-natal care, thus predisposing women to complications as normal contact with health service providers is disrupted. Pregnant and lactating women are also exposed to GBV due to reduced household income.

This project seeks to strengthen management of Emergency Obstetric and Neonatal care services in health facilities within the respective districts. The project will in addition, strengthen life-saving primary health care services by supporting Maternity Waiting Homes for high risk pregnant women in focus districts. Priority population groups for the lifesaving interventions will be women of reproductive age (15-49yrs) with a special focus on pregnant women and adolescent girls. 

The specific objective for the interventions is to decrease excess maternal mortality rate by 20% in 465,000 women in child bearing age in the identified 11 rural and 5 urban districts in Zimbabwe. 

Activities include 
1.	Rapid Health facility assessment and identification of women at high risk of developing obstetric complications
2. Supporting the developemnt of SRHR in emergency Operational Guidelines 
3.	Procurement, pre-positioning and distribution emergency RH kits, equipment and essential medicines
4.	Strengthening referral system to minimise delays in receiving skilled birth attendance
5.	Support health facilities to offer comprehensive Emergency Obstetric and Neonatal Care and cope with increased patient burden as a result of humanitarian crisis 
6.	Strengthening of health workers’ knowledge and skills providing Minimum Initial Service Package (MISP) for SRH in humanitarian/emergency
7.	Strengthen Maternity Waiting Homes’ capacity to provide antenatal care; serving as safe spaces for high risk pregnant women. 
8.	Provide technical support and quality assurance in the delivery of emergency obstetric and neonatal care services

project_name: Strengthening epidemic preparedness and response to drought affected areas in Zimbabwe.
project_objective:
The project seeks to contribute to the reduction of mortality and morbidity related to drought and disease outbreaks in drought affected areas of Zimbabwe through the provision of life-saving and emergency basic health services and interventions. The project will be done in collaboration with UNICEF, UNFPA, World Vision and other Health partners with the thrust of creating synergies among the agencies will be used to leverage health impacts.  
WHO interventions will seeks to strengthen epidemic preparedness and response for  3 million people in 52  drought affected districts in Zimbabwe. This will be achieved through supporting capacity enhancement of coordination structures at national, provincial and district levels. These structures include the Rapid response teams as well as the Civil protection committees at various levels. The project will also strengthen diseases surveillance for priority diseases conditions as well as malnutrition. To compliment surveillance efforts, the project will also support improving laboratory capacity through capacity building and procurement of reagents for the laboratory. Cases management for diarrhoeal conditions,  acute malnutrition and other drought related conditions and this will be carried out in collaboration with UNICEF. The project will also provide technical support for preventative vaccination campaigns which will be carried out in the 52 districts target for interventions. For improved programme quality, MOHCC  and health partners shall regularly carry out supportive visits to the facilities to ensure adherence to treatment protocols as well as reporting

project_name: Nutrition Emergency Response in Manicaland and Masvingo Provinces in Zimbabwe
project_objective: The nutrition emergency response aims to contribute to reduction in the prevalence of Global Acute Malnutrition  (GAM) in 6 districts, 3  in Manicaland Province namely Buhera, Chipinge rural and urban and Mutare rural districts and 3 in Masvingo Province namely Bikita, Gutu and Masvingo rural . The intervention will address six objectives that include providing leadership for a coordinated nutrition response, providing life-saving nutrition treatment of children affected by acute malnutrition, providing community level Infant and Young Child Feeding in Emergencies (IYCF-e) support to parents and caregivers of children below the age of two years, providing micronutrient supplements to children 6 to 59 months and pregnant women, improve decision making and effective nutrition response through strengthened data collection, reporting and information systems by at all levels and supporting distribution of essential nutrition commodities for prevention and treatment of acute malnutrition. Key indicators related to the six objectives will be tracked through Monitoring Evaluation, Accountability and Learning mechanisms in GOAL and Ministry of Health and Child Care's health information system. GOAL plan to prioritise key lifesaving actions whilst undertaking the necessary steps to better understand the evolving context, upon which to build supportive actions. In summary, the approach will include treatment for SAM & MAM in young children 6-59m through an expanded approach by supporting capacity building of health workers on treatment of acute malnutrition and supporting delivery of quality treatment services at health facility level. In addition, active screening for identification of acute malnutrition will be undertaken by community-based Village Health Workers (VHWs) following support for their capacity building on active screening. The VHWs then work with community leaders who will be engaged for social mobilisation of community to demand active screening and treatment services. Multiple micronutrient supplementation of high-risk groups, support for improved coordination at the district level and an IYCF-E training for health workers and VHWs will be supported. Review meetings at health facility and district level, to track progress and recommend key actions are an integral component of the response. Protection issues will be mainstreamed by ensuring that children identified with acute malnutrition at community and health facility level are further investigated for underlying protection issues through referral to Department of Social Services at district level and the Community Care Workers (CCWs) at community level and partners that are supporting protection issues directly in the districts of operation. In terms of Accountability to Affected Persons (AAP), GOAL will support the sensitisation of health workers on their role in AAP and support the proposal of mechanisms can be used at health facility level to ensure accountability. The Health Centre Committees (HCC) will be instrumental in handling the community issues. GOAL has a toll free line that will be shared at all levels for feedback to the organisation by affected persons.

project_name: Provision of essential non-food items and shelter assistance to most vulnerable families in north-west Syria
project_objective:
This project aims to support the SNFI response to the immediate needs of the most vulnerable displaced populations in northwest Syria through the (1) distribution of essential non – food items (NFIs) and (2) improve the basic infrastructure and shelter conditions in and out of camps. 

The distribution of NFI activities include: 

i.	Provision of essential NFI to at least 30,500 households (at least 183,600 individuals) in Northern Syria under the IOM direct distribution and rapid response mechanisms (RRM) in coordination with SNFI and CCCM Clusters (Sub activity 1.1.1). 

ii.	Providing procurement, storage and logistics support to the humanitarian partners operating inside Syria under the single source procurement pipeline (SSP) targeting around 40,000 kits to reach around 240,000 individuals (Sub activity 1.1.1)

iii.	Provision of at least 17,000 winter NFI kits and 102,000 winter clothing kits as complementary to the NFI package through in – kind and voucher modality reaching at least 102,000 individuals (Winterization) (Sub activity 1.2.1)

iv.	 Conduct pilot activities of multi-purpose cash assistance to the newly displaced families targeting around 1,800 households (at least 10,800 individuals) in the IDP locations where the needs are high and MPC is feasible considering the security, safety and other associated risks (Sub activity 1.1.1)


The basic infrastructure and shelter response will be done through:

i.	Replacement of 5,000 damaged family tents with new ones (Sub activity 1.3.2)
ii.	Ensuring 15,000 family tents are available to members of the CCCM and SNFI clusters for the contingency stock under the rapid response mechanisms (RRM) (Sub activity 1.3.2)
iii.	Provision of 1,000 Refugee Housing Units in IOM managed planned camp (Sub activity 2.1.2)
iv.	Rehabilitation of 2,000 unfinished shelter units (Sub activity 1.4.2)
v.	Repair of 3,000 damaged shelter units (Sub activity 2.1.1)
vi.	Repair of 1,200 damaged shelter units in collective centres (Sub activity 1.4.1)
vii.	Improving site infrastructure and facilities of 30 informal settlements. Infrastructure works include graveling of roads, graveling of tents ground as well as construction of drainage canals and culverts.  (Sub activity 1.3.2)
viii.	Winterization of 12,000 family tents through internal thermal insulation, external weatherproofing and ground raising and levelling (Sub Activity 1.2.2)

For the basic infrastructure and shelter component, the project will target 256,000 individuals living in Idleb and Aleppo governorates, northwest Syria with shelter solutions.

Overall, the project intends to reach 792,400 individuals targeting most vulnerable men, women, boys and girls and prioritize family members with high vulnerabilities according to the beneficiary selection criteria (IDP status, no source of income and support, persons with disabilities, elderly, female/single/child headed households) and identified priority geographic locations)

project_name: Food assistance for acutely food insecure households affected by climate shocks and economic crisis.
project_objective:
The highly volatile and rapidly deteriorating macroeconomic environment, combined with the poor agricultural season, continue to drive food insecurity in Zimbabwe. This year, the country is experiencing one of its worst food security crises in at least a decade. 
The 2018/19 agricultural season was characterized by the late onset of rains across the country and long dry spells.  To compound this situation, the country was hit by a devastating cyclone in March 2019, which caused severe damages to crop and infrastructure. Cereal production was estimated at 851,844 MT which is less than half the national requirement of 2.1 million MT. As of 21 November, the Government has stated that more than 800,000 MT maize are required to bridge the country’s grain deficit. Limited availability of foreign exchange to finance imports has created significant concerns for food availability in the country over the coming months with associated price increases further undermining purchasing power and food security for urban and rural households. 

To respond to the increased needs WFP intends to scale up assistance to reach 4.1m people (3.9m rural; 200k urban) classified as IPC 3/4 from January to April 2020 during the peak of the lean season and 1.5m (1.3m rural; 200k urban) people in May and June when the harvest will be starting and needs relatively reducing.  Further assistance will be provided from August to December 2020: an estimated 1m (800k rural; 200k urban) across August and September and 1.5 m (1.3m rural; 200k urban) between October and December 2020 as projections indicate below average precipitation for the current rainy season and a continued deterioration in macro-economic conditions suggesting that crisis conditions are likely to continue to affect portions of the population throughout the coming year. These figures will be revised based on the results of annual seasonal assessments in June/July 2020. 

 As part of this heightened response, WFP also intends to scale up coverage to reach all 60 rural districts in the country, including expanding coverage within already supported districts.

WFP stands ready to scale up assistance and is in the process of bringing food commodities into the country using a mix of local, regional and international procurement to meet the commodity requirement. 
The contracted transporter capacity is being doubled to reach 40,000 MT per month. In parallel, warehousing capacity is being adjusted in all locations.
In addition, WFP is engaging with 18 cooperating partners and augmenting its own staffing capacity in critical areas. Field Level Agreements are underdevelopment and on track to be ready in January for the scale up. Registrations are ongoing and partners are being trained on PSEA, Protection, SCOPE and other issues.  

WFP has a toll-free hotline, an on-site suggestion box and the active, visible presence of staff during the distributions. All complaints would be collected, referred and analysed on a timely basis and feedback provided to the complainant. WFP will adjust programmes based on complaints and feedback provided through these mechanisms.
Ad-hoc and regular monitoring will be conducted to assess any form of exploitation and manipulation of assistance including triangulation of data from the complaints and feedback mechanisms put in place. 
WFP and partners will continue to sensitize beneficiaries on the prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse and undertake dedicated trainings at Field Office level with WFP staff and Cooperating Partners.

project_name: Logistics Augmentation and Coordination to Support Humanitarian Operations in Syria
project_objective: WFP, as the lead agency for Logistics Sector, aims to oversee all the strategic objectives from the sector, namely: 1. provide logistics services (inclusive of surface transportation, transhipment, and warehousing) to humanitarian organisations responding to the Syria crisis; 2. maintain regional WoS interagency logistics coordination and information management in order to support the overall humanitarian response; 3. enhance the response capacity of humanitarian actors via dedicated logistics trainings and the procurement of necessary equipment; and 4. establish the United Nations Humanitarian Air Service (UNHAS) to provide safe, reliable and sustainable air access to beneficiaries for the humanitarian community, medical and security evacuations and facilitating the movement of light cargo where required.

project_name: Genral Food Assistance (GFA)
project_objective: WFP’s general food assistance covers the critical food needs of Syrian families across all 14 governorates.  Through GFA activities, WFP’s assistance ensures that basic food needs are met through a food basket that has a minimum of 1,500 kcal. In areas of high food insecurity such as North West Syria and the IDP camps of North East Syria, WFP aims to provide a 2,100-kcal basket.  As per the ongoing budget revision to the ICSP, WFP seeks to provide a monthly food ration to some 4.5 million people per month. General food assistance can be provided as  an in-kind food basket.. Given the increased food insecurity needs and the urgency to secure the GFA pipeline to ensure we can continue to reach 4.5 million people a month with a monthly food ration, for the purposes of this proposal WFP has decided to allocate this funding to GFA only.

project_name: Strengthening and provision of sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services for conflict-affected populations in Syria.
project_objective:
UNFPA will continue to work for the reduction of maternal and newborn morbidity and mortality as well as the provision of medical assistance and care to survivors of GBV. This will be achieved by ensuring (a) the availability, access to and utilization of integrated quality SRH services and information for women, men, girls and boys; (b) building the capacity of health workers and community health workers CHW; (c) reactivate and activate services in areas where no SRH services are in place; (d) ensure availability of essential equipment’s, medicines and supplies for delivery of SRH services and family planning;(E) Ensure delivery of complementary comprehensiveness service including the nutrition, MHPSS and NCD for targeted people in needs ;(F) strengthening referral mechanism with other actors and improve the coordination in national and sub national level.
UNFPA will take a Whole of Syria (WoS) approach with implementation taking place from Damascus and cross-border services from Turkey, achieving a country-wide response. . All 14 Syrian governorates will be targeted.
Vulnerable population groups in need to be targeted will include: Women and girls of reproductive age, Internally Displaced Population (IDP), host communities and returnees, adolescents as well as people living with disability (PwD).
The following key objectives will be pursed:
(1) Increasing access to life-saving and life-sustaining coordinated, equitable health services for those most vulnerable and in need:
• Increasing access to primary health care through the provision of essential primary health services to cover the health care needs of vulnerable populations, including Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, and Child Health (RMNCH).
• Improving access to secondary and tertiary health care for high risk pregnancy, emergency obstetric and newborn care (EmONC) cases, and acute cases which cannot access treatment in the area in which they reside, particularly rural areas.
• Strengthening and consolidating medical supply chains, ensuring availability of safe and quality medicines for essential primary health care, obstetric care, infectious diseases including HIV to prevent transmission from mother to child and family planning methods.Pre-positioning of emergency supply stocks at warehouse and health facility level in line with contingency scenarios for reduced access and increased level of hostilities requiring RH kits , pharmaceutical items and supplies.
• Supporting essential repairs, rehabilitation and equipping of health facilities providing public and specialized services, in particular in areas of most acute need , as well as facilities that receive referrals from areas of acute need.
(2) Strengthening health sector coordination and HIS, with an emphasis on enhancing protection and increasing access to health services and continue coordination within and across hubs, including thorough joint contingency and preparedness planning for changes in context.
(3) Engage in activities that support continuity of care, strengthening of community resilience, response to IDP movements and shifts in control; and beneficiaries participation all over the country.
UNFPA will continue to monitor the implementation of these activities based on the five principles of accountability to affected populations as well as UNFPA’s global results based monitoring framework. Monthly supervision visits will be done jointly with the partners in the national and sub national level by UNFPA staff and personnel subject to access and approvals. Third party monitors are used in the cross-border response.  Standardized tools including the supported services and supervision checklist are used to assess service availability/quality. Clinic registration data will be collated at least monthly. Beneficiary feedback (incl. complaints box, FGDs, exit interviews) will be collected where possible.

project_name: Providing life saving and resilience building interventions for vulnerable farming and pastoral communities in Darfur
project_objective:
The project will provide emergency agriculture and livestock-based livelihoods interventions and resilience building support for vulnerable farming and pastoral IDPs, returnees, and hosting communities in South, North, West, East, and Central Darfur states. Vulnerability of the target populations stems from the protracted crisis, the ongoing economic hardships at the macro and micro-levels and recent poor harvest because of localized droughts and pest infestations. This situation has led to high rates of acute and chronic food insecurity and malnutrition. FAO prioritized in a participatory manner 44 localities in the five states of Darfur based on the high degree of vulnerability to food insecurity and malnutrition.
This project will target 925,000 people among the most vulnerable communities including 277,500 returnees, 185,000 IDPs, and 462,500 residents. These interventions will benefit 283,050 women, 185,000 girls (less than 18 year of age), 271,950 men and 185,000 boys(less than 18 year of age). The proposed interventions are based on the basic and specific needs of the beneficiaries taking into account the factors of age and gender. The project will target about 35,000 elderly people among the adult population including persons with disabilities.
The project will follow the FSL Sector Strategy that follows the Multi-year Humanitarian Strategy adopted by the Humanitarian Country Team in Sudan for the period 2017-2020. The FSL Sector Strategy entails providing livelihoods-saving interventions and addressing the root causes of food insecurity and malnutrition to tackle all aspects of food security, including physical and economic access, availability and utilization of food and the stability of food systems through complimentary emergency life-saving and resilience building through agricultural and livestock-based livelihood interventions and income generating activities.
The project objectives are aligned with the FSL Sector objectives 1, which includes addressing immediate lifesaving humanitarian needs through emergency agricultural assistance including crop, livestock and veterinary inputs and extension services targeting 492,800 people. This will include as well building the capacity of governmental institutions and sector partners to improve preparedness and response for new emergencies. Under FSL Sector objective 2, the sector aims to restore and improve food and nutrition security and enhance self-reliance of the most vulnerable communities to cope with current and future shocks and stresses. Agricultural production will be improved through provision of climate-smart crop production, livestock and veterinary inputs and support to services. Similarly, small scale farmers will be targeted for reduced food losses and strengthened post-harvest techniques through improved food and crop storage and processing facilities. On and off farm livelihood assistance will be diversified and managed and coordinated to respond to food chain threats including animal and plant pests and diseases; In addition, communities will be involved in building, restoring and maintaining productive assets through cash and/or food for assets schemes. About 432,200 people (3,000 people will be targeted for cash transfer) will be targeted under Sector objective 2. Accountability to affected populations and environmental concerns will be mainstreamed into the proposed activities to reduce risk to GBV, respond to the needs of the target population, promote climate change adaptation measures and ensure implementation of environment-friendly interventions.

project_name: Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM): Mobility Tracking of IDPs, Returnees and other target populations in Sudan
project_objective:
In 2004, the International Organization for Migration began its Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) program to better support the Government of Sudan and its humanitarian partners. DTM was introduced in response to the need for accurate information on displacement and the identiﬁcation of beneﬁciaries for the delivery of humanitarian aid that arose in Sudan follow a series of crises that have affected Sudan since 2003. Following the implementation of DTM, IOM now has an established, accurate data collection system that provides displacement data in the areas most affected by conﬂict and disasters.

IOM has been working in close collaboration with the Humanitarian Aid Commission (HAC) and partners in the ﬁeld to establish a uniﬁed and systematic system to better track internally displaced populations and returnees in seven states in Sudan. Until 2018, IOM Sudan’s DTM program focused mainly on registration activities in response to requests from the Government and humanitarian partners to identify beneﬁciaries to better inform the delivery of humanitarian assistance (i.e. food vouchers by WFP). These registration activities have positioned DTM in Sudan as the key reference source of displacement data in the country.

As crisis levels within Sudan gradually reduce, and the situation broadly stabilizes the majority of the conﬂict-affected areas, there is a need to restructure the DTM program. Whilst there will continue to be a need to DTM to track displacement resulting from unpredictable events such as the ﬂooding in 2019, there are increasing  requirements in tailoring the operation to better suit the current situation of protracted displacement and return scenario. More speciﬁcally, there is the need to update displacement ﬁgures more frequently, comprehensively, systematically, and at regular intervals to ensure that data is continually collected, provides a meaningful resource and is available through IOM’s DTM system.

project_name: Providing Critical Multi-sector Support Services to Refugees

Promoting resilience building of vulnerable migrants and local communities to support improved  food and livelihood security through community based agriculture, livestock and income generating activities in Sudan
project_objective:
The project aims to strengthen the resilience and coping capacities of vulnerable migrants such as IDPs and returnees and their host community to enhance food and livelihood security as well as to mitigate the risk of malnutrition. This will be achieved through delivering agricultural, livestock interventions and alternative income generating activities. The planned activities will promote the synergy between agricultural production and nutrition requirements. The interventions will target the most vulnerable small scale farmers, IDPs, returnees and local communities with special attention to youths and women.  IOM will apply a right based, community centered approach to promote community initiative to respond to humanitarian needs and to ensure that planned interventions are met based on needs and rights of the vulnerable migrants and community to access to improved economic opportunities. 

The project will focus on eight localities and this includes: Umm Dukhun locality, Central Darfur, El Fasher locality, North Darfur, Geneina and Krenik localities, West Darfur, Rahad El Berdi and Um Dafug localities, South Darfur, Ghubaysh localitiy, West Kordofan State, and Doudeb locality, Red Sea State. Returnees, IDPs and local communities in these localities are vulnerable to food insecurity and limited livelihood opportunities due to limited purchasing power resulting from inﬂation and high food price. This contributes towards food insecurity alongside chronic and severe malnutrition. The identiﬁed localities suffered from the high prevalence in Integrated Food Security Phase Classiﬁcation (IPC) phase 3 (Crisis) and/or phase 4 (Emergency) further highlighting the need for timely and adequate livelihood interventions to address food insecurity, strengthen community resilience to protect lives, and move towards economic self-suﬃciency.

Under HRP 2020, this project ﬁts with the overall Outcomes 2. The planned interventions will include: (1) capacity training and inputs on agriculture for better local production addressing climate adaptation technique: (3) support sustainable livestock husbandry practice and veterinary services (2) small business support for youth and women on agriculture and other livelihood skills such as food processing activities. IOM has already established a good access to the most of target localities (Dourdeb, Krenik, Geneina, Um Dafug, El Fasher, Umm Dukhun) implementing community stabilization and durable solution initiative activities under UNDAF outcomes. The planned interventions will be delivered in a way to complement past and on-going activities implemented, thereby will support strengthening links between the HRP Outcome and UNDAF outcome.

project_name: Provision of lifesaving Sexual and Reproductive Health services to the most vulnerable populations in Sudan
project_objective:
It is vital that the suitable and timely Sexual and Reproductive Health SRH services are prioritized and made available in immediate as well as protracted crises, it is a mean for preventing morbidity and mortality and protecting the right to life with dignity. 
UNFPA jointly with partners, will ensure the provision of the Minimum Initial Service Package (MISP) for reproductive health in emergencies and transition to comprehensive SRH services as the situation allows.  MISP aims at reducing maternal and newborn mortality and morbidity, prevention and response to sexual violence, prevention of HIV transmission, reduction of HIV morbidity and prevention of unintended pregnancies, and sets the platform for comprehensive SRH services integrated in to primary health as soon as possible.  
All intervention of the MISP will be implemented simultaneously through coordinated actions with all relevant partners. In addition, the planned interventions prioritize the timely provision of Emergency Obstetric care and save delivery, support referral system, availability of and accessibility for Family Planning services, Clinical management of SGBV survivor’s, HIV and STIs prevention and response program, as well as timely access to Antenatal and postnatal care, and demand creation through awareness raising and educational activities. Morbidity such as Obstetric fistula will be given an especial attention by UNFPA. The intervention primarily targets women, girls in reproductive age, youth and adolescents, men and boys are also addressed.

project_name: Gender Based Violence prevention and response interventions to the most affected population in Sudan 2020.
project_objective:
UNFPA has a unique mandate to provide lifesaving support through coordination and implementation of integrated SRH services as well as GBV prevention and response.  UNFPA Sudan has committed to scaling up humanitarian response and national capacities to prevent and response to gender based violence, through effective, integrated and appropriate programs. The current changes in Sudan is opening new window for UNFPA as GBV sub sector lead and other humanitarian actors to introduce supportive environments in which the survivors rights and wishes are respected, their safety is ensured and they are treated and managed properly. In Sudan the main humanitarian needs resulted from different factors on top are the  insecurity and multiple conflicts namely in Darfur, BN and South Kordofan, add to that the  natural disasters inform of droughts and flooding as well as disease outbreaks. After a year of civil unrest and political change, humanitarian needs continue to rise. Some 9.3 million people – 23 per cent of the population – will need humanitarian assistance in 2020. The transitional government is prioritizing peace and ending the economic crisis, issues closely intertwined with the drivers of humanitarian need in the country. Women, children and elderly people represent almost 80% and remain most vulnerable. 
Through the proposed action, UNFPA will ensure that the affected population IDPs, returness, and vulnerable host community are actively engaged as partners in developing plans related to their protection and right based in nature. This approach involve direct consultation with women, girls, boys and men and those at risk to build community based protection networks.  Integration and strengthening of GBV services within the health facilities will be advocated for with the Health sector.

project_name: Livelihoods and Resilience for South Sudanese and Eritrean refugees in West Kordofan, South Kordofan White Nile and Kassala States.
project_objective:
Sudan is transition following deteriorating economic and political environment which saw the ousting of former regime and the establishment of a transitional government. In particular, the depreciation in Sudanese Pound and the hiking of prices of food and essential items, etc. have inevitably affected the lives and living standards of thousands of people including refugees who are currently struggling to make ends meet in their respective host communities across Sudan including South Kordofan State (SKS), West Kordofan State (SKS), White Nile State (WNS) and Kassala State. 

In September 2019, UNHCR population Dash Board estimates 859,286 South Sudanese refugees currently hosted in Sudan, out of which 364,269 are in SKS, WKS and WNS, while Kassala State hosts 124,125 Eritrean refugees. Hosing refugees in communities has occurred along with pressing needs thereby creating enormous pressure and competition in accessing available basic services and economic opportunities with triggers for conflicts if unabated. To make ends meet, refugees and vulnerable community members have resorted to ravaging forest resources such as the collection and sale of firewood, wild fruits, use of burnt bricks for shelter construction, etc. The situation has triggered the need for humanitarian assistance especially with fading absorption capacity of host communities. Unless something was done to abate the situation, it will reach a point where refugees and communities would no longer cope with the situation. Proposed intervention will focus on reducing the vulnerability of refugees (South Sudanese and Eritrean refugees) alongside other at risk groups affected by shocks, while seeking to support a gradual transition from humanitarian aid to self-reliance. Specific objectives are:
•	To improve refugees’ access to basic needs (food, clothes, medicine, shelter, etc.) through lifesaving emergency agriculture, temporal jobs and other sustainable livelihood activities.
•	To promote community resilience and enhance refugees’ access to lifesaving services through the provision of basic services and socioeconomic assets depleted as a result of overuse. 
•	To promote coexistence and social cohesion between refugees and different groups.
•	To support reforestation and renewable energy use in household meal preparation for refugees and host communities.

Intervention will support lifesaving through emergency agriculture and temporary job creation for refugees and host communities. The project will restore social services and socioeconomic assets depleted as a result of overuse due the presence of refugees in communities. The project will deliver social cohesion activities that will reduce friction and restore trust and confidence among refugees and other groups. 

Lessons from previous interventions informed that targeting individual refugees without the communities has limited impact and has potential to create conflict between refugees and host communities. Proposed intervention will be inclusive and community-based, ensuring direct support to refuges while enhancing the capacities of communities to sustain recovery and stability. 75% of assistant will go to refugees and 25% to host communities. This is a multi-year intervention that seeks for $22,189,000 to support 35,000 individuals (5,834 households) in four states.

Intervention will strengthen ongoing support by UNHCR and UNDP in targeted locations to maximize impact while paving way for humanitarian-development-peace nexus. Intervention will be area-based and multi-sectoral in approach.

Environmental safeguards will be incorporated in all aspects of the project activity to reduce vulnerability to climate change-induced risks. Intervention will promote improved natural resources management, efficient energy utilization and environmental protection through training on NRM and community environmental action plan (CEAP) development and implementation. The use of improved solar stove will be promoted.

project_name: Emergency Shelter and NFIs support to IDPs
project_objective:
The facilities are not self-sustaining and nor do they receive full support from the government; thus are dependent on shrinking support received from humanitarian partners 
UNHCR will continue to provide emergency shelter (ES) materials and non-food items (NFI) to people victims of newly displacedment. In situations of protracted displacement, UNHCR will provide ES/NFI support in case of new shocks, including natural disasters, floods or incidents of violence/attacks. Through policy advocacy with social protection stakeholders, primarily the Ministry of Security and Social Development and Ministries of Social Welfare, UNHCR will promote the integration of vulnerable IDPs in the social protection systems of Sudan, and the removal of legal or material discriminatory barriers to their access to essential protection services

project_name: Return, Recovery and Reintegration of Sudanese Refugees in Sudan
project_objective:
The conflicts in Darfur between 2003 and 2010 caused hundreds of thousands of Sudanese citizens to seek refuge in Chad where they were recognized as refugees on a prima-facie basis. They also found refuge elsewhere including South Sudan, Ethiopia, Egypt and other countries.  
With improvements in the security situation in most of the former conflict areas of Darfur, the Jebel Mara area and its ongoing armed clashes, being the exception, UNHCR anticipates as many as 20,000 refugees would register to return in 2020. The main return areas are Central, West and North Darfur. 
Therefore, UNHCR is expecting to facilitate their return from Chad. They will be going back to Central, North and West Darfur. It is also anticipated that majority of the Chadian refugees in Darfur will return to Chad, leaving only a small remaining residual group for which a local integration solution will be attempted. 
UNHCR and COR will continue to advocate the Local and Federal level authorities to facilitate access to land and documentation in Sudan, and families will be provided with cash grants for provision of shelter materials to re-establish their homes in Darfur. Individuals will be further provided with multi-purpose cash grants to facilitate the reintegration process and initiate livelihood opportunities.  After the provision of reintegration packages and protection services in the transit center, UNHCR and COR will facilitate safe and dignified movement of returnees from reception center to final return areas. The AGDM participatory assessment in return villages in West Darfur, has revealed the physical Security, SGBV and livelihoods as the major problem, followed by Education and community empowerment and self – reliance. 
Return areas in Darfur are generally underdeveloped and require reconstruction to ensure sustainable reintegration and peaceful sharing of resources and services among returnees and local communities.  As such, UNHCR will act as a catalyst for reintegration projects through UNHCR funded projects and existing coordination structures, including the Durable Solutions Working Group and Return, Recovery and Reintegration Sector, to improve access to basic services and enhance rule of law in return areas. In particular, returnees have indicated that water, education, protection and health are amongst their highest priorities. There is further need to enhance the capacity of communities to manage resources and resolve conflict peacefully, through maintenance of community-based protection networks, awareness raising sessions, and tailored community-based protection projects that benefit both return and host communities.

project_name: Réponse d’urgence aux besoins essentiels des ménages en insécurité alimentaire les plus vulnérables de la Grande Anse
project_objective:
Afin de répondre à l’urgence alimentaire et nutritionnelle et à la situation de vulnérabilité générale des ménages des communes d’ADH, Dame Marie et Les Irois, SI propose de conduire une intervention monétarisée en 2phases : un 1er round d'urgence composé de 2 distributions de cash à 4069 ménages et un 2nd round de 2 distributions « filet de sécurité »  de cash et coupons à 2035 ménages. 
En parallèle, le projet prévoit un dispositif communautaire favorisant l’acquisition et l’application de bonnes pratiques en matière d’alimentation, d’hygiène et de gestions des risques de désastres, afin de diminuer les vulnérabilités des ménages à la malnutrition et aux chocs climatiques récurrents. Cette activité met l’accent sur l’intégration et la participation communautaire tout en renforçant le rôle et l’implication des femmes dans la transmission et le partage des bonnes pratiques.
Enfin, SI participera à la mise en place d’une coordination efficace à travers l’autonomisation des autorités décentralisées sur la zone d’intervention. Les collecteurs de l’OSANGA travaillent actuellement en collaboration avec SI, et effectuent de relevés de prix sur huit marchés dans le département. Leurs capacités en termes de collecte de données de qualité, d’analyse et de remontée d’informations sont renforcées par l’organisation d’ateliers et un accompagnement continu. Les membres du BAC font également l’objet d’un appui afin d’accroitre leur implication dans les activités relatives à la sécurité alimentaire dans la zone. Les données collectées permettent l’élaboration conjointe de bulletins avec les institutions appuyées, favorisant la remontée d’informations au niveau national (CNSA).

project_name: Appui d'urgence  à la protection des moyens de subsistance des pasteurs et agropasteurs des régions de Tillabéry, Tahoua, Diffa, Agadez, Maradi et Zinder
project_objective:
Le projet vise à apporter une assistance aux ménages pastoraux vulnérables aux crises conjuguées (déficit pastorale et insécurité) à deux volets:   
⁕ Un volet urgence avec:
   -  Un appui conseil à travers des sessions de sensibilisation sur les conditions de déstockage, la formation sur l'amélioration de la valeur nutritive de la paille;
  - Un appui en aliment pour le bétail de 5700 tonnes à 38 000 ménages pastoraux et agropastoraux vulnérables, en nature ou sous forme de coupons après une analyse sommaire du contexte. Cela permettra aux pasteurs vulnérables, ayant en général au mieux une Unité Bétail Tropicale, d'acquérir une complémentation alimentaire couvrant les besoins d'animaux équivalants  à 10 petits ruminants (250 grammes/tête/jour) pendant 2 mois. En milieu rural, les petits ruminants sont notoirement reconnus comme une forme de thésaurisation sur pied pour les personnes vulnérables dont les femmes. Aussi, ces espèces y constituent le principal capital auquel les femmes ont un bon accès et un bon contrôle. Selon le Recensement Général de l'Elevage en 2007, près de 40% des ovins et de 55% des caprins appartiennent aux femmes et elles contrôlent les revenus issus de ces espèces dans 29.3% des cas (Enquête ECVMA 2011 de l'INS). 
  - 380 000 petits ruminants seront déparasités et vaccinés contre quatre pathologies dominantes au Niger (les charbons bactéridien et symptomatique, la Clavelée et la pasteurellose). En effet, les problèmes santé animale constituent l'une des principales contraintes de l'élevage au Niger, particulièrement celui des petits ruminants, exacerbées lors de crise.
  - Une distribution de CASH + d'un montant mensuel de 20 000 fcfa aux récipiendaires de l'aliment bétail pendant 2 mois pour prévenir une forte décapitalisation ou la vente partielle de l’aliment bétail reçu pour satisfaire d'autres besoins.

 ⁕ Un volet post urgence avec:
  - Un appui à l'autonomisation des personnes vulnérables (orphelin -enfant de moins de 14 ans ayant perdu son père-, femmes ou personnes âgées chefs de ménage, personnes vivant avec un handicap) par la distribution d'un noyau reproducteur de caprins. Cet appui leur permettra, au sortir de la crise, d’amorcer une activité pouvant conduire à leur épanouissement.
  - Activités Argent contre Travail : traitement de 6250 hectares aires de pâturage dégradées ou colonisées par des mauvaises herbes non ou peu appétées par les animaux et ouverture de 1750 kms de bandes pare-feu pour protéger les zones de bonne production.

⁕ Redevabilité et coordination des acteurs: 
  - Assurer la redevabilité par la mise en place ou redynamisation de comités villageois de veille pour le contrôle de la qualité de la mise en œuvre et la prise en compte des attentes des bénéficiaires;    
  - Renforcer la coordination des acteurs locaux pour une couverture efficiente des personnes en besoins;
  -  Appui au volet pastoral du groupe sectoriel de la sécurité alimentaire à travers particulièrement les évaluations, enquêtes, le système de veille et le partage d'informations relatives à l'élevage dans tout le pays ainsi que le renforcement de capacités sur les Normes et directives pour l'aide d'urgence à l'élevage (LEGS).

project_name: Promoting the inclusion and access of Children with Disabilities to education in the emergency context of the Gaza Strip
project_objective: The current context in the oPt is marked by imposed closures and the stop of peace negotiations between the Israelis and Palestinians. In the Gaza Strip, blockades and political divide continue to marginalize the population. In the 2020 Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO), the Education cluster estimates that children with disabilities are one the most affected by the protracted and acute crisis: they lack basic assistive devices that would facilitate their learning in the classroom and require psychosocial support (PSS) and remedial education. Since 2014, Handicap International (hereafter as HI) has strived to improve the access of children with disabilities to education in Gaza. In 2017, HI started directly supporting the capacity building of educational staff and implemented activities aiming to make schools more accessible. HI also provided specialized educational materials and developed technical guidelines on the inclusion of children with disabilities in education and developed an inclusive education practical manual. Besides, HI is supporting 3 special schools and 11 pre and primary mainstream schools in Gaza to develop child-friendly and accessible education environments, and to improve the delivery of adapted education services responding to children’s individual needs. In Gaza, the Middle Area and Rafah, HI develop emergency response plans providing psycho-social support, and organizes inclusive summer camps. Furthermore, HI closely collaborates with mainstream education service providers to build teachers’ capacities to adopt inclusive education strategies. Building on a two-fold strategy, the project’s objective is to increase the access to quality inclusive education for children with disabilities in improved education facilities. The first component focuses on community actors to identify and provide tailored services for out-of-school children with disabilities and their families to support children’s enrolment and continued attendance in school. The second component will aim at building the capacities of schools and teachers to respond to the needs of affected children. The project falls under the Humanitarian Response Plan’s (HRP) strategic objectives 2 and 3 and Education Cluster’s objectives 1) Increase equitable safe access to inclusive, quality educational services for vulnerable children and 2) Most vulnerable schools are supported in responding to potential emergencies through preventive measures, remedial programs and school-based psychosocial services. HI will financially and technically support three local implementing partners for the proposed project. The project will respond to the education cluster objectives through the identification of out-of-school children, the provision of personal support for children with disabilities: enhance their mobility, provide visual and hearing assistive devices, transportation, school kits, education materials and stationaries, school-based structured individual, and group psychosocial services. HI will also support the provision of holistic services through referrals to other stakeholders. Furthermore, HI will aim to develop an enabling educational environment through the provision of technical support for mainstream and special education service providers. These will be supported to respond to the needs of affected children through the development of adapted processes and tools benefiting both children with and without disabilities. HI will further provide educational materials, tools, and resources and create a welcoming and accessible educational environment for children with and without disabilities. The project will be implemented in partnerships with 3 local organizations in Gaza.

project_name: Treatment and Prevention of Malnutrition in Children Under 5 and Pregnant and Lactating Women & Girls in Sudan
project_objective:
The main objectives of this project are:

1. To ensure the provision of quality, lifesaving nutrition services for acutely malnourished children (boys and girls 6 - 59 months of age) and pregnant and lactating women (PLW) among highly vulnerable communities 
2. Improve equitable access to integrated program interventions for the prevention of under nutrition among affected communities

The project targets children aged 6–59 months and Pregnant and Lactating Women and Girls with specialized nutritious foods and social and behaviour change messages aimed at the prevention and treatment of acute malnutrition across selected states and localities in Sudan. 

A comprehensive package of food and non-food-based interventions are provided taking into account nutritional vulnerabilities. 

The proposed response from WFP is in line with the Nutrition Sector Strategy and with the Multi-Year Humanitarian Response Strategy of Sudan. Through this project, WFP will be responding to the nutritional needs of targeted beneficiaries under Outcomes identified by nutrition sector. 

With a particular focus on Do No Harm and Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) principles, WFP Sudan strives to enhance protection mainstreaming through the following priority areas: 1) Training and capacity building of key WFP and Cooperating Partners (CP); 2) protection risk analysis focused on safety, dignity and integrity of beneficiaries; 3) integration of protection indicators into program tools, notably Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E) tools; 4) design, implementation and adjustment of programs in line with identified protection concerns particularly for those disabled and with special needs; and 5) strengthened partnerships and coordination on protection issues.

project_name: Access to life-saving health services through strengthening local capacity to detect, prevent and control public health emergencies in all 18 States of Sudan
project_objective:
The World Health Organization (WHO) preparedness and response to health emergencies are aligned with the national health sector strategies and adheres to national and international standards. The focus of WHO and health partners will be providing life-saving free of charge health services to vulnerable populations affected by natural and manmade disasters through strengthening the locality and community level structures to prepare, detect and respond to all types of emergencies with public health consequences. 
The WHO in Sudan has well-established country office and 12 field offices located closer to the Federal and State Ministry of Health Offices across Sudan. Technical and operational support will be provided by the WHO to strengthen the SMOHs coordination and emergency response teams up to community level. The collection, centralization, analysis and dissemination of essential health data disaggregated by sex and age-groups will be maintained and strengthen by WHO field teams jointly with all partners. The WHO technical and cluster coordination team will ensure that the standard health cluster tools, such as Early Warning Alert and Response (EWARS), Health Resources Availability Monitoring System (HeRAMS), Who is doing What, Where and since When (4Ws), risk and vulnerability mapping, Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO), Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP), epidemiological briefings, periodic situational reports (SitReps) and health cluster bulletin are timely and regularly updated and utilized by health partners. 
The WHO procure and distribute free of charge medicines to support the NGOs and SMOH in dealing with humanitarian case load at all levels, while ensuring a rapidly revolving pipeline for addressing acute events in 2020. Rapid Response Kits (RRK) adapted to the protracted crisis in Sudan addresses specific needs of children (boys and, girls), women in general and women of reproductive age, men and elderly. In addition, medicines for case-management and laboratory regent for confirmation of outbreaks will be provided by WHO. Training of health workers on topics directly related to prevailing humanitarian situations such as on surveillance and case management and Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) will be provided based on the needs assessed. The project supports small repair and rehab of damaged health facilities; operational costs for scaling up the humanitarian health services as necessary. The project supports community mobilization to promote healthy behavior. Besides, the project adopts an integrated approach that facilitates access to health services to all age groups, male and female with their specific health needs adapted to the local cultural customs, including advocacy and synergic linkages with ongoing recovery-development interventions (GBV, FGM, Protection, FSL, WASH, Nutrition, NFI, and Education). 
Optimal capacity for early notification, investigation, confirmation and immediate response to public health threats (outbreaks) is another priority contributing to the health security of targeted groups and beyond. This is achieved through technical and operational support for EWARS, epidemic alert investigation and response operations by supporting the RRTs; supporting response vaccination campaigns and strengthening the routine immunization; providing reagents and medicines to fill in the gaps during eventual outbreaks. 
The overall target for the project is 5 million vulnerable communities and groups such as IDPs (1.3M), returnees, and children under five (860,000), pregnant women (2M), elderly (100,000) and people with disabilities in 112 localities of the 18 states in Sudan. The activities related to outbreak control are not restricted only to the 112 targeted localities, the WHO will intervene wherever the needs arise under its mandate for health security and protection of health.

project_name: Improve the quality and coverage of SAM inpatient care in 94 existing Stabilization Centers in Sudan.
project_objective: WHO project aims to decrease avoidable under five mortality and morbidity related to Severe acute malnutrition through improved access and quality of inpatient care for the Sever Acute Malnutrition (SAM) with medical complications in 94 stabilization centers Operating in health facilities. The project includes curative, preventive and promotive Measures in the same time. The activities will address the clinical life-saving interventions in Stabilization centers targeting the patients/children with SAM and the mothers/caretakers through IYCF counseling and young children nutrition awareness to lower relapse and prevent SAM cases in the same households. The project activities and costing factored in 49 SCs are supported by UNICEF (11 SCs) and Partners NGOs (38). The SCs Supported by NGOs will require only Medical kits/ secondary level and lab investigation Support, along with IYCF training and counselling, and UNICEF will cover 9% of the Caseload through the 11 SCs, most of them in big towns. Main activities: Training of the health and nutrition staff of 94 SCs (all except the ones Supported by UNICEF and NGOs) to include IPD SAM initial training (7 days) and refresher Training (3 days), provision of guidelines, Job Aids and IEC materials to all participants from the 94 SCs. WHO will procure and distribute to 94 SCs (all except the UNICEF Supported SCs) medicines (SAM inpatient Kits – secondary level care), lab reagents for Investigation essential for case-management, medical equipment and other supplies based on the needs identified together with MOH. To improve the quality of care and cure rate in SCs, WHO nutrition and public health officers present in all targeted states will conduct jointly with SMOH regular supportive supervisions in all targeted 94 SCs conducting on the job training, coaching, and adherence to the national treatment protocols. Routine nutrition surveillance at HF level/SCs, essential for trends and gap identification and effective planning of activities will be enhanced through training, provision of recording and reporting tools for 94 SC (all except UNICEF supported), and better integration into HFs reporting mechanism to promote sustainability. WHO nutrition team will provide technical and operational support to the MOH at federal and state levels to regularly analysis the data of SAM inpatient care services (using the agreed performance indicators) to identify the trends, and challenges dis aggregated by sex and age. The information will be disseminate to all relevant stakeholders through nutrition cluster bulletins, and briefing during the meetings led by UNICEF and MOH. Effective coordination of WHO with all partners (Nutrition, Health, food security) will promote an improved referral system between the SCs, TSFP, OTP, and community. Linkages with communities will be strengthened through raising awareness and social mobilization conducted by trained community mobilizers/CHW and MSG in coordination with other UN. The modalities and subjects for these activities will be guided by the community members suggestions collected through exit interview and focus group discussions during supervisions. The project activities also includes small repairs of 20 SCs in order to ensure better environment for work and improved hygiene in the SCs.

project_name: Improved access to safe water and vector control activities for the vulnerable, nutritionally affected and underserved population in 14  states in Sudan
project_objective:
This projects is aiming to prevent and reduce the avoidable mortality and morbidity due to water and vector borne diseases, and hospital acquired infection in Blue Nile, Kassala, Red Sea, Gadarif, North Darfur, South Darfur, West Darfur, Central Darfur, East Darfur, South Kordufan, West kordufan and White Nile. WHO as lead for vector control, will continue supporting MoH and partners to implement integrated vector management campaigns in response to acute outbreaks and increased vector population to mitigate / prevent imminent threats resulted from floods and displacement and keep on monitoring vector abundance and to ensure prevention of morbidity and moralities related to communicable diseases among Internally Displaced Persons and vulnerable population in Blue Nile, Kassala, Red Sea, Gadarif, North Darfur, South Darfur, West Darfur, Central Darfur, East Darfur, South Kordufan, West kordufan and White Nile; a comprehensive package of water quality and safety activities including community based integrated prevention of multiple WASH related diseases and control of vector borne diseases through breaking the mosquito life cycle and confine adult vector density and strengthen hazard control within health facilities.Water quality activities will be implemented by the MoH and WASH partners at state and national level with sustained support from WHO, complementing the UNICEF and WASH partners
intervention. This year, the focus will be at locality level, to promote efficiency by reducing
the cost of sample transport from field to states capital cities and enabling the local
authorities to conduct regular water sampling and testing in prioritized high risk locations. The newly established dashboard will provide different information on bacteriological and sanitary risk categorization and detailed status on the functionality of water sources. This will assist in identifying high risk areas and prediction of potential outbreaks to timely accelerate interventions to mitigate/ prevent the outbreak occurrence. Additionally, the functionality status mapping will provide data to partners in order to maintain, rehabilitate or replace water sources to increase access to sustainable drinking water supply. 
The main activities related to this component includes training of environmental health officers/workers (MoH and WES), community volunteers and hygiene promoters on water testing using portable kits; sanitary inspection of water sources; proper water sources maintenance and house-hold chlorination, treatment and storage. The results of the regular monitoring of water sources quality and sanitary conditions will allow timely identification of health threats and implementation of corrective measures through information sharing with all relevant partners. Close information sharing and consultations with
Health sector will facilitate the early warning on identified public health alerts related to water and vector transmission and joint planning of control measures. 
WHO comprehensive package of vector control activities includes; training of the environmental health officers, Community Health Workers from MoH/WES in the selected 21 localities/locations on the integrated vector management and entomological surveillance, printing of the IEC material on the common vector, technical and logistic support to vector control campaigns and vector surveillance mission. The implementation will take into account the specific demographics of the IDP camps in targeted states with high population density, and also be directed by health information data on prevalence, vector density and trends of the diseases.

Addressing the needs of Limb reconstruction patients in Gaza
project_objective:
This project aims to address the urgent needs of Limb Reconstruction patients in Gaza, especially those who suffered from complex LR injuries since the start of the Great Marches of Return (GMR) events.
 
This project is in rhythm with Strategic Objective #2 ""The basic needs of vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation are met through the provision of quality basic services and improved access to resources, in accordance with the rights of protected persons under IHL."", 
and Health Cluster Objective #1"": Ensure the availability, accessibility, acceptability and quality of essential lifesaving health services to vulnerable communities in Gaza and West Bank/EJ, including through health system strengthening, preparedness and community resilience building"". 

A year and half later after the start of GMR, many of those injured are still struggling with the devastating consequences of their wounds. They  are stuck in painful waiting while the effects of their injuries take an ever greater toll on them and their families.
However, this category of complex limb injuries has not been prioritized by organizations and have placed impossibly high demands on the Ministry of Health to deal with as these cases require years of treatment and are financially overwhelming. Plus, the skills' set available in Gaza are not able to meet such great numbers and complexity of injuries.

 Until recently, MAP has been the only active INGO since 2014 establishing LR services in Palestine (until eruption of GMR events) and have had huge successes in terms of LR interventions, this project is designed to meet the continuous needs of the very recent and late-complex limb injuries of the GMR as these far exceed any local capacity that exists in Gaza. According to the recent MOH report (September 2019), the number of live ammunition injuries in the GMR events reached 7,594; 87% of them are limbs injuries coming to a figure near 6,600 injuries (HC report, August 2019).
Of these, and according to latest estimations from health cluster, there are still around 1,700 patients who need LR treatment (HNC 2020 Monitoring Framework). 
As stated previously, this project will aim to reduce the suffering of the LR patients via increasing the frequency of the medical missions and the number of UK LR surgeons that MAP brings to Gaza and also via the supporting the local teams in Shifa and EGH with the needed supplies to perform the LR interventions locally.

project_objective:

Les activités du secteur logistique continueront de favoriser la coordination et le partage d’information logistique dans le but d’améliorer la prévisibilité, la rapidité et l’efficacité de la réponse logistique. 

Le secteur prévoit également de renforcer les efforts de planification d’urgence et la mise en place de mesures de préparation face aux risques de catastrophes naturelles et de crise sanitaire. 

Un soutien en matière de télécommunication d’urgence pourra aussi être prévu le cas échéant.

project_name: REVISED PROJECT- Food and Cash-based Assistance for Vulnerable Populations in Somalia
project_objective:
The September 2019 Food Security and Nutrition Analysis Unit (FSNAU) report estimates that 2.1 million people are in Crisis and facing acute food security while one million children under the age of five will remain acutely malnourished through end of 2019. Drought conditions since late 2018 to May 2019 and erratic 2019 Gu rains have contributed to the high levels of food insecurity, as many households have not yet recovered from 2017 drought. In most regions, crops failed leading to hunger for poor riverine and agro-pastoral households. Low production has led to below average food stocks and income from agricultural employment. In pastoral areas, livestock productivity has declined reducing access to milk and increasing debt among many poor households, which struggle to meet their food needs. Poor pasture conditions are reported in South-Central regions leading to livestock migration, while in Northern and Central Pastoral, livestock asset holding has drastically reduced due to previous droughts, thus reducing households’ ability to earn incomes from livestock sales to meet household food needs and purchase water for livestock. Delayed and below average 2019 Gu rains across Somalia have led to significant reduction of cereal production with harvests reported to be the worst since Gu’ 1995, at 68 percent lower than the long-term average (1995-2018).  Food prices have shown mixed trends across Somalia with up to 28 percent increase of local cereal prices, while imported food items have remained stable.  The food component of the Minimum Expenditure Basket (MEB) has increased over the past one year except in Northeast and Central regions (WFP,September 2019)
About 750,000 of internally displaced persons (IDPs) out of the 2.6 million estimated IDPs are in Crisis or Emergency. Approximately 258,000 people in urban areas are in Crisis or above and face food consumption gaps due to high cost of living and limited income earning opportunities. A WFP assessment conducted in July in seven IDP settlements in Galkayo town reported that IDPs face food insecurity, lack access to basic services such as water, education and health.  Majority of the households do not have access to credit and have limited access to income. Main expenditure costs are food, water, lighting and transportation to access basic services to the town.  The households surveyed indicated willingness to engage in alternative livelihood skills to build longer term resilience.
Nutrition surveys indicate persistence of widespread acute malnutrition in the country attributed to food insecurity, high morbidity, low immunization and others with a national median prevalence of Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) remaining serious (10-14.9%) over the past three seasons. A prevalence of Critical (15-29.9%) GAM was observed in 10 out of 33 population groups surveyed. 
WFP’s intervention aims to improve immediate access to food for vulnerable households and support resilience of vulnerable populations against shocks through unconditional and conditional food and cash-based transfers with the following outcomes
-Food-insecure people in areas affected by natural or human-caused disasters have access to adequate and nutritious food that meet their basic food and nutrition needs during and in the aftermath of shocks.  
-Food-insecure people in targeted areas are better able to withstand shocks and stresses throughout the year.
Based on 19/20 Deyr performance it is expected that the food security situation will improve in 2020. Considering food security trend analysis and needs covered by other food security cluster members, WFP proposes to assist 700,000 beneficiaries with relief assistance for the first 6 months a reduction of 30-35 percent compared to the target in the last quarter of 2019.    
A total of 980,000 people will be targeted to receive assistance to meet immediate food gaps, improve household food security, build household and community assets that strengthen livelihoods.

project_name: Safe and equitable access to inclusive education for 619,237 conflict-affected girls and boys age 3 to 17 years and an additional 15,000 youth (15+) in Adamawa, Borno and Yobe States of North East Nigeria
project_objective:
Overall Objective: 
Strengthen access and improve inclusive, quality and equitable basic education for 619,237 conflict-affected displaced, returnees, host communities, school-aged girls and boys aged 3 to 17 years and an additional 15,000 youth (15+) in Adamawa, Borno and Yobe states of North-East Nigeria.

Specific Objective: 
1.	Strengthen basic education for 619,237 children (ensuring 50% girls, 100,000 children who are 3-5 years old and 50,000 children from Tsangaya and Islamiyah schools ) through the provision of essential teaching, recreational materials, support to enrolment drive campaigns (EDC) and Girls for Girls (G4G).
2.	Improve the capacity of 10,100 teachers and volunteer teachers (at least 40% females) in psychosocial support, education in emergencies, special education, quality Early Childhood Development (ECD), classroom management and pedagogy.
3.	Increase access to safe learning spaces with gender-sensitive WASH facilities and water for the benefit of 400,000 children (50% girls).
4.	Provide access to learning, training and skills development for 15,000 youth (50% females; aged 15-24)
5.	Enhance the response and protection capacity of education service providers in school governance in emergencies through establishing and/or activating Monitoring of School-based Management Committees (SBMC) in targeted LGAs and building the capacity of 500 SBMC (40% females; 2,500 members) on SBMC effectiveness and provision of education services to out-of-school children, education-in-crisis, and education for vulnerable children including girls and children with disabilities with a focus on hard-to-reach areas.

project_name: Nutrition response in Niger: Saving lives of people affected by severe acute malnutrition while strengthening systems
project_objective:
Prevention and treatement of severe acute malnutrition in Niger: 
UNICEF's main support will consist in (i) providing nutritional and medical supplies (nutritional therapeutic products, drugs for systematic and specific treatment, materials, etc.) to 1,233 health facilities,  (ii) strengthening technical capacities of health staff and community workers in IMAM and IYCF, promotion of IYCF at health facility and community levels, monitoring and supervision of services providers, data collection, analysis and nutrition information sharing, and (iii) strengthening coordination at central and decentralized level. Throughout its interventions, UNICEF will contribute to strenghtening the national health system (supply chain, information system, etc.), in order to better link humanitarian action to longer-term development.

project_name: Shelter and NFI Assistance for IDPs and host community members in Northeast and Northwest Syria
project_objective: The proposed project aims to address emergency and more sustainable shelter and NFI needs of vulnerable households with acute needs (both IDPs and host community members) in Northeast and Northwest Syria. Specifically, ACTED will rehabilitate, through contractors, 850 households; 6000 in Ar-Raqqa and 250 in Idleb governorates. 1,150 households in Ar-Raqqa governorate will also be targeted with Cash for repairs interventions to conduct small rehabilitation works under ACTED supervision and support. In addition, ACTED will address the needs of newly displaced households through the provision of tents, emergency shelter kits and tents insulation kits to guarantee a shelter and dignified living conditions to these newly displaced individuals. Under this intervention, 1,175 households will be provided with tents across Al-Hasake, Ar-Raqqa, and Idleb governorates; while 5,600 emergency shelter kits will be distributed in Idleb and Northern Aleppo governorates. Idleb governorate will also be targeted with the distribution of 38,329 insulation kits across the eight camp clusters, to better equip the residents for winter. In addition, 2,650 NFI kits, composed of tarpaulin, jerry can, mattresses/sleeping mats, blankets (single and double), solar lamps, floor mat, stove, cooking pot, bowl for food, and cutlery, will be distributed across Idleb and Northern Aleppo governorates. 300 households will also be provided with cooking kerose stoves in Areesheh camp, Al-Hasake governorate. The intervention will target a total of 62,160 individuals, including 23,000 in Northeast and 39,160 in Northwest Syria; 13,763 men, 11,724 women, 19,804 boys, and 16,869 girls.
