project_name: Ensuring access to quality life saving GBV response and prevention services for Rohingya refugees and their host communities.
project_objective:
This proposed project is targeting Rohingya refugee and host communities in the affected areas of Ukhiya and Teknaf to ensure lifesaving GBV services  and prevention activities to mitigate the GBV.  The interventions will ensure the survivors centered approach to offer comprehensive GBV case management services, integrated SRH-GBV services, GBV prevention activities, PSS group activities, individual PSS support, MHPSS support for GBV survivors and women and girls at risk. Adolescent specific curriculum will be implemented to build life skill of the adolescent girls. GBV prevention messages, activities, lifesaving information, referral services to other service points for GBV and NON GBV survivors, structured skill development programme for women and girls through women lead Community centers, engaging men and boys through WLCC to GBV prevention programme, social mobilization activities through SASA methodology will be ensured in 20 locations of host and refugee setting.  GBV response programme will be ensured through women friendly spaces, and WLCC will be ensuring women empowerment through curricula based.  This project will have a focus on developing community-based protection groups, empowering community to provide a safe community for their women and girls. The project will target to include high risk populations  and marginalized groups into all the activities of GBV prevention and response. This year the project will expand into 16 new locations of host and refugee setting, therefore, a total of 39 locations the GBV response and prevention programmes will be implemented, where 10 WLCC offers training, and skill development programmes, engaging men and boys family mebers of trainees in GBV prevention programme through the centers. Knowledge  on disaster management, strengthening the facilities/service points to ensure the service delivery throughout disaster, activating emergency response unit (PERU, MMT) will be ensured. 
The proposed project will be coordinating with GBVSS , Child Protection Sectors, Livelihood sectors, site management, Sexual and Reproductive Health Working groups, GBViMS, Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) working groups, Communication With Communities Working Groups, Gender in Humanitarian  Assistance (GiHA) etc to ensure staff capacity, services, avoiding duplication, ensure referral pathway on a timely manner. 
In the overall project phase, data will be collected in a safe and ethical manner, Kobo software will be utilized for regular data collection, while GBVIMS and GBvIMS primero will be used for GBV data gathering. Client satisfaction surveys will be conducted with GBV survivors through GBV case management services, while non GBV survivors and trainees of the women lead community centers will also be part of this survey to understand about the satisfaction level of the services they receive. Regular safety audits, Community watch Group Meeting, Women Support groups interactive meeting with Camp Coordination groups will be conducted, to ensure community taking the lead of their own issues.  Skill assessment of the GBV case management staffs, Life skill facilitators and of the staffs who will be implementing SASA together will be done. Standard tools to be used to assess MHPSS services and activities. 
UNFPA will continue to pursue internal and external measures to protect beneficiaries from sexual exploitation and abuse (SEA) by members of the humanitarian community. Internally, UNFPA shall continue training all staff, Externally, sensitizes partners and others working in the humanitarian community about PSEA.  UNFPA will strengthen prevention and response to Sexual Exploitation and Abuse by ensuring availability of functional PSEA reporting and response mechanisms for UNFPA and its Partners.

project_name: Provision of comprehensive, specialized GBV services including case management, medical, psychosocial support and access to safe spaces for GBV survivors
project_objective: 9 months of conflict has led to multiple displacements, loss of livelihood opportunities, and destruction of social support systems and disruption of services. Though men and boys have been affected, women and girls are particularly facing multiple risks of GBV due to the ongoing conflict. An estimated 166,227 people displaces and at risk to protection issues. Due to the erosion of the protective structures both formal and informal vulnerability to violence, exploitation and abuse has become ever more acute. According to UNFPA implementing partners reports indicates incidents of GBV have increased as a result of the ongoing conflict in Tripoli and other cities; incidents ranging from sexual violence including rape, physical violence, denial of resources, opportunities and services, intimate partner’s violence/domestic violence and child marriage. However, the numbers don’t reflect the actual prevalence rates, due to fear of retaliation and social stigma, lack of specialized services including lack of trust in existing health services and providers as a barrier for help; survivors fear that they will not receive the care they need due to the attitude, lack of supplies and capacity of service providers. Displaced women and girls, women-child headed household, separated and unaccompanied girls and boys, orphans, women and girls living with disabilities and from marginalized groups at greater risk. As a result the primary objective of the proposal is to “Support the provision case management, medical, psychosocial support and safe spaces for GBV survivors”. Interventions at aims at scaling up UNFPA’s current response; to address the following forms of violence that are prevalent according to partners data; sexual violence including rape, domestic violence/intimate partner violence, forced/early child marriage, psychological abuse, denial of resources , opportunities and services ; as the primary focus for intervention. Due to the sensitivity nature of GBV and the low level of capacity on the ground; UNFPA will support health including sexual reproductive health services and safe spaces as an entry point for GBV services most notably clinical management of rape. Support the expansion of medical, psychosocial care, and by using health facilities as an integrated service hubs with facilitated referral to other services chosen by survivors of rape, child marriage, domestic violence/intimate partner violence, and psychological abuse among others to services such as legal, police and shelter. UNFPA through the reproductive health working group will work to expand the number of facilities that are providing GBV services through partnership and provision of drugs and equipment and through CMR trainings strengthen the health providers capacity to respond to survivors needs. These clinical and psychological services will be complemented with facilitated referral to other needed services chosen by the GBV survivor, such as legal, police, shelter, etc. The GBV case management services will be provided at all levels by the health workers and targeted service providers trained in GBV /case management including GBV referral; in GBV psychosocial counseling and in GBV data management.  Develop cities specific GBV referral maps/pathways with clear identified and trained focal points. support safe spaces; as a safe gateway that enable them to access information, reproductive health and GBV services in a non-stigmatized manner thus ensuring safety and dignity. communication materials will be developed to raise awareness on the availability of GBV health services as an entry point to GBV Services. GBV hotline will be another entry point for GBV survivors to reach out to the needed services of psychosocail and legal counseling.

project_name: Restoring access to quality education and protective learning environment for children in Derna
project_objective:
The proposed action aims to restore the access of boys and girls to quality education and a protective learning environment through capacity-building of teachers, the provision of catch-up classes, psychosocial support and recreational activities for children, awareness-raising and sensitization sessions, and the rehabilitation and repairs of damaged schools in conflict-affected areas in Derna. 
ACTED will enhance access to formal and non-formal education for vulnerable school-aged children affected by protracted crisis (Sector Objective 1) by providing catch-up classes to out-of-school and displaced boys and girls. Catch-up programs will address the priority needs of vulnerable children who are out of school, who are in enrolled in school but have fallen behind because of the conflict, from displaced families, as well from disadvantaged groups (girls, children with disabilities and additional needs, associated with armed groups, from minorities, from poorer socio-economic groups, etc.). ACTED seeks to bridge the learning gaps created by conflict-related disrupted access to education.  ACTED will also aim to address the physical and infrastructural barriers to safe and protective learning environments through the rehabilitation and repairs of educational facilities. The rehabilitation of the selected schools aims to create safe and inclusive learning spaces for children of all backgrounds and abilities.
Also under Sector Objective 1, ACTED will engage with local communities to enhance access to education in Derna. By conducting awareness-raising sessions for parents, caregivers and children on key issues pertaining to education and child protection, as well as to support building acceptance of the project and participation of beneficiaries. Awareness-raising sessions will focus on topics related to children enrolment in schools and the importance of prioritizing children’s education. 
To improve the quality of education services in protective learning environment (sector objective 2), ACTED will conduct psychosocial support and recreational activities. In a context where both parents and teachers noted signs of distress and psychological consequences from the conflict, these activities will respond to the children’s wellbeing needs through an integrated approach combining education and protection interventions. The activities will also seek the participation of parents and community members to contribute to reinforce family and community support systems and foster an enabling and supportive environment for young people, aiming at building resilience and social cohesion. 
To strengthen the capacity of teachers, education personnel and sector members to deliver a timely and coordinated education response (sector Objective 3), ACTED will conduct capacity-building of teachers on education, classroom management skills and on child protection. Doing so aims to address the issues of underqualification and underperformance of teachers reported in the assessment, in order to reinforce the quality of teaching in formal schools. This activity will also cope with the negative effects of the conflict on teaching staff, which limits their ability to create an inclusive and caring environment, by addressing issues related to their wellbeing and their emotional and psychosocial condition.
This action offers the opportunity to complement and expand existing programmes where ACTED has a demonstrated technical capacity in the East of Libya. To implement this action, ACTED will rely on its on-the-ground experience implementing education and child-protection projects in the East of Libya through its 2016 UNICEF-funded project, which operated child friendly spaces and provided psychosocial support (PSS) in six different areas of Benghazi. ACTED is also enhancing the resilience of and strengthening the protective environment of conflict affected children in Benghazi through its current UNICEF education and child protection project.

project_name: Improving access to essential basic health care services in conflict affected areas with low/no service coverage in Borno, Adamawa, and Yobe States.
project_objective:
The Ten years of conflict have made the humanitarian situation in the North East of Nigeria remains particularly challenging with an estimated 7.1 million people. 
Among this affected population, WHO estimates that approximately 5 Million people (including 613,783 children aged 0 to 59 months, 3.16 Million children between 5 and 18 years old, 525,740 adult women and 301,860 elderly) from 30 LGAs across the BAY States (46% of the total number of LGAs in this region) live in areas with no or low access to health services. This lack of access to health care services is driven by various factors that affect the capacity of the individuals to access adequate health services:
•	Lack of functioning health care facilities
•	Security constraints
•	Lack of referral mechanism
•	Cost
This low or no access to health services exacerbate the risks of increased mortality and morbidity within this population due to exposure to high level of vulnerabilities (disease outbreaks, lack of immunization, lack of treatment for common and complex ailment, etc.). 
Since 2016, the provision of life-saving services to the affected communities is a joint effort between the Government of Nigeria and international humanitarian community.
The lessons learned from previous and ongoing initiatives, the action will address the above mentioned context and needs with a view to reduce mortality and morbidity in areas with low and no health service coverage through increased delivery of and access to high impact health and nutrition services. This will be achieved through a three prone approach:
•	Providing to 724,662 people access to free comprehensive basic lifesaving in maternal and child health, mental health, gender based violence interventions and nutrition services for people in areas with low/no health service coverage in the BAY states through the Hard-to-Reach Mobile Health Teams (H2R MHT) and Community Resource Persons (CORPs) delivery platforms.

En effet, la protection des populations affectées par la crise centrafricaine reste un défi majeur, notamment concernant le mariage précoce des jeunes filles, les VBG, la déscolarisation ou non-scolarisation des enfants, le manque de documentation civile, etc. De plus l'assistance alimentaire fournie par l'aide internationale a drastiquement diminué alors que les besoins restent conséquents.

project_name: PROJECT REVISED- Delivery of integrated lifesaving nutrition services to boys and girls with wasting including pregnant and lactating women targeting in priority IDPs and rural communities
project_objective:
Despite substantial investment in the treatment of acute malnutrition, seasonal FSNAU assessments show that for many years the prevalence of acute malnutrition has remained above serious. The post Gu 2019 nutrition assessment findings showed marginal decrease in the median prevalence of Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) of 13.8% down from 14% of post Gu 2018 and 17.4% of post Gu 2017. The corresponding median SAM prevalence are: 2.3% (Gu 2019), 2.2% (Gu 2018) and 3.2% (Gu 2017). Current estimates indicate that 1 in 10 children under the age of five is acutely malnourished resulting in an estimate 1 million boys and girls of which 178,000 are projected to be affected by life threatening severe acute malnutrition while 830,000 are moderately malnourished. Further, 832,000 pregnant and lactating women are estimated to need nutrition assistance. 
Malnutrition appears worse in rural areas compared to urban areas: across rural areas assessed, the average GAM rate was 17.7%, compared to 12.1% in urban areas (non-displaced households). Similarly, the average SAM rate was 3.0% in rural areas compared to 2.1% in urban areas. IDP households are more likely to suffer from malnutrition than non-displaced populations.  The average GAM rate for IDPs is 18.0%, whilst the average SAM rate is 3.5 percent. IDP camps affected by critical GAM are; Galkayo 20% and Doloow 18.6%, Banadir 16 percent. Across regions, GAM and SAM rates varied: lower rates were observed in the relatively stable north-west of the country such as Woqooyi Galbeed, Awdal and Togdheer regions (8.7% GAM / 1.3% SAM;10.7% GAM / 1.9% SAM and 11.8%  GAM / 1.9% SAM respectively), with highest rates in Hiraan region (22.9% GAM / 5.0% SAM), followed by Bay (21.5% GAM / 4.2% SAM), Bakool (20.9% GAM / 4.4% SAM) and Gedo regions (20.4% GAM / 3.2% SAM). GAM rates also varied significantly at the district level, with average rates of above 22% in Belet Wayne, Jalalaqsi, Bulo Burto and Baydhaba districts, whilst average rates were less than 10% in Berbera, Gebiley, Xarardheere and Hargeisa districts
UNICEF recognizes that girls, boys, men, women and people with disabilities have different nutritional needs at different life stages with different capacities and risks in accessing nutrition services. Gender inequality exacerbates food insecurity, malnutrition and poverty in humanitarian crises. Although data from SAMRT survey conducted by FSNAU and other partners shows that malnutrition rate is higher in boys than girls, the latter have a higher admission rate than boys for reasons yet to be identified. Overall, children affected by severe acute malnutrition are nine times more at risk of death compared to those who are well-nourished. Therefore, this response plan is aligned to UNICEF’s new global narrative on wasting that seeks to focus both on protecting children from becoming wasted as well as caring for those who need treatment. Key interventions of this HRP will aim to deliver promotive and preventive services (Micronutrient supplementation, deworming, IYCF, PLW) and early detection and referral for treatment of SAM targeting in priority rural and IDP communities. In addition, UNICEF in collaboration with WFP will continue to provide care and treatment to children affected by MAM in hard to reach areas using the simplified protocol.  Out of the 178,000 children with SAM, UNICEF will target an estimated 133,500 (68, 085 girls, 65,415 boys) and 43,000 children with moderate acute malnutrition under the combined protocol for the management of acute malnutrition in close consultation with WFP. Through this HRP, UNICEF will procure nutrition supplies to IPs(e.g SHF,SHINE) with 25% buffer. Meanwhile, UNICEF OTP sites will provide a platform for the delivery of integrated multi stakeholder and multi sector services particularly WASH, C4D, Health and safety net. Drawing on the successes and lessons of previous years, UNICEF will continue to lead the cluster and the delivery of this response.

project_name: PROJECT REVISED- Strengthening the delivery of child protection services for boys and girls affected by conflict and other emergencies
project_objective:
The scope and range of protection issues affecting children in Somalia is ever widening and deepening due to the prolonged nature of the conflict. Children are exposed to persistent and extreme violence which includes recruitment and use by parties to the conflict. Population displacement due to chronic conflict, droughts and famines has resulted in the separation of children from their families, which exposes them to exploitation, violence and abuse children of IDPs and minorities are particularly vulnerable. Boys and girls continue to endure multiple protection risks and violations of their rights including physical abuse, psychosocial distress, family separation, sexual and gender-based violence (GBV). The proliferation of small arms and light weapons, a steady rise in the use of improvised explosive devices (IEDs) and widespread contamination of explosive remnants of war (ERW) are the results of the prolonged armed conflict in Somalia.
UNCEF will respond to the above needs in the following ways: 
•	Provision of psychosocial support services through open spaces reaching 100,000 (45,000 boys & 45,000 girls) children and 10,000 (5000 men and 5000 women) caregivers 
•	Provide community-based reintegration for 2200 (1700 boys & 500 girls) child formerly associated with armed forces/groups another vulnerable children 
•	Trace and reunify 8000 unaccompanied and separated children with their families (Boys: 5000 & Girls: 3,000) 
•	Raise awareness on the threats posed by unexploded remnants of war reaching 37,000 people (14,500 boys; 14,500 girls, 4,000 women & 4,000 men) 
•	Raise awareness on main CP concerns on child labour, child marriage and prevention of family separation to 200,000 people (80,000 boys, 80,000 girls, 20,000 men, women 20,000)
•	Train 1000 duty bearers and CSO on child protection and child rights (600 men & 400 women)

project_name: PROJECT WITHDRAWN - Increasing access to inclusive quality basic education for the most vulnerable crisis affected girls and boys including adolescents
project_objective:
Conflicts and climate change in Somalia have negatively impacted on the education needs of the affected girls, boys and adolescents. Lack of educational opportunities has left children in psychosocial distress, vulnerable and exposed to a range of socio-political risks and exploitation. This has increased the propensity for negative coping strategies, including engagement in child labour, forced and early marriage and recruitment into radicalism or criminal groups. 
More than half of the primary school-aged children (65% for girls and 59% of boys) have no access to education and gender gaps in enrolment and retention are also significant with girls facing specific barriers to education (Somalia Joint Multi Cluster Needs Assessments 2019). In addition, those accessing learning opportunities are not assured of continuation due to school drop-outs and closure of schools exacerbating protection risks.
Displacement continues to affect access to education for thousands of children. An estimated 108,000 school aged children of the 270,000 people have been newly displaced in Somalia between January to August 2019 (UNHCR Protection Return Monitoring Network). There are also cases of the displaced population suffering multiple and secondary displacements leading to disruptions in education cycle affecting both enrolment and retention apart from quality.
Somalia remained the country with the highest number of cases of the recruitment and use of children (Children and Armed Conflict Report of the Secretary-General 2018). Attacks on schools have had effects on access to education with a total of 2,228 boys and 72 girls, some as young as 8, were recruited and used by parties to conflict. In addition, there were 77 attacks on schools including killing, abduction and threats against teachers, destruction and looting.
UNICEF emergency education will work closely with Child Protection and WASH to promote an integrated approach. Attention will be focused on enhancing safe and protective learning environment that is gender and disabilities inclusive to meet the needs of vulnerable girls, women, boys and men for both displaced and host communities. In line with Education Cluster strategy, the project aims to deliver quality education and improve access to education services and learning opportunities in a safe and protective learning environment for the most vulnerable and marginalized girls and boys and at risk of exclusion. The project aims to target 130,000 (65,000 girls) across the country, among these 68,114 will be displaced children. 
UNICEF will deliver a comprehensive EiE interventions prioritizing education supplies, training of teachers and Community Education Committees (CECs), emergency incentives, provision of safe drinking water and supplementary school feeding, sanitary kits for adolescent girls among others. 
To ensure the protection of children, education response will be aligned to Education – Child Protection Integrated Response Framework. It will strive towards improved access to protection services to reduce vulnerabilities and strengthen safety of learners. This will be attained through strengthening child protection systems in schools, psychosocial (PSS) care and referral cases, PSS First Aid, create awareness on protecting children in and out of schools through child to child clubs, CECs and community leadership. This is aimed to ensure schools and the community support children’s physical, cognitive, social and emotional wellbeing. In addition, support for adequate WASH facilities and hygiene promotion activities with emphasis on health and hygiene and Acute Water Diarrhea (AWD) prevention at school level, will be undertaken for learners and teachers.  
Systems strengthening will be key in supporting MoE in strengthening management and coordination of education in emergencies. This is aimed to enhance long term sustainability, improved governance and enhancing education capacity to reinforce quality delivery of services.

project_name: PROJECT WITHDRAWN - Unconditional Cash transfers for Malnourished Children
project_objective: UNICEF proposes admissions into severe acute malnutrition therapeutic treatment as an entry point to target beneficiaries for emergency safety net cash assistance. This design aims at channeling assistance to the most vulnerable families using severe acute malnutrition (SAM) as a proxy for extreme vulnerability.  In addition, to prevent children from relapsing into acute malnutrition by addressing the multifaceted causes of malnutrition (including extreme poverty, lack of access to basic services, disease outbreaks, poor hygiene) and aiming to enhance impact of nutrition therapeutic interventions. Cash assistance could also help reduce related negative coping mechanisms such as sharing nutrition therapeutic commodities at household level. The program will also aim to build on current cash plus interventions including positive messaging in regards to nutrition and other targeted messages to change behaviours and social norms that may be contributing to vulnerability, extend community engagement, as well as accountability and feedback systems.  Geographical targeting will start with the areas where UNICEF is already providing cash assistance in Bay and Bakool and aims to be extended to rural areas in those districts, which may encourage return in safe areas and initial contributions to rebuilding livelihoods and resilience to shocks and crises. The selected household upon diagnosis of SAM, the mother or the regular care giver will be enrolled to the UNICEF supported therapeutic feeding centres. Upon admissions mother or the regular care giver will receive monthly cash assistance. The beneficiaries will be register in SCOPE allowing them to track beneficiary across the different type of assistance received. This would also enhance coordination efforts with other partner to avoid duplication of assistance being received (medical treatment vs cash transfers).

project_name: Enhanced access to quality education and skills development opportunities  for Rohingya and host community children, and adolescents affected by the Rohingya refugee crisis in Cox's Bazar District of Bangladesh.
project_objective:
UNICEF aims to reach 210,000 Rohingya children (3-14) with early childhood development and learning opportunities by maintaining the operation of 2,500 learning centres and establishing 500 new LCs under the Government of Bangladesh's ""Reaching Out of School Children"" project in collaboration with the World Bank. UNICEF will upgrade 230 existing LCs to 115 double-storey, medium-hazard structures, aimed at reducing the cost of repairs as well as contributing to increasing access to safe shelters for the refugee population in case of disaster. Additionally, 31,500 Rohingya adolescents will be provided with integrated life and vocational skills programme in multipurpose centres and secondarly level education using Myanmar National Curriculum as a pilot. The pilot will target 10,000 (out of 21,500) adolescents eligible to enroll at any of the four grades of  middle school (Grades 6 to 9) starting from the second quarter of 2020.   The curriculum will be delivered as prescribed by the national curriculum framework with adaptations where appropriate for the context of the camp and the needs of Rohingya children. This piloting will provide the formal educational opportunities to the Rohingya adolescents and this is expected to attract more adolescents and youths to prevent them from being vulnerable to trafficking, abuse, violence and anti social behaviours. 
In the host communities in Teknaf and Ukhyia, UNICEF will support access to improved quality of education 24,424 children (4-14) in pre-primary and primary schools. The support to host community will include system strengthening component aimed at enhancing the capacity of the district primary and secondary education office to accelerate access to equitable quality education.

project_name: Provision of equitable quality lifesaving and essential health services for Rohingya refugees and host communities children and women in Cox's Bazar
project_objective: UNICEF will provide quality, equitable and gender-sensitive maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health services, sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services including counselling and referral for GBV, with attention to people with disabilities. The project targets a vulnerable population of 418,117 people across the Rohingya refugee and host communities. To respond to the basic health and nutrition needs of Rohingya and host community women and children, UNICEF will continue providing harmonized health services through the 18health facilities in camps (5 PHCs, 9 HPs and 4 DCTs – two of which are hibernated) as well as strengthening government health facilities in adjacent host communities (2 union sub-centres and 16 community clinics). A special focus will continue to support the functionalization of Newborn Stabilization Unit (NSU) and kangaroo mother care in the Ukhia and Teknaf Upazila Health Complexes and the special newborn care unit (SCANU) at the District Hospital. Health interventions focus on providing comprehensive primary health care services through the Essential Services Packages (ESP) as per Government’s guidance, include maternal, newborn care, immunization, integrated management of childhood illnesses, nutrition, acute watery diarrhoea prevention and management, prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV services and community engagement. UNICEF will also strengthen the Health Management Information System (HMIS/DHIS2) through technical support and capacity building of services providers of all health sector partners including government counterparts. Maternal Perinatal Deaths Surveillance and Response (MPDSR) will be extended to cover Rohingya communities in camp in addition to host population. These activities will be implemented through partnership with Partners in Health and Development (PHD), and Research, Training and Management (RTM) International.

project_name: Communicating with communities with a provision of key life saving information through community engagement, social mobilization and strengthened accountability to the affected people
project_objective: Integration and institutionalization of C4D/Communication with Communities (CwC) approaches and interventions into health, nutrition, WASH, education, and child protection for sustained long-term and at-scale efforts. Strengthening the role of religious leaders towards increasing community ownership and participation in host and camps. Continued support to strengthen community accountability through information feedback centers and closing the community feedback loop. Promoting social cohesion and confidence-building in the host communities through community engagement interventions in Ukhiya and Teknaf Sub-districts. Supporting local governance structures to improve results for children at the community level through the Country Programme Local Governance for Children (LGC) program.

project_name: Provision of Life Saving Nutrition Interventions for Rohingya children, women, and vulnerable host population in Bangladesh through strengthening systems-based programming to ensure life-cycle based continuum of care
project_objective:
""The proposed activities by UNICEF aim to improve the coverage and the quality nutrition services and their use by the beneficiaries for the prevention and treatment of malnutrition in camps and host communities, using three strategies: (i) strengthening of systems; (ii) promotion of community- and facility-based nutrition interventions and (iii) integration of complementary nutrition-specific and nutrition-sensitive interventions. While the first strategy seeks to strengthen the existing systems by improving the human and institutional capacities, as well as strengthening partnerships with government and non-government organizations, the second strategy intends to improve community demand for services, outreach and participation in identifying and addressing causes of malnutrition and improve the quality of nutrition services at both community and facility level. Lastly, implementing complementary nutrition-sensitive and specific interventions will improve the impact, by contributing to addressing immediate, underlying and basic causes of malnutrition. 
Following a life-cycle approach and to break the intergenerational cycle of malnutrition, the main targets of these interventions are children under-five years (with a special attention to children under-two), adolescents (with focus on adolescent girls) and pregnant and lactating women (PLW) and the elderly. 
Key interventions will focus on screening and referral of malnourished children, in-patient and out-patient treatment of severe acute malnourished (SAM) children, growth monitoring and promotion (GMP), prevention and treatment of micronutrient deficiencies through micronutrient supplementation, promotion of optimum Infant and Young Child Feeding Practices (IYCF) and maternal and adolescent nutrition, through intensive social mobilization and behavior change communication. Support to livelihoods improvement, as part of resilience building (especially in host communities) will also be implemented. 
Throughout the implementation, a special focus will be given to gender and equity, to ensure fulfillment of human rights for any kind of vulnerable populations. Strenghtening coordination and partnerships with other institutions involved in the Rohingya response, as well as improving information systems, supporting nutrition suveys and assessments will also be an important aspect of UNICEF's interventions.""

project_name: Provision of WASH Services to vulnerable populations in Cox's Bazar District.
project_objective: The purpose of the intervention is to provide vulnerable populations with equitable access to safe water supplies, dignified and safe latrines and bathing facilities and to provide information on critical hygiene promotion information and training with the aim of changing behaviour away from potentially harmful practices. The provision of the services will focus on inclusive access for all and will consider especially the needs of women, children, the elderly and people living with disabilities. The target population are 241,754 Rohingya refugees living in 8 refugee camps and 150,000 Bangladeshi people living in Teknaf and Uhkia who are affected by the refugee influx.

project_name: Increase access to equitable quality essential health services for internally displaced persons (IDPs) and vulnerable population in South Sudan through provision of immunization core pipeline and use of the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM).
project_objective:
In line with our organisational Core Commitment to Children in Emergency, UNICEF will continue to provide the population of South Sudan especially children, pregnant and lactating women, with quality preventive, and curative services as well as outbreak response activities. The IRRM enables UNICEF, through direct implementation, to provide high impact lifesaving emergency response in inaccessible and conflict affected areas. UNICEF will ensure availability of core pipe line vaccines and cold chain supplies to respond to vaccine preventable disease outbreaks.

This project aims to increase access to quality equitable essential primary health care interventions through IRRM and provide a core pipeline to increase access to quality equitable immunization services by vulnerable populations living in host communities and IDPs living in Protection of Civilian Sites (POCs), formal IDP camps or host communities in conflict affected areas as well as refugee returnees.

The activities to be implemented are:
• Procurement and distribution of emergency vaccines.
• Procurement, distribution and maintenance of cold chain 
equipment.
• Technical support for improved vaccine and cold chain 
management
• Training of frontline partners of vaccine and cold chain 
management
• Conduct 30 IRRM missions

The expected beneficiaries of core pipeline supplies are  203,750 vulnerable children living in camps, PoCs, formal IDP camps or host communities in conflict affected areas and refugee returnees. The children will benefit from emergency vaccination to sure up their immunity to vaccine preventable diseases. Vaccines against measles, meningitis, and cholera as well as cold chain equipment and devices will be procured.

60,000 children are expected to be reached during the Rapid Response Missions. These will include children aged 6 months-15years who will be reached with immunization services and curative consultations and pregnant women who are expected to benefit from ANC services, tetanus toxoid vaccination, curative consultations and the provision of long-lasting insecticide treated nets (LLITN).

project_name: Improving WASH conditions in the Southern Governorates of Gaza Strip
project_objective:
In line with the WASH cluster objective #1 and country strategic objective #2, the action aims to ensure equitable, affordable and sustainable access to safe and sufficient WASH services with dignity for the un-served, underserved and most vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation in Gaza and the West Bank through ensuring basic WASH services for conflict-affected, un- or under-served and vulnerable populations and institutions in the Gaza Strip. The proposed intervention responds to the SDG #6. SDG6 aims to ‘ensure available and sustainable management of water and sanitation for all’ and includes targets for universal access to drinking water, sanitation and hygiene for all by 2030.

The project aims at reducing the public health and environmental pollution risks that may occur as a result of wastewater percolation from existing cesspits in the target locations in Rafah area. It will benefit nearly 12000 people of which 47% are women in four locations in southern part of Gaza namely in Al Salam Neighborhood South of Rafah, Msabbah Neighborhood North-East of Rafah, Al Fourkan Neighborhood in Rafah and Junian Neighborhood in East of Rafah area. Total number of beneficiaries in each location can be listed as follows: Al Fourkan 6000, Al Salam 1700, Msabbah 1600 and Junian 2700. Moreover, the project will indirectly benefiting all people in the target four locations through direct pollution prevention of their areas and also prevent groundwater pollution.

According to the information obtained from CMWU and PWA during the coordination meetings organized with them on 25 and 26 September 2018 respectively, these information were updated again on 29 September 2019 in coordination with PWA, CMWU and area focal point in Rafah (Islamic Relief – IRPAL) and they identified the four locations listed above which are in need of sewer system to connect more households in order to avoid flooding of wastewater to neighborhoods and to coastal aquifer. The need of each location can be summarized as follows: Al Fourkan needs 3000m UPVC sewer line and 100 concrete manholes and connecting 250 households. AL Salam needs 500 m UPVC sewer to connect 40 households while Msabbah and Junina needs 500 m each to connect 30 household in each one of them. Accordingly, the project will contribute by supplying and installing 4500 m of UPVC sewer lines, 150 concrete manholes and 350 house connection. Moreover, the project will also provide awareness and capacity building for local communities on best hygiene practices and will provide capacity building for municipal, CMWU and PWA staff (both male and female) on the operation and maintenance of wastewater sewer lines and wastewater operation and maintenance in general. The project will contribute also in closing down all the cesspits in the target locations to stop further pollution of aquifer and prevent public health risks, hence, reducing ensuring no harm principle.
The project design has considered gender mainstreaming and also mainstreaming of protection principles including meaningful access, safety and dignity. PHG will adhere to the protection principles throughout the implementation of the project and will develop protection monitoring, vulnerability mapping and impact assessment to ensure project compliance with these principles.
PHG will also implement the project and will be responsible for its overall management and reporting toward the donor. PHG will ensure the quality implementation and management of project in accordance with its ISO9001 - 2008 standards and will also ensure the timely implementation of the project in an efficient manner within the budget limit and will allocate relevant qualified human resources to implement it properly.

project_name: Humanitarian Coordination Assistance for the Syria Response Plan
project_objective: The 2020 Syria Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) sets out the framework within which the humanitarian community will respond to the large-scale humanitarian and protection needs in Syria throughout 2020 by flexibly leveraging the various response modalities. Leveraging these capacities and efforts under a single strategic framework, the plan aims to increase the effectiveness of the response by improving the identification of needs and gaps, reducing overlap and duplication, and monitoring of changes. The Humanitarian Coordinator for Syria and the Regional Humanitarian Coordinator for the Syria Crisis lead and coordinate humanitarian action inside Syria. . OCHA, in line with its global mandate, supports the humanitarian leadership in ensuring the effective coordination of the response inside Syria. To do so, OCHA maintains country offices in Syria and Turkey, and a regional office in Amman. OCHA requires sustained levels of funding to be able to maintain and further strengthen the effective coordination of humanitarian responses from these various offices, facilitate key coordination platforms, provide information management services, manage pooled funding, provide support for humanitarian access and civil-military coordination, provide public information and advocacy on the humanitarian situation, and support humanitarian leadership. The funding requirements reflect the needs of OCHA's three offices involved in the Syria response.

project_name: Peru - International Organization for Migration
Mécanisme de réponse rapide (RRM), médiation humanitaire et co-facilitation du cluster protection au Mali
project_objective:
Objectif principal: 
Améliorer les conditions de vie des personnes en situation de vulnérabilité aiguë suite à un mouvement de population ou une catastrophe naturelle, tout en améliorant la coordination du cluster protection et en contribuant à la protection des civils en situation de conflit. 

Résumé du projet: 
La situation humanitaire du Mali est caractérisée par des incidents sécuritaires liés notamment à l'activisme des groupes armés, les opérations militaires, les tensions intercommunautaires et la criminalité croissante qui complexifie de plus en plus l'accès humanitaire et notamment dans la zone frontalière ""des trois pays"", à savoir le Niger, le Burkina Fasso et le Mali. Déjà affaiblies par des problèmes de pauvreté chroniques, les populations civiles sont de plus en plus directement ciblées et contraintes au déplacement forcé. Selon les chiffres issus des alertes RRM sur les mouvements de population, entre janvier et novembre 2019, près de 300 000 personnes sous mandat RRM se sont déplacées. En dépit des interventions conduites par les partenaires RRM entre janvier et novembre 2019 près de 160 000 personnes sont toujours dans le besoin d'assistance. Cette action a pour but de renforcer le mécanisme de réponse rapide existant pour être en mesure de faire face aux besoins immédiats des populations affectées un conflit ou une catastrophe naturelle. Le projet va maintenir et renforcer la veille humanitaire ainsi que la coordination aussi bien au niveau régional que national. Une approche de médiation humanitaire d'urgence est conçue pour s'intégrer au RRM, notamment dans le cadre du volet de veille humanitaire, en renforçant l'aspect protection qui est aujourd'hui relevé comme un besoin principal et prioritaire.
Le projet a pour but la mise en place d'un mécanisme de réponse aux urgences en mesure d'alerter la communauté humanitaire sur l'existence d'une crise ; évaluer les besoins dans les secteurs de l'eau ; les articles ménagers essentiels ; et les besoins alimentaires ; et le cas échéant de déployer une réponse immédiate à ces besoins dans un délai de 15 jours après l'alerte.
Une attention particulière sera portée sur les personnes à besoins spécifiques (personnes en situation de handicap, les malades chroniques, les enfants chefs de ménages, les personnes de troisième âge) et la problématique « genre » pour assurer que les besoins spécifiques des femmes, filles, hommes et garçons de différents âges en situation de vulnérabilité aigue sont pris en compte (exemple l’accès aux kits de dignité pour les femmes/filles). Les femmes, filles, hommes et garçons ciblés seront associés au design de la réponse.
Les activités de médiation permettront de renforcer la composante de protection proactive des civils dans la réponse d'urgence, afin de prévenir ou mitiger les épisodes de violence affectant les civils, en proposant une approche participative et durable.
NRC poursuivra le soutien au cluster protection en terme de coordination au niveau national et régional pour mobiliser la participation des membres du cluster protection dans l'évaluation des besoins de protection et la coordination de la réponse apportée aux populations ciblées. NRC renforcera la méthodologie de travail des sous-groupes sectoriels actifs de protection et la qualité des documents stratégiques délivrés permettant d'orienter les actions de plaidoyer au niveau régional et national.
Cible: 160 120 individus (PDIs et communautés d'accueil)

project_name: Gender Based Violence
project_objective: ""The proposed 12-month project will be implemented directly by World Vision and target 9040 vulnerable individuals in camps 12, 13, and 19 of Cox’s Bazar to address protection and Gender-Based Violence (GBV) issues which will work towards the achievement Enhanced community-based protection systems to prevent and respond to GBV, particularly for at-risk and vulnerable women and adolescent girls. The Objective/ Outcome level actions will address change from an interlinked two-pronged approach focusing on both prevention and response as detailed under the activities sections below. Thus, the project will target women and adolascent girls who will be identified but also encouraged to receive services in a dignified manner, at the WV Women girl safe  spaces which will provide both target PSS/couneling. For any cases that require advanced service they will be referred to clinics through the referral system. Cognizent of the fact that at community effort is required to erradiate GBV and to mitigate any such issues n the camps, WV will faciliate and get buy in from commnuity leaders and faith leaders to educate people on GBV prevention, women rights and services that ensure safety and dignity of all benficiaries, among other relevant topics geared toward GBV prevention.

project_name: Healthcare support to the vulnerable Rohingya and host communities in Cox’s Bazar
project_objective: Save the Children (SC) will run eight Health Posts and one Primary Health Care Center (PHCC). These health facilities provide an integrated package of health, SRHR, nutrition, MHPSS, and WASH services in line with the Ministry of Health / Health Sector recommended minimum package of essential health services for primary health care facilities in the FDMN camps and are staffed by Doctors, Midwives, Paramedics, MHPSS specialist, Psychosocial Support Officer,  Clinic Aids, Maternal Child Health and Nutrition Promoters, and Community Health Workers (CHWs). SC carefully screens vulnerable children and their families for mental health issues, prevalent amongst the targeted population, as it can contribute to deteriorating the physical health of the already vulnerable people . This is done by creating awareness and building the capacity of staff to effectively detect, support and refer those in need and ensure those affected have access to equitable, comprehensive and essential primary health care services. With the operation and management of the 9 health facilities, SC aims to reach 109,301 individuals with consultations, and to provide them the primary health care services listed above. Healthcare providers at supported health facilities will also be re-trained on child protection basic concepts, child safeguarding, child rights, confidentiality and on how to be child/adolescent-friendly providers.

project_name: Strengthening Equitable Access to Inclusive, Quality Learning Opportunities and Community Support for Rohingya Refugee and Crisis-Affected Host Community Girls, Boys and Youth in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh
project_objective:
Plan International Bangladesh (PIB)’s education in emergencies (EiE) programme started in 2018 and, based on the learnings of two years into the response, will continue in 2020 to support across the 3 objectives of the Cox's Bazar (CXB) Edu Sector's JRP, corroborating equitable access to inclusive, quality learning opportunities and community engagement for girls, boys and youth in both camp and crisis-affected host communities in Ukhiya and Teknaf. In 2020, PIB will continue to support equitable access to culturally and age appropriate care, learning and development in a safe, protective and inclusive environment, spanning early childhood care and development (ECCD) to functional literacy, numeracy and life skills for older children, adolescents and youth. In camps, PIB will sustain its community-based learning facilities (CBLF) modality which has successfully engaged over 20,000 G & B as part of the 2019 JRP in different-sized facilities across different age groups, while ambitiously transitioning a portion of the learners into 10 LCs and piloting 2 two-storey LCs, conscious of the considerations of community acceptance and GoB approvals. Meanwhile, PIB will continue to support education in the crisis-affected host community (HC) building on its long experience with GoB across the country, and collaboration in CXB over 2019, particularly in ECCD.
Structured trainings for learning facilitators in camps and teachers in HC will aim to strengthen the quality of teaching and learning process for G&B across the age spectrum targeted by CXB Edu Sector, with regular monitoring of quantifiable and qualitative progress to feed into regular mentoring and on-the-job coaching. PIB adopts a pairing modality of learning facilitators from camps with HC Mentors, bridging the distance between both communities through capacity building initiatives. HC Mentors and education officials will be trained to provide better mentoring and supervisory support to learning facilitators and teachers for inclusive, quality education.
Strategically pivoting towards nexus programming, PIB will focus in 2020 on community-focused programmes to lobby community and authorities for support of education and mitigate sociocultural barriers to equitable access to quality learning opportunities. PIB will continue to support community ownership and engagement in G’s&B’s inclusive education by building capacities of Learning Facility Committees in camps to support equitable access to education, safeguarding and protection, including DRM and feedback, reporting and referral mechanisms. In addition, PIB contextualised and further developed a package for Parenting Education in 2019, with ECW/UNESCO funds and consultation of Edu Sector partners and GoB at national and local levels; this will be rolled out for awareness raising of caregivers of 0-8 G & B on child rights and protection, supporting G’s & B’s education, and tolerance and social cohesion. For caregivers of older G & B and/or youth, other resources will primarily draw on the Plan International global Adolescents in Crisis toolkits. Adoles. and youth will be supported to lead social cohesion initiatives to promote values of equality, tolerance and inclusion and foster a culture of peace within the camps and across with the HC.
PIB EiE team will continue to actively participate in the Edu Sector coordination platforms where the technical specialists are members of SAG and TWiG to ensure field-relevant inputs into strategic and technical discussions, as well as inter-sectoral linkages whether for certain vulnerable age groups as youth, supported through YWG, or crosscutting concerns such as CPSS and gender; PIB in fact volunteers for the role of GiHA focal point, and purposefully aims to incorporate gender and inclusion considerations for inclusive quality education as an organisational priority. Across all interventions, PIB’s programming will continue to link with GoB relevant stakeholders and Edu Sector guidance.

project_name: Basic healthcare, maternal and child care and awareness program for the Forcibly Displaced Myanmar Nationals and host communities in Cox’s Bazar District of Bangladesh
project_objective:
1. Providing basic medical services
a) Providing basic medical services
• Providing the OPD service and prescribing necessary medicine with the 24/7 emergency care. 
• Providing consultation and treatment for Non-Communicable Disease (NCD) patients and follow them up on every Tuesday.
b) Training by medical specialists
• Conducting training by medical specialists such as medical doctors, nurses, midwives either from DCHT HQ or/and PWJ every 3 months.
c) Data collection/analysis/monitoring
• Collecting the data regarding the diagnosis and prescription of the patients and report it to the health sector as needed.
• A specialist medical doctor monitors the prescription practice by using the data. The result of monitoring is shared through the monthly report or specialist report.

2. Providing maternal and childcare services
 Providing maternal and childcare services
• Gynecologists or midwives provide ANC/PNC services.
• Providing 24/7 labor and delivery support service
• Providing consultation regarding nutrition, and food which supplements the necessary nutrition for pregnant women and malnourished children
• Providing necessary vaccination for pregnant women and children
b) Providing family planning services
• Explaining family planning methods to all patients who come to the Hakimpara clinic, and providing the methods if the patients hope to practice it.
• Following up the patients who are practicing the family planning regularly to remind them to come to the clinic again in the appropriate timing.
c) Training by medical specialists
• Conducting training by medical specialists such as medical doctors, nurses, midwives either from DCHT HQ or/and PWJ every 2 months.
d) Monitoring
• DCHT HQ doctors or PWJ medical specialists conduct monitoring every 2 months.

3. Awareness program about health and hygiene
a) Awareness program about maternal and child health
• Conducting in 3 blocks in camp 14 and 2 areas in the host community
• Supporting the operation of awareness programs whose main actors are midwives/CHW/TBA. 
b) Selecting 3 target blocks of awareness program about sanitation and hygiene
• Detecting 3 blocks with the highest diarrhea case from the clinic database.
c) Selecting the topic of awareness program about sanitation and hygiene
• Conducting research in the targeted blocks and detecting the root cause of salience of diarrhea case. According to the research result, selecting the topic for the awareness program.
d) Conducting the awareness program about sanitation and hygiene once a month in each target block
• Conducting the awareness program about sanitation and hygiene targeting mainly children, collaborating with the learning center in Camp 14. After 3 months, selecting the hygiene promoters among Rohingya, and thereafter, the promoters lead the awareness program and cleaning event.
e) Distributing personal hygiene materials
• Distributing personal hygiene materials such as soaps, toothbrushes, and toothpaste, according to the topic of the awareness program.
f) Conducting the cleaning event once a month in each target block
• Conducting a cleaning event in 3 blocks in camp 14 once a month. PWJ leads the event in the first 3 months, and thereafter, the hygiene promoters take over the work. The cleaning event is held every month in each block.
g) Monitoring
• Conducting an interview with the residents in the target areas at the end of the project term. Assessing the change in the residents’ knowledge and practice from the survey result of the previous project.

project_name: Ecuador - International Organization for Migration

Regional - Argentina, Aruba, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Curacao, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Guyana, Mexico, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Trinidad and Tobago, Uruguay - International Organization for Migration
Ecuador - CARE International
Emergency and Lifesaving WASH Interventions to IDPs and Vulnerable People in North West Syria.
project_objective:

project_name: Delivering Integrated Sexual and Reproductive Health Services and Information for Crisis -affected population in South Sudan
project_objective:
According to the Health cluster strategy for 2020, it is estimated that 3,296,823 people in South Sudan will require humanitarian healthcare services in the whole of 2020.  However, the health cluster can realistically reach 2,049,990 people with various health care services in different parts of the country.  

In 2020, the health cluster intends to reach this target population using three main objectives in 2020: 1) Reduce excess morbidity and mortality of epidemic-prone diseases and health insecurities; 2) Improve access and scale-up response to integrated quality essential health care services to vulnerable populations; and 3) Increase access to services for survivors of SGBV, disabled and mental health disorders. These objectives are in alignment with HRP 2020 objectives and with UNFPA’s country programme outputs, especially the ones on humanitarian response 1) Increased access to Integrated Sexual Reproductive Health /Gender-Based Violence services including in humanitarian Response and gender and gender-based violence 4) Prevention and response to GBV and harmful practices. 

The situation of reproductive health, including the availability of commodities and supplies for the population affected by the crisis, remains dare. The implementation of the minimum initial services package for SRH is varied in scale and quality as you move across the country. Overall access to SRH services is limited due to poor health infrastructure and road network, limited availability of SRH commodities and limited skilled staff, among others. Antenatal visits and skilled delivery remain a significant challenge, with only 17% of pregnant women attending four visits and a chronic shortage of basic emergency obstetrics and neonatal services. The unmet need for family planning remains high at 24%. The needs for clinical management of rape and psychosocial services for survivors of sexual violence remains high while the mix of frequent population movements, lack of awareness among others provide a conducive environment for new HIV infections. 

Through this project, UNFPA seeks to serve two categories of affected populations namely: 491,998 women of reproductive age group (WRA) of whom we expect 71,000 deliveries, 34,900 WRA attempt to use modern contraceptives, 29,000 people seeking care for STI syndromes and nearly 9,000 cases of sexual violence who will seek care. On the other hand, UNFPA will seek to reach 471,498 girls and boy with HIV prevention services and information, adolescent sexual and reproductive health services and information among others   Overall, UNFPA seeks to reach 963,496 affected people with various forms of SRH services and information. The targets will be achieved through a well-coordinated mechanism for SRH at both the national and local levels.  

The main interventions to achieve the project purpose include, among others: 
a)	Ensuring availability of skilled staff and good quality infrastructure for the provision of integrated SRH/GBV, including emergency obstetric care services at static health facilities and through outreaches. 
b)	Conducting community dialogues and health education for women, men, families and community to increase awareness on benefits of safe sex, HIV prevention, family planning, ANC, PNC and delivery in a health facility by skilled birth attendants;
c)	Procuring, prepositioning, and distributing a whole range of RH kits and non-kit RH medicines and sundries essential for the delivery of RH services at the community, and health facilities including RH equipment for EmONC (delivery beds, examination couches, lighting, and others)
d)	Training service providers on essential lifesaving service areas like supply chain management and rational use of RH kits, MISP, CMR, PAC, FP, HIV prevention and universal precautions, and other lifesaving interventions.
e)	Producing and disseminating IEC materials.
f)	Supporting 24/7 referral system of complicated obstetric cases and GBV cases.
g)	Engage men and boys

project_name: Provision of essential health care services and psychosocial support to conflict-affected population in Northern Syria
project_objective:
DDD intervention will improve access to essential health services and psychosocial support for approximately 508,000 individuals in northwest Syria (catchment population as of September 2019). 

The intervention will contribute to improving access to comprehensive and inclusive healthcare services and to increase well-being of the conflict-affected population in Idlib and Aleppo Governorate, focusing on areas densely populated with IDPs, and continuously receiving new IDPs following conflict escalation in January 2020.

Direct Implementation by DDD:
In northern Idlib governorate (Harim & Idlib Districts):
-	5 PHCCs (Qah, Al Doaa, Al Jolan, Al Dana, Al Salam)
-	2 part-time PHCCs covered by 1 mobile team (Morek Alez and Deir Hassan)
-	2 mobile PHCCs available to respond to new health needs, currently responding to emergency needs in Sarmada and Kili.
-	1 mobile outreach team providing specialized home-based medical services for vulnerable households near DDD fixed PHCCs in Qah, Dier Hassan Cluster, and Al Dana town.

In northern Aleppo governorate (Afrin District)
-	1 PHC clinic in Jinderes;
-	1 PHC clinic in Afrin City;
-	1 PHC clinic in Celmeh, including normal delivery services (starting in second quarter of 2020)

Partners
DDD will work closely with partners to complement DDD direct implementation:
-	Idlib Health Directorate – 2 PHC clinics in Idlib city (Al Thawra and Al Jameea)
-	Aleppo Health Directorate – 3 PHC clinics (Kafr Noran, Kafr Naseh, and Kosnia), until March 2020.
-	Hand in Hand For Aid and Development – From January to March 2020, full support to Atmeh Maternity and Child Hospital. Starting from August 2020 until December 2020, support to 3 mobile clinics in northern Aleppo.

DDD and its partners maintain a flexible approach and adapt intervention according to priority needs defined in coordination with the Health Cluster. Emergency response to most vulnerable groups will be prioritized.

Between January and December 2020, DDD aims to provide a total of 387,320 consultations, consisting of 306,480 PHC consultations, 77,976 SRH consultations, and 2,864 MHPSS consultations. 

A total of 215,098 beneficiaries are expected to benefit from the project. In Idlib, it is estimated that about 75% of beneficiaries reached by the project are displaced individuals (living either in camps or out of camps) while 25% are part of the host population. This is due in part to the fact that certain health facilities are serving IDP camps or urban areas with strong presence of IDPs. In Afrin, beneficiaries of the project will be mainly host communities and IDPs living in informal settlements.

DDD recognize the specific needs of certain groups who face higher health risks or might have limited access to health services. In line with HNO 2019, these population are identified as children under five, pregnant and lactating women, at-risk pregnancies, individuals living with war-related injuries and disabilities, older people, people with functional difficulties, people living with chronic conditions and people affected psychologically by the conflict. 

DDD, as a member of Medecins du Monde (MdM) international network, has a proven track record in providing emergency and long-term medical care to conflict-affected populations in northwest. MdM has been responding to the Syrian crisis for since 2012, progressively increasing funding dedicated to the response. DDD currently runs one office in northern Idlib, located in Qah. The main operational base for DDD operations in NWS is in Antakya, in Hatay province.

The intervention is in line with the Humanitarian and Do No Harm principles and are adapted to comply with the EPHC Package developed by WHO and the Health Cluster.

project_name: Enhance protection environment and access to essential services for conflict-affected communities in East of Libya
project_objective:
Since 2011, Libya has been affected by political, security and economic volatility resulting to a governance vacuum, which has created significant security, rule of law, and social and economic consequences.
An estimate of 897,000 people (including internally displaced persons, returnees, non-displaced conflict-affected people, refugees and migrants) are considered to be in need of humanitarian assistance (HNO, 2020). The majority of people in need are found in urban areas of Libya while many of the most severe needs are in the southern Mantikas such as Al Kufrah. Key humanitarian needs reflect life-threatening risks from exposure, vulnerability and inability to cope with human rights violations, conflict, and deprivation of essential services and commodities. Thus, Libyan crisis is largely characterized by major protection issues. Based on its past years of experience, PUI places the protection in a focus of concern and has adjusted its programming to better response to the context’s evolution. To this end, PUI keeps taking concrete steps to reinforce the centrality of protection within its response with the goal to contribute to alleviating the suffering of conflict-affected populations in East of Libya. Specifically, the Action will aim to enhance the protection environment and improve access to essential services. During the 8 months, PUI will effortlessly continue to reach out and assist conflict-affected communities via the development of continuous protection need’s assessments, and the provision of health and protection-based direct assistance through the deployment of 4 outreach teams.
Throughout the Action, PUI will still work closely with authorities and partners to improve local capacities, acceptance and coordination of the intervention. Humanitarian principles will guide the Action to promote safety, dignity and rights of affected people, and mitigate exposure to additional risks through conflict sensitive and do not harm approaches.

project_name: Information, Counselling and Legal Assistance (ICLA) for Conflict Affected People in Eastern Ukraine
project_objective:
NRC will ensure that a greater number of the most vulnerable conflict-affected people in hard-to-reach areas have access to basic rights and humanitarian assistance, will help reduce vulnerability and increase resilience; Strengthen the capacity of government and civil society legal service providers to serve an increased case load of the IDP and conflict-affected population in need of assistance; 
Support economic and social well-being as a durable solution by providing IDPs with equal access to, and enjoyment of right to adequate standard of living without discrimination, including shelter, livelihoods and employment, effective and accessible mechanisms to restore housing, land and property rights, access to personal and other documentation and freedom of movement; Push for the adoption of legislation and practice promoting sustainability and protection in line with international standards. 
NRC ICLA in Ukraine aims to support persons affected by the conflict in eastern Ukraine (CAP), broadly defined as individuals who have suffered harm, including physical or mental injury, emotional suffering, economic loss or substantial impairment of their human rights and fundamental freedoms as a direct result of the conflict in eastern Ukraine. CAP include: IDP (registered or not); people at risk of displacement and people who are unable to flee; returnees; host families or communities. 

ICLA will endeavour to reach the most vulnerable within the above target groups, notably women/single headed households, especially with a large number of children, elderly (particularly living alone), people with disabilities or limited mobility, extremely poor and no-income families, people of pre-retirement age, people living in rural or remote areas. It is important to stress that this will include persons from GCA and NGCA, the latter being targeted through a range of modalities.
In addition to CAP, ICLA will target duty-bearer beneficiaries - central, regional and local legislative, executive and judicial authorities responsible for various aspects of the CAP issues, and other stakeholder beneficiaries - professional national associations/institutions (Bar Associations; Law Faculties Legal Aid Clinics, Secondary Free Legal Aid Centres) and nation-wide, long-standing NGOs, as well as local civil society organisations / initiatives / associations representing interests of conflict-affected people. Both of these target groups require sensitisation and capacity and institution building in order to cope with the displacement issues.

project_name: Protection of Children Strengthened
project_objective:
Children represent 54 per cent of the Rohingya refugee population in Cox’s Bazar (CXB) District (435, 679 children according to UNHCR-RRRC Family Counting data). Of these, 266,416 have been identified by the as children in need of immediate assistance by the Child Protection Sub-Sector.

The protection environment has become more complex with deteriorating security environment, which in 2019 particularly affected women’s and girls’ safe access to services, and conflicts with host communities. Based on UNHCR August 2019 settlement profiles, risk related to kidnapping, trafficking and violence were the three most perceived risks after natural hazards. UASC are at heightened risk of child trafficking, abuse and exploitation. Girls are of particular concern to protection actors as girls as disproportionately vulnerable to abuse, violence, sexual exploitation, and neglect. Boys have limited access to GBV services and have been found to be particularly vulnerable to child labour including worst forms of child labour. Other known prevalent risk factors for boys and girls include child marriage, child pregnancy and motherhood, domestic violence, as well as challenges to access to services for children with disabilities.

The project will be implemented through partnerships with established child protection agencies, which will improve access to quality child protection services through case management, Multipurpose Children and Adolescent Hubs and community based child protection structures. In line with the CPSS strategy of putting the community at the centre of the response, focus will be placed on scaling up and strengthening community child protection mechanisms such as community volunteers involved in prevention and response activities. Further engagement with influential community leaders as well as parents/ caregivers will be done to enhance community participation, ownership and sustainability of the programmes.

Specialised services will be provided for children at a higher risk of abuse, exploitation, neglect and violence taking into account Age, Gender and Diversity. Through targeted activities in existing safe spaces, the resilience and development of boys and girls especially adolescents will be strengthened; and specialized psychosocial support will be given to those in need, including psychologically distressed children. Community and child participation is key to protection of children and this project will provide capacity building through trainings and coaching to identified child protection structures as well as other stakeholders. Appropriate child friendly feedback mechanisms will be utilised throughout the project cycle in line with AAP principles.

 All activities will be coordinated through the identified child protection focal point agency in each camp and UNHCR’s active participation in and contributions to the Child Protection Sub-sector and Protection Sector coordination mechanisms and initiatives; and will be implemented with a multi-sectoral approach to ensure mainstreaming of child protection in all areas of the humanitarian response.

Some of the outcomes of the project include, but not limited to:
1. Increase in number of adolescents who participate in targeted programmes. 
2. Reduction in physical violence or psychological aggression experienced by children in homes, safe spaces and community. 
3. Girls and boys protected against harmful practices
4. Children have safe access to community spaces for socialising, play, learning, etc
5. Children have non-discriminatory access to national child protection and social services
6. Children with specific needs receive Age, Gender and Diversity appropriate services.

project_name: Evidence-based planning and programming for humanitarian actors in Syria
project_objective:
REACH, a joint initiative of IMPACT, ACTED and the United Nations Operational Satellite Applications Programme (UNOSAT), aims to facilitate evidence-based planning, technical advisory and coordination support for humanitarian actors in Syria by providing information management, technical advisory and coordination support to at least 225 humanitarian organizations. REACH will be leading on the implementation of project activities. More specifically, this will be done through the following activities:
•	Producing Monthly Humanitarian Situation Overviews in Syria (HSOS)
•	Emergency assessments on the humanitarian situation situation in Syria
•	Cash and markets assessments in collaboration with CBR-TWG
•	Camps and sites profiling and mapping
•	Remote sensing to support IDP site identification and shelter counts
•	Technical advisory to the humanitarian coordination structure, among other towards the successful implementation of the 2020 Syria MSNA
•	Thematic assessments/specialised assessments to meet information gaps

REACH has designed this intervention based on feedback from humanitarian actors and seven years of experience in implementation in Syria. REACH maintains regular discussions with Whole of Syria coordination structures including the deputy regional humanitarian coordinator, OCHA, clusters/working groups, and the NES forum, and sits as well at the ICCG in Turkey and the ISWG in NES/Iraq. Additionally, REACH is part of the NGO Forum and the SIRF and also joins the SIRF Policy and Advocacy working group. These engagements enable a timely and efficient identification of information needs and gaps as well as opportunities for partnerships and collaboration. Activities included in this proposal have thus been designed based on these interactions. For example, conversations with the NES Forum, OCHA, SSWG and CCCM cluster have confirmed a general lack of information on camps and sites in northern Syria, which was flagged as of particular concern given the worsened emergency situation in both NWS and NES. REACH Camps and Sites sweeps conducted in 2019 in NWS also revealed a significant number of sites that were not yet registered by the CCCM cluster, which outlined an information gap and a need to support CCCM processes.

This project is already fully funded, but may require additional top-ups later in the year.

IMPACT is a leading Geneva based think-and-do-tank, created in Switzerland in 2010 on the initiative of ACTED and firstly operationalised in 2012. While autonomous organizations, IMPACT and ACTED operate together thanks to a formalised global partnership. Together, IMPACT, ACTED and UNOSAT set up the REACH program in order to promote and facilitate the development of information products that enhance the humanitarian community’s decision making and planning capacity. IMPACT is the lead-organization in REACH and hosts the REACH global team in its Geneva HQ. As sister organizations, IMPACT and ACTED coordinate on field implementation. In all field operations of the REACH program, ACTED provides operational support (security management, office space, cars, national HR recruitment, etc.), while IMPACT provides strategic and programmatic oversight through its global team and is in charge of the validation and dissemination of reports, and external relations
