project_name: Primary health care services for vulnerable children and women in Syria
project_objective:
With the continuation of conflict into the ninth year, the basic health status of women and children in Syria remains precarious, with a fragile health sector. This situation has been exacerbated by the disruptions to allied sectors, such as food security, water, sanitation and hygiene which have further compounded the prevailing vulnerabilities. This proposal from UNICEF aims to support the provision of basic lifesaving curative, preventive and promotional health services, while enhancing  early recovery  and resilience of the sector by contributing to strengthening the service delivery partners, platforms and community systems. It is also conceived with a view to promoting the complementarity of the contributions of other sector sections within UNICEF ( Nutrition, WASH, Education and Child protection) and other sector key sector partners ( UN agencies, NGOs etc).
A total of more than 5 million women and children will directly benefit from the package of services, focusing more on the highest severity areas in all governorates as defined by the health cluster. Program effectiveness shall be enhanced by applying a conflict and risk informed lens to planned interventions, and the promotion of the participation of affected populations.
UNICEF will implement the planned activities through MOH, and local 21 NGOs who will run 36 fixed health centers and 47 mobile medical teams, and will monitor the implementation of those NGOs through programmatic field visits and financial monitoring visits by UNICEF staff in the different hubs as feasible and by the third party facilitators & monitors. A special format for the field visit report is already developed by UNICEF and used by all supervisors, facilitators and monitors. For MOH; the monitoring is usually done jointly with MOH staff and WHO officers to monitor the proper implementation of the vaccination campaigns and the routine vaccinations in health centers and mobile vaccination teams, feedback is given to MOH with focus on the safety of injections, communication with parents and proper management of vaccines and cold chain.
The planned activities will include all targeted vulnerable children under the age of five years and women in child-bearing age, including disabled children and women (15% of the population), and the IPs will report separately the number of disabled children and women reached with the different interventions.
Health workers are oriented on GBV and PSEA, and the services is designed to be protective for vulnerable girls and boys and women. Female doctors and nurses are always available in health centers and mobile medical teams.
Communities are engaged in the design of the project through focus group discussions, and feed back through the field visits by staff and third party monitors and facilitators. Several tools have been developed, and the results are taken into consideration to further improve planning, prioritization and the quality of supplies. The feedback from families has been very useful to further improve the quality and the type of items distributed.

project_name: Health Response to the COVID-19 pandemic in Cox's Bazar District
project_objective:
""The project aims to reduce the morbidity and mortality from COVID-19 through rapid detection, diagnosis, and prevention of the spread of the novel coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2), caring for those affected and breaking the chain of human-to-human transmission. 

IOM will establish 4 SARI isolation and treatment facilities with the total bed capacity of 250 with the provision of isolation and treatment services to forecasted 6,000 cases in 9 months. Initially, existing 4 PHCs will be upgraded for limited scale isolations (total 11 bed capacity) to enable the isolation and referral of initial suspected cases and while infrastructural development for the larger facilities will continue. Existing health posts will be upgraded for appropriate patient screening and triage. 100 mid-term shelters at camp 20E will be repurposed for quarantine of contacts of COVID-19 cases during low incidence phase with the view to early containment of the outbreak. In the high incidence phase, the facility will be converted into a 200 bed isolation facility for mild cases. Additionally, IOM will support government health facilities in Ukhiya, Teknaf, Cox's Bazar Sadar and when needed in broader Cox's Bazar (including Maheshkhali, Ramu and Chakaria) with structural support, human resource and logistics for case management and infection prevention and control.

To establish a prompt and effective referral system for COVID-19 cases and contacts, IOM will lead a dispatch and referral unit along with designate ambulances and vehicles. Three ambulance disinfection points will be established for safe cleaning and decontamination of ambulances carrying COVID-19 cases.  IOM will also support effective surveillance through participation of its skilled staff in rapid investigation teams and community health workers in contact tracing.

In parallel, IOM will undertake the procurement of necessary items, including prepositioning of commodities, PPE and medicines for patient management at dedicated isolation facilities, Rapid Investigation Teams and dispatch and referral unit including ambulances. The operation of the four Isolation and Treatment Centers (ITC) will require continous supply chain management for appropriate medical and other logistic supplies as well as the recruitment of large number of additional medical and support personnel as per WHO guidlines. Ensuring that all personal have the required amount of PPE to minimize risks of contamination and that ITCs are equipped with the necessary equipment and medicines will be a key focus of our procurement and supply chain teams. Additional human resources, including medical officers, nurses and cleaners will be engaged to strengthen IOM existing medical teams. 

IOM will set-up mini laboratories in the isolation and treatment centers for common laboratory investigations including X-ray with portable machines. Laboratory testing facility for novel corona virus, when feasible, will be established at IOM ITCs. IOM considers using GeneXpert testing for COVID 19 in the proposed laboratories.

To ensure Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) procedures, protocols and systems will be established and monitored for effective response to COVID-19. Notably IOM will subject all supported 35 existing health facilities and the four ITCs to the IOM IPC Checklist to monitor medical team compliance with IPC measures. Through the network of Community Health workers of the implementing partners, IOM will ensure health risk communication and community engagement. 

During preparedness mode, MHPSS activities will focus on increasing the capacity of IOM team members including volunteers to deliver basic psychosocial support (e.g. psychological first aid (PFA), basic counselling skills, and stress management skills)

project_name: Provision of camp coordination and camp management services, coordination and capacity-building to support displacement-affected communities in South Sudan.
project_objective:
ACTED concurs with CCCM cluster objectives to continue core camp management activities in PoCs and camp settings, expand mobile CCCM capacity, engage with coordination mechanisms, and to engage deeper with the capacity building of NNGOs. In line with these objectives, ACTED plans to directly respond to the needs of 81,367 IDPs through the following interventions:
1.	Response to the needs of 31,367 IDPs located in Juba PoCs (29,429) and Bor PoC (1,938) through static CCCM interventions. 
2.	Response to the needs of some (50,000) of the approximately 1.2m IDPs (OCHA) residing outside of formally recognized camp-like settings through 10 mobile CCCM-led missions. 
3.	Support to a coordinated response and advocacy for the needs of IDPs through hosting the Camp Management and Camp Coordination (CCCM) cluster co-lead.
4.	Capacity-building to NNGOs. 

1.	Static Responses:
As of September 2019, the total of number of civilians seeking safety in Juba UN House was 29,429, and in Bor PoC 1,938 (CCCM cluster).As camp manager, ACTED will provide residents and partners with CCCM support aimed at improving living conditions and effective delivery of services. Activities include:
•	Strengthening community governance mechanisms
•	Ensuring accountability through communication and community engagement (CCE)
•	Site maintenance improvements
•	Service provision coordination
•	Information management
Under RSRTF funding, ACTED intends to respond to the recommendations of the Secretary General’s 180 day report by expanding capacity in protection (particularly HLP) and by working with the PoC service providers to expand provision in the peri-PoC and urban areas, equalizing historic service imbalances. 

2.	Mobile Responses:
Of the approximately 1,465,542 IDPs in South Sudan (OCHA, September 2019), only around 18% or 278,206 resided in PoCs and collective sites (CCCM cluster, September 2019). ACTED’s mobile responses will target hard-to-reach displacement-affected populations outside of camp or camp-like settlements.
ACTED intends to conduct at least 10 mobile missions in 2020, which will be CCCM-led quality, information-driven, multi-sectoral interventions that help people adapt to disaster and prepare to transition towards self-reliance. 
Activities will include:
•	Multi-sectoral assessment and CCCM site profile assessment
•	Establishing and strengthening community governance mechanisms
•	Ensuring accountability through CCE
•	Site maintenance improvements
•	Service provision coordination
•	Information management
•	Contingency planning and emergency preparedness
As many of targeted locations demonstrate severe emergency needs across sectors, advocacy to other partners and clusters is prioritized. To streamline this process, ACTED also intends to leverage multi-sectoral funds (S/NFI, FSL and WASH) to deliver a more comprehensive and holistic response. 
Interventions target a whole ‘displacement-affected community’ (IDPs, host community, returnees and local polity) with CCCM activities. Protection staff accompany mobile missions to support coordination with protection partners. Where protection gaps exist, ACTED will collaborate with mobile protection partners for joint missions.

3.	Coordination:
ACTED will host the CCCM cluster co-coordinator, supporting improvement of participation in coordination mechanisms. ACTED will continue to work closely with the CCCM cluster and other parnters to coordinate all activities, including strengthened collaboration with SFPs.

4.	Capacity-building:
ACTED is in discussion with the NGO Forum to deliver a comprehensive package of training to NNGOs in South Sudan, in Juba and nationwide. This will focus on supporting capacity for all humanitarian responses, including specific training on CCCM. ACTED trains local authorities and local NGO partners on CCCM in all responses. ACTED will soon support Health Link, an NNGO, with their new mobile CCCM activities, and we will expand this focus on mobile CCCM capacity building.

project_name: Colombia - iMMAP
Seasonal food support to 30,000 local vulnerable populations in the Far North Region
project_objective:
Through the project WFP will provide seasonal food assistance to the most vulnerable local populations in targeted areas of the Far North regions. Assistance will be delivered through unconditional in-kind food distributions for 6 months. In-kind food assistance will support households’ access to adequate and nutritious food, therefore prevent them from adopting negative coping practices. The half ration of the in-kind distributions will provide 1,050 kcal energy per day per person. The food basket and the daily rations will comprise 175g cereals, 50g pulses; 17.5g vegetable, and 2.5g salt.

WFP food assistance in-kind will contribute to ensure food security of the households during the period of hardship. During food distribution special attention will be paid on households with people specific needs and necessary support will be provided taking into consideration of the situation of the head of the household (whether male or female or child); the presence of a person with specific needs (pregnant woman, elderly person, disabled person etc.) in the household also has an impact on food security. Regular monitoring activities will be conducted during food distribution and monthly data collected against performance indicators for reporting. During post distribution monitoring, attention will be paid on the role played by men, women, girls and boys including decision-making on food consumption and food security in the household. Targeted vulnerable local populations will be closely involved in various stages including beneficiaries targeting process, food distribution also through complaints and feedback mechanisms they could freely express their views and concerns on the project implementation. In line with WFP accountability to affected populations, beneficiaries’ complaints are treated respectfully, and their views are considered for projects adjustment. WFP together with local authorities and partners, conducts assessments to identify most vulnerable people among the local populations to be considered in the projects based on vulnerability criteria. These criteria include household size, presence of under-5 children, the elderly and handicapped, women-headed households, assets. Women and men will be equal participants, decision-makers and beneficiaries to enhance resilience. WFP ensures that women, men, girls and boys are involved in various stages of the project from conception to evaluation. For the conception of projects, beneficiaries’ opinions are regularly consulted through focus group discussions, gender and protection evaluation field missions, post distribution monitoring exercises and others. These gave beneficiaries opportunities to state their preferences for food items and transfer modalities and opinions on targeting criteria.

project_name: Asset creation project to support Early recovery and Resilience for 50,000 people through livelihood activities in crisis-affected areas in the Far-North region
project_objective:
The Project aims to improve access to food and contribute to improving social cohesion and building resilience of vulnerable and food insecure communities affected by the Boko Haram crisis and violence in the Far North region. This project will address immediate food needs of 50,000 vulnerable people including returnees and local populations that are severely affected by Boko Haram attacks disrupting economic, agricultural, and pastoral activities in the Far North region. The implementation of livelihood activities, Community-based Participatory Planning (CBPP) sessions are carried out together with local community members (both women and men) to identify actual needs and priorities of the local communities that will support the affected populations to come up with their own response strategies and build resilience. This people-centered approach ensures the provision of effective solutions together with beneficiaries and reduce the dependency on relief. 
Assistance through for FFA, will be implemented using cash modality and in-kind Food for three months. Therefore, the cash transfer value is aligned with the in-kind food ration. It considers beneficiaries' food preferences for the commodities and prices on the local market. The transfer value is calculated based on the identified food gap and is designed to assist beneficiaries to reach the recommended minimum calories intake of 2,100 Kcal per person per day. The use of cash-based transfers is expected to improve the cost-effectiveness of WFP's operations, while seizing the economic opportunities of local markets, with particular consideration for the beneficiaries’ choice and dignity. 
WFP will collaborate closely with Government technical ministries, cooperating partners and communities to ensure project implementation and sustainability. Nutrition, Gender and protection issues are taken into consideration at all the stages of the project elaboration, implementation, monitoring and evaluation. Gender and protection risk analysis will be carried out and the most vulnerable will be targeted, including female-headed households, pregnant and lactating women, persons with disabilities.
Project sites will be in secure areas and at convenient distance from the homes of the beneficiaries.
To support smooth project implementation and ensure sustainability, capacity strengthening sessions will be organized for all stakeholders on gender and protection policy, project management, monitoring and nutrition.

project_name: Emergency Shelter and Non-Food Item  (ES/NFI) Assistance in South Sudan for Medair’s Emergency Response Team (ERT)
project_objective:
The project aims to meet the basic life-saving ES/NFI needs of affected populations due to conflict or violence within South Sudan. It is part of an emergency response so can take place in any location at short notice. The target is to reach 40,000 individuals who are deemed the most vulnerable using both the cluster’s and Medair’s vulnerability criteria. Medair will target newly displaced persons, protracted displaced persons, returnees and vulnerable host communities. Within these groups the most vulnerable will be defined as sharing limited resources, over-burdened households, people with disability, female headed households, pregnant and lactating females etc. Medair puts AAP and protection mainstreaming at the core of all programming to ensure meaningful access to services and to protect the safety and the dignity of beneficiaries.

With ongoing violence throughout South Sudan Medair continues to see many people still displaced and most having left their homes with no items and in some cases homes have been looted and burned down. IDPs are then sharing resources with already vulnerable host households often meaning multiple families will share 1 saucepan, 1 mosquito net, 1 blanket etc. Medair aims to address this by responding to sudden onset displacement due to violence. Medair will complete an effective analysis of the populations needs using the clusters analysis tools. An analysis (using tools such as the stakeholder analysis, a protection risk analysis, research, observation and Medair field teams’ findings) takes place to then discuss if an intervention is appropriate and what interventions are possible. The communities are then involved in discussions to help determine the intervention needed to best suit the needs alongside Medair teams. 

Once an intervention is confirmed Medair then works closely with the ES/NFI cluster and IOM to receive items needed for the distribution in a timely manner for beneficiaries. Medair set up a community distribution committee made up of representative community members to discuss the appropriate and safe way to distribute to allow meaningful access. Guidelines are given on the selection criteria and this is disseminated to communities and the teams are available to answer questions on this. A safety audit is completed to make sure the distribution site is safe and accessible. 

Throughout the distribution the Medair team makes sure representative casual labourers are used and then there is a clear and well organized complaints feedback mechanism so any issues are resolved swiftly on the day. Following the distribution, Medair teams will complete exit interviews so they remain accountable to the populations, they can deal with any urgent issues whilst in the field, they can identify any furthers gaps or needs and for internal lessons learnt. Anytime between four weeks and 3 months a PDM will be completed to fully assess the impact of the intervention and if the community feel that their most basic needs have been met and if this was done in a safe and dignified manner. 

The Medair team then report to the cluster, donors and sometimes communities on findings from the intervention and will also share with other partners and cluster if further needs have been identified that Medair are unable to respond to. This means Medair programmes remain accountable and transparent to all involved.

project_name: Provision of life saving Shelter and Non-Food Items (SNFI) for the most vulnerable conflict and otherwise-disaster affected people in South Sudan.
project_objective:
DRC’s SNFI project  will (i) provide emergency SNFI support to crisis-affected populations in hard to reach locations across South Sudan  and (ii) provide life-saving and life- sustaining shelter support to the most vulnerable groups within Malakal PoC. Support will be provided  through a mobile approach, using teams stationed in Juba and Malakal, and through DRC’s static presence in Malakal PoC. All responses will be based on comprehensive SNFI assessments incorporating protection risk analyses. DRC will aim to the cluster recommended  26% cash modalities and the remaining 74% with in-kind modalities depending on feasibility, appropriateness, and value-for-money determined through comprehensive protection risk assessments and market analysis.
DRC will aim to reach 45,000 individuals who are in need  of life-saving SNFI assistance. Targeted individuals will be prioritized  through a needs-based approach considering IDPs, host community, returnees, and other population groups. Within the target populations, individuals with particular protection vulnerabilities including pregnant and lactating women, unaccompanied children, elderly people in need  of support, and people with disabilities, will be prioritized  in accordance with SNFI cluster guidelines. Close coordination with the SNFI sector will be maintained to ensure DRC’s activities complement and feed into wider sectoral strategies for the wider South Sudan  response. 
DRC mobile response team is composed of Protection, S/NFI, WASH and CCCM sectors and DRC as a protection focus agency to mainstream Protection, Gender Based Violence (GBV) mitigation and prevention and AAP to enhance the overall quality of S-NFI response in 2020. According to shelter-NIF cluster strategy, DRC will participate in joint missions among others to avoid duplication and better coordination among the Shelter-NFI cluster partners and other clusters.

DRC Malakal Protection team is already implementing Housing, Land and Property (HLP) support in Upper Nile state and providing high-quality counseling on HLP legal rights and civil documentation/registration, freedom of movement and basic access to social services to community members in Malakal town and in the PoC. DRC consider HLP under the protection due to its complexity but Shelter/NFI team will access support from HLP team to enhance S-NFI qualitative response.  

DRC will ﬂexibly draw on both its own funds to procure distribution items and the SNFI cluster pipeline as most appropriate to ensure an eﬃcient and timely response. In accordance with SNFI cluster priorities, there will be an ongoing focus on monitoring, evaluation, assessment, and learning  (MEAL) activities through post-distribution monitoring activities and integrating quick monitoring exercises conducted for all distributions done by mobile teams and by our static oﬃces in Malakal and new ones that DRC may open  in 2020.

project_name: Colombia - Stichting War Child
Inclusive Emergency Assistance to Crisis-affected Populations in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh
project_objective:
The proposed response aims at providing direct comprehensive services at HH, hospitals and HF levels including specialized MHPSS, Physical and Functional Rehab and SRHR through a twin-track approach. 
- Multi-sectorial mobile units composed of Social Workers, Nurses, Physiotherapists and Psychologists identify and provide tailored and individual assistance to the most vulnerable persons, especially the persons with disabilities and their caregivers who might be excluded from the community safe spaces due to mobility issues, distance or social norm barriers. Through a unique home-based intervention and integrated outreach teams, composed of a Rehab and a PSS Officer, persons with injuries and/or disabilities receive home-based Rehab and PSS services. SOPs are implemented to frame this intervention, to define the eligibility criteria (only for persons who cannot access HF). An internal and external multi-sectorial referral system is facilitated to ensure timely emergency assistance for the most vulnerable individuals.
- Support to Gov hospitals and health facilities (HF) both in the host and the refugee communities. Physiotherapists provide direct comprehensive Rehab services in the HF and build the HW capacities through trainings and mentorship. HI has 11 fix points equipped with Rehab equipment and ran by 11 teams that includes Physiotherapist and PSS Officers providing Rehab and PSS services to those with enough mobility to access the HF. Finally, the Rehab team provides assistive and mobility devices and other specific items (crutches, bedsore mattresses…) when necessary, to people with physical and functional limitations in order to improve their mobility, enhance recovery for person with injury and prevent further complications. Training and advices are provided to persons them and their caregivers on basic home-based rehab and proper use, maintenance and repair of mobility devices. 
Individualized PSS aims at reducing the symptoms faced by individuals with chronic and long-term disabling conditions. PSS services focus on individual assessment to create personalized care plans to increase their functionality and enable individuals that face psychiatric or distress symptoms to take part in group activities to support their social skills whilst learning coping mechanisms. For those in need of specialized psychiatric support, HI PSS staff provides basic counseling combined with referral and follow up of medication continuation at home/center level. PSS Officers work with caregivers to alleviate their distress and ensure that persons with disabilities who require daily rehabilitation care understand the necessity of modern care services compared to traditional healers. 
HI Nurses focus their outreach support on the following health issues: wound care, bedsores care, ANC and PNC. HI Nurses provide maternal care for women who cannot access HF, including the prevention and detection of pregnancy-related risks and complications. The Nurses then refer to the nearest HF and follow up to ensure they received the necessary services. HI raises awareness on the risks to deliver at home encouraging pregnant women to attend a HF for the delivery, ensuring an integrated and complementary response. Pregnant women with mobility issues are regularly followed by HI Nurses, who control their vital signs and ensure a healthy pregnancy by providing basic advices to the pregnant women and young mothers who cannot attend the HF or the fix points. 
HI has been present in Cox’s Bazar for more than 12 years and is part of the Health sector, including MHPSS WG and the ADWG the aim of which is to the aim of which is to mainstream Age and Disability across all sectors through trainings on data collection (WGSQ), the types of impairments, barriers and facilitators.
Along with a strong standardized CRFM which uses different channels including individual and group feedback sessions and a hotline, HI ensures the respect and promotion of its PSEA policy.

Unconditional food assistance through cash based transfers to 15,000 IDPs in the Far North region

In line with WFP Cameroon Country Strategic Plan (CSP 2018-2020), life-saving assistance will be provided 15,000 IPDs that moved from their villages located along the border with Nigeria and settled in safer places within the Far North region.  The food assistance to the beneficiaries will be delivered through monthly unconditional cash transfers the ration is 8,580 XAF per beneficiary to support them to access adequate and nutritious food. A six months full ration assistance will contribute to prevent the IDPs from adopting negative coping strategies during the farming period. 
For the conception of projects, beneficiaries’ opinions have been considered through focus group discussions, gender and protection evaluation field missions, monitoring exercises. In line with WFP Cameroon Country Strategic Plan (CSP 2018-2020), life-saving assistance will be provided Nigerian refugees in Minawao camp. Multi-sector refugee assistance for Eritrean, Ethipian and South Sudanese refugees in East Sudan and North Darfur
project_objective: This project targets vulnerable refugee and host communities in three different States: North Darfur, Kassala and Gedaref with multi-sector activities. In North Darfur, the project is part of the South Sudanese refugee response in Al Lait locality and targets 300 individuals with livelihood and resilience support. As part of the  Eastern Sudan refugee response (Eritrean and Ethiopian refugees), the project targets 128,546 individuals in El Fashaga locality in Gedaref State and and Wad El Helew locality in Kassala State. The individuals are targeted with multi-sector activities, including the following areas of intervention: (child) protection (700 beneficiaries), WASH (92,436 beneficiaries), Livelihood (930 beneficiaries), Energy/Environment (300 beneficiaries) and direct support through NFI distributions (7,000 beneficiaries). The project aims to to respond to the humanitarian needs of the target population as well as strengthening their resilience to become self-sustaining and enhance peaceful coexistence. Mass hygiene messaging though radio as well as recreational activities for youth groups (football tournaments, cultural events) will benefit both host communities and refugees alike.

project_name: Coordinated support to the NGO Forum members to improve and save lives
project_objective:
Although the R-ARCSS resulted in improved security and opportunities for recovery, due to the cumulative impacts of conflict, destroyed livelihoods and persistant localised insecurity, 7.1 million people in 2019 were in need of humanitarian assistance. With the government having limited capacity to responds nearly 90% of assistance is provide by international and national NGOs. There is need for NGOs to share information on learning from humanitarian and development programmes, understanding of government policies and regulartory processes regarding providing humanitarian assistance. NGOs, particularly national NGOs lack access to security information to allow for for planning and ensuring safety and protection of staff and beneficiaries. National NGOs ofthen lack capacity to engage in coordination mechanisms to share learnings to improve programming. Coordination needs to be considered to minimise misunderstandings between NGOs, UN agencies and government, and, inevitably, a reduction in the available services for beneficiaries and improve the operating environment for humanitarian agencies. 
Concern will continue to host the NGO Forum to support NGOs to contribute to principled and effective humanitarian assistance in South Sudan by members. The NGO Forum will provide information sharing for members on learnings to improve humanitarian and development approaches and forging collaborations between the INGOs and national NGOs. Security information will be compiled and shared with members to allow for planning of humanitarian and development programmes to ensure safety and protection of members’ staff and beneficiaries. The NGO Forum will coordinate collective voices of  NGO members for common positions; and joint advocacy for enabling environment operating in South Sudan. Capacity of national NGOs will be reinforced through providing capacity building for NGOs through providing humanitarian training; sharing best practices in humanitarian delivery and information exchanges.

project_objective: Le projet s’inscrit dans la continuité des actions mises en oeuvre dans la région de Tombouctou depuis 2014 sous financement ECHO dont les projets mis en oeuvre en de 2017 à 2019. DRC propose de contribuer à la réduction de la vulnérabilité économique, alimentaire et nutritionnelle des ménages très pauvres et vulnérables. L’approche multisectorielle incluant la protection transversale sera reconduite et approfondie afin d'assurer la sécurité des bénéficiaires, de minimiser les effets négatifs de l'aide humanitaire et d'adapter les activités aux changements contextuels. L’action se concentrera sur les besoins d’urgence tout en renforçant les aspects de résilience, essentiels pour assurer un impact maximal. L’objectif est de poursuivre la transition amorcée depuis 2017 de l’aide humanitaire vers des actions de développement et de planifier ainsi une stratégie de sortie responsable et progressive en mettant l’accent sur les besoins de Protection des ménages du Nord et Centre du Mali. project_name: Provision of lifesaving reproductive health care and GBV prevention and response services for Southern Sudanese refugees in khartoum, White Nile, South Kordofan , West Kordofan, East Darfur, refugee and asylum seekers in Khartoum (Urban Situation), Central African Republican (CAR) refugees in South Darfur and Eritrean and Ethiopian refugees in Kassala and Gadaref in East Sudan.
project_objective:
Given the current situation in Sudan the refugee population and other migrants and asylum seeker in different states are at risk of GBV and Sexual and reproductive health SRH problems and complications due to insecurity, limited access to health care services, low economic status and lack of livelihood opportunities, lack of community awareness, combined with negative coping strategies. UNFPA in 2020 will support integrated GBV and SRH life-saving prevention and response services for South Sudanese refugees,  refugees and asylum seekers in Khartoum, Ethiopian, Eritrean asylum seekers in the east  and CAR refugees in South Darfur, with focus on women and girls, men and  boys. 

Khartoum presents a diverse and complex migration profile of Eritrean, Ethiopian, Congolese, Syrian and Yemeni. UNFPA objective in this project is to address GBV prevention and response needs including the SRH consequences among the urban refugees in the prioritized localities of (Jabal Aulia, Khartoum, Sharq El Nile, Um Durman and Umm Badda as well as the Open Area) through the planned activities: Support immediate GBV/SGBV prevention and response services, community-based protection networks, Community outreach activities, Host community sensitization, and trafficking prevention and response services, and supporting provision of clinical management of rape  CMR services to survivors. So far the GBV referral pathways builds on the availability of existing services including medical treatment of survivors (CMR).  Vulnerable host communities living near to the targeted population will be considered in the response. 

In East Sudan  UNFPA objective is  to address GBV prevention and response and SRH needs among the Eritrean and Ethiopian refugees in the prioritized localities  El Fashaga (Um Gargour camp), Khashm Ghirba (Kilo 26 and Girba camps),Wad Sherifey camp; Wad El Helew (Shagarab I, II and III camps ). project_name: Provision of comprehensive and live saving sexual reproductive health services for rohingya refugees and host community in Cox's Bazar
project_objective:
To improve equitable access to and utilization of quality lifesaving and comprehensive sexual reproductive health services for refugees and host communities, UNFPA will continue to strengthen sexual reproductive health and rights of women and girls. UNFPA will ensure continuous availability of sexual and reproductive health commodities and equipment through improved supply chain management, including family planning methods to meet contraceptive needs of refugees and host communities. Capacity building will continue for healthcare providers on sexual and reproductive health, gender-based violence, adolescent health, obstetric fistula screening, newborn care and cervical cancer screening. Minimizing loss of life cannot be achieved without sustaining funding for emergency and specialized health care referrals.  A robust referral mechanism will be implemented for both the camps and host community through trainings and knowledge exchange among the health care providers/midwives and implementation of a functional hospital rotation plan. Maternal and neonatal death surveillance will be expanded to help identify and address avoidable mortality factors.
The interventions planned under this project will ensure timely access to essential live saving and comprehensive sexual and reproductive health services to Rohingya refugees and host community in Ukhiya and Teknaf Sub districts of Cox’s bazar district. The project aims at addressing the priority sexual and reproductive Health including ensuring the minimum initial service package (MISP) for reproductive health in crisis and now transitioning to comprehensive SRH for the affected population 
Of the 1.3 million people targeted in the JRP, this project will focus on those 406,108 refugees and host communities which includes women of reproductive age that are facing critical life threatening situations in the Teknaf and Ukhiya sub-districts of Cox’s Bazar. These women of reproductive age are at constant and immediate-risk of pregnancy related complications and will need urgent and immediate care. 
The project also seeks to improve and maintain the quality of SRH facilities, strengthened referral pathway and safe access to 24-hour rapid transfer of all life-threatening emergencies, maintaining continuous supply of life saving SRH commodities including family planning services, scale up quality midwifery led care across the camps by providing mentorship support to the service providers through capacity building program, strengthening community based SRH services and behavioral change approaches by ensuring that quality SRH information and services are available near the communities. 
Bangladesh as a country being prone to natural disasters and ranked 13th in the world in the risk for natural disasters with flooding and cyclones ranking the highest. The project will also take into consideration the contingency planning and needs to respond to sexual reproductive health and rights during natural disasters. Less than two year ago, this same area of Bangladesh, including Cox’s Bazar and Chittagong, was ravaged by Cyclone Mora bringing widespread flooding and damaging winds affecting over 3 million people. 
The project will be implemented under the auspices of SRH Working Group under the Health Sector, which provides technical guidance and support to partners to ensure that the projects are implemented in an integrated manner as per the international standards and at par with nationals.

project_name: Improving access to and provision of life-saving maternal and reproductive health services and information to most vulnerable communities in the West Bank.
project_objective:
This project is aligned to HNO 2018-2020 Cluster Strategic Objectives 1 & 2. UNFPA and its and implementing partners (IPs); Ministry of Health (MOH) and Palestinian Medical Relief Society (PMRS) aim to save women’s lives and ensure that, women, men and girls living in Bethlehem, Jenin, and Hebron (H2 and Area C), have access to essential maternal and reproductive health (RH) services, counselling and information, including on well-being and protection from gender based violence (GBV).

This will be achieved through filling gaps in RH services, including access to essential maternal health care and RH service provision and preventing excess mortality and morbidity by;
1) Ensuring a continuum of care and provision of life sustaining RH services, counselling and information including strengthening community preparedness.
2) Provision of essential life-saving maternal health equipment and supplies.
3) Implementation of MISP and training on emergency obstetric care, safe birth etc.
4) Actively engaging communities, strengthening their resilience, supporting coping mechanisms, sensitization, awareness raising and outreach of life saving approaches for RH, including maternal health.
5) Support linking and informing communities to available services with a special focus on marginalized communities and groups including the disabled, elderly etc.

This project is primarily meant to address the immediate response to urgent and critical needs of pregnant and lactating women (around 4,216), especially those living in areas recognized by OCHA as high and medium vulnerable communities (60,310 in area C of Bethlehem, H2 and Hebron). It will also support women of reproductive age (7,245), men (5,175 adults aged 22 years and above), and other vulnerable adolescents; boys (3,060 aged 11-18 years) and girls (5,220 aged 11-18 years), and strengthen the preparedness and resilience of the community and health system for absorbing shocks, saving lives and recovering from crises.

MOH shall serve as the backbone and main partner for specialized service provision, particularly secondary health care, including emergency obstetric care, safe birth, and high risk pregnancy management and follow up. PMRS, in close collaboration with Village Council Committees, will use mobile clinics (MCs) to conduct community based RH interventions through service provision and awareness raising in the target areas. 

UNFPA will strengthen RH care and complement UNICEF and WHO interventions targeting <5 and neonates, including nutrition activities. UNFPA will synergize activities for maximum benefit for pregnant and lactating women, women in reproductive age, men and adolescents, to utilize the complete package of life sustaining interventions available. UNFPA will coordinate closely with UNICEF, WHO, and other partners through the Health Cluster and bilateral coordination meetings that already occur on a regular basis to ensure synergies and avoid duplication. This entails sharing information, coordinating activities for target communities & facilities, and reviewing and verifying equipment and supplies to be procured; to ensure alignment with common frameworks and cooperation plans i.e. Every Newborn Action Plan (ENAP 2017-2020).

The project objectives and activities are aligned with the 2020 health cluster HRP strategy, including responsive and remedial components and is guided by the UNFPA Arab States regional framework for resilience and the UN strategy for Hebron and latest OCHA multi-sectoral needs assessment.  UNFPA aims to improve access to RH services and information, through a strengthened continuum of care, MISP implementation at the primary health care level, support to mobile clinics, reinforcement of referral pathways, increase of community awareness and preparedness for emergencies, and increase of resilience for women, men and girls in these communities.

Support to and integration of mine victims in eastern Ukraine
project_objective:
As the armed conflict in eastern Ukraine continues, available data on landmine/explosive remnants of war (ERW) casualties continues to document frequently occurring accidents. In the period between June 2014 and June 2019, a total of 958 landmine/ERW accidents were recorded by DRC-DDG from open news sources. From the total of 1,767 individual casualties recorded, 1,644 were adults (1,098 landmine/ERW accidents) and of these, more than 460 casualties constitute adult civilians - 390 casualties were registered in Luhansk and Donetsk regions of which 50% in NGCA.

In August 2018, DRC-DDG, with support from UNICEF, developed and launched a six-month pilot project assisting child landmine/ERW survivors in Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts where the highest numbers of casualties have been recorded. The project has four key components which are closely linked to the Mine Victim Assistance (MVA) core pillars as defined by the UN: data collection including needs assessment, the establishment of response methodology, provision of direct assistance through the case management and strengthening of the protective environment for survivors. 

A notable achievement of the project was the completion of the child landmine/ERW needs assessment, conducted by DRC-DDG during the period between Sept-Nov 2018, which covered the GCA of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts. The findings of the assessment conveyed the profiles of child landmine/ERW survivors, their path from the moment of accident to recovery, existing gaps and barriers in the process of rehabilitation and capacities of service providers (governmental and non-governmental) to meet the needs in accordance with the six pillars of MVA (defined in the UN Policy on Victim Assistance in Mine Action): (a) data collection, (b) emergency and continuing medical care, (c) physical and other rehabilitation, (d) psychological and psychosocial support, (e) social and economic inclusion, and (f) laws and public policies. 

The findings of the pilot project informed the need for continuation of the MVA intervention and a 10-month project was launched in Mar 2019 with a key development which included the change in the scope of the intervention resulting in equal assistance for both, families with child survivors and adult survivors of mines/ERW who are also primary caregivers of children. 

The action is formed by the UN Policy on Victim Assistance in Mine Action and built around five key components all inspired from this. 
The 1. component envisions strengthening of communication between national governmental actors and local service providers through the facilitation of joint meetings, round tables discussions to ensure the provision of better support to the mine/ERW victims and their families. The 2. component consists of direct support to victims through case management and targeted individual assistance (in cash or in-kind). Victims will be closely followed by DRC-DDG staff who will ensure needs are met to the largest extent possible which includes: emergency and ongoing medical treatment, psychosocial support, physical rehabilitation (e.g. prosthesis) and social/economic inclusion. Part of this support will be secured through referrals and follow-up with relevant governmental/non-governmental services. The 3. component aims at strengthening national capacities through completion of a detailed physical rehabilitation assessment (focusing on technical aspects of prosthesis production and physiotherapy). In the 4. component, DRC-DDG will deliver a number of trainings in the selected communities (targeting schoolteachers, school children, and key community representatives) on how to improve inclusion of persons with disability into social and economic life. Following this, community-based initiatives focusing on such inclusion will be supported where the effects are deemed to be highest. Finally, to complement this, advocacy efforts will be reinforced to promote the needs assessment report recommendations.

project_name: Management and Monitoring of Emergency Response, and Enhancing Safety and Security
project_objective:
Management coordination is essential to enable UNRWA to deliver timely and effective humanitarian assistance. The project consists of three main components: management and monitoring of humanitarian response, safety and security, and repair and maintenance of UNRWA premises in the new accessible areas. In April 2019, UNRWA received authorization to start carrying out works to its installations in camps previously not accessible (Dera’a and EinElTal camps).
One of UNRWA’s main priorities in 2020 is to resume its service in the new accessible areas to better respond to the needs of Palestine Refugees (PR) and ensure capacity in place to provide the service particularly in light of the spontaneous returns of IDPs and Refugees to camps and gathering areas. Contrary to the principle of the inviolability of UN premises, UNRWA facilities in Syria have suffered extensive damage throughout the conﬂict. Many PR camps have seen major hostilities, particularly Ein el Tal (Aleppo), Dera’a (South) and Yarmouk (Damascus) oﬃcial and nonoﬃcial camps, which have sustained large-scale destruction. In 2020, UNRWA will continue to focus on resuming its core services in areas where access has resumed and civilians are spontaneously returning. UNRWA will also make sure that beneﬁciaries and staff, including persons with disabilities, have safe access to its facilities by maintaining and rehabilitating its programme and operational support premises and community centres.
In order to ensure effective delivery of services as well as the support of operations in the logistic and administrative ﬁelds, deployment of local and international staff based in the target locations is essential. Considering the scale of the humanitarian needs, UNRWA will continue to require dedicated technical staff to manage, support and monitor multisectorial activities as well as emergency operations in Syria. International dedicated experts (humanitarian oﬃcers, monitoring and evaluation specialists, donor relations oﬃcers) will continue to be deployed at the main oﬃce to increase programme quality and neutrality. Adequate staﬃng is essential for UNRWA to implement its operations, especially with regard to direct implementation, as well as to ensure an eﬃcient coordination with all stakeholders and to enhance advocacy on behalf of PR. 
Since the onset of the conflict, UNRWA has made significant investments in the safety and security of its staff, assets and facilities and security procedures. UNRWA requires funding to maintain and strengthen the existing security infrastructure. In 2020, the main investments will continue to focus on security personnel staﬃng costs, the procurement of security equipment and services, and uniforms for security staff. These investments will enable UNRWA to facilitate and provide security support for over 600 field missions conducted yearly in a medium to high-risk security environment, and to conduct security risk assessments of its installations. In order to ensure that UNRWA facilities are compliant with minimum operating security standards, the Agency will conduct security risk assessments on targeted facilities and will carry out necessary physical enhancement works to ensure a safe and secure environment for its staff and beneciaries accessing assistance and services. In addition, UNRWA plans to ensure the installation of a closed-circuit television (CCTV) room and Internet Protocol (IP) surveillance cameras at its oﬃces in Damascus and Central area. UNRWA will continue to train its staff in Safe and Security Approaches to Field Environment (SSAFE) and will also provide are safety training. Finally, through its commitment to ensuring gender considerations in security management, and recognizing that women are more exposed to risks of GBV, UNRWA in Syria will maintain a Women’s Security Awareness Training (WSAT) programme for UNRWA female staff members.

project_name: Provision of Emergency Education Services to Palestine Refugee School Children in Syria
project_objective:
•	Cost per beneficiary: $616 
•	UNRWA reached 50,143 through educational activities.
In 2020, UNRWA will continue to provide quality, inclusive and equitable education services to up to 51,000 Palestine refugee children enrolled in 103 UNRWA schools located in Damascus, Rif Damascus, Aleppo, Hama, Homs, Latakia and Dera’a. A number of schools still operate on a double-shift basis. Since the beginning of the conflict, the number of UNRWA-managed schools has decreased from 118 to 103 in the 2019 / 2020 scholastic year, due to access constraints and damage or destruction creating a severe for the rehabilitation of premises. UNRWA will employ approximately 1,700 teachers, including daily paid teachers to cover possible gaps created by the conflict. The Agency will also continue its Education in Emergencies (EiE) interventions, including the implementation of recreational activities, the provision of Summer Learning activities; the engagement of parents through awareness-raising sessions on violence / GBV, ERWs, and career guidance for their children; and the strengthening of the identification and management of Psychosocial Support (PSS) cases in schools; and continued capacity-building for education staff. To address the anxiety and stress generated by the trauma of conflict, group and individual PSS counselling sessions facilitated by professional counsellors will be available throughout the academic year to students in UNRWA schools. UNRWA will be executing awareness-raising sessions for parents and children on disability inclusion, violence against children, GBV and ERW; career guidance for students; and capacity development for education staff using other funding streams. 

In 2020, UNRWA will work towards the resumption of educational services in newly accessible areas or areas of increased returns, including Yarmouk/Yalda should conditions allow, and Dera’a and Ein el Tal camps. Construction works will be undertaken depending on the availability of funding to ensure students, including children with disabilities, have access to safe and secure UNRWA premises. With the authorization received to carry out works in Dera’a camp, UNRWA will prioritize the reconstruction of schools in this area to ensure the provision of education services to the increasing number of returning Palestine refugees.

project_name: Provision of Life-saving Healthcare Services to Palestine Refugees in Syria
project_objective:
The provision of health care inside Syria remains hindered by the widespread damage and destruction of health facilities, insufficient human resources and access constraints in some areas. While the general cost of living, including of health services, has dramatically increased since 2011, the ability of public and private hospitals and clinics to respond to the needs of the population has decreased. As a result, the vast majority of Palestine refugees in Syria have become increasingly dependent on UNRWA for the delivery of healthcare services. 
In 2020, UNRWA will continue to deliver quality primary health services through 17 health clinics, six health points operating in areas of displacement of Palestine refugees and two mobile clinics which are deployed according to needs. UNRWA health facilities provide a range of primary medical services, including out-patient consultations, immunization services, growth monitoring, provision of medicine, gynecology consultations, laboratory services, non-communicable disease care, maternal and child health care, dental and MHPSS services.  
Furthermore, the Agency provides support to Palestine refugees seeking secondary and tertiary health care through a system of referrals to public, private and NGO hospitals. UNRWA subsidizes 75-95 per cent of the total cost of treatment for referred patients, depending on the socio-economic status of the patient. UNRWA will continue to ensure that patients have adequate access to essential medical supplies and drugs,and will strive to maintain contingency stocks of medical supplies and drugs to address any emerging situation. 

Finally, the Agency will focus its efforts on the resumption of health care services in newly accessible areas and in areas of spontaneous return. Those areas will include the South (Dera’a camp, Muzeirib, Jillin) and the South Damascus area where accessible (Yarmouk/Yalda) as well as main gatherings, depending on access and based on needs. Should funding become available, UNRWA will also reconstruct its health facilities that have been completely destroyed by the hostilities in selected locations to ensure that Palestine refugees have access to services. The Agency will continue to deploy its mobile clinics, to sustain the provision of medical and dental services to refugees in areas where facilities are not fully operational. UNRWA will also equip rehabilitated health centres with confidential spaces for patients facing protection concerns, including cases of gender-based violence (GBV) and violence against children. 

UNRWA has an internal Results-Based Monitoring system, with indicators tracking the progress of activities and impact of interventions for all programmes, including the Health Programme.  Data is entered on a monthly basis by focal points, and Quarterly Monitoring Review meetings are conducted to analyze the data, measure achievements, and address shortcomings and challenges. In addition, mid-year results review and annual results review meetings are held with the involvement of implementing programmes and management at Field and HQ levels to ensure lessons are extracted and fed back into the design of programmes and strategies. Regular field visits are carried out by programme senior staff to monitor day-to-day operations and delivery of service. Third-party-monitoring exercises and external evaluations are also conducted periodically in coordination with donors and the Evaluation Division of HQ.

project_name: Provision of In-kind Food Assistance to Vulnerable Palestine Refugees in Syria
project_objective: UNRWA estimates that 418,000 Palestine refugees in Syria will continue to require humanitarian assistance in 2020.  Food insecurity continues to negatively affect the Palestine refugees who depend on UNRWA assistance to meet their minimum food needs. To mitigate the impact of poverty and food insecurity, the Agency will provide in-kind food assistance to up to 135,000 Palestine refugees including those belonging to the following categories of extreme vulnerability: families headed by a person older than 60 years; families headed by a person with disability and people with disabilities; families headed by a female; and orphans.  Palestine refugees affected by acute emergencies, including newly displaced persons and those directly impacted by new or increased hostilities, and families and individuals spontaneously returning to newly accessible areas that were severely affected by the conflict and/or lacking basic services will also be eligible for in-kind support based on needs. The Agency will continue to monitor the availability of food on the markets and will retain operational flexibility to adjust to a changing context as appropriate.

project_name: Prevention and treatment of malnutrition in under 5 boys and girls in Yobe, Borno and Adamawa states
project_objective:
The humanitarian crisis in the Northeastern Nigerian States of Borno, Adamawa and Yobe (BAY) continue as hostilities between government security forces and non-state armed groups enter their tenth year. Civilians still bear the brunt of the conflict that has resulted in widespread displacement, destruction of infrastructure and collapse of basic services including nutrition. With an estimated total population of 13.04 million, in the three NE states – the states hardest-hit by the conflict - remain the epicentre of the humanitarian crisis. Conflict and the consequent displacement results in disrupted livelihoods, food insecurity and population overcrowding, which in turn increase the risk of malnutrition and mortality in affected populations. 

The Nutrition and Food Security Surveillance (NFSS) conducted in the Northeast Nigeria in October 2019 showed that while the overall nutrition situation in the BAY states is gradually improving, the situation is still very volatile and highly responsive to seasonality. The survey findings showed that the prevalence of Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) in Adamawa, Borno and Yobe was 7.2 per cent, 8.1 per cent and 11.5 percent respectively. This is further compounded by the presence of sub-optimal child care and feeding practices which was found to be below 60% in the three states.

Based on analysis from the 2020 Enhanced Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) of the conflict affected population, it’s projected that 289,197 boys and girls below 5 years will suffer from Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM), out of this total UNICEF’s Nutrition Sector is targeting 255,619 SAM cases for treatment. 

To overcome the challenge of malnutrition in the North-eastern states of Nigeria, UNICEF nutrition interventions will be focused on the below interventions;

	Procuring, managing and prepositioning nutrition supplies for effective management of SAM. A total of 306,743 cartons (including a 20% contingency) of RUTF will be procured to cover the sector target of 255,619 boys and girls aged 6-59 months and any unforeseen upsurge in needs. This will cover the entire 2020 sector needs as UNICEF is the sole pipeline agency for the procurement of RUTF.
	Timely detection, referral and treatment of children with severe acute malnutrition in the conflict-affected states of Borno (51,172), Adamawa (19,200) and Yobe (31,876). This is 40% of overall sector target for SAM treatment. The remaining 60% will be undertaken by other sector partners with UNICEF providing the required RUTF.
	Promoting uptake of recommended child feeding and care practices among 107,797 pregnant and lactating women in the BAY states (25,770 in Adamawa, 64,266 in Borno and 17,764 in Yobe.
	Strengthening the capacity of government, partners and the community to identify and treat malnutrition in Borno, Adamawa and Yobe states 
	Conducting nutrition programme assessments to identify barriers and boosters in access and developing suitable measures to ensure maximum programme coverage in all prioritized locations.
	Strengthening Nutrition Surveillance to determine the evolving nutrition situation that will further inform the response implementation strategy and location prioritization
	Coordinating and information management of the collective in the nutrition response in the three states.

UNICEF has planned to mobilize and generate $28.7 million funds to accomplish the planned activities for children and women in North-east Nigeria

project_name: General Protection for Refugees and Host Communities in Cox's Bazar District
project_objective: DRC will continue its effort in improved accountability to the affected population (AAP) and enhancing community engagement, ensuring participation and representation of diverse Rohingya and host communities to build resilience and promote ownership of the programming. Building on 2019, 2020 will continue to focus on internal and external protection mainstreaming and capacity-building for field-based staff, contributing to an overall improved protection response across sectors in Camp 2E, 2W, 5,6,7,10,11,12,13,14. Critical individual protection issues will be addressed through case management, including referral and individual protection assistance (IPA), ensuring a tailored customised support. Protection monitoring will enable adaptability and a community-based approach on identified trends, concerns and needs and complement to evidence-based advocacy. Through community-based programming with existing and trusted community groups community-led programming will continue in its efforts to build community resilience and community-led advocacy. 2020 will further focus on social-cohesion within and between communities to foster social-cohesion and community-led conflict resolution and peacebuilding mechanisms.DRC is directly involved and a participant in the PSEA network and ensured a PSEA focal is in place. DRC works very closely with government counterpart Camp in Charge (CiC) in community level action planning and implementation. For protection, the protection team engages with the CiC offices and CiC's themselves to discuss and update on the protection environment, concerns and the protection community-led projects. At host community level, all DRC activities are informed and coordinated with the UNO offices in Rajapalong and Palongkhali. At Cox Bazaar level, DRC SMT regularly interacts with the District Commissioner, RRRC and other government agencies to ensure that DRC projects are supported and coordinated. Furthermore, as part of its sustainability strategy, DRC is currently conducting a comprehensive local partner mapping and selection exercise as part of its partnership strategy to expand its programming with national and local partners for the camp.

project_name: Réduction de la  mortalité infanto-juvénile liée à la malnutrition (Tillabéri, Tahoua, Zinder et Maradi) et réduction de la morbidité des populations des zones de conflit (Tillabéri, Tahoua et Maradi)
project_objective:
L'objectif du projet est de réduire la morbidité infanto-juvénile particulièrement liée à la malnutrition et à ses complications et aussi de renforcer le mécanisme RRM pour faire face aux futures crises/chocs. 

Dans un premier temps le projet se concentre sur l'aspect nutrion pour lutter contre la malnutrition aigue sévère en assurant un appui aux structures de santé existantes pour améliorer la prise en charge des enfants atteints de malnutrition. Cet appui sera fait dans 6 CRENI (Abala, Ayérou, Tchintabaraden, Tassara, Mirriah et Dakoro) et 31 CRENAS (6 à Abala, 3 à Ayérou, 3 à Tchintabaraden, 3 à Tassara, 2 à Tillia, 7 à Mirriah et 7 à Dakoro) par les actions suivantes : une prise en charge de qualité  des enfants MAS de moins de 5 ans en ambulatoire dans les CRENAS appuyés, appui au système de référencement des cas compliqués  vers les CRENI;Appui en RH, Intrants et petits équipements ;  Poursuivre les essais clinique de OPTIMA pour la prise en charge simplifiée de la MA pour les enfants de 6-59 mois dans le DS de Mirriah (CSI de Guirari et Gaffati) ;Favoriser une intégration durable de la PEC de la MAG par les autorités sanitaires du pays à travers le plaidoyer et la prise en charge d'une partie des RH;

D'autre part le projet vise à renforcer le mécanisme de réponse aux urgences (RRM), assurer une réponse d'urgence en cas de crise sanitaire, humanitaire ou catastrophes naturelles et faciliter l'accès aux soins des populations vulnérables (réfugiés, déplacées et populations hôtes) dans les zones affectées par les conflits (frontière Mali -districts sanitaires de Abala, Ayérou (Tillabéri), Tillia, Tassara, Tchintabaraden (Tahoua) par les activités suivantes : 
veille humanitaire et sanitaire, suivi des alertes, formations de relais commmunautaires/lanceurs d'alertes, déploiement des cliniques mobiles, offre du paquet de soins de santé primaire, référencements, formation, prédisposition du kit EPREP, stock de contingence, équipes d'urgence, intervention sous les 7 jours suivant la confirmation d'une alerte, appui en RH, intrants et petits équipements aux services de santé maternels des hôpitaux de district de Abala, Ayérou et Tchintabaraden ainsi que dans les 31 CSI couverts.

project_name: Enhancing the protection environment for crisis affected populations in NW Syria through provision of integrated protection services
Providing humanitarian WASH assistance and improving basic WASH infrastructure in IDP sites in north-west Syria.
project_objective:
This project aims to support the WASH response and the immediate needs of most vulnerable displaced populations in the northwest of Syria by providing emergency WASH assistance in camps and improving the basic WASH infrastructure and WASH conditions in IDP sites in northwest Syria through:

i) Improving access to drinking water by rehabilitating 15 water systems and installing connections to IDP camps.
ii) Rehabilitation and construction of 15 sanitations systems in informal IDP sites.
ii) Provision of temporary water supply, solid waste management, desludging, water storage tanks and garbage containers to newly displaced and/or highly vulnerable
populations living in 30 IDP camps.
iv) Operational support to 270 latrine units including water trucking, maintenance, solid waste management and desludging

The project will contribute to the two objectives of the WASH cluster which are:
•  Support to water, sanitation/sewage and solid waste management systems to ensure regular services for affected people in Syria.
•  Deliver humanitarian WASH supplies, services and improve hygienic behaviour and practices of most vulnerable people 

Overall, the project aims to support 220,000 beneficiaries with humanitarian WASH assistance and improvements to basic WASH infrastructure in and out of camps in NW
Syria. Project locations are Harim, Dana and Salqin.

project_name: Integrated Emergency Food Security and Livelihoods Protection Project for IDP and Host Communities in Unity, Lakes and NBEG
project_objective: The objective of this project is to enhance emergency food production through complementary vegetable and crop seeds and fishing and livestock support for households classified in Crisis (IPC 3) or worse food insecurity in Panyijiar(Unity), Aweil East (NBeG), and Rumbek Center(Lakes) Counties. IRC will provide immediate, short term to recovery livelihood protection support to the food insecure and vulnerable households beginning 2020 lean season. To augment household recovery and resilience, the program will mainstream conflict sensitivity and disaster risk reduction support to at-risk households focused on improving crop, livestock and fisheries production and bolstering resilience towards recurrent shocks in the community. Cash-based activities will be used to boost vulnerable households’ income and purchasing power while engaging in rehabilitation and building household and community productive and disaster risk mitigation assets. In pursuit of program objectives, the following activities will be implemented: (a) Engagement community and local leaders to confirm needs and agree on selection criteria and register beneficiaries. (b)Distribute emergency (short term maturing) agricultural inputs/kits (seeds and tools) through input trade fairs (ITF) to farmers including in-kind pipelines from FAO. ITFs will be utilized to promote restocking (sheep and goats assets) and backyard poultry targeting households with malnourished mothers and children and most vulnerable households including flood and conflict-affected female-headed households and the elderly. (c) Market informed Cash-Based Activities targeting rehabilitation of community prioritize economically viable assets supported through conditional cash transfer activities providing income opportunities and boosting the purchasing power of food insecurity households and the use vouchers to access needed inputs- seeds and tools and livestock during ITFs or food. (d) Capacity building to county-level extension agents (CAHWs, AEA), crop/pastoralists and fisherfolks on sustainable production skills, post-harvest handling technologies and climate-smart agronomy demonstration gardens set up within the community. Value addition and marketing shall be stimulated through improved post-harvest handling, proper storage at household and community level – including granaries, fish preservation skills and local cereal market structures established through cash-based interventions. In collaboration with FAO and local government, mass livestock vaccinations are envisaged for households restocked and in suspected disease outbreaks. The IRC will mainstream gender equity and promote gender inclusiveness, allowing for the most vulnerable women, girls, boys, and men to participate and realize benefits for their wellbeing. Participatory monitoring and evaluation will be boosted through routine consultation of community, local leaders and authority from start. Beneficiary identification and selection (BIS) include agreeing on affirmative action to register at least 70% of female beneficiaries under the project. An inclusive community-led project feedback and complaint mechanism consisting of a committee’ set up to foster equal chances for female and male beneficiaries to voice their complaints and feedback. Complementarity will be promoted through integration (nutrition, protection, and health) including registration of referred vulnerable persons facing intersectional needs e.g- chronic illness and diseases, acute food insecurity, malnutrition, and flooding. Overall the IRC will reach 33,825 (17,759 Women, 57,610 Men, 5,919 Girls, 2,537 Boys; 10% of the most vulnerable households’ classified in IPC Phase 3 or worse food insecurity in Panyijiar (7,188), Rumbek Canter (9,237) and Aweil East (17,400). By program type: 33,825 through ITFs, 6,765 through cash vouchers, 16,913 through production skills training (50%), 5,500 through restocking and livestock vaccination and 18,000 through fisheries support.

project_name: Provision of critical support to the health care system in Syria
project_objective:
The project will reach those most at risk (IDPs, host communities, returnees) by supporting health facilities mainly located in areas where large number of IDPs are living including inclusive facilities easing access for people with disabilities (PWDs), dialysis centres providing services to the chronically ill, and facilities providing life-saving trauma and other medical services. Also, throughout this project, GBV survivors will be supported by more capable health facility staff and referral mechanisms at the supported health facilities.

The Project has following main components:
	4 Mobile Emergency Units will be supported by stipends, running costs, equipment, drugs, and disposables.
	6 PHC centres will receive stipends running costs, equipment, drugs and disposables.
	2 dialysis centres will receive stipends, running costs and dialysis sessions.
	1 cardiology centre will receive drugs, disposables, stipends and running costs 
	30 PHC centres will receive equipment, drugs and disposables (without stipends)
	150 healthcare staff will be trained in data management, warehouse management, orientation on the complaint mechanism, GBV case management, protection, and inclusion.
	Maintenance of the healthcare facilities in the promotion of inclusion and the strengthening of established referral systems for GBV cases will be carried out to promote protection.

IR Syria Mission in Turkey is involved in various national and international coordination settings, i.e. as member of the NGO forum which includes most of the INGOs working to support communities inside Syria through Turkey. IR in Turkey takes part in UNOCHA coordination activities to coordinate with all other actors working inside Syria. Within the health sector, IR Syria Mission is an active member since its launch in Southern Turkey. IR Syria Mission team regularly attends the relevant clusters meetings conducted on monthly basis where they share the 4Ws in order to update on the progress of all ongoing projects. IR also reports on the UN-Financial Tracking System (FTS). IR Syria has also actively participated inside the country in regular coordination meetings and has good relations with the local councils, authorities and health directorates and coordinates with various community-based organizations in the areas in order to be able to update the data on access, beneficiary numbers and safety regulations frequently.

Moreover, IR coordinates with local communities of different areas inside Syria to share information about their needs and ongoing responses on the ground. IR coordinates with various community-based organizations and other local actors like the local councils and health directorates inside the areas of intervention in northern Syria in order to share updates about the accessible routes to guarantee that assistance reaches the target beneficiaries and to ensure the safe passage for project deliverables as well as staff.
 The project aims to provide a complete service delivery package including trauma, non-communicable diseases and referral support. This includes but not limited to provision of drugs, disposables and equipment to the targeted health facilities to treat range of diseases such as respiratory illness, Dermatologic conditions, acute diarrhea, Chronic illnesses (diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, kidney) Anemia, antenatal care and surgical procedure. 
IR has 2 MEAL officers and 2 MEAL assistants in Syria to provide progress monitoring. Field reports in the form of monthly progress reports as well as feedback received from the main stakeholders and from the targeted community will be shared through regular Skype meetings between field staff in Syria and management staff based in Turkey and actions will be taken accordingly. Also IR will ensure to have a robust complaint and feedback mechanism.

project_name: Conflict affected population in Libya including migrant and refugees have improved access to lifesaving and comprehensive primary, reproductive and mental health care services
project_objective:
The IRC will provide primary and reproductive healthcare services by deploying mobile medical teams (MMTs) to existing MoH Primary Healthcare Centers and will maintain referral pathways between different levels of care. MMTs will provide standardized packages of primary and reproductive health services, including antenatal and post-natal care, which are aligned with the EPHS for Libya using WHO protocols and guidelines. Clinical packages also include healthcare for children and the management of childhood illnesses as well as mental health services. SGBV case workers will be trained alongside the health staff on clinical care for sexual assault survivors (CCSAS) and mental health gap action plan (mhGAP) to promote comprehensive care.

MMT activities will be complemented by robust community outreach activities. This strong link between the community and the PHCs allows for better follow up of cases and successful referrals. In addition, the IRC will procure and supply medicine, medical equipment and supplies, laboratory equipment, nutritional supplies, necessary furniture, and other supplies such as toiletries, stationeries, etc. to all supported facilities. The IRC will work to strengthen its existing referral systems with local and international actors to maximize the number of people who receive appropriate next levels of healthcare, including specialized care for complicated pregnancies and birth. 

The IRC will complete minor rehabilitations of healthcare facilities to increase their capabilities to deliver the full range of services outlined in the EPHS package and ensure compliance with MoH and WHO standards. Ensuring that all facilities meet the standards for infection prevention and control is a key priority and the IRC will support MoH to make sure that all healthcare workers have sufficient knowledge and skills to protect themselves and their patients. This will likely entail the development of SOPs and trainings for staff. All training materials will be available in Arabic and English from MOH & WHO, MSF, IMC.

The IRC will provide technical training and assistance to effectively respond to emerging health needs and improve general health seeking behaviors. Technical training will cover topics such as specific disease management and adherence to treatment protocols, standard training packages related to health in humanitarian settings and minimum standards of services in crises, as well as psychological and traditional first aid. Additional trainings related to project management, specifically related to management health information systems, emergency preparedness and response, reporting into and monitoring early warning systems, and best practices in pharmaceutical management will also be provided to staff to grow their capacity to manage complex health programming.
