project_name: PROJECT REVISED- Shelter Assistance for Persons Affected by Conflict and Natural Disasters in Somalia
project_objective: In the midst of increasing displacement caused by conflict and natural disasters in Somalia, AVORD is submitting this proposal with the aim of enhancing the living conditions of affected communities through provision of NFIs, emergency and transitional shelters and Community Infrastructure. Program activities will target 6,700 households (40,200 persons) from affected communities in need in Banadir, Bay, Bakool, Lower Shabelle, Middle Shabelle, Hiiraan, and Galgaduud. Combined, these regions host 1,085,000 IDPs, or 42% of the entire IDP population in Somalia (OCHA HNO 2019). Where market conditions allow, AVORD will use a cash/voucher modality for implementation. Otherwise, in-kind modality will be used during which AVORD will distribute NFIs and emergency shelter kits directly to beneficiaries.

project_name: PROJECT REVISED-Foster equitable access to multi-sectoral services and durable solutions for the Internally Displaced People in Somalia
project_objective: In the midst of increasing IDP caseload in Somalia, AVORD is submitting this proposal with the aim of enhancing the living conditions of the Internally Displaced People (IDPs) through enhanced coordination, access to information and multi-sectoral services at site level, site maintenance, and durable solutions. Proposed interventions will covers IDPs in need in Banadir, Bay, Lower Shabelle, Hiiraan, Gedo and Galgaduud. Combined, these regions host 1,337,000 IDPs, or 51% of the entire IDP population in Somalia (OCHA HNO 2019).

project_name: PROJECT REVISED-Provision of Sustained CCCM Support for IDP Settlements in Somalia
project_objective:
Despite above average Gu rains in certain areas of Somalia, the delayed rains have prevented the population from planting crops in time for harvesting and has resulted in poor harvests. Cities and major towns are still the most favorable destinations for the majority of the affected population that lost their livelihoods. Despite numerous efforts to reach rural and unreached communities humanitarian aid remains largely concentrated in urban areas. Insecurity and protracted drought still do not allow safe and dignified returns for the affected population, while eviction continue to be a major protection issue for displaced populations and prevents work towards local integration. Self-settled sites remain exposed and more prone to hazards related to site layout such as fire and floods, but also other protection concerns related to overcrowded spaces and lack of privacy. Even in urban settings, humanitarian assistance is provided in a discontinuous way, with poor quality service delivery or the absence of exit strategies.

Camp management remains key to ensure coordination of service provision, underpinned by reliable, strong and regular information management, in order to ensure identification of gaps, advocacy for the needs of affected population, as well as monitoring of evictions risk and service delivery to minorities and marginalized groups. The participation of affected populations is lacking in many aspect of the delivery humanitarian assistance. In response to this, camp management is crucial to empower affected populations through dissemination of information on delivery of humanitarian assistance and in supporting inclusive and representative community governance structure. Moreover, it monitors service delivery by other partners. In order to reach displaced sites in rural or unreached areas, whenever security conditions allows, ACTED will adopt a two layers approach. Mobile teams will visit sites weekly in urban areas, providing a full range of camp management activities whereas for rural areas, the team will mix remote site monitoring with in person visit (every one or two months). The teams will collect information on needs, provide support through capacity building of governance and Communication with Communities (CwC) while focusing on quick impact projects for the community to account for the absence of service providers.

project_name: PROJECT REVISED-Providing Gender Sensitive Emergency WASH Services to Vulnerable IDPs, Drought Affected Agro-Pastoral and Host communities in Somalia/Somaliland
project_objective:
Providing gender sensitive Emergency WASH services to drought affected IDP and Hosting communities in Somalia and Somaliland. ARC is proposing an emergency WASH project with DRR component interventions in the regions of Banadir, Lower Juba, Middle Shebelle, Sool, Sanaag, and Togdheer regions in South Central and Somaliland regions. In strategy of ARC for implementation of this project, steps are planned to mobilize and socialize communities, especially community leaders/religious leaders so that women will be provided with the opportunities of contribution to implementation of proposed WASH activities. Such opportunity of interaction of women in the development and decision making affairs will have an impact on further gender dynamics to improve their condition and impact on Gender­Based violence (GBV), particularly for girls and young women, the lack of access to gender segregated latrines leave them vulnerable to sexual violence, which frustrates efforts for them to lead a healthy and productive life. This is a major concern as well as one of human rights in IDP camps in Somalia/Somaliland. This means that many girls and young women live in constant fear as there are no toilet facilities for them, hence they are often forced to relieve themselves in relatively villages peripheries during the early hours of the morning or late at night, when the likelihood of sexual assault or violence is higher, hence one of many triggers for open defecation. 

ARC will provide an effective gender-responsive programming as per ARC’s Age, Gender and Diversity (AGD) standards and the Global WASH Cluster agreed gender policy in the Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) sector. ARC will take into account several gender sensitive points into WASH intervention but not limited to reduce walking distances to latrines and install solar lights to rebel sexually abusive groups and empower adolescent woman/girls by providing gender segregated toilets and information and fundamental life skills in hygiene promotion and safe sanitation. 

ARC targets over (60,146) beneficiaries, comprising 6,668 IDPs and 26,566 drought affected agro-pastoral and host community across these regions, with breakdown of Female 15,625 (12,294 women + 3331 girls) and Male 11,287 (9,087 men + 2,200 boys) through WASH infrastructure and services. This emergency WASH project will be integrated with Health; Nutrition, Protection and Livelihood sectors to have greater impact on the lives of the affected communities. The linkage to health component will ensure a comprehensive approach to reduce morbidity and mortality associated with diseases resulting from deficient sanitation conditions, lack of access to safe water, and low level of good hygiene practices. Most importantly, ARC will focus on increasing access to safe water by improving the water infrastructure. This includes protecting shallow wells from contamination or pollution in Kismayo, Banadir, Afmadow, Togdheer, Sool and Sanaag regions through rehabilitation of strategic boreholes by installing hybrid solar water pumping system, construction of water storage facilities and water distribution networks/extensions to health facilities, construction of water catchments and zero coliform by providing water treatment tablets to target household and water quality monitoring and inspections. 

ARC’s WASH technical designs adhere to SPHERE standards, mainstreaming of gender considerations, including IASC guidelines for GBV Interventions in Humanitarian settings, WASH, securing access to the elderly and those with special needs (disabled people) as per Handicap International Guidelines, and to the environmental considerations.

project_name: PROJECT REVISED-WASH Response to Drought and Displacement Affected Population in Sool and Bay Regions of Somalia
project_objective:
Approximately 2.7 million people require access to WASH support in Somalia. In drought affected regions, water scarcity and inadequate quality are leading causes of displacement and conflict. Of the people in need and highly vulnerable, a large percentage are children, women and the elderly, who critically lack access to clean water and are acutely at risk of gender-related violence and high morbidity and mortality due to water-borne disease outbreaks. Many households lack access to adequate sanitation leading to frequent open defecation while safety of people, particularly women and children to access latrines and water points remains a serious concern and a serious risk for exposure to violence. IDPs in particular are the most impact by an inability to access WASH services. Most of the primary IDP settlements are in Crisis or Stressed in Laas Cananood and Baidoa. 

In this context, ACTED will implement a WASH cluster-specific intervention for IDPs and rural communities in areas affected by drought aiming to 1) Provide reliable and sustainable access to sufficient safe water, based on identified strategic water points and construction of new boreholes; 2) Establish an appropriate system for the management and maintenance of facilities, with different groups contributing equitably; and 3) Enhance community sanitation.

project_name: PROJECT REVISED- Providing equitable access to quality curative and preventive nutrition services for the vulnerable population
project_objective:
To address the high rate of malnutrition, ARC will support curative and preventive nutrition interventions to treat children under five (U5) and pregnant and lactating women (PLW) with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) and moderate acute malnutrition (MAM). Services include nutrition screening, targeted supplementary feeding programme (TSFP) and outpatient therapeutic programme (OTP). All interventions will be aligned with MoH, WHO guidelines/protocols and Somalia integrated management of acute malnutrition (IMAM) protocols. 
Nutrition services will be co-located at the MCHs noted in sub section Management of acute malnutrition Co-location of nutrition and health services will help ensure that children U5 a cross both genders and PLW presenting for health services are screened for nutrition and likewise those presenting for nutrition services can be referred and easily access primary, maternal, and child health services, as needed. Considering all genders, all children U5 presenting at the MCH will be screened and if necessary, referred for admission to the TSFP or OTP per the IMAM admission criteria. SAM cases presenting with medical complications will be referred to the nearest stabilization center (SC).  ARC is also planning to combine the nutrition and health nursing staff to foster more integration across health and nutrition activities at the facilities. 
The linkage to WASH and health components will ensure a comprehensive approach to reduce morbidity and mortality associated with the compound effect of diseases resulting from poor sanitation conditions, lack of access to safe water, and malnutrition. To increase the impact, the nutrition project will be coordinated also with ARC Protection and Livelihood projects.
ARC will closely coordinate with MoH and respond in locations where gaps in nutrition services have been identified. ARC will ensure the participation of the local communities, with special attention to participation of women, in decision making throughout the project cycle to strengthen community acceptance and ownership. Throughout the lifetime of the project, ARC will work with the MoH to pave the way for a proper phasing out at the end of the project.

project_name: PROJECT REVISED- Food Security and Livelihood support to drought and conflict affected communities in Eastern Somaliland
project_objective:
The humanitarian crisis in Somalia is among the most complex and protracted emergencies worldwide. Growing conflict across the country and simultaneous environmental hazards, such as recurrent droughts, hamper the livelihoods of Somalia’s 12 million people.

The assessments by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), Food Security and Nutrition Analysis Unit (FSNAU) and Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWSNET) (Post Gu, 2019) also indicate that, without humanitarian aid, up to 2.1 million people across Somalia (including Somaliland) will face severe hunger through December 2019. FEWSNET and FSNAU findings further anticipate the livelihood zones of Eastern Somaliland to be at high risk and to slide from phase 2 (stressed) to phase 3 (crises) or phase 4 (emergency), within the next months. Widespread malnutrition persists across Somalia and one million children are expected to be acutely malnourished over the next year, including 180’000 children who are likely to become severely malnourished in case the humanitarian community fails to scale up its support. Finally, the analysis projects more than 2.6 million people to be internally displaced across the country, in either rural or urban settings.

Also, an assessment (March 2019) by Candlelight with one of its partners revealed that poor food security levels in Togdheer and Sool was partly due to poor food access; the dietary diversity for households is limited to only 3 food items or less, composed of mainly carbohydrates. Also, based on the analysis, most of the children between the age of 6-59 months suffering from acute malnutrition were mostly from families with limited income or in which the parents were not engaged in any income generating activity at all. The study concludes that providing lifesaving food assistance by means of Conditional or Unconditional Cash Transfer will improve access to food for the most affected families in the proposed target villages. The analysis also stresses the importance of women as main caregivers and their potential to act as key players in humanitarian aid.

The proposed project’s intervention logic will put emphasis on relieving the distress suffered by affected families, preventing their situation from getting worse and strengthening collective resilience mechanisms.
Against this background and in line with the Food Security Cluster guidelines, the project aims at providing lifesaving and resilience building assistance to the most vulnerable and affected families. The overall objective of the suggested project is that the food and livelihood security situation of vulnerable IDP and host community families in Eastern Somaliland is stabilized and communities are more resilient towards adverse weather conditions and conflict. In order to achieve the objective, the project offers: a) unconditional and conditional cash transfers for improved access to food and b) agriculture and livelihood support activities (Trainings, quality seeds support and animal restocking) 

Cash has been prioritized based on Candlelight’s previous experience and best practices in cash transfer programming. Cash especially unconditional is an ideal intervention because of the freedom and dignity it gives to the beneficiaries, its limited administrative requirements and reduced risk. Conditional cash transfers support to achieve a range of objectives and will result in increased access to food, short term employment opportunities and re-building of communal infrastructure. Assessments by Candlelight and other agencies reveal that in most of the villages, markets and small shops can easily cope with the demand for food created by the cash transfers; thus boosting the local markets.

The project will target 11,060 beneficiaries (Men, Women, boys and girls) and will have a duration of 12 months (January 2020 – December 2020) to allow families to recover from adverse weather conditions.

project_name: PROJECT REVISED- Support for Life Saving, Protection, Recovery and Resilience Project for Vulnerable Populations in Galmudug, Banadir and Lower Shabelle Regions.
project_objective:
Two successive rain seasons, that is Deyr rains (October- November) 2018 and Gu rains (April-May) 2019 have registered below average amounts (FSNAU Port Gu report 2019). Leading to water deficit and poor pasture conditions (FSNAU Technical Release September 2, 2019) for pastoralist livelihood groups in Central Somalia. This has resulted in Galgadud Region being among areas classified as being in Crisis (IPC Phase 3) while other Mudug Region’s rural region areas falls in the category of areas classified as being in Stressed. Central Somalia has yet to recover from the significant livestock loss occurred during the 2016/2017 drought, with the many drop- out pastoralists identified as being reliant on labor as an alternative income source after losing their animals as CPD Market Assessments for Hobyo, Adado and Dhusamareb undertaken with the support of Diakonie Germany (for Hobyo District) and Somalia Stability Fund project for Adado and Dhusamareb Districts Indicate. The availability of saleable animals’ remains among the local pastoralists is low, constraining the ability of poor households to feed their families and purchase water for their animals. The pastoralist populations in Galmudug Regions (i.e. Galgadud and Mudug Regions) shall require livestock related interventions to enable them access water, pasture as well as veterinary care critical for the survival of theirs herds. CPD proposes the provision of integrated interventions to support the pastoralists with supplementary feeding, basic veterinary care and water trucking for animals, alongside collapsible tanks to hold and supply water in strategic locations.  
In Lower Shabelle Region, the successive rain seasons failures have led to a below average harvest being realized for the Gu 2019 season crop (50 percent below the long-term average according to June 2019 Monthly Rainfall and NDVI Report). The region has also faced intensified conflict as the Federal Government forces and AMISOM have intensified their war against the Non-state actors in control of many of the Districts and locations in Lower Shabelle Region. The combined effects of poor harvests, increased food prices, low cereal to animal exchange rates will increase food access difficulties and also subsequent capacity of the farms to produce as they have reduced farm incomes. Women and children have borne the brunt of the noted food access challenges with localized high malnutrition rates being observed within the IDP camps. There is also a window of opportunity created in the newly liberated areas in Lower Shabelle Region especially among the agro-pastoral and riverine livelihood groups which require support to rehabilitate their farms, farming inputs and trainings and also the rehabilitation of irrigation canals damaged through many years of deliberate destruction and also lack of maintenance.
IDP Populations in Mogadishu, Adado (in Galmudug Region) and Galkayo (in Mudug Region) are among those indicated as being in Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or Stressed (IPC Phase 2). The IDPs will need lifesaving unconditional cash transfer, skills training and start-up capital for alternative livelihood means especially for women from women headed households. The cash transfer will support the women and youth from resorting to unsustainable and vulnerable survival livelihood means. CPD through information generated by Vulnerability Assessment Survey in Mogadishu’s Dayniile and Dharkeynley Districts in January 2019 indicated that  87% of the interviewee IDP households have 1-3 children under 5 years in the family and 52% of the interviewed households have 1-2 over 60 years old members in their families. At the same time though many of the IDPs rely on waged labour for their livelihood (57% of HHs), the incomes from waged labor at an average of US $50 per months was below the recommended Minimum Expenditure Basket for Banadir which is currently at US $93 (MEB for urban markets September 2019).

project_name: PROJECT REVISED-Provision of primary and secondary heath services to emergencies and conflict affected communities in Gedo and South West Regions, Somalia
project_objective:
There is dire need to sustain the provision of services, which is currently declining since HDC has been under the gap and has affected effective services in 8 facilities, thus exposing the populations to significant health risks and making it hard to access quality health services. Similarly ,we have been providing  CEmONC services in Bardhere Hospital  through support of UNFPA and Ministry of Health (Federal Government) and came to an end in June 2019 further causing gap. To also ensure increase access to services, we intend to support CEmONC services and secure access to referral services in Elwak District hospital where only BEmONC services are currently available though with no funding support. Populations around Elwak are forced to travel hundreds of Kilometers to access health services or referral services and in many instances have to cross borders to Wajira nd Mandera of neighbor country or BaardhereCEmONC servicedue to limitation of services. 
Since 2019, we took over management of Berdale MCH previously under Swisso Kalmo where are  currently providing IPTCS services vices to the communities (host)and the IDPs/persons displaced most pf whom were affected by drought and conflicts. There are many health needs in Baidoa as estimated populations of displaced populations stand at 323,000 persons in 48 IDP camps. The health needs are alarming due to the high populations and recurring shocks, including constant disease outbreaks and common illnesses. We are seeking to enhance the support of services through Berdale MCH which sits close proximity with IDP camps and convenient to access services which will focus in strengthening access to quality health services to the most vulnerable populations who are forced to travel far and wide to seek medical facilities as well will cover hard to reach communities who are still inhibited to accessing services due to insecurity in some locations.
This project seeks to reach over 48713 person (6029: girls; 5565: boys; 26083: women and 11036: men)) through provision of health services in 4 districts including Bardhere, Elwak, Doolow and Baidoa to populations including IDPs and hard to  reach communities , conflict and drought affected people by ensuring access to Universal Health Care covering primary and secondary health care through 8 facilities, 2 in Bardera District which is Bardhere District Hospital, Ali cato MCH/Habala Adey IDP,4 facilities in Elwak which include Elwak District Hospital, Dhamasa MCH, Geriley MCH and Husqurun, one facility in Dollow which is Doolow MCH and Berdale MCH in Baidoa through the provision of  services including outpatient consultations for both males and females (boys and girls included), child health services, immunizations for both children under five and Women of Child Bearing Age; Reproductive health services  including Family planning promotion and integrated method mix counseling and service delivery, Focused Antenatal Care (including complete physical examination of the mother and her foetus, systematic screening for syphilis, urine analysis; hemoglobin as well as establishment of delivery plan including referrals when appropriate, Sexually Transmitted Infections and HIV Testing and Counselling which shall enhance Emergency Obstetric and Neonatal Care Services. We intend to provide the BEmONC and CEmONC services through Bardhere District Hospital and in Elwak Hospital, where we are currently providing similar services in the former facility. Reproductive health campaigns shall also be conducted in Baardhere and Elwak District to improve access to sexual health services.  
Five mobile outreaches shall also complement the services in static facilities to ensure adequate and equitable access to health services in Bardhere Hospital, Doolow MCH, Elwak District Hospital, Geriley MCH, and Berdale MCH to reach the vulnerable populations including IDPs.

project_name: PROJECT REVISED- Prevention and Response to violations with focus on child protection and GBV in flood and conflict affected areas in Beletweyne & Buula BurteyDistrict.
project_objective:
In response to the displacements in the Hiran region due to prolonged drought, conflict and expecting flooding, HIWA is proposing response with mobile teams providing combined Protection support services to both IDPs and host communities. In this project, HIWA will provide emergency GBV and child protection services to vulnerable, newly displaced boys and girls in Beletweyne and Buula Burtey districts, in both IDP and host communities.

To ensure the most vulnerable are reached, HIWA will target 16,342 newly displaced women, men, girls and boys from both IDPs and host communities. This project will fill gaps in service provision where government and humanitarian support is currently insufficient. Provision of services in general and protection services, in particular, have been significantly challenged by the limited access. As a result, HIWA aims to support the current situation in Beletweyne while preparing for the possible influx of people following the expected rain.

HIWA is proposing the following interventions to expand lifesaving GBV, protection and child protection services to vulnerable populations in Hiran Region. The complexity of the operating environment requires multifaceted approaches that are tailored to each location including: 

1. Mobile GBV and Protection emergency response services in Beletweyne and Buula Burtey during the flooding which will expand protection and GBV emergency response through teams based in both districts. The proposed intervention is designed to: 

•	Capacity building on Clinical Management of Rape Survivors (CMR)
•	Safety audits in priority areas to review cluster response implications for girls, boys, women and men living in the camps
•	Increase women and adolescent girls’ access to life saving GBV case management psychosocial support (PSS) services and protections to reduce risks of GBV. 
•	Integrate protection monitoring and mainstreaming into the GBV intervention to improve the overall context analysis and integration of protection principles in the intervention that will be scaled up to respond the identified needs. 
•	Enhance understanding and analysis among humanitarian actors on the protection context and needs. HIWA will utilize existing internal emergency response capacity to staff these teams to provide timely, effective and efficient GBV and protection responses during the project period 

2. Child Protection interventions in the target districts the child protection intervention has been specifically designed to be integrated within HIWA’s existing protection program in Hiran region, which are aimed at strengthening community¬ based protection mechanisms and facilitating access to information and appropriate services. 
•	Through existing, Community Protection Committees, provide a platform to provide family tracing and reunification, alternative family care and arrangements including community-based support to identified UASC.

project_name: PROJECT REVISED- Improving and strengthening protection services through prevention and response to gender-based violence (GBV), and mitigation of child protection risks in emergencies (CPiE) for the displaced communities of Middle Shebelle, Lower Shebelle, Lower Jubba, Banaadir, Bay and Bakool regions of Somalia.
project_objective: The project seeks to strengthen case management through direct service provision to survivors of gender-based violence (GBV) and unaccompanied and separated children (UASC), including children at risk of being recruited by armed forces or armed groups (CAAFAG). The interventions aim at direct services and referral services for where a holistic approach is necessary. This includes providing training and mentoring to GBV and CP staffs from INTERSOS and implementing partners (IPs). GBViE and CPiE aim to provide immediate lifesaving assistance to vulnerable populations. Beneficiaries will receive comprehensive case management and psycho-social support (PSS) - including emergency care, referral to INTERSOS medical teams trained on clinical management of rape (CMR). Additionally, access tailored material assistance, basic emotional support, and follow up on all services (direct and referrals). Capacity building of duty bearers including formal and informal authorities to strengthen and improve identification. Considering current approaches, the emphasis is on scaling up prevention and response services to survivors of GBV and children who have been separated from their families (by restoring the family links/family tracing efforts) who are the primary duty bearers. Commitment to participate in strengthening service mapping to facilitate appropriate referrals and through coordination and maintaining links necessary in service delivery. Comprehensive services to survivors as well as unaccompanied and separated children (UASC) at risk, in the long run, ensure the protection of children from recruitment by armed forces or armed groups (CAAFAG) and even use of girls in and by armed group/forces (gender-based violence (GBV)). The project will further strengthen protection monitoring in areas of settlement of returnees and IDPs through community-based protection monitors (or advocates) working with CSOs to ensure that quality evidence-based reports about protection issues and human rights violations in a systematic collection of protection-related data to inform better response and advocacy.

project_name: PROJECT REVISED-Provision of quality essential lifesaving and life sustaining health services to vulnerable group including IDP and returnees in Middle Shabelle, Bay and Bakool
project_objective:
Somalia remains in a state of chronic catastrophe characterized by a complex political environment, extreme poverty, food insecurity, conflict and instability. This has led to poor access to basic health services, recurrent disease outbreaks, food insecurity and high malnutrition rates, a lack of safe water supplies, and significant rates of population displacement.
Furthermore, the humanitarian needs have increased drastically due to limited rain, large-scale displacement, lack of access to basic services and, at its root, ongoing conflict and significant displacement from rural to urban areas, because of the above-mentioned condition this project responds to the current health needs in the drought and conflicts affected populations in the targeted regions.
Provision of quality essential lifesaving and life sustaining health services in Middle Shabelle, Bay and Bakool regions with focus on women, children, neonates and other vulnerable groups and strengthen the local capacity to deliver evidence-based and cost effective services based on the Integrated Primary Health Care Approach with BEmONC services and enhanced referral system for severe medical conditions and Obstetric complication in the targeted area of intervention.
The health sector in Somalia especially the targeted districts is in critical condition with very poor Health indicators. The high-risk groups of the direct beneficiaries are U5 (55,492) Under 1 yr (72,125), Pregnant women (13,492) in the targeted areas of intervention.

The project aims at reducing morbidity and mortality of undeserved communities of Bay, Bakool, Middle Shabelle and Banadir regions (Baidoa and Dinsoor in Bay, Wajid and Hudur in Bakool and Jowhar and Bal’ad in Middle Shabelle) with focus on children under 5 years and pregnant and lactating women through the provision of life saving emergency Health services by supporting Health Facilities and Mobile clinics supported by a network of Community Volunteers (CVs). The proposal will follow on the priorities set by the Humanitarian Technical Clusters and Somalia Humanitarian Fund (SHF) for emergency interventions by supportingﬁxed health facility per district (Baidoa, Diinsoor, Waajid, Hudur, Jowhar and Bal’ad) and mobile teams with a network of CVs. The ﬁxed facilities will provide PHC with integrated BEmONC and further referral for secondary health services. More so, INTERSOS will engage 20 CVs in every district of implementation. The Primary Health Care Package includes Curative consultations, Sexual Reproductive Health (SRH), Integrated Management of Childhood Illnesses, Immunization, screening of under ﬁve children and PLWs immunization (for both routine and supplementary vaccines), provision of Medical supply, Health Education massage for 104,832 in the target location.
The project will deploy Basic Life Support (BLS) ambulances equipped with basic medical supplies to all targeted locations. The BLS ambulance will provide referral services from the outreach to the ﬁxed facilities and those requiring secondary health care will be referred to secondary healthcare providers ensuring rapid transportation of critical cases (priority will be given to under 5 children and pregnant women with Obstetric complications). The project will establish an eﬃcient outreach and referral mechanism from community level to primary health services and for primary to secondary health services, through a network of CVs and the BLS capacity for the transport/stabilization of critical patient. The community volunteers will do screening, assessing and identifying the sick patient and severe ill person to refer to the hospital for further diagnosis and treatment. This will ensure to fasten the referral process and provide efficient and effective basic life support during the referral process to the hospital in which will provide a trained community volunteers and in support with the nurses to maintain and secure the life of the ill patient before the referral is done.

project_name: Provision of life-saving nutrition interventions to the most vulnerable women of reproductive age and children under 5 years in the occupied Palestinian territory
project_objective:
The objective is to respond to the cluster objective to ensure the availability, accessibility, acceptability and quality of essential lifesaving nutrition interventions that will address the needs of the most vulnerable target group identified by the Cluster. Target groups include most vulnerable pregnant women, women of reproductive age and children under 5 years (U5) suffering from malnutrition. 

The project will address critical gaps in the health sector response for maternal and child nutrition services in the West Bank (Hebron H2 and Area C) and the Gaza Strip. It will address life-threatening micronutrient malnutrition among the most vulnerable women of reproductive age and U5 children including moderate and severe wasting through provision of appropriate infant and young child feeding (IYCF) counselling, food and nonfood items, including essential micronutrients and treatment jointly delivered by UNICEF, WFP and Save the Children.

UNICEF will procure and deliver the annual requirement of essential micronutrients such as Iron and folic acid (Iron 65mg + Folic Acid 0.4 Tablets) for at least 36,000 pregnant and lactating women (PLW) (Gaza: 24,000; WB:12,000) and Iron syrups for 40,000 children aged 6 to 59 months (girls: 19,600; boys: 20,400) in Gaza and the West Bank (Gaza: 30,000; WB: 10,000) who are attending the Ministry of Health (MOH) and NGO facilities.

WFP will provide U$ 40 Unconditional Cash Transfers (e-voucher) on a monthly basis for most vulnerable PLW and mothers of children (2-5 years) with high anemia and micronutrient deficiencies, to purchase healthy food and WASH kits, to meet their increased nutritional needs. To synergize efforts and have a comprehensive Maternal Infant Young Child -Emergency project, WFP will target 900 PLW (600 in Gaza and 300 in the West Bank) and mothers of children (2-5 years old) for e-vouchers, who will receive supplements from UNICEF, in addition to 100 men and 100 children. The provision of the Unconditional Cash Transfers will be complemented with Behavior Change activities to increase the dietary impact of the cash. 

WFP will target 600 women, 50 children (girls: 25) and 50 men in the Gaza Strip; as well as 300 women, 50 children (girls: 25) and 50 men in Area C and H2 in Southern Governorates of the West Bank. 

In the Gaza Strip, Save the Children (SCI) will focus on building the capacity of 80 selected health workers (female: 60) in providing quality maternal and infant and young child nutrition services, including maternal nutrition, IYCF counselling and detection and management of moderate and severe malnutrition. The support will help detect and treat cases with moderate and severe wasting (2,000 U5 children) (girls: 1,000) and provide basic equipment and supplies to ensure and support quality nutrition services (5 nutrition clinics) in access restricted areas of Gaza (ARAs). The SCI component will provide counselling and support services for pregnant women and mothers of children under age 2 (Gaza: 2,200 PLW). Special attention will be given to infants who are not breastfed (<6 months), a group that is at particularly high risk of mortality and morbidity (Gaza: 200 infants under 6 months) (girls: 100) with the provision of individual counselling, home visits, appropriate infant formula hygiene and breastmilk substitute (BMS) kits in line with the IYCF in emergencies (IYCF-E) operational guidance 2017. 

Total beneficiaries (including U5 children, PLW, health workers and men) will be 81,600 (UNICEF: 76,000; WFP: 1,100; SCI: 4,500). It is estimated that 39,100 high-risk women (UNICEF: 36,000; WFP: 900; SCI: 2,200); 42,300 U5 children (UNICEF: 40,000 (girls: 19,600; boys: 20,400); WFP: 100 (girls: 50); SCI: 2,200 U5 children (girls: 1100)); 80 health workers (60 females); 20 protection case workers (10 males); and 100 men (under WFP Behavior Change activities) will benefit from urgently needed lifesaving nutrition interventions.

project_name: INCREASED ACCESS TO COMMUNITY- AND FACILITY-BASED NUTRITION SERVICES TO STRENGTHEN THE RESILIENCE OF CHILDREN
project_objective:
Up to 2.1 million people across Somalia are expected to face food consumption gaps, high acute malnutrition, or depletion of assets indicative of Crisis (IPC Phase 3)1 or worse outcomes through December 2019. Moreover, an estimated one million children under the age of five are likely to be acutely malnourished through mid-2020. Sustained and large-scale humanitarian assistance, which is planned and likely through September, is currently preventing more severe outcomes in many areas. In the absence of humanitarian assistance from October to December, however, food security is expected to deteriorate. Current high levels of food insecurity are driven by drought conditions from late 2018 through mid-May 2019, exacerbated by below-average and erratically distributed rainfall during the 2019 Gu season (April-June), which began late and finished early. Many households are still recovering from the severe 2016/2017 drought or have been affected by conflict, and 2.6 million people remain displaced. The Gu cereal harvest failed in most regions, leaving most poor agropastoral and riverine households unable to meet their minimum food needs given significantly below-average food stocks and income from seasonal agricultural employment. In pastoral areas, the impact of the drought on livestock led to a lack of access to milk, and many poor households have accumulated large debts while struggling to feed their families and rescue their remaining livestock. Although the 2019 Deyr (October-December) rains are forecast to be average to above average, the positive impact on food security will not be realized until late 2019. However, seasonal production activities will mitigate more severe deterioration during this period. These findings are based on the 2019 post-Gu seasonal food security and nutrition assessment conducted across Somalia during June-July 2019 and subsequent analyses, jointly led by the Food Security and Nutrition Analysis Unit for Somalia (FSNAU, a project managed by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations) and the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET, a project funded by USAID) and carried out with the active participation of Government institutions, UN and NGO partners.
The prevalence of acute malnutrition in Somalia is likely to deteriorate from February 2019 to June 2019 due to significantly below average livestock production, sales income and constraining food purchases. An estimated 1 008 500 children under the age of five years (total acute malnutrition burden) will likely face acute malnutrition through June 2020, including 178 400 who are likely to be severely malnourished.
The program target population of all the target region is 323,978(64,796 <5, 29158 PLWs.
According to the 2019 Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) for Somalia, more 3 million people require urgent and essential healthcare services. Women and children are particularly exposed to elevated health risks; access to birth spacing services is limited, while 98% of women experience Female Genital Mutilation/Cutting (FGM/C). Somalia has the world’s highest child mortality rate and the sixth highest lifetime maternal death risk in the world, although most maternal deaths are preventable. The risk of childhood mortality is highest in the neonatal period, accounting for approximately 45% of death among children under age five. 
Mercy-USA will identify, refer and treat children suffering from severe acute malnutrition through community- and facility-based approaches in Hiran-Bulaburte and Mahaas,Banadir- Yaqshid, Kahda, Karan and Daynile,Mudug- Hobyo,Galgadud- Abudwak, Balambale and Dhusamareb.
Complicated cases of SAM will be referred 4 SCs in all the regions and MAM to TSFP centres managed by Mercy-USA. Mercy-USA will manage 29 fixed OTP sites and subcontract 2 fixed sites to Banadir Consortium Efforts will be made to ensure integration of OTP and TSFP sites where possible. Mother-led MUAC approach will bed used for referrals.

project_name: PROJECT REVISED- Sustained Livelihoods for Improved Food Security  in  Jubaland, Galmudug and Banadir Regions
project_objective:
The sustained IDP and Host community Livelihoods project will be implemented in Jubaland state, Galmudug and Banadir  Regions. It will target and benefit  23,000 individuals in need. This will be achieved through the provision of seasonally appropriate agricultural inputs, emergency livestock assistance, livelihood diversification for women and the youth, improved post-harvest practices, response to food chain threats, protection of rangeland and development of income-generating activities. To facilitate immediate access to food for vulnerable communities living in areas with severe acute food insecurity, 720 households (4320 people) in Kismayo, Mogadishu, Dollow and Dhusamareb will receive food vouchers  All cash rates will be based on the rates as set by the Cash working group of Somalia.  Conditional and unconditional cash transfers will increase the purchasing power for targeted households to access food commodities available in the local markets for at least 3 months as they recover their assets. The cash is a digniﬁed approach to supporting these beneﬁciaries to make choices of types and quantities of food to purchase. Conditional transfers to 840 households will ensure that agricultural canals and river dykes are rehabilitated. Post Distribution Surveys will be conducted to monitor the use of transferred and the benefit it has brought the families.      

1,560 households( 9360 individuals) will be supported to develop or restore their agricultural livestock production through the provision of farm inputs (seeds tools and fertilizers to mention but a few) and provision of basic treatment of 28,800,000 livestock. 140 women will be supported to diversify their livestock production to take up poultry keeping for household consumption and commercial benefits to the households.  150 women and youth will also be supported to establish income-generating activities while 90 youth will be supported to take up technical courses that will broaden their opportunities for self-employment.  In a bid to reduce the number of people living in acute food insecurity, 850 farmers and pastoralists will be facilitated will SMART  agricultural and livestock production skills through demonstration farms established through the proposed project and provision of agricultural extension services. Protection of rangeland in Abudwak, Dhusamareb, Dollow, Belet Hawa and Kismayo will be conducted through trained community-based natural resource management committees. This project is will be implemented in a 12 month period.

project_name: PROJECT REVISED-Enhanced coordination and self management of IDP camps for newly displaced and protracted internally IDPs in Banadir, Lower Shebelle, Lower Jubba and Gedo Regions
project_objective:
This project intends to strengthen CCCM site management structures in Banadir, Lower Shebelle and Gedo Regions with increased coordination among the service providers within the settlements and host community to streamline humanitarian service delivery. The project shall also ensure that the population can access key services through ongoing advocacy to the partners with a special emphasis on people with specific needs. Through this project, NoFYL shall work in close coordination with the local authority to strengthen the existing governance structure and fill in the identified gaps while encouraging the active participation of both IDPs and the host community’s leadership. The project shall further promote building a sustainable relationship between the host communities and IDPs through strengthening the leadership capacities of IDPs and the host community. The project aims to improve living conditions and reduce protection concerns in Banadir, Lower Shebelle, and Gedo Regions, encourage free movement of IDPs and partners around the sites.

Through this project, NoFYL will address the cluster’s overall objective of improving the living conditions inside IDP sites and facilitate the immediate and targeted delivery of services to the displaced population.  Cluster coverage will be expanded through NoFYL capacity to carry out assessments and monitor the displacement conditions in target locations where there are currently no CCCM coordination structures in place or no IDP assessment of any kind having been conducted in the last one year. Coverage will also be expanded through coordination meetings with camp committees and camp leaders.

The cluster’s primary monitoring tool, the detailed site assessment (DSA) will be utilized to gather baseline information on multisectoral issues and trends on displacement and monitor areas with camps and camp¬like settings and where there is a likelihood of displacement because of the ongoing conflict, flood/natural disaster. To immediately address needs and gaps and monitor areas where new displacement is reported, NoFYL will draw on field monitors to strengthen response capacity. 

NoFYL will implement emergency site improvement projects to minimize risks of exclusion and high incidence of protection violations in IDP sites, as well as achieving durable solutions. NoFYL will also conduct settlement planning training for settlement leaders; create coordination structures and SOPs for emergency displacements; conduct capacity building training for government actors and relevant stakeholders; establish/reinforce community mechanisms for communication channels among others. Gender and protection will be mainstreamed in all program activities. Variations in gender, areas of origin, physical ability and age that affect vulnerability and coping strategies are identified and taken into account for planning to prevent their situation from deteriorating even further. Additionally, contingency plans are developed and put in place to ensure NoFYL can quickly adapt to and respond to changing humanitarian needs on the ground. Lastly, NoFYL will develop systems to strengthen community self-management to promote durable solutions for displaced people in sites.

project_name: PROJECT REVISED- Provision of assistance and support to survivors of gender based violence and Unaccompanied/ Separated boys and girls prevention services in Banaadir, Lower Shebelle, Lower Jubba and Gedo Regions.
project_objective:
Based on the analysis of the current drought situation in the target regions, NoFYL intends to extend its protection program to contribute towards enhancing protection, increasing safety and promoting the dignity of conflict-affected women, men, girls, and boys, in Banaadir, Lower Shebelle, Lower Jubba and Gedo Regions. These areas are currently concerned by prolonged drought, displacement, and voluntary return movements and, with the intensification of the military operations around AS control areas, it is expected that a high number of newly displaced people and/or newly accessible people will be imminently in need of critical assistance.

The overarching objective is to contribute towards enhancing the first line and second-line overall GBV and child protection response capacity, through the deployment of specialized mobile teams composed of Social Worker, Case Manager, Health Worker, and IDTR Officers, for increased identification and service delivery. 

This assistance will be provided where there is currently very limited access to GBV and child protection services and to provide tailored and effective assistance where it is needed most, NoFYL will:
1. Conduct Rapid Protection Assessments to identify the most urgent needs after new displacements and to tailor the subsequent provision of services;
2. Establish mobile Child-Friendly and Youth Friendly Spaces (CFS/YFS) providing psychosocial support, awareness-raising activities, non-formal education, and recreational activities to vulnerable IDP children in underserved locations. The CFS/YFS will also act as a platform to identify particularly at-risk children.
3. Provide specialized child protection case management to at-risk children identified through RPAs and the CFS/YFS. The guiding strategy will be twofold: combining collection, analysis and dissemination of relevant information through community outreaches; and direct support of identified cases through comprehensive case management (including case management for boy and girl survivors of GBV; case management for unaccompanied/separated minors-IDTR and ensuring appropriate follow up and providing alternative care where necessary)
4. Capacity building of other NGOs and other CP organizations for continuity of these critical services that are currently not available or not to the extent needed in the target locations.
5. Distribution of emergency kits and engagement with communities to build community-driven GBV/child protection mechanisms.

NoFYL will be the overall lead for this project and will work closely with other agencies, NoFYL has been working in the area for over 10 years and have good knowledge of the area and rapport at the community level.

project_name: PROJECT REVISED- Lifesaving humanitarian and recovery assistance is provided to the disaster affected communities of Somalia
project_objective:
The proposed lifesaving and life sustaining interventions will include provision of Multipurpose cash transfer, conditional cash transfer and launching of safety net program. Whereas recovery interventions will focus on engaging youth in skill development program for livelihoods diversification, establishing small enterprises, improved agricultural production and livelihoods assets building & protection through cash for work in the long term.   These initiatives will not only help beneficiaries to deal with the negative coping strategies on immediate basis rather will also help communities to recover from shocks through improved asset based resilience, enhanced capacities and strengthened linkages. Livelihoods and Food Security will continue to engage with other actors including humanitarian agencies working in the areas, public / private sector institutions and local authorities to promote cash programming for synergized support. NRC has already in place signed framework agreements with the Telecom companies in each of the operational areas. E transfer using telecom services are swift, safe and ensure upholding dignity of the beneficiaries. 

Vocational skills development will help in creating market sensitive job opportunities for unemployed women and youth. Under the safety net programs; NRC will conduct research to identify poorest of the poor households and will register these households for safety net program. Registered poorest HHs will be provided with monthly safety net support as per CMWG recommended transfer values. NRC has adopted localization approach in program operational areas and the complementing integrated programs funded by various donors are being implemented in clustered villages. So identified and registered HHs Where appropriate will benefit from a companion program for awareness raising around good nutrition sensitive intervention, BCC, safe food preparation, access to diverse food, improved hygiene practices and diversified livelihoods options. These companion programs will ensure that poorest HHs have improved capacities and access to food and income sources.  Likewise, Small farmers will be provided with agricultural inputs including (Training, cereal / pulses / horticultural crops seeds and Tractor tillage hours) for improved agricultural production and access to nutritious horticultural crops.  NRC will make sure to implement cash transfer programs (CTPs) considering seasonality, agricultural calendar and fluctuating market prices. Resilience building initiative will help beneﬁciaries to sustain shock, protecting and conserving natural resources on which they bank and making informed decision. NRC will support targeted populations especially communities in hard to reach areas to meet their basic food and non-food. In the long run this will help in peace building.

project_name: PROJECT REVISED-Durable and Sustainable WASH Interventions for AWD, Drought Affected and chronically under-served host, displaced and disaster affected populations in Somalia
project_objective: Project aims to increase access to sustainable safe water, adequate sanitation facilities and hygiene education for drought affected population and areas that are high risk of AWD/Cholera due to extremely low water and or sanitation coverage in Somalia. Long-term displaced populations in prioritized locations will be provided with durable solutions to WASH services where land is availed by the government. Access to safe water will be increased through construction and or rehabilitation of water sources including 8 boreholes (3 new), 17 shallow wells, 1 river water intake system with water treatment, 1 desalination system using existing sources and extension of piped water network. New borehole construction will be preceded by hydrogeological survey and safe pumping regime will be designed. River water intakes will be preceded hydrological study. In all cases, an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) will be undertaken for new water sources and mitigation measures put in place for negative impacts. All water systems will be equipped with distribution infrastructure and hybrid energization systems. Pipeline extensions will also be made. Taps stand will be located within a radius of at least 500m to reduce distance and enhance security of women and girls. Project will also construct 1 major improved water dam in locations that lack other options. All well heads will be raised at a minimum 0.5m to reduce risk flooding and contamination. Water committees comprising men and women from all community groups including the minority and the marginalized will be trained on management, operation and maintenance. Local technicians will be trained and provided with O&M tools to undertake repairs whereas consumers will pay for the technician’s services. For major water supply in urban areas, Private Public Parternship (PPP) management system will be adopted. Adequate sanitation in 4 rural villages will be provided through construction of sanitation facilities, using Community Led Total Sanitation approach when feasible. Project will construct 400 latrines for families reintegrated through the durable solutions. NRC undertakes sanitary surveys periodically to identify contamination risks for timely mitigation. All latrine will be installed with handwashing equipment and community sensitized to use soap for handwashing. Design of infrastructure will take into consideration the needs of special groups in the community including the disables, old, children to ensure they have equitable access to the services. Life-saving WASH interventions will be implemented in case of sudden disaster to reduce the related mortality and morbidity especially among children. This will be through temporary provision of safe water through direct delivery or restricted cash depending on context and market functionality, provision of hygiene kits through cash or in-kind, household water treatment and/or point of use water treatment to 3000 hhs, construction of 450 simple design emergency latrines, latrine emptying (450 latrines) and safe fecal sludge disposal and hygiene promotion. Schools and health facilities will be provided with private space for menstrual hygiene (60 institutional latrines). All latrines will be raised above ground level to reduce the risk of flooding during rains. Women and girls will be involved in identification of sites for facilities to ensure their safety and security is taken into account. Latrines will be gender separated, provided with lockable doors and handwashing equipment. Solar street lights (35 posts) will be provided near water points and latrines to improve the security and safety of women and girls especially in crowded IDP settlements. Throughout the implementation period the beneficiaries will be provided with adequate information on NRC’s complaints, response and feedback (CRFM) mechanisms to enable them channel complaints or share feedback to be incorporate as necessary.

project_name: PROJECT REVISED-Sustainable Access to Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene Services for Vulnerable Populations in Jowhar, Middle Shabelle region of Somalia
project_objective:
In January 2019, Polish Humanitarian Action (PAH) received requests from community leaders and PAH’s community-based DRR teams that nine villages, located in Jowhar West, were experiencing complete water sources dry up and were forced to travel between 8-15 km to collect water each day. The villages, namely, Buulo Maxamud, Khalafow, Guumeys, Gumarey, Guumeysta, Caliwarabey, Duray, Maryan Keynan, Dhay-Gawan are mainly pastoralists and agrarian communities practicing on a small scale. They are highly dependent on rain to fill the water canals connecting them to the Shebelle river. These canals, are their source for not only drinking and domestic use but also for irrigation and livelihood purposes. Based on the initial assessment conducted in February 2019, PAH identified that without humanitarian intervention, the villages were at risk of slipping into IPC 3 & 4 status. In response, as of February, PAH has been provided water via trucking due to their WASH vulnerability and food insecurity and lack of available WASH infrastructure in the area; coupled with high population density and the absence of a permanent water source as evidenced by the attached needs assessment report. 
PAH is submitting this proposal to increase the resilience and recovery capacity of these at-risk communities in the long term to prevent further deterioration and higher severity of needs. Moreover,, the project will complement the ongoing nutrition project with the objective of contributing the reduction of morbidity and mortality among moderately malnourished under 5 children and PLW in Jowhar district. 
The exact activities prioritized based on the allocation strategy (SO4 “Increase resilience capacity of at-risk communities and promote complementary interventions of development partners in social services” and WASH cluster objective to “provide sustainable access to safe water and sustainable sanitation services” to support the integrated approach include:
•The provision of sustainable access to safe water through the construction of strategic water infrastructure. Namely, the construction of a borehole, identified with a hydro-geological survey and environmental impact assessment. In line with the strategy, the borehole will have equipped with Gen-set and other infrastructures such as Water kiosks, and animal troughs. 
•Borehole construction will be followed by the extension of existing water infrastructures through pipelines and the construction of 4 water kiosks in a strategic location in the villages targeted in this proposal. This will increase access to water in a sustainable and functional way as well as mitigate the Gender-Based Violence and protection risks associated with women and girls walking a long distance to fetch water. The villages targeted are Buulo Maxamud, Khalafow, and Guumeys.
•Construction of 12 handpump shallow wells in 6 villages: Gumarey, Guumeysta, Caliwarabey, Duray, Maryan Keynan, Dhay-Gawan. The depth of the shallow wells will be increased to 15m to ensure that water is available during the dry season.
•PAH will establish gender-balanced water committees to manage water points and ensure equity of access, functionality, and sustainability. The committees will additionally uphold disease mitigation measures such as borehole shock chlorination, sanitation surveys, and site cleaning to ensure the safety and continuity of services of the water facilities beyond the project period.
•Access to adequate sanitation will also be ensured through the construction of communal latrines, which will be designed in line with the protection guidelines (covered with a roof, solar light, lockable from inside and outside). Hygiene promotion and hygiene kits distribution activities will be conducted for a period of 6 months. Hygiene promoters will be hired and trained on the door to door hygiene promotion sessions and reporting tools to ensure monitoring of the progress of the campaign.

project_name: PROJECT REVISED-Emergency Health Service Provision in Banadir, Hiraan, and Gedo Regions of Somalia
project_objective:
Relief International (RI) will increase access to and utilisation of primary health care services by pregnant and lactating women and girls (PLWG) and children under the age of 5 years in Banadir, Hiraan, and Gedo regions of Somalia. RI aims to improve health seeking behaviour, including attitudes towards skilled delivery and hygiene in the target communities.

Delayed, and poor performing Gu rains across Somalia have led to widespread crop failure and reduced livestock productivity. The 2019 Gu harvest in southern Somalia is the lowest output since 1995. Repeated climatic shocks, including more frequent and prolonged dry conditions and episodic flood events, undermine food security, compounded by widespread insecurity, displacement, and poor access to basic services including nutrition, water, and sanitation increase morbidity. Humanitarian access remains a challenge across southern Somalia where main roads connecting Bulo Burte to Jalalqsi remain blockaded and attacks on government buildings in Ghabaharey and Belet Hawa heighten fear of al-Shabaab attacks impede vulnerable populations’ access to lifesaving health and other humanitarian assistance. As localized insecurity and access deteriorated in parts of Banadir, Gedo, and Hiran, prolonged harsh dry conditions imperilled food security and nutrition outcomes, and access to water and sanitation at household level decreased precipitating a marked uptick in the number of consultations at health facilities in the target communities as compared to the same period in 2018. To date, RI have conducted 125,460 primary health consultations; Over 7000 for acute diarrheal diseases (ADD) and 16,364 acute respiratory infections (ARI). Despite a promising start to the Deyr season (October – December), three successive failed harvests in Hiraan and other parts of southern Somalia has undermined household resilience and will require the urgent scale-up of the humanitarian assistance to avert a further deterioration.

Aligned to the health cluster strategic objectives, RI will address the health needs of displaced and rural PLWG and children under the age of 5 in need of immediate and sustained health interventions. RI currently supports 12 static health centres in the target regions that provide a comprehensive package of health and nutrition services. Women and children comprise the majority of patients seen at the health facilities. Data collected from RI’s health centers reveal that in many cases, women and children in need of health and nutrition services travel long distances. In Hiraan, RI found, in July 2019, that 30% of patients travelled more than 10km to reach health facilities. These journeys invariably expose these vulnerable groups to protection risks, as they traverse through unfamiliar and insecure environments. Anchored to static health facilities, RI will deploy mobile health and nutrition teams to serve underserved host and internally displaced communities outside the main urban hubs. These mobile teams will increase access to lifesaving primary health services, including ante- and post-natal care, and integrated management of childhood diseases for those unable to access the static health facilities in Gedo, Hiraan and Banadir. These health interventions will help decrease morbidity rates and overall mortality by simultaneously addressing poor nutrition and WASH status among the target populations. 

The health service provision at the supported static facilities with the mobile teams will reach 100,440 PLWG and children, predominantly from IDP and underserved rural and remote households.

project_name: PROJECT REVISED- Improve access to food and enhance livelihoods for vulnerable populations in Bay region, Somalia
project_objective:
In the Bay region, the number of acutely food insecure People (Rural, IDP and Urban Combined) who are Most Likely (October-December 2019) includes 218,000 People who are in IPC Phase 2, 196,000 in IPC Phase 3 while 71,000 in Emergency IPC Phase 4 (FSNAU September 2019). In the absence of assistance during the October- December period, food security is expected to deteriorate in central Somalia and some parts of the South including the Bay region. Emergency (IPC Phase 4) is most likely in the Bay-Bakool Low Potential Agropastoral livelihood zone, given the severity of Gu food deficits. 

In response to this, READO in line with the FSC & HRP 2020 objectives aims to improve households’ immediate access to food through conditional and unconditional cash transfers in Baidoa, Hudur and Dinsoor districts in the Bay region. Also, READO will protect and restore livelihoods, related food and income sources, through the provision of seasonally appropriate livelihood inputs provide livelihood inputs/training and technical support in rural and peri-urban settings.

project_name: PROJECT REVISED-Essential and Life-saving Integrated Health Assistance for Vulnerable Populations in Somalia
project_objective:
The project will provide essential and life-saving integrated health assistance to vulnerable communities in Awdal, Bakool, Banadir, Bari, Bay, Galgaduud, Hiran, Lower Juba, Mudug, Nugaal, Sanaag, Sool and aims to reach a total of 265,800 IDPs and host communities  of the cluster target in the targeted geographies. 
The project will seek to contribute to a 5% reduction in excess morbidity and mortality rates from crisis-driven diseases and outbreaks among target vulnerable communities by end of 2020 while scaling up provision of regular health services and providing safe, dignified and meaningful access to life-saving assistance (provided directly or through referral) with sensitivity to age, gender and disability status.
This will be achieved by supporting the Somalia governments and communities to be able to delivery essential package of health free services to communities with acute humanitarian needs using development programs as a platform for immediate responses. The required budget for the delivery of the project is USD 3.6 million.

project_name: PROJECT REVISED - Integrated lifesaving treatment and prevention of acute malnutrition among children U5 and PLW in Somalia
project_objective: The objective of the project is to improve access to  quality lifesaving nutrition services through integrated prevention, treatment and rehabilitation, services for acutely malnourished children (boys and girls 0-59 months of age) and pregnant and lactating women (PLW) among the most affected communities in addition to  strengthening  the capacity of  national staff to respond

project_name: PROJECT REVISED- Strengthening community engagement on GBV response and prevention in Banadir and Lower Jubba regions.
project_objective:
This project seeks to address dire humanitarian needs of protection for the IDPs and poor host communities in Banadir (Kahda, Daynile and Dharkaynley districts) districts) and Kisamayo of Lower Jubba Region.   The project is planned to include the protection mainstreaming guidelines to ensure that the beneficiaries access humanitarian aid at convenient time and points considering place of distribution as well time.  The project will involve all the target stakeholders to avoid conflicts and to facilitate effective targeting and inclusion of the most vulnerable households in the target locations.  
SCC proposed project will be implemented in a period of 12-months to benefit 2250 women, girls and men in Banadir and Kismaiyo.  The project aims to sustain the provision of emergency protection and lifesaving services to reduce risks for women and girls at the target locations.  The intervention will contribute to build resilience and restore dignity for the beneficiaries to gain control of their lives through the provision of case management and material support for the affected women and children in the target villages and IDP Camps.
The proposed project resulted to recurrent conflicts and drought that is widespread in rural-urban forcing the target communities to dislodge in search of services and livelihood opportunities hence increasing displacement in Banadir region and Kismayo .  While there is a considerable number of refugees returning to Kismayo villages and IDPs that presents significant protection challenges, particularly for women and children, as households lose traditional socio-economic safety nets and frequently experience extremely poor living conditions in Internally Displaced Persons (IDP) sites. There are significant information gaps on the specific protection vulnerabilities faced by IDPs and host communities in these regions and SCC outlined the need for strengthened system-wide data collection, analysis and data management across the protection sectors in banadir and Lower Jubba regions.  The intervention will include the following activities:
Activity 1.1: Awareness raising forums and campaigns for individuals targeted with rights-based public outreach and awareness-raising activities.
Activity 1.2: Capacity building on protection for duty bearers, service providers and community leaders.
Activity 1.3: train and establish Community-based protection committees in Banadir and Lower Jubba regions. 
Activity 1.4: Provision of training to GBV/Health workers to ensure clinical care for sexual assault survivors accesses health facilities with trained GBV/Health staff. 
Activity 1.5: conduct gender forums involving local authorities, law enforcement, women representatives, traditional community leaders, state duty bearers, service providers and community leaders engaged on protection.
Activity 2.1. provision of life-saving assistance to rape survivors through Cash voucher support to cope with post-trauma stress.
Activity 2.2:  Dignity kit distribution to women and girls of reproductive age (15-49Yrs) including rape survivors.
Activity 2.3:  Provision of solar lanterns to female households in the IDP camps.

project_name: Provision of essential quality PHC services to the vulnerable and the neglected population in NES
project_objective:
UPP will address the urgent and life-saving health needs, as well as basic acute needs of primary health care in 4 different areas, including non-communicable diseases. 
UPP and KRC will support four Primary Health Care Centers (PHCs) established between 2017 and 2019. These 4 sites were identified due to their strategic value of service delivery points covering a heavily underserved catchment area of 214,000 people (PIN data, December 2018). According to UPP/KRC historical consultation pattern, approximately 40,000 direct beneficiaries accessed the facilities in 2019.

project_name: Life-Saving and Life-Sustaining Emergency and Seasonal SNFI Assistance for Conflict Affected Populations In Idleb and Aleppo Governorates.
project_objective:
The proposed action will respond to emergency, displacement S/NFI needs and protect the well-being and thermal comfort of conflict-affected highly vulnerable IDPs and host communities in North West Syria (NWS). This will be achieved through an integrated programme of assistance focused on providing targeted, emergency S/NFI assistance to newly displaced households and winterization assistance to the most vulnerable households in areas with greatest severity of winter need. Whenever possible, complementary Food Security assistance will be provided to SNFI beneficiaries. 

Funding is secured to provide immediate, emergency and / or winter assistance to 9,102 vulnerable households newly displaced by the latest conﬂict escalation, of  which an estimated 26,760 male (14,745 boys) and 27,852 female (15,291 girls) as summarised below. Please note for activities implemented by the Lead Partner, our submission shows only the caseload and budget to be implemented by our organisation. The Lead Partner will input their planned activities to the HPC separately, to ensure no duplication in targets reported.
In partnership with INGO and funded by ECHO: Multi-Purpose Cash Grants (MPCGs) to reach 1,163 IDP households + in-kind NFI kits for a further 1,000 HHs. Based on S/NFI Cluster and Cash WG guidance, beneﬁciaries are anticipated to use 15% of MPCG assistance to meet NFI needs.
 
In partnership with INGO and funded by DfID: In-kind NFI kits to respond to the winter and displacement needs of total 2,639 households.

project_name: Emergency health services to internally displaced persons and vulnerable host communities in Jonglei and Eastern Equatoria States
project_objective:
Multiply displaced communities face significant health challenges in parts of Jonglei and Eastern Equatoria, which prior to the conflict had limited or no access to health care services. The project seeks to provide access to essential lifesaving health care services to vulnerable populations focusing on the major causes of morbidity and mortality in the counties of Ayod, Duk, Twic East, Pigi and Fangak (Jonglei); and Kapoeta South, Kapoeta North and Kapoeta East (Eastern Equatoria State)

CMD aims at fostering improved access, prevent, detect and respond to epidemic prone diseases, improve resilience among vulnerable populations and deliver an integrated response cutting across health, WASH, Nutrition, food security and protection. The project will implement and expand essential primary health care emergency clinical packages targeting the most vulnerable, carry out preventive health measures through immunization targeting children, PLWs and <5s. Working alongside health cluster leads; CMD will implement outbreak investigation and response in the targeted locations while mainstreaming accountability to affected populations. 
An expanded program will include HIV/AIDS/TB care and reproductive health (RH) services including SGBV. CMD will implement integrated response for severe acute malnutrition with medical complications especially in locations with high cases of malnutrition as well as implement integrated response for epidemic prone communicable diseases including diarrheal, vector, Viral Hemorrhagic diseases with WASH/Nut/FSL. Emergency health protection for people with disabilities will be provided across all project locations. 
In the locations of Ayod, Fangak, Kapoeta South, North and East, CMD will carry out referrals for Comprehensive Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care (CeMONC), minor trauma and surgery, and work with development health partners to scale up integrated response to SAM with medical complications. 

The project will directly benefit 8,333 people (51% female, 48% IDPs, 45% vulnerable host communities, 7% returnees and other groups in the locations of Ayod, Duk, Twic East, Pigi and Fangak (Jonglei); and Kapoeta South, Kapoeta North and Kapoeta East (Eastern Equatoria State)
