project_name: Protecting Civilians through Humanitarian Mine Action in Syria
project_objective:
The humanitarian crisis in Syria has been exacerbated by the widespread use of explosive ordnance. Explosive ordnance poses significant risks and require different mitigation strategies to reduce their impact on the civilian population and the humanitarian sector delivering aid and relief to those in need. While the full scale of contamination is not known, preliminary findings for the 2020 Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) estimates that one in three communities report some form of explosive contamination, affecting some 11.5 million people. The presence of contamination in essential civilian infrastructure, agricultural lands, homes and roads is a lethal barrier to safe movement which: deprives civilians from accessing essential basic services; hampers the delivery of humanitarian assistance; endangers those seeking refuge from violence or returning to areas affected by the conflict; and precludes the resumption of livelihood activities. A comprehensive humanitarian mine action response is thus a humanitarian necessity and a vital precursor for the delivery of humanitarian aid and early recovery.
The overall aim of UNMAS project “Protecting Civilians through Humanitarian Mine Action in Syria” is to reduce the impact of explosive hazards on the civilian population and humanitarian workers in Syria through effective sector coordination and the implementation of humanitarian mine action activities across Syria, in line with humanitarian priorities as identified in the Humanitarian Response Plan, and within the framework of agreements between the Syrian State and UN agencies, funds and programmes, as well as Security Council resolution 2504 (S/RES/2504, 2020) . Since the opening of the UNMAS Damascus office in October 2018, one of the key focus is on the development of the Humanitarian mine action sector and capacity enhancement of civilian actors to conduct mine action operations within the Government controlled areas. As such, UNMAS will work on the advancement of humanitarian technical mine action standards and frameworks to support the development of a Syrian civilian capacity, ensure humanitarian needs-based prioritization in line with the HRP, and the expansion of humanitarian mine action activities from risk education to explosive hazard survey, marking and clearance related activities. Under this project, in accordance with this humanitarian response plan, UNMAS will lead, manage and coordinate humanitarian mine action activities: risk education, victim assistance and clearance as defined by International Mine Action Standards (IMAS). The delivery of risk education, tailored to age, gender, localized threats and activity patterns of different at-risk groups, is a critical, life-saving activity for raising the awareness of civilians and humanitarian personnel about the dangers posed by explosive hazards, thus directly contributing to HRP strategic objective 1: “Save Lives” and strategic objective 2: “Enhance Protection”.  As the Syrian crisis has been characterized by large-scale conflict and displacement, survey, data collection, and mapping are critical to informing on localized threats, humanitarian programming, and needs-based prioritization, as well as the expansion of clearance to remove the contamination threats facing civilians, particularly in high-priority areas. Furthermore, UNMAS will support the expansion of victim assistance and provision of specialized services for persons with disabilities, in particular survivors of explosive hazards and their families, thus contributing to strategic objective 3: “Increase Resilience and Access to Services”.

project_name: Emergency child protection prevention and  response for the internally displaced persons, returnees and most vulnerable host communities in Lakes, Jonglei, Eastern and Central Equatoria States, South Sudan.
project_objective:
The Project aims at reducing the exposure to and ensure timely protection from violence, abuse, neglect and exploitation for at-risk IDP, returnees and host community children and their families through enhanced access to child protection services in Lakes, Jonglei, Eastern and Central Equatoria States, South Sudan.

The project will provide life-saving child protection prevention and response services through provision of Comprehensive case management services and referrals for children with critical protection concerns (750 boys and 750 girls); Psychosocial Support (PSS) activities (4000 boys, 4000 girls, 800 men and 1600 women); Training of staff, volunteers and Government officials on CP (168 men and 168 women); Child protection awareness raising and outreach (5500 men, 6500 women,7000 boys, 8400 girls) and Strengthening of community-based child protection mechanisms to prevent and respond to child protection concerns (132 men and 132 women. In total, the project will target 40,040 most vulnerable individuals (13,150 girls, 11,750 boys, 8,470 women and 6,670 men). The project will be implemented Plan’s existing field locations of Eastern Equatoria (Kapoeta East); Lakes (Rumbek Centre and Rumbek East); Central Equatoria (Yei) and in Jonglei (Pibor). The project will target IDPs, returnees as well as vulnerable host communities. Plan International will coordinate closely with the Child Protection Sub-Cluster and UNICEF in implementing this project. Further, in the different field locations, Plan will work closely with other child protection partners (Save the Children, DRDA, TDH, IPCS, GREDO) to avoid overlapping and duplication of efforts. For instance, will work in different payams or bomas from other CP actors in the target locations. Plan will also coordinate with CP partners through referrals of CP cases.

project_name: Cash Emergency for Disaster Affected Residents and Nutrition (CEDAR & NUT)
project_objective: The project aims to expand cash based assistance for individuals affected by the Beirut blast through a 3 months-cycle of MPCA (food portion and basic needs) based on nutrition-sensitive vulnerability criteria as entry point for targeting, coupled with guidance to safeguard nutrition security for vulnerable HHs (special focus to infants and proper use of breastmilk subsitutes). The targeted population will be from all nationalities as per needs and will focus on caregivers of children under 2, pregnant and lactating women, female-headed households, older people and people with special needs who may not have the capacity to provide healthy foods for themselves and their families as well as needed health access with the exacerbated vulnerability caused by the blast. MPCA receivers will be 900HH for a total of 4.500individuals (Disagregated 0-2 years: 100 females; 100 males/ 3-17 years: 450 females; 450 males/ 18 to 64 years: 1900 females; 1000 males/ 65+ years: 300 females; 200 males). The proposed intervention builds on a planned Emergency Cash Assistance (ECA) program under Action Against Hunger for HHs with similar vulnerability criteria residing in Karantina and Mar Mkhayel (% of existing caseload) while including areas with the highest presence of socio-economically vulnerability such as Borj Hammoud and Dawra (Data source: OCHA, MapAction 13/08/20, LRF, UNICEF UN-Habitat).

project_name: Increase access to health services for most at risk older people and people with disabilities affected by the Beirut port blast
project_objective: In response to the Beirut explosion that happened on the 4th of August, HelpAge International is proposing a project that will contribute to improved access to primary healthcare services for most-at-risk older people and persons with disability living in the affected areas through 1) two roving medical teams of general physicians and nurses providing home-based essential healthcare services in partnership with Amel Association International and Makassed Association, 2) referring older people and persons with disabilities to relevant services based on their needs and ensuring their access, and 3) equipping three of the affected primary healthcare centers in Bachoura, Msaytbeh, and Horj with appropriate PPEs to mitigate the risk of COVID19 infection. The project will be linked up with other projects implemented by HelpAge under the Protection and WASH sectors to complement the intervention and ensure a comprehensive response to the emerged needs.

project_name: Increase protection and access to services for most at risk older people and people with disabilities affected by the Beirut port blast
project_objective: In response to the Beirut Explosion that happened on August the 4th and based on a needs assessment, HelpAge International is proposing a project to reach out to older people and persons with disabilities affected by the explosion and support them to access services focusing on their protection needs. The project will target a total of 800 older people and persons with disabilities living in the affected areas through 1) identifying the most at risk and provide them with information on health and protection services, 2) raising their awareness on Covid-19 prevention measures, 3) referring them to health and protection services including support to transportation, 4) home visits by trained community volunteers for home-bound older people to support them in their daily living activities and provide them with psychosocial support, 5) provision of multipurpose cash assistance to most at-risk households with older people, 6) provision of psychological one-on-one counseling and psycho-social support through home visits by psychologists, and 7) operating an MHPSS hotline and referring to in-clinic consultations for older people and other household members in need for further intervention. The project will be linked up with other projects implemented by HelpAge under the Health and WASH sectors to complement the intervention and ensure a comprehensive response to the emerged needs.

project_name: Improved and Specialized Child Protection Services to Rohingya and Host Community Population
project_objective:
The Project aims to continue to provide protection to vulnerable girls and boys in camps and in the host community through specialized child protection services, case management, strengthening Community-based Child Protection Mechanisms and capacity building of protection actors. Focus remains on the vulnerable children at risk or survivor of child abuse, child labour, child marriage and trafficking and on particular groups (e.g. unaccompanied and separated boys and girls, children with disabilities and/or child survivors of sexual abuse).

Services will be provided through implementing partner Terre des hommes (Tdh) in camp 13, 20, 20 extension and in the host community in Ukhia/Palong Khali, and by direct implementation of IOM in camp 9 and 23. In camp 7,9,17, 18, 20 extension and camp 23 IOM Child Protection runs Child Friendly Corners in  Women and Girls Safe Spaces. The CP team also engages with IOM GBV, Counter-Trafficking and General Protection Sub-units as part of integrated protection approaches. With a cross-cutting approach IOM CP cooperates with other sectors  (e.g. MHPSS/ Health, Shelter, WASH, Site Management, Transition and Recovery Division, ) to mainstream child protection, disability and to promote peaceful co-existence and to strengthen the PSEA and Feedback mechanisms.

The prevention and response closely interlinked with Community-based protection to enhance sustainability, accountability and community participation and especially to enable children to be instrumental in improving the quality of their life and mitigating risks and dangers in their community and living environment. The Project also has a strong emphasis on supporting children and their caregivers/families with Mental Health and structured Psychosocial Support services and with comprehensive Case Management services, utilizing the safe spaces run by IOM or its partners as access points to the beneficiaries

IOM is committed to monitor the situation and activities in the camps to ensure safe multi-sectoral programming, including monitoring to mitigate the risks of exploitation and child labor and to protect beneficiaries from sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA). IOM provided training on PSEA to staff and appointed PSEA Focal Points within each camp where complaint and feedback mechanism, as well as referral mechanism are in place for reporting. 

IOM ensure accountability towards the Rohingya community and continuously investing and developing accessible, reliable and data-protected electronic Community Feedback Mechanism (CFM).  IOM Site Management currently is piloting a new inter-agency CFM system for collecting, referring, analyzing, and replying to community feedback. Child Protection is working closely with IOM Site Management to reach out to generally underrepresented groups like boys and girls in different age groups (with special focus to adolescents) in a child-friendly way through organizing FGDs periodically to give a voice for the younger population about their concerns and feedback.

Coordination: IOM has been strongly committed to child protection inter-agency efforts and has contributed to the development of several CP technical documents, key message campaigns and adaptation of materials for inter-agency child protection trainings. IOM CP contributes to the CP Sub-Sector, CP Case Management Technical Working Group, GBV Sub-Sector and co-chairs the Counter Trafficking Technical Working Group and PSEA Network. 

IOM Child Protection programme aims to establish durable and sustainable solution through strengthening community child protection mechanism through inclusive and diverse community participation (including boys, girls, and children with disabilities). IOM also contribute to institutional capacity strengthening building of NGOs, local authorities and law enforcement agencies and to the advocacy to promote children’s rights to have access for informal and formal structures and services of Government of Bangladesh.

project_name: Gender-Based Violence Prevention and Response in the Rohingya Refugee Response: Mitigating Risks, Supporting Survivors and Addressing the Root Causes
project_objective:
In line with commitments to the global Call to Action on Protection Against Gender-Based Violence in Emergencies, IOM’s GBV in Crises (GBViC) Operational Framework and in accordance with the IASC Guidelines for Integrating GBV Interventions in Humanitarian Action (2015), IOM will continue to develop its comprehensive GBV intervention focused on three key pillars: 1) Survivor-centered support, 2) Risk mitigation and 3) Addressing root causes that perpetuate GBV. 

In line with the 2020 JRP’s three strategic objectives and two of the GBV sector’s objectives, most of the activities described in this proposal will be jointly implemented by IOM and its local partner, PULSE Bangladesh. IOM and PULSE teams will work alongside each other, through Women and Girls’ Safe Spaces (WGSS) and the emergency transitional shelter and at the community level through ten facilities across nine camps. IOM directly implements case management and supports the day-to-day operations of the WGSS. PULSE teams work as activity animators, community mobilisers and also manage IOM’s emergency transitional shelter for GBV and trafficking survivors. 

The WGSS provide non-stigmatizing case management entry points where women and girls can safely access individual case management and life saving services, including temporary accommodation through an emergency transitional shelter, as well as streamlined referral pathways for health, legal, MHPSS and self-reliance opportunities for women and girls. To mitigate risks, prevent GBV and empower women and girls, the WGSS provides age-appropriate and structured psychosocial and educational activities, life-skills and vocational learning, forums for information sharing and learning, including targeted awareness on SRH and radio listening groups, amidst a wide-range of recreational activities. Through close linkages with IOM general protection, child protection and counter trafficking teams, women and girls are empowered to manage their own safety and protection. 

IOM will also focus on diversity of need, mapping health posts and confidential spaces to ensure non-stigmatising access for male and LGBTI survivors, persons with disabilities and child survivors as needed. IOM caseworkers will strengthen counselling support, referral and follow up of such cases working through an integrated approach with IOM Health teams. IOM GBV will refer identified cases – for example general protection cases, child victims of trafficking, other child protection cases, in need of specialized services to IOM’s integrated protection specialists or other protection partners. 

IOM will scale up coaching and capacity building to PULSE, particularly in regards to shelter management, in line with its localization strategy whilst providing specialized services, capacity development and systems strengthening in GBV and Counter Trafficking (58% by PULSE, 42% by IOM). IOM and PULSE will also scale up their work with their community groups, advocates and volunteers going into 2020 to ensure sustainability and a community-based approach. 

IOM and PULSE will focus on GBV mainstreaming across sectors and within emergency preparedness and response efforts. IOM GBV Caseworkers will continue to support as part of interagency response structures and Mobile Medical Teams. IOM is as an active contributor to the GBV Sub-Sector and its related task teams. 

IOM is an active member of the GBV subsector and related task teams, including: GBV Case Management, GBV IMS, Male Engagement, Women’s Leadership and GIHA. IOM also co-chairs the Counter Trafficking Technical Working Group and the PSEA Network. IOM senior GBV staff also support interagency training on PSEA and SEA case management as a pool of facilitators working to support the PSEA Network in Cox’s Bazar to ensure capacity building in quality survivor-centred direct assistance.

project_name: Strengthening Community-level Protection Outcomes for Refugees and Host Communities and Ensuring Access to Protection Services for the Most Vulnerable to Mitigate the Gravest Forms of Harm and Risk.
project_objective:
The Rohingya, who sought refuge in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh are in dire need of Protection and other life-saving humanitarian assistance. Among the 910,000 Rohingya in the camp settlements, women and children comprise approximately 78%, and 31% of the families have persons with specific needs. Most Rohingya in the camps continue to be in immense need of humanitarian services and face formidable challenges, although they have found a safe haven and demonstrate resilience. The lack of a refugee protection framework in Bangladesh leave the Rohingya vulnerable to harm, abuse and exploitation and expose them to serious protection risks. Their restricted mobility, coupled with limited access to civil documentation and formal livelihoods and education, render most of them dependent on humanitarian aid, stymie sustainable solutions, and weaken the protective environment. Violence, criminal activity, the threat of natural disasters caused by the monsoon and cyclone seasons, wide-spread poverty, and limited access to scarce resources impact Rohingya and host community populations.  
In response, the protection project that IOM proposes herewith for the 2020 JRP has interlinked activities under the Protection Sector’s strategic objectives 1, 2, 3, and 6.  The cross-cutting activities that IOM will conduct focus on community-based protection at the camp-level through direct interaction with beneficiaries, awareness raising and sensitization; case management for extremely vulnerable individuals and victims of human trafficking; protection monitoring activities; and protection mainstreaming through capacity building activities. IOM will use existing facilities in Camps 8E, 8W, 9, 18, 19, 20, 20Ext, 23, 24, and 25 for activities linked to Sector Objectives 1, 2, 3 and 6.  Many of the counter-trafficking activities that IOM will conduct in 18 camps and 10 host communities aim to achieve the Sector’s third objective, along with sustainable impact and improved social cohesion. 
Drawing on experiences from the IOM Protection programme that has expanded considerably since 2017, IOM has conceptualized and will implement the activities for 2020 according to age, gender, and diversity needs of the affected population in Cox’s Bazar. IOM’s approach to Inclusion will identify, understand and support the affected segments of Rohingya and host community populations through meaningful access, participation, and engagement in decisions and action that directly impact the well-being of the individual, family, and community. 
For disaster preparedness, IOM will work with Site Management, WASH and Shelter Sectors to identify and relocate with consent extremely vulnerable individuals before a disaster. For disaster response, IOM will verify the needs of EVIs, who are in collective centres after a disaster, and coordinate services. IOM will serve as the focal point for the Protection Emergency Response Units in 8 camps.
Most activities described in this proposal will be directly implemented by IOM Protection staff. The IOM counter-trafficking team is mobile and covers the entire district. Some activities will be conducted by IOM through a few implementing partners that contribute a specific expertise and complement but do not duplicate IOM’s Protection presence or work. IOM will continue to serve as the Protection focal point in 8 camps, be a proactive member in the PWG, the PW Task Team, the PSEA Network, and co-chair with UNHCR the Protection Sector’s Anti-Trafficking Working Group.      
IOM programming will benefit 99,082 Rohingya and host community men, women, boys, girls, older persons, persons with disabilities, and persons with diverse sexual orientation, gender identity, and expression in Cox’s Bazar in a way that does not harm, assists based on needs, and prioritizes respect for human rights, safety and dignity.""

project_name: Coordination: ISCG Secretariat, Ukhiya Coordination Hub, and ACAPS Analysis Hub
project_objective: Provision of core coordination functions to enable a coherent, effective response for Rohingya refugees and their host communities. The aim of the Analysis Hub is to support decision-making through research and analysis which contribute to a shared understanding of the Rohingya crisis. The Rohingya response is a data rich environment. The Analysis Hub will contribute to the provision of impartial, independent research and analysis to aid and support programmatic and operational decision making and contribute to a single and impartial analysis of needs.

project_name: Accountability and Engagement of Affected Populations in All Communities
project_objective:
IOM leads the CwC Sector, serves on the Strategic Advisory Group, and implements a comprehensive set of CwC activities across all IOM Site Management Camps directly and through partners. In coordination with IOM Site Management, dedicated outreach and community engagement teams routinely hold meetings with key stakeholders, runs audio-listening programs, conduct awareness raising sessions, holds consultations, and operate a CFM system from dedciated Feedback and Information Centres. These activities are all designed and implemented with active participation and inclusion of different Rohingya populations and have been redesigned to improve their impact and overall effectiveness. IOM’s community engagement volunteers routinely conduct outreach sessions and community meetings with different community leaders and stakeholders on a range of health, DRR, WASH, Site Management and protection related needs. Women, girls, boys and disabled populations’ information and particular needs are met through community outreach teams, who ensure their feedback is entered in the system, and are targeted with specific and gender, age, and disability appropriate information sessions. Regular consultations about different needs and issues within the Rohingya population are conducted and disseminated on a regular basis in accordance with AAP best practices to ensure affected populations voices are included at all stages of relief delivery. IOM also ensures commitment to the Accountability commitments of the Grand Bargain through a harmonized CFM system that provides routine analysis and overview of community feedback to different actors and sectors within the response. In 2020, IOM will bring on-board other Site Management partners into a harmonized CFM system and work to support the CwC Sector in developing standardized referral pathways and data fields for community feedback within each sector in order to improve overall accountability and operational effectiveness of responding to community feedback. 
This work will coincide and support facility monitoring and consolidation of services according to the Macro Site Development plan; IOM will work closely to support and coordinate CwC services and activities across the IOM AoR. IOM’s JRP plan was prepared in close coordination with the Government of Bangladesh and the RRRC. Regular meetings and consultation are held with all relevant Government stakeholders on a routine basis. Activities in the field are conducted in close coordination will all relevant camp level actors and IOM’s CwC program is conducted through and alongside IOM’s Site Management coordination and Site operations programming. IOM operates these activities in a harmonized approach in coordination with other IOM programming units covering a range of sectors and key issues, including health, disaster preparedness, site management, and WASH. In the event of reduced JRP funding, IOM will continue to implement standard CwC activities and funding but will reduce scope of its activities and number of field staff and volunteers implementing activities.

project_name: Improvement of WASH services for the most vulnerable populations in Ukhia and Teknaf Upazila of Cox’s Bazar District, Bangladesh
project_objective:
The project will implement activities as per the following description to achieve the objective of people in need having access to water and sanitation. Here below the three subsectors of intervention are presented:                                                                                                                      Water Supply: In accordance with the WASH Sector’s Water Plan, the IOM WASH Unit has identified key locations to prioritize the construction of new solar-powered piped water networks (Camp 20, 20 Ext, and 23), in order to provide safe, chlorinated water to the populations living there. Operation and maintenance of existing tubewells will continue, and new Tube Wells (TWs) will be drilled where needed to meet gaps. Operation, maintenance and monitoring of existing large-scale water networks (Camp 12/19 and Camp 24), as well as existing tube wells, will continue to ensure critical water supplies, and emergency stocks will be procured to prepare for cyclones or other natural disasters. To address potential long-term impacts, technical studies will be conducted on groundwater resources for both refugee and host communities, as well as on water supplies to address chronic shortages in the Teknaf camps, with a view to finding durable solutions.

Sanitation: Construction of durable latrines that minimize desludging and health risks will be undertaken in both refugee and host communities. These include provisions for gender-inclusivity, as well as improved access and usability for Persons with Disabilities (PwD). This approach will also be followed to upgrade existing latrines. New Decentralized Wastewater Treatment Systems (DEWATS) will be constructed to address coverage gaps, and operation of existing systems will continue. Older wastewater treatment systems and communal latrines will be upgraded to improve treatment and disposal, and to minimize exposure risks for community members and sanitation workers. Additional bathing facilities will be constructed, and drainage of existing facilities will be improved. The approach to solid waste management will be strengthened by focusing on reduction and recycling of waste produced – promoting household waste separation, large-scale composting, and recycling of plastics.

Hygiene Promotion and Epidemic Control: Critical supplies of hygiene items (soap, water containers, Menstrual Hygiene Management (MHM) materials, etc.) will be provided, together with community education and mobilization activities targeting all age and gender groups at the household and community level. Mass cleanup campaigns and camp-wide celebrations for Global WASH days will be conducted to improve engagement and ownership of camp hygiene conditions. Strong monitoring and community feedback mechanisms will be implemented to ensure immediate identification and response for any WASH-related health risks, and emergency response stocks will be maintained in case of any Acute Watery Diarrhea (AWD) or other outbreaks.

project_name: Strengthening resilience of the displaced Rohingya Refugees and affected  populations  through collaborative  Learning, and informal production and market networks
project_objective:
IOM’s approach promotes self-reliance initiatives through integrated skills development & links to opportunities. Skills & in-kind assistance support enable adolescent youth (boys & girls), & adult Rohingya men & women to maximize their participation in emerging camp set up economic networks & adjoining host communities of informal markets to which they are connected to enhance their  well-being. 
Food & nutrition security of both refugee & host community remain is a key concern. Vulnerability is  shown by the Fill-the Nutrition-Gap Analysis (WFP oct 2019) which  indicates 1 of 2 children in immediate host communities are malnourished.  IOMs existing programmes support collaborative production initiatives through the provision of tools, fertilizers, improved vegetable seeds to groups of  Rohingya & host community households.  
A Social Cohesion Trends & Dynamics Baseline conducted by one of IOM’s partner, United Purpose, has attributed rising crime to joblessness among youth. Concerns over threats to safety of Rohingya in certain camps  have led to relocation of Rohingya households (United Purpose, June  2019). Similarly, IOM End Line Assessment (October 2019 shows 40% of respondents attribute tensions to gaps in access to livelihoods & life-saving support.  
While facilitating continued emergency & life-saving support to the Rohingya, IOM invests in building human  capacities of refugees to cope & maximize market environments within camps set ups & immediate co-existing host communities. In host communities, the adoption of market-oriented livelihoods strategies is a dimension IOM seeks to promote sustainable incomes, household capital & market linkages. This will be implemented in the following ways;                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  -Promoting the development of vocational/technical skills for Rohingya in camps to tap into the opportunities for social & economic well-being while fostering peaceful coexistence for Rohignya and Host Communities immediately next to camps. 
-Promoting collaborative production initiatives through,
 a) Supply of tools, basic production equipment, improved seeds & functional literacy & market skills development of 3700 affected host community households coexisting with Rohingya in camps & in adjoining locality of camps. This will aim to maintain production from homestead farms, fish ponds, & vegetable crops; as well as livestock initiatives.
 b) training & distribution of assets & tools to 5,000 Rohingya (mainly 3,000 women & 2000 male)  to participate in production of vegetables & basic agriculture produce  on available land alongside their host counterpart, as well as small scale assets transfer for livestock micro initiatives;
-Promotion of Peaceful coexistence initiatives:
This will involve the support to 25 networks of 250 women Social Entrepreneurs in camps & in adjoining host communities for promoting sustainable practices. The objective is to enhance Women’s self-help & promote their central role in conservation as primary users of land & natural resources.  This initiative will recover eroded lands through adapted tree plantation on 1000 hectares of land. Both Rohingya & host community women compete in gathering of fuel wood, cultivate most of the vegetable products on available lands in & around the camps & therefore are key agents of knowledge sharing towards positive community attitudinal change. This activity builds on lessons of IOM’s Women Income Generation Support Project (WINGS) which has shown that women empowered by exposure to market-oriented trainings often use their skills & creativity to build their own models of economic & social empowerment while contributing to social harmony (IOM WINGS Oct 2019).

project_name: Protecting Health of Refugees and Local Communities in Cox’s Bazar- an Emergency Health Care  Services and Health Systems Strengthening Project
project_objective:
In addition to continued need to provide lifesaving assistance to the refugees (Women, boys, girls, men and alternative gender identity), IOM seeks to expand its scope of work to strengthen the health systems to the local communities. By October 2019, IOM and its partners is supporting: 04 Community Clinics, 08 PHC, 10 Health Post and 02 Upazilla Health Complex serving about 350,000 refugees-and will continue to do so in 2020. IOM will ensure adequate staffing, provision of essential medical supplies, and 24/7 emergency referral systems through 12 vehicle ambulances. 
On coordination, IOM seeks to maintain support to the health sector coordination at camp level by continuing the deployment of 5 Camp Health Focal Persons
Overall, IOM supports 350 CHWs accounting for about 24% of the coverage. IOM will support local NGOS to implementing the Community Health interventions and ensure. Besides, IOM will also support local NGOs (under selection) to scale up access to Palliative Care services. In Camp 10, one HP is to be refurbished from bamboo infrastructure to semi-permanent sandwich pannels.

IOM requires additional funding to maintain delivery of lifesaving quality services through the networks of health facilities and CHW without which, over 25% of the population would be left without access to essential comprehensive primary health care services.

project_name: Responding to the Health Needs of the Host and Rohingya Communities through the Production of Hygiene Materials
project_objective: In addition to the health impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic in Bangladesh, there are long-term effects on socioeconomic factors as a result of the health crisis. While needed to save lives, restrictions on movement and trade have crushing effects on local and national economies. Incomes of vulnerable people are disrupted; businesses shrink or close; supply chains are impeded, and hundreds of millions of people are losing their jobs in the informal and formal sector, resulting in loss of access to the cash or credit needed to buy life essentials. Highly vulnerable individuals who already live in poverty and rely on daily or wage labor are struggling to buy food, maintain access to safe housing, purchase health and hygiene supplies, or meet other basic needs as they lose crucial income. The project will focus on the health response through utilizing local capacity in the production of hygiene materials such as cloth-masks, hand sanitizer and PPE. In line with the Food Security Sector (FSS) Strategic Response, IOM will ensure host communities, front line health responders, local government authorities and government law enforcement are equipped with preventive hygiene materials to mitigate the spread of the COVID-19 pandemic.

project_name: Communicating COVID-19: Community-led Approach to COVID-19 Engagement
project_objective: IOM will respond to the COVID-19 crisis in both the Rohingya camps and the host communities within Cox's Bazar District through a community-led engagement approach that places affected populations at the forefront of the response. Firstly, IOM will conduct large scale consultations across the affected populations to ensure different perspectives and needs of men, women, boys and girls are reflected within all sectors of the response. IOM will also launch an interactive-voice-response (IVR) hotline to disseminate information and collect feedback from the affected populations. IOM will support this and other awareness raising work with content that is developed through engagement and participation from the affected population. Finally, IOM will support local community-led initiatives to respond to the COVID-19 crisis at all stages of the response.

project_name: Shelter and NFI support for vulnerable IDPs, returnees and host communities in Tripoli, Benghazi, Ajdabiya and Derna
project_objective: NRC will provide shelter and Non-Food Items (NFIs) support to vulnerable IDPs, returnees and host communities through the following modalities: in Tripoli, NRC will distribute NFIs and rehabilitate communal shelters which are hosting IDPs, while in Benghazi, Ajdabiya, Derna, NRC will rehabilitate communal and household-level shelters in IDP camps as well carry out shelter rehabilitation in urban environments (Benghazi/Derna) through the provision of upgrades/repair of sub-standard buildings.

project_name: Provides a joint platform to facilitate the work of INGOs operating in Libya.
project_objective:
The INGO Forum is an independent network of 21 INGOs implementing humanitarian programs / in the process of setting-up operations to respond to the needs of vulnerable population living in Libya.

It provides a joint platform to facilitate the work of INGOs and help members to efficiently and effectively address key issues of common interest.

The Libya INGO Forum exists primarily to serve the needs of its members and to act in their interest for the betterment of serving beneficiaries. The Forum objectives include the following:

Information Sharing: To ensure that there is effective and transparent sharing of information relevant to both Forum members and external stakeholders.

Coordination: To coordinate INGO exchange, learning and resource-sharing through meetings, Working Groups and through relationships with external stakeholders.

Policy/Advocacy: To represent the interests of the members in external meetings, policy discussions, advocacy meetings and documents, as well as to lobby on issues of common interest.

Representation: To consistently represent the interest of members with external stakeholders.

project_name: Safe and inclusive learning environments for Syrian children
project_objective:
The project aims to provide improved quality and protective learning environment for Syrian boys and girls in 10 schools in Idleb and Aleppo Governorate. These schools are located in the areas where there is high proportion of out of school children. As per the non-structured interviews with school management, 30% of primary school age children (5-17 years) are out of school. Non-availability of education supplies (school bags, stationary, uniform), child labor, increase trend of early marriages and inappropriate learning facilities are common factors contributing to high percentage of out of school children. A complete Back to School campaign will be run in the targeted communities. Community volunteers (teachers) will be recruited and will receive monthly stipend to facilitate this campaign. This campaign will sensitize the parents and caregivers about the importance of education and will bring back 2000 children into targeted formal schools. All the children in the targeted schools will be provided with student kit. The sensitization campaign will continue throughout the project period to mitigate the risks of school drop outs. The targeted schools will be provided with student kit and education supplies (text books) and furniture as per the need. 120 teachers and school management staff will be identiﬁed for monthly stipend. These teachers will also include psycho social trainers. The teachers and administrative staff will also be trained on child protection and psychosocial support. The teaching staff will conduct regular classes in the targeted schools and individual/group psychosocial sessions and recreational activities will be conducted. In additional minor school repair and rehabilitation will be conducted specially to improve WASH facilities in schools. Provision of prefabricated classrooms to ensure that education space is suitable for learning. The provision of conducive learning environment, improved enrolment rates, psychosocial support, education supplies, student kit, school rehabilitation and regular classes are expected to contribute positively in the overall child development as well as attendance and school performance. The project is aligned with the objectives and priorities as set by Humanitarian Response plan. This project will also contribute to the No lost generation initiative by enrolling the out of school children and providing them with protective learning environment
A Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability and Learning (MEAL) Framework will be developed to enable continual improvement during implementation and decision making with an emphasis on accountability systems for information sharing and handling feedback/complaints. An indicator tracking tool will be developed, along with a detailed plan for data collection, entry, analysis and reporting on the indicators. Regular monitoring of a core set of activities will be carried out to ensure the quality of implementation, thereby contributing to the achievement of the overall impact of the project. Tools/checklists will be developed with a specific section to enable follow up on key issues arising from the activity monitoring process. 
Islamic Relief has an accountability system that will focus on information sharing, participation, and complaint and feedback mechanisms. A system will be in place to share information and gather/respond to feedback from beneficiaries to effectively improve the quality of the action's design and implementation, and strengthen the relationship and acceptance by stakeholders.
A learning and knowledge management system will be established to ensure the generation, capture, dissemination, and application of the action's learning. Ongoing monitoring findings, best practices, and lesson learned will be captured to generate knowledge. A database will be in place to capture these for further dissemination among project stakeholders.

project_name: Integrated health, WASH, nutrition, FSL and protection support to IDPs, returnees and host communities
project_objective:
The IRC plans to deliver an integrated emergency health program of primary healthcare, nutrition and WASH activities, with an expanded essential package that ensures delivery of sexual, reproductive, maternal and newborn health, child health including immunization, non-communicable diseases, mental health and psychosocial support, and communicable disease control, including where relevant outbreak surveillance and response. For nutrition, the IRC will deliver a complete CMAM package. IRC will set up and/or strengthen existing case management services for moderate and severe acute malnutrition for children and pregnant and lactating women (PLW). The IRC will ensure the existence of active Stabilization Centers, OTPs, TSFPs, and community activities to raise awareness, and screen and refer malnourished children and PLW. The IRC’s WASH program will provide lifesaving WASH services, minimizing hazards related to seasonal flooding, and responding to water-borne and vector-borne disease outbreaks. WASH activities will be delivered at the health facility and community level comprising of safe water supply, sanitation, waste management, hygiene promotion, and vector control. 

FSL - The IRC will provide emergency food and agricultural assistance as well as longer term agricultural and non-agricultural livelihoods support. The IRC will consider modalities of cash, vouchers, in-kind and training packages (for agricultural support). The IRC will layer immediate food assistance needs with agricultural support focusing on those in IPC classifications 3 and 4. In smaller villages the IRC will assess 100% of the population in need and consider a blanket distribution assistance approach to prevent creating tensions within the community; while in urban areas the IRC will work with local relief committees / local organizations to support in the identification of vulnerable households. 

Child Protection - The IRC will work on community-based child protection systems, expanding access to and quality of specialized services, including case management services, with focus placed on UASC and CAAFAG. IRC will establish Safe Healing and Learning Spaces (SHLS) and Supporting Adolescent and their Families in Emergencies (SAFE) program spaces for adolescents. SHLS is a secure, caring place where children and adolescents can learn and be protected, for stronger social and emotional skills and reductions in violence in the home.  Both programs use a Parenting Skills Intervention which improves parents’ stress management.  IRC will also train local actors on child protection minimum standards.

Protection Rule of Law - IRC will establish community-based protection (CBP) programs which integrate participation, empowerment and resilience. The project will seek local capacities, perceptions of problems and ideas about solutions, and work with community actors to support, activate and expand the capacities for self-protection. The IRC will build the capacity in protection core concepts and safe identification and referrals, protection risk analysis, non-violent conflict resolution, and participatory action planning. The IRC will establish community structures and training of focal points. 

GBV Prevention and Response - The IRC will deliver services to meet women and girls’ needs in response to violence working with health and social service providers, and providing direct case management. The IRC will train GBV caseworkers in guiding principles and survivor-centered approaches, and will establish private spaces to receive survivors. The IRC will ensure safe, confidential storage of all client information. IRC will also do service mapping and develop referral pathways as well as psychosocial services and prevention activities. The IRC will work with women’s groups for provision of basic psychosocial services. The IRC will establish safe spaces for women and girls to exchange information and get support. 
All projects will work toward a RRR approach over time.

project_name: Improve access to basic WASH services in BN, SK, SD and Khartoum
project_objective:
In South Kordofan, Blue and White Nile, South Darfur and Khartoum states, GAH conducted needs assessment in November 2019 to review the humanitarian situation. The assessment covered the localities of Provision of WASH services to the vulnerable communities in El Damazine in Blue Nile, Dimso in South Darfur, Abujubeha in South Kordofan, Bantiue and Om Bada in Khartoum States in Sudan. The rainy season has affected all Sudan states significantly this year, heavy rainfall during the month of August that occurred in different areas resulted in massive flooding, there by affecting most parts of the various states throughout the Country. According to the findings of the assessment reflected that there humanitarian needs in these areas, 50% of those people who are without access to basic water services are considered in severe need, 40 to 60 percent of assessed boreholes and 70% of the hand pumps are destroyed, people are traveling long distance to collect water (30 minutes to 8 hours), 39% of the Sudanese population have access to limited sanitation services as per the revised S3MII. 23% of those people who are without access to limited sanitation are assumed to be in severe needs, 80% of the assessed population are not practicing proper hand washing practices during critical times, In addition, only 4% to 20% of the assessed households have latrines and the remaining percentage are practicing open defecation including the IDPs, host communities and SSR. They suffer from lack of enough safe drinking water and basic sanitation facilities and inappropriate hygiene practices. According to the State Ministry of Health (SMoH), the international NGO (INGO) and the World Health Organization (WHO) report, lack to Safe drinking water, poor sanitation and inadequate personal hygiene practices the major causes to Acute Water Diarrhea (AWD) and Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) to children in the targeted Areas.
This confirmed that water quality is a public health issue among the targeted communities. The planned intervention is needed to contribute to reduce morbidity and mortality associated with WASH related diseases among IDPs, host communities and vulnerable groups, especially children under 5 years and pregnant/lactating mothers and elderly. Additionally GAH conducted assessments in 2019 to rural targeted areas to identify the most critical WASH needs and there is urgent need of WASH services as well as other needs like health and immediate food and non-food items assistance. In 2019, based on focus group discussion GAH collect information in targeted areas and localities, The main finding of these assessment are summarized as follows, The main assessment findings in WASH sector highlight needs for (i) safe drinking water by repairing the existing Hand pumps, Haffirs and upgrading some to mini-water yards, (ii) support sanitation/hygiene including school sanitation/hygiene, and (iii) explore options for new water supply sources. The socio-economic situation in the targeted areas had been broadly affected by the conflict in South Sudan and Civil wars in Darfur as the entire displaced populations sought refuge in villages within the targeted areas putting additional pressure on existing available WASH facilities, hence posing a threat of possible conflict outbreak among different communities, people currently depend on unprotected open water sources for drinking water and these sources are not protected, and water declines significantly during the dry season.

project_objective:

project_name: Addressing Critical Winterization Needs of the Most Vulnerable Households in Eastern Ukraine
project_objective:
With the conflict in eastern Ukraine entering its sixth year, an estimated 3.5 million people are in need of humanitarian aid. Cyclical vulnerability to winter depletes household resources and negatively impacts agricultural activities, wherein households are often unable to adequately access necessary heating materials. From previous cash projects, ACTED has recorded compounding vulnerabilities: food consumption decreases during winter as negative coping strategies are used more often due to the diversion of household funds to cover costs of heating. With few economic opportunities available to vulnerable households with people with disabilities, elderly and/or homebound members, financial means are especially limited leading up to and during winter months, resulting in systemic inability to adequately prepare for the harsh winter. Increasing heating costs have not reflected the current income gap and inability to meet minimum subsistence requirements for most of the targeted beneficiaries, wherein the average income is significantly low at UAH1305 and falls to UAH684 for HHs with unemployed pre-pensioners (representing 40% and 21% respectively, of minimum actual subsistence level (2018 average: UAH3263 [Ministry of Social Policy]). Additional vulnerabilities include protection-related risks, which increase closest to the LoC, where notably 89% of households within 5km of the LoC reported shelling as being a main concern and 28% of HHs perceived the presence of mines and unexploded ordinances (UXOs) in their communities, impacting daily life and shelter needs.
As per the Shelter Cluster's 2019-20 Winterization Guidance, heating remains a top priority for assistance to areas within 5km of the LoC. The project accordingly aims to meet the basic winterization needs of vulnerable households in Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts in government-controlled areas (GCA) of eastern Ukraine, primarily households with people with disabilities and elderly people. Through direct cash or in-kind assistance, valued at 8,000 UAH/household (covering 50% of seasonal needs as per Shelter Cluster Winterization Guidelines), beneficiaries in isolated settlements along the Line of Contact (LoC) will receive or be able to purchase necessary heating fuel for essential survival during the harsh winter months. The proposed intervention leverages ACTED's experience providing cash assistance (cash for food security, cash for winterization, multi-purpose cash) in all raions/cities bordering the LoC since 2018 and ACTED's expertise as an active cash programming partner (incl. as co-lead of Ukraine's Cash Working Group). For in-kind donations, ACTED will leverage its global expertise and the experience of its partners in Ukraine – including under the ECHO-funded ACCESS Consortium. The intervention will ensure that settlements chosen for cash distribution include those with functional market access to fuel (or those connected to gas heating lines) and stable prices in order for assistance received to be most impactful – where those conditions are not met, in-kind assistance will be provided.

project_name: Providing lifesaving multi-purpose cash assistance to the most vulnerable conflict-affected populations close the Line of Contact
project_objective:
The protracted conflict in Eastern Ukraine is well into its sixth year, and multiple attempts at ceasefires having yielded little respite overall. In 2019 so far, conflict intensity does seem to be on a downwards trend, with a decrease in the number of civilian casualties as compared to earlier years. However, the great majority of conflict-related incidents – 94% (INSO data) – continues to take place within 5km on either side of the Line of Contact (LoC), meaning that populations in these areas continue to be disproportionately affected, on a quasi-daily basis, by the conflict and associated protection risks. REACH has also illustrated how the LoC, in essence a de-facto border, has disconnected GCA urban peripheries from their NGCA urban centres now located in NGCA, disrupting pre-conflict networks and hindering access to markets and services, especially health care and employment. Analyses of humanitarian trends in 2018 and 2019 have confirmed that needs in GCA are correspondingly higher in areas closest to the LoC, especially within 5km. Protection risks related to shelling and mines, food insecurity, damage to property and barriers to accessing basic services (incl. healthcare) are more pronounced for populations living within 5km of the LoC as opposed to those living within 5-20km, and those living beyond 20km (REACH 2018, 2019). Overall, while core humanitarian indicators assessed in 2019 show a slight amelioration as compared to 2018, this is not evenly distributed: populations within 5km of the LoC, a substantial proportion of whom have overlapping vulnerabilities (e.g. elderly with a chronic illness, households with multiple children and members with a disability, etc.), continue to have severe humanitarian needs. 
Notably, Ukraine is also experiencing overall inflation, which is reflected in the steady increase in the actual minimum subsistence level: this translates into constantly increasing food prices – 7.8% increase in 2019, projected increase of 6.9% in 2019 (National Bank of Ukraine). Incomes of vulnerable populations, especially those living in the 5km area – noting disproportionate representation of pensioners and pre-pensioners – struggle to follow. The gap between incomes and prices is especially pronounced in winter, with food and fuel costs rising sharply during this season, thus decreasing even further ability to meet basic needs and increasing the use of negative coping strategies.
In response to this situation, ACTED will implement this project in continuation of 2+ years of Multi-Purpose Cash (MPC) distribution, to provide the most vulnerable conflict-affected individuals residing close to the LoC in Donetsk and Luhansk (GCA) with the means to cover their critical needs and protection requirements through MPC grants. Focus will be on the most vulnerable groups, who do not have sufficient income to cover these needs, including women headed households, households of elderly, and households headed by pre-pensioners who are not eligible for pensions. Other vulnerable categories identified through the vulnerability assessment may also be targeted, in line with ACTED’s selection methodology which is based on a cumulative vulnerability approach approved by the CWG and adapted by ACTED to the Ukrainian context.

project_name: Food Assistance for Households affected by the Beirut Explosion
project_objective: In line with the Lebanon Flash Appeal food security sector objective to enhance food security through immediate life-saving food and nutrition security assistance, this project will provide in-kind food assistance for 500 households directly affected by the Beirut explosion in  Nabaa area of Bourj Hammoud, Mount Lebanon. In-kind food assistance will distributed on a monthly basis for 3 months. The amount provided will cover 50% of the full daily requirement of 2,100 kcal/person/day. ). This cluster-recommended ration size in emergency situations has been adjusted from 73% to 50% to as assessed households were found to still have access to enough resources to supplement the food parcel with fresh fruits, vegetables, bread and dairy products – all of which are generally considered part of the households daily diet –  which are not possible to include in the in-kind parcel. In order to ensure that households will be able to prepare the food assistance provided by distributing kitchen non-food items based on household needs assessments. In order to account for differences in household size two different food packages will be available, one for families up to 3 members (30%) and one for households with four or more members (70%). The project will target vulnerable households from all nationalities impacted by the explosion including Syrian refugee, Lebanese and other refugee and migrant worker households. Selection criteria will prioritize female-led households, elderly and and those with special needs (chronically ill, persons with disability, elderly headed households) with delivery mechanisms to be adapted as appropriate to ensure accessibility.  This project will scale up an existing 12-month food assistance project for 1,000 households in blast affected neighbourhoods including Nabaa. The majority of personnel and general operating costs for this project will be covered by the funding already secured for that project.

project_name: Couverture des besoins essentiels, la relance des moyens d'existence et la protection des populations affectées par la crise alimentaire et nutritionnelle dans le Lac et le Bahr El Gazal :  HIP2020

project_objective:

The project also aims at addressing vulnerability of women and girls by distribution of Dignity Kits as well as information materials on GBV risk mitigation and available services as well as on COVID-19 specific mitigation measures. Building on the findings of study on Integrating   for cash and voucher assistance (CVA) into GBV program conducted by UNFPA Lebanon (August 2020), UNFPA with its partners will ensure the provision of CVA targeting women and girls at high risk of GBV or GBV survivors with an aim to reduce household tensions by contributing to household needs, to pay for safe alternative accommodation and for GBV survivors to meet urgent needs. Outreach activities will be conducted to facilitate access to the GBV services for women and girls as well as to increase awareness of men and boys on GBV risks and mitigation to have them as allies based on ""do no harm"" approach. UNFPA will support its partners to establish and scale up existing hotlines for provision of remote specialized services. Support to existing Women and Girls Safe Spaces (WGSS) managed by UNFPA partners will be further strengthened and linkages with sexual and reproductive services will be reinforced. UNFPA and its partners will continue to conduct GBV safety audits to ensure that programmes are accountable to the needs of people in a way that promotes their safe and dignified participation and engagement in decisions affecting them. UNFPA will enhance partner capacity on Prevention from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA). Based on the PSEA protocol developed for Lebanon, feedback and complaints mechanisms are in place and UNFPA will ensure response to unethical behavior by humanitarian workers as per agreed code of conduct. UNFPA will ensure that staff and partners are aware of PSEA standards and will keep raising awareness on SEA risks.  The social workers and mobile team members at the WGSS will be deployed only after going through training and having relevant/required skills on survivor-centered approach for GBV case management and emergency psychosocial support. Mobile teams are also oriented on Psychological First Aid (PFA), community outreach, and both have critical tenets of ‘do no harm’ approach. All partners and staff working on the projects, including frontline workers, will be further capacitated through supervision and mentoring on survivor-centered approach; basic protection skills, whose main tenet is ensuring a ""do no harm"" principle.

project_name: Improving food security and livelihoods of vulnerable households affected by conﬂict and natural disaster in Blue Nile, North Darfur and Kassala states
project_objective: The project interventions are intended to lead to increased food security & strengthen community resilience to climate shocks &conflict through enabling sustainable increases in agricultural and livestock productivity & adopting alternative livelihoods which will decrease competition over natural resource. The ultimate beneﬁciaries of the project are mainly the farmers and pastoralist, IDPs, returnees & poor residents in Blue Nile, North Darfur and Kassala states (around 580790 people). Agricultural tools, drought resistant seeds & seedlings, vegetables and horticulture will be provided to increase household food production. Promotion of climate smart & resilient crops & livestock production systems, protection of livestock based livelihoods in pastoral & agro pastoral community through provision of emergency livestock assistance, livestock watering, restocking with goat & poultry; awareness raising on the important of healthy diet in addition to women training on food processing for malnutrition, these inputs will build the capacity of the targeted communities to achieve their own food security & improve their livelihoods by increasing their production & income to better able them to withstand future shocks, droughts & other natural disasters. Solar powered women farms will enable produce quality diversified food items for household consumption and income & will reduce work load compared to currently practiced irrigation methods. Establish women saving & loan groups & support it with clean fuel (LPG cylinders & stoves) to establish revolving funds thus reducing wood collection work load & negative health impacts of indoor pollution. Process of women farms will be supported by nurseries, business management & agro processing trainings, linkage to markets & solar lights for safe gathering and mobile charging. The project will support assets protection and increase the ability of the target communities to decrease post-harvest losses & increase their resilience to shocks through provision of cash for work & cash for assets. The project will facilitate regeneration of ecosystem through a range of activities that aims to increase access to water, pasture and forestry which in the past directly contributed to conﬂict between farmers and pastoralists. Training will be provided on the management of these resources and environmental conservation techniques. The project will support the formation & reinforcement of farmers’ groups & community based associations strengthen their institutional capacity and consolidate their links to government service providers & other actors; to facilitate delivery of other project activities. For example, the training & technical support will be provided through these groups. The Project will apply participatory approaches for prioritizing & planning community needs to ensure that community planning & service delivery is tailored to local needs. More over the project will arrange to raise community awareness on themes other than production of the value chain products, including gender, protection & environment. As with elsewhere in the three targeted states men & women have different and unequal access to agriculture and livestock production inputs and technology (women represent about 49% of the total population yet are responsible for more than 65% of agriculture and livestock livelihood activities); therefore the project will ensure that everyone in the affected community women, girls, boys and men have a voice in the development & implementation of the project & have access to opportunities that the project gives. Restocking with livelihoods kits, vegetable growing & marketing will enable women and youth to better engage in income generating activities and production process. The project will be run in environment friendly pattern, saving natural resources & increase target population awareness about environment issues through discussion & orientation sessions.

project_name: Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene Promotion Amongst IDPs, Returnees and Host Communities in Rural Areas of Kassala, Blue Nile and North Darfur states
project_objective:
The planned community based WASH interventions will help to create sustainable access to sufficient quantities of safe drinking water at institutions and community levels, and assist to promote best sanitation practices and hygiene behavior. This will be coordinated with line ministries at state and federal levels. This will also include implementation of CLTS, water quality and quantity in participatory fashion in coordination with targeted communities. In addition capacity building of targeted communities in sanitation and water infrastructure management To ensure sustainability and continuity of services.
Nutrition sensitive WASH interventions will be ensured through prioritizing areas with high malnutrition rates and providing sufficient quantities of clean water for households’ consumption as well as improving hygiene at community level in order to reduce the associated health hazards and avoid further deterioration in nutritional status especially among U5 Children and PLW.
The project will rehabilitate, upgrade and establish water infrastructure (water yards, miniwater yards and hand pumps) to improve people’ access to safe drinking water in the three targeted states. Locations of water points will consider women accessibility (selected in consultation with women). To improve the efficiency and reduce the negative environmental impact; the project will establish/ replace/upgrade diesel operated water yards by solar pumps.
Associated women and men WASH committees will be established and trained to manage and maintain rehabilitated/established water sources (resourced from user fees) in order to enhance the sustainability. Women consultation in site selection and participation in water management committees will be a condition to ensure women interests are reflected. Water monitoring systems those include water testing and treatment will be established for the different water points under the WASH committees’ management to ensure water safety. Water harvesting infrastructure will also be introduced to improve water supply systems (e.g. Simple Check dams). Hygiene campaigns will be organized to raise awareness about sanitation and hygiene at community and institution levels (e.g. school hygiene promotion clubs and teachers training on CHAST). WASH package will also include public and schools latrines and hand-washing facilities. These basic services are vital for keeping people healthy and productive.
Availability and accessibility of safe drinking water will reduce work load and risks of violence on women and girls. Number of gender-sensitive communal latrines will be constructed in schools, health facilities and markets; the multi-cubical latrines will be provided with hand washing facilities and solar lanterns for protection and safety.
Protection measures will be ensured through these solar lighted and separate latrines for women and girls.

Improve food security and resilience to climate change for vulnerable communities in Aroma, North Delta, Telkok and Hamashkoraib localities of Kassala State
project_objective:
Kassala is one of the most vulnerable states in Sudan to extreme weather phenomena, droughts and floods in particular. Long periods of drought cause loss of crop and livestock, reduce the amount of groundwater, wear down forests and increase the risk of wild fires.
The consequences on the livelihood of the local population are disastrous and add to the already precarious living conditions.
Kassala region is one of the poorest and most marginalized in the country despite the good potential for agriculture and livestock and is location nearby important commercial hubs.
Kassala bases its economy on agriculture and pastoralism.
The recurrent and prolonged periods of drought, accompanied by sporadic torrential rains that cause flooding and destruction of the vegetation cover, increasingly deteriorate the subsoil, reducing its capacity to absorb water.
In addition, the quality of the soil has been ruined by the mesquite, a plant introduced in the '80s for its fertilizing properties.
The local diet is very poor (consisting mainly of sorghum and vegetables) and the parcels of land are too small to meet the needs of families. Communities therefore depend on the purchase of food at the market, where prices are extremely volatile and rise dramatically as a result of droughts or floods (which cause the loss of crops and livestock with a consequent reduction in the supply of products on the market). This is aggravated further by the devaluation of the local currency.

project_name: Basic Needs Support Programme Through Provision of NFIs and Cash Transfers
project_objective:
The widespread poverty and on-going hostilities combined with high commodity prices and destruction of housing stock have left many families unable to provide for the basic needs of the children including adequate clothing, especially during the winter time and before the beginning of school year when the families endure even higher costs of living. This is particularly true for families who have been displaced several times and continue to live in dire conditions. The main objective of UNICEF’s Basic Need Support Programme is to support families to respond to the essential needs of their children. The programme has two components: (i) The in-kind assistance through the provision of children clothing kits, and (ii) Cash assistance during winter time and prior to the school year. 
In 2020, UNICEF replaced its e-voucher programme with an unconditional cash transfer to support vulnerable families cope with the economic hardship and increased cost of living during the winter time and prior to the beginning of the school year. 
While the distribution of in-kind winter clothing packages targets children in the hard-to-reach, IDP camps and remote rural areas, the cash transfer programme targets vulnerable families in impoverished urban areas where competitive markets are reasonably accessible. The objective is to provide the families with the choice to decide on the essential items that they need in order to meet their children’s needs. Respecting people’s choice and dignity and enhancing the programme effectiveness are at the heart of this cash transfer programme.
This project aims to reach 590,000 children in the 0-14 age group with seasonal clothing kits and cash assistance, prioritizing children in hard-to-reach areas as well as impoverished urban areas in both government and non-government controlled territories.
