project_name: Multi-Pillar Mine Action Response for Libya
project_objective:
Recurrent fighting in Libya since 2011 has led to widespread contamination from explosive hazards, often in urban, densely populated areas. Even when active hostilities come to an end, the dangerous contamination continues to pose a considerable threat to civilians, impedes the return of displaced persons, and significantly impacts the ability of humanitarian and development actors to implement activities towards early recovery and stabilization. The outbreak of hostilities in 2019, which was concentrated on, but not limited to, the greater Tripoli area, has only exacerbated the threat from explosive hazards.

The Libyan national capacity to mitigate the threat through clearance activities, Risk Education (RE), and Victim Assistance (VA) interventions is insufficient in comparison to the growing threat to the population. With the existing managerial and coordination capacity in place, governmental and non-governmental actors have a solid base for programme growth, yet are lacking qualified personnel, equipment, and technical expertise to scale up to meet the demand. This project includes an Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) component, as well as three components that focus predominantly on the enhancement of technical skills and physical capacity of established local actors.

project_name: Emergency GBV Prevention, Mitigation & Response in Conflict-Affected & High Risk Areas in South Sudan 2020
project_objective:
In line with the Protection Cluster Objectives 1&2 (ensure provision of critical protection-related assistance and specialized services; and prevent and mitigate protection risks through enhanced preparedness), the project seeks to (1) reduce suffering of women, girls, boys, and men who have experienced various forms of GBV, (2) provide GBV prevention and risk mitigation measures that address priority needs of women, girls, boys, and men in need, (3) ensure access to livelihood support and economic resources to reduce vulnerability and mitigate GBV, and (4) strengthen risk analysis and vulnerability assessments – reflecting GBV Sub Cluster’s overall strategy and objectives. 

The project targets locations in Tier 1 (Twic and Aweil East), Tier 2 (Yambio, Nzara, Renk, Malakal), and Tier 3 (Juba, Fashoda, Tambura and Ulang). 

Briefly, project activities include: GBV case management (including specialized, individual, and group PSS), legal advice to survivors to facilitate access to justice, and safe referrals to services (including medical and health care providers for CMR services, safety, access to justice, livelihoods, and other support services). World Vision (WV) will continue to work through existing and establish new WGFS, serving as a self-referral point for services, but also as a space for prevention and risk mitigation activities, in line with South Sudan Guidelines for WGFS. Building on the work of the WGFS, and in line with best practice, WV will continue to move towards and integrate livelihood and income generating activities at WGFS, conducting financial and literacy training to complement the skills learned. Further prevention and risk mitigation activities will include, broad awareness raising, information on access to justice, service mapping, referral pathways, and work with community stakeholders and change agents (community leaders, faith actors, women and youth representatives, protection committee representatives, etc.) who will share messaging further. WV will integrate SASA! and EMAP models more broadly (having started this work in 2019) across interventions to facilitate knowledge, attitude, and behaviour change that is community-led and transformative. Dignity kits will be distributed to women and adolescent girls (prioritizing new displacements, female-headed households, disabled women and girls, pregnant and lactating women, survivors of GBV, among others, as reflective of community demographics and need) alongside messaging on: GBV prevention and response services available, menstrual health and hygiene management, sexual and reproductive health and rights, etc. Finally, interventions will be informed by safety audits and safety perception mapping, to be conducted on an ongoing basis (and particularly as the changing context dictates); such tools will not be exclusive to GBV interventions, but mainstreamed across WV’s interventions, particularly in Food Security and Livelihoods, Shelter / NFI, Health and Nutrition. 

The project reflects the unique needs of people in need, committing a gender marker that sees significant contributions to gender equality (including across age groups), prioritizing the needs of disabled populations (reflective of strong protection mainstreaming), and accountability to targeted communities (engaging stakeholders and conducting broad consultations to inform interventions and ongoing monitoring). The project design prioritizes a Do No Harm approach with an explicit intention to address protection issues experienced by women, girls, boys and men, specifically GBV, recognizing that respect for human rights and increasing gender equality are enablers of the South Sudan humanitarian response strategy. 

Finally, WV maintains zero tolerance for sexual exploitation and abuse, and has a robust Child and Adult Safeguarding Policy and approach to realize this at a national level across South Sudan and globally.

project_name: Improving WASH Situations in marginalized rural Area “C” of the West Bank
project_objective:
The project aims at securing sufficient and safe drinking water quantities for 345 households (2,377 individuals) of the targeted communities and families living in Area “C” of the West Bank for household purposes, including 1,134 women and girls.
The initiative responds to needs highlighted in the 2019 HNO and it is also fully in line with the oPt. Response plan, contributing to the WASH Cluster Objective 1: ensuring equitable, affordable and sustainable access to safe and sufficient WASH services for the most vulnerable communities. Access to safe WASH service is a main concern in the West Bank, specifically In Area C, where around 95,000 people receive less than 50 liters of water per capita per day, while over 83,000 people receive bad quality drinking water or are unconnected to a water network.
The initiative has been endorsed by PWA, it is in line with the PWA Strategic Plan (2017-22) and in compliance with the Water Master Plan for Area C. The action is in line with the Sustainable Development Goals, specifically contributing with “Goal 6: Ensure access to water and sanitation for all”.
Further, the initiative allows to reduce and more effectively address the core vulnerabilities of people in need, increasing water access for unconnected and underserved communities in area “C” of the West Bank, precisely in Ras al Tin and Wadi As Seeq in Ramallah Gov., AL Farisiya, Al Hadidiya, Hammamat al Maleh, Humsa, Khirbet Samra and Mak-hul in Tubas Gov. and in Turat al Mujdarin (al A'uja), in Jericho & Al-Aghwar Governorate.

project_name: Ensuring accessibility and quality services for health centers in Hebron H2 and raising hygiene and health awareness
project_objective: The proposed action is based on the 2018 – 2020 Humanitarian Response Plan strategic objective 2: “The basic needs of vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation are met through the provision of essential services, in accordance with the rights of protected persons under IHL”. It is also in line with the Health Cluster second strategic objective: “Ensure the availability, accessibility, acceptability and quality of essential lifesaving health services to vulnerable communities in Gaza and West Bank/EJ, including through health system strengthening, preparedness and community resilience building”; and WASH Cluster first strategic objective: “Ensure equitable, affordable and sustainable access to safe and suﬃcient WASH services with dignity for the unserved, underserved and most vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation in Gaza and the West Bank”. This proposition is based on ACTED assessments, extensive consultations with the Ministry of Health in Hebron and other key stakeholders including OCHA’s Head of Office in South and the partner HWC (Health Work Committees), a Palestinian non-profit organization with extensive experience in providing health services in H2, and follows the recommendations of both Health and WASH clusters. The project will aim to ensure the quality of WASH facilities within health centers in the old city of Hebron, H2 through WASH facilities rehabilitation and WASH and Protection training of staff. It will also aim to provide health services for people in marginalized communities of Hebron H2 and raise awareness on hygiene practices among women. The needs assessed in terms of lack of health services in H2 community have been already identified in 2019 and confirmed as still valid and unmet in 2020 by the Health Work Committees. New needs, which have been identified and assessed by ACTED between August and September 2019, have seriously emerged in terms of rehabilitation of WASH facilities inside the target health centers in H2 area in Hebron.

project_name: Strengthen WASH and Shelter preparedness and response capacity for the most vulnerable families in the North Gaza Governorate
project_objective:
The proposed action is in line with 2019 WASH Cluster Objectives 1 and 3 and Shelter Cluster Objective 2. The action works at community level and HH level according to a comprehensive WASH and Shelter strategy aiming to strengthen the communities capacities through repairing/upgrading of HHs’ main structures facilities (WASH and Shelter), provision of winterization assistance and NFIs to vulnerable HHs at risk of exposure or affected by natural or manmade hazards and improving of service provider’ capacities to mitigate and respond to flooding. At community level, the action will act through life-saving emergency WASH response interventions and preparedness to the most vulnerable communities (improvement of drainage water systems, domestic water accessibility and reducing hazards for private/public hygiene). This will also enhance service providers’ preparedness capacity and support communities’ resilience building against protracted threats and chronic vulnerability, especially in terms of Health and WASH. At HH level, the action will act through rehabilitation and/or upgrading of shelters, distribution of winterization kits, HH wastewater connection and hygiene promotion activities to reduce the exposure of targeted beneficiaries to both man-made and natural disasters, and risk of water borne diseases and health problems, by enabling them to live meeting adequate standards. 
Providing adequate shelter will contribute to reduce and mitigate the effects, vulnerabilities and risks associated with living in Access Restricted Area (ARA), especially for women, children, elderly and people with disabilities (PwDs). Shelter rehabilitation and upgrading will contribute to empower communities, in terms of coping capacities and protection response mechanisms, enhancing their capacities to respond to protracted crisis and reinforcing the local capacities as mitigation and preparedness to environmental and man-made hazards. 
The project will address the needs of most vulnerable HHs living in substandard overcrowded housing units, improving the accessibility to adequate and safe WASH and shelter conditions, protecting from the effects of extreme climate, and promoting safety, privacy, and hygiene best practice, creating a safer environment to cope with environmental threats.  
The proposed intervention will target 18 localities in the North Gaza, Gaza and Middle Area Governorates, specifically Beit Lahia, Beit Hanoun, Jabalia, Jabalia Camp, Umm Al Nasser, Al Mughraqa, Ezahra, Juhor ad Dik, An Nuseirat, An Nuseirat Camp, Az Zawayda, Al Bureij, Al Bureij Camp, Al Maghazi, Al Maghazi Camp, Deir al Balah, Deir al Balah Camp, Al Musaddar and Wadi as Salqa, directly benefiting 41,402 HHs, meaning a total of 264,970 individuals (70,120 girls, 73,242 boys, 54,741 women, 56,682 men, 10,186 elderly including 18808 PWDs) and 662,427 indirect people as catchment area. This action is in line with the PWA Storm water management policy and considered high and urgent priority by CMWU for ensuring access to essential services strengthening the population to cope with protracted threats, and works as an emergency time critical response, which is not currently addressed by CMWU and PWA intervention due to funding constraints. The project includes the following activities based on the protection egg model: Responsive (57.4% of the budget): connection of households to the municipal wastewater system; enhancing of operation of 11 water wells and 17 wastewater pumping stations; Remedial (34.2% of the budget): repairing/upgrading of 150 HHs main structures facilities (WASH and Shelter); hygiene and environmental health awareness campaign and distribution of 711 hygiene kits; Environmental building (8.4% of the budget): Provision of protective clothes and tools; Cleaning and inspection of 5 stormwater collection ponds, 24 wastewater pumping stations, gully traps and wastewater networks.

project_name: Integrated Protection Approach to address WASH and GBV Concerns of Vulnerable Groups in Deir Al Balah Governorate
project_objective:
The project aims at improving the access to safe and equitable WASH services and appropriate GBV response mechanisms during emergencies and shocks in accordance with the dignity of the underserved and most vulnerable communities of the Middle Area in the Gaza Strip. The project targets the most vulnerable communities of the Middle Area with particular focus on families whose children were identified to receive case management services (according to the national child protection referral system), families whose children affected by GMR related violence, and GBV survivors.
The objective of this action is consistent with the assigned objectives of the WASH Cluster 2020 HRP, objective 1: “Ensure equitable, affordable and sustainable access to safe and sufficient WASH services in accordance with the dignity of the unserved, underserved and most vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation in Gaza and the West Bank"". In addition, this action is consistent with the assigned objectives of the Protection Cluster 2020 HRP, objective 2:” Protection response mechanisms are in place to prevent and mitigate the effects of the occupation and conflict-related violence”. The project activities include two main components (1) WASH component, and (2) GBV component. Under the WASH component the following activities will be implemented: (1.1) Distribution of functional and safe Roof Storage Tanks (1000 liters’ capacity), (1.2) Distribution of functional and safe Potable water storage tanks (200 liters’ capacity), (1.3) Rehabilitate sanitation facilities for 300 households to meet SPHERE standards (age, gender, and culturally sensitive WASH facilities, and adequate to the needs of people with disabilities); (1.4) Hygiene promotion activities, (1.5) Hygiene kits distribution, (1.6) Maintenance/installation of sewer lines, and (1.7) installation of houses sewage connections. Under the GBV component the following activities will be implemented: (2.1) Provide case management and referral services, (2.2) Counselling Services (Individual and group counseling), (2.3) Distribution of dignity kits, (2.4) Awareness raising on GBV, (2.5) provide legal services, and (2.6) training of non-GBV specialist, WASH staff, on GBV detection and referral

project_name: Primary health care and emergency medical services provision to the population living in GCA within the 5km zone from the contact line in the Luhansk and Donetsk regions
project_objective:
1. Establishment of 5 standard emergency medical care posts at the 5 exit-entry checkpoints (EECPs) to provide primary health care and emergency medical care to people crossing the contact line both ways.
2. Establishment of 6 mobile emergency medical care teams (6 emergency medical vehicles) attached to each medical post at EECPs to provide primary health care and emergency medical care to people living in the GCA within the 5km zone from the contact line. Each mobile team would function within an operational zone of 200 km2 (20 km lengthwise on either side from the EECP and 5 km in depth from the contact line).
3. Establishment of the Call Center, a unit for collecting information about the people’s need for medicines and humanitarian aid in the so-called ‘gray zones’, in order to promptly respond to risks or events hazardous to the health of the target groups.
4. Establishment of approximately 100 workplaces for the population of the Luhansk and Donetsk regions through full or partial employment of health care and trade jobs professionals, regardless of their age or gender, in the project.
The project focuses primarily on target groups living in isolated settlements in the GCA within the 5km zone from the contact line. Medical assistance will be provided to everybody on the basis of medical ethics and medical secrecy, regardless of gender, age, race, nationality, linguistic choice or presence of mental illnesses, including to the LGBT community representatives and people with HIV/AIDS.

project_name: Urgent response to increase access to safe water and improve WASH services in public facilities to prevent public health risks
project_objective:
This project (approved 2019 HRP HPSE19-WSH-150683-1) will support critical public facilities in the Gaza Strip (GS) in maintaining safe and sufficient drinking water and adequate WASH services to reduce public health risks (Strategic Objectives 2 and 3 and WASH Cluster Strategic Objective 1). Interventions will focus on improved water quality and basic sanitation in the communities, schools, and health institutions. 
 
The proposed intervention builds on the detailed assessments completed by Norwegian
Refugee Council (NRC) and Action Against Hunger (AAH) in 2017. These assessments were  updated by AAH in 2018 on the WASH needs/gaps in public desalination plants, schools and health institutions operated by CMWU, MoEHE, and MoH and mid-2019 on WASH facilities in 4 public trauma hospitals (Aqsa, Beit Hanoun, Abu Yousef Al Najjar hospitals and Nasser Medical Complex); and Islamic Relief Palestine (IRPAL) interventions for rehabilitating desalination plants in schools and health facilities. Based on these, critical interventions will be made through a hardware approach (construction, minor rehabilitation/maintenance, and procurements related to WASH services and water quality) and soft component solutions (capacity building of technical staff in Operation Maintenance (O+M) of small-scale desalination plants/RO-units, Hygiene ToT for school health coordinators, and awareness raising for truckers/consumers of publicly supplied drinking water about safe water handling).  
 
Based on the evidence from assessments, including AAH’s 2018 assessment of public desalination plants, other work completed in the WASH Cluster’s Water Quality Working Group (WQWG), and AAH’s 2019 assessment of 4 public trauma hospitals treating GMR injured patients, tailored advocacy and awareness messaging will be conducted to hold accountable duty bearers on the right to safe water. The partnership between AAH as the lead of the WQWG and NRC as the previous lead, and with strong advocacy capacity within each organisation, will maximise the outcomes of advocacy campaigns and water quality interventions. The proposed intervention ensures protection mainstreaming as it is guided by protection principles and is taking into account safety and dignity; meaningful access; accountability as well as participation and empowerment.

project_name: Integrated COVID-19 WASH Response to the Rohingya  and Host population in Cox’s Bazar
project_objective:
""WaSH project is continuing to ensure inclusive and equitable provision of life saving water and sanitation services building on infrastructure already constructed in the previous phase in 2019 (in the Camp no,14 and 15 and host community) and strengthening behaviour change communication (BCC) by encouraging community-based collective measures. 
 There are two main routes of transmission of COVID-19: respiratory droplets and direct contact. Respiratory droplets are generated when an infected person coughs or sneezes. Droplets may also land on surfaces where the virus could remain viable and thus, the immediate environment of an infected individual can serve as a source of transmission (contact transmission). The provision of safe water, sanitation, hygienic living and environmental conditions are essential to protect human health during all infectious disease outbreaks, including the COVID-19outbreak. Hand hygiene, personal and social hygiene are key elements in preventing this disease to spread. As of today, a lot of aspects of COVID-19 prevention and control are still unclear, including implications related to WASH interventions (like virus persistence on surfaces or sewage). 

  The previous phase of the intervention has contributed to an increase in the appropriate usage of handwashing. Almost 79% of the respondents from the end of project evaluation reported that handwashing points installed under the project were utilized for hygiene maintenance. In terms of safe and inclusive access to water, the water point accessibility for PWD, pregnant women, adolescent girls and aged persons has been enhanced. The increase in ease of accessibility for pregnant women rose from 6% in baseline to 48%, similarly, for adolescent girls, it improved from 24% to 83%. So, maintenance of these essential WaSH facilities and services are vital to reduce the risk of disease outbreak.
Bear in mind the gravity of the issue, CAID will continue to ensure lifesaving water and sanitation services to the Rohingya and host communities in 2020. Focus will be provided to address the key challenges facing WaSH service such as congestion at water points, unequal distribution, inclusive access and protection concerns in bathing cubicles and latrines.""

project_name: PROJECT REVISED- Unconditional Cash Assistance to Improve Immediate Access to Food for Vulnerable Households in Southern Somalia and Somaliland
project_objective:
The 2019 Gu rains were the 3rd driest on record since 1980s, resulting in widespread crop failure and accelerated decline in livestock productivity, pushing communities in the worst-affected areas into acute food insecurity phase or worse. A spike in drought-induced displacement continues as rural communities flee to urban areas and increased military activities, insecurity and clan conflict further amplify displacement. As of September 2019, 2.6 million people remain displaced.
Rainfall in most of central and southern Somalia was 25-40% below average and the Shabelle and Juba river levels remained very low. An increase in rainfall from mid-May to mid-June led to improved browse and water conditions in northern and southern Somalia. However, the short duration, low amount and erratic distribution of the rains, as well as low river levels, led to significant reductions in area planted and yield of cereal crops. Severe acute malnutrition rates among children are increasing, mainly among IDPs. With an estimated 1 million children under 5 likely to be acutely malnourished through mid-2020.
According to FAO, an estimate 5.4 million Somali face acute food insecurity through September 2019; this includes 2.1 million people in Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and Emergency (IPC Phase 4).
FSNAU estimates national maize and sorghum Gu production are expected to be 68% of normal in agropastoral areas, leaving most poor agropastoral and rivering households unable to meet their minimum food needs due to below-average food stocks and income from seasonal agricultural employment. Despite some improvements in herd sizes and livestock body conditions after the onset of the Gu rains, pastoral households are still recovering from extended impacts of the 2016/17 severe drought, contributing to poor food security outcomes. 
The average number of beneficiaries reached with food assistance from January to May 2019 declined 47% compared to those reached from August to December 2018, according to FSNAU.
Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected to be widespread in northern and central agropastoral and pastoral livelihood zones as distressed sales of livestock will outpace births. However, seasonal milk availability and restored livestock body conditional and value, along with agricultural labor opportunities will offer some food and income. Emergency (IPC Phase 4) is most likely predicted in Guban Pastoral livelihood zone as births will not occur until Dec-Jan and in Bay-Bakool Lower Potential Agropastoral livelihood zone given the severity of the Gu food deficits.
This project is aimed at improving the ability of vulnerable HHs to meet their basic needs and reduce consumption gaps through life-saving humanitarian Unconditional Cash Transfers (UCTs) in the most vulnerable communities in Southern Somalia and Somaliland. The project will target populations in IPC 3, 4 and 5 and especially female-headed HHs, heads of household with disabilities and elderly headed households. Support will be provided through monthly multi-purpose cash transfers to 8,900HHs via Mobile Money Transfer.

project_name: Integrated nutrition, food security and protection to enhance household food security and livelihoods for conflict affected communities in Mayendit County - Unity state
project_objective:
Unity State emerged as the most highly contested area with the worst humanitarian crisis since the start of the conflict. The communities had to move to very remote areas most which were swamps to escape the fighting and all forms of livelihood initiatives like agriculture were abandoned, livestock raided and used as food for the armed groups leaving the population unable to meet the most basic food and nutritional needs especially of the children, lactating mother and pregnant women. 
The USA factsheets released in July 2019 reported over 17000 returnees came from neighbouring Sudan between April and June out of which 2000 reportedly settled in Leer County alone. The same report indicates that the driving force for their return is the perception of relative calm in their original counties and insufficient basic services like health and education for their families in Sudan.
Reports from RRC officials in Mayendit County indicate that many returnees are living in Markuel, Luom and Dablual in Mayendit County. Reports from the assessment undertaken by Mobile Humanitarian Agency (MHA) indicate that 8000 returnees were recorded in Adok and Thonyor Payams in Leer County in June 2019 of which 20% are children. The same report mentioned 5831 returnees in Dablual in Mayendit County alone. As the report states, these returnees do not have anything left to re-establish themselves apart from expecting handouts from the humanitarian actors in the area. 
This project will target the 17,000 returnees in Southern Unity who are in need of humanitarian assistance and protection and rebuild their livelihoods. The fact that food security situation is very acute, households rely on nature for their survival in terms of alternative food sources. This will not only provide the much-needed supply of protein foods but it will act as a source of income when due training is given to the fisher flocks to learn simple fish preservation. The presence of the water bodies will also be essential in establishment of the demonstration farms for vegetables by providing irrigation water. It should be noted that Christian Aid and its partner UNIDOR will also train beneficiaries on psycho social targeting the nutrition voucher and unconditional cash vouchers beneficiaries.

project_name: Food Security and Livelihoods Project
project_objective:
In North Darfur,  GOAL works closely with the Ministries of Agriculture and Animal Resources in Khartoum and in North Darfur as well as FAO on identifying needs, gaps in coverage, and on programme implementation. In addition, GOAL remains an active participant in the FSL Cluster at both national and state levels  where FSL programming is implemented, including North Darfur. GOAL’s FSL programming is closely integrated with other sectors, especially nutrition, health, and protection through targeting vulnerable households (including affected by malnutrition, people living with disabilities, and women-headed households) in catchment areas of supported clinics. GOAL will also incorporate protection and women’s empowerment approaches. With OFDA funding, GOAL proposes to focus on the IDP populations in Kutum Town as well as Kassab and Fata Borno Camps near Kutum, and complementary funding (SHF) will be used to reach vulnerable host communities in Kutum and Al Waha localities to ensure all relevant communities have their needs addressed. Activities are closely coordinated with other FSL actors in North Darfur to eliminate any duplication of effort. Through the FSL Cluster and Cash Working Groups, GOAL incorporates and shares lessons learned and harmonized approaches to livelihoods activities in order to maintain high technical standards in its work.
In South Kordofan, GOAL will work with Village Development Committee (VDC) in areas where they are already established and functional. If the VDC are not available, GOAL will work community leaders to form a VDC consisting of community leaders, influential community members (such as teachers, health workers, religious leaders etc.) as selected by community members. A close effort will be made to ensure that gender representation is observed in the composition of VDC members. And then, GOAL will work with the VDC to identify 200 households in each locality (400 total) to benefit from the first and second phase distribution. The first 100 households will receive 3 local species female goats per family directly from GOAL in the first phase of distribution and this group will make commitment with the VDC to pass on the first generation to the remaining 100 households. The commitment will be between among the first phase beneficiaries, VDC and the second phase beneficiary. This means each beneficiary from the second phase is tied with specific households from the first phase. Male goats will be distributed to the VDC and managed by them to ensure that they are accessed equally by all recipients of female goats. 

GOAL will identify and support existing Community Animal Health Workers (CAHWs) in the targeted areas to provide training and ongoing monitoring and care for the distributed animals. GOAL will provide refresher training to CAHWs and facilitate their work, in particular by supporting their transportation to rural and IDPs areas, as the lack of vehicles or resources for transport has been identified as a major challenge to effective support for animal welfare services across South Kordofan.

project_name: Platform for Accountability to Affected Populations in Libya
project_objective:
Ongoing political instability, conflict and insecurity in Libya, has resulted into a protracted crisis, leaving 893,000  people in need of assistance. As a cross cutting issue in a protracted crisis providing Accountability to affected populations has been a challenge with many members of the affected community unable to find information and provide feedback about humanitarian services. A common feedback mechanism has been established which has four main objectives:
i.	Access to Information
o	Enabling affected populations  to easily access vital information related to humanitarian aid;
ii.	Feedback Mechanism
o	Enabling two-way communication between the affected population and the humanitarian community; including receiving and referring issues of sexual exploitation and abuse 
iii.	Trends Analysis
o	Providing humanitarians with insight into communities’ key concerns, needs and challenges based on region, gender and age to help humanitarians take better informed programming decisions;
o	Informing future community engagement program design and interventions;
o	Supporting the provision of trends analysis to key government counterparts through the sectors and sub-sector leads when appropriate.  
iv.	Accountability and Efficiency
o	Facilitating collective accountability to affected populations and consolidating limited resources that are currently only available to humanitarian organizations individually while putting the affected populations at the centre of humanitarian response.

project_name: Food Assistance for migrants outside of detention centres in Libya based on face-to-face/web-based surveys analysis
project_objective:
WFP and its partners are currently assisting approximately 100,000 vulnerable populations on a monthly basis in Libya. These include IDPs and Libyan host communities in the three regions of Libya.

In November 2019, WFP started its pilot of providing assistance to migrants in Libya. The most food-insecure non-detained migrants have been identified in close partnership with IOM Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) Unit and Migrant Resource and Response Mechanism (MRRM) Unit. The pilot assistance has reached some 12,000 migrants outside of detention centres for the first two months.  To protect targeted migrants from risks of being detained or harassed, special arrangements will be put in place for the food assistance. Instead of calling them to come to collect their entitlements at one designated place on designated distribution dates, the targeted migrants receive their monthly entitlements through door-to-door or outreach modalities. 

Based on the success and lessons learnt, WFP looks to streamline the food assistance for 12,000 vulnerable migrants outside of detention cetnres into the Humanitarian Response Plan 2020 as one of the key activities under the Food Security Sector.  

To enhance the quality and the impact of the assistance, building on the successful collaboration between IOM and WFP, including release of the WFP-IOM joint-publication on Migrant Food Security in Libya, WFP looks to strengthen the collaboration with IOM in joint analysis of IOM's face-to-face flow monitoring surveys on food security WFP’s web-based Migration Pulse surveys.

project_name: Rapid Response Mechanism
project_objective:
The Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) responds to emergency needs when there is rapid, medium to large-scale population displacement. The RRM is an interagency multisectoral response mechanism implemented jointly by 04 UN agencies: IOM, UNFPA, UNICEF and WFP. The RRM relies on DTM (Displacement Tracking Matrix) for rapid assessment and data verification.The RRM is implemented jointly with a number of national and local NGOs. 
The mechanism aims to deliver immediate, life-saving supplies to families and individuals on the move as they flee conflict including those located close to military frontlines, delayed at checkpoints, or stranded in between. In Libya, the RRM was first used to respond to the humanitarian needs of IDPs in Tripoli. The first distribution took place on 11 April 2019 in Ain Zara (the university dorms and Al Asmaa school). Since then, the RRM has provided one-off assistance packages composed of food parcels, immediate response rations, blankets, mattresses, hygiene kits, dignity kits, baby kits as well as PSS services to over 7,233 families (over 35,000 people). RRM responded to the population displaced following conflict in the western area and Murzuq as well as people affected by the floods in Ghat. The RRM has reached out to affected people in 25 municipalities, 12 mantikas in 2019. 
In 2020, RRM aims at providing assistance to 12,000 families (60,000 affected people) across the 04 humanitarian sectors.

project_name: Enhancing resilience of conflict-affected population for future crises in eastern Ukraine through community mobilization
project_objective:
PCO3. Improve social cohesion and resilience of conflict-affected people, including IDPs, through community-based protection and identification of durable solutions 
Community mobilization project aims to support grassroots initiatives of vulnerable communities to increase resilience for future development. All project activities are based on the analysis of issues, and prioritization of protection risks and solutions in every particular community. Community mobilizing component seeks to empower communities to develop their own community-based coping mechanisms, to exercise their rights, and to find solutions for the most pressing issues in their communities. Communities will mobilize themselves when they have trust and confidence in the process and when they see benefits emerging from their own efforts.
Once communities are selected based on assessments conducted by the project team, PIN will select key community volunteers/activists to participate in a training on project development. The training will be conducted in each of the communities and includes a three-hour session conducted by the project team, during which topics such as Protection, Safeguarding, CRM are presented as well. 
The communities will be selected based on the following process: At the start of the project, PIN will disseminate the information in community meetings, cluster meetings as well as among local administration. Applications will be invited, with the project team also offering support to any community that might require assistance with the applications. Afterwards, the internal selection committee will create a shortlist based on the applications received. Only applications tackling Protection-related issues will be considered.
The key community volunteers/activists will be selected through a dialogue with local authorities from the selected communities.  Prior to the training, the community volunteers/activists’ representatives should identify key needs within their community that can be addressed with an external financial assistance. During the training, participants will acquire an overall understanding and basic skills in project cycle management for community-based projects, and will get acquainted with the application procedure for PIN funding. Each community will develop their own proposal with assistance from the project team as needed. Once PIN has approved the proposal, a contract will be signed, and materials/funds will be provided/disbursed for the project to be implemented.
PIN is responsible in front of the beneficiaries in terms of the main following accountability commitments and prioritizes:
-	Accountability to affected population: PIN involves people affected by crisis in key decisions and processes that affect them, and have effective communication and feedback channels that engage all sectors in a community.
-	Leadership/Governance: compliance response mechanisms that are integrated into project proposals, strategies, monitoring and evaluations, trainings and performance tracking management, partnership agreements etc. 
-	Information Provision: accessible and timely information to beneficiaries on organizational procedures, structures and processes that affect them to ensure that they can make informed decisions and choices, and facilitate a dialogue between an organisation and its beneficiaries over information provision.  
-	Beneficiaries’ Feedback: actively seek the views of affected populations to improve policy and practice in programming, ensuring that feedback and complaints mechanisms are streamlined, appropriate and robust enough to deal with complaints about breaches in policy and stakeholder dissatisfaction.
-	Non-discrimination: PIN ensures that all vulnerable groups of women and girls, men and boys, have access to the assistance.

project_name: Emergency Food Security and livelihood assistance to conflict affected population in Northeast Nigeria
project_objective:
The regions surrounding the Lake Chad basin have been embroiled in a decade-long conflict with the three North East Nigerian states of Borno, Adamawa and Yobe (BAY) bearing the brunt of the violence. The conflict has severely disrupted food production systems resulting in high levels of displacement and extensive human and socioeconomic losses. According to the Recovery and Peacebuilding Assessment (RPBA) undertaken by the World Bank in 2016, the conflict has resulted in losses of USD 3.7 billion caused by the destruction of farmland, animals and infrastructure. Acute food insecurity persists at alarming levels. Findings of the October 2019 Cadre Harmonisé analysis highlight that, between October and December 2019, approximately three million people in the BAY states will face acute levels of food insecurity (Phase 3
and above).Moreover, the prevalence of acute malnutrition is high, with GAM rates in Yobe (11.5 percent), Borno (8.1 percent) and Adamawa (7.2 percent) under pressure. As a result, the mortality rate in all three states is equally under pressure.
FAO has had a permanent presence in the BAY states since 2015, implementing lifesaving interventions in the form of emergency food security, nutrition and livelihoods support to IDPs, returnees and host communities affected by the crisis. Despite these ongoing efforts, without sustained and expanded humanitarian assistance the number of people experiencing acute food insecurity is projected to increase by up to 50 percent by the onset of the 2020 lean season (June – August).
The overall objective is to improve food security and nutrition among conflict-affected communities through the restoration, protection and promotion of sustainable and environmentally friendly Agro-Sylvo-Pastoral-based livelihoods. This will be achieved via the distribution of essential inputs/assets and capacity building targeting vulnerable households in both rural and urban / peri-urban communities; the creation of sustainable livelihood opportunities and decent employment in the agriculture, livestock and aquaculture sectors; and the promotion of value addition via the formation of cooperatives, group savings and loans, and market linkages. In addition, Safe Access toFuel and Energy (SAFE) will be promoted
More specifically, the proposed intervention includes the following activities:
• Support to land preparation including distribution of rainy season and dry season kits (seeds and fertilizer) for crop production as well as essential inputs for backyard vegetable gardening to restore/protect agricultural livelihoods and promote household nutrition.
• Animal restocking targeting women and youth with goat, sheep and poultry packages for income generation and improved nutrition.
• Vaccination campaign to control animal diseases aimed at protecting livestock-based livelihoods; biosecurity/biocontainment training for disease control, food safety and animal welfare to key associations/groups of animal workers.
• Distribution of aquaculture kits (tanks, feed, fingerlings) to unemployed fisherfolk linked with the provision of fish processing assets (smoking kilns) and training to vulnerable women’s groups.
• Distribution of assets (bulls and ploughs) and training to unemployed rural youth to promote entrepreneurship in land development services.
• Establishment/upgrading of fuel-efficient stove production centres and distribution of fuel-efficient stoves to households facing heightened protection and health risks; mitigate poor energy access and adoption of negative coping strategies.
More Specifically the proposed intervention includes the following activities;
• Organization of beneficiaries into local agribusiness cooperatives supported with training and seed money towards establishing group savings and loans to promote upscaling and resilience building

project_name: Emergency shelter and non-food item assistance for IDPs in Borno State
project_objective:
Under the proposed Action ACTED aims to deliver critical emergency shelter and non-food item assistance to vulnerable and conflict-affected IDPs in Borno State. In alignment with core objectives of the Shelter and Non-Food Item Sector, the project will address immediate shelter and NFI needs faced by new arrivals, while ensuring equitable and safe access to life-saving assistance for vulnerable and newly internally displaced persons (IDPs). In order to provide immediate relief to IDPs, ACTED proposes to build on its long-standing experience as a Shelter and NFI implementing partner in Borno State, through engagement of its dedicated Shelter and NFI Team, in order to provision emergency aid in coordination with the Sectoral response. The Action will strengthen the overall humanitarian response to address urgent needs faced by new arrivals, by individuals living in protracted displacement without access to shelter repair, and IDPs living in vulnerable makeshift shelters, by delivering Bama type emergency shelters, and non-food item assistance. The Action aims to contribute towards the significant decrease of protection risks faced by displaced families that lack access to basic and essential shelter and household needs by reducing exposure resulting from inadequate privacy and protection from the elements, and reducing correlated negative coping strategy adoption rates. 

ACTED anticipates that the Action will directly benefit a total of 16,000 beneficiaries, based on a five-person household average, within Dikwa, Mafa, Maiduguri, and Monguno LGAs.

project_name: Emergency camp coordination and camp management assistance, and critical risk mitigation for IDPs in Mafa, Maiduguri, and Dikwa LGAs, Borno State
project_objective: ACTED will deliver critical camp coordination and camp management assistance to vulnerable and conflict-affected persons living in camp settings in Mafa, Maiduguri and Dikwa in Borno State. The proposed Action will be delivered in order to deliver robust coordination and information sharing mechanisms at camp level in order to strengthen targeted and evidence based humanitarian intervention activities. The Action will further serve to implement critical risk preparedness, mitigation and response strategies, ensuring immediate access to life-saving assistance for IDPs in the event of a rapid onset emergency, through the development and implementation of emergency preparedness and response plans. The intervention approach is derived from the two core pillars of participatory governance structures in order to ensure the inclusion and elevation of beneficiary voice into humanitarian planning and response is systematically conducted, and on ensuring accountability to affected populations for the delivery of transparent and accountable humanitarian interventions. ACTED will thus deliver a comprehensive CCCM package through static and experienced Teams in the target camp locations, benefitting a total of 83,384 IDPs living in camp settings in Mafa, Maiduguri and Dikwa LGAs. In addition, ACTED will conduct mobile CCCM, enabling emergency response to informal settlements facing critical CCCM gaps, ensuring that basic coordination and management structures are in place. Mobile CCCM services will be delivered across the BAY states, anticipating to benefit up to 20,000 individuals.

project_name: Supporting WASH for Conflict Affected Populations in Borno and Yobe States
project_objective:
The Supporting WASH for Conflict Affected Populations in Borno and Yobe States project proposed by GREENCODE is as result of WASH gaps currently experienced and observed in IDPs and host communities in Jere, Konduga, Nganzai and Mongonu LGAs of Borno state and host communities in  Gaidem, Damaturu LGAs of Yobe state 
Currently, GREENCODE assignment in in Kaga, Konduga, Jere and Mongonu LGAs of Borno state shows gaps in sanitation facilities (inadequate latrines and dysfunctional ones), open defecations, inadequate access to water supply as well as menstrual hygiene kits.
The proposed GREENCODE project is aimed at improving ongoing WASH services  in LGAs in Yobe and Borno state with critical WASH Needs. In this project GREENCODE in a timely manner as well as grant equitable access to safe water through water trucking where necessary as temporary measures for some days,  repairs of water points (hand pumps and motorised solar powered borehole), promote hygiene and sanitation services, undertake partial and full repairs of dysfunctional latrines and showers,  public health promotion activities and WASH NFIs, with a specialized provision hygiene kits that include menstrual hygiene products, particularly re-usable sanitary pads.
The project is targeting to reach 17,000 persons with 15 liters of water daily and 2,500 women and girls of reproductive age with girls will be targeted specially for menstrual hygiene management. People living with disability will be mainstreamed into both targets. 
The project objectives are;
i). To increase safe and equitable access to enough quantity of water for drinking, cooking and for personal/domestic hygiene purposes for both formal and informal camps hosting new arrivals and host communities/returnees in Yobe and Borno states.
ii). To promote good hygiene practice (user friendly and gender appropriate kits) among the new arrivals in both formal and informal camps in the project locations/LGAs.
In achieving this GREENCODE with donor grant will be trucking water daily to IDP locations (new arrivals and host communities with water crisis) in LGAs in Borno and Yobe states for 90 days,  drilling of   new boreholes, rehabilitation of both hand pumps and  solar motorized borehole, train and facilitate proper hygiene /health education activities using the two major language (Hausa and Kanuri), for proper understanding aimed at improved knowledge, attitude and practice of the people, GREENCODE will adopt the use of cartoons/pictorial messaging during the hygiene promotion sessions as tool for in promoting lifesaving behavioural change. Also, the project will provide specialised hygiene kits that include menstrual hygiene products particularly re-usable sanitary pads for women and girls of reproductive age.
In line with WASH Sector priority, GREENCODE will continue to assess and undertake repairs of sub and super structure of latrines and showers in LGAs for both states. 
GREENCODE in the past 5 months has been responding WASH needs in Borno state, but the needs are overwhelming and need more actors and resources. Through the provision of life saving WASH activities, GREENCODE will contribute to mitigate the risk of cholera outbreak as the two states has in recent past experienced outbreak of Cholera and this intervention will help checkmate future occurrence. 
Protection interventions will be mainstreamed into the project and maintain in all the project cycle. Also, SGBV and child protection will be part of the training during WASH Committee and Hygiene promoters’ training. The hygiene/health promotion will be designed taking into account disposal of used menstrual hygiene products, accessible to children and the physically disabled, sex dis-aggregated. The lock down order and restrictions on movement has confined people to their homes which makes it difficult for children to cope with. This is because they are vulnerable to domestic abuse which may likely happen. project_name: Provision of Food Assistance, Livelihood support and access to Fuel efficient Technologies to Vulnerable IDPs and Host Communities in Borno State.
project_objective:
This project will undertake food assistance, livelihood projects and provision of access to SAFE to affected persons in Jere, MMC, Ngala and Rann (Kala-Balge) in Borno State. According to Food Security Sector 2020 Humanitarian Response Plan, Food access remains a challenge due to relapse of the security situation and fresh waves of displacement, and continued food assistance for conflict-affected Households is needed. Borno State in the North-East region is largely affected by insurgency and has left most vulnerable crises-affected people in need of access to timely and appropriate Food assistance, including fuel and energy-related support to meet their immediate Food needs and Livelihood support. Access to humanitarian assistance has improved throughout the State, though periodic access constraints have persisted notably in many parts of the State. Despite this improvement, Crisis and Emergency remain widespread, and an estimated 1.75 million affected persons are targeted for assistance and support in the year 2020.
Food assistance and livelihood/access to SAFE projects will contribute significantly to:
1.	The prevention of common diseases: having healthy community that will have strong immune system to fight infections.
2.	Children learning properly when they have food available either at home or in schools: once there is food in households, girls and boys are allowed to attend classes than when there is no food in the house.
This project will include a Wet Feeding component which is going to provide emergency response and act as first responder to new arrivals in the selected LGAs in Borno State through:
•	Preparation and distribution of the meals to feed the new arrivals for 120 hours in the reception center.
•	Provision of cooking fuel to new arrivals who are able to cook for themselves.
•	Provision of follow ups and referrals for therapeutic feeding program.
The project will target an improvement in household food security, with the average number of meals consumed by both adults and children increasing from below 2 meals to nearly three meals (2.7). Household dietary diversity will also improve with households consuming a more varied diet.
At the field level, this project is going to have protection monitors to ensure effective systems are in place for preventing and responding to acts of sexual exploitation and abuse. Identifying protection threats enables us to harmonize and fine-tune our food security activities in order to address, mitigate or reduce these threats. 5% of the total Budget for this project will be channeled towards protection mainstreaming.
At the programmes level, SHO will ensure Accountability, Participation and Empowerment by achieving the following:
•	Making sure beneficiaries know they have a right to equitable and safe assistance, and where and how to obtain it.
•	Consulting Men, Women, Boys, Girls, the elderly, and persons with disabilities/specific needs to understand their needs and preferences for location, assessment, design, and methodology of assistance.
•	Communities and beneficiaries will be involved in planning, implementing, monitoring and evaluating of programmes so they can make informed decisions. SHO will be transparent in their objectives with beneficiaries and non-beneficiary communities, as well as with the government and other Stakeholders.
•	A complaints feedback mechanism will be established with a view to improving programming, assisting in understanding beneficiary and community perceptions, promoting beneficiary empowerment and assisting in the early detection of problems such as targeting, misconduct including sexual exploitation and abuse, food diversion and fraud. 
•	Ensuring that Food or livelihood committees are representative of all groups within the community (e.g. gender, age, ethnicity, socio-economic group, etc.).
•	Monitoring and Evaluation will be done to track implementation and outputs.

project_name: PROVISION OF INTEGRATED SHELTER, CCCM AND NFI SUPPORT TO IDPs IN BORNO STATE
project_objective:
The project aim at providing integrated CCCM, shelter reinforcement kit, NFI, and shelter repairs to meet the need of the most vulnerable households in need of shelter support in Maiduguri, Jere and Rann. 
The project will engage the POCs with carpentry training on shelter repairs and maintenance which is aimed at providing them with livelihood support through the cash for work strategy to enable them get cash to cover their needs.
This project will target 35,000 beneficiaries for the CCCM support, Emergency Shelter construction, shelter reinforcement/emergency shelter kit and NFI kits to fill gaps in IDP camps situated in Jere.
More so, their poor living conditions does not allow any privacy and consequently even the protection of the most vulnerable (mostly single women and children) is not guaranteed.
Furthermore, The CCCM project will improve the quality of management of the women, men, boys and girls IDPs within the camp settings, monitor and assist those out of camps and some vulnerable persons in host community. The project will support systematic follow up of the IDPs and returnees new arrivals particularly vulnerable women and girls. The project seeks to provide quality services during the registration process and will ensure that reception facilities are equally accessible to women, men, boys and girls newly arrived. Camp managers will ensure proper relocation of new arrivals from the reception centres to the shelters constructed taking into account the needs of the most vulnerable. Through this project, CCCM interventions will also provide monitoring and making referrals  and report on all protection gaps and needs to be addressed by different sectors in order to improve the living conditions of women, men, girls and boys displaced. The CCCM project will promote the participation of the IDPs based on age, gender and diversity in the life cycle of camps particularly care and maintenance of infrastructures, small scale drainage, etc. In case of Rann, the Reception center will be reactivated providing the basic needs of new Arrivals.

project_name: Improving reproductive health services in conflict affected Area (Rann-Kala balge)
project_objective:
The aim of proposed project is to provide lifesaving sexual and reproductive health care services to IDP, host community and new arrivals in kala-bale LGA and more particularly Rann.
The project aims to contribute to respond to the needs of the targeted communities in terms of reproductive health in Rann (Borno state) through two main components:

1. Support the community through Registered Midwives Practical Observational Skills Training of Traditional birth attendants (TBAs) and Community Health Extension Workers (CHEWs) to provide safe
clean delivery services and support for exclusive breastfeeding to women in a bid to reduce maternal and neonatal mortality and morbidity.
TBAs and Community Health Extension Workers (CHEWs) are lay health workers trained by the Ministry of health (MoH) to carry out healthcare delivery through a task shifting model. Both are usually in the center of delivering modern, traditional and cultural maternal health related interventions and are usually well respected in the community.
A massive gap in the delivery of maternal health care interventions and programs by trained health care professionals exists in Rann due du the insurgency in the first quarter of 2019. Registered midwives will conduct practical training to TBAs and CHEWS, whilst conducting basic antenatal and postnatal care, detection and recognition of danger signs of pregnancy and delivery. TBAs and CHEWs will be provided with clean delivery kits, registered and mentored on how to use the kits for optimum coverage of clean safe deliveries. Midwives will also mentor TBAs and CHEWs to take on case management of women during post-natal period and encourage exclusive breastfeeding for at least six months as a minimum standard. A doctor will visit the area once or twice a week to provide supportive supervision and treatment for complicated cases if appropriate medications are available or certify medical referrals depending on the security situation to the secondary health care in Cameroon

2. Support the community to prevent excessive amount of anticipated Measles disease outbreak cases during the harmattan season that may threaten and further destabilize health care system of the area.
his component seeks to enhance health promotion for disease prevention through awareness raising campaigns in the community.

project_name: COVID19 - Provision of Adequate Living Spaces and NFIs to People in Displacement and Return areas in Borno, Adamawa and Yobe States
project_objective:
This project will target IDPs and returnees in three affected states, Yobe, Adamawa and Borno with provision of emergency shelters, Non-food Items (NFIs), transitional and shelter repair kits as protection live-saving assistance aligned with Shelter/ NFI/ CCCM Sector strategic objectives for the HRP 2020. Providing IDPs, Returnees and Host Communities with living spaces represents an essential intervention in reducing the impact of the COVID-19 crisis, and it is a critical first step to reducing vulnerability that preserves the ability of the most vulnerable and affected people to meet their basic needs which are now further exasperated by the pandemic. It is critical to ensure that PoCs are supported to recover their wellbeing and dignity in a protective environment where they can enjoy full exercise of their rights including to adequate shelter.  

Provision of shelter assistance will also allow for decongestion of camps which is one of the vehicles of COVID19 facing IDPs living in camps. In highly congested camps and settlement, social distancing is not possible hence putting IDPs at high risk of contracting the disease.

project_name: School Feeding Programme to support 52,000 school children in Logone et Chari, Mayo Sava and Mayo Tsanaga divisions in the Far North Region
project_objective:
The school feeding activity is implemented in the Far North region targeting the most crisis affected divisions of Logone and Chari, Mayo Sava and Mayo Tsanaga. The objective of the project is to provide school meals to 52,000 children to encourage and promote school attendance. Many children have been out of school for many years due to insecurity children in the targeted divisions,thanks to various humanitarian support some children have timidly started going to school. The project will contribute to maintain those who are already in the school till the completion of the primary school cycle. Through the project, daily hot meals will be provided to all the children during 165 days of the school year, to encourage them to attend and stay in schools throughout the school year, thus contributing to improve their nutritional status as well as to protect them and limit their exposure to terrorist groups. Some 52,000 school  children will be assisted through in-kind modality. 
Food commodities will be delivered to schools and meals will be prepared for the children at school. Parents and communities will complement with various items including water, fire wood and cooking services and other locally produced food. The food basket and daily rations for the in-kind assistance are; cereals (140g), Pulses (40g), Oil (15g) and salt (3g). To support the implementation of the project, capacity strengthening sessions on school feeding management, food storage, gender and Protection, will be organized for school canteens managing committees and other partners and actors involved in the school feeding project. These include members of Parent Teachers Associations, mothers’ associations and Government staff form the Ministries of Basic Education, agriculture, Health, Women affairs and social Affairs.

project_name: Prevention of under nutrition among children 6  23 months, pregnant and lactating women in vulnerable districts in the  Far North  region

project_name: Provision of Quality Lifesaving Nutrition Intervention to conflict affected communities in Borno and Yobe State
project_objective:
The conflict in northeastern Nigeria continues to undermine social stability and economic development due to the scale of displacement disrupted livelihoods and diminished agricultural production due to the protracted nature of the crisis. This has a consequential impact on food security and nutrition situation. The conflict has also further affected the health system with less than 30 per cent of health facilities remaining functional in Borno State, where malaria is endemic and diarrhoea and other diseases affect the population regularly and are often life-threatening.  

Based on the NE Nigeria Nutrition and Food Security Surveillance Round 8 (Preliminary report) in Oct 2019, the prevalence of global acute malnutrition (GAM) remains at serious levels in several domains, particularly in Borno and Yobe states.  Based on WHZ the prevalence of Global Acute Malnutrition in Borno was 8.1 (7.0-9.4 CI) while 11.5 (9.6-13.7 CI) in Yobe. Whereas the prevalence of SAM in Borno was 0.9 (0.6-1.4 CI) and Yobe 1.5 (1.0-2.2 CI). Some of the drivers of malnutrition were poor dietary diversity, low rates of exclusive breastfeeding (particularly in Yobe), the incidence of common childhood illnesses (fever, diarrhoea, cough etc.) and poor water, sanitation and hygiene practices. The high influx of IDPs and the high malnutrition rates among newly arrived children as they have been deprived of humanitarian assistance for several years may also contribute. The nutrition situation is likely to worsen due to poor hygiene and sanitation conditions, especially in host communities disease outbreaks such as measles, and the influx of newly displaced populations.

project_name: Promoting rights and supporting emergency protection needs in MMC, Jere, Monguno, Gujiba and Michika in Borno, Yobe and Adamawa States
project_objective: The overall situation in northeastern Nigeria, can still be characterized as dire with IDPs, returnees and host community members all facing acute life-threatening risks to safety and dignity. Following nearly ten years of attacks by Armed Opposition Groups (AOGs), families have been displaced numerous times following either failed attempts at return to areas of origin or the spreading of violence into new areas. , Populations as a result of conflict and displacement face grave protection risks and violations such as exploitation and abuse, arbitrary and extended detentions, family separation, restrictions on freedom of movement and insecurity. These are then further exacerbated by insufficient access to basic services and psychosocial distress. The ongoing conflict and continued displacements in the northeast particularly affect the most vulnerable populations, including the elderly and chronically sick, persons with physical and mental disabilities, female and child-headed households, unaccompanied or separated children, adolescent boys, pregnant and/or lactating women and people returning from captivity. Violations and sexual abuse against women and children are widespread. The IRC will provide holistic Protection services to meet the large number of households with high protection needs. Throughout its intervention the IRC will ensure protection mainstreaming, inclusive program design for persons with specific needs, and attention to gender sensitivity.

PROJECT REVISED - Integrated Relief and Recovery for Drought Affected people in Awdal, Sool and Nugal regions of Somalia.
project_objective:
Up to 2.1 million people across Somalia are expected to face food consumption gaps, high acute malnutrition, or depletion of assets indicative of Crisis (IPC Phase 3)1 or worse outcomes through December 2019. Moreover, an estimated one million children under the age of five are likely to be acutely malnourished through mid-2020. Sustained and large-scale humanitarian assistance, which is planned and likely through September, is currently preventing more severe outcomes in many areas. In the absence of humanitarian assistance from October to December, however, food security is expected to deteriorate. Current high levels of food insecurity are driven by drought conditions from late 2018 through mid-May 2019, exacerbated by below-average and erratically distributed rainfall during the 2019 Gu season (April-June), which began late and finished early. Many households are still recovering from the severe 2016/2017 drought or have been affected by conflict, and 2.6 million people remain displaced. The Gu cereal harvest failed in most regions, leaving most poor agropastoral and riverine households unable to meet their minimum food needs given significantly below-average food stocks and income from seasonal agricultural employment. In pastoral areas, the impact of the drought on livestock led to a lack of access to milk, and many poor households have accumulated large debts while struggling to feed their families and rescue their remaining livestock. An estimated 2.6 million people across Somalia remain internally displaced. Post-Gu assessment results indicate that most of the 14 major Internally Displaced Person (IDP) settlements are in Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or Stressed (IPC Phase 2) in the presence of humanitarian assistance. In the absence of assistance during the October- December period, food security is expected to deteriorate in most of northern and central Somalia and some parts of the South. Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected to be widespread in northern and central agropastoral and pastoral livelihood zones, as distressed sales of livestock will outpace births and result in stagnant or declining livestock herd sizes

project_objective:

project_name: Provision of quality education services for children and adolescents in Northern Syria.
project_objective:
According to the 2019 Humanitarian Needs Overview, 6.07 million school-age children (5-17 years) are in need of education assistance. The highest numbers of children in need in Aleppo (1.1m), Rural Damascus (0.91m) and Idleb (0.83m).
The severity of needs was calculated for the education sector in each community in Syria, based on variables in the three subjects of education access, quality of education and education systems strengthening, together with inter-sector indicators for severity of need based on access to and intensity of conflict in each community. Access indicators include enrolment rate, attendance rate, proportion of school-age children who are internally displaced persons and/or returnees, availability of learning facilities, and availability of teaching and learning materials; quality of education indicators include the availability of teachers, and percentage of teachers receiving a salary/incentives; the education system strengthening indicator includes professional development for education actors. the greatest severity of education needs (severity 4-6), in terms of number of people in need (children and education personnel) are Idleb (0.89m) and Rural Damascus (0.68m) and Aleppo (0.63m). 
SC will target 85% subdistricts with a 4, 5 or 6 severity. The areas for implementation in Northwest Syria (NWS) were selected based on numbers of out-of-school children and the capacity of the hosting communities to accommodate them within existing schools. Vulnerability criteria also prioritizes newly displaced children, unaccompanied and separated children (UASC) and children with disabilities. The locations selected, based on the 2019 HNO education severity scale, averaged a 5 of 6 severity. The number of people in need for protection services is 342,078 newly displaced individuals as of November 2019, and 2,425,649 total IDP’s in the NW, which includes many of our target areas . This number continues to grow as there has been a sharp increase in displacements in the NW of Syria. In Northeast Syria (NES), SC’s Education team has worked in five camps - Newroz, Roj, Al hole, Areesha, Washokhani These camps include very different groups of populations such as Iraqi refugees including Arabs and Yezedians, Syrian IDPs and foreign families).

SC recognizes the need for having a gender balanced recruitment and training strategy to ensure that dialogue with communities, implementation of activities, and coordination with stakeholders take the needs of both genders into consideration. An estimated 50%+ of the targeted children are girls, but girls will still be explicitly targeted and prioritized for inclusion. Though retention rates for boys can exceed girls by secondary schooling, initial enrolment rates reflects girls less often reached. SC teams identify barriers to participation and inclusion and implement measures to mitigate these, for example by separating parent/community group meetings, where cultural norms dictate to facilitate female participation; or by ensuring males are also recipients of our key messaging on education as they are usually the gatekeeper in household level decisions. In addition, diversity must be considered very carefully, especially regarding religion, ethnicity or nationality. The contents of education activities must be neutral and suitable for all children in the learning space.

This action is in line with SC Whole of Syria strategic plan. In NWS SC is co-leading the Education Cluster together with UNICEF and in NES SC established and has led the Education Working Group (EWG) for the education sector coordination since 2017.
