project_name: Mitigation of Threat Posed by the Presence of Explosives in Palestine
project_objective:
The ongoing security situation in Palestine remains volatile and unpredictable. In Gaza, new rounds of military escalations and exchanges of fire result in the increasing presence of remnant explosive hazards (ERW). The ongoing escalations continue to leave behind thousands of items of ERW. These residual outbreaks of armed clashes further increase ERW contamination in Gaza and are becoming more frequent and exacerbate a security environment already on the brink of another full-scale conflict. 
UNMAS aligns with its Country Programme Strategy in contributing to two outcomes: 1. The UN, and its humanitarian partners in Gaza, maintain critical functions, uninhibited by explosive hazards. UNMAS is the only provider of specialized explosive ordnance disposal (EOD) capacity that is permitted to operate in Gaza by the Gazan and Israeli authorities. UNMAS continued presence has been requested by the Palestinian and Israeli authorities, the UN Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator, OCHA, UNRWA and UNDP. UNMAS continues to provide ERW mitigation measures to UN and humanitarian partner sites to ensure that vulnerable communities are protected and prepared against the threat of explosive hazards from past, present and future escalations in conflict. 
UNMAS Palestine maintains an emergency EOD presence in Gaza to remove and destroy ERW posing a threat to Gaza communities. This allows UNMAS to be ready for a rapid response during potential conflict and to maintain an Emergency Response Preparedness Plan (ERPP) to ensure access for the Humanitarian response in any future Gaza conflict. 
Outcome 2: Conflict affected people know how to mitigate the risk of explosive ordnance. An  individual’s risk of exposure varies on factors that include where they live and work and the information they have at hand. ERW risk awareness is critical to mitigating the threat posed to civilians. UNMAS Palestine has identified two types of educational activities that are required in the specific context of Gaza. After several years of community engagement with beneficiary stakeholders and local partners they have developed targeted curricula which consider the needs of different gender and age groups as well as persons with disabilities: (i) risk education provides information for civilians to protect themselves from existing ERW threats, (ii) Conflict Preparedness and Protection (CPP) is a novel form of risk education providing resilience training to prepare for future escalations, and is critical to avoid civilian casualties. To address COVID-19 restrictions, remote delivery methodologies have been developed as well as dual messaging addressing ERW and pandemic mitigation.  Informal street session with social distancing measures have also been utilised.
In the West Bank, UNMAS works with the National Mine Action Authority, Palestinian Mine Action Centre (PMAC) to enhance their capacity to provide risk education to vulnerable communities in the West Bank and to address the needs of victims of ERW accidents. There are 16 minefields and over 46 identified areas with recorded ERW contamination that pose a 
risk to shepherds, farmers, women and children. Lack of resources has impacted PMAC ability to coordinate EORE in the West Bank and provide age, gender and disability appropriate risk education where needed. Victim Assistance (VA), is the pillar of mine action that meets the short, medium and long-term needs of women, girls, boys and men who have been injured by explosive ordnance and addresses affected families and communities.  UNMAS works to support PMAC in developing their capacity in addressing this requirement. UNMAS has consulted, via a number of workshops, in 2019, to develop a project that will assist PMAC to develop and implement an EORE strategy in the West Bank, that is inclusive of the varied needs of women, men and persons with disabilities; and training of training to women volunteers for EORE, with a special focus on children in the West Bank.

project_name: Mitigating explosive hazard threat in north-east Nigeria.
project_objective: More than 1.5 million individuals are exposed to the risk of Explosive Remnants of War, landmines of an improvised nature, and other Improvised Explosive Devices in Borno, northern parts of Adamawa, and eastern parts of Yobe. After over a decade of the ongoing conflict in North-East Nigeria, intense fighting between the Nigerian army and Non-State Armed Groups resulted in the widespread contamination of the area by explosive hazards. The presence of explosive hazards is affecting the population and humanitarian actors, restricting freedom of movement, safe access to villages, and rebuilding of key infrastructures, and arable land. Given the widespread explosive ordnance (EO) contamination and prevalent use of improvised explosive devices (IEDs), to include landmines of an improvised nature, by non-state armed groups, the 2020 Humanitarian Needs Assessment identifies 1.5 million people in need of mine action in north-east Nigeria. The majority of people in need are in Borno State, the epicenter of the crisis. The presence of explosive hazards was a barrier to access land for agricultural activities. The lack of access is exacerbating food insecurity and will continue to do so until mine action activities can be undertaken. Many IDPs in Borno State are intended to be resettled to their places of origin by the government of Borno. The Borno State Return Strategy emphasizes “IDPs and returning refugees must be protected from violence, (…) mines, and unexploded ordinances and any other threats to their rights and security”. Minimal conditions include inter alia, that they must be protected from explosive hazards. This year alone, in Borno, Adamawa, and Yobe (BAY) states, 224 explosive incidents were registered, 195 IED incidents, and 29 Explosive Remnants of War (ERW) incidents, resulting in 145 civilian casualties. Nigeria has been reported in the landmine monitor (data 2019) as the country with the fifth most Explosive Ordnance casualties. UNMAS Nigeria supports national capacities, including the security sector and civil society, and coordinates the mine action response in northeast Nigeria as it is crucial that the immediate threat posed by explosive ordnance to civilians and humanitarian and development actors is mitigated. To ensuresustainability, UNMAS is also committed that relevant national and local entities should be able to manage the explosive threat, based on an accurate understanding of the scale and scope of explosive ordnance contamination. In response to these challenges, UNMAS developed a project that aims at providing prevention of incidents, through capacity building of national and state authorities as well as local NGO/ Civil Society Organizations via Training of Trainers (ToT) for Explosive Ordnance Risk Education (EORE) and Non-Technical Survey (NTS), enhancement of existing national capacity by providing targeted training for security forces on Improvised Explosive Device Disposal (IEDD), and response to incidents through Advanced Emergency First Responder Course (EFR) and Individual First Aid Kit (IFAK) training and victim assistance (VA) referral mechanism.

project_name: Community-based protection response to IDP and conflict-affected communities in Ukraine
project_objective:
After six years of armed conflict in Ukraine, the Minsk Agreements, which outline the basis for peaceful settlement of the conflict, remain unimplemented. As long as the armed conflict continues, along with its consequences of civilian casualties, damage to housing and critical infrastructure, contamination of mines/UXOs, significant restrictions on the freedom of movement and disruption to normal life, people living along both sides of the line of contact will have emergency humanitarian needs, especially for shelter repairs, NFIs, protection, health, heating and water.  While many prefer to remain in their homes, regardless of the ongoing conflict, those most at risk from the conflict must be offered reasonable alternatives so that they can live in greater safety. The main protection needs relate to physical protection from the effects of armed conflict, access to social and economic rights, documentation, HLP rights, as well as SGBV and child protection. 

In line with its Protection mandate, Multi-Year Multi-Partner Protection and Solutions Strategy for Ukraine, and Country Operations Plan UNHCR will continue to address the protection needs of IDPs and persons, affected by the conflict, with particular focus on the persons residing on the both sides of the contact line. In doing so, UNHCR will partner with government, NGOs and communities. With its leading role in Protection and Shelter, UNHCR will continue to contribute to the broader humanitarian response within the framework of IASC for the entire crisis-affected population.

In the protection sector, UNHCR will conduct protection monitoring, particularly along the contact line and at EECPs.  UNHCR will provide protection counselling, legal assistance and representation.  UNHCR will support community-based groups and build the capacity of local protection actors, such as community centers and providers of social and administrative services, to deliver support to conflict-affected populations and to build partnership with community-based organizations, with a focus on persons with specific needs.  In 2021, UNHCR will mobilize community participation in SGBV prevention and response. Persons with specific needs will receive individual protection assistance, using a cash-based modality wherever possible; as a component of comprehensive individual case management, including social accompaniment to assist persons access public services.  Persons with psycho-social assistance will receive psychological assistance. UNHCR will advocate for the adoption and implementation of laws and policies that protect the rights of IDPs, as well as conflict-affected persons living in areas along the line of contact, and in NGCA. ; In addition, UNHCR will support measures that ease movement across and along the line of contact. Protection by presence will be provided through a robust field presence along the line of contact and in NGCA. 

Throughout the response, particular attention will be given to minorities, older persons (who are disproportionately women), as well as persons with disabilities, since their needs receive less attention from other protection actors. 

UNHCR will operate a hotline for IDPs and conflict-affected persons. Hotline operators will provide protection counselling and make referrals to services. All complaints will be forwarded to UNHCR for follow-up. UNHCR will continue to assess all partners’ capacity to prevent and respond to cases of SEA, and support partners to implement best practices. As part of AAP, UNHCR will conduct a participatory assessment with IDPs and conflict-affected persons in 2021 to assess both protection risks and community capacities.

project_name: Increase access to quality education for refugee returnees, poor host community and IDPs
project_objective:
Access to education continues to be inadequate, with only 30 % of children aged six-13 years are enrolled in primary education and only 26 % of children aged 14-17 years are enrolled in secondary education. According to education cluster needs analysis 2021 an estimated 1.4 million school-aged children (45% girls) need humanitarian assistance, out of these children,1,139,632 are children from non-displaced families and 300,398 are children from displaced families.  According to UNHCR PRMN, an estimated 893,000 people have been displaced in Somalia between January and August 2020, of which 357,200 (40%) are school-aged children. According to Education Management Information System (EMIS) 2018/2019 systems across the country (FGS, Puntland & Somaliland), one million children are enrolled in schools which is 21% of school age children.

In addition, Somalia is also home to 35,884 refugee returnees’ school-aged children who need education support in 2021. This number excludes another 9,927 refugee returnees projected to return to Somalia in 2021. Due to limited livelihood opportunities for families of these children, parents cannot afford to meet the education cost; hence concerned children miss the opportunity to access quality primary and secondary education. There is a need to explore approaches to expand the reintegration of refugee returnees into the public schools.  There are limited intermediate/ secondary education opportunities for IDPs and returnees. Tradition, culture and religion make it difficult to reach the grass-root level, and females are constrained from expressing their ideas and needs.

In addressing the key gaps and needs identified in the Cluster Needs Analysis and other assessments outlined above, UNHCR will assist IDPs, poor host community and returnees in accessing education through provision of education grants and scholastic materials to the parents of each returnee child enrolled in school, parents will receive a cash grant for the school going child through mobile money transfer, The support shall be based on school term modality, whereby parents received cash grant of $ 30 per child. This will be paid in one or two installments.
 
In addition, UNHCR will support existing schools in areas of return to increase their absorption capacity, including; provision of scholastic materials, teaching and learning materials, and rehabilitation of school infrastructure (classrooms, construction of gender specific latrines, playgrounds and provision of sporting facilities/items, water points/hand washing sinks, etc.). UNHCR will also conduct teachers' training and awareness raising for Community Education Committees on child protection and mitigation of COVID-19 impacts. In coordination with the Ministry of Education and other relevant actors, UNHCR will also support interventions aimed at greater school attendance and retention of students, in particular of girls, including through providing sanitary and hygiene items to girls attending school.
Inclusion will be key to UNHCR’s approach; as such, UNHCR will support the Ministry of Education in integrating returnee children into the national public-school system in order to prevent the continuation of NGO-managed parallel systems.  Overall, UNHCR will work closely with the Ministry of Education and the Education Cluster, adopting a local area-based approach, where the emphasis is placed on supporting existing systems to increase capacities. UNHCR will support 46,034 students of returnees ( 25,319 boys,20,715 girls ) of which 4,603 (2,531 boys, 2,072 girls) are verified as living with various disability and they have difficulties in accessing education including lack of disability-friendly services in the schools, lack of qualified teachers and infrastructural challenges like ramps, UNHCR will work with partners to provide friendly services to children who are living with specials needs like training teachers on brails and providing assistive devices.

project_name: Contribution à la protection globale des populations affectées par la crise sécuritaire et humanitaire au Burkina Faso
project_objective: Depuis 2015, le Burkina Faso traverse une crise sécuritaire sans précédent à la suite d’attaques de groupes armés (GA) qui s’étendent notamment sur les régions du Sahel, de la Boucle du Mouhoun, du Nord, du Centre-Nord, du Centre Est, des Hauts-Bassins, des Cascades et de l’Est. L’activisme des GA, les opérations militaires de l’Etat, des forces régionales et internationales, et l’opérationnalisation des volontaires pour la défense de la patrie (VDP) ont provoqué progressivement des déplacements massifs de population dans presque toutes les régions du pays. Au 10 Novembre 2020, le Burkina Faso comptait 1.049.767 personnes déplacées internes (PDI) dont plus de 770.000 enregistrées sur une base individuelle par le CONASUR. 94% de ces PDI sont dans les régions du Centre Nord, Sahel, Nord, Est, Boucle du Mouhoun et Centre Est. Le Burkina Faso traverse ainsi une crise de protection du fait du nombre de PDI; de multiples déplacements que subissent les ménages; de l’inaccessibilité à certaines populations le long des frontières avec le Mali et le Niger; de certaines fragilités préexistantes à la crise notamment des conflits intercommunautaires souvent autour de la bonne gouvernance et celle foncière particulièrement; des tensions inter communautaires accentuées par des suspicions d’affiliation de certaines communautés aux GA ou aux milices armées ; de la présence dans ces régions de PDI, retournés Burkinabè, réfugiés, et communautés hôtes très vulnérables ayant tous des besoins de protection et vivant dans des zones avec un faible accès aux moyens de subsistance accentué par la crise sanitaire du COVID 19. Les PDI et leurs communautés d’accueil font face à l’insécurité, l’inaccessibilité ou la faible accessibilité aux vivres, à l’eau, à l’éducation, à la santé, au bien être psychosocial et aux moyens de subsistance dans des communes déjà fragilisées par l’impact du changement climatique. Dans sa stratégie du Sahel central, l’UNHCR a réaffirmé son accompagnement aux gouvernements dans leur gestion des populations affectées par la crise avec des activités de Protection, Education, Abris/Articles Ménagers Essentiels (AME), Energie et Environnement. Ces priorités définies par l’UNHCR sont en lien avec le plan d’actions prioritaires du programme d’urgence pour le Sahel-élargi, un programme gouvernemental visant à réduire l’impact de la crise sur les populations civiles, et à rechercher le développement et la bonne gouvernance. Fort de cette analyse de la crise de protection au Burkina Faso, de l’existence des cadres d’action de l’UNHCR et du gouvernement du Burkina Faso, et de sa volonté d’accompagner le cluster protection dans la réalisation de ses objectifs sectoriels dans le cadre du HRP 2021, l’UNHCR propose ce projet de protection des populations affectées par le conflit dans les 6 régions prioritaires autour de: L’enregistrement des PDI en soutien au CONASUR afin d’assurer que ces PDI puissent bénéficier d’une protection et d’une assistance humanitaire optimale ; La documentation des PDI, retournées et autres communautés vulnérables pour leur faciliter l’accès aux droits fondamentaux et leur éviter des violations de droits et libertés ; Le monitoring de protection qui complète l’analyse issue de l’enregistrement et qui tient compte de la mobilité des PDI ; L’engagement communautaire et la redevabilité qui sera renforcée dans tous les domaines d’intervention pour garantir la participation, l’inclusion, la communication avec les communautés et la redevabilité, l’éducation à la paix ; La protection contre les violences basées sur le genre (VBG) et la protection de l’enfant (PE) avec des activités de prévention, de mitigation de risques, de réponse multi sectoriels aux VBG et à la PE y compris l’assistance juridique et judiciaire ; La facilitation de l’accès consensuel et sécurisé des PDI à la terre au niveau individuel et collectif pour leur protection et pour une cohabitation pacifique.

project_name: Provision of essential primary health care to remote and vulnerable communities of Palestine refugees in the West Bank
project_objective: UNRWA's proposed intervention aims at ensuring the provision of primary health care for vulnerable Palestine Refugees in the West Bank.  Through the deployment of mobile heath teams, the project will provide essential health services to vulnerable and remote communities in Area C and East Jerusalem whose access to health services was significantly reduced due to access and movement restrictions exacerbated by the context of COVID-19 pandemic. Furthermore, the action will help preventing the spread of COVID-19 by distributing awareness raising material on best practices on how to prevent the transmission of the virus.

project_name: Emergency Health and MHPSS in Gaza
project_objective:
The global outbreak of COVID-19 is putting further pressure to the already overstretched health system in the Gaza Strip. UNRWA continues to provide essential primary health care services to 1.3 million Palestine refugees in Gaza, with adjusted approach with risk mitigation measures to provide services safely amidst COVID-19 outbreak. The public health system is overstretched responding to COVID-19 emergency, and expanding the capacity of the health services to absorb increasing needs is necessary to ensure access of vulnerable population to health services. Meanwhile, UNRWA’s ability to respond to emergency health needs in Gaza is greatly constrained by the tight funding situation compromising its ability to respond if necessary. 

In light of these conditions, this proposed intervention aims to support the provision of critical healthcare needs for Palestine refugees in the Gaza Strip, while alleviating the pressure on public health system, through: (1) ensuring access to secondary and tertiary health services for poor refugees,   (2) providing life-saving medicines , (3) hiring emergency surged staff to cope with increasing needs  and new interventions designed in response of COVID-19, (4) providing healthcare services adjusting COVID-19 emerged needs including telemedicine, the home delivery of medicine, triage system in all health centers and enhanced measures including strict use of PPEs,  (5) providing necessary assistive tools to children with special needs , and (6) providing mental health and psychosocial support especially women and people affected by COVID-19 emergency .

project_name: Restoring Women’s Dignity in Conflict Resettlement Areas
project_objective: WASH Hygiene Promotion: Support to girls and women, PSN, IDP, and hosting communities in hygiene NFI in the resettlement and or hosting areas by (i) distribution of women’s dignity and hygiene kits, and hygiene promotion as preventive measures against diarrheal diseases and COVID -19, (ii) access to water in quantity and quality for families, Access to appropriate sanitation and hygiene facilities, including management of solid waste and (iii) safe programming.

project_name: Support to the Food Security and Nutrition Analysis Unit (FSNAU) of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)
project_objective:
Given the precarious food security, nutrition and livelihood situation across Somalia, conducting timely assessments and analysis on a regular basis and continuous monitoring of the situation remains vital. At present, the Government of Somalia has limited institutional and technical capacity to generate and provide such data. To fill this gap, the FAO-led Food Security and Nutrition Analysis Unit (FSNAU) provides critical and timely information and analyses on the food security and nutrition situation in Somalia to a broad range of stakeholders.  FSNAU information and analyses facilitate and support effective evidence-based decision-making in support of humanitarian, recovery and development interventions. 

FSNAU identifies food insecure populations by livelihood and by district, pinpoints the specific challenges facing vulnerable groups, including women in achieving food security, and reports on the population’s nutritional status to support targeted interventions. In addition to its early warning function, FSNAU carries out relevant baseline livelihood studies for an improved understanding of underlying causes of food, nutrition and livelihood insecurity. Gender analysis is an integral part of FSNAU’s data collection analytical process. FSNAU also provides food security and nutrition related technical and institutional capacity development support to Somali government institutions and other key actors.

In 2021, FSNAU will continue to provide information and analysis on the current and emerging food security and nutrition situation in Somalia in a manner that supports prioritization and targeting of appropriate food security and nutrition response interventions. FSNAU will also provide additional information through its Early Warning Early Action Dashboard in order to support timely and prioritized response. Staff of relevant government institutions at Federal level, Federal Member State level and Somaliland will also be trained and supported to participate in seasonal food security and nutrition assessments and analyses.

FSNAU information products are disseminated through the FSNAU website (www.fsnau.org), mailing list and through regular as well as ad hoc presentations to stakeholders, including the Somalia Humanitarian Country Team.

The main beneficiaries of the information and analysis generated by FSNAU under this project will be government line ministries, UN agencies, local and international NGOs and resource partners. Indirect FSNAU project beneficiaries will be the millions of food insecure people and acutely malnourished children who are expected to benefit from humanitarian assistance and livelihood support provided by the Government, UN agencies, local and international NGOs and resource partners.

FSNAU and REACH provide complementary information and analysis to IASC Clusters in and the HRP/HNO process in Somalia. FSNAU primarily provides information and analyses that support the Food Security and Nutrition Clusters and REACH provides support to the other IASC clusters in Somalia.

project_name: Provision of Integrated Emergency Health and Nutrition Services for internally displaced persons and host communities in the North West Region of Cameroon
project_objective:
This project will be implemented in 4 health districts and 8 health facilities: HD Njikwa (IHC Konda and Oshie), Bengwi HD (IHC Bamunka and CMA Babessi). Stabilization centers in District Hospitals will be support. 
Nutrition:
Maternal, infant and young child nutrition in emergencies:
In order to ensure that good nutrition practices do not deteriorate and that poor practices are improved, IMC will conduct a mapping of existing activities and platforms that can be used for strengthening and improving Integrating Maternal Infant & Young Child Nutrition (MIYCN) practices; set up mother support groups as a platform for improving MIYCN practices (including identification and training of lead mothers and CHWs to supervise and support the lead mothers); conduct nutrition education sessions within communities to improve nutrition practices; carry out IYCF IEC during ANC/PNC visits; conduct individual counseling for mothers with breastfeeding or complementary feeding problems by a trained counselor; train of health staff, CHWs and lead mothers in MIYCN practices and education techniques; and conduct cooking demonstrations. 

b.	Sub-sector 2:  Management of acute malnutrition
IMC proposes to implement a CMAM program to ensure quality treatment of acute malnutrition following the Cameroon national protocols and international recommendations for providing treatment of acute malnutrition in the COVID-19 context.

Treatment of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) without medical complications in the Outpatient Therapeutic Program (OTP): Treatment of SAM will be implemented in OTP sites in the revitalized health centers and nutritional supplies for the OTPs (RUTF) will be provided by UNICEF. The program will be strengthened through technical support and capacity building activities such as training and supportive supervision to enable the OTP program sites and staff to treat cases appropriately. The OTP will take place on a bi-weekly basis due to COVID-19 and will use ready-to use therapeutic foods (RUTF) and routine medication as per Cameroon protocols (antibiotics, vitamin A, folic acid, anti-helminths, and anti-malarials if required).

Treatment of SAM with medical complications in the Stabilization Centers (SC): SAM cases with medical complications will be referred to Bamenda where SCs are fully functioning with support from different humanitarian actors. IMC will cover costs related to the referral including transport, medical bills and feeding during hospitalization. 

Outreach in the community: CHWs will inform the communities about malnutrition and the available treatment programs, conduct routine screening of children aged 6-59 months, trace absentees and defaulters and conduct home visits for problematic cases in order to reduce defaulter rates and increase access in the communities. The CHWs will also be responsible also for facilitating the distribution of iron/folic acid, vitamin A supplementation, MYICN education sessions, cooking demonstrations, and participation in national deworming campaigns. 
Health:
International Medical Corps’ implementation strategy for health activities will target four health districts in the North West region and provide support to eight public health facilities with basic essential services. The choice of the Mbengwi, Njikwa, Ndop and Fundong health districts and the targeted health facilities have been motivated by the number of those in need (IDPs, returnees and vulnerable host population); the needs and gaps identified at the health facility and community level, including access as well as the presence or absence of other partners and NGOs. As insecurity and the influx of IDPs have reduced access to quality health care in the targeted health districts, IMC’s focus will be to improve the provision of primary care through training, formative supervision, deployment of staff, identification and support of CHWs and donations of medical equipment and drugs.

project_name: Improving access to essential health services among vulnerable migrants and host communities in Lebanon
project_objective: This project aims to support vulnerable individuals overcome barriers to accessing healthcare in Lebanon, while also supporting Lebanon’s ailing health system against pressures linked to deteriorating economic conditions and against the continued challenges posed by COVID-19. The project will provide essential health services across the continuum of care either through an implementing partner where a gap exists or in close coordination with partners already providing the services.These services are at the level of primary Healthcare, the advanced diagnostics, ER and hospital coverage. All interventions will be closely coordinated with MOPH, WHO, the Health sector and the active partners. The selection of supported facilities is based on the geographical distribution of migrants and is done in close collaboration with MOPH–PHC department aiming at expanding the partners existing support. The PHCs providing specialized services will be prioritized. The modalities follow the existing support schemes by providing subsidized consultation fees for the available pre-defined packages in addition to the running costs incurring from the additional working hours. Focus will also be given to providing mental health support as well as reproductive health support to the most vulnerable migrants. Above activities will be reinforced by supporting 2 hospitals to continue with their essential services focusing on a migrant-dense area. The selection of the 2 hospitals is based on the discussions with MOPH and partners planning to provide such support as well as with the Health sector.  The support will entail providing its operational needs on an emergency basis to continue with its operations. Facilities with psychiatric wards, OPD and vaccination center will be prioritized. Finally, the project will continue supporting the COVID-19 response in complementarity with the existing support.Homecare support for vulnerable migrants will be strengthened through 2 homecare teams, one covering BML and the South and one covering Beqaa and the North.  The team is composed from a practitioner, a community healthcare worker and a social worker. This team will provide medical care and follow up as well as health education and necessary support to the patient, his caregivers and family. Each team will be able to cover 25 patients at a time. Those 2 teams will be assisted with one mobile team of a nutritionist and a physical therapist to cover the post-COVID rehabilitation needs of a smaller number of patients. Under the COVID section, IOM will as well support the cost of PCR testing requested for vulnerable migrants to undertake surgeries or be admitted to mental health facilities or shelters. IPC trainings for all frontliners are planned and supported under the C19RM successful application that will be channeled through the Middle East Response funded by Global Fund which IOM is the primary recipient. A network of community mobilizers will be engaged in accordance with the sector guidance and equipped with the necessary trainings and materials to deliver quality, integrated health messaging including COVID 19 prevention and vaccination. Communication will be done following different channels and in the different migrant languages. Upon the request of multiple partners and noting that many partners are new to migrant programming; IOM aims to provide a cultural adaptation training. The main objective is to render the services migrant friendly and accessible to this vulnerable group. Building on IOM’s active work with the national IHR focal point to assess the POE’s in regards to COVID 19 preventive measures and the gaps identified and in close coordination with UNICEF, IOM aims to strengthen the COVID 19 preventive measures  5 key POE: Masnaa, Qaa, Aaboudieh, Aarida, Bokayaa  by strengthening MOPH capacity at the said POE through deployment of Port Health Officers in addition to the development and implementation of relevant SOP and a TOT for non-health actors

project_name: Building the resilience of conflict- and COVID-19-affected communities in Ukraine’s Eastern Conflict Area through livelihood restoration and socio-economic early recovery
project_objective:
The action will contribute to enhanced resilience of vulnerable communities affected by conflict and the COVID-19 pandemic through livelihood restoration and recovery activities aimed at strengthening food security and supporting employment and self-employment of IDPs, returnees and most vulnerable social groups.

IOM will use a variety of approaches to boost individual, household and community income-generation on both sides of the contact line. All activities will be tailored to the assessed needs, location, socio-political context and level of access granted. IOM will support individuals working in the following economic spheres: retail, production, agriculture and services.

Self-sustenance grants will be directed to communities residing along both sides of the line of contact (LoC), focusing on isolated areas with limited livelihood opportunities. Self-sustenance grants are meant to assist households scale up their self-subsistence activities, which can both enhance their food security and allow them to produce additional food products for small scale income generation. 

Support will be provided to micro businesses to boost their income and employment capacities, through the procurement of necessary equipment, improvement of managerial and technical knowledge, as well as coaching and mentoring. The aim of these grants will be to reduce operational costs, maintenance expenditure and also the risk of failure due to sudden shocks in the marked, such as those induced by the COVID-19 pandemic.

To further support most vulnerable conflict-affected communities, IOM will invite SME’s to submit proposals for employment creation and for socio-economic early recovery. These grants will specifically target activities that will enable job creation for most vulnerable social groups in conflict-affected areas, as well as businesses that have a wide impact on the local community. 

Lastly, as piloted in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, IOM will continue its MPC support to vulnerable livelihoods beneficiaries. 

Additionally, IOM will support beneficiaries in increasing the production capacity of their businesses as well as to ensure that their business remain functioning and less affected by the impact of COVID-19 outbreak, enhancing the quality of their produced goods and provided services through the development of business education plans. After having identified needs, business owners will be able to attend education classes on various topics such as crises management, gender, environment, access to finance, customs rights, official employments, taxes, etc. that will be listed in the education plans agreed with each beneficiary separately.  IOM plans to launch a hotline for entrepreneurs who are willing to receive up-to-date information on changes in the legislation, governmental projects for entrepreneurs and taxes. In case the hotline workers will not be able to address the issues and concerns raised by the entrepreneurs, the callers will be redirected to other hotlines run by the government, NGOs, INGOs and UN-agencies.

project_name: ENHANCING PREPAREDNESS AND RESPONSE CAPACITY  TO DISEASE DUE TO NATURAL DISASTER IN AT-RISK COMMUNITIES IN BURUNDI
project_objective:
Burundi is facing a crisis that combines the devastating effects of natural disasters and burden of communicable diseases in the country. It is located in an earthquake-prone geographic zone of the Great Lakes, thereby increasing the risk of the country to be affected by a catastrophic event. Natural disasters due to climate change such as floods and storms have negatively impacted the country through repeated displacement. Occasionally, dangerous storms involving violent winds and torrential rains cause severe damage to property and populations, particularly in rural areas.
According to the latest DTM data, at the end of August 2020, the number of IDPs identified in Burundi’s 18 provinces stood at 131,336 (28,333 households), of which 83 per cent were displaced due to natural disasters , including a majority of women (55%). Using Emergency Event Tracking figures, IOM estimates that between August 2018 and August 2020, 8,969 houses were totally destroyed and 17,075 houses were partially destroyed due to climatic events (142 torrential rains, 12 severe landslides, 65 strong winds, 7 main destructive floods and hail). The protection monitoring reports of UNHCR show that a majority of returnees did not have access to their houses and did not have viable income-generating activities – leaving families with the critical need to find emergency shelter with negative impact on the health status. 
At the end of June 2020, the number of IDPs identified in Burundi’s 18 provinces stood at 136,610 (29,384 households).
Climate change also presents significant direct and indirect risks to public health. Many aspects of health are also influenced by climatic and weather conditions and should be considered in this response. A direct link to health includes illnesses from increased frequency and severity of extreme weather events such as precipitation, flooding, droughts, and storms. The ongoing cholera outbreak that was declared in December 2018 started from Rumonge. The outbreak is linked to heavy rains that caused flooding and consequently contamination of water, which allowed it to spread. Malaria is also a major public health issue in the country and was the second leading cause of mortality in Burundi in 2017. 
In 2018, there were approximately 3.1 million reported cases of malaria or approximately 8,500 cases per day Cases increased especially during the rainy season, which is a factor that is often linked to flooding resulting in standing water that creates breeding sites for mosquitoes. Given the struggling public health system in Burundi, capacity strengthening of the local health systems is essential in order to increase resilience and adapt to the changing climate’s effect on health. Finally, On January 23, 2019, 162 cases of malaria, including 2 deaths, were reported in Rumonge and Bujumbura Mairie and more than 90% of the cases were identified in Rumonge.
The ongoing worldwide COVID-19 pandemic, which started in China in Hubei province, has not spared the Republic of Burundi. The first cases of COVID-19 were declared on the 31st of March 2020. As of 10th, December, a total number of confirmed cases is 732 with 2 associated official deaths. 
WHO has recommended several measures including but not limit to, social distancing.  Displaced people, such as those located in Gatumba internal displaced sites,   are more vulnerable to COVID-19 because they are living in high densely populated where social distancing, addition to the lack of sanitation can be challenging. 
Moreover, internal displaced people are exposed to violence, belongings and family member’s loss which can have grave impact on mental health. When the internal displaces status is combined with the fear of contracting communicable disease including coronavirus, anxiety, depression, sleep disorders, psychological distress and post-traumatic stress disorder will increase and impact well-being and daily activities.

project_name: Water, sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) support to health and social institutions in Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts to enhance safe and qualitative service delivery
project_objective:
This project aims to support health and social institutions (hereafter referred to as SIs) in the field of WASH in Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts to enhance safe and qualitative service delivery to conflict-affected communities by providing hygiene kits, WASH-related equipment and hygiene items. 

A well-functioning WASH infrastructure is crucial for the health and wellbeing of the conflict-affected communities in Eastern Ukraine. The protracted conflict has not only caused direct damage to this infrastructure but has also aggravated the tight funding situation, a situation which has been further affected by the COVID-19 pandemic. This threatens to disrupt services but also increased the risks SI staff members are exposed to.

In order to alleviate the pressure on these facilities, IOM will distribute COVID-19 hygiene kits, including information leaflets on COVID-19 protective measures and hygiene practices, to 175 SIs. As IOM is currently responding to 175 institutions in NGCA/GCA, IOM will approach current receiving institutions to see if top-up kits are required.  In addition, WASH-related equipment will be procured, delivered and installed at 80 SIs to facilitate their work and reduce the risk of infections. As elderly people are particularly vulnerable and underserved, the project also foresees the distribution of adult diapers to 125 SIs. Hygiene kits are in line with cluster guidance and will include cleaning tools, disinfection material in line with WHO recommendations for COVID-19, washing powder/fluid to allow turnover of communal use items (linens /plates/cutlery) and some personal use items identified by SI that assist in the management of individuals with mobility issues and those who are bed ridden to make hygiene management easier. These will enable the facilities to maintain the increased cleaning schedules that are advised by WHO and local legislation to help mitigate against the spread of COVID-19.  

Identification of institutions in GCA will be done through coordination with WASH cluster primarily with secondary coordination with health clusters in relation to IPC based on relevant cluster gaps analysis. These locations and institutions will be further coordinated with regional and local authorities to ensure that most in need locations from the oblast perspective are being considered. Sanitary equipment procured will be determined through a needs assessment at the institution level to ensure that it is necessary and appropriate. Hygiene kit content will be based on cluster guidance and advised through PDM results and revised needs assessments at the facility level. In NGCA, given the restrictions, IOM will leverage IP knowledge of the operating environment and needs assessments where possible to advise on both hygiene kit content review and sanitary equipment provision.

project_name: Enhancing the capacities of medical and social institutions as well as EECPs to meet the urgent health needs of conflict- and COVID-affected populations in ECA
project_objective:
This project aims to support conflict-affected populations as well as medical and social workers in Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts by contributing to a reduced risk of infection with COVID-19 and improving access to medical care.
The protracted conflict in Eastern Ukraine continues to have a negative impact on medical institutions (MIs, including hospitals and health care centers) and social institutions (SIs, including those working with the elderly, disabled persons or orphans), which are highly dependent on scarce public funding. In the GCA and NGCA alike, insufficient funding is leading to a lack of essential equipment and consequently reduces MIs’ and SIs’ capacity to provide necessary (and often lifesaving) care to the most vulnerable . 
The already dire situation has been exacerbated by the severe consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic. Institutions across the targeted intervention area need personal protective equipment (PPE) to reduce the risk of infections among their staff and avoid undue limitations of their critical work. Furthermore , limited awareness of COVID-19 preventive behaviour and a lack of social distancing increase the risk of transmission for the general population.
Through this project, IOM will provide medical and other equipment to MIs and Sis based on a thorough needs assessment to be jointly conducted with local authorities; In addition, IOM will distribute PPE to MI and SI employees and social workers in the targeted institutions, further to raising awareness on the risks of COVID-19 as well as preventive behaviour among SI staff; and provide health-related equipment   and support to Entry-Exit Checkpoints (EECPs) to reduce the risk of infection. IOM has already provided PPE to EECPs and is currently providing medical equipment to Stanitsa Luganska. The proposed activities are a scale up of current interventions in light of gaps identified and the continued threat of COVID 19. 

IOM will primarily target SI staff for PPE assistance given their engagement with vulnerable COVID 19 groups including the elderly, people with disabilities and people with chronic diseases. Their ability to act as vectors places these groups at extreme risk of contracting COVID 19. This concern was raised by the Ministry of Social Policy to IOM as the earliest cases within their staff was contracted on a home visit and subsequently spread due to lack of proper equipment. 
Further, regional authorities and assessments conducted with SI indicated that there was a need for small scale life support equipment at SIs to assist residents struggling to breathe until appropriate medical care is able to reach them. Due to the nature of the groups in residential care (elderly, individuals with severe disabilities and chronic diseases) they are more vulnerable to the impact and reportedly less of a priority to move as they are already in care.
EECP will also be targeted due to the continued concern over them acting as vectors. Humanitarian partners have consistently raised concerns over the management of crossings and lack of sufficient assistance. This places border guards (SBG) and those crossing at risk which is a high percentage of elderly in normal times.  The ability of EECP staff to ensure safer practices and have life saving equipment on site increases their ability to better manage the needs and safety of vulnerable groups crossing the LoC. As such EECPs will be provided with PPE and other equipment gaps identified during previous assessments, these have included defibrillators and other emergency primary care equipment and relevant first aid and trauma care training. IOM assessments identified that despite the presence of humanitarian first aid points the working hours are insufficient and ambulances can take over half an hour to arrive. As such, SBG need both training and equipment to manage the needs outside of humanitarian first aid points working hours.

project_name: Mitigating negative impact of COVID-19 pandemic on  human trafficking, exploitation and abuse among the most vulnerable communities in Eastern Conflict Area
project_objective:
The project aims to mitigate the exacerbating impact of COVID-19 on human trafficking  exploitation and abuse among vulnerable population in Eastern Conflict Area of Ukraine (ECA) by providing holistic and tailored social protection assistance to community members (including men, women and children) and though carrying out prevention activities.  

The severe decrease of economic opportunities in Ukraine and ECA specifically due to COVID-19 pandemic in addition to the protracted conflict, compounded by ramping unemployment rates, scarcely efficient social services and precarious social safety-nets, had already increased the strain on the most vulnerable groups within displaced and host communities, who were often left with no choice but resort to negative coping mechanisms. As a result, the most fragile social segments are left vulnerable to drivers of instability and to protection risks including vulnerability to trafficking in persons, exploitation and abuse – as well as more prone to resort to undesired migration and/or other negative coping strategies. Furthermore, not all types of protection and assistance needed by VoTs returning to Ukraine or (potentially) exploited in the country are available from the State.

In order to mitigate growing risks of human trafficking, exploitation and abuse in ECA, IOM aims to ensure access of vulnerable population to comprehensive rehabilitation and reintegration assistance tailored to individual needs of beneficiaries. IOM will leverage protection partner networks and capacities of the state-led National Referral Mechanism in the conflict area to offer assistance in safe and confidential manner. IOM’s activities include legal aid, medical care, mental health and psychosocial support, financial support, vocational training, and other types of assistance to (potential) victims of trafficking, exploitation and abuse. Concurrently, IOM will carry out preventive measures raising awareness about risks of trafficking and exploitation and providing contacts of the currently operating hotlines , which provide information on safe migration and employment as well as providing further referrals to protection assistance for vulnerable population. Furthermore IOM share information on regular/safe migration and employment, prevention of trafficking and exploitation within youth, unemployed, newly graduates from vocational and technical schools etc.

project_name: Provision of Emergency and essential health services for IDP and Host communities in Burdhubo and Luuq Districts, Gedo Region.
project_objective:
Access to adequate health services, particularly for women and children, is significantly restricted by social barriers, poor infrastructure, low service quality, high levels of insecurity, and a limited number of health facilities and trained health workers. Relative security in Burdhubo and Luuq towns provides an opportunity to improve health services in both districts significantly. This proposal focuses explicitly on the urgent health care needs existing in Burdhubo and Luuq districts (Northern side), to be implemented over one year. 

The project targets 37,048 (18,820 female, 18,288 male, 2,595 boys and 2595 girls, and 739 elderly) beneficiaries from both host and IDP communities with healthcare services, out of which 1,852 beneficiaries are people with disabilities. This project will directly contribute to the Health cluster objectives of reducing excess morbidity and mortality due to disease outbreak driven by climatic shocks and conflict, contribute to improvement in the physical and mental well-being of the population affected by conflict and displacement, improve case management and referral services for survivors of sexual or gender-based violence and improve equitable access to quality emergency and essential health services. The proposal is also aligned to the Ministry of Health (MoH) strategic plan Objective 1 and 4, which focuses on improving the Somali population's health, focusing on maternal and child health and the cluster objectives. 

Towards this end, Trocaire will work jointly with the Ministry of Health and Community Health Committees to improve staff and health facilities (static and outreach) to provide essential healthcare. This will include building the capacity of   MoH team and Community Health Committees to provide these services fully in the near future, equipment of health facilities, widening the reach by breaking geographical, infrastructural, cultural and economic barriers to access to health, investing in prevention measures through vaccination exercises and community awareness-raising, and prepositioning of supplies in anticipation for a crisis.

The programme's intended impact is to: Contribute towards improved health, particularly for women of childbearing age and children under-five, by providing health care services at the targeted facilities in Burdhubo (2 health facilities) and Luuq Districts (2 health facilities). The programme builds on Trócaire's 28 years of experience operating in Gedo. It will work closely with the Ministry of Health and the community through community structures- District Health Boards (DHBs)-, to provide quality healthcare services that meet MoH and Health cluster standards. The DHBs are community-based governance structures that have proven to be an effective and sustainable model in delivering healthcare services in the region. This programme complements Trócaire's existing programme providing the EPHS in Four districts (Belet Xaawo, Dollow, Garbaharey, and Luuq) of Gedo.

project_name: Provision of Life-Saving Emergency Shelter and Non-Food Items Assistance in Sudan
project_objective:
This project will ensure that the most vulnerable populations affected by conflict or natural disasters with specific needs have timely access to Emergency Shelter (ES) and Non-Food Items (NFI) assistance. This project contributes to the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) Strategic Objective 1: Provide timely multi-sectoral life-saving assistance to crisis affected people to reduce mortality and morbidity; and Strategic Objective 2: Contribute to building resilience to recurrent shocks and improving vulnerable people’s access to basic services. 
IOM proposes to purchase and preposition 30,000 NFI kits and 20,000 Emergency shelters as a preparedness measure for addressing the needs of newly displaced and vulnerable people with special needs in the protracted displaced populations in 14 different states. Emergency Shelter and Non-Food Items assessment missions will Utilize DTM Data to select the most vulnerable households to be assisted with Emergency Shelter and NFI kits. IOM will also transport the emergency shelters and Non-Food items for the distribution locations. Distribution will be provided to the most vulnerable populations in selected states through close coordination with ES/NFI sector lead and partners as well as government bodies to ensure consistency in provision of assistance and to mitigate assistance duplication. As a final stage IOM will Undertake Post Distribution Monitoring mission to monitor usage of the distributed items after 2 to 4 weeks of the distributions.

project_name: UNICEF Humanitarian & Recovery WASH response in Eastern Ukraine 2021
project_objective:
UNICEF intends to support the Coordination in the WASH sector, essential to strategize and optimize the intervention of all actors in WASH.
After reviewing different assessments, keeping in view the situations in East, needs, capacity and comparative advantage, UNICEF is planning to respond the needs of 0.8 million individuals in the two conflict affected areas of Donetska and Luhanska oblasts (GCA and NGCA) and Ivano-Frankivsk, Chernivtsi and Zakarpattia Oblasts in western Ukraine, with provision of safe drinking water, improving access to safe sanitation and hygiene supplies, dissemination of critical water and hygiene related messages on communities located on both side of contact line in the two oblasts of  Eastern Ukraine, and to respond actively to the COVID-19 emergency. 
This will be implemented through the water utility companies (centralized network of primary and secondary water suppliers) and decentralized structures (in NGCA). A particular focus will be made on WASH in social institutions (education/health facilities) on both GCA and NGCA.
The different activities take into account the gender, age and disabilities specificities and promote equality, especially on gender. People reached with more than one activity are only considered once to avoid duplication in counting beneficiaries.
The COVID-19 pandemic has furthered hampered the situation in Eastern Ukraine, for the conflict-affected population, suffering from the restriction of movement, the resulting economic crisis and being more and more directly affected by the disease. Institutions such as Health centers, Social institutions, educational facilities, are deeply impacted, depleting the level and quality of services too be provided to the population.
Also, Western Ukraine was part of the regions where people were among the first affected by the pandemic; Roma populations, often amid difficult conditions, are at particular risk; UNICEF proposes to support their HHs directly and through the public services the Roma frequent (health centers, social institutions, educational facilities…), and insist on hygiene messages (COVID-related, but also, menstrual hygiene etc.).

The total amount for the project is 6,245,044 USD, to provide assistance to 814,506 people.

project_name: Saving Lives and Livelihoods in Rural Somalia
project_objective:
Somalia faced a growing number of threats to its food security in 2020, starting with the ongoing Desert Locust crisis, followed by COVID-19 first reported in March, severe flooding between April and September and poor rains forecast for the Deyr 2020 season. Based on latest projections, 2.1 million Somalis are in IPC Phases 3 and above through December 2020. Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of the La Nina developing, which tends to trigger dry conditions in Somalia. If the forecast below-average Deyr rains (Oct-Dec 2020) is followed by below-average or delayed 2021 Gu rains (Apr-Jun), this could lead to a rapid and substantial worsening of the humanitarian situation. 

Rural populations are at a high risk of further deteriorating food security, given the direct and indirect impacts of these threats on rural livelihoods, related assets, food production and income. FAO’s proposal responds both to the lifesaving and life-sustaining needs of rural populations in IPC Phases 3 and above, against a Population in Need (PiN) of 3.1 million people prioritized for Food Security Cluster (FSC) assistance under the 2021 HRP. FAO’s planned activities will directly support 103,850 households in IPC 3-4 under both FSC Strategic Objectives (SOs), while further delivering support to protect food security in Somalia at a wider scale through countrywide animal health campaigns, among other activities. 

Under SO1, to improve access to food, FAO will deliver lifesaving cash assistance to 76,300 rural households, including IDPs, in the form of Cash+, UCT and CFW activities delivered through FAO’s e-Platform for Mobile Money and Livelihood Assistance. All cash-based programmes include trainings on good nutrition practices, covering infancy to old age.

Under SO2, to protect livelihoods, FAO will provide in-kind and technical support to anticipate, mitigate and respond to food security threats across Somalia’s rural livelihood zones, including the delivery of integrated cash and livelihood support to 53,500 households targeted for Cash+ interventions under SO1 (while supporting an additional 7,550 households with agricultural inputs only). FAO’s planned Cash+ activities combine cash transfers with tailored livelihood support packages to assist rural families out of hunger sooner. Alongside cash transfers, the assistance packages will protect and restore the livelihoods of households in IPC Phases 3-4 by providing: (i) farmers with quality inputs to produce a nutritious variety of food crop (cereal, pulse and vegetable seeds, storage bags, fertilizer and irrigation/tractor services, where appropriate; (ii) pastoralists with nutrient-rich feed blocks and deworming to improve livestock productivity especially milk supply; and (iii) coastal communities with a variety of basic fishing gear and processing equipment to improve catch and consumption.  

Also under SO2, in anticipation of drought conditions in early 2021, FAO will also strategically position water bladder tanks and provide nutritive animal feed blocks to protect the small milking animals of up to 20,000 pastoral households impacted by scarce pasture from dry conditions and/or locust damage. Countrywide livestock vaccination and supportive treatment campaigns will further protect livestock assets belonging to at least 2.2 million men, women and children. Preparedness for animal health emergencies will be enhanced through strategic stocking of vaccines and related supplies (PPR), and training to local partners in Livestock Emergency Guidelines and Standards (LEGS), antimicrobial resistance, disease surveillance and reporting, among others.

project_name: UNICEF Education in Emergencies Response 2021
project_objective: UNICEF’s response will serve children and teachers in conflict affected areas of eastern Ukraine with essential interventions that will ensure continuation of education in the time of COVID-19 pandemic and address immediate and cumulative impacts of the protracted armed conflict. 75,000 boys and girls will benefit from a range of activities that ensure their access to safe, inclusive and enabling learning environment and improve quality of teaching and learning. Over 60% of these boys and girls live and learn in Non-Government Controlled Areas (NGCA) where humanitarian needs are most severe. 500 schools on both side of the Line of Contact (LoC) will be supported with implementation of COVID-19 infection prevention and control protocols. 450 education professionals in NGCA and GCA will be trained on identified priority topics that enable them to deliver conflict-sensitive, risk-informed and life-skills-based education. UNICEF will work with the Ukraine Education Cluster partners to support the Government in implementation of the Safe Schools Declaration commitments to protect schools during the armed conflict.

project_name: UNICEF Maternal and Child Health Emergency Response 2021
project_objective: UNICEF proposes to enhance access to the conflict-affected population in Eastern Ukraine to quality maternal and child health services by strengthening capacity of health workers, increasing access to basic and essential Maternal and Child Health services, increasing awareness of IYCF practices and immunisation, and provision of supportive services for PLHIV, children and adolescents. UNICEF also proposes to respond to the current COVID-19 crisis in affected areas in Eastern Ukraine by supporting health facilities essentially through the procurement of supplies and equipment needed for the ongoing outbreak, as well as to provide facilities and health workers with skills, knowledge and resources for optimal infection prevention and control measures.

project_name: Conflict and Disaster-affected Children have Access to Inclusive Quality Education
project_objective: The project objective is to improve access to inclusive quality basic education for 37,226 girls and 42,941 boys, including children with disabilities, who are affected by conflict and natural disasters in 9 localities in North Darfur, Kassala, and White Nile states. This will be accomplished through improving facilities and furnishing schools affected by heavy rains and floods. The school facilities will be designed, constructed, and maintained to be resilient to flooding. The learning will be supported by the provision of teaching and learning supplies, recreational materials, as well as menstrual health and hygiene kits for adolescent girls. Safe water and sanitation facilities will be constructed that are gender sensitive and friendly for children with disabilities and teachers/PTAs will be trained on COIVD-19 School Protocol. Teachers will be trained on Package for Teachers in Crisis Contexts and provided teaching supplies. PTAs will be strengthened to participate in school governance, develop School Improvement Plans, and carry out awareness raising activities on the rights of all children to education and identifying and addressing oppressive norms that hold girls and boys back. The target schools will be linked to child protection, psychosocial services, and child protection referral pathways will be established.

project_name: Monitoring de protection et assistance aux populations affectées par la crise dans les régions du nord et du centre du Mali.
project_objective:
Le HCR met en œuvre le système de monitoring de protection, en partenariat avec AMSS, dont l'objectif principal est d’améliorer l'environnement de protection des populations civiles dans les régions du Mali, touchées par le conflit, en renforçant la collecte, l'analyse et la diffusion d'informations, ainsi que son utilisation par les acteurs humanitaires et de développement. Le projet comprend 4 piliers, à savoir : 1) la prévention et le renforcement de la résilience communautaire ; 2) la collecte et le partage d’information sur les violations de droits humains et les risques de protection ; 3) le référencement pour la prise en charge des victimes ; 4) le plaidoyer pour le respect des droits. Le système de monitoring de protection couvre les régions de Tombouctou, Gao, Kidal, Ménaka, Mopti, Ségou. Il repose sur 57 moniteurs, 188 points focaux communautaires, 168 membres de 42 comités locaux de protection communautaire. 
Le monitoring de protection est désormais un outil inter-agence au service de la centralité de la protection. Il offre une fenêtre unique de collaboration et de partenariat permettant de déterminer les violations de droits humains, mais également d’orienter la réponse et le plaidoyer de l’ensemble du Cluster Protection.
Le lien essentiel entre le monitoring, la prévention et la réponse doit être assuré. Ainsi, le HCR renforcera sa réponse aux besoins de protection des personnes déplacées internes. Cette réponse s’articulera autour de plusieurs axes à savoir notamment la lutte contre les Violences Basées sur le Genre, le soutien aux Personnes ayant des Besoins Spécifiques, le Renforcement du cadre légal de protection des PDIs au Mali.   En outre, le HCR contribuera à la coordination et à la gestion des sites de déplacement en collaboration avec les autorités maliennes à travers la DNDS et l’OIM.

project_name: Renforcement de la coordination et du plaidoyer humanitaire au Tchad
project_objective:
Le projet vise à renforcer le rôle de OCHA dans la mise en œuvre de son mandat et son rôle auprès des partenaires humanitaires et gouvernementaux au niveau des fonctions coordination, gestion de l’information et plaidoyer. Le bureau national d’OCHA à N’Djaména et ses trois sous-bureaux régionaux à l’Est (Abéché) au Sud (Goré) et la province du Lac (Baga Sola) mettent l’accent sur l’opérationnalisation de ses fonctions y compris en assurant une lien entre les activités humanitaires et de développement (nexus) en vue de promouvoir une solution durable visant à ne pas perpétuer une situation de dépendance humanitaire. Dans le cadre de cette nouvelle façon de travailler outre l’opérationnalisation du nexus, le lien avec les objectifs commun des programmes développement, paix et sécurité sera mis en avant. L’accent est aussi mis sur le renforcement de la coordination civilo-militaire afin de faciliter l’accès et la protection des civils.

Le projet a pour but de renforcer la coordination d’une réponse humanitaire rapide et efficace afin de sauver des vies et protéger les personnes affectées par les situations de crises au Tchad. Une coordination humanitaire rapide et correctement évaluée au niveau des besoins de la population affectée permettra aux acteurs humanitaires de mieux identifier et répondre aux besoins humanitaires, de renforcer la préparation de réponse aux urgences à travers le renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et plus spécifiquement l‘Equipe humanitaire pays, la coordination inter-clusters, la coordination civilo-militaire, les clusters et les mécanismes de coordination au niveau de terrain.
Le projet vise aussi à assurer le plaidoyer humanitaire à travers l’analyse des besoins faites par l’ensemble de la communauté humanitaire et ses partenaires en vue une compréhension commune des problématiques auxquels fait face le Tchad, ses causes profondes, l’impact sur les populations. OCHA jouera un rôle clé dans la création d'espaces de collection et d'analyse et gestion d’informations, pour assurer une stratégie de réponse coordonnée menant à des actions humanitaires répondant aux besoins les plus aigus et être mieux préparé face aux urgences soudaines. Le projet permettra également d’assurer conjointement avec la communauté humanitaire le plaidoyer en faveur du respect des principes humanitaires, de la protection des civils, de l'accès humanitaire et pour la mobilisation et l'allocation efficace de ressources humanitaires.

Un accent a été mis sur la mise en œuvre des plans d’action de la redevabilité envers les populations affectées (AAP), la PSEA et la préparation aux urgences en plus d'intégrer une attention au genre et de renforcer la centralité de la protection.
Un plaidoyer pour plus de visibilité des résultats tangibles au niveau de la réponse facilitant la mobilisation de ressources pour les différentes crises au Tchad (mouvement de population – crise du Bassin du Lac Tchad, insécurité alimentaire et malnutrition, urgences sanitaires) est aussi défini comme une priorité dans ce projet 

OCHA continuera de jouer également un rôle moteur dans le renforcement du lien entre les acteurs humanitaires et de développement et la transformation de la réponse humanitaire, en lien avec les engagements pris au Sommet humanitaire mondial de 2016 et ceci à travers la nouvelle façon de travailler (NWOW) et le renforcement de l’utilisation de la modalité de transfert monétaire.
