project_name: COMMUNITY BASED PROTECTION, SGBV PREVENTION & CHILD PROTECTION RESPONSE IN MUDUG AND GALGADDUD REGIONS
project_objective:
Decades of prolonged conﬂict and insecurity, drought and massive displacement in Mudug and Galgaduud regions have placed women, girls and children in extreme vulnerability and at increased risk of gender-based violence (GBV), during the 2020 dyer rains Mudug region was one of the most affected, with very high levels of displacement and food insecurity. Children are being used for a range of military purposes: ground combat, assassinations, intelligence collection and logistical support. Female and child-headed households remain at risk of sexual violence, abuse and exploitation. For CAAFAG, it is estimated that there are between 3,000-5,000 CAAFAG in Somalia, but these are only estimates; actual numbers could be larger. Grave violations against children are expected to continue with the ongoing military offensive and prolonged conflict. While the humanitarian response has stabilized ﬂoods and famine affected populations, perpetual external shocks limit the population’s access to basic services causing ﬂuctuating levels of vulnerability. As a result, women and children are forced to adopt risky and sometimes harmful coping strategies, including collection and sale of ﬁrewood and payment of debt through forced marriage. Pressure for survival intensiﬁes the potential for intimate partner violence. Furthermore, the modalities of aid assistance have sometimes exacerbated vulnerability and risk of exploitation. WISE is proposing the following interventions to lifesaving GBV and protection services to at risk population in Galmudug state of Somalia. The proposed interventions are designed to increase women and adolescent girls’ access to life saving GBV case management psychosocial support services and protection to reduce risks of GBV, integrate protection monitoring and mainstreaming into the GBV intervention to improve the overall context analysis and integration of protection principles in the intervention that will be scaled up to respond the identiﬁed needs. WISE will utilize existing internal response capacity to staff these teams to provide timely, effective and eﬃcient GBV and protection response during the project. This will provide much needed humanitarian services in mudug and Galgaduud to areas without GBV and protection services.
Since early 2020 through WISE’s existing programming, and in line with protection cluster ﬁndings, WISE has noted increasing and targeted attacks against women and girls with growing levels of sexual violence perpetrated. These are linked to the escalating insecurity, militarization of political leadership and mobilization of armed groups. Girls are particularly vulnerable to multiple forms of violence and have limited support systems and access to information. Based on the programming experiences in Galkayo, Dhusamareb and Adaado the majority of girls are out of school, experience growing levels of sexual violence abductions, sexual harassment, early and forced marriage, sexual exploitation and abuse and have restrictions placed on their movement by their families. 400 GBV cases were reported by women and children over the last 10 months (GBVIMS, December 2019-August 2020); 39% were rape and 48% were physical/domestic violence. Over the last year WISE has been building capacity in case management and provision of support to rape survivors However, due to post-rape kits pipeline gaps no rape survivors were provided with post rape treatment, there are currently no safe shelters or material support for survivors to access services. It is necessary to improve the quality of care by; reception of GBV cases, referral services and material assistance and safe shelter support. Communities, authorities and humanitarian actors lack awareness of GBV risks and consequences and have limited practical involvement for GBV prevention and response.

project_name: Child Protection for most affected IDP, returnees and host community children and care givers in Somaliland, Puntland, South West State and Jubaland
project_objective: Somali children are described to live in one of the least protective environments in the world due to the cyclical occurrence of the man-made and natural disasters. This scenario has broken down the child protection systems and structures and weakened the capacity for delivery of services in spite of the concerted efforts of community, government, donors and partners. COVID-19 pandemic, floods and the locust invasion in 2020 has further exacerbated child protection risks due to their impact on household livelihoods thus exposing children to negative coping mechanisms like child labour, separation, FGM and child marriage. Access to CP services such as psychosocial support activities ceased with government sanctioned lockdowns to prevent COVID 19 spread. The goal of this project is to ensure boys and girls including those with disabilities, facing life- threatening risks of abuse, neglect, violence, exploitation, and severe distress have access to well- coordinated and disability, gender- sensitive quality child protection services by 2021. To deliver on this, WVI seeks to focus on prevention, mitigation and response interventions in Somaliland, Puntland, South West State and Jubaland where the organization has a physical presence with ongoing interventions on CP, health, nutrition WASH and FSL.  Under prevention, awareness raising and capacity building of child protection structures at the front line is emphasized while creating a linkage with the formal reporting and referral pathway. Dialogue forums with different community people groups such as caregivers, teachers, faith leaders as well as duty bearers will be used to strengthen child protection awareness at the community level. Child to child interventions including school club activities will be used build lifeskills and increase knowledge on child rights. Skills for self-protection in emergency situations will also be imparted through IEC materials and school club activities. Caregivers, parents and teachers will be targeted with positive parenting messages and non-violent discipline techniques to address the corporal punishment and other forms of violence at the household level and at school. Negative coping mechanisms to emergency situations such as child marriage, separation, child labor and trafficking will be prevented through cash based assistance to households with children at risk of abuse including those headed by caregivers with disability. Through the Channels of Hope Child Protection model, WVI will continue to work with faith leaders to tackle difficult topics around cultural practices that disadvantage the girl child such as FGM and child marriage. In close collaboration with existing local networks, policy advancement in child protection with different government line ministries at state level will be supported. Under mitigation, community-led safety audits and mapping of most vulnerable households with children at risk of violence will be done with an aim of ensuring risk mitigation mechanisms that are disability-sensitive are in place. Community level disaster risk reduction plans with an early warning system embedded alongside a communication plan targeting children and caregivers including those with disabilities will be disseminated through IEC materials and community meetings. Under response, individual specialized services through case management e.g. for Unaccompanied and Separated Children (UASC) will be done while collaborating with existing mechanisms for family tracing and reunification efforts. To strengthen reporting and referral, the use of the toll free line 364 will be popularized alongside setting up child help desks and dialogue forums with children at school level to identify those in need of care and support. Mental health and psychosocial support interventions will be prioritized for children and care givers including child friendly spaces, support groups etc.COVID-19 control measures will be integrated during activity implementation

project_name: Facilitating recovery and durable solutions through protection and HLP interventions
project_objective:
Recovery and the pursuit of durable solutions remain a daunting prospect as local communities across Somalia continue to grapple with the legacy of decades of war. The challenges confronting displaced communities in Somalia are entrenched and cumulative. While meaningful strides are being made by the government and international partners to address the displacement situation, these efforts are being continually reversed and/or undermined by generalized inadequate protection of HLP rights, including widespread evictions. A little over 200,000 individuals have been evicted across Somalia in 2019 alone (HLP Subcluster). Forced or otherwise, evictions have an enormous impact on the victims’ dignity, physical security, livelihoods, and most importantly, their search for durable solutions to displacement. In addition to the enormous cost in humanitarian investments, the consequences range from secondary displacements and total destruction of livelihood strategies and assets to the disruption of established life routines and social networks. 

Widespread tenure insecurity and general inadequate legal and policy frameworks remain the primary underpinning factors. Still, development-induced evictions, inability to pay rent and dispute over ownership between competing landowners are among the reasons most cited for evictions. Eviction as a problematic
phenomenon remains a foundational imperative to addressing the issue of displacement in Somalia in a realistic, comprehensive, and sustainable way. It suffices to conclude that efforts to strengthen protection and contribute to durable solutions to displacement in Somalia will be incomplete and/or undermined without addressing the issue of eviction concurrently and systematically.

It is within this broader strategic framework that the current project, which seeks to facilitate enhanced protection of displaced communities from evictions, has been conceptualized. Project services and customized assistance packages will benefit 196,100 individuals in 21 districts across 15 regions. In terms of delivery modalities and outputs, the overarching objectives of the project will be achieved through a combination of complementarily reinforcing set of actions that are framed around the following eight core pillars.

1.	Strengthening ongoing eviction monitoring systems to enhance analysis, data availability, and usability.
2.	Scaling up and consolidating eviction risk mapping to inform advocacy and response.
3.	Supporting proactive engagements to negotiate improved tenure arrangements and/or facilitating dignified relocations for populations of concern.
4.	Mitigating protection risks exacerbated by evictions by providing different forms of tenure security support to displaced populations, including facilitating the issuance of documentation at both household and group levels. Documentation will also seek to reduce risks to HLP assets on which local livelihood initiatives are dependent.
5.	Supporting extremely vulnerable victims of evictions cope with post-eviction stress (PES) through the provision of multi-sectoral cash assistance, specialized counseling, and legal assistance services.
6.	Mobilizing and supporting the government’s effort to address evictions, including robust engagement with landlords, gatekeepers, and community leaders.
7.	Facilitating access to information designed to assist IDPs access services, navigate complex procedures, and utilize existing remedies in areas of displacement to enhance their protection.
8.	Strengthen coordination, as well as the functional and operational capacity of the HLP sub-cluster.

project_name: Provide emergency and livelihood support to protect and strengthen Resilience of vulnerable Rural, Urban Poor and IDP populations in Somalia
project_objective:
Driven by the impacts of climatic shocks and insecurity over the last two years, large-scale destitution and displacement continue to diminish food access and limit recovery efforts of the most vulnerable populations. While little rainfall has been experienced since May, the combined effects of flooding, and Desert Locust and other crop pest infestations have adversely impacted the 2020 Gu season crop production, with production dropping 40 percent lower than the long-term average for 1995-2019, according to FSNAU estimates. This is further exacerbated by the rapidly spreading Corona Virus (COVID-19) pandemic, which has led to market and transportation disruptions, as well as decline in remittances, livelihood opportunities and humanitarian assistance, directly affecting food security and affordability. As a result, 3.5 million people are expected to be in crisis and emergency (IPC3&4) through 2021 and in dire need of humanitarian assistance (HNO, 2020). Around 2.6 million IDPs living in over 2000 sites, in crowded living conditions in urban and semi-urban areas, are among the most at risk to COVID-19, and in dire need of immediate and long-term assistance. Additionally, the total acute malnutrition burden or Somalia is estimated at 849,900 children under the age of five years likely facing acute malnutrition through August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished. (FSNAU, September 2020)
The project focuses on the delivery of basic lifesaving and protection/restoration of livelihoods of the target population with a special focus on all locations with FSC prioritized persons in need, including IDP camps and host communities that are classified in IPC Phase 3 & 4 in terms of response. 
The project is aimed at improving the ability of vulnerable HHs to meet their basic needs, supports protection and recovery of livelihood assets through life-saving UCT, animal treatment services, provision of locally preferred high quality seeds kits and trainings, and rehabilitation of community productive assets through CFW to support the resilience of vulnerable populations against shocks and prevent them from slipping into acute food insecurity. The proposed project aims to target at least 12,585 HHs (75,510) agro-pastoral and IDP households in Baidoa, Banadir, Belet_Xaawo, Burco, Cabudwaaq, Doolow, Luuq and Owdweyne districts in crisis and emergency with delivery of life saving interventions in line with the strategic objectives of the HRP and FSC response plan.
The project is informed by the centrality of protection and a gender, age and diversity-sensitive approach which is mainstreamed throughout the project cycle. Moreover, the project reflects the principles of COOPI Protection Policy and is built consistently with COOPI Protection SOPs and Protection Mainstreaming guidelines. The project will be guided by the principles of DO NO HARM, ensuring safety and dignity of target population is upheld and at the same time providing for accountability, participation and empowerment. 
In summary the following activities will be carried out:
1.	Provide UCT to 4,285 HHs that are faced with severe levels of food insecurity (crisis and emergency) with the aim of increasing immediate access to food for 3 months.
2.	Rehabilitation of community productive assets through CFW targeting 1,900 vulnerable HHs.
3.	Provision of locally preferred high quality seed kits, trainings and fuel for irrigation for 900 flood affected female and male headed vulnerable riverine farmers in Gedo region.
4.	Provision of locally preferred high quality seeds kit (drought tolerant) and trainings for 2,500 female and male headed vulnerable agro-pastoral farmers in Bay region.
5.	Emergency livestock treatment (treatment and deworming) campaigns for animals belonging to 3,000 HHs will be dewormed and treated against endemic &prevalent diseases.

project_name: Improving food security and resilience building in Somaliland
project_objective:
Project background and purpose 
Somalia’s population is currently experiencing multiple shocks including desert locust upsurge that started in late 2019 in many parts of the country; riverine and flash floods that affect the food security, livelihoods and safety of farmers and people living in flood-prone, populated areas and the novel coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic that is having severe health and socio-economic impacts. Based on the cumulative, combined impacts of multiple shocks, FSNAU and FEWS NET projected in May 2020 that around 3.5 million Somalis would be in Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and Emergency (IPC Phase 4) through at least September 2020. An additional 3 million Somalis were anticipated to be Stressed (IPC Phase 2) and engaging in negative coping strategies to meet their food and non-food needs. Analysis of household food security survey data collected in the July/August 2020 post-Gu assessment resulted in reduced estimates through December 2020. However, anticipated La Niña conditions are associated with an elevated likelihood of consecutive below-average rainfall seasons, and Somalia faces a high risk that drought conditions will develop by early 2021 while desert locusts could exacerbate crop and pasture losses. As a result, a high proportion of the population that is projected to be Stressed (IPC Phase 2) in October-December 2020 could deteriorate to Crisis (IPC Phase 3) in early 2021. The Food Security Cluster projects an average of 3.5 million Somalis to be in Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and Emergency (IPC Phase 4) through 2021.

Against the above background, the purpose of the proposed project is that the food security situation of vulnerable and affected households in Somaliland is stabilized and households are more resilient towards drought, desert locusts scourge and other shocks. Specifically, the proposed project will contribute to two objectives including; 1: Improving access  to food through conditional and unconditional transfers and 2: Provide seasonal livelihood inputs support (agriculture and livestock). These will be achieved through conditional and unconditional cash transfers, rehabilitation of communal assets and agricultural inputs support. 

Target beneficiaries 
The project will target at risk and affected populations in rural areas including farmers, agro pastoralists, pastoralists and rural IDPs and host communities to whom humanitarian assistance is key to prevent them from further deterioration of their food security and nutrition situation. In total the project will target 1,450 households  (10,150 individuals) in the districts of  Owdweyne in Togdheer region and Talex and Xudun in Sool regions of Eastern Somaliland and Zeylac district in Awdal region of Western Somaliland. Priority will be given to households headed by disabled persons or elderly persons without support, poor female-headed households, poor households with malnourished children under 5 years and poor pregnant and lactating women, who are at increased risk of malnutrition. The project will be implemented between January to December 2021. 

The criteria for selection of the beneficiaries will be guided by food insecurity levels (IPC 3 and 4, based on latest FEWSNET and FSNAU analysis), Structural vulnerability or social status including minority groups, IDPs, women or child headed households, elderly or persons with disability, and families with malnourished children under 5 years

project_name: To improve the living conditions and protection of IDPs at site level in Banadir, Lower Shebelle, Lower Jubba, and Gedo Region to ensure equitable access to services and assistance of all persons in need, with a clear focus on moving toward attaining durable solutions.
project_objective:
According to HNO 2020, an estimated 709,000 new displacements were reported from January to December 2019, mostly to urban areas, where displaced people move to private IDP sites with poor living conditions and little access to basic services. There are over 2,000 recorded IDP sites across Somalia. Approximately 85 percent of the sites are informal settlements on private land and about 74 percent of them are in urban areas according to the Detailed Site Assessment (DSA). According to the DSA, over 70 percent of IDPs in informal sites lack access to information about their rights and available services. Displaced communities, especially new arrivals, people with disabilities and women need access to information and representation in the community governance structure to make informed decisions about how to receive services and potential solutions to displacement. This year (2020), Somalia has seen serious flooding which have forced hundreds of thousands of people to flee their homes amid risks of COVID-19. According to UNHCR more than 150,000 Somalis have been forced to flee their homes since late June, including some 23,000 in the last week of July, due to flash and riverine flooding in the Southern regions of Somalia. As of 19 May (OCHA), ongoing flash and riverine flooding in Somalia has affected about 919,000 people, of whom 412,000 have been displaced and 24 killed, in 29 districts. 

The displaced people in informal sites in Banadir, Lower Shebelle, Lower Jubba, and Gedo Region are in greatest need of CCCM services to improve the living conditions and protection of IDPs at the site level. The target areas have been through successive years of drought and conflict, leaving the population vulnerable to shocks and inhibiting a sustainable return to places of origin. The displaced population in these areas are living in precarious conditions with their basic needs not met due to inconsistent service provision and exclusion with all existing coordination and management mechanisms at site level being informal, with most sites managed by landlords and gatekeepers limiting accountability and adherence to minimum standards. While ensuring equitable access to services and assistance of all persons in need, NoFYL will ensure to enhance the accountability of affected populations through community participation and consistent engagement with a focus on moving toward attaining durable solutions. 

NoFYL intends to scale up its CCCM program to contribute towards strengthening camp coordination and camp management to improve the living conditions and protection of IDPs at the site level by ensuring equitable access to services and assistance of all persons in need. All the project activities will be carried out to maximize community participation and enhance the accountability of humanitarian actors to the affected population. NoFYL will coordinate with relevant responders and mobilized towards providing sectorial assistance to those identified as very vulnerable at the site level. Together with the established site governance, NoFYL will carry out service monitoring activities aimed at highlighting service gaps, and ensuring that minimum standards are being adhered to at the site-level. To ensure that sites are safe and hygiene conditions are ensured NoFYL will provide training on-site maintenance and site planning to camp committees to strengthen their capacity, Support community-led site maintenance activities to ensure the upkeep of sites through cash for work activities, distribution of tools to site maintenance committees. The project will also support maintaining inter-sector complaints feedback mechanisms (CFMs) at the IDP site-level.

The project will be implemented in 4 regions, including Banaadir, Gedo region covering Beletxaawo and Ceelwaaq districts, and Lower Juba covering Kismayo. The project will target 60 sites in total targeting an estimated IDP population of 64,000 to be verified through the detailed site assessments.

project_name: Strengthening protective environment and enhancing access to HLP rights for displaced populations in Banaadir, Jubaland, Hiraan, and Lower Shebelle.
project_objective:
The situation in most of Somalia is highly variable. Women and young girls are still exposed to continue protection risks or other forms of exploitation and abuse, due to several social and cultural factors exacerbated by displacement and lack of resources generalized insecurity and limited access to support networks, in particular, lack of specialized service providers addressing HLP issues and lack of information regarding available services prevent even the most basic support for vulnerable IDPs and the host population. Moreover, there are still gaps in preventing and responding to HLP issues along with the limited availability of national skilled human resources with the required knowledge and background. Access to areas where populations are known to be in severe distress is highly restricted. In this scenario, the role of national NGOs like NoFYL, who has the broadest and deepest reach and can access difficult areas, is crucial.

Protection, monitoring and response mechanisms with regards to land, housing and property is lacking in most of the protection programming. Most often legal Aid services, land, houses and property rights are not prioritized hence leaving big gaps in the protection response mechanism. There is poor coordination among protection and response service providers, especially on land, housing, and property rights. Furthermore, the protection response mechanisms have limited or no provision of free legal aid services to IDPs, survivors of GBV and HLP.

Therefore, this project seeks to improve and strengthen coordination among service providers and to enhance protection and response mechanism for IDPs on land, housing and property rights. These will be achieved through eviction monitoring, prevention and response services, improved referral pathways, on spot monitoring and response to assist IDPs to reclaim housing, land and properties, awareness-raising, free legal aid, and innovative and sustainable alternative dispute resolution mechanisms.  The project will ensure individuals affected by displacement receive support assistance to improve their tenure security situation and address post-eviction complications including enhanced capacity to Prevention and response to evictions.

During the needs assessment phase, data will be disaggregated by gender, and by age. NoFYL will collect gender disaggregated data by sex and age of relevant data related to the project activities and ensure that all segments of the affected population including children and adolescents at risk, female HHs, elderly, disabled, have equal access to project services and that targeted support to advance gender equality is based on a gender analysis. The programme will meet the distinct needs of women, men, girls and boys. NoFYL shall apply gender segregated community based activities at the safe spaces enabling women and girls to address their specific concerns, priorities their needs and appropriately inform the development of proposed activities. 

Cognizant to promote equity, NoFYL shall endeavor to provide equal chance, inclusiveness and participation of minority members of the community as well as disabled groups in the locations and entrench transparency in recruitment of beneficiaries, capacity building, empowerment and resource sharing to achieve a comprehensive community engagement. Active participation of individuals with special needs will be pursued to identify, support and strengthen the coping mechanisms that beneficiaries often create to protect themselves against threats to their safety and dignity, and also foster beneficiaries’ self-esteem and development of skills. Case workers selection, orientations and will also consider gender sensitivity including both men and women. All this will ensure gender issues and equity are addressed as well as offer services as per the community acceptable practices.

project_name: Logistics Cluster Support to Humanitarian Partners in Somalia
project_objective:
This project endeavours to fulfill the Logistics Cluster’s mandate to support humanitarian partners in reaching affected populations in the context of the ‘triple threat’ COVID-19, Locust and Floods emergency.  Somalia’s operating context is particularly complex due logistics infrastructure and continued insecurity as well as restrictions on border crossings; and although Somalia is reasonably accessible by air, the cost of air operations is extremely high – and often is a deterring factor for several organisations and partners. 
In 2020, as a consequence of the COVID-19 pandemic, commercial and humanitarian supply chains remained under strain due to limited accessibility which has significantly restricted the transportation of passengers and vital cargo for the humanitarian community. Therefore, this project aims to strengthen the humanitarian community's ability to save lives and address needs through timely and reliable logistics services, facilitation of operational coordination and information sharing, thereby facilitating the efficient and rapid transportation of urgent relief items for the humanitarian community's emergency response operations.

project_name: Prevention of undernutrition amongst children under 5 and pregnant and lactating women and girls in vulnerable health districts of the East, Adamawa and North regions affected by the CAR crisis
project_objective:
WFP’s programme focuses on preventing malnutrition amongst the most vulnerable populations through strengthening supplementary feeding with focus on the first 1000days. The programme activities include: Screening for malnutrition and referral of severe cases for treatment, Social and behavioral change communication in favor of appropriate infant and young child feeding practices and other Family practices, distribution of specialized nutritious food to children aged 6-23months and and MAM children aged 24-59Months for treatment of moderate acute malnutrition(MAM) and

project_name: Life-saving integrated food security and livelihoods support for Somaliland and Puntland communities
project_objective:
The project is responding to humanitarian needs of drought, covid 19 and locust affected community in target locations of Puntland and Somaliland through cash injection to address the immediate food needs of the people. Cash transfer programming will be used to reach households that are in IPC 3 and above. While focusing on life-saving interventions, the project will also support recovery and resilience building of the people where possible. 
Findings from FSNAU  2020 post-Gu seasonal food security and nutrition assessment conducted across Somalia during July and August 2020 indicate that Due to the combined effects of widespread and severe flooding, Desert Locust infestation, socioeconomic impacts of COVID-19 and the cumulative impacts of previous shocks, up to 2.1 million people across Somalia are expected to face food consumption gaps or depletion of assets indicative of Crisis (IPC Phase 3)1 or worse outcomes through December 2020 in the absence of humanitarian assistance. In addition, 849 900 children under the age of five are likely to be acutely malnourished through August 2021. 
Desert Locust continues to pose a serious risk of damage to both pasture and crops at least until the end of 2020. The 2020 Deyr (October-December) rainfall season is likely to be below average to average across the country, which could lead to drought and trigger a worsening of the humanitarian situation if the 2021 Gu (April-June) season rainfall is also delayed or performs poorly.

The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the Somalis’s economy is significant impacting on poor urban and IDP households, as well as pastoralists in northern Somalia, namely Puntland and Somaliland.  External remittance flows from the Somali diaspora constitutes 1.4-2 billion USD every year and contribute 23-32 percent of Gross Domestic Product, according to the World Bank. However, after the onset of COVID-19, money vendors report that the volume of cash transactions declined approximately 30-40 percent from March to June 2020
Improving food availability through support to agricultural production in Awdal and Nugal  and introducing it in Sool and Sanag regions of Somalia is seen as an entry point to diversify pastoral livelihoods of those two regions. This plan involves also supporting communities’ recovery and livelihoods diversification interventions through livestock support with vaccination and treatment and Improving Agricultural Production/Food Security. 

Livestock production was severely affected by the drought leading to substantially reduced herds; which is the country’s prime investment especially in rural communities. The mains reasons leading to the death were water shortages and lack of pasture.  In view of this situation the project will explore fodder production combined with campaigns on livestock treatment. These include promotion of carrying capacity for sustained production. These actions will be coupled with Cash for Work activities which will be used for communal asset development linked to crop and animal husbandry. 

In times of shock and more critical food insecurity, Oxfam will utilize cash and voucher assistance to reach to the most affected households impacted by triple threats of drought, covid or locust  to meet the immediate emergency needs of at risk communities. cash is the preferred option for Oxfam to reach to people in remote areas, it is faster, sacure and easy to cover at scale. cash and voucher assistance also helps people to have flexibility on their needs and decision, choice and have multiplier effect on the economy

project_name: Provision of safe, secure and dignified shelter and sustainable solar energy support to Rohingya refugees and crisis-affected host communities in Teknaf Upazilla, Cox's Bazar District, Bangladesh.
project_objective:
To address the identified critical needs of the Rohingya refugees facing the deterioration of shelters and the lack of adequate internal lighting, as well vulnerable host communities facing a lack of adequate shelter and access to sustainable energy sources; the twelve-month NRC Shelter Programme will provide safe and dignified shelter and energy solutions to Rohingya refugees in the camps, and vulnerable crisis-affected populations in the host communities of Teknaf Upazilla, Cox's Bazar District. 
In the Rohingya refugee camps, NRC will distribute TSA II kits as part of the Shelter Sector’s TSA II blanket coverage strategy and distribute SHS kits that will target the most vulnerable in the Rohingya communities. Throughout the process, the shelter beneficiaries will be engaged through awareness campaigns, training, focus group discussions and feedback sessions, including training and awareness on DRR. NRC will also contribute technical and operational capacity in emergency circumstances and will ensure DRR shelter coverage of TDKs in Camp 25 as part of 2021 monsoon preparedness. NRC Shelter will also provide repair and maintenance to all other NRC Programme facilities in the camps and host communities, ensuring that they remain in good condition and they are accessible to all PSNs. All repair and maintenance costs will be provided by the relevant NRC Programme user of the facilities.  
In the host communities, NRC will offer cash-based shelter assistance for household repair or upgrades and distribute SHS kits to the most vulnerable members of the community. NRC will engage the host communities in all levels of the decision-making of the activities, to promote ownership and increase the empowerment of vulnerable and marginalised individuals. NRC will also provide training and awareness on DRR, to increase the host community’s resilience during emergencies.  
NRC will undertake these activities using a professional training team that will be fully trained in gender and disability inclusion and PSEA. Gender equality will be mainstreamed throughout the project and each of the activities will include sensitization activities on abandonment of gender-based violence (GBV) and the promotion of women and girls’ rights. NRC will also ensure that there is an independent and impartial complaints mechanism availble for all activities. Alongside meeting minimum internal and ISCG Shelter Sector standards, NRC will conduct this intervention following the latest Covid-19 guidelines for distributions, ensuring that vulnerable Rohingya refugees and host communities are shielded from the risk of catching the virus whilst receiving shelter assistance. 
NRC will at all times coordinate all activities with the Shelter Sector, other partners operating in the camps and the SMSD Sector.
NRC Information, Counselling and Legal Assistance (ICLA) programme will support the HLP TF with HLP assessments, development of guidance notes and advocacy papers as identified by the HLP TF in its workplan and HLP Strategy 2020-2023. NRC M&E will provide access to an independent and impartial complaints feedback mechanism. Furthermore, NRC Shelter will undertake all repair and maintenance construction works for NRC Education Rohingya and host community learning facilities.

project_name: Providing life-saving WASH assistance to the most vulnerable disaster affected populations and increasing access to sustainable WASH services for the chronically under-served host and displaced populations in Somalia.
project_objective:
Project aims to provide live-saving WASH assistance to disaster affected displaced and
non- displaced population in order to reduce the excess morbidity and mortality rate from
preventable crisis-driven diseases and public health outbreaks among most vulnerable
people. The project will continue to restore access to safe and equitable basic WASH
services in targeted locations in a dignified manner. Lack of adequate WASH services to
the population is a main cause of spread of Acute Diarrheal Diseases (ADD), leading to
malnutrition in the country and contributing to increasing the existing stunting rate of
25.3% in children below 5 years of age.
Access to safe water will be increased through construction and or rehabilitation of water
sources including 8 boreholes (2 new), 20 shallow wells, 2 river water intake system with
water treatment. New borehole construction will be preceded by hydrogeological survey
and safe pumping regime will be designed. River water intakes will be preceded
hydrological study. In all cases, an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) will be
undertaken for new water sources and mitigation measures put in place for negative
impacts. All water systems will be equipped with distribution infrastructure and hybrid
energization systems. Pipeline extensions will also be made. Taps stand will be located
within a radius of at least 500m to reduce distance and enhance security of women and
girls. Project will also construct 2 major improved water dams in locations that lack other
options. All well heads will be raised at a minimum 0.5m to reduce risk flooding and
contamination. Water committees comprising men and women from all community
groups including the minority and the marginalized will be trained on management,
operation and maintenance. Local technicians will be trained and provided with O&M
tools to undertake repairs whereas consumers will pay for the technician’s services. For
major water supply in urban areas, Private Public Parternship (PPP) management system
will be adopted. Where possible NRC will partner will local private investors to establish
sustainable water sources and equip them with SmartTAPs to enhance revenue collection
and accountability. Project will construct 400 latrines for families reintegrated through the
durable solutions. NRC undertakes sanitary surveys periodically to identify contamination
risks for timely mitigation. All latrine will be installed with handwashing equipment and
community sensitized to use soap for handwashing. Design of infrastructure will take into
consideration the needs of special groups in the community including the disabled, old,
children to ensure they have equitable access to the services. Life-saving WASH
interventions will be implemented in case of sudden disaster to reduce the related
mortality and morbidity especially among children. This will be through temporary
provision of safe water through direct delivery or restricted cash depending on context and
market functionality, provision of hygiene kits through cash (3000 HH), construction of
550 simple design emergency latrines, latrine emptying (450 latrines) and safe fecal
sludge disposal and hygiene promotion. Schools and health facilities will be provided with
latrines offering private space for menstrual hygiene (200 institutional latrines). All
latrines will be raised above ground level to reduce the risk of flooding during rains.
Women and girls will be involved in identification of sites for facilities to ensure their
safety and security is taken into account. Latrines will be gender separated, provided with
lockable doors and handwashing equipment. Solar street lights (35 posts) will be provided
near water points and latrines to improve the security and safety of women and girls
especially in crowded IDP settlements. Throughout the implementation period the
beneficiaries will be provided with adequate information on NRC’s complaints, response
and feedback (CRFM) mechanisms.

project_name: Essential Support to the Health Sector North Syria
project_objective:
SAMS Health program for the year 2021 comes in line with the Health Sector objectives 1&2&3: Increase access to life-saving and life-sustaining coordinated, equitable humanitarian health services for those most vulnerable and in need; Strengthen health sector capacity to prepare for, detect and deliver a timely response to disease outbreaks, including COVID-19 and Strengthen health system capacity to support continuity of care, strengthen community resilience, and respond to IDP movements and changes in context. In this program, SAMS will prioritize the reduction of morbidity and mortality through improving the access to quality health care (primary and secondary, specialized services, mobile clinics, and an ambulatory system, COVID-19 response) in 36 health facilities within NWS and Al Hasakeh and Ar Raqqa governorates. SAMS will support facilities on different levels including coverage of staff incentives, running costs, provision of pharmaceuticals and other medical and non-medical commodities, rehabilitation/maintenance of the HFs. SAMS will provide recruitment support, capacity building, and medical supervision to ensure the HFs are staffed with qualified medical personnel and to enhance compliance with standard treatment protocols. 
SAMS will provide the following services at the primary healthcare level: RH services (ante-natal care, post-natal care, family planning, normal deliveries, gynecological consultations, and clinical management of rape), Integrated management for child illness, EPI, communicable and non-communicable diseases, Nutrition, MHPSS, health awareness, and basic laboratory and radiology services. Services at the secondary health care level will include gynecologic surgeries and cesarean sections, trauma management, major surgeries, hospitalization services, blood transfusion, hemodialysis, and ICUs, in addition to COVID-19 response (CM, Triage, PPE/IPC, CHWs). This program will also provide cancer treatment to Breast, colon, Hodgkin, and non-Hodgkin Lymphoma patients, Cath Lab, Pathology, GI endoscopy, Dental services, Paediatric ALL, ICU, NICU, PICU, Kidney transplant medications. Additionally, SAMS will support the ambulatory system (10 ambulances, part of which will be dedicated to transferring COVID-19 patients). SAMS will sustain the support for rehabilitation in Sejjo, Termanin, and Afrin. In addition, as part of SAMS focus on contributing to its goal of increasing the capacity of the health care professional in NWS through advancing SAMS’ investment in its medical education program: Supporting Residents Doctors; Supporting Midwifery Education in NWS; Supporting Nursing Education.
Similar to all SAMS projects, SAMS will seek all efforts possible to coordinate with all health actors through the Health Cluster whether through the routinely gathered data in 4Ws and HeRAMS. or through its constant participation and active membership within the following TWG: COVID-19 TF, SRH, MHPSS, Non-Communicable Diseases, SIG, Midwifery Capacity Building Strategy for NWS, Secondary Health Care, and Drug Supply Line, in addition, to coordinate with other NGOs on the referral, and the contribution to DHIS2, notwithstanding its membership in the NGO Forum, SNA, and other bodies. SAMS always coordinate and consult its operations with the HDs.

project_name: Humanitarian Action for Saving Lives through Livelihood (HASLL)
project_objective:
Climatic shocks have become a recurring phenomenon in Pakistan, exposing the population to food and nutrition insecurity. Pakistan ranks 8th on long-term climate risk index of 2019, and is prone to climate-induced disasters (floods, snowfall, drought, and locust). Vulnerable communities have witnessed multiple climate-induced disasters in previous few decades with the increased frequency and intensity.  In a country, where 25 percent of the country' population lives below the poverty line, multiple shocks including recent COVID-19 outbreak have further deteriorated the  socio-economic indicators.   
With this backdrop, Islamic Relief aims to provide support the most vulnerable communities in targeted districts of Chagai, Noshki, Pishin and Washuk (Baluchistan), Thatta/Sujjawal, and Badin (Sindh), North Waziristan, South Waziristan, Orkazai, and Khyber districts (Khyber Pkhtunkhwa). Targeted districts fall under HRP with prevailing multiple socio-economic vulnerabilities. 
The immediate humanitarian assistance will include livelihood assistance through conditional cash disbursement, promoting resilient livelihood initiatives, restoration of affected on and off-farm livelihood, and capacitating youth with entrepreneurship and technical skills. 
Proposed action will be implemented in close coordination with the relevant district and provincial authorities/mandated institutes ensuring ownership, linkage development and long-term uptake of the interventions. 
Islamic Relief will adapt participatory approach while ensuring inclusion of persons with disabilities, women (prioritizing women headed households and PWDs), elderly, young boys and girls, and children under the age of five.   
The proposed interventions will contribute to the overall humanitarian response in Pakistan, with an effective mainstreaming of DRR and protection. Proposed action is in alignment with the Government’s Strategic Preparedness and Response Plan and Global Humanitarian Response Plan (GHRP) to address the direct  and indirect immediate humanitarian consequences of the multiple disasters across Pakistan. 
Beneficiary targeting strategy of the proposed action is in synergy with the Pakistan 2021, Humanitarian Response Plan's targeting strategy. Multiple  vulnerability criteria will be employed in the disaster affected communities to target the most vulnerable segments of society/individuals. 
A total of 112, 105 individuals (including approximately 4,484 persons with disability), will be benefitted with the proposed activities. Further desegregation of beneficiaries is as under;
Total: 112105 individuals
Male: 43474
Female:42234
Boys: 13474	
Girls: 12922

project_name: Protection of the basic livelihoods of communities and people acutely affected by protracted crisis to cope with the threats and shocks through cash assistance
project_objective:
This project contributes to strategic objective three of the HRP 2021, (particularly SO 3.5 and SO 3.6 in Food Security Sector), by enhancing food security for highly vulnerable non-refugee population affected by conflict and COVID-19 pandemic in Gaza Strip through improving access to diversified, sufficient and nutritious food. 
Based on recent IRPAL assessments and consultations with key stakeholders, and the recommendations of the ministry of social development (MOSD), it was found that there is a food security gap among vulnerable populations that should be addressed urgently in the short and medium term. 
The intervention builds on previous SIDA funded projects in the food security sector implemented by IRPAL, and IRPAL’s long experience and efforts in the field of reducing food insecurity through cash-based interventions (CBI). This modality (CBI) proved to be highly effective in ensuring tailored assistance that meets the distinct priorities and needs of women, men, girls and boys in different age groups of beneficiaries, while respecting their dignity and autonomy and strengthening their resilience against future shocks. Specifically, the project’s overall goal is to contribute to enhancing food security of highly vulnerable non-refugee population affected by conflict and COVID-19 pandemic in the Gaza Strip, by the two essential components: 
- CFW opportunities: this will provide temporary employment opportunity with conditional but not restricted cash assistance for one member of 400 food-insecure HHs for 5 months creating a total of 44,000 paid working days. The estimated number of direct beneficiaries will be 2,240 including 746 women, 746 men, 374 girls and 374 boys, among them 112 PWDs. The project will target 200 graduates (who will be placed at CSOs & private sector companies) and 200 labourers (who will be placed at small-scale farms and food manufacturing factories). Supporting the agricultural sector will improve the availability of, and access to local foods. Females will be encouraged to enroll to increase the women participation and engagement rates in the labour market. The participants will be paid average daily wages of 50 ILS (40 for laborers and 60 for graduates) for 22 working days which means average monthly income of 1,100 ILS (approx. $320).
- Food Vouchers: this will provide monthly unconditional but restricted monthly cash assistance to 1,200 households for a period of 6 months (6,720 direct beneficiaries including 2,240 women, 2,240 men, 1,120 girls, 1,120 boys, among them 336 PWDs) that will improve their food intake and dietary diversity. The cash provided will be adjusted to the family size and based on the average of monthly food expenditures estimates.
The nomination and selection of HHs will be from the available databases of IRPAL, MOSD and local actors. The HHs of the worst score of socioeconomic vulnerabilities with high food insecurity levels and eroded coping capacities, will be selected and higher priority will be given to FHHs, HHs with protection concerns and HHs with members who are elderly, chronically ill, or PWDs. Approximately 50% of the beneficiaries will be women or girls and 5-7% will be PWDs. The selection of CFW beneficiaries will be based on specific criteria like; persons above 18 years old breadwinner of a family with no regular source of income, unemployed, recent graduate or unskilled labourer, non-refugee. Nominated candidates will be cross-checked with UNRWA, Ministry of Labour, MOSD, FSS Cluster and peer institutions.
Finally, IRPAL adheres to protection principles and good practices as guided by the humanitarian standards (CHS, SPHERE, etc.) with special focus on accountability to beneficiaries, applying complaint systems, access to assistance with dignity and gender equality. Also, IRPAL adheres to PSEA (Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse) among its staff and hosting institutions through orientation before the start of the project implementation.

project_name: Nutrition program aimed at reducing morbidity and mortality related to acute malnutrition in Lower Juba and Baidoa in Somalia
project_objective:
Nutrition situation in target areas remain fragile with unstable  state following presence of aggravating factors that trigger high levels of acute malnutrition.
Afmadow and Kismayo in Lower Juba are areas with persistent high acute malnutrition rates. Both areas have IDP and urban poor as vulnerable populations whose state are affected by multiple aggravating factors . In the last season these factors have included: disease outbreaks, especially measles and AWD cholera, acute household food insecurity which was heightened by COVID 19 prevention measures among IDP and urban poor and  displacement mostly through floods and military offensive in neighboring districts contributing to migration into these districts. In Afmadow acute malnutrition state is stressed.GAM among Kismayo IDP and urban is 12.2 and 11.4 receptively. SAM rates however remain high at 2.6 and 3.2 respectively. Acute malnutrition among PLW in Kismayo is stressed (FSNAU<2020).
Baidoa IDP remain some the most vulnerable in Somalia (Reach IDP profile 2019). IDP
numbers continue to increase due to a number of factors including conflict, insecurity,
flooding and drought among others. In January 2020, the first influx of IDP fled from
Tooswayne to Outskirts of Baidoa town following clashes with Al Shabaab community
leaders on forced taxation and child recruitment. As a result, belongings of the
community members were looted including grain storage and business centers, forcing
the people to flee empty handed. In June 2020, armed conflict broke out
again in Toosweyne village causing communities to flee to IDP camps. More IDPs continue to arrive at camps straining resources and increasing vulnerability to acute malnutrition. By end July 2020, an estimated number of 4,500 households have moved to IDP to find shelter, security, healthcare and food .These IDP reported  high household food insecurity, poor access to nutrition services with high SAM rate, poor integration with health and high risk to COVID 19 infection (OCHA led Multisector assessment report,September 2020). 
WRRS is currently implementing integrated health and nutrition interventions in Afmadow and Kismayo that it intends to sustain in 2021. In all locations both mobile and fixed
services will be offered. Mobile teams will cover rural areas where services hardly reach
while fixed facilities will cover the town areas and IDP sites where the population can
easily access services. CHW will also be employed to ensure  the population is encouraged to use these services and that some services are offered at village/community level.
 In Baidoa, WRRS is implementing a camp management project covering most new IDP. Having identified the huge nutrition gap in camps, WRRS plans to scale up and include integrated  nutrition and health interventions in the camps where it has operational presence.
In all location Food security, WASH and protection activities will also be integrated.All sites will offer treatment of acute malnutrition (MAM and SAM) and prevention services for both children under 5 and PLW.
Project will also include : identification and referral of protection victims, prevention of COVID
19 and hygiene promotion with distribution of hygiene kits and risk communication.
Proposed interventions will also include all gender groups, marginalized groups and the
disabled who are often left out or given unequal treatment. Disabled will participate at all
levels of the project cycle. Staff will be trained on disability inclusion as to to eliminate
discrimination . APP and protection will also be mainstreamed. All data will be
dis aggregated according to gender and disability.The project will adhere to set
government policy and guidelines and any other MoH protocol, while observing
international health guidelines.
Coordination will be ensured with health actors and those from other sectors.

project_name: Emergency health to disaster affected populations in Somalia
project_objective:
CARE plans to implement and integrated lifesaving integrated health and nutrition  services to IDPs and disaster affected populations targeting  58,500 children U5 years (boys and girls) and pregnant and lactating women living in Bari, Sool , Sanag,Bari  and Lower Jubba  regions covering 10 districts (Bosaso, Badhan, Lasqoray, Ceelafweyn, Erigavo, Ainabo, Dhahar, Lascanod, Talex and Kismayo). project will complement ongoing interventions by CARE responding to the effect of floods, locust and COVID 19 pandemic. 
This The Project will be implemented through support to static Health facilities and mobile services for hard to reach populations to improve access to essential health care. CARE will work with relevant ministry of health authorities to strengthen local capacity and sustainability of project. CARE will provide equitable access to integrated health and nutrition services at both health facilities and through mobile teams. The health team will be comprised of two qualified nurses, two midwives, an auxiliary nurse, a registrar and a community health worker (CHW). This team will provide preventative and curative health services including outpatient consultations (especially for sexual and reproductive health,common childhood illnesses including diarrhea, acute respiratory infections, influenza, malaria, measles, and pneumonia). The team will refer complex or severe cases to the nearest district hospital where the patient will receive free medical care, as well as basic laboratory testing for malaria, common infections, etc. The mobile teams will provide the same services through an outreach modality working in different villages each day with weekly follow-up schedules. Nurses will use the Somalia treatment guidelines as well as the IMCI guidelines translated into the local language to diagnose and treat patients according to the country protocol. CARE will pay the incentive of one medical doctor at each district hospital so that all referred patients including survivors of Gender Based Violence (GBV) can assess free medical inpatient care as well as emergency obstetric care. In addition to routine health services, MCH clinics will also act as a hub for the storage of vaccines to be administered by the mobile teams.  Medical supplies for mobile teams will likewise be stored at the MCH clinics.  CARE will also support workers at these front-line health care facilities to gather health data from the population and report to the MoH using the MoH’s Communicable Disease Surveillance and Response Early Warning and Response Network (EWARNS). CARE will also support health management information systems by submitting monthly district level health reports to the MoH’s DHS 2 tool. CARE will use standard infection prevention and control procedures (IPC) as outlined by WHO . In all HF CARE will; Encourage Health workers to have a high level of clinical suspicion; establish a well-equipped triage station at the entrance to the facility, supported by trained staff; institute the use of screening questionnaires according to the updated COVID-19 case definition. This measures will enable contact tracing and follow up. In addition, CARE will put visible signs in public points within HF reminding patients with symptoms of COVID-19 to alert the Health workers and also install hand washing stations to be used by all patients before coming for services. CARE will also support the transportation costs of the referral in order to make the referral pathway effective. Through linkages and support from CARE's existing counsellors will support GBV cases will referred. CARE will compliment this project with existing funding from OFDA,FFP, DFID on health and nutrition and address gaps not covered by the project.  CARE’s activities will benefit both women and girls, as well as boys and men, to ensure that their unique needs are covered. Age, sex, and vulnerability criteria disaggregated data will be used to track inclusion, promote accountability

project_name: Provision of basic and lifesaving nutrition curative and preventative services to drought affected populations in Sool , Sanag, Bari and Lower Juba regions.
project_objective: The nutrition situation in the country is serious and has not improved since last year and recent FSNAU Post Gu 2020 assessment reported a median GAM rate of 13.8% which translated to almost 1 million children expected to be malnourished in 2021, out of these 162,000 will suffer from sever form of acute malnutrition (SAM) and 800,000 will be moderate malnourished  (MAM). The malnutrition  situation in CARE operational areas range from  serious to critical with  9-16.2 % in Sool and Sanag regions, 15.8% in Bosaso IDPs and 12.4% in Kismayo IDPs according to the latest FSNAU Post Gu 2020 assessment. The malnutrition situation is likely to worsen in pastoral areas and amongst IDPs as they face higher shock of seasonal food insecurity. From October to December 2020, food insecurity is expected to deteriorate among poor households with limited livestock or low capacity to cope with harvest losses as well as IDPs who are unable to meet their minimum food needs without external assistance. IDPs and pastoral communities are vulnerable to high food insecurity across the regions and this is mainly due to low purchasing power, lack of diversified income sources, leading to food scarcity, irregular meals and this also contributes to high diseases incidence resulting from lack of appetite and poor feeding practice and poor child spacing. Childhood morbidity is also leading to malnutrition as a result of poor hygiene and access to clean water. The water scarcity in the northern regions has triggered high water prices which are further expected to worsen during the dry seasons. CARE has also conducted IYCF KAP survey in Sep 2020 across 5 districts in Sool and Sanag and has found sub-optimal feeding practices which are further exacerbating the malnutrition situation in these areas.  In light of this and to continue building on the gains made in 2020 CARE will continue to implement an integrated nutrition and health intervention which will also be linked with other CARE wash and food security programs. This integrated nutrition and health program will consist of several components and cover both curative and preventative interventions targeting 30,000 children U5 years (boys and girls) and pregnant and lactating women living in Bari, Sool and Sanag regions covering 10 districts (Bosaso, Badhan, Lasqoray, Ceelafweyn, Erigavo, Ainabo, Lascanod, Talex and Kismayo). The intervention will provide access to basic and emergency nutrition and health services through support to key MOH staff at mobile and fixed clinics to enable delivery of outreach services. Nutrition activities will include identification and screening of acute malnutrition at both the community level and facility level; admissions into OTP, TSFP and SC services; referral of complicate cases; micronutrient supplementations including Vitamin A and IYCF counselling and promotions services at community and facility level. In addition to beneficiaries will also receive basic health services including outpatient disease consultations and treatments; referral of complicated cases for inpatient care; EPI immunization; antenatal and postnatal case service; referral to BemoC services and delivery by skilled birth attendants.  CARE will partner with MOH and WASDA and support 33 fixed sites in Badhan, elafweyn, Erigavo, Lascanod, and Afmadow and 40 mobile sites in Bosaso, Ainabo, Badhan and Taleh  in Puntland, Somaliland and Juba land.  Pandemics such as COVID-19 present more opportunities for exploitation and abuse. As the need for aid increases, with supply of and access to aid decreasing simultaneously, these unequal power dynamics are exacerbated further. Concurrently, due to the restrictions placed on movement, domestic violence, intimate partner, and gender-based violence are also likely to increase. As a result of these vulnerabilities CARE will train all its staff on PSEA in the nutrition centres in order for them identify and refer  risk groups and know what signs to look out for.

project_name: Program on Increased Access to Education Services for Vulnerable Girls and Boys in Lower Juba and Gedo Regions
project_objective: This project is designed to ensure that most vulnerable crisis-affected children and youth - including children living with disabilities - have access to safe, protective, inclusive and continuous learning opportunities in Gedo and Lower Juba Regions of Somalia. In achieving this, the intervention will implement a set of integrated actions aimed at increasing access and retaining these vulnerable learners in school whilst ensuring they are able to access lifesaving learning within a protective environment. The 10,000 learners (5,000 girls, 5,000 boys) will primarily be targeted from IDPs and vulnerable host communities. Of these targeted beneficiaries, the project will deliberately target 1,000 children living with disabilities, 50% of whom will be girls. The project proposes a set of integrated activities consisting of: construction/rehabilitation of learning spaces with child friendly and inclusive WASH facilities, provision of 5,000 litre water tank to schools, Enrollment awareness campaign, cash voucher assistance for vulnerable learners, provision of teaching and learning materials, incentive payment for teachers, emergency school feeding and provision of sanitary kits for female learners. Disability mainstreaming will also be targeted, to ensure CwDs are able to access inclusive education. In order to strengthen the capacity of education actors to deliver effective and coordinated EiE preparedness and response in Lower Juba and Gedo regions, the action will train teachers on inclusive, protective and socio-emotional teaching and learning and psychosocial support; CECs on school management, child protection and school safety. MoE staff at State and District level will be trained on emergency preparedness and response planning and coordination. In Gedo and Lower Juba, protection related issues have been identified as one of the hindrances to safe access to protective learning environments. These include the presence of armed personnel at checkpoints on the road to school, as well as at the school premises. GBV on the way to school and back is also another concern, in addition to lack of fences and gender sensitive WASH facilities, which particularly impacts girls’ access to education. Cultural practices e.g. FGM, early marriage and child labor also causes children to not enroll in schools or drop out prematurely. Marginalization and discrimination of children is prevalent and access to education for children from marginalized groups, CWDs and girls is being hampered. To respond to these challenges, the project will establish referral system in schools and community-based Child Protection Mechanisms for quick and efficient referrals of children with protection needs. This will include training, mapping of services and focal points within community and school (community child protection committees, School Management Committees, school Child Protection focal points); Provision of community and school based PSS to the affected children and their families through CFS, school clubs, community groups activities, procurement of recreational and dignity kits.; Case management – for Unaccompanied and Separated Children through documentation, immediate care, referrals and family tracing and response to GBV survivors & capacity building and life-saving messaging on prevention of family separation, child recruitment Risk Education, and other protection concerns- for teachers, community members, CP committees. The action will provide and support safe and free education that will help mitigate the impact of conflict and disasters by giving children and families a sense of normalcy, stability, structure and hope for the future, especially post-COVID. Disability mainstreaming will also be ensured in the action, by deliberately increasing efforts to identify barriers, risks and enablers for CwDs, and will disaggregate data by disability; consult closely with CWDs and address the additional risk they face in accessing education.

project_name: Provision of integrated treatment and prevention of Acute Malnutrition to reduce morbidity and mortality in children less than five years as well as PLW in priority areas in Sanaag, Togdheer, Waqooyi Galbeed and Awdal Regions - Somaliland.
project_objective:
rt community mobilization and screening as well as micro-nutrient supplementation for PLW (multiple micro-nutrients and Iron folate) and Vitamin A supplementation for children between 6-59 months. It will also provide de-worming for children 12-59 months and pregnant women in the 2nd and 3rd trimester as well as counselling and promotion on infant and young child feeding compounded with health and hygiene promotion. Moreover, measles immunization will be provided to infants living within the catchment areas of the target health centers who are not immunized against measles. Systematic defaulter tracing for immunization services will also be conducted at community level. 

In order to strengthen the accountability with affected population, we will introduce Mother-led MUAC approach to increase detection, identification and early referral of malnourished children. ANPPCANSOM will train mothers to use MUAC tapes to enable mothers screen, detect oedema and self-referral of their children to nutrition sites.

ANPPCANSOM is committed to ensuring that protection of beneficiaries and do not harm principle is prioritized into all program responses. Protection principles will be integrated into the project in order to improve the nutrition service delivery and guarantee the protection of the population from exposure to threats related to humanitarian assistance by empowering beneficiaries to claim their rights, and to prompt duty-bearers to comply with their obligations.

ANPPCANSOM is accountable to the women, men, boys and girls whose lives it aims to improve, and places this responsibility at the core of its programming. ANPPCANSOM is committed to ensure that people receiving support participate in and influence all steps of the program life-cycle, including initial assessment, project design, beneficiary selection, implementation, monitoring and evaluation. We will open up effective feedback channels as well as complaints and response mechanisms to enable ANPCPANSOM and its partners know what impact programs are having on beneficiaries and intends to incorporate feedback or address problems rapidly, including prevention of sexual assault and exploitation while enabling the deprived, disadvantaged and the marginalized to have a voice.

project_name: Provision of life saving emergency response intergrated with MHPSS program and EWAR to vulnerable populations in Banadir, Mataban, Balcad and Jowhar district of Hirshabelle state and Dusumareb and Quraceel of Galmudug region.
project_objective:
Primary health care visits and vaccination coverage have sharply declined in Somalia amidst the COVID-19 pandemic, raising concerns that vaccine preventable diseases such as respiratory infections and acute watery diarrhoea (AWD) as well as malnutrition could be going untreated, all while floods have forced people from their homes. While the healthcare system’s resources are already limited and overstretched, this development could easily degenerate into a public health.
More cases of AWD are being reported in children under five years old, who are particularly vulnerable to disease, especially if their immune systems are compromised. Critical gaps in Balcad, Marka  and Wanlaweyn where no WASH assistance has been received despite high risk levels for acute watery diarrhoea  (AWD). Aamin is currently implementing mobile service project funded by SHF reserve allocation 2020 in Balcad district. We as well are implementing SHINE project under consortium led by ACF through support of DFID in Banadir region. Aamin Ambulance provides a twenty four hour, unparalleled free ambulance service in Mogadishu, Somalia. July-Sept 2019, Aamin ambulance transported and facilitated 638 affected people (427 female, 211 male) within the ten districts covered by the SHINE project. This was a significant increase compared to last quarter by 284. The increase can be attributed to increased awareness of the availability of the free ambulance service in the ten districts. Aamin ambulance seeks to bridge the gap of unreliable health and emergency response system through this free ambulance and first aid system to the people of Mogadishu. We take cognizance of the needs the vulnerable in the community and hence our project also plays focus on the needs of the vulnerable including women and children. Through a recent needs assessment conducted by Aamin ambulance, it was established that over 2100 expectant mothers in our target districts are in need of maternal health services (including referrals) to ensure a safe pregnancy and delivery, emergency obstetric services. The situation is even life threatening when the mothers are in need of these emergencies during the wee hours of the night. Our emergency project hence seeks scale up efforts in ensuring that no woman or new-born dies during birth by avoiding prolonged labour. Aamin ambulance has 16 fully equipped ambulances staffed with qualified and well trained professionals to provide pre-hospital care to patients. The project in Mogadishu with plan to expand operations to three other states. in this Aamin ambulance will targets 22,270 people with mobile OPD consultation treatment of common illness, incidences, and early referral  for further treatment and care. Aamin Ambulance will adopt mobile clinic strategy to reach out to vulnerable people in IDPs areas and bring service close to their community. The team will provide Out-patient services to the people at the convenience of their villages. We will go to remote area, we will attain the set target and deliver high quality service the community has been yearning. ambulance will bridge it by bringing service close to the people and providing free referral services for people in critical condition. Scale-up early warning and response (EWAR) and case management of epidemic prone diseases through surveillance. The project will adopt a health informatics software that will display real time reporting, transmission and processing of epidemiological data for timely detection, verification and prompt public health response. Integration of Mental Health/Psycho-social Support (PFA) services, community engagement, and health education to community members to enhance identification and referral of persons of concern in need of MHPSS while also conducting a focused MHPSS intervention through trained social workers. Conduct psycho-education sessions for persons in need, including raising awareness on key protection risks faced by PSNs i.e discrimination, stigma
