project_name: School Meals Programme to support 72,000 school children in Logone and Chari, Mayo Sava and Mayo Tsanaga Divisions in the Fra North Region
project_objective:
The school meal activity is implemented in the Far North region targeting 72,000 school children in the most crisis affected divisions of Logone and Chari, Mayo Sava and Mayo Tsanaga. The project aims to provide school meals to 72,000 children to encourage and promote school attendance. A consequence of the Lake Chad Basin crisis, many schools were closed leaving thousands of children out of school for many years mainly in the targeted divisions. With the improvement observed in the security situation in the areas and thanks to the humanitarian support from UN agencies, and NGOs many children have been able to go back to school. The project will contribute to maintain those who are already in the school till the completion of the primary school cycle. The project will consist of providing daily hot meals to all the children during 165 days of the school year, to encourage them to attend and stay in schools throughout the school year, thus contributing to improve their nutritional status as well as to protect them enrolment by the terrorist groups. 
Food commodities will be delivered to schools and meals will be prepared for the children at school. Parents and communities will complement with various items including water, firewood and cooking services and other locally produced food. The food basket and daily rations are; cereals (140g), Pulses (40g), Oil (15g) and salt (3g). During the implementation special attention will be paid to children with disabilities. Their food will be collected and served in at their sitting place.
Various actions will be put in place to support the implementation of the project.  Capacity strengthening sessions will be organized on school feeding management, food storage, gender and Protection, for all actors involved in the school canteens management including other partners operating in the targeted division such as local councils, Parent and Teachers’ Associations, mothers’ associations and Government staff form the Ministries of Basic Education, agriculture, Health, Women affairs and social Affairs. In addition, Mothers' associations will trained on nutrition aspects using locally available food.

project_name: Support for resilience building to 47,500 vulnerable persons in the East, Adamaoua and North Regions through assets creation.
project_objective:
The influx of Central African refugees in the East Cameroon region has accentuated the vulnerability of these host populations in terms of precarious living conditions, access to socio-health infrastructure and means of subsistence. This situation has created pressure on the available natural resources and on the services offered, which are already largely insufficient. Localities such as Mandjou and Boulembe are experiencing strong demographic growth and are facing enormous difficulties in resilience, however preventing them from finding lasting solutions. Among these, we can cite: very severe cassava rots which compromise the yields of family farms, an upsurge in agro-pastoral conflicts between breeders and farmers, uncertainty of the savings resulting from market gardening production due to bad weather, To this must be added the growing problems of under-education of young people and the delay in the evolution of mentalities both among nationals and among refugees which cloud the prospects for development and social cohesion. The most exposed vulnerable populations are women (53.5% of the refugee population) and children aged 0 to 11 who constitute 44% of the refugee population. Almost 34.4% of refugees and 15.5% of host populations are in a situation of food insecurity (severe and moderate). The significant increase in the availability and diversity of local food productions, then the establishment of means of preventive control against white flies and cassava rots and finally the reframing of the agricultural calendar according to the climatic and environmental specificities of the villages in order to ensure market gardening activities throughout the year are the main challenges in our intervention areas. Considering the massive and sudden arrival of refugees from the Central African crisis in 2004, 45% of food consumed by households in these villages has been imported. Local productions (cassava, corn, vegetables) are not yet significant in meeting local household food demands.
According to the assessment made by WFP, humanitarian solidarity partners (UNHCR, International Solidarity, FAO, PLAN CAMEROUN ...) and sectoral (MINADER, MINEPIA, MINPROF, MINEPAT, MINFOPRA, MINEPDED ...) accompanied by a Participatory Community Plan held in 2018 and 2019 showed that in these villages on the vulnerability of populations, 30% of the population is very vulnerable; 50% have a medium vulnerability level and 20% a moderate vulnerability.
The main activity of the populations noted during exchanges with local communities, held throughout our coverage area, is the cultivation of cassava, to which is grafted that of corn, peanuts, market gardening, petty trade, fishing, breeding.
In view of the situation mentioned above in terms of food imbalance which has generated rampant insecurity and a shortage of food availability in line with the ever-continuing demographic growth within communities which, at the end of the consultations, one major solutions had been to enable them to meet their own nutritional needs through the establishment of agro-pastoral activities; the provision of small agricultural equipment; quality seeds and openness to small trade, which justifies a need for support on the technical itineraries recorded. Hence the project will support the increase in agro-pastoral production in the East.
This intervention is in line with the consolidation of the assets carried out between 2018 and 2019 on the one hand and with a view to building resilience capacities within the beneficiary populations: food security, nutrition and social cohesion of somewhere else.
These activities, effectively put together, will constitute a march towards an integrated agriculture that can contribute to the achievement of the Zero Hunger Objective by 2030 according to the agenda that Cameroon and the other UN member countries have adopted and which constitutes the mission of the World Food Program.

project_name: Unconditional food assistance to 48,800 CAR Refugees in the East, Adamaoua and North Regions (CBT)
project_objective: In the Eastern regions, the insecurity caused by the socio-political crisis in CAR since March 2013 has forced many Central Africans to seek refuge in neighbouring countries. Cameroon has been the main destination of this displaced population because of the 800 km of border it shares with CAR and also the cross-border ethnic affinities between the two countries. According to UNHCR (November, 2019), 292,863 CAR refugees from different arrival waves (2003, 2008 and 2014) are settled in the East, Adamawa, and North regions of Cameroon, mainly in the rural areas. 30% of these refugees live in 7 refugee sites while the remaining 70% live in more than 100 localities across 23 communes in these three regions. This refugee population is largely made up of children, young people and women. This demographic pressure has resulted in increased vulnerabilities, and a trio-crisis of humanitarian-peace-development challenges. The findings of JAM conducted from November 2018 to May 2019 revealed that 81% of refugees are highly vulnerable, about 58.9% of refugees are in need for immediate food assistance, out of which 38.9% need livelihood support. Overall food consumption is acceptable among refugees (63 %) and host communities (79 %), with distributed food consumption patterns across regions. The consumption rate of inadequate diets was reported by 35.7 % , 33.8% and 31.2 % of households respectively for Adamawa, North and East. Despite this stability, the refugee households rely on unstable food sources, mainly food assistance, humanitarian cash transfers and gifts. The presence of CAR refugees has greatly increased pressures on natural resources and basic social infrastructure that were already precarious. Competition over scarce resources and the consequent tensions between refugees and host communities, farmers and herders have led to an increase in food needs, as well as a deterioration in the provision of basic social services and severe environmental degradation. The multifaceted assistance provided by the Government of Cameroon and humanitarian actors is still far from optimal to ensure sustainable food security and basic needs for this population. This is due to several factors, including the persistence of insecurity in CAR (and the worldwide multiple crises which have shifted donors’ interest from the situation in CAR. This has led to a decline in resources for CAR refugees in Cameroon. A UNHCR survey (June 2018) of 4,000 people in refugee sites and host villages in the East and Adamawa regions indicates that 74% of CAR refugees (70%) prefer local integration in Cameroon as a durable solution rather than returning to their home country, mainly due to insecurity in CAR. This situation is especially of concern since, according to the 2019 JAM for CAR refugees, these population groups are worse off than host communities. Assessments also report that vulnerable local populations have had to resort to negative food-related coping strategies, reducing the number of meals (to one meal a day) and quantity of food consumed by adults in order to feed the children. A survey carried out by UNHCR-WFP in Eastern Cameroon in September 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic negatively affected income-generating activities of CAR refugees, causing supply difficulties, reducing economic activities, limiting access to fields, reducing access to seeds and other agricultural inputs, due to restrictions on movement. Due to resource shortfalls, WFP has been providing 50% food rations which has negatively impacted the food consumption of CBT beneficiaries and significantly increased the chances of households moving from the acceptable to the poor or borderline group (PDM, November 2020). Through this project, WFP is planning to provide unconditional cash transfers to the CAR refugees to ensure they can cover their food and nutrition needs and, therefore prevent them from resorting to negative coping mechanisms which would deepen their vulnerability.

project_name: Protección y asistencia humanitaria para víctimas del conflicto y la violencia armada en los departamentos de Chocó, Antioquia y Córdoba (2021-2022).
project_objective:
La acción tiene como objetivo responder a nuevos eventos de desplazamiento forzado y/o restricciones de movilidad y confinamiento, generados el conflicto y violencia armada en el norte de Colombia en las sub-regiones de Urabá, Norte de Chocó, Antioquia y Bajo Cauca; así como la respuesta insuficiente de las autoridades locales y nacionales frente a los escenarios de emergencia humanitaria. El contexto humanitario de la región objetivo está dominado por una lucha permanente entre los grupos armados por el control de los territorios estratégicamente importantes y corredores de economías ilícitas como contrabando y narcotráfico. A medida que las extintas FARC se están retirando después de su desmovilización, los grupos armados (ELN y BACRIM) están ampliando su control territorial, reconfigurando la violencia y causando nuevos desplazamientos, hostigamientos, homicidios y limitaciones de la movilidad.

Teniendo en cuenta las necesidades humanitarias identificadas, se adopta un enfoque integral (que combina los diferentes sectores de intervención). La protección de las comunidades establecidas, es el objetivo principal de la acción que establece una sinergia entre la protección como enfoque transversal en todas las actividades y con actividades específicas para aumentar la resiliencia de la comunidad frente a los riesgos existentes y fortalecer sus capacidades organizativas con un enfoque adicional de construcción de paz.

project_name: Improved access to Life Saving basic Health services for vulnerable boys, girls, men and women in Nugaal, Sool, Lower shabelle, Bakool, Hiraan and Banadir regions in Somalia.
project_objective: The proposed project targets 15  districts in 6 regions of Somalia namely  Nugaal region (Garowe District), Sool region (Hudun and Boame districts), Bakool region (Hudur, Elberde, Rabdure, and Wajid)  Lower Shabelle (Afgoye district), Hiran region (Beletweyn, Bulo burto and Jalalaqsi districts) and  Banadir (Kahda, Hodan, Abdiaziz and Waaberi). The project aims to cover the health needs of drought/conflict affected women, men, boys and girls in the target locations by providing curative and preventive basic lifesaving health services among the communities by Action Against Hunger. COVID-19 preventive measures will be adhered during implementation. Protective gear will be provided to health care workers during the service delivery to minimize disease transmission as well as capacity building on Infection Prevention & Control, and COVID-19 case management. The project is planned to reach a total of 167,190 (81,923 M & 85,267 F) for a period of 12 months.  The project will provide services through one hospital in Afgoye district, one referral health centre in Elbarde district, and in fourteen health centres, in addition to fourteen primary health units, in line with EPHS package. Additionally, the health facility committee and community-level health service provision will be strengthened in the project target location with a full representation of key community stakeholders including people living with disability. The project will be linked with other interventions (Nutrition, WASH & FSL) in the same location in order to provide a holistic package to the target beneficiaries.

project_name: Scaling-up and providing integrated protection services to IDPs and vulnerable communities including people with disability in in Gedo and Lower Jubba Regions of Jubbaland State in Somalia.
project_objective:
The project activities will support the provision of appropriate and efficient child protection and GBV services as well as raising awareness on prevention of child protection, GBV, and harmful practices in the two regions including hard-to-reach areas. Services including Medical, Psychosocial support and case management will be offered. Material supports such as dignity kits and solar lights will be provided to both adults and children. The project will also work on recovery and resilience of survivors and their families-This will be done through capacity building, involvement of communities in protection activities, and through provision of Cash-Based Intervention (CBI) to enhance self-reliance and resilience of survivors and at-risk groups. SEDHURO plan to conduct awareness raising through community meetings, dialogue sessions and out-reach sensitisation campaigns. 

The project will provide CMR training to HW. The content of the CMR training will cover legal, psychological, medical and involvement of communities for better collaboration for the help of survivors. Health providers will also be trained to be compassionate and provide emotional support to survivors. The training also intends to roll out the CMR protocol, endorsed by the ministry of health in December 2015.SEDHURO will assess the capacities of health clinics before they receive the kits with respect to their capacity in the provision of reproductive health services including family planning, antenatal care, normal delivery care, or management of STIs.

The project will establish community-based mechanisms for prevention and response of separation of children and Gender Based Violence against children and women to enhance grassroots identification, prevention of and response to child protection concerns. 

Case management process will be initiated for all unaccompanied children, including provision of interim family–based care, family tracing and reunification. The vulnerabilities of UASC will be assessed based on the individual circumstances of each child including the type of separation, the duration of separation, contact arrangements, the suitability of care arrangements, child’s age, gender, children with disabilities and the child’s best interests. Following this assessment an appropriate care plan will be developed. CP officers will work with CPC and coordinate with other agencies involved in way-stations management, IDP camp management, food distribution points, madarasa/school teachers, medical facilities to identify UASC. Identification of UASC will also take place in outlying villages to ensure maximum coverage and response. This will be done with the informed consent of the children.
CFS will ensure children have a safe place to gather for play, for self-expression and learning. To enhance ownership and resilience and the likelihood of sustaining the longer-term impacts of psychosocial interventions, CFS will be established and operated in a way that engages or strengthens support systems within families and communities. 
The project will provide specialized social service and/or mental health care for parents with MNS disorders and support for the wellbeing and coping ability of parents, raising awareness of distress reactions of children in emergencies, according to age and developmental stage and further promoting positive parenting knowledge and skills among caregivers. They will be introduced through discussion and dialogue sessions parenting messages that improve relationship with children under their care with Focused care for distressed parents/caregivers, including PFA to be provided.

Public broadcasts of key protection messages will be conducted twice per week for four weeks during the first quarter of the programme and twice per month for the rest of the programme. These broadcasts will cover 200,000 people within the IDP camps and host communities and ensure broad based knowledge and awareness.

project_name: Providing life-saving and sustainable WASH service to underserved IDP communities in Somalia
project_objective:
ACTED is implementing a market-based project in six largely underserved and high-WASH risk IDP sites in Bardera, including Bulo Ceesan, Bulo Garass, Liban, Xabalcadey, Horseed and Kulmiya IDP sites, and is serving approximately 44,280 individuals. To ensure the sustainability of this action, ACTED is collaborating with the private sector to extend existing water networks to these communities and where necessary construct new water assets. The activities aim to meet both the acute and long-term needs of the vulnerable IDP communities, whilst establishing relationships with the private sector for continued maintenance and operation of these assets.
ACTED throughout project implementation will ensure all gender, persons of disability are included during consultation and in  WASH management committees. In selecting beneficiaries, ACTED will give priority to female headed households, households led by persons with disability and households with lactating or pregnant women.

project_name: Enhanced access to quality emergency and essential lifesaving health services for crisis affected populations living in Galkcayo, Hobyo, Abduwak, Afgooye and Beletweyne Districts through improved case management and efficient referral system.
project_objective:
The health situation in Galkayo, Hobyo, Afgooye, Belatwyne and Abduwaak districts seem to be worsening due to the compounded negative impacts of covid-19, flooding, desert locust infestation and lack of basic health services. The average morbidity rate among under-five children in these districts is 19% while the coverage for vitamin A is 59.8% with coverage for measles vaccination standing at 61.5% while the clear water access is only 28% (CESVI progress report, 2020). COVID 19 pandemic has an adverse effect on the service delivery where access to health and nutrition services of the population has been greatly hampered. The impacts of these threats not only led to aggravation of the shocks but also
exacerbated the challenges of the vulnerable groups. 
To address the challenges enumerated above, CESVI will implement a life-saving health interventions through 7 static and 5 mobile Health clinics to increase access to basic health services. This action will address endemic diseases like pneumonia, anemia, acute watery diarrhea and ARI which are the leading causes of infant and child mortality in the target villages. CESVI will provide primary, and referral health care, with special attention to maternal and child health, including basic emergency obstetric care (BEmONC), Expanded Program on Immunization. This project will create demand for health services including family planning, antenatal care services and delivery at health facilities through sensitization of the communities by trained Community health workers on the importance of these services.
Health mobile clinics will serve IDP camps and villages in the far flung villages to deliver quality primary health care services to populations without a static MCH in close proximity. Moreover, Health facilities will be equipped (after minor rehabilitations) with essential drugs, vaccines and post- rape treatment drugs including medical equipment. Further, this intervention will enhance a referral system from primary to secondary health services and TB services and from nutrition to health services and vice versa. 
Community Health Workers (CHW) will be engaged as part of the emergency response team to actively act as first responders for health and nutrition issues. They will play a key role in the referral system ensuring better access to health care services for the population in general, but for the most vulnerable in particular.
Monitoring of activities and epidemiological surveillance will be maintained and strengthened through strong partnership with MoH and using official and revised HIMS MoH tools to support identification of risks, monitoring of incidence and to increasing efficiency towards timely response to health programs. Community health workers appointed as part of MCH staffs will be will be equipped with skills on alert thresholds for epidemic diseases as per WHO standards. They will be issued with cell phones and in the course of discharging their duties of promoting community awareness, they will also act as sentinels to detect any change in the context in terms of emergency, epidemic outbreaks and relay information to CESVI senior Health staff who will immediately contact the MoH and WHO for case verification to facilitate immediate response.
To prevent AWD/cholera epidemic outbreak, hygiene promotion campaigns will be organized regularly throughout the action within the target villages.
The project will provide trainings targeting thematic areas such ANC and BEmONC, drugs consumption and GBV/Protection mainstreaming among others. Joint supportive supervision will also be undertaken with MoH as per of efforts to build their capacity.

project_name: support to vulnerable food insecure holds in Somalia through provision of essential livelihoods packages
project_objective:
According to FSNAU/ FEWSNET September 2020, acute food insecurity and malnutrition conditions exist in Somalia at alarming levels due to multiple shocks that negatively affected livelihood assets of the most vulnerable households. GU seasonal flooding and Desert locust upsurge contributed to loss and damage to property, housing, farmland and infrastructure. Also, social economic impacts occasioned by COVID 19 pandemic significantly contributed to food insecurity in Somalia. Social unrest in some parts of the country led to unprecedented levels of population displacement and disruption of livelihoods forcing hundreds of thousands to adopt negative coping mechanisms. Although livestock holding and milk availability is improving generally in Somalia, however, protracted droughts over the years combined with desert locust manifestation resulted drastic decline of livestock herd size holding among pastoral and agro pastoral households in Somalia leading to increased destitution and displacement in rural setups. 
401, 136 people are in emergency (IPC 4) of which 31% are rural population, 8% urban, 61 IDPs and urban population, while 3,048,080 people are in crisis (IPC 3) of which 24% are non-displaced rural population, 51% urban population while 26% are IDPs/ urban/ rural population (FSNAU/FEWSNET December 2020). Projection estimates shows that over 3.5 million Somalis will be deprived to access essential food and non-food needs in 2021 if current food indicators persist. According to FSNAU post GU report released on 30th of September 2020, Galgadud and Lower Juba  regions of Somalia has combined population of 6,000 people in in emergency (IPC4) from July to September 2020. Additional 7000 People are projected to be in (IPC 4) from October to December 2020. The report further revealed that an estimated 30,000 people in the same regions are in crisis (IPC 3), while putting projection figures at 39,000 from October 2020 to December 2020. Without sustained large scale humanitarian assistance worse food security outcomes 
The proposed intervention seeks to respond to the food needs of the affected households in Galgaduud and Lower Juba regions of Somalia with essential livelihood packages such as cash, voucher, livestock treatment and feed in order to strengthen and protect the livelihood assets of the poor and most vulnerable households.HOD currently implementing livestock activities with FAO Galgaduud. HOD seeks to use integrated food security packages which will respond to both immediate and the long term needs of the affected population. The intervention will support 2,100 households with total population of 12,600 persons (Women 3110, men 1285, boys 3765, and girls 4340). The transfer value will be based on the current regional MEB. The proposed project is cost effective because 80% of the project budget will go to the project beneﬁciaries making the project cost effective. Accountability on cash tracking will be achieved through the use of vouchers which will contain the name and unique identification of each beneficiary. A competitively selected Money vendor will also be engaged to process payments for beneﬁciaries in order to reduce risk associated with the cash and to enhance accountability in the cash transfer process. The use of cash is informed by the availability of well-functioning market system. It also responds well to local needs during crisis. A post distribution assessment for the beneﬁciaries will be done to verify how much cash each received and the use they have put the cash to. A feedback mechanism/grievance mechanism will also be put in place for beneﬁciaries to reach out for any support. Frequent spot checks will be done to verify whether beneﬁciaries are receiving the right amount. Market data will be collected on regular basis to monitor cash impact on the market

project_name: Improving dignified living conditions and protection of Crisis affected IDPs, returnees living in informal settlements in Bay and Lower Shabelle and Middle Shabelle Regions, Somalia
project_objective: The project is aimed at providing appropriate support to ensure dignified living conditions for  26000 displaced person (10816 women, 9984men, 2600 boys and 2600 boys) at the informal settlements in Bay, lower Shabelle and Middle Shabelle Regions Somalia. The targeted IDPs including people with disabilities are living precariously in crowded informal settlements in Bay, Lower Shabelle and Middle Shabelle Regions, Somalia. The recent climate shocks and insecurity affected IDPs are living  under very poor and deplorable conditions in unplanned informal settlements with limited access to basic needs owing to inconsistent and unreliable service provision coupled by cases of exclusion from accessing humanitarian assistance. Women, girls and people with disabilities are further affected by unplanned nature of the IDP sites that limit them from accessing essential services such as latrines located within the sites which compromise their safety. The situation is exacerbated by poor coordination and management structures at the settlement owing to the fact that they are managed by gatekeepers who are not accountable and further keeps demanding for favors from them in the face of fears of rampant evictions. The highlighted plight calls for need for timely and appropriate site improvements to enhance safe and secure access to critical services available within the sites particularly for women, girls and people with disabilities in addition to very strong need for site-level coordination and management systems to ensure equitable access to services and increase protection of displaced persons. Furthermore there is need for information sharing with meaningful consultation and participation of affected IDP communities and People with disabilities to ensure their dignified living conditions sustainable impact

project_name: Assistance nutritionnelle aux personnes résidant dans les 6 régions du Burkina Faso affectées par l’insécurité
project_objective:
Malgré les efforts notables qui ont été réalisés au Burkina Faso dans le domaine de la nutrition et de lutte contre la malnutrition, cette dernière demeure un problème majeur de santé publique. Le pays connait une situation sécuritaire qui continue de se détériorer de façon significative sur l'ensemble du territoire avec pour corollaire un déplacement massif continue de populations, mais aussi un accès limité aux soins de santé primaires qui a été exacerbé par l’impact indirect de la pandémie à la COVID-19 qui n’a pas épargnée le Burkina Faso depuis Mars 2020. En effet, presque un tiers des structures de soins sont fermées (28%), dont plus de la moitié concerne les régions du Sahel et Centre Nord, et plus de la moitié des structures accueillent des PDIs. Les résultats de l’enquête rapid SMART de Juillet et Octobre 2020  dans les communautés et sites d’accueil de grand effectif de personnes déplacées internes a révélé une situation nutritionnelle critique des enfants de 6 à 59 mois ainsi que des femmes enceintes et femmes allaitantes (FEFA) chez les PDIs mais aussi chez les ménages hôtes,. La prévalence de la malnutrition aigüe globale dépasse le « seuil d’alerte » OMS de 10% dans un grand nombre de communes avec des facteurs aggravants ou surpassait ke seuil d’urgence/critique de l’OMS de 15% dans certaines communes des régions du Sahel et du Centre Nord. 
Au regard de ce contexte, et de la faible couverture de la prise en charge globale de la malnutrition aigüe, le PAM fournira une assistance nutritionnelle d’urgence, avec une approche multisectorielle, sous forme d’un package d’interventions complémentaires et synergiques comprenant l’extension des activités de prévention de la malnutrition,  le traitement de la malnutrition aiguë modérée, le renforcement de capacité des agents de santé communautaires y compris dans le traitement au niveau communautaire et la Communication pour le Changement Social et Comportemental (CCSC).
Pour les activités de prévention, le PAM fournira un appui nutritionnel sous forme de « rations de protection » nutritives et enrichies à 160 023 enfants âgés de 6 à 23 mois (IDPs et Pop Hotes) et à 55 546 FEFA. Cela permettra de réduire les risques de malnutrition ainsi que les risques d’aggraver davantage la situation nutritionnelle des femmes en période de vulnérabilité, vecteur principal pour de faible poids de naissance et malnutrition intergénérationnelle. Cette intervention spécifique tout en permettant de réaliser des dépistages actifs de la malnutrition aigüe puis en orientant précocement les sujets diagnostiqués malnutris vers les structures de prises en charge appropriées est une opportunité pour renforcer les connaissances des participants sur les bonnes pratiques alimentaire, d’hygiène, assainissement en vue de leur adoption. 
Le PAM appuiera également la prise en charge curative « intégrée » au niveau des structures de soins mais aussi au niveau communautaire des enfants de 6-59 mois et des femmes enceintes ou allaitantes présentant une malnutrition aigüe modérée. Pour ce faire, les structures de prise en charge étatiques seront approvisionnées en intrants nutritionnels adaptés, à savoir, pour assister 153 474 enfants âgés de 6 à 59 mois et 52 687 FEFA  pendant trois mois. Pour renforcer la prise en charge de la malnutrition aigüe sévère dans les centres de récupération et d’éducation nutrition, le PAM prévoit apporter une assistance alimentaire à 10 533 mères d’enfants MAS hospitalisés. 
Les activités se dérouleront sur une période de 12 mois. 
Le présent projet qui adressera les besoins des populations déplacées, hôtes et vulnérables, vise à contribuer à la réduction de la morbidité et de la mortalité infantile et maternelle, à travers une amélioration de la couverture de prise en charge préventive et curative de la malnutrition et à la promotion cohabitation pacifique entre ces populations.
Le projet représente une partie des besoins totale du PAM sur cette activité.

project_name: Programme de cantines scolaires d’urgences au profit des élèves déplacés de 5 régions à haut défi sécuritaire du Burkina Faso
project_objective: L’insécurité croissante et continue qui prévaut au Burkina Faso depuis 2015 s’est traduite par la fermeture au 10 mars 2020, de 2 512 écoles, affectant 349 909 élèves et 11 219 enseignants. A la rentrée scolaire 2020-2021 on dénombrait 2 206 écoles fermées. Suite à la COVID-19 le gouvernement a ordonné la fermeture de 20 754 établissements scolaires affectant 5 130 730 d’élèves et 122 810 enseignants et personnels éducatifs. Les régions du Sahel, du Centre-Nord, de l’Est, du Centre Est, du Nord et de la Boucle du Mouhoun constituent les zones à haut défi sécuritaire du pays.  En réponse à ces deux crises majeures, le PAM a mis en œuvre à compter de 2019, un programme d’alimentation scolaire en situation d’urgence afin d’assurer la protection des enfants et faciliter leur accès à l’alimentation et à la nutrition. Ce programme d'alimentation scolaire en situation d'urgence, cible les élèves déplacés en priorité qui ont été réinstallés avec leur famille dans des zones sécurisées des régions affectées par l’insécurité. Il vise à sauver des vies tout en contribuant à l’accès et au maintien à l’éducation de base des enfants par la fourniture de repas scolaires nutritifs et la protection des moyens d’existence de leurs parents. Il contribuera à la réduction des obstacles à l'éducation de base des enfants notamment ceux des filles vivant dans les régions Sahel, du Centre-Nord, de l’Est, du Nord et de la Boucle du Mouhoun et complètera les initiatives sectorielles existantes visant l’amélioration des indicateurs de l’éducation.

project_name: Improved learning , early childhood and skills development opportunities  for crisis affected Rohingya and host community children, adolescents and youth in Cox's Bazar District.
project_objective:
UNICEF will support improved access to learning, early childhood and skills development opportunities for 296,065 (50% girls) refugee crisis affected children, adolescents and youth aged 3-24 years, including 260,043 in the camps and 36,022 in Teknaf and Ukhyia upazilas of Cox’s Bazar District. 

In the camps, UNICEF will sustain operational cost of 2,645 learning centres and support capacity building of teachers, technical officers and programme officers to enable them effectively support the delivery of improved learning for 226,035 (50% girls) children and adolescents aged 3-14 years using the learning competency framework and approach (LCFA) as well as the Myanmar curriculum for students in Grades 6 to 9 and Grades 1 and 2. UNICEF will upgrade 115 existing LCs to a double-storey, medium-hazard structures, contributing to increased access to emergency shelters for the refugee population in case of disaster and providing safe and protective learning environment for children. In addition, 34,008 refugee adolescents and youth (15-24) will be supported with secondary education (10,000) based on the Myanmar curriculum and vocational skills development (24,008) programmes.  UNICEF also support capacity building of partners on inclusive education, learning outcomes assessment and the use of education technology solutions to enhance the delivery of education services as part of the COVID19 response and recovery. 

In the host communities in Teknaf and Ukhyia, UNICEF will support 36,022 children, adolescents and youth to access improved quality preprimary and primary education (28,818 children) and vocational skills training (7,204) programmes for out of school adolescents and youth. The support to host community will include system strengthening component aimed at enhancing the capacity of the district primary office on evidence based planning to enhance acceleration of access to equitable quality education. Schools will be supported to safely reopen and provide continuity of learning with appropriate safety measures in place. UNICEF will provide grants to schools to support implementation of school improvement plans in collaboration with school management committees.

project_name: Strengthened Protection for Children in Rohingya camps and Host Communities
project_objective:
In coordination with the CPSS and relevant sectors, the Project will prevent and respond to abuse, exploitation, violence (including GBV) and neglect of children in targeted communities, adopting a socio-ecological approach that recognizes the roles of children, families and communities in the protective environment and builds on their inherent strengths. The Project will contribute to systems-strengthening that ensures children have access to a continuum of care that bridges the humanitarian-development nexus.
The project will reach 160,864 boys (48%) and girls (52%) including CwD (10%), adolescents, and unaccompanied and separated children with high quality services. The project will leverage significant programming experience in Cox’s Bazar to provide PSS, life skills-based learning, pre-vocational training (such as ‘greening’ initiatives), social cohesion and resilience, and recreation activities. The Covid19 pandemic will see community outreach mobilizers, volunteers and community groups will playing a crucial role. The support to adolescents will recognize their capacities as agents of positive change.  108,873 men (48%) and women (52%) will benefit from positive parenting support, protection awareness and social mobilization through CBCPCs. Overall, 75% of beneficiaries will be from camps and 25% from host communities. Interventions will follow a survivor centered, Do No Harm approach that minimizes stigma. AAP, complaints and feedback mechanisms will be embedded in all activities. 
Services will be delivered primarily through Multipurpose Centers and Social Hubs. Through an integrated approach, the Project will prioritize case management with trained personnel linking and facilitating children’s referral to specialized services, the quantitative and qualitative scale-up of CBCPCs, and bolstering protection at the household level will be bolstered through guidance to parents and caregivers. PSEA will be afforded the highest consideration.
The Project will build the capacities of government; strengthening the social workforce, improving information management through roll-out of CPIMS+, and accelerating birth registration in through upgraded systems and trained personnel.

project_name: Increased access to community- and facility-based nutrition services in Banadir, Galgadud, Mudug, Hiraan, and Togdheer regions in Somalia.
project_objective:
Mercy-USA for Aid and Development intends to set up a project to address the urgent nutrition needs in Banadir, Galgadud, Hiran, Mudug and Togdheer regions of Somalia.  Since the collapse of Somalia's central government in 1991, repeated conflict in conjunction with poor food security, limited healthcare and nutrition service availability and has resulted in Somalia having among the worst health-related indicators in the world.
According to FSNAU-FEWSNET-2020-Post-Gu-Technical-Release, 2.1 million people across Somalia are expected to face Crisis or worse (IPC Phase 3 or higher) outcomes between now and December without sustained humanitarian assistance. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC Phase 2), bringing the total number of people facing acute food insecurity to 5.1 million. Humanitarian assistance must be sustained through December 2020 to prevent Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or Emergency (IPC Phase 4) outcomes for 2.1 million people. 
Mercy-USA will provide treatment of Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) and Moderate Acute Malnutrition (MAM) through IP (Inpatient Therapeutic), OTP (Outpatient Therapeutic) and SFP (Supplementary Feeding) services in line with the Basic Nutrition Service Package (BNSP) at up to 39 facilities and related outreaches. Mercy-USA will train and support nutrition workers to identify, provide lifesaving treatment and follow-up on cases of malnutrition. Mercy-USA will also integrate preventative services including providing Infant Youth and Child Feeding (IYCF) counseling and micronutrient supplementation at MCHs. Community-level social mobilization will be done to promote healthy nutritional practices, including campaigns for micronutrient supplementation, deworming, and improved feeding practices. The Mother-led MUAC approach will be used for referrals.
Mercy-USA will ensure that people with disabilities participate in the implementation of project activities by ensuring that they are represented in all community meetings. The project will consult with PWDs about location, design, safety, and facilities' appropriateness. During project implementation, segregated focus group discussions will be held with the community to identify gender inequalities, discuss all the genders' needs, and understand the risks faced by PWDs in accessing nutrition services. Activities will target to address these needs during program implementation. 
Access to children with disabilities and their caretakers and/or disabled pregnant and lactating women will be ensured and increased through outreach activities and behavioral change communication campaigns.
During routine and regular program monitoring and evaluation, Mercy-USA staff will collect disaggregated data by disability, age and gender to monitor the impact of programs on vulnerable groups. Mercy-USA, during both monthly and quarterly reviews and analysis of data, will seek to monitor the inclusiveness of programming by comparing achievements versus available population data.

project_name: Provide immediate lifesaving Basic Nutrition Service Package support to <5 children boys, girls and pregnant and lactating mothers in Ceelwaaq, Baardhere and Garbaharey in Gedo region.
project_objective:
In 2020 Somalia have major shocks that great affected service delivery and livelihoods these included infestation of desert locust, flash floods and Corona Virus Pandemic. According to (Somalia-2020-Post-Gu-Seasonal-Food-Security-and-Nutrition-Assessment-Findings-30-September-2020)  Currently (July September 2020 an estimated 1.3 million (i .e people in IPC Phases 3-4) people have food consumption gaps, even in the presence of humanitarian assistance this number is expected to increase to 2.1 million people between now and the end of the year due to multiple risk factors . At the national level, the median prevalence of Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) has remained Serious (10–14.9%) over the past three seasons (11.8% in 2020 Gu, 13.1% in 2019 Deyr and 13.8% in 2019 Gu). Urgent treatment and nutrition support are required for approximately 849 900 children under the age of five years (total acute malnutrition burden), who will likely face acute malnutrition through August 2021, including 143 400 who are likely to be severely malnourished. Integrated interventions should be provided to support recovery and prevent deterioration in the nutrition situation.
Internally displaced persons (IDPs), majority of whom are poor and live in urban areas in desperate conditions, have limited livelihood assets and coping options and rely more heavily on external humanitarian assistance. As a result, a significant proportion of IDPs continue to face moderate to large food consumption gaps. Some of the urban poor across Somalia who struggle to make ends meet also continue to face moderate to large food consumption gaps. For both groups (i.e. IDPs and urban poor), the socioeconomic impact of COVID-19 was a factor, associated with a decline in remittances, increased food prices, and a decline in employment and other income-earning opportunities in urban areas. 
 HDC intends to scale up lifesaving nutrition intervention with the treatment of severely acute malnourished children(SAM cases) both complicated an uncomplicated cases for children n(6-59 months) and moderately malnourished cases on both <5 and Pregnant and lactating women through 6 fixed outpatient therapeutic program in  and 6 mobile services which will cover other smaller pastoral villages in the surrounding areas of  Ceel Waaq, Baardhere, and Garbarey  districts .The project shall strive to integrate basic nutrition services packages that will includes of nutrition education on infant and young child feeding for Pregnant and lactating mothers on Nutrition, hygiene and health promotion, support mother to mother, vaccination, micronutrients supplementation for children <5 and pregnant and lactating women. The project will identify the target beneficiaries, children <5 and pregnant and lactating mothers through screening and community sensitization and awareness campaign through community health workers .Through the proposed project HDC project will support 2000 boys, 2000 girls and 1200 pregnant and lactating women in then project area, It will also capacity build the community health workers, project technical staff on integrated management of acute malnutrition (IMAM),infants young child feeding best practices(IYCF),Nutrition, health and hygiene promotion (NHHP) as well as conduct caregivers infant and young child feeding practices (IYCF) promotion session for better information dissemination to the caregivers in the project area.

project_name: Strengthening the Protection of vulnerable girls, women, boys and men affected by conflict and climatic shocks in Somalia
project_objective: Women and children are disproportionately affected by violence, emergencies and displacement, which exacerbates the protection risks faced, especially those in IDP populations who are at grave risk of exploitation, violence and abuse and are vulnerable to a range of protection concerns and bear the brunt of these vulnerabilities resulting in negative coping strategies. Groups such as women-headed households, unaccompanied children, socially marginalized and discriminated communities are at particular risk and face further protection concerns.  Many children are exposed to risks adopt negative coping strategies including enlisting into armed groups/forces and other harmful activities like criminal gangs and substance abuse among many. According to the GBV AOR, 95% of all incident reported in 2019 were women and girls while 76% of these were from displaced communities. Further, due to cultural barriers and weak protection institutions, inequality and disrespect of women and children’s rights continue with dire results such as separation of families, unwanted pregnancies, transmission of STI’s and mental disorders among others. The objective of the project is to strengthen the protection of most vulnerable girls, boys, women and men including people with special needs affected by conflict and climatic shocks by reducing risks and vulnerabilities and increasing community capacities. It will employ participatory and right based approaches, survivor- centre approach, AGD approach and community-based approach which will involve, inclusion of the target population; refugees/asylum seekers, migrants, IDPs and most vulnerable host communities in addition to local authorities in the project cycle. The project aims to build and strengthen local capacities within the community and support them to establish a protection framework to prevent and respond to violations. It will focus on improving capacity for immediate response to violations and remedial action as well as strengthening the protective environment in Somalia.On immediate response, the action will aim to address acute protection needs of girls, boys, women and men, stemming from violence, including GBV, child rights violations, as well as coercion, and abuse. Using a survivor centered multi-sectoral approach DRC, vulnerable women and girls will receive GBV services through Women and girls safe spaces, psychosocial support (PSS) and case management. To enable recovery and restore dignity of individual and community victims of violence, neglect, abuse and exploitation and to improve positive coping strategies and prevent further violations, DRC will establish child friendly spaces through which psychological first aid support will be provided. In addition, material assistance and livelihood skills training for GBV survivors will also be provided. On environment building, DRC will reinforce formal and community institutions for better legal and community-based protection of vulnerable groups from violence, coercion and abuse. Key to achieve this objective, activities will include awareness-raising and outreach among communities on protection issues, capacity building and training for stakeholders on GBV, CP and HLP. In addition, DRC will map out civil identification documentation required in Somalia to obtain/access government services such as ID's, passports, title deeds as well as birth and death certificates. The information will be disseminated to strengthen governance structures and to support service delivery to affected populations. On advocacy, DRC will strengthen coordination of protection services and enhance advocacy on protection with relevant stakeholders. Key activities will include strengthening of referral pathways, mapping of service providers and Protection Monitoring of rights violations. DRC will further identify and provide protection-oriented support to people with disabilities. The proposed action will reach 55,700persons (3500G, 3500B, 24000M & 24700W).

project_name: Sustainable and Emergency Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene interventions for emergency affected and vulnerable populations in Somalia
project_objective: The humanitarian context in Somalia has remained fragile; the impact of the prolonged 2016-17 drought and subsequent hurdles, like poor Deyr rains in 2018 (October-December), an unusually hot dry Jilaal season in 2019 (December-March), and abnormal, erratic rainfall during the same year's GU rainy season (April-June).  flash flooding has also affected 540,000 people across Middle and Lower Juba, Bay, Lower and Middle Shabelle, and Hiraan; 370,000 have already been displaced. Climatic shocks, combined with other persistent drivers of needs - such as armed conflict and/or displacement - have left around five million Somalis in need of humanitarian assistance (HNO overview 2020 OCHA). In Banadir region, a rapid assessment of recent flood damage to WASH infrastructure and facilities conducted on 17 July by the WASH Cluster found that 130 latrines have been damaged or destroyed, affecting over 1,200 people, in IDP sites in Kahda, Daynille and Garasbarley districts. IDPs are currently residing in urban and peri-urban informal crowded settlements, with insufficient access to WASH services that raise protection and health concerns. DRC proposes to undertake a life-saving and sustainable assistance to 131,250 individuals (18,375men, 21,300 women, 41,892 girls, 44,733boys, 5,250 EVIs) Disaster-Affected Communities IDPs, returnees, refugees and host communities through provision of emergency and sustainable WASH interventions (water, sanitation and hygiene) geared towards improved well-being of people and prevention of morbidity and mortality from WASH-related disease outbreaks.  DRC will prioritize the displaced in affected by droughts, floods and armed conflict but excluded humanitarian assistance, in DRC operational areas particularly those experiencing shortage of water and communities; and service levels are putting the health and of populations at risk. Interventions will focus on marginalized families and vulnerable female-headed households. DRC will also include Persons with disabilities challenged physical access and information in WASH interventions. DRC will carry out Joint analysis prior to implementation to inform the neediest sites and priorities. Predetermined beneficiary selection criteria will be used to reach the most vulnerable HHs/individuals. Gender will be mainstreamed into the project through the specific consideration of the different needs of women, men, boys and girls during the design of activities. Life-saving WASH interventions include; water trucking where there is no safe water source, fabrication and distribution of portable water tanks, emergency latrine, sanitation and hygiene kits and rapid hygiene promotion and durable WASH solutions of improved and equitable access to safe, of adequate yields. DRC will rehabilitate or construct water supply infrastructures such as strategic boreholes focusing on optimizing outputs through upgrading, rehabilitations/ of shallow wells, water networks, water supply schemes extensions or surface water catchment systems, Berkads/Hafir Dams.  DRC will engage the community’s ability for O&M of sources and assess water sources available to choose suitable water supply technology. DRC will encourage existing water source owners – both private and government, to extend water services to the settlements of DACs. Gender-balanced and inclusive committees water will be established for smooth O&M of water facilities. Hygiene promotion awareness will be done to enhance WASH behavioral change on key WASH behaviors andCovid19 prevention and distribute 3000 household hygiene kits, IEC messaging and dissemination, mass media awareness sessions and campaigns. For sanitation, DRC will encourage a market-based approach – looking at creating demand for latrine construction and building capacity of the supply side to ensure enterprise-creation and therefore sustainable services. DRC will construct gender segregated latrines, provide tools and support solid waste management.

project_name: Provision of urgently needed lifesaving Health and Nutrition interventions for vulnerable women, boys and girls in Gaza
project_objective:
The project is to respond to the Health Cluster Objective 1 “Ensure the availability of acceptable and quality essential healthcare services to vulnerable communities across oPt” and Objective 2 “Strengthen the healthcare system's capacity to respond to emergencies and build community resilience through health system strengthening, preparedness and community resilience building”.

This project aims to provide urgent response to immediate health needs by ensuring access to health and nutrition services for the most vulnerable patients (pregnant, lactating women, neonates and children under the age of ﬁve, both boys and girls) through the provision of medical supplies, malnutrition treatment and targeted outreach postnatal home visiting services. Additionally, the intervention will provide essential COVID-19 medical supplies (laboratory tests, infection prevention and control items and PPEs) to build the capacity of the health system to timely and effectively respond to the outbreaks of new and re-emerging infectious diseases.

The project will respond to two key components of the Health and Nutrition cluster response plan: a) Health Cluster partners will scale-up the COVID-19 response through technical support to the health authorities as well as procurement of supplies, laboratory testing, infection prevention and control, surveillance and contact tracing, case management; b) Health Cluster partners will provide primary and secondary healthcare, including preventive health services, through enhanced monitoring of shortages of medicines and other essential supplies; capacity-building for enhanced quality of life-saving healthcare; and support to preventive programs and diagnostic services. This will include procurement of essential medical supplies to increase the availability of drugs, disposables, and medical equipment to ensure accurate diagnostics and treatment for high risk pregnant and lactating women, including victims of or at risk of Gender Based Violence (GBV), newborns and children under the age of ﬁve (boys and girls) across the ﬁve governorates in the Gaza Strip. Furthermore, access to quality newborn and child health care will be improved through further enhancement of health workers’ (doctors and nurses, both females and males) capacity on lifesaving health interventions, including essential newborn care, and provision of early intervention services to children with developmental delays and disabilities and strengthening communities’ preparedness, response and resilience, especially during crises. The project will be implemented in close coordination with Health Cluster partners including WHO, UNFPA, international and local NGOs to ensure complementarity of the interventions for the improvement of maternal, newborn and child health care.

The total number of women and children that will beneﬁt from the HRP funding will be 78,450 across the ﬁve Gaza governorates over a twelve-month period. It is estimated that 47,000 high-risk women and caregivers and 31,000 children under the age of ﬁve (15,810 boys and 15,190 girls) and 450 health professionals (doctors and nurses; female 60 per cent and 40 per cent males) will beneﬁt from urgently needed lifesaving health interventions.

project_name: MHPSS for most vulnerable groups in Donetsk and Luhansk
project_objective:
Please note: 
- duration of the project as submitted to the donor is 2 years, all budgetary figures, targets, beneficiary data given here apply to 9 month, = April - Dec. 2021
- negotiations with the donor are underway

Needs: In an evaluation of studies on mental health in conflict contexts, WHO concludes that at any given time (of the conflict) about 22% of those affected suffer from depression, anxiety, post-traumatic disorders, bipolar disorder or schizophrenia. 13% suffer from mild forms of depression, anxiety and PTSD, 4% from moderate forms and over 5% from severe forms. 

In a policy brief, the UN points out that people with serious mental illnesses live 10 to 20 years shorter than the respective average life expectancy of the population. 

The Ukraine Humanitarian Response Plan 2020 (HRP 2020) estimates that almost 40% of the inhabitants of the Donetsk and Lugansk regions have had traumatic experiences that can result in stress, depression, anxiety and PTSD. A study by the University of Birmingham in 2018 already concluded that 20.2% of IDPs and 12.2% of the general population have moderately severe or severe anxiety attacks. The prevalence of depression was 25% for IDPs and 14% for the general population.  
Against this background, the project contributes to improving the psychological condition of those affected - measurable according to standard psychological indicators. The measures planned for this project focus on individual specialized psychosocial support measures. Further measures will be implemented in the area of community-based psychosocial support/psycho-education as well as further training and supervision of professionals. All services are harmonised with the international standards of the UN Inter-Agency Working Group on Mental Health. 

Beneficiaries: It is planned to reach 4400 project beneficiaries in Donetsk and Lugansk oblasts. At least 75% of them live within 20 km on both sides of the contact line. The remaining 25% reside beyond the 20km line and are people in need particularly affected by the conflict (ex-combatants with problems of domestic violence, IDPs etc.). By Washington Group Criteria (long list of questions) people living with (severe) depression, fatigue, PTSD or anxiety are considered persons living with a disability. A further target group are the health workforce in order to protect them from exhaustion and mental distress.

Objectives: 
The project contributes to all 3 Health Cluster Objectives. 
1) Reduce infectious disease transmission and hospitalization rate by supporting the healthcare system,
2) Improve access of conflict-affected population to essential healthcare services, incl. MHPSS
and 
3) Improve capacity, sustainability and quality of healthcare services.

They are able to reach out to people from all geographical zones. Recently the provision of phone and online-services shows an increase of clients from NGCA. Phone consultations also reach people affected by COVID19, incl. health care workers. Hotlines are already in place.
