project_name: Providing Quality Integrated Primary healthcare including reproductive healthcare services to conflict affected IDPs and host communities in Borno, Adamawa and Yobe States
project_objective:
The IRC’s health response interventions will continue to align to the Health Sector response objective to provide access to life-saving and life-sustaining humanitarian health assistance to affected IDPs, returnees and host population; to establish, expand and strengthen communicable diseases outbreak prevention and response systems; and to strengthen access to health care, health system recovery and build humanitarian and development linkage.

IRC’s health program locations cover 14 LGAs in BAY states. MMC, Jere, Monguno, Gwoza, Bama, Mafa, Konduga, Askira Uba and Magumeri LGAs in Borno state, Michika in Adamawa and Damature, Gujiba and Gulani in Yobe.

The IRC, being the implementer and of the leading NGO in Monguno and MMC/Jere LGAs in providing health care service) will work closely with the Health Cluster and SMOH, community and other cluster partners to directly implement the health response in this two (MMC/Jere and Monguno) LGAs.

The IRC interventions will include:
• Maintain primary health care services in targeted areas through provision of basic equipment, drugs, medical supplies, basic lab equipment and supplies and reproductive health supplies
• Communicable disease control and outbreak response including supplies
• Support immunizations via fixed and mobile health clinics targeting returnees, displaced people, and other vulnerable groups including emergency mass vaccination campaigns
• Capacity building interventions will include
• Emergency preparedness and communicable disease control and outbreak response
• Community based interventions including awareness raising, hygiene promotion, education and participation in health-related issues
• Support to referral system for emergency health care
• Support to minor rehabilitation and repairs of health facilities.

The IRC will continue with both internal and external collaboration with Nutrition, Women empowerment and protection (WPE) WASH, and other Sectors / health actors for a coordinated response interventions

project_name: Specific and sensitive health emergency response for host and displaced populations in Borno State, Nigera.
project_objective:
This project aims to improve access to free comprehensive Primary Health Care (PHC) including Nutrition, Mental Health and Psychosocial Services (MHPSS), Sexual and Reproductive Health (SRH) and Gender Based Violence (GBV) services for conflict affected populations in Maiduguri, Jere and Damboa Local Government Areas (LGA), Borno State, Nigeria. Through the organisations Emergency Response Mechanism (ERM), MdM is ready to respond in other LGAs of Borno State, based on humanitarian needs and security. 

MdM has been active in Nigeria since August 2016 in the fields of PHC, nutrition, GBV, SRH and MHPSS. MdM aims to respond to the emergency situation caused by the violent armed conflict in the North-eastern part of Nigeria. 

In order to follow the dynamic of IDPs movements in Borno State and adapt timely to changes, 3 modalities of intervention will be implemented and closely monitored: 

●	MdM clinics in IDP settlements and informal camps
●	Revitalization and strengthening of Primary Health Care services in MoH facilities
●	An Emergency Response Mechansim 

This project will scale up MdM capacity in the field to ultimately reinforce its emergency healthcare intervention to respond to the immediate needs of the target population. In terms of operational approach, MdM will consider first direct support to the Nigerian Ministry of Health (SMoH) and State Emergency Management Agency, wherever health facilities are still available or functional, in reinforcing care management capacities and quality of care. If health facilities are not available, MdM will set-up a temporary clinic to cover the essential and most urgent healthcare needs of the affected population. Activities will be coordinated with other stakeholders active in the state, through continued coordination mechanisms at local level and throughout MdMs involvement within the relevant Sectors.

project_name: ACAPS-NPM Analysis Hub
project_objective: The aim of the Analysis Hub is to support informed humanitarian & development decision-making through research and analysis, contributing to a shared understanding of the Rohingya crisis and improved accountability to the affected populations. The Analysis Hub will support response actors in designing and accessing thorough analysis of the complex drivers of needs and the inter-sectoral relationships between needs, which would better inform response priorities and take into account the perspectives of the affected population. The Analysis hub will continue its support to different sectors and partners with customized technical support for data collection and analysis based on requests. This includes the ongoing support to the Joint Needs Assessment and J-MSNA frameworks. Specifically, NPM will carry out Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) flights covering all Rohingya refugee settlements. The UAV imagery will be used to produce maps and Digital Elevation models for operational actors, to identify natural hazard risks and to monitor changes in site conditions and development.

project_name: Post/emergency and primary health care services and environmental health in NES – Phase 2+3
project_objective:
The Phase 2 of project aims at supporting the emergency response to the Syrian humanitarian crisis though a combined humanitarian and stabilization intervention, divided in 2 connected components in the Health and WASH in health. The health sector response aims at supporting the provision of emergency, primary and secondary health care services, including primary care activities in Deir ez-Zor, ar-Raqqah, Aleppo and al-Hasakeh Governorates and to Covid-19 case management response in preselected hospitals. 
The WASH component aims at consolidating and where needed establishing the safe system of healthcare waste management in several healthcare facilities in the Governorates of Deir ez-Zor, ar-Raqqah, Aleppo and al-Hasakeh. This will allow to strengthen the Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) activities carried out in all targeted health facilities and it is part of the Covid-19 response in NES. This action will also contribute to promote safe and sustainable human settlements for Syrian IDPs and local population in North-East Syria (SDG no. 11).
With the overall aim of reducing morbidity and mortality among affected populations through coordinated and timely emergency health and WASH services, the action has 2 specific objectives: 
- SA1: Guaranteeing access to emergency and primary health care services to Syrian IDPs and locals in NES, with particular attention to the most vulnerable cases, including Covid-19 preparedness and response.
- SA2: Consolidating and increasing availability of health waste management and IPC services in healthcare facilities in Deir ez-Zor, ar-Raqqah, Aleppo and al-Hasakeh.

The Phase 3 of the project aims to target in-camp and out-of-camp high-need/neglected areas with a comprehensive and integrated package of primary health care services, specialized assistance for PWDs, health waste management, and community outreach. 
The modality of response will focus on strengthening the existing referral mechanism among partners and towards external services and other humanitarian actors providing assistance in targeted areas.  IPC and Health Waste Management (HWM) activities will be mainstreamed in several UPP/KRC healthcare facilities, in continuity with Phase 2 and previous projects and in coordination with other WASH and Health NES actors. Major focus will be on implementing partner’s capacity building, with the aim of consolidating and strengthening the functionality of the already installed systems of HWM.

project_name: Soutien au mécanisme de réponse d’urgence (RRM) dans les cercles de Koro et de Bandiagara
project_objective:
Le projet entend soutenir le déploiement des réponses aux déplacements de population à la hausse dans la région de Mopti. En effet, la région de Mopti enregistrait en octobre 2020 un total de 131 150 personnes déplacées internes (PDI) ce qui correspond au double du nombre de PDI à la même période en 2019 (61 083 PDI en octobre 2019). L’assistance auprès des ménages déplacés comportera l’allocation de kits NFI et COVID-19 d’urgence et de complément permettant de renforcer les capacités de réponse rapide des acteurs RRM de la région. A noter que compte tenu des risques de propagation de la COVID-19, les acteurs RRM ont adapté leurs pratiques opérationnelles afin de prendre en compte les mesures de prévention de l’exposition des communautés affectées par les crises, des partenaires ou encore du personnel humanitaire. 
Par ailleurs les kits NFI ont été renforcés pour inclure : 700gr savon, 1 tasse à manger, 1 tasse à soupe, 1 gobelet en plastique. Les kits NFI et COVID-19 seront ainsi composés de 15 articles : 2 Couvertures  dimension: 200cm x 240cm, bords: plié et cousu; 2 nattes en plastique en polypropylène d'une taille minimum de 180 X 90 cm; 2 moustiquaires imprégnée d'insecticide Taille minimum de 190X180X150cm; 1 pagne: tissu en coton, 4-6 yards  ( wax) ; 1 Seau plastic de 10 litres avec couvercle Ne plie pas sous le poids ; 1 savon de toilette pour l’hygiène corporelle (en kg); 1 Savon pour lessive/vaisselle (marque BF ou Fanico en Kg) ; 1 Marmite en aluminium, 7 litres Production locale encouragée; appellation locale ""7kg"" ; 1 Marmite en aluminium, 5 litres Production locale encouragée; appellation locale ""5kg"" ; 3 Tasses à manger Diamètre minimum de 40cm, hauteur de 15cm. Avec couvercle. 100% aluminium. Marque loured ; 3 Tasses à soupe/sauce Diamètre minimum de 20cm, hauteur de 12cm. Avec couvercle. 100% aluminium. Marque loured ; 6 Gobelets plastique 0,4 litres ; 1 louche acier inoxydable, capacité minimum 100ml, longueur minimum 30cm, pièce unique non magnétique ; 1 bâche plastique dimension : 5x4m, marque de référence “Bouare lion Bâche” ; 1 Sac polypropène 90kg et d'une taille de minimum de 74 x 116 cm.
A travers cette intervention, ACTED compte appuyer 3200 ménages déplacés, soit 19 200 personnes (9600 hommes et 9600 femmes). Le nombre total des bénéficiaires pourra évoluer dans les cas où les prix des articles fluctuaient énormément sur le marché, ou encore si les coûts logistiques sont supérieurs aux coûts moyens estimés. 
En outre, les mouvements de population se prolongeant bien souvent plus d’un mois (réponse RRM), et même plus de trois mois (réponse post RRM Distribution de vivre de WFP), ACTED propose à travers ce projet de distribuer un second kit NFI dans un délai de 4 à 6 mois suivant l’intervention RRM initiale afin de remplacer le kit usagé remis lors de celle-ci. Ceci concernera les déplacés toujours sur le site et sur la base des listes RRM validées par les SLDSES.
Les activités programmatiques de monitoring post intervention devront permettre de mesurer l’impact de ces différents scénarios sur la qualité de l’assistance, le changement dans les conditions de vie et la satisfaction des personnes affectées en rapport avec l’assistance.
Par ailleurs, grâce à son rôle de point focal de la veille humanitaire à Koro et Bandiagara, ACTED pourra contribuer à la coordination des interventions humanitaires dans la zone en facilitant la remontée d’information et le partage des bonnes pratiques. 
Pour chacune des évaluations rapides multisectorielles RRM menées, une analyse qualitative (contextuelle mouvements de population, causes et effets sur les conditions de vie des populations affectées) et semi-quantitative (ampleur chiffrée des populations affectées et seuils de vulnérabilité sectoriels) seront prises en compte. Les techniques de collecte des données consisteront en une combinaison d'observations directes, interviews individuelles d’informateurs clés, groupes de discussion et documentations secondaires.

project_name: Assistance médicale et nutritionnelle à la population touchée par la crise dans la région de Menaka
project_objective:
L’objectif global des cinq derniers projets financés par l’OFDA est de contribuer à la réduction de la morbidité et de la mortalité de la population touchée par les crises dans le centre et le nord du Mali en améliorant l’accès à des soins de santé et de nutrition de qualité. Les objectifs spécifiques sont les suivants :
 
1)	To améliorer  l’accès à des soins médicaux gratuits de haute qualité pour les femmes enceintes et allaitantes, les enfants de moins de 5 ans, les personnes déplacées à l’intérieur du pays (PDI) et l’ensemble de la population de la région de Menaka où le système de santé est incapable de fonctionner sans aucune aide humanitaire.
2)	Réduire la morbidité et la mortalité des populations touchées par la crise humanitaire dans la région de Menaka dues à la malnutrition en améliorant leur état nutritionnel et leur accès aux services nutritionnels.
La crise dans le nord du Mali exige la continuité des interventions humanitaires de Médecins du Monde (DoTW) dans la région de Ménaka. Selon l’OCHA (HNO/HRP 2020), la crise multidimensionnelle qui a touché le Mali depuis 2012 n’a pas vu de signes de résolution malgré les efforts déployés. En 2019, l’ampleur de la crise a encore été accentuée par la propagation de la violence à grande échelle et l’insécurité dans tout le centre du pays. Les populations sont exposées à une criminalité croissante, à la prolifération des armes légères et de petit calibre et à la présence de groupes armés qui font preuve d’une violence extrême et de conflits au niveau communautaire.

Certains problèmes critiques ont été identifiés, notamment les suivants :

●	Les populations des zones touchées par la crise sont touchées par des chocs violents caractérisés par la détérioration de la situation sécuritaire mettant en danger leur bien-être physique et mental, entraînant plus de 200 000 personnes déplacées fin décembre 2019.
●	Les conflits et les catastrophes naturelles ont eu un impact considérable sur les populations et mettent en danger leur bien-être physique et mental.
●	L’explosion des alertes du Mécanisme  d’intervention rapide (RRM), qui est le baromètre clé de la gravité de la crise humanitaire.

Compte tenu de l’évolution du contexte, les modes d’exploitation et les objectifs ont changé.
Avec ce projet, MdM BE continuera de s’appuyer sur son programme de nutrition sanitaire dans le nord du Mali, en adaptant son intervention aux résultats des études et des enquêtes qu’il a menées et en intégrant les leçons apprises au cours des années 2017-2020 pour améliorer la qualité du programme. 
Les activités continueront de renforcer la résilience en renforçant les capacités de 28 structures de santé (27 CSCom et 1 CSRéf). L’action poursuivra son objectif d’améliorer la résilience des structures de santé visant à un désengagement progressif de l’aide accordée par MdM à ces structures qui sera atteint par les deux tiers avant 2025, selon le MdM au Mali plan stratégique de six ans. Cela ne sera possible que si le contexte politique et sécuritaire permet une reprise progressive par les autorités. MdM continuera d’appuyer les mécanismes d’orientation et d’évacuation des communautés vers le CSCom et le CSRéf ou vers l’hôpital de Gao.
Dans le même temps, la composante communautaire sera particulièrement renforcée pour faire face à la situation nutritionnelle critique (taux de malnutrition aiguë mondiale (GAM) de 15,3 % bien au-dessus du seuil de 10 % fixé par l’Organisation mondiale de la santé (OMS), ainsi qu’à la nécessité de détecter les signes de danger chez les femmes enceintes, mais aussi les cas de violence sexiste (GBV) pour leur prise en charge précoce.

project_name: Multi-disciplinary Rehabilitation and mental health-psychosocial support services for conflict affected populations and support to health structures in Syria.
project_objective:
The project aims at reducing vulnerability and improving physical and mental well-being of crisis-affected population with particular attention to specific vulnerabilities linked to Disability, Gender, and Age (DGA). The organization’s action focuses on providing multi-disciplinary health services tailored to the needs of people with physical and functional limitations and their caregivers through direct intervention or through the support of local partners in North-West, North-East and GoS-controlled parts of Syria. The intervention includes provision of multidisciplinary physical rehabilitation services (including the provision of assistive mobility devices, prostheses & orthotics and education sessions for caregivers) and the psychosocial support services to physical rehabilitation beneficiaries and their caregivers. Furthermore, to ensure continuity of the tailored treatment plans Tele-rehabilitation/Tele-PSS sessions in case of access restrictions, due to COVID-19. Improving access to services through referral and accessibility work into health structures. These services help in recovery of physical rehabilitation beneficiaries and support the caregivers in a holistic approach in order to alleviate stress, fatigue and other psychological impacts related to their responsibilities. The organization mainstreams COVID-19 Key messaging in the activities package according to WHO Guidelines. 
In GoS- controlled areas and North-west Syria the intervention include the provision of Mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services to people suffering from psychological distress without having physical rehabilitation needs. MHPSS services include psychological first aid, psych education, and individual and/or group session therapy. Noting that in GoS- controlled areas, the organization focuses on developing rehabilitation services in areas where services are not available.
Concerning the DGA mainstreaming, all activities and delivered services are prepared based on a rapid assessment to study the sensitivity of the context and ensure inclusion of Persons according to DGA. This includes the promotion of equal opportunities for people with different needs and abilities. Conditional cash for transportation is also provided to patients and caregivers according to individual assessed needs based on pre-defined criteria. HI will closely coordinate with the Cash working group in the targeted hub to align the common standards and guidance. conditional cash will be provided to patients and/or caregivers based on individual assistance and HI criteria taking into account socioeconomic, travel, clinical factors.
The health staff assess the needs case by case based on fixed criteria. The cash is conditioned to the attendance of patient to the treatment sessions aiming to ensure the finalization of the treatment plan. In parallel, the organization provides support to its local health partners through technical, financial and managerial support and the capacity building tailored to the needs of partners, to ensure the quality of the delivered services and the sustainability of impact. While the outreach teams reach out to IDPs; and underserved communities; as well as persons who are incapable of reaching the service centers.  

In addition to the rehab and inclusion specialist support to the health clusters, by guiding through several session on how to implement DGA inclusion principles and how to identify vulnerability risks. In addition to trainings related to understanding needs of persons with disabilities mainly women.

project_name: Projet d'accès aux services de santé nutrition et de secours d'urgence aux PDI et population hôte dans le Yagha
project_objective:
La province du Yagha est l’une des provinces du Sahel qui a été calme sur le plan menace sécuritaire mais par la suite elle a connu d’importants incidents en 2019 et début 2020 qui a engendré des déplacements de population avec fermeture de formations sanitaires. En effet, au mois d’octobre 2019, des menaces d’agents de santé et des acteurs communautaires ont impacté fortement les services de santé entrainant la fermeture de formations sanitaires (13/17 CSPS. Au 25 Octobre 2020, sur 20 formations sanitaires la province du Yagha enregistre la fermeture de 2 CSPS et 17 fonctionnant à minima 17 privant environ 18 028 personnes de soins essentiels de base (Source : Ministère de la Santé). Le déplacement des populations a empêché les travaux champêtres occasionnant en 2020 une période de soudure plus précoce.
La pandémie à la covid-19 est venue aggraver la situation sanitaire et nutritionnelle déjà précaire en raison de la prévalence élevée (2.6%) de la malnutrition aigüe selon les résultats de l’enquête SMART 2018. Au 22 Novembre 2020 le Sahel 29 cas de covid-19 ont été enregistrés dont 2 cas pour le Yagha.
La psychose est générale et touche aussi bien le personnel de santé que la population. Ce qui a perturbé le  dispositif de soins engendrant une baisse de l’accès aux soins.  
L’intervention, qui est une continuité d’un projet en cours, va renforcer le système de santé pour maintenir un bon niveau de soins tout en améliorant l’accès.

project_name: Protection of Palestine Refugees Affected by Armed Conflict and Forced Displacement in the West Bank (including East Jerusalem)
project_objective:
The impact of over 50 years of continued military occupation in the West Bank on the protection of Palestine refugees is wide-ranging. Palestine refugees face a range of serious protection threats, including: threat to life; liberty and security; destruction or damage to homes and other property; forced displacement and restrictions on freedom of movement and access to natural resources, markets and other livelihood opportunities.

This action is based on UNRWA's protection mandate for more than 860,000 Palestine refugees in the West Bank. Particular focus is given to the needs of Palestine refugees living in 19 refugee camps, where the Israeli Security Forces conduct repeated military operations. The action seeks to address the acute needs of numerous Palestine refugees exposed to conflict-related violence and the risk of displacement and/or forcible transfer.
The project has two key aims, (1) to enhance the protective environment for Palestine refugees exposed to protection threats through protection advocacy - through persuasion, mobilisation and denunciation, and based on monitoring and documentation of protection incidents, including alleged IHL and IHRL violations. This advocacy aims to promote both protective policies and practices as well as the accountability of duty bearers.

The second aim (2) is to respond to protection threats, linked in particular to the risk of displacement and/or forcible transfer, but also conflict related violence more generally - mitigating the consequences of these and reinforcing the resilience of affected persons. This is achieved through a combination of shelter support to refugees who have been displaced and/or who have had their homes damaged or demolished, and through the provision of targeted case management to these individuals. Shelter support is provided through cash transfers, case management services are provided to affected persons through dedicated protection social workers. Cash assistance addresses immediate needs linked protection threats, whilst case management services improves access to other UNRWA services and specialised partners, and reinforces the resilience of affected persons.

This action works directly towards to two of the strategic objectives under the HRP:

STRATEGIC OBJECTIVE 1: The rights of Palestinians living under occupation, including those living under the blockade and other restrictions, are protected, respected and promoted in accordance with International Humanitarian Law (IHL) and International Human Rights Law (IHRL), while duty-bearers are increasingly held to account. 

STRATEGIC OBJECTIVE 2: The basic needs of vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation are met through the provision of quality basic services and improved access to resources, in accordance with the rights of protected persons under IHL.

project_name: Enhancing Access to Equitable & Inclusive  Education in Emergencies
project_objective: The project intend to ensure that children of school going age have access to equitable and inclusive education even during emergencies.  World Vision Zimbabwe (WVZ) will focus on (1)supporting most vulnerable children to enroll and attend school (2) support school feeding to encourage school attendance and improve the health status of pupils and (3)implement complimentary WASH activities for schools to have safe drinking water .The project will target  3 districts with an overall severity of 5 in  Matebeleland South (Gwanda, Insiza, and Mangwe). (WVZ has presence in ALL these districts implementing other projects  hence this project will  be  complimentary. This project will focus on (1) supporting 101,540 (50.262 boys & 51.278 girls) most vulnerable children ( 3-18years)  to ensure that they  enrol and attend school,(2) support school feeding to boost school attendance as well as improve the health status of 101 540 pupils and (3)  implement WASH in schools activities for improving schools access to  safe drinking water for 16,467. The project will also incorporate cross cutting issues like Gender, Pyscho- social services (PSS),  Disaster Risk Reduction ( DRR), Child Safeguarding and Protection in Emergencies, Children feedback meetings, Teacher training on emergency sensitive teaching and learning activities will also be incorporated.

project_name: Provision of quality child protection services for the most vulnerable, at-risk children and their caregivers in Syria
project_objective:
SC's programming combines immediate relief with the restoration of basic social support services through the delivery of multi-sector responses that integrate child protection (family tracing and reunification, case management and resilience to the impact of conflict and crisis), and MHPSS support to affected populations. Protection concerns are caused and compounded by crisis and displacement, and their acute impact on safety and wellbeing of children is at the core of Save the Children’s commitment and response. Furthermore, ongoing security challenges inside the camps increase psychosocial insecurities of a population which has already resorted to multiple negative coping mechanisms.

Amidst such significant humanitarian need, Save the Children is prioritizing the continuation of its child-centered, gender-sensitive integrated protection and MHPSS interventions responding to the absence of safe spaces to play and express themselves and the acute individual risks faced by the most vulnerable children, particularly UASC and child survivors. For caregivers across Syria, there are almost no opportunities to acknowledge and gain support for the aggregate stressors of displacement, poverty and persistent insecurity, and the ways in which this affects their individual coping capacity and the ways in which they care for their children. The proposed activities draw upon Save the Children's global technical expertise, the evidence base and minimum standards for child protection in emergencies, deep local insights and commitment from a team of experienced frontline staff, and learning from previous projects inside Syria.

Case management and care of UASC: Child protection case management (CPCM) will be delivered by a set of trained and supervised case management staff, in line with the inter-agency CPCM SOPs, and supported by best practice and tailored guidance from SC’s Steps to Protect Common Approach to case management. SC will continue its leadership in the CPIMS+, which went live in late 2020 and strengthens quality service provision and coordination. Where appropriate, SC will explore to deliver cash for protection activities to improve the wellbeing of vulnerable children. The modality and CVA approach will be adapted to the local contexts, and the specific vulnerabilities the programme aims to address. 

Community awareness raising and community-based child protection: Parents and caregivers will participate in group-based parenting skills and peer support sessions, drawing upon SC’s Parenting without Violence Common Approach. This will include targeted sessions for mothers of babies and toddlers to foster early attachment and build knowledge on early childhood development and nutrition. Children and adolescents will also have the opportunity to participate in creative and recreational activities in SC’s Child Friendly Spaces (CFSs). Participation will be further supported through child and youth clubs on topics and themes selected by the children and adolescents themselves. SC will continue to collaborate with and learn from community-level child protection actors and structures, including the child and youth clubs mentioned above, Child Protection Committees (CPCs), as well as other existing groups. SC will provide capacity building in the safe identification and referral of vulnerable children, psychological first aid, and child protection in emergencies.

GBV: Where possible, child survivors of SGBV will be able access case management services delivered by child protection case management staff. SC will scale up capacity building on GBV mainstreaming to all staff to mitigate and more effectively respond to GBV, including safe referrals and case management for child survivors. 

In accordance with SC’s minimum standards, a gender, age and disability sensitive approach will be used across program components so that the different needs of girls and boys of all ages and abilities are effectively addressed, especially CLwDs.

project_name: Protection of Rohingya Refugees in Bangladesh and Promotion of Community Cohesion
project_objective: UNHCR will ensure the centrality of protection and protection mainstreaming through inclusive coordination and leadership of the humanitarian response. UNHCR will work with the Government to give Rohingya refugees a legal identity through registration and documentation, which will serve as the foundation for protection, program delivery and solutions, while pursuing community-based protection responses and providing essential services in the areas of MPHSS, GBV prevention and response, child protection, and legal assistance. UNHCR will remain a central player within interagency disaster preparedness efforts for the monsoon and cyclone seasons and in addressing the challenges brought on by COVID-19. UNHCR will bolster inclusion through support to host communities, addressing the broader challenges that undermine protection space while promoting peaceful coexistence and social cohesion. Reinforcing accountable government leadership of the response will be an important component of inclusion, and UNHCR will continue to support capacity development across the operation. UNHCR will empower Rohingya refugees by building community capacities for leadership, self-management and engagement with the Government and the humanitarian community, including through the election of refugee representatives and involving refugees from all parts of the community in a range of community-based protection programs. Within the current government policy framework, UNHCR will advocate for greater access to education and economic inclusion, so that young refugees retain hope and become a constructive force in the community. UNHCR’s solutions strategy necessarily takes into account the Government’s policy that voluntary repatriation is the only feasible solution for Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh. While promoting conditions needed for voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable return in Myanmar, large scale returns are not likely to take place in 2021. UNHCR will work to improve protection conditions and quality of life for refugees in Bangladesh pending solutions, building upon the framework for responsibility sharing provided by the Global Compact on Refugees.

project_name: Integrated Education in Emergencies Response for Crises Affected Children in Bay and Bakool regions of Somalia
project_objective:
Bay and Bakool regions are among the most affected regions in Somalia by protracted droughts, flash floods and locust swarms, causing high displacement and acute humanitarian needs. Baydhaba hosts high number of IDP (392,274 IDP) and has 110,905 primary school aged children. About 91,259 children (36,504F; 54,756M) are estimated to be in schools, while 162,239 are out of school children (OOSC) and 1,381 are IDP children with disability (CWD). In Diinsoor, 14,112 are primary school aged children, among those only 3,135 (1,163F; 1,972M) are enrolled in 8 primary schools, with 10,977 being OOSC and 226 CWD. In Ceel-barde there are 1,720 primary school aged children, with only 698 (414M;312F) enrolled in 3 public and IDP schools, while 1,032 (568M; 464F) are OOSC and 50 children are CWD. In Xudur, only 4,384 children (2,436M;1,948F) are currently enrolled in the 16 public and IDP schools, while 10,692 children (5,988M; 4,705F) remain out of schools and 151 are CWD (FCA needs assessment 09-10/20).

Major findings of FCA assessments in the four districts showed enormous shortage of accessible and gender friendly infrastructure such as latrines, handwashing facilities and classrooms, lack of learning and teaching materials, and inadequate number of qualified teachers especially female teachers. Girls face tremendous barriers in accessing to education due social norms that restrict their enrolment, retention and movement. The existing education system also reflects the persistence of these norms and does little to promote change in perception, attitude and behaviours. Children with disabilities met significant challenges such as strong stigma, discrimination and misconceptions, limited disability friendly infrastructure, poor learning environment and lack of specialised teachers trained in special education needs. Caregivers also faced with challenges in covering foods, school fees, uniforms and scholastic materials. Many of IDP children face significant health risks and psychological distress. Child protection and safeguarding mechanisms in schools are weak, due to lack of protection knowledge and relevant trainings among key education personnel. This has compromised the safety and well-being of the children, especially for girls and CWD in accessing education. 

Aligning with the 2021 Somalia Humanitarian Response Plan, Education Sector Strategic Plan and Covid-19 Emergency Response Plan for Education, the initiative aims to restore and maintain access to safe, protective, inclusive and continuous learning opportunities for crises and emergency affected primary school boys and girls in Bay and Bakool regions of South West State of Somalia. The project will put a strong emphasis on an integrated approach to education focusing on access, quality of education, protection, child safeguarding, gender equality, conflict sensitivity, and disaster risk reduction (DRR) in the design, approach and activities. 

The project will remove barriers to primary education for 7,365 affected children (3,314F;4,051M), prioritising children from the most vulnerable groups such as IDPs, girls, CWD and destitute host community children. About 736 children with disability (331F;405M) will also be targeted (10%). Particularly, 40% IDP children, 60% destitute host community children and 45% of girls will benefit from the support.
 
FCA will partner with GREDO to implement some components of the project, particularly in relation to rehabilitation and construction of infrastructure, community mobilisation and protection mechanisms in schools. FCA will engage Somalia Institute for Special Education Needs and Disability (SISEN) for capacity building on inclusion and SEN for teachers, MoE and other education personnel. 

FCA has excellent capacity to scale up the approach and apply best practice in the four target locations built on its ongoing EiE response in Bay and Bakool regions and solid expertise as a well-known and trusted Finnish education actor.

project_name: Comprehensive Child Protection Services for Children, Adolescents and their Caregivers in the Northeast Nigeria.
project_objective:
The continued insecurity and increased action of armed opposition groups (AOGs) in North East Nigeria has resulted in widespread civilian displacement, destruction of critical infrastructure and the collapse of basic services. According to the 2020 Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) 7.9 million people require assistance across the Borno Adamawa and Yobe (BAY) States , an 11% increase since 2019. The insurgency has displaced an estimated population of 1.7 million persons displaced form their home communities with Borno, Adamawa and Yobe (BAY) States worst affected.
The continued conflict has seen new arrivals and displaced populations residing in over-congested formal and informal camps without the ability to meet their basic needs. Of those affected by these realities, children and adolescents continue to face high protection risks as child-headed households, unaccompanied and separated children (UASC), children living with disabilities and adolescent girls and boys. These risks are exacerbated by other emergencies such as fire outbreaks, floods and infectious disease outbreaks and are further compounded by a lack of adequate services. Recently, the COVID-19 outbreak and its attendant concerns has led to family separation, isolation, stigmatization, bereavement and loss of livelihood, further worsening the vulnerability of children, adolescents and their caregivers. 
The IRC is proposing a comprehensive and community-based approach to addressing identified child protection needs drawing on its expertise in child protection programming and over five years presence in the Northeast. The IRC Protection response will focus on providing case management through direct services and linkages to specialized services as well as structured age and gender sensitive Psycho- Social Support (PSS) for children, adolescents and their caregivers who have been affected by the insurgency, COVID-19 and its related issues.
IRC Child Protection (CP) intervention will provide specialized case management services to UASC, former CAAG and other children and adolescents (including children living with disabilities) that have suffered or are at risk of abuse, exploitation, neglect and violence. This response will also create linkages to specialized services that will cater for the particular and immediate needs of children and adolescents arising from the effect of COVID-19 on the one hand and those associated with the humanitarian crisis in the BAY states on the other. This response will be closely coordinated with the IRC GBV, Protection and Rule of Law (PRoL), Health, Nutrition and WASH services together with Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE) activities, mainstreamed through a collaborative approach while also working closely with other Child Protection partners. The IRC tool kits for Socio-Emotional Learning (SEL), Supporting Adolescents and their Families in Emergencies (SAFE) and the Families Make the Difference (FMD) parenting skills, which have been adapted to meet the COVID-19 preventive measures of physical distancing, will be used to meet the psychosocial needs of children, adolescents and their families. The adaptation of these activities – while observing the preventive measure of social distancing - aim to provide children and their caregivers’ with the much needed social and emotional support, helping them manage the stress they face daily as a result of their displacement, loss of homes and livelihoods and COVID-19 associated stress. The intervention will also strengthen community led structures which will support the IRC Child Protection team in implementing these activities in their communities. To enhance its area of coverage, the IRC will partner with identified National Child Protection NGOs across the BAY states.

project_name: Improved access to safe and inclusive care to children in Derna and Benghazi.
project_objective:
The proposed action aims to improve the access of boys and girls to safe and inclusive caring  environments in Derna and Benghazi through capacity building of child protection and education actors, the provision of PSS and recreational activities for children and caregivers, awareness-raising and sensitization sessions and the provision of case management for children in need of specialized child protection services. 

In Benghazi, ACTED will strengthen the capacity of child protection and education actors as well as non-child protection actors – including Libyan national/local authorities and CSOs - by providing capacity-building trainings on child protection and PSS. The training topics will mostly cover PSS to children, child psychology, children’s rights, child development and children’s well-being, including child protection and the identification of child protection risks and concerns. ACTED will also deliver dedicated sessions to address the topic of inclusion, non-discrimination and access to services for non-Libyan populations, life skills and social emotional learning as well as case management and referral pathways. Through these sessions, ACTED will help strengthen participants’ capacity to identify, monitor and respond to child protection issues. 

ACTED will also conduct PSS recreational activities in Benghazi, responding to children’s wellbeing needs through an integrated approach combining education and protection interventions. These activities will also be group-based and individualized PSS support will be provided where needed to the most vulnerable children and their parents and caregivers. In a context where both parents and teachers noted signs of distress and psychological consequences from the conflict and because of the recent COVID-19 outbreak, these activities will respond to the children’s wellbeing needs. The activities will also seek the participation of parents and community members to contribute to reinforce family and community support systems and foster an enabling and supportive environment for young people, aiming at building resilience and social cohesion.

ACTED will engage in both cities, with local communities to conduct awareness-raising sessions for parents and caregivers and children on key issues pertaining to child protection, psychosocial support, as well as to support building acceptance of the project and participation of beneficiaries. Awareness-raising sessions will also focus on topics related to children enrolment in schools, COVID-19 and the importance of prioritizing children’s education. 

In both cities, ACTED will incorporate a case management system for children in need of specialized services or assistance. The child protection case management system will address the needs of vulnerable children experiencing or at risk of abuse, violence, neglect and exploitation. In the context of Benghazi and Derna, ACTED’s case management unit will pay particular attention in identifying children-at-risk, children with disabilities with protection concerns, children working in hazardous environments and exploited, child and adolescent survivors of SGBV, as well as adolescents who were formerly recruited by armed groups.

project_name: Provision of protection services for displacement and conflict-affected Libyans and non-Libyans in Tripolitania
project_objective:
The proposed intervention aims at strengthening the protection environment of conflict and displacement-affected Libyans and non Libyans in Tripolitania area. 
Proposed services include protection monitoring, aiming at providing timely protection information and evidence to on-going and future interventions, critical information sharing and awareness raising, individual protection assistance (IPA), group and individual PSS, and case management services. These will target internally displaced persons and returnees, as well as migrants, asylum seekers and refugees in need of humanitarian assistance through a rights-based and community-based approach. 
A combination of modalities, including cash and in-kind assistance, individual and collective services, direct and indirect delivery methods will be used to provide tailored and needs-based protection services to the groups of concern.

project_name: Supporting evidence-based and accountable humanitarian service provision to conflict-affected populations through the implementation of the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) in the North-West, South-West regions of Cameroon
project_objective:
In the NWSW, a socio-political crisis erupted in 2017. What started as corporatist peaceful protests against a perceived encroachment of the regions’ cultural practices and autonomy turned into an armed conflict between the government defense forces and Non-State Armed Groups (NSAGs), triggering very dynamic and massive internal displacements and related humanitarian needs. Since December 2019, a significant spike in military operations is forcing more individuals to flee their homes as property destructions as well as human rights violations are being reported on a regular basis. According to the HNO for 2021  , violent conflict in the south-west and north-west regions has displaced more than 700,000 people.  Since the beginning of the year, IOM’s Emergency Tracking Tool (ETT) has identified more than 90,000 new forcibly displaced persons and around 30,000 returnees, mainly linked to violence and school closures related to COVID-19 governmental measures. IOM’s latest ETT dashboards have highlighted the increasing trends of recurring short-term displacements characterized by individuals seeking refuge in makeshift shelters or agricultural structures in the surrounding bushes of their villages. Priority needs, as indicated by displaced populations through the ETT assessments include protection, access to food as well as shelter and non-food items. Access in NWSW for humanitarian actors continues to be an issue, with frequent ad-hoc road blocks and Monday ‘Ghost-towns’ having a considerable impact on the maintenance of reliable and effective humanitarian assistance. 
IOM, as the only actor present in these regions with the capacity, expertise and access to certain areas to conduct comprehensive assessments on displacement trends and statistics, was asked by OCHA and the Humanitarian Coordinator to carry out multi-sectoral needs assessments (MSNA) in NWSW. The data from MSNA is shared with more than 30 operational humanitarian actors and is used as the primary data source for the update of the Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) and Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP). Data that is produced and disseminated through the IOM DTM methodology has become the key source of information on internal displacement across both crisis-affected regions and is used by humanitarian partners for vital planning purposes. The last partner survey conducted in late 2019 stated that 95% were either ‘very satisfied’ or ‘satisfied’ with the data supplied, with 95% also stating that they either want more DTM data or the same amount for coordinating their activities. Comprehensive assessments provide humanitarian actors with reliable data on the number and location of displaced populations (IDPs and returnees), which contribute to a better understanding of the displacement trends and most pressing needs. 
In light of the above, IOM seeks to continue providing the humanitarian community with information on displacement trends and most pressing sectoral needs of conflict-affected populations in these two regions. IOM will continue its data collection activities with additional rounds of displacement tracking, Emergency Tracking Tools, Multi-Sectoral Needs Assessments as well as the general informal support to the humanitarian community in North-West, South-West with ad-hoc information requests and situational analysis. A range of information products will be distributed throughout 2021 depending on partners’ needs, from the Emergency Tracking Tool to help coordinate partners’ emergency response to sudden displacements, to larger scale Multi-Sectoral Needs Assessments (MSNA) that will fit into wider Humanitarian Country Team planning. 
All these activities will contribute to better availability of data to allow for better evidence based programming  with more informed and appropriate crisis response based on accurate and up to date information made available.

project_name: Sustain Shelter/NFI Cluster's capacity to enhance access to safe and appropriate shelter and NFI solutions for vulnerable populations in South Sudan
project_objective: Through the effective management of South Sudan's S-NFI core pipeline, IOM will strengthen the S-NFI cluster's capacity to respond to protracted and emerging humanitarian needs in locations with the greatest needs. The complex operating environment indicates that the provision of in-kind supplies will continue to constitute a key response modality for lifesaving responses in areas affected by emergencies, such as sub-national violence and the heavy seasonal flooding of the past two years. Under the Humanitarian Response Plan 2021, IOM will continue its commitment to support the S-NFI Cluster Pipeline through the provision of key shelter and NFI  supplies to benefit a total of 819,000 (75% of the total target of 1,085,000)  people in need. Procured supplies will be prepositioned in various logistic hubs throughout the country. The distribution will be prioritized to directly benefit vulnerable people affected by displacement, conflict, natural disaster, disease outbreak, famine/food insecurity, and GBV risks.

project_name: Support evidence-based humanitarian response and inform resilience, transition and recovery programming through provision of integrated data and analysis on IDPs, returnees and multi-sector household needs
project_objective: The project will provide the humanitarian community with timely, accurate and actionable data and analysis to enable a fair and evidence-based humanitarian response and inform resilience, transition and recovery programming. Key deliverables will include a regularly updated location- and area-level baseline on the presence, number and needs of IDPs and returnees across the country; biometric data management for fair, effective and targeted delivery of humanitarian assistance; representative multi-sector data on household needs and vulnerabilities in urban areas that will feed into South Sudan’s inter-agency multi-sector needs assessment (MSNA); and regular updates on population mobility at key internal transit hubs and border points.

project_name: Provision of Emergency WASH Services for Vulnerable IDPs in Banadir, Middle shabelle and Galgudud region of Somalia
project_objective:
The continuation of protracted crises in Somalia, now compounded by the effects of Covid-19, Floods and droughts has resulted in massive challenges pertaining to Water, Sanitation and Hygiene. Approximately, 4.6 million Somalis are still in need due to insufficient access to portable water and inadequate sanitation services of the affected population in many districts, thus negatively affecting the country’s public health and the dignity of highly vulnerable and displaced communities. This spike in numbers compared to 2020 is mainly exacerbated by the situation developed as a result of Covid-19 and its rapid transmission. Lack of adequate WASH services to the population is a main cause of spread of Acute Diarrheal Diseases (ADD), leading to malnutrition in the country and contributing to increasing the existing stunting rate of 25.3% in children below 5 years of age. It is also a cause of relapse (ADD) when treated patients and children returning to their communities where safe water and sanitation coverages are limited, resulting in limited sustainability of health programs.  
According to JMCNA, 53% of the IDPs face challenges in terms of access to WASH services in Somalia (53% as highest pertaining to access to soap and handwashing facilities). As Somalia’s vulnerability to climate change is projected to increase especially with the upcoming La-Nina where there is a likelihood of drought, the country might be further affected by water scarcity, which calls for a stronger collaboration between the humanitarian and development partners to work on collective outcomes. Furthermore, issues related to access to WASH facilities for vulnerable groups including persons with disabilities, elderly, women, boys and girls is an ongoing challenge. It requires availability of reliable data, extensive consultations and community engagement on planning and design while considering unique needs of each group.
The proposed project is designed to boost the ongoing lifesaving assistance and will target the most vulnerable displaced, floods, and drought-affected communities in Banadir, Galgadud, and Middle Shabelle regions of Somalia. At the moment, IDPs and urban poor and rural communities are among the most vulnerable groups in the society. Since the capacity of the local community to address their needs is very weak it is clear that the increasing number of IDPs and urban poor in crisis requires an urgent comprehensive action to support the target populations. The project responds to urgent humanitarian needs including (1) Deliver life-saving WASH assistance to reduce acute needs among the most vulnerable settlements and communities (2) Reduce the risk of violence against women, children, and vulnerable groups when accessing WASH services, and (3) Provide or restore sustainable access to safe water and adequate sanitation services in targeted communities and institutions. 
Further, the target population will be involved in activities planning, implementation, and monitoring. Special attention will be given to women, children, and the elderly, and people with disabilities during the designing and construction WASH activities (i.e. 15% of all latrines will have disability-friendly features and will be constructed close to their shelters to ease access). Moreover, women will be part of WASH committees and will be represented in all community structures to empower them. Minority groups and female-headed households likely to face exclusion will be part of community-based committees to represent the voice of the minorities. Distribution sites will be pre-selected by target population and hygiene kits contents shared with beneficiaries allowing them to understand their rights and entitlements. Different distribution modalities will be used where protection concerns are mitigated and reported if they occur. The household-level distribution will be employed if people with disabilities and the elderly cannot access distribution sites.

project_name: CCCM and Information Management Support to Improve Living Conditions of Drought Affected Rural and IDP populations in Somalia
project_objective: ACTED’s proposed action will response to the needs of IDPS and rural communities in Baidoa, Kismayo, El-Afwayne, Badhan, Diinsoor and Buurhakaba districts who are impacted by floods and drought, lack sustainable livelihoods and at risk of displacement. This project will establish, reinforce and strengthen governance, management and coordination mechanisms at appropriate levels; Increase site safety through site maintenance and improvement works; and capacity build Camp Governance, CCCM stakeholders and local authorities working towards self-management.

project_name: IMPROVING SOCIAL COHESION AND COMMUNITY WELLBEING IN CONFLICT-AFFECTED AREAS OF MALI
project_objective: The proposed project will improve psychosocial wellbeing and social cohesion in the conflict-affected areas of Mopti and Timbuktu regions. HI will target a total of 16,000 direct beneficiaries in 56 communes of the regions of Mopti and Timbuktu, including 3,681 people in need of PSS, also benefiting from IGA (184 beneficiaries), kits (920 beneficiaries) and rehabilitation of safe spaces (2,945 beneficiaries). In addition, HI targets 484 community focal points, 560 members of local protection committees, 216 members of local peace committees, 8,400 beneficiaries of direct information and awareness raising sessions on social cohesion and 2,700 beneficiaries of community projects (in 18 communes). HI estimates that 83,390 persons will be reached through mass media information campaigns on social cohesion and peaceful cohabitation.

project_name: Medico-nutritional assistance to populations affected by the socio-political crisis in Anglophone areas, North West Region, Cameroon
Améliorer l’accès aux soins de santé par le renforcement des activités à  base communautaire des populations affectées par le conflit dans la région  de Tillabéri, Niger
project_objective: ALIMA/BEFEN propose d'agir sur la prévention, la sensibilisation et la mise en place de mécanismes de référencement au niveau primaire. Nous appuierons également la prise en charge (PEC) des populations vulnérables à travers un renforcement des acteurs en communauté, ainsi qu’un renforcement des agents de santé pour la PEC des pathologies prioritaires. Nous assurons également l’augmentation de la couverture de santé par des cliniques mobiles dans les zones enclavées et éloignés. Dans l’objectif de garantir un continuum dans la PEC des cas de référencement Malnutrition Aiguë Sévère, les urgences pédiatriques et grossesses compliquées, un appui au niveau secondaire de soins sera apporté à la maternité, à la pédiatrie et au CRENI. Enfin, Les cas référencés dépassant la capacité de PEC au niveau des districts seront référés aux hôpitaux de Tillabéri et Filingué.

project_name: Inclusive specialized (Rehab, PSS, SRHR) services for vulnerable persons including persons with disabilities in Cox's Bazar Rohingya camps and host communities
project_objective:
HI will continue its 12+ years of broad support for refugee and host communities by addressing the immediate acute and chronic health needs of refugees and host communities through multi-sectoral mobile units, center-based services and a strong referral pathways. 
The proposed intervention will be delivered through a twin-track approach: 
- Multi-sectorial mobile units composed of qualified Nurses and Midwives, Physiotherapists, PSS/ Protection Officers, and social workers will be deployed to identify and provide tailored and individual assistance to the most vulnerable, especially the persons with disabilities and their caregivers who might be excluded from services due to mobility or social barriers.  Integrated outreach teams (PSS + Physiotherapist) deliver home-based services focused on education for beneficiaries and their caregivers on safe, effective exercises and interventions.
- At HI service centers, teams support beneficiaries with enough mobility to access the facility with rehabilitation, PSS, basic healthcare, through nurses and protection. The Rehabilitation team provides assistive devices and other health items when necessary to people (adults/children) with physical and functional limitations in order to improve their mobility, enhance recovery, and prevent complications. Training is provided to persons and caregivers on basic home-based rehabilitation and proper use, maintenance and repair of mobility devices. 
- In home-based and center-based services, Nurses will support beneficiaries with: wound care, bedsores care, ante and post-natal care. A key focus will be to provide maternal care for women who cannot access health facilities (i.e. women and girls with disabilities), including the prevention and detection of pregnancy-related risks and complications. Nurses refer to the nearest Health Facility and follow up to ensure they received needed specialized services. 
- Support to government hospitals and health facilities both in the host and refugee communities. Physiotherapists will provide direct comprehensive Rehabilitation services within the Health Facilities and will train and mentor health workers.
- PSEA principles are mainstreamed through all activities through extensive training of all staff and volunteers using PSEA Network materials and recommendations. Feedback is regularly elicited through comment boxes, a dedicated hotline for host and refugee communities, community discussions and 1:1 interviews. A dedicated Focal Point to receive complaints is installed in the Cox base to coordinate with camp level team leaders to ensure referral for needed services and ensure survivor advocacy as needed. 
HI is currently implementing four projects that addresses above mentioned health services funding under different donors. To provide the service for the host community people, HI support 5 hospitals It includes Cox's Bazar Sadar hospital, Ukhiya Upazila health complex, Teknaf Upazila health complex, MSF hospital and IOM hospital with rehab staff (physiotherapist) provide services in those facilities. Both host community people and beneficiaries from the camps can receive services from these facilities.
-HI welcomes complaints and feedback from the beneficiaries to integrate beneficiaries views in the project activities. HI MEAL team leads the complaints, feedback and response mechanism. Currently different complaints and feedback collection modalities exists in both host communities and camps. Modalities are face to face interviews, group discussions, hotline and feedback box. Based on the sensitivities of the complaints HI provide solution as soon as possible.

project_name: Provision d’une assistance médico-nutritionnelle de qualité des populations vulnérables et renforcement du système de santé primaire dans les zones affectées par les crises au nord et au centre du Mali
project_objective:
Première Urgence Internationale intervient dans la région de Gao à Ansongo depuis 2014 et dans la région de Mopti à Bandiagara depuis 2019. PUI a mis en œuvre plusieurs interventions dans les domaines de la santé, de la nutrition et de la protection afin d’améliorer l'accès des populations vulnérables aux soins de santé primaires et la sécurité nutritionnelle. A travers ce projet PUI compte continuer l’appui d’urgence à la prise en charge des personnes les plus vulnérables (femmes enceintes et allaitantes et enfants de moins de 5 ans) en délivrant le paquet minimum d’activités (PMA), assurer l'approvisionnement des CSCom en intrants médicaux (médicaments, matériel et consommables médicaux), la vaccination, le référencement des cas de complications, l’appui à la santé de la reproduction, lutter contre la malnutrition, le déploiement de cliniques mobiles. 
Les efforts consentis en première phase permettent à PUI d’aller plus loin dans l’appui au fonctionnement du système de santé en proposant une aide modulée suivant l’évaluation de performance des CSCom, le renforcement des capacités des agents de santé, des ASACO ainsi que du réseau communautaire pour améliorer l’accès à la santé primaire. La communication et les sensibilisations sur les Pratiques Familiales Essentielles, le COVID-19, l’hygiène, l’éducation à la santé etc. resteront des activités phares étant persuadé que l’amélioration du niveau de santé passe par la communauté.
La protection est également au cœur des préoccupations de PUI notamment dans la lutte des violences basées sur le genre. Des comités de soutien aux VBG seront créés pour améliorer les sensibilisations, les identifications et le référencement (la création des comités se fera en collaboration avec la coordination du cluster/sous-cluster concerné, afin de les faire entrer dans le mapping interactif des mécanismes communautaires existants et éviter les doublons/trop de comités dans certaines localités). En plus d’une prise en charge médicale et psychologique les survivantes seront appuyées dans leur réinsertion économique. 
Enfin, la multiplication des mouvements de population a encouragé Première Urgence Internationale à se positionner au nord et au centre comme un acteur clé en santé dans le cadre du mécanisme de réponse rapide (RRM).
L’objectif de ce projet est ainsi double. Il vise à la fois à appuyer les activités en soins de santé primaire dans 25 aires de santé afin d’assurer la permanence de la couverture de santé dans le cercle d’Ansongo et de Bandiagara, tout en renforçant les capacités des acteurs du système de santé (Equipe Cadre de District (ECD), Equipe CSCom, communauté)  en vue d’un transfert progressif des compétences de gestion, de suivi, de supervision et de formation, quand les prérequis seront  présents (niveau de compétence, ressources humaines et financières, infrastructure, procédures). Cet accompagnement passera à la fois par la formation continue dans le cadre de la fourniture de services de santé de qualité, mais aussi par des formations. Par ailleurs, dans le cadre de la fourniture des services de santé, Première Urgence Internationale applique la gratuité ciblée pour les groupes vulnérables, en accord avec les textes législatifs maliens en vigueur.
En parallèle la collaboration étroite avec les autorités sanitaires locales continuera et contribuera à renforcer le leadership, la capacité de suivi et de gouvernance de ces derniers.

project_name: Support to and integration of mine victims in eastern Ukraine
project_objective:
As the armed conflict in eastern Ukraine continues, available data on landmine/explosive remnants of war (ERW) casualties continues to document frequently occurring accidents. In the period between June 2014 and June 2019, a total of 1126 landmine/ERW accidents were recorded by DRC-DDG from open news sources. From the total of 2060 individual casualties recorded, 1,909.

2018-2019, with support from UNICEF DRC-DDG implemented MVA project. The project covered four out of six core pillars as per the UN Policy on Mine Victim Assistance (MVA) in Mine Action*: (a) data collection including needs assessment, (b) establishment of response methodology, (c) provision of direct assistance through the case management and (d) strengthening of the protective environment for survivors. 
* UN Policy on Victim Assistance in Mine Action: (a) data collection, (b) emergency and continuing medical care, (c) physical and other rehabilitation, (d) psychological and psychosocial support, (e) social and economic inclusion, and (f) laws and public policies.

A notable achievement of the project was the completion of the child landmine/ERW needs assessment, conducted by DRC-DDG during the period between Sept-Nov 2018, which covered the GCA of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts. The findings of the assessment conveyed the profiles of child landmine/ERW survivors, their path from the moment of accident to recovery, existing gaps and barriers in the process of rehabilitation and capacities of service providers (governmental and non-governmental) to meet the needs in accordance with the six pillars of MVA (defined in the UN Policy on Victim Assistance in Mine Action): (a) data collection, (b) emergency and continuing medical care, (c) physical and other rehabilitation, (d) psychological and psychosocial support, (e) social and economic inclusion, and (f) laws and public policies. 

The findings of the pilot project in 2018 informed the need for continuation of the MVA intervention and a 10-month project was launched in Mar 2019 with a key development which included the change in the scope of the intervention resulting in equal assistance for both, families with child survivors and adult survivors of mines/ERW who are also primary caregivers of children.  

The action is formed by the UN Policy on Victim Assistance in Mine Action and built around five key components all inspired from this. 
The 1. component envisions strengthening of communication between national governmental actors and local service providers through the facilitation of joint meetings, round tables discussions to ensure the provision of better support to the mine/ERW victims and their families. The 2. component consists of direct support to victims through case management and targeted individual assistance (in cash or in-kind). Victims will be closely followed by DRC-DDG staff who will ensure needs are met to the largest extent possible which includes: emergency and ongoing medical treatment, psychosocial support, physical rehabilitation (e.g. prosthesis) and social/economic inclusion. Part of this support will be secured through referrals and follow-up with relevant governmental/non-governmental services. The 3. component aims at strengthening national capacities through completion of a detailed physical rehabilitation assessment (focusing on technical aspects of prosthesis production and physiotherapy). In the 4. component, DRC-DDG will deliver a number of trainings in the selected communities (targeting schoolteachers, school children, and key community representatives) on how to improve inclusion of persons with disability into social and economic life. Following this, community-based initiatives focusing on such inclusion will be supported where the effects are deemed to be highest. Finally, to complement this, advocacy efforts will be reinforced to promote recommendations, developed as part of the Needs Assessment report.

project_name: Strengthen the collective humanitarian response through effective, agile and efficient coordination, based on humanitarian principles
project_objective: Five years after the opening of a country office, OCHA in Cameroon has become instrumental among the humanitarian and development community. As needs continue to grow, OCHA has a key role to play in the coordination of the humanitarian response as well as by liaising with key stakeholders to maintain humanitarian space and advocate for the rights of those directly affected by the three crises within the country. The complexity and magnitude of the three concurrent humanitarian crises requires coordination adapted to the different contexts and based on humanitarian principles. The continuous high humanitarian needs in Cameroon highlight the importance of strong coordination mechanisms capable of supporting an effective emergency response in line with humanitarian principles. The HCT under the leadership of the Humanitarian Coordinator will continue to provide overall strategic guidance to the humanitarian community, ensure that humanitarian principles are respected and maintain high-level engagement with relevant Government interlocutors. OCHA Cameroon will contribute to a better funded, more strategic humanitarian response that mainstreams protection, and is carried out in complementarity to development action. OCHA will continue to provide essential services to the humanitarian community in Cameroon, including the coordination of the Humanitarian Programming Cycle, the dissemination of key information products and the facilitation of joint multisectoral needs assessments. OCHA will continue to promote the development of a shared analysis of the distinct needs, vulnerabilities and risks by supporting gender-sensitive data collection and analysis. Playing the role of lead agent in the implementation of several specific results of the HCT’s gender in humanitarian action roadmap (2021-2022), OCHA will help the operation increase the quality and efficiency of its response, in line with the IASC gender policy. OCHA’s presence in Yaoundé, Maroua, Buea, Bamenda and Kousseri will enable it to provide critical coordination support on regional humanitarian needs analysis and response activities and promote consistency between field operations and strategic decision-making bodies. Coordination services will focus on improving capacity to address operational challenges on the ground, including through reinforced data collection and information management – particularly on access constraints to facilitate real-time solutions to access challenges. Existing rapid response mechanism will be further strengthened to ensure coordinated, dignified and timely assistance to affected populations. OCHA’s central role also allows the organization to promote the centrality of protection, Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) and the humanitarian-development-nexus. OCHA will use its comparative advantage to facilitate humanitarian access and civil-military coordination and will continue to build the capacity of local responders.

project_name: ADRA Integrated Refugee Response for Urban populations (Khartoum) and ADRA SSR response in White Nile camps.
project_objective:
The project aims at responding to the protracted needs of refugees through strengthening the community based mechanisms and responses. An instance of this is protection whereby ADRA will capitalize on the existing systems and mechanisms in the community, further enhancing their understanding and ability to address protection concerns through capacity building. Furthermore, ADRA will ensure an integrated approach in assistance. This is one of the main reasons that ADRA has prioritized specific locations. Access to water supply especially in the new extensions in Al-Jamya and El-Keshafa are important to counter both COVID-19 and other waterborne diseases. An assessment by ADRA shows that nearly 78% lack access to clean water in those camps.  Assessment also indicated that nearly 91% of SSR prefer household latrines as they are more private and easier to clean and maintain.
To address the emerging Ethiopian Crisis, ADRA will provide emergency water supply, and NFI assistance in the camps in Gedarif and Wad Almahi. ADRA will also compliment this with Emergency NFI Shelter assistance.

project_name: UNICEF Life Saving Nutrition Interventions Targeting Most Vulnerable Population (IDPs and Vulnerable Residents) Across Sudan
project_objective:
Sudan has one of the highest rates of malnutrition in the region, around three million children under 5 suffer from acute malnutrition out of which an estimated 570,000 have severe acute malnutrition (SAM) (Draft HNO 2021). Through this project, UNICEF aims to increase equitable access and utilization of quality nutrition curative and preventative services for acutely malnourished children (boys and girls 6-59 months) and pregnant and lactating women (PLWs) among highly vulnerable populations including IDPs and vulnerable residents. In 2021, UNICEF will continue to support the provision of nutrition curative interventions through strengthening the quality of services and scaling up Outpatient Therapeutic Program (OTP) while working also on securing pipeline for essential nutrition supplies such as Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF), therapeutic milk, Resomal, OTPs drugs & Anthropometric measurements). Through this UNICEF will target around 330,000 children suffering from SAM and will procure 396,000 RUTF cartons. To ensure early identification and referral of children with acute malnutrition, UNICEF will work on strengthening outreach activities through activation and training of new and existing community structures, including community outreach volunteers and Mother Support Groups (MSGs). 
UNICEF will also support the provision of other specific nutrition interventions through the promotion of infant and young child feeding (IYCF) practices. In 2021, UNICEF will continue to exert efforts in scaling up IYCF program to ensure the counselling of 990,000 pregnant women and mothers and caregivers of children less than two years (0-23 months). At the community level, IYCF counselling will be carried out by MSGs, while at the health facility level one-on-one IYCF counselling will be carried out by trained health care/IYCF counsellors. UNICEF is working on strengthening the linkages between CMAM and IYCF program, to ensure that SAM children upon discharge from the OTP are referred for nutritional counselling through community-based MSGs & vice versa.
To alleviate the risk of micronutrient deficiency in women and children, UNICEF will continue to provide vitamin A supplementation targeting 6,770,972 children (6-59 months) and iron foliate supplementation targeting 990,000 pregnant and lactating women.
Through this project, UNICEF will continue to support health system strengthening through efforts to strengthen supply chain management of nutrition commodities at all levels (national, state, locality and facility level). Besides building the capacity of front-line health workers and other CMAM related cadres on CMAM program and CMAM monitoring to ensure the delivery of high-quality nutrition services. UNICEF will also support the strengthening of nutrition information systems to provide accurate and timely data from OTPs and MSGs.

project_name: Inclusive Humanitarian Assistance, Health and Protection Response for the Most Vulnerable, Crisis Affected Persons in Libya
project_objective:
The goal of this project is to enhance the wellbeing and safety of conflict affected population in Libya with improved and more inclusive access to services. The project will target highly vulnerable, crisis-affected internally displaced persons (IDPs), returnees and host communities living in Tripoli, Misrata and Benghazi districts as well as local and national service providers. 

The project will improve physical and functional independence and psychological wellbeing of the most vulnerable, conflict-affected persons with functional limitations and their caregivers thanks to an integrated approach to rehabilitation services, alongside raising awareness on risks posed by Explosive Ordnance (EO) for conflict affected population as well as promoting a more inclusive humanitarian action within coordination bodies, humanitarian community and partners. Finally, it will also seek to enhance the capacities and empower local and national services providers and institutions.
