project_name: Improving living conditions of the most vulnerable population in both camps and communities through provision of shelter and winterization assistance.
project_objective:
This project has been designed to responds to the needs for humanitarian life-saving shelter and NFI assistance to IDPs and host community HHs in Azaz, Albab, Dana, Maaret Tamsrin, Harim, Armanaz, Atareb, Idleb, Kafr Takharim, Mhambal and Qourqeena subdistricts in Aleppo and Idleb governorates targeting 7500 HHs (37500 individuals, 9750 Men, 10500 Women, 8250 Boys, 9000 Girls).

The locations are prioritized as per the HNO 2021 data and according to prioritization of BINAA to the location as per the eld teams’ communication with the local councils and their eld visits to some villages and camps.

The project will target the IDP’s sites in the targeted locations, (5000 HHs (25000 individuals); Men 6500; Women 7000; Boys 5500; Girls 6000) in order to improve living conditions for conflict affected IDP HHs though supporting IDPs sites with emergency response activities like NFI distribution (5000 Heaters and 320 liters/HHs of heating fuels), tent winterization, insulation, levelling, graveling pathways (over 150 camps).

For targeted communities in mentioned subdistricts, BINAA will provide shelter repair and functional upgrades for damaged houses valued at an average of $650 for 1500 HHs (7500 individuals) (1950 Men, 2100 Women, 1650 Boy, 1800 Girl) (60% IDPs and 40% HC). The repair works will enable the target communities to use local materials and work through local contractors to improve their living conditions, fostering a sense of ownership, responsibility, and resilience while supporting local markets. BINAA will also working on upgrading 250 unfinished buildings accommodated by 1000 IDPs HHs (5000 individuals) (1300 Men, 1400 Women, 1100 Boy, 1200 Girl) and providing safe and dignified housing conditions. valued at an average of $850 for each HH.

Shelter repair beneficiaries will be IDP and HC HHs living in an inadequate shelter that does not meet minimum SPHERE minimum standards for square meters of covered living space per person and has inadequate privacy or protection from the elements, settlement planning and WASH facilities. We will target HHs that have light to medium damage but remain structurally sound. Works include doors and windows repair or replacement, partition installation, sealing cracks and holes in walls, and WASH facilities repairs. The works will ensure increased privacy between male and females, host and hosted families that enhance gender sensitive response. Furthermore, for HHs with disabled persons, additional works will be included to respond to their needs by including disability friendly entrance and toilet facilities (e.g. use of a simple ramp with a handrail for using wheelchairs at the building entrance and seating provisions for toilets). The unfinished buildings rehabilitation varies between the number of rooms in each unfinished building, installation of masonry partitions, repair of WASH facilities within the building. To enhance gender sensitive response, necessary adaptations that particularly affect women and girls will include appropriate lighting, separate toilets and showers for men and women, accessible facilities for people with disabilities (disability friendly entrance and toilet facilities), areas for bathing, washing of clothing, and partitions to create spaces for different households and additional partitions within households to create privacy for men and women.

To participate in the project HHs and building owners should agree on the terms of assistance and sign a contract that allows the IDP household to stay for one year for free to ensure that HLP guidance are considered and utilized. To bene t from the project, all beneficiaries should present valid HLP documents that verify the ownership of properties.

project_name: Recovery of Local Economy and Promotion of Social Cohesion in Northern Syria
project_objective:
The project contributes to supporting social and economic realities in Al-Bab subdistrict in the NW of Aleppo and in Salqin in NW Idlib for a period of 12 months. It directly targets 2,125 BNs (50% M&50% F, 1010 IDPs & 1010 HCs (161 returnees), %6 PWDs) from both subdistricts with different types of modalities. 
The project has two key tracks, with many links and integration between them in a way that maximizes the impact of the intervention.

FIRST TRACK: The social track that aims to empower the local communities and enhance social cohesion in both targeted subdistricts through:
-	Building the capacity of two local development committees LDCs (one in each subdistrict) in community development and conflict-sensitive community initiatives.
-	Providing guidance and consolation services to LDCs in developing 3 community initiatives in each subdistrict  (2 to support social cohesion and one to support the community) and then reviewing the initiatives proposals according to the finings of “participatory market assessment” (PMA) and the social cohesion assessment. After that, provide micro-grants to the approved initiatives as per the initiatives plans.
-	An extensive assessment of social “connectors” and “dividers” to identify the factors affecting social cohesion in the targeted subdistricts from social, economic, legal, and NGOs intervention aspects.
The findings of the assessment will be organized in a comprehensive report and disseminated to internal and external stakeholders, and hold a conference to present the main findings to the service providers in the targeted subdistricts, e.g. INGOs and NGOs, to benefit from the findings.

SECOND: The economic track that aims to improve the access of targeted communities to livelihoods and basic services through:
-	Conduct a Participatory Market Assessment PMA to identify community priorities by engaging the L communities and LAs in assessing key value chains in their communities, market analysis, community assets, mapping services. LDCs, who have been trained in participatory evaluation, are involved in managing this evaluation.
-	Based on PMA, and the high coordination with local authorities and service providers in the two targeted subdistricts, providing 300 beneficiaries from most vulnerable groups (50% F&50%M, 150 IDPs & 150 HCs (20 returnees),  7% PWDs) access to short-term employment in a manner that helps them meet their essential needs through work in the rehabilitation of socio-economic structures and societal initiatives. This, in turn, contributes to improving the access of targeted communities to basic services. A referral mechanism for labor will be established with prioritization of rehabilitation of socio-economic infrastructure.
Based on PMA, 100 BNs are supported to establish or expand their small enterprises and 100 BNs to start-up their vocations. This support will be through the provision of business development skills (BDS) and training vocational training courses, remotely. Guidance and consultation services will also be provided to BNs during the development of their business plans and during implementation. 200 micro-grants (cash, vouchers, and/or in-kind) will be awarded to the 200 beneficiaries based on the evaluation and approval of their business plans.

As BNs participated in project designing phase already, so again, while implementation: the partners will ensure that project is introduced to the L community and LAs including goals, activities, duration, location, and criteria of selecting BNs. To ensure well introduction process, it will include: consultation sessions with LAs, seminars with the L community, sessions with BNs, flyers, social media posts, road posters, and banners. Several project activities, for example: community assessment and community initiatives, are designed to be BNs an essential part of the outputs and implementation in addition to support the M,W and PwDs to ensure non-discriminatory and dignified access.

project_name: Provision of sustainable life-saving WASH services to the most vulnerable IDPs in Idleb
project_objective:
The project aims at targeting the most vulnerable people in 3 camps in Idleb governorate to ensure the sustainability of service provision through a holistic approach to meet the urgent need of 12363 IDPs (2268 men, 2918 women, 3317 boys, 3860 girls).
The project will be implemented by Alseeraj for development and healthcare - SDH, through the intervention, SDH will use its resources and previous experience in the distribution of hygiene kits, hygiene promotion campaigns, rehabilitation of existing latrines, establishment of water network, sewer network and provision of clean drinking water, solid waste management, construction of latrines, and bathing facilities.
The project will include one round of distribution hygiene kits and one round of complimentary hygiene items in respond to COVID-19 for 2139 families to maintain the level of personal hygiene among IDPs living in those camps. Hygiene kits contents are designed to meet the need of the IDPs and the WASH cluster standards.
Moreover, this project will cover the solid waste management activities on daily basis in 3 camps which includes the distribution of 246 (100 L) solid waste container across targeted camps. The collected waste will be dumped in a formal dumping sites in Sarmada sub-district.
The project will provide safe water for drinking and personal hygiene to 12363 IDPs in 3 camps by water trucking for the first two months of the project, meanwhile SDH will be working on a more sustainable solution by building a water network within the camps and provide the water from a nearby water source (Public well), SDH will also build a central water tank nearby the targeted camps to ensure the continuous flow of water. SDH will ensure the water quality by chlorinating the water at source in addition to water quality testing in the main tank and at household level. 
The project will ensure that each person receives 40 L/Day of safe water as per the latest WASH cluster recommendation. SDH will pay special attention to the water quality, and make sure that water is chlorinated, and it meets the WHO standards (0.2 and 0.5 mg/l FRC) before distribution and at the household level. This activity will include installing a water tabs which will be used during the water trucking phase, and will be connected to the water network later. 
the project will also cover the construction of 152 latrine blocks (456 cells) to ensure IDPs have safe access to sanitation facilities while employing the latest recommendation by the WASH cluster (25 people per latrine). the latrines design will take special consideration of protection issues as it is provided with lighting system working on solar panels to ensure safe access during the dark hours. Out of the constructed latrines 4 cells will be dedicated to cover the needs of 66 people with special needs in the targeted camps. The project will also conduct maintenance for the 40 existing latrine cells in the 3 camps. The constructed latrines will be connected to the nearby main sewage system to avoid constructing of septic tanks and for safe disposal of sewage waste. 
152 bathing facilities will be constructed as well taking into consideration the gender sensitivities by separating the facilities for men and women. The bathing cells will be part of the sanitation facilities, in which each block will contain 3 toilets and one shower. (detailed sketch will be attached to the proposal.
In case of any probable new displacement waves to targeted camps, SDH will report to WASH Cluster about the deviation in number of targeted beneficiaries reached in each site of implementation.

project_name: Provision of food assistance in northwest Syria
Preventing, mitigating and responding to protection risks to the most affected population in South Sudan facing the highest severity levels
project_objective:
The overall objective is to prevent/mitigate the impact of violence on communities, and to increase the protection of population affected by conflict and/or disasters. NP will conduct direct protection, violence prevention, enhancing community protection structures, and supporting humanitarian response through protection mainstreaming advice/training and assessments. 

In light of the protection and GBV needs, NP will respond to direct physical violence through direct protection services (patrols, protective accompaniment or referral to services). These measures will deter violence and ensure safe access to services by survivors. Referral pathway strengthening further help monitoring/responding to protection concerns. 

Risk prevention includes controlling rumor so communities can make informed decisions about how to respond protection crisis – thereby reducing tension and displacement. Workshop/advocacy targeting communities and key stakeholders will help transform attitude and secure community participation in risk prevention/responses. 

Building communities capacity to self-protection is critical to amplifying project effectiveness, relevance and accountability. It also ensures communities are resilient to, and can recover from violence/harms without NP’s presence. Concretely, EWER training/assessment – focusing on existing coping strategies – will support communities’ capacities in identifying and responding to protection risks especially in high-risks locations. Community protection structures will also be trained and involved in project activities; this will lead to greater community participation in identifying/enacting effective, relevant and sustainable protection strategies. By drawing members from different community segments, NP encourages inter/intracommunal interaction and participation of marginalised groups; this in turn promote social cohesion and overall inclusivity in community decision-making processes. 

Inter/intracommunal violence has to be diffused before escalation. At NP fieldsites, there had also been reports of returnees and host communities tension as the two compete for resources. In response, NP will facilitate dialogues and meetings between parties, community members/leaders, local security actors and authorities. These will lead to enhanced understanding and trusts between parties, resolve issues before they escalate, and minimise risks of harm in case of violence. In line with the aforementioned local capacity building approach, violence prevention, protection and response workshops will also be provided to communities, using training manuals on peacebuilding, Unarmed Civilian Protection (UCP) and conflict mitigation.

Finally, to facilitate centrality of protection in humanitarian operations, NP will provide training/technical advice to partner agencies when there are identified gaps. NP will also use its unique access to provide regular assessments on ongoing protection crises, and thereby provide critical information to humanitarian responses. 

NP has static teams in Central/Western Equatoria, Unity, Upper Nile, Jonglei, Western Bahr el Ghazal and Lakes. Mobile team deployment is coordinated with the Protection Cluster, and once response is triggered by PC’s clear criteria, mobile teams can be immediately deployed to where violent conflict happens or where there is no presence of protection actors to respond. 

NP has unique expertise in facilitating community-driven protection. Teams are embedded in community and present 24/7 to address protection needs. NP relies on strong relationship-building, resulting in community trust and acceptance that helps NP negotiate unique access to areas. NP staff includes advisors in protection, women peace & security, social cohesion, safety and security and M&E: guiding NP to be effective and efficient whilst ensuring safety. Operational support systems are in place to ensure effective and timely actions for programming and reducing operational risks.

project_name: Mine Action in Northwest Syria
project_objective:
The HALO Trust will continue to deliver an integrated Mine Action approach in northwest Syria involving Explosive Ordnance Risk Education (EORE), Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD), Non-Technical Survey (NTS) and Victim Assistance (VA), delivered both directly and through three implementing partners.
HALO and its implementing partners will provide EORE to men, women, boys and girls, with a focus on community members most at risk of accidents (including children, teenagers, IDPs, agricultural workers and rubble removal workers). HALO will also continue to deliver ‘Training of Trainer’ (ToT) workshops to NGO workers and Community Focal Points to improve the relevance, integration, and reach of EORE messaging across all communities and relevant humanitarian sectors. Incorporation of COVID-19 messaging to EORE sessions will continue throughout 2021 and HALO will provide COVID hygiene kits to EORE beneficiaries. 
In Q4 2020, HALO completed its contamination impact survey work in all accessible communities in northwest Syria, improving HALO’s awareness and understanding of explosive ordnance (EO) contamination in the region. This has created opportunities for HALO to advance its survey activities to improve its Mine Action response in the region. Disposal teams will dispose of all accessible surface and sub-surface EO items (excluding minefields and IEDs) in accordance with priorities determined by the HALO Operations room. The primary method of disposal will be via thermite flares, with the outcome being the detonation or burning of EO items in a controlled and safe manner  by suitably qualified field staff, mindful of team safety and the safety of local communities. EOD permanently removes the lethal threat posed by EO. At this point in time, disposal activities do not extend to minefields or IEDs, due to the technical nature of these items.
NTS activities will validate previous explosive ordnance survey data with an emphasis on suspected minefields, IED fields, and multiple EO-contaminated areas (notably sub-munitions). NTS provides information for disposal and clearance operations and informs where Mine Action resources should be prioritised. Lastly, NTS provides local authorities, humanitarian actors, the Gaziantep cluster network, and the donor community with a greater understanding of EO threats, including specific locations.
HALO will also expand its EOD activities, through its Turkish implementing partner, to all accessible districts in Turkish-administered northern Aleppo, including Afrin. This will permanently remove the threat of explosive ordnance contamination to community members and IDPs, preventing further accidents and allow land, infrastructure and resources to be used safely and productively.  HALO will also incorporate into operations full clearance activities to tackle minefields identified and mapped during prior NTS work.
The support to survivors of EO accidents will continue through a Victim Assistance (VA) component implemented by HALO and one of its partners. This will include the provision of prosthetics and orthotics, physiotherapy, nursing, psychosocial services and multi-purpose assistance delivered by three rehab centres between January and February, and two centres between June and December 2021. HALO and its other partner will also provide victim assistance case management services, providing referrals to specialised services for survivors of EO accidents.
HALO acknowledges the requirement to avoid activity duplication within the MASC as well as addressing gaps in providing EORE (to children, adults, CFPs, and NGO Focal Points), NTS and EOD. This will be achieved through ongoing and regular coordination with other members of the MASC, as well as engagement with local authorities, communities, and other NGOs throughout the implementation of the project. Both HALO and its implementing partners are active MASC members (and HALO is co-chair) and regularly submit 4Ws to the cluster.

project_name: Improved resilience and food security, and strengthened livelihoods opportunities for vulnerable displacement-affected population in Syria
project_objective:
NRC’s project will contribute to Early Recovery and Livelihoods (ERL) sector HRP objectives 1, 2 and 3. NRC will implement its ERL activities through a combination of direct and partner-led modalities, with aim to build resilience of displacement-affected population by providing a pathway from acute food needs to their greater self-reliance and livelihood recovery. Geographic areas will be targeted based on the severity and scale of needs, inter-agency coordination at hub-level (including the Cash Working Group), and access. NRC will provide ERL assistance to vulnerable conflict and displacement affected populations, including IDPs, refugees, returnees and members of host communities suffering the effects of the conflict. 

1.	Emergency Response: Objective: Vulnerable households can meet basic needs and reduce negative coping strategies, as well as to ensure protection of their productive assets.
To ensure that displacement affected households can meet basic needs and reduce negative coping strategies, and to ensure protection of their productive assets: 
- Unrestricted Cash Based Assistance, as a primary response modality to empower households to define and attain their own specific needs whenever appropriate.
- Information and Behaviour Change: CBA will be accompanied by information about the importance of dietary diversity and nutritious dietary choices to increase the impact of CBA in promoting FS outcomes.

2.	Economic Recovery:  Objective: Vulnerable households achieve self-reliance through own-food production and/or income generation.
To facilitate the transition of displacement affected populations from humanitarian assistance to self-reliance. NRC will support economic recovery of households so they can restore their ability to produce food, while for non-agricultural population NRC will use market-based approaches to facilitate access to demand driven income generation activities. 
- Local Food Production: targeted grants (cash or in-kind) to support local production of food by conflict affected population. Grants will be accompanied by training in food production techniques. 
- Income Generation Activities (IGA): NRC will facilitate access to IGA through: (1) Cash for Work activities that will ensure access to temporary income and employment opportunities, (2) Grants (cash / in-kind) to support income generation and (self) employment, and (3) Basic business skills training.  

3.	Inclusive Markets:  Objective: Households achieve resilience through sustainable livelihoods and inclusive markets.
To promote the development and access to inclusive markets that enable displacement affected populations fully restore their sustainable livelihoods. 
-	Sectoral Market Based Support: Development of agricultural livelihoods via provision of targeted grants, supported with training, mentoring, and market access.
-	Market Access Support: Employment Facilitation, Entrepreneurship, Local Capacity Strengthening and Infrastructure Rehabilitation.

project_name: Emergency vaccination and preventative animal health services for small-scale herders affected by the Syria crisis to keep livestock alive, healthy and productive.
project_objective:
The United Nations (UN) estimates the number of crisis-affected people in need of humanitarian assistance in Syria to be 14.2 million (48.7 % male and 51.3 % female), of which almost six million are in acute need. The above figure of people in need includes 6.7 million protracted internally displaced persons (IDPs); estimated 320,000 spontaneous IDPs return; 480,000 Palestine refugees and the rest overburdened host communities. More than 70% of the population in need of humanitarian assistance are accessible from within Syria.  
Overall, 12.4 million of people are estimated to be food insecure (including 1.27 million severely food insecure and 9.5 million moderately food insecure) and 1.9 million at risk of food insecurity. In this context, FAO has designed a project to assist 217,000 small-scale herder households (equivalent to 1,300,000 people) in Syria. The objective of the proposed action is to protect the livestock assets of these vulnerable herders through the provision of vaccinations and treatment of livestock. The expected project outputs are:
Output 1. Access to veterinary services to protect against and treat transboundary animal diseases (TADs) and common livestock diseases increased to benefit 217,000 herders. The output aims at providing animal healthcare, vaccinations against foot-and-mouth disease (FMD), Enterotoxaemia and treatment against ecto endo parasites (as per sector response package under emergency livestock vaccination and treatment).common and urgent diseases  
Output 2. Capacity of veterinarians and veterinary technicians for vaccination and treatment of livestock strengthened. This output aims at training of veterinarians and veterinary technicians and equipping them on TADs and zoonotic diseases control and eradication.
It is expected that the support to protect livestock assets through improving access to animal health services against TADs and common livestock diseases and enhancing the capacity of veterinarians and technicians to conduct vaccinations will help ensure the survival of the remaining livestock herd while increasing their productivity, which will lead to improvement of livelihoods, increase local availability of food, support self-reliance and improve the food  and nutrition security of small-scale herders in Syria, especially the most vulnerable.

project_name: Scaling up health facilities and community based interventions for maternal and child nutrition and lifesaving interventions in NW Syria
project_objective:
QRCS aims to continue integrating nutrition-related activities into the health facilities and community levels are currently operating. The intervention is intended to support the nutritional status for children under 5 years of age (boys and girls) as well as pregnant and lactating women, caregivers including people with disabilities across northwest Syria through the integration of the preventive and curative nutrition-related activities into primary facilities across NW Syria that are operated by QRCS in Idleb governorate (Darkosh, Zardana, Bennsh, Fos-Zuf, Ein El-Bayda, Haranbush, Qah, Harim, Ma'arrat Tamsrin and Salqin), and rural Aleppo (Al-Bab). QRCS will implement programmatic adjustment in the context of COVID-19 to protect health care providers, mitigate the risk of infection and ensure continuity of life-saving nutrition services. The service package entails:
1- Facility-based and outreach messaging about infant and young child feeding IYCF practices.
2- Nutritional assessment for pregnant and lactating women and children under 5 years of age (Application of mid-upper arm circumference MUAC and Z-scores among other assessment tools) in addition to family MUAC approach and referral of undernourished cases to the appropriate facility as needed.
3- Nutrition counselling for pregnant and lactating women, in terms of the infant and young child feeding practices for children 0-23 months.
5- Outpatient and inpatient management of moderate and severe acute malnutrition cases of children under 5 years of age.
6- Deployment of rapid response teams and nutrition mobile clinics to detect malnutrition cases and provide treatment.
7- Distribution of preventative and curative nutrition supplements for PLWs and children under 5
The project will contribute to the protection of the most vulnerable groups of women, men, girls and boys in all age groups especially 26,400 children under 5 (boys and girls), 17,400 PLWs and 1750 disabled people in the targeted communities, moreover beneficiaries have been involved in the project designing and implementation through close coordination with local council also beneficiaries will be engaged in evaluation through satisfaction survey and complaint mechanism.

project_name: Providing enhanced protection and resilience for most vulnerable men, women, boys and girls in camps and IDP sites in NW Syria
project_objective:
The project aims at providing integrated services to enhance resilience and protection from fire risks, and protection risks and to promote safe and dignified living conditions for IDPs living in camps and IDP settlements, especially for women, adolescent girls, the elderly and people with disabilities in NW Syria, sub-districts of Dana, Maaret tamsrin in Idleb and subdistrict of Azaz in Aleppo.

The project will target 35 IDP sites (which are also targeted by other shelter and protection components to ensure complementarity) with 9636 HHs, 54683 individuals, mostly women and children disagregated as 11695 men, 12782 women, 14348 boys and 14581 girls with about 3512 PWDs, 14217 children under 5 and 2197 elderly people above 60 years old.
Selection of sites is done in coordination with SNFI and CCCM clusters, local authorities and camp management and based on needs assessment after ensuring HLP rights through due diligence process according to relevant clusters guidelines. 
SDI will be keen to adhere to IASC standards and international principles in relation to GBV, PSEA, and inclusion and accessibility of people with disabilities. The project will ensure the formation of IDP committees in these sites including the participation of women and PWDs. Coordination with all the abovementioned stakeholders and committees will be maintained throughout the project cycles to ensure active participation and accountability. Camp management and different committees in the camps with receive awareness-raising on safety & security, Covid19, complaint mechanism, GBV, PSEA in addition to camp management and cross-cutting issues through sessions, training and banners, which be available to all camp residents. Multi-sectoral gap analysis will be conducted and submitted regularly to CCCM cluster.
To ensure the safety of IDPs and enhance protection against fire incidents that might happen on large or small scale. The intervention will focus on two aspects in consistence with Fire Response TF guidance:
1. Increase the awareness of IDPs residing in those camps on safe practices against fire incidents from small to large scale, causes and harmful effects; the targeted age/sex groups will include children and women.
2. Set up fire units within targeted camps and equipping them with necessary tools (fire kits); in addition to selecting one of out of every 75 IDPs, (total 730 IDPs) voluntarily to be trained on firefighting of fire ranged from low to medium scale by a technical team from SCD (Syrian Civil Defense).
The project will also include the maintenance of basic infrastructure in camps such as clearing drainage channels, replacing/refiling fire extinguishers and light repair to latrines, lighting, water tanks, fence...etc.

The project will be handed over to existing camp management and/or existing committees upon project closure after ensuring that the site management is acquainted with accountability and humanitarian principles, site management, maintenance in IDP sites, safety & security and existing CCCM Syria cross-border cluster tools and guidelines and provide open channels with CCCM to keep regular reporting of needs, ISIMM, displacement figures and other key information requested by CCCM through the training provided by SDI.

Prioritization of activities: All activities are life-saving and crucial to the survival and dignity of IDPs residing in the IDP camps. In case of underfunding, SDI will be obliged to reduce the number of camps targeted within this intervention. However, these camps will continue to be at risk of fire and suffer from bad living conditions due to lack of infrastructure and facilities maintenance in addition to lack of governance/participatory management thus affecting the dignity and rights of most vulnerable individuals.

project_name: Provision of Multipurpose Cash to Vulnerable Palestine Refugees in Syria
project_objective:
UNRWA plans to provide up to 418,000 Palestine refugees with cash assistance to meet their basic needs, including food, non-food items (NFIs) and shelter. The Agency will continue to provide this assistance based on a targeted approach introduced in 2019, prioritizing refugees assessed as most vulnerable with a higher cash transfer. In 2021, it is expected that around 140,000 Palestine refugees will be assessed as most vulnerable based on the four vulnerability categories used by UNRWA (female headed households, families with persons with disabilities, families headed by an older person and unaccompanied minors/orphans). 
Our cash transfer values were calculated while designing our Emergency Appeal 2021 intervening during the last quarter of 2020. The values were mainly based on a poverty line assessment for Syria, undertaken by the Relief and Social Service department at UNRWA HQ, and were also discussed with the CWG at the time. Based on this assessment, which adjusted the abject poverty line to USD 32, our cash transfer values were set to USD 27 per person per month for tier 1 (most vulnerable categories) and USD 16 tier 2 (remaining caseload of vulnerable Palestine refugees). These values may be considered as ceilings for our cash transfer based on our poverty line assessment. In reality and based on funding patterns and forecast, we expect to provide an average of USD 14 per and USD 9 per person per month for tier 1 and tier 2 respectively. This would amount to SYP 35,000 and SYP 22,500 per person per month respectively or SYP 175,000 and SYP 112,500 per month for a family of five, which is within the range of the CWG recommendation. 3) We plan to cover twelve months of assistance in 2021. We deliver our assistance in rounds of cash distribution depending on fund availability and taking into account cash flow considerations and donor requirements for the different grants. The cash distribution round is usually launched once the needed funds are secured for the full round based on the adjusted amounts (USD 14 and USD 9 per person per month). We are about to complete the first round of 2021, which will cover the needs for three months. We are planning to launch two other rounds in July and October 2021, which shall cover the remaining 9 months (5 months for one round and 4 months for the other).
M&E plan:
UNRWA plans to conduct two post-distribution monitoring exercise in June and December 2021 after the first and the third (final) round of cash distribution. UNRWA does not have the leverage to hold PDM surveys after every single round due to limited resources and in view of the long approval process from authorities. In addition to PDM, UNRWA also has a result based monitoring (RBM) system which tracks a number of indicators for all programmes and interventions including cash assistance. Quarterly management review (QMR) meetings involving relevant staff, including senior management, are held to track and assess the indicators. Mid-year result review (MYRR) and annual result review (ARR) are also conducted with departments at HQ to add another layer of scrutiny and to provide an overall overview of achievements and challenges. Project associates are deployed to cash distribution points to monitor the process on the ground and address any issues that may emerge on location. Humanitarian Officer for cash assistance provides overall support and supervision and UNRWA, with the help of the Emergency Operational Support Team with UNRWA Syria. Monitoring visits are conducted by EOST staff and by senior management on a regular basis. Area offices in Damascus, Aleppo, Homs and Dara’a are also closely engaged in the overall process of cash assistance. Finally third party monitoring exercises are often commissioned by prominent donors.
UNRWA has been providing cash assistance through multiple FSPs in the same area since 2013 and we didn’t face problem as such. UNRWA send the SMS to each family mentioning the name of the specific FSP.

project_name: Provision of life-saving healthcare services to Palestine Refugees in Syria
project_objective:
In Syria, the public health system has been exhausted by ten years of conflict, not only because of the destruction and damage of many health facilities, but also due to the displacement and migration of professional health workers. 
With the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, rising patient numbers are adding pressure to the fragile health system. Healthcare workers are particularly exposed to COVID-19, underscoring the risk of the already-overstretched healthcare capacity to be further compromised.
Within such context, the 438,000 Palestine Refugees (PR) who remain in Syria have become increasingly reliant on UNRWA for the provision of primary healthcare services and for subsidizing access to secondary and tertiary healthcare.
In 2021, while adapting its services to the COVID-19 preventive measures in place to protect both beneficiaries and staff, UNRWA will provide over 810,000 primary health care consultations through 25 health facilities, including 2 mobile clinics to sustain the provision of medical and dental services to refugees in areas where facilities are not fully operational. Besides, UNRWA will continue to subsidize access to secondary and tertiary healthcare services (including COVID-19 treatment) for around 12,000 cases through a network of partnered hospitals and private laboratories. UNWA will also subsidize COVID-19 testing and treatment for Palestine refugees.

With regard to COVID-19 preventive measures, UNRWA will continue operating a triage system at every health center, by which patients with fever and / or respiratory symptoms are quickly identified and supported by a dedicated medical team equipped with PPE. For COVID-19 suspected cases, laboratory tests (not PCR tests) are conducted at the health center and the patient is then transferred to a public hospital for further analysis. 
Beside, telemedicine will continue to be provided through a hotline set at each health center and managed by a medical officer in charge of addressing patients' medical queries.  Another hotline is managed by clerks to book appointments in order to avoid overcrowding at the center. UNRWA is also regularly reaching out to the community to raise awareness about the importance of having an appointment booked before coming to the health center. 
All patients visiting the health centers are required to use disinfection liquid at the entrance and to keep physical distance with one another in the center's premises. This is reminded by all health staff as well as billboards and advertisements set on the building's walls.

project_name: Provision of lifesaving integrated Gender Based Violence and Sexual Reproductive Health prevention and response services for Rohingya refugees and host communities in Cox's Bazar
project_objective:
UNFPA will continue to promote, coordinate and provide accessible, confidential, survivor-centered services to address GBV in line with the Inter-Agency Standards for GBV in Emergency Programming. In all UNFPA 23 supported Women Friendly Spaces (WFS) and selected 15 health facilities, case management, mental health and psychosocial support services, clinical management of rape, family planning services and counseling, treatment of sexually transmitted infections and emergency referrals will be provided to GBV survivor and vulnerable women and girls.  UNFPA fosters social cohesion by working in both refugee (80%) and surrounding host communities (20%). 
Prevention and mitigation strategies, mechanisms and initiatives to support community-based interventions in line with IASC principles and guidelines and AAP principles will be strengthened. The project will ensure community engagement and awareness aiming at mobilizing communities, including youth and men utilising SASA methodology to address negative social norms and to prevent and respond to GBV in a safe and timely manner.  As women and girls continue to face protection risks, advocacy and communication for change will be implemented to guarantee their dignity and safety. To ensure the safeguarding of beneficiaries, UNFPA will continue to collaborate with the PSEA network to reinforce Sexual Exploitation and Abuse reporting and response mechanisms and conduct training on SEA. 
The GBV sub sector will enhance engagement with other sectors and government for integration of GBV prevention, mitigation and response programming for quality services of GBV survivors using Inter-Agency Minimum Standards. The sub sector will expand comprehensive GBV prevention and response programs for women, and girls, focusing on case management and multi-sectoral referral systems. UNFPA will continue to mainstream GBV interventions for DRR in its Disaster Response emergency preparedness and response plans, through specialized capacity building PERU team and ensure a contingency stock of dignity kits. 
Capacity will be enhanced on the IASC GBV Guidelines to sector leads, government stakeholders, MoWCA, Bangladesh Police, implementing partners and fostering effective coordination in planning, implementing and monitoring essential GBV risk mitigation actions in all humanitarian response and services. This will be supported with regular community based GBV risk monitoring and joint safety audits. The JRP 2021, will deliberately target disability inclusion in GBViE response.

project_name: Projet de renforcement de la prevention et réponse aux violences basées sur le genre en faveur des populations affectées par les situations humanitaires dans les provinces de Kirundo, Cankuzo, Ruyigi et Bujumbura rural
project_objective:
Selon l'aperçu des besoins humanitaires 2021,les violences basées sur le genre (VBG) constituent un problème important pour toutes les couches de la population au Burundi mais elles affectent particulièrement les personnes les plus vulnérables. Ainsi, l’analyse des données sur les incidents de VBG rapportés par les acteurs humanitaires montrent une augmentation des cas parmi les populations.Par ailleurs,l’accès aux soins spécifiques n’est que très partiellement garanti sur le territoire, la plupart des centres de santé n’ayant pas le personnel formé ni les médicaments adéquats pour prendre en charge les survivant-e-s. Selon les évaluations conduites après les inondations de Gatumba, les 4 formations sanitaires proches des sites de déplacés ne disposaient pas de kits post viol ni de personnel formé et dédié à la prise en charge clinique des cas de viol.
Le projet s’aligne aux deux objectifs sectoriels (objectifs 1.1 et objectif 3) Protection du plan de réponse humanitaire 2021 pour le Burundi notamment:
Objectif 1 : Assurer un accès et une  réponse immédiate et multisectorielle aux services de protection  en faveur de 297, 947 personnes ciblées, y compris les survivants de VBG,  les enfants séparés et non accompagnés avec une attention particulière aux personnes à besoin spécifique
Objectif 2 : Renforcer les capacités de résilience des PDI, rapatriés et communautés cibles à faire face aux chocs par les activités liées aux solutions durables/ résilience / relèvement précoce
Objectif 3 : Améliorer l’accès aux services de protection pour les personnes cibles via le renforcement de mécanismes communautaires et nationaux
Il sera question principalement de fournir les services holistiques de prise en charge aux personnes victimes de violences par un accès aux services psychosociaux, compris les services psychosocial et médical, hébergement d’urgence et de prévenir l’impact et risques des violences basées sur le genre  parmi les populations touchées par les situations humanitaires (catastrophes naturelles, conflit) par les sensibilisations, les formations, la distribution des kits de dignité et assistance en cash aux ménages les plus vulnérables dirigés par les femmes.
Afin de répondre aux besoins les plus urgents de VBG le projet se focalisera sur les résultats suivants : 
1. Les survivants de VBG ont accès à des services médicaux, juridiques et psychosociaux spécialisés, socio-économiques en fonction de leurs besoins; 
2. Les Communautés (CDFC, OSC, etc…) ont les capacités nécessaires pour prévenir, répondre et réduire les risques de VBG dans les zones affectées; 
3. Les capacités de résilience des femmes et filles sont renforcés grâce à l’accès aux opportunités socio-économiques (surtout des ménages dirigés par les femmes et filles) via l’assistance d’urgence en cash
4 ; Les femmes et filles en âge de procréer les plus vulnérables ont accès aux kits de dignité
5. Les communautés sont sensibilisées sur les risques de VBG et comment les prévenir pendant les situations humanitaires
En effet le projet contribuera à la protection et l’accès aux services d’urgence de prise en charge pour les survivantes de VBG. Il va également renforcer l’engagement et les capacités communautaire à la prevention et réponse aux violences basées sur le genre à travers les formations et sensibilisations des membres des communautés, leaders communautaires, les autorités locales, les organisations locales sur les questions de VBG et thèmes connexes. Enfin le relèvement économique des ménages car cela contribue efficacement dans la prévention des VBG. Un focus sera également mis sur la prevention contre la COVId-19 afin de susciter l'engagement individuel et collectif surtout parmi les déplacés. La sensibilisation sur la prevention contre les violences conjugales et domestiques sera également renforcée. Les équipements de protection individuels seront mis à la disposition des beneficiaires.Il s'agit entre autre des masques, dispositif des lavages de mains,etc

project_name: Education in Emergencies – Improve access and learning for children in the most vulnerable schools of the West Bank, including East Jerusalem
project_objective:
The proposed project will contribute to improving children’s access to quality education in selected schools in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem. The selected schools were prioritized by the Ministry of Education and NRC, in the most vulnerable areas in Area C including East Jerusalem. The proposed project is in line with the MoE Strategy and Plan to guarantee children’s right to education, including the return to school plan, due the COVID- 19 strategy. The project- fits under a multi-year NRC education intervention of integrating psychosocial support in formal education, and supporting the MoE distance education efforts. The project aims to target 66 most vulnerable schools to support children through: i) Provision of  psycho-educational “Better Learning Program” (BLP), NRC PSS flagship programme institutionalization process, by training a new cohort of BLP Master Trainers, General Directors and subject supervisors; and capacity building of teaching and non-teaching staff in MoE schools; ii) Provision of emergency kits to the 66 schools; awareness sessions for parents on PSS and mental health; and provision of a “Supporting the Supporter” package for teaching and Non-teaching staff that are in need; and  iii) Strengthen the capacities of teachers and supervisors to carry out remedial/catch up classes for children that are not active in virtual classes and who are stuck in disrupted academic functioning, including by providing tablets to specific group the most vulnerable children; printing self-learning materials; and rehabilitate the schools’ ICT infrastructure. The distance learning component, will be implemented in full coordination with the Ministry of Education, at national, directorate and school level, to have a clear criteria on ICT equipment distribution, the use of tablets, including the different programmes and content to be utilized. NRC will also distribute the equipment to teaching and non-teaching staff in coordination with the MoE. NRC will develop clear procedures and SOP with the MoE on how to distribute and use the ICT equipment for teaching, non-teaching staff and students.

project_name: Strengthen provision of PHC across Syria.
project_objective:
WHO will continue supporting primary health care activities in Syria through both mobile teams and fixed primary health care facilities to ensure the delivery of the integrated Essential Health Service Packages (EHSP) to the population of Syria, while ensuring last mile coverage through integrated PHC network and access to healthcare to those in need who live in hard-to-reach areas. Estimated number of health facilities to be covered 500 fixed and MMUs along the country. Yet, the direct distribution is not applicable for PHCs, as the shipments are dispatched directly to MOH central level, and distribution tables are prepared by MOH based on their priorities.

It is imperative to enhance national health resilience and to reactivate public health canters’ by supporting the rehabilitation of non-functioning public canters, to repair extensive damage to crucial infrastructure, support ongoing medical training for human resource for health ,sustain availability of EML (medicines/equipment) and to undertake ongoing needs’ assessments to fulfill the gaps on the mid- and long term.

To ensure system strengthening the following programmatic areas will be in focus of the implementation of this project:
- Ensuring Access to Essential Primary Health Care Services
- Integrated Health Service Delivery/ PHC network
- Referral System
- Capacity building - trainings on a range of topics, such infection prevention and control, facility cleanliness and patient safety, pharmacy & warehouse management, facility management and standardized reporting through DHIS2. 
- Health Information Systems - trainings on a range of topics, such infection prevention and control, facility cleanliness and patient safety, pharmacy & warehouse management, facility management and standardized reporting through DHIS 2.
- Quality of service provision.
- NCD integration 
- TB integration into the delivery of EHSP
- Community health integration into the delivery of EHSP.
-Nutrition linkage: The provision of EHSP inclines Nutrition services, with focus on prevention of malnutrition among PLWs (Pregnant & Lactating Women) and U-5, health promotion acclivities, community-based interventions.
-GBV linkage: GBV first line support is part of the integratory services provided at the level of PHCs and community, after supporting health and community workers with capacity building, in collaboration with MHPSS programme and RH, basically through integrating with psychological first aid and psycho-social skills for COVDI19 responders.
It is important to mention here that due to SYP devaluation, the cost of rehabilitation and furniture from local markets was tripled, and thus the targeted PHC is reduced; still this is crucial support on the long term towards UHC and free of charge PHC services. Also to mention here that the number of operational mobile medical units, including medical teams supported is reduced compared to 2020 , as the final list of NGOs to be supported by WHO is under assessment by NGO unit along the country, the reassessment of qualified NGOs to be ready by end of July 2021. The planned MOUs in the 2nd half of 2021 is 20 , and this will bring the total supported NGOs to 30.

project_name: Apoyo a los servicios básicos de salud materno-infantil en los estados priorizados y fortalecimiento del programa nacional de inmunización.
project_objective:
La recesión económica y la disminución de la inversión en Venezuela han llevado al deterioro de la infraestructura y los servicios públicos, siendo salud uno de los sectores más golpeados en todos sus niveles. 
Si bien no contamos con informes actualizados que analicen las causas de muerte tanto en recién nacidos como en sus madres, resulta evidente la relación que esto tiene con el elevado número de servicios que no pueden ofrecer la atención básica para el parto y para el cuidado de los recién nacidos. Los resultados de una encuesta de UNICEF en 49 establecimientos de salud, incluidos 21 hospitales, en los estados de Bolívar, Zulia, Miranda y Distrito Capital sugieren una falta general de medicamentos y suministros; uso oportunista de antibióticos; un número inquietantemente bajo de enfermeras de cuidados neonatales, entre otras preocupaciones. Esto se ha agravado por la falta de limpieza y desinfección de los entornos neonatales, lo que aumenta el riesgo de mortalidad y morbilidad. También hay daños estructurales significativos en las instalaciones junto con la disponibilidad limitada de agua, que empeora durante o después de los frecuentes cortes de electricidad. 
La situación actual en Venezuela también amenaza la continuidad y la cobertura de las actividades de inmunización rutinaria, resultando en el resurgimiento de brotes de enfermedades prevenibles por vacunación como el sarampión y la difteria. Las principales razones del debilitamiento de la inmunización sistemática son la insuficiencia de los recursos financieros y el deterioro del sistema de la cadena de frío, debido en gran medida a los frecuentes cortes de electricidad.
A través de este proyecto, UNICEF contribuirá a que 125,668 mujeres que asisten a control prenatal reciban un paquete integrado básico de atención prenatal que incluye la detección de embarazos de riesgo y la prestación de servicios como suplementos de hierro, pruebas del VIH, profilaxis del paludismo y prevención de la transmisión del VIH de la madre al hijo; los niños y niñas recibirán atención integrada y diagnóstico de los lactantes con el VIH en ambulatorios prioritarios, al tiempo que se asegurará que se
establezcan vías de derivación funcionales a la red de hospitales para que reciban una atención más alta o especializada aquellas personas que lo necesiten. Además, en coordinación con la OPS/OMS, para 2021 UNICEF adquirirá y distribuirá vacunas para la poliomielitis (bOPV, IPV), el Sarampión/Parotiditis y Rubeola, la Tuberculosis, la Fibre amarilla, la difteria (Td y Pentavalente) y la Hepatitis B. Estas vacunas correspondientes al Programa Ampliado de Inmunizaciones, cubrirán una población infantil de alrededor de 1.286.959 niños menores de 5 años a nivel nacional, asegurando las dosis del esquema básico y los refuerzos del año y los 5 años de edad para dicha población. UNICEF continuará fortaleciendo la capacidad de la cadena de frío a través de reparaciones de infraestructura, instalación de equipos tales como generadores de energía, aires acondicionados, sistemas eléctricos y de alarma, etc., en almacenes a nivel central y estatal. UNICEF también diseñará e implementará campañas intensivas de comunicación y movilización social en colaboración con la OPS/OMS y el Ministerio de Salud para satisfacer la demanda de vacunas de inmunización de rutina.

project_name: Atención nutricional de niños y niñas menores de 5 años, mujeres embarazadas y en periodo de lactancia en 11 estados para reducir el impacto de la pandemia COVID-19
project_objective:
La atención nutricional propuesta por Unicef está dirigida a niños y niñas menores de 5 años, madres embarazadas y en periodo de lactancia - MEL, ubicados en zonas de alta vulnerabilidad en los estados de Zulia, Lara, Falcón, Delta Amacuro, Amazonas, Bolívar, Táchira, Apure, Miranda, Sucre, Distrito Capital y Delta Amacuro, - priorizados por el HRP. La atención nutricional con intervenciones según los protocolos de atención simplificado y medidas de prevención para el personal de salud y nutrición, de acuerdo al contexto de COVID-19 incluye las siguientes acciones:
1.Prevención de la desnutrición aguda y otras formas de desnutrición. se enfocarán en las siguientes intervenciones: a. 500,000 Niños, niñas y MEL que reciben atención de servicios de nutrición preventivos y de tratamiento a la desnutrición- a 400,00,000 niños, niñas menores de 5 años, y 100,000 MEL; b. Desparasitación a 305,000 niños y niñas de 2 a 14 años y 11,900 embarazadas en 2T y 3T de gestación, c. Suplementación con micronutrientes a 395,000 niños y niñas de 6 a 59 meses y 105,000 MEL; d. Prevención de la desnutrición aguda en 60,000 niños y niñas con riesgo de desnutrición aguda y 17,850,000 mujeres embarazadas con bajo peso gestacional; e. Consejería en alimentación del lactante y el niño
pequeño a 80,000 familias de niños y niñas de 0 a 23 meses de edad; 2. Tratamiento de la desnutrición aguda y deficiencias de micronutrientes. La atención se realizará con los servicios de salud ambulatorios y hospitalarios adscritos a las autoridades únicas de salud y MPPS, respectivamente, incluye el a. Tratamiento ambulatorio a 10,550 niños y niñas con desnutrición aguda moderada y severa sin complicaciones y apoyo en la transición al manejo ambulatorio. 
3. a. 1,500 personal de salud y nutrición en emergencias prevención y tratamiento de la desnutrición y prácticas adecuadas para la Alimentación del Niño Pequeño en Emergencias (IYCF-E por sus siglas en inglés) con enfoque multisectorial (salud, nutrición y WASH) durante la emergencia
b. 500 de personas de organizaciones gubernamentales y no gubernamentales capacitadas en temas de fortalecimiento del monitoreo y reporte de temas del estado nutricional de los niños, niñas y MEL.

project_name: Mejora de acceso de la población vulnerable a servicios básicos y resilientes de agua, saneamiento e higiene
project_objective:
En el contexto actual, es necesario implementar acciones para evitar el colapso de los servicios de agua y saneamiento a nivel rural, urbano y peri-urbano, y aumentar la percepción de riesgo de las comunidades y su resiliencia frente a un servicio discontinuo en cantidad y calidad. Se trabajará reforzando el nexo emergencia desarrollo, como Fase 2 a la intervención inicial. Con el proyecto, se trabajará en dos líneas:
-	Fortalecer el apoyo en operación y mantenimiento a las instalaciones rehabilitadas durante 2020 y recuperar otros servicios críticos de abastecimiento de agua potable y sistemas de saneamiento en las comunidades; y dotarlos de mecanismos resilientes para evitar el colapso, incluyendo apoyo en operación y mantenimiento, control y tratamiento del agua. Esto se realiza principalmente a través de la rehabilitación de los sistemas de bombeo, los sistemas de cloración, y elementos críticos de las instalaciones (dosificadores, generadores eléctricos, etc.). Igualmente se ampliará la respuesta hacia proyectos comunitarios para aumentar la tasa de conexión domiciliaria y la continuidad del servicio. 
-	Empoderar a las comunidades en la adopción de prácticas básicas de higiene y de tratamiento y conservación del agua en el hogar; a partir de estrategias de comunicación basadas en evidencia y la distribución de elementos esenciales de higiene. Incluye la elaboración de estudios KAPs e investigaciones para adaptar las estrategias, así como acompañamientos más sostenibles en el tiempo para acompañar los cambios de percepción de riesgos.  
Con el proyecto, se abordarán causas inmediatas y estructurales para mejorar los sistemas de abastecimiento de agua potable y los servicios de saneamiento. Se priorizarán acciones de impacto inmediato, tales como:
-	Diagnóstico de las instalaciones estratégicas e identificación de las acciones prioritarias, bajo enfoque de resiliencia.
-	Rehabilitación de fuentes existentes de agua subterránea para abastecer a hospitales y camiones-cisternas; incluyendo sistemas de cloración.
-      Mejora de los sistemas de bombeo, rehabilitación, generadores eléctricos, bombeo solar, etc.
-	Rehabilitación y fortalecimiento de fuentes superficiales existentes. 
-	Instalación y conexión de tanques pulmón en puntos estratégicos.  
-	Reparación de tramos estratégicos de las redes de distribución.
-	Distribución de agua en puntos estratégicos.
-	Apoyo para control y monitoreo de la calidad del agua.
-	Distribución de tabletas purificadoras y promoción de buenas prácticas en tomas de agua informales.
-	Instalación de generadores eléctricos en puntos estratégicos para asegurar el bombeo de agua en contingencias eléctricas. 
-       Apoyo en operación y mantenimiento de las instalaciones de abastecimiento de agua potable, incluyendo formación e incentivos. 
-       Preparación y respuesta a emergencias, incluidas emergencias en salud pública como COVID19
Considerando las dificultades de acceso a servicios básicos, con todo lo que significa en términos de cantidad, calidad y continuidad, es necesario reforzar las etapas últimas de la cadena de consumo agua potable, donde la atribución recae principalmente en el usuario. En este sentido, se priorizarán las siguientes actividades: 
- Análisis de las estrategias implementadas durante 2020 y generación de evidencias para informar las estrategias de 2021. Implementación de la Estrategia de Comunicación para el Desarrollo para la promoción de prácticas de higiene adecuadas adaptadas al contexto, basadas en evidencias, incluido COVID19.
- Distribución de productos básicos de higiene y de tratamiento y conservación del agua en el hogar para las familias más vulnerables.
- Incluye actividades de comunicación de riesgos, actividades de abogacía como el Día Mundial de Lavado de manos, formación de formadores, y fortalecimiento de las estrategias comunitarias para dar continuidad a las acciones de promoción.

project_name: Mejorar y expander los servicios de Protección para NNAs y cuidadores, afectados por la situación humanitaria en Venezuela, en el marco de la respuesta COVID-19
project_objective:
A través de la presente intervención UNICEF se propone continuar a apoyar las diferentes
instituciones del sistema de Protección de NNA en brindar servicios y programas a NNA y
sus cuidadores afectados por la situación humanitaria, exacerbada por los efectos de la pandemia, con un enfoque de género, edad e
inclusión. Las actividades implementadas contribuirán para alcanzar los 3 objetivos
estratégicos del Plan de Respuesta en estas componentes: OE1: UNICEF y sus aliados
brindarán servicios de apoyo psicosocial individual, grupal y atencion remota a NNA en riesgo y
cuidadores; OE2: UNICEF y sus aliados facilitaran el acceso a certificados y registros de
nacimiento en hospitales, unidades sanitarias y en comunidades con un enfoque también
a NNA de población indígena; OE3: UNICEF y sus aliados contribuirán a fortalecer los
mecanismos institucionales y comunitarios para prevenir, mitigar y responder a los riesgos
de protección de los NNA y sus cuidadores afectados por la situación humanitaria, de acuerdo a los
principios humanitarios y al respeto de los derechos humanos. UNICEF trabajará también
apoyando la coordinación inter-cluster a través del Área de Responsabilidad de NNA y sus
actividades con un enfoque en armonización de abordaje en las diferentes temáticas
diseminando las Normas Mínimas y promoviendo procedimientos estándar en temáticas
estratégicas como la gestión de casos y el cuidado alternativo.
A través del proyecto UNICEF en alianza con sus aliados implementará las siguientes actividades:
• Fortalecimiento de instituciones del Estado y ONGs en temáticas de protección de NNA
incluyendo Normas Mínimas, gestión de casos, salud mental y apoyo psicosocial, prevencion y respuesta a la violencia basada en género, cuidado alternativo, trata y trafico entre otras.
• Expansión de la oferta y calidad de servicios de protección para NNA en riesgo que
incluyen entre otros: gestión de casos por los Consejos de Protección, acompañamiento de
casos por parte de equipos multidisciplinarios de ONGs, apoyo en emisión de certificados y registro de nacimiento, apoyo a adolescentes en conflicto con la ley.
• A nivel comunitario, UNICEF y sus aliados trabajaran fortaleciendo los conocimientos
sobre temáticas de protección de NNA incluyendo la prevención de la separación familiar y la prevencion de la violencia, incluyendo la violencia basada en genero, la prevencion del embarazo adolescente,
y la diseminación de informacion sobre los servicios y programas de protección existentes.

project_name: Integrated access to quality basic education in a protective and inclusive environment for crisis affected children and youth in Somalia/Somaliland
project_objective:
Attendance rates continue to be low and attributed to a variety of factors such as lack of appropriate learning facilities, no or minimal learning materials, untrained teachers and overcrowded classrooms. 
Covid-19, conflict and natural disasters has further aggravated the situation and continues to undermined socio-economic development of communities and created vulnerabilities that demand lifesaving initiatives and reducing priority to education. Despite various efforts by international donors and NGOs out of school children face extra protection related risks, including forced recruitment, abuse, child labor and early marriage; thus, access to protective education can provide children a safe space. In some areas especially, rural areas there are no schools’ and where schools exist, they lack qualified teachers, water, sanitation and school feeding programmes. A Joint inter-cluster assessment conducted in September, 2020 in Hiran, 15% of the respondents mentioned that they do not have schools or learning spaces in their settlement.
Education committees lack capacity (financial & human) to manage schools effectively. Gender disparities exist in access to educational opportunities with boys being favored. Many families, when faced with costly school fees choose to educate boys rather than girls as the girl will be married off hence no benefit of educating her. 

A recent assessment in Hiran showed that 39% of school going age children do not attend school because their parents cannot afford books even if school is free. 34% of the respondents also said they are out of school due to fees being unaffordable. According to a study by the Ministry of Education and Higher Education (MoEHE) in Puntland, children with disabilities are subject to neglect, abuse, stigma and discrimination, negative attitude and exclusion. Families of persons with disabilities are often faced with similar barriers of stigma, segregation, refered in derogative names and lack of access to services and opportunities. Many children with disabilities do not attend school and are kept at home. The barriers faced by these children are huge and are additional to those they already face due to conflict, gender or refugee status. 

The project will target locations with most marginalized and deprived communities (displaced and extremely poor host communities) through an integrated approach in Beletweyne, Banadir; Bossaso, Butrinle, Caluula, Bandarbeyla; Berbera, Boroma, Burco, and Buuhodle, 22000 (South Central Somalia, 9300 (50% girls); Puntland, 6,500 (50% girls); and Somaliland, 6,200 (50% girls) with 10% being children with disabilities across. 90 (30:30:30) schools per area will be targeted across Somaliland, Puntland and South Central Somalia.   
The project through community mobilization will focus on inclusion in education services, school infrastructure and learning environment to ensure friendly children spaces (classrooms and WASH facilities) for children with disabilities. Community sensitization activities, will promote value of educating girls to boost enrollment and retention of girls in school. This will be complemented by girls' involvement in school clubs, girls' forums and provision of sanitary kits to girls. The project will also ensure inclusion of female teachers and female CEC members in capacity building activities to ensure the female voice is heard. Massive public awareness on covid-19 prevention will be conducted through pictorial print messages which will be printed and distributed to all supported schools.
SC will construct temporary learning spaces for expansion, rehabilitation and furnishing of classrooms and gender segregated latrines with handwashing facilities accessible to children with disabilities and girls, provision of top up incentives for teachers and supply of Covid 19 kits including thermometers, masks and hygiene kits.

project_name: ESSCOD (Expanding and Strengthening Surveillance and Communicable Diseases Outbreak Preparedness and Response Systems in Adamawa, Borno and Yobe states)
project_objective:
The overall goal of WHO’s activities in the area of Health Management Information Systems (HMIS) remains to support the government in data gathering and utilization for evidence-informed policy making across all pillars of the health system, especially in the area of health financing. In 2021, the WHO will organize workshops with SMoH representatives to identify information priority areas and conduct baseline studies to analyze the maturity level of the HMIS to measure them. The studies’ results will inform joint planning to strengthen state capacities. 
WHO will advance the SMoH capacity for information gathering, reporting, and management through training for state Disease Surveillance and Notification Officers (DSNOs/ADSNOs) on DHIS 2 usage, data collection, reporting, and processing at all levels of the state health systems. To advance electronic data utilization, WHO will support the states with the necessary infrastructure. At the SMoH level, WHO will facilitate workshops on evidence-informed policy making, planning, and budgeting and leverage these workshops to support the development of the states’ AOPs for 2022.

In addition, WHO will support the monitoring of service platform functionality by conducting HeRAMS assessments across the BAY states. In Adamawa and Yobe, the HeRAMS assessments will be complemented by a health service quality assessment, adapted from the Service availability and readiness assessment (SARA) methodology. To support the Borno state government in the relocation process of IDPs to safe areas with adequate health service coverage, WHO will conduct a rapid assessment in the area of Human Resources for Health. In addition, WHO aims to finalize a health workforce registry and link it to HeRAMS. Furthermore, WHO will improve the suboptimal data collection on mortality and Adverse Event Following Immunization (AEFI) at all levels of the state health systems. 

Risk communication 
Risk communication and community engagement
Effective risk communication is the key to prevent risky behavior among populations. It is especially important to prevent outbreaks of infectious diseases from becoming epidemics, e.g. by promoting physical distancing or personal hygiene during the COVID-19 pandemic. In 2021, WHO will continue to strengthen the local capacities to conduct effective risk communication by training journalists across BAY states on health reporting during outbreaks, but also by engaging social media influencers as well as mobile and stationary service providers. In addition, WHO will provide proactive risk communication material tailored to specific beneficiaries like IDPs and other vulnerable groups through different platforms, including house-to-house campaigns, social media, and radio.
Outbreak Preparedness and Response
The BAY states continue to experience outbreaks of epidemic-prone diseases, including measles, meningitis, viral hemorrhagic fevers, and cholera. WHO will continue to support the BAY states in the prevention, detection, and response to these hazards, including through response vaccination campaigns for Polio and other infectious hazards. To prepare for outbreaks, WHO will support the SMoHs in developing response plans for epidemic-prone diseases and preposition medical supplies and commodities for case management and case-based surveillance 

In 2021, the WHO will engage in strengthening laboratory capacities across all three BAY states to improve early detection and response capacities.  To this end, WHO will provide training to public health laboratory staff in the diagnosis of epidemic-prone diseases like Cholera and Meningitis, but also on quality management as well as biosafety and security. Besides, laboratories will be provided with equipment and reagents for safe and sound sample storage and testing. Finally, training will be provided at LGA levels to ensure safe sample collection, packaging, and transportation.

project_name: Enhance the resilience of the vulnerable Gaza Population through WASH Support to Fragile and under-served Communities to mitigate the impact of COVID-19
project_objective:

Furthermore, this project is aligned to the WASH cluster HRP objective 2: Ensure equitable, affordable, and sustainable safely managed access to sufficient WASH services for the most vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation in Gaza and the West Bank and objective 3: Strengthen WASH preparedness and response capacity to the most vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation in Gaza and the West Bank, to reduce threats and cope with emergencies and shocks.
The project’s overall objective is to contribute to strengthening the capacity of essential WASH services for the vulnerable population threatened by the ongoing Covid-19 crisis in the Gaza Strip, while the specific objective of the project is: To provide an appropriate, integrated WASH response for vulnerable communities and households affected by the ongoing Covid-19 crisis including women, children, girls and boys in fragile and critically under-served communities. The objectives are in line with the needs identified in the humanitarian need overview (HNO) and Oxfam’s recent assessments.
