Total estimated number of people the organization reached in 2020 = 49,145

UNRWA in Syria continues to support the education of Palestine refugee students despite the conflict and
displacement. In responding to the COVID-19 crisis, the Agency relied on its Education in Emergencies (EiE) approach, reconceptualised in the following areas:
Continuity of Learning, Psychosocial Support (PSS),  Security and Safety, and Health and Hygiene issues. Below is a description of the key elements of the response in Syria for 2021:

1) Continuity of Learning:

Students and Installations 
In 2021, UNRWA will continue to deliver basic, quality and inclusive education to almost 51,000 Palestine refugees through 102 schools managed by the Agency across Syria, of which 39 are running on a second shift in buildings on loan from the Ministry of Education, to compensate for UNRWA schools that have been destroyed or severely damaged by the conflict. UNRWA will cover the cost of additional temporary staff hired to address the increasing needs that have arisen due to the compounded crises.

Nature of Learning
Back-to-school kits and stationery will be procured and provided to students at the beginning of the academic year to alleviate some of the economic burden faced by parents. Summer learning activities will also be sustained. These interventions have become an integral part of UNRWA’s EiE modality, delivering academic, extracurricular and psychosocial support activities to students during the summer months. Conducting summer learning will be contingent on the COVID-19 situation in the country during summer 2021. In addition, support classes will be organized for 9th Grade students. While schools in Syria re-opened on 13 September 2020 for in-person education, the growing number of COVID-19 confirmed cases amongst education staff and students across the country over the last quarter of 2020 highlights the challenges of preventing transmission in schools. During emergency situations (including pandemics), Palestine refugee children may be unable to access their regular schools, leading to a risk of interruption of their education. UNRWA has developed a self-learning programme to provide UNRWA students with access to age-appropriate, relevant, and safe self-learning material that is in line with UN values and humanitarian principles. The Agency has recently launched a Digital Learning Platform  to enhance this process and materials for the platform are being developed for UNRWA students from Grades 1 to 9 in Syria.

2) Hygiene and Physical Safety:
A number of training sessions, incorporating COVID-19 prevention measures, will be conducted for teachers and principals on topics such as Gender Based Violence (GBV), Child Protection, and Addressing Violence against Children (AVAC). Similar training sessions will be delivered to parents through parent-teacher associations (PTAs), which will continue to play a pivotal role in developing a holistic approach to education for Palestine refugees. Reusable masks will be procured and distributed to students and teachers. In addition, disinfectants and sanitizers will be provided to schools to ensure proper hygiene practices are in place.

3) Psychosocial Support:
UNRWA will also continue to provide psychosocial support to address the additional stress created by the COVID-19 pandemic, by deploying psychosocial counsellors in all of its schools with the aim of providing individual and group counselling and support to students and teachers, in addition to the provision of recreational activities, if the context allows. Psychosocial support and awareness raising sessions on COVID-19 will also be delivered in classrooms and/ or through remote modalities.

project_name: Provision of primary health care services for vulnerable children and women in Syria
project_objective:
Due to the ongoing 10-year crisis, movement and the corrosion of public services and infrastructure, there is increased risk of disease outbreaks. More than half the population now lives in poverty, with around 8 million people becoming poor since the beginning of the war  https://unstats.un.org/unsd/publications/statistical-yearbook
. The basic health status of women and children in Syria remains precarious, with a fragile health sector. This situation has been exacerbated by the disruptions to allied sectors, such as food security, water, sanitation and hygiene which have further compounded the prevailing vulnerabilities. The COVID-19 pandemic also contributed to the increased poverty and vulnerability of children and women due to the lock-down and interrupted social services. The economic crisis and devaluation of the local currency also added to the vulnerability of Syrian children and women who are not able to pay for the essential health and nutrition services. This proposal from UNICEF aims to support the provision of basic lifesaving curative, preventive and promotional health services, while enhancing early recovery and resilience of the sector by contributing to strengthening the service delivery partners, community systems through supporting local NGOs and community volunteers, and support health system strengthening interventions including information system for primary health care and immunization. The project is also conceived with a view to promoting the complementarity of the contributions of other sections within UNICEF (Nutrition, WASH, Education and Child protection) and other key sector partners (UN agencies, NGOs etc).
More than 5 million women and children will directly benefit from the package of services, focusing on the highest severity areas in all governorates of Syria as defined by the health cluster. Programme effectiveness shall be enhanced by applying a conflict and risk informed lens to planned interventions, and the promotion of the participation of affected populations. The accountability towards affected population (APP) is integrated throughout the programme cycle.
UNICEF will work in 262 sub districts, 163 are with severity scale 3 or higher and 99 are in lower severity scale but they are hosting IDPs and they need to be supported for the essential maternal and child health services including immunization. 
The support to primary health care and immunization programme will strongly support resilience through building strong health information system, building strong cold chain system for vaccines allover the country, building national capacity on vaccine management and quality vaccination services. In addition to the rehabilitation of health facilities as needed.

project_name: Improve equitable access to preventive and curative nutrition services for under five years children and pregnant and lactating women in Syria.
project_objective:
Under the Nutrition sector framework, this project aims to provide preventive and curative nutrition services for under five years children and pregnant and lactating women in Syria with a special focus in high severity areas and IDPs camps inside Syria. UNICEF will work in 247 sub districts, out of which 243 are with severity scale 3 or higher. The services will be delivered through fixed and mobile teams run by our implementing partners (IPs) which include Local and International NGO’s and Government health directorates. UNICEF will provide IPs with essential lifesaving nutrition supplies to treat and prevent malnutrition and prevent deaths among vulnerable children and women especially during the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic and the devaluation of local and household economy. Nutrition services will also focus on raising awareness among vulnerable mothers and caregivers on prevention of malnutrition, breast feeding and improving Infant Young Child Feeding practices. The project will also provide capacity building for health staff and community volunteers to ensure quality service delivery. At the national level support will focus on strengthening the system to provide services through producing strategic documents (Nutrition Strategy, IYCF guidelines) and evidence generation to inform programming (e.g. Nutrition surveillance, Iodine deficiency survey among school children
6-12 years).
To address accountability to affected populations the project will establish a face to face key informants’ interviews using mentors to assess needs, satisfaction and gaps in the nutrition services among affected population. The project will also arrange for virtual meetings with the mothers of children of the age 0-5 years to ensure taking their opinions and views on the nutrition services provided to them. Mothers will be trained on MUAC screening and identification of acute malnutrition and how, where and when to refer their children to care.

project_name: Emergency protection initiative for the most vulnerable returnees and IDPs of Rural Aleppo
project_objective:
The action proposed by AVSI is focusing on measures capable of coping with the situation of displacement and spontaneous return in South-Rural Aleppo, Zarbah district, in Syria caused by exposure to conflict. The intervention is in line with HRP objective one in providing life-sustaining humanitarian assistance to the most vulnerable people and objective two in enchanting the prevention and mitigation of protection risks. 
With this proposal, AVSI is seeking the protection of civilians through a comprehensive response based on the specific needs in the area, on the lessons learned of previous actions and benefitting also from the coordination and complementarity with existing projects put in place by the partners in the same geographical area. The project wants to answers to the basic needs of the population through an unconditional cash assistance in order to ensure that the families will be able to cope with their basic needs after the return, to support families they have lost their income and at great risk of negative coping mechanism, to support IDPs and separated members of HH, to provide an opportunity to cover protection gaps in age-gender-disability sensitive households, to support GBV cases, etc. . In collaboration with Syrian Commission for Family and Population Affairs (SCFPA), the cash assistance will be completed by GBV actions, PSS activities, safe identification and referral and mine awareness. All activities will be implemented following Covid-19 prevention measures. This intervention has been planned with the active participation of the target community through an assessment conducted in January 2021. The action will be directly managed and implemented in partnership with the Ministry of Social Affairs and Syrian Commission for Family and Population Affairs (SCFPA), the latter already guaranteeing to AVSI the access to the area.

project_name: Promoting access to food and livelihood opportunities for IDPs, returnees and vulnerable households in Syria
project_objective:
The aim of the project is to support self-resilience of HHs in Rural Damascus, Hama, Homs, Aleppo and Dar'a through distribution of food rations, agro-kits and poultry kits as well as organization of market driven income-generating activities. The Project will strengthen resilience of the affected HHS and reduce the dependency on aid of the most vulnerable Syrian population living in the proposed governorates. The project will contribute to the Sector Objective 2 “Support self-reliance of affected households by protecting and building productive assets and restoring or creating income generating opportunities to save and sustain lives” in order to reach 1.2 million HHs in 2021. 
To decrease the dependency on food assistance and to promote the self-resilience and consequently the dignity of beneficiaries, the project is aiming to support 15,000 HHs. The main modality of implementation will be through distribution of in-kind assistance, while whenever possible this modality will be changed with restricted vouchers or cash-based assistance. 
Support to small scale food production will be done through provision of agricultural inputs, poultry kits or food rations. Agricultural inputs will be delivered to those families who have an access to their land, ensuring that lands are free of UXOs, while in the areas still UXOs affected or for the families who do not possess land, poultry kits will be delivered. Food rations or food vouchers will be provided to the most vulnerable individuals that do not have access to a land and/or could not be involved into the rehabilitation of the agricultural or livestock activities. Market driven income-generating activities (IGAs) will target mostly women with proven interest in starting an IGA. The trainings will be organized for selected beneficiaries in cooperation with specialized institutions, the participants who attended the whole
training and passed the final exam will receive a small grant to start their own production.
In the process of beneficiary’s selection specific focus will be on returnees and local population (host communities). Special attention will be given to female headed HHs, elderly, HHs with People with Disabilities, unaccompanied children and to those groups who have only limited access to income to cover the family food needs and are forced to adopt negative copying mechanisms, unskilled or seasonal workers for instance. 
During the preparation and implementation of the activities, COOPI will ensure the coordination with local authorities and robust participation of the communities giving them a voice to express desired modalities of implementation (the design of similar projects have been already successfully tested by COOPI in Dar’a and Nashabiyeh). Coordination will be ensured with the FSA Sector and its members but also with international and national actors active in the same villages in order to harmonized the response, avoid overlapping and to promote synergies. Synergies will also be promoted by COOPI through other projects submitted to HRP 2021 taking place in the governorates of this project.

project_name: WASH integrated emergency response for vulnerable communities in newly accessible and underserved areas in Aleppo and Deir-Ez-Zor.
project_objective: WWGVC plans to intervene in Aleppo and Deir-Ez-Zor governorates restoring community services in newly accessible and underserved areas. A set of interventions identified is to provide sufficient access to safe water to 65,600 people in need, allowing communities to cope with the expected increasing number of returnees. Water systems are out of service or partially functioning and unable to guarantee sufficient standards. The light rehabilitation of 5 pumping stations and sections of damaged water networks will ensure access to water to host communities and possible newcomers. Whereas the light rehabilitation of 5 learning centers/schools and 27 WASH facilities will facilitate safe and inclusive access to schools. Hard component activities will be integrated with awareness campaigns on hygiene promotion (HP) and Covid-19 preparedness and prevention for the most vulnerable communities. The action also includes capacity building to technical staff of the Water Board (WB).

project_name: Management and Monitoring of Emergency Response, and Enhancing Safety and Security
project_objective:
Management, coordination and monitoring of activities, and deployment of professional staff are essential for UNRWA to deliver timely and effective humanitarian assistance, to ensure efficient coordination with relevant stakeholders and to enhance advocacy on behalf of Palestine refugees. 

While the vast majority of posts needed to deliver the mandate of the Agency in Syria will continue to be filled by Palestine refugees and Syrian nationals, UNRWA will maintain some international capacity, particularly specialist staff in the fields of humanitarian response, monitoring and evaluation, and grants management. 

UNRWA will continue to conduct safety and security trainings for its staff across Syria, including on COVID-19 safety measures. UNRWA has made significant investments in the safety and security of its staff, assets and facilities  despite financial challenges. In 2021, the Agency will continue to focus on security personnel staffing costs, the procurement of communication devices such as VHF radios, as well as the procurement of PPE for security staff in response to the COVID-19 pandemic. These investments will enable UNRWA to facilitate and provide security support for over 600 field missions in 2021 in a medium to high risk security environment, and to conduct security risk assessments of its installations. 

In order to ensure that UNRWA facilities are compliant with minimum operating security standards, the Agency will conduct security risk assessments on targeted facilities and will carry out necessary physical enhancement works to ensure a safe and secure environment for its staff and beneficiaries accessing assistance and services. In addition, UNRWA plans to install a closed circuit television (CCTV) room and Internet Protocol (IP) surveillance cameras at its offices in Damascus and Central areas. UNRWA will continue to train its staff in Safe and Security Approaches to Field Environment (SSAFE) and will also provide fire safety trainings. Finally, through its commitment to ensuring gender considerations in security management, and recognizing that women are more exposed to risks of GBV, UNRWA in Syria will maintain a Women’s Security Awareness Training (WSAT) programme for UNRWA personnel.

Finally, under this project, UNRWA will also sustain the operational needs of support departments, including HR, Administration, Procurement and Logistics. UNRWA has also included a budget for the minor repair and maintenance of UNRWA facilities to ensure safe and functional delivery of services for both beneficiaries and staff.

project_name: Protection services and interventions for Palestine Refugees in Syria
project_objective:
In 2021, UNRWA will continue to provide critical protection assistance to Palestine refugees. It is anticipated that the vulnerabilities of Palestine refugee will further increase due to COVID-19 and the current economic situation.  
The Agency will seek to improve the protection of Palestine refugees in Syria through various interventions:
-	Mainstreaming protection within UNRWA services will remain a priority. Corresponding to needs, protection training, including on disability inclusion, GBV, PSEA, addressing violence against children, will be delivered to a wide range of staff and volunteers. 
-	Dedicated programmatic responses will be implemented through regular service-delivery and stand-alone initiatives to support the needs of vulnerable populations including those related to psychosocial distress. Areas most affected by conflict-related violence as well as displaced and returning populations will be prioritized.
-	Legal support services will be offered while prioritising women and children experiencing GBV by assisting them in obtaining civil documentation and referrals to external partners. 
-	Mine risk awareness campaigns will continue throughout the country targeting students and other community members, with a specific focus on areas of spontaneous returns. 
-	Protection monitoring, reporting and advocacy will continue to be prioritised through the participation of UNRWA in global protection mechanisms and the international human rights system (IHRS). This will be done through the interaction with relevant stakeholders, including the protection sector of the Humanitarian Country Team (HCT) in Syria. In parallel, UNRWA will focus specifically on monitoring the return of Palestine refugees displaced within and outside Syria.
In a cross-cutting approach, UNRWA will continue to strengthen Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) by systematically increasing the participation of Palestine refugees in programme identification, design, delivery and lesson learning. Feedback will be sought on programme quality and to assess Palestine refugees’ satisfaction with the services provided. This will help UNRWA to implement programmes that are of higher quality, with greater and more sustainable impact.

project_name: Enhancing Coordination of Humanitarian International NGOs (CHINGO)
project_objective:
The INGOs forum in Cameroon (CHINGO) was established in June 2019 with the objective to enhance collaboration and coordination between INGOs and between INGOs and external stakeholders (line ministries, UN agencies, donors, civil society organizations) engaged in the humanitarian response to populations affected by the three on-going crises in Cameroon.
Under the strategic guidance of its Steering Committee and the leadership of its coordinator, the INGO forum will specifically aim at enhancing information-sharing between INGOs, notably to build common positions, improving representation of INGOs and joint advocacy and contributing to the overall humanitarian coordination architecture. The project includes various services to INGOs, including trainings for INGOs and partners’ staff, sharing of experience and lessons learnt, and facilitation and support on issues of common interest. CHINGO also engages with external stakeholders and provides a collective voice for INGOs as well as an entry point for requests to INGOs. Advocacy and communication activities aim to support better understanding of the assistance provided by INGOs in Cameroon, identify and propose solutions to challenges faced by INGOs in humanitarian operations and increase the visibility of the crises in Cameroon with the overall objective to better respond to humanitarian needs of populations affected by displacement.

project_name: Restoring disrupted livelihoods for Palestine Refugees in Syria
project_objective:
UNRWA Technical and Vocational Education and Training Programme (TVET) will continue to provide short-term courses at Damascus Training Center in addition to Homs, Aleppo, Daraa and Lattakia training centers, based on availability of funds. As demand for TVET services grows, the Agency will continue its efforts to better link students with the job market in an effort to increase employability rates of graduates.
Building on 2020 learning and good practices in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the courses will be delivered through a mixed-modality (in-class or online) or remotely (online) to avoid overcrowding in classrooms. Self-learning resources will be made available to students. Hygiene measures and physical distancing will be ensured across all TVET premises. 
Finally, depending on the availability of funds, UNRWA will explore the feasibility of conducting small-scale cash-for-work initiatives in 2021 mainly focusing on job placements supporting works in camps and Palestine refugee gatherings.

project_name: Essential healthcare support for the vulnerable Rohingya refugees and host communities in Cox’s Bazar
project_objective: Save the Children (SC) will deliver comprehensive healthcare services over a 12-month period in 8 camps of Ukhia and Teknaf, Cox’s Bazar to ensure that Rohingya refugees and host communities have access to essential primary healthcare services through health posts (HPs) and primary healthcare center (PHCC), including SRHR, nutrition, MHPSS, and WASH services in line with the Ministry of Health and Health Sector recommended minimum package of essential health services. In responding to COVID-19, SC will also provide quality healthcare to moderate to severe cases of COVID-19 through continuing Severe Acute Respiratory Infection Isolation and Treatment Centre (SARI ITC), and CBS in line with sectoral guidelines for COVID-19 patients in the communities. All health facilities are staffed by doctors, midwives, MHPSS workers, paramedics, clinic aides, maternal child health, IYCF-E counsellors and nutrition promoters and community health workers (CHWs). Clinical services will be complemented with a programme of strengthened health promotion communications and community engagement to encourage timely access to healthcare and address existing fears around access. This will include the promotion of COVID-19 preventive measures and the identification and referral of suspected COVID-19 cases to appropriate health facilities. SC will procure personal protective equipment (PPE), pharmaceuticals, medical supplies, equipment and non-medical supplies. All staff and volunteers will be trained and re-trained on child protection basic concepts, child safeguarding, child rights, and confidentiality and on how to be child/adolescent-friendly providers. SC will strengthen community outreach activities for identification of suspected COVID-19 cases, referrals to the appropriate health facilities, and promotion of COVID-19 preventive measures with key health messages. The project will cover all operational services for 8 health posts, 1 primary healthcare center (PHCC), 1 severe acute respiratory infection isolation and treatment center (SARI ITC) and community-based surveillance (CBS) to ensure uninterrupted healthcare services during multiple outbreaks including COVID-19 and disasters. SC will engage PHD as a local partner to localize the interventions. The core scope of work includes support to two health posts in Ukhia with related healthcare services. PSS services will be provided under the technical guidance and supervision of SC. As a partner, PHD will be responsible for field level operations, financial management and regular reporting. SC will strengthen the Upazila Health Complexes (UHCs) and Community Clinics (CCs) in Teknaf to minimize the adverse impacts of COVID-19. SC will expand IPC measures as stated in National Guideline for Health Care Provider On Infection Prevention and Control of COVID-19 pandemic in Healthcare Setting and support health facility to select one focal point following ‘National Preparedness and Response Plan for COVID-19’ to ensure IPC protocols are in place and implemented according to the set plan.

project_name: Preventing and responding to child protection concerns of affected boys, girls and their families in Cox's Bazar
project_objective: Save the Children (SC) will operate an integrated child protection programme in Cox’s Bazar and aim at strengthening protective factors and reducing risk factors at every level of the socio-ecological framework. In 2021, through partnership with 3 local NGOs, SC will maintain critical interventions and services including case management, adolescents and PSS programming, with a focus on protecting the most vulnerable children, including UASC, child headed households, married and house bound girls and children with disabilities. Interventions will seek to address ongoing risks posed by COVID-19 and target the most vulnerable boys, girls and their families based on evidence and input from affected communities. Child participation, eliciting the views of boys and girls across age, ability and protection concern will be an integral part of designing, implementing and monitoring of programme components. SC will also continue to enhance capacity of parents and caregivers on positive parenting as well as strengthening the community based child protection mechanism for creating an enabling and protective environment for children in both camps and host communities. Through maintaining and establishing services in both refugee camps and host communities, critical gaps in service delivery will be addressed, and social cohesion strengthened, by targeting inequity of access to services which is a driver of conflict.  In 2021, SC will place a greater emphasis on supporting the host communities and especially focus on addressing the worst forms of child labor and supporting indigenous children. Moreover, SC will focus on strengthening the child protection systems that support a child. This will include partnerships in an effort to strengthen technical capacity, and work closely and collectively with duty bearers and service providers in both camps and host communities to see children's rights realized. Multiple accountability mechanisms will be applied to ensure that feedback is actively collected, whilst ensuring the safety and dignity of the beneficiaries.

project_name: Assistance en Eau, Hygiène et Assainissement (EHA) aux populations affectées par la crise humanitaire causée par les conflits dans les régions du Centre Nord et du Sahel au Burkina Faso
project_objective:
Les populations de la région du Centre-Nord sont sévèrement affectées par la détérioration de la situation sécuritaire liée à la présence des Groupes d’opposition armés (GOA) entrainant des mouvements de populations continus. Plus de 74% des personnes déplacées sont installées dans les régions du Centre Nord et du Sahel (766 836 IDPs) majoritairement dans des familles d´accueil. Ces zones sont déjà fragilisées par une insuffisance des ressources naturelles et une situation de crise alimentaire chronique, accroissant ainsi le risque des maladies hydriques et de conflits liés à l’accès aux pâturages et à la gestion des points d’eau. Oxfam et ses partenaires l’Alliance Technique d’Assistance au Développement (ATAD), l’Association pour le Gestion de l’Environnement et le Développement (AGED) mènent une réponse d´urgence multisectorielle dans les régions du Centre-Nord et du Sahel depuis décembre 2018. Depuis lors, les actions menées par les équipes sur place couplées à des analyses de données permettent de réaliser une évaluation approfondie des besoins des populations, en incluant une dimension genre.
Outre les multitudes de crises (le défi terroriste, les exactions et massacres de populations civiles, la crise humanitaire qui touche plus de deux 2,5 millions personnes dont plus de 1 030 000 déplacés, et les nombreux conflits sociaux dans les administrations publiques), le Burkina fait face au péril de la pandémie du COVID-19 depuis mars 2020. 
La situation dans les régions du Centre Nord et Sahel, théâtre d’importants mouvements de populations, favorise la propagation rapide de l’épidémie car le déplacement interne de populations augmente le risque d'infection de la population en raison de la densité et des mauvaises conditions de vie, de l’incapacité à garder la distance physique. Les niveaux d'assainissement et d'accès à l'eau potable sont très faibles, ce qui constitue un facteur aggravant dans la transmission des maladies 

En 2021, sur la base de ces évaluations OXFAM et ses partenaires entendent continuer leurs actions dans ces deux zones à travers le projet intitulé « Assistance en Eau, Hygiène et Assainissement (EHA) aux populations affectées par la crise humanitaire causée par les conflits dans les régions du Centre Nord et du Sahel au Burkina Faso». Ce projet est une réponse humanitaire aux besoins des populations affectées par la crise sécuritaire qui vise à assurer une couverture des besoins urgents et prioritaires en eau, assainissement et hygiène des populations déplacées et des communautés hôtes.
Le projet est basé sur les principes et normes humanitaires (CHS, SPHERES), et intégrera les aspects suivants :
Protection: Une analyse des pouvoirs et une analyse des risques sera réalisée afin d’identifier les menaces pour les différents groupes vulnérables (filles, femmes, jeunes, personnes handicapées et vivant avec le VIH/SIDA) parmi les populations IDPs et hôtes vulnérables. Les analyses de risques seront réalisées de façon participative afin d’assurer l’appropriation et l’autonomisation progressive des populations IDPs et hôtes.
Nexus : Le projet est aligné avec le triple Nexus (humanitaire – développement – paix) car Oxfam intègre cela dans sa stratégie. Il créera ainsi des liens avec les actions de relèvement et de développement en cours dans les régions ciblées, notamment entre les aspects de développement du leadership humanitaire local et la gouvernance locale. Par ailleurs, Oxfam associe la question de la consolidation de la paix qui sera un pilier de la stratégie de réponse d´urgence pour 2021. Cet aspect permettra sur le long terme, de promouvoir un environnement favorable à la pacification au Burkina Faso.

project_name: Strengthening Protection Interventions in Support of the Most Vulnerable in Gaza
project_objective:
The global outbreak of COVID-19 is putting further pressure to the lives of people in Gaza who have already been facing years of humanitarian crisis under the on-going blockade, coupled with the impact of recurrent hostilities and deteriorating socio-economic situation in Gaza. The restrictions on daily life activities as a result of the measures enforced by the local authority to prevent the spread of the virus are having severe impacts on lives and livelihoods, leading to exacerbated pre-existing protection risks and negative coping mechanisms. In particular, these risks are intertwined with heightened MHPSS needs, the potential for an increase in GBV and SEA, and a lack of access to legal support by vulnerable women amidst sporadic closures of the courts. 
In order to mitigate these risks, UNRWA proposes to:
a)	conduct protection training to 200 staff members focusing on child protection, protection of people with disabilities, and protection of the survivors of gender-based violence (GBV) to ensure the protection mainstreaming incorporating protection principles and promoting meaning access, safety and dignity in all UNRWA services.
b)	organize a campaign to better inform the available services and access to UNRWA’s internal MHPSS services as well as external specialized MHPSS services for 8,000 Palestine refugees
c)	organize a multifaceted campaign to employ the recommendations outlined in the IASC’s Interim Technical Note on the prevention of SEA amidst COVID-19 targeting 150 staff for ToT and 1,000 people in the community. These include the reduction of risks, prevention, strengthening safe and accessible reporting channels, coordination and providing support and protection.  
d)	support the provision of legal services as well as other social interventions to approximately 1,000 Palestine refugee women in partnership with community based Women Programme Centres (WPCs) located across the Gaza Strip
e)	engage in a minimum of 25 advocacy initiatives to the international community.

project_name: Emergency Cash for Work in Gaza
project_objective: Access to food in Gaza remains a challenge for a majority of refugees struggling with deteriorating socio-economic condition compounded with the COVID-19 emergency. Soaring rates of unemployment and limited income are key drivers to poverty and food insecurity among the population. Through the Cash for Work intervention, UNRWA aims to support Palestine refugees in Gaza coping with protracted threats and shocks, and mitigate food insecurity through offering short term employment opportunities to approximately 14,000 poor Palestine refugees. These will be equal to more than 1,430,000 work days, and will inject over US$ 17.6 million into households, generating almost 5,000 full time job equivalents (FTEs). The short term job opportunities will include more than 10,000 unskilled positions, more than 3,800 skilled positions and around 170 professional positions. Amidst COVID-19 emergency, UNRWA developed a Standard Operation Procedures to ensure that beneficiaries under cash for work programming have access to enhanced occupational health and safety norms for the work they agree to undertake. It identifies the functions and manner in which the Cash for Work modality can be deployed for UNRWA activities in a pandemic environment safely and in a dignified manner in order to continue providing income generation opportunities to refugees to achieve livelihood objectives.

project_name: Mitigate flooding risks and improve access to hygiene in vulnerable communities in Gaza Strip.
project_objective:
The project has two main components: 
1)	Strengthening of WASH services for vulnerable households in North Gaza.   This intervention is in line with WASH Cluster objective 2 “to ensure equitable, affordable, and sustainable safely managed access to sufficient WASH services for the most vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation in Gaza.
2)	Flood mitigation interventions at community infrastructures level in Gaza.  This activity is in line with Objective 3 “to strengthen WASH preparedness and response capacity to the most vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation in Gaza to reduce threats and cope with emergencies and shocks”.  
In North Gaza the project will be implemented in partnership with Beit Lahia Development Association (BLDA). The household component of the project aims to improve the hygiene condition of the vulnerable families through rehabilitation and upgrading of WASH facilities including improving the water storage capacity for 240 HHs (Alsyafa, Al Amal, Al shayma ,Al Salateen and Izbit biet Hanoun), to improve the HHs hygiene knowledge and practices and with a distribution of  family hygiene kits.  Moreover, SC partner will distribute 240 family hygiene kits to the target families with the most vulnerable girls, boys, women, men, elders and people with disabilities. SC in coordination with the partner will develop hygiene awareness messages in coordination with the WASH cluster. The project partner will deliver the awareness messages through home visits in parallel with the distribution of the hygiene kits. 
The project will select the beneficiaries in Gaza based on their vulnerability through socioeconomic and protection assessment conducted through home visits. Beneficiary selection will prioritize vulnerable groups such as female-headed households, HHs with malnourished children and HHs with dependent(s) suffering from chronic disease, injury or disability, children suffering from multiple child protection concerns and those receiving case management services.  
SC will consult the Community Protection Committees (CPCs) and youth group in the selection of the beneficiaries and the planned working modalities with the targeted HHs.
To mitigate the flooding risk in critical flooding areas, SC already coordinated with Costal Municipality Water Utility (CMWU) and PWA to identify the needs of the required intervention. SC will prepare the engineering design in close coordination with CMWU for the construction of new storm water pipeline in Beit Hanoun to install 550 m of storm water pipeline and rehabilitate the infiltration basin in Mashro’ Biet lahia. The intervention will help approximately 10,000 people in the most vulnerable group to enhance their ability to survive, prevent or alleviate the risk of deteriorating their health and dignity. 
To ensure full integration with other WASH actors, SCI will closely coordinate with the WASH cluster and Hygiene Working Group in designing the awareness messages focusing on hygiene and flooding management at the HHs level to strengthen their mitigation abilities to these kinds of risks.
To ensure no-harm, SCI will conduct strong community engagement to ensure regular exchange of information, consultation on priorities and preferences and transparency for preventing tensions amongst community members. The overall project implementation will be adapted to the recent COVID-19 national and international guidelines to minimize the risk of transmission. SCI commits to Do No Harm through ensuring all areas of SCI’s work are designed and resourced appropriately to minimise the opportunities for perpetrators to act exploitatively and to maximise the safety of those engaging with our programming and otherwise involved with SCI.

project_name: Strengthening Community-Based Protection for Refugees and Host Communities in Cox’s Bazar
project_objective:
IRC seeks to continue its implementation of  a Protection and Rule of Law Project that encompasses, Systematic Protection Monitoring, Legal assistance, Community Based Protection and Protection Mainstreaming. The modality of implementation will be a hybrid of direct implementation and through its Partner BLAST. 

IRC will identify community level protection risks and individual protection needs for direct intervention, referral, and specialized services in five camps (1E. 1W, 15, 16, 21). Using existing community structures and coordination with other humanitarian actors, the IRC will engage communities to identify the protection risks of greatest concern in the community exploring the causes, consequences and reflecting on existing prevention and response strategies.  IRC/ Partner Legal Officers will conduct gender sensitive mediation services, provide mediation services to address non-criminal cases within the camps at IRC legal hubs/appropriate community structures in a manner consistent with fairness, equality and accessible to women.  

IRC in Partnership with BLAST will engage in quality awareness raising on access to justice procedures, avenues for alternative dispute resolution and access informal/formal justice mechanisms. In addition, build capacity of key community members such as Maji, Justice Committees on conflict resolution. Within the Host community, IRC will implement through BLAST. IRC activities will be implemented through a protection mainstreaming lens, promoting safety, dignity, and meaningful access, participation of Women, girls and Elderly, and empowerment of beneficiaries. 

IRC will implement a solid community feedback mechanism in both Host and refugee community. IRC will ensure the project is adopted to observe COVID-19 preventive measures. In it design and Implementation, the Project will consider DRR and environmental aspects in the design and programming such action would include Continuous assessments of risks associated with disaster and COVID-19. All staff involved in the project implementation will be periodically trained on PSEA and conform to the guidelines and Policy on Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse.

project_name: Children and youth in Rohingya and host community are safe in their homes and communities and receive gender-sensitive support when they experience harm, they are socially and economically empowered and engaged in building peace and social cohesion.
project_objective: IRC Bangladesh is implementing its integrated child protection and youth development program since the beginning of the Rohinga Influx. The program covers both camp and host community (1E, 1W, 5, 8E, 15, 22, 23 and 25 and all 11 unions in Tecknaf and Ukhiya). Our interventions are designed to prevent and respond to sexual abuse and exploitation of children and adolescents with case management services, psychosocial support, economic empowerment, community-based protection mechanism and CSO capacity development. For case management IRC has trained case worker (60% female) who are professionally skilled in addressing diversity and inclusion in service delivery. Structured Safe Healing and Learning Spaces (SHLS) provided for psychosocial support to children age 6-10 year and adolescent age 11-19 years. Caregivers are also supported with structured positive parenting curriculum to support children recovering distress situation. Adolescent empowerment program includes both social and economic skills development opportunity for adolescent achieving positive coping mechanism and building social cohesion. The environment, DRR and COVID risk and awareness is at the center of program content development and delivery.  IRC has its’ adapted module ready and tasted to implement in a situation of pandemic. Local partners and CSOs are supported with capacity development initiative to better work with children and youth. IRC’s integrated program approach (protection, GBV and health) ensure comprehensive services to the clients, especially to the SGBV survivors. External coordination and representation in sub-sector and task forces is our key priority for sustainable changes. Client centered complaint mechanism is established to do no harm (complaint box, hotline, child friendly reporting) and clients are part of project design and evaluation. Direct beneficiaries are children and young people who are at most risk of abuse and exploitation age 10-24 years with equal representation of boys and girls including 7% children and young people with disability.

project_name: Protecting and responding to women and girls against the consequences of GBV by empowering  them and engaging men and boys as allies
project_objective:
The project will be operating in IRC’s 5 existing WGSS’s known as Integrated Women’s Center (IWC) and 2 BEmONC centers to ensure women and girls are protected from and treated for the consequences of GBV and have access to comprehensive, quality GBV response and prevention services in a safe, dignified and confidential manner. All activities are implemented in close consultation with women and girls, supported by strong community engagement through community volunteers. 
IRC will provide GBV case-management including PSS and referral service as lifesaving support to GBV survivors. Besides that, IRC will train service providers to strengthen adherence to regularly updated, confidential and timely interagency referral systems. IRC will also continue to provide integrated SRH services in the IWCs including FP and voluntary contraception; safe MR including post abortion care; and management of STIs and CMR. In addition, IRC will have a resident legal officer who will provide legal counselling to GBV survivors.  

IRC will deliver prevention and empowerment activities to reduce acceptance and prevalence of GBV through awareness raising; listening sessions; community-led activism; and dialogue sessions with community leaders using the SASA! model to address GBV-driving norms. EMAP program which works constructively with men to examine the gendered impact of conflict and power dynamics in household will be introduced. Women and girls will regularly benefit from life skills and empowerment activities. Girl Shine curriculum will be used to provide adolescent girls with skills and knowledge. EA$E (Economic and Social Empowerment) will be implemented to challenge gender norms about financial decision making. 

IRC will conduct safety audits which will document protection risks informing advocacy with community leaders and other stakeholders. IRC will set up GBVIMS to harmonize data collection, data storage and analysis, safe and ethical sharing of reported GBV incident data.

project_name: Gender-based Violence (GBV) Prevention and Response for Conflict-Affected Population in South Sudan
project_objective:
The GBV prevention and response program of International Medical Corps (IMC) in South Sudan aims to empower communities and build resilience through promoting social and behavioural change to address the root causes of GBV in the country. Leveraging on the vast experiences, gains and successes of IMC in implementing GBV prevention and response interventions through FCDO-HARISS program, this project will be continued to implement in the states of Western Bahr el Ghazal (Wau IDP Camp and County), Upper Nile (Aburoc IDP camp in Fashoda County, and Malakal PoC and County), Unity (Nyal County), and an additional location in Jonglei (Canal/Pigi County). It will directly benefit about 27,146 vulnerable women and girls across the target locations.

One of the project’s key priorities is to further strengthen core services to GBV survivors and vulnerable women and girls in the aforesaid intervention sites. These services include quality case management using a survivor-centered approach, along with psychosocial support to enhance healing and recovery. IMC works to ensure that survivors’ holistic needs are met by providing multi-sectoral services, referring to health centers for clinical management of rape, to legal justice services and to other kinds of support based on the needs of survivors.

IMC, together with the Women Center Management Committees, will further strengthen the existing Women and Girls Friendly Spaces in Aburoc, Malakal, Nyal and Wau, and establish new spaces in Payams/Bomas, which are far from the existing spaces of IMC within the said counties. Empowerment, awareness and recreational activities ranging from age-appropriate PSS, life skills and soft skills activities as well as curriculum-based GBV awareness sessions on GBV core concepts and information on services to integrated awareness sessions are being provided by IMC’s trained GBV staff, in cooperation with the medical and MHPSS teams.

Similarly, temporary spaces/tents will be set-up across in Canal/Pigi County for psychosocial support services, including Psychological First Aid and counseling for vulnerable women and children. Due to volatile security, continued displacement and weather-constrained access of many areas in Canal/Pigi, IMC will form and deploy four Mobile Protection Units, which will be integrated in the Mobile Medical and Nutrition Units of IMC, which will rotate in various remote areas on a pre-determined schedule, providing an integrated health, nutrition and protection services. 

IMC will also scale-up its implementation of holistic community engagement strategies on the promotion of long term positive change in the targeted communities. IMC will use the GBV community mobilization tool called SASA! to help communities rethink about “power” and the positive use of power, and EMAP to ensure men engagement with accountability to prevent GBV. 

Furthermore, IMC aims to support more vulnerable women and GBV survivors with economic empowerment and livelihood activities through building their business skills, helping them to start small scale businesses, and encourage them to save though strengthening of existing and/or forming new Village Savings and Loans Association groups. These are proven effective strategies to fully realize the economic potential of women.

Finally, in order to ensure sustainability of the project and ownership by the community, especially of the WGFSs, IMC will continuously train Women’s and Adolescent Girls’ Committee Members on key Protection Concepts, GBV principles and referrals as well as basic knowledge on MHPSS and PFA. Bi-weekly consultations on specific topics, as well as joint quarterly safety audits, will serve to inform programming, community adaptions of safety measures and support as well as advocacy through coordination fora with key stakeholders to improve the safety measures in the target communities.

project_name: Addressing the Specific Protection Needs of Persons with Disability and vulnerable populations affected by crisis and natural disasters in South Sudan.
project_objective: The project goal is to address identified critical protection concerns and gaps through service delivery (identification and assessment, targeted protection assistance, comprehensive case management (including individualized care plans, accompanied referrals, and advocacy), capacity building and strengthening of community-based protection mechanisms through protection monitoring and increased focus on integrated general protection-MHPSS activities for the most vulnerable population in South Sudan.

project_name: Multi-Sectoral and Rapid Needs Assessment
project_objective: ACTED (REACH) proposes interventions under the Coordination and Common Services (CCS) cluster in-line with the 2020 HRP Sectoral Objective 1; “Strengthen joint needs analysis and strategic response planning for effective and well-coordinated humanitarian action”. The proposed intervention is multi-sector needs assessment (FSNMS+), to inform the 2022 Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) and Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP), building on the successes of the 2020 FSNMS+ collaboration, as well as a set of rapid needs assessments following the identification of areas of acute humanitarian need by using the MSNA, REACH Areas of Knowledge (AoK) data collection, and our Integrated Needs Tracking (INT) system and the Shocks Monitoring Index (SMI). Rapid Needs Assessments will be conducted in these areas, feeding into the wider response through the NAWG, ICCG and NGO forum, strengthening the relationship between reliable data and humanitarian intervention.

project_name: Emergency Food Security and Livelihoods for flood affected Households in Upper Nile
project_objective:
Heavy rain and flooding created historical overflow of the Nile and Sobat Rivers since July 2020, creating the worst flooding in 60 years. The flood destroyed homes and livelihoods of people - damaged settlements, agriculture (crops and cattle), horticulture, and market access which are crucial for peoples’ livelihoods. 40% of the crops and vegetable gardens in GOAL operational areas have been affected and no yield has been harvested during harvesting in 2020. People are also displaced and feared to turn to negative coping mechanisms such as informal borrowing, selling productive assets, and depletion of working capital which might be used to protect from the impact of the disaster. The  flooding crisis came at the back drop of very grim hunger situation in these areas, where already 163,000 were suffering from acute and severe hunger (about 70% of population in Baliet, and 85% in Ulang) (IPC Phases 3, and 4). And 59,462 in IPC4. This situation was further impacted by the current economic downturn and higher inflation rates, in addition to food price hikes exacerbated by the impact of COVID-19 pandemic. The floods severely affected the opportunities for income generating schemes leading to loss of household income and inability to afford food and meet basic needs. Negative coping mechanisms of poor and most affected households have been reported, such as taking fewer meals per day (mostly amongst women and girls), selling assets or borrowing money at high rates to purchase food items, causing unmanageable debt. The flooding also resulted in increased incidences of human diseases such as malaria and acute watery diarrhoea that will affect productivity and deplete savings in the form of increased medical expenses – this will further contribute to household vulnerability and reduce resources available for purchasing food.
GOAL is requesting access to the HRP to cover the immediate needs of 25,800 vulnerable individuals severely  affected by the current flooding of the Sobat river. The individuals targeted will be from existing GOAL beneficiaries who have been flood affected. The flooding affected 68,502 people in Baliet  and Ulang counties. Under the GOAL programme, GOAL has been providing support to build the resilience of 160,000 people in Melut, Baliet, Ulang, Rubkona, and Panyinjar counties since 2016. Prior to the current flooding GOAL program has been implementing various flood risk preparedness and mitigation activities including: dissemination of Early Warning Information, and  development of an early response strategy to mitigate the impact of flooding, stakeholders coordination, formation of flood response committees, identification of most vulnerable people and high-risk areas; distribution of empty sacks to aid dyke construction, dyke construction and monitoring implementation of flood response actions. This request for HRP is sought as the scale and magnitude of the current flooding and livelihood crisis it has compounded requires additional interventions to help vulnerable households meet their immediate needs, reducing the hunger gap and mitigating negative coping mechanisms. This intervention will also provide support to host communities that had to cope with people displaced. 
There is a significant gap in the response to these needs. WFP food distribution covers only 50% of the monthly  households’ food needs. This presents an urgent need for emergency livelihood interventions. The HRP will support households through Cash for Assets to address their immediate food needs, while building assets, such as constructing flood control dikes that will improve their livelihoods, reduce risks and impact of shocks, increase food productivity, and strengthen resilience to natural disasters. The cash for assets will be conditional cash transfer with two components of conditionality – engagement on Cash for Asset, to rebuild community assets, for able bodied households; and mandatory attendance on trainings.

project_name: Provision of Community Based Management of Acute Malnutrition to Under Five Children and Pregnant and Lactating Women in the Former Upper Nile, Warrap, Western and Central Equatoria states in South Sudan
project_objective:
In South Sudan, an estimated 1.9 million people are anticipated to suffer from acute malnutrition in 2021, including 313,391 children (163,913M,149,476F) with severe acute malnutrition (SAM), 1,078,867 children (562,697M, 516,170F) with moderate acute malnutrition (MAM), and 483,383 pregnant and lactating women with acute malnutrition (AM-PLW).124 In addition, some 21,000 out of 286,000 refugees in Maban, Pariang, Juba and Yambio counties are anticipated, and 483,383 pregnant and lactating women with acute malnutrition. IPC Acute Food Insecurity and Acute Malnutrition Analysis for December 2020, an estimated 6.35 million people (52.6% of the population) faced Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse acute food insecurity, of which 2.1 million people faced Emergency (IPC Phase 4) acute food insecurity. During the same period 4,000 people were likely in Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5) acute food insecurity, out of which 11,000 were in Pibor Administration Area, and 13,000 were in Tonj North County in Warrap state. Malnutrition needs are greatest in Jonglei, Upper Nile, Lakes, Warrap and Northern Bahr el Ghazal states where number of acutely malnourished children under-five and PLW caseloads are highest, also with more than 50 per cent of their respective population facing Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse acute food insecurity.

World Vision International(WVI) will implement lifesaving nutrition intervention in Warrap, Central Equatoria, Western Equatoria and Upper Nile.  The proposed nutrition project will be integrated with health, WASH, protection and FSL activities. Through the 2021 HRP, World Vision will prioritize life-saving treatment services targeting children under five years of age, PLW, and chronically ill persons as the most vulnerable groups to acute malnutrition due to their increased biological and physiological needs. Prevention activities that address the immediate and underlying causes of malnutrition will be enhanced. The response will expand on nutrition specific interventions, as well as reinforce integration and linkages with other clusters to address key drivers of malnutrition: food insecurity, sub-optional child care and feeding practices, morbidity, and lack of safe water and sanitation. It will prioritize areas where high prevalence of acute malnutrition, conflict and displacement coexist.

In 2021, WVI  intends to achieve the following nutrition cluster objectives:  1) Reduce morbidity and mortality, as well as suffering from protection threats and incidents, of most vulnerable populations in severity levels 4 and 5; 2) Ensure safe, equitable and dignified access to critical cross-sectoral basic services to enable populations meet their basic needs in locations of severity level 4 and 5; 3) Enable vulnerable people to recover from crisis, seek solutions to displacement, support returns and build resilience to acute shocks and chronic stresses through targeted programming to support coping capacities and livelihoods in prioritized areas.

To materialize the nutrition cluster objectives, WVI  will provide lifesaving nutrition emergency interventions through CMAM and maternal infant and young child nutrition practice by targeting under 5 children and pregnant and lactating women (PLW) in the former Warrap, Upper Nile, Central Equatoria and Western Equatoria states. The proposed emergency nutrition interventions will be implemented in the communities, at the Outpatient Therapeutic Programme (OTP), Targeted Supplementary Therapeutic Programme (TSFP), and Stabilization Centers (SCs). WVI is requesting USD 2,149,701 to reach 51,049 people for this sector.

project_name: Fortalecimiento comunitario y asistencia humanitaria a personas con necesidades específicas en comunidades priorizadas de Venezuela.
project_objective:
El proyecto tiene como objetivos la prevención, mitigación de riesgos y protección de la población en 86 comunidades priorizadas de Venezuela. Se trata de un proyecto multisectorial  que trabajará en función a la respuesta y prevención del COVID-19 de forma transversal en todas las intervenciones, así como la mitigación del riesgo de la violencia de género.

Protección: ACNUR brindará orientación y asistencia psicosocial y material a personas en movilidad y asistencia legal a personas en riesgo de apatridia; apoyará a las estructuras comunitarias en la organización de iniciativas solidarias, las cuales podrán consistir en actividades de promoción de derechos y medios de vida. Se llevarán a cabo capacitaciones sobre identificación de riesgos, enfoque diferencial, rutas de atención, prevención de enfermedades (incluidas enfermedades crónicas, como el VIH/SIDA) y purificación y tratamiento del agua e higiene a las estructuras comunitarias, las cuales diseminarán mensajes claves a sus comunidades. ACNUR apoyará mesas de información móviles sobre temas de protección, manejadas por ONGs. ACNUR también proveerá asistencia material a personas con necesidades específicas, especialmente a la niñez en riesgo y a personas sobrevivientes de violencia de género.

Alojamiento, Enseres y Energía: ACNUR construirá o rehabilitará espacios de alojamiento temporal de personas en movilidad y casas seguras para sobrevivientes de violencia de género; también apoyará la gestión de estos espacios y proveerá enseres a personas con necesidades específicas. ACNUR realizará capacitaciones a las comunidades sobre construcción segura y rehabilitará espacios comunitarios y mejorará viviendas de las familias de acogida de personas en movilidad. Por último, ACNUR distribuirá lámparas y paneles solares, entre otros enseres.

Educación: ACNUR realizará dotaciones de material docente para las escuelas y kits escolares para los alumnos y clases de nivelación para niños, niñas y adolescentes fuera del sistema escolar, de manera que puedan incorporarse a la educación formal o a programas vocacionales para jóvenes.

Agua, Higiene y Saneamiento: las intervenciones en agua, saneamiento e higiene que llevará a cabo el ACNUR y sus socios, se centran en la promoción de derechos y el empoderamiento comunitario; buscando generar soluciones que permitan una cohesión en algunas de nuestras comunidades priorizadas, a través de actividades técnicas y de formación que permitan una operación de Protección con un componente de WaSH conexo y la prevención del COVID-19.

project_name: Provisión de salud primaria y psicosocial en las comunidades de origen, transito y destino en Venezuela
project_objective:
El impacto reciente de la pandemia mundial de COVID-19 exacerbó la situación sanitaria grave del país, ya deteriorada significativamente debido a la crisis socio-económica y humanitaria de Venezuela, debido a una escasez de medicamentos, equipos médicos, personal capacitado, suministro irregular de agua y saneamiento.

La OIM brindará acceso a la atención primaria de salud a través de equipos de salud móviles especializados, mediante el cribado de casos con síntomas sospechosos de COVID y otras enfermedades, así como el control de enfermedades no contagiosas (Diabetes, Hipertensión, Asma y EPOC), tratamientos curativos básicos en el área de medicina general (que aborda principalmente enfermedades transmitidas por vectores como la malaria, pero también enfermedades parasitarias, transmitidas por alimentos, transmitidas por el agua), pediatría, ginecología y primeros auxilios psicológicos.

La OIM organizara campañas de sensibilización y prevención de VIH/SIDA, TB, ITS, y temas ligados a salud sexual y reproductiva en las comunidades priorizadas, en coordinación con las autoridades locales y con las redes de salud. Eso será complementado por la formación y despliegue de brigadas de salud para fortalecer la atención primaria, a través de evaluaciones de salud y tratamiento básico, además de referimiento de casos en comunidades.

Las actividades de apoyo psicosocial fortalecerán esta respuesta: equipos interdisciplinarios serán formados y desplegados en las comunidades identificadas, para brindar apoyo psicosocial, a través de evaluación, orientación, promoción de salud mental, y actividades recreativas para abordar necesidades psicosociales y fortalecer las redes comunitarias en las zonas identificadas.

Los equipos móviles de salud estarán compuestos por profesionales de la salud, de los cuales médicos especialistas en medicina general, pediatría, ginecología, psicología, enfermeras y un/a promotor/a. La IOM formará líderes comunitarios y trabajadores en salud para fortalecer la educación sobre el tema de salud a los beneficiarios tanto en las comunidades como a migrantes en movilidad, y para la identificación y referimiento de casos de salud primaria y psicosocial a servicios existentes. Los TSC servirán como puntos focales para identificar las necesidades y facilitar la prestación de servicios profesionales de las ferias de salud y la realización de sesiones educativas sobre promoción de la salud, prevención de enfermedades y vigilancia de la salud de la comunidad (identificación de personas con enfermedades febriles y/o síntomas respiratorios o cutáneos). Los promotores deben ser miembros de las comunidades seleccionadas para el desarrollo de las jornadas médicas.

La OIM ha identificado una escasez aguda de los medicamentos más esenciales, incluidos analgésicos suaves, antibióticos, antiparasitarios o antidiarreicos y suplementos vitamínicos para mujeres embarazadas y lactantes. El servicio de vigilancia médica incluye la provisión de medicamentos, suplementos nutricionales, derivaciones a hospitales y sensibilización sobre problemas de salud en las comunidades objetivo.

La OIM identificó 8 centros de : 1.Hospital José Gregorio Hérnandez (Amazonas); 2.Hospital Vera Zurita y 3.Caicara del Orinoco, Ambulatorios 4..María Isabel Farias, 5..La Urbana, 6..Sakoroken (Bolívar); 7..Ambulatorio de Guariquen, 8.Hospital Santos Aníbal Dominicci (Sucre), con problemas de corte de energía, ubicados en áreas de intervención de OIM, incapaces de operar equipos vitales de salud como servicios de rayos X y resonancia magnética. Los constantes cortes de energía han provocado también pérdidas de medicamentos y otros productos médicos que necesitan refrigeración.

Se proporcionará generadores y otros insumos de salud (motores para embarcaciones de emergencia existentes, ambulancia terrestre, tanque de agua, generador, tanque contenedor para oxígeno) y PPE a los establecimientos de salud en las comunidades donde operan los líderes comunitarios.

project_name: Mitigar, prevenir y responder a riesgos de protección incrementados debido a la crisis de COVID-19 a través de espacios seguro y campaña de sensibilización
project_objective:
Con la crisis consecuente al brote de Covid-19, los casos de VBG incrementaron progresivamente, debido a la convivencia con el agresor y el círculo de violencia que persiste por mantenerse durante la semana radical de cuarentena. Como parte de su respuesta, con el fin de proveer servicios multisectoriales seguros, de calidad, y que salvan vidas que estén disponibles para las personas vulnerables y las personas en riesgo para abordar las consecuencias y los efectos de la crisis en Venezuela, la OIM construirá y/o instalará tres espacios seguros en comunidades con alta incidencia de incidentes o riesgos de protección, en: San Cristóbal, Maracaibo y Santa Elena de Uairen. Los espacios seguros son lugares estructurados que proveen un punto de entrada seguro y de empoderamiento para mujeres y niñas con el fin de acceder a información, servicios especializados, referencias a servicios de salud y protección, así como otros servicios a determinar, dependiendo de las necesidades manifestadas por las mujeres y niñas de las comunidades seleccionadas. En los espacios seguros las mujeres y niñas pueden buscar, compartir y obtener información, acceder a servicios, espacios de expresión, proteger su seguridad física y emocional, ser referidas a servicios de salud, protección y otros especializados, mejorar su bienestar psicosocial, crear una red segura comunitaria que reducen el aislamiento y refuerza la integración de estas en la vida comunitaria. Servicios en los centros también incluyen la provisión de formaciones profesionales para desarrollar una variedad habilidades específicas como, por ejemplo, la fabricación de jabón, tecnología de la información, sastrería/costura, estética, repostería, etc. Los servicios que se proveerán en los centros dependerán de las necesidades destacadas por las mujeres y niñas de las comunidades seleccionadas. IOM establecerá un punto focal en cada centro.

En estos espacios se garantizará un contexto apropiado de servicios de mitigación de riesgos, orientación y referencia a servicios de asistencia especializada a los que les gustaría acceder a sobrevivientes de Violencia basada en Genero (VbG), así como víctimas de trata y otros abusos con el fin de reponerse del incidente ocurrido. Esto incluye apoyo psicosocial con el fin de guiar a las sobrevivientes de VbG y de trata y tráfico en el proceso de recuperación y recibir información sobre los servicios disponibles. Bajo los principios de derechos humanos, genero, edad y confidencialidad, específicamente la OIM hará: 1. Valoración de caso detectado y preparación para la entrevista. 2. Entrevista tomando en cuenta en principio de no hacer daño y otros relacionados a la seguridad física de la víctima potencial y la de su familia inmediata, 3. Análisis y valoración de riesgo para la persona y su familia, 4. Plan de Intervención inmediata: acceso servicios básicos: atención psicológica, ropa, abrigo, albergue, alimentación, salud primaria, seguridad. La OIM cuenta con herramientas internas que serán la base para la atención de los casos detectados en el marco de este proyecto. El manual de identificación de vulnerabilidad, así como el manual de protección a víctimas de trata orientaran la asistencia y protección a la victimas detectadas o las personas en mayor riesgo de serlo.  

OIM se hará cargo de la gestión de estos centros y del fortalecimiento de capacidades del personal para brindar atención de calidad. OIM también llevará a cabo referencia a otros servicios especializados cuando así sea necesario, incluyendo a apoyo psicosocial. 

Para responder al desafío de la falta de conciencia sobre riesgos de protección y de método de mitigación y prevención, la OIM trabajará para crear un entorno más seguro a través de campañas de sensibilización sobre mitigación y prevención de riesgos de protección como VbG, trata y tráfico en puntos de alta confluencia y tránsito para alcanzar grupos de edades, genero, vulnerabilidades diferentes.

project_name: Education in Emergencies in Hama
project_objective:
* All areas targeted by the project has severity above 4 as per the Education severity scale. 
*Average cost per beneficiary is around 200 usd per child including 2 NFE cycles, school rehabilitation, school materials, cash for education and protection related activities. 
* 5 % of targeted beneficiaries have disabilities. 
* Total funding FCA received in 2020  339,174.78
* Total estimated funding FCA received so far in 2021  2,143,623.91
* In 2020 FCA Syria Country Programme has reached 35 575 (direct) beneficiaries (18 292 women, 17 283 men)
The project is part of the FCA work in Hama that is partially funded by SHF/OCHA and ECHO grants. 

From April 2017 to May 2018, the Syrian government forces gradually advanced in the northern parts of Hama, which led to the changes of control in those areas. From September 2019, with the improvement in the security situation, the government allowed displaced people to return to their homes. Though most of the towns are severely damaged and the basic services are not available, many families left areas they sought refuge in and returned to their homes. Though the MoE has made some efforts to open classes in the existing schools for returning students, most of the schools are not prepared to receive students - they do not have WASH facilities, doors, windows, fences, or teaching tools and equipment. 
FCA has conducted its assessment in five areas of Hama Governorate in January 2021 and found that the number of out of school children in the 5 targeted communities is about 1358 (MoE, Municipalities). The assessment also included the conditions of ﬁve schools in the areas that witnessed a large displacement movement: Karnaz, As-Saan, Kawkab, Halfaya, and Bredage. Based on the information from the local authorities in the targeted locations, the large number of families did not enroll their children in schools, because children of absence of schools, overcrowded schools and children are working to support the families and depend on negative coping mechanism such as early marriage.
The aim of the proposed Action is to improve access to a safe and inclusive education for out of school children and children at risk of dropping out in Hama. The project will be implemented in 5 schools and will serve the communities surrounding those schools. To improve access to quality education, the project offers a systematic package of the activities that tackle various barriers to education - absence of functional schools or their poor physical conditions, absence of dignified WASH facilities, poverty, years of missed education, long distance to schools, poor quality of education, and protection issues. In 5 schools, 62 classrooms and 17 WASH facilities will be rehabilitated, thus creating a safe learning environment. A Cash for Education intervention will promote education of children who are engaged in child labour or are at risk of early marriage. The project will last for 12 months and will include 2 cycles of NFE classes that will allow children that have been out of education to catch up to 2 academic years of education and create conditions for return to formal education. FCA will organize trainings for teachers in EiE modules and TiCC package that include pedagogy skills + practical skills for teachers and include a skills in dealing with the students and positive discipline and classroom management , PSS as well as general student centered pedagogy to increase their professionalism and prepare them for the NFE classes. Protection events, PSS and referral of severe protection cases to specialized services will be also organized through building the capacity of schools. We expect that majority of OOSC children receiving NFE will  enroll in formal education. 
The project builds on FCA experience in EiE in Syria and particularly on its latest work on EiE in Hama.

project_objective: Le projet vise à contribuer à la réduction de la mortalité et de la morbidité des populations touchées par les crises à l'est et au sud du Tchad en renforçant la surveillance des maladies à tendance épidémique et à apporter une réponse rapide permettant de sauver la vie de toutes les populations vulnérables (hommes, femmes, enfants, garçons et filles)

project_name: Prise en charge médicale des complications de la malnutrition infantile et Information et sensibilisation sur l’importance des 1000 premiers jours dans les services de pédiatries des Délégations Sanitaires Provinciales du  Barh El Gazel, Batha, Guéra, Hadjer Lamis, Kanem, Lac, Ouaddai, Wadi-Fira, Ennedi Est et Mayo-Kebbi Est.
project_objective:
La malnutrition au Tchad contribue d’une manière directe ou indirecte à plus de 43% des cas de décès des enfants de moins de cinq ans en augmentant le risque de décès précoce à travers plusieurs maladies. Un enfant sur huit meurt avant d'atteindre l'âge de 5 ans et les principales causes de cette mortalité sont liées aux maladies infectieuses telles que le paludisme (20.4%), la pneumonie (15,7%) la diarrhée (13,5%) etc. avec la malnutrition comme facteur contributif majeur.
Des épisodes répétés de malnutrition aiguë (émaciation) chez les enfants, entraînent à long terme des déficits de croissance et de développement (retard de croissance) suscitant une mauvaise performance scolaire entre autres. Chez les grands enfants et les adultes, l’effet persistant de la malnutrition augmentent le risque de maladie chronique et peut se manifester par la réduction de l’aptitude physique qui peut entrainer une baisse de la productivité dans leur travail.
 Selon les résultats de l’enquête SMART 2020 conduite au niveau national, la malnutrition aigüe globale affecte 10% des enfants âgés de 6 à 59 mois dont 2.1% de forme sévère alors que la malnutrition chronique ou retard de croissance affectent environ un tiers d’entre eux (30,5%).
Bien que les résultats de l’enquête SMART 2020 révèlent au niveau national des taux de malnutrition moins élevés comparativement aux précédentes enquêtes,  cependant il existe encore des disparités très importantes entre les provinces et les différentes zones géographiques dont les zones sahéliennes et sahariennes sont les plus affectées.
Selon les projections du Cluster nutrition, 16 provinces sont considérées comme prioritaires sur la base d’extrapolation des données de SMART 2019 et 2020 prenant en compte la prévalence de la MAG (≥15%)  et de la  MAS(≥2%) au-dessus du seuil critique et du taux de décès brut(1 décès/10000 pers/jour) et du taux de décès des moins de cinq ans( 2 décès/10000 pers/par jour) relevant d’une situation grave. La plupart de ces 16 provinces sont presque situées dans la ceinture sahélienne qui sont affectées depuis des années par la crise alimentaire et nutritionnelle. 
Les projections Cluster Nutrition révèlent que 292 278 cas de MAS  sont attendus en 2021 parmi lesquels 29228 seraient des cas compliqués. Les taux élevés de mortalité rétrospective chez les moins de 5 ans observés lors de l’enquête SMART  dans les provinces du  Lac , Tibesti et Hadjer Lamis ( ≥2% )  seraient principalement dus à l’impact des maladies transmissibles d’une part et  d’autre part  au statut de malnutrition qui affaiblit la capacité des enfants à lutter contre les maladies transmissibles et les épidémies.
Plusieurs causes concourent à la détérioration de l’état nutritionnel de la population : les plus immédiates sont un apport alimentaire insuffisant, des maladies et les mauvaises pratiques de soins dans les ménages. En effet, environ 16% des enfants âgés de moins de 6 mois seraient allaités exclusivement au sein en 2020.
Les mesures prises pour stopper la propagation et le contrôle du virus de COVID-19 ont eu des effets sur la capacité de ménages à maintenir le niveau optimal de sécurité alimentaire, d’économie et d’accès aux services sociaux de base. Les structures sanitaires et communautaires, vu leur faible capacité ont aussi des difficultés à offrir des services de qualité tout en respectant les orientations COVID-19. 
De plus, les provinces de la bande sahélienne sont les plus touchées par le manque d'accès aux services de santé de base. La plupart des villages de ces provinces sont situés à plus de 30 km des centres de santé et certains à environ 100 km. Plus de 20% de la population est nomade, ce qui a entraîné un faible accès aux services de santé de base. Le manque d'accès aux services de santé de base est la principale raison qui explique les taux élevés de mortalité infantile (133/1000) et de mortalité maternelle (860/100 000).
