project_name: Supporting the humanitarian community in Ukraine in fulfilling their own mandates through the provision of essential humanitarian access, security coordination and information services including flash reporting, periodic analysis and briefings, safety related statistics, immediate expertise, and crisis management assistance.
project_objective:
The action assists humanitarian aid organizations in fulfilling their mandates through the provision of essential access and security coordination, information services and the availability of expertise. As a result, NGOs and humanitarian partners will better understand, design, and manage their operational capacity and to improve humanitarian access while reducing the risks that will confront them.

The monitoring mission provides scheduled and on-demand services. INSO reporting targets audiences are operating or planning to operate in areas of high risk and local engagement.

The mission delivers a monthly analytical report which includes thematic topics and analysis, data and trend information and mapping, and flash alerts and security reports. Monthly meetings will take place at NGO hubs or in an online format during the COVID-19 pandemic. Members can access to our independent security advisors for data, research and expert technical advice, and assessments. Coordination and representation on common and prevalent issues within the beneficiary and partner group, and with authorities, such as civil-military representatives, is a structural component of the mission.

Monitoring services:
• 24/7 Threat Warning System (Flash alerts) and security reports on conflict and access incidents affecting the humanitarian community;
• Monthly analytical reports;
• Monthly meetings;
• Independent Security Advisory services.

Our standardized collection and verification of data feed the INSO Ukraine database of 54,885 conflict and access incidents (affecting humanitarian action) verified and recorded between August 1, 2015, and October 2020 (as of October 22 2020). INSO Ukraine data informs INSO’s global information products, such as INSO Key Data Analysis and Safety and Access Review, reaching 1,048 organizations worldwide (approximately 10,000 email recipients).

INSO services are free of charge. INSO does not and will not charge NGOs to become members or to access any INSO services.

Since beneficiaries are organizations, not individuals, issues of gender balance will not arise. In addition, most of our beneficiaries are working with highly vulnerable people.

The NGO community in 2015 directly requested the action, and the modified action agreed in 2018 by members and donors. 

We expect that NGO safety will remain vulnerable in areas affected by conflict and specifically for frontline NGOs. INSO Ukraine is a scalable response and, where resourced sufficiently, can respond if needs increase. INSO Annual planning 2021 will determine the continuation of the action and similar cost.

The mission focuses on Donetska and Luhanska regions of Ukraine and will maintain its coordination office in Kyiv to engage partners at the capital level. INSO deploys field monitors at locations in Donetska and Luhanska Oblasts.

project_name: Emergency Cash Assistance for the Most Vulnerable Palestine Refugees in Gaza
project_objective: The global outbreak of COVID-19 is putting further pressure to the already deteriorating socio-economic situation in Gaza. The restrictions on daily life activities as a result of the measures enforced by the local authority to prevent the spread of the virus are having severe impacts on lives and livelihoods, leading to significant increase in need for assistance. UNRWA continues to provide in-kind food assistance to more than 1 million Palestine refugees in the Gaza Strip, covering a part of daily caloric needs, yet the COVID-19 emergency has added further struggles to the people. The population has already been facing years of humanitarian crisis, and many people are relying on daily labour and casual work to secure their minimum requirements, which are heavily affected by COVID-19 restrictions. The families with high dependency ratios, including those with children, elderly and headed by females or persons with disability, are particularly at risk, as they are more likely than others to suffer from poverty or other forms of deprivation. Through this project, UNRWA will provide one-off multi-purpose cash assistance of US$40 to 180,000 vulnerable Palestine refugees identified by its multi-dimensional vulnerability criteria of identified cash-strapped groups including female-headed households, households headed by an elderly person or an adolescent, persons with disability, and persons with special requirements.

project_name: Improve access of basic health care services to the under-served and marginalized socio-economic groups by strengthening primary healthcare systems in the context of COVID-19 pandemic
project_objective:
CHEF International proposes a one-year project addressing basic curative and preventive health care issues. The project will cater to the immediate needs most vulnerable populations, especially women, adolescent girls, children and persons living with disabilities who have become more vulnerable in the current situation of COVID-19 pandemic. The project goals:  a) to improve access of under-served and marginalized socio-economic groups to basic curative and preventive health care services, b) to assist the government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in strengthening primary healthcare system in the targeted areas.  
CHEF is already closing working with provincial and district health departments. Through this project, CHEF will work with 60 BHU’s of 3 districts (Mardan, Charssada, Bunner) of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The proposed project will enhance the capacity of targeted health facilities in treatment of the patients in safe & infection prevention & control (IPC) environment on prevailing health conditions such as communicable and non-communicable diseases. 
The project will mainly have two components i.e. (1) provision of health care services along with free medicines, delivery kits and free prosthetic and orthotic; (2) Community Outreach through Education and Awareness.  To support the women and girls of the target population, a free helpline will be provided for psycho-social support and MNCH support for expecting mothers. The GBV and sexual harassment will also be managed through the helpline by providing them mental psychological support as well as refer them to the relevant specialists’ authorities, if needed. A strong referral mechanism will be established from community to first level care facility (FLCF) & from FLCF to secondary or tertiary level care facility by ensuring dedicated transport ambulance services in target communities specifically for mothers and children.
CHEF will identify Persons with Disabilities within each locality and provide them assistive technology devices as CHEF’s contribution to the project.   

Trainings and capacity building activities will target 1500 medical health workers including doctors, paramedics, LHWs, LHVs, DPOs disease surveillance officers, vaccinator & psychologists to prevent, identify and refer the COVID patients to designated COVID treatment centers.  Further 300 LHV’s & LHWS will receive training on Birth preparedness and prevention of complications in COVID pandemic situation. 
CHEF International will sensitize the local communities on primary health issues through a robust education and awareness campaign. CHEF will develop and publish Brochures and Pamphlets on topics such as how to live a healthy life, MNCH, Hygiene and social distancing, family planning, and managing Stress and anxiety.  Radio messages and cable TV adverts will also be utilized to reach out to the masses. 
In each Health facility CHEF will provide COVID-19 related PPEs such as gowns, masks, hand sanitizers and disinfection materials for health facilities.

project_name: Provision of comprehensive (preventive and curative) nutrition and health services for vulnerable children under 5 and PLWs in Akkar and North Lebanon, and conducting a SMART survey at national level
project_objective:
This Project is designed to provide life-saving nutrition services in poor neighborhoods with high density of Lebanese, Refugees and Migrants in vulnerable situation through both community and facility-based interventions including:
1.Infant and young child feeding (IYCF) practices optimization, micronutrient supplementation distribution, and reporting of blanket distribution of Infant formula
2. Screening, referral, and treatment of malnutrition (SAM without complications and MAM) among children under 5 and PLW 

The project will contribute to saving lives of the most vulnerable people, children under 5, in addition to PLWs by providing coordinated, accessible nutrition services and informative data to derive recommendations needed to inform the nutrition sector response in the country.

The project will target 41,237 people (Host communities, Syrian Refugees, PRS/PRL and migrants) in Akkar and North Lebanon disaggregated as follows: 15,956 Pregnant and Lactating Women (PLWs) & 25,281 Children under 5 (13,002 girls - 12,279 boys).

19 localities will be targeted through the support which will be provided to 8 non-supported Primary Healthcare Centers (PHCs) in high populated areas in the targeted Cadasters in the North & Akkar.

6 outreach staff (3 IYCF counselors and 3 Community Health Workers) will be based out of each PHCs to provide visual screening, referrals and IYCF services for PLW and children under 5. These outreach teams will work in parallel and direct coordination with the selected health facilities in the targeted areas. 
Staff will assess the nutritional status of children under 5 and distribute nutritional supplies to them as needed. Additionally, IYCF services will be provided.

Moreover, an assessment of the nutritional status of children aged 6-59 months in order to generate information for an improved response by conducting a SMART survey. The SMART survey will be conducted at national level across all 8 Lebanese Governorates + the camps. The overall objective of the survey is to conduct a nutrition assessment representative at the national and governorate level to determine the nutrition status of children under 5 years of age, maternal nutrition status for pregnant and lactating women as well as critical IYCF practices. The survey results will be used to derive recommendations needed to inform the nutrition sector response in the country.

A pre and rapid coordination combined with referrals will be put in place whenever the team identifies any sign of abuse or violence among children under 5 and or mothers. All cases of violence against women and children will be referred to the pre-identified health facility and signaled to the relevant sector.

This response will adopt the safety recommendations in the COVID-19 context.

Coordination with the nutrition sector, UNICEF, MoPH and IOM will be ensured throughout the project. Mercy-USA will also coordinate with IOCC and Al Midani and other stakeholders to avoid any overlap of activities, and to ensure a wider coverage of targeted populations including migrants, and to ensure a harmonized coordinated response. The Migrant Presence Monitoring exercise being finalized now by IOM will be shared with Mercy-USA which will give a good understanding about migrants’ geographical distribution. 

This project will empower mothers and HH members through training them to screen their own children for malnutrition by teaching them how to use color-coded Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) tapes.

Hence this project will contribute to sector specific objectives through:
- The provision of life-saving nutrition services in high needs and remote locations through both community and facility-based including screening, referral, treatment, micronutrient supplementation and infant and young child feeding (IYCF); 
- An assessment of the nutritional status of children aged 6-59 months in order to generate information for an improved response by conducting a SMART survey.

project_name: Integrated protection assistance for vulnerable IDPs, Returnees and Host Communities in Aleppo, Dar'a, Idleb, Hama, Homs and Rural Damascus
project_objective: In  line with needs and priorities identified in HRP 2021, COOPI aims to give continuity and expand integrated protection services to support the affected populations of Aleppo, Dar'a, Idleb, Hama, Homs and Rural Damascus Governorates, to respond to the substantial gap in the delivery of protection services in the targeted areas. COOPI response will focus on three key results: 1) Improve the protection response through a community-based protection approach 2) Safely identify protection threats and facilitate access to specialized services and 3) Strengthen protection mainstreaming across all its sector of intervention, including food security, livelihood and early recovery. To strengthen communities’ self-protection mechanisms and ensure sustainability, COOPI will support community-led initiatives and the establishment of community-based structures, such as women committees, that proved to be effective in identifying and mitigate CP, PSS and GBV issues in remote areas. Direct engagement of communities will also mitigate the impact of COVID-19 on the restriction of movements and access to remote areas by COOPI staff. Community members will be involved in the dissemination and delivery of tailored risk education messaging to mitigate the risks posed by explosive contamination by increasing the community’s response capacity. Specialized services, such as case management, will be consolidated in the urban areas of Aleppo and in Rural Damascus, where static facilities are operational since 2019, and expanded in Hama, Homs and in cross-line areas (Sheikh Maqsoud - a Kurdish Self-Administration neighborhood of Aleppo city and Abu Duhur - Idleb) mainly through mobile intervention. COOPI intends to enhance the services related to victim assistance, HBR for PwD and home-based care for elderly already implemented in Aleppo. Acknowledging the challenges related to data management and protection and the lack of specialized service providers in the 6 Governorates, COOPI will continue ensuring the direct implementation of case management services, including the management and referral of GBV survivors and the engagement of men and boys in the risk prevention and mitigation activities. As identified in the HRP, COOPI will focus also to respond to the harmful coping mechanism related to child labour that has been detected in all areas of intervention and that necessitate an integrated assistance, including the support of families to meet basic needs with FSL activities. COOPI foreseen to include voucher assistance to prevent protection risks, to respond to ongoing protection concerns and/or to complement protection programs, depending on the needs assessed in each location and the market availability. The activities could be related to provision of vouchers for general or in-kind assistance, vouchers for PwD in order mitigate stigma and contribute to their inclusion in the community or voucher assistance to community-based structures. COOPI will ensure protection mainstreaming in its multi-sectoral response, with a particular focus on safe distribution modalities, AGD approach and focusing on highly vulnerable groups in the definition of eligibility criteria and in targeting. PSEA will constitute a cross-sectoral priority to be addressed and eradicate, while ensuring COOPI staff and third parties to be trained, and to report it and to protect people. MEAL system and the data collection methodology, that already provide disaggregated data for specific services, will be further strengthen and integrated in all activities, to strengthen monitoring, reporting and analysis and to adapt the project implementation. COOPI will put additional efforts to collect data related to disabilities, victims of EO and UASC to inform the humanitarian community. Complaints and feedback mechanisms will be designed, available and adapted to be accessible by the specific community groups, for beneficiaries to express on accessibility, adequacy and equity of services.

Emergency Food Assistance for Syrian Households (EFASH)
project_objective:
The overall objective of the Emergency Food Assistance for Syrian Households (EFASH) project is to improve the overall food security among vulnerable Syrian households. This will be achieved through the provision of food vouchers to vulnerable communities of men, women, boys, girls and people with disability by providing an approximate of 70 percent of their monthly food requirements.  
Priority locations where ADRA has operational presence and ongoing programs include Rural Damascus, Homs, Aleppo and Deir Al Zour are also in alignment with the Food Security and Agriculture Sector. Exact locations will be selected in close coordination with local partners such as the Syrian Arab Red Crescent (SARC), WFP, FAO and the FSA sector. Prioritization will be given to areas with high food security severity scales such as Northern Rural Homs, Aleppo and Rural Damascus (Duma), presence of IDPs/returnees and areas with limited previous interventions (such as newly accessible areas). 
Duma is located in East Ghouta, Rural Damascus and was heavily involved in the conflict. It was besieged from 2013 until it came under Government of Syria (GoS) control in 2018. The area is still heavily controlled with access restrictions for those wishing to enter and leave. According to ADRA assessments in Duma city and surrounds, levels of food insecurity remain high, especially with the most recent economic hardships faced during 2020. From those assessed, 57% had an unacceptable food consumption score, 73% reported that they had not enough food to meet their family needs in the past 12 months and an average dietary diversity of 8 . The major issue faced by much of the population is access to food commodities, rather than availability, with the average monthly household income found to be only $40 . 
Northern rural Homs, encompassing Al Rastan, Telbisa and Teldu was also under siege until 2018 when it became accessible to humanitarian intervention. The area was heavily damaged, including to basic infrastructure, housing and farming land. The population have been slowly returning since that time. Despite being an agricultural area, the levels of food insecurity remain high, due mostly due to limited livelihood opportunities and widespread poverty (average monthly income of $31 with an average of $94 of debt ) with high levels of disability. 72% reported that there were months they did not have enough food to meet their family needs, with 59% having an unacceptable food consumption score . 
The city of Aleppo (Jabal Saman) was spilt between opposing forces until 2016 that extensively damaged local infrastructure and resulted in mass displacement. What was once the most populous city in Syria, Aleppo became home to the highest number of individuals classified as food insecure. As a highly populated urban area, the market is fully functional, although the most vulnerable lack sufficient funds to access sufficient food commodities. 

A total of 10,000 food insecure households will be targeted to receive eight months’ worth of food assistance of the twelve-month program through a food voucher directly given to beneficiaries equivalent to the amount of $70, to redeemed from local contracted venders, the voucher will be specific to a range of nutritious food item list endorsed by the FSA sector. All activities of the project will be aligned with the FSA sector SO1 response package and will be aligned with WFP through bilateral discussions. 
Distribution of the food vouchers will contribute to positive outcomes in livelihoods of the beneficiaries allowing them to spend their income on their other needs such as health and education.

project_name: Improve Access to Comprehensive Health and Emergency Services for Pregnant and Lactating Women and Children under five years in Syria
project_objective:
Sustaining and expanding essential, quality health services at primary care levels remains critical to addressing health needs of affected populations. Protracted crisis has left just 64% of hospitals and 52% of primary health care centers (PHCs) fully functional. Up to 70% of health workers have left Syria and many others have been injured or killed. 37% of the affected population require reproductive, maternal, neonatal and child health services, and at least 15% require mental health and psychosocial services with infrastructure and referral systems inadequate to cope with these needs. The health system is unable to respond to the high trauma, mental health and rehabilitation needs. This is causing physical hardship and mental trauma which in turn complicate women’s, fetal and infants’ health in pregnancy and increases risks during delivery. Overall, there is a lack of available, qualified and trained staff, with limited financial means to support supervision and referral services, and community-based interventions relating to MHPSS, child and maternal health and nutrition. Access constitutes a distinctive barrier to health care in areas with high severity scores, including those that recently witnessed changes of control like North East, North West, and parts of Southern Syria. The health system in Damascus and Aleppo is overburdened with hosting the largest internal displacements from within Syria, and by acting as the main reference point for referrals.
AAH proposes a two-pronged approach to meet the priority needs from the 2020 HRP focusing on immediate lifesaving support together with sustainability efforts, integrating health systems strengthening and infrastructure provision of primary care and essential public health functions, including NCD, nutrition, MHPSS and GBV while identifying appropriate referral modalities to ensure local capacity can meet the different needs of women, men, girls and boys. Vulnerability criteria is based on highest severity, needs assessment, (including prioritization of IDPs, returnees, population hosting displaced persons, and people with socioeconomic hardships), contextual volatility and strategic presence of AAH. Monitoring and beneficiary data will be disaggregated by sex, age and marginalized groups, including disabilities. To increase sustained access to health services, AAH will identify emergency small-scale rehabilitations to reinstate safe and dignified condition of services. The intervention will be completed with the provision of basic furniture, medical supplies and equipment. PHC staff will be trained on integrating primary health care services (including MHPSS, nutrition, NCD, and GBV) with activated supervisory visits to ensure adequacy of implementation. Community Health Workers will also be trained to integrate and deliver MHPSS, GBV, nutrition and NCD prevention at the primary healthcare centers, community and household levels within the selected health districts. The project will intervene at multiple levels within the targeted health districts, including primary static and mobile healthcare facilities. A comprehensive MEAL plan is designated to support collection and tracking of sex and age disaggregated data in line with proposed health interventions and is undertaken directly by MEAL in collaboration with health and nutrition department. Monitoring methodologies include needs assessments, baseline and end line, and activity monitoring. Systematic collection of information on gender roles and responsibilities, gender relations and decision-making dynamics, access to and control of resources, and social norms will be done. Qualitative interviews and satisfaction surveys will complement monitoring activities to examine the project’s effect on social dynamics in communities and pathways of change. Focus group discussions and key informant interviews with stakeholders, such as health facility workers and beneficiaries, at key points and midway through program cycle.

project_name: Education support for IDP’s, Host community and Returnees students and education personnel in Deir Ezzor, Dar’a, Hama, Homs, Ar-raqqa, Aleppo and Sweida
project_objective:
* All the sub-districts that we are targeting is within the severity 3,4,5 by that the percentage will be 100% with the mentioned severity.
 * The estimated cost per beneficiary is 5$.
* According to RSRP field assessment that the proposed project will cover 15% of total people with disabilities within the targeted areas.
* As for 2020 RSRP received fund of $ 280,000 for implementing Education services.
* For 2021 RSRP has received fund of  $ 835,783 for implementing Education services.
* During 2020 RSRP through implementation of projects have reached 2024 of affected people in need fo Education support.
Considering the complicated impact of the 2020 situation in the conflict-related displacement area of intervention in early 2020 and the longer-term impact of the COVID-19 pandemic - 78% drop in value of the Syrian currency in just one year (to SYP 3,030/US$1 on informal market (WFP, December 2020)). This generated additional needs for IDPs and results 2.4 million children out of school. The key reasons why children were not able to receive proper education was that schools were not accessible  in their area, schooling has not being affordable, children labor is common to support the family household and  schools are either damaged, non operative or used for non-education purposes. The mission was done knowing the general sector assessment and conducted in coordination with the local direatorate of education (DOE).

project_name: “Strengthen Microplanning in High Risk Union Councils in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in Pakistan”
project_objective:
NIDA will aim to enhance national EPI goals to reach and immunize every child by strengthening of microplanning in high risk and poor performing union councils of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province  through capacity building of health facility staff, and monitoring and evaluation activities.

The province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) has a population of 35.53 million1, and is divided into seven divisions: Bannu, Dera Ismail Khan, Hazara, Kohat, Malakand, Mardan and Peshawar. Each division is further divided into districts and there is a total of 35 districts in the entire province. Moreover, the seven Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA): Bajaur, Khyber, Kurrum, Orakzai, Mohmand, North Waziristan and South Waziristan have also been included as Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Merged Districts (KPTD) in the province.
The overall health indicators of the KP province are compromised due to double burden of communicable and non-communicable diseases, superimposed with challenges of inaccessibility, weak health system, high out-of-pocket expenditure, security issues, natural calamities like flash floods, heavy snow prone mountainous areas and precarious health condition of children and mother.

The Department of Health, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa effectively and efficiently contributes towards Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) by adopting various measures to achieve Universal Health Coverage. The child health interventions are mainly planned at the grassroot level with community participation and stakeholder’s engagement.

Continued efforts for universal immunization of under five children against vaccine-preventable diseases is one of the best practices contributing towards preventing neonatal, infant and child mortality. The access to each child is ensured by using the Reaching Every District (RED) Strategy. However, the Routine EPI service delivery, yet need an intensive support to address common obstacles to increase immunization coverage such as sub-optimal microplanning for immunization service delivery in remote districts, low quality and unreliable service, inadequate monitoring, and supervision of health workers.
The EPI indicator of <80% PENTA-3 coverage in remote and far-flung union council of 27/34 districts in seven divisions of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province for the period of Jan-Sep 2020 is alarming. 

Project Goal
Reach and immunize every child by strengthening of microplanning in high risk union councils of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.

Project Objective
The project objectives are to:

1.	Strengthen microplanning in high risk and poor performing union councils by capacity building of health facility staff at 300 health facilities’ to update micro plans responding to the coverage enhancement requirements especially in the hard-to-reach areas and high-risk districts
2.	Adapt and translate the microplanning curriculum.

project_name: Cash-based assistance to most vulnerable and food insecure households in the Gaza strip
project_objective: The project will increase food security for 15 localities communities in the eastern and northern areas of the Gaza strip through provision of e-vouchers for food commodities. The project will target 15 localities in the eastern and northern areas of Gaza five governorates through provision of e-vouchers for food commodities. The intervention will be integrated with SCI-nutrition and child protection current interventions and will provide a database for the potential beneficiaries. It will also contribute to addressing malnutrition, particularly with children and will increase the impact of our health/nutrition interventions. Applying a cash-based voucher modality will empower food insecure households to prioritize and meet their own needs while enhancing their access to sufficient food intake.  The intervention will target 4,000 vulnerable HHs (approx. 22,000 people) with e-vouchers. SCI will target exceptionally vulnerable HHs such as HHs with members with disability, children under 5, pregnant or lactating women, infants, child/female-headed HHs, and HHs of extended size only. The E-voucher value is expected to cover 100% of HHs` food needs factoring in coping strategy practices that they may use to complete their needs such relying on less preferred and less expensive foods, borrowings and assistance from relatives or host families and use of available savings.  The project is in line with   Country Strategic Objective 3 (SO3) and FSS objective 2 “Households suffering from limited access to food and to income opportunities are able to meet their basic food needs” and will respond to the root cause in malnutrition resulted from increase in poverty and high food insecurity impacted by the reduction in per capita income and the rise in unemployment.

project_name: Integrated psychosocial support and child protection services for the most affected boys and girls in Gaza, especially those impacted by COVID-19 and its repercussions on families in Gaza
project_objective:
This project will support the delivery of quality, integrated child protection and psychosocial support services to the most vulnerable boys and girls aged 4-18 in Gaza, especially those affected by COVID-19. The pandemic has affected all aspects of life in Gaza, including child protection needs and services. The project will ensure that 12 family centres and 30 outreach sites in Gaza are fully operational, responding to the pressing mental health and psychosocial as well as child protection needs of affected children. Service delivery will be targeted to the most affected locations and the most vulnerable children through a coordinated continuum of services in Gaza. Each family centre will be connected to a community-based child protection committee that informs the family centre of community needs and acts as a focal point for identifying vulnerable children for referral. Family centres will operate through established Community Based Organizations (CBOs) and outreach sites, and will assess/screen and refer children for further services through:
1) a case management approach for the worst affected;
2) referral of complex child protection cases to child protection services (relevant stakeholders and Civil Society Organizations (CSOs); and
3) referral of children with further psychosocial support needs to more specialized psychological support services. Services will also strengthen outreach capacities to detect and link up children in need with service providers, whilst providing mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) support through the family centres.

This project is in line with and contributes to the Protection Cluster Objective Two, which calls for putting in place protection response mechanisms to prevent and mitigate the of the occupation and conflict related violence.

The proposed project will also be implemented in synergy with other sectors implemented by World Vision in the target locations such as health, nutrition, WASH, gender and protection related programming.

project_name: Promouvoir la protection des civils par l’engagement des Acteurs Armés Non Etatiques et des communautés en faveur du respect des normes humanitaires au Mali
project_objective:
La protection des civils au Mali a été mise à mal par la crise depuis 2012. Ce phénomène a eu des conséquences dramatiques pour la sécurité humaine, mais aussi l’accès aux services essentiels, y inclus, lorsque nécessaire, aux systèmes de référencement.  Le présent projet vise à accroitre l’engagement des AANE en faveur de la protection des civils, à travers une meilleure appropriation des normes humanitaires, et à les inciter à s’engager publiquement et concrètement pour le respect de leurs obligations vis- à -vis des populations civiles. Sur la base de l’hypothèse selon laquelle les communautés informées de leurs droits sont plus à même de les défendre, le projet vise également à accroitre la connaissance des communautés sur les normes humanitaires et à les équiper afin qu’elles puissent effectuer un plaidoyer adéquat si nécessaire. Plus largement, la logique d’intervention vise à renforcer la protection des civiles. L’objectif général de ce projet est de « Contribuer à la protection des civils et des personnes hors de combat et l’amélioration de l’accès humanitaire ».  
Son objectif spécifique  est « Les AANE et communautés se mobilisent en faveur du respect des normes humanitaires y compris par la signature d’actes d’engagement, l’émission de déclarations unilatérales et le plaidoyer ».  
Le spectre du projet touche tout autant la protection de l’enfant et de l’éducation, de la mission médicale que la prohibition de la violence sexuelle et basée sur le genre. Il comprend également une composante accès humanitaire. 

La zone de mise en œuvre est : Mopti, Gao, Tombouctou, Ménaka, Kidal.

En ce qui concerne les AANE ciblés, l’Appel de Genève s’attend à ce qu’ils 

-	s’approprient les normes humanitaires d’une manière générale et spécifiquement les thématiques abordées : protection de l’enfant, de la mission médicale, de l’héritage culturel, de la lutte contre les violences sexuelles ;  
-	prennent des engagements en faveur de la facilitation de l’accès aux acteurs humanitaires intervenant dans les zones sous leur contrôle ; 
-	participent à la réflexion en faveur de la protection et de l’accès humanitaire.

Ces trois actions permettraient ainsi un meilleur engagement en faveur des normes humanitaires et garantiraient le droit des populations civiles vulnérables à accéder à l’action humanitaire.
Corolaire indispensable de la sensibilisation, formation et de l’engagement des AANE, l’Appel de Genève ciblera également les communautés vivant sous le contrôle des AANE dans les localités suivantes : Mopti, Tombouctou, Gao, Ménaka et Kidal. L’Appel de Genève sensibilisera ainsi les populations civiles aux normes humanitaires à travers des campagnes de mass media et des sessions de sensibilisation et de formation visant plus spécifiquement les personnes d’influence (religieux, notables, représentants des communautés…).
L’Appel de Genève accompagnera également les communautés dans des initiatives ponctuelles visant à assurer le respect de leurs droits. La nature de ces initiatives sera définie par les communautés elles-mêmes, et l’Appel de Genève s’assurera que le principe de Ne Pas Nuire est respecté. Ces initiatives peuvent recouvrir : l’organisation de forums de discussions regroupant leaders communautaires et représentants des AANE et reporting de cas de violation du droit aux points focaux des AANE chargés de la collaboration avec l’Appel de Genève.

project_name: Provision of Camp Coordination and Camp Management assistance to displaced persons in Malakal PoC, collective sites and outside of camps settings in Malakal and Unity State
project_objective:

Through this project DRC aims to contribute to the following CCCM HRP strategic objectives:

-	Ensure predictable and coordinated delivery of service, provision of information aimed at improving the quality of integrated services for the displaced populations in camps and camp like settings

project_name: Shelter assistance to Returnees and IDPs In Syria
project_objective:
DRC intervention will particularly be focused on providing access to basic, safe, and dignified Shelter solutions, and  having access to sufficient and safe water for domestic use which will assist in  enabling access of the most vulnerable population groups to safe and dignified shelter solutions which contributes to the 2020 Shelter HRP Objective2: “Contribute towards the resilience and cohesion of communities and households by improving housing and related community/public infrastructure.”
The conflict-affected population is assisted in compliance with the Sector and MoLAE standards. DRC seeks to engage with other DRC sectors to complement DRCs work this coordination and complementarity mechanism needs to be expressed accordingly between the shelter activities and achieving the principles of protection DRC will achieve this through the following outcomes:
1. Increased access to adequate gender- and disability-sensitive shelter, water, and hygiene infrastructure
among conflict-affected persons in Dara'a, Homs, and Aleppo.  
DRC aims to provide life-saving and life-sustaining shelter support through addressing overburdened communities with a high ratio of returnees and, members of host communities and IDPs in the rehabilitation of partially damaged apartments,  DRC is aiming for a multi-sectoral integrated intervention of Shelter, Education and WASH sectors to increase access to life-saving emergency and life-sustaining assistance while also transitioning to more resilience/early recovery-oriented activities in selected locations of intervention to maximize the impact of humanitarian actions, and enabling access of the conflict-affected population to safe water for drinking and domestic use and safe excreta.  A total of 15,00 beneficiaries and 30 PWDs will be reached out in different locations with a 3 and above severity scale.
DRC’s programme strategy is realized through two programme objectives which are responding to emergencies and addressing solutions to protracted displacement. When combined, these can provide a basis for a comprehensive response in all phases of the displacement cycle transitioning.
DRC will respond to emergencies where sudden population movements cause conflict-affected populations to be living in conditions posing immediate life-threatening risks as well as address needs arising due to the covid-19 pandemic. 
IDPs assistance follows SHELTER Sector Standards will be provided in collective shelters, and private unfinished/demolished buildings in both, urban and rural areas. Newly displaced populations get prioritized as an emergency response including COVID 19 response, according to the Sector’s directive. The intervention will concentrate on areas where DRC has a current presence.
Selection of targeted beneficiaries will be done by DRC in close coordination with MoLA and SARC with verification of needs and beneficiaries by DRC. DRC will liaise with the Mukhtar, with any humanitarian actors present in the area, and with local residents to identify HHs, ensure coordination and avoid any overlap. DRC staff will have free access to move around the target areas scoping houses and approaching HHs directly to explain the scope of the intervention and offer to conduct an initial technical assessment. Initial technical assessments will provide an understanding of each family’s situation/vulnerability and determine the feasibility of works.

DRC will prevent, mitigate, and respond to risks aggravated by the COVID- 19 pandemic, contributing to a strengthened protective environment for conflict and displacement affected individuals that are facing a sudden onset, a recent emergency that gives rise to an urgent WASH risk that they are unable to overcome.
DRC will respond to emergencies where sudden population movements cause conflict-affected populations to be living in conditions posing immediate life-threatening risks as well as address needs arising due to the covid-19 pandemic.

project_name: Shelter Assistance for IDPs, Returnees and vulnerable host communities in Aleppo, Rural Damascus, Homs, Hama,  Al- Hassakeh, Dier- Ez-zor  and Dara’a
project_objective:
Through the proposed intervention, Secours Islamique France (SIF) will directly contribute to the Shelter Sector’s objectives of Syria by supporting the sustainable rehabilitation of housing and related public infrastructures in Rural Damascus, Dara’a, Hama, Homs, Al- Hassakeh, Dier- Ez-zor and Aleppo Governorates. SIF is in coordination with local authorities to gain access to Al-Hassakeh. The sub districts in these governorates are selected based on their level of accessibility and the severity of needs as per the 2021 Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) Syria and SIF’s field assessments. After a comprehensive needs assessment, consultations with the local community, related authorities and taking into account the sector priorities, SIF’s proposed interventions are:

(1)	Rehabilitation and repair of damaged houses and (2) Provision and Installation of doors and windows (Shelter Package). A total of 4,000 beneficiaries will be reached through the proposed intervention. SIF meal team will conduct an assessment to establish which type of assistance  will be provided to the beneficiaries, according to their needs and vulnerability.  

SIF will continue to adopt protection mainstreaming approach in the design and implementation of this project. As part of the proposed action, SIF will consider threats of physical attacks and landmines in the selection of the locations, ensure clarity on HLP ownership of private houses in order to avoid eviction as well as involve local authorities in site planning and selection to avoid issues and ensure consent and participation from municipalities, governorates and the MoLAE. Specific needs will be addressed through including door locks and lighting, especially in WASH facilities, to better protect women and girls, particularly single women and female-headed households. SIF will also ensure that infrastructures are accessible to persons with disabilities and older persons, and safe for small children. Housing will be secured for unaccompanied children and, whenever possible, SIF will proceed to referrals to ensure the monitoring of the situation of boys and girls by specialized agencies. SIF will take into account local capacities and encourage the contractors in recruiting workers from local communities. SIF ensures participatory approach in all project cycle phases including the planning, project design, implementation and the monitoring phase. The MEAL team will put in place a complaints and feedback mechanism.
