project_name: Prevention, treatment and management of malnutrition through provision of integrated nutrition services in Lower Juba, Gedo and Galgaduud
project_objective:
Somalia’s public health system has significantly underperformed due to longstanding conflict and instability. In addition to this, the combined effects of widespread and severe flooding, desert Locust infestation, socioeconomic impacts of COVID-19 and the cumulative impacts of previous shocks have contributed towards the deterioration of production outputs and social economics increasing vulnerabilities of households. These cumulative factors have significantly impacted the state of nutrition in children, women and men.  
The median Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) prevalence has remained Serious (10–14.9%) for the past three consecutive seasons (11.8% in 2020 Gu, 13.1% in 2019 Deyr and 13.8% in 2019 Gu). Based on the nutrition survey analysis and projections conducted by FSNAU and partners in June and July 2019, High levels of acute malnutrition continue to persist. Urgent treatment and nutrition support are required for approximately 849,900 children under the age of five years who will likely face acute malnutrition through August 2021, including 143,400 who are likely to be severely malnourished.
For population groups that registered a high prevalence of acute malnutrition, contributing factors include high morbidity, low immunization and vitamin-A supplementation, poor care practices and food insecurity. One contributing non-food security factor to consistently poor acute malnutrition is the incidence of measles as well as Acute watery diarrhea(AWD)/cholera, due to unprotected water use and poor WASH practices. According to joint WHO and Somalia Federal Ministry of Health reports, nearly 1,257 measles cases were reported from January to August 2019, keeping the outbreak at epidemic levels. In the same period, 1,909 cases of AWD/cholera were reported, an increase of 48% from the number of cases reported in June to August 2018, but 31% lower than same time in 2017 drought year. More than 250 cases were reported in August 2019. There is concern for increased waterborne disease in October due to ongoing flooding and contamination of water sources.
In Lower and Middle Juba, falling livestock prices limiting household income. Given ongoing dry conditions through September, livestock body conditions have further deteriorated and income from sales is even lower than reflected in August prices. Poor households are unable to access adequate food to meet basic needs and are expected to be in Crisis (IPC Phase 3)
Population groups classified as Crisis (IPC Phase 3) in our project area of interest are 5,460 in badhadhe, 32,459 in Afmadow, 120,352 in Kismayo, 34,905 in Buaale, 34,905 in JiIlib ,14932 in bardheere, 60,471 IN Garbaharay and 6760 In Ceel waaq require interventions aimed at reducing food consumption gaps, eradicating acute malnutrition, saving lives, and protecting and saving livelihoods. In the Integrated interventions we intend to provide activities to support recovery and prevent deterioration in the nutrition situation.
ADA is well positioned to implement the management of severe Acute Malnutrition both with and without medical complication since it already has well established four health facilities which will host static nutrition centers and also the outreach nutrition teams. ADA actively participates in nutrition cluster coordination meetings at regional level and closely co-ordinates with individual nutrition partners in referring the active cases. ADA also has currently been working closely with the community through community health workers who will take lead in ensuring timely identification and referral of Malnourished cases from the IDP camps.
The project will target 18,299 direct beneficiaries from the community who will benefit indirectly from the project from improved services and improved nutrition and hygiene practices.

project_name: Provision of basic and life-saving WASH services in Galmudug, South West, Hirshabelle States and Benadir region of South-Central Somalia
project_objective:
The continuation of protracted crises in Somalia, now compounded by the effects of Covid-19, Floods and droughts has resulted in massive challenges pertaining to Water, Sanitation and Hygiene. Approximately, 4.6 million Somalis are still in need due to insufficient access to portable water and inadequate sanitation services of the affected population in many districts, thus negatively affecting the country’s public health and the dignity of highly vulnerable and displaced communities. Lack of access to water and adequate sanitation in schools is also a factor contributing to poor school attendance. In historically drought-affected districts, lack of access to water for humans and for livestock remain one of the leading causes of displacement, conflict and diseases. 

According to JMCNA, approximately 8.9 million people are affected by the prevalent poor WASH conditions in Somalia. The population in need of adequate WASH services in 2021 includes approximately 1.16 million IDPs 3.36 million host communities, 53,906 Returnees and 28,002 Refugees. 

According to a Joint Rapid Assessment carried out in Galmudug State in May 2020 by the government and humanitarian partners including CPD, five IDP settlements hosting 2,000 households (12,000 people) have partially or completely lost their shelters following a heavy storm in Adado. The affected IDPs settlements include: Badbaado, Kulmiye, Karama, Daryeel and Xeeb. Moreover, 700 vulnerable households (4,200 people) from the host community also lost their shelters and household items. The multi-agency assessment indicates an estimated 68,000 internally displaced people (IDPs) who are in urban and peri urban areas in Galgaduud region have WASH needs. Most of the IDP’s do not have access to safe drinking water with the only option being unprotected berkads, putting women and children at risk as they are mostly the handlers of water in the household. New IDP’s lack sanitation facilities leading to open defecation, compromising the security and privacy of women and girls. 

The proposed interventions will include piping of water from the strategic boreholes to IDPs and vulnerable host communities in the rural areas through cash for work for digging trenches and laying pipes. It will also include rehabilitation of 12 water pans through cash for work across the target areas, provision of water bladders in IDP camps, construction of strategic boreholes, shallow wells, gender-segregated latrines for under-served public primary schools and public health facilities and hygiene promotion activities.

Persons with disabilities face additional challenges and barriers. Barriers include environmental barriers, which inhibit access to WASH facilities, as well as social barriers, leading to discrimination within communities and further aggravating the risk of exclusion to WASH services. Water and sanitation facilities such as latrines will be accessible to people with disability and this will be done through design and construction of disability-friendly facilities. Considering the figures above, there are correlations between districts that have a limited access to water and sanitation and account for a high proportion of total incidence of AWD across Somalia.

CPD is targeting 29,580 people and train management committees in order to avoid over reliance on unsustainable means of accessing clean water by using long term high yielding well managed community boreholes. Committees will also be established to maintain clean sanitation facilities, as well as scale up hygiene promotion initiatives to help minimize AWD/cholera outbreaks during the rainy seasons when there is flooding. Management committees will be inclusive by ensuring representation of women, youth and persons living with disabilities. These marginalized groups will also be consulted in all project phases including design and implementation. Covid-19 regulations and guidelines will be adopted in the project implementation.

Food assistance needs in Somalia are already high with an estimated 3.5 million people in rural livelihood zones, urban areas, and IDP settlements in need of food assistance. In riverine areas, farmers have suffered from multiple flood events during the Gu and Hagaa 2020 seasons, which damaged Deyr 2019/20 off-season crops and Gu 2020 main season crops. As a result, the main Gu harvest in July/August is significantly below average in these areas. While the floods disrupted recessional cultivation activities and inundated crops, the rains are supporting late planted Gu main season crops and Gu off-season crops and alleviated fears that the forecast of a below-average Hagaa season would deplete soil moisture and negatively affect off-season crops. In general, farmers have benefitted from improved access to water for irrigation. Worryingly however, the damage to road infrastructure and market access, have adversely affected terms of trade with higher prices of maize, and significantly lowering the prices for goats and daily labour wage rates by up to 30 and 102 per cent below the five-year average. 
WRRS will seek to offer response to the needs that has affected both the host community and the IDPs who have sought to take refuge in these proposed areas. This will be attained through improvement of HH access to food by provision of unconditional and conditional cash transfers to the beneficiaries of the targeted district of Bay and lower Juba. Besides this those who are pastorals will receive restock of animals offered with the vaccination, and poultry support with major focus of the female headed HH which will be accompanied by capacity building on best farming practices; veterinary care and pest control. The need to offer sustainable access to livelihood assets in hard to reach areas of Lower Juba and Bay will remain crucial and need urgent humanitarian response especially after the flood that has caused a lot of damage to the previously restored livelihood.

project_name: Increased access to community- and facility-based health services in Banadir, Galgadud, Mudug, Hiraan, and Togdheer regions in Somalia.
project_objective:
Mercy-USA for Aid and Development intends to set up a project to address the urgent health needs in Banadir, Galgadud, Hiran, Mudug and Togdheer regions of Somalia.  Since the collapse of Somalia's central government in 1991, repeated conflict in conjunction with poor food security, limited healthcare and nutrition service availability and has resulted in Somalia having among the worst health-related indicators in the world.
According to FSNAU-FEWSNET-2020-Post-Gu-Technical-Release, 2.1 million people across Somalia are expected to face Crisis or worse (IPC Phase 3 or higher) outcomes between now and December without sustained humanitarian assistance. FEWS NET’S research shows the NMME forecast has a strong capability to predict below-average rainfall during the October to December 2020 rainfall season in East Africa. Combined with the persistent threat of desert locust and COVID 19 pandemic, the impact of below-average rains on crop and livestock production is expected to lead to widespread deterioration of the crisis situation in northern and central pastoral areas and southern agropastoral areas in the absence of sustained assistance. There is an urgent need for a scale-up of the current response to ensure preparedness and increase resilience of the most vulnerable people i.e. already health compromised refugees, internally displaced persons and all for whom everyday sanitation, access to clean water, and the ability to practice social distancing may be virtually impossible.
This project will be a multi-sectoral initiative that is itself fully integrated into a broader humanitarian response crossing all sectors, implemented by Mercy-USA, other NGOs, other humanitarian actors, government actors, and the communities themselves. The project will be integrated to the maximum possible extent with local government entities, including the District Commissioner and head of government department in the district.
Mercy-USA will deliver primary health care services through 39 Maternal and Child Health Centers (MCHs). Mercy-USA will be facilitating the provision of medicines, supplies and equipment to the health facilities through UNICEF, while working together with the Ministry of Health (MOH) in each respective region to ensure standard provision of care and to build local capacity. Mercy-USA will train and support healthcare staff and Community Health Workers (CHWs) at each MCH facility to diagnose and treat common illnesses, provide safe pre-natal and post-natal care, and support vaccination and other health services. Mercy-USA will also promote local health, family planning counseling, safe-motherhood and safe-childhood initiatives through community sensitization. 
Mercy-USA will ensure that people with disabilities participate in the implementation of project activities by ensuring that they are represented in all community meetings. The project will consult with PWDs on the location, design, safety, and facilities' appropriateness. During project implementation, segregated focus group discussions will be held with the community to identify gender inequalities, discuss all the genders' needs, and understand the risks faced by PWDs in accessing health services. Activities will target to address these needs during program implementation. 
Access to children with disabilities and their caretakers and/or disabled pregnant and lactating women will be ensured and increased through outreach activities and behavioral change communication campaigns.
During routine and regular program monitoring and evaluation, Mercy-USA staff will collect disaggregated data by disability, age and gender to monitor the impact of programs on vulnerable groups. Mercy-USA, during both monthly and quarterly reviews and analysis of data, will seek to monitor the inclusiveness of programming by comparing achievements versus available population data.

As of September 30th, 2020, the nutrition cluster partners reached 244,727 boys and 287,318 girls aged 06-59 months covering 66% of HRP targets. Of which 190,366 are severely acute malnourished children, 341,679 moderately acute malnourished children and 104,017 PLW admitted. In order to improve the situation, integrated programming and linkages to (WASH, Health and FSL) are needed and through early action and preventive interventions to the high risk groups the situation can be addressed effectively. A Critical (4-5.6%) prevalence of Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) was observed in the Riverine livelihood of Beletweyne district and in urban Beletweyne. Morbidity among children was high (≥20%) in 15 out 33 population groups surveyed. However, Crude Death Rate and Under-Five Death Rate were relatively low in most areas. Integrated interventions should be provided to support recovery and prevent deterioration in the nutrition situation. Hiraan, Bay and Bakool region were considered hotspot areas with a projected Critical GAM prevalence, indicated by a weight-for-height z-score of 15-29.9% or by a Mid-Upper Arm Circumference below 125 mm of ≥10%, IDP areas of concern are Baidoa and Beletweyne is an urban area of concern for acute malnutrition and need of urgent nutrition and health support interventions This project therefore target to reach a total 9,000 vulnerable boys, girls and pregnant and lactating women through an integrated response around Nutrition. It is intended to mitigate the physical and protection consequences of drought on populations and communities directly affected in Bakol, Bay and Hiran region, in particular, Ceelbarde, Rabdhure, Baidoa and Beletweyne town. The main objective of this project is to provide integrated lifesaving emergency Nutrition services to 9,000 drought affected direct beneficiaries and intends to achieve the following, capacity building of nutrition staff on IMAM. Referral of malnourished children with complicated cases will be done to the Outpatient Therapeutic Programme (OTP) centers and directly linked with primary health care services managed by HIDIG and other actors in the program areas thus providing more holistic opportunity to the target beneficiaries HIDIG will closely coordinate with Local MOH as well as Federal level MOH and social mobilizers, elders all involved in activities on mobilizing communities. To support increase access to basic nutrition services in the area

project_name: Provision of Emergency health care services for the vulnerable communities in Balcad District of Middle Shabelle, Garasbaley and Shangani District of Banadir Regions Somalia
project_objective: Through this proposed project, Aid Vision will operationalize one health facility and further scale up Garasbaley and Shangani MCH that will offer life-saving primary health care services that includes but not limited to: free consultation and treatments for both under-fives and over five at the outpatient departments, immunization services, early detection and treatment of communicable diseases, free 24hours skilled, Free antenatal and postnatal care, early detection and treatment of communicable diseases both at the facility and community level by the trained health care workers. Through this initiative, community health workers will also be engaged who will active case finding, defaulter tracing, COVID-19 awareness, hygiene promotion and messaging for the hard to reach area in the target districts, further Capacity build trainings will be conducted for both qualified staff as well as community health worker to ensure quality services are offered to the vulnerable communities in the target area. For purpose of the sustainability of the project, Aid Vision will employ community based participatory approach through strengthening community capacity by capacity building own staff, local Authority staff, MoH staff and training of CHWs and established community health committees while observing gender inclusion in the top leadership of the designed committees. This approach ensures at the end of the project a strong cadre of community-based structures are built for community ownership and sustainability of the program. Further, Aid Vision will closely work with other agencies in the region by collaborating with other humanitarian key stakeholders in the area of Nutrition/WASH/Education/Food security and protection for better coordination and avoid duplication.

project_name: Provision of quality lifesaving curative Nutrition care services in Balcad Districts of Middle Shabelle Region, Garasbaley and Shangani District of Banadir Region.
project_objective:
According to HNO 2021, Despite 2020 Gu season performance rated as favorable in terms nutrition outcomes, an estimated 2.3 million people including children <5 years, pregnant and lactating women across Somalia will require lifesaving curative and preventive services. It is projected that 1.6M require preventive services while 1.4 need preventive services. Worst affected are IDP populations who account for 511,706 of the total population in need, 15% of who are persons living with disability. This is attributable to their deep seated vulnerability to arbitrary eviction and displacements due to perennial conflicts and cyclic floods and attendant food insecurity. The nutritional vulnerability of PLWs, girls and women in IDPs and urban poor communities are further exacerbated by lack of access to basic livelihood and other social sector facilities such as primary health care services, access to safe drinking water and sanitation services.
A post Deyr Assessment conducted by FSNAU revealed that GAM levels in 24 assessed IDP sites assessed had 18 sites rated as either critical or serious, an indication of how IDP children are disproportionately affected and their need for immediate lifesaving interventions.
Somalia 2020 Micronutrient Survey shows increased susceptibility of mothers and children to malnutrition. The survey discloses that approximately 40.2% of non-pregnant women and 47% of pregnant women are anemic and similarly around 43% children below five years are anemic, revealing a serious public health challenge. The report further reveals that uptake of IYCF practices is below acceptable levels of less than 20% and the same is true for minimum dietary diversity, hence recurring infections among malnourished children thereby resulting in poor or non-response to treatment and mortality if left untreated.
In light of the above, Aid Vision proposes a 12-month quality and inclusively lifesaving curative and preventive nutrition care services aimed at supporting communities in Garasbaley and Shangani districts of Banadir Region and Balcad District of Middle Shabelle Region. The project intends to conduct facility and community-based screening for severe acute malnutrition for children aged 6-59 months and pregnant and lactating women (PLW) and provide treatment of acute malnourished children 6-59 months (6400 children between 6-59 months and 2888 pregnant and lactating women) at the outpatient therapeutic centers linked to the health facilities to curb Malnutrition in the targeted districts. Further, micronutrient supplementation to PLW mothers and children 6-59 months for treatment and prevention of malnutrition, Routine individual IYCF counselling services will be conducted for PLW mother attending the facility; children aged 6-59 months will be supplemented with vitamin A, capacity building of health facility and community workers(Boys, girls, men and women ) on appropriate IYCF counselling services  to mothers attending the facility, conduct training for the facility workers as well as community nutrition workers(10 male and 10 female ) on integrated Management of Acute malnutrition(IMAM) Guidelines to ensure basic nutrition package are provided. The centers will also develop referral pathway to link patients in need of specialized care to other centers. To enhance community capacities and nutrition service uptake, community based approaches like Mother-Led MUAC screening will be adopted. Aid Vision will closely work with other partner agencies, government line ministries and local authorities in the region to better coordinate humanitarian interventions and prevent duplication.

project_name: Improved access to equitable Food Provision targeting the vulnerable and the at-risk and Food Insecure, Drought Affected, IDPs and Host Communities in Garbaharey, Gedo Region - Somalia.
project_objective:
Garbaharey district, in Gedo Region, continues to face a number of food insecurty related challenges. There are 49,394.32 people in need (PiN) falling within the IPC 3 & 4 according to Food Security Cluster. The eratic weather patterns and repeated crop failures have routinely depleted assets and contributed to lack of sustainable livelihood opportunities effectively affecting the resilience programs.

Food security is an important element in the stability and health of the people in Garbaharey, Gedo Region. Food insecurity has thus been consistered a worrying priority by different actors within the Gedo riverine and pastorals areas. This adds to the insecurity challenges which straddles the district. As such, the project seeks to increase food security for the at risk communities in Garbahare host and IDPs by integrated food-related multipronged interventions including screening, provision of food referrals, and awareness. The project aim is to reduce malnutrition, ameliorate severe effects, or fatalities associated with lack of adequate and nutritious food to the at-risk population especially Pregnant and Lactating Women and their children between 6 - 59 months.

A very important element of the project is building resilience through provision of relevant skills to increases self-reliance, enhance self-sustenance and provide cutionary livelihood activities against shocks. The targeted are the IDPs and those whose assets and sources of livelihood were destroyed affected by prolonged drought and demonstrate susceptibility to food deficiency diseases. Identification is done through standard screening processes and capacity building to PLW to undertake MUAC screening methodologies. Periodic screening, coordination with the local actors including the local administration.

project_name: Emergency livelihoods and nutrition assistance to improve resilience of the crisis-affected population in the North West and South West regions of Cameroon
project_objective:
Since the onset of the anglophone crisis in 2018, the situation has further deteriorated with the invasions of NSAGs on the population such as kidnappings with ransom demands, executions, destruction of property and infrastructure, the destruction and burning down of schools and hospitals. This situation has therefore led to a massive displacement of people fleeing the armed conflict and famine towards neighbouring Nigeria and to safer areas.
According to September 2020 SITREP of OCHA, with more than 705 8000 IDPs, 360 5000 returnees and 609 000 Cameroonian refugees in Nigeria and  increasing number of causalities on the military side, non-state actors and civilian end as well. A major national dialogue was organized last September 2019 to provide a solution to this situation; however, this has yielded no results so far because most of the resolutions taken were rejected by the Non State Armed groups (NSAGs). This has led to an increase in violence as could be observed especially with the approach of the regional election planned for December 6, 2020 and Municipal/Legislative elections which took place in February 9,2020 . These events are characterized by an increase in the number of ghost town days and armed conflicts.
“Cadre Harmonisé” results conducted in Cameroon in October 2020 showed that 1076257 people in the North-West and South-West regions are food and nutritionally insecure (crisis to emergency phases). This represents 24% of the population of the North-West and South-West and in the 10 regions of Cameroon that was analyzed, an average of 21.8% of the total population falls within the crisis to emergency phases. With continuous humanitarian aid, anticipated peace and next agricultural season running good, it is expected that the number of people suffering from food insecurity would have decreased by the end of the 2021 farming season but remains very worrying.Moreover, the current conflict has plunged the North West and South West regions into a drastic slowdown of economic activities in general, and agro pastoral production in particular. 
The priority of this project is to revamp the livelihoods and productive assets of internally displaced people, PWD and their host communities by setting up and monitoring highly productive micro-units of high-nutrient agro-pastoral products with high potential for financial revenue. It is reported that more than 80% of those affected by the crisis have experienced a continuous deterioration in their living standards and conditions for more than four years. In this deteriorating scenario, the scarcity of food in quantity and quality is highly noticeable. For example, the total quantity of meat (beef, egg, fish, poultry, etc.) available decreased from 27 kg/capita/year before the crisis to less than 20 kg/capita/year in these regions. In the same regard, a decrease is observed in the availability of staple foods such as maize, vegetable, cassava, plantain, and children's foods (FAOSTAT, 2019). In order to reverse the ongoing situation, the project aims to improve the food security vulnerable population in these regions by implementing sustainable vegetables, eggs, roots and tubers production systems. On the other hand, by providing a sustainable means of livelihoods, the project also aims to reduce the wide use of negative coping mechanisms enrolment of youths into armed groups, women vulnerability, PWD, IDPs and promote dialogue and governance in peace finding solutions and implementation.

project_name: Emergency WASH Support to Internally Displaced People (IDPs) and Host Communities in North and South West Regions of Cameroon
project_objective:
Under the first strategic objective of Cameroon HRP 2021, the WASH Sector has planned to provide services as per the agreed standards for immediate, early and short-term response, to address context specific WASH needs of NWSW regions of Cameroon. As per UNICEF’s project, under Cameroon HRP 2021’s Outcome, UNICEF plans to provide lifesaving assistance to people newly displaced by conflict using early recovery approaches to improve the overall access to WASH services, connecting the need for short-term emergency interventions with long term solutions and applying development principles by working directly with local communities to facilitate ownership and accountability. UNICEF seeks to improve and sustain access to safe water in target communities in South West and North West regions, and on improving and sustaining access to safe sanitation facilities and hygiene messages addressing malnutrition related risks and enhance the resilience of affected population to unexpected events or hazards e.g. disease outbreaks

Data collected about the situation through the 2020 MSNA, MIRA and Emergency Tracking Tool (ETT) were used to design the project. According to specific information gathered during assessment visits, IDPs are in urgent need of:
- Water supply systems as a majority have been neglected and in need of repair/rehabilitation to increase community’s resilience to disease outbreaks.
- Knowledge of good water, sanitation and hygiene practices including COVID-19 prevention as basis for survival
- WASH kits (family kits, menstrual kits and water treatment kits)
-Household water treatment techniques 
-Open Defecation Free environment
- Adequate personal hygiene for health improvement


Based on the actual situation, UNICEF plans to conduct the following WASH intervention:
- Support hygiene, sanitation and environmental health promotion, as well as awareness about COVID-19 prevention and water quality in affected areas and host communities;
- Increase access to safe drinking water through community training of water management committees, rehabilitation or construction of water sources, small water supply networks and distribution of household water treatment kits;
- Provide WASH kits to ensure a clean environment, maintain contingency stock for cholera and ensure adoption of good water, hygiene and sanitation practices;
- Ensure promotion of menstrual hygiene.
The response targets 380,000 IDPs and host communities. Proposed interventions will be implemented with other key sectors with priority focus on nutritional, protection and health related issues. Other partners will be involved in the WASH response; this includes local and International organizations. UNICEF will make two staff members available for the WASH response coordination and provide technical support to actors involved in carrying out the emergency WASH response during the intervention. Specific needs will receive special attention, as well as beneficiaries’ protection during the emergency WASH intervention, particularly at sites where internally displaced populations are gathered.

project_name: Scaling Up Emergency Nutrition Response in North West and South West Region of Cameroon
project_objective:
UNICEF Nutrition planned nutrition response aims at scaling up critical lifesaving interventions for treatment of severe forms of wasting and prevention of under nutrition in North West and South West Regions. The planned response is in tandem with the nutrition cluster HRP 2021 strategy and response framework.

UNICEF will support the screening of children under-5 for acute malnutrition and appropriate treatment. UNICEF will advocate and explore adoption of simplified approaches to management of acute malnutrition to improve coverage to care for children suffering from wasting. UNICEF will also explore provision of cash to cover for the transportation expenses of caregivers seeking “inpatient” treatment of SAM treatment. Family MUAC/Mother MUAC approach will be scaled up to enhance early identification of SAM . Preventative actions that will include promotion of infant and young child feeding in emergencies (IYCF-E), deworming prophylaxis and micronutrient supplementation - Vitamin A supplementation (VAS) and iron folate supplementation with the aim of addressing micronutrient deficiencies. For 2021, UNICEF will also focus on ensuring equitable access of iron/folic acid supplementation and deworming prophylaxis by pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers - with special attention to pregnant adolescent girls. 

To reinforce partners and the community’s capacity to deliver basic nutrition services to affected communities, UNICEF will support training of additional Trainers of Trainers (ToT) at regional level who will later cascade the training at the health district levels. Furthermore, alternative approaches of capacity development to complement the conventional classroom training will be explored and tested e.g use of short videos, On Job Training. To inform evidence-based programming, the nutrition information system will be strengthened. A rapid nutrition assessment (RNA) will be conducted in the 2nd quarter of 2021, in accordance with guidance on resumption of surveys in the context of Covid 19 Pandemic and this will to complement Programme data. UNICEF will strengthen the supply chain management with focus on prepositioning of nutrition inputs (RUTF, F75/F100), IEC Materials, drugs and anthropometric equipment at health districts level to ensure continuity of services in the event of movement restrictions. Furthermore, UNICEF will continue strengthening nutrition cluster coordination and enhance multisectoral collaboration with other nutrition sensitive clusters (Health, Food Security, WASH and protection) to maximise optimal nutritional outcomes.

UNICEF nutrition response will apply the principle of “do no harm” and mainstream aspects related to gender, protection centrality, age, gender, disability and Accountability to Affected Population (AAP). Nutrition trainings will incorporate sessions these cross-cutting issues. Interventions will be also be adapted in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic and enhanced with integrated Communication for Development (C4D) capacities.  

UNICEF will partner with organizations that have a better level of operational capacity, access to and acceptance by populations in need. Intervention will use of static health structures, mobile clinics, rapid response mechanism (RRM) and comprehensive child response (CCR) approaches to access the affected population both in accessible and those in hard to reach remote areas.

The target groups will include boys and girls under-five for screening, referral, children with SAM, Vitamin A supplementation and deworming prophylaxis. Adolescent, pregnant and breastfeeding will be targeted for the iron and folic acid and deworming prophylaxis. Health workers will be targeted for trainings on SAM management (mobilize, screen and refer acutely malnourished), information Management (DHIS II) and IYCF-E.

project_name: Addressing food insecurity of conflict-affected communities in Northern Syria.
project_objective: The proposed project aims at improving food security of conflict-affected communities in Northeast and Northwest Syria, with an approach geared at saving lives with emergency assistance, and increasing resilience at household and community level with improved food production capacity and livelihoods opportunities. This will be achieved through a combination of different interventions at the individual and community-level. At the individual level, emergency responses will be delivered through distribution of in-kind food baskets and Ready-to-Eat Rations, as well as Cash-for-Work and Cash-for-Food schemes, benefiting 51,242 individuals, including recently displaced persons. This emergency response will complement multiple rounds of recurrent, monthly food assistance, which will constitute the core of the intervention, reaching 232,800 beneficiaries in and out of camp through cash, voucher, or in-kind modalities for at least 8 months. In addition, ACTED will enhance food production at HH level, through kitchen and home garden kits, enhancing individuals' food security.  Both emergency and monthly activities will be completed by Nutritional Awareness Sessions, targeting all beneficiaries regardless of the modality through which they received support, which will strengthen HHs’ ability to make informed choices regarding nutritional values. ACTED will also target farmers and livestock holders with longer-term support, delivering voucher assistance to redeem seeds, fertilizers, polytunnels and tools, and training on climate-smart agriculture and best practices. At the community level, ACTED will rehabilitate communal agricultural assets, including bakeries and mills, as well as irrigation networks. These interventions will benefit both farmers (who will have increased access to water for irrigation through network rehabilitation) and communities (who will be able to access good quality bread through bakeries rehabilitation). All project activities will be designed in a way that enables resilience to be built at a local level and that builds the capacity of men, women, boys, and girls to access basic items and meet basic needs themselves. Specifically, at the household and community levels, ACTED will support men and women in building their own capacities to meet their basic needs so that they are more resilient and better able to access commodities and services in the future. Lastly, ACTED will work in coordination with local technical department with the aim of building their capacity to provide essential services for communities. This project is estimated to benefit a total of 344,319 individuals. ACTED will rely on a variety of selection criteria depending on the assistance modality, including recent displacement, no access to similar food assistance prior to the intervention, low economic status/conditions, food assistance not covering household needs, absence of regular income source, etc. Criteria such as market accessibility and labor opportunities in each area of implementation will determine assistance modalities between in-kind and voucher/cash. For business grants support, beneficiaries will selected on the basis of application presenting a business plan.

project_name: Emergency WASH response and Building Resilience to crisis affected Syrian men, women, boys and girls in Syria
project_objective:
Building on experience of project interventions in Syria since 2013, Oxfam continues to work with local authorities  in responding to the vulnerable populations’ WASH needs  in districts/subdistricts of Aleppo, Hama, Idlib, Rural Damascus, Dar’a and Deir Ezzor, based on assessments, severity of needs  and in response to further emerging needs in NES and NWS. The subdistricts that will be targeted by this project have all been heavily affected by conflict and require WASH support.  OXFAM conducted integrated WASH and EFSVL assessments from January 2021 to date covering over 50 communities through group discussions and key informant in three governorates. This includes consultations with LNGOs, INGOs, secondary data and the Humanitarian Needs Overview 2021.  The project is designed to meet specific lifesaving needs around water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) strongly aligned to the WASH Sector. It is gender mainstreamed, with a response strategy overarched by a community engagement approach suitable to access and security challenges; implementation engages trusted community structures, experienced local site engineers, carefully screened private contractors, community-based volunteers and identified local partners, and strong collaboration with other actors.  
The total estimated population, as per UN-OCHA datasets in these sub-districts, is over 1.1m people. OXFAM targets the timely response to emerging rapid onset emergency needs in hot spots and potential flashpoints, new returns, new displacements, affected by COVID-19, economic issues, and the current returned areas with persisting WASH needs. The target locations proposed are according to severity of humanitarian needs and number of populations in need which will be adapted to the evolving ground context, access and people's movement. The project aims to support lifesaving WASH interventions that additionally pay attention to ensuring locally sustained maintenance of repaired existing WASH systems:  The objectives of the project are; 1): support to water, sanitation/sewage and solid waste management systems to ensure regular services for affected people in Syria; 2): deliver humanitarian WASH supplies and services, and improve hygienic behavior and practices of most vulnerable people; 3) WASH coordination structures facilitated and enhanced; and 4) improve WASH facilities and services in institutions to minimize sub-standard WASH conditions of the most vulnerable people in Syria. The type of interventions strongly aligns with: SO1, SO2, SO3 and SO4 which captures the sector efforts to respond and assist local water establishments in restoring WASH services to basic functionality for communities, schools and community health facilities. Oxfam will target all age groups for water and sanitation interventions.  Hygiene interventions, will target   carers,  women, adolescent girls and school  children. Accurate disaggregation of population data will be collected from relevant ministries and actors to ensure coordinated and relevant data and appropriate interventions during WASH assessments and interventions.  Oxfam has a unique MOUs with several ministries gaining  trust, strong relations and approval of interventions. Bi-monthly meetings at the MoWR allow insight and agreement for selection of prioritized possible activities and discussion of operational challenges. This project’s close alignment with the HRP in terms of outcomes, activities and methodology is a reflection of Oxfam’s close engagement with the Sector, particularly through strategic discussions and information sharing throughout 2019 and 2021.

project_name: Safe access to sanitation services and hygiene promotion for un-connected vulnerable communities and people hosted in the quarantine centers across the Gaza Strip
project_objective:
This project which is proposed to be implemented in 2021 by Action Against Hunger (AAH) and the Charitable Future Society (CFS) across the Gaza Strip aligns with Strategic Objectives 2 and 3 as well as the WASH Cluster Objectives 2 and 3. 
On one hand, the project aims to support vulnerable families (including women, men, girls and boys, elderly and people with disability and specific needs) who depend on cesspits only to discharge their wastewater. Through connecting families of Al Fukhkhari, Maan, Alstar and Jawrat Alluwt communities to an adequate wastewater drainage system, the different interventions aim to protect individuals from being in contact with flooded wastewater during the winter season due to the accumulation of stormwater in the cesspits flooding in the streets and in hospitals and schools. This will further help prevent the risks of infections and diseases from flooded wastewater and other health-related issues. A public awareness campaign targeting newly connected households will spread messages on safe water handling, improving the capacity of families in targeted areas to address hygiene practice issues at household level. This awareness campaign will include information on COVID-19 mitigation measures, to contribute to the efforts to limit the spread of the pandemic in the occupied Palestinian territory (oPt).
On the other hand, the project will provide wastewater collection and discharge systems for targeted quarantine centers (QCs), hosting returnees to the Gaza Strip during their mandatory isolation period to mitigate the spread of COVID-19, avoiding municipalities to evacuate cesspits. Disinfection units will be added to prevent the virus to propagate through wastewater.
In addition, AAH will carry out a technical study to pilot new techniques to improve access to WASH services in the community water facilities, with support from the Water Quality Working Group (WQWG) and key actors in the WASH sector. 

The proposed intervention is guided by AAH Gender and Protection policy and AAH staff endeavor to streamline safety and dignity in all humanitarian interventions. Accountability and participation will be ensured through interviews and focus group discussions and through applying AAH’s thorough Feedback and Complaint Mechanism.

project_name: Most vulnerable schools and students, boys and girls, in Gaza and the West Bank provided with emergency supplies to continue learning
project_objective:
The project responds to Cluster Objective 3 “Children and school staff in vulnerable schools are supported in preparing and responding to emergencies.” The Education Cluster estimates that 503,927 people (47% females) need Education in Emergencies humanitarian assistance across the West Bank and Gaza. The estimated figures reflect an increase in the need for humanitarian assistance in 2021. This is based on an analysis of trends over the recent five months which revealed a marked deterioration in the overall humanitarian situation in oPt due to the Covid-19 pandemic. More families have been pushed into poverty, undermining their ability to afford basic education supplies and increasing the risk of school dropout. 

The project will support over 30,000 poorest students in West Bank and Gaza aged 6-17 (50% girls), who may be at risk of dropout due to poverty, to continue in their education by providing basic, urgent supplies including school bags, and winterization items such as school uniforms, warm clothes, and shoes. The provision of the winterization items to children will be through the e-voucher programme with WFP to allow the targeted beneficiaries the option to select their own supplies. In the past, distribution of school uniforms was done through schools and the feedback from beneficiaries was that the children felt stigmatized by their peers as poor children. Providing options to the families to procure the uniforms through e-vouchers would minimize stigmatizing children in that their peers will not know those benefitting from the free uniforms. The target vulnerable households will be selected from the database of relevant authorities, cross referenced with the vulnerable community assessment list developed by UNICEF and relevant authorities and verified by the OCHA list of hardship cases. Priority will be given to female-headed households, households with children with disabilities and households with children affected by the Great March of Return. Due to a lack of an operational budget, 421 schools in Gaza are starting the new school year without basic teaching and learning supplies and struggling to afford basic stationery, paper and chalk. These schools will be supported with basic teaching and learning supplies. 

The COVID-19 emergency has further exacerbated the already existing vulnerabilities created by an unprecedented fiscal crisis for the Palestinian Authority (PA) which worsened after the PA’s decision of not receiving tax collected by the Israel as a response to the threat of annexation. The education sector has particularly been hit hard affecting over 1.4 million children in both the West Bank and Gaza. Schools are unable to provide the necessary school hygiene materials to operationalize the guidelines for Safe Schools Operations.  In this context, 600 schools (179 in the West Bank and 421 in Gaza) will be supported with school hygiene kits to help them operationalize safe schools protocols in their schools.

project_name: Strengthening the Delivery of Integrated Primary Health Care Services to Vulnerable Populations in BAY States
project_objective:
This project is designed to build on gains achieved from providing improved integrated PHC services in supported vulnerable communities in Borno, Adamawa and Yobe states. These states are share borders with Cameroon, Chad and Niger respectively and are the most affected in the 11-year armed conflict that has seen over 2.1 million persons internally displaced with over 1 million refugees in the neighboring countries. The majority of IDPs in Borno are in host communities in camp-like settlements and around 15% in IDP camps characterized by congestion and other specific challenges and vulnerabilities with an already suboptimal functioning health service, poor and inadequate shelter and poor hygiene conditions.
Escalating clashes between armed actors in this protracted complex crisis is a major driver of displacements towards garrison settlements especially in Borno state.
Intercommunal conflicts are also major cause of displacements especially in Adamawa state. The effects of these stressors are made manifest in the health indices (U5MR, NMR, MMR, SAM rates) and other socioeconomic indices (literacy rates, food security index, etc). The BAY states are also prone to natural disasters such as droughts and flooding and consequent environmental degradation coupled with poor water and waste management, the possibility of disease outbreaks such as Cholera is very high as experienced in Adamawa State in 2019.
All these causes, contributing factors and effects are made much worse considering the COVID-19 pandemic which has affected the region as well. The pandemic affected access to health facilities and stretched already limited resources as health partners struggled to respond effectively to the novel disease that has claimed over 1 million lives globally. In the BAY states as of 29 November 2020, a total of 1,123 confirmed cases had been recorded including 63 deaths, 26 active cases and 1,034 recoveries. Borno is the worst affected with 758 cases and 36 deaths.
The BAY states suffer from a greatly debilitated health system which is currently being strengthened through close collaboration between humanitarian actors and government with significant gains over the past two years. It is therefore critical that the COVID-19 outbreak readiness and response strategies, plan and operations are strengthened and extended to all persons regardless of status and ensures inclusiveness as well as protecting and sustaining the progresses made in health systems strengthening (HSS)
 
through a multisectoral approach.
UNICEF in partnership with the state government agencies (SPHCDAs and SPHCMBs) and the State Ministries of Health of the BAY states will continue to provide integrated primary health care to locations with high and moderate humanitarian needs and continue to support HSS in the rest of the states. We will focus on how to reach people in need including returnees, support the states to implement interventions that will enable transition from emergency phase to development in some LGAs, partner with INGOs that are present on the ground and provide strategic technical assistance in building capacity for resilience at the community level. We will review existing supplies and focus on the critical component. We will leverage resources through convergence with other sections within UNICEF and other sectors at the state, LGAs and community levels.
The following objectives will be met through the project:
1.	Support the provision of basic essential quality health care services to vulnerable populations.
2.	Support the timely disease outbreak response through active participation in EOC activities.
3.	Support improved access to health care strengthening health system recovery, enhance resilience, and promote humanitarian-development linkages.
4.	Support mitigation of the risk and contain the spread of the COVID-19 pandemic and decrease morbidity and mortality in IDP camps and host communities.

project_name: Critical Humanitarian Water, Sanitation and Hygiene Services in Emergency-affected Communities in North East Nigeria (Borno, Adamawa, and Yobe) and other States
project_objective:
UNICEF is both a service provider under the partner presence rationalization in the sector and the provider of last resort (POLR). The largest response is in NE Nigeria (Borno, Adamawa and Yobe states) where protracted armed conflict has continued to force displacement of population into camps and camp-like settlements for more than a decade.  In other regions, the need for response arise from sporadic conflicts, natural disasters like floods or risks of outbreaks/spread of infectious diseases such as cholera, which is endemic in Nigeria, and the recent covid-19 or other hazards.   Gaps also arise as a results of new population displacements or diminished capacity/departure of other humanitarian WASH partners. As a service provider, UNICEF is optimizing the water production and distribution, increasing attainment of the required minimum standards.  UNICEF is rolling out the approach of urban type network water distribution in deep field LGAs with high yielding boreholes and high-density population of displaced persons or returnees and host communities.  This approach will support decongestion in camps and expansion of WASH services to schools and health/nutrition facilities.   UNICEF will also expand cash in wash programming for hygiene kits and other WASH NFIs.

Through this project, UNICEF will have specific target populations in needs in IDP camps in Borno State, specifically in Maiduguri Metropolitan City and 10 LGAs (Bama, Dikwa, Gwoza, Jere, Kara Balge, Konduga, Mafa, Mobbar, Monguno, and Ngala), whilst in Adamawa and Yobe, and possibly other states, the target population will be determined by locations where needs will arise.  UNICEF will adhere to the SPHERE standards and scale up the sustenance of the services as needed. 

To meet the demands of the POLR responsibility, UNICEF may need to mobilize additional resources.  Through this project UNICEF will provide the initial lifesaving response to fill the gaps, prioritizing areas receiving newly displaced people or under an outbreak of cholera, hepatitis or other WASH-related diseases including covid-19. UNICEF will strive to sustain the basic initial WASH services until further response becomes available from other sector partners.  The project is also aimed at sustaining critical humanitarian water, sanitation and hygiene services to displaced population affected by protracted armed conflict in NE Nigeria (Borno, Adamawa and Yobe States: target 5,540,800 people) and emergency affected population in four states including other locations.  500,000 of the target population are at risk of covid-19 infection.    

The project objectives and targets are:

1) Affected people have safe and equitable access to safe water for domestic needs, as per SPHERE standards. This objective aims at scaling up sustainable water supply coverage in IDP camps to reach 15 litres per person per day. Target: 624,000 people.
2) Affected people have sustained access to safe water for drinking, cooking and personal hygiene.  Target 1,261,670 people.
3) Affected people have safe and dignified access to gender and disability-sensitive facilities at a rate of 20 users/pit for latrines. This objective aims at scaling up sustainable sanitation coverage in
IDP camps to reach latrine coverage standard of 20 users per latrine. Target: 229,320 people.
4) Affected people sustainably access clean, disinfected and desludged latrines.  Target 875,520 people.
5) Affected people reached with key hygiene messages.  This objective aims at reaching 1,985,000 people in IDP camps and host communities and other affected locations with risk informed behaviour change communication messages in 2021.
6) Affected people living in camps and camp-like settlement reached with critical WASH supplies and/or cash for NFIs. This objective will also cover WASH supplies to newly affected people in all locations with initial response hygiene kits. Target: 500,000 people.

project_name: Integrated nutrition response for the prevention and treatment of malnutrition among children, adolescents and women of reproductive age in conflict affected BAY States.
project_objective:
According to the Nutrition and Food Security Surveillance Round 9 (NFSS IX) and the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification Acute Malnutrition analysis 2020 (IPC AMN), the nutrition situation in Borno and Yobe State is classified as Phase 3 (Serious) and Adamawa at Phase 2 (Alert) level, with Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) levels of 13.6% in Yobe, 10.7% in Borno and 7.5% in Adamawa. The nutritional situation is expected to deteriorate further due to worsening of the immediate and underlying causes including increased displacement, sub-optimal childcare practices and feeding environments, food insecurity and the socio-economic impact of COVId-19.

To overcome this challenge of malnutrition, UNICEF nutrition interventions will aim at reducing malnutrition through the provision the lifesaving treatment services for Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) whilst strengthening malnutrition prevention measures amongst children aged below 5 years, adolescent girls and boys, pregnant and lactating women. Specifically, this will include;

	Direct interventions for treatment: Procuring, managing and prepositioning nutrition supplies (Ready to Use Therapeutic Food, essential routine medicines, anthropometric equipment and data tools) for effective management of SAM. A total of 295,288 cartons of RUTF will be procured to cover the sector target of 295,288 children aged 6-59 months who are envisaged to suffer from SAM in 2021. Timely detection, referral and treatment of children with SAM in Borno (116,257), Adamawa (60,209) and Yobe (118,822). This is 100% of overall sector target for SAM treatment as UNICEF will provide all the required RUTF needs for the collective nutrition response. UNICEF will provide Mid Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) tapes to all pregnant and lactating women to necessitate scale up of family MUAC approach.

	Direct preventive interventions: Promoting exclusive breast feeding among children aged below 6 months , improving the consumption of quality diets for children, adolescents and women of reproductive age, iron folic acid supplementation for adolescents and women of reproductive age group, Vitamin A supplementation and deworming among children and adolescents.

	Indirect promotional interventions: Promoting uptake of optimum maternal, child feeding and care practices among 361,470 Borno (153,213), Adamawa (106,962) and Yobe (101,295). pregnant and lactating women in the BAY states. This represents 60% of sector targets. This will be done through community-based support groups as well as facility-based approaches.

	Strengthening nutrition governance; integration of nutrition information within the health  information system, supply integration with health as well as technical capacities of government, partners and community to prevent, identify and treat malnutrition from a life-cycle approach.

	Strengthening Nutrition Surveillance to determine the evolving nutrition situation that will further inform the response implementation strategy and location prioritization. 

	Coordination and information management of the collective the nutrition response in BAY States.

UNICEF has planned to mobilize and generate $39.8 million funds to accomplish the planned activities for children and women in North east Nigeria.

project_name: Integrated Protection assistance for conflict affected boys and girls including Women and Men.
project_objective: SC proposes a one-year integrated CP programming with Nutrition in Borno state. High nutrition and protection needs, heightened by C-19, requires SC to continue supporting vulnerable communities in Jere and Konduga LGAs, while expanding to Mafa LGA, where high needs and service delivery gaps require immediate intervention. Due to recent increases in protection needs and risks faced by girls and boys, SC plans to: (i) reinforce existing CP Committees (CPCs) in Jere and Konduga, and establish new ones in Mafa. (ii) SC will continue to provide PSS to improve wellbeing of vulnerable girls and boys. SC will establish 2 new and support 6 existing CFSs, where structured, age- and gender-specific recreational and social activities will be held. To mitigate spread of C-19, SC also adopted a house-to-house approach to provide PSS. SC Plans to reach 10,000 Children in 2021 with psychosocial support activities including to reinforce the PSS activities with HEART approach which is an evidenced based Programme to improve the wellbeing of children affected by the conflict through healing and education through Art. SC plans to reach 1500 Children with case management service provision including those at risk of GBV, survivors of SGBV, CAFAAG etc.

project_name: Improved access to adequate housing and community infrastructure in Libya
project_objective:
NRC’s shelter program in Libya seeks to improve the living conditions and physical protection and well-being of conflict affected populations and internally displaced persons through the maintenance and rehabilitation of houses for vulnerable families residing in or intending to return to damaged or substandard houses in urban settings, the rehabilitation works will focus in improving protection from the elements, physical security and safety as well as improving access to functioning sanitation facilities and water. The intervention will aim at supporting a total of 160 households divided between Benghazi and Tripoli. 

The program will also promote improved access to basic services through the investment in rehabilitating and upgrading community infrastructure such as health facilities, power utilities, roads, or communal buildings providing essential services to the public. This component of the program will be mainly focused in Tripoli in areas that have been heavily affected and damaged by the conflict during the past year. The Program will aim at providing infrastructure solutions in three neighborhoods benefiting an estimated 1,500 individuals.

In Tripoli the program will also promote safe and dignified returns of IDP’s that remain unable to return due to the physical conditions of their shelters or due to the lack of adequate community infrastructure.

project_name: Emergency FSL intervention to Vulnerable Populations (IDPs, Returnees and Host Communities) in South Sudan
project_objective:
In South Sudan 6.35 Million people (52.6% of the population), 5.82 million (48.3% of the population) and 7.24 million people (60% of the population) were projected in October to November 2020, December 2020 to March 2021 and April to July 2021 respectively to faced crisis (IPC phase 3) or worse acute food insecurity. An estimated 24,000 people were classified in Catastrophe (IPC phase 5) acute food insecurity, of which 89,820 people in Tonj North County of Warrap state are in IPC phase 5 (IPC South Sudan Oct 2020 - July 2021). Almost half of Tonj North County have a convergence of high needs related to food insecurity, protection and WASH due to inter-communal conflicts.  Livelihood needs in Kajo-Keji, Terekeka and Kapoeta East are dire given that they are classified as IPC 4. The proposed intervention aims to saves lives, enhance early recoveries and build community resilience by addressing the main drivers of vulnerabilities because apparently unresolved conflicts leaves these areas extremely fragile. With the advent of COVID-19 with lockdown the already ailing economy drastically went down making the already vulnerable population lose their livelihoods and ability to feed their families. It is widely appealed that in order to save lives and avert total collapse of livelihoods in the affected counties, particularly those with the populations in catastrophe IPC Phase 5 and Emergency IPC Phase 4, there is an urgent need for immediate scale-up humanitarian assistance. 
The intervention will seek to support 41,850 vulnerable people with emphasis on access to food emergency livelihoods deprived during conflict and floods. IRW will provide food items, unconditional and conditional cash transfers in all areas of intervention except Tonj North where delivery of food items to the beneficiaries will be through Voucher. To further strengthen resilient livelihoods income diversification the project will provide pathways for communities to recover and adapt to climate variability. Activities will provision of inputs for crop and vegetable production, distribution of livelihood kits with farming tools (hoes, moloda, rakes) crop seeds (groundnut, maize, sorghum, cowpeas), and vegetable seeds (tomatoes, onion, eggplant, Okra, kale, kudra, Amaranth). IRW will also conduct basic training in agronomic- and post-harvest practices, and emerging threats such as trans-boundary crop diseases.
Enhancing household resilience will be through capacity building including trainings on modern livestock management and milk handling and processing to increase production, Community Animal health Workers (CAHWs) will be trained and provided start up kits for management of livestock diseases. The CAHWs are specifically work on livestock and poultry.  Trainings will be done by facilitators contracted from the department of Livestock at state level because they use local languages understandable by beneficiaries.  Some households will benefit from Re-stocking of livestock program to replace the animals which were killed or died during the crisis as registered and confirmed by the local beneficiary community themselves during open meetings; Distribution of fishing kits and training on fish preservation and marketing during fishing seasons in river areas. Training of Community Agricultural Extension Workers (CAEW) who specifically deal with crops by providing extension services to farmers benefiting from the in order to increase agriculture production.
The intervention is expected to reinforce and strengthen protection of the various groups affected by the conflict. Livelihood roles are expected to change to include women as decision makers in household income generation hence reducing the risks of SEA accosted with poverty. IRSS will conduct FSL based protection risk analysis to mitigate all risks to various groups women, girls and children and the marginalized of the affected group. Awareness on GBV, sexual exploitation and child abuse and exploitation.

project_name: Restored lives with dignity of  refugees and vulnerable host communities through provision of basic services in WASH, Livelihoods, Education, Health and Nutrition, Protection and Shelter /NFIs in Blue Nile, West, North, and South Kordofan, Gadaref states
project_objective:
This project is aimed to provide basic services of WASH, Livelihoods, Education, Health and Nutrition, Protection and Shelter /NFIS in all settlement sites and localities. The project will run for 12 months in El Fashaga and EL Fawo localities in Gadarif state targeting 13851 direct beneficiaries and 7400 indirect beneficiaries in WASH and education sector while in Blue Nile State targeting 3,780 direct beneficiaries and 2,400 indirect beneficiaries in WASH and FSL sector in Ed Damazine Ar Rusayris localities. Besides this project will target 28,864 direct beneficiaries and 7,541 indirect beneficiaries who have been affected by conflict, yearly flooding with poor agricultural practices, poor access to quality nutrition services and poor health seeking behavior and dilapidated wash, hygiene and sanitation services in the Shikan, Algoz and Dilling Localities of greater Kordofan which are prone to problems of food insecurity, poverty and environmental degradation.
In West Kordofan project will mainstream protection activities to address the urgent needs of 33,604 South Sudan Refugees and 6,014 vulnerable host communities in Kailak, El Mairam, Lagawa and El Nuhud Localities through a comprehensive packages of Education, WASH, and FSL & livelihood services ensuring target groups basic needs are addressed.
Recent Ethiopian refugees’ influx is increasing and so for more than 45 thousands had fled to Sudan from Ethiopia. These refugees are accommodated in UM Rakoba camp, village 8 in Gadarif and COR/UNHCR is looking to identify a new settlement site to accommodate upcoming refugees. Under this project IRW will extend its support in WASH, Education, FSL, Shelter/NFIs, Protection and CVA in all these camps in Um Rakoba, village 8 and newly identified site by the government. Project aimed to reach around 10,000 beneficiaries including male 57%, female 43 %, children 45 % and elderly people by 4% among the Ethiopian refugees in camps. 
 The proposed project will complement and linked to existing IRS projects in the proposed project sites and will include rehabilitation of WASH facilities, supporting hygiene and sanitation facilities, quality education to refugees and host communities, providing quality health and nutrition services in targeted area, providing refugees and vulnerable host communities farmers with seeds and tools, protection services and ensuring sustainable environmental practices,. Cash transfer program is also part of strategy to grant unconditional cash grant to eligible Ethiopian refugees families in camps in Gadarif state. IRS will coordinate the project activities with other partners and respective government departments in the project sites including UN agencies such as COR, UNHCR, UNICEF, WFP, FAO, UNOCHA and WHO and other humanitarian actors.

project_name: Cash Based Assistance in North West Syria
project_objective: The IRC will target some of the most vulnerable families in NW Syria through multi-purpose cash assistance. The IRC will aim at supporting families meet their most urgent basic needs through a one off cash assistance of a 100 USD, that is the full amount of the SMEB value. The IRC will monitor local markets pre and post project implementation to ensure the functionality of local markets as well as post distribution monitoring to ensure meeting project objectives or families’ meeting their most urgent needs.

project_name: Creation of income generating opportunities for vulnerable people through market driven vocational training programs in Aleppo and Deir-Ez-Zor
project_objective: In line with the priorities of the HNO and identified gaps and needs in the selected areas, the project aims at improving livelihood opportunities of vulnerable unskilled workers in Aleppo and Deir-Ez-Zor Governorates, such as women heads of households (HH) and young adults between 18 and 35 years old breadwinners of the family. The intervention will be implemented in rural areas of Aleppo and Deir-Ez-Zor. These are considered extremely poor and economically affected areas, in high need of support. The action is designed to train people providing them with knowledge and tools; they will be eventually re-inserted in the work market, boosting the local economy and assuring the sustainability of the intervention. Beneficiaries will be identified through a comprehensive and participatory approach, which involves also the analysis of data collected by WWGVC in the same areas in the past years through the conduction of non-formal education activities. The typology of the trainings, with 3 to 6-months length, will be decided through an initial market study to identify the most successful topics, with the involvement of  local/national authorities. Trainees will be provided with individual professional kits allowing them to self-create their job. Specifically, the intervention is composed of two phases: (i) plan, design, and conduction of vocational trainings to identified 800 beneficiaries, and (ii) facilitate their regular employment access through linkages with workplaces and distribution of individual professional kits. The target of the intervention are adults breadwinner of the families, identified as the most vulnerable and in need of such support. The identification phase will rely on the analysis of data collected through previous WWGVC implemented projects about families with out-of-school children. Specifically, the intervention will privilege households with out-of-school children due to economic reasons, and/or with children at risk of dropping out, aiming not only to create a job opportunity, but also to facilitate the children’s school re-insertion and/or school retention. The initiative will have an impact that will not only directly benefit the head of households, but dramatically improve the economic condition of their entire families, with positive impacts to close relatives and neighborhoods.

project_name: Strengthening and scaling up emergency protection services for the flood affected populations through gender-based violence (GBV) prevention and response in Benadir and South West State
project_objective:
Somalia continues to face triple humanitarian threats; desert locust, floods and the COVID-19 Pandemic. Among the 5.2 million in need in Somalia this year, 3.5 million are women of reproductive age. Although some COVID-19 restrictions have been eased in the country, the food insecurity situation has already deteriorated due to the ongoing locust infestation. The triple crises have exacerbated pre-existing vulnerabilities of women and girls and affected livelihoods for the poor families and internally displaced persons in most parts of the country. Also, the number of women and girls facing abuse including sexual violence has significantly increased due to restrictions on movement, as well as economic and social stresses induced by the COVID-19 pandemic. According to GBV IMS report about 1599 GBV incidents from January to February 2020. Out of the 1599 Incidents, 72 percent accounted for intimate partner violence, sexual assault accounted for 12 percent and rape 13 percent, psychological emotional abuse at 9 percent, physical assault at 52 percent, forced marriage at 4 percent and denial of resources and opportunities at 9 percent. Sexual violence, particularly rape within the drought and conflict hot spots account for 15 percent. 75 percent of the GBV survivors are IDPs and 97 percent of these are female. Furthermore, the protection cluster has concerns that the protective environment for the IDPs and civilians affected by the drought and conflict remains weak and requires strengthening to respond.
The proposed project is designed to provide immediate lifesaving services and risk mitigation to GBV survivors and vulnerable women and girls in the IDPs and host communities affected by floods, droughts and conflicts in Daynile, Dharkenley, Kahda districts of Mogadishu, and Afgoye and Marka district of lower shabelle Region through the following interventions: - Provision of Clinical Care for Sexual Assault survivors (CCSAS), Case management (CM) Psycho social support (PSS), tailored material support including emergency support for safe spaces and dignity kits to survivors of GBV and extremely vulnerable women affected by the floods and conflicts. Addition, SOYDA will provide transport cost to GBV survivors to facilitate access to post exposure prophylaxis in different health facilities. This project will strengthen service mapping to facilitate appropriate referrals, coordination and linkages in service delivery to ensure quality comprehensive services to gender-based violence (GBV) survivors
SOYDA is one of the few organization actively providing GBV/CP services and case management in Lower Shebelle supported by SHF. 173 GBV cases were reported over the last 8 months (SOYDA GBVIMS, January 2020- August 2020); 32% were rape and 48% were physical/domestic violence. Over the last year SOYDA has been building capacity in case management and clinical management of rape survivors (CMR). Currently there are no safe shelters or material support for survivors to access services. It is necessary to improve the quality of care by 1) CMR technical support for health staff in the two operational hospitals, 2) reception of GBV cases and provision of comprehensive case management, 3) supply and management of post-rape drugs in coordination with UNFPA And MoH, 4) material assistance and emergency support at the women friendly spaces intended to improve the protective environment and respire their dignity. 
Communities, authorities and humanitarian actors have limited knowledge awareness of GBV risks and consequences and have limited practical involvement for GBV prevention and response. Non-GBV humanitarian actors across all sectors, and the local government authorities have identified this gap in knowledge and practice. Although SOYDA have been working with GBV AoR to establish referral system and increase awareness of services in target areas, there is still a need to strengthen engagement of communities, service providers and authorities

project_name: Providing life-saving WASH assistance and restoration of access to safe and equitable basic WASH services to most vulnerable communities displaced by conflicts, drought, floods, and diseases , living  in Lower juba, Middle Shebele, Banadir, Sool and Sanaag  region of Somalia/Somaliland
project_objective:
In the context of the current multi-faceted emergencies (increased risks of flooding, protracted conflict, droughts, Covid 19, Cholera/AWD Outbreaks and the projected La Nina phenomena expected in Somalia, ARC proposes this emergency WASH project to target IDPs and most vulnerable host communities living in Kismayo, Benadir, lascanod,Xudun, Telex,  Afmadow, Balcad, Badade , and El-Afweyne district with aim of saving lives and reducing morbidities associated with WASH-related diseases. ARC understands that internal displacements are the key driver of humanitarian needs in Somalia. Many IDPs and Poor vulnerable Host communities are currently residing in Urban and pre-urban informal crowded areas with insufficient access to water and Sanitation. According to JMCNA assessment done in August by REACH, 53% of the IDPs face challenges in terms of access to WASH services in Somalia. The situation of IDPs and non- IDPs vulnerable host community members are complicated by frequent forced evictions meted on them leading to disruptions of access to critical  WASH services and  loss of gains made on access to these essentials services. According to an assessment done by ARC in Mogadishu in September 2020, more than 7000 IDPs households were forcefully evicted from their homes in Kaxda district, Benadir in the past three months. Ongoing conflicts and riverine flooding along Juba and Shebelle will continue to displace more people to major towns. In Sanaag and Sool regions, persistent clan conflicts, insecurity and recurring droughts are the major cause of displacement of people in the region.
Cognizant of these contexts,  ARC will provide emergency water trucking to  12000 (2000HH) Drought- affected IDPs and vulnerable pastoral communities living in drought-prone areas of lascanod, xudun, telex and Celf-Afweyn districts for a period of two months as the agency will find and  rehabilitate alternative water sources for the affected people. 20 critical shallow wells will be rehabilitated and protected targeting IDPs and Non- IDPs vulnerable communities and settlements from Kismayo, Kaxda &Darkenley (Banadir), lascanod, Cel-Afweyne and Telex. ARC will also conduct Disinfections and chlorination of floods affected wells.
