project_name: Ensuring availability of Essential health services with strengthening of disease monitoring including COVID-19 prevention and response, for the disaster  affected and high disease burden districts of Pakistan
project_objective:
Pakistan is a disaster-prone country mostly faced with floods, droughts, earthquakes and is currently passing   through the second wave of COVID-19 pandemic. The ongoing COVID19 Pandemic has further deteriorated the situation as the country is faced with both direct and indirect morbidities and mortalities due to COVID pandemic. COVID-19 cases are the highest in Sindh and Punjab provinces and certain urban areas of Balochistan followed by KP.To date, the total number of cases notified since the beginning of the outbreak is 488,529 with 10,350 deaths (CFR: 2.12%).

Most recently, heavy rains in Pakistan in august 2020 resulted in devastating floods affected many districts in Sindh and Balochistan province resulting damages to infrastructure and properties and population displacement. Sindh is the highly affected province followed by Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa respectively. Literature reveals that global warming, unpredicted heavy rains and floods, population displacement due to natural and man-made disasters result in outbreaks of water and vector borne diseases resulting in high morbidity and mortality. Most districts of Balochistan, Sindh and KP are more prone to natural emergencies, already show poor development indicators including health. The country has suffered approximately $18 billion in damages and losses from natural disasters over the past decade. It has been estimated that nearly 3 million people are affected by disasters in Pakistan each year; the annual economic impact of floods – which affects 77% of all Pakistanis affected by disasters – is estimated between $1.2 billion to $1.8 billion, equivalent to 0.5% to 0.8% of Pakistan’s GDP. 
Due to the unexpected flooding situation in Sindh, on 25th august 2020 emergency was declared in 20 of the 29 districts in the province. In Sindh 2.2 million people have been directly or indirectly been affected by the flooding with 77,337 houses fully damaged and 137,007 partially damaged in 15,233 villages. 
The second most affected province is Balochistan where torrential rains lashed 22 districts of Baluchistan province on Saturday 7 August 2020 caused flooding and damaged bridges and highways, cutting off highways Gwadar-Karachi, Quetta-Jacobabad from main cities. Initially, it has been reported that Jhal Magsi, Jafferabad, Sibi, Harnai, Naseerabad and Kachi Districts areas are badly affected by the floods. 
Health related effects in flood affected areas of Sindh revealed that 15% of the health facilities are nonfunctional. The nonfunctional facilities are more based in the rural settings, compared to urban. The provision of round the clock (24/7) services in the functional health facilities of the flood affected areas is 57%, while 43% have services availability only at morning times. Reproductive Maternal and Neonatal Child Health (RMNCH) services for pregnant women have also been affected in various districts, while 43% of the pregnant women have no access to the health facilities. The average time required to reach the nearest health facility including RMNCH services has almost doubled in both the urban and rural flood affected areas due to damage to infrastructure; roads, bridges and limited public transportation which has also increased the monetary costs for the households while some residents are expected to delay seeking health care due to financial limitations, which would negatively impact the communities.
Alongside with this, other diseases continue to impact the health status of the affected populations. As of 1st October 2020, a total number of 1,964 confirmed dengue cases has been reported out of 81,379 suspects from all four provinces and Capital city (ICT) of Pakistan. Sindh province reported highest number (n-1087) of dengue cases which constitutes 55 % of total cases of the country (n-1964), Baluchistan province reported second highest number of cases (n-766) constituting 39% of total cases of the country (n-1964) while Khyber Pakhtunkhwa a total 260

project_name: Enhancing preparedness and response capacity for prevention and control of potential epidemic of high threat pathogens in Syria
project_objective:
The prolonged humanitarian crisis in Syria combined with the challenges brought on by the COVID-19 pandemic and its economic impact has severely affected the health system in Syria and increased the risk of potential infectious diseases outbreaks. Since the onset of conflict in 2011, the country has suffered from deterioration of living conditions and environmental conditions, breakdown of control measures, collapse of the health system and decrease in health workforce, and inadequate surveillance and detection of cases, as well as difficulties in access to health facilities and to affected populations.  The Early Warning and Response System was established in response to the Syrian Crisis, with the objective of addressing the increased potential for communicable disease outbreaks.  EWARS has been considered as one of main source of data for monitoring and response to disease outbreaks in Syria.   The number of sentinel sites increased and reached to 1360 in 2021 and covered public and private health facilities across the 14th Syrian governorates.  Although EWARS has become well established in the country and had largely replaced the main national routine surveillance system, however, new concerns about the spread of infectious diseases, especially emerging diseases such as COVID-19 or pandemic influenza, have emphasis the importance of enhancing the early warning and rapid response surveillance system in addition to the existing routine surveillance system.   This project aims to improve the availability of descriptive disease epidemiology data, outbreak early detection and response, provide data required for assessment of disease prevention and control interventions, in addition to improve the information system of surveillance by using a web-based interface with integration of other vertical surveillance systems to detect unusual events that might signal an outbreak.  The project also aims to enhance the country’s capacities for timely laboratory confirmation, as outlined in the international health regulations (2005), and to facilitate the transfer of safe and appropriate diagnostic technologies, practices and training to laboratories in the zones of emergence of these diseases. The successful detection, characterization and tracing of transmission and the subsequent management and control strategies of these disease outbreaks require accurate laboratory confirmation. However, there are major gaps in basic laboratory diagnosis for common epidemic-prone diseases and in biosafety and biosecurity practices in the public health laboratories.
Proposed activities include the support prevention and control of epidemic prone diseases through the provision of lifesaving medicines for communicable diseases. Activities also include the support in enhancing laboratory capacity for timely diagnosis and response to potential epidemic of high thread pathogen, expand the EWARS coverage in hard to reach and remote areas, and develop electronic application for routine surveillance system. 
The project will contribute in reducing the burden of infectious diseases and will cover cost effective interventions for the prevention and early detection of outbreaks. This project will be implemented through close coordination and consultation with MoH, health directorates at the governorates and district levels. the project will also contribute in strengthening the capacity of health partners through capacity building and technical support activities for surveillance and lab officers. and will ensure the availability of reliable disease surveillance data, and secure treatment and case management  of Infectious disease.

project_name: Assistance humanitaire en BNA et abris d’urgence aux ménages sinistrés par les inondations dans les régions de Diffa, Maradi et Tillaberi
project_objective: Le projet d’assistance humanitaire en BNA et abris d’urgence aux ménages sinistrés des inondations vise à couvrir les besoins en abris et BNA pour les victimes des inondations dans les régions de Tillabéri, Maradi et Diffa. 5,000 ménages, soit 35,000 personnes, seront ciblées pour une assistance en bien non alimentaire (BNA) et 2,000 ménages, représentant 14,000 personnes, recevront une assistance en abris d’urgence. La mise en œuvre de la réponse va se faire à travers le mécanisme de collaboration existant entre le gouvernement et les acteurs humanitaires. Afin de préserver le caractère life-saving de la réponse, UNICEF et son partenaire de mise en œuvre DGPC (par ailleurs acteur clé des évaluations et la collecte des données inondations) veillerons à répondre aux besoins des ménages ciblés dans un délai maximum de deux semaines. Pour cela, les pré-positionnement des kits devront se faire avant la fin du mois de mai 2021. Les coûts logistiques liés au transport des kits jusqu’au niveau régional seront assurés par UNICEF.  UNICEF appuiera la DGPC et/ou le MAH/GC pour couvrir les coûts de transport des kits des régions vers les sites sinistrés et lies ciblage, déploiement et distribution.

project_name: Gender-Based Violence (GBV) Risk Mitigation, Prevention and Response: mitigating risks, supporting survivors and addressing the root causes
project_objective:
In line with IOM’s GBV in Crises Operational Framework and the 2020 JRP’s three strategic objectives and two of the GBV sector’s objectives, IOM will develop its multi-sectoral GBV programming working with Rohingya refugees and host communities focused on three pillars: 1.) survivor-centered support, 2.) risk mitigation and 3.) addressing root causes that perpetuate GBV. IOM will provide specialized services and multi-sectoral support via its case management entry points embedded throughout 11 Women and Girls Safe Space (WGSS) across 10 sites working alongside its local partner PULSE. The WGSS ensure that women and girls can safely access multi-sectoral services, including safety via referral to IOM´s emergency safe shelter. 

To mitigate risks, prevent GBV and empower women and girls, the WGSS provides age-appropriate and structured psychosocial and educational activities, life-skills and vocational learning, forums for consultation, information-sharing and learning, including targeted awareness on GBV, sexual and reproductive health, menstrual hygiene management, life skills and vocational training, psychosocial support, risk and resilience building, and awareness-raising working with an extensive network of community volunteers, male advocates and other community champions, and ensures community feedback using tested tools and satisfaction surveys.  IOM and PULSE provide a wide-range of static interventions and community-level interventions focused on GBV prevention and risk mitigation, and community sensitization working with men, boys, women, girls and specifically targeting groups with diversity of need including male survivors and persons with diverse sexual orientation, gender identity, and expression. Such approaches also ensure safe referrals for male and gender-diverse survivors with jointly mapped counselling spaces in collaboration with other IOM Protection teams in community facilities where appropriate to ensure safe and non-stigmatizing case management services. IOM will also ensure capacity building and training in GBV working with local authorities and as part of community-based disaster risk reduction efforts.

project_name: Junto a ellas: Fortaleciendo mecanismos integrales de respuesta a la VBG para mujeres y niñas (incluye ejecución 5 meses 2021)
project_objective:
Las medidas para contener el COVID-19 y sus efectos y las devastadoras consecuencias de los huracanes ETA Y IOTA están impactado significativamente los proyectos de vida de las mujeres y niñas de Honduras, especialmente aquellas que viven en condiciones de mayor vulnerabilidad y que confrontan diversas discriminaciones y violencias interseccionales. Estas nuevas presiones han contribuido a profundizar las desigualdades preexistentes al generar presiones adicionales con pocas ofertas de solución a las vulnerabilidades previas en los sistemas sociales, políticos y económicos. En todos los ámbitos, desde la salud hasta la economía, desde la seguridad hasta la protección social, los impactos de COVID-19 se han exacerbado para las mujeres y niñas simplemente en virtud de su género (Policy Brief UN Women, 2020). Análisis recientes en Honduras evidencian los retrocesos significativos en los indicadores o condiciones estructurales relacionadas con la feminización de la pobreza, y los que inciden directamente en los factores de riesgo y aquellos protectores conexos a la VBG, los cuales particularmente se ha agudizado. Esto se debe, por un lado, a que las mujeres se ven obligadas a permanecer en sus hogares con sus agresores, en un momento donde las tensiones económicas se han incrementado y en donde el acceso a los canales de denuncia y servicios se han debilitado (Care & ONU mujeres, 2020). Por el otro, los repertorios de violencia de grupos criminales en las zonas más vulnerables contra las mujeres (por ejemplo, amenazas, extorsiones, femicidios, violencia sexual) no han disminuido y por el contrario, también debido a las restricciones de movilidad y de servicios, se ha limitado el acceso a las mujeres a denunciar y ser atendidas (ídem). Partimos de reconocer el valor de las mujeres de diferentes edades, etnias, clases sociales que confrontan estas violencias. También y con un rol protagónico, la respuesta se construye con la participación de organizaciones de mujeres, feministas y de sociedad civil situadas en los territorios, quienes pese a un escenario adverso han impulsado importantes logros para la defensa de los derechos de las mujeres. A su vez, las instituciones nacionales y locales, responsables de brindar protección y dar respuesta a los derechos de las mujeres son actores clave para el impulso de las estrategias que busquen mejorar las condiciones de las mujeres y su igualdad en términos de derechos.  El proyecto desarrolla acciones de atención inmediata a las mujeres a la vez que impulsa sostenibilidad fortaleciendo e instalando nuevas capacidades en instancias proveedoras de servicios. Las mujeres sobrevivientes de VBG recibirán servicios psicosociales integrales y acompañamiento, fortaleciendo su capacidad para identificar y exigir respuestas efectivas y que respondan a los estándares de calidad del paquete de servicios esenciales. Además se realizarán acciones para fortalecer los mismos desde OMM y organizaciones locales y sus procesos de comunicación, coordinación intersectorial y atención, gestión de casos, rutas de referencia.
Pondrá en marcha mecanismos de apoyo a sobrevivientes para reactivación de sus medios de vida, desde una perspectiva de atención para la transformación mejorando sus capacidades vocacionales y mapeando los servicios que contribuyan a crear y restablecer sus medios de vida para superar situaciones previas de vulnerabilidad. 
Parte importante de esa transformación, para reducir vulnerabilidades previas, se fomentarán escuelas y espacios de reflexión feminista, se impulsarán formaciones para actores comunitarios y una campaña masiva de comunicación y sensibilización orientada a promover cambios concretos en cuanto a la situación de VBG.
Finalmente, también se trabajará con actores/as que contribuyen de manera indirecta o directa en la ocurrencia y persistencia de la VBG: empresas; miembros de las fuerzas de seguridad; iglesias, establecimientos educativos y la sociedad en general.

project_name: Assistance en eau, Hygiène et Assainissement pour les populations déplacées et les populations hôtes affectées par la crise sécuritaire au Burkina Faso.
project_objective:
La situation humanitaire au Burkina Faso a été l'une des crises à la croissance la plus rapide de 2019. Le nombre d'incidents violents de sécurité a considérablement augmenté par rapport aux années précédentes. Le nombre de déplacés internes est passé de 87 000 en janvier 2019 à 1,013,234 en aout 2020 (dont 55% d'enfants). On estime que 95%  des PDI vivent dans des communautés d'accueil, 22%  des ménages vivent directement dans des familles d'accueil, ce qui a considérablement accru la pression sur les infrastructures communautaires de base réduisant ainsi la capacité des communautés à satisfaire leur besoin.
En 2020, face au besoin en WASH des populations affectée dans les 5 régions prioritaires , Unicef adresse dans sa réponse qui, au mois d’octobre 2020, a permis d’atteindre d’apporter l’accès à l’eau à 151823 personnes affectés sur 370 000 personnes prévues, l’accès à l’assainissement à 101 703 personnes sur 483 100 personnes prévues, 477142 personnes ont eu accès à l’hygiène dont les kits d’hygiène de dignité sur 483 100 personnes. L’assistance se poursuit malgré les problèmes d’accès humanitaire engendrant la réticence des entreprises dans la réalisation des travaux, l’impact COVID qui ralenti la mise en œuvre des projets et la capacité opérationnelle limitée de certains de nos partenaires.
Pour 2021, l'UNICEF continuera sa réponse humanitaire WASH au Burkina Faso dans un cadre multisectoriel à travers les partenariats, une coordination sectorielle et intersectorielle et une collaboration avec le gouvernement. UNICEF renforcera également sa participation au Mécanisme de réponse rapide, en collaboration avec les organisations non gouvernementales compétentes et les organismes des Nations Unies, grâce à un appui technique et à des achats.

Dans le cadre HRP 2021, le cluster WASH a identifié une cible de 1 600 000 personnes pour les 6 régions prioritaires (Centre Nord, Nord, Sahel, Boucle du Mouhoun, Est et Centre Est). Unicef ciblera 50% de la cible du cluster avec ses partenaires dans le cadre de l’action globale des acteurs WASH.

Le principal objectif du programme WASH de l’UNICEF dans les interventions d’urgence en 2021 est la prévention des maladies hydriques dans toutes les communautés touchées par des crises humanitaires. Pour ce faire, l'UNICEF fournira de l'eau potable, construira / réhabilitera des infrastructures d'assainissement et organisera des séances de sensibilisation à l'hygiène (y compris la distribution de kits d'hygiène). Également dans le cadre du contexte COVID 19 UNICEF assurera le renforcement des bonnes pratiques d’hygiène et les mesures de prévention et de contrôle des infections dans les établissements de santé, les écoles, les espaces publics et les communautés vulnérables afin de réduire l’exposition et la transmission du COVID-19.
Les interventions WASH combineront l'urgence et la réponse rapide, avec des stratégies de renforcement de la résilience à moyen terme. Les interventions se feront en concertation avec les autres acteurs dans le cadre de la coordination régionale et nationale pour optimiser les ressources et avec l’implication des DREA qui contribueront dans la supervision et la qualité des ouvrages

project_name: Improving Access to Lifesaving Integrated Emergency Primary Healthcare Services to IDPs and Host Communities in States of Warrap, Upper Nile and Western Equatoria,  in  South Sudan
project_objective:
The protracted armed conflict since December 2013 has resulted in multiple, acute, and chronic needs among the conflict affected population in South Sudan, further stretching their coping capacity. Some 8.3 million people in South Sudan are estimated to be in need of humanitarian assistance in 2021. These include 8,000,000 South Sudanese women, men, girls and boys and 310,000 refugees and asylum seekers.  The people of South Sudan have limited access to optimal health services due to ongoing conflict, flooding and an underdeveloped health care system. Because of the weakened health system compounded by multiple shocks, it is estimated that in 2021 4.9 million South Sudanese will have their health and wellbeing impacted. The health facilities which are operational face challenges of delivering the complete basic package of health-care services. The absence of services means that cases needing emergency obstetric care, as well as tuberculosis, HIV/AIDS and mental health issues go largely untreated, causing increased morbidity and mortality. Through the 2020 Humanitarian Response Plan, World Vision International (WVI) South Sudan will provide emergency lifesaving health interventions which will be integrated with nutrition, WASH, protection and FSL activities. Additionally, the emergency health intervention WVI intends to implement will focus on sexual gender based violence (SGBV), clinical management of rape (CMR), mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS). Owing to the high mortality rate of under 5 children (90.7/1000), maternal mortality rate (789 deaths/100,000 live births) in South Sudan, World Vision will provide also maternal and child health interventions, mainly skilled birth attendance, prevention of post -partum hemorrhage, ante natal care, post-natal care, basic and comprehensive emergency neonatal and obstetrical care (EMNOC), Sexual and Reproductive Health/ family planning service and Expanded Programme Immunization (EPI) and quality management of Severe Acute Malnutrition with medical complication.

World Vision will ensure that there is continuum of case for under 5 with complicated SAM so that they have access to OTP and TSF facilities run by nutrition partners, including World Vision who is a provider of Community Based Management of Acute Malnutrition (CMAM) and Maternal Infant Young Child Nutrition (MIYCN) practice. World Vision will ensure that people with disabilities and mental disorders have priority access to emergency health services and are included as vulnerable groups owing to their high risk during emergencies. The response plan will be prioritized based on epidemiological profile of disease outbreaks, cholera hot spot locations, measles outbreaks, malaria seasonality. The emergency lifesaving response World Vision will provide will be done in line with the recommended health cluster emergency clinical services package for primary healthcare units, primary healthcare centers, county hospital, mobile medical team, and Integrated Community Case Management (ICCM). These interventions will be in line with the South Sudan Ministry of Health’s policies and guidelines, namely basic package of health and nutrition services, Boma Health Initiative, sexual and reproductive health, immunization guidelines and health policy of the Republic of South Sudan.
This project plans to reach 90,250 people with a budget of USD 3,000,000 over one year.

project_name: Access to Justice for Migrant Domestic Workers
project_objective:
Access to Justice for Migrant Domestic Workers addresses the needs of migrants as identified in the 2021-2022 Emergency Response Plan for Lebanon, with a focus on migrant domestic workers, most of whom are women. The intervention will advance the ERP strategic objective of enhancing timely, unhindered, and equitable access to protection assistance for migrants.   This will be achieved through the provision of direct legal aid for migrant domestic workers, including information, assistance and representation. In addition, and strategic litigation will be employed to challenge the overall legal framework that facilitates the oppression and exploitation of migrant domestic workers. Through this double-faceted approach, the intervention will meet the ERP goal of delivering emergency assistance to the most vulnerable populations while supporting the transition to sustainable approaches and linking to non-humanitarian frameworks. 
 
The living and working conditions of migrant domestic workers in Lebanon are shaped to a large degree by the sponsorship system known as Kafala, which ties the legal residency of a migrant to their employer, giving the employer undue control over the migrant’s life. Kafala excludes migrant workers from the protection of the Lebanese labour law, and fails to meet international human rights and labour standards.   The ERP identifies some of the abuses migrant workers face under Kafala as including violence, exploitation, overwork, restricted movement and non-payment of wages. The grave conditions of migrant domestic workers have been worsened by recent events in Lebanon, with assessments indicating that half of all migrants today are unemployed.   
 
The protection of vulnerable migrants has never been more imperative amid ongoing current crises. The present action will empower migrant domestic workers to seek their rights using available legal and protection mechanisms, by employing a two-pronged approach. First, the project will provide direct legal aid, including information, counselling, mediation, assistance and representation, to resolve issues such as unpaid wages, violence or abuse, and the provision or replacement of civil documentation. LAW will employ its existing networks within migrant domestic workers groups, official affiliations and coordination mechanisms with local and international stakeholders, including IOM, Al Makan Shelter, Concern Worldwide, and ARM organization, and related Embassies to implement an organized outreach strategy in order to reach the widest vulnerable migrant groups. Legal aid will attempt to secure adequate remedy for violations suffered. Informational legal awareness posts through social media will be used to empower a large audience of migrant domestic workers to recognize their rights under Lebanese law and according to universal human rights standards. 

Second, the project will seek to precipitate sustainable change in the protection status of migrant domestic workers through strategic litigation and awareness campaigns.  LAW will utilize its expertise in creative lawyering and strategic litigation to mount a strategic litigation case on behalf of a migrant domestic worker, complementing the first case filed in 2020 on behalf of an Ethiopian migrant domestic worker. Strategic litigation will be used to set and strengthen precedents for the criminal prosecution of abusive sponsors and recruiters. LAW will use social media platforms to generate public interest in the case, creating public pressure for delivering an effective outcome, and contributing to the ongoing transformation in attitudes and behaviours in relation to the exploitation of migrant domestic workers. The litigation will be complemented by a coordinated strategy targeting key stakeholders and decision-makers including civil society actors, legal actors, and representatives of migrant country-of-origin embassies.

project_name: Enhance resilience of food insecure rural population in areas with high concentrations of returnees and internally displaced persons in Syria
project_objective:
The United Nations (UN) estimates that the number of crisis-affected people in need of humanitarian assistance in Syria is 14.2 million people (48.7% male and 51.3% female), of which 6 million people are in acute need. This figure above on people of need includes 6.7 million protracted internally displaced persons (IDPs); an estimated 320,000 spontaneous IDPs return; 75,000 refugees return; 438,000 Palestine refugees and the rest overburdened host communities. It is estimated that more than 70% of the number of people in need of humanitarian assistance are accessible from within Syria.  
Overall, 12.4 million people are estimated to be food insecure (including 1.27 million severely food insecure and 9.5 million moderately food insecure) and 1.9 million people are at risk of food insecurity. 
In this context, FAO has designed a project to assist 42,378 crisis-affected households through support to vegetable and poultry production (equivalent to 254,268 people) in Syria. The objective of the proposed action is to enhance the resilience of the food insecure rural population in areas with high concentrations of returnees and IDPs. Project outputs include:
Output 1: Income generating capacities and access to alternative sources of revenue for crisis affected farmers households are increased.
It is expected that the project support will improve the food security and nutrition status of crisis-affected, small-scale farmers. Specifically, the project will aim to diversify diets through increased income and creation of employment for the most vulnerable household members, especially for women and youth, which will lead to improvement of livelihoods, increase local availability of food, increase self-reliance and improve food and nutrition security of crisis-affected households, especially the most vulnerable

project_name: Renforcement de la résilience des populations déplacées, des retournées et hôtes vulnérables dans la région de l’Extrême-Nord Cameroun
project_objective:
La région de l’Extrême-Nord du Cameroun fait face à des contraintes structurelles et sociales qui la classent d’une grande fragilité du fait de son exposition aux aléas climatiques et environnementaux. La région a subi consécutivement deux années d’inondation. Les actions de la secte boko Haram sont venues amplifier cette situation de fragilité et le COVID19 en moindre mesure, mais, à accentuer notamment sur les zone semi rurales et urbaine Les jeunes sont majoritaires (60%) et sont sous employés (86%) par conséquent sont en proie à la secte Boko-Haram. Les personnes vivant avec handicap généralement exclues des activités de développement constituent plus de 10% de la population. La récente analyse cadre harmonisée (octobre, 2020) dénombre 641 948 personnes en besoin dont plus de la moitié sont les femmes (51%), situées en phase 3 et plus. Alors que l’ensemble des acteurs humanitaires cibleront 167 617 personnes en situation d’insécurité alimentaire, la FAO, à travers ce projet, déroulera une réponse ciblant 41 904 personnes.  
Le présent projet de renforcement de la résilience des populations déplacées retournées et hôtes vulnérables vise à améliorer la capacité d’adaptation des populations vulnérables face à l’insécurité alimentaire. Il sera mis en place dans quatre départements à savoir Logone et Chari, Mayo-Sava, Mayo-Tsanaga et Mayo-Danay. Le projet se propose d’appuyer 6000 ménages, soit en moyenne 36 000 personnes. La réponse se déclinera suivant 2 axes d’intervention. L’axe de production céréalière avec un support en cash inconditionnel pour assurer les besoins alimentaires et non alimentaires tout en préservant l’actif productif et un second axe centré sur l’élevage et le maraîchage de contre saison en vue de développer des revenus supplémentaires. 
Les résultats attendus de ce projet sont les suivants :
-	Les ménages vulnérables de la zone d’intervention ont constitué des stocks de consommation alimentaire à travers la production agricole : il s’agira pour les ménages de relancer leur production agricoles en disposant assez de ressources pour satisfaire les besoins alimentaires et autre en saison de production.
-	Les ménages ont développé les sources de revenus supplémentaires à travers la production animale (petits ruminants et volaille) et le maraîchage: les ménages développeront les activités d’élevage et du maraîchage pendant le temps libre pour mieux les occuper et améliorer la productivité pour s’en servir comme source de revenus supplémentaires pour ne pas seulement compter sur la production agricole. Dans cette logique, la production agricole pourrait couvrir les besoins de la prochaine campagne

project_name: Strengthening sexual and gender-based violence prevention, risk mitigation and inclusive, survivor-centred response services
project_objective:
The project aims to 1) improve the quality, accessibility and safe referral of existing response services for survivors, especially linkages between case management, medical and legal services 2) mitigate the risk of both sexual and gender-based violence through multi-level and cross-sectoral capacity building (including on PSEA) and community-led (especially by women and girls) initiatives and 3) prevention through sustained, evidence-based programming that changes the social norms undergirding violence against women.  Highly vulnerable, underserved populations will be targeted.

UNHCR and partners’ approach is community-based and survivor-centred, with refugees—especially women and girls—engaged as active agents and emerging leaders within their communities. We will increase women and girls’ participation in decision-making and leadership by building their confidence and capacity with skills building and training, engaging female refugees in our community-based protection work and engaging men and boys as allies in promoting gender equality. Key components include safe spaces, life and vocational skills, PSS, community volunteers, male role models, women-led initiatives, women’s leadership training and SASA! Together. 

UNHCR and partners will continue to provide case management and psychosocial support services for survivors of sexual and gender-based violence, with special attention to strengthening the survivor-centred care practices within the multi-sectoral referral network and increasing accessibility for, and capacity to serve, target populations. Service delivery modalities have been adapted for risk mitigation, including for COVID-19 and natural disasters. Key components include capacity building for case management, PSS, health, legal and law enforcement service providers.

Promoting the centrality of protection and an age, gender and diversity approach, UNHCR and partners will invest in AAP with community-based complaints mechanisms, SEA risk mitigation through protection mainstreaming across sectors and targeting highly vulnerable populations. Target populations include child and adolescent survivors, male survivors, adolescent girls, gender diverse populations and individuals engaged in sex work in host and refugee communities, and persons with disabilities.

project_name: Improving Access to WASH Facilities and Services to Rohingya Refugees and Host Community
project_objective:
The project is designed to contribute to a reduction in WASH-related public health risk through improved access for refugees and affected host communities in the area of water, sanitation, and hygiene promotion.  
In 2021, UNHCR will ensure notably through capacity building the finalisation of the 54 networks in UNHCR-managed camps covering 345,000 refugees. UNHCR and partners will continue maintaining, operating, and upgrading the existing stock of water infrastructure and the development of a large-scale, unified urban-based water system for UNHCR camps along with Teknaf and its host community and will further provide technical support to the sector and DPHE, particularly for the water supply monitoring programme.

UNHCR and partners will continue to support urban scale sustainable sanitation infrastructure, looking to cover all 14 UNHCR camps by end of 2021. Develop and get approval for integrated household latrines and bathing areas to be adopted as the standard in all new transitional shelter designs covering 3,000 households. Increase shared household latrine coverage and bathing area, especially for women and children, and bring coverage rates to UNHCR standards with iron frame bathing areas. Faecal sludge treatment will be increased with a mix of large off-site units and increased use of small-bore sewerage and appropriate cost-effective on-site disposal. UNHCR will ensure a more effective solid waste management systems and infrastructure and further enhance hygiene promotion activities with community engagement and reduce partner support in favour of refugee ownership.

Infrastructure construction and service delivery would mainstream community engagement within the Age, Gender, Diversity (AGD)/ Protection lens for better project outcomes and sustainability ensuring equal access for Rohingya refugee women, men, boys and girls living in camps, and affected host communities to adequate safe drinking water and for domestic purposes as well sanitation and hygiene facilities.

project_name: Protection of Children Strengthened
Protection and targeted assistance to promote resilience and solutions for IDPs and non-IDP communities and refugee returnees.
project_objective:
The project aims to strengthen a rights-based protection response for IDPs and non-IDP communities, as well as refugee returnees, in particular those most vulnerable through stronger advocacy, life-saving protection and assistance activities, evidence-based programming with the focus on developing and building the capacity of affected communities to cope and recover and better position them for the attainment of durable solutions. Improving coordination and quality of assessments and monitoring will also be key components of the project. The project also foresees benefiting the entire displaced population through continuous advocacy and support in the area of Law and Policy, fostering the successful engagement with relevant authorities and partners with a focus on the approval and implementation of the new IDP Law. This activity will be built upon efforts by UNHCR that in 2020 culminated in the Somalia accession to Kampala Convention and development of draft IDP Law that is aimed to domesticate it.   
UNHCR will continue to make the best of its key membership of the protection cluster and ensure regular reporting to the clusters’ 5Ws and strong participation and contribution in the different clusters’ working groups to ensure coordination and complementarity of interventions, avoiding duplication with other members and ensuring regular sharing of protection reports with the cluster. 
Many IDPs in protracted displacement remain in situations with no progress towards durable solutions and suffer from systemic marginalization. Access to life-saving assistance and basic services, such as education and health, exclusion from services provided by government are other factors that contribute to heightened protection risks faced by displaced and other conflict-affected populations. Sexual and gender-based violence also remains a critical protection concern for IDPs. A significant proportion of IDPs are members of minority groups lacking the protection of major clans. COVID-19 pandemic has further exacerbated pre-existing risks and vulnerabilities. In Somalia internally displaced persons (IDPs) have been facing despicable acts of man-made violence including forced evictions and natural hazards which have led to multiple displacement and limited access to durable solution opportunities. Many newly displaced IDPs still remain in need of assistance. Many of the IDPs reside in overcrowded areas with poor living conditions and limited security provision. The basic needs of IDPs are often not met due to inconsistent service provision, exclusion from accessing services, or from the sheer absence of services due to poor targeting of settlements. Forced evictions remain one of the most severe and prevalent protection threats, particularly for IDPs and poor households, due to an underdeveloped regulatory framework, hampered access to justice, low awareness of and respect for HLP rights, and a weak protective environment. It is anticipated that opening of the borders and lifting some of the COVID-19 travel restrictions can lead to an increase of number of returns as compared to 2020 that will bring overall number of returnees in the Somalia that will be in need of variety of protection services to 109,989. Many returnees choose not to return to their areas of origin, preferring to settle in urban areas. Many of these contribute to and suffer the results of pressure on basic services, further compounded by recurrent influxes of IDPs. Any intervention will be vulnerability and needs based.  While there is increased effort to promote sustainable return and re-integration, a substantial number of returnees have limited access to basic services, precarious or no physical security and are constantly exposed to myriad protection risks that proposed project will seek to address. The project includes a sustainability/handover component where feasible, particularly in the areas of Law and Policy, as well as community mobilization and NNGOs engagement.

project_name: Protection et assistance multisectorielle aux réfugiés, demandeurs d’asile, rapatriés et personnes à risque d’apatridie au Mali
project_objective:
Depuis 2018, la Commission Nationale Chargée des Réfugiés et le HCR enregistrent une augmentation croissante du nombre de réfugiés au Mali en raison de l’insécurité au Sahel, nécessitant une réponse interagence et multisectorielle. En 2021, l’opération du HCR au Mali planifie les chiffres de population suivants : 75 000 réfugiés, 35 000 nouveaux rapatriés et 18 500 personnes à risque d’apatridie. Les activités de réponse à ces groupes de populations seront orientées autour de trois axes, qui reflètent sa stratégie de protection et de solutions pluriannuelle et multipartenaires 2018-2022 :

-	Axe 1 : 100% des réfugiés, demandeurs d’asile et personnes à risque d’apatridie ont accès à la protection internationale au Mali dans un délai et des conditions d’accueil optimal 

-	Axe 2 : 100% des réfugiés, demandeurs d’asile, rapatriés et personnes à risque d’apatridie ont accès aux services sociaux de base et aux moyens d’existence et d’autosuffisance dans leurs zones d’accueil, à travers le renforcement des capacités nationales et locales

-	Axe 3 :  Les réfugiés, demandeurs d’asile, rapatriés et personnes à risque d’apatridie reçoivent l’accompagnement requis en vue d’une solution durable effective en fonction de leurs besoins de protection

Le HCR se donne pour objectif d’ici à 2022 que les réfugiés, les rapatriés et les personnes à risque d’apatridie aient accès aux systèmes et services locaux et soient de plus en plus autonomes, tandis que des solutions globales et durables seront trouvées pour au moins 40% de ces personnes.

Ce projet, qui reprend l’ensemble des activités planifiées par le HCR pour les réfugiés, demandeurs d’asile, rapatriés et personnes à risque d’apatridie doit aboutir à cet objectif. Les activités clés prioritaires peuvent se résumer autour des éléments suivants :

-	pour les réfugiés et demandeurs d’asile : 1) Répondre rapidement et efficacement aux nouveaux déplacements en soutenant les efforts proactifs visant à favoriser la cohésion sociale et à renforcer la capacité du Gouvernement à coordonner la réponse aux réfugiés et à fournir une protection internationale aux réfugiés nouvellement arrivés du Burkina Faso et du Niger, dans les zones frontalières, tout en renforçant les activités de surveillance aux frontières. 2) Assurer l'accès à l'asile, l'intégrité de la protection des réfugiés et des demandeurs d'asile et la préservation de l'espace de protection par les autorités maliennes dans le contexte d'afflux massifs et de mouvements mixtes. 3) Soutenir la mise en œuvre de solutions durables, y compris le processus d'intégration locale des réfugiés en situation prolongée. 4) Soutenir l'accès à l'état civil, aux documents d'identité et à la nationalité. 5) Mettre à jour les plans d'urgence de l'opération nationale en tant qu'exercice prioritaire et en tant que mesure de préparation aux situations d'urgence, en y associant les principaux acteurs et partenaires. 

-	pour les rapatriés : réaliser les priorités du Gouvernement en se concentrant sur 1) Permettre aux réfugiés maliens de prendre une décision éclairée concernant leur retour potentiel ; 2) Faciliter l'accueil de 35 000 réfugiés maliens de retour au pays ; 3) Assurer leur réintégration socio-économique multisectorielle durable en 2021, sur la base de 5 principes avec une approche centrée sur la nature : Protéger, Répondre, Inclure, Tenir pour responsable et Résoudre.

-	pour les personnes à risque d’apatridie : en soutien à l'engagement du Gouvernement d'éradiquer l'apatridie au Mali ; 1) Continuer à préconiser la naturalisation des réfugiés de Mauritanie en situation prolongée, comme solution durable et comme effort pour réduire l'apatridie; 2) Soutenir l'introduction de procédures de détermination de l'apatridie pour permettre au Gouvernement de quantifier la question au Mali ; 3) Assurer le suivi des recommandations de l'étude sur l'apatridie conclue en 2020 ; 4) Soutenir la mise en œuvre du plan d'action national contre l'apatridie.

project_name: Increased access to and quality of lifesaving preventative and curative primary health care and integrated nutrition, including integrated services for people with physical disabilities and essential GBV protection services for vulnerable conflict affected populations.
project_objective:
This project aims to reach 181345 target beneficiaries (excluding overlap), building on the experience, expertise and relationships from its previous project cycles to reach the most vulnerable and in-need, and with protection mainstreaming and sustainability at the core of its programme. Medair will focus on rehabilitating and/or re-equipping primary healthcare facilities in areas with high needs, prioritizing hard to reach and newly accessible areas, as well as rehabilitating a maternity ward. Given the high needs and likely reduction in the presence of other actors. Following infrastructure rehabilitation and/or re-equipment, a 12-month programme of monitoring visits and capacity building training for staff will maximise the quality of service provision.

The community health programme (CHP) will target key health, hygiene and nutrition behaviours through messaging at household level in the clinic catchment population.
For the 8 PHCCs rehabilitated and/or re-equipped by Medair in 2020, the supervision, training and CHP will continue into 2021. Medair plans to rehabilitate and/or re-equip up to 6 PHCCs during 2021, as well as one maternity ward.

Additionally, 2 hospitals will be provided with necessary measures for COVID-19 prevention and management, including training for all health care staff, PPE for visitors, and equipment to support COVID-19 ICU beds.

MHPSS services, healthcare for people living with disabilities and initial support of GBV cases will be integrated into the services provided by the PHC facility. Nutrition screening and treatment will also be integrated-details of this have been submitted separately as per sector guidance.
Service provision is by existing public sector health staff. Medair Health Officers (4) conduct field visits and training. Support staff consist of Health Coordinator, Health Advisor and senior management.To ensure sustained access to healthcare, Medair will exit the location at the end of the support period by handover of each PHCC to national or regional health authorities.

Medair provides capacity building training for both clinic staff and CHWs working in the clinic catchment area. 615 healthworkers and 430 CHWs will be trained in 2021. The training package for both is extensive, and delivered over a 12 month period by Medair staff, qualified MOH staff, and external trainers. Medair provides transport /accommodation costs for trainers if needed. Healthworker training comprises 28 days per governorate (140 training days in 2021), covering key gaps (RH (ANC, PNC, FP), mhGAP, PFA, Disability inclusion, NCDs, and IMCI) and COVID-19. 
CHWs receive 8 days of initial training and 6 refresher days, delivered per clinic (98 days total during 2021) . Supervisors also attend M+E days. Topics include ANC/PNC, nutrition, MHPSS awareness, PFA, hygiene, communicable diseases, NCDs, GBV awareness, and disability awareness. CHWs will also identify up to 395 PLWMIs in order to support them with Assistive Devices.

Consultation target calculated based on catchment population, a clinic utilization rate of 1 and number of months Medair will support service provision.

project_name: Emergency support to income and dietary diversification of crisis-affected population through household level vegetable and poultry production
project_objective:
The United Nations (UN) estimates the number of crisis-affected people in need of humanitarian assistance in Syria to be 14.2 million (48.7 % male and 51.3 % female), of which almost six million are in acute need. The above figure of people in need includes 6.7 million protracted internally displaced persons (IDPs); estimated 320,000 spontaneous IDPs return; 438,000 Palestine refugees and the rest overburdened host communities. More than 70% of the population in need of humanitarian assistance are accessible from within Syria.  
Overall, 12.4 million of people are estimated to be food insecure (including 1.27 million severely food insecure and 9.5 million moderately food insecure) and 1.9 million at risk of food insecurity. In this context, FAO has designed a project to assist 98,300 crisis-affected households through support to vegetable and poultry production (equivalent to 589,800 people) in Syria. The objective of the proposed action is to improve the food security and nutrition of vulnerable crisis-affected households. Project outputs include:
Output 1: Increased capacity for vegetable production for 54,150 households.
The output aims at increasing the vegetable production of 54,150 vulnerable households (of which 16,245 are women-headed) through the provision of full vegetable production packages, which include vegetable seeds/seedlings, drip irrigation networks, and organic fertilizers.

Output 2: Increased capacity for poultry production for 48,735 households.
This output aims to support 48,735 vulnerable households (of which 15,162 are women-headed) to engage in poultry production for both consumption of poultry products and as part of income generating activities.

It is expected that the project support, through provision of vegetable and poultry inputs and associated training, will diversify the diets of the targeted households and at the same time, the sale of vegetable and poultry products will increase household income and create employment for the most vulnerable members of the households, especially for women and youth. It is expected this will lead to improvement of livelihoods, increased local availability of food, increased self-reliance and improved food security and nutrition of crisis-affected households, especially the most vulnerable.
This project will enhance household production of vegetables and poultry to increase dietary diversity and micronutrient consumption. The project will provide inputs to improve household food availability and income generation through backyard poultry production and vegetable production). Household-level farming is an activity often undertaken by women that will benefit from this intervention, and they will be prioritized in the selection process. This support will be complemented by training and capacity building to strengthen the technical skills of beneficiaries and improve their food production and income generation capacities for food and nutrition security. Household food production activities (vegetables, poultry.) will also benefit vulnerable groups with limited access to land such as IDPs, the landless rural population, and urban and Semi-urban populations. 
Support provided to agricultural production will help alleviate the scarcity of food commodities and reduce dependency on imports and food aid. A close partnership with other UN agencies, such as UNICEF, UNDP, WFP and IOM, will further contribute to creating synergies between using agencies comparative advantages and improve the food security and nutrition of targeted households

project_name: Providing quality and comprehensive GBV Prevention and Response Services in Misrata and Benghazi
project_objective:
IMC will continue to implement GBV prevention and response services in Benghazi and in Misrata, which include the provision of specialized GBV case management services based on a survivor-centered
approach.  IMC has established awareness and case management services in Misrata and Benghazi and intends to expand to ensure comprehensive services in line with GBV guiding principles and a survivor centered approach through static (women and girl safe spaces (WGSS)), mobile and remote service delivery modalties. The main target population will be women and girls but men and boys will be engaged in awareness sessions to facilitate social behaviour change. To ensure complementary services under this project,
health staff will also be trained on GBV core concepts and safe referrals of GBV cases to GBV
caseworkers. IMC will also maintain a field-level referral system with other nongovernmental
organizations (NGOs) and actors providing relevant services like emergency cash
assistance, child protection, and shelter. IMC will train community based focal points to support community based awareness and referrals and work closely with local organisations to ensure local ownership and support. Moreover, local partners will be trained on GBV case management and awareness and life skills curricula, such as the adolescent toolkit.
IMC will provide the target communities with increased knowledge on their health rights, including SRHR, and service availability. In addition to the GBV team, also the health and MHPSS staff will be trained on Protection and GBV concepts and ensure gender balance of staff in facilities with clear referral pathways in line with the IASC Guidelines for Integrating GBV Intervention in Humanitarian Actions and the IASC Gender Handbook for Humanitarian Action, giving clear guidelines to increase inclusive access and reduce barriers to care. IMC will continue to collect disaggregated sex and age data and conduct focus group discussions and key informant interviews with both mixed and single-sex groups and, when possible and relevant, with different age groups as well as with people with disabilities, to gather vital information and to allow for deeper analysis of the gender and inclusion implications that activities and services offered by IMC have in the specific areas of intervention and to ensure adjustments are made accordingly and continuously throughout the program cycle.
