The project will provide information, counselling and legal assistance, integrated capacity building and collaborative dispute resolution to achieve this. The project will also work to strengthen capacities of civil registries and local authorities.

The WASH response will ensure that the most vulnerable refugees have access to safe drinking water and sanitation through household level interventions, support water safety plans from the distribution points up to the point of use and provide family shared emergency latrines and vector control interventions. The response will further upgrade/ expand small-scale water infrastructures for both host community and refugees, increase the water supply, improve the water quality which will consequently reduce conflicts over scarce natural resources. Market-based approach will be utilised to effectively meet people’s WASH needs.

The shelter action will undertake the provision of adequate shelters and NFI for refugees, rehabilitation/repairs of existing shelters to ensure minimum protection against the elements,  and replenish and/or issue essential NFI kits for the most vulnerable groups. The response will additional support the establishment of communal infrastructures to facilitate social cohesion and integration with host communities. Household-level energy interventions will mostly focus on solar solutions. The action and precise response modalities will be informed and driven by a market systems analysis.

The EiE intervention and support will focus on enabling refugee and vulnerable host community  boys and girls of school age to gain access to timely, safe and quality education through addressing multiple barriers preventing their education. Structural upgrades, rehabilitation of schools, WASH facilities and distribution of essential hygiene supplies and teaching and learning materials will be a key component. 

The action will establish a Digital Community Hub (DCH) which will serve as a two-way communication platform with people of concern. Information distributed through the platform will include life-saving and life improving awareness-raising messages as well as information on how to access services. Similarly, people of concern will be able to ask questions, raise emergency alerts, communicate their needs and obtain referrals for services, and voice complaints or feedback via the hub. 

The project will assist the most vulnerable refugee households to meet their basic needs through multi-purpose cash. The project plans to support these new arrivals with half the value of the MEB for a period of 6months. A market assessment will be undertaken before the proposed cash intervention.

The response will target the most vulnerable refugees living in camps, camp-like, out-of-camp and urban settings in White Nile and Gedaref and those in formal or informal settlements in South Kordofan. Beneficiary targeting, within refugee communities and their nearby hosting communities, will be done by applying socio-economic vulnerability criteria.

project_name: Access to housing, land and property rights, legal identity including civil documents for displacement affected individuals in Darfur and South Kordofan.
project_objective:
IDP’s, and returnees in Sudan face significant challenges accessing documentation as well as housing, land and property. Conflict over land and natural resources in Darfur and South Kordofan regions have resulted in massive destruction of property and displacement. Rampant secondary occupation and ongoing disputes over land and natural resources have been identified as a major cause of conflict and hindrance to attaining durable solution in the return context. Inability to access legal identity and civil documents additionally gives rise to various protection concerns including; limited access to essential services, livelihood and employment opportunities. 

The project to be implemented by ICLA department (Information, Counselling and Legal Assistance) aims at supporting displacement affected communities to claim their rights through promoting the exercise and enjoyment of housing, land and property rights and facilitating increased access to legal identity and civil documentation. The project will focus on creating awareness on HLP rights aimed at advancing security of tenure and supporting dispute resolution processes and structures. The project will draw on a three-fold approach which aims to 1) ensure that displacement affected communities are better informed about their HLP and legal identity rights through information sessions, information education and communication (IEC) materials, mobile counselling, individualized legal assistance and collaborative dispute resolution 2) enhance understanding amongst authorities, community leaders, and humanitarian actors on HLP rights and the importance of legal identity and civil documentation and 3) promote HLP mainstreaming through adoption of due diligence approach before humanitarian interventions which have an implications on land use and ownership. 

To complement the above, ICLA staff will organize mobile group information sessions to increase awareness about HLP rights and the procedures that must be followed to replace documentation that has been lost or destroyed. Following these group information sessions, displacement affected individuals who express the need will receive individualized counselling tailored to their specific circumstances on the procedural and administrative requirements necessary to access HLP and/or legal identity or civil documents. Information and counselling sessions will also touch on the processes involved with accessing legal identity documents as these are frequently linked to HLP rights. NRC will also be available to facilitate referrals for displacement affected individuals who have protection related concerns that are not related to ICLA’s thematic areas of intervention.

The project will undertake legal research and assessments to build on the understanding of housing land and property issues and access to legal identity and civil documentation in-country. ICLA will undertake HLP and collaborative dispute resolution mapping assessment in Darfur and as well as detailed ICLA assessment South Kordofan. These assessments will look into the legal framework governing HLP and legal identity and civil documentation, identify key issues and provide conflict sensitive recommendations for effective programming and policy influence in Sudan.  

The project will target vulnerable displacement affected populations including; IDP’s, returnees, host community and conflict affected communities in Darfur and South Kordofan. Access to HLP rights and legal identity documents are gendered issues with regularly recurring instances of gender inequality regarding ownership of housing, land and property and access to legal documentation. This project will target 60% of female beneficiaries to address this gendered gap.

project_name: WASH assistance for displacement affected populations in Southern and Eastern Sudan
project_objective:
With this project NRC will ensure that most vulnerable displacement affected populations living in camps, camp-like, out-of-camp and urban settings will have access to safe drinking water and sanitation facilities and will be supported to achieve positive behavioural changes through effective hygiene promotion campaigns.  
NRC WASH programmes will offer a progressive and phased response approach with a focus towards longer-term goals and durable solutions. Where appropriate, upgrading/expansion of existing water infrastructures will be promoted, along with the development of sustainability plans. Market-based solutions for sanitation and hygiene items will be the preferred option. WASH programme will target primarily displaced population in neglected, hard-to-reach locations in Khartoum, White Nile, South Kordofan and Gadaref.
The WASH objectives will be achieved through an integrated approach with Shelter, LFS, ICLA, Education and CM programmes. 
Emergency Response:
Newly displaced populations will be targeted with WASH response to enhance their access to safe drinking water and sanitation through household level interventions. For the water component, the programme will focus on the Water Safety Plan from the distribution points up to the Point of Use, including proper water collection, handling, treatment and storage (adequate water containers and household level water treatment systems complemented by relevant awareness sessions). The programme will be complemented by family-shared emergency latrines and vector control interventions to minimize high-risk practices and reduce faecal and vector-borne diseases transmission, contributing to improve the health and dignity of the affected communities. 

Longer-term goals and Durable Solutions:
The populations living in protracted displacement or returned to areas of origin will be primarily targeted with upgrading/expansion of small-scale water infrastructures, benefitting both the displaced and the hosting communities with longer-term impact. The interventions will aim at increasing the water supply and improving the water quality and in parallel will reduce potential social conflicts generated by the sharing of already scarce natural resources. The sanitation response will primarily promote the CLTS approach in alignment with the Sudanese WASH sector strategy. Sustainability plans, engaging local water authorities and target communities on the facilities’ Operation & Maintenance through the creation Water and Sanitation Users Committees will strengthen the response. To complement the communal/infrastructural components, market-based activities will be promoted to meet effectively people’s WASH needs and contribute towards market rehabilitation and community resilience.

Integrated (multi-sectoral) Response:
The WASH response will be highly integrated to the other Core Competency programmes to ensure longer-term goals and greater impact. In particular, synergies will be ensured with ICLA on HLP issues and community engagement around durable solutions; Shelter to strengthen the overall scope of creating home and building communities; Education on supporting WASH in School programming and contribute to create safe learning environments; LFS to support agricultural and market-based livelihood programmes; CM on Communication with Communities for greater engagement of the target communities on both household and communal level response.

project_name: Restoration of Livelihoods for rural and semi-urban Communities in Eastern Equatoria State, South Sudan
project_objective:
The project aims to enhance the self-reliance of vulnerable communities in Eastern Equatoria State. This is achieved, on the one hand, by increasing their household income and food production and, on the other hand, by facilitating access to drinking water and water for agricultural use. The project thus contributes to removing the constant threat of food and nutrition insecurity.  

The project supports farming families to increase their agricultural production in a sustainable way. Caretakers of malnourished children are supported to create kitchen gardens for vegetable production. The project also focuses on the creation of other income generating activities (promotion of fair and inclusive value chains). Furthermore, the project improves access to drinking water and water for agricultural use. It also supports various schools to improve their sanitation facilities and to increase the knowledge about hygiene and environmental protection through the innovative Blue School approach.

project_name: ​PROVISION OF PROTECTION AND HUMANITARIAN ASSISTANCE SERVICES TO MIGRANTS IN VULNERABLE SITUATIONS
project_objective: The project’s aim is to provide a range of protection services to migrants in need, strengthen links between targeted community groups and services available, and enhance knowledge on migrant population groups in Lebanon. Services will target both male and female migrants, with a higher caseload of the latter group due to their increased number in country. Beneficiaries will typically be working age, between 18 and 40 years old. The services that IOM will deliver, either directly or through partners, include legal assistance, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), safe and temporary shelters for vulnerable migrants, provision of non-food items, multipurpose cash assistance (MPCA), and voluntary humanitarian return. These services will be made accessible to migrants by scaling up IOM’s pre-existing case management services, supporting enhanced capacity of, and referral with partners, strengthening translation and interpretation efforts to diminish language barriers facing migrants, and expanding community-level networks to strengthen targeted communities’ awareness of and access to IOM and partner services, as well as wider issues of concern. Finally, enhancing knowledge of migrant populations will involve nationwide data-collection efforts via key informant interviews in order to inform humanitarian planning. The project will be implemented by the IOM in partnership with civil society organizations (CSO) and community-based initiatives, with some services such as shelter, legal assistance referred from IOM. IOM will work with local service providers to strengthen their capacity, to enhance the overall protection network available for migrants in Lebanon. Onward referral to multisector assistance such as food or health support will be mainstreamed across the project.

project_name: Protecting vulnerable communities by improving their abilities to cope with the effects of armed violence through Psychosocial Support and Child Protection activities
project_objective: The objective of the project is to provide children and adolescents with the tools and space to improve their mental and psychosocial wellbeing, identify and manage stress, and develop positive coping mechanisms in order for them to better cope with the stress and potential trauma that they are likely facing in their daily lives. Structured and sustained PSS activities targeting children/adolescents will be conducted in DCAs Child Friendly Spaces through art, music, drama, sports, story-telling, games and activities aiming to develop feelings of safety and trust. Adolescents who are unable to attend the CFS will be reached with awareness sessions focusing on stress management in their schools, sports clubs and/or youth centres. Additionally, parents/caregivers of children and adolescents receiving support will be provided with awareness sessions focusing specifically on child protection issues.

project_name: Saving lives and enabling safe and sustainable returns through the provision of Risk Education, Survey and Clearance
project_objective: The objective of the project is to provide life-saving Risk Education to at-risk populations in Northeast Syria (Aleppo and Ar-Raqqa governorates), in concert with Non-Technical Survey (NTS) and Clearance activities specifically enabling people who have been displaced to safely return to their homes and land. This is in line with the HRP Protection objective 4: “Reduce the impact of explosive hazards [ related to strategic objectives,1, 2 and 3]” and will contribute to addressing the high levels of explosive hazards contamination across NES (according to the 2021 HNO 1/3 of communities are contaminated).

project_name: Amélioration de la protection des civils au Mali
project_objective:
Dans le but de prévenir et d’atténuer les conflits récurrents qui entrainent les déplacements des populations, mais aussi en vue d’atteindre les déplacés/refugiés les plus vulnérables dans les zones difficiles d’accès, NRC envisage de mettre en place un projet de médiation humanitaire pour l’année 2021 dans les regions de Mopti, Tombouctou, Gao et Menaka.

La strategie de réponse repose sur 5 pilliers : 

1)	Une approche communautaire primant la participation et l’inclusion de toute personne affectee  ou impliquée dand le le conflit. Les interventions se dérouleront selon les priorités identifiées par les communautés, et c’est elles qui seront les premiers responsables de la mise en œuvre des solutions aux conflits identifées et acceptées par tous.

2)	Une comprehension approfondie des dynamiques conflictuelles et enjeux de protection à travers des analyses sensibles au conflit et de protection. Ces analyses, qui incluent des ateliers de collecte de données et formation et des entretiens de groupe et individuelles, s’appuient sur des outils précis. Ils servent à informer non seulement une éventuelle intervention de médiation, mais sont partagées au sein de NRC au Cluster Protection pour décider de la meilleure approche à adopter et renforcer la compréhenision du programme de la situation.

3)	Un renforcement, intégration et complémentarité avec les autres programmes NRC (ICLA, Education, LFS) pour apporter des solutions appropriées. Au moment de l’analyse il peut se révéler qu’une réponse autre que la médiation est prioritaire. De même, les solutions mutuellement acceptables trouvées par les parties au conflit a travers la médiation peuvent nécessiter l’intervention d’autres programmes NRC. De plus, les capacités d’analyse, communcation et facilitation des équipes médiation peuvent être mise a disposition des autres départements ou cela peut s’avérer d’une valeur ajouté.

4)	La mise en œuvre de processus de médiation humanitaire pour prévenir et attenuer des conflits, renforcer l’accès aux populations vulnerables et aux services sociaux de base, de renforcer la compréhension entre les parties au conflit, et génerer une confiance mutuelle entre NRC et les communautés. L’experience de plusieurs médiations humanitaires conduit au Mali entre 2018 – 2020 démontre que le processus de médiation (alert-analyse sensible au conflit – prémediation – mediation – suivi) contribue a une amélioration du sentiment de sécurité et sureté des participants, une amélioration de la compréhension entre les parties, et que le processus de médiaton et les médiateurs sont perçus comme essentiel à l’atteinte de ces resultats. Cette situation a dans plusieurs cas améliore l’accèes aux services sociaux de base et l’accès pour les acteurs humanitaries.

5)	Assurer le suivi des interventions pour préserver et renforcer les acquis, mais aussi comprendre et évaluer l’impact des interventions. L’engagement auprès des communautés ne fini pas à la conclusion du processus de médiation, mais nécessite un suivi de la mise en œuvre des solutions et, si nécessaire, des interventions (formations, dialogues, etc) pour préserver ces acquis. Il est aussi essentielle d’evaluer et comprendre, a travers un processus de suivi des outcomes, l’impact de l’intervention sur la situation et la communauté


Pour faciliter application de cette nouvelle approche de resolution des conflits et pour des raisons de la pérennisation des solutions durables, des formations sur les outils de gestion de conflit dans leurs communautés seront dédiées aux mecanismes traditionnels de resolution des conflits existants et aux organisations d’agriculteurs et d’éleveurs. 

Ces formations vont contribuer a  restaurer la cohésion sociale et le vivre ensemble entre agriculteurs et éleveurs et entre autres acteurs en conflit . Elles permettront également d’atténuer considérablement les conflits récurrents entre éleveurs et Agriculteurs dans les zones d’interventions de NRC.

project_name: Access to health for individuals in Lebanon
project_objective: The project aims at providing access to primary health care and providing COVID 19 homecare to individuals affected by the crises in Lebanon. The intervention will be rolled out through primary health care centers and mobile care teams operated by Amel. It will target 9000 individuals over a duration of 12 months through facilities (centers and mobile) that were not supported by other response plans prior to the launch of the ERP. Consequently, the project will respond to the additional demands for healthcare, in particular the ones expressed by the vulnerable communities including migrants and Lebanese, as per the PHC package defined by the health sector / MOPH. It will also contribute to the COVID-19 plan through homecare mobile unit support. The approach towards targeting will be balanced and contribute to the vision of ensuring universal access to health for all the populations affected by crises in Lebanon, with a clear focus on Lebanese and migrants, as per the ERP rationale.

project_name: Food Assistance for Lebanese in South and Nabatieh areas
project_objective:
The ERP acknowledges that estimates of extreme poverty also known as “food poverty” amongst the Lebanese stand at 36% (1.38 million). Food security has become a major threat to the Lebanese and migrant community in general and specifically to the female-headed households, lactating, and pregnant women, and households with people with disabilities. As it is also expected to remove what is left from current subsidies “Lebanese and migrant households are unable to rely solely on social safety nets to cushion the impact of these shocks”. Despite existing systems and collaborating efforts of local and international communities, needs are exponentially increasing. 
The proposed project under the LHF 2021 1st standard allocation, responds to vulnerable Lebanese families that have found themselves unable to meet their food security needs and critically food insecure as a result of the deteriorating situation of the country. After the passing of yet another year since the beginning of the Lebanese crisis, Lebanon is still facing the quadruple challenge of economic, political, social and health crises. Despite the collaborative efforts of local and international communities, needs are exponentially increasing thus, there still remains Lebanese families that are in need of emergency assistance at least during the coming months to cover their food and health needs. By conducting several assessments through our work in South and Nabatieh areas it was identified that there are approximately 500 HH in need of food assistance/
DPNA will work on providing 500 families in the areas of South and Nabatieh (after validating the criteria through an endorsed survey in compliance with WFP and Ministry of social affairs – MOSA- standards) that fall under at least one condition of the targeted vulnerability criteria of this allocation with in-kind food assistance for a period of 6 months. Also, under this project DPNA will distribute for a period of 2 months in-kind food assistance for COVID-19 positive cases referred by DPNA’s call center (endorsed by UNICEF and MOH) and collaborating municipalities. The second activity will be achieved through the establishment of a contingency stock of food kits. Through these two components we would contribute to the strategic food objective of the allocation which is the provision of immediate life-saving food assistance to meet growing and critical food needs of vulnerable Lebanese and migrant workers, not covered under the LCRP.

project_name: Provision of Medical Supplies for Hospitals and Expanded Coverage for Migrant In-Patient Hospital Care
project_objective:
Aligned with ERP Health Sector Objectives 1 and 2, SAMS will: 1) address the critical hospitalization needs of at least 100 migrants as a result of the pandemic and Lebanon’s socio-economic situation; and 2) procure and distribute PPE to five hospitals within SAMS' referral network, based on assessed needs. Note, hospital selection will be done in coordination with the Health Sector and nominated by Mr. Hisham Fawwaz - MoPH focal point. With regard to provision of critical life-saving hospital care, SAMS will provide financial top-up contributions to support the patient share, diagnostic care, and the non-covered cost (material) to vulnerable migrants, as well as the mandatory PCR tests associated with these hospital admissions.  Medical vulnerability criteria will be established in coordination with IOM, ICRC, Caritas and other key stakeholders, to determine which migrant patients will receive financial top-up contributions. With regard to payment modality, there will be no transfer of funds to patients. Rather, contracted hospitals that have been vetted by SAMS will submit invoices to SAMS for review and payment for costs of around $1,000 per patient on average. The cost of $1,000 per patient was determined in coordination with LHF and IOM, based on experience with hospitalization cost coverage for patients. In case patients with catastrophic illness require more support (ie. complications/longer-term support), SAMS will strive to cover the cost in full, negotiating also with contracted hospitals. Only patients that SAMS has pre-approved for treatment will be supported under the project.

The project will decrease protection concerns for patients, including the confiscation of ID and legal documents, the long separation of patients from their caregivers, refusal of the hospital to admit or discharge the patient because of medical debt, and the refusal to release the bodies of deceased patients through MOUs with hospitals that name SAMS as the responsible party for payment rather than the patient. As a secondary outcome, this project sustains hospital functionality during Lebanon’s confluent crisis while strengthening their administrative procedures for future patients. This will contribute to COVID mitigation and the protection of both patients and health workers in hospital settings via PPE provision and PCR testing for admitted patients. All activities will be closely coordinated within key stakeholders within the Health Sector - MOPH, IOM, OCHA, Health Sector WG NGO members, and hospital focal points.

This proposed response addresses the immediate needs of migrants, prioritizing the most vulnerable through temporary solutions, with the aim to mitigate the rapid deterioration of social and economic conditions while contributing financially to strengthening Lebanon’s public health system via income opportunities. As a complementary measure, SAMS will support hospitals with PPE as a means to respond to COVID needs of patients. 

As an immediate result: 100 migrant patients experiencing severe economic hardship will access previously unavailable medical care while being alleviated of any protection concerns associated with hospital admissions (such as document confiscation and refusal to admit/detention in hospitals due to a lack of payment). 5 hospitals, selected in coordination with the MOPH based on needs, will receive PPE- 250,000 facemasks, 100,000 gloves, 125,000 headcovers, and 40,000 shoe covers, procurement of which has been hindered due to staff shortages and inability to pay suppliers due to a lack of hard currencies and reduced imports into Lebanon. 

As a long term result: Hospitals will benefit from additional income and patient bills paid to avoid further MOPH deficits.

This project is currently 81% funded; the gap remains for provision of PPE support to five hospitals.

project_name: Nutrition Support and Awareness to Mothers and Children in Bekaa, Beirut, Mt. Lebanon, and North
project_objective:
As part of the intervention, RI aims to improve nutrition outcomes and practices, including attitudes towards breastfeeding, Infant and young Child Feeding (IYCF), hygiene practices, nutritionally balanced diets for pregnant and lactating women and children under two, and adolescents. These activities will be implemented across Bekaa, Beirut, Mt. Lebanon, and North for vulnerable Lebanese and migrant communities. RI will engage the community and expand knowledge and ensure lasting effects through the training of local NGO staff on early detection of malnutrition through screening.

Prolonged, economic deterioration, social and political tensions, and major food shortages continue to undermine food security and access to basic needs and services, limiting access to nutritional diets and knowledge of nutrition practices. Households (HHs) containing Lebanese and migrants across the country have been pushed into severe economic difficulty. With limited financial capabilities, HHs are unable to seek or obtain the critical nutrition services required, have limited access to necessary nourishable foods, are limited in movement due to major fuel shortages, and have limited employment prospects. Such circumstances mean HHs prioritize other needs and children and pregnant and lactating women are placed at increased risk. According to recent data collected, poor nutritional practices are becoming more widespread and common against the backdrop of the unfolding humanitarian situation.  As illustrated in the Needs and Vulnerability Assessment of Migrants in Lebanon report by IOM (May 2021), poor nutritional health among migrants is common with 60% of 674 respondents recording low dietary diversity. Likewise, Lebanese are struggling, 80% of Lebanese are now classified as poor, directly impacting nutrition outcomes, impacting expenditure on diets and being forced to purchase inferior foodstuffs and limiting daily food intake. According to the World Bank, GDP declined by 20.3% alone in 2020, and economists at Bloomberg reported a 400% increase in food prices.

RI determined targeting rural areas such as Tripoli  Akkar, Bekaa, Baalback and El Hermel, due to the fact that these areas host a large population of vulnerable Lebanese with limited access to health and nutrition services, aggravated with the overall devastating economic situation. In addition to Baabda, an area known of its vulnerability and crowdedness with vulnerable Lebanese and migrants. RI will continue to coordinate with IOCC to ensure a strong referral mechanism for malnutrition cases. This will be done across all areas of intervention and will include referral and follow up on malnourished cases identified through screening at the community of PHCs to the malnutrition treatment centers supported by IOCC.

Aligned to the nutrition cluster strategic objectives, RI will contribute to addressing the growing humanitarian needs, by targeting 3,000 individuals, made up of children and pregnant and lactating women.

project_name: Integrated community based child protection interventions in Rural Damascus
project_objective: IMC will continue its current programming implemented within its community center (RAC – Recreational Activity Center) in Jaramana and 2 mobile teams (currently deployed in Babella, Yalda and one collective shelter in Damascus). As IMC proposes to open a Community center in Babella,   RAC will continue providing PSS structured and non-structured activities including non-formal education and skill development (literacy, English and Arabic courses), social and recreational activities (handcraft, music, sport, theatre, art), targeting children, adolescents and their parents divided in groups according to their age and interests. A rehabilitation and inclusion program will also continue to be implemented targeting children with disabilities and their parents. Other positive parenting skills programs such as Early Child Development (ECD) programs, Caregivers Skills Training (CST) will continue to be offered at the RAC and at IMC PHC clinic in Jaramana, where also case management services are offered. Information and awareness activities as well as training on different child protection topics will continue to be conducted to support the beneficiaries and their communities to establish positive coping mechanisms, reduce protection related risks and enhancing their resilience. Within the mobile teams, IMC will continue provide case management services including referrals and PSS structured and non-structured activities, similar to those mentioned above for RAC (although no parenting skills programs will be implemented) as well as awareness and information activities. At the proposed community center, IMC plans to provide similar package of services as those currently offered at RAC, in addition to CP case management services. The center will constitute a safe space where boys and girls (in addition to mothers who will be engaged in certain activities with their children) can meet for social and recreational activities and obtain integrated protection services ranging from education and livelihood support to PSS and Child Protection interventions, in accordance with their needs. The services provided in the center will aim at empowering children and their families to cope with the consequences of the crisis and strengthen their resilience while at the same time strengthening the capacities of the community to prevent and respond to child protection concerns. When dealing with CP cases, the case managers will focus on the needs of the child and his/her family, ensuring that concerns are addressed systematically and in consideration of the best interests of the child, building upon the child and his/her family’s natural resilience and ensuring the child’s meaningful participation and family empowerment throughout the process, with the overall goal of ensuring safety for the child.

project_name: GBV prevention and response programming in Rural Damascus
project_objective:
IMC plans to establish a Women and Girls and Safe Space (WGSS) in Babella sub district, Rural Damascus. The center will work as entry point for identification of GBV related concerns, representing a safe space for beneficiaries to access confidential support through case management, psychosocial and referrals services. At the same time, the center will be offering a range of structured and non-structured evidence based activities, aimed at enhancing awareness, prevention and response about GBV concerns. Women and girls will be able to express and exchange concerns and experiences with their peers and qualified counselors, which will be crucial in enhancing prevention mechanisms while ensuring confidential and appropriate responses are provided when needed. Beneficiaries will be able to determine their interests in terms of PSS activities that the center will offer, which in turn will enhance their active participation. Women and girls and the community overall will be consulted in an effort to better understand the main risks as well as the types of community support systems existing before the crisis and how they have changed over the years. 
IMC has been working in Babella and Yalda over the past months through a mobile protection team in spaces offered by the communities, mostly targeting children, youth and women. The team offers PSS structured, non-formal education and recreational activities in addition to case management services. Internal referrals are made for medical services offered by IMC medical mobile team also working in the same areas. 
Based on its experience, IMC recognize that the establishment of a WGSS would further encourage and promote active participation of girls and women, offering a safe space for them to interact and discuss about topics of their interest. Furthermore, IMC team will work to raise information and awareness on GBV related topics, to strengthen community protection and support mechanisms. To this end, IMC also plans to organize and conduct capacity-building activities to community members and volunteers (these will be involved in the implementation of some activities at the center). 
Aside from the WGSS, IMC plans to continue its case management and awareness and information activities within IMC primary health care facilities, both static and mobiles.

project_name: Whole of Syria (WoS) Education assistance for vulnerable and out-of-school children and youth
project_objective: War Child Holland (WCH) and its consortium of six Syrian implementing partners will provide an education response to 10,000 highly vulnerable children in communities in Northwest (Idlib and Aleppo governorates) and Northeast Syria (Deir ez-Zor and Raqqa governorates) across a 12-month action. Recognising the interconnection between protection and education, the action will increase access to non-formal education and strengthen the protection of vulnerable girls and boys who are out of school or at risk of dropping out, to build their resilience and provide a pathway back into a safe and protective environment in school and within their communities. The action will include non-formal education interventions including Accelerated Learning Programme (ALP) for out of school children; guided self-learning modality for informal settlements with no access to learning spaces to keep children connected to learning; remedial and homework support for children at risk of dropping out; effective teacher professional development through a coaching system; and material support in terms of stationery and light rehabilitation. The action will adopt an integrated approach through developing the capacity of teachers on child protection and enhancing the accessibility and safety of the school environment. This prevention and response approach will address immediate and urgent identified risks to access to education while contributing to long-term change.

project_name: Améliorer l’accès aux soins de santé primaire et nutritionnels en ambulatoire et en hospitalisation au Tchad
project_objective:
ALIMA et son partenaire Alerte Santé ont pour objectif de contribuer à la réduction de la mortalité des enfants de moins de 5 ans dans les régions sanitaires de N’Djamena et du lac à Liwa et à contribuer à la réduction la morbidité dans la région sanitaire de Liwa à travers des soins de santé primaire adaptés.   

Le projet apportera une assistance nutritionnelle à travers la prise en charge médico-nutritionnelle de 71102 enfants de moins de 5 ans dans la province de N’Djamena et 10770  dans la province de Liwa, des activités de sensibilisation à la malnutrition aigüe sévère et le renforcement des capacités de professionnels de santé. 
 
Dans la région sanitaire de N’Djamena, le projet appuiera la prise en charge de la MAS en ambulatoire dans les centres de santé appuyés et en hospitalisation à l’UNT HATC. La prise en charge des enfants MAS en ambulatoire s’effectuera dans 10 UNAs (AKS, Goudji, Atrone, Hille Houdjadj, Angabo, Diguel Est, Diguel Nord, Goudji Charafa, Zafaye Est et Zafaye Ouest) avec la mise en place d'un circuit unique permettant le dépistage systématique de la MAS. 
Dans la région sanitaire de Liwa au Lac, le projet appuiera la prise en charge de la MAS en ambulatoire dans les cliniques mobiles se rendant dans les sites de déplacés ainsi que les postes fixes appuyés par le projet (Djil Kory, Mananara, Kangara, Doudeye, Daboua école, Fadatou, Foul Foul, Kindikou Fodi Oudou, Amma et Diamerom) et en hospitalisation à l'UNT de l'hôpital de district de Liwa. 
Le renforcement des soins de santé communautaire sera mis en place avec des activités de porte à porte pour le dépistage précoce de la MAS ainsi que la sensibilisation sur les PFE et le covid-19. 

 A Liwa, le projet apportera  également une assistance de soins de santé primaires aux populations déplacées affectées par les multiples crises de la région du Lac afin de développer l'accès à des soins de santé primaire gratuits et de qualité pour tous. 
Dans la région sanitaire de Liwa au Lac, le projet appuiera le renforcement des soins de santé communautaire dans les sites de déplacés appuyés (Djil Kory, Mananara, Kangara, Doudeye, Daboua école, Fadatou, Foul Foul, Kindikou Fodi Oudou, Amma et Diamerom) avec des activités de porte à porte pour la PECADOM (des cas simples de paludisme, diarrhée et IRA) et fournira des soins de santé primaire (cliniques mobiles, soins de santé curative, santé de la reproduction). 

Pour la mise en œuvre de toutes les actions du projet, les capacités des agents de santé seront renforcées en tenant compte du contexte de la pandémie de covid-19.

project_name: Réponse nutritionnelle des populations affectées par les crises récurrentes dans les districts sanitaires Mao, Mondo, Nokou et Rig Rig Province du Kanem , Tchad
project_objective:
Le projet vise la réduction de la mortalité des enfants de moins de 5 ans dans la région du Kanem à travers l’amélioration du statut nutritionnel des enfants de moins de 5 ans et des femmes enceintes et allaitantes par les activités spécifiques et sensibles à la MAS avec la mise en place d’un paquet d’activités préventives à travers la stratégie 1000 jours. De façon plus spécifique, l’intervention vise l’amélioration de la couverture et de l’accès à une prise en charge préventive et curative gratuite et de qualité des principes pathologies de l’enfants dont la MAS, le renforcement du dépistage et du référencement des enfants
malnutris aigus par l’approche PB-mère oedème, l’amélioration de la demande, du recours et de la disponibilité des soins néonataux et obstétricaux d’urgence dans la zone ciblé par le projet, et le renforcement du paquet minimum Wash dans les centres de santé, le  renforcement de la mobilisation communautaire , la promotion des pratiques familiales essentielles (PFE) à travers des stratégies de communication prenant en compte les spécificité socio-culturelle des zones d’intervention. L’intervention couvrira 37 aires de santé dans les districts sanitaires de Mondo et Mao, Rig Rig  et Nokou.
La dimension genre sera intégrée à chaque étape du projet, pour les bénéficiaires directs, indirects à travers une approche participative, afin de répondre de façon adaptée aux besoins de l’ensemble de la population

project_name: Améliorer la santé et l'état nutritionnel des ménages vulnérables et déplacés dans le district sanitaire de Bagasola (GAC, Province du Lac)
project_objective:
S'appuyant sur son expérience dans les réponses aux besoins humanitaires aigus, Concern propose un projet d’une année, afin de réaliser un renforcement des services essentiels de base dans le District sanitaire de Bagasola. Le projet proposé ciblera en particulier les femmes et les enfants affectés par la crise humanitaire ou souffrant de malnutrition. Ce projet intégré appliquera une approche sexo-spécifique et sensible aux conflits afin d'accroître la capacité, l'accès et l'utilisation des services de traitement des maladies infantiles, de la malnutrition, ainsi que des infrastructures d’eau et assainissement. L’approche visera à sauver des vies et à réduire la morbidité des groupes les plus vulnérables, qui sont le plus souvent des femmes, des garçons et des filles de moins de 5 ans parmi la population déplacée et hôte. Ce résultat ultime sera atteint grâce à deux résultats intermédiaires, qui permettront d'atteindre à terme 20 000 personnes (6 120 filles, 5 880 garçons, 3 000 hommes, 5 000 femmes et filles de plus de ans).  

Dans le cadre de ce projet, Concern travaillera avec les populations déplacées et les communautés d'accueil afin de réduire les tensions dans l'accès aux ressources. Concern promeut avec diligence la diversité dans le recrutement du personnel et forme le personnel à l'égalité des sexes et à la protection contre l’exploitation et les abus sexuels (PSEA). Les personnels de santé formés dans le cadre de ce programme seront sensibilisés aux approches qui leur permettront de fournir un appui sensible aux conflits. Concern restera également en contact et en coordination étroite avec d'autres acteurs clés, notamment la communauté locale au sens large, les agences des Nations Unies, les prestataires de services, les ONG et le gouvernement, afin de garantir que nos approches en matière de ciblage et de programmes sont appropriées, sûres et adaptées aux besoins des populations affectées.

project_name: Appui multisectoriel dans les provinces du Lac et du Kanem auprès des populations déplacées et des populations hôtes
project_objective: L'action prévoit d'apporter une réponse multisectorielle aux besoins des populations de la province du Lac, dans les départements du Fouli et de Kaya ainsi que dans la province du Kanem, dans le département du Nord-Kanem. Les taux d’insécurité alimentaire très élevés dans les deux provinces concernées amènent ACTED à intervenir sur des renforcements de la sécurité alimentaire au moment de la période de soudure afin d’atténuer les chocs que cette période peut engendrer dans les ménages vulnérables. Un appui sous format de distributions de vivre ou de transfert monétaire en fonction des possibilités évaluées dans la zone sera apporté. Face à des chocs récurrents, la population sera soutenue pour mettre en place des systèmes de réduction de risques des catastrophes afin d’en limiter les impacts. ACTED fera le lien entre les secteurs WASH et Sécurité alimentaire comme établie dans les stratégies sectorielles des deux clusters qui investissent pour articuler leurs actions afin d’apporter une réponse la plus pertinente, et cohérente possible. Afin d’assurer de manière holistique l’amélioration de la sécurité alimentaire et par corolaire de la malnutrition, des appuis en Wash in nutrition et au niveau des communautés seront apportés dans le Nord-Kanem et auprès des populations hôtes dans le Lac. Pour les deux départements du Lac, ACTED interviendra auprès des sites de déplacés pour renforcer leur accès aux points d’eau et garantir les besoins en eau des bénéficiaires. La promotion de l’hygiène et assainissement auprès des bénéficiaires dans leurs pratiques quotidiennes sera également réalisée. Les besoins des populations hôtes en point d’eau autour des sites d’intervention d’ACTED seront également pris en compte afin d’assurer une réponse globale et favoriser la cohésion entre tous les groupes présents. ACTED prévoit également dans son intervention de soutenir les populations sur l’éducation en urgence au sein des sites des déplacés de la province du Lac. ACTED prévoit d’apporter une réponse qui lie le secteur Wash et éducation. Ainsi un appui aux écoles pour favoriser le respect de l’hygiène menstruelle des filles sera réalisé. La réponse d’urgence permettra de fournir les éléments de bases pour assurer aux bénéficiaires un accès minimum aux infrastructures éducatifs pour favoriser l’accès à une éducation pour tous. Les actions sont élaborées en coordination avec les autres acteurs humanitaires et de développement présents sur le terrain. Un point d’attention sera apporté de manière transversale sur l’ensemble de nos actions pour garantir la protection des bénéficiaires.

project_name: Providing Lifesaving NFIs and Shelter Support in North of Syria
project_objective:
The program provides life-sustaining shelter and NFI support and contributes towards the resilience and cohesion of communities and households by improving housing and related community/public infrastructure. Targeting both IDPs (70%) and host communities (30%) involves activities; 3,000 standard NFI kits distribution (3,000 HHs) and winterization components such as distributing (500,000 L) heating fuel to 1,667 HHs, and (2,000) stoves to 2,000 HHs and (25,000) winter clothes kits for 25,000 children both gender. As well as providing restricted cash for house rent services (1,000 units) for those IDP vulnerable groups and prioritizing female or child-headed households and elderly people and considering people with disabilities (1,000 HHs; 5,000 individuals).
This program includes 2,500 house rehabilitation activities which will target both IDPs and host communities (2,500 HHs; 12,500 individuals), this activity includes rehabilitating partially damaged units through ceiling repair, walls buildings and holes ﬁxing, doors and windows, infrastructure, electricity network, and solar panels, plastering, plumping and providing the water tank. This component will be guided by the shelter rehabilitation guidance published by the SNFI cluster in 2018 and ensuring that HLP documentations are well carried out in parallel with ﬁeld coordination with the relevant local councils

The program will seek feedback from both male and female beneﬁciaries and fully interact with both genders to ensure equitable access and equal opportunities.

project_name: Enhance  The Mental Health and Medical emergency services at Gaza Emergency Departments
project_objective:
Médecins du Monde – France (MdM-F) is operating in Gaza since 2002,  working mainly in the fields of emergency preparedness and response, mental health, and psychosocial support in addition to reproductive health.  Gaza is facing a deep economic and humanitarian crisis, which stems from 13 years of blockade, continuing internal political division, and the accompaniment of chronic electricity and water shortages and recurrent escalations of hostilities. As a result, access to health for this population has witnessed almost a reversal.
MdM is an active member of both the Health and Nutrition cluster and the Protection cluster. Among the last years, MdM contributed to the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) and in this case more specifically to the HCT Response Plan. 
The proposed intervention is contributing to the health cluster objective 1: Ensure the availability of acceptable and quality essential healthcare services to vulnerable communities in oPt related to the strategic objective 2. 
MdM-F is focusing its intervention on strengthening the capacities of the health system and the community to deal with emergencies. The proposed intervention aims at enhancing the mental health and medical emergency services at the hospitals and community levels. 
At the hospital level, the intervention will aim to increase the capacity of the health staff at 5 emergency departments on the mental and medical flow chart that was designed and validated by the Ministry of Health (MOH) in previous MdM interventions. MdM will ensure the continuation of the mental health integration at the emergency department of Al Aqsa hospital (both medical staff and 5 psychologists) as part of the MOH strategy and following the approved WHO approach as it was previously agreed between WHO and MOH that MdM will on WHO approach using the mhGAP . At the community level; MdM will work with a local partner to ensure the delivery of MHPSS services to the communities in Beit Hanoun through technical support taking into consideration COVID-19 adaptations, needs integration, and mainstreaming in all level of interventions.
MdM is in working with both MoH and Health cluster to coordinate its intervention and to ensure the effectiveness of our actions as well as to avoid duplication
This intervention complements the Palestinian Ministry of Health (MoH), as the main provider of health services in Gaza they are responsible for the supervision, regulation, and control of all health services. Finally, MdM – France, MdM - Switzerland, MdM-Spain , MAP UK, and WHO have coordinated their proposals in order to avoid any duplication.

project_name: Supported community-based awareness on settler violence and related military operations in Area C
project_objective:
The need to strengthen, improve, and increase awareness among exposed communities on reporting and documenting settler violence incidents has been widely identified. Moreover, the need to increase community participation and feedback on the type of responses necessary has been highlighted. Lastly, the essentiality of holding the international community and duty bearers accountable towards the affected communities in terms of IHL and IHRL violations resulting from settler-related incidents has been highly documented as well. Based on the above-identified needs, the purpose of this project is to actively facilitate the participation of communities and ensure their contribution to the methods of mitigating and/or preventing the risk of settler-related incidents. Thus, the resilience and self-protection capacity of the communities most exposed to violence will be supported.

To achieve the above, the project will target 354 direct beneficiaries in identified vulnerable communities, while the entire population of these 53 communities is estimated as indirect beneficiaries. The action, implemented by PUI and Al Haq will contribute to the protection cluster strategic objective SO1: “Increased respect for International Humanitarian Law (IHL) and International Human Rights Law (IHRL) and accountability for violations” and will be both remedial and environment building in nature. The project contains four layers of action designed to support the communities and the inter-cluster mechanism led by OCHA. This mechanism was established with the support of PUI and OHCHR, to trigger and coordinate protection as well as material responses to SV incidents. In this framework and beyond the response side, OHCHR and PUI agreed that there is still a need for a deeper analysis of the settler related threats.

The first part of the action will focus on strengthening policy and advocacy efforts. The second part will supplement the first part by strengthening alerting skills at the community level to support the OCHA inter-cluster SV tracking mechanism. The targeted communities are considered to be heavily impacted by SV, but without having incidents comprehensively recorded and triggered in the existing tracking tool. The communities targeted are either located close to new outposts that are thus expected to face severe threats of settler violence and military related operations, or are identified by key stakeholders as highly affected by settler violence, but with a very limited documentation incidents in the inter-cluster tracking tool.

The third part of the action will target clusters of communities identified as highly affected by SV “hot-spots” and exposed to the same sources of threats arising from specific settlement and outposts. The project will facilitate joint discussions on the threats of SV (similar in types and origin) - to foster collective reflection on possible methods of mitigating threats and holding duty bearers accountable.

Lastly, the fourth part of the action will aim at addressing internal community protection risks identified, through the provision of targeted awareness raising and capacity building activities. This layer of intervention addresses the intersectionality of needs of different groups of people within the community face (e.g. PwD, FHHs, etc.). To further reinforce local resilience and self-protection, it is of utmost importance to also address internal protection related risks and threats.

Identification of needs for capacity building & activity implementation will be planned and coordinated together with community members, putting great attention to the community representation reflecting the wide range of characteristics in terms of age, gender and diversity (AGD). The action will specifically emphasize women participation in identifying protection threats, & decision making processes on designing collective strategies, including ways to tackle specific risks faced by diffrent groups of people.

project_name: Conflict-affected households in North Syria provided with access to sufficient and safe WASH services and improved hygiene conditions
project_objective:
Mercy Corps (MC) will respond to priority needs with life-saving and life-sustaining WASH assistance across the governorates of Al-Hasakeh, Aleppo, Ar-Raqqa, Deir-ez-Zor and Idleb. 
MC will work on improving access to basic Water and sanitation services through the delivery of water trucking, SWM, Desludging and the rehabilitation of water supply infrastructure in IDP locations and areas with a high number of IDPs and returnees, and areas we anticipate significant inward displacement (Ar-Raqqa and DEZ, Dana, Daret Azza and Atareb in Idleb and north Aleppo). In NW, MC will continue providing a full WASH package camps and IDP sites, which includes COVID related interventions, Water Quality monitoring and treatment and hygiene education. Hygiene education, using carefully tailored messages, and the distribution of hygiene and COVID kits will complement the other WASH interventions. Through ongoing Coordination with WASH cluster, working groups, local councils and other agencies, MC will be coordinating its response in relation to the gaps identified and associated needs. In 2021, a special focus will be given by MC to seek solutions for operation and maintenance (O&M), through support to local committees and water authorities directly after the completion of water supply rehabilitation. MC will work actively to identify and implement water trucking sustainable solutions and cost efficient sanitation management in the targeted IDP locations. Internal water supply networks, water tanks and toilets will complement more comprehensive HH shelter activities, providing safe and dignified accommodation standards for displaced and for those who have chosen to return. MC will also distribute multi-purpose cash assistance to conflict-affected households based on regional SMEB values, which include hygiene items.

project_name: Assistance en abri d’urgence et articles ménagers essentielsaux populations déplacées affectées par la crise dans le Sahel, le bassin du lac Tchad et le Nord-Ouest Nigeria
project_objective:
Depuis 2013, la situation instable dans le bassin du lac Tchad et les conflits dans le nord du Nigeria ont entraîné des déplacements prolongés dans la région de Diffa.  L’insécurité croissante dans les trois États de Nord Nigeria de Sokoto, Zamfara et Katsina a engendré de nouveaux déplacements forcés dans la région de Maradi avec plus de 23,000 PDIs en date d’octobre 2020. En outre, les combats récurrents entre les groupes armés non étatiques, les forces militaires et les groupes ethniques dans le nord du Mali ont entraîné de récurrents déplacements internes depuis 2018, avec plus de 140,000 IDPs dans les régions de Tillaberi et Tahoua. La détérioration de la situation sécuritaire à la frontière avec le Burkina Faso a également conduit à des déplacements internes de population à l'intérieur du pays. 
De plus, les conditions de vie des populations rurales et urbaines au Niger sont régulièrement affectées par les aléas climatiques de plus en plus imprévisibles et difficiles à surmonter à cause de leurs caractères intenses et dévastateurs (inondations, incendies, sécheresses, etc.). Spécifiquement en 2020, les fortes pluies ont occasionné d’importants dégâts et perte, faisant plus 39,655 ménages sinistrés soit environ 342,263 personnes. 

Laissant derrière elles leurs maisons, leurs biens essentiels, leurs stocks alimentaires, leurs moyens de subsistance (bétail, matériel de pêche) souvent pillés ou détruits, les déplacées vivent dans des conditions précaires sur leurs lieux de déplacement. L’urgence sanitaire causée par la pandémie Covid-19 a accentué d’avantage la vulnérabilité de certaines catégories de personnes déjà fragiles (PBS, les personnes de 3eme âge, etc.). Le manque d’abris décents les expose aux intempéries et à une promiscuité accrue qui n’est pas favorable pour respecter les mesures de distanciation sociale.  En effet, la précarité des abris et la promiscuité sur les différents lieux d’hébergement créé un climat propice (particulièrement pour les PBS, les femmes et les filles), aux tensions, aux violences sexuelles et aux differentes risques sanitaire (palu, covid19, etc.).

De ceux qui précèdent, le HCR propose de répondre aux besoins humanitaires dans les Region de Diffa, Maradi, Tahoua et Tillabery, en ciblant les populations en situation de vulnérabilité aigüe suite à un mouvement de population, à savoir les populations déplacées, les familles d’accueil, et les populations autochtones particulièrement vulnérables. Le projet vise à fournir une aide d'urgence immédiate avec des abris adéquats et des AME à 47,500 personnes, soit 9,500 ménages touchés par les déplacements forcés.  À moyen terme la réponse d'urgence facilitera l'accès à des conditions de vie plus décente et contribuera la diminution de certains risques de santé de protection pour les populations affectées dans le secteur Abris-BNA. 

La résilience face aux conditions météorologiques difficiles pour les matériaux composants les abris d’urgence reste un défi de taille pour le secteur ABNA. Ainsi, ce projet va aussi répondre au besoin en abri des extrêmes vulnérables ménages affectées par les déplacements prolongés et qui nécessite un appui régulier pour le renouvellement ou le renforcement de leurs abris.   
La réponse sera principalement centrée sur les ménages et est basée sur leur vulnérabilité. Une priorisation des plus “vulnérables parmi les vulnérables” se fera également en prenant notamment en compte les vulnérabilités spécifiques liées à l’âge, à la diversité, au genre, ou à d’autres besoins spécifiques (situation d’handicap, femmes chefs de ménages, enfants/mineurs séparés, et non accompagnés, minorités ethniques et autres). à travers un mécanisme d’entraide communautaire, ces personnes bénéficieront d’un soutien supplémentaire dans le cadre des activités notamment un appui pour les transports des kits et la construction des abris.

project_name: Holistic child protection intervention in Wadi Khaled and Ras Baalbek, and judicial protection in Bekaa and Baalbek-Hermel
project_objective:
Lebanon was hit by unprecedented ascending multiple crises at a time, which is negatively impacting the lives of boys and girls living on its soil. More of 80% of the Lebanese, PRL and migrant populations are under the poverty line, leading to exposing children to child labor in its worst forms as schools are closed, or became inaccessible. Lebanese children are more and more in need of an adequate response as other response plans failed to compensate the emerging need, since targeted areas were linked to the presence of Syrian refugees, leaving the host and other cohorts in other areas underserved. 
All proposed activities are long awaited by the affected populations, given the fact that the needs are exponentially increasing since the onset of the financial crisis. himaya first suggests implementing an integrated package of community based and focused psychosocial activities, addressed to both children and parents as well as case management services in Akkar, specifically in the most vulnerable areas of Wadi Khaled. According to interviews conducted with several decision makers in the region, some villages in Wadi Khaled didn’t get any support from NGOs since 2016. Furthermore, as per Unicef field focal point and the CP sector coordinator in the North, there is a big gap in child protection services in the region, especially in Hnaider, Amayer, Kneiseh and Majdal, knowing that these villages are listed in the high priority localities to implement an integrated approach. Community members identified the stateless people, especially children as the most vulnerable and marginalized groups in Wadi Khaled society. Children are deprived from their basic rights: Their right to play and the right for a descent education. Community members mentioned that a huge number of children are exposed to different kind of abuse: Neglect (Children left in the streets with no safety measures taken), sexual harassment (for boys and girls), Child Labor, Child Marriage, and Violent discipline. Furthermore, a big tension is highlighted between the Lebanese and Syrian children.  
Another intervention is proposed in Ras Baalback, a forgotten area calling for himaya's help, via its community based groups such as the scouts. Few children were recently referred to himaya's office in Kaa for case management, and the absence of local actors is a concern. Parents are in distress, as their monthly salaries are currently worth less than 40 usd and they cannot endure severe conditions anymore. Finally, an extremely important component is to cover in both Bekaa and Baalbek- Hermel governorates, which is the judicial protection of children as himaya is mandated to cover this service.

project_name: Increasing access to child protection mechanisms and psychosocial support services for vulnerable children and families in Lebanese and Palestinian Communities
project_objective: The proposed intervention aims to strengthen the provision of Child Protection (CP) services and Child Protection support to the children and families affected by the crisis among the Lebanese and Palestinian communities. It will be built up on existing projects, benefiting from the long-lasting experience of TDH IT in preventing and responding to protection threats of the refugee and Lebanese children and from the experience of the organization in working with Palestinian communities in Lebanon. Targeted beneficiaries will be supported with the provision of full cycle quality CP prevention (Awareness, Community based PSS, Caregivers Program) and response services (Focused PSS and Case Management) in vulnerable localities particularly affected by the crisis in Beirut, Mount Lebanon and Baalbeck-Hermel Governorates, as well as in Palestinian refugee camps across Lebanon. The outreaching process will make use of the Vulnerability and Capacity Assessment - including household/door-to-door visits, FGDs, semi-structured discussion and KII - and of internal/external referrals in coordination with the other humanitarian actors based in the areas of intervention.  The ‘I Am Here’ methodology is also in use to support staff in identifying and responding to the needs of adolescents, children and their caregivers for the development of inclusive and holistic outreaching processes. The intervention will be implemented both through TDH IT direct implementation and through the involvement of local organizations, benefiting from their technical skills and added values in providing PSS through alternative modalities (e.g.: sports, arts, yoga). Such a collaboration has been piloted by TDH IT through previous initiatives with successful achievements in terms of child protection mainstreaming, outreaching new typologies of beneficiaries and addressing related vulnerabilities. Among targeted Palestinian camps, the intervention will be fully implemented through local organizations, already collaborating with TDH IT in the provision of NFE services to increase Child Protection in Education integrated approaches and mainstreaming. Community engagement initiatives will be organized in all the locations mentioned with the goal to increase awareness on raising Child Protection threats (especially focusing on child labor, early marriage and violence against children) and on the activation of related prevention and response mechanisms. The modality of implementation will be adapted to the emergency situation in the country and can be carried out face-to-face, remotely or blended, through the use of ad hoc tools (interactive sessions, videos and games, arts to be implemented via remote) and the use of online platforms (WhatsApp, Zoom, conference calls). Specific COVID-19 awareness sessions and RCCE activities will be delivered throughout the intervention in line with the MoPH/health sector recommendations.

project_name: Strengthening CP and GBV response services  in underserved areas in South and Nabatieh within the framework of ERP 2021-2022
project_objective:
Within the framework of the ERP 2021-2022, Tdh in consultation with their local partner organizations Sanabel Al Janoub (SJ), SAMA, Al Ghad and Human Charity for Relief and Development (HCRD) have jointly developed a project to strengthen the Child Protection (CP) and Gender-based violence (GBV) response services for the most vulnerable Lebanese, Palestinian Refugees from Lebanon (PRL) and migrants in remote and underserved areas in the South and Nabatieh Governorates.

The proposed intervention will take place in the Governorate of South, particularly in Saida and Tyre districts, covering 30 cadasters and in the Governorate of Nabatieh, specifically in Bent Jbeil and Nabatieh Tahta districts, covering 9 cadasters. In addition, the project will target five Palestinian Camps of South (Bourj Chamali, Al Bass, Rashdieh, Ein el Helwi and Mieh Mieh). 

The locations were identified and targeted in consultation with the Union of Municipalities in Tyre, Saida, Sarafand and Nabatieh, Popular Committees and Child Protection Networks (CPNs) in the five Palestinian Camps and based on the recent needs’ assessments of the local partners that highlighted the gaps in terms of CP/GBV services, trends, and vulnerabilities of the targeted populations. Furthermore, the previous prevention and outreach activities within the Social Behavioral Change Initiatives of Tdh in South and Nabatieh were factors that supported the identification of the locations and pointed out the areas with the highest CP/GBV needs. 

The specific localities were also selected based on Tdh and partners’ ability to access remote and underserved areas (such as Bent Jbeil and Nabatieh) and areas that project’s partners have more than 44 years constant presence and working experience. 

The primary purpose of the project is to provide a life-saving response in a context of significantly increased needs due to complex humanitarian crisis in Lebanon. Tdh and local partners have identified the vulnerability criteria through needs assessments, CP Realtime Monitoring Reports, analysis of the recent referrals but also using as a baseline the data from the case management specialized services of the previous and/or ongoing projects that target partially the CP/GBV concerns of Lebanese and PRL populations. As a response, the project is proposing to target the most vulnerable individuals with the following criteria: 1. Children exposed to neglect, psychical, psychological, and emotional abuse, exploitation, including all types of child labour, 2. Children separated by their parents/caregivers or at risk of separation due to COVID19, medical or socioeconomical reasons, 3. Children exposed to poverty, malnutrition, hidden malnutrition, and school’s drop out due to socioeconomical situation in Lebanon. 4. Children in conflict and in contact with Law and exposed to substance abuse. 5. Children (girls and boys) and young women (until 24 years old) exposed to GBV, including child marriage, sexual abuse, intimate partner violence and domestic violence. 6. Female single headed households with children.

This project will provide specialized response services to GBV cases, including Case Management, provision of Emergency Cash Assistance (ECA), Legal Assistance, as well as Focused PSS sessions to vulnerable individuals. The project will have a holistic approach, including Community-based PSS sessions in Safe Spaces and distribution of Dignity Kits within prevention activities. Moreover, specialized response services related to CP cases will be provided such as Case Management, referrals to the cash assistance under the Haddi program, and focused PSS sessions for children and caregivers. Community-based PSS sessions, Positive Parenting sessions for caregivers and Social behavior Change/child protection initiatives will be also implemented during the project duration of 11 months.

project_name: CARE Integrated GBV Response
project_objective:
The project aims to reinforce an effective protection environment and to reduce the risk of GBV for girls, boys, men and women from Lebanese, PRL, and Migrant communities.

The project will build on GBV prevention and response mechanisms currently in place, as it will continue to provide multi-sectoral response to GBV and upscaled prevention services through improving community engagement. CIL with its local partner will provide a comprehensive package of services for GBV survivors through the implementation of case management, emergency cash assistance, protection cash assistance, PSS, awareness raising activities, legal services, and distribution of dignity kits. 

This package will be combined with community outreach, which will involve stronger community engagement and will ensure a timely access to services. 

Beneficiaries with specific needs, survivors of GBV or women and girls at risk of GBV will be identified to benefit from project services. Identification of beneficiaries will happen through: outreach, external referrals, internal referrals, self-referrals through the helpline, referrals from partners. 

A combination of targeting methods will be used in order to improve access and inclusion. A specific vulnerability criteria of targeted beneficiaries with specific protection risks will be put in place in order to ensure the identification of “most at risk” individuals especially for the selection of beneficiaries under the emergency cash assistance activity, example of prioritized most at risk or most vulnerable groups: women head of household, women and girls with limited or no access to SRH services, women with medical needs, elderly women, PWDs..etc  

The project aims to achieve two main outcomes:  1) To reduce the risk of GBV through prevention services and strengthening community engagement ;2)To mitigate the impact of GBV through improving access to response services and activating referral pathways The project will also promote accountability through strengthened coordination, community participation, improved access to information about PSEA, and prevention and response through service provision.

Project services will be provided through a combined approach of static (in partner(s) community centers) and mobile services in different areas: Beirut, Mount Lebanon, Akkar, Tripoli and Beqaa, combining both approaches will enable a better access to services and eventually improved response.

project_name: Education for Lebanese and Migrant in North Lebanon
project_objective: The main purpose of this project is to ensure children that are out-of-education or are affected by the economic crisis are provided relevant, inclusive and quality education adhering to national and international standards on education in emergencies and child protection. The target population in this project is the most vulnerable children and youth and parents/caregivers from Lebanese and Migrant backgrounds in North Lebanon and Akkar. The project aims to provide learning support, food, referral to other sectors, SGBV and protection awareness sessions and procurement of learning materials to the targeted groups. Moreover, the project include 1000 most-vulnerable children enrolled in catch-up learning support programs addressing learning losses in public schools. The project includes a main outreach component to identify out of Education Children, refer children and youth to basic services and implement awareness sessions to children and youth on the importance of education and being in education. The number of target group ranged across activities as identified in cluster/sector later.

project_name: Access to learning for out-of-education children with and without disabilities
project_objective:
Access to learning continues to be a challenge for over 1.2 million children in Lebanon due to the economic crisis and COVID-19 pandemic; the Ministry of Education and Higher Education estimates an influx of 100,000 children from the private sector to the public. Furthermore, a significant percentage of children with disabilities struggled to follow remote learning last year and were left out of education. The challenge to access learning becomes more complex to these children due to stigma and limited capacity of the education system to respond to their needs [Based on the consolidated analyses done by the ERP Lebanon – Education sector regarding the situation of access to education in Lebanon]. Prior to the crisis and pandemic, children with disabilities already faced exclusion. According to UNESCO (2021), children with disabilities are 2.5 times more likely not to access remote learning and to drop out when schools re-open [Consolidated information from sources such as GPE, World Bank, UNESCO, and UNICEF (2020, 2021) on how the COVID-19 pandemic has disrupted education around the world including Lebanon]. This project therefore aims to mitigate these challenges and specifically aims to provide access to learning to 3,000 out-of-education Lebanese and migrant children with and without disabilities, aged 6-14. The logical framework developed by the National Education Sector in Lebanon defines and guides the development of this project’s objectives and targets. However, HI emphasizes on targeting children with disabilities based on its institutional capacity on disability inclusion in Lebanon and globally. This then provides the organization the benefit of responding to the needs of children with disabilities who remain the most marginalized group in accessing learning. Notwithstanding, HI recognizes the importance of targeting children without disabilities as well, children from the same households or neighborhoods of children with disabilities. To achieve its objectives and targets, this project will invest on two major interventions.
First is the identification and referral to basic services including education of out-of-school children with and without disabilities. HI’s trained outreach workers will identify children at the community level. The data gathered from the identification exercise will then support HI in defining specific interventions to respond to children’s needs and barriers faced, as well as to facilitate their referral. The second intervention of providing direct assistance to children with and without disabilities, and their caregivers to support continued learning will then take place. In this project, HI will focus on direct assistance, namely: cash for education, assistive technologies, learning kits, and psychosocial support. HI will ensure continued learning by developing personalized support plans identifying children’s needs with corresponding low-cost solutions. Through outreach, these plans will then be monitored periodically via home visits and phone calls; they will include activities that provide children and parents/caregivers with training sessions on digital literacy, focusing also on practical skills such as connecting to WiFi/mobile data, signing up/creating accounts, and joining online classes. Finally, the personalized support plans will outline the provision of PSS activities to children and parents/caregivers, including the adaptation of existing PSS curriculum through theater plays, interactive learning, and training sessions. To ensure meaningful and efficient delivery of these direct assistances, HI will establish processes at different levels. Furthermore, HI’s outreach workers will follow up on learning retention among children with and without disabilities. Finally, data and evidence generation will be a prioritized under this project. HI will then ensure dissemination of these data and evidence to government and partners to facilitate scale up or replication.
