project_name: Emergency School Feeding Programme
project_objective:
Based on the success and learns learnt from the first two years of the Emergency School Feeding
Programmes in Libya in 2019 [HLBY19‐EDU‐151894‐1] and 2020 [HLBY20-EDU-162711-2], where more than 20,000 School-aged children has been reached with whether on-site school meals or alternative Take-Home-Rations when schools closed because of the COVID-19 pandemic. WFP will expand the complementary school meals programme as means to ensure children’s access to food in times of crisis and enhance diets through increased micronutrient intake. Assistance will take into account protection and safety, COVID-19 precautions, and where possible, contribute to their broader protection and community awareness. In 2020, the school rations including nutritionally‐fortified date bars, which are culturally‐acceptable, programmatically‐feasible and can contribute to enhanced micronutrient intake among children, were actually provided to over 18,379 school-aged children (Onsite feeding or Take-Home-Rations) against the original plan of 20,000 school‐aged children.

In 2021, WFP plans to reach 41,000 school-aged children in need for Education Sector's assistance, out of which 20,000 school-aged children will be prioritized for the humanitarian-oriented assistance under the Humanitarian Response Plan 2021. This programme could also support and strengthen the current formal education system and advocate towards a safe back to School, in order to allow a greater and at scale-reach of those already in school, girls and boys out of school or at risk of dropping out and those who are most vulnerable in the society, minority groups including (but not excluded to) girls. It will also help promote and encourage the enrolment of the children of the migrant populations in urban settings. The programme would review implementation arrangements to assure  COVID-19 precautionary measures, strengthen synergies with education and livelihood sectors and increase nutrition sensitivity, gender sensitivity, local procurement and community ownership. This would promote community infrastructure, rehabilitation, and reconstruction ﴾including schools and health centres﴿ as well as promote the reintegration of displaced populations and returnees, with special attention paid to the different needs of women and men.

While implementing the Emergency School Feeding under the HRP 2021, WFP will invest its resources in the capacity strengthening to enable national and local authorities to respond, and foster schools’ resilience to acute shocks and chronic stresses stemming from existing and future crises through strengthened coordination, evidence-based needs analyses, and strategic preparedness. WFP will also work with the Ministry of Education in conducting awareness raising sessions for the local Education officials and school representatives on nutrition and cross-cutting issues such as gender, GBV, environment and the prevention of Sexual Abuse and Exploitation (PSEA).

The project will be monitored by the local Education officials and WFP’s Third Party Monitors. The outputs data will be collected by WFP through the partners’ monthly distribution reports, and the outcomes will be assessed the Post-Distribution Monitoring on an annual basis.

project_name: Strengthening national disease surveillance with a focus on COVID19, TB and HIV
project_objective:
The overall objective of this project is to strengthen capacity of Ministry of Health, National Center for Disease Control and health sector partners for rapid detection of public health risks and events with a focus on COVID19/TB/HIV, prompt risk assessment, notification and response through enhanced sentinel surveillance, event based surveillance and community surveillance structures. Furthermore the project will support the collection, processing, analysis and dissemination of critical health information including disease surveillance data and access to the availability of life-saving services.
The project is in line with objective 3 of the health chapter of Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP). It is also in line with strategic objective 1 of the same document.
In this project, WHO will address the capacity gaps to ensure compliance of all health facilities and sentinel sites with the minimum standards of disease surveillance reporting with a focus on COVID19, ILI/SARI and TB/HIV surveillance. Vulnerable groups including migrants, returnees, displaced families and poor host communities will remain the direct beneficiaries of the project as it will detect, respond to and contain outbreaks at an early stage.
Considering the potential for rapid and exponential growth of COVID-19 outbreaks, new cases and clusters should be identified and reported as rapidly as possible, and data should be included in any relevant epidemiological analyses within 24 hours of diagnosis. National authorities should include COVID-19 as a mandatory notifiable disease with requirements for immediate reporting.
Surveillance systems should be geographically comprehensive, and surveillance for vulnerable or high-risk populations should be enhanced. This will require a combination of surveillance systems including contact tracing for all levels of the health-care system, at the community level, in closed residential settings and in other vulnerable groups.

project_name: Accès à l'Éducation des Enfants affectés par la Crise sécuritaire dans les Régions du Nord et de la Boucle du Mouhoun au Burkina Faso
project_objective:
Le projet s’inscrit dans un contexte marqué par une insécurité caractérisée par la fermeture d’écoles due aux attaques terroristes perpétrées dans certaines communes du Yatenga, du Lorum du Sourou et de la Kossi. Les écoles ciblées pour ce projet relèvent des communes de ces provinces. L’affluence de ces personnes déplacées internes( PDI) dans ces zones implique nécessairement une augmentation de la demande en terme d’éducation. C’est pourquoi, nous envisageons renforcer les capacités de 25 écoles susceptibles d’accueillir ou ayant accueilli des enfants déscolarisés en situation de déplacement interne pour les réintégrer dans les différentes écoles primaires et établissements du post primaire et secondaire des communes ciblées. 
Le projet vise à garantir l’accès à une éducation de qualité, inclusif et protecteur pour 11 250 élèves dont 3900 élèves EDI déscolarisés ou à risque du primaire (50% de filles) et 1950 élèves EDI dont 200 filles du post-primaire qui ont été accueillis dans 25 écoles ciblées dans les écoles des communes ciblées du fait de l’insécurité dans la zone du Nord et de la Boucle du Mouhoun. Au-delà des enfants, l’action compte renforcer les capacités de 150 enseignants / enseignantes et encadreurs pédagogiques. Mais au préalable, il importe d’apporter un soutien psychosocial aux 11 250 bénéficiaires ciblés et un appui psychologique à 50 enfants en vue de réduire le choc et la détresse psychologique subis. Pour réussir ce projet, il faudra nécessairement impliquer les acteurs et partenaires de l’éducation en l’occurrence les municipalités, les OSC / ONG intervenant dans l’éducation dans les communes cibles, les membres des APE/AME/COGES estimés à 175, à travers des cadres de concertation. Ces instances seront des opportunités de capacitation de ces acteurs sur la prévention et la gestion des situations d’urgence afin d’améliorer les conditions de vie des enfants déplacés en renforçant les familles d’accueil (hôtes) sur la parentalité. Pour rendre les enfants plus résilients face à la situation, il est prévu un accompagnement de 11 250 enfants et adolescents sur les compétences en survie.
Educo mettra le projet en œuvre en consortium avec l’Association Tabital Lobal dans la region du Nord et l’Association Donnons nous la main (ADM) dans la Boucle du Mouhoun

project_name: Shelter Assistance for vulnerable populations in Burundi, and returning households
project_objective:
This project aims to address the needs of vulnerable returnees, IDPs, and host communities in Burundi, focusing in priority in the provinces neighboring the United Republic of Tanzania, where most returns are expected by UNHCR for the year 2021: Kirundo, Muyinga, Cankuzo Ruyigi, Makamba and Rutana. 
These areas host the largest numbers of returnees, with important needs of shelter/NFI as well as livelihoods. Reintegration assistance through shelter will provide a comprehensive approach to assisting the most vulnerable beneficiaries. The primary stakeholders are identified as not only those people returning through the VolRep program, but also spontaneous returnees, IDPs and host communities to facilitate a holistic approach, as well as to enhance the social cohesion in these communities. 
Partnerships with NGOs, local leaders, civil society, and the broader UN family will be upheld and strengthened through the implementation of this project. Given the existing gap in overall funding from development partners in Burundi that focus on returns and reintegration through shelter construction, the aim is to provide services that build upon previous projects in line with donor priorities.

project_name: WaSH Joint National Emergency Response (JNER)
project_objective:
JNER is a common appeal by 13 WaSH NGOs, constituting the majority of non-UN active sector partners. Modalities are adapted from crisis-sensitive components of the HawkaMaa-EU development project consortium. Coordination at the sector level was led/facilitated by the coordination team, which encouraged collective action, and which is also invited to support the implementation of the JNER. 
The ERP acknowledges that public services are “overstretched and underdeveloped due to years of under- investment” and adopts a “system approach” to maximize reach and cost effectiveness while minimizing inter/intra-community (including host-refugee) tensions and adverse effects of parallel services on public utilities. JNER reinforces this approach by tackling the two main components of water service provision, production and distribution, across three categories of localities/communities; those served by Water Establishments (WE), others by municipalities, and those unserved by public systems. It assumes that UNICEF, as sector lead and owing to its capacity will provide the necessary consumables (notably fuel and chlorine) and maintenance required for continued operation of priority pumping stations. 
Recognizing that water production does not guarantee its effective and equitable delivery due to blockages, bursts, pressure imbalances, and faulty operation fittings and regimes within networks and exclusion of households and communities from coverage altogether, JNER will primarily tackle distribution problems to ensure the minimum standard of safe water (35 l/c/d) is received by the most vulnerable communities and key outbreak-prone institutions. This entails addressing urgent maintenance requirements of WE and municipal networks. Unserved communities/households will be served through temporary water trucking or private pumping systems. Against referrals from the Health and Food Security sectors, JNER will implement a rolling Hygiene Kit distribution activity. Also, it’s relevant to mention that in line with the LHF strategy, ACF, GVC and DPNA will provide 2824 WASH kits to mitigate hygiene risks for a duration ranging between 6 to 8 months in Akkar, South, and Bekaa benefiting approximately 13,500 individuals.
Participation will be subject to partners’ proven access, capacity, and readiness to implement timely interventions. This will be enhanced by inviting them to participate in joint national tenders soon to be launched by WW-GVC under HawkaMaa-EU and establishing framework contracts with infrastructure contractors and suppliers. Similarly, LebRelief will lead a joint national tender for hygiene items, as well as use Hawkamaa-EU (which has dedicated funding) to provide (with ACTED and LEWAP) capacity building for local NGOs. 
National coverage will be ensured through a geo-split akin to that employed within the refugee (IS) response, adopting a wider unit of WE branch/section jurisdiction to ensure compatible coordination scales in line with the vulnerability assessment adopted by the Water Sector Stabilization Thematic Group, except for Hygiene Kit distribution which is divided by District/Caza. JNER will coordinate nationally to (re)allocate funding dynamically as the understanding of vulnerability evolves with incoming analysis.

JNER will refer access challenges due to public production systems to UNICEF and offer to accompany assessments and interventions. Off-grid renewable energy for pumping stations will be exceptionally considered where feasible to help break WEs’ perpetual ‘energy crisis mode’. JNER will prioritize service recovery/improvement in collaboration with public entities by providing the necessary resources while maintaining direct oversight, reinforcing rather than undermining community trust in the public sector. This is critical to support the wider drive to reinforce public institutions, but JNER will stop short of providing them with direct support, conscious that the “ERP is strictly of humanitarian nature”.

project_name: Enhance the income of vulnerable and poor female and male farmers in the most affected areas of the Gaza Strip.
project_objective:
Project Objective:
Is to enhance the income of vulnerable and poor female and male farmers in the most affected areas of the Gaza Strip.

Project Summary :
The project is mainly assisting vulnerable and poor female and male farmers by providing them with one or more of the following services:
*	Rehabilitation of open lands
*	Rehabilitation of existing water wells run by electricity or fuel
*	Installation of solar systems for agricultural water wells
*	Rehabilitation of existing water ponds
*	Rehabilitation of greenhouses 

The project activities will be implemented all over the Gaza strip. NDC will partner with two local registered cluster NGOs who have extensive agricultural experience to implement the project. In addition, the project activities will be completely coordinated with the Ministry of Agriculture and the Food Security Sector.

The estimated number of direct beneﬁciaries is 1075 farmers (At least 175 female farmers and 900 males' headed household) while the total number of the farmers and their families is 5912. The estimated total budget for the project is $ 2,320,400.

The project's objectives match the HRP 2021 oPt, Strategic Objective country #( 3): The ability of vulnerable Palestinians to cope with the protracted crisis, including environmental threats, is supported, while solutions to violations and other root causes of threats and shocks are pursued.


Furthermore, the project is speciﬁcally in line with the Food Security Sector (FSS) objective
#(1) The livelihoods of vulnerable households are protected, and their resilience, food security and productive capacity restored/enhanced.

project_name: Increase innovative access to quality and inclusive education in safe environment for conflict affected children in North-East Nigeria
project_objective:
This action is proposed to support affected children including out of school, those at risk of dropping out and koranic school (children, teachers, parent, school infrastructure, etc.). Main focus will be made on creating and maintaining the protective learning environment for children and teachers, as well as strengthening their knowledge and skills cope with threats and attacks; special focus will also be put on developing and expanding relevant non-formal and informal education opportunities for children and adolescents. Through this action’s support, parents will be at the centre of awareness sessions on the importance of education which will also be applied to support parents and communities in enrolling and retaining their children in school and learning centers.
This action will target children, girls and boys (3–17 years) affected by the protracted crisis in Northeast Nigeria, especially in Borno (Askira/Uba, Monguno, and Konduga LGAs), Adamawa (Hong and Michika LGAs). Plan international has strong presence in these locations. And this action will leverage on previous and existing  interventions.
Also, this action is designed in line with Northeast EiE Working Group objectives to provide access to inclusive quality basic and vocational skills opportunities to conflict-affected children and adolescents.

Equitable access to safe and protective learning environments shall be facilitated through the Construction of (classrooms, latrines and water points), school facilities built and used by all students, girls and boys, including children living with disabilities. Access to quality alternative education adapted to the needs of girls and boys (3-17 years old) who are out of school because of the crisis shall be reinforced through learning or training activities. Rights of girls and boys shall be protected from immediate and future threats through access to conflict-sensitive education, disaster and conflict risk reduction, strengthening psychosocial coping and protecting schools from attack.

project_name: The Access Coordination Unit - Facilitating Access of Humanitarian and Recovery Actors in the oPt
project_objective:
Access challenges differ greatly across the oPt, primarily due to the range of political and administrative measures implemented by Israeli and Palestinian authorities. Access and movement restrictions are severe, widespread, costly and difficult to overcome. They increase the impoverishment and vulnerability of Palestinian women, girls, boys, and men within the oPt, and directly impede humanitarian and development operations. They make reaching vulnerable communities difficult and compromise the quality of programming and impact the effectiveness of humanitarian and development interventions. These restrictions which have profound gendered and protection impacts on different vulnerable groups, have been accentuated by the measures imposed by relevant authorities since March 2020 to contain the spread of C19. 
The Access Coordination Unit (ACU) provides a more systematic approach to these challenges and improves access of humanitarian personnel and goods in Israel and oPt including Gaza and the WB. Overall, 56% of ACU's UN staff beneficiaries are female (3350 from 6000). Working over all access points, the ACU provides direct engagement and advocacy with relevant authorities as well as direct and timely support, information and advice to international organizations and their personnel. The ACU also facilitates the movement of Palestinian staff serving at duty stations around the world, supporting family reunification and career development of humanitarian personnel. 
The ACU formulates common policies with a coordinated approach to alleviate constraints to access and to negotiate changes to access policies and procedures with the relevant authorities including Israel, the PA, Gaza authorities, Egypt and Jordan. 
The ACU currently supports the work of 24 UN agencies, over 200 NGOs, and 65 diplomatic missions whose access to populations in need is impeded by a series of political, physical and bureaucratic restrictions on access and movement imposed by authorities. In addition, an estimated 2.45 M Palestinians in need of assistance throughout the WB and Gaza will indirectly benefit through the more efficient and timely delivery of humanitarian assistance.
One of the primary services of the ACU is a 24/7 access hotline where staff can call the ACU to conduct real-time interventions with relevant authorities to resolve access incidents at checkpoints and crossings for both personnel and goods. The ACU also manages the ACULive mobile app which has 255 active users from 80 organizations, and which enables humanitarian and development personnel and agencies in the oPt to obtain timely and effective access information, guidance and support.The ACU also provides information and advice on procedures for obtaining visas, permits, project approvals and materials coordination as well as conditions and accessibility at checkpoints and crossings via the hotline and beneficiary-specific mailing list which includes 631 individuals working in UN, NGOs, and Diplomatic delegations.
During emergencies and contingency situations, the ACU deploys to key field and coordination centres to conduct access and civil-military coordination with the relevant authorities. During the July-August 2014 escalation, the ACU facilitated evacuation of over 1,300 foreign and dual nationals from Gaza to Jordan as well as coordinating other humanitarian activities. ACU coordinated the exit of dual nationals from Gaza during the C19 restrictions, as well as the entry and exit of humanitarian personnel. The humanitarian locations notification system developed by the ACU was launched in 2019 and contains over 500 locations that are regularly shared with the Israeli authorities. 
Finally, information, analysis and messaging on restrictions to humanitarian space are made publicly available to support advocacy efforts undertaken by the humanitarian community and other stakeholders with regards to access of the civilian population to basic service provision.

project_name: Strengthen capacity and increase access to health care, GBV and MHPSS services in Bor South, Duk, and Twic East counties
project_objective:
The project aims to strengthen the capacity of the public health system in delivering quality primary and secondary health care, with integrated GBV and MHPSS services. In close collaboration with the County Health Departments (CHDs) and State Ministry of Health (SMoH), MdM will support 41 health facilities across Bor South, Duk, and Twic East counties by providing regular supervision, monitoring, and training to the health and MHPSS/GBV personnel and supplying the necessary drugs, equipment and materials. Through Sudan Medical Care (SMC), an experienced local NGO, mobile medical units (MMUs) will be deployed to hard-to-reach locations and displaced populations. MHPSS and GBV services will be integrated through counselling services at PHCC and hospital level with awareness-raising and referral activities at community level, complemented by a remote MHPSS hotline. This intervention design which combines static with mobile health facilities, as well as remote support, and offers integrated protection services, provides an inclusive, accessible, and holistic approach to health care. The community-based component of the Boma Health Initiative (BHI) and MHPSS/GBV community facilitators makes the project embedded in local structures and contributes to long-lasting impact. 
The project is targeted towards meeting the basic health, MHPSS and GBV needs of the population in Bor South, Duk, and Twic East counties, with a particular focus on vulnerable persons, such as women of reproductive age, pregnant and lactating women, at-risk pregnancies, children under 5, and people with particular needs and vulnerabilities across physical and mental wellbeing, living standards and coping mechanisms, such as displaced people, returnees, and host community members.

project_name: Mejorando la Seguridad Alimentaria y Nutricional  de las familias afectadas por la crisis humanitaria.
project_objective:
Acción contra el Hambre (ACH) cuenta con experiencia en la implementación de proyectos en diversas áreas rurales en el ámbito de acceso al agua potable, el saneamiento y la higiene; salud, nutrición, seguridad alimentaria, gestión de riesgos y atención y respuesta a la emergencia. Centra su trabajo en mejorar las condiciones de vida de familias vulnerables afectadas por la situación de crisis humanitaria como consecuencia de los diferentes fenómenos climáticos (sequía, los desastres naturales, el cambio climático) y la situación de violencia generalizada, entre múltiples amenazas y, en consecuencia, el hambre 
El proyecto tendrá una duración de 18 meses, diseñado para ser implementado en 2 etapas: La primera etapa en 2021 y una segunda etapa en 2022. Se realizarán transferencias monetarias condicionadas y no condicionadas, cada grupo familiar recibirá al menos 2 transferencias monetarias, de forma diferenciada de acuerdo con el número de miembros del hogar, principalmente para la cobertura de alimentos y medios de vida. La cantidad inversión por familia será de $50 y la máxima de $250.00. Se priorizarán los grupos de familias con mayor vulnerabilidad. Se identificará a las familias vulnerables que tienen habilidades y condiciones para restablecer sus medios, se consideraran los rubros agrícolas y no agrícolas, la entrega se condicionara a paquetes de insumos agrícolas o bien, mediante el apoyo con capacitaciones técnicas que les permita generar ingresos de manera independiente (albañilería, carpintería, fontanería, electricidad, etc.) y que a su vez les proporcionen mejores oportunidades de acceso a empleo. 
Estas actividades se realizarán en el departamento de Cortes, específicamente en los municipios de Choloma, San Pedro Sula, La Lima, Villanueva y San Manuel Cortes y en el departamento de Yoro, específicamente en el municipio de El Progreso, lugares en donde Acción contra el Hambre tiene experiencia con diferentes financiamientos, lo que ha permitido contar con conocimiento del contexto, así como con las alianzas a nivel municipal y departamental con diferentes instancias de Gobierno, organizaciones no gubernamentales, actores de la sociedad civil y actores comunitarios como principales aliados.

project_name: Child-centered humanitarian response in Protection, Education and Emergency Assistance (with integrated WASH) for Colombian conflict-affected victims and migrants in Nariño.
project_objective:
Address the basic needs of displaced families and improve the protection and education outcomes for Colombian children and their families affected by the armed conflict in Tumaco, El Charco, and Barbacoas in the department of Nariño 
O1: Strengthening children and communities’ resilience and coping mechanisms in areas affected by armed conflict and enhancing community based protective mechanisms. 

O2: Boys and girls with urgent protection needs are identified, receive psychological first aid and are referred to relevant services.  

O3: Out of school children and children at risk of dropping out, including those with disabilities, are supported to access quality, safe learning environments through provision of flexible, non-formal education. 

O4: Teachers and other education personnel are supported to deliver inclusive, child centered education and develop skills to support children´s psychosocial well-being. 

O5: Internally displaced families affected by conflict are provided with emergency assistance to address their immediate needs

project_name: Emergency WASH Response for Forcibly Displaced Myanmar Nationals
project_objective:
Caritas Bangladesh (CB) aims to provide sector endorsed all WASH activities in camp 4 (F-block) and camp 17 (B-block) covering a total of 2,928 HHs. The major activities include construction of latrine, deep tube-well/water networks and bathing spaces, repair and maintenance of latrine, tube-well and bathing spaces, water quality test, hygiene promotion, solid waste management and desludging of latrine. 
Within the camp and host community area, 28% of bathing facilities are out of order due to unavailability of water facilities, uncleanliness, distance from the shelter, no privacy, and broken door/fence and drainage problems. CB will conduct necessary repair and maintenance of the facilities. More than 65% of people use communal bathing facilities. Most of the people do not have designated bathing facilities, and thus use tube-well platforms. On the other hand, around 35% of latrines are non-functional and not in use due to a lack of privacy/no separation between men and women, toilets being full, not being safe (no door, no lock, etc.), and being too far away. Repair of latrines will be done with sector standard design and effective coordination and communication will be maintained with other actors of WASH sector. These challenges around latrines and bathing places especially affect women because they did not feel safe using the facilities at night and there was no segregation of facilities for men and women, a problem due to cultural norms. Additionally, females’ s menstrual hygiene needs are largely unmet. Also, COVID-19 is a major risk within the camp which will be addressed in hygiene promotion as the targeted population will receive hygiene kits and awareness sessions. Moreover, the potential diseases in the camps (i.e. AWD) are major concerns which will also be addressed in coordination with other actors. 
In a joint agency gender analysis on the response, children and adolescents also raised concerns about safety when accessing WASH facilities. Girls were prevented from using latrines that were being used by both men and women, due to the lack of segregation and privacy. Girls also had problems with long queues, overcrowding and the lack of lighting at night at latrines. With the WASH related activities, greater emphasis will be provided to ensure safe and dignified access to WASH facilities. Boys raised concerns around the proper maintenance of latrines and lack of lighting and felt unsafe when using wells because of the long queues. All girls surveyed felt that fetching water from tube wells was unsafe because of the distance from home.

project_name: Emergency Livestock and Agriculture-based Livelihood Assistance for most crisis-impacted communities in Syria
project_objective:
This project will target the most vulnerable small scale farmers, mainly IDPs, returnees and hosting communities in, Hama, Aleppo and Rural Damascus governorates which are per the HNO for 2020 have expressed most need for income-earning opportunities, fuel, food and health services.  The thematic geographic focus of the project is based on the vulnerability of population, accessibility to basic services and livelihoods opportunities, the rate of displacement or returns, and the highest severity scale.
Interventions will include:
(1) Provision of training on agricultural practice with the aim of increasing knowledge and skills for better and environmentally, and economically sustainable agricultural production; (2) Provision of agriculture input and farming tools to restore agriculture productive capacity; (3) Support sustainable livestock husbandry practice; (4) Support food processing activities based on local agricultural production, coupled with support for market access (value chain development).
The type of assistance provided will be based on the beneficiaries' identified needs as well as their ability to participate in/benefit from the intervention.
Targeting and Vulnerability criteria: severely food unsecured; IDPs; HHs hosting IDPs; HHs with children under five years old and/or pregnant women and/or lactating women; FHHs; HHs with no productive assets, or functional means of income/ reliable source of income; Elderly headed HHs; HHs headed by chronically ill members or headed by physically challenged heads; 9- HHs not receiving adequate assistance from other sources; HHs meeting other vulnerability criteria as identified by the communities .
Specific criteria for livelihood assistance:
For the support of sustainable livestock husbandry practice proposed activities, UNDP will exclusively target HHs who have livestock and/or experience in livestock management, access to grazing land, availability of labor for livestock activities and willingness to maintain livestock.
For the provision of agriculture input and farming tools, UNDP will target HHs who have agriculture land and sources of water but must be the small holders.
For the support of food processing activities based on local agricultural production, UNDP will target beneficiaries with minimum required Know-How and have access to agriculture input and market. The estimated number of beneficiaries is 1500 distributed as follows: 200 persons will benefit from the provision of training on agricultural practice; 600 persons will benefit from the provision of agriculture input and farming tools; 600 persons will benefit from the support of sustainable livestock husbandry practice; 100 persons will benefit from the support of food processing activities.

project_name: Promoting community safety and individual rights
project_objective:
Given the current Syrian context, there is a need to integrate support to legal awareness and legal counselling, GBV prevention and response and mine-risk education into the humanitarian response as part of the protection cluster in order to address immediate and longer-term needs to rebuild communities. In this regard, UNDP will contribute towards the following outcomes and activities: 
(1)	Promotion of Social Cohesion through utilising UNDP Peace Agents
a.	Use the platform of agents of change established by UNDP’s social cohesion team. The team of volunteers trained on community mobilisation, social engagement and community level dialogues will work with the target communities in order to harness harmony, sense of co-existence and respect for the rights of others in order to promote social cohesion among host communities, IDPs and returnees. These will support the following interventions from (as moving from being passive beneficiaries to active partners.
(2)	Increased capacities to address GBV through prevention and responsive action at the community level within safe environments 
a.	Preventive measures and activities: 
1.	Conduct outreach and GBV awareness raising activities for the general public (GBV defined, COVID-19 impact of GBV, rights and legal consultation, survivor response, etc.)
2.	Support women networking as part of peer-to-peer support – whereby women network members are the entry point to their communities, and start meaning participation (digital bloggers to amplify the voices of women during the COVID-19 crisis and community participation) in women’s movement and leadership in preventing violence. These women are provided skills enhancement to lead designing, developing and implementing their own community-based initiatives. 
3.	Men and boys Engagement through dialogue and awareness sessions to be aligned to eliminate violence against women and girls. 
4.	Conduct Campaign – create the demand for behavioural change. 
b.	Responsive measures and activities 
1.	Support to victims of GBV related response services (MHPSS Mental health psychosocial support – holistic support which covers psychiatrist, psychology family counselling and sociological support who is responsible for adopting the referral system, documentation and legal consultation and referral) for survivors of GBV.
2.	Coordinating and working with local municipalities and concerned directorates to prevent and respond to violence and discrimination against women and girls. 
(3)	Increased knowledge of rights and access to justice at the community level
a.	Provide Legal Awareness (know your rights, channels to access justice, women’s rights, children’s rights, civil documentation and HLP) for the general public. 
b.	Support Legal Aid clinics to address the many social-legal issues faced by the general public.  
(4)	Increased knowledge of mine-risk safety at the community level
a.	Provide mine risk education sessions for the general public.
b.	Widely disseminate Mine-risk materials. 
UNDP will target 13 locations in need of humanitarian support while targeting 40,000 individual beneficiaries. 
See Annex 1 for further information on Project implementation, methodology and target communities

project_name: Emergency Food and Livelihood Assistance to the Crisis-Affected Families Through the Appropriate Modality
project_objective: Through the proposed project Oxfam plane to enable the most vulnerable families in the targeted subdistricts to have access to the essential food items. Depending on local market functionality, people preferences, and availability of appropriate FSPs, distribution modality will be though cash, noting that Oxfam had performed market assessment in several communities in the proposed subdistrict and found that cash modality is preferable and feasible. Oxfam will provide up-to 8 rounds of cash transfers to 6,800 HHs, at least 30% of which will be headed by females. Oxfam will try to equip the targeted most vulnerable people with skills and assets that enable them to build their capacities to produce food / generate income in a sustainable manner, so they become less dependent on the humanitarian assistances. This will benefit a total of 38,000 individuals in acute need. The monthly distribution value will be according to the CWG recommended cash for food value. Based on the last updated values (February 2020), the cash for food values will be 22 USD, 15 USD, and 15 USD per month per capita for Aleppo, Rural Damascus and Deir ez Zor respectively. Based on Oxfam assessments, the average family size in Aleppo and Deir ez Zor is 5, while the average in Deir ez Zor is 7. Therefor, the cash for food values that will be distributed are: 66 USD, 46 USD and 63 USD in Aleppo, Rural Damascus and Deir ez Zor respectively.  The transfer will be made in Syrian Pound using the  equal to 70 USD using the Central Bank preferential exchange rate at the time of distribution.  The transfer value might be changed based on the discussions within the CWG. Oxfam will coordinate with other humanitarian actors to avoid overlapping in and ensure complementarity in geographical targeting, their coordination will be done through FSA Sector, CWG and even through bilateral meetings. According to the FSA Sector guidelines, the assistance will be provided to the food insecure assessed families. The assistance will be provided for up to 8 months Oxfam will make sure to engage the communities in the selection of the most vulnerable families. Therefore, Oxfam will form a community committee where at least 50% of participants will be women. The committees will be responsible in identifying the most vulnerable families. If the security situation and Covid 19 measures allow, Oxfam will perform 100% physical verification, if not, Oxfam will rely on random representative sampling approach. The aid delivery process, impact and market prices will be monitored regularly.

project_name: Safe Enabling Learning Environments: A Shared Responsibility
project_objective:
Purpose:
•	Deterioration of Families’ Economic Conditions
The economic, financial, political, and pandemic crises in Lebanon, have affected every aspect of children’s lives, including education, nutrition, and mental health. According to the assessment “Children’s future on the line” conducted by UNICEF on June 2021, nine per cent of families sent their children to work, 15 per cent stopped their education, and 60 per cent had to buy their food on credit or borrow money.
The outlook of the future is grim. The World Bank says the economy looks likely to contract by a further 9.5 per cent in 2021 and has warned that there is “no clear turning point in the horizon” (Lebanon Economic Monitor, Spring 2021). The longer children in Lebanon are out of school, the higher the possibility that they will experience violence and exploitation, including child labor and child marriage. The increasing socio-economic pressure on families in Lebanon during the economic and COVID-19 crisis, increases this possibility. The increased pressure on children to support their families may lead to an increase in psychosocial distress and negative coping mechanisms.
•	Migration from Private to Public Schools
In the scholastic year 2020-2021, around 54,000 students transitioned from private to the public schools. MEHE estimates that another 50,000-60,000 Lebanese students will transfer from private to public schools during the SY 2021/2022, resulting in 100,00- 120,000 Lebanese students migrating to public schools. This will pause additional challenges to an already stressed system. A hiring freeze of teachers in public schools has been in place for around 2 years. With the rapid increase in number of students in public schools, human resources are required to match the demand. However, due to the unprecedented diminishing value of the LBP, teacher salaries in the public system are now valued at less than 1 USD per hour, which is pausing yet another serious risk of teachers leaving the schools or be on strike more often.
The purpose of this project would be to provide direct community support measures to most vulnerable Lebanese and migrant children to retain them in education and to ensure that students affected by the economic crisis are provided relevant, inclusive and quality education adhering to national and international standards on education in emergencies and child protection by ensuring that schools have maintained their basic educational resources, including adequate human resources.  Ana Aqra is suggesting the “Safe Enabling Learning Environments: a Shared Responsibility” project as part of the Lebanon emergency response plan. 
Ana Aqra strives to make learning accessible to all children and works to support the education sector and the public school to respond to the specific needs of all children as well as empowering partnerships to partake in the responsibility for the safe and enabling learning of girls and boys.

Targeting criteria, intervention and mechanism:
This project will support 10,000 girls and boys and 75 public schools, including those receiving learners transferred from the private sector. The project activities will include provision of funds to ensure that students affected by the economic crisis are provided relevant, inclusive and quality education adhering to national and international standards on education in emergencies and child protection. The project will also ensure that schools will receive necessary stationery, books, and funds to cover operational costs and adequate human resources. It will also ensure school retention of most vulnerable girls and boys by providing them and their caregivers with direct community support program, including remote awareness sessions, remote PSS/SEL activities, responsive caregiving and remote basic and digital literacy to parents /caregivers, assistive technologies for children with disabilities, cash for education support and food parcels during the academic year 2021-2022.

project_name: Access to lifesaving mental health services in Lebanon
project_objective:
Suicide is a pressing health concern worldwide, with over 800,000 people dying by suicide yearly. Since the Covid-19 pandemic, related uncertainties, fears, and health measures led to increase in suicide and associated mental disorders. In 2020, 150 people died by suicide in Lebanon, a low- to middle- income country facing social, political, and economic collapse since October 2019. Despite the impact of mental health activities launched via non- profits such as Embrace, a local non- profit that promotes mental health and suicide prevention, resources remain restricted while community needs exponentiate. Today, people in Lebanon are experiencing severe livelihood risks and absence of basic life necessities including medication, gasoline, and food. These burdens, in addition to the stressors of the pandemic, come as a detriment to citizens’ mental health and are especially magnified for those with predisposition or pre-existing mental illnesses. Additionally, hundreds of people are still grappling with the mental, emotional, and financial consequences of the Beirut explosion which continues to manifesting through trauma symptoms and loss of hope. 

From this project Embrace expects to increase the capacity of both the National Lifeline and the Mental Health Clinic. The current national situation exacerbates the risk factors individuals live on a daily basis further increasing their risk of mental health symptoms and problems, which in return necessitates the need to strengthen community prevention services. The project intends to support the growth of the National Lifeline as a service that has been very well adopted by the community and is under high demand to become a 24 hour service as it currently operates for 21 hours. This service is operated by specialized volunteers trained on active listening and collaborative problem solving for intervention in suicide crises. The current situation has deteriorated the progress and/or treatment of individuals with mental illnesses. Mental health services are no longer affordable, resulting in an increased demand for funded mental health services, usually provided through non- profits, with long waiting lists and limited resources. Additionally, the purchasing power of individuals has dropped dramatically and rapidly, causing them to view mental health as a luxury while prioritizing basic living supplies and bills. The project intends to increase the mental health clinical capacity to respond to the growing community need and respectively sustain a strong impact, while playing a crucial role in the economic recovery of Lebanon, given the link between mental health and one’s ability to function productively in their community and society. Following Embrace’s mandate, this project intends to increase its inclusivity of communities with disabilities and their access to mental health services. The budget lines that are presented as full costs needed for the time frame of the project and to complete the activities presented. Shared costs are those of human resources that complete tasks relevant to the project activity but also tasks in other programs out of the scope of this project and accordingly not billed here.

project_name: Respuesta integral en seguridad alimentaria y nutricional de emergencia para la población más vulnerable afectada por la crisis en Venezuela
project_objective:
Acción contra el Hambre-ACH trabaja en Venezuela atendiendo las necesidades humanitarias de los grupos más vulnerables con riesgo de desnutrición aguda: niños y niñas (particularmente menores de 5 años), mujeres gestantes y lactantes, personas con discapacidades, adultos mayores y en particular población indígena. Son agravantes para estas personas la situación de pobreza y sus limitaciones de acceso a alimentos, a condiciones higiénico-sanitarias adecuadas, de acceso a la salud, la educación y el trabajo. La desnutrición y el deterioro de la salud repercuten en una mayor exposición a factores agravantes como la violencia -especialmente la de género, embarazos adolescentes, infecciones de transmisión sexual-ITS, o criminalidad. Las estrategias de sobrevivencia pueden llevar a reducir la ingesta calórica o de nutrientes, a la venta de activos, y hasta a la emigración. 
A través del HRP, ACH brindará una respuesta humanitaria integral y multisectorial para reducir el sufrimiento y ayudar a salvar vidas humanas, identificando casos de desnutrición en sus diferentes niveles, y a las familias más en riesgo; a través de su programa nacional 2021 y según el marco regional en intervenciones articuladas, complementarias e integrales en los sectores de: 1) Nutrición: sensibilización y consejerías; prevención, detección, tratamiento de la desnutrición aguda, y derivación de los casos con complicaciones médicas; capacitación en el manejo preventivo de la desnutrición aguda a nivel comunitario. 2) Salud: atención en salud primaria con equipos médicos, insumos, medicamentos a menores de 5 años y mujeres gestantes y lactantes. Además un enfoque en salud mental con atención en primeros auxilios psicológicos y salud sexual y reproductiva a través de la sensibilización y entrega de métodos anticonceptivos, especialmente para las madres y adolescentes. 3) Seguridad Alimentaria: distribución de alimentos/transferencias monetarias/cupones/soporte para la producción de alimentos, apoyo en actividades para resiliencia con actividades agrícolas y de medios de vida, formaciones en seguridad alimentaria. 4) WASH: acceso a servicios básicos de agua, saneamiento, e higiene, en instituciones educativas, centros de salud, centros comunitarios como comedores sociales y vicarías a través de la distribución de kits de higiene (familiares, de higiene menstrual, de productos de limpieza y desinfección, etc.), promoción de prácticas clave de higiene, rehabilitación/ reparación/ reingeniería de sistemas de abastecimiento de agua y de saneamiento en comunidades. 5) Protección y género: sensibilizaciones a adolescentes, mujeres y hombres sobre prevención de violencia basada en género, nuevas masculinidades y derechos sexuales y reproductivos; establecimiento y/o fortalecimiento de espacios seguros para mujeres y niñas; atención psico-social para personas en riesgo y protección para mujeres en riesgo de VBG. 
En todos los sectores se trabajará de manera multisectorial en la medida de lo posible y con un abordaje a nivel comunitario; siempre en coordinación con organizaciones humanitarias, y de manera funcional con instituciones locales, en particular con escuelas y centros de salud.

project_name: Provision of integrated and comprehensive primary healthcare services for vulnerable populations in Lebanon
project_objective:
The proposed project aims at improving access to quality, affordable and comprehensive primary health services for vulnerable populations in Lebanon. Given the current deteriorating economic situation in Lebanon – vulnerable populations have become more at risk of being unable to access healthcare in Lebanon. These populations include Lebanese, Palestinian refugees residing in Lebanon, and migrants that are becoming increasingly unable to afford or access healthcare in Lebanon. This compounded with a potential fourth wave of the COVID-19 on the horizon – immediate intervention is required in order to ease the health impact on beneficiaries as well as ensure continuity of operations for Primary Healthcare Centers (PHCCs).

For health activities, IMC will work with 4 PHCCs: Al Moasat PHCC (South), Al Amir Medical Center (Akkar), Nahda Bedawi (Tripoli) and Bar Elias PHCC (Bekaa). These centers have been selected due to the high density of vulnerable Lebanese as well as a considerable size of migrant populations in the areas. Our data has shown a 9% increase in demand for IMC services by vulnerable Lebanese in July 2021 in comparison to the same month the previous year. The support to these 4 PHCCs will include: increasing the hours of operations for PHCCs by 4 hours a day 5 days a week by providing salary support for physicians, nurses, data entry clerks, and other personnel and running costs, secondly, donating essential acute medications as per the Ministry of Public health (MoPH) essential medication list, lastly, IMC will be providing PPE’s for the healthcare providers at the PHCCs in order to be able to provide high-quality services in a safe manner for both the health staff and the beneficiary. IMC will be recruiting and training Lebanese HOVs from the target population in order to disseminate and provide health awareness on IMC services to vulnerable Lebanese communities and migrants - as well as identify cases requiring primary healthcare and referring them back to the PHCC. 

IMC Mental Health and Psycho-Social Support (MHPSS) team currently support 20 Case Management (CM) teams based in 20 PHCCs across Lebanon aiming to strengthen the integration of MH into PHCCs. CM teams consist of full-time case managers, part-time psychotherapists and psychiatrists. MH services including PSS with case managers and consultations with psychotherapists and psychiatrists are provided to beneficiaries free of charge to beneficiaries from all nationalities and age groups. Cases that require hospitalization are referred to MH psychiatric wards. Under this project, IMC is proposing to complement MHPSS provided at the 20 centers by procuring additional psychotropic medications to be provided as part of MH case management services to the MH beneficiaries from the target population group including Lebanese and migrants as well as assisting coverage of inpatient care when needed. No additional budget is needed for either specialized services or running costs and these medications will be used to complement the services provided for free. Case managers will be able to conduct closed group awareness raising sessions for the target community (which will also target PwDs) to decrease stigma and promote accessibility to MHPSS services. 

IMC is planning to procure acute and psychotropic medication which will be donated to the PHCCs. IMC will coordinate with MoPH to complement quantities and try to plug gaps in the MOPH supply chain. IMC patients (14,400) will also benefit from MoPH medications. IMC will run a detailed assessment, quantities will be shared with MoPH for coordination of numbers and specifying the number of PHCCs to be covered as well as the duration of coverage and timeframe. At the PHCC level, medications will be dispensed free of charge and only upon medical prescriptions. IMC has partnered up with agencies that can help with international procurement and will be actively using this chain of supply rather than rely on local markets.

project_objective: Save the Children y ASONACOP, ambas organizaciones no gubernamentales, la primera enfocada en respuesta humanitaria y la segunda en promover y fortalecer las redes de atención en protección con estrecha colaboración de los Consejos de Protección del Niño, Niña y Adolescente, se proponen ayudar a los niños y niñas en edad escolar más vulnerables que se enfrentan a riesgos de protección de la infancia en el hogar y la comunidad, tales como maltrato, agresión física y verbal, rechazo, violencia psicológica y negligencia; así como a sus representantes. En este sentido, las acciones inmediatas buscarán fortalecer el sistema de protección comunitario e institucional con una lógica doble: hacer disponibles servicios de atención psicosocial en las comunidades con fortalecimiento de mecanismos de referenciación y fortalecer las capacidades de los Consejos de Protección Locales para que puedan atender los casos derivados a sus servicios y ellos puedan operar y hacer la remisión fuera se necesitase atención más especializada, como penal o legal. Los profesionales de la red de protección pública (Consejos de Protección) ofrecerán sesiones de PSS a los niños vulnerables, incluidos los niños abandonados, los UASC, los supervivientes de SGVB, los padres (jóvenes) y los cuidadores (ancianos) directamente afectados por la crisis. El enfoque de la articulación con el proceso de gestión de casos de base comunitaria que el equipo de Save y el socio establecerán en cada estado facilitará la identificación permitiendo que los casos complejos sean remitidos a la atención especializada disponible y aquellos que no puedan ser atendidos in situ mediante equipos multidisciplinarios en terreno coordinados por ASONACOP. Asimismo, es establecerán espacios amigables para la infancia, en donde se podrán realizar actividades de sensibilización con NNA en temas de derechos de la infancia y VBG. El trabajo en la crianza positiva, masculinidades positivas, prevención del abuso y explotación sexual serán abordados con madres, padres y cuidadores, entendiendo el incremento en violencia doméstica e intrafamiliar. Apalancándose en el sistema de protección local, la dotación de insumos de trabajo y el fortalecimiento técnico permitirá que estas instituciones tengan mejor capacidad de respuesta; sin embargo, la carga de trabajo será distribuida con equipos multidisciplinarios en terreno que realizará jornadas grupales o individuales de atención psicosocial a NNA y víctimas de violencia de género.

project_name: Respuesta nutricional para prevención y tratamiento de Desnutrición Aguda en población materno-infantil en departamentos de la zona Norte de Honduras
project_objective:
Acción contra el Hambre (ACH) cuenta con experiencia en la implementación de proyectos en diversas áreas rurales en el ámbito de acceso al agua potable, el saneamiento y la higiene; nutrición, seguridad alimentaria, gestión de riesgos y atención y respuesta a emergencias. Acción contra el Hambre centra su trabajo en mejorar las condiciones de vida de familias vulnerables afectadas por la situación de crisis humanitaria como consecuencia de los diferentes fenómenos climáticos (sequía, el impacto de los huracanes, inundaciones asociadas), la situación de violencia generalizada,  entre múltiples amenazas y en consecuencia el hambre.
La propuesta de proyecto “Respuesta nutricional para prevención y tratamiento de Desnutrición Aguda en población materno-infantil en departamentos de la zona Norte de Honduras” se enfoca en el manejo ambulatorio, la prevención, tratamiento y atención de la desnutrición aguda en niñas y niños menores de cinco años, mujeres embarazadas y en período de lactancia, mediante la mejora de la vigilancia y el tratamiento nutricional, fortalecimiento de capacidades del personal institucional de salud por medio de formaciones sobre el uso de los protocolos nacionales simplificados de manejo de la desnutrición aguda (utilización de cintas MUAC y estándares de crecimiento, específicamente peso para la talla) y entrega de equipamiento e insumos para los establecimientos de salud (equipo médico, antropométrico, micronutrientes y alimentos terapéuticos listos para consumo); así mismo, propone el   fortalecimiento de capacidades de voluntarios comunitarios (agentes de cambio) para la identificación temprana y oportuna de niños y niñas con desnutrición aguda, sensibilización a familias sobre prácticas adecuadas de alimentación, nutrición e higiene infantil, promover la utilización de la metodología Family MUAC y dar soporte nutricional a través de la metodología de Escuelas de Campo de Seguridad Alimentaria Nutricional (ECASAN) incluyendo el enfoque de desviación positiva, en estos espacios se promueven prácticas de alimentación y cuidado infantil e higiene para la mejora de prácticas de cuidado del niño y niña pequeños, a través de la metodología aprender haciendo. También se propone brindar soporte con alimento complementario a niños y niñas menores de 5 años, mujeres embarazadas y/o en período de lactancia que se encuentren en riesgo de padecer desnutrición , para mejorar su estado nutricional.
Estas intervenciones se planifican llevar a cabo en tres departamentos de Honduras: Cortés, Yoro y Atlántida.

project_name: Safe and protective education services for vulnerable children and adolescents in Guatemala
project_objective:
In the context of Covid-19 border closures have meant families are often stuck and in need of humanitarian assistance and children often face stigmatization, social exclusion, violence and extreme poverty, especially returnees. In Guatemala, hurricanes ETA & IOTA left unprecedented damages, with nearly 500 schools affected and a growing number of students without access to formal or non-formal education, delaying school reopening in 2021. Through this action UNICEF will create opportunities for children exposed to high levels of violence in communities that include returnees or displaced families, through the provision of multiple pathways to education, access to quality learning materials and
psychosocial support that facilitate staying in school. UNICEF will include the provision of WASH in schools to ensure a safe “back to school”. UNICEF will work to reintegrate children that have been out of school in 2020 and prevent their school desertion once schools open. For children, C-19 has essentially meant the loss of one year of learning. Urgent action is paramount to ensure access to education for the most vulnerable children currently at risk of losing a second year of education. This would have a devastating impact on their right to learn and thrive, and children will face increased exposure to violence both if their families stay or embark on a dangerous migration route. The departments of Alta Verapaz, Izabal and Quiché are among the most impacted by Eta and Iota. With schools reopening school´s repairs are urgent, especially with regards to safe WASH facilities which are mandatory for reopening. Through the proposed action UNICEF´s support to the Ministry of Education will increase the number of students that benefit from a restored school infrastructure and WASH facilities an ensure opportunities for education continuity.
