project_name: Strengthening the Delivery of Integrated Primary Health Care Services to Vulnerable Populations in BAY States
project_objective:
This project is designed to build on gains achieved from providing improved integrated PHC services in supported vulnerable communities in Borno, Adamawa and Yobe states. These states are share borders with Cameroon, Chad and Niger respectively and are the most affected in the 11-year armed conflict that has seen over 2.1 million persons internally displaced with over 1 million refugees in the neighboring countries. The majority of IDPs in Borno are in host communities in camp-like settlements and around 15% in IDP camps characterized by congestion and other specific challenges and vulnerabilities with an already suboptimal functioning health service, poor and inadequate shelter and poor hygiene conditions.
Escalating clashes between armed actors in this protracted complex crisis is a major driver of displacements towards garrison settlements especially in Borno state.
Intercommunal conflicts are also major cause of displacements especially in Adamawa state. The effects of these stressors are made manifest in the health indices (U5MR, NMR,MMR, SAM rates) and other socioeconomic indices (literacy rates, food security index, etc). The BAY states are also prone to natural disasters such as droughts and flooding and consequent environmental degradation coupled with poor water and waste management, the possibility of disease outbreaks such as Cholera is very high as experienced in 2021.
The BAY states suffer from a greatly debilitated health system which is currently being strengthened through close collaboration between humanitarian actors and government with significant gains over the past two years. It is therefore critical that the COVID-19 outbreak readiness and response strategies, plan and operations are strengthened and extended to all persons regardless of status and ensures inclusiveness as well as protecting and sustaining the progresses made in health systems strengthening (HSS)
through a multisectoral approach.
UNICEF in partnership with the state government agencies (SPHCDAs and SPHCMBs) and the State Ministries of Health of the BAY states will continue to provide integrated primary health care to locations with high and moderate humanitarian needs and continue to support HSS in the rest of the states. We will focus on how to reach people in need including returnees, support the states to implement interventions that will enable transition from emergency phase to development in some LGAs, partner with INGOs that are present on the ground and provide strategic technical assistance in building capacity for resilience at the community level. We will review existing supplies and focus on the critical component. We will leverage resources through convergence with other sections within UNICEF and other sectors at the state, LGAs and community levels.
The following objectives will be met through the project:
1. Support the provision of basic essential quality health care services to vulnerable populations.
2. Support the timely disease outbreak response through active participation in EOC activities.
3. Support improved access to health care strengthening health system recovery, enhance resilience, and promote humanitarian-development linkages.
4. Support mitigation of the risk and contain the spread of the COVID-19 pandemic and decrease morbidity and mortality in IDP camps and host communities.

project_name: Northeast Nigeria Nutrition Response 2022
project_objective:
The Nutrition response in 2022 will prioritise implementation of the nutrition lifesaving activities (inpatient, outpatient, and targeted supplemental feeding programmes) and targeting of LGAs with high rates of GAM (above 10%) such as MMC/Jere, Nganzai, Bama, Machina. Hard-to-reach areas (such as Gubio, Rann, Magumeri), areas with large IDP  and returnee populations (like Monguno) and high-risk/inaccessible locations such as Marte LGA will also be prioritised for nutrition assistance. 
UNICEF will primarily target acutely malnourished children and PLW who are at a significantly high risk of death. The nutrition response will also target the total under-five and PLW with preventive nutrition services e.g. micronutrient supplementation to ensure levels of acute malnutrition are not above average thresholds, and to also reduce morbidity and mortality. The response will prioritise households with persons living with disabilities, who face barriers in accessing health, nutrition and WASH services and are disproportionately food insecure due to high levels of exclusion. 
The nutrition status of the targeted population in the BAY states significantly deteriorates during the period from May-August every year, which is the lean season and coincides with the rainy season. The season is characterised by very high rates of acute malnutrition with medical complications due to poor food access and a high prevalence of diarrhoea and malaria. UNICEF will need to adequately prepare for the lean season period by prepositioning supplies, increasing the overall sector capacity to treat acute malnutrition with a focus on inpatient care and IYCF-E
The nutrition response in BAY states will be contextualised in 2022 based on the following categorisation: 
1. Protracted crisis e.g north and central Borno LGAs where the rates of acute malnutrition are high, worsened by poor access to food and health systems. The approach in these areas will include INGO/NNGO direct support to the affected population, and prioritisation of lifesaving nutrition activities. 
3. New emergencies – locations of new crisis and fluctuations such as relocations, displacements and spike in acute malnutrition. The approach will focus on the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) with a focus on lifesaving activities. 
4. Hard-to-reach / inaccessible areas – locations with limited humanitarian footprints and access e.g Gubio and Magumeri. The approach will include RRM and remote management strategy (where feasible) with a focus on life-saving interventions. UNICEF will also strengthen the implementation of nutrition interventions through local organizations or community-based structures to implement nutrition services in hard-to-reach/inaccessible areas. 
UNICEF response is primarily through services and in-kind deliveries. UNICEF will employ the use of cash and voucher assistance (CVA) to fill the nutrient gap in the Nutrition/Food Minimum Expenditure Basket to ensure that populations have access to a varied diet e.g CVA for meats and vegetables. 
The nutrition status of the affected population is an outcome of various underlying issues including access to health, WASH, food security, child protection, and gender issues. The main cause of acute malnutrition among children and women in BAY states is the high morbidity rates. High diarrhoea prevalence is the major cause of acute malnutrition among the IDPs and urban poor population due to the prevailing poor hygiene and sanitation conditions worsened by congested living conditions. The response will strengthen the integration of nutrition-sensitive interventions including WASH, food security, health, livelihoods and child protection, and gender-based violence risk mitigation.
UNICEF will prioritise projects that include basic nutrition packages such as integrated treatment of acute malnutrition (SAM and MAM) and prevention services including integration with WASH, food security, health and protections services.

project_name: Critical Humanitarian Water, Sanitation and Hygiene Services in Emergency-affected Communities in North East Nigeria (Borno, Adamawa, and Yobe) and other States
project_objective: UNICEF is both a service provider under the partner presence rationalization in the sector and the provider of last resort (POLR). The largest response is in NE Nigeria (Borno, Adamawa and Yobe states) where protracted armed conflict has continued to force displacement of population into camps and camp-like settlements for more than a decade. In other regions, the need for response a rise from sporadic conflicts, natural disasters like floods or risks of outbreaks/spread of infectious diseases such as cholera, which is endemic in Nigeria, and the recent covid-19 or other hazards. Gaps also arise as a results of new population displacements or diminished capacity/departure of other humanitarian WASH partners. As a service provider, UNICEF is optimizing the water production and distribution, increasing attainment of the required minimum standards. UNICEF is rolling out the approach of urban type network water distribution in deep field LGAs with high yielding boreholes and high-density population of displaced persons or returnees and host communities. This approach will support decongestion in camps and expansion of WASH services to schools and health/nutrition facilities. UNICEF will also expand cash in wash programming for hygiene kits and other WASH NFIs. Through this project, UNICEF will have specific target populations in needs in IDP camps in Borno State, specifically in Maiduguri Metropolitan City and 10 LGAs (Bama, Dikwa, Gwoza, Jere, Kara Balge, Konduga, Mafa, Mobbar, Monguno, and Ngala), whilst in Adamawa and Yobe, and possibly other states, the target population will be determined by locations where needs will arise. UNICEF will adhere to the SPHERE standards and scaleup the sustenance of the services as needed. To meet the demands of the POLR responsibility, UNICEF may need to mobilize additional resources. Through this project UNICEF will provide the initial lifesaving response to fill the gaps, prioritizing areas receiving newly displaced people or under an outbreak of cholera, hepatitis or other WASH-related diseases including covid-19. UNICEF will strive to sustain the basic initial WASH services until further response becomes available from other sector partners. The project is also aimed at sustaining critical humanitarian water, sanitation and hygiene services to displaced population affected by protracted armed conflict in NE Nigeria (Borno, Adamawa and Yobe States: target 5,540,800 people) and emergency affected population in four states including other locations. 500,000 of the target population are at risk of covid-19 infection.

project_name: Projet d'assistance alimentaire  et nutritionnelle d'urgence aux populations les plus vulnérables en insécurité alimentaire sévère pendant la période de soudure
project_objective:
Près de 5,3 millions de personnes (51% de femmes) souffrent d’insécurité alimentaire dont 1,8 million en insécurité alimentaire sévère. Selon le cadre harmonisé de novembre 2021, la situation alimentaire a connu une légère dégradation avec une baisse de production céréalière de 1,5% et plus en baisse (3,3%) dans la zone soudanienne. Les résultats prévisionnels de la campagne agricole 2021/2022 présagent une baisse de la production agricole par rapport à 2020 et à la moyenne quinquennale justifiée par plusieurs facteurs dont la mauvaise répartition des pluies dans le temps et dans l’espace, les séquences sèches de longue durées (jusqu’à 25 jours) ont été constatées dans la bande sahélienne et les inondations par endroit surtout dans la bande soudanienne.  La hausse de prix des céréales et la détérioration des termes de l’échange bétail/céréales et cultures de rente/céréales affectent également la consommation alimentaire, l’état nutritionnel et l’évolution des moyens d’existence. Cette situation affectera plus de 3,6 millions de personnes qui sont actuellement dans la phase sous pression et font face à la dégradation de moyens de subsistance pour avoir un accès minimum aux services sociaux de base et risquent de basculer en phase crise.

La malnutrition reste préoccupante au Tchad avec une prévalence de 10,9% de malnutrition aigüe globale et 2% de malnutrition aigüe sévère. Environ 3,65 millions de personnes ont besoin d’une aide nutritionnelle, soit une baisse de 3,9% par rapport aux 3,8 millions en 2021. Le nombre d’enfants à risque de malnutrition aiguë globale (MAG) est passé à 1 668 150 dont 334 649 de cas de malnutrition aigüe sévère (MAS). En outre, 198 493 femmes enceintes et allaitantes sont à risque de malnutrition aigüe.  Alors que le taux de malnutrition aigüe globale est de 10, 9% dont 2% de malnutrition aigüe sévère au niveau national, la situation est bien préoccupante dans 17 de 23 provinces qui ont déjà surpassé les seuils d’urgence de 10% de malnutrition aigüe globale et de mortalité. Parmi les 17 provinces 07 ont atteint et dépassé le seuil critique de 15% (Batha, Barh El Gazal, Salamat, Ennedi Est, Ennedi Ouest, Wadi Fira, Kanem). Selon les résultats de l’enquête SMART 2021, le taux de malnutrition aigüe sévère n’a pas varié entre 2020 (2,1%) et 2021 (2%) et dépasse le seuil de 2% dans 05 provinces (Batha, Barh El Gazal, Chari Baguirmi, Ennedi Ouest et Kanem). 

L’analyse IPC (Integrated Food Security Phase Classification) de la malnutrition de 2021, a montré que sur les 57 unités d’analyse (5 provinces et 52 départements), 4 provinces et 27 départements sont en situation nutritionnelle sérieuse à critique avec près de la moitié des enfants de moins de 5 ans (47%) vivant dans ces provinces et départements. En outre, la projection montre une détérioration continue de la situation nutritionnelle, notamment durant la période de soudure (juin à septembre 2022) où 5 provinces et 29 départements seront en phase sérieuse à critique.

Durant la période de soudure 2022 (juin à septembre), le PAM planifie appuyer 820 172 personnes avec une assistance alimentaire inconditionnelle pour quatre mois avec rations complètes dans les provinces du Barh el Gazel, Batha, Kanem, Lac, Ouaddai, Salamat et Wadi Fira. Cette assistance alimentaire sera combinée à une assistance nutritionnelle de 4 mois afin d’assister 61 513 enfants de 6 à 23 mois ainsi que 41 009 femmes enceintes et femmes allaitantes issus des ménages bénéficiant de l’assistance alimentaire. De plus, des activités de prévention de la malnutrition seront réalisées, telles que session ANJE, bonnes pratiques familiales, etc.

project_name: General Food Assistance (GFA)
project_objective:
As highlighted in the 2022 HNO, Syria continues to suffer from multiple and complex socioeconomic difficulties - continued effects of the Lebanese economic crisis, tightening of unilateral coercive measures and consequences of the Covid-19 pandemic. The protracted crisis, now in its 11th year, is exacerbating food security and livelihood needs for many families across the country, further eroding the resilience and recovery prospects. These factors have triggered unprecedented inflation rates of basic commodities, including basic food items, pushing additional people into food insecurity. The Syria Food Security and Agriculture sector has identified the overall people in need for 2022 – of food insecure and those at risk of food insecurity – to be estimated at 13.9 million, with 12 million facing acute food insecurity and 1.9 million at risk of sliding into food insecurity. The acute food insecure include 1.9 million people living in camps and deemed to be 100% food insecure. WFP’s GFA covers the critical food needs of Syrian families across all 14 governorates. Subject to availability of funds, WFP’s GFA will ensure that food needs are being met through a food basket planned to have a minimum basic caloric value, across modalities from 2,100 kcal per person per day for the most food-insecure, like the IDP in camps in Northeast Syria, 1,700 kcal per person per day for beneficiaries assessed as severely food insecure or living in camps in Northwest Syria, to 1,300 kcal per person per day for beneficiaries assessed as moderately food-insecure. Target beneficiaries include the most vulnerable crisis-affected population groups. These include the need based IDPs settled in camps or host communities, IDP returnees, host communities, and poor rural and urban households. In total, WFP Interim Country Strategic Plan aims to target 7.75 million food-insecure people each month in 2022 and 2023, including the severely food-insecure (1.3 million); 50 percent moderately food-insecure (4.7 million); and all need based IDPs living in camps and informal settlements across the north-western and north-eastern governorates (1.7 million). This plan to target 7.75 million food-insecure people each month in 2022 is costed at US$985,564,157.

WFP is completing the nationwide Vulnerability Needs Assessment (VNR) exercise, to allow effective prioritization of assistance to households identified as most vulnerable. The VNR exercise will enhance the currently used ""Beneficiary Selection Tool"" by applying indicators that more accurately capture vulnerability status compared to relying only on demographic characteristics.

The operational context in Syria continues to present a complex risk climate. WFP applies the organization's enterprise risk management policy and internal control framework that enables WFP to address and monitor risk and opportunities proactively. Some examples of risks that WFP continues to address cover deteriorating economic and security conditions, inconsistent access to affected population, increasing number of people in need of assistance and impact of COVID-19 pandemic. These risks challenge the safety and security of staff, personnel and beneficiaries, and compromise efficient programme implementation. To address these challenges, WFP continuously reviews its internal and external operating environment, update its risk register, and actively identifies solutions to address current and emerging risks to enable the programme to deliver on its objectives.

With large population unable to cover basic needs and dependent on humanitarian agencies for assistance, PSEA risks resulting from power dynamics between affected population and responding agencies are also at risk of increasing. WFP will continue its work with UN agencies participating in the PSEA network and its partners to ensure that in-place PSEA policies and protocols are fully adopted, implemented, including capacity building, and establishing mechanisms.

project_name: Support scale-up of preventative and curative nutrition services for children under five and women in Somalia
project_objective:
Humanitarian needs continue to rise in Somalia due to the protracted political crisis, armed conflict, climate change implications, desert locust infestation, and COVID-19 pandemic. Based on FSNAU Gu Assessment carried out in June and July2021, an estimated 3.5 million people in Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and Emergency (IPC Phase 4) between October and December 2021 due to multiple risk factors. The post Gu 2021 nutrition assessment has 
indicated critical malnutrition situation among the IDPs in Banadir, Baidoa, Bossaso, Hargeisa and
Galkayo. The post Gu 2021 nutrition assessment findings also showed marginal decrease in the median prevalence of Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) among children aged 6-59 months of 11.1 % down from 11.8% of post Gu 2020 and 13.8% of post Gu 2019. Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) prevalence among children aged 6-59 months is estimated at 1.5% in 2021 down from 1.8% in 2020 post Gu. Despite improvements in prevalence of acute malnutrition among children aged 6-59 months, still an estimated 1.28 million children aged 6-59 months are expected to face acute malnutrition between August 2021 and July 2022, including 295,515 severely acute malnourished children. Urgent nutrition and health support are required to address their needs. Under 2022 HRP, UNICEF and implementing partners will target an estimated 236,222 SAM children (120,474 girls and115,748 boys) i.e.  80% of the SAM burden and 1,142,002 pregnant and lactating women ie. 75% of the total needs. UNICEF will ensure provision of nutrition services through life cycle approach. Target nutrition sites will function as a platform for the
delivery of integrated multi sector services particularly Nutrition, Health, WASH, C4D, CP/GBV and referral for other services in collaboration with other sectors/organizations. UNICEF recognizes that girls, boys, men, women and people with disabilities have different nutritional needs at different life stages with different capacities and risks in accessing nutrition services. UNICEF and implementing partners will support preventive and lifesaving nutrition interventions through provision of maternal, infant and young child nutrition (MIYCN), treatment of children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM), capacity building and robust information systems nationwide. UNICEF as sole provider for SAM nutrition supplies, will ensure to procure nutrition supplies to nutrition cluster partners including SHF recipients, SHINE and BRICSconsortia. The estimated total cost of delivering the UNICEF nutrition HRP project is estimated at USD 40,627,208 for the year 2022.

project_name: Providing Life Saving Treatment and Prevention Nutrition Services to the Vulnerable Communities in Somalia
project_objective:
Food and Nutrition context in Somalia
Decades of conflict and natural disasters including repeated droughts and seasonal flooding followed by limited government and institutional support have had a profound negative effect on the food security situation and social service sector in Somalia. Nearly seven in ten Somalis live on less than USD 1.90 per day,  the sixth-highest poverty rate in sub-Saharan Africa. Poverty is both widespread and deep, particularly for households in rural areas and internally displaced person (IDP) settlements. The number of food-insecure people experiencing long-term stress is trending upwards, indicating that chronic food insecurity persists, requiring sustainable solutions. Recurrent climate-related shocks and political instability are key drivers of food insecurity and pose continuing risks to crop production and food access. Malnutrition in Somalia is driven by a combination of factors such as recurrent food insecurity, child illnesses, high morbidity, micronutrient deficiencies, low immunization levels, poor access to clean water and sanitation, poor hygiene practice, gender inequality and discriminatory sociocultural attitudes leading to poor care practices. Based on the latest Post Gu FSNAU assessment (September 2021), it is estimated that a total of 3.5 million out of the 15.8m people face acute food insecurity (IPC 3 and above – crisis or worse)  until December 2021. At the national level the median prevalence of Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) has remained at a serious level of 11.1%. Approximately 1.2 million children under the age of five are likely to be acutely malnourished, including 295,515 who are likely to be severely malnourished. In addition to this, around 245,909 Pregnant & Lactating Women (PLWs) will be at risk of acute malnutrition. 

Acute malnutrition is a major public health problem in Somalia. It affects disproportionately children under the age of five, as well as Pregnant and Lactating Women (PLWs), especially among IDPs, vulnerable (agro) pastoralist communities and those living in areas affected by flooding. Morbidity among children is high (≥ 20%). Out of a total of 40 surveyed population groups 18 recorded high morbidity presence of above 20%. 
Vitamin A supplementation and Measles vaccination remains low <40% in several population groups. 

TB prevalence remains one of the highest globally with Somalia in the top 10 countries with high TB burden (262 per 100,000 population) while the HIV prevalence remains <1% however with high stigma and discrimination levels at 94%.

Project activities
The World Food Program is the leading UN agency in Somalia in fighting hunger. In Somalia, WFP together with the Ministry of Health (MoH), nutrition cluster and the partners, supports nutrition service delivery and prevention. WFP collaborates with the MoH and UNICEF to offer an integrated package of nutrition and health, following the revised MoH IMAM guidelines for treating acute malnutrition in Somalia.

WFP will cover both treatment and preventive nutrition services including:
•	Targeted Supplementary Feeding Program for 665,846 moderately acute malnourished children 6-59 months; 173,746 malnourished Pregnant and Lactating Women (PLW), 10,794 malnourished People Living with HIV on ART treatment and malnourished TB patients.

project_name: Maternal, Infant and Child Nutrition Emergency Response in South Sudan.
project_objective:
According to FSNMS+ round 27 in 2021 and County based SMART survey results, 26 counties in six States (Jonglei, Unity, Warrap, Upper Nile, Northern Bahr el Ghazal (NBeG), and Eastern Equatoria) have Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) prevalence above the emergency threshold of 15 percent (very high acute malnutrition level- WHO classification). In 2021, the high level of food insecurity and malnutrition are compounded by new shocks related to the COVID-19 disease, unprecedented, localized conflicts and floods that affects large parts of the country especially in Jonglei, Warrap, Unity, Upper Nile and Western Equatoria states.
In 2022, an estimated 2.02 million people in South Sudan (SS) will be at risk of acute malnutrition, including 302,163 children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM), 1,037,432 children with moderate acute malnutrition (MAM), and 675,710 pregnant and lactating women with acute malnutrition (AM-PLW). 


South Sudan continues to grapple with persistent nutrition insecurity stemming largely from disabling socio-economic and political conditions, exacerbated by a long history of shocks, including years of conflict, droughts and flooding as well as suboptimal maternal and childcare practices and gender disparities on the one hand and widespread and repeated episodes of childhood illnesses on the other hand. Since March 2020 the COVID pandemic has affected the entire country, negatively impacting food security and uptake of health and nutrition services.

The cumulative effect of many years of conflict, displacement, economic meltdown, and lack of basic services perpetuates the underlying causes of malnutrition, thus limiting the impact of treatment. Acute malnutrition is attributed to persistent high food insecurity, poor maternal nutrition and poor infant and young child feeding practices, as well as high morbidity due poor sanitation, lack of safe water and limited access to quality health services.

In response, UNICEF will collaborate with actors in health and WASH sectors to reinforce preventative activities and treat children under five with severe acute malnutrition. These activities will include securing safe water through: rehabilitation of non-functioning boreholes; distribution of water treatment kits to secure safe water; hygiene promotion through distribution of soap; early childhood development (ECD); counselling on appropriate infant and young child feeding (IYCF) practices; promotion of kitchen gardens and cooking demonstrations  to ensure adequate physical and cognitive developments; malaria testing and treatment; vaccinations, micronutrient supplementation and deworming to boost immunity; and community engagement to encourage greater utilisation of available services. 

To improve community participation and awareness among caregivers and other community stakeholders, UNICEF will use multiple channels to mobilise communities around key behaviours to prevent undernutrition through network of CNVs (community nutrition volunteers) and MtMSG (mother to mother support groups). 

Given the current nutrition situation and in response to humanitarian needs in South Sudan, UNICEF and nutrition implementing partners plan to reach an estimated 2.02 million people in South Sudan (SS)at risk of acute malnutrition, including 302,163 children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM), 1,037,432 children with moderate acute malnutrition (MAM), and 675,710 pregnant and lactating women with acute malnutrition (AM-PLW). The estimated total cost of delivering this UNICEF nutrition project is US$ 54M to ensure timely and adequate availability of essential nutrition life-saving supplies at point of use to treat the 241,662 children. UNICEF, as the core pipeline manager, still need $8.5 million to procure and distribute 130,000 cartons of ready to use therapeutic food (RUTF).

project_name: Increase access to equitable quality essential health services for internally displaced persons (IDPs) and vulnerable population in South Sudan through provision of immunization core pipeline and use of the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM)
project_objective:
In line with our organizational Core Commitment to Children in Emergency, UNICEF will continue to provide the population of South Sudan especially children, pregnant and lactating women, with quality preventive, and curative services as well as outbreak response activities. The IRRM enables UNICEF, through direct implementation as well as in partnership with IPs, to provide high impact lifesaving emergency response in inaccessible and conflict affected areas. UNICEF will ensure availability of core pipe line vaccines and cold chain supplies to respond to vaccine preventable disease outbreaks.
This project aims to increase access to quality equitable essential primary health care interventions through IRRM and provide a core pipeline to increase access to quality equitable immunization services by vulnerable populations living in host communities and IDPs living in Protection of Civilian Sites (POCs), formal IDP camps or host communities in conflict affected areas as well as refugee returnees.
The activities to be implemented are:
• Procurement and distribution of vaccines for emergency response .
• Procurement, distribution and maintenance of cold chain 
• Technical support for improved vaccine and cold chain management
• Conduct 10 IRRM missions
• Procurement and distribution of anti- snake venom 
• Procurement and distribution of LLINs
• Procurement and distribution of Health Emergency Kits, Clean Delivery Kits and items for diarrhea (IEHK2017 basic unit kit and Supl.1-medicines kits, AWD Periphery Kit drugs), malaria and Pneumonia prevention and treatment 
The expected beneficiaries of core pipeline supplies are 650,000 vulnerable children aged 6 months-15years (323,988 Female; 326,590 Male) living in camps, PoCs, formal IDP camps or host communities in conflict affected areas and refugee returnees. The children will benefit from emergency vaccination to sure up their immunity to vaccine preventable diseases. Vaccines against measles, and traditional childhood vaccine. UNICEF will also support repair and maintenance of the damaged cold chain equipment and devices as well as replacement of the non-repairable equipment to ensure the continuity of the vaccination services.
The curative consultations will be provided for an estimated 28,000 children (13,972 female; 14,028 male) during the Rapid Response Missions. These will include children aged 6 months-15 years who will be reached with immunization services and curative consultations and pregnant women who are expected to benefit from ANC services, tetanus toxoid vaccination, curative consultations and the provision of long-lasting insecticide treated nets (LLITN).
Under the IDP response through IRRM, provision of Emergency Maternal and Newborn care will prioritize provision emergency health kits for obstetric emergencies during curative consultations. Also mainstreaming GBV referrals and strengthening the referral pathway for Psychosocial first aid.

project_name: Strengthening roll out of COVAX vaccination in Syria
project_objective:
UNICEF in coordination with WHO will support MOH to continue COVID-19 vaccination through the COVAX facility and through other bilateral donations.  UNICEF is contributing to most of the ten pillars of COVID response:
Pillar 1: Coordination, planning, financing, and monitoring
Pillar 2: Risk communication, community engagement, and infodemic management
Pillar 3: Surveillance, epidemiological investigation, contact tracing, and adjustment of public health and social measures
Pillar 4: Points of entry, international travel and transport, mass gatherings and population movement
Pillar 5: Laboratories and diagnostics
Pillar 6: Infection prevention and control (IPC), and protection of the health workforce
Pillar 7: Case management, clinical operations, and therapeutics
Pillar 8: Operational support and logistics, and supply chains
Pillar 9: Strengthening essential health services and systems
Pillar 10: Vaccination
UNICEF will focus on the procurement, importation, shipment and transport of vaccine doses to arrive in Syria, improving cold chain system, capacity building for the health workers, and risk communication, community engagement & generating demand. It also includes monitoring and evaluation 
This project aims to ensure availability of sufficient cold chain equipment and proper infrastructure and storage to store the COVAX vaccines allocated to Syria as agreed with GAVI with COVAX facility. This equipment will be part of the countrywide cold chain system used for routine immunization programme as well as supporting the COVAX vaccines at different levels. This will contribute to the resilience and strengthening of the health system through building strong infrastructure for routine vaccination prog, COVAX vaccines, and any future vaccines needed to respond to public health emergencies.
The project will strengthen the capacity of health staff and increase the outreach skills. It will contribute to the improvement of the quality of vaccination services through real-time data collection for monitoring of cold chain and communication interventions.
The project will ensure effectiveness of all received COVAX doses until reaching final beneficiaries as MOH is now targeting all citizens 18 years of age and above. Women and men with disabilities will be reached through outreach mobile vaccination teams through which they will have access to the registration & vaccination services. Women and men with disabilities are among the priority groups for COVAX vaccination.
The project will focus on protection of health workers while performing their duties to vaccinate the targeted population through providing them with personal protective equipment and preventing the negative effects of medical waste on human health and the environment by providing incinerators. 
The project also includes a series of advocacy events (workshops, webinars, orientations) with professional associations, influencers and NGOs, government officials through partnership agreements with NGOs, professional associations and education institutions for capacity building, community engagement and crisis communication. This will be done in coordination with Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE) task forces in all hubs, including the North Eastern Syria (NES) RCCE task force. Local NGOs are playing a vital role in RCCE and will be supporting all community-based awareness activities & demand generation interventions. Also included is a partnership with media agencies to conduct evidence driven media campaigns, evidence generation & behavioral insights to support the implementation of national roll-out action plan. The project includes operational activities to transport COVAX vaccine in NWS, monitoring and evaluation for all interventions including for the outreach activities.
UNICEF will work in all subdistricts, including NES & NWS. This includes 270 SD with 181 of them in severity 3 & 4, and 89 in severity 2, but UNICEF will cover all with the vaccination.

project_name: Strengthening Child Protection interventions for girls and boys most at risk of violence, abuse, neglect and exploitation across whole of Syria
project_objective:
In line with the CP Area of Responsibility (AOR) Strategy and the “No Lost Generation” framework, UNICEF will enhance equitable access to quality CP services with a resilience focus, including for Survivors of abuse, violence, neglect and exploitation as well as children with disabilities, targeting 117 high severity sub-districts (3 to 5) and 38 low severity ones.

UNICEF’s CP Strategy in 2022-2023 includes:
• Addressing behavioural, social, cultural and economic determinants of CP violations as a prevention approach.  
• Improving the reach and quality of specialized CP services
• Capacity development of CP responders
•  Monitoring, evidence generation and advocacy 

UNICEF will support the delivery of integrated programming that will encourage social transformation, prioritizing:
• Structured and sustained CP MHPSS and EORE programmes
• Specialized integrated CP services including case management for survivors of violence, exploitation, neglect and abuse (child labour, CAFAAG, child survivors of GBV, child marriages, justice for children, birth registration and unaccompanied or separated children amongst others) 
• Parenting programmes to promote positive child rearing skills and experience for caregivers
• Elimination of violence against children, including GBV prevention and empowerment for girls, boys and women, prevention of violence in schools, homes and communities.
• Awareness-raising on CP risks
• Capacity development of CP responders and social workers

UNICEF will generate evidence to inform the humanitarian response and advocacy including setting up an information management system for case management. UNICEF will embrace new delivery modalities and implement cash transfers aimed at child protection outcomes for vulnerable families. UNICEF will also continue to support the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism on grave violations against children.

CP services will be delivered by partners based on minimum standards and IASC guidelines. 7,200 CP and social workers will be trained on case management, MHPSS, EORE, advocacy, evidence generation and coordination across sectors for a comprehensive CP response.
 
UNICEF will support MHPSS for 364,000 children to benefit from improved mental health and social wellbeing. UNICEF will equip 61,500 parents and caregivers with skills to provide a stimulating and safe environment at home, including reduced violence.  

Violence prevention is a key priority. Family violence prevalence is high for girls 12-17 years (47%), boys 12-17 years (44%), boys below 12 (45%) and girls below 12 (44%) (UNICEF 2018). UNICEF will work to protect children from violence and abuse through prevention activities in schools, homes and communities and providing survivors of violence with child-friendly and gender sensitive services. Support will be provided for PSEA mechanisms to protect beneficiaries and build the capacity of humanitarian actors. PSEA programming will be implemented with the Protection Sector AORs.

Based on HNO 2021, one in three communities in Syria is reportedly contaminated by explosive ordnance. One in four victims is a child (Joint MA & CP Analysis, 2020). EORE messages will be provided to 1,460,000 children and adults through humanitarian actors and public service providers using static facilities and mobile teams. UNICEF will build the capacity of partners to provide quality EORE that is age, gender and disability appropriate and to provide child victims with assistance.
 
UNICEF will strengthen the justice system to ensure that children in contact with the law victims, offenders or witnesses are protected through child-friendly, gender-sensitive services, that are community-based and family focused.

As Lead Agency for the CP AOR, UNICEF will ensure coordination needs at Hub and WOS levels. Two UN-led and one INGO-led coordination hubs in Damascus, Gaziantep and NES, as well as a WOS overall coordination system, to ensure coherence across the CP response.

project_name: Integrated Social Protection Programme for Children with Disabilities
project_objective:
The economic collapse and the significant reduction in Government’s social spending have led to the complete breakdown of critical national social protection programmes, including the pre-conflict programme for people with disabilities. This has left many families unable to provide for the basic needs of their children, in particular families caring for children with severe disabilities.

Children living with severe mental and/or physical disabilities, are today the most socially and economically vulnerable group of children in the country. They are more likely to be poor than others and have more difficulties in accessing services. UNICEF’s monitoring surveys point to multiple deprivations and the hardship that children with severe disabilities and their families face.  For example, over 70 % of children with severe forms of disabilities are out of school (UNICEF PDM 2021). They are often discriminated against and face greater risks of abuse, harassment and violence. Families with children with severe disabilities have even less opportunities to provide for their livelihoods. – mainly because of the full-time care requirements, the disruption of social care services and social stigma. 

To respond to this situation, UNICEF is implementing the Integrated Social Protection Programme for Children with Disabilities. It is the largest social protection interventions for children with severe disabilities in Syria. The intervention promotes an integrated social protection model with links to public services, with a view to prepare the ground for a future transition from an emergency response to a nationally owned social protection scheme. Since the programme began in 2016, over 30,000 CWD in eight governorates have been reached. 

The programme enhances the resilience of the most vulnerable families and strengthens the continuum of humanitarian and early recovery intervention through an integrated response, which combines regular and un-conditional cash transfers with case management services to facilitate the referral of CWD to available social services and increase their social inclusion. For a 24-month period, families of CWD receive a regular quarterly transfer of US$ 40 per month or US$ 120 per quarter. Each child is followed throughout the period by a dedicated and trained case manager. While the cash help families meet the basic needs of children and the households, the case management component facilitate the referral of CWD to available social services, increase their social inclusion and respond to their specific protection concerns. Therefore, the case management is a vital component that seeks to empower families to better respond to the needs of their children, beyond the life of the cash transfer intervention.

In 2021, three baseline monitoring surveys for the CWD programme were conducted in Homs, Al Hassakeh and Hama governorates. The results of the surveys conducted have indicated the positive impact of the programme on targeted beneficiaries. Key highlights of the PDM survey in Homs indicates high level of satisfaction with the payment modality (86 % satisfied/very satisfied) and increased investment in children after receipt of the first quarterly transfer with a 57 % increase in spending on education for the child and a 48 % increase in the spending on healthcare of the child. It also demonstrated high level of satisfaction with the services provided by case managers (82 % satisfied/very satisfied) in addition to increased access to disability cards (9 % of children without disability card were issued a card).

In 2022, the programme aims to reach 13,000 CWD and their families with regular cash transfer and case management services in seven governorates Dier-ez-Zor; Hassakeh; Aleppo; Hama; Homs; Rural Damascus and as Sweida. Similar targets are planned for 2023.

Accountability to beneficiaries’ is ensure through two main channels: UNICEF centralized redress and grievance mechanisms; and regular monitoring survey

project_name: Water, Sanitation and Hygiene Sector Coordination and Enabling Environment
project_objective:
The Syria crisis is one of the most complex humanitarian crises in recent memory. Humanitarian assistance is provided by a large variety of active actors on the ground, operating both from within Syria and from neighbouring countries. Coordination hubs have been established, in Damascus, Gaziantep, and NES, with WOS in Amman, that ensures common strategies and best use of resources from the different hubs. 
WASH needs of affected populations will continue to be high across 2022 and 2023 with sector partners expected to provide quality emergency WASH services and maintain WASH facilities and infrastructure. WASH needs will largely be influenced by, but not limited to: 
•Water scarcity and drought-like conditions – The evolution of the situation will heavily depend on the sufficiency of winter precipitation, the ability to fill in the dams along the Euphrates River through an increase in the flow to water, which will impact hydropower generation and functionality of water systems powered by them. Nevertheless, proper aquifer recharge, affected by years of over-extraction and drought-like conditions, will not be achieved by a single year’s sufficient winter precipitation.
•Energy supply crisis – the evolution of the situation will largely depend on the level of winter precipitation and related ability to resume normal hydropower generation as well as on the availability of fuel for fossil-fuel power plants, water supply systems, or solid waste management services. If intermittency and further degradation of electricity supply to WASH systems continue, this will trigger a further increase in the people in need of WASH assistance.
•New displacements:  New displacements may also be triggered by hostilities or economic or water crises.
•Population living in IDP sites: population in last resort sites continued to increase despite little to no major hostilities taking place in 2021. This may be partially linked to ongoing economic or water crises, and to the closure of collective centers. Due to funding decrease, trend deterioration of the WASH conditions in IDP sites may be expected. 
•Returnee movements: no major change is expected due to political stasis. Nevertheless, there are areas experiencing a higher level of returns (returns from Al Hole camp, returns to the areas around the frontline in the northern part of rural Latakia, Idleb, Aleppo). This trend is likely to continue, with the returnees facing lower levels of access to WASH services than residents 
As Sector/Cluster Lead agency for the WASH Sector, UNICEF must ensure that sectoral coordination needs at Hub and at Whole of Syria levels are met through appropriate support.  There are also growing needs to create an enabling environment allowing for the Government of Syria and more specifically the Ministry of Water Resources to be more involved with existing coordination structures as the currently the wash Sector is the leading structure that coordinates between WASH partners and managing the sector activities, with minimum engagement of Ministry of Water Resources (MOWR). The sector will try this year to work closely with MOWR to encourage its management team in the ministry for more engagement in leading the sector activities possible and with data collection processes at different levels. This project presents accordingly the activities and related budget allowing to fulfill these coordination tasks and the development of this enabling environment, thus, to ensure following objectives: 
•	Increased predictability of geographic coverage and sectoral responsibility 
•	Demonstrated accountability (for sector-wide performance). 
•	Increased field level capacities to address gaps. 
•	Quality and uninterrupted WASH services.
•	Maximized coordination and partnership and buy-in from the major humanitarian actors to ensure a more strategic and coherent response in support of national led efforts.  
•	Advocacy efforts to ensure that the sector needs are appropriately funded

project_name: Lifesaving Wash Emergency Response and restoration of basic WASH services to enhance resilience and to ensure equitable and sustainable access to Water and Sanitation in Syria
project_objective:
The proposed project will help mitigate service degradation due to physical damage to water and sanitation infrastructure in Syria and enhance its climate change resilience. The challenge for the Syrian WASH Sector will be to identify strategic entry points to resume WASH service delivery. If this is not dealt with in a timely manner, there will be a ""vicious cycle"" whereby insufficient maintenance services, damage and destruction, and non-delivery of services compound on each other, leading to unrecoverable WASH infrastructure and services. The WASH sector is significantly affected by climate change and environmental degradation. Each stream of UNICEF’s humanitarian WASH response in Syria presents opportunities to act on climate, energy, and environmental issues in order to deliver more sustainable results. The “vicious cycle” of cumulative impact on all three components (people, hardware, and consumables) during the current protracted armed conflict in Syria may lead to a situation that is too technically difficult or simply too expensive to reverse. UNICEF will therefore repair and rehabilitate critical parts of water supply systems and infrastructure while being guided by the principle of “Minimum reliable services for All – rather than All services for Some”. The projects supported will be guided by the findings from needs-based vulnerability mapping. Several criteria will be used for the project identification and selection both from an overall and participant perspective, including cost per participant, level of project complexity, neutrality, accessibility, severity scale, number of returnees, quality and quantity of water, and sanitation services currently available. 
Most rural and urban areas in Syria are witnessing electricity shortages, which have affected the operation of water systems. Electricity generation has severely declined in 2021 and is at its worst levels since the beginning of the crisis.  Most wells, water pumping stations, and main water tanks, especially in rural areas depend on diesel generators, which makes them more vulnerable to outages, price gouging, and the inability of Water Boards to secure the required amounts of fuel to operate wells, water pumping stations, and main water tanks. UNICEF is committed to the longer-term sustainable restoration of water services not only by conducting the rehabilitation of damaged infrastructure but also by using solar power as an alternative solution for the electricity and fuel shortage, where it is possible in affected areas, to ensure the provision of clean water to people in need. 
UNICEF will continue providing life-saving WASH interventions such as emergency provision of safe water, sanitation, and solid waste facilities and services, WASH-related supply (non-food items-NFI) distributions as well as improving hygienic behavior and practices of the most vulnerable population. Preparedness actions and contingency planning will also be kept up to date and at sufficient levels to enable timely response to emerging needs considering anticipated rapid changes in the level of access and possible new mass displacements, that might affect northwest and/or north-east of Syria. Cash Voucher Assistance (CVA) will be promoted in the northwest, as an alternative to supplying hygiene kits and/or other WASH services.
The proposed project aims to reach at least 14,762,285 beneficiaries located in 214 subdistricts (64% are high severity areas) in 2022 which represents 82% of the total people in need for 2022.

project_name: Expanding Social, Civic and Economic Engagement and Social Cohesion Interventions for Conﬂict-Affected Adolescents and Youth in the Syrian Arab Republic
project_objective: In support of the ERL Sector (Strengthened Communities and Participation), UNICEF through this project in 2022&2023, will further support its Generation Unlimited initiative and No Lost Generation Agenda by empowering vulnerable adolescents and youth (10-24 years), female and male and those with disabilities, to access social, civic and economic opportunities for skill development and engagement (including participation in social cohesion initiatives) with the objective of contributing to enhancing resilience and social cohesion. UNICEF will build on strategic partnerships, integration and at scale programming focusing on the most vulnerable adolescents to strengthen skills development, employability and meaningful engagement (factoring COVID-19 focused approaches) through friendly spaces and mobile teams. The proposed project will support young women and men to have better access to civic, social, and economic opportunities for skill development and engagement and to unleash their potentials and increase their learning, leadership, and employability opportunities. UNICEF will promote the active and meaningful participation of young people brought together from different ages, genders, abilities and cultural and educational backgrounds to be agents of positive change in their communities. UNICEF will work in the following three pillars and related interventions: (1) Provide access to services and skills-building for adolescents and youth for enhanced employability. (2) Strengthen social, civic and economic engagement of adolescents and youth and foster volunteerism and social cohesion-building. (3) Support young entrepreneurs to start their own project projects through seed funding. UNICEF will continue strengthening the capacity of local partners including services providers, youth workers and young volunteers to improve the quality of provided services and enhance the evidence generation. UNICEF will support the scalable and sustainable approaches with national partners including integrated centers & platforms. In this project, UNICEF will give priority to adolescents and youth in the newly accessible areas in Dara’a. Since the end of September 2021, the humanitarian situation and access to Dar’a Al-Balad and towns in Dar’a have progressively improved. These will include Rural Damascus, northern Homs, southern Hama, east and northeast of Aleppo, Deer EZzour and Idleb. UNICEF will expand its support to young people in NES, focusing on returnees and displaced people in Raqqa and Hasakah, including those in camps, collective shelters and urban settings. During 2021, IDPs have begun returning from the camps to their places of origin in Raqqa. Projects engaging young people will be essential needs for their effective integration in their communities. In addition, since 2014, many young people have been staying in camps and collective shelters. They do not enjoy the freedom of movement and face other risks, thus offering them activities that will enhance their skills and allow them to catch up to their peers in terms of skills and non-formal education. UNICEF will focus on the most deprived areas in rural and urban areas. These will include camps (Hol, Roj, Newroz, Areesha, Mahmoudli) in Hasakah and Raqqa, the collective shelters in Haskah city, and the rural areas in Hasakh Qamishli, Malikia, Yaroubia, and Raqqa Governorate. The programme will coordinate with and support other UNICEF programmes to ensure interventions are tailored to the particular needs of young people. The programme will implement activities for young people affected by, or at high risk of, emergencies or the socio-economic situation, to acquire the right skills, become empowered and resilient community members who help their communities to cope with emergencies. Life-skills and citizenship education for these adolescents will equip and empower them to act as both participants and catalysts of change in their community as volunteers and peer influencers.

project_name: Expanding Skills Building for Conﬂict-Affected Adolescents and Youth in the Syrian Arab Republic
project_objective: In support of the Education Sector, UNICEF through this project in 2022& 2023, UNICEF will further support its Generation Unlimited Initiative and No Lost Generation Agenda by empowering vulnerable adolescents and youth (10-24 years), female and male including those with disabilities, to have access to age and gender sensitive, learning and skills building opportunities for improved learning, empowerment, and employability. UNICEF will build on strategic partnerships, integration and at scale programming focusing on the most vulnerable adolescents to strengthen skills development, and employability (factoring COVID-19 focused approaches) through adolescent-friendly spaces and mobile teams. UNICEF will support access for young girls and boys to multi-sectoral services and opportunities, including technical vocational and education training (TVET), employability skills and life skills and citizenship education. UNICEF will support integrated approach to gender and age-appropriate service delivery maintained strong focus on promoting development and participation of adolescents and youth in north-east Syria, Aleppo, Dara’a, Rural Damascus and Hama. The project will support the access of young people to skills-development programming that is comprehensive and reaches the most vulnerable adolescents, especially those not in Education, Employment and Training, IDPs and returnees. The project will promote alternative pathways and learning beyond schools and implement 21st century skills-development programming. The project will support development of foundational, transferrable, technical and vocational, and entrepreneurship programming to prepare adolescents better for their future, and to unleash their potentials and increase their learning, leadership, and employability opportunities. UNICEF will promote the efficiency and effectiveness in TVET education services nationwide through (i) expanded access and service delivery; (ii) enhanced quality and relevance of TVET provision; and (iii) improved TVET systems including strengthen the capacity of service providers and evidence generation. The project will target the most marginalized adolescents and youth groups in particular those who are out of school, the poor, those from child- or female-headed households, returnees, IDPs, youth in the camps, adolescents with disabilities, and young people affected by the crisis. The project plans to reach a total of 400,000 young people in Rural Damascus, north Homs, south Hama, Idleb, Dier-ez-Zor, east and north-east Aleppo, and other locations. This includes the newly accessible locations such as Dara’a Al-Balad and towns in Dara’a where the security situation has been improved, a new generation of young people, who have been lost for more than 10 years, has appeared. Through this project, UNICEF will expand its support to young people in NES, mainly for the focusing on returnees and displaced people in Ar-Raqqa and Al-Hasakeh, including those in camps, collective shelters and urban settings. During 2021, IDPs have begun returning from the camps to their places of origin in Ar-Raqqa. Projects engaging young people projects will be essential needs for their effective integration in their communities. In addition, since 2014, many young people have been staying in camps and collective shelters without freedom of movement and facing other risks, thus offering them activities that will enhance their skills and empower them to be agents of positive change in their community. UNICEF will focus on the most deprived areas in rural and urban areas include camps (Hol, Roj, Newroz, Areesha, Mahmoudli) in Al-Hasakeh and Ar-Raqqa, the collective shelters in Al-Hasakeh city, and the rural areas in Al-Hasakeh Qamishli, Malikia, Yaroubia, and Ar-Raqqa. The project will implement the activities for the young people affected by the crisis to acquire the right skills, become empowered and resilient community members.

project_name: Assistance multisectorielle pour les populations réfugiées et hôtes de l'Adamaoua et de l'Est
project_objective:
L'intervention intégrée proposée par ce projet répond aux conséquences de la crise centrafricaine dans les régions de l'Adamaoua et de l'Est aux besoins urgents des communautés en termes de protection et de sécurité alimentaire et moyens de subsistance. En effet, la protection des populations affectées par la crise centrafricaine reste un défi majeur, notamment concernant le mariage précoce des jeunes filles, les VBG, la déscolarisation ou non-scolarisation des enfants, le manque de documentation civile, etc. De plus l'assistance alimentaire fournie par l'aide internationale a drastiquement diminué alors que les besoins restent conséquents
En vue d'assister les populations affectées par la crise, ainsi que de maintenir la cohabitation pacifique et la cohésion sociale avec les communautés hôtes, bien que la pression sur les ressources et sur les services augmente, cette intervention permettra d'appuyer la réduction des stratégies de survie négatives et de favoriser l'accès aux moyens de subsistance basé sur les vulnérabilités des individus et des ménages à travers l'intégration avec l'action déjà en cours de renforcement des mécanismes de protection à base communautaire et d'amélioration de l'environnement protecteur.

project_name: Atención nutricional de niños y niñas menores de 5 años, mujeres embarazadas y en periodo de lactancia a nivel nacional y focalización a estados priorizados por el HRP.
project_objective:
La atención nutricional propuesta por Unicef está dirigida a niños y niñas menores de 5 años, madres embarazadas y en periodo de lactancia - MEL, ubicados en zonas de alta vulnerabilidad a nivel nacional, y focalización en los estados priorizados por el sector de nutrición del HRP, apoyando principalmente a través de la implementación directa en centros de salud. La atención nutricional incluye las siguientes acciones:
1.Prevención de la desnutrición aguda: se enfocará en las siguientes intervenciones: a.Tamizaje del estado nutricional - a 700,000 niños, niñas menores de 5 años; b. Tratamiento antianémico para 80,898 niños y niñas de 6 a 59 meses y MEL; c. Desparasitación a 4,400,000 niños y niñas de 2 a 14 años y embarazadas en 2T y 3T de gestación. Suplementación con micronutrientes a 520,800 niños y niñas de 6 a 59 meses y 373,921 MEL; e. 23,351 de mujeres embarazadas y en periodo de lactancia con bajo peso que reciben tratamiento.
2.Tratamiento de la desnutrición aguda y deficiencias de micronutrientes. La atención se realizará con los servicios de salud ambulatorios y hospitalarios adscritos a las autoridades únicas de salud y MPPS, respectivamente. Incluye el a. Tratamiento a 60,397 niños y niñas con desnutrición aguda moderada y severa con y sin complicaciones y apoyo en la transición al manejo ambulatorio. c. Tratamiento de la anemia nutricional en 89,898 niños, niñas menores de 5 años y MEL. 
3. Mejorar el acceso a los servicios de salud y nutrición de alta calidad a través de apoyo técnico calificado y provisión de insumos y equipo nutricional. a. 10,120 personal de salud y nutrición capacitados para la prevención y tratamiento de la desnutrición b. 800 centros de atención nuricional fortalecidos con insumos y equipos nutricionales.
4.  Promocionar y apoyar prácticas adecuadas para la Alimentación del Niño Pequeño IYCF por su siglas en inglés, con enfoque multisectorial a. 344,311 mujeres embarazadas, madres, padres y cuidadores de los niños y niñas menores de 5 años que reciben orientación en prácticas claves de Nutrición a través de las consultas nutricionales, las Redes Sociales y otros canales de comunicación. b. Entrenamientos de entrenadores en nutrición en emergencias prevención y tratamiento de la desnutrición y prácticas adecuadas para la Alimentación del Niño Pequeño en Emergencias (IYCF por su siglas en inglés) con enfoque multisectorial (salud, nutrición y WASH) a socios implementadores de Unicef. 
c. Fortalecimiento del monitoreo y reporte de temas del estado nutricional de los niños, niñas y MEL y capacitaciones en a personal de salud y de socios implementadores.

project_name: Access to Education for Refugees, IDPs and Host Communities in Ruweng (Parieng), South Sudan
project_objective:
Ruweng Administrative Area  currently hosts about 124,000 Sudanese refugees and at least 4,868 internally displaced persons(IDPS) who have moved from Benitu due to the flooding. This has posed increased challenges to the already stretched service delivery point in the area. Available records from the Area Ministry of Education indicates that 83 learning facilities in the Administrative Area are currently not operational due to lack of paid teachers. Additionally safe learning environment remains a huge challenge with over 90%  of all learning centers in the area are temporary structures.. This intervention is geared at providing education for learners in the host communities of the Ruweng Administrative Area (Parieng). Below are the goal and three principal objectives of the proposed intervention:
Goal: Increase access to inclusive quality education for host community children especially girls and children with disabilities

Objective1:
Improve equitable access to safe and protective education services for 4550 emergency affected IDPs, returnees, spontaneous refugees, and host community children including children with disabilities and youth (girls and boys).

Objective 2:
Improve the quality of gender and disability-inclusive education services and teachers' capacity to protect the wellbeing of all children and prevent the negative impact of the emergencies on learning environments.

Objective 3:
Strengthen/enhance the education system’s response capacity of the school community and national/local education actors to mitigate the impact of existing emergencies on learners, teachers, and communities

Target:
Some of these refugee learners will be hosted by within the existing refugee schools located in the Ajuong Thok and Pamir refugee camps and will therefore together with the refugee learners directly benefit from this intervention 
•	4,264 learners (2,132F, 2,132M) at ECD, primary & secondary levels 
•	76 (20F, 56M) teachers and head teachers 
•	 200(100F,100M) executives and members of PTAs/SMCs/BoGs
•	10 (3F, 7M) Area Education leadership members

project_name: Increase Food Access and Enhance Resilience to Most Vulnerable people under IPC4  Twic East, Duk and Bor South counties, Jonglei State, South Sudan
project_objective:
Food Security and Livelihoods (FSL) project is targeting natural disaster/flood and conflict (compounded by inter-clan, inter-tribal violence and cattle raiding) affected most vulnerable IDPs, and Returnees and host communities who have been affected over the past one year. LWF plans to reach 4500 HHs (27000 Individuals )and additional 690 Individuals  (total of 27690 Individuals) from IDPs, and Returnees communities in Twic East, Duk  and Bor South counties through supporting emergency food production and building capacities of people and households’ level to build resilience to better respond to shocks. This project will contribute to strategic objective 1 (Specific objective 1.1) and Strategic Objective 3(specific objective 3.1) of the South Sudan and Humanitarian Needs Response Plan (HRP 2022). The project intends to reduce the food insecurity and malnutrition through enhanced emergency food production via distribution of seeds, agricultural tools, fishing kits and poultry for the most vulnerable people but also to build resilience slowly reducing the dependency on food and agricultural inputs through training & capacity building on-farm production, with demonstration plots and kitchen garden created also in proximity of schools and health facilities to be of example for the community; awareness on nutritious food consumption and food waste management, capacity building on saving and income generation.
The project will ensure the sustainability of its outcome through working together with customary institution, line departments, women groups, youth groups, and local administration from beginning of the project.  
The project activities will be implemented in consideration of preventive measure to prevent the spread and transmission of COVID-19.

project_name: Enhancing Protective Environment for displacement affected communities in Ethiopia
project_objective:
Ethiopia continues to experience critical humanitarian needs and displacement, exacerbated by recurrent crises caused by environmental and conflict drivers. The multiple crises in Ethiopia have affected the ability of humanitarian organizations to respond quickly and in a meaningful manner, as well as the capacity of affected communities to deal with multiple shocks and secondary displacement. In addition, the conflict in northern Ethiopia has led to a significant increase in internal displacement, as well as spillover effects creating increased tensions in Amhara, Afar, and Somali regions, and heightening the targeting of ethnic groups in different parts of the country. 
IDPs and IDP returnees face substantial protection risks, including threats of human rights violations before and during displacement, lack of meaningful access to essential services, loss of HLP rights, including civil documentation, and protracted displacement with high risks of secondary displacement or lack of durable solutions. Protracted displacement also serves as a conflict driver, due to increased tensions with host communities around resource scarcity, local integration, and inequalities in service provision. 
As such, DRC proposes a comprehensive protection response to support populations affected by crises, inclusive of those affected by conflict, violence, disasters, or climate change, and those at risk of displacement; this includes host communities, IDPs, returnees, and refugees in and out of camp settings. DRC's programming will focus on supporting displacement-affected populations in Tigray, Somali, and Gambella region, as well as refugee and returnee response in Addis Ababa; further, DRC will provide an integrated protection and emergency response to affected communities in Afar or elsewhere through a mobile response capacity.

project_name: Increased access to quality health, nutrition and MHM services, through intergrated, community-based mechanisms, especially for women and children under 5.
project_objective: In 2022, Tdh will ensure an evidence-based health package which fulfils the essential health services for refugee and host communities in an equitable manner while ensuring accessibility and quality. Tdh primary health care facilities will avail health promotion, preventive services curative services, and access to secondary/ tertiary referrals. Systematic community-level health promotion and preventive services will continue to be rolled out through community health workers linked to the primary health facilities. Curative services will encompass IMCI, SRHR which includes, ANC, PNC, Normal delivery, B-EMONC, Preterm new-born and sepsis management, post-abortion care, Menstrual regulation, Td vaccination IFA supplementation, obstetric fistula screening and referral, voluntary counselling and testing for PMTCT and MHPSS as a multi-sectoral approach with tdh cp response which includes psychological first-aid, identification and referral of persons with mental needs, management of mental health priority conditions by mhGAP trained clinician, referral of severe casse, psychosocial interventions provided by a trained psychologist, counsellor’s, community awareness workshops, psychoeducational activities such as self-care and risk factors reduction, group psychosocial activities and individuals psychosocial services, in addition to general communicable and non-communicable disease curative services, which includes standard triage including nutrition screening, first aid, treatment of emergency cases, outpatient services. Referrals are sustained to ensure intra-camp and outside camp referrals for secondary and tertiary health care. For child health Tdh, in coordination with GOV, will provide routine immunization and individual growth monitoring and provide IYCF counselling to mothers and systematic detection of acute malnutrition among children 6 to 59 months and PLWs. Additionally, clinical diagnosis and management of anaemia among the targeted beneficiaries and referral of PLW, SAM and MAM children 6 to 59 month to OPTS or TSFPs according to nutritional status and treatment guideline will be actioned. Tdh will also continue to provide a family planning service that includes short- and long-term methods together with the community sensitization outreach program, in line with Tdh’s child protection response.  Other services, such as Oral and eye care, will be explored to be provided in an integrated manner in close collaboration with primary and secondary health care providers. An important focus will be on the vulnerable groups including pregnant and post-natal women, new-born, under 5 years child including those with malnutrition, and persons with disabilities. Tdh health program also focused on adolescent health which includes adolescent-friendly service, IFA supplementation, Menstrual Health Management (MHM) through a gender-responsive, adolescent-friendly PHC service, in coordination with Tdh’s Child protection team. As Tdh’s commitment to mainstreaming GBV prevention and response messages on community-level, the Health response has a particular focus on GBV survivors, including survivor identification through referrals, self-reports, accompaniments, health provider suspects injury or condition that can be linked to violence, assessment and care for survivors of associated minor injuries, clinical management of rape survivor, also the treatment of prophylaxis of STI, emergency contraception, post-exposure prophylaxis, TT and Hepatitis B vaccination, follow up and consent-based referrals for other services. B laboratory services will also be provided among the beneficiaries. Tdh health program also looks after health care waste management.

project_name: Inclusive specialized (Rehab, PSS, SRHR) services for vulnerable persons including persons with disabilities in Cox's Bazar Rohingya camps and host communities
project_objective:
HI will continue its 12+ years of broad support for refugee/FDMNs and host communities by addressing the immediate acute and chronic health needs of refugees and host communities through multi-sectoral mobile units, center-based services and a strong referral pathways. The proposed intervention will be delivered through twin modality:
1.	Multi-sectorial mobile units composed of qualified Nurses and Midwives, Physiotherapists, PSS officers, Protection Officers and social workers will be deployed to identify and provide tailored and individual assistance to the most vulnerable, especially the persons with disabilities and their caregivers who might be excluded from services due to mobility or social barriers. This mobile teams deliver home-based services focused on education for beneficiaries and their caregivers on safe, effective therapeutic exercises and interventions.
2.	Static points: Multidisciplinary teams support beneficiaries with rehabilitation, PSS, basic healthcare through nurses and protection. Training is provided to persons and caregivers on basic home-based rehabilitation and proper use, maintenance and repair of mobility devices. Group sessions on MHPSS and assessment for protection beneficiaries take place.
-In home-based and center-based services, Nurses will support beneficiaries with: wound care, bedsores care, ante and post-natal care. A key focus will be to provide maternal care for women who cannot access health facilities (i.e. women and girls with disabilities), including the prevention and detection of pregnancy-related risks and complications. Nurses refer to the nearest Health Facility and follow up to ensure they receive needed specialized services.
- Support to government hospitals and health facilities both in the host and refugee communities to provide rehabilitation services. HI coordinates at Age & Disability Working Group (ADWG) as co-founder to provide services to unserved camps if disability specific services are required. HI also have modality of outreach rehabilitation team to serve the areas where HI doesnot serve on regular basis.
- PSEA focals are assigned at each site offices who ensure PSEA principles are mainstreamed through all activities through extensive training of all staff and volunteers using PSEA Network materials and recommendations. Feedback is regularly elicited through suggestions boxes, a dedicated hotline for host and refugee communities, community discussions and 1:1 interview. A dedicated Focal Point to receive complaints is assigned in the Cox’s Bazar base to coordinate with camp level team leaders to ensure referral for needed services and ensure survivor advocacy as needed. 
HI is currently implementing four projects that addresses above mentioned health services funded by different donors. To provide the service for the host community people, HI support 5 Health Facilities. It includes Cox's Bazar Sadar hospital, Ukhiya Upazila health complex, Teknaf Upazila health complex, KTP MSF-OCA-331 and IOM Leda-200 with rehabilitation staff (physiotherapist) provide services in those facilities. Both host community people and beneficiaries from the camps can receive services from these facilities.
HI welcomes complaints and feedback from the beneficiaries to integrate beneficiaries’ views in the project activities. HI MEAL team leads the complaints, feedback and response mechanism. Currently different complaints and feedback collection modalities exists in both host communities and camps. Modalities are face to face interviews, group discussions, hotline and feedback box. Based on the sensitivities of the complaints HI provide solution as soon as possible.
Provision of basic nursing & SRHR services (ANC, PNC, FP awareness) through individual, family and group sessions to women, men, boys and girls with significant focus on vulnerable people (persons with disabilities, pregnant women, older persons, chronically ill and who could not access the facilities etc) in the camps.
