project_name: Shelter and NFI Assistance for IDPs and host community members in Northern Syria
project_objective:
The proposed project aims at addressing emergency and more sustainable shelter and NFI needs of vulnerable households with acute needs (both IDPs and host community members) in Northeast and Northwest Syria.  

The intervention will target a total of 123,625 beneficiaries under shelter activities, and 153,004 beneficiaries under NFI activities across Northwest and Northeast Syria for a total budget of 5,472,963$ including 4,209,680$ of program budget. To note, some beneficiaries will receive more than one type of assistance. As a result, some of them if will double-counted under the activities in section 4. 

In Northwest Syria, ACTED will provide fuel for heaters to better equip the residents for winter in A’zaz and Idleb sub-districts for 111,095 individuals for 1,148,474$ (program budget). Under this intervention, the same number of camp residents will also receive emergency NFI kits -composed of, for example, tarpaulin, jerry can, mattresses/sleeping mats, blankets, solar lamps, floor mat, stove, cooking pot, bowl for food, and cutlery - as well as winterization kits, to guarantee shelter and dignified living conditions to newly displaced household, for 196,296$ (program budget). Through contractors, ACTED will rehabilitate private off-camp shelter units to 600 individuals in A’zaz sub-district for 131,046$ (program budget). In addition, ACTED will rehabilitate shelters in-camp to 500 individuals in Jarablus sub-district for 135,061$ (program budget). In addition, 750 individuals out-of-camp will benefit from shelter repairs for 255,409$ (program budget) and ACTED will provide multi-purpose cash Assistance for winterization to 15,000 individuals in Aleppo governorate, for a total amount of 266,051$ (program budget). 

In Northeast Syria, ACTED will provide fuel and heaters to 14,433 camp residents across Areesheh camp, Al-Hasake governorate, to better equip the residents for winter for a total amount of 829,868$ (program budget).  In Serekaniye camp, Al-Hasake governorate, ACTED will distribute fuel and heaters to 12,476 camp residents for a total of 291,840$ (program budget). 
These camp residents will also benefit from installation and maintenance of fire safety points, for 11,333$ (program budget). In Ar-Raqqa governorate, ACTED will rehabilitate household shelters for dignified living conditions to 10,680 beneficiaries in out-of-camp areas for a total of 1,365,650$ (program budget). 

ACTED will take into account the different risks and concerns affecting women, men, girls and boys and people with disabilities when designing this intervention. With regards to the latter, ACTED will ensure that the distributions are conducted respectfully of the needs of the most vulnerable, with specific distribution lines dedicated to women and elderlies. ACTED will also conduct the distributions directly at the HH level when needed. As for the shelter rehabilitation activity, ACTED will ensure to select the HHs also based on vulnerability, with consideration for income and/or demographics. ACTED will develop BoQs for each shelter based on technical shelter assessments. The assessment of the shelter will take into consideration privacy needs, as well as specific needs for people with disabilities when relevant and particular works will be incorporated as necessary. This will ensure safe and dignified living conditions to the targeted HHs in the area of intervention.

project_name: Increased access to emergency and sustainable water, sanitation and hygiene support by displacement affected populations in Somalia
project_objective:
The population of people in need of humanitarian assistance in Somalia has been on a steady increase. Estimates show that of the 7.7 million people in need in 2022, 6.4 million will be in need of Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) support. Repeated cycles of drought and floods, further exacerbated by the spread of COVID 19 and resurgent conflict in the country, have resulted in disease (cholera/Acute Watery Diarrhea (AWD) outbreaks, severe water shortage, inadequate and non-functional water sources and sanitation facilities, and poor water supply systems. Those affected include refugees, refugee returnees, internally displaced persons (IDPs), host communities who DRC refer to as displacement affected communities. Among these groups are individuals with particular vulnerabilities such as women and girls, children, persons living with disabilities, the elderly and members of minority groups. Assessments conducted by the WASH Cluster, for example, point to the specific and growing vulnerabilities of women and girls who are at high risk of gender based violence (GBV) as they travel long distances to fetch water for household consumption due to insufficient and inadequate WASH facilities. 
In light of these challenges, DRC proposes to support 236,050 individuals (34,342 men, 39,809 women, 83,604 boys, 78, 295 girls) through provision of emergency and sustainable WASH interventions that will improve water access, reduce the risk of mortality and disease, and improve overall WASH outcomes. DRC will prioritize flood prone and drought risk areas in Somalia and especially those not receiving sufficient WASH support. Furthermore, DRC will streamline gender and disability in its programming ensuring that the specific needs and vulnerabilities of women and girls and persons living with disabilities are catered to. Prior to commencing any implementation, DRC will conduct a needs assessment that will feed into the final project locations and priorities. This will also feed into the beneficiary selection criteria that DRC will adopt that will ensure only the most vulnerable groups are targeted. Through this proposed response, DRC will provide both emergency and longer term sustainable access to WASH Support. Under emergency response, and informed by the drought projections of 2022, DRC will undertake emergency water trucking especially in areas where people rely on rain water to avoid displacements, fabrication, provide hygiene and sanitation kits, construct disability friendly emergency latrines, and conduct rapid hygiene promotion. In a bid to support more sustainable water access, DRC will rehabilitate critical water supply infrastructures such as boreholes with a clear focus on optimizing outputs through upgrading of water supply systems. As part of its market based approach to WASH, DRC will establish partnerships with private and government water source owners to extend water services to settlements to areas where displacement affected communities reside. Community members will then be trained on the operation and maintenance of rehabilitated WASH infrastructure as part of building buy in by the community as well as increasing a sense of ownership within the community. In DRC’s experience, this has resulted in more care and upkeep of rehabilitated assets and longer-term service of these assets. Where distribution of hygiene kits is seen to be a more emergency type of intervention, hygiene promotion is considered to be a longer-term intervention that seeks to influence positive behavior uptake regarding personal and community sanitation and hygiene. In light of the current third wave of COVID 19, DRC will distribute hygiene kits coupled with COVID 19 message shared in mass media and through Information, Education and Communication (IEC materials). Lastly, DRC will support the desludging of latrines and construction of new latrines and handwashing stations that will support solid waste management and promote good hygiene and sanitation

project_name: Provision of emergency and durable shelters and NFIs to displacement affected communities in Somalia
project_objective:
The Humanitarian Needs Overview estimates that 3.6 million people will be in need of Shelter support in 2022. This includes both IDPs and non-IDPs and remains a concern for 58% of the entire IDP population in Somalia. Key concerns under shelter include overcrowding, lack of security, and poor shelter conditions with majority of those living in IDP sites lacking permanent tenure to land thus increasing their risk for forced evictions. Lack of access to income is also a key concern for the most vulnerable as they often lack the necessary finances to put up adequate shelters thus necessitating the need to provide emergency shelter and non-food items. This remains particularly crucial especially in hard to reach areas of Somalia. 
The ongoing conflict and floods in parts of Somalia has resulted in damages to shelter among other critical infrastructure, and with the resulting displacement, populations often find themselves living in dangerous and unsustainable shelters. Those that are displaced for a shorter period with the intention and capability of returning to regions of origin often need emergency shelter kits while those that have been displaced for a longer period of time would require more durable shelters. Although access to shelter and housing is an issue that cuts across the different groups, IDPs remain particularly vulnerable due to their lack of tenure and displacement status. 
As such, DRC will target a total of 103,800 displacement affected communities (DACs) through provision of emergency shelter kits (ESK), non-food items (NFIs), transitional shelter and durable shelter solutions. DRC defines DACs as people affected by displacement internally and those that are returning seeking for reintegration. Therefore, DRC targets new IDPs, the IDPs in protracted situation, returnees and host communities. DRC understands that the primary displacements in Somalia is as a result of natural disasters and man-made conflict; but also, secondary displacements are now a common reality due to military offensive. These displacements are the key driver of humanitarian shelter needs in Somalia. IDPs remain in need of Shelter and NFIs support for protection from harsh climatic conditions, overall improvements to their living conditions and improvement to their chances to access livelihoods and durable solutions. On the other hand, DRC targets Host Communities – to ensure peaceful coexistence between the local population and target groups and also because many of them are equally vulnerable and in need of humanitarian assistance. For IDPs in protracted situation, DRC offers transitional shelter assistance. This also includes negotiating for extension of land lease/tenure to allow for a longer stay until full re-integration is sought. Returnees are also targeted with durable housing solutions in which case DRC proposes permanent shelter. For permanent shelter, DRC will ensure an integrated approach where other needs - WASH, shelter, livelihood, and protection are included in the settlement planning. Therefore, DRC will target newly displaced populations with emergency shelter and NFIs. For IDPs in protracted situation and returnees, DRC will seek transitional shelter and durable solutions respectively. Where cash based intervention or voucher is sought, DRC will undertake registration based on AGD and vulnerability criteria through an electronic system. Then DRC will undertake a verification exercise whereby beneficiaries will be screened to see if they meet set criteria. The list of beneficiaries selected shall be shared with a mobile money transfer company operated by telephone service providers. The cash shall be released in two tranches of 70% and 30% respectively for both NFIs and ESKs. This shall minimize risk of cash being used for other activities not related with shelter but also to make sure the cash goes to the right beneficiaries.

project_name: Protecting vulnerable communities by improving their abilities to cope with the effects of armed violence through Psychosocial Support and Child Protection activities
project_objective: The objective of the project is to provide children adolescents, and adults with the tools and space to improve their mental and psychosocial wellbeing, identify and manage stress, and develop positive coping mechanisms in order for them to better cope with the stress and potential trauma that they are likely facing in their daily lives . Structured and sustained PSS activities targeting children/adolescents will be conducted in DCAs Community Safe Space (CSS) through art, music, drama, sports, storytelling, games and structured activities aiming to develop feelings of safety and trust. Moreover, provision of case management in the case basis and need basis will conducted. Adolescents who are unable to attend the CSS will be reached with awareness sessions focusing on stress management in their schools, sports clubs and/or youth centers. Additionally, parents/caregivers of children and adolescents receiving support will be provided with awareness sessions focusing specially on child protection issues. Individuals who require further assistance will be referred to specialized mental health services for follow up. Furthermore, DCA will facilitate a new intervention, support groups, where beneficiaries can help each other by discussing some of their problems and successful coping skills.

project_name: Improving nutritional status of children under two years of age and PLW through integrated health and nutrition services
project_objective:
Save the Children International (SCI) will implement preventive nutrition services through 8 health posts in 8 camps. The nutrition program will target pregnant and lactating women (PLW) and under-five children with a special focus on two children who attended the health post for any occasion. SCI will follow the “IYCF-E Multisectoral framework for action” for designing an integrated service model with Health and Child protection sector. Management of non-breastfed (NBF) children will be one of the priorities with appropriate logistics support. SCI will maintain referral linkage with Integrated Nutrition Facilities (INF) for identified malnourished cases. SCI will continue leading the IYCF-E technical group and provide strategic guidance to the nutrition sector for evidence-based decision making and partner’s capacity building on IYCF-E and CMAMI.
The nutrition program comprises of nutrition assessment of all the PLWs and under two children, nutrition education and counselling on IYCF-E, cooking demonstration, and referral of identifying malnourished cases to INF or stabilization centre. Community awareness sessions will be organized with community influential (Imam/Majhi) for creating a community support system. Gender roles and negative practices that restrict optimal nutrition behaviour will be highlighted during these sessions. Transformative gender role targeting support for unpaid care tasks and mobility will be focused during household negotiated counselling and group awareness sessions. Knowledge to practice transformation requires repeated contact and counselling support. SCI will utilize health post visit as an additional contact opportunity and emphasized nutrition promotion and ensure referral. In targeting, the nutrition coverage gap of around 20% is considered and SCI will report service received and only new case referral for avoiding duplication error with existing INF coverage.  
SCI will continue its technical assistance to implementing partners in managing NBF children and required lifesaving logistics will be distributed to specific cases following all the regulations and technical protocols. Capacity building and on-job training on CMAMI and NBF management will be organized with support from nutrition sector partners. 
Inclusion of PWD is one of the priorities and health posts included nutrition corners will be made suitable for their access and comfort for service seeking. Community workers will ensure that PWDs are practising the optimal nutrition practices and berries can be minimized through regular household visits. 
SCI is a member of the PSEA network. SCI will give importance to the protection from and responding to sexual exploitation and abuse. SCI has a strong reporting and monitoring mechanism to identify PSEA cases. SCI will conduct periodical training, awareness sessions for the staff, volunteers, and other stakeholders on PSEA policy.  
SCI will lead IYCFE TWG as before and provide advisory support to the nutrition sector on generating evidence-based strategic guidance and implementation modalities on IYCF-E.

project_name: Prevent and reduce morbidity and mortality of Rohingya refugee and host communities through quality primary healthcare in Cox’s Bazar
project_objective:
Save the Children will deliver an inclusive, gender responsive & comprehensive healthcare services and will reach around 90,277 beneficiaries through 8 HP and 1 PHCC & SARI ITC over a 12-month period in 8 camps of Ukhiya and Teknaf, Cox’s Bazar to ensure that diverse Rohingya refugees and host communities have equitable access to essential healthcare services. This Health facilities will deliver primary health care service with special focus on 24/7 emergency care, sexual, reproductive, maternal, neonatal, child and adolescent health; mental health and psychosocial support and noncommunicable diseases in line with the MoH and Health Sector recommended Minimum Package of Essential Service Package. Along with regular health consultation, PHCC will offer IPD service with 15 beds (5 child, 5 male, 5 female); laboratory; PMTCT; BEmONC service with 5 bedded maternity unit & SGBV services (CMR, IPV and Domestic Violence). All this health facility will offer integrated services with Nutrition (IYCF-E), WASH(IPC) and Child Protection by ensuring coordination and referral in between, establishing a child friendly corner considering Do no harm policy. To ensure IPC measure and safe disposal practice to avoid chance of infection, a dedicated IPC focal will work closely with facility level IPC committee and provide necessary guidance aligned with IPC WG and MoH. Considering living with COVID-19 strategy, SCI PHCC & SARI ITC will merge to manage COVID-19 cases through its 20  COVID-19 dedicated beds along with regular PHCC operation. Overall, this center will act as a multifunctional outbreak center where other communicable diseases (AWD, Measles, Diphtheriae, etc) will be managed along with the COVID-19. As per the guidelines, health facilities are staffed by Doctors, Midwives, Medical Assistant, Nurse, Dispenser, MHPSS officer, clinic aides, IYCF-E counsellors and MCHN promoters. Clinical services will be complemented with health promotion and community engagement activities through a robust community health workers(CHWs) to encourage timely access to healthcare and address existing challenges in the community level. SCI CHWs will work in their catchment area of 8 different camps in Ukhiya, Teknaf and its surrounding host communinty as organized by Community Health Working Group(CHWG) to avoid service overlapping with other partners and CHWs will visit around  17546 House Hold. Community based surveillance(CBS) will be continued by CHWs to identify COVID-19 patients in the communities. All staff and volunteers will be trained on CP, child safeguarding and PSEA. To enhance clinical excellence, team will be trained on prevention & management of communicable & non-communicable disease, IMCI, IPC and on other identified needs. There will be 2 Mobile Medical team (MMT) aligned with Emergency Preparedness Response Working Group (EPRWG) will be providing services in any emergency health response following any natural or manmade disaster. All the health facilities will be accessible and environment friendly for all age group and also for PWD by ensuring ramp, disable friendly latrine, triage area, signage, lighting and skilled workforce to prioritize and manage geriatric population and PWD. 
SCI has a robust MEAL system and according to the Program’s Logical Framework, develop a MEAL plan including Monitoring Plan that specifies indicators, data disaggregated by sex, age and disability etc. Data will be managed internally using SCI’s web-based Information Management System (IMPACT) and externally with EWARS and DHIS2. In regards of Accountability to Affected Population(AAP) , SCI is applying multiple channels for Feedback Response and Reporting Mechanism i.e Hotline, Partner Led Data Collections, Help Desk & Exit Interview.

project_name: Expansión y fortalecimiento de atención institucional-comunitaria multi-sectorial para niños, niñas, adolescentes y sus familias en Venezuela.
project_objective:
SC y socios proponen una intervención multidisciplinar en los estados de Anzoategui, Zulia, Miranda, Distrito Capital, Delta Amacuro y Sucre, para atender a las necesitades de NNA de manera holística.
La implementación tomará en cuenta los hallazgos de análisis de género y de necesidades previamente desarrollados por la organización, así como un plan de acción que permita adaptar la respuesta a las necesidades diferenciadas y evidenciadas por edad, sexo y discapacidades.
El proyecto se enfoca en los sectores de protección, educación, nutrición y salud, WASH y seguridad alimentaria. 
Las acciones inmediatas buscaran fortalecer el sistema de protección comunitario e institucional, generando mayor atención psicosocial en las comunidades, consolidando los mecanismos de derivación y fortalecer las capacidades técnicas y operativas de los CPNNA para que presten servicios con mayor capacidad y calidad. Se facilita la gestión de casos a NNA con riesgos de abuso infantil y en coordinación con el sistema de protección se dará respuesta a sus necesidades. Se facilitará apoyo psicosocial individual a los casos que lo requieran. Se ofrecerán servicios de gestión de casos con riesgos de protección identificados (incluida la violencia sexual y de género), con referenciación a otros servicios e instancias del Sistema de Protección infantil, cuando sea requerido.
En educación, se fortalecerán capacidades técnicas en los docentes comunitarios y de educación formal de inicial, primaria y bachillerato, así como al equipo directivo, en INNE, Educación en Emergencia, Participación Infantil y Juvenil, Escuela Segura, educación inclusiva, aprendizaje acelerado y significativo, didáctica de la lengua y la matemática, a fin de contribuir en la formación de líderes proactivos, resilientes y comprometidos en desarrollar estrategias curriculares que respondan a necesidades diferenciadas de grupos vulnerables en contextos de emergencia. Asimismo, se fortalecerán capacidades técnicas y operativas a 7 Centros Alternativos de Aprendizaje, a fin de garantizar una atención segura y de calidad a NNA sin acceso a la educación o con desafíos para disfrutar de este derecho, quienes posteriormente con apoyo especializado e inclusivo son reinsertados en el sistema escolar formal.
En Nutrición, entendiendo que la desnutrición aguda es una de las principales causas de mortalidad para los niños menores de 5 años (U5), y los efectos en su desarrollo matriz, psicológico y cognitivo son a larga plazo, y que la mujeres/adolescentes en gestación o lactancia son una población en riesgo de sufrir malnutrición con efectos negativos en su salud y de sus bebes, las intervenciones de SC y socios se enfocan en disminuir la vulnerabilidad y a fortalecer las capacidades de recuperación a través de incrementación del acceso a los servicios de nutrición en la comunidad para evaluación, prevención y tratamiento, teniendo en cuenta las barreras de género, conflicto y pandemia, en el fortalecimiento de la capacidad de respuesta de los servicios de nutrición y salud pública (se dara soporte para prevencion de covid19 para el personal de salud que atendera a los NN con desnutricion aguda complicada que ameriten hospitalizacion); en el mejoramiento del conocimiento y las prácticas de alimentación a Lactante y Niño Pequeño y Lactante en Emergencias (ALNP-E).
De manera transversal, SC y socios trabajaran con las comunidades para fortalecer el desarrollo comunitario de servicios públicos de Agua, Saneamiento y Higiene, fortalecer el empoderamiento de las comunidades para prevenir, responder y mitigar riesgos de VBG y PSEA, incluyendo el manejo clínico de VBG. En SA se apoyarán a los hogares con casos de desnutrición y presencia de PLW, derivados del componente de nutrición, con asistencia alimentaria como complemento a su recuperación y/o fortalecimiento. Se estima la entrega mensual de kits de alimentos básicos durante 5 meses en paralelo a las actividades a las actividades de nutrición

project_name: Providing Access to Life-Saving and Essential Primary Health Care Services for Conflict Affected and Vulnerable People in Eastern Equatoria, Jonglei and Warrap States.
project_objective:
Save the Children (SC) will support essential health care that prevents and reduces excess mortality and morbidity in crisis-affected populations with a focus on the core areas of emergency health response: communicable diseases, reproductive health, non-communicable diseases, injury, and first aid care, mental health, nutrition and community health activities, surveillance and control of epidemic prone diseases in vulnerable communities in Kapoeta North, South and East in Eastern Equatoria State; Akobo, Nyirol and Uror counties in Jonglei State, and Tonj East, North and Twic in Warrap State. Save the Children has presence in these locations that need to be strengthened to ensure life-saving healthcare services.
This will be achieved by supporting the State Ministry of Health (SMoH) and County Health Department (CHD) and in coordination with the health cluster through static and mobile health facilities and community outreach supporting the Boma Health Initiative. SC will coordinate the response with the RRC as well as with the health clusters and other actors in the areas to consider the need for initial assessments. 
Objectives:
1. Improve equitable access to life-saving essential quality health care services including maternal, child and adolescent health, sexual and reproductive health, treatment common illnesses, disability, MHPSS and GBV health services to crisis affected populations.
2. Reduce excess morbidity and mortality by timely detection and coordinated response to epidemic prone diseases
3. Enhance resilience and promote humanitarian-development linkages to strengthen health system recovery and coping mechanisms

SC will target beneficiaries with primary health care services through supporting existing static sites and by supporting mobile clinics in hard to reach locations including MHPSS and sexual and reproductive health care services. The project will target 338752	total beneficiaries desegregated into169, 219	male and 169,533 female and will also target persons with disability, host communities and IDPs. SC will support MOH in delivering quality and cost effective healthcare services, health system strengthening, capacity building of staff at national level, state level including the CHD as well as coordination activities.

project_name: Provision of Integrated lifesaving Nutrition interventions to conflict affected populations in Jonglei, Eastern Equatoria states and Abyei administrative area in South Sudan.
project_objective:
Through the proposed response, Save the Children International will provide integrated lifesaving nutrition service to the population in Akobo West, Budi , Bor, Kapoeta, Lopa Lafon, Magwi, Nyirol, Torit Counties, and Abyei administrative area. The aim of this is to reduce suffering, morbidity, and mortality related to malnutrition among vulnerable populations, SCI's proposed response will focus both treatment and preventative approaches, using community-based management of acute malnutrition (CMAM) and infant and young child feeding (IYCF) approaches. SCI Emergency nutrition programs will include. i) Community mobilization to increase access and coverage of CMAM services, ii) Treatment of children and PWLs with acute malnutrition through inpatient and Outpatient therapeutic programs. iii) blanket Supplementary feeding program. iv) Institutional feeding program (IFP), v) Maternal dietary supplementation, vi) Promotion of optimal IYCF through mother-to-mother support groups. vii) Improving Dietary Diversity through household kitchen gardening, viii) Strengthen nutrition information systems and operations research to ensure an evidence-based response, ix) Building capacity for frontline nutrition workers and institutions at all levels. SCI will work through communities to promote, protect and support recommended IYCF practices through one-on-one counselling and group message and counselling. Besides the CMAM and behaviour change interventions, SCI will implement cash transfer intervention in selected areas targeting families of severely malnourished children and SAM PLW to maximize the program's nutrition outcomes and reduce the relapse of acute malnutrition among under-five children and PLW. Through this response, SCI will support 104 static OTP/TSFPs and eight stabilization centres integrated with health facilities. The service will be delivered through static and outreach/mobile facilities for remote and hard-to-reach areas in the targeted project locations. SCI will work with MOH, UNICEF and WFP to secure timely provision of Nutrition supplies necessary for Nutrition Service Delivery. SCI will reach 73,683 under-five Children and 66,992 PLW. 
SCI will make deliberate efforts to enhance coordination and integration with the Health, WASH, FSL, Protection and Education clusters to address the causes of malnutrition through a multi-sectoral approach that aims to reduce vulnerabilities, prevent malnutrition and build resilience among the vulnerable people. Specific multi-sectoral activities are to increase access to safe water and sanitation, promote critical WASH messages, and integrate early childhood development strategies in nutrition treatment sites. Kitchen gardening, screening and treating of malaria, managing diarrhea, and mainstreaming child protection and gender-based violence risk mitigation will also be promoted at the nutrition sites.y. SCI will also support hygiene interventions to improve nutrition outcomes and reduce risk of hygiene-related morbidities
SCI will monitor the nutrition situation and the needs of the affected people through KAP survey, SMART surveys, monthly nutrition programme data collection and analysis, and joint field monitoring visits. Spot checks, supportive supervision and monitoring visits will monitor service delivery and engage with the community and other stakeholders to gauge evolving needs. Community nutrition volunteers will be supported to undertake household visits, conduct regular screening of malnourished children and women to ensure timely detection and treatment, and report on a monthly basis. Data collection tools and analysis will be strengthened to enhance monitoring of integrated services

project_name: Continuité de l'éducation et de la protection des enfants affectés dans la région de Tillabéry
project_objective:
Ce projet vise à garantir que les filles et les garçons des régions touchées par la crise de Tillabery (30 écoles dans les départements de Gotheye, Tera et Ayorou) continuent d'avoir accès à une éducation de qualité, protectrice et inclusive. Le projet contribue aux résultats suivants :
1. Accès et continuité : Les filles et les garçons âgés de 7 à 14 ans de la région ont accès à des espaces d'apprentissage sûrs, protecteurs et inclusifs.
2. Qualité et protection : Les enseignants et les communautés de la région de Tillabéri sont dotés des compétences pertinentes pour assurer un apprentissage de qualité et protecteur pour tous les enfants.
3. Coordination et plaidoyer : La réponse à l'éducation dans les situations d'urgence est bien coordonnée, cohérente et répond aux besoins holistiques des garçons et des filles, des femmes et des hommes touchés.
Le projet proposé vise à assurer un accès continu à des opportunités d'apprentissage de qualité pour 11 066 enfants d'âge scolaire (dont 5 643 filles, 465 enfants handicapés et 7746 enfants déplacés), y compris les enfants non scolarisés dans les communautés affectées par les fermetures d'écoles à Tera, Gotheye, et Ayorou.
Pour une meilleure prise en compte des besoins des enfants handicapés, SCI établiera une collaboration avec la Fédération Nigérienne des Personnes Handicapées (FNPH) au niveau national ainsi qu'avec la coordination régionale de  Tillabéri. Ces oragnisations  assureront l’appui technique nécessaire aux autres structures d'implémentation du projet  et garantiront la participation des enfants et jeunes handicapées dans l’action. Ils  contribueront également au plaidoyer nationale pour l’inclusion dans enfants handicapés dans l’action humanitaire.

project_name: Preventing and responding to child protection concerns of affected boys, girls and their families in Cox's Bazar
project_objective: Save the Children (SC) will operate an integrated child protection program in Cox’s Bazar and Its aim is to strengthen protective factors and reduce risk factors at every level of the socio-ecological framework. All of the activities will be adhered to protection principle like Do No Harm, non-discrimination, protect from abuse and violence and ensure participation and access to rights. In 2022, through the partnership with four local NGOs, SC will maintain critical interventions and services including case management, adolescents, and PSS programming, with a focus on the most vulnerable children including UASC, child headed households, child marriage and pregnancy, children with disabilities, domestic violence, and child labor. Based on evidence and input from affected communities, interventions will seek to address the ongoing risks posed by COVID-19 and target vulnerable boys and girls and their families. Child participation and eliciting the views of boys and girls across age, ability, and protection concerns will be an integral part of designing, implementing, and monitoring program components. As earlier, SC will work to mainstream an age, gender, and diversity (AGD) approach throughout the planning, implementation, and reporting processes for the interventions. For different age of children SC has different time slot in MPCAC, activities designed considering the age range of the children, materials procure and distribution with age sensitive specification and size. SC Volunteers are oriented to identify children with disability and prioritize them to include in child protection programming of SC. Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) will be included into the plan of SC. The respective staffs of SC will represent in the PERU of respective camps. They will be trained and will be involved in different responses and awareness raising initiatives for community people like disseminating awareness raising messages, making the community people being alert before cyclone, ensuring safety security from any other natural disasters. SC will also continue to build the capacity of parents and caregivers in parenting without violence, as well as strengthen the community-based child protection mechanism in both camps and host communities, to create an enabling and protective environment for children. It will include scaling up capacity building of community-based groups and volunteers through training and coaching on CP concerns, increasing their engagement in prevention and response activities. In both Rohingya and host community, the engagement of influential leaders, parents/caregivers, and children will be continued to enhance the participation, ownership, and sustainability of the program. Through maintaining and establishing services in both refugee camps and host communities, critical gaps in service delivery will be addressed and social cohesion will be strengthened, by targeting inequity in access to services, which is a driver of conflict. In 2022, SC will emphasis on supporting the host community, especially with a focus on strengthening the CP systems. This will include partnerships to strengthen technical capacity and work closely and collectively with duty bearers and service providers in camps and host communities. SC will give importance to the protect from and respond to sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA). SC will conduct periodical trainings, awareness sessions to the staffs, volunteers and other related stakeholder on PSEA policy. SC will also work to strengthen the coordination among different stakeholders to engage them in the child protection system to improve the accessibility of CP services. SC will continue coordination with CPSS, PWG in a regular basis and participate in different committees and working groups. Multiple accountability mechanisms will be applied in line with the AAP principles to ensure that feedback is actively collected, whilst also ensuring the safety and dignity of the beneficiaries.

project_name: Child protection assistance for the most vulnerable, at-risk children in Syria
project_objective:
SC’s child protection intervention is: 1) Children and adolescents have increased resilience and access to violence prevention and response services; 2) Caregivers, community members and other sector staff have strengthened capacity to protect children/adolescents, and support their healthy development and resilience.  SC’s intervention aims to improve the safety and wellbeing of girls and boys through individual case management for the most at-risk, including UASC, children with disabilities, child survivors, as well as children affected by armed conflict and armed groups (CAAFAG).  Case management is the entry point to support the needs of UASC, including Syrian, Iraqis and third county nationals, and FTR is initiated by caseworkers in coordination with relevant protection actors. For children without parental care and in line with interagency SOPs, SC trains foster families, supports existing informal care arrangements, and identifies alternative forms of care when foster families are not available, such as supported independent living or ICCs, as a last resort. Case management is also a vital service for CAAFAG and an area of focus for SC to ensure that released or excluded children access the holistic services and individual support for reintegration. CVA for child protection through case management is being piloted in community settings. Training, coaching and supervision for caseworkers is a key part of delivering quality case management, and the Steps to Protect rollout includes a focus on supervision, as well as on feedback and accountability.  

  

SC reaches children and adolescents through inclusive age and gender-sensitive group activities to foster psychosocial support, stress processing and resilience. In the absence of safe spaces in both camps and communities, a range of static, mobile and integrated child-friendly spaces (CFSs) offer group activities designed for creative expression, to develop protection knowledge and life skills, as well as strengthen an environment of trust. These spaces provide an entry point for community engagement as a hub for protection-related information and referrals, such as for children involved in child labor. Based on assessed needs and in consultation with children and caregivers, SC + partners will deliver structured PSS curricula. A targeted effort will be made to engage children with disabilities. 

  

For the trusted and responsible adults in children’s lives–caregivers, teachers, community members and service providers, SC builds their knowledge and skills to communicate with children, identify risks facing and take action to increase children’s safety. SC will continue its rollout of the Parenting without Violence (PwV) Common Approach, with an focus on caregiver self-care and stress management alongside positive parenting practices. SC will offer sessions for mothers of young children and incorporate a focus on early childhood nutrition (delivered in tandem with nutrition colleagues) as well as outreach to caregivers of children with disabilities. PwV encourages promotion of positive parenting messages and gender equality through community structures, such as Child Protection Committees and Parent/Teacher Associations (PTAs). These structures have been supported previously and will be sustained in the proposed period. Community members and other sector staff will be targeted with capacity building on safe identification and referral, basic MHPSS including PFA, GBV and PSEA, as well as CPMS. Efforts will be made to build capacity of SC staff and partners to include children and caregivers with disabilities.  Community members, including children, will identify the risks and develop awareness raising initiatives.  To mitigate the risk of GBV, SC will conduct targeted GBV awareness sessions with adolescents and caregivers using an adapted GBV prevention toolkit to improve knowledge on root causes and consequences of GBV and accessing available GBV response services.

project_name: Facilitating the creation of a favorable protection environment in Darfur
project_objective:
This project aims to facilitate the creation of a favorable protection environment in Darfur (with particular focus on North and West Darfur) to bring positive impacts on the lives of at least 45,000 crisis-affected population, including internally displaced persons (IDPs) and returnees. The proposed outputs and activities will contribute to all 3 Protection Cluster objectives of the 2022 Humanitarian Response Plan as well as Objective 1 and 2 of Gender-based violence (GBV) Cluster.

In North Darfur, the project will target Kabkabiya locality (Sortony and Kabkabiya town), Dar Es Salam locality (Shangil Tobaya and Abu Zereiga), El Fasher locality (Korma and Kusa), and Kutum locality (Hashaba). In West Darfur, IOM will target Kerenik locality (Abu Naema, Fedus, and Mazrub) and Geneina locality (Anjimi, Gokar and Noro). 

In relation to Protection Objective 1 and GBV Objective 1, IOM will aim to improve access of vulnerable crisis-affected people, especially that of girls and women, to protection services including GBV response services. IOM will strive for improving their access to life-saving services, such as primary healthcare and non-food items (NFI) in coordination with IOM’s Health and NFI teams. IOM will also work towards strengthening the capacity of GBV service providers through trainings and deployment of social workers and psychologists. These psychologists will be also available for providing psychosocial support (PSS) to other crisis-affected population in the target areas.

To contribute to Protection Objective 2, IOM will engage in capacity building of informal mediators and dispute resolvers so as to improve the crisis-affected people’s access to community-based dispute resolution mechanisms. IOM will work with the existing committees in the communities, including, but not limited to, Native Administrations, Peaceful Co-existence Committees, Agricultural Protection Committees as well as community leaders and representatives from other community-based organizations including women’s and youth groups, and those belonging to farmers and herders. IOM staff will also contribute to “protection by presence” through monitoring the protection situations in concerned locations and collect relevant information on protection needs, gaps and trends for advocacy, programmatic and ad hoc assistance purposes.

Through this project, IOM will coordinate with its other projects under key programme areas in the target States, such as Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) and emergency response as well as with WASH and health activities, to ensure effective synergies between programme activities. In addition, IOM will work in close coordination with international and national partners to ensure project’s efficiency and effectiveness. Besides, IOM with its partners and DTM teams operating in field locations will enhance protection monitoring and help in verifying the most vulnerable households to be assisted on a priority basis.

Concerning Protection Objective 3, IOM will support the local government to strengthen their capacity and resources to improve birth registration of IDPs and service provision to people with disabilities through the provision of office equipment, capacity building trainings, and facilitating regular visits of government staff to remote areas to provide the services for the concerned population. For the activity related to civil documentation, IOM will closely coordinate with the Civil Registry and UNHCR in the target states to maximize complementarity and to avoid duplication. 

In relation to the GBV Objective 2, IOM will support the establishment and/or reactivation of women’s groups and Women Centres in the target areas to ensure safe platforms are available for women and girls’ engagement and their access to the information on protection services including GBV response services. Community awareness raising sessions, life skills/recreational activities will be organized as part of Women Centres activities.

project_name: Provision of Life-Saving Emergency Shelter and Non-Food Items Assistance in Sudan
project_objective:
This project will ensure that the most vulnerable populations affected by conflict or natural disasters with specific needs have timely access to Emergency Shelter (ES) and Non-Food Items (NFI) assistance. This project contributes to the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) Strategic Objective 1: Provide timely multi-sectoral life-saving assistance to crisis affected people to reduce mortality and morbidity; and Strategic Objective 2: Contribute to building resilience to recurrent shocks and improving vulnerable people’s access to basic services.
IOM proposes to purchase, preposition, and distribute 20,000 NFI kits and 20,000 Emergency shelters as a preparedness measure for addressing the needs of newly displaced and vulnerable people with special needs from the protracted displaced populations in 14 different states. Emergency Shelter and Non-Food Items assessment missions will utilize Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) data to select the most vulnerable households to be assisted ES/NFI kits. IOM will also transport the emergency shelters and non-food items to the distribution locations. Kits will be distributed to the most vulnerable populations in selected states through close coordination with ES/NFI sector lead and partners as well as government bodies to ensure consistency in provision of assistance and to mitigate assistance duplication. As a final stage IOM will undertake post distribution monitoring missions to monitor usage of the distributed items after 2 to 4 weeks of the distributions.

project_name: Renforcement de la résilience et de la cohésion sociale des personnes déplacées et des communautés d’accueil affectées par les crises dans les zones de Bagasola, Daboua et Liwa dans la province du lac Tchad
project_objective:
La province du Lac au Tchad fait face à une série de crises sanitaires, sécuritaires, alimentaires et nutritionnelles. Ainsi, les incursions de groupes armés non étatiques dans la zone ont provoqué des mouvements constants de population, une réduction de l'accès humanitaire et un rétrécissement de l'espace civique, avec pour corollaire l'exacerbation de la vulnérabilité des populations qui y vivent. Selon la matrice de suivi des déplacements de l'OIM de juillet 2021, 401 511 personnes déplacées à l'intérieur de leur propre pays (IDP) ont été enregistrées suite à la crise sécuritaire dans la région et vivent dans 228 sites de déplacement et villages d'accueil. Au cours de la même période, 47 % des personnes déplacées n'ont pas reçu d'aide alimentaire, ce qui a entraîné de nouveaux déplacements à la recherche d'aide. Entre juin et août 2021, le nombre de personnes au stade de la crise de famine (phases 3 à 5) a été estimé à 157 842, soit environ 24% de la population de la province de Lac. Cette situation alimentaire et nutritionnelle risque de se détériorer davantage cette année en raison de l'imprévisibilité des précipitations et de la volatilité du contexte sécuritaire
Selon les analyses de l'AEM de mars 2021, les départements de Fouli et de Kaya font partie des départements tchadiens analysés qui auront des déficits de survie. La province du Lac reste exposée au risque de propagation d'épidémies (choléra, Covid-19) en raison de sa position géographique. Les taux d'accès à l'eau potable et aux installations sanitaires sont encore faibles dans la zone d'intervention, respectivement 68% et 17% (selon la matrice de suivi de la mise en œuvre 2021 d'Oxfam). La pratique de la défécation en plein air reste courante, ce qui représente un risque par rapport aux maladies transmises par voie fécale-orale.
D'après les résultats de l'enquête de base (21 juin 2021) dans la région de Lac, 77% des membres de la communauté ne disposent pas de latrines et défèquent en plein air, ce qui expliquerait les 72% d'enfants et 69% d'adultes qui ont souffert de diarrhée dans les deux semaines précédant les enquêtes.
En juin 2021, la situation de protection a été marquée par une série de conflits communautaires dans plusieurs régions de la province du Lac. Suite à ces conflits intra-communautaires et intercommunautaires, 40 cas d'agressions physiques, 12 homicides/meurtres et 11 cas de pillage et de destruction de biens ont été rapportés. Ces incidents liés aux conflits communautaires dans les sous-préfectures de Bol, Bagasola et Liwa représentent 42% des 151 cas de violations des droits de l'homme enregistrés pendant la période sous revue.
Le projet ciblera 53 200 personnes - 31 920 déplacés internes - 21 280 hôtes - 11 278 femmes, 10 002 hommes, 16 918 filles et 15 002 garçons - dans toutes les zones d'intervention (Bagasola, Daboua et Liwa dans la province du Lac), couvrant ainsi 13% de la population affectée par la crise pendant cette période (401 511 personnes). En même temps, elles recevront différentes formes d'appui (urgence, développement et paix) pour faire face à leur vulnérabilité de manière cohérente.
Les actions de cash transfert permettront d’atteindre un total de 18 608 personnes dont 9.862 personnes et 8.746 personnes. Un total de 2648 personnes en phase 3 du Cadre Harmonisé dont 1.403 femmes et 1245 hommes de Kaya et Fouli bénéficieront de l’assistance par le cash transfert inconditionnel. Parmi les déplacés internes et populations retournés se trouvant les départements de Kaya et Fouli, un total de 15.960 personnes dont 8459 femmes et 7501 hommes pendant la période de soudure. Deux formations sur la redevabilité seront organisées au profit des différentes parties prenantes impliquées dans la mise du projet. Ceci pour les équiper à mieux prendre en compte les questions de redevabilité dans l’intervention à mettre en place.

project_name: ​PROVISION OF PROTECTION AND HUMANITARIAN ASSISTANCE SERVICES TO MIGRANTS IN VULNERABLE SITUATIONS
project_objective: The project’s aim is to provide a range of protection services to migrants in need, strengthen links between targeted community groups and partners, improve the quality of services available, and enhance knowledge on migrant population groups in Lebanon. Services will target both male and female migrants, with a higher caseload of the latter group due to their increased number in country. Beneficiaries will typically be working age, between 18 and 40 years old. The services that IOM will deliver, either directly or through partners, include legal assistance, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), safe and temporary shelters for vulnerable migrants, provision of non-food items, multipurpose cash assistance (MPCA), and voluntary humanitarian return. These services will be made accessible to migrants by scaling up IOM’s pre-existing case management services, supporting enhanced capacity of, and referral with partners, strengthening culturally appropriate outreach to large migrant groups, including translation and interpretation,, and expanding community-level networks to strengthen targeted communities’ awareness of and access to IOM and partner services, as well as wider issues of concern. Additionally, IOM will provide training to partner organizations in case management, identification of vulnerable migrants and victims of trafficking, and Psychological First Aid, as well as other important thematic areas such as migrants with diverse SOGIESC and rights of migrants with regards to detention. Finally, enhancing knowledge of migrant populations will involve nationwide data-collection efforts via key informant interviews. The project will be implemented by the IOM in partnership with civil society organizations (CSO) and community-based initiatives. Provision of or onward referral to multisector assistance such as food or health support will be mainstreamed across the project.

project_name: Assistance Alimentaire d'urgence aux personnes vulnérables_Mali
project_objective:
Couvrir les besoins immédiats des populations vulnérables à l'Insécurité alimentaire dans toutes les regions affectés du Mali par les conflits, secheresse, inondations. Ce projet sera mis en oeuvre au niveau à travers les partenaires coopérants, qui seront supervisés par les équipes sous bureaux du PAM sur terrain afin de delivrer une assistance de qualité et à temps aux bonnes personnes. Les modalités d'assistance seront selectionnées sur base de i) l'analyse de contexte, ii) la faisabilité opérationnelle, iii) analyse cout-efficacité et iv) analyse cout efficience afin de choisir les modalités/mechanismes de transferts les plus adaptés: Cash, Mobile money, Voucher, Vivres. 
le ciblage des zones prioritaires sera guidé par le CH en mettant l'accent sur les cercles en Phase 3 et les communes seront identifiées sur base du Système Expert du SAP. le PAM s'appuiera sur le guide méthodologique de ciblage afin d'identifier les villages les affectés et donner le pouvoir decisionnel aux communautés de selectionner les ménages les plus vulnérables. 
Plusieurs catégories de bénéficiaires sont concernées par cette reponse d'urgence: personnes résidentes vulnérables, personnes deplacées/réfugiés, personnes vulnérables en communautés hôtes, personnes affectées par les inondations. 
Cette intervention veillera à l'application des domaines transversaux notamment la politique du PAM en matière de genre, rédévabilité et Protection. 
Un plan de suivi-évaluation sera préparé pour mesurer les outputs/Outcomes tout au long du processus afin de mieux guider dans la prise de décision et améliorer l'assistance aux populations affectées. 
En termes de partenariat, le PAM continuera à renforcer les systèmes gouvernementaux dans la préparation et reponses aux urgences conformément au dispostif national de Sécurité Alimentaire à travers notamment le Comissariat à la Sécurité Alimentaire, le Développement Social et la Proection Civile. 
L'utilisation des nouvelles technologies sera un point central afin de renforcer la redévabilité envers les bailleurs et les bénéficiaires afin d'éviter toute duplication entre bénéficiaires et fournir une assistance efficace et éfficiente.

project_name: Strengthening protection environment through Improving access to General Protection services and building capacity of vulnerable Rohingya refugees and Host communities in Cox’s Bazar
project_objective:
DRC will continue to provide general services for the prevention and response of a range of protection risks observed in the camps. Direct case management services will be provided by strengthening synergies and integration with other protection areas (child protection and GBV) and other non-protection sectors (wherever possible and appropriate). These include among other individual protection assistance (IPA), referrals to specialised services, PFA. Capitalizing on past accomplishments, DRC will continue to invest in strengthening engagement with community-based protection mechanisms. This will include further capacitating existing community groups to identify, prevent and respond to protection risks, including through community-led awareness and sensitization, case management follow-up and referrals, protection monitoring and community-led peacebuilding and conflict resolution initiatives. 
DRC will ensure its programmatic response is based on evidence that is context-specific and on a disaggregated analysis of age, gender and diversity (AGD). Accordingly, DRC will strengthen its protection monitoring activities to inform protection monitoring and advocacy work. This will include further capacitating staff and volunteers to collect data on a range of risks, including CP risks currently not monitored, and improve the sampling methodology to ensure data is systematically collected on specific vulnerabilities such as PwDs, single-headed households, sexual minorities.  To strengthen its commitment to AAP and ensure a right based and AGD approach is implemented across its program cycle DRC will also seek to increase representation of diverse groups in its community structures to increase effective participation of more marginalised groups such as PwDs, women and adolescent girls in decision-making processes around issues that concern them. In addition, the pool of community volunteers will be diversified to expand participation of women volunteers. DRC caseworkers will continue to coordinate interventions with existing complaints and feedback mechanisms to avoid overlaps and duplication of assistance. This includes communicating and coordinating with the CFRM and CFP for every case management client to ensure he/she has not already been supported with assistance as well as referring all relevant non-protection cases to the CFRM/CFP. 
DRC has a zero-tolerance policy to sexual abuse and exploitation. DRC is an active member of the PSEA Network and has a PSEA policy and an internal mechanism to report SEA concerns. DRC is arranging PSEA trainings to all of its staff and volunteers in the next weeks and regularly shares data on SEA with the Network. DRC is also an active member of the PWG and associated sub-sectors. Going forward, DRC intends to ensure more regular sharing of protection monitoring data with the PWG and sub-sectors in the form of summarised overviews of risks observed in the camps, continuing to comply to routine reporting requirements by the sector and ad hoc requests on information that may arise. DRC will also continue delivering protection mainstreaming training to non-protection actors according to the resources and guidance provided by the sector with the goal of facilitating meaningful access to assistance provided by the DRC and other actors, ensuring that humanitarian assistance and protection activities do not harm, that actors respond appropriately to instances of violence and coercion, and that refugees are assisted.
Finally, DRC will continue to coordinate with RRRC and CiCs. Coordination aims to ensure timely access, to avoid resource gaps and duplications.  Advocacy briefings are conducted regularly with the CiCs to raise awareness on the importance of protection interventions and report on DRC’s work in the camps. DRC will continue to support in developing government officials' capacities in the area of protection and its importance during an emergency.

project_name: Humanitarian coordination and provision of CCCM-integrated responses to displacement-affected populations in Juba and Bor former PoC sites (semi-static) in hard-to-reach areas (mobile)
project_objective:
According to the South Sudan CCCM Cluster HNO 2022, 1.64 million people are currently IDPs in need of CCCM assistance across South Sudan. After a sudden shock, IDPs often gather in informal displacement sites in extremely precarious conditions, most of the time without access to basic services and information, and with limited decision-making power on issues that affect their daily lives and their future. These gathering places are often characterized by an increased exposure to security risks and protection needs, particularly for the most vulnerable groups. Poor living conditions; lack of financial resources and limited access to basic services can lead to outbreaks of disease, increased prevalence of GBV or domestic violence, and tensions between population groups within the informal camps. Likewise, overcrowding could led to challenges in maintaining safe levels of hygiene and sanitation. Continued political uncertainty, coupled with the increased risks of climate change has also largely resulted in the inability of the international community to return these IDP’s to more suitable locations and an unwillingness from the camps inhabitants to leave. Regarding Bor and Juba former PoC camps, as of February 2022, 2,745 IDPs resided in Bor IDPs Camp, 7,299 in Juba IDPs Camp 1 and 24,255 in Juba IDPs Camp 3. Since the transition from former PoCs sites under UNMISS management to conventional IDPs site under the South Sudanese government responsibility in November 2020, the 2,745 residents of Bor IDPs camp have continued benefitting from essential services provision. The RRC offices of Jonglei at State and County levels have taken up the camp administration responsibility after the transition and are well involved, present and committed in the camp activities. However, the state and county authorities are facing limited resources to fully take over the camp administration responsibility. ACTED will aim at reinforcing the local authorities’ resources and abilities in Jonglei, while continuing to build capacity of camp leadership representatives, leading to the full handover of the Camp management responsibilities to the Community Members Committees and Camp administration role to RRC office in Jonglei by the last quarter of 2022. On the other hand, the 31,554 residents of Juba IDPs Camp 1 and 3 have faced a drastic decrease of essential service provision since the transition from former PoC sites under UNMISS management to conventional IDPs camps under the leadership of the South Sudan Government. Since the transition and re-designation of roles over to the government of South Sudan the RRC office has not yet taken over the responsibility of the camps.
ACTED is aiming to continue to work to design a road map for RRC’s take over and to work closely with Juba IDP camps service providers. ACTED would continue to engage in discussions with key actors and communities impacted to take active role in several fora including the Durable Solutions Working Group. During the semi-static phase, ACTED is planning to provide in-kind support to local authorities, including RRC, that are facing a lack of resources to take over the camp administration role, while enhancing the camp leadership skills. Therefore, ACTED will continue implementing CCCM interventions in line with the following cluster objectives: CO1: Improve living condition of IDPs by facilitating safe, equitable and dignified access to cross-sectoral humanitarian services, including CCCM CO2: Enhance the protective environment, respond to vulnerable population with priority on addressing protection gaps and strengthen the predictability and effectiveness of multi sectorial interventions at site level CO3: Support vulnerable IDPs to recover from the crisis by strengthening community self-management, build resilience to promote solutions for displaced people in sites.

project_name: Improving short-term and long-term food security and livelihoods access in Jonglei, WBeG, Lakes, Upper Nile, through provision of unconditional food assistance, investment in food production assets, and utilization and strengthening of local capacities.
project_objective:
In line with the FSL cluster strategy for 2022, ACTED will contribute towards improving food security of over 712,536 beneficiaries through provision of in-kind and cash food assistance, enhancing emergency food production though distribution of livelihood kits and reducing dependency on food and agricultural inputs through resilience building activities such as training and market support functionality. Millions of South Sudanese remain displaced across the country following years of violent conflict that resulted in one of the most devastating humanitarian crises in recent history. Based on the latest IPC analysis and projections until July 2021, 60% of the population living in South Sudan is critically food insecure with 7.2 million people estimated to face high levels of acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above). Specifically, 4.668 million people are facing crisis (IPC Phase 3), 2.413 million people are facing emergency (IPC Phase 4) and 108,000 people are facing catastrophic (IPC Phase 5) food insecurity  As such, the needs across South Sudan have severely increased, driven by flooding, insecurity, population displacements, declined crop production, diseases and pests, the economic crisis, the effects of COVID-19, limited access to basic services, and the cumulative effects of prolonged years of asset depletion and loss of livelihoods.  The project activity will be in line with the cluster Objectives “CO1: Provide food assistance to prevent famine and improve food consumption, dietary diversity and coping strategies for vulnerable populations (in IPC 5, 4 & some 3)

CO2: Enhance emergency food production through complementary vegetable and crop seeds and fishing and livestock support (in IPC 3, 4 & 5)

CO3: Reduce dependency on food and agricultural inputs to support and strengthen households’ ability to absorb shocks (implemented across all 78 counties)
