-Installation of solar light panels for site and IDPs units in Zoghara and A’rima sub-districts reaching to 850 IDP HHs (4250 Individuals) disaggregated by gender (842 men, 1,071 women, 1309 girls and 1029 boys)
-Build the capacity of the IDPs and host HHs  through provision of shelter mentoring sessions for HHs with skilled workers (piloting the approach) for 50 HHs disaggregated by gender (47 men, 51 women, 82 girls and 70 boys) in Idleb, A’zaz and Albab sub-districts. 
The project will be aligned with the cluster guidelines. Shafak intends to increase its input to the cluster and ensure new experiences like solar panel installation and cash for shelters are shared. The project has been partially secured in funding for 2022 while the remaining amount will be advocated for to be funded by other donors for 2023.

As for 2023, according to Shafak's strategy and fund availability, it is expected to implement similar activities reaching approx. 130,000 individuals. During Activities implementation, Shafak will maintain good coordination with the SNFI cluster through monthly submission of 4ws, contribution to the winter planning and floods response actions.

project_name: Respond and mitigate the protection risks of the most vulnerable women, men, girls and boys in NWS through provision if integrated protection services.
project_objective:
In 2022, Shafak Organization proposes to mitigate and respond to the protection risks faced by the conflict-affected people in Jabal Samaan, Jarablus, Al-Bab and Azaz districts in Aleppo governorate, as well as in Harim, Jisr-Ash-Shugur, Ariha and Idleb districts in Idleb governorate through a community centers and protection mobile teams.

The purpose of this project is to empower local communities and conflict-affected individuals in North West Syria, and support their role in building society and in determining their future by provision of protection services and emergency protection services to 107,570 IDPs and host community members, through five community centers, two protection tents and 25 mobile outreach teams. The provided protection services will comprise both mitigation and response services as well as specialized and non-specialized protection services.

The proposed project will offer gender and age appropriate general protection service including, structured PSS, recreational and MHPSS activities, case management involving life-saving assistance to vulnerable people in ensuring their access to existing services, referral to specialized and non-specialized services, awareness raising on protection related topics, life skills and vocational training to enhance the community resilience and livelihoods opportunities, legal assistance and legal awareness raising session of HLP and CSD through qualified and well-trained legal teams, protection monitoring, as well as supporting community committees. 

Shafak will maintain gender-balanced team in all its projects in order to facilitate the access of all gender groups to the services in line with the humanitarian principles. Moreover, training on HLP and CSD will be delivered to partners’ legal staff and community actors in Syria and Turkey by specialized legal staff in accordance with the protection cluster and HLP TWG guidance and SOPs.

These services will be offered to vulnerable IDPs and host community members with particular emphasis on quality services to the following groups:
• Women headed households
• Children headed households
• UASC, CAAFAG and Child labor
• PWDs
• Elderly women and men
• Family has children at risk of child labor
• UASC and orphans who are being cared for by another family.
• New IDPs who fled their home and have no financial means

In case of emergencies, the project activities will be shifted to respond to the emergency protection needs of new displaced people delivering the protection emergency package like: PFA, referrals and case fund support to respond to the urgent needs of IDPs.

Shafak will establish community committees from the same communities and train them on protection topics such as; CPMS, Safe identification and referral and communication skills to enable them identify and refer people in need to the case management team. 

The activities will emphasize equity and non-discrimination, reinforcing the basic social and human rights of participants while taking into consideration the cultural, historical and social specificities of targeted populations. All static centers will be rehabilitated and well equipped to be disabled-friendly spaces.

COVID-19 precautionary measures will be taken in line with WHO, Global Protection Cluster and the Protection Cluster’s Guidance, including strict enforcement of physical distancing, minimizing of participants per activity to maximum eight people and maintaining the social distancing between BNFs and staff, the use of personal protective equipment (PPE) by staff/beneficiaries.

As for 2023, according to Shafak's strategy and fund availability, it is expected to implement the same activities with the same size and budget.

project_name: Building Resilience, Enhance livelihoods and Reduce food insecurity and inability to meet basic immediate needs among conflict-affected households (HHs) living in NWS
project_objective:
The projects intends to provide a multi-faceted response in an integrated and coherent way. Shafak's proposal is designed to supporting farmers and livestock herders needs of the vulnerable IDPs, returnees and HCs. Over 2022, the project comprises the following key intervention areas:

Activity1: 5600 Targeted winter crops farmers (wheat and barley) are able to resume and restore agricultural activities, to  increase household income and improve consumption through provision of agriculture start-up kit that contribute to the cost of  : i)  agricultural inputs, including improved access to water; pest control, harvesting and V) extension services, VI) purchasing wheat.

Activity2: 2000 Targeted olive trees are able to resume and restore agricultural activities, to  increase household income and improve consumption through provision of agriculture start-up kit that contribute to the cost of  : i)  agricultural inputs, including improved access to water; pest control, harvesting and V) extension services.

Activity3: 1000 Targeted forage crops farmers are able to resume and restore agricultural activities, to  increase household income and improve consumption through provision of agriculture start-up kit that contribute to the cost of  : i)  agricultural inputs, including improved access to water; pest control, harvesting and V) extension services.

Activity 4: 6500 Targeted households are able to increase household income and maintain livestock activities through: i) provision of livestock inputs (500 kg of fodder per beneficiary 1500 beneficiaries) ; ii) associated training, iii) vaccination campaigns per health care calendar (4 campaigns, 200,000 head per campaign owned by 4,000 households).

Activity 5: 4000 Targeted households stabilize, maintain or increase their income through Cash-for-Work activities, which build and strengthen community related value chain infrastructure , disaster risk reduction, mechanical pest and vole control and olive trees harvesting, purification of wheat fields, and afforestation.

Activity 6: Rehabilitation of related value chain infrastructure, irrigation channels, Markets,  Mills, bakeries, storage, fodder mixers, feeder roads and silos.

Activity 7: Graduation Business Grants: 500 Small-Micro Enterprises through provision of business skills training and financial or in-kind support with value ranging from 500 to 1000 USD. Selected beneficiaries will have access to financial services, in addition to improving job skills and linkages to the job market. The identified participants will receive Business Development Skills training (BDS)including operations and financial management(food processing, production, agriculture and livestock enterprises.

Activity 8: 5000 HHs to be supported with regular food basket over 8 rounds.

Activity 9 : 15000 HHs to be supported with Cash/voucher based on populations preference and market dynamics

Activity 10 : 15000 RTEs to be distributed as response to emergencies and shocks

Activity 11: 2000 MT of flour to be distributed to bakeries to subsidize bread prices.

As for 2023, according to Shafak's strategy and fund availability, it is expected to implement the same activities with the same size and budget.
It is worth mentioning that  about 50% of 2022 budget is secured up to date of this submission.

project_name: Support self-reliance of affected households ,protecting the productive assets and restoring or creating income generating opportunities.
project_objective:
This program aims at supporting the resilience of the conflict affected people in northwest Syria, particularly in Idleb and Aleppo governorate. Shafak's proposed action is designed to contribute to supporting the transition to the early recovery phase, as it supports the targeted communities with long-term assistance activities, programs that focus on building/restoring the communities' infrastructure, local economic empowerment, and initiatives that ensure engagement and participation of the community in recovering from the protracted crisis. Over 2022, this program will achieve its objectives through the following:

a)Temporary Employment: 5000 vulnerable HHs within the targeted communities are supported through temporary income generation opportunities through Cash for Work activities.
Cash-for-Work activities will enable the provision of 5000 temporary labor opportunities focusing on the rehabilitation of community-identified projects related directly or indirectly to agriculture and community infrastructure, also Cash-for-Work activities will help the beneficiaries to meet their essential needs, be involved in the labor market and break the cycle on unemployment and retrieve self-confidence of the affected populations. 

b) Establishing or expanding Small-Micro Enterprises through provision of business skills training and financial or in-kind support with value 750 USD to 1000 selected beneficiaries and access to financial services. in addition improving job skills and linkages to the job market. The identified participants will receive Business Development Skills training (BDS) including operations and financial management. The trained participants will be requested to submit their business plans which will be reviewed by a committee from Shafak. The grant will be delivered in two tranches. The identified beneficiaries will receive facilitation for the creation of savings and loan groups using the Village Savings and Loan Association (VSLA) methodology.

c) Financial Services:  Facilitating the Establishment of 10 Village Savings Loaning Associations (VSLAs) to improve access to financial services. An estimated 10 Savings and Loan Groups, each consisting of approximately 10-15 members, will be facilitated to establish. The groups will constitute a common fund for members to save and borrow to finance a business or pay for life expenses. Groups will follow a standard savings and loan groups methodology; however, this will be adapted to the Syria context. Participants will elect their own group leaders, set their own rules. Individuals opt to join a group and identify their own members. 

d) Providing vocational and skills training to 400 youth, men and women applicants and then support successful trainees (Expecting 300 trainees) with small-scale cash grants to enable them restart/initiate their small enterprises, each grant total will be 750 USD on average (between 600-900 USD) per beneficiary.

e) 400 HHs, Graduation Approach: Support self reliance of vulnerable households from those supported with Cash for food. The The Graduation approach will include also ,market facing skills , transfer of productive asset, financial services through VSLA, mentoring and Coaching, and  Referral mechanism.

f) Rehabilitating the local economic, public and social infrastructure (20 Projects) through linking with the Cash-for-Work activity or through service providers. Each project cost will be about 15000 USD.

g) Supporting local community and social cohesion initiatives: Through forming community engagement team representing the different segments in the community. develop community action plans and identify the prioritized initiatives to be supported through the appropriate modality. 

As for 2023, according to Shafak's strategy and fund availability, it is expected to implement the same activities with the same size and budget.

project_name: Provision of safe and equitable access to formal and non-formal education services for conflict-affected girls and boys in NW Syria.
project_objective:
As a strategy for 2022, Shafak, in line with education cluster’s objectives and in coordination with involved authorities and stakeholders, intends to focus on achieving two main goals for a total of 43,712 5-17 yr. school children (20,545 boys; 23,167 girls, including 1088 CWDs) and 1,536 education personnel (736 males, 800 males):
1) Scaling up access to formal and non-formal education for Syrian crisis-affected children: Access strategies will include small-scale rehabilitation of damaged schools and establishment of other safe temporary/alternative learning spaces through a gender-sensitive and disability-friendly approach. 
a)- Formal education activities in 56 schools targeting approximately 34,496 students (16,213 b; 18,283 girls; 5-17 yr. old) through classroom learning modality (with plan B to resort to distance learning modality, based on developments of COVID 19). This intervention will minimize the risk of students dropping out, where monthly incentives to teachers will be provided, as they don’t have any alternative fund in addition to provision of education materials for students and teachers and providing schools with necessary operational costs (including heating for winter and school safety equipment). As education is one of the very basic children’s rights Shafak is planning to provide access to education for children with disabilities by providing transportation services and improve school environment by provide targeted assistance within the schools in order to encourage these children to continue their education and integrate them with their peers.
b)- Non-formal education opportunities and pathways back to inclusive education at age appropriate levels are increasingly required to address the complex learning needs of children through classroom learning modality (with plan B to resort to distance learning modality, based on developments of COVID 19), making use of 4 BTL campaigns conducted for that end. Thus, non-formal education will target school girls and boys (aged 8-12 and gender disaggregated) to fill in existing needs, where 24 Non-Formal education centers will be supported targeting approximately a total of 9,216 children (4332 b; 4884 g; 5-17 yr. old) to provide SLP and catchup for 2416 children (1136 b, 1280 g) in addition to remedial classes for 6800 (3196 b, 3604 g) along with PSS sessions; the PSS activities will be selected from I-Deal curriculum; the curriculum used for non-formal Activities will be curriculum B that combines two academic years in one, SIG for remedial and Self Learning Material books.
2) Enhancing the quality of formal and non-formal education within a protective environment. Teachers will be equipped with the skills in non-formal education modalities, child-centered pedagogy, and positive classroom management to cope with overcrowded classrooms, address and accommodate host community, displaced and returnee children within their classes, in addition to regular monthly conducted PTA sessions.
Stakeholders in the project implementation site, including children, adolescents and older persons, including PwDs and their opinions are taken into account while developing the project design, implementation of activities so that they have better access to humanitarian services and information in accordance to their specific situation.
The intervention will make sure that children engaging in child labor or recruited for military purposes, or living with older or disabled caregivers or adolescent girls at risk of early or forced marriage are given special attention and have their own space to participate in the project activities and are properly referred as per child protection sub-cluster guidelines.
As for 2023, according to Shafak's strategy and fund availability, it is expected to implement the same activities with the same size and budget.

project_name: Protection of crisis affected vulnerable families in NW Syria through the provision of Community-based and Specialized Child Protection services, as well as reducing the threat of Explosive Remnants of War (ERW)  by the provision of Risk Education activities.
project_objective:
Child Protection:
During 2022, Shafak organization will respond to the increased child protection concerns of the crisis affected children including CWDs through center-based activities in five Child-Friendly Spaces and 19 community outreach teams deployed in Harim, Jisr-Ash-Shugur, Ariha, and Idleb districts in Idleb, and Azaz, Al-Bab and Jarablus districts in Aleppo. Total number of BNFs targeted 45000(4000M, 6500W, 17250B, and 17250G).
Shafak will provide CP case management and referral in the targeted locations targeting children with CP concerns. CM services will be complemented with the provision of emergency case funds and CVA to respond to the immediate and urgent needs of children including CWDs.  Shafak will submit the CM tracker to CPSC on regular basis. The following CP vulnerability criteria and concerns will be considered for CM and IPA support: 
1-	UASC 
2-	Child labor including its worst forms
3-	CAAFAG
4-	Early Marriage 
5-	Child headed household 
6-	Domestic violence 
7-	Severe Psychological distresses

Moreover, age and gender-appropriate MHPSS and structured and non-structured PSS activities for children and adolescents will be organized in and out of the CFSs. Different curricula will be used such as; IRC PSS manual, I DEAL, and Child Resilience.
Positive parenting skills sessions will be provided to caregivers to reduce the physical and humiliating punishment of children in the home, and improve the capacity of parents and caregivers to practice positive parenting.

In addition, Shafak will target the communities with awareness-raising activities on PSEA, child rights, and CP issues. Thus, messages will be tailored to gender and age needs in target locations to ensure gender sensitivity and also that messaging is relevant to children at special age levels.

Finally, Shafak will strengthen the capacity of local communities about child concerns by establishing 20 CPNs covering all age and gender groups in the targeted communities to prevent and respond to CP needs at the community level. And secondly, train key persons in those communities and the workers in care centers, schools, hospitals who are in direct contact with children about the CPMS, PFA, and Safe Identification and referral. Shafak will adapt the CFSs and the static facilities to be accessible and friendly for CWDs through establishing ramps and toilets for CWDs.

As for 2023, according to Shafak's strategy and fund availability, it is expected to implement the same activities with the same size and budget.

Mine Action:

Shafak will deliver a comprehensive Risk Education. This project will be a continuation of Shafak's work in the Explosive Remnants of War Risk Education ERW - RE program in Idleb and Aleppo. 
During 2022, and under the ERW-RE part of the project, 4 RE teams who have already been trained by Shafak, will target 5200 individuals (400M, 1000W, 1900B, and 1900G) including IDPs and host communities in Idleb and Aleppo providing school-age children with RE activities, and materials to inform them about the dangers of ERW. Shafak will also provide RE material to adults, putting up posters about the ERW risks in the public streets and communities to increase awareness of ERW threats. 
Moreover, the RE (ToT) Trainers will provide RE training to Community Focal Points (CFPs) in affected communities, and RE teams and other workers from NGOs across all humanitarian sectors, to improve the relevance, integration, and reach of RE messaging across NW Syria. 

COVID-19 precautionary measures will be taken in line with WHO, Global Protection Cluster, and the Protection Cluster’s Guidance, including strict enforcement of physical distancing, minimizing of participants per activity, and maintaining the social distancing between BNFs and staff, and the use of PPE.

Shafak plans to implement similar activities during 2023 and reach the same target.

project_name: Provision of WASH services to the affected people in Aleppo and Idleb Governorates
project_objective:
Over 2022, the intervention plan will focus on immediate emergency life-saving WASH interventions and support the resilience of existing WASH systems (water supply and sewer networks, wastewater treatment, solid waste management) and WASH in institutions, such as schools and healthcare facilities, ensuring coordinated and cohesive response and provide comprehensive WASH services for affected people in northwest Syria living in IDP sites and host communities. 

The intervention will focus on providing emergency WASH services in the short term and provide a sustainable service in the long-term to the affected people in Aleppo and Idelb governorates. Shafak through this intervention will provide emergency WASH services for 620,000 individuals living in camps and communities. Shafak will provide full package WASH emergency services to provide rapid responses and strengthen the community resilience to adapt to living conditions in the affected communities
The intervention plan will ensure safe access, availability to basic WASH services, and quality assurance based on WASH cluster guidelines and COVID-19 mitigation measures for the planned activities. The intervention will comprise the following components:

a) Rehabilitation/upgrade of 20 water pumping stations including equipping the stations with electrical and mechanical equipment and installing renewable energy systems to reduce the running costs benefiting 100,000 Individuals. In addition, support Water Association Units (WAUs) through providing monthly running costs for the stations (fuel, chlorine, engine oil, and incentives for workers) and promote a cost recovery system. As well as train the local communities and apply water safety plans.

b) Provision of WASH emergency services for 400,000 individuals living in camps including water trucking and water quality monitoring, water containers, construction/ repair of emergency latrines, providing cleaning materials for latrines and latrine cleaning, desludging of septic tanks, and solid waste management.

c) Rehabilitation of sewage networks to connect the remote sites, camps, public facilities (schools and health centers) in addition to replacing the damaged sewer lines benefiting 75,000 Individuals.

d) Rehabilitation of water networks to connect the remote sites, camps, public facilities (schools and health centers) in addition to replacing the damaged water lines benefiting 30,000 Individuals.

e) Supporting the local operators and municipalities to continue the garbage collection and disposal of the waste from 20 communities (around 220,000 individuals), schools, health centers, and surrounding IDPs sites. This support will cover providing fuel for garbage vehicles, and maintaining/repair of the broken ones in addition to supporting workers’ incentives. Also, rehabilitation of 10 dumpsites.

f) Conducting hygiene promotion sessions about the improvement of hygiene practices and behaviors for 60,000 individuals.

g) 50,000 hygiene kits (approx. 300,000 individuals) will be distributed to the IDPs and host communities who don’t have the capacity to secure hygiene materials.

h) provision of WASH services to 5 education centers and 5 health facilities. 

Shafak will ensure support the innovative solutions as possible in its proposed interventions for dealing with water drought issues through supporting solar-powered systems, wastewater treatment. In addition to applying environmental improvement projects through developing solid waste management treatment and elevating the bad impacts of neglecting SWM support.

As for 2023, according to Shafak's strategy and fund availability, it is expected to implement the same activities with the same size and budget.

project_name: Multi-sectoral response to vulnerable individuals and refugees in Khartoum, Gedaref and Blue Nile States, Sudan
project_objective: For Integrated Protection in Gedaref and Blue Nile, specialized Women’s Protection and Empowerment (WPE) prevention and response services will be delivered to support women and girls at risk, such as elderly women, pregnant women, breastfeeding women, women and girls with disabilities, and female headed households (HHs). The project will support the integration of reproductive health and WPE services so that gender-based violence (GBV) survivors can access safe and timely clinical care for the harmful health consequences - both physical and emotional. The project will also deliver Child Protection (CP) services to ensure that children are safe in their homes when they experience harm. The IRC will provide access to quality services and a robust CP response inclusive of case management and Safe Healing and Learning Spaces (SHLS) where the IRC's Social and Emotional Learning (SEL) curriculum will be implemented. The IRC will also engage community members to further mitigate potential risks for children and adolescents. Additionally, the IRC will introduce activities to assist in reducing the risk of water-borne diseases and vector control within the catchment areas of the supported Health Facilities through risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) activities by involving IRC Integrated protection. The IRC will target the refugees in both Blue Nile and Gedaref states, affected by WASH-related diseases and outbreaks as well as flooding and malnutrition, to address their dire needs in terms of WASH support. The IRC prioritizes gender and protection as cross-cutting themes across all areas of intervention to ensure that services are equally accessible and safe for clients and that the unique needs of individuals are addressed. especially children under 5 and pregnant, lactating women (PLW), and people with disabilities. WASH activities will be bolstered by life-saving, integrated health and nutrition services to reduce excess morbidity and mortality for the refugee population. This will be done through primary health care facilities and referral of complicated cases to secondary facilities. The health package will include reproductive, maternal and child health services, treatment of communicable and non-communicable diseases, mental health and psychosocial support, emergency preparedness and response including response to COVID-19 pandemic. The IRC will provide life-saving treatment for severe acute malnutrition (SAM) and moderate acute malnutrition (MAM), referrals to stabilization centers and counseling of pregnant and lactating women (PLW) on infant and young child feeding (IYCF). The IRC will work directly in the camps to provide services, and through established Ministry of Health (MoH) facilities to scale up services to refugees in urban areas. Refugee HHs in Tuneydbah camp will also receive one round of multipurpose cash assistance (MPCA) to meet their basic needs. The transfer value will be distributed as per the guidelines of the Cash Working Group. The IRC will use the strategy of blanket coverage and cover around 21,000 refugees in Tuneydbah camp in Gadaref state.

project_name: Adequate Shelter Solution for vulnerable households in Gaza
project_objective:
The project responds to the Shelter/NFIs Cluster’s Objective n. 1 “Displaced populations are provided support that mitigates immediate harm and ensures adequate and safe temporary shelter solutions”, and Objective n. 2: “Vulnerable households exposed to harsh weather and protection concerns are supported to meet basic needs and enhance their coping capacity”. This is linked to HRP 2022 SO.1; “The rights of Palestinians living under occupation, including those living under the blockade, and other restrictions, are protected, respected and promoted in accordance with International Humanitarian Law (IHL), and International Human Rights Law (IHRL), while duty-bearers are increasingly held to account”. and HRP 2022 SO.2; “The basic needs of vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation are met through the provision of quality basic services, and improved access to resources, in accordance with the rights of protected persons under IHL”. 

 The overall project objective is to ensure that 630 most vulnerable HHs (3840 individuals) from Gaza, North Gaza, and middle area Governorates are supported with adequate temporary and durable shelter solutions that meet their basic needs and enhance their coping capacity. 350 of these HHs are at immediate risk of eviction from rented shelters and suffer from deteriorated socio-economic situation and protection concerns. The remaining 280 are vulnerable HHs living in substandard housing conditions without essential protection against harsh climate and are exposed to protection concerns. The proposed response will be tailored on the HHs’ needs including:1) Cash-for-rent and legal support to 350 vulnerable HHs in rented accommodation according to MoSD database who are repeatedly exposed to the risk of eviction for their inability to pay the rental costs. This includes provision of cash-for- debt re-payment for cases identified during the case-by-case legal counselling sessions, or at high risk of imminent imprisonment due to being forced to sign promissory note. The cash for rent will cover 4-months’ rent fees including electricity and water bills and will be provided through phased cash payments.2) Provision of cash for essential  items for 210 vulnerable HHs living in the above-mentioned conditions and who lack essential equipment (gas stoves, cylinders, refrigerators, bedding sets, etc.) due to poverty or selling their essential assets. The support will be tailored to the actual needs considering beneficiaries’ priorities, and will be paid through cash transfer based on agreed BoQs. 3) Shelter rehabilitation and repair of 80 substandard housing units will be supported to secure minimum requirements of waterproofing, hygienic living space, privacy, and protection from weather extremes up to the basic shelter cluster minimum standards, to ensure physical and climate protection, to enhance the living space conditions, and to improve privacy. 4) Provision of in-kind sealing-off materials and winterization NFIs for 200 HHs at risk of exposure to harsh weather conditions particularly  people living in ground floors and houses located in low depression areas near the valleys or adjacent to Sewage Water pumping stations.  

5) Provision of hygiene kits and hygiene awareness material for all the 630 vulnerable families targeted in the above activities, to enable adequate personal hygiene and protection against C-19. This project is designed in consultations with NRC local partner, the Shelter Cluster and the Ministry of Public Work and Housing (MoPWH) to fill the current gap in short-medium term response and coordinated with active shelter partners to avoid duplication and ensure fair distribution of the limited humanitarian funds among affected communities across Gaza Strip.

project_name: Information, Counselling and Legal Assistance (ICLA) to protect the rights of Palestinians in the West Bank (including East Jerusalem)
project_objective: Provision of information, counselling and legal assistance to Palestinians in Area C and East Jerusalem affected by violations of their rights, including housing, land and property rights, residency rights, access to basic services and freedom of movement.

project_name: Improving equitable access to inclusive, quality learning opportunities, community support and strengthening education sector
project_objective: In 2022, PIB will continue providing support to improve access to quality, gender-responsive and inclusive learning opportunities in a safe and protective environment for Rohingya refugees and host community children, adolescents and youth (aged 3 to 24 years). PIB will continue education interventions in camps and host communities through direct implementation and local implementing partners. PIB will sustain its community-based learning facilities (CBLF) modality and establish and refurbish new ECD, LCFA, Myanmar Curriculum and Youth Functional Literacy facilities. Project learning facilities will benefit from improved WASH facilities through setting up hand washing stations, distribution of basic hygienic , MHM kits and COVID19 preventing materials. Facilitators and learners for the project LF will be jointly identified with community members and financially supported through 2022. This project includes an evident disability inclusion focus, aiming to identify and assess disability status of learners attending learning facilities and cater individualized support for those most vulnerable, including conditional cash transfer to reduce learners drop out. In 2022, PIB will assure the quality of the project’s learning opportunities through updating and upgrading teaching and learning modules for our various education levels, ensuring inclusion, gender sensitiveness and SEL is mainstreamed across our learning facilities. PIB will build the capacities of SBK, LCFA, MC ,FLN, host primary and secondary school teachers/facilitators and sector education partners on gender responsive pedagogy, inclusive education, theme-based training, crisis sensitive education and planning  to become better teachers and improve learning outcomes of refugee and host communities’ learners. PIB will also identify and build the capacities of Rohingya women to become Myanmar Curriculum teachers and create a pool of female facilitators. In 2022, PIB is planning to incorporate technology-based teaching and learning approaches in a sample of learning facilities across the various educational levels to assess its impact and benefits on students' learning outcomes. To ensure students learning progress is assessed and tracked, PIB will conduct regular learning assessment and an individualizes progress tracking system put in place. In this JRP 22, PIB will continue to support the community engagement and capacity strengthening of Education Sector partners and affected communities to enhance their participation in the education of children, adolescents and youth. Key community stakeholders, parents and members of the learning facilities committees will be trained on gender, girls education, disability inclusion, child protection and safeguarding. PIB will also train LF management committees on DRR to jointly design emergency preparedness and response plans to equip LF and communities with required skills to respond to potential emergencies. Furthermore, PIB education partners will be benefiting from capacity building on gender responsive pedagogy, SEL, inclusive education and crisis sensitive education planning and management.

project_name: Children Are in Peace
project_objective:
PLAN International Bangladesh will focus on vulnerable and at-risk children, survivors of violence, abuse, neglect and exploitation, adolescents and youth through three interlinking components – quality case management, community-based child protection and CP system Strengthening. The proposed project will include adolescent life skills, community engagement in everyday peace and social cohesion building. The services will ensure boys, girls and adolescents in camp and host communities are safe and protected from violence, abuse, neglect and exploitation with special consideration on gender and disability. These activities will be aligned with Self-Reliance and Resilience.
Age appropriate, gender responsive and timely individual Case Management Services will be provided for vulnerable CAYs targeting unaccompanied and separated children, child-headed households, children in psychosocial distress, children with specific needs, and child survivors of GBV.
CBCP activities will be structured through feedback from community consultation and participation to ensure inclusion and ownership by both the host and the refugee community. The interventions will ensure inclusion of CAYs, persons with disability and the youths. Community-level interventions will include promoting social cohesion and strengthening self-protection of children. Addressing harmful practices and attitudes, Plan will invest in active community participation and positive parenting.
Keeping AAP in account PIB will ensure that child friendly feedback mechanisms are in place with strong emphasis on PSEA and Child Safeguarding through direct consultation with children and community people. The contact number of PSEA and safeguarding will be well informed to wider community. PIB will also ensure its partners have PSEA policies and the same is implemented.
PIB is committed to coordinating the response through active participation in sectors such as Protection, Education, GBV and Child Protection Sub-Sector and other working groups like Strategic Working Group (SAG), CMTWG to ensure meaningful access, prioritization of safety and integration of services.  The services offered will be in line with CPMS, interagency tools and SOPs, CPSS strategy and will be ensured through structured training enhancing competencies in providing quality gender-responsive and timely services. This project will also include a contingency plan for natural disaster with giving importance on environment.
PLAN will also keep close connection with Government officials including capacity strengthening initiatives at different stage of project that will bring positive outcomes on the lives of the children.
This project will carry out A participatory research on social cohesion, facilitate and support dialogue and trust-building activities in pilot locations of host and camp. Workshop with duty bearers (government officials and local authorities), community leaders, parents, teachers and religious leaders in both community groups on developing a basic understanding of everyday peace, social cohesion, social trust and public accountability will also take place. Undertaking capacity-strengthening and training activities for national and local institutions, actors and partners on conflict sensitivity, everyday peace, social cohesion and peace-building will be the important aspect of this project.
Plan will undertake several assessments such as baseline, midterm, impact assessment and will collect disaggregated data including people with disability.
The project will priorities resourcing and capacity building of local partner for quality implementation in both camps and host community.
The project falls within Plan International’s development and humanitarian framework for Bangladesh in which sit several tools, such as The Plan International Bangladesh Country Strategic Plan, The Cox’s Bazar JRP 2021; CPSS strategy 2021, J-MSNA Refugee and host communities – Protection (Findings, 08 November 2021) etc

project_name: Lifesaving Support to Most Vulnerable Host Communities and Rohingya Refugees in Teknaf and Ukhiya Upozilla of Cox's Bazar District.
project_objective:
""The project incorporates with both the Rohingya refugees and the extremely vulnerable host communities in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. The camp side activities This Activity will support 750 Rohingya refugees HHs with Community Cooking and Learning Centres (CLC) and Gender Based Violence (GBV) awareness funded by World Vision Hong Kong and New Zealand-MFAT. CLCs complementary safe spaces for women and men to engage with services, learn and hear relevant messaging mainly Kitchen Gardening, Nutrition food preparation, Pastry making, IYCF, GBV, DRR, Child and Mother care to improve safety for women and children. Also empower Lead Mothers to capacities and support community others people. Provide Vegetable gardening training and inputs to involve women in kitchen gardening to support fresh vegetable for family nutrition.
On the other hand, at host communities will address the short-term food security crisis and medium-term livelihood recovery needs of most vulnerable 5229 HHs. Targeted HHs will be drawn from Ukhiya and Teknaf Upozilla with priority given to villages adjacent to refugee settlements while simultaneously addressing other social dynamics such as women’s mobility restrictions and income generating restrictions by engaging males in the same communities through building awareness on GBV prevention through men care group. Vulnerable will be provided home gardening and off farm IGA training and input vouchers to purchase home gardening tools and certified seeds for nutritious food production. Trainings by government extension workers will be facilitated to provide ongoing support for project beneficiaries beyond the project lifetime. HHs will be supported with financial literacy training and business plan development for income generating activities (IGA), along with multi-purpose cash transfers to start/ enhance IGAs. 
Another segment of the project will be working to support vulnerable HHs in Ukhiya and Teknaf Sub-Districts in Cox’s Bazar to lead them out of poverty.  Especially 2880 ultra-poof HHs will be receive productive assets and strengthen producer group and local market place construction and ultra-poor family link with service provider.
""

project_name: Rehabilitation services for Rohingya Refugees and Host Community in Cox’s Bazar Bangladesh
project_objective:
Women with disabilities often face additional, severe disadvantage due to discriminatory norms and perceptions of their low value and capacity. They are at more risk of abuse and have little access to rehabilitation. Persons with disabilities face attitudinal and physical barriers and are often excluded and not consulted. Lack of experience of field staff to interact with people with disability further exacerbates their failure to access essential information. Older persons face restrictions to participation (like language or literary barriers) that prevent them from accessing information services.  Gender Equality and Social Inclusion will be a significant cross cutting issue, ensuring marginalised groups (including women, girls, older persons, people with disabilities and LGBTIQ+) actively participate in the Activity. The project will incorporate strategies to address gender equality and social inclusion issues as follows:
• Particular attention paid to ensuring meaningful participation and input from particularly vulnerable women and girls, e.g. providing girls and women with disabilities with reasonable accommodation, assistive devices, and other means to access activities, equally contributing to participation processes.
• Data disaggregated by gender, age, and disability to monitor participation of marginalised groups. 
• CBM-CDD will proactively capture systematic feedback of beneficiaries with disabilities and set strategies to remove barriers accordingly. 
• Female rehabilitative service providers and volunteers from the host community employed who speak the same language.
• All staff receive refresher training on CBM/CDD gender and safeguarding/child protection policies and codes of conduct.
The project will create access to rehabilitation in primary health care. While there are now multiple health service providers operating in the camps and host communities, rehabilitation service provision for people with different medical conditions, including various Neurologic (e.g., stroke, spinal cord injuries), Orthopedic (Osteoarthritis, Cervical Spondylitis), and Pediatrics Conditions (Cerebral Palsy) is limited to the availability of a few organizations only representing a significant gap. The provision of accessible Home Based Rehabilitative (HBR) services will improve the health outcome & quality of life of people with disabilities in the camps and host communities. The proposed rehabilitation services include Physiotherapy, Occupational Therapy, Speech & Language Therapy, Eye Screening, Hearing Screening, provision of assistive devices (including orthosis and prostheses,) & home adaptation.  The project will make strong links with other (primary) health care providers to create a strong referral system for those patients who need primary health care services.  
CBM with local partner the Centre for Disability in Development (CDD), will implement the programme based in camp 15, camp 16, and mobilize to other unreached camps upon request & agreement by mainstream health actors. In the host community, CBM & CDD will implement the project in the Jaliapalong Union.  The project will be gender inclusive and will cover all age range people while ensuring added focus on women with disabilities.
Recognizing the significant gap in rehabilitation services that exits in the camps & host communities, the project will advocate for integrating rehabilitation components within the existing healthcare system and share example of good practices on Health & Rehabilitation.  Among the community peoples, persons with disabilities specially women with disabilities are more vulnerable and deprived from services. By considering this issue, CDD will form Rehab team by equal number of male & female staff.  
Considering frequent natural disasters, the project also includes a 5% contingency budget based on a risk compliance contingency plan followed by the CBM crisis modifier approach align with Mobile Medical Team (MMT) during emergencies.

project_name: UNICEF Life Saving Nutrition Interventions Targeting Most Vulnerable Population (IDPs and Vulnerable Residents) Across Sudan
project_objective:
The nutrition situation in Sudan in 2022 is projected to remain at elevated high levels, the nutrition sector has estimated that 3.9 million children under five and pregnant and lactating women (PLW) will need humanitarian assistance to meet their nutritional needs. Through this project, UNICEF aims to increase equitable access and utilization of quality nutrition curative and preventative services for acutely malnourished children (boys and girls 6-59 months) and PLWs among highly vulnerable populations including internally displaced people (IDPs) and vulnerable residents. In 2022, UNICEF will continue to support the provision of nutrition curative interventions through strengthening the quality of services and scaling up Outpatient Therapeutic Program (OTP) while working on securing pipeline for essential nutrition supplies such as Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF), therapeutic milk, Resomal, OTPs drugs and anthropometric measurements. Through this UNICEF will target around 330,000 children suffering from severe acute malnutrition (SAM) and will procure 396,000 RUTF cartons. To ensure early identification and referral of children with acute malnutrition, UNICEF will work on strengthening outreach activities. UNICEF will also support the provision of preventative nutrition interventions through the promotion of infant and young child feeding (IYCF) practices. In 2022, UNICEF will continue to exert efforts in scaling up the IYCF program to ensure the counselling of 990,000 pregnant women and mothers and caregivers of children less than two years. To alleviate the risk of micronutrient deficiency in women and children, UNICEF will continue to provide vitamin A supplementation targeting 6,520,335 children (6-59 months) and iron foliate supplementation targeting 990,000 PLWs.

Through this project, UNICEF will continue to support health system strengthening through efforts to strengthen supply chain management of nutrition commodities, besides building the capacity of front-line health workers and other CMAM related cadres on CMAM program and CMAM monitoring to ensure the delivery of high-quality nutrition services.

project_name: Syrian Communities Assistance in Livelihood and Early-recovery (SCALE)
project_objective:
The SCALE project will respond to the vulnerable needs of vulnerable Syrian communities in Deir AL Zor, Homs, Idlib, Hama and Lattakia. These areas have been considered to have many people with needs where services, resources and assistance are limited. As a result, substantial responses are needed to reduce the suffering of those who have lived through considerable hardship, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic.
The objective of the SCALE project is to improve the access of men, women, boys and girls, including people with disabilities, to essential services in the governorates mentioned above.
The SCALE project will benefit 435,000 highly vulnerable individuals, in 2 years, including 121,800 men, 121,800 women, 95,700 boys and 95,700 girls, by supporting to maintenance and improvement of equitable access to basic services through rehabilitation of electricity networks, water networks, solar street lights, and increase in access to Livelihood and job opportunities through providing livelihood grants and repair of shops.
The proposed activities are under objective 1 of the ERL Sector log frame (Support the Maintenance & improve equitable access to basic services) activity 1.1  (Rehabilitation of basic electricity), indicator 1.1.2 (# Km electrical networks rehabilitated), activity 1.2 (Promote/support the use of renewable energy), indicator 1.2.1 (# KWA generated from solar panel per month), activity 1.9 (Rehabilitation water stations), indicator 1.9.1 (# of water stations rehabilitated) and objective 2 (Increase access to Livelihood and job opportunities), activity 2.3 (Create long and short-term work opportunities), indicator:2.3.1 (# # of longer-term jobs created), and indicator 2.3.3 (# of jobs created during the rehabilitation of public and private infrastructure).
ADRA will prioritize areas that include the most significant number of children under five years, women of reproductive age (15 – 49 years), older persons (age 60 and above), displaced persons –including refugees, IDPs and returnees, and persons living with disabilities.
ADRA will further prioritize sub-districts with the highest severity scale (3 and above), dense urban settings, areas with lower/ limited functional facilities.
Where possible, ADRA will select the areas where ADRA is already present to provide an integrated approach, including the sectors of WASH, Livelihood, food security or education.

project_name: Population affected by forced displacement increase ability to exercise and enjoy HLP rights and achieve durable solutions in Far North region of Cameroon
project_objective:
The main objective of this project is to improve access to housing, land and property rights for returnees, displaced persons, refugees and host communities in Mayo-Sava, Mayo-Tsanaga and Logone-et-Chari divisions in Far North region of Cameroon. 
Violence perpetrated by armed groups in the Far North of Cameroon has led to forced displacement of populations and caused many human rights concerns. In Round 22 (March 2021) of the DTM , 82,586 households of 514,747 individuals (43% male, 57% female) were identified, including 341,535 IDPs (68%), 48,902 out-of-camp refugees (10%) and 124,310 returnees (22%). According to Round 22 report, returns have continued to increase at a slower pace since 2019 but were high between January and March 2021 (7,869 households) for only three months, compared with 10,927 for the whole of 2020. Reasons for 40% of return are access to arable land.
During 2021, 1287 HLP cases (50,97% of women) were followed up in the Far North in 20 villages by the NRC’s team. The cases identified related to the lack of property documents, forced eviction, secondary occupation, inadequate houses, insufficient arable land, access deprivation.  Another HLP issue in the Far North is related to military operations conducted by the Cameroon army against NSAG. Those military operations affected around 7500 persons who were either evacuated from their homes or whose access to their farming lands was blocked. It is also important to note the rise in inter-community conflicts over the insufficiency of natural resources, which have caused, for example, the forced displacement people in the Logone-et-Chari in 2021.
NRC will reinforce its response and provide support to displaced populations and vulnerable host communities to access their HLP rights. NRC will deliver information, awareness and counsellings sessions to IDPs, returnees, refugees, and host communities on HLP issues.  .
Additionally, NRC will provide legal assistance to conflict-affected population (IDPs, refugees) in need of securing their HLP rights. NRC will assist vulnerable individuals to obtain signed agreements from local authorities and traditional leaders (chief of villages) for beneficiaries at risk of forced eviction . Priority will be given to female heads of household, widows, displaced persons, and vulnerable or affected host community members. This process will contribute to the prevention of forced evictions. 
Furthermore, NRC will build the capacity of local and traditional authorities on HLP issues, including through the provision of training and coaching on HLP rights and CDR (Collaborative Dispute Resolution), to strengthen their HLP response. NRC will also train humanitarian actors operating in sectors such as shelter, WASH, education, and food security. This will help ensure that these sectors prioritize land tenure agreements instead of the direct and customary land transfer in their interventions and prevent or solve land-related conflicts. For due diligence approach, NRC will work with beneficiaries of Livelihoods and Food Security (LFS), Shelter, Wash and Education programmes to secure access to land. In order to avoid or reduce forced evictions, NRC will assist Shelter, Wash, LFS beneficiaries to access land with increased security of tenure. 
In order to strengthen the coordination and give further visibility to the needs of affected populations with regard to access to land, housing and property, NRC will lead the HLP Area of Responsibility. This will also contribute to an integrated and multi-sectoral response to HLP from national and local authorities, as well as humanitarian actors.  
NRC will advocate for the HLP rights of conflict-affected populations to be respected. Workshops with relevant government officials and humanitarian actors at national and regional levels will be held in order to enhance the access to HLP rights for forced-displaced persons.

project_name: Protective and adaptive Education Approaches for Children in Emergencies (PEACE)
project_objective:
In recognition that conflict-affected primary school-aged children in Nigeria, Niger, and Cameroon face major challenges to accessing quality education and protection services, IRC Deutschland proposes to partner with ECHO under the Pilot Programmatic Partnership to deliver the 3-year PEACE project. PEACE takes an integrated and adaptive approach to education and child protection, to support 171,065 school-aged boys and girls, their carers and educators, most affected by crisis across target countries to access and learn in safe educational environments. The PEACE evidence-based approach towards improving educational access, quality, and safety builds on previous IRC programming and includes: 
1.	Four core models to expand access to formal and non-formal education that is conflict-sensitive and designed to support children who are most in need;
2.	Support to caregivers and communities so that they may more fully ensure girls’ and boys’ safety, access, and learning; and 
3.	Capacity building of teachers and facilitators in order to improve the quality of instruction and provide safe learning environments for children. 
Child protection measures are integrated throughout PEACE, from individual case management support to individual and group psycho-social support activities for caregivers and children. 
In light of the COVID 19 pandemic, PEACE will adapt programming to ensure the continuity of child protection and learning support in safe environments, as well as COVID-19-specific messaging related to health and or WASH.

project_name: Improved food security and livelihoods of IDPs, returnees and vulnerable host communities in South Sudan
project_objective:
In line with the South Sudan 2022 Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) and the FSL Cluster priorities, NPA will support vulnerable and food-insecure Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs), returnees and vulnerable host communities in IPC 4 locations in Canal/Pigi, Fangak, Pochalla & Bor South Counties of Jonglei State, Rumbek East, Rumbek Center, Cueibet, Yirol East, Yirol West and Awerial Counties of Lakes State, Terekeka County of Central Equatoria State and Kapoeta North County of Eastern Equatoria State. The targeted communities in the identified counties will be supported to improve their food security and livelihoods through provision of timely and appropriate main season and dry season inputs/kits (Crop, vegetable and fishing), training in improved agronomic and fishing practices. In addition, NPA will support food-insecure with cash transfers in Rumbek East and Rumbek Center Counties in Lakes State with cash transfers to address their food needs. NPA’s emergency assistance and livelihoods support aims at saving lives and averting total collapse of livelihoods in the target Counties. The provision of agricultural and fishing inputs/kits, training in agricultural production and fishing is expected to improve the food production and in turn the food security of the target households (HHs) thus supporting them to recover from crisis and placing them on an accelerated path to early recovery and resilience to acute shocks. NPA’s response will address the food security and livelihoods needs and priorities identified in the South Sudan 2022 Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO).

NPA seeks to support 105,056 HHs (630,338 individuals) in the targeted Counties with livelihood kits and cash transfers to address food insecurity. Some of the kits will be provided by FAO and some procured by NPA. Training on improved agronomic and fishing practices, marketing and group dynamics will be done through model farmers and fisher folk who will undergo a Training of Trainers (ToT) and subsequently cascade the knowledge and skills to the farmers and fisher folk in their communities. The knowledge gained from these trainings will improve the agricultural and fishing practices of the target HHs thus improving food production, addressing their immediate food security needs and building their resilience to future shocks. The provision of cash transfers and agricultural inputs and fishing kits and subsequent enhancement of food production and fishing is expected to contribute to improvement of the Household Diversity Score (HDDS) and Food Consumption Score (FCS) of the target HHs. COVID-19 preventive and mitigation measures will be mainstreamed throughout all activities to prevent spread and transmission of the virus. The proposed interventions are aligned to the FSL cluster objective 1: CO1: Provide food assistance to prevent famine and improve food consumption, dietary diversity and coping strategies for vulnerable populations (in IPC 5, 4 & some 3) in a way that prevents the spread & transmission of COVID 19 and Objective 2: Enhance and sustain emergency food production through complementary vegetable and crop livelihood inputs, fishing and livestock support in a way that prevents the spread & transmission of COVID 19.

NPA will employ a community-based beneficiary selection approach which will entail establishing Project Management Committees (PMC’s) to lead the selection of eligible beneficiaries based on the beneficiary selection criteria. Vulnerable HHs with severe food insecurity including female, child, disabled/chronically ill headed HHs; persons living with or at risk of HIV/AIDS and survivors of Gender-Based Violence (GBV) will be targeted in this project.

The target communities will be the prime movers of the implementation process through engagement in the project. Through various means, NPA will gather feedback from the target communities and stakeholders to improve project implementation.

project_name: Humanitarian food security and livelihoods support to vulnerable groups in Sudan, covering Blue Nile, Central Darfur, North Darfur, Red Sea, South Kordofan and West Kordofan.
project_objective:
The humanitarian crisis has been growing as Sudan is facing high inflation rates that raised the number of food insecure people and deepening poverty level. The number of people falling before poverty line has grown rapidly, which needs swift response. It has also reduced the capacity of the state in availing basic services to its residents. The COVID-19 pandemic has added more burden to the exiting challenge, by contributing to slowing down of the economic growth, loss of jobs and reduction in remittances flowing in to the country. Sudan has been doing an economic reform which includes to remove subsides on fuel, food and medicine. As result of this, the prices of the goods are going up and more people are finding it hard to access basic food and medical services. The increment on fuel prices has contributed to higher production cost for irrigated farms, directly contributing to increased food costs. 
This project will include range of activities from filling food gaps using cash and voucher, to supporting for improvement of production (crop and animal) by providing or strengthening the purchasing power of the affected people through cash and voucher assistances. The quality of seeds will be checked for germination and purity tests, and inputs that fit to the existing climatic conditions will be introduced. The livestock sector will focus on restocking and providing veterinary services. Community members will be trained and supplied with essential medical equipment/drug for wider coverage of vaccinations and controlling of potential disease outbreaks. Trainings on post-harvest management, to reduce the loss that is currently happening and demonstrations on improved farming systems will be included. Income generation activities will benefit youth and some small scale business people, to re-activate the local economy and assisted with up-to-date market information sharing. The cash and voucher assistance (CVA), will support vulnerable groups to fill the monthly food gaps, to cover 50% of the MEB. And the early recovery activities will provide improved seeds and tools, in collaboration with local universities and research centers. This will pave the way for adaptable and sustainable food production in the near future. Affected families will be supported on enhance production skills and reduce the post harvest loses. Swift and timely support for the most affected families, will play critical role in stopping from worsening food insecurity and begins with recovery to grown their own foods.

project_name: Enhancing Targeted Humanitarian Response Through Beneficiary Data Management
project_objective:
For more than three years, the province of Cabo Delgado in northern Mozambique has experienced attacks by Non-state Armed Groups (NSAGs), causing over 700,000 people to be internally displaced. Attacks have increased in severity and frequency since they began in October 2017, with continued increases in violence and subsequent displacement in 2020 as well as a significant rise in internal displacement following launched attacks in Palma Sede from 24 March 2021.
Vulnerable populations including women, children and the elderly are particularly impacted. In addition, humanitarian service delivery faces challenges. In the face of constrained humanitarian access, it becomes increasingly important to address the highest priority needs effectively and efficiently with a targeted approach. Quality and robust information is required to support effective inter-cluster coordination integrated response missions, and to enable partners to implement critical humanitarian response activities This project enables IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) to establish IDP verification and registration efforts for the purposes of humanitarian response. In developing a centralized and regularly maintained digital platform – the proposed project is designed to maximize operational impact and support more effective and efficient resource mobilization, whilst strengthening partnerships with the wider humanitarian community. Beneficiary verification and digital registration for the purposes of humanitarian response will additionally support accountability over resource mobilization/allocation across humanitarian partners through 

The overall objective of this project is to strengthen accountability and targeted humanitarian response through list activities:   

1.	Scale-up of IDP verification and registration across sites and host communities, including the provision of technical support in mapping and identifying IDPs hosted in urban settings. Technical support will be provided for purposes of planning for humanitarian assistance
2.	Development of Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), inclusive of updated Community-Feedback mechanisms, revised Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) messaging and protection referral pathways-to fit the evolving context. Technical Assistance to verification/registration will also be adapted to align with minimum standards outlined in Verification/Registration Checklists drafted by the, including improved technical assistance in registration of conflict-affected populations (in line with Checklist outlined by Cabo Delgado Technical Working Group).
3.	Expanding training sessions to government technicians (INGD, SDPI), local leadership, the local community, relevant committees, and relevant non-government stakeholders, including newly established NGOs active in Cabo Delgado), among others

To distinguish the different kinds of exercises in this project
•	Verification is used to refer to a preliminary exercise whereby beneficiary identity is confirmed
•	Registration of verified caseloads via digital platform (BRaVE or SCOPE)

project_name: Emergency Health and MHPSS response for conflict affected populations in Cabo Delgado and Nampula, Mozambique
project_objective: Ensure access to and continuity of essential primary health and MHPSS services, emergency referrals and outbreak response for vulnerable displaced people and host communities. This will be implemented through an integrated community-based approach in Cabo Delgado and Nampula provinces and through the deployment of mobile clinics and mobile brigades.

project_name: Strengthening Evidence-Based Humanitarian Planning Through the Continuation and Expansion of the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) in Northern Mozambique
project_objective:
For more than three years, the province of Cabo Delgado in northern Mozambique has experienced attacks by Non-state Armed Groups (NSAGs), causing over 700,000 people to be internally displaced. Attacks have increased in severity and frequency since they began in October 2017, with continued increases in violence and subsequent displacement in 2020 as well as a significant rise in internal displacement following launched attacks in Palma Sede from 24 March 2021.
The DTM is an information system and set of tools developed to gather and analyses data to disseminate critical multi-layered information on the mobility, vulnerabilities, and needs of displaced and mobile populations that enables decision makers and responders to provide better context-specific and tailored assistance. In Mozambique, the DTM can add value in attending to the needs of displaced populations through the continuation and reinforcement of its comprehensive information management platform designed to provide accurate and up-to-date information to Government and humanitarian actors and, in fine, improve the overall humanitarian response. Monitoring tools are methodologies are designed to ensure representations of affected populations include the specific needs/vulnerabilities of persons with disabilities, elderly, separated/unaccompanied children, pregnant women as well as persons with chronic diseases.
In addition to being systematically deployed in medium to large-scale humanitarian response operations, DTM has also proven to be highly effective as a preparedness tool (the mapping of potential evacuation and displacement sites and the establishment of data collection mechanisms before a disaster strikes).
Building on IOM’s established DTM presence in the northern region, IOM proposes to continue its operations by strengthening coverage capacity and teams on the ground. In this phase, responding to the complex mobility trends and intentions of disaster and conflict affected communities, IOM will continue its current operations and further improve its methodology through: 
List Activities:
1.	Bi-monthly Baseline assessments
2.	Weekly Emergency tracking Overviews/Ad Hoc Movement Alerts
3.	Bi-monthly Multi sectoral site assessment/Population count
4.	Ad hoc Return assessment
5.	Ad hoc Thematic Surveys

IOM further proposes to continue capacitating relevant focal points from the provincial level (governor’s office technicians, INGC, Provincial Directorate of Gender, Children and Social Action) on information management, data collection and other DTM components. Through coordination with relevant focal points operating in Cabo Delgado, Nampula and Niassa- data protection, general protection, disability, and inclusion as well as PSEA standards in data collection efforts will be incorporated in refresher training modules. All capacity building efforts will be complemented by operational and technical support for information management exercises, both recurring or ad hoc, conducted by Government counterpart’s representative of men and women. 

Overall People Targeted (1,538,000 individuals, indirectly) with 52% Non IDPs, 48% IDPs and 33% Returnees (migrants, refugees)

Vulnerable Groups Targeted: Children under 5 years (21% of total targeted population), School Age Children 5-17 years (3%), Elderly 60+years (5%) and Persons with special needs/vulnerabilities (15%)

After capacity development (short and long term), the young people, girls and young women from the will be supported for enterprise development or job placement. The project included demand specific employment and entrepreneurship strategies considering the sustainability aspects. The target people will also be linked with the Government extension departments, training institutions and other scopes in the private sectors. Inside the camps, the household will be supported for effective self-reliance activities that will prepare them to return back to Myanmar. 

GAM: The project will reach to the 10,000 women and 2300 men both in the host and refugee communities. The target people are selected from the bottom layer of the population considering their economical vulnerability and as well as deprived for gender negative stereotypes in the society. The gender transformative approach in the project will contribute for their food security, control over resources, decision making process and finally in the role sharing at households’ level. This strategy will ensure male engagement and diversity also.  

In addition, specific needs of women and people with disabilities have been highlighted in the design and linked to the proposed interventions, that will help reduce access barriers for girls, boys, adolescents, women and men awareness raising and sensitization activities that target negative gender-based norms and values in the project area.

project_name: Lifting Healthy, Empowered and Protected Girls and Women in Cox’s Bazar (LEAP).
project_objective:
LEAP is informed by proven, evidence-based approaches, programmatic lessons and consultations with stakeholders, including girls, boys, women, men, community leaders, partners and government actors. Though the project duration is 30-month and projected budget is $6.8 million for whole working areas but under the provision of JRP, the project will cover 6 locations including two camps in partnership with PHD and the projected budget is $1.62 million for proposed JRP period  (an estimated 10% in camps). The project will employ a rights-based health services , gender-transformative (GT) and three-pronged strategy to: i) improve the individual and collective agency and resilience of adolescent girls and young women to exercise their SRH and protection rights (1100); ii) strengthen health systems to provide sex- and age-responsive quality health and protection services (1200); and iii) enhance the capacity of local women's rights organizations (WROs), including girl-led organizations (GLOs), and youth-led organizations (YLOs) on evidence-based advocacy for GARI health and protection services while advocating for long-term change for evidence-based GARI SRH, SGBV and MHPSS services and programming (1300). Improved, integrated SRHR outcomes for girls have shown to contribute to better lifelong outcomes in education, protection, livelihoods and overall wellbeing (Brookings, 2016). LEAP’s multi-sectoral and feminist approach works across health and protection sectors to strengthen horizontal linkages while integrating women and girl's agency throughout and engaging WROs/GLOs and YLOs as  influencers to improve accountability for GARI SRH and SGBV services and policies.  

Aligned with national and local humanitarian, health, protection and GE policies and strategies, as well as the SDGs and Canada’s Feminist International Assistance Policy (FIAP), LEAP will contribute to poverty reduction by targeting marginalized groups in Rohingya camps and host communities facing multifaceted dimensions of exclusion. In partnership with three local implementing partners and one key technical partner, LEAP will directly reach more than 79,000 people, including 49,873 females, in four Unions in Ukhiya and Teknaf sub-districts, as well as two Rohingya refugee camps (7,000).
