project_objective:
The unique socio-economic conditions of the blockade, with its movement restrictions and destruction of productive capacity, are further compounded by repeated cycles of conflict and political instability, undercutting employment and livelihood opportunities in the Gaza Strip. UNRWA’s emergency food assistance provides a critical humanitarian lifeline responding to the basic needs of over one million Palestine refugees, tempering food insecurity and improving access to food. It accounts for approximately 200,000 Palestine refugee families including families with persons with disabilities and female headed households. On quarterly bases, eligible families receive a unified food basket that is composed of a range of basic food commodities.
Through its well-established monitoring system, UNRWA will continue to evaluate the food distribution system including the distribution modality that follows strict safety and security measures responding to changing environment around unpredictable situation, while guaranteeing a consistent support to Palestine refugees in Gaza.

project_name: Darna Al-Aman (Our safe home) phase 2
project_objective:
Darna Al-Aman project was successfully launched in 2021 and aimed to support safe return of Raqqa’s civilian population through protection and health integrated services and the set-up of safe spaces for Women and Girls and for Children respectively, as well as GBV and CP response. Funding is being sought for follow up Action and continuity of essential services.
The protection component includes enhancement of WGSS, adjacent to the Raqqa Hospital, and a CFS, acting also as entry point for women, girls and boys allowing better access to services including integrated CM. The holistic and integrated approach leverages on reproductive health to ease access to protection services. Services targeting women and girls include informative sessions, PSS and life-skills activities, GBV CM services, and referral to other existing services. Moreover, parenting skills sessions and sessions for young mothers during breastfeeding will be provided, also through the support of medical staff. The programme supports a CFS, when IP staff provide PSS, life-skills and recreational activities aimed at young children and adolescents, specialized CM services for CP cases, and awareness sessions for caregivers and community members on CP risks.
A key element of the action will continue to be UPP's Capacity Building plan including integrated training, supervision and mentoring for protection, medical and nonmedical staff. To ensure high standard services, all the staff will be trained/receive refreshers on PSEA, Safeguarding, CoC, CP, WPE, GBV Core Concepts, safe identification and referral of cases, etc. Refreshers for health staff will also be included for CMR training to improve the management of these cases within 72 hours.
The project tries to address gender and age markers. The intervention is based on a thorough needs analysis and a participatory approach through programme lifecycle. The widespread GBV, SEA, child labor, trauma and the stigma resulting from all this kind of issues are taken into account into the project design. The Action seeks to address the specific needs of women, men, boys and girls, including persons with disabilities, female headed households and older persons; regular consultations with persons with specific needs, including persons with disabilities, will be conducted throughout the project implementation to ensure inclusion and to tailor the activities according to the specific target group. UPP staff will conduct regular Protection Mainstreaming assessments in the safe spaces and in the health facility to ensure that assistance is provided in a safe, dignified, accessible and participatory manner. If necessary, infrastructure adaptations will take place to guarantee access to services to children/persons with disability. UPP and IPs staff are trained on Disability & Inclusion and activities are adapted to the needs of the different groups. Outreach activities will ensure involvement of hard-to-reach groups. Key messages will be developed through consultations with community members, including persons with disabilities, to ensure adaptation to the context and to the needs of different groups. Data collected is disaggregated by age and gender (SAAD). 
Continuity for CM will also be guaranteed, and the satisfaction of the beneficiaries will be measured thanks to anonymous surveys, internal and external referrals database, feedback and complaint boxes.
The expected result is to reach up to 17.400 community members with integrated protection services, including outreach, awareness sessions and campaigns, informative sessions, PSS and recreational activities. Moreover, at least 100 women and girls survivors or at risk of GBV and 120 children at risk will received specialized CM services. As per the capacity building, the target is 32 staff members including UPP and IP staff.
The intervention will foster synergies among medical staff and protection staff, and a closed cooperation between Health, CP and GBV WGs and CM TFs.

project_name: Information, Counselling and Legal Assistance to Rohingya and Host Communities in Realization of Rights to Legal Identity and HLP Rights.
project_objective:
NRC ICLA will be implementing activities across 16 camps and 8 unions ensuring protection and gender mainstreaming. ICLA will work with the Camp-in Charge’s, UNHCR and other actors in camps to secure identity and documentation of Rohingya refugees through existing registration and documentation guidelines. NRC will also work with Ukhiya and Teknaf government authorities e.g. UNO office, UP office to host communities. The project designed to positively increase access to the documents required for accessing essential services and to the records of vital events, which can also be used as a proof of facts (e.g. age and identity) in the case of return or resettlement. The project also aims at mitigating and addressing tensions between the Rohingya and local communities generated by the HLP disputes. 

To fulfil the Accountability to the Affected population (AAP) principles, targeted objectives will be achieved through the provision of information, counselling and assistance based on individual needs, to enable target beneficiaries to overcome legal, procedural, and documentation challenges, including the referral to specialized case management actors as it may be required. Improvement of the relationships between refugees and host communities, and within the Rohingya community itself, will be mainly achieved through the building of capacity of actors within the recognized dispute resolution structures to identify and address (or refer to the NRC) the HLP disputes. Key staff, volunteers, and other stakeholders, including target communities whenever possible, will be involved to identify existing and emerging threats to safety, dignity and rights faced by different sex and age groups among the refugee and the host populations. Special attention will be paid to threats and vulnerabilities generated or exacerbated by COVID-19 and the associated containment measures. This information will be analyzed and used for evidence-based advocacy and will also be shared externally with other protection actors and stakeholders. ICLA field teams will continue the deployment of ‘mobile legal clinics’ – portable canopy tents, equipped with folding furniture and some basic equipment in the targeted 16 camps. NRC will also maintain “help desks” at the camp 2E, 8W, 10, 17, 21 and 22 CiC offices, as well as ICLA hubs at the camps 4, 21, 25 and 26, based in the premises rented from local community residents (meeting the due diligence requirements), accessible by both refugees and host communities. 

Four Protection Mainstreaming principles – a) safety, dignity, no harm, b) meaningful access, c) accountability and d) participation & empowerment will be promoted throughout the project implementation; while the Complaints and Feedback Mechanism (hotline for complaints and feedback) will be constantly upgraded in line with the NRC CFM Policy and the NRC CFM Handbook. NRC has also engaged the PSEA Network to train camp volunteers during inductions, and NRC has a designated PSEA focal point for reports concerning NRC staff. NRC ICLA will be an active participant within interagency disaster preparedness efforts for the monsoon and cyclone responses and in addressing the challenges brought on by COVID-19. ICLA team will coordinate with PERU teams in camps during any emergency to support on the registration, documentation and other related services.  NRC staff will continue working closely with the CiC office, site management, and protection focal points so that services are be tailored to reflect camp needs, in order to avoid duplications and create synergies, including the continuous development of efficient and effective referral mechanisms.

project_name: Integrated Inclusive and Protective Education and Child Protection Services in Bentiu IDP Camp
project_objective:
Given the current state of flooding in Rubkona County and much of Unity State, many families and households have been displaced, instability and fear within communities has settled, and increasingly smaller spaces of dry land are available to accommodate the competing priorities. Under such conditions, Mercy Corps proposes to leverage school infrastructure and institutional standing to enhance quality and inclusive education while expanding child protective factors of schools through intentional interventions and mainstreaming.
Mercy Corps will work to improve the equitable access to safe and protective education and community-based child protection services for 34,427 school-age children (18,049 boys and 16,378 girls), and raise the awareness and capacity of their parents and caregivers, teachers and school personnel, and other frontline and community workers who currently live in the Bentiu IDP Camp (data provided by IOM DTM population count, January 2022). 
Under the Education arm of the proposed project, Mercy Corps will support schools in enrolment of school-age children while continuing to accelerate enrolment and attendance of female pupils and children living with disabilities. To better ensure that this, Mercy Corps will work with school and community leadership to identify key barriers to education and work to remove them through targeted back to learning campaigns and events while also making schools safer and more accessible through rehabilitation of TLS blocks and school-based WASH services. Based on prior activities and community feedback, Mercy Corps will procure and distribute age-appropriate teaching and learning material, ECD kits, and recreational equipment to school locations to benefit learning and wellness outcomes. Mercy Corps will train teachers on pedagogy and inclusive teaching methodologies as well as child wellbeing and child protection mainstreaming. Mercy Corps will work with P8 school leavers through life skills and intermediary vocational development. Finally, Mercy Corps will work with school leadership structures, community partners, and education officials to strengthen emergency response capacity and mitigate the impact of emergencies on learners, teachers and communities. 
Under the Child Protection arm of the proposed project, Mercy Corps will seek to strengthen community-based child protection case management and referral services while continuing to increase engagement and capacity at the school level to identify and direct possible cases and through updated Bentiu IDP Camp referral pathways for child protective—and other protection—services. Mercy Corps will also continue to scale up Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) services in schools to ensure school spaces are protected and child friendly. Mercy Corps will work with school leadership to fit schools for multi-purpose functionality as child friendly and recreational spaces outside of the school day and as centers to enable children to enjoy the fullness of childhood. As such, Mercy Corps will tap into the resources of PTA committee members and community leaders to train them on CPiE and activate awareness campaigns and events to highlight the need for MHPSS and child wellbeing. Mercy Corps will similarly train select teachers and other frontline workers in MHPSS focused and non-focused approaches to enact low-level interventions at the school and community level while referring or elevating more specialized cases to appropriate partners. Working with local community members, Mercy Corps will continue to explore and support the revitalization of traditional games and activities to compliment the organization’s evidence based and tested MHPSS and life skills curriculum for children and adolescents. Mercy Corps will train select staff in case identification and management for children tailored to their specific needs, including the needs of unaccompanied and separated children, or child headed households.

project_name: Improving access to Comprehensive Child Protection services to support children, adolescents and families affected by conflict and violence in Pibor, Rumbek Center and East, Rumbek North Cueibet, Wulu, Yei, Kajokeji, Lainya, Morobo, Magwi, Torit, Kapoeta north &South, Malakal, Counties in South Sudan
project_objective:
The project will be implemented in Central and Eastern Equatorial, Jonglei, Lakes, Upper Nile and Western Equatorial states in the highlighted counties. This aim to improve access to comprehensive CP services including GBV and linkage to multisectoral services to benefit  children, adolescents and caregivers. Plan  has presence in the proposed locations. 2 counties (Pibor and Kapoeta South) are ranked severity 4 while the rest are under level 3. 65,000 beneficiaries (18,550 girls, 16,450 boys, 15,900 women, 14100 men). Out of 35,000 children targeted, 10000 (6000 girls, 4000 boys) are adolescescents while 15% of beneficiaries are persons  living with disability.

Beneficiaries profile includes those living in remote, insecure and hard to reach areas, IDPs, Retunees, host community , pastoralists, vulnerable adolescents including girl mothers, elderly caregivers, female headed households, UASC among others. 

Key protection risks addressed are school drop out, early and forced marriage and GBV, child labor,  family separation and neglect, prevention of recruitments, psychosocial distress and other MHPSS issues, support for persons living with disability, dangers and injuries, access to justice and access to multisectoral services.

Plan strategies to address the issues includes provision of age  gender responsive comprehensive case management including FTR, alternative family based care, cash assistance, NFI  and dignity kits to address complex needs, PSS-MHPSS for children/caregivers, positive parenting and life skills education, CP/GBV capacity building for staff, volunteers, community structures and stakeholders, tailored community awareness and dialogues on harmful cultural practices, GBV prevention and CP monitoring and coordination with actors, mainstreaming diverse feedback mechanisms including integrated helpdesks to address CP risk PSEA/safeguarding. Plan will collaborate  with Government, community structures, UNICEF, Protection cluster, CPAOR, CPWG, CMTF, UASC, PSS/MHPSS, GBV and CAAFAG WG. Others includes WASH, Education, PSEATF, shelter, WASH Etc. for service deliver.

Mixed static and mobile programming approaches including face to face and remote modalities will be integrated to allow adopting to changing needs and context especially deep field locations to support beneficiaries. Key interagency guidelines and Plan manual will be utilized for quality programming which includes revised CPMS standards, IA CM/CP/FTR/ SOPs, IA PSS working group PSS manual, CFS standards among other guidelines. 

Plan will also adopt gender transformative approach, rights based, child/survivor centered approaches to programming to address root causes of child violation and GBV to shift community attitudes and negative behaviors that harm children. Gender/disability inclusion trainings will enhance access for persons with disability. Activities integration will be prioritized in Nutrition, Education, GBV, Food Assistance, WASH to holistically address diverse needs of beneficiaries including elderly. 

COVID-19 measures will be observed per Ministry of Health/MHPSS guidelines to keep beneficiaries/ staff safe. AAP and feedback mechanisms will be integrated to address issues affecting boys, girls, men, women and enhance women and girls access to information through integrated and child friendly desks in CFS, schools, Nutrition sites etc., use of phones, girls symposiums, community feedback sessions.

safety audits, safeguarding risk assessment, community risk mapping and safe planning will strengthen centrality of protection/Protection monitoring to mitigate risks for beneficiaries and strengthen protective environment of children. Sustainability strategies includes capacity strengthening of community structures on CPIE creating pool of change agents and linking to development programs for resilience and working with NNGOs IPCS, GREDO, CHADO,SSADO and MOGCSW (Government) for planning handover and transitioning  beyond this project.

project_name: Provision of Emergency Education Services to Palestine Refugee School Children in Syria
project_objective:
In 2022 and 2023, UNRWA will continue to deliver basic, quality and inclusive education to almost 50,000 Palestine refugee students through 102 schools managed by the Agency across Syria, of which 39 are running in second-shift in buildings on loan from the Ministry of Education to compensate for UNRWA schools that have been destroyed or severely damaged by the conflict.

While schools in Syria re-opened on 2 September 2021 for in-person education, the growing number of COVID-19 cases amongst education staff and students across the country over the last quarter of 2021 highlights the challenges of preventing transmission in schools, particularly given overcrowded classrooms. Therefore, throughout the year, UNRWA will remain ready to shift to a remote or blended learning modality. Self-learning materials will continue to be updated and be available to all students.

UNRWA, through its Education in Emergencies (EiE) programme, helps to ensure that Palestine refugee children can continue to access education, even in times of emergencies. Below is a description of the key elements of the response in Syria for 2022:

1) Support to Student Access to Education: Back-to-school kits (including school bags) will be provided at the beginning of the next academic year (2022/2023); stationery will be procured and provided to students at the beginning of the 2021/2022 second semester in January 2022, to alleviate some of the economic burden faced by parents. UNRWA, will also support students returning to damaged camps such as Yarmouk and Ein el Tal by providing transport (contracted buses) to take them to schools in nearby areas. 

2) Psychosocial Support: UNRWA will continue to provide PSS to address the additional stress created by the COVID-19 pandemic. Psychosocial counsellors will be deployed in all Agency schools to provide individual and group counselling and support to students and teachers. 

3) Safe and Secure Learning Environment: A number of training sessions, incorporating COVID-19 prevention measures, will be conducted for teachers and principals on topics such as GBV, child protection and addressing violence against children (AVAC). Similar training sessions will be delivered to parents through parent-teacher associations (PTAs), which will continue to play a pivotal role in developing a holistic approach to education for Palestine refugees. 

Reusable masks will be procured and distributed to students and teachers. In addition, disinfectants and sanitizers will be provided to schools to ensure proper hygiene practices are in place. UNRWA will also conduct minor repairs to some UNRWA school facilities that require urgent maintenance. 

4) Sustaining Quality Teaching and Learning: Through this appeal, summer learning activities will be organized, contingent on the COVID-19 situation in Syria during summer 2022. In addition to academic support, the programme would include extracurricular and PSS activities to students. Support classes will be organized for Grade 9 students in preparation for official end of cycle exams. 

Printed copies of self-learning materials (SLM) will continue to be updated and made available to all students in the event that access to the Agency's Digital Learning Platform (DLP) is not available. Where needed (i.e., during school closures), UNRWA will support/subsidize internet and SMS costs for students and teachers (up to 50,000 students and 2,000 education staff), and will provide tablets/mobile devices for Grade 9 students and teachers (up to 4,550 students and 210 teachers). 

Through this project, UNRWA will cover the cost of additional temporary staff hired (up to an estimated 271 daily paid teachers and school attendants) to address the increasing needs that have arisen due to the ongoing crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic.

project_name: Primary and Secondary Health Care Support for Conflict-Affected and Displaced Populations in NES
project_objective:
With an estimated 12.4 million people in need of humanitarian health services this year, the already-disrupted health system in Syria remains under tremendous strain from concurrent emergencies: the ongoing crisis, the COVID-19 pandemic and the worsening economic situation in the country, all of which pose increased risks to health.  At the start of 2021, the Health Sector remains focused on three response priorities defined through health system, monitoring and community feedback. The IRC will deliver comprehensive lifesaving primary health care services and support to secondary level health facilities through direct and partner implementation. The IRC health 
services will reach an estimated target 132,900 vulnerable conflict-affected individuals in Raqqa, Hasakeh and Deir ezZor through 6 health care interventions including 4 static primary health care clinics (four will deliver BEmONC services), 5 mobile medical units (MMU), community health outreach and two COVID treatment centres. The targeted location includes 2 health centers in DreEzZor governorate 8 in Raqqa governorate and 9 in Hassakeh. The IRC will work in 2 static health facilities in Der Al-Zor to provide primary health care services via partners relief international in Al-Raqqa and Der Al-Zor. The static health faculties with BEMONC activities in Der Al-Zor will be supported by the Local health authoritysecondary health care (hospitals) support will be provided via partners in Al-Raqqa, Al-Hasaka and Der-Alzor, 2 MMUs in Al-Hasaka (Derek MMU, and Al-Sor MMU in Al-Hasaka Local health authority. The MMUs support will be direct support via IRC. The two isolation centers in Al-Hasaka and Qamchli will be supported by partners with local ministry of health. The IRC will be scaling nutrition health services to include extra areas as Raqqa PHCC, and MMU units in Der Alzor rural areas (Shagra). The IRC primary health care intervention integrates community health and reproductive health services and they are provided in line with the essential health service package for northern Syria and WHO guidelines for Syria. This includes prevention and management of communicable and non-communicable diseases (NCD)s, integrated management of childhood illnesses (IMCI), reproductive, maternal and child health, clinical care for sexual assault survivors (CCSAS), provision of pharmacological and nonpharmacological mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), health education and risk communication and community engagement (RCCE), and COVID-19 risk mitigation measures with strict adherence to standard infection prevention and control measures (IPC). The IRC will also continue support with COVID-isolation units and its work with implementing partners. The IRC will adopt two referral mechanisms: Internal NGO intersectoral pathway (Health- Protection-ERD), at the health facilities level between the health components (Health- MHPSS- Reproductive health-community health) and external referral pathway from the MMU and static clinics to secondary health care centers. The referral between the IRC component is tracked and documented through referral tracking tools and focal points from each component who are following the case through regular meeting. For the external referrals, the IRC uses the ambulances to transport the beneficiaries to the secondary health care and receive documented feedback about the case through accompanying medical personnel. The IRC will also contribute to disease surveillance through systematic collection, analysis and reporting of health data and weekly reporting through the Early Warning and Alert Reporting System (EWARS) to inform and support outbreak preparedness and response. In light of the COVID-19 pandemic, the IRC will aim to increase support to COVID-19 isolation units and integrate its screening, triage, and referral protocols 
throughout its health interventions. The IRC will expand (RCCE) across its health programming.

project_name: Protection and prevention services to the most vulnerable children (boys and girls) and their caregivers in the West Bank including East Jerusalem, and monitoring of protection incidents in Israel and the State of Palestine
project_objective:
This project will ensure 7,577 of the most vulnerable Palestinian children (5,525 boys and 2,052 girls aged 12-17 years old) exposed to conflict-related violence, and 4,775 caregivers are reached with protection, impact mitigation, rehabilitation, and prevention services in the West Bank. It will also foster increased respect for IHL and IHRL and accountability for violations against children through documenting and monitoring violations to inform advocacy and increase accountability.

This project is in line and contributes the three strategic objectives of the humanitarian response plan and to the Protection Cluster's first and second objectives that aim to increase respect for IHL, IHRL, and accountability for violations as well as ensuring that protection response mechanisms are in place to prevent and mitigate the effects of the occupation and conflict-related violence. 

The main objective of this child protection project is for children in the West Bank to be safe, protected, and secure from violence, exploitation, and grave violations. The project will:
•	support initiatives to engage vulnerable and at-risk children positively in structured recreational, educational, awareness-raising, life skills, and resilience-building activities to improve their resilience and coping mechanisms. 
•	support awareness-raising for vulnerable families and communities regarding children’s right to protection; preventing and responding to Violence Against Children (VAC); and the impact of stigma, social exclusion, and bullying caused by COVID-19  
•	support vulnerable children affected by conflict-related violence and their families with integration and rehabilitation services especially structured counselling and mental health and psychosocial support including through helpline services. (Level 3)
•	support monitoring, data analysis, and reporting on grave violations trends related to child protection concerns in Israel/Occupied Palestinian Territory (the WB) to provide evidence and inform advocacy. 
•	support legal assistance for children affected by conflict-related violence. 

Ensuring compliance with PSEA principles and procedures, implementing partners and project beneficiaries will be oriented on sexual exploitation and abuse and will receive information on UNICEF email, as well as other interagency channels including SAWA Free toll number, social media platforms, and WhatsApp to report on PSEA.

project_name: Enhance access to quality, timely and confidential services for GBV survivors and strengthening coordination for GBV mitigation and prevention in Somalia
project_objective:
GBV incidence continues to worsen in due to multiple displacements, forced evictions, loss of livelihoods, disruption of social and community protection systems due to floods, droughts, sacking of communities by Alshabab with significant impact on the lives and well-being of women and adolescent girls. GBV risks and exposure includes distance to water points, Schools, markets and GBV service sites. Lack of lockable latrines, poor lighting in IDPs camps and overcrowded shelters/lack of privacy.  Media and programme reports of gang rapes, homicide, forced abortion of young pregnant adolescents, attempted suicide of rape survivors and increasing levels of FGM are common place. The recent displacement in Lasánod aggravated the situation for women and girls.  More women and girls including elderly have been left without food and shelter. The displacement is coming at a time when Somali authorities are facing difficulties in containing the spread of COVID19 virus. 

Women and girls living in IDP Camps are more prone to sexual violence and abuse than those living in host communities with a better housing infrastructure and service sites and markets. The JMCNA 2021 informs that 13 percent of households were concerned that girls in host communities and 17 per cent in IDP camps were exposed to sexual violence and harassment, while 16 per cent (host community) and 18 per cent (IDP) households were concerned that girls were to be forcibly married. In addition, it was indicated that 29 percent of respondents lacked proper bathing facilities, 26 per cent poor lighting, and 14 per cent privacy in shelter; 31 per cent lacked lockable latrines; 93 per cent use common latrines that are far or not in proximity. Similarly, the GBVIMS report from January – June 2021 indicates 62 per cent of the reported GBV incidents were physical assault, 11 per cent rape, 10 per cent sexual assault, 8 per cent denial of resources, while 6 per cent psychological/emotional abuse, and the remaining 4 per cent percent forced and early marriage.

Safety concerns of adolescent for adolescent boys and men continue to worsen with severe food insecurity and prevailing armed and communal conflicts. They are subject to kidnap, forceful recruitment by armed groups. Women and adolescent girls are relying on direct cash and voucher assistance to meet basic survival and material needs to improve their resilience to mitigate/escape GBV. Given the widespread food insecurity in Somalia, there may be a possibility of vulnerable women and adolescent girls exchanging sex for food. Reliance on cash support is providing a buffer for poor families but may also contribute to rising intimate partner violence with divergent priorities for families on where to invest the cash support. Increasing population in need for GBV services, limited services provision to cover the landscape of needs is a major concern for the GBV humanitarian response in Somalia. 

UNFPA interventions will target the displaced and non-displaced communities including all age groups, women and girls living with disabilities, widowed and divorced women, married adolescents and women and adolescent girls from minority clans. Some of the key interventions will include: 1) Support access to comprehensive multi sectoral GBV services (medical, legal, psychosocial) for 6000 women and girls. 2) Strengthen the capacity/and mobilize 200 PSS counsellors; 150 health workers to provide timely, quality, and confidential PSS and rape treatment. 3)  Support the establishment 6 GBV one-stop centers in South West State, Banadir and Lasanod. 4) Provide 2,000 dignity kits and 36 post rape kits dignity protection for women and girls and treatment of rape. 5) Support 600 women and girls’ survivors of GBV with cash voucher assistance and grants for livelihood.

project_objective:
Teniendo en cuenta las necesidades humanitarias crecientes, particularmente en zonas donde el conflicto y la violencia armada son permanentes y están causando graves afectaciones a la población, el Secretariado Nacional de Pastoral Social / Cáritas Colombiana (SNPS/CC), de la mano con las Pastorales Sociales Locales de Apartadó, Pasto, Tumaco, SEPASVI, Florencia y San Vicente del Caguán, con el apoyo solidario de Cáritas Alemana y financiero del Ministerio Federal de Relaciones Exteriores de Alemania; adelantan acciones para la transferencia de capacidades orientadas a la protección y autoprotección de la población indígena, afrocolombiana y campesina en las comunidades del norte del Chocó, Nariño, a través del reconocimiento de capacidades que facilitan la identificación y gestión de los riesgos existentes en sus territorios.
Se hace especial énfasis en la vulnerabilidad frente al riesgo de accidentes por artefactos explosivos (Minas Antipersonal -MAP, Municiones Sin Explosionar -MSE y Trampas Explosivas -TE), así como desastres, dando también una respuesta a través de bienes de ayuda humanitaria en materia de seguridad alimentaria y agua e higiene.
Así mismo se acompaña de manera holística a los sobrevivientes de MAP, MSE y TE, y sus cuidadores desde los diferentes componentes en las regiones priorizadas por el proyecto. La atención a los sobrevivientes, familiares y cuidadores, se inscribe en una estrategia de desarrollo humano integral que consiste principalmente en asesoramiento jurídico para los afectados y apoyo psicosocial. Los sobrevivientes de los accidentes de las minas suelen sufrir discapacidades de por vida y también sufren consecuencias psicológicas y traumas.

project_name: Strengthening Humanitarian Coordination and Common Services in Sudan
project_objective:
According to the 2021 Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) some 14.6 million people – 31 per cent of the population – will need humanitarian assistance in 2022. This is a 1.2 million increase compared to 2021. Overall, the number of people in need in Sudan in 2022 is the highest in the past decade. The transitional government is prioritizing peace and ending the economic crisis, issues closely intertwined with the drivers of humanitarian need in the country.
While incidents of fighting have reduced considerably in recent years, the situation of people displaced due to decades of conflict remains unresolved. Some 2.9 million IDPs, 1.2 million refugees, 0.9 million returnees and 9.6 vulnerable residents continue to need humanitarian assistance and protection support, both in camps and host communities. Pockets of armed conflict continue in Darfur, and sporadic inter-communal conflicts also continue. 
Across Sudan, basic services are lacking, and natural disasters, like floods, affect people each year. But it is a deepening economic crisis, following years of stagnation and little investment in already-weak public services, that is driving worsening food insecurity, deteriorating healthcare, and other needs across Sudan. 

In 2021, Sudan faced a worsening economic crisis that will continue to drive humanitarian needs into 2022, even as the transitional government works toward economic reforms. While the transitional government is committed to stemming the economic crisis, reforms have already involved subsidy cuts which  have a further impact on families who are already struggling to cope. Basic service provision, already weak and underdeveloped, has been dangerously degraded by the economic crisis. This has affected people directly, impacting households’ ability to buy food and cover basic needs. It has also deepened already existing needs – including among existing vulnerable groups like displaced people, returnees, and refugees – and may cause new people to fall into humanitarian need

project_name: Assistance en Eau, Assainissement et Hygiène pour les déplacés et les communautés hôtes affectés par le conflit dans 3 régions du Burkina Faso (Sahel, Nord, et Centre-Nord)
project_objective:
L’aggravation de la crise sécuritaire au Burkina Faso depuis 2015 et la multiplication des incidents dans 6 régions depuis juin 2018 dues au conflit qui oppose les groupes d’opposition armés et les forces armées burkinabé d’une part et au conflit communautaire d’autre part, a occasionné des mouvements de population sans précédents au Burkina Faso (principalement dans le Sahel, le Centre-Nord, le Nord et l’Est) et a contribué à la dégradation de la situation humanitaire. Selon les derniers chiffres publiés par OCHA, le nombre de déplacés internes aurait atteint 1 407 685 personnes en Septembre 2021. Depuis le début de la crise, on a pu observer que les populations affectées ont tendance à se déplacer vers les centres urbains où ils sont pour la plupart accueillis par la communauté hôte ; ce qui occasionne une forte pression sur les infrastructures en eau et assainissement et ne favorise pas l’application des bonnes pratiques d’hygiène. Selon les MSA réalisées par SI en 2021 dans ses zones d’intervention, il apparaît que 68% des ménages PDIs enquêtés n’ont pas accès à au moins 15L/j/pers d’eau salubre et que 67% utilisent des latrines non hygiéniques ou défèquent à l’air libre.
SI est présente au Burkina Faso depuis Octobre 2018 et a déjà réalisé 247 réhabilitations de points d’eau, 3355 latrines d’urgence et communautaires, réhabilité 21 latrines institutionnelles dans les écoles, réhabilité les infrastructures d’assainissement dans 11 centres de santé, distribué plus de 37 000 kits d’hygiène pour les déplacés (dont 2700 via l’approche coupons et 1140 via transfert monétaire) et 1000 kits d’hygiène pour les enfants malnutris, sensibilisé près de 240 000 personnes aux bonnes pratiques en termes d’EHA.
Fort de cette expérience et d’une connaissance approfondie du contexte, SI propose de répondre aux besoins de    79 000 personnes affectées à travers la réalisation d’activités en Eau, Assainissement et Hygiène dans les sites d’accueil des déplacés et dans les communautés hôtes.

project_name: RÉPONSE MULTISECTORIELLE AUX RÉFUGIÉS
project_objective:
La protection internationale des réfugiés et demandeurs d’asile est au cœur du mandat du HCR (Haut-Commissariat des Nations Unies pour les Réfugiés - UNHCR), qui , en appuyant le Gouvernement du Burundi à travers l’Office National pour la Protection des Réfugiés et Apatrides (ONPRA) , s’assure que les activités d’identification des demandeurs d’asile aux frontières et leurs accès à la procédure de détermination du statut de réfugié, en particulier dans les centres de transit (CT) de Cishemere et de Rumonge ainsi que dans les camps de réfugiés et en milieu urbain, soient de qualité, afin de préserver le caractère civil et humanitaire de l’asile et de garantir la prise en charge des personnes vulnérables y compris les enfants non accompagnés et séparés, et les survivants des VBG.
Jusqu’au 31 Décembre 2021, la population totale des réfugiés et demandeurs d’asile (DA) enregistrés au Burundi est de 85 801 personnes (50,5% femmes et filles ; 49,5% hommes et garçons). La plupart d’entre eux a fui les violences dans les provinces du Sud et Nord Kivu en RDC. 37% de cette population vit en milieu urbain et 63 % sont reparties dans cinq camps : Kavumu, Bwagiriza, Kinama, Musasa et Nyankanda. Avec environ 400 nouveaux DA qui arrivent par mois, ainsi que, considérant les récents développements en RDC, le nombre des réfugiés au Burundi pourrait atteindre à environ 100 000 avec 5000 Demandeurs d’asile en 2022. L’installation des réfugiés sur les sites tiendra compte de la protection de l’environnement, aussi dans le souci de préserver un équilibre harmonieux avec les populations hôtes.
Le HCR Burundi continuera à travailler avec l'Office Nationale de Protection des Réfugiés et Apatrides (ONPRA) afin - d’améliorer les procédures d'asile et de détermination de statut des demandeurs d'asile et des réfugiés. En termes de protection, le HCR continuera à plaider pour que l'ONPRA garantisse une totale liberté de mouvement ainsi que d'autres droits et libertés fondamentaux aux réfugiés qui résident légalement sur son territoire, et qu'ils mettent fin aux arrestations et détentions arbitraires ; - et de réaliser le potentiel d'autonomisation des réfugiés tout en continuant le plaidoyer pour un cadre plus favorable à leur intégration locale qui restera une priorité. Un effort sera fait pour une meilleure autonomisation des réfugies orientée vers leur coexistence pacifique avec la population d’accueil. Le projet « Turikumwe » de la Banque Mondiale, avalisé par le HCR a pour objectif premier la promotion de projet communautaire des Refugies avec des Burundais. Dans le même ordre d’idée, le HCR Burundi, inclut dans ses projets d’intégration, la prise en charge de 20% de la population vulnérable local. Cette autonomisation se fera par le biais de projets novateurs conformes aux Objectifs de Développement Durable (ODD) et par un soutien ciblé aux initiatives en faveur des réfugiés dans les camps et en zone urbaine, incluant également les populations d'accueil, y compris les rapatriés et les personnes déplacées. L'opération du HCR au Burundi continuera à fournir des formations et à mener des campagnes de sensibilisation pour atténuer les attitudes négatives du public à l'égard des réfugiés, et pour augmenter les espaces de coexistence pacifique entre les communautés. L'enregistrement continu mettra à jour les données disponibles sur les réfugiés et les demandeurs d'asile au Burundi. Les données recueillies permettront d'affiner les recommandations de protection et de concevoir des solutions plus durables pour les bénéficiaires. Les femmes, pour des raisons sociales, sont souvent exclues de la possibilité d'exercer des activités génératrices de revenus. project_name: Increased access to nutrition sensitive food security and livelihood support to strengthen the resilience of crisis-affected vulnerable communities in Jonglei and Warrap States.
project_objective:
The proposed 2022 FSL cluster HRP highlights the gaps identified among vulnerable communities affected by crisis and in IPC 4 to 5, particularly limited access to improved high yielding vegetable and crop seeds, limited tools for farming, limited access to cash for essential food and HHs needs and inadequate fishing equipment. The project aim to provide immediate lifesaving intervention for crisis affected vulnerable communities by targeting  58,973 Fangak,15,683Tonj East and 42,609 Pibor which are  117,264(56,521m, 60743f) people (Host 50%, IDPs 30% and Returnees 20%) and 10% disable people which are in crisis due to insecurity, yearly flooding, drought and were the farming practices among the predominantly peasantry communities are very poor culminating in to problems of food insecurity, poverty and environmental degradation.
The action will provide conditional cash assistance for most vulnerable households during the 6 months lean season to enable HHs community asset creation however enabling continues access to diversified food and HHs needs. Targeted HHs provided with vegetable and crop kits for cultivation ensuring continuous access to food for a long period of time, fishing kit to complement household food needs during floods times since most flooding in this areas comes with fish mean while supporting continues fishing in areas close to rivers as fish is a rich nutritious protein source for consumption and surplus sold for income generation by the community. The project will ensure year round production of vegetable crops through recession irrigation practices during dry season and diversification of the livelihood activity options among the vulnerable communities, increasing dietary diversity for the farming community and the fishing groups. The project aimed at complimenting the current interventions in an effort to prevent an even more severe food shortage as well as strengthening the coping capacities of the vulnerable communities with special focus given to people with disabilities and chronically sick to make sure they are not left out including pregnant and lactating mothers. The project inputs will be procured and transported to the field to the field with timeliness of delivery of these inputs  very critical. Capacity building support will be conducted for selected beneficiaries and continuous practical sessions through the central demonstration gardens learning sites within the communities including health/nutrition centres. The cash beneficiaries will be trained on creation of community dykes to prevent flooding within their gardens. The project seeks to create synergies with other thematic areas such as Wash, health and nutrition of AAH and other implementing partners on ground through integrated approach. The program will also integrate with nutrition project focusing on areas of food preparation, utilization and cooking demonstration and technically supporting rolling out of training by establishment of kitchen gardens for the targeted groups. 
The project will benefit the most vulnerable households (IDPs, disable, Child-headed, chronically sick, PLW, Elderly and Female-headed households) which account for the 27.9 % households under IPC 4 and 5 suffering crisis and acute food insecurity and at high risk of malnutrition as food insecurity is likely to continue affecting these counties negatively.
The project will ensured continuous collaboration with key stakeholders including the government ministries at both county and state level to be part to support ongoing activities.
The project will target at least 60% women for support, as women are the most vulnerable group mostly involved in farming activities. The project considers Do No Harm principles by encouraging environmentally friendly activities including strategies to improve soil fertility, water tolerant crops such as rice and drought tolerant crops such as sorghum/millet will be promoted and awareness on protection against GBV provided.

project_name: Local Food production (seed distribution: cereals, legumes and vegetables) with capacity building
project_objective:
The overall estimated Sector PIN for 2022 – of food insecure and those at risk of food insecurity – is estimated at 13.9 million, with 12 million facing acute food insecurity and 1.9 million people at risk of sliding into food insecurity. The acute food insecure figure includes 1.9 million people living in camps and deemed to be 100 percent food insecure.  The water crisis in Syria has resulted in a deterioration of the food security situation for thousands of people, most notably farmers – further reducing primary food production. The continuity of socioeconomic difficulties has driven more people into food insecurity. The 2020/2021 rainfall season was significantly poor and erratic, in terms of temporal and spatial distribution, combined with a significant delay in the onset of rainfall. This was further worsened by several successive seasonal dry spells and an early cessation of rainfall, with the last rains being received in mid-April 2021. This significantly affected critical crop growth and development, especially grain filling. The seasonal constraints were also coupled with significant shortages and high cost of agriculture inputs, including diesel fuel, which resulted in limited access to water and ability to provide supplementary irrigation.
In this context, FAO has designed a project to assist 228,571 vulnerable crisis-affected food insecure farming households (equivalent to 1,371,429 people) in Syria. The objective of the proposed action is to improve access to staple foods for vulnerable farmers through increased cereal and pulse production. 
The project outputs include:
Output 1: Access to agricultural inputs to facilitate production of cereals, pulses and vegetables for 225,571 households increased. 
The response package under this output will be in line with sector recommendations for provision of 200 kg of wheat/barley seeds (adequate to plant 1 ha), 15kg NPK 10:10:10 (adequate for 0.5 ha). Or 25 to 30 kg of various legume seeds (adequate to plant approximately 0.4 0.5 ha) or 15-20 kg per dunum for vegetable will be provided per household. 

Output 2: Skills for cereal and pulses production of 228,571 targeted households enhanced. 
This output aims at building the capacity of the 228,571 households that will benefit from cereal and pulses production inputs. Beneficiaries will trains to support use of the inputs and the training programme will be built on the following FAO concepts: “Save & Grow”,

project_name: Improving access to protection services for vulnerable women men boys and girls through community based protection.
project_objective:
Somalia’s protracted humanitarian crisis is characterized by ongoing conflicts, climate-related shocks, communicable disease outbreaks and weak social protection mechanisms. The 2022 Humanitarian Needs overview highlights that 7.7Million people in need (5.5M non- internally displaced people, 2.2 Million Internally displaced people, and 0.16M refugees and asylum seekers) an increase from the 5.9 Million recorded in 2021. 
The 2022 HNO people in need for the General Protection is 2.7 million, of whom 63 per cent are children, and 49 per cent are women and girls. From January to August of 2021, the Protection Return Monitoring Network (PRMN) reported conflict as the main driver of displacement. Insecurity and conflict contribute to protection challenges such as physical attacks and threat to life, arbitrary arrest and detention, kidnapping, sexual assault, child recruitment, amongst others. This situation is exacerbated by the limited availability of basic services, and support for the victims of abuse. 
Oxfam will make direct implementation and at the same time will work local NGO partners in the implementation of the response. 
The proposed Protection package aims to increase the resilience, capacities and protective environment of the targeted communities by strengthening community-based protection mechanisms through capacity building, improving access to information and available services, awareness raising, service mapping, and referrals toward mitigating risks (including SGBV), especially for women and girls. Community-based structures, including Community Protection Volunteers, Women’s Forum, Community Committees and duty bearers will play a key role in the project. A protection analysis will be conducted in the target locations to identify existing (strategic and practical) needs and dynamics, vulnerabilities, and threats faced by women, men, boys, and girls. 
Though the community based protection approach a community lighting initiatives will be implemented during the action to improve community safety and dignity and reduce protection threats faced by crises affected communities speciﬁcally women and girls in IDPs settlement and vulnerable host communities. Other materials including wheelbarrows will be provided to most vulnerable households to reduce work burden resulted by changing gender roles due to the crises which make the work of women and girls more demanding, e.g fetching water and ﬁrewood collection which in most cases they travel in long distances. In addition this material provision will reduce the frequency of risk exposure and will contribute community cohesion to strengthen community self- protection mechanisms.
Mapping existing services will improve access to information, establishing protection reporting mechanisms, a referral system, and training community volunteers to reduce protection vulnerabilities while increasing the capacities of the target population, who will be able to make informed decisions. Further the action will establish women forums to balance traditional male dominated structures and create safe space for women and girls discuss protection issues. The  issues identiﬁed by women groups will then be incorporated systematically into Community Action Plans for further actions and advocacies aiming to strength women’s engagement in community decision making process to address speciﬁc issues affecting them.Oxfam is fundamentally committed to ensuring accountability to affected people. Women, men, girls, and boys within target beneficiaries will be directly involved at all stages of the project cycle in order to encourage community ownership and participation in project activities. Gender protection analysis will be carried out to inform program implementation. Separate consultations will be conducted for different gender groups including persons with disabilities , clan affiliated minorities and other marginalized groups including women and girls.

project_name: Réponse aux besoins urgents en Eau, Hygiène et Assainissement (EHA) et amélioration de l’accès aux services EHA au profit des populations affectées par la crise humanitaire causée par les conflits dans les régions du Centre Nord et du Sahel au Burkina Faso
project_objective:
Les régions du Centre-Nord et du Sahel durement touchées par la crise sécuritaire comptent parmi les plus affectées par les crises humanitaires et constituent à elles seules plus de 68% (960022 PDIs) des PDI (personnes déplacées internes) du pays. La présence de ces PDIs majoritairement installées dans des familles d´accueil affecte l’accès aux services WASH déjà fragilisé par une insuffisance des ressources notamment en eau et des défis structurels accroissant ainsi le risque des maladies hydriques et de conflits liés à l’accès à l’eau. Oxfam et ses partenaires mènent une réponse d´urgence multisectorielle dans les régions du Centre-Nord et du Sahel depuis décembre 2018. Depuis lors, les actions sont menées par les équipes sur place couplées à des analyses de données permettent de réaliser une évaluation approfondie des besoins des populations, en incluant une dimension protection et genre.
Avec la conjugaison de la crise humanitaire résultant des différentes crises sécuritaires et la pandémie du COVID-19 depuis mars 2020, Burkina Faso comptera plus de 3,4 millions de personnes dans le besoin humanitaire WASH.
La situation dans les régions du Centre Nord et Sahel, théâtre d’importants mouvements de populations, favorise la propagation rapide de l’épidémie car le déplacement interne de populations augmente le risque d'infection de la population en raison de la densité et des mauvaises conditions de vie. Les très faibles niveaux d'assainissement et d'accès à l'eau potable constituent un facteur aggravant dans la transmission des maladies 
En 2022, sur la base de ces évaluations OXFAM et ses partenaires entendent continuer leurs actions dans ces deux zones à travers le projet intitulé « Réponse aux besoins urgents en Eau, Hygiène et Assainissement (EHA) et amélioration de l’accès aux services EHA au profit des populations affectées par la crise humanitaire causée par les conflits dans les régions du Centre Nord et du Sahel au Burkina Faso ». Au regard de l’ancrage de la crise humanitaire et l’absence de perspective de retour des PDIs, ce projet vise à assurer une couverture des besoins urgents et prioritaires en EHA des populations affectées (hôtes et PDI) tout en améliorant l’accès aux services EHA dans les zones d’accueil pour faire face aux conséquences des afflux continus de PDIs
Le projet est basé sur les principes et normes humanitaires (CHS, SPHERES), et intégrera les aspects suivants :
Protection: Une analyse des pouvoirs et des risques sera réalisée afin d’identifier les menaces pour les différents groupes vulnérables (filles, femmes, jeunes, personnes handicapées et vivant avec le VIH/SIDA) parmi les populations IDPs et hôtes vulnérables. Ces analyses seront réalisées de façon participative afin d’assurer l’appropriation et l’autonomisation progressive des populations IDPs et hôtes.
Nexus : Le projet est aligné avec le triple Nexus (humanitaire – développement – paix) car Oxfam intègre cela dans sa stratégie. Il créera ainsi des liens avec les actions de relèvement et de développement en cours dans les régions ciblées, notamment entre les aspects de développement du leadership humanitaire local et la gouvernance locale. Par ailleurs, Oxfam associe la question de la consolidation de la paix qui sera un pilier de la stratégie de réponse d´urgence pour 2022. Cet aspect permettra sur le long terme, de promouvoir un environnement favorable à la pacification au Burkina Faso.
Le leadership humanitaire local : Oxfam au Burkina Faso assure la promotion du rôle des organisations locales et des collectivités territoriales dans le travail humanitaire comme priorité : délégation de la mise en œuvre des actions humanitaires aux partenaires; recrutement et mise à disposition de staff programmatique et support pour les partenaires dont la bonne connaissance de la zone et des acteurs locaux permettra de favoriser l’acceptance des actions avec les communautés et les autorités locales.

project_name: Seguridad alimentaria y medios de vida para la población afectada por la situación humanitaria en Venezuela
project_objective:
El proyecto está conformado por cuatro ejes principales, basado en las necesidades identificadas, población vulnerable y la experiencia de intervenciones actualmente implementándose. NRC tiene la capacidad de adaptar y ampliar sus proyectos, aportando y proponiendo: 

A) Proveer de insumos, herramientas y asistencia técnica que ayude a mejorar la producción y construcción de capacidades en centros educativos que tienen componente técnico agropecuario, con niños, niñas y adolescentes, así como las comunidades aledañas. Esto conlleva el fortalecimiento del modelo productivo orgánico, auto-suficiente y sostenible que sirva de modelo para replicar a nivel de pequeños productores. Entre otras cosas se contempla la entrega de ganado vacuno, ovino, porcino, pollos y gallinas, sistemas de producción de queso; ordeños mecánicos; restauración y rehabilitación de espacios para pasto, siembra, gallineros, jardines, semilleros, viveros, dotación de semillas, tanques de agua y sistemas de riego; alimentos para ganado y animales de granja. Así como todo tipo de apoyo en el área técnica agropecuaria, emprendimiento y capacidad técnica para jóvenes, en sinergia y de forma complementaria con otros proyectos sectoriales ASH, educación, protección, bajo el modelo integral de intervención de NRC. 

B) Concienciación en hábitos de vida saludables y apoyo técnico a hogares en riesgo de inseguridad alimentaria (réplica de modelos productivos exitosos, construyendo capacidades, sostenibilidad y auto-producción ecológica). Se promueve un cambio cultural respecto a hábitos saludables a través de una intervención integral y complementaria, para ayudar en la toma de conciencia sobre la importancia de una buena alimentación, preparación y cocinado, huertos familiares y comunitarios, comedores y ollas comunitarias para personas en tránsito, personas de la tercera edad y/o niños, entrega de semillas, mejora de riego, cultivos y métodos alternativos. 

C) Apoyo a las escuelas y familias de los alumnos: niños y adolescentes. Trabajo conjunto y complementario con proyectos de educación (comedores escolares) en la que se alcanza la mejora de la asistencia escolar, unido a la mejora en las condiciones de seguridad alimentaria de las familias y comunidad. Integral y articulado con proyectos de protección y ASH. 

D) Distribuciones de bolsas de alimentos. Dirigidas a grupos más vulnerables identificados, NRC distribuye una canasta de alimento para atender los gastos calóricos necesarios para 2 o 3 meses de una familia con 4 personas en promedio. Particularmente, las modalidades de asistencia se adaptarán según las necesidades de la población y respetando cualquier riesgo sanitario que pueda afectar a los beneficiarios.

project_name: Mejora de los servicios esenciales de Agua, Saneamiento e Higiene de las personas en situación de desplazamiento afectadas directa o indirectamente por la situación humanitaria
project_objective:
NRC Venezuela tiene como objetivo reducir riesgos de salud pública y la prevención de enfermedades relacionadas con el agua y el saneamiento inadecuados, garantizando el acceso al derecho al agua y al saneamiento, reduciendo los riesgos de protección ligados a la situación humanitaria en Venezuela. El programa ASH propone modalidades de (a) respuesta de emergencia, (b) respuesta con soluciones duraderas basada en un enfoque comunitario, y (c) una respuesta Integrada con otros programas de NRC tales como: Educación e ICLA. 

 

La respuesta ASH de NRC continuará incluyendo la provisión de un mínimo de servicios ASH durante la Respuesta de Emergencia (COVID-19 y crisis humanitaria venezolana). Por otro lado, durante la Respuesta con Soluciones Duraderas se pretende mejorar la resiliencia en comunidades meta, fomentando la participación de comunidades en el diseño e implementación del programa, desarrollando sus capacidades locales, y asegurando la sostenibilidad del programa. 

 

La componente de AGUA incluirá: (a) Provisión de agua segura (a nivel del hogar) a través de kits de tratamiento de agua para el hogar y/o kits de manejo de agua) y rehabilitación y sistema de tratamiento de agua a nivel comunitario; (b) Provisión de capacitación y sensibilización (tratamiento, calidad del agua y uso seguro). 

 

La componente de SANEAMIENTO incluirá: (a) Provisión de baterías de baños y duchas culturalmente apropiadas, desagregados por género y estaciones de lavado de manos. Las instalaciones se ubicarán en áreas públicas o institucionales en zonas clave de flujo migratorio; (b) Provisión de kits NFIs de saneamiento (mantenimiento / limpieza); (c)Provisión de contenedores de basura para gestión de residuos sólidos. 

 

La componente de HIGIENE incluirá: (a) Provisión de kits de dignidad e higiene, junto con sensibilizaciones sobre su uso apropiados; (b)Provisión de campañas de sensibilización sobre higiene personal, prevención de enfermedades, higiene menstrual y protección; (c) Creación, capacitación y sensibilización de comités ASH en colegios y comunidades que servirán como apoyo a la promoción de higiene. La respuesta ASH de NRC pretenden ser Integradas a otros programas como el de Educación que apunta a una mejora de la calidad de la educación, inclusivas e integradas con el programa ASH centrándose en la mejora de la infraestructura ASH, para garantizar las instalaciones satisfagan las necesidades de todos los grupos de NNAs, profesores y personas con discapacidad.

project_name: Support in rebuilding resilience of the most vulnerable conflict and disaster-affected people through improving access to appropriate shelter and lifesaving Non-Food Items (SNFI)s services across South Sudan.
project_objective: Through a multisectoral approach and the static team based in the field area, DRC will improve access on Shelter and Non-Food Items Services to the most affected vulnerable women-headed households, the elderly, persons with specific needs boys and girls across South Sudan. The project targets to mitigate exposure to weather elements and disease-causing vectors through the provision of cash and voucher assistance for Shelter and NFIs, provision of in-kind Non-Food Items assistance using the DRC static team based in Malakal, and emergency SNFI support and emergency shelters to crisis-affected populations in hard-to-reach locations across South Sudan. Through the multisectoral teams, the project will manage to safeguard the right to an adequate standard of living to promote safety and dignity through addressing specific needs of women, girls, boys, and men. According to the shelter-NFI cluster strategy, DRC will continue supporting coordination and participating in joint missions to avoid duplication to improve resource sharing and timely response. DRC will seek the support of the SNFI cluster Core pipeline with SNFIs items to support the affected populations. DRC will adhere to the SNFI cluster guideline and priorities, focusing on responses guided by assessments and further post-distribution monitoring to allow feedback and learning for project and response improvement.

project_name: Flexible Mine Action response supporting emergency, recovery and resilience needs in South Sudan
project_objective:
DRC will deploy 2 highly mobile Multi-Task Teams (MTTs), to respond to urgent threats to physical safety, dignity, freedom of movement and access to humanitarian assistance within communities. Additionally, DRC will deploy 5 Teams focused on delivering Explosive Ordnance Risk Education (EORE) to conflict-affected communities to further mitigate risks of explosive hazards. The proposed project aims at:

•	Providing immediate lifesaving assistance to address the urgent protection needs of the most vulnerable (including women, children, elderly, disabled and survivors of ERW in conflict) in hard-to-reach areas.
•	Enhancing prevention and preparedness programming to mitigate risks and strengthen resilience
•	Enabling durable solutions for IDPs and other affected populations

Tasks that will support the humanitarian response in the country will be prioritized through the following key activities:

•	Non-Technical Survey (NTS) and Technical Survey (TS) – NTS and will be conducted to target and prioritize clearance according to humanitarian need. Surveys will be conducted using a mixture of key informant interviews and household questionnaires held with the local population and authorities. NTS will determine the likely locations and density of ERW contamination in target locations, whilst assessing the impact of these hazards on vulnerable populations in any given location. TS (using detectors) will be used upon discovery of an area with a high concentration of explosive hazards.
•	Manual Mine Clearance (MMC) / Battle Area Clearance (BAC) - the MTTs will be able to act as a MMC / BAC capacity, performing static clearance activities across larger, clearly defined areas (identified through the above data collection activities and technical survey as appropriate).
•	Explosive ordnance disposal (EOD) – once NTS has determined the nature of the threat, technical capacities within the teams will be deployed to remove and destroy identified hazards.
•	Explosive Ordnance Risk Education (EORE) – all teams will contain a capacity to deliver risk messaging, toraise awareness about how to recognize dangerous items. as the risk education will emphasize safe practices that should be followed, and high risk behaviour that should be avoided in relation to mines and explosive remnants of war.

project_name: Creating a Protective Environment for People of South Sudan through safeguarding, respecting their rights and finding solutions
project_objective:
In response to identified priority needs of and protection service provision, DRC will deliver this integrated protection (General Protection, HLP, GBV, and Child Protection) project with solutions mainstreamed for conflict and displacement affected communities. The aim is to creating a protective environment for women, men, girls and boys of South through safeguarding, respecting rights and finding solutions. DRC will implement protection activities including in hard to reach locations through both static, outreach and mobile modalities. In doing so DRC aims to contribute to the overarching intersectoral strategic objectives for the 2022 HRP through contributing to the protection cluster strategic objectives too.
The proposed sub-sectors and activities will ensure provision of critical protection related assistance through an integrated approach to address priority needs of targeted communities, women, men, girls and boys in hard-to-reach and priority geographical areas. The project will mainstream durable solutions whilst enhanced protection assessments and monitoring will inform protection and overall humanitarian response. 
DRC also currently has 2 Mobile Protection Teams that respond to emergencies in hard to reach locations where there are limited services and high needs thus under GP. These mobile teams will also provide General Protection services. The target locations are country wide, hard-to-reach and recommended by the Protection Cluster for short response or semi-static response – in coordination with the Cluster. The Mine Action under Humanitarian Disarmament and Peacebuilding (HDP) has two highly Mobile Task Teams (MTTs) and Five teams who will be deployed to focus on delivering Explosive Ordinance Risk Education (EORE). GBV prevention and response activities will be implemented through static and outreach in Unity and Upper Nile State. Child Protection activities by DRC will be implemented through partners focusing but focusing in Jonglei State and Greater Pibor Administrative Area. Proposed activities in this integrated protection project are as follows: 
1.	Protection monitoring, assessments and analysis. This with include Non-Technical Surveys (NTS) and Technical surveys (TS) under MA, safety audits, conflict analysis, and rapid gender and inclusion analysis for the project.  
2.	Manual Mine Clearance (MMC)/Battle Area Clearance (BAC); Explosive Ordinance Disposal (OED); and). 
3.	Information Dissemination and Awareness raising on rights, entitlements, assistance opportunities GBV issues, Child protection issues, HLP rights, available services, Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA), Peacebuilding issues, etc. 
4.	Strengthening community-based protection structures like women committees, Community Protection Committees, community-based protection networks, Community based child protection structures and networks. 
5.	Comprehensive Case Management (GBV) and (CP) and provision of psychosocial support
6.	Integrated GBV prevention and response with GBV risk mitigation 
7.	Individual Protection Assistance (IPA) in-kind of material or cash.
8.	 Comprehensive Case Management for GBV survivors and Child Survivors. 
9.	Supporting community co-existence, facilitating peacebuilding dialogues, 
10.	Capacity building of staff, partners, and local authorities and leaders on GBV core messages, CPiE, Peacebuilding, ADR, HLP, according to available IASC standards, PSEA Cluster SOPs, DRC tools, among others.
Evidence-based programming and advocacy across the response in will be supported through regular protection monitoring and protection assessments based on pre-identified triggers, with mechanisms to ensure inclusion of persons with specific needs such as persons living with disabilities, elderly people, young men at risk, adolescent girls at risk, and female headed households. 
DRC will integrate community-based protection in refugee and livelihoods programming in Jamjam. DRC will support safe programming.

project_name: Prestación de Servicios de Prevención, Respuesta y Apoyo que salvan vidas en Salud Sexual y Reproductiva y Violencia Basada en Género para las mujeres y adolescentes más vulnerables en 10 estados priorizados de Venezuela.
project_objective:
El proyecto plantea proteger y garantizar el acceso  a los Derechos de Salud Sexual y reproductiva y al derecho a vivir una vida libre de violencia de las mujeres y adolescentes más vulnerables, incluidas embarazadas afectadas por la crisis, a través de una estrategia intersectorial para la prestación de servicios esenciales de SSR y prevención y respuesta a la VBG que salvan vidas y promueven el bienestar, en 10 estados priorizados  de Venezuela (Anzoátegui, Apure, Bolívar,Delta Amacuro, Distrito Capital, Miranda, Sucre, Táchira y Zulia) alcanzando a un total de  544.633 personas.  El proyecto está alineado con los objetivos sectoriales OE1.1 y OE 1.2 del Clúster de salud y O.E 1 y E.O.3 del Clúster de Protección. 

Está acorde a la estrategia  concertada del Ministerio del Poder Popular para la Salud para la  disminución de muertes maternas. Dando continuidad a  acciones realizadas desde 2019, para el fortalecimiento del Sistema Público Nacional de Salud,  mejorando  el acceso a los servicios de SSR a  oportunos y de calidad a 350.800 mujeres , para la prevención de morbimortalidad materna, embarazo no deseado, infecciones de transmisión sexual (ITS),disminución de la  Sífilis congénita , transmisión vertical del VIH, y violencia sexual. Se pretende dejar capacidades instaladas en  27 hospitales y 81  centros de la red de Atención Primaria en Salud promoviendo los servicios y suministros, a través de reforzar capacidades del   talento humano a  3520 personal de salud,  provisión de anticonceptivos,  equipos, insumos, medicamentos, pruebas diagnósticas rápidas , EPP y ejecución de  las rehabilitaciones necesarias para disponibilidad de agua y luz en la atención de emergencias obstétricas. Se incluyen acciones para la respuesta intersectorial a la VBG en el MCVS  con el  acondicionamiento  de los espacios ,dotación de insumos, medicamentos, PEP Kit  y capacitación al personal que brinda la atención.

Se pretende facilitar el acceso a estos  servicios integrales de respuesta multisectorial a la VBG desde un enfoque centrado en la persona sobreviviente, con énfasis en la violencia sexual, mientras se reducen y mitigan los riesgos de VBG. 
Se beneficiará directamente a 68.962 personas [46731 mujeres], [10.210 niñas] y adolescentes], [46.731 hombres] y [4480 son jóvenes], a través de 5 objetivos estratégicos: 
1)Proporcionar asistencia y servicios de protección especializados, incluyendo gestión de casos, apoyo psicosocial y orientación jurídica a 3290 sobrevivientes. 
2) Fortalecer los mecanismos y capacidades de prevención de la VBG en comunidades y el cambio comportamental de 49.862 personas a través de estrategias de prevención de la VBG. Asimismo, se estima cubrir las necesidades esenciales de higiene y salud reproductiva de mujeres y adolescentes mediante la distribución de 15.000 KD y empoderar a las comunidades en materia de SSR mediante sensibilizaciones en DSSR. 
3) Contribuir a la restauración de los medios de vida y mejorar la resiliencia de 150 mujeres a través del establecimiento de 13 ESMN.
 4)Fortalecer las capacidades de 660 personal humanitario y de instituciones públicas, en enfoque centrado en las sobrevivientes y la entrega de asistencia material a 130 instituciones públicas para la respuesta a la VBG. 
5) Fortalecer los mecanismos de coordinación de las intervenciones de GBV, la actualización regular de las rutas de remisiones y POEs, creación de grupos temáticos de trabajo y armonización de la data de VBG a través del roll out del sistema GBVIMS en Venezuela. 
 
Asimismo,  se fomentará la resiliencia comunitaria a través de acciones que permitan mayores niveles de información y participación, con sensibilización e información en temas de promoción de la SSR, signos de alarma durante el embarazo, prevención de Covid 19, integrando los enfoques de género, edad y diversidad.

project_name: Asistencia humanitaria en agua y promoción de la higiene por emergencia para 5 municipios del corredor seco de Guatemala.
project_objective:
La respuesta se enfocará en 5 municipios de 2 departamentos del corredor seco de Guatemala donde los sistemas de agua fueron dañados por eventos naturales o ampliaciones para el mejoramiento de los mismos. La implementación será a través de socios nacionales o locales que coordinarán y fortalecerán a las municipalidades y comunidades buscando que mejoren sus capacidades de respuesta a emergencia, vincularse al desarrollo con sistemas de información pertinentes y oportunos en cuanto a WASH se refiere. 
Se realizarán sistemas de agua y saneamiento sostenibles con participación activa de las partes, que incluyan el enfoque de resiliencia, vinculado con actividades de cambio de comportamiento de manera inclusiva y participativa. La orientación del proyecto es a personas con mayor vulnerabilidad como población rural, mujeres, niñas y personas con
discapacidad.
Además, se coordinará con los clústeres de nutrición, salud, educación y protección para generar una respuesta cohesiva e integral y generar sinergia con las otras acciones que se integran dentro de este proyecto, las principales acciones se realizarán en conjunto con
UNICEF y ONU Mujeres.
Las acciones más relevantes son:
- Fortalecimiento de capacidades para la sostenibilidad de los sistemas a funcionarios municipales de WASH, responsables de AOM de sistemas comunitarios e integrantes del hogar en sistemas unifamiliares.
- Rehabilitación, mejora y construcción de sistemas de agua a escala familiar y comunitaria.
- Mejora de la calidad de agua en sistemas en hogar, comunidad, escuelas y
establecimientos de salud.
- Promoción y vinculación del triple nexo en acciones WASH relacionados con captación de agua lluvia, uso de recursos hídricos, tratamiento de aguas para consumo y residuales para reciclado.
- WASH en escuelas y establecimientos de salud abordando las necesidades de higiene menstrual.
- Campañas de comunicación para promover la práctica de hábitos de higiene, desinfección, uso y manipulación del agua.
