project_name: Early recovery support to conflict-affected communities across Northern Syria
project_objective:
The proposed project aims at restoring rural and urban livelihoods for conflict-affected communities across Northern Syria. ACTED will provide a variety of support modalities in targeted communities, including short-term income opportunities through Cash-for-Work schemes; sustainable restoration of basic services and value chain through the repair, installation and rehabilitation of key assets including productive assets, such as irrigation canals, water stations, roads and schools; livelihoods support and market recovery through grants and training to small-to-mid-scale businesses as well as farmers and livestock holders. ACTED will continue its Area-Based Approach in six communities across Northern Syria, providing multi-sectoral assistance and building the capacity of local stakeholders toward community-driven response plans focused on early recovery and resilience-building. ACTED aims to reach a total of 621,151 individuals through this project in 2022. By fostering early recovery across areas of intervention where needs are acute, ACTED will also contribute to limiting pull factors into IDP camps.

With regards to road rehabilitation, ACTED will also conduct rehabilitation works on certain roads connecting IDP camps in Northwest Syria, ensuring safe and continued access to these camps by residents, service providers, and relief organizations. With regards to grant support to businesses, ACTED will deliver small-scale grants ranging from 500 to 1,000 USD to micro-businesses as well as small-scale agri-businesses, while larger, transformational businesses will receive on average 6,210 USD.

For cash-based approaches, ACTED will coordinate through the relevant Cluster / Working Group with other aid providers operating in its areas of implementation, so as to ensure harmonization in the value of the assistance distributed, thereby avoiding creating tensions or undesirable pull factors. ACTED will systematically conduct assessments and consult local stakeholders prior to implementation. ACTED will apply this approach for cash-for-work schemes, ensuring the relevant of proposed activities to local needs  and avoiding the disruption of the local labor market, as well as for business support schemes, ensuring that supported businesses are connected to local, functioning markets with an existing demand. In all areas where cash-based modalities are rolled out, ACTED will avoid creating tensions at the community and households levels through community engagement in the form of representative Focus Group Discussions ahead of implementation.

project_name: Addressing food insecurity of conflict-affected communities in Northern Syria
project_objective: The proposed project aims at improving food security of conflict-affected communities in Northeast and Northwest Syria. This will be achieved through a combination of different complementary interventions at the individual household and community-level. At the household level, emergency responses assistance will be delivered through distribution of in-kind food baskets, Ready-to-Eat Rations and Cash-for-food assistance, reaching 76,334 individuals overall, including recently displaced persons. In addition, ACTED will enhance food production at HH level, through kitchen and home garden kits for 858 HHs, enhancing individuals' food security. These activities will be completed by Nutritional Awareness Sessions which will strengthen HHs’ ability to make informed choices regarding nutritional values. ACTED will also target 33,132 farmers and livestock holders with longer-term support, delivering agricultural inputs to redeem seeds, fertilizers, polytunnels and tools, and training on climate-smart agriculture and best practices. ACTED will also provide solar energy equipment to two water pumping stations to ensure the pumping of water into irrigation canals, necessary for agriculture. All project activities will be designed in a way that enables resilience to be built at a local level and that builds the capacity of men, women, boys, and girls to access basic items and meet basic needs themselves. Specifically, at the household and community levels, ACTED will support men and women in building their own capacities to meet their basic needs so that they are more resilient and better able to access commodities and services in the future. Lastly, ACTED will work in coordination with local technical department with the aim of building their capacity to provide essential services for communities. This project is estimated to benefit 193,312 individuals overall.

project_name: Protecting Civilians through Humanitarian Mine Action in Syria
project_objective:
The humanitarian crisis in Syria has been exacerbated by the widespread use of explosive ordnance (EO), posing significant risks and requiring different mitigation strategies to reduce its impact on the civilian population and the humanitarian sector delivering aid to those in need. While the full scale of contamination is not known, preliminary findings for the 2022 Humanitarian Needs Overview estimate that around 10.2 million, that is to say, 1 in 2 people is at risk from EO, and a third of communities are potentially contaminated. EO contamination in essential civilian infrastructure, agricultural land, roads, and private property is a lethal barrier to a safe movement which deprives civilians of accessing essential basic services, hampers delivery of humanitarian assistance, endangers those seeking refuge from violence or returning to their areas, and precludes resumption of livelihood activities, thus amplifying the social and economic crisis aggravated by the COVID-19 pandemic. A comprehensive humanitarian mine action response is a humanitarian necessity and vital precursor for delivering humanitarian aid and early recovery.
Mine action is a key humanitarian priority and enabler for the wider humanitarian response and is  critical enablers for safe delivery of humanitarian assistance, The overall aim of UNMAS project is to reduce the impact of EO on the civilian population and humanitarian workers through effective sector coordination and implementation of humanitarian mine action activities, in line with humanitarian priorities as identified in the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP), and within the framework of agreements between the Syrian State and UN agencies, funds and programs, as well as Security Council resolution 2585 (S/RES/2585, 2021). Under this project, in accordance with the HRP, UNMAS will lead, manage and coordinate humanitarian mine action activities as defined by International Mine Action Standards (IMAS). All components of humanitarian mine action (risk education, victim assistance, survey and clearance) remain critical, but in 2022-2023, UNMAS will focus on expanding survey and clearance, as the only way to permanently remove the threat posed by EO and subject to access and funding. UNMAS will also continue the  delivery of EO Risk Education (EORE), tailored to age, gender, localized threats, and activity patterns of different at-risk groups,  a critical, life-saving activity for raising the awareness of civilians and humanitarian personnel about the dangers of EO, thus directly contributing to HRP strategic objective 1: “Save Lives'' and strategic objective 2: “Enhance Protection.”  As the Syrian crisis has been characterized by large-scale conflict and displacement, survey, data collection, and mapping of EO are critical to informing humanitarian programming, needs-based prioritization, and the expansion of clearance to remove the contamination threats, particularly in high-humanitarian priority areas. UNMAS will support the expansion of victim assistance also and the provision of specialized services for persons with disabilities, including survivors of EO and their families, thus contributing to strategic objective 3: “Increase Resilience and Access to Services”

project_name: Education in Emergency Integrated support of vulnerable boys and girls in Syria
project_objective: INTERSOS Action tackles identified problems and unmet needs through an EiE response targeting the most vulnerable population in areas with high severity conditions in Hama, RD, Idleb Governorates where INTERSOS is already present with protection and health interventions. In line with 2022-2023 Syria Education Sector Response Plan, the Action aims to improve 1) safe and equitable availability and access to formal and NFE services; 2) enhance the quality of formal and Non Formal teaching and learning; 3) enhance education system and communities’ to support a timely, coordinated and evidence based education response. During 2022-2023 INTERSOS aims at outreaching a total number of 18070 beneficiaries (B7502; G8128; M1220; W1220). The programme is starting in January 2022 and will be continuing throughout 2022-2023. INTERSOS is building on evidence-based support of the formal school system in Syria provided in the 2nd half of 2021 and on its extensive expertise in the delivery of NFE in the Middle East region. INTERSOS is currently working under a bilateral MoU signed with MoE in June 2021 and under the broader MoU with SARC. INTERSOS carries out integrated actions where Protection and CP principles are mainstreamed along with GBV preventive messages. INTERSOS work through multiple approaches promoting boys and girls ACCESS to formal and NFE through: hard components (school rehabilitations, provision of emergency prefab classrooms, furniture), SLP, remedial classes (after school for children at risk of drop out and in learning center for OOSC), adolescents' clubs. INTERSOS promotes an inclusive environment enhancing access and structural accessibility (including WASH) of CwDs (1250) and providing the community with the skills to support CwDs inclusion in the learning environment. Education and hygiene kits are delivered to all the children enrolling in the classes (stationary and SLP). INTERSOS is focusing on girls’ continuation of learning preventing adolescent girls drop out also through the distribution of adolescents’ dignity kits. Classes are arranged based on a flexible schedule to accommodate the needs of children supporting the family with work/house chores. Regular classes are alternated with PSS group sessions and individual counselling is provided in order to promote boys and girls’ wellbeing and retention. QUALITY of teaching and learning is promoted through training to formal and NFE personnel on Active Learning, Inclusive Education, Curriculum and Planning, Pedagogy, Teachers’ role and well-being, CP principles (last 4 subjects are already included in INEE standard TiCC training). INTERSOS has developed a response strategy based on a strong COMMUNITY-BASED APPROACH coupled with a robust capacity building programme to enhance the quality of services delivered to the affected individuals. PTAs are established and/or supported and their members trained on: CP elements, PSEA, Safe identification and referral, education outreach and monitoring, gender mainstreaming in education. Once trained they become the first initiators of: i. PTAs led initiatives and ii. Back to Learning (B2L). Through consultations with the community and HHs assessments, the education outreach volunteers identify OOSC and individual causes for being OOS. Such methodology promotes the definition of individual pathways for re-enrolment through NFE. Finally, INTERSOS is fully integrating health and hygiene promotion and infection prevention and control in its action providing holistic knowledge and capacities to the targeted schools through training and awareness and promoting the knowledge and respect of the school Health Protocol. INTERSOS targets the most vulnerable boys and girls at risk of drop out and OOSC privileging overage students, adolescents’ girls and boys, IDPs and CwDs based on clear vulnerability criteria with an holistically integrated response with Protection, Health (MHUs school visit) and ERL.

project_name: Assistance d'urgence aux personnes déplacées dans les régions de Tahoua et Tillabéry
project_objective: Dans le cadre du HRP 2021, partant de la stratégie du GTABNA et en étroite collaboration avec le Ministère de l’Action Humanitaire, l'OIM poursuit l'objectif général de contribuer à l'amélioration les conditions de vie des populations. En particulier des populations déplacées vulnérables victimes des crises armées et l'activisme de GANEs spécialement dans les zones frontalières, dans les régions de Tahoua et de Tillabéry, par la fourniture d'abris d'urgence et de Biens Non Alimentaires. En tant que Co-Lead du Cluster,  l'OIM va contribuer au  renforcement de la coordination du Groupe de travail Abris et Biens Non Alimentaires, renforcer la collecte des informations, d'informer les intervenants sur la localisation, la nature et l'ampleur des besoins exprimés, sensibiliser les partenaires et membres du secteur à mener les activités dans le respect de la stratégie du secteur et les principes humanitaires et d'appuyer les services étatiques locaux dans leurs rôles de coordination et suivi des activités du secteur. La situation sécuritaire dans les régions de Tahoua et Tillabéry étant toujours volatile, le GTABNA reste attentif à tout mouvement de population et suit la situation au travers des annonces de sécurité, les MSA de RRM et le monitoring de protection du cluster protection fournissant les informations indicatives à la réponse en abris d’urgence et Biens Non Alimentaires.  Partant de la cible du HRP 2022, le secteur abris et bien non alimentaire mettra à disposition 7 000 kits abris d’urgence et 7 000 kits BNA en vue de répondre aux nouveaux mouvements de population, aux mouvements secondaires ainsi qu'au renouvèlement des abris détériorés des ménages. L’assistance basée sur la vulnérabilité ciblera également les familles hôtes vulnérables. Sur base de la stratégie du Secteur abris/BNA et dépendamment de la faisabilité, les interventions pourront se faire en transfert monétaires conditionnels. Cette modalité offrira la réduction considérable des coûts logistiques qui sont très élevés en période hivernale à cause du mauvais état des routes et permettra de résoudre le problème d’accès lié à l'insécurité qui retarde les interventions. Les activités de la réponse d'urgence se conformeront aux Principes de Protection transversales et au Cadre institutionnel de l'OIM de lutte contre les violences basées sur le genre en situation de crise (GBV), intégrera des mesures visant à assurer la sécurité, la dignité et le bien-être de la population touchée. Ce projet s'inscrira dans le respect des principes humanitaires et portera une attention particulière au principe ne pas nuire, de sécurité et non-discrimination. Les activités du projet seront mises en œuvre dans le respect soutenu des règles de lutte contre la COVID-19 par l'observation de mesures barrières telles que le port du masque, le lavage des mains, le respect de la distanciation sociale afin d'endiguer tout risque de contamination et de propagation de la maladie auprès des bénéficiaires. Dans le cadre de la redevabilité des sessions d'information sur le projet seront organisées avec les bénéficiaires, la phase d'évaluation des besoins sera réalisée de commun accord avec les populations dans les communes ciblées, la communication avec les communautés et les autorités locales sur les critères de ciblage seront organisées et après intervention, les feedbacks de la communauté cible seront collectés à travers des évaluations post-distribution et des séances de discussion de groupe séparées par genre et âge avant et après l'assistance. Aussi, en tant qu’acteur humanitaire, l'OIM et ses partenaires de mise en œuvre s’assureront que les actions n’induisent aucune tension ou problème dans la zone et n’exposent pas les bénéficiaires en affichant les compositions de kits BNA et Abris. A cet effet, une collaboration étroite sera faite avec les acteurs de protection pour un suivi de prêt de toute question de protection. Le coût total du projet sera de 4 161 500 USD.

project_name: Ensure equal access to protection services for vulnerable IDPs, Returnees and host communities in Aleppo, Raqqa, Idleb, Dar’a, Hama, Homs and Rural Damascus
project_objective: In 2022-2023, COOPI aims to respond to the main protection concerns identified throughout protection program implementation and need assessment with local communities, IDPs and returnees. The response will be focused on 4 strategic Objectives: 1. Improve protection of population affected by the crisis through community-based and individually targeted protection interventions and through advocacy with duty bearers; 2. Improve access to quality and life-saving GBV response services for GBV survivors and women and girls at risk and put measures in place to prevent and mitigate risks of GBV; 3. Minimize the impact of explosive ordnance for communities most at risk; 4. Increased and more equitable access for boys and girls to quality child protection interventions in targeted locations in line with the CPMS in Humanitarian Action. COOPI response will be based on a community-based and participatory approach involving the affected population in actively participating to the decision-making process, focusing on the establishment of community committees, that, with the guidance of COOPI staff, will work on the identification of protection risks within their communities to address them appropriately. To reach an equal access for boys and girls (0-17) to quality child protection interventions, COOPI will support community-based child protection responses for girls and boys in targeted locations, including provision of MHPSS services for girls, boys and caregivers, parenting programmes, awareness-raising and establishment of groups/committees to ensure the community’s active participation to prevent and respond to child protection issues. The combination of these activities, aims to develop a long-term positive practice through the targeted populations with effects on the whole community. Psychosocial assistance will be also provided in order to cope with stress relief/PTSD. For women and children will be provided quality and life-saving response services, including case management, and COOPI will contribute to reinforce referral pathways. CVA modality will be considered to meet specific protection needs, and to mitigate risks related to GBV, child labor, child marriage, and disability. CLIs will be also promoted and implemented as more efficient tool for protection risk’s prevention and response. Our team will work through mobile team interventions to guarantee assistance also to the most vulnerable populations in rural, underserved areas. For example, therapists will reach out for home-based rehabilitation and distribution of medical in-kind assistance to the most vulnerable PwDs and survivors of landmine and ERW, to provide physical rehabilitation through COOPI specialized therapists, to reduce the physical and psychological implications of EO traumas and overcoming impairments, economic loss, social marginalization, limiting the enjoyment of their basic human rights. Mental therapists will provide individual counselling and to provide a lifesaving support. In addition, COOPI response will have a focus on risk education, due to the presence of EO that our team has assessed in several areas targeted. Awareness and campaigns will be conducted in the communities to reach all beneficiaries’ age and sex groups and to allow them to reach economic, social and health development, mitigating the likelihood of exposure to accidents leading to permanent injuries or loss of life. Intervening in multi- sectoral response, COOPI will ensure protection mainstreaming across all sectors, with particular attention to safe distribution modalities, gender, age and diversity approach and focusing on highly vulnerable groups in the definition of eligibility criteria and in targeting the assistance. Moreover, the SEA will constitute a cross-sectoral priority to be addressed and eradicate, while ensuring COOPI staff and third parties to be trained, to recognize and to report such violations, to do no harm and to protect people affected by the crisis.

project_name: Building Resilience and Mitigating Protection Risks in Conflict-Affected Areas of South Sudan
project_objective:
This IOM Protection project aims to contribute towards the achievement of the Protection Cluster Objectives 2.4 and 2.5.
The project seeks to build resilience among the most vulnerable i.e. women, children, persons with disabilities and the elderly among others. Building the resilience of the most vulnerable against the surrounding crisis including subnational violence and climatic shocks will help to reduce their vulnerabilities. The building of the resilience will be done through mitigating the risks and addressing the violations experienced by the vulnerable members of the community. The project will focus on providing cash assistance or individual protection assistance (IPA) to those facing protection risks or those who have survived protection violations. The cash assistance will target the vulnerable in areas affected by subnational violence and climatic shock hotspots such as Warrap, Jonglei, Central and Eastern Equatoria.  The counties to be targeted include Twic, Tonj North and South, Wau, Jur River, Rubkona and Mayom. The project will also continue raising awareness on protection and conducting protection monitoring in hot spots of conflict and climatic shocks.
IOM aims to contribute to strengthening the humanitarian response to GBV  through building national capacities to implement GBV prevention and response programming based on the Interagency GBV minimum standards. 
The HLP Rights component seeks to continue addressing the contextual situational analysis, legal environment and judicial system as the potential tools to better lives of persons faced with HLP related challenges and or issues. It’s evident that the law and legal institutions are charged with the mandate of protecting the dignity of Property Holders and in doing so, fortify those most vulnerable to HLP issues.
The target group consists of IDPs, Host Communities, Returnees and Vulnerable groups in various categories like widows, PWDs, paralegals, elders, regulatory and supportive institutions staff who can help escalate and advocate for the upholding of the dignity of the right holders especially the vulnerable groups and PWDs as the most affected by the impact of continued discrimination in society and violations of their HLP rights as entitled to.
IOM also intends to particularly target Regulatory and Supportive Institutions so that they can represent cases of HLP rights violations among the most affected and vulnerable groups.

project_name: Survey of contaminated areas along the Somali-Ethiopian border
project_objective:
The HALO Trust’s (HALO) ultimate goal is to clear Somalia’s landmine contaminated border with Ethiopia, in order to improve access to water, pasture, and infrastructure, and promote peacebuilding. Somalia’s landmine contamination is a legacy of 40 years of sustained conflict, and it threatens the recovery of Somalia’s most fragile rural communities. This contamination restricts access to water, pasture, and other essential services, in regions where clan conflicts and grievances exacerbate an already desperate competition for resources. This contamination has resulted in recent and severe accidents, killing civilians and destroying livelihoods. So great is the need for landmine clearance that some communities have attempted their own demining, without training, safety equipment, or adequate detection equipment. 

The project seeks funding to support the deployment of non-technical survey teams along the Somali-Ethiopian border. Non-technical survey (NTS) is the process through which a team gathers information on the presence and impact of mines and other explosive ordnance, without using any specific capital equipment or technical process. The NTS relies on a range of discussions with key informants like affected communities, ex combatants, or explosive ordnance victims. This process gathers important information that will help the team decide whether the area is indeed contaminated; and what the boundaries of the suspected hazardous area are. It also helps gathering information on the type of contamination in the area, which will affect the clearance method chosen in the future.

NTS is a vital element of the mine action sector, as it allows operators and authorities to have an accurate picture of the contamination landscape in the country. It can then be used to effectively plan, prioritize, implement and monitor all explosive hazards activities such as clearance and risk education. Delineating the dangerous areas can also save lives and alleviate suffering, by clearly indicating where the hazardous areas are. Until 2021, most NTS focused on localised areas along the Ethiopian-Somali border in the South West, Hirshabelle and Galmudug States. Little is known about the contamination in Puntland and Jubaland State and extending survey activities there will enable the mine action operators and the Somali Federal Government to have a better grasp of the work needed. In addition, there are still many knowledge gaps regarding the contamination in South West, Hirshabelle and Galmudug States, and this grant will allow for a more comprehensive survey of the area, including remote locations.

The project seeks to deploy 8 NTS mobile teams along the Ethiopian border between January and December 2022 (12 months). Each team will be composed of 4 members (1 man, 3 women), and will roam around the region to identify and map potentially hazardous areas. Geodata will be shared with the Somali Explosive Management Authority (SEMA), to help them build a comprehensive picture of the contamination. In addition, the teams will provide crucial risk education and awareness sessions to all communities visited, in order to minimize the likelihood of explosive hazards-related deaths and accidents.
The overarching objectives of this project are to:
•	Enhance security and stability, as well as reduce risk of death and injury to individuals and communities;
•	Improving the knowledge of the contamination landscape in Somalia, for all mine action operators; and
•	Help SEMA improve their planning and monitoring capacities.

project_name: Improving access to Civil Documentation and upholding HLP rights of IDPs in Cabo Delgado
project_objective: Displaced households in Cabo Delgado often lack legal documentation, including civil and property documents. This can have far-reaching implications in terms of their ability to fully enjoy freedom of movement, access basic services or secure land tenure rights. NRC will address this through a 2-prong approach. Firstly, the ICLA programme will support displacement affected households in obtaining legal identity documentation through the establishment of mobile legal clinics providing information, counselling and referral to relevant Government authorities. Secondly, through the co-chairing of the HLP Area of Responsibility (AoR) Working Group, NRC will provide leadership, technical support and capacity building to the humanitarian community, in an effort to mainstream HLP into assessment tools used in localities where HLP issues of highest prevalence and concern are reported. NRC will carry out joint HLP field assessments with the HLP AOR co-chair, Protection Cluster, and other humanitarian actors.

project_name: Les populations affectées par la crise au Mali bénéficient d'une assistance adaptée à leurs besoins en matière de documentation civile dans les régions de Gao et de Mopti.
project_objective:
Dans le souci de promouvoir les droits à la documentation civile et d'identité juridique des PDI, des communautés d'accueil touchées par le déplacement et des autres groupes vulnérables dans les régions de Gao, Tombouctou, Mopti et Ménaka, NRC à travers son programme d'information, de conseil et d'assistance juridique (ICLA), entreprendra des activités facilitant l'accès à la documentation civile et d'identité juridique et garantissant la protection des droits fondamentaux. 
Les solutions proposées s’alignent à la fois aux objectifs stratégiques 1, 2, 3 et 4 du cluster protection (HRP 2022) et correspondent aux résultats 3 et 5 de Protection. 
ICLA organisera des campagnes de sensibilisations sur l'importance de la déclaration civile et d'identité juridique ;  fournira des conseils juridiques aux PDI en vue de les aider à surmonter les obstacles les empêchant d’exercer leur droit à la documentation civile et d'identité juridique, apportera une assistance juridique pour l'obtention des actes de naissance et cartes nationales d'identité, et renforcera les mécanismes communautaires et les services techniques en charge de l'établissement des actes de naissance. De même, le programme ICLA apportera son assistance sur sollicitation d’autres acteurs humanitaires intervenant dans la même région et suivant l’analyse de la situation sécuritaire par NRC. ICLA portera une attention particulière aux femmes et filles dont le taux d'enregistrement reste faible dans ces zones précitées. ICLA favorisera l'approche inclusive et participative pour les communautés cibles en facilitant les dialogues communautaires contribuant à identifier les obstacles à l'exercice de ces droits. En outre, les acteurs humanitaires et les décideurs seront ciblés pour le renforcement des questions de plaidoyer. L’action ICLA ciblera au total 17 990 sur 2 876 867 personnes de la population en besoin de protection ciblée par le secteur de la Protection Générale.

project_name: Contribuer à améliorer l'accès à une éducation inclusive et de qualité dans un environnement d'apprentissage sûr et protecteur pour les enfants affectés par les conflits dans les regions de Tillaberi, Tahoua et de Diffa.
project_objective: Ce projet vise à lever les barrières qui empêchent les filles et garçons d’accéder à une éducation de qualité dans un environnement sûr et protecteur grâce à un programme d'Education en Urgence dans les régions de Tillaberi, Tahoua et de Diffa. Dans ce cadre, 250 écoles primaires seront appuyées dans les Régions de Tahoua et de Tillabéry et 40 écoles dans la Région de Diffa. Des réhabilitations, constructions de classes évolutives et de latrines seront effectuées afin de garantir que les espaces d'apprentissage soient adéquats pour accueillir le nombre croissant d'enfants inscrits. Des formations et un accompagnement pédagogique tout au long de l’action seront proposés aux enseignants en lien avec les services techniques pour améliorer la qualité des enseignements. Les enseignants situés dans des zones difficilement accessibles seront appuyés via l’approche vidéo-coaching. Des dotations de kits scolaires pour les élèves et de ressources pédagogiques pour les enseignants seront effectuées. Le projet travaillera par ailleurs avec les communautés pour les sensibiliser sur l'importance de l'éducation, surtout des filles et des enfants en situation d'handicap et renforcera les structures éducatives communautaires pour qu’elles puissent qu’elles appuient l’élaboration de plans de gestion des risques et la mise en place de code de conduite dans les écoles. Les enseignants recevront également une formation pour mieux répondre à la détresse des enfants - approche « École sûre », identification de la détresse psychologique et gestion du stress, premiers secours psychologiques et appui psycho-social. Des bibliothèques itinérantes seront créés dans les trois régions afin d’offrir aux enfants un accès facilité à des ouvrages éducatifs mais aussi ludiques.  Afin de favoriser la réintégration de 5400 enfants précocement exclus ou n’ayant jamais intégré le système scolaire, 180 classes passerelles seront mises en place au sein des écoles formelles appuyées. Dans les régions de Tillabéry et de Tahoua, un programme d’apprentissage par la radio sera mis en place dans les zones où les écoles sont fermées du fait de la situation sécuritaire. La collaboration avec des structures communautaires ainsi que les formations d´enseignants accroitront la durabilité de l´intervention par une mobilisation et un ancrage communautaire. L'accent sera mis aussi sur la responsabilisation des structures communautaires et sur la capacité des enseignants en termes d’encadrement des filles afin d’améliorer la rétention ainsi que le niveau des acquis scolaires des filles.

project_name: Provision of lifesaving assistance and sustainable solutions through safe Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) services, for people in crises and their host communities in multiple regions in Somalia.
project_objective:
IOM WASH is proposing to contribute to lifesaving of access to safe and equitable basic WASH services to overall 281,400 beneficiaries from vulnerable Internally Displaced Persons (IDP) and host-communities in multiple regions in Somalia. 

Specifically, the project will target 168,840 Non displaced people (children 104,681; women 27,014; Disabled 25,326; and elderly 11,819) and 112,560 displaced populations (children 69,787; Women 18,010; Disabled 16,884; and elderly 7,879)
IOM will rehabilitate 60 strategic water sources for multi-use (human and animals) and further 55 community berkads (water reservoirs) that will provide continued, equitable, safe, sufficient and sustainable water to regions, targeted by the cluster, prone to natural disasters.
IOM further proposes to construct 3,300 new emergency sanitation facilities (following cluster specifications) targeting populations without access to basic sanitation and hygiene.

The project will also strengthen the capacity of the Federal Government of Somalia and Federal Members States, community leaders and water committees/technicians for better coordination with government authorities and communities and sustainability of the constructed/ rehabilitated WASH infrastructures. In addition, the project will nurture community participation in good hygiene practices through training and community sensitization campaigns.

The project is aligned with protection mainstreaming to ensure safety and dignity of affected populations without causing harm. Affected populations and all relevant stakeholders including men, women, boys, girls, elderly and people with disability will be involved in decision making throughout the project activities/cycle. Furthermore, the project will be a part of an IOM integrated emergency response program and resilience building, where possible, efforts will be made to integrate IOM health, nutrition, shelter, CCCM and protection activities.

project_name: COVID-19 response:  stopping the spread of the virus and mitigating the impact of the pandemic on mental health among Palestine refugees in the West Bank
project_objective:
This project focuses on UNRWA's comprehensive response to mitigate the spread of COVID-19 and protect Palestine refugees and health care workers in the West Bank from the virus while continuing to provide primary health service and addressing the needs of the most vulnerable.
The response includes measures to prevent the spread of COVID-19 during primary health delivery at UNRWA health centers through: A) infection prevention and control measures and protection of the health workforce, B) COVID-19 vaccinations; C) continuation of of essential health services with adaptation of services to limit exposure to the virus or isolation for pregnant and lactating  women, NCD patients and persons with disabilities; D) mitigating the impact of COVID-19 on mental health; E) community outreach and awareness raising on COVID-19 mitigation measures and; F) training and support to PSEA and complaints mechanisms.

project_name: Providing Information, Counselling and Legal Assistance (ICLA) and enhancing the protection of civilians affected by conflict and displacement in Syria
project_objective:
The NRC protection response will be two-fold: (1) the direct provision of information, counselling and legal assistance (ICLA) to PACD and (2) increased knowledge and capacity to respond amongst duty-bearers. In addition, ICLA will identify emergency response capacities and multi-sectoral integration with NRC Shelter, WASH, Livelihoods and Food Security (LFS), and Education programmes. NRC will prioritise IDPs, returnees, host community members as well as Iraqi refugees, Palestine refugees, stateless individuals and individuals at risk of statelessness including third-country nationals (TCN). Through the delivery of a multi-faceted response, NRC will focus on the protection of rights to legal identity and civil documentation (CD); housing, land and property (HLP); employment and labour; and access to essential services. Geographic areas will be targeted based on the severity and scale of needs, inter-agency coordination at hub-level, and access.
(1) Provision of Direct Assistance: For 2022/2023, NRC direct services will be aimed at PACD who face legal challenges in relation civil documentation, HLP, employment procedures and accessing essential services. Key needs include the issuance of basic civil documentation such as birth, marriage and death certificates which are necessary in order to access education, health care and humanitarian assistance. NRC will further prioritize the most vulnerable, taking into account gender, age, disability, ethnicity and/or religion. This includes a focus on children and youth without proof of legal identity and female-headed households (FHH) with missing or deceased spouses who require confirmation of their legal status and that of their children. HLP information and counselling will aim to protect security of tenure and legal assistance will seek to prevent forced evictions.  Information and counselling activities may involve home visits to reach beneficiaries who are otherwise inaccessible to increase inclusivity for differently-abled persons. NRC will increase its support to key community stakeholders, including local civil society actors, on collaborative dispute resolution (CDR) techniques, such as mediation and negotiation. NRC will continue to carry out HLP due diligence to support Shelter and WASH, Education and Livelihoods interventions. NRC will launch interventions related to community awareness and training arounds the rights of children.
For all NRC and other humanitarian activities, ICLA will advocate and emphasize that civil documentation should not be considered a prerequisite to receive assistance.  (2) Increased Knowledge and Capacity to Respond: NRC will continue to undertake legal analysis and research and will additionally provide technical assistance to community leaders, duty-bearers and humanitarian partners through training modules on legal identity, HLP, collaborative dispute resolution (CDR) and employment law. Community leaders who will benefit from capacity building interventions may include formal and traditional authorities such as Mukhtars, Sheikhs, lawyers/jurists, female leaders and representatives of vulnerable groups. NRC will continue its support for the resolution of HLP disputes through CDR techniques such as mediation and negotiation, and will explore the potential for such techniques in employment or labour disputes. Guidance and advice on HLP due diligence procedures will be provided to other NRC programmes, such as Shelter and WASH, as well as the broader humanitarian sector through continued leadership and coordination in in the HLP Technical Working Groups. Across interventions, particular emphasis will be placed on the rights of women and girls, as well as the rights of persons with disabilities. NRC will continue to input activities into 4Ws, as often as requested, to ensure accurate protection service mapping. NRC will further review all awareness raising and training materials on a quarterly basis to update as needed.

project_name: Livelihood based Emergency Response for drought affected IDP population in Adadle, Gode, Kelafo, and Mustahil Woredas of Shebele Zone, Somali Region
project_objective:
The proposal is in line with the HRP 2022 project module designed to prevent further deterioration of food security and protect livelihoods of vulnerable households who has been the worst drought since four decades after loss three consecutive rain seasons. ADRA will implement under this proposal three major livelihoods in four Woredas (Adadle, Gode, Kelafo and Mustahil) of Shebele Zone Somali Region.
1-	Provision of Emergency Agricultural Input (locally adoptable Maize seeds and Sudan grass seeds for fodder production with fuel for irrigation and necessary Farm tools for Total population of121,799 people in (Adadle 34350 people), (Gode 24,950 people), (Kelafo 39,975people), and in (Mustahil 22,524 people).
2-	Provision of emergency Animal health intervention Livestock treatment, CAHWs training, Voucher system implementation, livestock disease surveillance Livestock Vaccination campaign for Total population of 81,636 people in (Adadle 2,746 people), (Gode 24,566 people), (Kelafo 39,974 people), and (Mustahil 14,350 people).
3-	Provision of Emergency Livestock feed intervention Seed for fodder production and Concentrated Animal Feed provision for a Total People of 128,713 people in (Adadle 54,258 people), (Gode 25,140 people), (Kelafo 34,975 people), and (Mustahil 14,350 People).
The project will target where ADRA has a permanent presence implementing Humanitarian Livelihoods long term programs while responding to the recurrently arising humanitarian emergencies in the target area. This is in line with the recent document of the HRP 2022 location and activities prioritization Guide for the Clusters. 

To achieve this objective, ADRA will focus lifesaving interventions for 7 months with possible Cluster decision of flexibility to adjust in case of new life threatening crises occurs. To ensure smooth implementation and complementarity ADRA will closely coordinate with the DRM-ATF Cluster, Federal, Regional and zonal authorities, and other operational partners in the targeted communities as the needs are massive and will require concerted efforts. Continuous monitoring will be undertaken in the implementation period to ensure all emerging trends are captured and reported to stakeholders. Community participation will be incorporated during the project design with women and children needs emphasis who mostly form a great percentage of the displaced populations. This approach will continue in the project implementation and lessons learnt incorporated in future responses.

In addition, ADRA will establish a protection committees involving men, women, a community leader, Religious leaders, a representative from the local authority and the police aimed to raise awareness on sexual violence and its impacts in the community; connect GBV and HIV; denounce any abuses of human rights; and share knowledge on how people could protect themselves. 
Humanitarian crises increase the risk that GBV will occur—compounding the challenges already faced by people. Girls and women are disproportionally affected by Livelihoods and Food security issues that arise during humanitarian emergencies. Forced to travel long distances to Aid Items distribution points with existing sanitation facilities often lacking privacy, lighting, or locks—they are at increased risk of sexual assault and harassment. Livelihoods and Food security scarcity can create tension in the home and heighten the possibility of domestic violence. And a shortage of culturally appropriate and accessible NFIs/Dignity Kits supplies, services and other support materials can increase all of these risks. ADRA’s proposed emergency Livelihoods and Food security NFI/Dignity Kits intervention will be integrated with gender-based violence (GBV) protection, mitigation and reduction activities, that will play a critical role in enhancing the safety and well-being of those most vulnerable people affected by humanitarian crises.

project_name: Appui à la prévention et la prise en charge de la malnutrition aiguë des enfants de 6 à 59 mois et aux femmes enceintes et allaitantes dans les zones en situation humanitaire au niveau national
project_objective:
La situation nutritionnelle demeure préoccupante et se dégrade dans les zones affectées par l’insécurité.
Les résultats de l’enquête Nutritionnelle réalisée avec la méthodologie SMART en Octobre 2021, ont montré une prévalence de la (MAG) à 9,7% dans 12 régions sanitaires (L’enquête n’a pas considérée la région du Sahel suite à l’insécurité) contre 9,1% en 2020 dans tout le pays. Les régions du Centre, du Nord et du Plateau-Central ont enregistré les plus forts taux de MAG respectivement 12.1, 11.9 et 11.3 %..

Les principaux facteurs associés à la malnutrition au Burkina Faso sont principalement les maladies, les apports alimentaires insuffisantes chez les enfants, les pratiques inappropriées d’alimentation du nourrisson et du jeune enfant, l’insécurité alimentaire, le faible accès à l’eau potable et les conditions inadéquates d’hygiène. Les facteurs aggravants de la malnutrition sont l’insécurité politique, les épidémies et la pandémie de COVID-19, le déplacement internes des populations, la réduction de l’accès aux services sociaux de base dont les services de santé etc.
 En effet, selon les résultats de l’analyse du cadre harmonisé sur l’ insécurité alimentaire de Novembre 2021, de Juin à Aout 2022, 2 196 110 de personnes seront en insécurité alimentaire avec en plus de 05 provinces sur les 8 déjà en crise en période courante (Sanmatenga, Komondjari, Tapoa, Kompienga et Loroum), 06 autres provinces pourraient tomber dans une situation de crise alimentaire durant la période de juin à août prochaine si rien n’est fait. 436 393 personnes dans trois (03) provinces de la région du Sahel (Soum, Séno et Oudalan) basculeraient en phase 4 « urgence » en situation projetée si rien n’est fait. Cette classification est relative à la dégradation de la situation sécuritaire (augmentation du nombre de PDI, augmentation significative de la criminalité, fermeture de formations sanitaires ou fonctionnant à minima, forte dégradation des moyens d’existence des ménages, etc.), au taux élevé de la malnutrition, à l’impact ""moyen à important"" sur l'activité principale habituelle. 

  Au 31 octobre 2021, le pays comptait 1 481 701 personnes déplacées internes dont 906 963 (61,21 pour cent) sont des enfants et 333 244 (22,49 pour cent) des femmes provenant majoritairement des régions du Sahel (34.4 pour cent), du Centre-Nord (34,4 pour cent) de l’Est (9.9 pour cent) et du Nord (9,6 pour cent).En novembre 2021, près de 1264100 personnes n'ont pas accès aux soins médicaux et nutritionnels car 103 centres de santé sont fermés et 288 offres des services restreints. La plupart des centres de santé fermés se trouvent dans la région du Sahel et dans la région du Centre-Nord. 

 Cependant des stratégies telles que les approches simplifiées pour la prise en charge de la malnutrition aigüe, la délégation des taches aux agents de santé à base communautaire, la stratégie PB à domicile sont mises en œuvre avec l’appui de l’UNICEF et d’autres partenaires pour assurer la continuité des services.

L’appui de l’UNICEF à travers ce projet consistera à mettre en œuvre un paquet intégré de services de prévention et de prise en charge de la malnutrition aigüe à travers le dépistage de la malnutrition aiguë (y compris PB à domicile), la promotion et le conseils l’ANJE en situation d’urgence, y compris la communication sur l’hygiène et la stimulation cognitive et l’appui à la référence vers les centres de santé des malnutris dépistés. Un appui ciblera également le renforcement de la prise en charge de la malnutrition aigüe sévère, la coordination du secteur de la nutrition ainsi que la surveillance nutritionnelle.
En 2022, l’UNICEF assure la disponibilité de 90% des intrants thérapeutiques au niveau national. Le reste de 8% est assuré par le gouvernement.

project_name: Scaling up primary health care services including Expanded Program of Immunization allover Libya
United Nations Humanitarian Air Service
project_objective:
Since 2018, the security situation in Burkina Faso drastically deteriorated with the
expansion and intensification of activities of non-state armed groups (NSAGs), exploiting
pre-existing inter-communal tensions. A further escalation was observed in 2020 and 2021, with a
greater toll on human lives and on vulnerable populations. The non-state armed groups
(NSAGs) are fragmented, with multiple internal players; and there are increased external
players linked with the regional dynamics (i.e. Central Sahel countries). This has led to
massive population displacements and has had a severe impact on already vulnerable
populations.
As of October 2021, over 1.4 million persons have been displaced and new displacements are reported daily. The security situation has had repercussions on the overall food and nutritional security of the country. Food security and nutritional situation has been impacted by the growing crisis affecting
vulnerable populations. 
The unprecedented humanitarian emergency will left 2.6 million persons in need of
humanitarian assistance during the 2022 lean season – according to the last Cadre Harmonisé.
Health services, schools and markets have been closed due to growing insecurity in
several parts of the country, seriously affecting the population’s ability to sustain healthy
lives.  COVID-19, and measures taken by the Government from March 2020, added another layer of
vulnerability.
Humanitarian access to vulnerable populations in need of assistance is restricted by
threats posed by non-state armed groups, counterterrorism operations, the presence of
Improvised Explosive Devices (IEDs) planted on roads and the damage or destruction of
key road infrastructure (bridges targeted in attacks in the Sahel region for instance). In
addition, access is hindered by restrictive counter-terrorism legislation preventing
negotiation with NSAGs. Many humanitarian actors have left areas which remain
impeded by serious access constraints. To safeguard neutrality and the perception of it,
humanitarian workers in Burkina Faso do not use military escorts, particularly since the
national Security Forces (FDS) remain the primary target of armed groups.
In order to support the planned humanitarian response and enable access to the populations in need and project implementation sites, UNHAS aims to provide a safe,
effective and efficient passenger air service to the entire humanitarian community and
their implementing partners, principally NGOs, UN agencies, red cross/crescent movement,
donor organizations and diplomatic missions.
UNHAS will be used to deliver assistance to hard-to-reach areas were people are the most vulnerable. 
Another crew is available since 2021 to allow 7/7 days coverage. Depending on the level of resources, another helicopter could be available to increase the operations in hard-to-reach areas.
The service is accessible to all humanitarian actors upon registration transporting personnel or
cargo aimed to support targeted populations.

project_name: Restoring Disrupted Livelihoods and Supporting Early Recovery Efforts for Palestine Refugees in Syria
project_objective:
Over ten years of crisis in Syria has drastically eroded the living conditions of Palestine refugees and Syrian nationals alike. The rapid depreciation of the Syrian pound accompanied by staggering inflation levels, the impact of Lebanon's financial and banking crisis, and the tightened trade restrictions imposed on the country since June 2020, have all contributed to a worsening of the socio-economic conditions. The COVID-19 pandemic has led to additional stress on basic services that has impacted the livelihoods of Palestine refugees and Syrians. 
To support Palestine refugee youth access to employment opportunities, the UNRWA TVET programme will continue to provide short-term courses to 850 students in Damascus, Dera’a, Homs, Aleppo and Latakia, offering a variety of specializations that respond to the needs of the local market. Short-term courses (three months on average) are designed to strengthen technical skills, with minimal financial costs to the refugee students, to improve their prospects of accessing the labour market. 

In 2022, UNRWA will also expand its provision of long-term courses, usually only offered at the Damascus VTC, to its TVET centres in Dera’a, Homs, Aleppo and Latakia. This is in response to the increasing demand of refugee youth in these areas for similar courses and to promote equal access for all Palestine refugees to livelihood opportunities to support their resilience. 

Depending on the trajectory of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2022, the TVET programme is ready to adjust to either remote or blended (in-person and remote) modalities for course delivery. Internet packages will be procured for students and staff to support this approach when needed. Hygiene measures, including the provision of masks to students and staff, and the distribution of sanitizers to all TVET centres will also be put in place to mitigate the risk of exposure and spread of COVID-19.  

The various components of UNRWA's interventions in 2022-2023 will also contribute to supporting refugees who have spontaneously returned to their places of residence either internally or from other countries. Where possible, UNRWA will aim at restarting services in camps that were heavily destroyed during the conflict (Dera’a, Yarmouk and Ein el Tal) through the rehabilitation of the Agency’s installations (including schools and clinics) in these camps.

project_name: Provision of life-saving healthcare services to Palestine Refugees in Syria
project_objective:
The public health system in Syria has been degraded by a decade of conflict and remains extremely vulnerable as a result of the displacement and migration of qualified professionals and the widespread destruction and damage to health facilities. The COVID-19 pandemic has further strained existing capacity. Therefore, Palestine refugees will continue to rely heavily on the Agency for health care. 

UNRWA's 25 health facilities in Syria (including 23 health centres and health points located in Palestine refugee camps and two mobile clinics) provide a range of primary health services, including out-patient consultations, immunization services, infant and child growth monitoring, dispensing of medications, gynaecology consultations, laboratory services, NCD care, maternal and child health care, dental and MHPSS services. The two mobile clinics will be deployed to areas affected by conflict or localized tensions where refugees are facing movement restrictions and to locations where Agency health facilities have been damaged or destroyed during the conflict.

UNRWA will continue to subsidize access to secondary and tertiary care (including COVID-19 treatment) for around 9,000 refugee cases (400 COVID-19 cases and 8,600 non-COVID-19 cases) through a network of partnered hospitals and private laboratories. This intervention has become increasingly critical as families’ ability to afford hospitalization services continues to decrease. The support provided by UNRWA will cover between 75 and 95 per cent of the costs, depending on the level of vulnerability and availability of funds. 
Dedicated support will be provided to persons with disabilities through the provision of prosthetic devices, including hearing aids for the elderly. Persons with long-term disabilities as a result of conflict-related injuries and in need of physiotherapy will be referred to external partners in community-based organizations. It is estimated that 8,000 physiotherapy sessions will be required.
In 2022, UNRWA will also conduct minor repairs to some of its health facilities that require urgent maintenance. This does not include facilities covered under the Emergency Repair, Rehabilitation and Maintenance of UNRWA Installations section in this appeal.

Under this appeal, the Agency will also continue to respond to the COVID-19 emergency through subsidizing COVID-19 testing for 2,400 Palestine refugees. As in 2021, COVID-19 testing will be extended to UNRWA health and non-health staff to contain the spread of COVID-19 and ensure the safety of Agency staff and the refugees they serve. In addition, UNRWA will continue to ensure that health centres are equipped with PPE to protect patients and frontline staff, and that disinfectants and sanitization materials are also available at all facilities
.
Since May 2021, UNRWA has been responsible for administering COVID-19 vaccinations for all United Nations (UN) staff and partner NGOs in Syria as part of the UN vaccination campaign, which has contributed significantly to the inter-agency COVID-19 response. UNRWA is also planning to vaccinate Palestine refugees if government approval is secured. This appeal will support the recruitment of five additional staff for the vaccination campaign and the establishment of a cold room in Damascus to store the vaccines.

project_name: Emergency and Relief Intervention - Nutrition Activities in South Sudan by Medair
project_objective:
Medair will continue multi-sectoral intervention in its proposed catchment area and ERT intervention. The total targets for 2022 based on Medair’s mapped catchment populations and at least 60% coverage in all areas will be 3545 SAM admissions, 8787 U5 MAM, and 8213 PLWs. Medair will continue to integrate MIYCN at both community and health and nutrition site levels and will support VAS in Medair’s catchment areas when no other actors are conducting. The proposed interventions in the plan align with the strategic and sector objectives and contribute to increasing equitable access and utilization of quality preventative, lifesaving, early detection and treatment of malnutrition and program monitoring, analysis, and utilization of nutrition information.
In Renk, there has been a consistent nutritional emergency for many years with the last GAM measured in June 2019 alarmingly high at 32.1%. Medair is the only nutritional actor in the county and has been doing multisectoral programming—health, nutrition and WASH. After seven months of program suspension due to insecurity, Medair abled to re-enter to Renk since December 2021 and on process of initiating multisectoral intervention in selected areas. As effort of re-entry Medair conducted pre-implementation MUAC screening in five selected sites (Saraya, Anbayok, Geiger, Shemedi and Jelhak) in December 2021 and found a proxy GAM rate of 14.4% for U5 and 21.4% for PLW. Medair is hoping to start at small scale and monitor the situation for possible scale up depending upon access and security and to implement over at least a 1-year period. 
The 2022 FSNMS+ estimates GAM rate in Leer County as 19.2% (SAM 6.1%). But, in the mass MUAC screening conducted in August 2021, the proxy GAM rate was 7.9% (SAM 0.6%). Medair is the major nutrition actor covering a catchment population of 41,200 in Leer County (6) and 1 site Luol in Mayendit County. Medair is continuing multisectoral programming—community health, nutrition—CMAM and MIYCN via Care Groups (CG) WASH, and MHPSS to address some of the underlying factors.
In the recent IPC classification (HNO 2022) Pibor was classified as IPC 5, “famine likely” with extremely critical levels of acute malnutrition. In 2022 nutrition cluster prioritized Pibor as one of the neediest areas with no significant improvement from last year situation. Medair continues to run the SC and set up multisectoral programming in Gumuruk and Lekuangole (est population of 55,126 (Feb 2021 OCV Campaign). OTP and TSFP services will continue be covered by Plan and JAM. As part of Medair’s health and WASH programming Medair will set up a community CG network which will cover MIYCN and other public health topics as well as ensure Mother’s MUAC is established and well linked to Plan and JAM’s services through referrals. Health facilities will also conduct nutritional screening and referral of U5 and PLWs as part of BPHNS. As no actor is addressing at risk infants <6 mo, Medair will continue exploring integrating MAMI with the health services in 2 PHCUs. To avoid duplication, Medair will continue to coordinate activities with JAM/PLAN to manage all the coexisting illness referrals. Medair will continue supporting minimum WASH packages and child friendly spaces and early child development activities will be promoted.
ERT continues to respond to emergency levels of acute malnutrition by establishing CMAM services to address the most lifesaving needs, in areas with high GAM and low program coverage. The RRTF in collaboration with the NC gives input on priority areas and intervention modalities in scenarios characterized by agreed triggers where other actors are absent or unable to fully intervene. The team will work with the partner on the ground to identify areas for capacity building for quality service delivery. The team will provide nutrition emergency services for up to 3 months and thereafter handover services to an identified partner before exiting.

project_name: Provision of life-saving quality and age appropriate sexual and reproductive health services including basic and comprehensive emergency obstetric and newborn care to internally displaced persons and host communities in Somalia.
project_objective:
The Somali population continues to face combined impact of recurring stress factors including drought, desert locusts, political uncertainty, COVID-19 restrictions, and an upsurge in conflict which have deepened and widened poverty conditions in Somalia, compounded pre-existing vulnerabilities. The secondary economic and humanitarian consequences of COVID-19 in 2020-2021 are estimated to have been more significant than the health consequences of COVID-19. The vulnerability exposure of the population has increased due to these multiple stress factors with seven in ten Somalis currently living in poverty. The number of people in need of humanitarian assistance has increased to 7.7million and 2.9million persons are internally displaced across the country. 
Somalia’s health system is inadequately equipped to provide a minimum amount of coverage for equitable access to health care, resulting in increased morbidity and mortality. Somalia is among the highest rankings in infant and child mortality rates with respectively 76.6 and 121.5 per 1000 live births. The maternal mortality rate (692 deaths per 100,000 live births) and the fertility rate (average of 6.9 children per woman) are also among the highest in the world, while 79% of all births are home delivered without skilled assistance. Access to birth spacing services remains limited, and up to 99 percent of women experience Female Genital Mutilation/Cutting (FGM/C) (SHDS, 2020). Displaced persons and persons with disability reported particularly high access barriers to food, nutrition, health, water, protection, sanitation, and hygiene services within IDP sites. Reports have shown that the low level and difficult access to health services in the IDP sites in Baidoa and Kismayo tends to particularly disadvantage women and their ability to access maternal healthcare and personal hygiene Also the COVID-19 epidemic is also exacerbating gender-based violence (GBV). COVID-19-related restrictions led to the termination of several GBV services. Women, adolescents, girls, and children account for 95 per cent of survivors who reported GBV occurrences in 2020, with 75 per cent coming from displaced populations. 
In this regards, UNFPA interventions will ensure access to life-saving maternal and reproductive health information and services for the affected women and girls as well as men and boys in IDPs and in hard-reach locations including persons with disabilities. The project will contribute in the prevention and management of consequences of sexual and gender based violence such as unintended pregnancies, increased acquisition of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and increased transmission of HIV through compassionate, confidential and competent care to the survivors among displaced and host communities in the crisis affected population. The following are the specific objectives of the intervention:
•	Ensure access and utilization of quality and age appropriate emergency obstetric and newborn care services and information to IDPs and host communities including persons with disabilities in the affected locations.  
•	improve availability of a range of long-acting reversible and short-acting contraceptive methods in the EmONC facilities of the affected areas
•	Support the capacity of service providers on mental health and psychosocial support (MPHSS) for pregnant and lactating mothers and adolescent girls affected by the humanitarian crises in Somalia.   
•	Enhance the capacity of managers and service providers for sexual and reproductive health in Minimum Initial Service Package (MISP) and clinical management of rape (CMR) 
•	Support the procurement and the distribution of Emergency Reproductive Health Kits (ERH Kits) to deliver quality health services.

project_name: Protection and targeted assistance targeting IDPs and vulnerable non-IDP communities and refugee returnees
project_objective:
The project aims to strengthen a rights-based protection response for IDPs and non-IDP communities, as well as refugee returnees, in particular those most vulnerable through stronger advocacy, life-saving protection and assistance activities, evidence-based programming with the focus on developing and building the capacity of affected communities to cope and recover and better position them for the attainment of durable solutions. Improving coordination and quality of assessments and monitoring will also be key components of the project. The project also foresees benefiting the entire displaced population through continuous advocacy and support in the area of law and policy, fostering the successful engagement with relevant authorities and partners with a focus on the approval and implementation of the new IDP Law. 
UNHCR will continue to make the best of its key membership of the protection cluster and ensure regular reporting to the clusters’ 5Ws and strong participation and contribution in the different clusters’ working groups to ensure coordination and complementarity of interventions, avoiding duplication with other members and ensuring regular sharing of protection reports with the cluster.

project_name: Shelter and NFIs Assistance to Crisis Affected Populations in Somalia
project_objective:
In 2022, UNHCR will target affected populations including; newly displaced populations, IDPs currently living in protracted situations, refugee returnees, and affected host communities with adequate shelter and basic household items. This will be done through the provision of Non-Food Items (NFI kits), Emergency Shelters, and where feasible transitional and durable shelter solutions through different modalities including in-kind and through cash.
The Somalia Joint Multi-Cluster Needs Assessment (JMCNA) 2021, reports the living standard gap of Shelter and NFIs to be at 84%. According to the same assessment, the most commonly reported priority need of more than half of the affected population is still shelter or housing due to poor shelter conditions, lack of space, poverty and lack of security of tenure. The critical indicators that were considered in the calculation of the severity of the POCs in the sector were access to safety of enclosures, technical performance of shelters and the access to vital household NFIs. In addition to these indicators, others that were also considered were living conditions including overcrowding, functional domestic living space, occupancy status, and security of tenure.
In response to the identified needs in the HNO 2022, UNHCR plans to distribute NFI Kits to 56,800 households in kind/cash, provide emergency shelters to 20,000 households, transitional shelters to 800 households and permanent shelters to 600 households. The project will target 340,800 individuals with NFI kits, 120,000 individuals with emergency shelters, 4,800 individuals with transitional shelters and 3,600 individuals with permanent shelters. NFI, emergency shelters and transitional shelter assistance will be provided in cash or in kind and the response modality will depend on the availability of items in the local market, access to the locations, user preference and associated protection risks. Permanent shelters will be provided in kind through implementing partners.
As per the HNO, it is reported that a total of 237 IDP sites hosting 593,058 individuals were congested with associated health risks and fire outbreaks. These overcrowded sites are not planned, leading to the increased risk of fire outbreaks, spread of diseases including COVID 19, relatively higher GBV related incidences and flooding due to the absence of adequate drainage systems. In response to this, through an ongoing inter-cluster initiative between the Shelter Cluster and the CCCM Cluster, UNHCR will provide settlement planning and infrastructure support in 49,500 individuals in sites to be identified by the shelter cluster basing on the level of risk and feasibility of the project. This infrastructure support will be done to ensure site decongestion through settlement extensions and implementation of basic site planning principles where feasible. 
UNHCR will carry out Post Distribution Monitoring (PDM) and ensure the utilization of the Complaints, Response and Feedback Mechanism for each project. The PDM exercise will be conducted 4-6 weeks after NFI and ESK distribution to analyze the impact of the projects, level of beneficiary satisfaction and establish the lessons learnt for future programming.
UNHCR will target a total of 469,200 vulnerable individuals of the 3.6 million persons identified as in need of shelter assistance. Of the targeted individuals, 84,456 women, 65,688 men, 218,849 children, 18,768 elderly and 93,840 disabled individuals. UNHCR will also incorporate 93,840 vulnerable individuals from the host community and 375,360  vulnerable POCs as part of its target group. The targeting will occur based on UNHCR and Shelter Cluster assessments for those most in need and highly vulnerable. Activities will be implemented in Bari, Banadir, Bay, Lower Juba, Gedo, Mudug, Hiraan, Nugaal, Middle Shabelle, Lower Shabelle and Woqooyi Galbeed regions.
UNHCR will implement and monitor the activities through the support of Implementing Partners.

project_name: Emergency Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene interventions for emergency affected and vulnerable populations in Somalia
project_objective: The objective of the project is to provide lifesaving emergency water supply, sanitation and hygiene promotion services for conflict, drought, flood and Covid-19 affected people, vulnerable host communities and people in disease prone areas, mainly women and children including strengthening of communities’ resilience to cope with the impact of emergencies and recurrent shocks. During the proposed emergency WASH project design and implementations women and girls will be consulted and WASH facilities will be designed and located to ensure the specific needs like privacy, safety and dignity of women and girls. In addition, the project is also targeting to reduce the risk of violence against women, children and vulnerable groups while accessing water and sanitation facilities by providing gender segregated and disability friendly WASH facilities and establishing water supply facilities within 500 meters’ distance of the settlements and sanitation facilities within 50 meters. The emergency WASH response will also be implemented by considering the needs of people with disabilities. People with disabilities will be represented in the community consultation process, beneficiary identification and on design and location of WASH facilities. In addition, a certain percentage of emergency WASH facilities will be constructed with disability friendly components like ramps and support facilities to cater for people with disabilities.

project_name: Intervention médicale d'urgence pour réduire la morbidité et la mortalité chez les personnes déplacées, les retournés et les populations hôtes dans l'est et le sud du Tchad
project_objective:
Résumé du projet
Le projet vise à contribuer à la réduction de la mortalité et de la morbidité des populations touchées par les crises à l'est et au sud du Tchad en renforçant la surveillance des maladies à tendance épidémique et à apporter une réponse rapide permettant de sauver la vie de toutes les populations vulnérables (hommes, femmes, enfants, garçons et filles)

project_name: Production alimentaire d’urgence en soutien aux populations vulnérables (déplacés internes, refugiés, ménages très pauvres) victimes de chocs (crises et catastrophes naturels) dans le nord et le centre du Mali.
project_objective:
La Mali est confronté depuis plus d’une dizaine d’année à une situation d’insécurité qui met à mal l’ensemble de sa structure économique particulièrement dans les nord et sud du pays. Une des conséquences majeures de cette situation est le déplacement d’une proportion importante dans des zones mieux sécurisées. Selon le DTM de juillet 2021, 377.781 personnes o nt été identifiées comme déplacés internes. Les principales zones de déplacement de personnes sont Bamako, Gao, Kayes, Kidal, Koulikoro, Ménaka, Mopti, Ségou, Sikasso, Tombouctou. En plus des problèmes de sécurité, il s’est ajouté une saison agricole de moyenne à mauvaise. Selon le cadre Harmonisé de novembre 2021, les déplacements inhabituels de population, la baisse des transferts monétaires et de réduction des activités économiques particulièrement dans les centres urbains en rapport avec la COVID-19 dans les zones d’accueil des migrants, l’épuisement précoce de la biomasse, engendreront la dégradation des moyens d’existence dans l’ensemble du pays. Selon le Cadre Harmonisé, en situation projetée de juin à août 2022 : 12 zones seront en phase crise (Ansongo, Bourem, Gao, Ménaka, Nioro, Bandiagara, Bankass, Djenné, Douentza, Koro, Niono et Gourma Rharous) ; 17 zones en phase sous pression (Diéma, Abeibara, Kidal, Tessalit, Tin Essako, Nara, Tenenkou, Youwarou, Baroueli, Macina, Ségou, Tominian, Yorosso, Diré, Goundam, Niafunké et Tombouctou)
Le présent projet a pour objectif d’apporter une assistance alimentaire à travers une production alimentaire d'urgence. Cette intervention sera basée sur un accès immédiat aux intrants agricoles et d'élevage afin de soutenir et restaurer la disponibilité alimentaire, la diversité alimentaire et réduire les stratégies d'adaptation négatives. Les populations cibles de cette intervention sont les déplacés internes, les réfugiés et les ménages les plus vulnérables des communautés hôtes. L'intervention contribuera à la réalisation de l'objectif stratégique 1 du plan de réponse humanitaire (PRP) 2022 : Sauver et préserver la vie et la dignité d'au moins 80% des populations vulnérables affectées par une crise humanitaire ou par des catastrophes naturelles à travers une assistance multisectorielle en nature et en cash adressant leurs besoins vitaux et de survie y compris le monitoring de protection dans les cercles prioritaires des régions nord, centre, sud et ouest selon les droits fondamentaux d’ici fin 2022

project_objective: Le Tchad accueille depuis plusieurs années un nombre important de réfugiés dans la province du Lac, les zones du Sud et de l’Est, soit plus de 481,000 réfugiés. Cette population, pour laquelle les perspectives de rapatriement dans les pays d’origine sont très limitées, continue à bénéficier d’une assistance humanitaire dans les secteurs essentiels et vitaux tels que l’assistance alimentaire, la nutrition, l’eau, la santé, l’éducation et la protection. Le PAM apportera une assistance alimentaire d’urgence aux populations réfugiées Camerounaises, Nigériennes, Centrafricaines et Soudanaises . Cette assistance alimentaire est adaptée aux vulnérabilités des ménages réfugiés vivant, entres autres, dans les provinces du Lac, Logone Oriental, Mandoul, Moyen Chari, Salamat, Ouaddai, Sila, Wadi Fira et Ennedi Est. Une stratégie de transition vers le renforcement de la résilience / self reliance des réfugiés et des communautés hôtes a été développée et est mise en oeuvre afin de les appuyers à moyen et long terme. Le PAM soutiendra les réfugiés “les moins vulnérables” et les communautés hôtes par la création et la réhabilitation d’actifs productifs, ainsi que par des transferts monétaires et des kits de moyens de subsistance pour encourager l’agriculture, l’élevage, et le commerce.
