To further improve the contribution of WASH to the achievement of health outcomes, the proposed WASH response will invest improvements of  behavioral change through advocacy of attainment of community  ownership of projects to prolong the lifespan & sustainability of projects for  access to WASH facilities in health care facilities and other public institutions, the project intends to complement with Action Against Hunger Health and Nutrition projects in hard to reach areas to reach the elderly, disable and vulnerable person are included and targeted in activities,  Overall, the project envisages to reach 70,000 individuals (19,809M, 19180 F,15,505 B and 15,506 G) including 7,111 people living with disabilities for a period of 12 months in Bakool, Bay, Lower Shabelle,  Nugaal,  Banadir, ACF WASH project will be gender  sensitive through inclusion of women in WASH committee and are represented in crucial roles, are consulted in the design of the project especially during the planning,design and distribution of MHM kits to understand  women and girls preference & functionality of the products in the local  markets, The project will adopt protection mainstreaming in WASH  and that latrines are gender segregated and with a barrier screen for privacy   and WASH facilities are disable friendly through construction of ramps during distribution of WASH Kits triage sort of mechanisms will be adopted to give priority to those who cannot stand in line for long periods, such as older persons, persons with disability, unaccompanied children, pregnant and lactating women, so that they wait for less time. Community hygiene volunteers and community health workers will be trained and work closely with the targeted communities and ensure that WASH minimum at health facilities are attained and the project linked with other interventions(FSL, Health & Nutrition)  supported by  Action Against Hunger for optimal impact of the project

project_name: Provision of Emergency and sustainable  WASH Services for Vulnerable IDPs and communities in Banadir (Kaxda and Deynile), Middle Shabelle (Balcad and Jowhar) and Galgadud region of Somalia (Adado, dusmareb and Guricel district).
project_objective:
The continuation of protracted crises in Somalia, now compounded by the effects of Covid-19, Floods and droughts has resulted in massive challenges pertaining to Water, Sanitation and Hygiene. 
An estimated 6.4 million people, 40 per cent of the Somali population need emergency life-saving WASH assistance of which 3.5 million will need safe drinking water, 5.1 million sanitation services, and 6.4 million hygiene supplies. 16 per cent of these are females, children for 64 per cent and the elderly for 4 per cent. This presents an increase of 39 per cent from 2021, in which 4.6 million were estimated to be in need of WASH services across Somalia. This increase is due to adjusted population figures of Somalia, in combination with continuous failed rainy seasons, which are expected to further strain existing limited WASH services, especially in rural areas424. The population in need of WASH services in 2022 includes approximately 1,619,415 IDPs and 4,818,944 vulnerable host communities. Estimated that 6,058,603 people (38 per cent) in the Severe category” lack access to safe water and proper sanitation services and are highly vulnerable to AWD and cholera and around 379,757 people (2 percent) are in “extreme condition as they access water directly from rivers and surface bonds, practice open defecation and lack access to soap and other essential hygiene materials and are susceptible to communicable diseases.
The proposed project is designed to boost the ongoing lifesaving assistance and will target the most vulnerable displaced, floods, and drought-affected communities in Banadir, Galgadud, and Middle Shabelle regions of Somalia. At the moment, IDPs and urban poor and rural communities are among the most vulnerable groups in the society. Since the capacity of the local community to address their needs is very weak it is clear that the increasing number of IDPs and urban poor in crisis requires an urgent comprehensive action to support the target populations. The project responds to urgent humanitarian needs including (1) Deliver life-saving WASH assistance to reduce acute needs among the most vulnerable settlements and communities (2) Reduce the risk of violence against women, children, and vulnerable groups when accessing WASH services, and (3) Provide or restore sustainable access to safe water and adequate sanitation services in targeted communities and institutions.
Further, the target population will be involved in activities planning, implementation, and monitoring. Special attention will be given to women, children, and the elderly, and people with disabilities during the designing and construction WASH activities (i.e. 15% of all latrines will have disability-friendly features and will be constructed close to their shelters to ease access). Moreover, women will be part of WASH committees and will be represented in all community structures to empower them. Minority groups and femaleheaded households likely to face exclusion will be part of community-based committees to represent the voice of the minorities. Distribution sites will be pre-selected by target population and hygiene kits contents shared with beneficiaries allowing them to understand their rights and entitlements. Different distribution modalities will be used where protection concerns are mitigated and reported if they occur. The household-level distribution will be employed if people with disabilities and the elderly cannot access distribution sites.

project_name: Rapid Response Mechanism 2022
project_objective:
Ce projet est un mécanisme de veille, alerte, coordination, pré positionnement de stocks et réponse de dernier recours en MPC (à des fins alimentaires principalement), NFI, abri, et EHA.
Les alertes sont déclenchées par les 90 points focaux disséminés dans tout l'Extrême Nord, à partir d'un seuil minimal de 20 ménages déplacés. En lien avec la coordination humanitaire (OCHA) et les sectoriels, et après validation (triangulation) de l'alerte, une évaluation mutisectorielle des besoins est réalisée. Le RRM coordonne aux côté de OCHA la réponse et en dernier lieu prévoit une intervention dans les domaines cités plus haut, intervention qui doit se tenir 22 au plus tard après la validation de l'alerte par le coordinateur du RRM. Un effort sera mis dans le RRM 2021 sur la protection transversale (référencement contre référencement des cas de protection) et un plaidoyer élevé et constant pour optimiser la couverture des gaps de besoins par l'ensemble des acteurs humanitaires présents dans la zone (mise en place d'un Géoportail).
Le ciblage se basera sur des critères de vulnérabilité révisés avec chaque groupe sectoriel (vulnérabilité alimentaire, matérielle, sociale, etc). Les activités prennent en compte le genre (à travers la distribution de kits d'hygiène pour les femmes, des FGD non mixtes, etc) et la redevabilité (mise en place d'une hotline) Notons également que lors des évaluations, les enfants malnutris seront identifiées, recensés et référencés au centre de prise en charge le plus proche.
Enfin, à des fins de pérennisation, d'acceptation et d'ancrage, une OSC encore à identifier sera formée et appuyer pour accompagner le RRM dans la conduite d'enquête terrain et d'activités liées à la redevabilité (PDM, PIM, etc)

project_name: Emergency and regular food assistance for the assessed food insecure households in NWS through appropriate modality (Food basket, Ready to Eat Rations, Cooked meals, Food voucher, Bread distribution and cash for food) (FSL SO1)
project_objective:
Throughout 2022 and 2023, VO is planning to implement comprehensive food security interventions applying a variety of modalities (In-kind, Cash, and vouchers) to address the needs of the different groups with proper modality.
The proposed project will effectively contribute to improving food security status to the assessed food insecure people through life-saving and life-sustaining food assistance through improving food consumption, dietary diversity, and avoiding negative coping strategies. the planned activities to be implemented during 2022 and 2023 are the following activities:
1.	Emergency Food assistance distribution for HHs of crisis-affected IDPs through proper modality (Cash - In Kind)
2.	Cooked meals provision for COVID-19 positive confirmed cases admitted in 2 CCTCs in NWS
3.	Regular Food assistance per modality (in-kind, Cash, Voucher) for HHs
4.	Provision of free and subsidized bread for IDPs individuals and host communities.

More over; in terms of the implementation activities, Violet is planning for cash and vouchers modalities whenever possible for regular food assistance to ensure markets revival in the targeted location with taking into consideration, market functionality/proximity/capacity, also functionality of financial service providers in the targeted location. the value of the voucher will be according to FSL and CWG recommendation for the food assistance which is currently 60 USD per HH based on their last update on this regard, and in the meantime, VO will consider in-kind modality for regular food assistance where there are low-functionality of the markets in the targeted areas to increase food availability in the targeted locations, the weight of the in-kind food basket (when applied) will be based on the WFP recommended food basket composition and FSL cluster response packages .
Regarding beneficiaries targeting, VO will still consider blanket distribution to the camps residents based on the current cluster recommendations, and applying faire eligibility and vulnerability criteria when it comes to food distribution off-camps.
Based on the situation/context analysis, VO will ensure considering the best suitable modality all of the food assistance , then if voucher, then Violet will ensure proper and enough vouchers distribution and redemption period, and if in-kind, then the distribution will be through setting distribution points in the targeted location based on recent updated VO distribution SOPs during COVID-19 context.

Out of the total project total amount (4,185,000 USD), the below amounts are already secured: 

- 120,600 USD is secured for emergency food assistance during 2022 covering RTEs and cooked meals
- 590,940 USD is secured for the regular food assistance. 
- 86,250 USD is secured for the Provision of free and subsidized bread for IDPs

In total, 677,910 USD is already secured. Moreover, 1200,000 USD is in the pipeline.

project_name: Provision of life-saving Shelter and Non-Food Item (NFI) support to vulnerable populations in Somalia
project_objective:
For HRP 2022, IOM will contribute to the cluster objectives namely: CO#1: Ensure that persons affected by conflict and natural disasters have protection from the weather and privacy through provision of shelter and NFIs; and CO#2: Vulnerable displacement and disasters affected populations have access to transitional or durable shelter, enabling safer and more dignified living standards and preventing recovering communities from slipping back into humanitarian need; through provision of: (1) NFI support to 10,000 newly displaced households through in-kind (through contingency stocks – 5,000 kits) and Cash-Based Interventions (CBI)); (2) Emergency (3,000 households (HH)), transitional (1,000) and permanent shelter (250) support through mix methods of in-kind and CBI; (3) Mainstream risk and resilience into project activities through infrastructural support and site de-congestion activities (500 HH). Interventions will focus on Baidoa, Dollow and Kismayo.

Somalia is at the crossroads of mixed and complex migration flows, often resulting in internal and external displacement due to ongoing conflicts, climate-related shocks, communicable disease outbreaks and weak social protection mechanisms. It is estimated that the pressing need for shelter has persisted and worsened into 2021; the 2022 Humanitarian Needs Overview for Somalia estimates that 3.6 million people are in need of shelter and NFI assistance with 2.7 million of these categorised as displaced population with 573,000 being newly displaced with an increasing trend of migration to urban centres related to climatic shocks, insecurity and better livelihood opportunities.

For the 2022 HRP, IOM will focus on providing 60,000 individuals with NFI support through a mixed method of in-kind and CBI support through contingency stocks and direct implementation respectively. A further 24,000 individuals will receive shelter support either emergency, transitional or permanent shelter using in-kind or CBIs. The unit cost for durable shelters is 3,000 USD. Finally, 3,000 individuals will receive infrastructure support under umbrella of risk reduction activities or site decongestion.

project_name: Amélioration de la qualité et de la coordination de la réponse aux situations d’urgence
project_objective:
Le Mali comme la majeure partie des pays de la zone Sahélienne, est confronté à une crise humanitaire depuis plusieurs années qui tend à s’aggraver au lieu de diminuer. Parmi les principales causes, il peut être citer les conséquences des changements climatiques qui frappent durement les pays de la zone avec des phénomènes comme l’irrégularité des pluies, les inondations, les sécheresses localisées ou généralisées. A ces phénomènes, il faut ajouter les épidémies comme le cholera ou encore la COVID 19. En effet, Afin de lutter efficacement comme la pandémie de la COVID 19, les pays de la zone sahélienne dont restreint les mouvements des populations, fermer des marchés ou encore instaurer des couvres feu. Ces mesures ont négativement impacté les revenus des ménages les plus vulnérables. De même, du fait des mesures de restriction liées à la COVID 19, les transferts monétaires des Maliens de l’étranger vers leurs familles restées au pays ont diminué de manière significative augmentant par la même occasion la vulnérabilité des populations. Mais c’est la situation d’insécurité qui prévaut dans le nord et le centre du pays qui est à la base de la plus grande crise humanitaire actuelle. En effet, un grand nombre de ménages ne sont pas en mesure de se rendre dans leurs champs pour cultiver du fait de l’insécurité qui règne. De même, du fait de la fermeture de nombreux marchés itinérants de fait de l’insécurité, les ménages ne sont plus en mesure vendre leurs surplus de récoltes ou de se ravitailler. Mais la conséquence la plus visible de cette situation d’insécurité est le déplacement d’un grand nombre de ménages principalement issus du milieu rural. Selon le DTM de septembre 2022, ce sont 401.736 personnes déplacées internes soit (69.696 ménages) qui ont été enregistrés sur l’ensemble du territoire malien. Les zones d’installation de ces personnes déplacées internes sont les suivantes, Bamako, Gao, Kayes, Kidal, Koulikoro, Ménaka, Mopti, Ségou, Sikasso. 
Afin de répondre à ces différentes situations d’urgence, plusieurs organisations développent des projets qu’ils mettent en œuvre au profit des ménages affectés. Cependant, force est reconnaitre qu’il y a souvent un manque de préparation et un déficit de coordination sur le terrain. 
Le présent projet vise à répondre à cette faiblesse de la réponse aux situations d’urgence en renforçant les capacités des organisations sur la préparation et la réponse mais également en renforçant la coordination entre les acteurs de la réponse humanitaire.

project_name: Provide lifesaving, equitable, dignified, safe and sustainable access to basic WASH services for vulnerable populations affected by drought and conflicts in Bardheere District of Somalia
project_objective:
The project aims at providing lifesaving equitable as well as dignified, safe and sustainable access to basic WASH services for the vulnerable populations that are affected by drought and conflicts in Bardheere district of Somalia. In submitting proposed activities under the WASH cluster, the project aims at improving access to safe water through the extension of water distribution networks to drought affected settlement as well as host communities in the villages of Geriley, Darussalam, Dalsan, Dadshimbir, Dhomadhere, Jawhar, Wadajir in Bardheere district. in the Gedo region.

The current drought situation is worsening the already dire humanitarian situation in Somalia. According to the Food Security and Nutrition Analysis Unit’s (FSNAU) projection, almost 3.5million Somalis may endure food insecurity or depletion of livelihood assets, indicating a crisis level (IPC Phase 3) or even worse by the end of 2021. 
The country is experiencing its third consecutive below-average rainfall season since late 2020, which is worsening the current drought conditions, particularly in the Southern, Central and Northern parts. According to FAO/SWALIM, these areas have received little to no rainfall since June due to delayed October to December 2021 Deyr rains.
The widespread dry conditions have resulted in increased human suffering and livestock deaths, with severe drought impacts reported in Jubaland, SouthWest and Galmudug states (Central regions) and parts of Puntland. 
In Gedo region, a severe drought impact was reported especially in Bardhere and surrounding areas. The drought-affected people urgently need water assistance. 
Access to safe WASH facilities will also remain an issue of concern, especially for children, women and vulnerable groups, such as persons with disabilities. More than 8.9 million people are affected by poor and deteriorating WASH conditions in Somalia, which have been further exacerbated by the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic affecting people’s health and livelihoods. The WASH Cluster estimates that 3.3 million people are in severe and extreme need of humanitarian WASH assistance and 1.1 million people are in catastrophic need of assistance. Water is also an enabler for agricultural and livestock production systems, for sanitation and hygiene, and helps to prevent conflict and stabilize communities.
Dry conditions will contribute to the likelihood of crop losses and deterioration in pasture and water availability in some areas.
The proposed activities will focus on the rehabilitation of strategic water sources as well as installation of water distribution networks, encouraging safe hygiene practices at the community level through awareness campaigns, and hygiene kits distribution including female specific hygiene items( sanitary materials) where sourcing for these kits shall be done through the use of local vendors.
This project will focus on Wadajir, Geriley, Dadshimbir, Dalsan, Darusalam  Jowhar and Dhomadhere villages of Bardhere district of South Central Somalia where access to basic WASH services is very limited due to the servere droughts, locusts invasion, Covid-19 pandemic which continues to disrupt livelihoods and the constant conflicts due to scarcity of water and pasture resources affecting particularly girls, children, women, edlerly and disabled people. The project will focus on IDPs and vulnerable host communities, small scale farmers whilee putting the marginalized populations into consideration.

project_name: Providing Food Security and Livelihood Assistance to the most vulnerable communities in Gedo, Lower Juba and Galgadud regions
project_objective:
According to FSNAU Post-Gu Technical Report released September 2021, indicates that from Oct–Dec 2021, food insecurity is expected to further deteriorate among poor rural, urban, and displaced populations including Galgadud, Gedo and Lower Juba regions due to the impacts of anticipated, below-average 2021 Deyr (Oct-Dec) season rainfall, continued insecurity and other food security related risk factors, including rising food prices and cost of living, declining availability of milk for both consumption and sale, and a likely reduction in agricultural employment opportunities during the forthcoming Deyr season.
Furthermore, FSNAU Post-Gu Technical Report –September 2021, points out that estimated 55,290  people in Galgadud region including Abudwak district are experiencing food crisis/or IPC 3 and estimated 3,900 people in the rural parts are in IPC 4, translating to about 13% of total in Crisis and Emergency as percentage of total population. In Gedo region a significant number of people (66,080) are in IPC 3 and 6,430 people are in the IPC 4, translating to about 15% of total in Crisis and Emergency as proportion of total population. As for Lower Juba region, encompassing Badhadhe district, an estimated 93,830 people are in IPC 3 and 8,840 of the population are in IPC 4, representing about 12% of the total population. 

Cluster Objective 1: Improve access to food for 3.1 million of people facing severe acute food insecurity including million IDPs, 2 million non-displaced people and persons with disabilities in 64 districts. ADA will aim to improve immediate access to food to at least 5,250 households. 

Cluster Objective 2:  Protect livelihoods and related food sources for 830 000 farmers, pastoralists, agro pastoralist and 163 000 rural IDPs across Somalia through emergency agriculture, livestock, and other livelihoods support. ADA will ensure to  protect  and  restore  livelihoods  related  to  food  and  income  sources at least 3,500 households will be reached.

The planned project activities are;
Activity 1: Community mobilization, identification of 10 water catchments and household that are vulnerable but can provide labour for deepening and expansion of productive facilities. 
Activity 2 Procurement and provision of seeds to agro-pastoralist farmers (12kg sorghum, 10kg cowpea and 10 Kg maize) for 3,500 farmers at least 30% women.
Activity 3 Training of farmers on good agronomic practices including conservation agriculture reaching 10% of the target farmers.
Activity 4: 5,250 agro-pastoralist households have increased access to productive assets through rehabilitation of water catchments.
Activity 5: Desilt community water catchments through Cash for Work to increase water storage by 4,200,000lts seasonally in each pan in respective village. The water catchments will provide water for human and livestock and enable the local population to concentrate on crop production.

The livestock will have enough water for drinking, having enough water available to livestock allows for optimal animal performance and health. High water in-take, and the more an animal drinks, the more the milk production and better animal performance. The availability of milk and meat obtained from the livestock, will mean that the household's income will be better, since the households have substitutes to either trade the livestock or sell the direct consumption outputs such as milk or meat, thus the household will utilise the money obtained from such action in many ways, which will consequently enhance the food security situation of the households. 
Activity 6: Conduct post distribution monitoring in each cycle of CFW payments to beneficiaries and food distribution, where at least 5% of the target beneficiaries will be interviewed.
Activity 7: Conduct crop yield assessments for the planted crop stages.
Activity 8: At least 3,000 animals comprising of goats and cows will be supported in animal interventions including support in treatment.

project_name: Provision of emergency WASH services to drought and conflict affected populations in Gedo, Galgaduud and Lower Jubba regions of Somalia.
project_objective:
Somalia is currently undergoing drought conditions with rains having failed/sub-optimal while some areas have had seasonal flooding. This situation is compounded by diseases outbreaks and conflict related displacement which further contributes to the increase in the number of people in need for WASH services. COVID-19, Acute watery diarrhea as well as cholera outbreaks have eroded the previous gains made in the provision of sustainable WASH services to the most vulnerable in Somalia. Recent studies show that rural areas and hard to reach districts have shown a significant increase in the number people in need attributed to increasing vulnerability due to limited access to water and sanitation among rural areas and IDP sites. Access to improved sanitation facilities in the target areas is very low with the JMCNA 2021 study showing  that 57 percent of households do not have access to improved sanitation facilities. Additionally, 23 per cent of people across Somalia still defecate in the open, 49 per cent of which are in rural areas. Due to the drought, water sources are far from the households and this predisposes women and girls to GBV cases and assault while the disability affected population is fairing far much worse with their situation increased by these factors. Active in Development Aid which has been active in the target areas plans to target 15,000 vulnerable populations in Gedo and lower Jubba as well as Galgaduud regions of Somalia out of the estimated 333,848 people in need of WASH services. The projects key activities will include provision of emergency water services through water tracking, rehabilitation of existing water sources, rehabilitation and construction of household/communal and institutional latrines as well as hygiene promotion. each location will have water committees who will be chosen by the target communities following the WASH guidelines and will be trained on proper water management. The project will be implemented to ensure all members of the community including persons with disabilities have equal access to WASH services. ADA is similarly submitting HRP proposals in nutrition and livelihood in the same target areas hence the project will be integrated and have synergy with these other thematic areas. ADA will engage with the
community through FGDs for the different sexes and ages to ensure accountability and that their needs are catered for and able to benefit from the project. To ensure people with disabilities benefit equally from the project, ADA will design disability friendly infrastructure such as ramps, safer latrines, hand washing facilities among others. Data on usage of WASH services by the people with disabilities will be collected and shared with cluster/donor.

project_name: Provision of Emergency shelter Kits and Non Food Items to the most Vulnerable IDPs and the Host community in South and Central Regions of Somalia
project_objective: According to the JMCNA 2021, shelter is one of the top three priority need of more than half of the entire population and of 58 percent of IDPs. An estimated 3.7 million people need shelter and NFI assistance mainly due to poor shelter conditions, overcrowding and lack of space, poverty, and lack of security of tenure. Those in need of shelter and NFI assistance include displaced and non-displaced populations. Conflict, drought, flooding, evictions and cyclones are the key drivers of displacement, which in turn exacerbates humanitarian shelter and NFI needs. Natural disasters are one of the main causes of displacement and therefore accelerate migration from rural to urban and peri-urban centers that started decades ago. Urbanization is rarely organized through urban planning and multiyear plans. Women and girls living in sub-standard and overcrowded shelters are particularly vulnerable. They tend not to feel safe in makeshift shelters which do not offer privacy and sufficient protection from weather elements and increase the risk of gender based violence. Juba Foundation conducted a quick assessment that aimed to ascertain the needs of over 50,000 beneficiaries in the targeted regions, it was noted from the assessment that women and girls are at risk of disaeses as most of them live in makeshift shelter and face the risk of eviction, there is no land tenure security. It is with this in mind that Juba foundation proposes to intervene and provide emergency shelter kits to 3000 HHs  (18000 individuals both women, men, boys and girls) 4000 HHs with Non Food Items (24,000 women, men, boys and girls) and also construction of 400 transitional shelter) in Lower Shabelle, Lower Juba, Galgaduud, Hiraan, Bay and Bakool Regions. Juba foundation will conduct a market assessment in the target areas to establish the functionality of the markets and the availability of the commodities, this will be done to ascertain the modality that will be used for delivery of the Non Food items and ESK. Where feasible vouchers will be used.

project_name: Strengthening and improving the protective environment for the  most vulnerable IDPs and Host communities in South and Central regions of Somalia
project_objective:
According to UN OCHA 2021 Somalia Humanitarian Needs Overview Protection risks are increasing and the need to centralize protection throughout response activities to the most vulnerable is vital
Elevated protection risk exposure Protection concerns remain at the centre of the humanitarian crisis with a diverse range of protection issues in Somalia, including violations of international human rights and humanitarian law. At least 1.1million internally displaced persons (IDPs) and other vulnerable people, notably women, children, minorities, the disabled, child and female-headed households, survivors of violence, abuse and exploitation (particularly children), or older persons without support structures, are exposed to protection risks, such as forced evictions, discrimination based on status, child rights violations and child labour, family separations and gender-based violence (GBV), such as rape and sexual assault, due to conflict and protracted displacement as well as natural hazards. Settlements are often ungoverned, or governed by gatekeepers, overcrowded and displaced people have limited access to protective shelter, safe water and sanitation facilities as well as other basic needs.
Based on ongoing reports from UNHCR PRMN’s partners in the field, new displacements About 
1,780households (approximately 10,700individuals) displaced by drought were recorded as arriving in various parts of the country High levels of displacement lack of social support systems and family breakdown mean children are at high risk of separation from their families which puts them at risk of trafficking, sexual exploitation. Separated and unaccompanied (UASC) girls are often “hidden” as a result of being absorbed into community structures often taking on the burden of domestic labour and child care. The current droughts in the target areas requires action to prevent family separation and respond when separation does occur through the provision of comprehensive IDTR and case management services for UASC.
JF will establish a complaint and feedback mechanism that will support the beneficiaries in accessing the services and recording their complaints and feedback regarding the project. The project will implement Protection monitoring activities and conduct service mapping, the organization will work with the local authorities to improve protection service provision in the target locations. The organization will conduct safety audits, this will include also child safety walks in 20 IDP sites and the reports will be shared with the relevant stakeholders. High risk IDP sites will be targeted with this activity.
The aim of this project is to respond to the drought by providing CP services in the target regions to protect child rights and safety, prevent critical deterioration of their physical and mental health and promote their short and longer-term well being. The activities to achieve the above includes: Monitoring of Child Recruitment in camps and host communities, Identification Documentation, Tracing and Reunification (IDTR),legal aid services, recreational activities and psycho social services, interim care services, reintegration services and referrals to other sectors as well as supporting expansion the Community-Based Child Protection (CBCP), Material assistance such as Clothing, dignity kits, solar lamps. The project will also focus on creation of awareness on GBV, Establishment of referral pathways, Distribution of Dignity kits to GBV victims and survivors. Support psycho social services among other activities.
The project will also focus on filling the information gaps on  Housing land and property Juba foundation will work with the local authorities to prevent the risk of Eviction and especially for the most vulnerable IDPs, people living with disabilities and the most vulnerable women and child headed HHs in the project target area. JF will also provide HLP services in the project target areas.

project_name: Provision of Livelihood Support and Farm Inputs to Crisis-Affected IDPs in Banadir and Farmers in Middle Shabelle of Somalia.
project_objective:
Protracted political instability, continued population’s displacements, ongoing armed conflict, and enduring environmental stress have rendered many of the country’s estimated 15.7 million people to be acutely food insecure. It is projected that drought will be one of one of the primary drivers of food insecurity in the country in 2022. This is largely attributed to the La Nina condition experienced in the greater Horn of Africa region.

2021 witnessed a delayed start, early end, and erratic rainfall distribution of the Gu rainfall season as a result, cumulative rainfall was below the 40-year average across much of the country, especially in central and southern Somalia. Forecasted La Niña conditions are associated with an elevated likelihood of consecutive below-average rainfall seasons, and Somalia faces a high risk that drought conditions will develop by early 2022.

According to Post- Gu assessment done by FSNAU and FEWS NET in September 2021, 3.5 million persons would be in Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and Emergency (IPC Phase 4) through to December 2021, if urgent humanitarian assistance is not provided. Of this, 1.1 are Internally Displaced Persons who are likely to face moderate to severe food consumption gap. 640,000 persons of the 3.5M people in need of urgent food assistance are facing significant food gap, this is envisaged to continue until late in 2021. Further 3.7M people in IPC Phase 3 (stressed) that engaged in negative coping strategies to meet their food and non-food needs may push the total of acute food insecure population to 7.2M by December, 2021.

Cyclic climatic shocks and perennial conflicts are negatively impacting on traditional rural livelihoods resulting influx to urban centers. This is expected to continue in 2022 further exacerbating food insecurity that already biting in the country. It is projected that girls and women will be disproportionately impacted if urgent and deliberate interventions are not put in place. Girls and women are likely to take on opportunities to place food on their families’ tables, fetch water and other duties that would not only burden them but also put them at risks of violations and exploitations. 

Other drivers of food insecurity include lack of information by minority and marginalized groups stemming from lack of consultation and participation in decision making, pushing the included groups to the brink of starvation.

Impact of COVID-19, crippling poverty levels, and protection concerns; particularly among
vulnerable groups like Internally Displaced Persons, women headed households, girls, elderly and minority communities and persons with disabilities are likely to exacerbate food consumption gaps among urban communities.

Aid Vision proposed project is aimed at providing access to lifesaving and sustaining food security and livelihood interventions to 9,000 crisis affected population in Banadir and Middle Shabelle Regions, Aid Vision has presence in the two regions for over two decades and established networks of community structures and local authorities. The project will provide Cash Based interventions, rehabilitation of farming infrastructure, provision farm inputs, irrigation support, training of farmers on contemporary farming techniques and provision of agricultural extension services. It is envisioned that the interventions will go a long way in not only improving food security in the target regions but also enhance community resilience to shocks in future.

project_name: Provision of Emergency Lifesaving Water, Sanitation and Hygiene services to Flood and Conflict Affected Communities in Benadir and Lower Shabelle Region.
project_objective:
The situation in the Banadir and Lower shabelle region remains volatile and uncertain due to limited development coupled with recurring climatic shocks, such as drought and conflict give rise to high levels of need among affected populations. Daynile and Kahda districts IDP sites are hosting a Total of 61,727 Households or 263,783 Individuals, and 50,146HHs or 190,308 individuals respectively were assessed and mapped as per Detailed Site Assessments (DSA) conducted in Banadir in march 2021 by the REACH initiative. Among the IDPs targeted are vulnerable new Displaced populations of around 7,686 and 4,995 individuals in Daynile and Kahda whom they arrived in the past three (3) months, which is equivalent to 12,681 are displaced between December 2020 - March 2021 due to drought and conflict. In this, almost 60 -70 percent of the total population in kahda and Daynile are severe and extreme conditions for WASH intervention as per the DSA report in April 2021. 
The Proposed project will contribute to increased investment to address the water infrastructure development gaps through rehabilitation of existing water sources and expanding the supply networks to improve access by reducing access in needs to safe and clean water and improved sanitation of most vulnerable and underserved communities living in floods affected areas in Daynile, Kahda districts in Mogadishu and Merka, Wanlaweyn and Afgooye district of Lower Shebelle region. A total of 18,700 flood affected men, women and children including the 15% disabilities, marginalized communities and IDPs will bene t safe drinking water and will have access equally throughout the project period. SOYDA in collaboration with the local authority, partnership with main water vendors in rural villages in target districts, will provide emergency water voucher to the 7,440 (1808 men, 1,536 women, 2,048 boys and 2,048 girls) targeted beneficiaries including people with disabilities and marginalized communities in the targeted IDP camps, which they can redeem for water at the specified water vendors (water trucks). The action also includes to hire water truck of a capacity of 6,000 liters of safe water to the targeted locations. Each voucher can be used to redeem specified quantity of safe water of 7.5 liters per person per day for a period of 30 days. The project will build the capacity of 10 WASH Committees (composing 4 men and 3 women per Committee) shared equally men and women on operation and maintenance of developed water infrastructures shall be throughout the project implementation period, to ensure the sustainability of the developed water facilities after the project is faced out. SOYDA will make sure that men, women, girls and boys including people with disabilities and marginalized community have equal access to the rehabilitated/constructed WASH services. SOYDA will upgrade/rehabilitate two boreholes equipped with hybrid to improve its water quality and reduce its running cost, in order to receive the community their water needs at an affordable cost. SOYDA will replace the engine powered boreholes in to hybrid system and construct 8 water kiosks nearer to the IDP settlements supplied water through piping network to avoid the risk of rape against women and girls in target districts. The project will provide reliable and sustainable access to environmental sanitation through construction of 200 IDP latrines in target districts. The latrines will be gender separated and flood proof with lockable doors and hand washing basins. construction of latrines will be implemented through market-based programming. 
The project will ensure the participation of people with disability in all decision-making processes and ensure WASH- related information is in formats that people with different types of disabilities can understand and as well will consider disability groups in the design, monitoring and evaluation of development and emergency WASH interventions through disability mainstreaming

project_name: WASH assistance for droughts affected vulnerable communities.
project_objective: Project interventions are enabling the easy access of sustainable water services for vulnerable settlements/households include (displaced and none-displaced and persons with disabilities) in floods and severe-drought hotspot districts in Sanaag, Togdheer and Awdal regions of Somaliland, of whom currently accessing temporary water trucking, distant shallow reservoirs, and unprotected shallow wells that are not functional throughout the year.  In response, basic water supply systems to be restored through rehabilitation of existing water-facilities and provision of new sustainable water sources to decrease the effects of disproportional affects of droughts, and barriers of accessing sustainable WASH services.

project_name: Access to lifesaving education in emergencies for Crisis affected children including children with disability in Bari and Sool regions.
project_objective:
The impact of the ongoing flooding compounded by economic and social impacts of COVID-19, escalated conflict, and forecast of below average rainfall from May to November 2021 may result in further deterioration of humanitarian outcomes for affected communities through 2022. In a context like Somalia where teachers are under qualified, classrooms are overcrowded, and materials and facilities are scarce, teachers are often using verbal or physical punishment of children to maintain control of the classroom. This behavior affects children negatively and hampers their learning outcome and well-being. Additionally, barriers to access to education for children with disabilities are considerable. The low enrolment of children living with disabilities can be explained negative attitude towards children with disabilities and unavailability of favorable learning environment compounded by untrained teachers on inclusive education. Schooling provides essential learning and when schools close, children and youth are deprived opportunities for growth, development and cognitive. Those who are greatly affected include girls, IDPs and Rural children who tend to have fewer educational opportunities beyond school. According to JMCNA findings the regions with the highest proportion of school-aged children in need of humanitarian assistance are in Southern and Northeastern areas. In Bari region, 63% of school-aged children in Qardo, 62% in Qandala and 61% Calula. Despite the advantages female education brings (increased economic productivity and increased awareness of rights) girls face a unique set of barriers that prevents them from going to school, including many cultural and economic hurdles, some of the reasons cited by Somali parents and teachers for gender disparities in education are: the inadequate number of female teachers, lack of gender-segregated latrines, and inaccessible schools amidst conflict and heightened insecurity. The project will, through its community sensitization activities, will specifically promote the benefits and value of educating girls, to boost the enrollment and retention of girls in school. 
TASS proposes to address this gap through an integrated approach by ensuring that 18,000 (9,450 boys and 8,550 girls) school-children and particularly girl child and children with disabilities are able to access quality education in schools through the provision of inclusive basic education package in a protective learning environment combined with life-saving activities such as: Rehabilitation of 25 Classrooms, Provision of protection activities as per the Integrated Education-Child Protection Response Framework including establishing community dialogues in both IDPs and host community settlements to raise awareness on mitigating risks and all kinds of child abuse practices to enhance children’s access and retention in education, Provision of emergency teaching and learning materials to 18,000 (9,450 boys and 8,550 girls) Provision of teachers incentives -240 (40% female), Provision of Clean drinking water- 18,000, Provision of school feeding- 18,000 (9,450 boys and 8,550 girls), Provision of Teacher training- 240 (40% Female), CECs on school management, child protection and school safety and Provide training to Education Cluster partners and MoE staff (10M and 10F) on emergency preparedness and response planning and coordination, additionally TASS in Collaboration with MOE department of special needs will coordinate with identification of needs specific to boys, girls particularly children with disability and children from IDPs in ensuring better protective environment to all learners. The project will be implemented in 7 Districts in bari and Sool regions including Bari (Bossaso, Caluula, Iskushuban, Qandala, Qardho) and Sool region (Taleex and Xudun) targeting 18,000 (9,450 boys and 8,550 girls) including Children with disability, IDPs and Vulnerable host communities specially in hard-to-reach areas.

project_name: Child protection intervention to Vulnerable crisis affected boys and girls including children with disabilities in Hard-to-Reach Areas of Sool, Bari, Sanaag, Nugaal and Mudug Regions
project_objective: Crisis affected populations who are underserved are at great risk of Child violation, sexual exploitation and abuse, and forced/early marriages are usually the consequences in this insecure and unstable setting with weak rule of law, scarce of opportunities to sustain the daily lives and limited access to the quality multi-sectoral services. The project will be targeting boy and girls in hard-to-reach areas including children with disabilities as they are especially vulnerable and report a very high level of unmet needs. They are the most vulnerable, marginalized and at-risk group within Somalian society as a result of the numerous attitudinal, environmental, and institutional barriers they face. The proposed project will provide of age, and gender sensitive structured mental health and psychosocial support services to girls and boys, including adolescents, children with disabilities, provide caregivers with psychosocial support, parenting messages, positive parenting and other kind support leading to improved relationships with the children under their care, provision of individual case management services that meets their unique needs to the identified girls and boys, including adolescents, children with disabilities at risk, Reintegrate girls and boys released from armed forces and groups with their families/communities and provided with adequate care and services, reunification of identified separated girls and boys with their primary caregivers or in appropriate alternative care, Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism (MRM), Training CP actors [social workers, community volunteers, government officials, field coordinators], Community awareness on child protection and Conduct referral mapping. Optimizing Child Protection outcomes through meaningful integration with other sectors and providing various forms of support to caregivers and families of children facing protection risks in order to enhance their capacity to care for and protect their children. Awareness raising activities will target 15,000 community members including PLWDs with a wide range of prevention messages and awareness sessions including on recruitment/CAAFAG, SGBV, harmful practice, family separation, and Children’s rights. The project will be implemented in the hard to reach areas of Bari (Bandarbeyla and Iskushuban) Mudug (Galdogob and Jariiban) Nugaal (Burtinle and Eyl )Sanaag (Laasqoray) and Sool( Taleex and Xudun)

project_name: Provision of essential primary health care services to Crisis Affected people in hard to reach areas in Bari, Mudug, Nugaal, Sanaag and Sool Regions
project_objective:
According to Human Development Reports (undp.org) The population of Somalia consistently experience some of the worst health outcome indicators in the world, the average life expectancy is estimated to be 51.5 years (UNDP’s Human Development Reports) addtionally Somalia is among the countries with the highest rankings in infant and child mortality rates of, respectively, 76.6 and 121.5 per 1,000 live births. The maternal mortality rate (692 deaths per 100,000 live births) and the fertility rate (average of 6.9 children per woman) are also among the highest in the world, 79 per cent of all births are home delivered without skilled assistance. Overall, 99 per cent of Somali women have undergone female genital mutilation, 64 per cent of these having suffered the Pharaonic type. Overall, only 11 per cent of children aged 12-23 months are fully vaccinated, around 19 per cent of children in urban areas have received all basic vaccinations, while this is the case for less than 1 per cent of children in nomadic areas (FINAL SHDS Report 2020). The inadequate comprehensive and reliable epidemiological and disease information from all districts makes it difficult to ascertain the extent of gaps in service provision and burden of disease across the country and effectively plan for response among actors. To estimate the health needs indicators, a combination of health status, health resources, and contextual factors were considered.
For People living with disabilities (PLWD) not only is COVID-19 a significant direct risk to health, but it has added to the mental suffering of the population, causing anxiety, fear and driving stigmatization. The nature of the pandemic and some of the measures used to control it have increased vulnerability especially to gender-based and interpersonal violence for persons living with disabilities (PLWD) in their access to care. Those most vulnerable to health risks are PLWDs and those with mental health disorders. Particularly People living with disabilities (PLWD) become more vulnerable when healthcare is inaccessible and of poor quality. 
In the proposed Project TASS will respond to the most urgent needs for 25,000 beneficiaries including People living with disabilities (PLWD), The services including emergency clinical service provision, community health care and maternity (supporting ANC, PNC, normal delivery, Basic emergency obstetric and newborn care (BEmONC) services and newborn care, outbreak investigation and response for epidemic prone diseases and the provision of essential medical supplies. SGBV, protection services to support MHPSS services and CMR in the health facilities through case management, training staff on MHPSS and CMR and conducting Community dialogue on the prevention of GBV and Harmful social norms
Minority groups and People with diability, who are often omitted from humanitarian assistance, will be participate at all phases of the project cycle. The project will also strive to include all age and gender groups. To ensure staff have capacity to promote these while ensuring protection, all staff will be trained in PSEA, social mobilization and disability inclusion in programs. Strong monitoring will ensure realization of this with all data disaggregated by age and gender Gender will be mainstreamed throughout the project: data will be disaggregated by sex and age whenever possible and activities will be tailored to respond to the specific needs of women, girls, men and boys affected by crisis in three targeted Districts of Sool region. The needs of girls and women in conflict will be taken into account by tailoring specific training to the female health workers and by strengthening the referral mechanism to assist women and girls who have been subjected to sexual gender-based violence. The access to integrated lifesaving emergency health services will be particularly ensured for pregnant and lactating women, U5 children and PLWDs.

project_name: Strengthening and Improving the protective environment for the most vulnerable internally displaced populations and host communities through gender-based violence prevention response and mitigation mechanism in Bari, Nugaal, Sanaag, Sool and Mudug Region
project_objective:
The protection crisis in Somalia continues to be characterized by a multi-faceted armed conflict. It is also compounded by the persistent drought, governance challenges, weakened resilience and economic vulnerability of families and communities. Both protracted and new displacement have resulted in undignified living circumstances with severe protection implications for affected men, women, and children.
Boys, girls and persons with disability continue to endure multiple protection risks and violations of their rights including family separation, GBV, physical abuse, psychosocial distress, child labour, wide spread recruitment and use of children by armed groups, forced displacement, limited access to humanitarian assistance due to insecurity and/or discriminatory practices and exploitation. This situation is exacerbated by the limited availability of basic services, weak governance, negative social norms, and persistent marginalization. Psychosocial wellbeing is built on safety and access to basic services which are fundamental to children’s growth and development. 
The proposed project is designed to support the crisis affected populations (Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) and host communities including marginalized and People living with Disability) in Bari, Nugaal, Sanaag, Sool and Mudug Regions, through: 1) Provision of age appropriate and quality services of clinical management of rape in GBV one stop centers that meet the minimum standards to 1200 (1,100 women and girls and 100 Men and Boys) 2) Provision of age-appropriate psychosocial support for FGM/GBV in existing GBV one stop centers and women and girls' safe spaces that meet the minimum standards to 1200 women and girls including PWDs 3) Provision of recreational and livelihood skills including GBV/RH education sessions in Women and Girls safe spaces to 1200 women and girls, 4) Provision of age appropriate and gender responsive legal aid support/Education and information to 1200 vulnerable women and girls including PWDs & Marginalized, 5) Provision of dignity kits, menstrual hygiene kits and solar lanterns to 1500 vulnerable women and adolescent girls (including those living with disabilities and from minority clans) 6) Provide capacity building to national actors (government officials, security personnel, NGOs ) and cluster field coordinators with knowledge on implementing GBV mitigation, coordination , response strategies and PSEA for vulnerable women and girls (including PLWDS and minority clans) 7) Conduct Mass community awareness for women, girls, boys and men (including those with disabilities and from minority clans) reached with key GBV/FGM information on service availability, prevention and mitigation of GBV/FGM. This shall therefore increase accessibility to quality and coordinated GBV services for drought and conflict affected communities in in Bari, Mudug and Sool Regions and strengths resilience among the vulnerable populations including Internal Displaced Population (IDP) and poor host community through awareness. While implementing the activities we will work closely and use the existing structures to strengthen the coordination with stakeholders/clusters, partners and government structures and /or women and girls’ friendly spaces and avenues. TASS shall ensure confidentiality in reporting and referral mechanism through its qualified and professional staff who will improve services accessibility to women and children in target locations and provide comprehensive protection services. Minority groups and People with diability, who are often omitted from humanitarian assistance, will be participate at all phases of the project cycle. The project will also strive to include all age and gender groups. To ensure staff have capacity to promote these while ensuring protection, all staff will be trained in PSEA, social mobilization and disability inclusion in programs.

project_name: To provide access to basic child protection services including child friendly spaces and tracing, reunification or alternative care for UASC to the affected children.
project_objective:
The proposed project will increase child protection activities that will work to consolidate
efforts that ensure services reach the most deserving and vulnerable children’s groups.
This project is aligned with the UNICEF child Protection strategy note and will contribute to
the overall goal of “2022 - 2025, children are protected from all forms of abuse, neglect and
exploitation. It targets the most vulnerable in society including UASC and at-risk ones and
the strategies proposed will not only mitigate risks, but will also work towards resilience
building, and sustainability through investing in community structures CBCPCs knowledge
building. ARC has expertise in protection and currently leads the Protection Sub Regional
Cluster in Sool and Burao of Somaliland with close coordination of UNHCR and NDRA and
chairs the GBV Working Group Sub Cluster in Kismayo and co-chair the regional protection
cluster in Jubbaland in collaboration with MOWGFA AND UNHCR in hosting all protection
meetings with the Ministry in Jubbaland. ARC have strong programmes, community
acceptance and accessibility to the proposed locations. The intervention will also include
activities for adolescents between the age of 14 and 17 years old in order to address the
unique needs of this group. Despite adolescence being the most important stage for
children in terms of making critical choices in life, interventions available for this group
remain limited across Somalia. As a result, early parenthood, dropping out from school,
recruitment into armed groups and making un-informed choices in life are predominant
challenges. 1,200 IDP children (650 girls; 550 boys) drawn from the above IDP camps will
benefit from psychosocial and life skill development activities at safe spaces. 360
children will benefit from case management; 500 adolescents (300 females; 200 male)
identified from the above IDP camps will benefit from mentorship programs. 10,000 IDP
children (6,400 girls; 3,600 boys) from the above IDP camps will benefit from improved
child protection environment as a result of improved awareness on child protection,
monitoring, reporting and referrals among the wider community in their camps. 15,000
adult IDPs will benefit from awareness campaigns and sensitization initiatives on child protection. child protection networks created/enhanced across the locations of
intervention. 20 child protection service providers including INGOs, local NGOs, formal
schools, Qur’anic centers and Maternal and Child Health Clinics workers will be trained. ALIGHT will deploy trained Psychosocial Counsellors at the Child Friendly Spaces to support the social workers deliver one on one daily counselling services to the traumatized children affected by Tigray crisis and have lost social connections and parents. Children will be provided with appropriate conducive, confidential, compassionate environment to express their emotional stress and trauma. 1200 Children under the age of 18 will be targeted with structured   PSS sessions and parent and foster parents will be engaged in specific designed session to enhance their mental wellbeing and reduce the chances of the critical mental health issues as a result of the crisis. Through adult structured sessions, daily therapy sessions will be coordinated under the Psychosocial sub sector under GBV.  ARC will endeavor to ensure a standardized approach for case management (including IDTR for UASC), PSS and reporting within the targeted Tigray child protection network. This effort will be beneficial for designing more appropriate and timely responses for children, benefit data collection and analysis, advocacy work and in general strengthen coordination and complementary of actions among partners who are engaged for the protection of children in Tigray. ARC, will coordinate mapping of where children have come from, building linkages with the stakeholders there for reunification will be implemented.

project_name: Provision of equitable access to quality lifesaving treatment and prevention of acute malnutrition among children (6-59months) and  pregnant and lactating women (PLW) in Somalia
project_objective:
Acute malnutrition persisted high in Somalia, at the national level, the median prevalence of Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) has remained Serious (10–14.9%) over the past three years. According to Food Security & Nutrition Analysis Unit (FSNAU) Post Gu Assessment in July 2021, the overall median Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) in Somalia remained Serious (11.1% weight-for-height z-score). The drivers To address the high rate of acute malnutrition and considering gender inequality and all other inequalities in Somalia, ALIGHT will provide equitable access to quality preventive and life-saving curative nutrition services through systematic identification, referral and treatment of acutely malnourished cases, support curative and preventive nutrition interventions to treat children under five (U5), pregnant and lactating women (PLW) with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) and moderate acute malnutrition (MAM). The need assessment and proposed assistance is tailored towards all gender, age groups and those with disabilities. Services include nutrition screening, targeted supplementary feeding programme (TSFP) and outpatient therapeutic programme (OTP) as well as management of SAM children with medical complications at stabilization centres. All interventions will be aligned with MoH, WHO, WFP and UNICEF guidelines/protocols and Somalia integrated management of acute malnutrition (IMAM) protocols through capacity building to the qualified staff and CHWs on IMAM, IYCF and CommCare COVID putting the COVID-19 protocols into consideration. ALIGHT will improve access to life-saving preventive nutrition services with an integrated health response and protection mainstreaming for vulnerable population groups focusing on appropriate infant and young child feeding practices in an emergency, provision of supplementary products, micronutrient interventions and optimal maternal nutrition services will be co-located at the MCHs to help ensure that children U5 across both genders (69498 males and 72335females) and PLW presenting for health services are screened for vaccination, nutrition and likewise those presenting for nutrition services can be referred and easily access primary, maternal, and child health services, as needed.
 Considering all genders, all children U5 presenting at the MCH will be screened and if necessary, referred for admission to the TSFP or OTP per the IMAM admission criteria. SAM cases presenting with medical complications will be referred to the nearest stabilization centre (SC). ALIGHT is also planning to combine the nutrition and health nursing staff to foster more integration across health and nutrition activities at the facilities while undertaking protection mainstreaming. The linkage to WASH and health components will ensure a comprehensive approach to reduce morbidity and mortality associated with the compound effect of diseases resulting from poor sanitation conditions, lack of access to safe water, and malnutrition. To increase the impact, the nutrition project will be coordinated also with ALIGHT WASH, Protection and Livelihood projects. ALIGHT will undertake SMART or IYCF survey for evidence-based intervention and Strengthen nutrition situation coordination, monitoring and surveillance, analysis and utilization of early warning information for timely coordinated response Regularly updating the ONA and sharing 3W Matrix, ALIGHT will closely coordinate intervention with the cluster, MoH and respond in locations where gaps in nutrition services have been identified. ALIGHT will ensure the participation of the local communities, with special attention to the participation of women, in decision making throughout the project cycle to strengthen community acceptance and ownership. Throughout the lifetime of the project, ALIGHT will work with the MoH throughout the lifecycle of the project by sharing information and supporting joint support supervision to pave the way for a proper phasing out at the end of the project.

project_name: Provision of life-saving WASH assistance and restoration of access to safe and equitable basic WASH services to drought, conflict, floods and diseases outbreaks affected most vulnerable communities including displaced, non- displaced populations and Institutions from Lower juba, Benadir, and Sool  region of Somalia/Somaliland.
project_objective:
In the context of the current multi-faceted emergencies (increased risks of flooding, protracted conflict, droughts, Covid 19, Cholera/AWD Outbreaks, Alight proposes this emergency WASH project to target IDPs and most vulnerable host communities to save lives, restoring access to basic wash services, and reducing morbidities associated with WASH-related diseases. The project will target worst – affected districts such as Kismayo, Benadir, Afmadow, lascanod, Telex, Badade , and Xudun.
Alight understands that droughts and protracted conflicts are the key drivers of internal displacements and also the humanitarian needs in Somalia. Many IDPs and Poor vulnerable Host communities are currently residing in Urban and pre-urban informal crowded areas with insufficient access to water and Sanitation. According to JMCNA assessment done in August by REACH, 53% of the IDPs face challenges in terms of access to WASH services in Somalia. The situation of IDPs and non- IDPs vulnerable host community members are complicated by frequently forced evictions meted on them leading to disruptions of access to critical WASH services and loss of gains made on access to these essential services.  According to JMCNA 2021, 39 per cent of vulnerable people in Somalia do not have access to sustained, improved and safe water sources for drinking and other domestic uses, while 84 per cent still walk for more than 15 minutes to the nearest water source. Due to these constraints, one in five Somalis does not have enough water per day to cover their basic needs for both drinking and domestic use.
Cognizant of these contexts, Alight will provide emergency water trucking to 12000 (2000HH) drought-affected IDPs and vulnerable pastoral communities living in drought-prone areas of Lascanod, Xudun, Telex and Afmadow districts for two months as the agency will find and rehabilitate alternative water sources for the affected people. 12 critical shallow wells will be rehabilitated and protected targeting IDPs and Non- IDPs vulnerable communities and settlements from Kismayo, Kaxda & wartanabada (Banadir), Lascanod, Telex. Alight will also conduct Disinfections and chlorination of floods affected wells. 
Alight will Provide 10 Strategic boreholes in drought-prone locations in Lascanood, Telex, and Xudun and Afmadow district with generators, submersible pumps, cable wires and control panels to ensure drought affected peoples have access to safe, adequate and reliable water.
ARC will establish 6 Pipeline water extensions to identified IDPs Camps and non- IDPs camps including the construction of elevated water storage tanks, installation of solar-powered systems and water kiosk with a minimum of 6 taps to ensure increased access to adequate water by the IDPs and Non-IDPs. Alight will construct/rehabilitate 600 gender-segregated, disability-friendly communal latrines for IDPs and vulnerable host community members who have no access to any sanitation facilities. Alight will construct sex-Disaggregated, Disability Inclusive 40 Institutional latrines with water and Handwashing facilities for 24 target schools and 15 health centres.
 Hygiene promotion will remain a key component of the intervention to prevent the spread of Covid-19 and other WASH-related diseases through risk communications and community engagement promoting behaviour changes.  2000 Hygiene kits and basic MHM kits will be provided to adolescent girls in schools and villages/camps. Alight will target approximately 48, 000 beneficiaries from North and south-central Somalia (7488 women, 5823 men, 12165 boys, 12165 girls, 9201 disabled, and 1158 elderly people). Alight will consult men, boys, girls, elderly, and people with disabilities on their needs and preference regarding the type, Design and location of the water and sanitation facilities to address barriers relating to access. Alight will involve women, boys, girls and disabled people in the project monitoring and their feedback will be sought.

project_name: Provision of Life Saving assistance to the disaster affected communities in Somalia
project_objective:
Recurrent drought has severely and directly affected communities whose sources of food, income and water are diminishing and increasingly at risk. This has led to HH food insecurity, sharp increase in debt levels among poor HHs and poor animal health and produce. 
A delayed and poor Deyr season, worsened drought conditions in the target regions resulting in majority of HHs having inadequate access to food and water while staple food and commodity prices have risen at an average of 8.5% in Gedo and 24% in Bay regions over the past year (COOPI PNA, Oct 2021). From October to December 2021, food insecurity is expected to further deteriorate among poor rural, urban, and displaced populations due to the impacts of anticipated, below-average 2021 Deyr (October-December) season rainfall, continued insecurity and other food security related risk factors, including rising food prices and cost of living, declining availability of milk for both consumption and sale, and a likely reduction in agricultural employment opportunities during the forthcoming Deyr season.
The project focuses on the delivery of basic lifesaving and protection/restoration of livelihoods of the target population with a special focus on all locations with FSC prioritized persons in need, including IDPs and host communities that are classified in IPC Phase 3 & 4 in terms of response. 
The project is aimed at improving the ability of vulnerable HHs to meet their basic needs, supports protection and recovery of livelihood assets through life-saving UCT, animal treatment services, provision of locally preferred high quality seeds kits and trainings, and rehabilitation of community productive assets through CFW to support the resilience of vulnerable populations against shocks and prevent them from slipping into acute food insecurity. The proposed project aims to target at least 6,600 HHs (39,600) pastoral, agro-pastoral and IDP HHs in Bay, Banadir, Gedo and Togdheer regions in crisis and emergency with delivery of life saving interventions in line with the strategic objectives of the HRP and FSC response plan.
The project is informed by the centrality of protection and a gender, age and diversity-sensitive approach which is mainstreamed throughout the project cycle. Moreover, the project reflects the principles of COOPI Protection Policy and is built consistently with COOPI Protection SOPs and Protection Mainstreaming guidelines. The project will be guided by the principles of DO NO HARM, ensuring safety and dignity of target population is upheld and at the same time providing for accountability, participation and empowerment. COOPI prioritizes respect for the rights, dignity and safety of the people affected by crisis and is committed to taking account of, giving account to, and being held to account by the populations benefiting from the intervention. During implementation, the beneficiary women, girls and the disabled will be included in decision making processes and in monitoring so as ensure that the most marginalized and vulnerable are represented and have influence.
In summary the following activities will be carried out:
1.	Provide UCT to 3,100 HHs that are faced with severe levels of food insecurity (crisis and emergency) with the aim of improving immediate access to food for 3 months.
2.	Rehabilitation of community productive assets through CFW targeting 1,000 vulnerable HHs.
3.	Provision of locally preferred high quality seed kits, trainings and fuel for irrigation for 500 flood affected female and male headed vulnerable riverine farmers in Bele-Hawa Gedo region.
4.	Provision of locally preferred high quality seeds kit (drought tolerant) and trainings for 1,000 female and male headed vulnerable agro-pastoral farmers in Burhakaba district, Bay region.
5.	Emergency livestock treatment (treatment and deworming) campaigns for animals belonging to 1,000 HHs will be dewormed and treated against endemic &prevalent diseases.

project_name: Response to immediate and sustainable access to safe and equitable basic WASH services in Somalia
project_objective: The high humanitarian needs in Somalia are driven by seasonal floods, severe drought conditions, acute water diarrhoea/ cholera outbreaks exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic. According to 2022 HNO, The population in need of WASH services in 2022 is estimated at 1,619,415 IDPs and 4,818,944 vulnerable host communities. Access to basic water supply in Somalia is 37% in rural and 79 % in urban areas. The JMCNA assessment report 2021 approximates that 39% of the vulnerable people in Somalia do not have access to sustained, improved and safe water source for drinking and other domestic uses, while 25 per cent still walk for more than 15 minutes to collect water from a nearest water source. In addition, 16% of households do not have access to enough drinking water while 45% reported having no access to soap, while more than half of HHs reported lacking access to improved latrines and menstrual hygiene materials. CCCM cluster reports indicate that the majority of those most acutely affected are vulnerable groups; women, elderly, refugee returnees, minority groups and people living with disability (PLWD), putting further stressing affected families and limiting their ability to cope. In October 2021, Ministry of Water and Energy-Jubaland (Gedo Regional Office) and Regional WASH Cluster (Gedo Region) needs assessment report indicates that the drought situation in Gedo region is continually deteriorating. This has worsened in Doolow where estimated 5,244 household have no access to clean and adequate water Doolow due to displacements during recent inter clan conflicts in 17 riverine villages. The same scenario exists in Luuq District where more than 7, 120, HHs living in northern and south rural villages are also in need of basic WASH services including specific appeal for hygiene kits and sanitation tools. The inadequate access to water and sanitation services are particularly prevalent across the majority of congested IDP sites compared to host communities, which in turn leads to higher rates of acute diarrheal and other water-borne diseases, increasing the risk of malnutrition and disability. Further, aggravating the recurrent drought situation in Somalia, the Somalia Water and Land Information Management SWALIM reports that around 40% of existing water supply systems are non-functional mainly due to weak water supply management resulting to affected populations to depend on water trucking. For the year 2022, COOPI proposes to address the immediate Water, Sanitation and Hygiene needs of the severely affected people while sustaining ongoing response in Doolow, Luuq, Owdweyne, Baidoa and Banadir through activities aligned with the Humanitarian Programme Cycle for 2022. As part of the intervention, COOPI will purposefully target PLWD during identification of beneficiaries, design and build facilities to ensure accessibility to all, ensure Water Management Committees include at least one member with disability and that WASH campaigns are all inclusive.

project_name: Strategic Provision of Integrated Nutrition support to improve Basic Nutrition services and strengthen social service provision, resilience and improve Governance for enhanced service delivery and community based public health interventions benefiting 6-59 months children and PLW in Garbaharey district of Gedo Region.
project_objective:
Garbaharey district is one of the most affected in the ongoing analysis of nutritional situation in Gedo Region and by extension Somalia. Somalia 2021 Post Gu Seasonal Food Security and Nutrition Assessment indicates that in Jubba pastoral the number of children with MUAC < 12.5 CM (%) is 13.8% and MUAC < 11.5 CM (%) of 3.4% and the child morbidity rates of 27.8% one of the highest in the country. Already, the federal government and the Jubbaland government have declared drought of a serious concern and national disaster which must be confronted with adequate response mechanism.
The project aim is to increase access to basic nutrition services among PLW and children between the age 6 - 59 months in Garbahare district, in Gedo region, Somalia. To accomplish this feat, it will conduct screening and provision of life saving and preventive nutritional supplements to the children and the PLW. Furthermore, facility and community based (BNSP) program will cover both curative and preventative interventions targeting children U5 years (boys and girls) and pregnant and lactating women.

The project will facilitate identification, referral and treatment of cases of SAM at facility-based as well as mobile OTP teams. All the while, the project will refer complicated cases of SAM to SC and MAM to TSFP. The project will also include routine deworming and immunization services. The organization runs MCHN and provides drugs to PLW at their facility in Garbaharey run by a trained and qualified pharmacist. As such provision of these aforementioned nutritional services will also be overlaid by the strengthened health services at the MCHN which has also been strengthened to cover mild and moderate health complications for children and PLW. Furthermore, the organization has provided access to drugs at the MCHN chemist and entered into agreement with several suppliers to ensure adequate requisite support is available at all points in time. This will provide a full package of community and facility-based nutrition, health and WASH services. Preidentified caregivers will be trained equipped to provide counselling on Maternal, Infant and Young Child Nutrition (MIYCN) to strengthen the resilience of PLW and improve nutrition of infants between 0-23months. Moreover, the project will ensure children betwee 6-59 months receive vitamin A supplements in the first quarter.

To emphasize on the resilience aspect, provision of sustainable skills in WASH & hygiene to support the prevention of infection and/or fatalities related to poor hygiene especially in PLW will overlay. Women will be capacitated on breastfeeding and Infant Young Feeding Program (IYFP), which are key sustainability and resilience approach as well as basic hygiene programs.

The organization will also work in synergy and coordination with other actors at the cluster and field level to ensure referrals, information sharing, feedback and coordination provide effective management of nutrition within the district. The organization will continue its partner-level attendance of meetings and sharing important data.
