Beneficiaries selections will be targeted including the vulnerable communities. The focus will also be made on women-headed households as well as vulnerable families in IDPs. The beneficiaries' selection process will be inclusive and conducted after extensive social mobilizations and communications about the project. Special focus will be made on the disabled through supportive framework for movements and access. For other forms of visibilities, the organization will make intentional effort to identify people with special needs in the community and prioritise their nutritional and health needs during the social mobilization, screening and profiling the beneficiaries.

project_name: Provision of integrated management for severely and moderately acute malnutrition among boys, girls and PLWs Hiran, Bay and Bakool regions Somalia
project_objective: The persistence of widespread acute malnutrition in Somalia due to a combination of factors, including food insecurity, high morbidity, low immunization and vitamin-A supplementation, and poor care practices. According to the latest findings of 2021 post Gu results of FSNAU, the median prevalence of Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) at the national level has remained at a serious level of 11.1 per cent   weight-for-height z-score. Based on this analysis and the latest population figures, the cluster estimates that in 2022 around 1.2 million children, under the age of 5 years, will be at risk of acute malnutrition and will therefore need emergency nutrition services urgently. Out of this, 295,515 children under the age of 5 are likely to be severely malnourished and around 986,000 children will be moderately acute malnourished (MAM).In addition to this, around 245,909 PLWs will be at risk of acute malnutrition. A total of 463,204 pregnant and lactating women are estimated to be in need of either preventive or curative emergency nutrition assistance. In this regard, it is estimated that around 629,567 children between 6 to 23 months and 283,305 PLWs will be at greater risk as well. The total number of IDPs that need nutrition services will be around 0.3 million including women and children.High levels of acute malnutrition continue to persist driven by several factors, including high morbidity, below sphere immunization and Vitamin-A supplementation, poor childcare practices, inadequate access to clean/safe drinking water and acute food insecurity. Consequently, the country is facing a Triple Threat of Desert Locust, flooding’s and the global pandemic COVID-19 contributing towards the deterioration of production outputs, social economics increasing vulnerabilities of households. These culminations result in impact on the states of acute malnutrition situation affecting children and women. A Critical (4-5.6%) prevalence of Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) was observed in the Riverine livelihood of Beletweyne district and in urban Beletweyne. Morbidity among children was high (≥20%) in 15 out 33 population groups surveyed. However, Crude Death Rate and Under-Five Death Rate were relatively low in most areas. Integrated interventions should be provided to support recovery and prevent deterioration in the nutrition situation. Hiraan, Bay and Bakool region were considered hotspot areas with a projected Critical GAM prevalence, indicated by a weight-for-height z-score of 15-29.9% or by a Mid-Upper Arm Circumference below 125 mm of ≥10%, IDP areas of concern are Baidoa and Beletweyne is an urban area of concern for acute malnutrition and need of urgent nutrition and health support interventions This project therefore target to reach a total 9,000 vulnerable boys, girls and pregnant and lactating women through provision of outpatient therapeutic and supplementary feeding intervention. It is intended to mitigate the physical and protection consequences of drought on populations and communities directly affected in Bakool, Bay and Hiran region, in particular, Ceelbarde, Rabdhure, Baidoa and Beletweyne town. The main objective of this project is to provide integrated lifesaving emergency Nutrition services to 9,000 drought affected direct beneficiaries and intends to achieve the following, capacity building of nutrition staff on IMAM. Referral of malnourished children with complicated cases will be done to the Outpatient Therapeutic Programme (OTP) centers and directly linked with primary health care services managed by HIDIG and other actors in the program areas thus providing more holistic opportunity to the target beneficiaries HIDIG will closely coordinate with Local MOH as well as Federal level MOH and social mobilizers, elders all involved in activities on mobilizing communities. To support increase access to basic nutrition services in the area

project_name: EMERGENCY SHELTER & NFI ASSISTANCE TO IDPs & HC IN GEDO AND LOWER JUBA
project_objective:
The project is aimed at providing life saving support to vulnerable IDPs and Host Communities families living in makeshift shelters & with limited access to basic non-food items in Gedo & lower Juba. The project will target those who have continuously been affected by either, the prolonged flooding, displacements due to conflict, drought, forced eviction & the inability to repair or replace their shelters owing to their poor economic situation. 
The proposed intervention will support 24,000 vulnerable individuals (4,000 HHs with average size of 6) including 18,000 IDPs (75%; 3,000 HHs) & 6,000 individuals from the host communities (25%; 1,000 HHs) (out of the 62,304 individuals targeted by the cluster (CLSHL/CO1) in the country), as they are also in dire need of timely life saving & life-sustaining emergency shelter support since they don't have ability to repair or replace their shelters. This will be realized by ensuring their access to adequate and dignified shelter solutions through an in-kind response modality where 4,000 basic NFI kits and 4,000 cluster standardized Emergency Shelter Kits will be provided.  The target beneficiaries will include; 7,200 men-30%, 10,080 women-42%, 3,360 girls-14% and 3,360 boys-14%. In addition, the beneficiaries selection exercise will try to ensure that about 60% of the targeted HHs will be women/child-headed, 17% has elderly people & 15% of them will have at least one persons living with disability.
The project will adhere to the cluster recommendations to ensure the provision of a habitable covered living space that provides a healthy living environment, enabling the beneficiaries’ to have & enjoy privacy, dignity & protection. The intervention will mainstream gender issues & ensure that the needs of women, men, girls & boys are taken into account especially during critical decision making levels from the initial consultations stage on the needs to the designing & construction/rehabilitation of the shelters.
To promote community participation,  HAPEN will ensure active & meaningful engagement of community groups in all aspects of the project cycle from needs assessment, beneficiary selection, response planning & monitoring. This will promote an informed implementation approach that will enable reaching the most vulnerable & needy individuals. While to promote inclusivity of all the affected groups, HAPEN will engage representatives from all the minority groups during key activities such as beneficiaries identification and selection. Accountability to the affected population will be ensured by providing the target beneficiaries with a platform of airing their views & perception with regards to the project. This will be achieved through rolling out a comprehensive feedback, complaints & response mechanism which will be easily accessible to all beneficiaries. This will include among others, a complaint Hotline number that will be displayed on project display materials and also awareness-raising sessions to ensure target population are informed on how they can voice their concerns to project management & raise any positive or negative suggestions. 
Accountability to resources will be ensured by developing a comprehensive M&E plan which will entail a baseline survey, technical tracking sheets for distributions, post distribution and construction monitoring, weekly/monthly progress reports, monthly financial reports and a project completion report. After the provision of the NFIs to the targeted population, a PDM exercise will be conducted to inform and assess the effectiveness & efficiency of the intervention. Furthermore, a PCM will also be conducted to assess the quality & standard of the shelters constructed. The M&E plan help to ensure the effective implementation of project activities, assess if the required quality standards are met and help in monitoring the progress in line with agreed milestones and targets.

project_name: Provision Of Emergency Life-Saving Primary And Secondary Health Care, For Crisis Affected Populations In Baardhere, Dollow, Garbaharey And Ceel-Waaq Districts In Gedo Region
project_objective:
The population of Somalia consistently experience some of the worst health outcome indicators in the
World, the average life expectancy is estimated to be 51.5 years. Somalia is among the countries with the highest rankings in infant and child mortality rates of, respectively, 76.6 and 121.5 per 1,000 live births. The maternal mortality rate (692 deaths per 100,000 live births) and the fertility rate (average of 6.9 children per woman) are also among the highest in the world, 79 per cent of all births are home delivered without skilled assistance. These is further compounded by the prevailing prolonged humanitarian crisis characterized by ongoing conflicts, climate-related shocks, communicable disease outbreaks and weak social protection mechanisms (Humanitarian Needs Overview -2022). Since the beginning of 2020, four additional shocks have contributed to a deterioration of humanitarian conditions: Extensive floods, Desert Locust infestations, the COVID-19 pandemic and ravaging drought currently been experienced in Gedo region particularly in Bardhere, Dollow, Ceel-Waaq and Garbaharey districts of Gedo region.

 According to Humanitarian needs overview 2022, Over 6.56 million Somali people require lifesaving essential Healthcare in 2022. Excess mortality in Somalia is driven primary by malnutrition, disease outbreaks (e.g., COVID-19, AWD/cholera, measles, malaria) and violence; as well as non-communicable disease including complications of pregnancy and chronic disease. These are compounded by displacement due to conflict and natural disasters and lack of preventative and curative healthcare. Lifesaving physical trauma care services are scarce, and the available mental health and psychosocial support services do not keep up with the substantially increasing need. Availability and access to appropriate health care for persons living with a disability, estimated to be at least 15 per cent of the population, remain dramatically insufficient.

project_name: Improve living conditions of Internally Displaced People (IDPs) through site development, care and maintenance and decongestion initiatives in Afgoye, Wanla Weyne and Marka (lower Shabelle region), Dhusaamareeb (Galgaduud region) and Mogadishu (Kahda, Daynile, Dharkeenley) Banadir region
project_objective:
Conflict, drought, COVID-19, and flooding are only a few of the major shocks that have uprooted at least 2.9 million Somalis. In urban, semi-urban, and rural locations around the country, the bulk of displaced persons have self-settled in over 2,400 substandard and unplanned IDP settlements. Persons who have been displaced to these locations are living in dangerous situations, with the majority of them not being able to meet their basic needs due to inconsistencies in service delivery or being denied access to humanitarian aid. More than 80% of sites are informal settlements situated on private land, with the bulk of sites located in metropolitan areas, according to the CCCM cluster's comprehensive site assessment findings (DSA) and site verification assessments.
In Somalia, internally displaced persons (IDPs) are the most vulnerable population group: Somalia's IDP population continues to exhibit traits that make them more vulnerable than people living in host communities, whether they are urban or rural. Factors like as deplorable living conditions in settlements, inclusion challenges, and overall disenfranchisement in obtaining key services continue to be common among IDPs, making it even more challenging for these populations to achieve substantive change. Persons with disabilities (PWDs), members of minority clans, women, and youth are among the populations in IDP camps with the most pressing needs, and they face significant challenges to receiving humanitarian aid, preventing them from living in dignified conditions.
Therefore, the overall goal of the proposed initiative is to improve the living conditions and general security of IDP population in the camps, as well as provide fair access to services and assistance for all those in need. Through this, the initiative is anticipated to strengthen safe access to multi sectorial services at site level through improved site management and coordination. Secondly, the project will improve living conditions of displaced people through site development, care and maintenance and decongestion initiatives. Lastly, the project is anticipated to strengthen community self-management and access to information for displaced populations.
The outcome of the initiative is to have site- level information available and shared with stakeholders.  The activities that will generate this outcome include; conducting site verifications on bi-annual basis, establishing or updating service mapping of partners operating in various sites at the target districts.  Carry out service monitoring activities on monthly basis aimed at highlighting service gaps at the site-level and ensuring that minimum standards are being adhered to.
The second outcome is to have activities aimed at improving site-level living conditions administered across the regions targeted by the project. This will include; providing trainings on-site maintenance and site planning to camp committees; supporting community-led site maintenance activities to ensure upkeep of sites (cash for work, site maintenance committees, distribution of tools); implementing emergency sites improvement activities to minimize protection risks and ensure safety in sites (flood mitigation, fire prevention). Administer joint stakeholder site decongestion activities allowing for short-term improvements in settlement standards, minimizing protection threats and ameliorating COVID-19 transmission. Conduct safety audits annually to inform site improvement activities and to illustrate targeted initiatives that sector agencies should administered
Lastly, the project aims at ensuring that all sites in the target districts have a governance structure in place that serves to fulfil the needs of the displaced population. This will be achieved by undertaking mapping of existing community structures; providing core trainings (CMC Training Package) to community governance structures; identifying and supporting governance structures, encouraging participation.

project_name: Provision of Integrated Emergency WASH Services in Diinsoor and Bardale
project_objective:
This project will respond to the need of the most vulnerable displaced and host communities of 20,000 individuals (women = 6,500, men=4,400, boys= 4,200, girls = 4,780, PWD= 120) in Diinsoor and Bardale to cope with worsening humanitarian situation in these regions that now compounded by the effects of Covid 19 droughts which has resulted in massive challenges pertaining to Water, Sanitation and Hygiene. communities from these districts are still in need due to insufficient access to portable water and inadequate sanitation services of the affected population in many districts, thus negatively affecting the region’s public health and the dignity of highly vulnerable and displaced communities. 

Lack of enough WASH services to the population is a main cause of spread of Acute Diarrheal Diseases (ADD) in IDPs in the project target regions, leading to malnutrition in the country and contributing to increasing the existing stunting rate of 25.3% in children below 5 years of age. It is also a cause of relapse (ADD) when treated patients and children returning to their communities where safe water and sanitation coverages are limited, resulting in limited sustainability of health programs.

IRW through this intervention will identify distribution locations through in-depth assessment, and Relief Distribution Committees (RDCs) will be established at each distribution site, to facilitate the identification of the most vulnerable households and their needs, through community participation. This activity will also imply training of the beneficiaries on household water treatment, which will be conducted house-to-house by trained community hygiene promoters. The project activities will also include Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) with women and girls in order to identify collective water points with secure location and access. At the same time, Water Management Committees (WMCs) will be established and trained in each area, which will be responsible for the maintenance of water points identified.

Through this intervention will conduct rehabilitation/improvement of existing water points and construction/ rehabilitation of sanitation facilities, in order to make them secure, protected and gender-appropriate (gender-segregated latrines with provision of locks and doors). This will include other FGDs, 50% with women and 50% with men. These activities will be paired with community sensitization on the use and maintenance of safe water sources and appropriate sanitation facilities, and on the use of correct hygiene and sanitation practices, e.g. the need of washing hands at critical moments, food preservation and proper storage of water safe for drinking, and discourage defecation, especially near open water sources. Community sessions of hygiene promotion will be conducted in common spaces in various locations, accessible by all categories of marginalized persons, by trained hygiene promoters in the course of one year.

project_name: Livelihood Support for vulnerable IDPs and poor Host Communities in Mudug and Galgadud Regions-Galmudug State of Somalia.
project_objective:
Mercy Corps proposes a project on Livelihood Support targeting vulnerable IDPs and poor host communities in Mudug and Galgadud Regions of Galmudug State of Somalia, with the aim to contribute to the achievement of FSC strategies and objectives aligned to the HRP 2022. The project will benefit a total of 4,120vulnerable and marginalized households (1,100 Men, 1,500 women, 600 boys, 920 girls) in IDPs and host communities in Galkayo, Hobyo, Caabudwaq and Caadado Districts. The proposed intervention will improve immediate access to food, provide livelihood inputs (Livestock), and skills training for new livelihoods for the communities. Access to immediate food assistance will be provided through Conditional and Unconditional Cash transfers in forms of the multipurpose cash assistance and food vouchers to meet their basic needs and to protect and restore livelihoods, related food, and income sources. Communities will also participate in the rehabilitation and establishment of community infrastructure such as water catchments, and feeder roads, whereby they will receive cash-for-work and pastoral households will receive livelihood assets in form of livestock restocking for restoration. Technical vocational skills training will also be provided as a form of building new livelihoods.  The project targets the most vulnerable populations categorized as facing IPC Phases 3 and 4.
The proposed project is cognizant of the current food security context of Galmudug region of Somalia. According to FSNAU and FEWS NET, Post-Gu Assessment in September 2021 projected that nearly 3.5 million Somalis would be in Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and Emergency (IPC Phase 4) through at least December 2021, in the absence of humanitarian assistance. That includes 1.1 million internally displaced persons who will face moderate to large food consumption gaps through late 2021. Out of the total 3.5 million people in need of urgent food assistance, 640,000 people face significant food consumption gaps. In addition, 3.7 million people are classified in IPC phase 2 (Stressed), engaging in negative coping strategies to meet their food and non-food needs, bringing the total number of Somalis experiencing acute food insecurity to 7.2 million by late 2021. In addition to, majority of the estimated 2.9 million IDPs across Somalia are poor with limited livelihood assets, few income earning opportunities, low communal support, and rely heavily on external humanitarian assistance. As a result, one-third of internally displaced persons (in both rural and urban settlements) face moderate to large food consumption gaps through late 2021. The COVID-19 pandemic and related containment measures seem to affect the urban poor population more than rural poor population. As a result, the urban poor face moderate to large food consumption gaps, partly due to a slowdown in economic activities in urban areas and the rising costs of food and other essential non-food items. 
Mercy Corps field assessments in target regions revealed the deepening effect of frequent droughts and conflicts, which have led to high food consumption gaps and loss of livelihood assets. There is urgent need to address the food insecurity and livelihood threats for the IDPs and communities in the region. As the food security situation in Galmudug state remains tenuous, Mercy Corps sees an urgent need to respond and save lives, alleviate human suffering, and reduce the social and economic impact of the humanitarian crisis. This will reduce acute humanitarian needs and excess mortality among the most vulnerable by providing lifesaving and sustaining integrated assistance. The project will consider all gender groups and disability needs in implementation and will maintain accountability to the population through ensuring community feedback mechanisms and adherence to policies.

project_name: Emergency safe water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) crisis support for affected vulnerable populations in Bay, Bakool, Lower Juba, regions of Somalia.
project_objective:
The proposed project aims to improve the living conditions and wellbeing of vulnerable displaced and host communities who are affected by conflict and other natural disasters including drought and floods in Bay (Baidoa) Bakool (Hudur) and Lower Juba (Kismayu) of Somalia. This will be through emergency WASH interventions to benefit 85,000 Individuals (20,400 men, 28,900 female, 17,000 boys, 18,700 girls). This will contribute to the HRP 2022 strategic objectives by delivering life-saving WASH assistance to reduce the acute need among the vulnerable IDPs and communities; reducing protection risks against women, children and vulnerable groups accessing WASH services; and providing and restoring access to safe water and adequate sanitation services in the targeted communities. Prioritized activities include: 1) emergency water trucking for vulnerable communities to access water, 2) enhancing sanitation services through the construction of deslugible gender-segregated and disability-friendly communal/ shared latrines in congested IDP camps and host communities, 3)Delivering basic sanitation by enhancing COVID-19 response, construction of handwashing stations and pipeline water networks, establishing solar lamps for increased safety when accessing WASH services, hygiene promotion and awareness, and enhancing of menstrual health and hygiene for girls by distributing hygiene kits, 4) increasing emergency safe water supply through rehabilitation and/ or construction of shallow wells, boreholes (including solar-powered to lower the cost of groundwater abstraction), rehabilitation/ construction of storage tanks and communal taps, and strengthening the capacity of WASH committees in managing water sources and to ensure water safety and quality. Community hygiene promoters will also receive training to undertake house-to-house hygiene education.

The proposed intervention is based on the background of the Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) in 2022.  An estimated 6.4 million people in Somalia need humanitarian assistance, with  40 percent needing emergency life-saving WASH assistance of which 3.5 million will need safe drinking water, 5.1 million sanitation services, and 6.4 million hygiene supplies. 16 percent of these are females, children for 64 percent, and the elderly for 4 percent. This presents an increase of 43 percent from 2021, in which 4.6 million people were estimated to need WASH services across Somalia. Rural areas and hard-to-reach districts have shown a significant increase in the number of people in need compared to last year this is also attributed to increasing vulnerability due to limited access to water and sanitation among rural areas and IDP sites. According to the JMCNA 2021, the population in need of WASH services in 2022 includes approximately 1,619,415 IDPs and 4,818,944 vulnerable host communities. Populations in the target locations and especially those in crowded IDP settlements that lack water and sanitation facilities are at high risk of water-related disease outbreaks, Cholera/AWD, and COVID-19. There is an urgent need to support them through increasing access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene. The provision of water will also prevent further displacements and conflict over water resources. 

Mercy Corps will ensure community participation in targeting.  In general, Mercy Corps will ensure that, as WASH activities are implemented, the contextual issues of different needs of men, women, boys and girls, taking into account age, gender, and diversity (AGD) factors, including social background and disability. To ensure that the aged population and PLDs have good access to water and sanitation services, MC will consider them during the design stage. Moreover, accountability to the affected population will be ensured through the community feedback mechanism and Mercy Corps Policies.

project_name: Increasing Access to Food and Improving the  Resilience and Food Security of Crisis Affected IDP and Non-IDP Communities in Jubaland, Banadir and Galgudud
project_objective:
The project will benefit 1,360 households (8,160 persons who include 3,006 IDP Households and 5,154 vulnerable non-IDP households- 1,799 men, 1,873 women and 4,488 children).   These beneficiaries will include IDP communities in Banadir, Kismayo, Dollow and Abudwak; agro-pastoralists smallholder farmers in Dollow and pastoralists from Abudwak.  The project also purposes to target 816 persons with disabilities with the planned interventions. These beneficiaries include 2,226 Displaced persons, 954 persons belonging to the host communities and 318 persons living with a disability. This figure also includes 1,749 children. 430 households including IDP and non-IDP households, who are food insecure, will be targeted. 200 of these households will receive unconditional cash transfers worth $ 124 each for three months. project_name: Provision of Essential Camp Coordination and Camp Management services and Protection of Sites residents for newly displaced and protracted internally IDPs Regions of Banadir, Galmudug, Lower Jubba and Gedo.
project_objective:

project_name: Provision of  Shelter assistance to displacement affected communities including poor host communities in Somalia
project_objective:
This project will focus on improving the physical protection and dignity of IDPs, refugee returnees and poor host communities across all parts of Somalia through distribution and provision of locally purchased Non Food Items (NFIs) and Emergency Shelter Kits (ESKs) through cash/voucher/in-kind modalities and construction of Transitional and/or Permanent Shelters through community driven or owner driven approaches (where appropriate). To avoid decongestion, settlement (re)planning training will also be conducted and Post Construction Monitoring (PCM) exercises for Shelters and Post Distribution Monitoring (PDM) exercises for NFIs & ESKs will also be conducted. NRC will also ensure participation in infrastructure mapping exercises led by Shelter cluster or any other partner.
For the beneficiaries’ selection and registration, NRC will use an electronic mobile data collection tool called Kobo tool box, which provides an accurate and real time data. The data received through Kobo is easily manageable and transferable. 20% to 30% Poor host community members will be selected to ensure 'DO NO HARM' and other humanitarian principles including humanity, neutrality, impartiality and independence. Similarly, 5 to 15% Persons With Disabilities (PWDs) will also be condisered in each project.
For the provision of NFIs, each HH will be provided with a cash of $100 as per cluster agreed standard NFI kit while for the provision of ESKs, each HH will be provided with a cash of either USD 247 (for ESK Type-1 with a size of 380 cm x 550 cm) or USD 213 (for ESK Type-2 with a size of 360 cm x 440 cm) depending upon the area of land available. If the area available is less, ESK Type-2 will be selected esle ESK Type-1 will be proiratized. The cash for ESKs will be distributed in two subsequent installments (50% as first installment and remaining 50% as second installment). NRC will acquire the services of local telecom companies (viz. Hormuud telecom in South and Central Somalia and Somtel & Golis in Puntland and Somaliland) for the cash transfers. NRC will provide a complete list of selected beneficiaries to respective telecom companies for their cross checking purposes. This list will include all details of selected beneficiaries including their telephone numbers and token numbers. After reviewing and cross checking, respective telecom company will transfer specified amount of money to selected beneficiaries through mobile transfer facility. Beneficiaries will be selected through predetermined beneficiary selection criteria prioritizing the Extremely Vulnerable Individuals (EVIs) including female and single headed HHs, orphans, chronically ill, aged and child headed households. Gender will be mainstreamed into the project through the specific consideration of the different needs of women, men, boys and girls during the design of activities. The project will ensure that all participants have equal access to resources and training. Monitoring and evaluation will be based on gender, age and diversity dis-segregated data. NRC will target total 78,000 individuals (50% females) consisting of 15,000 in South and Central Somalia, 10,800 in Jubbaland, 32,400 in Puntland and 19,800 in Somaliland through different Shelter interventions throughout the year 2022. NRC staff will ensure that the provided cash is to be utilized for intended purpose by coordinating with the beneficiaries and conduct follow up visits with the support of the community leaders, local authorities and the relevant cluster partners. 
A Post Distribution Monitoring (PDM) exercises for NFIs and ESKs and Post Construction Monitoring (PCM) exercises for Tranisitional and/or Permanent Shelters will be conducted to analyse outcomes, the beneficiaries’ level of satisfaction and draw lessons learnt for future programming.

project_name: Strengthening protection and durable solutions in Somalia through an integrated and holistic Housing Land and Property (HLP) response
project_objective:
The Housing, Land and Property (HLP) challenges confronting displaced communities in Somalia are protracted and multifaceted limiting access to and impacting the enjoyment of HLP rights. The centrality of Housing, Land and Property (HLP) is a key component of achieving sustainable durable solutions to displacement. Despite increased prevention efforts, over 100,000 individuals have been forcefully evicted across Somalia in 2021 alone and 1,054,306 persons in a span of five years (HLP Sub cluster 2021). The HLP challenges are created by repeated and protracted displacement in urban areas that are exacerbated by the high demand (in the context of rapid urbanisation, investment and development) and rocketing land prices. This has been compounded by competing claims on land coupled with limited legal and policy frameworks around HLP rights, inadequate technical and functional land registries or departments.  And yet, evictions, forced or otherwise result in widespread protection risks, impact victims’ dignity, livelihoods, physical safety and reverses incremental gains made in attaining sustainable durable solutions. 
Further to this, the shelter situation in Somalia is critical, coupled with limited public land available to establish new settlements. 85% of informal settlements are constructed on private land (CCCM Cluster, 2020). Moreover, tenure insecurity remains widespread, leading to an alarming rate of forced evictions countrywide. Most informal settlements are either without formal documents or written land tenure agreements or have in place some form of short-term arrangements (Shelter Cluster, 2020). In addition to this, IDPs who lack legal identity documents, specifically nationality documents and civil registration such as birth certificates are disproportionately affected. There is increasing evidence that legal identity is linked to HLP rights. Land owners are increasingly demanding for proof of identity as a prerequisite for accessing HLP. The project seeks to facilitate enhanced protection of displaced communities from Housing Land and Property violations including but not limited to forced evictions. 
Through holistic and integrated assistance packages, this Project will benefit 500,000 individuals (women, girls, boys and men, including persons with disabilities) in 21 districts across 15 regions around the following seven complementing actions. 
1. Strengthening access to documentation for displaced persons including women, girls and persons with disability through a comprehensive analysis and response to documentation needs.
2. Strengthening of ongoing eviction monitoring systems and expanding eviction risk mapping to collect, review and analyze data.
3. Supporting proactive engagements to negotiate improved tenure arrangements and/or facilitating dignified relocations for populations of concern. 
4. Mitigating protection risks exacerbated by HLP violations such as inadequate access to housing, and forced evictions.
5. Supporting extremely vulnerable victims of evictions cope with post-eviction stress (PES) through the provision of multi-purpose cash assistance, specialized counselling and legal assistance services. 
6. Strengthening Eviction taskforce members, and supporting government’s effort to address evictions, including robust engagement with landlords, gatekeepers and community leaders.
 7. Facilitating access to HLP and legal identity information, legal services, awareness campaigns and, communication materials.
8. Strengthen coordination as well as the functional and operational capacity of the HLP sub cluster.
9. Invest in research, studies, analyses and assessments related to HLP, legal identity and other protection specific issues identified through this response 
10. Conduct evidence based advocacy and policy influence on thematic areas identified through data and evidence generated during the course of implementation. 
11. Ensuring access to justice for IDPs is a priority, in line with the HLP AoR

project_name: Provision of life-saving WASH assistance to drought and conflict affected communities and improvement of health standards for the IDPs, and Host Communities in Mudug and Nugaal in puntland state of Somalia.
project_objective:
To increase access to life-saving sustained safe drinking Water, Gender-sensitive sanitation facilities, and promotion of good hygiene practices to support 8,500 people including PWDs in Galkacyo, Burtinle, Garowe, Galdogob, IDPs, and Host Communities in crisis and/or emergency affected Women, Girls, Boys, and Men. These groups shall be involved at the various project stages from planning to actual implementation to ensure their views and needs are fully captured. The project's cluster objective 1 will require 65% financial requirements while Cluster objective 2 will require 35% project finances for efficient and successful implementation.
This will be achieved through increased access to adequate, safe, and sustainable water following the rehabilitation and construction of flood-proof water infrastructure proposed under this project, improvement of access to gender-sensitive sanitation food-prone prone settlements, and promoting a culture of good hygiene practices in order to reduce the related protection and disease risks especially among women, girls and children in the targeted locations. As an initial lifesaving intervention, PMWDO will prioritize the provision of vouchers for hygiene kits to 2000 extremely vulnerable households to increase their household water storage capacity thereby reducing the frequent trips to water points, which will as a result reduce congestion at the existing facilities. Within the first 5 months of the project, PMWDO will establish and capacity build water committees and rehabilitate 10 strategic water infrastructures whose combined water supply will benefit 8,000 individuals. To ensure improved quality of the water both at households and supported water points, PMWDO will undertake initial tests and regular water treatment at the source (bucket and batch chlorination). Further, PMWDO will provide water treatment tablets to 2000 vulnerable households who will be sensitized about household water treatment and safe storage. PMWDO will utilize the capacity of the local market by promoting market-based programming in WASH through the use of vouchers (for NFIs) and contracting suitable construction services from the local market following extensive market assessments and monitoring. In order to improve the hygiene knowledge and practices among the target populations, PMWDO will determine the hygiene knowledge and practice gaps through KAP surveys, one (baseline survey) at project inception to inform approaches to awareness-raising and composition of emergency hygiene kits to be distributed to the most vulnerable households. An online KAP survey will be conducted towards the end of the intervention to gauge the impact made in water, latrine, environmental and personal hygiene, and in general, behavior change. To ensure community ownership and sustainability, PMWDO will help establish 10 water resource management committees 50 members (30 women and 20 men) water source management committees. Where possible, a technician from each village and a representative from the local administration will be incorporated into the committee. All the members will be trained in basic operation, maintenance, troubleshooting, and orderly access to the source. The training will be conducted jointly by PMWDO staff, Ministry of Energy, Water and Natural Resources staff, and the private sector (suppliers of spare parts). To instill a sustained culture of good hygiene practice, the project will train and effectively engage the existing 24 community health volunteers recruited from the targeted villages to enable mainstream hygiene promotion activities into the communities. The hygiene promotion intervention is expected to benefit 8500 individuals.
PMWDO seeks to improve access to safe and affordable water and clean sanitation facilities in rural communities and sites where the internally displaced have settled.

project_name: Strengthening coordination and self-management in IDPs settlements of Bosaso, Qardho, Garowe, Armo, Burtinle, Laasqoray and Ceelafwayne through improved coordination mechanisms
project_objective:
The project’s goal is aimed at improving the living conditions and protection of IDPs in Bosaso, Garowe, Gardo, Armo, Burtinle, CeelAfweyn and Laasqoray by ensuring equitable access to services and assistance of all persons in need, with a clear focus on moving towards durable solutions and enhancing GBV prevention and response.

The proposed project will be an extension of the ongoing Camp coordination and Camp Management (CCCM) Project being implemented by PSA and funded by UNHCR in Bosaso, Qardho,Armo, Garoowe and Burtinle with full participation of the displaced and host communities that are estimated population to be 170,660, with 13 camps in Bosaso (72,659), 20 IDPs camps in Garowe (31,273), 6 IDPs camps in Qardho (6146), 3 IDPs camps in Burtinle ( 4825) and 4 IDPs camps in Armo (3800).

Internally displaced persons (IDPs) in Somalia are struggling to cope with forced evictions, lack of opportunities, harsh livelihoods, water shortages and inadequate health-services. The country is a home to over 2.6 million IDPs.  An estimated 1.3 million people were displaced in Somalia. In 2021, more than 60 per cent of the total IDP caseload (about 1.6 million) are considered to be the most vulnerable and require life-saving humanitarian assistance. Close to 80 per cent of those displaced are women and children. 

IDPs are fronted with a lot of challenges comprising inadequate physical shelter structures in IDP camps, inadequate lighting in IDP camps, lack of/and inadequate locks for latrines are also secondary factors that predispose women and girls to sexual violence and abuse. In Puntland, women and girls in drought-affected communities with already have pre-existing emergencies such as the COVID-19 pandemic.


On disability inclusivity, PSA under the project will ensure that the rights of persons with disabilities are put into consideration throughout the project implementation; we will also ensure feedback and complaints mechanisms are designed to ensure accessibility for persons with disabilities. Including our staff trained on inclusion of persons with disabilities and ensuring that measures to overcome barriers by any group are addressed. In addition, we will engage regularly with Persons with Disabilities to increase understanding of the general situation of persons with disabilities, barriers to accessing services and assistance, capacities and existing coping mechanisms, and actions that humanitarian organisations can take to strengthen inclusion.


The project will ensure that all participants have equal access to resources and training. Monitoring and evaluation will be based on gender, age and diversity disaggregated data. An additional settlement mapping exercises from the previous one conducted by PSA will be conducted to get the information of all targeted settlements for necessary services in place and gap analysis, with our ongoing project we have noted various gaps that need to be addressed in the next phase of project, during our assessment the IDPs prioritized the following needs as urgent.

•	Rehabilitation of solar lights 
•	Construction of IDP community centres 
•	Garbage collection and site maintenance such as constructing drainage systems 
•	Advocacy of Land and support relocations to public land when appropriate

Under the project, PSA will target 13 IDPs camps in Bosaso (72,659), 20 IDPs camps in Garowe (31,273), 6 IDPs camps in Qardho (6146), 3 IDPs camps in Burtinle ( 4825), 4 IDPs camps in Armo (3800),  7 IDPs camps in CeelAfweyn (8905) and 12 IDPs camps in Laasqoray (10,129) as well as the host community.

project_name: Lifesaving food and Livelihood assistance for drought and affected community in Lower Juba region of Somalia.
project_objective:
According to the 2022 HNO A total of 7.7 million Somali women, men and children are estimated to require humanitarian assistance in 2022. With 2.9 million people estimated to be internally displaced throughout the country, of these, 2.2 million require urgent humanitarian assistance. IDPs are chronically more food insecure and vulnerable than host communities. Somalia continues to grapple with multiple shocks that exacerbate existing acute food insecurity and acute malnutrition. The failure of the 2021 GU rains put the pastoral and the agro-pastoral livelihoods in one of the worst crisis. The COVID-19 pandemic and associated socioeconomic impacts also contributed to the food insecurity situation in Somalia. As a result, the FNSAU post GU assessment projected 3.5 million Somalis would be in Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and Emergency (IPC Phase 4) through at least December 2021, in the absence of humanitarian assistance. That includes 1.1 million internally displaced persons who will face moderate to large food consumption gaps through late 2021.
Lower juba is one of the worst affected region by the protracted drought. The ministry of Humanitarian and disaster management of Juballand estimated over 60% of the animals in Juballand have perished due to lack of water and pasture. With no alternative livelihood or coping strategy left, over 11 cases of suicide were also reported in Jubaland. Besides, Kismayo alone host an estimated 90,000 new and protracted IDP’s in 144 sites (CCCM Cluster), displaced by multifaceted conflicts, floods, drought and government evictions. This intervention thus targets IDPs, urban poor and poor agro-pastoral households that have been hit by the successive droughts, conﬂict, Desert locust, COVID-19 and displacements and are in dire need of immediate food assistance and livelihood support. 
SFH will address the immediate household food needs in the target locations through direct unconditional cash transfer activity targeting 500 most vulnerable IDPs and pastoral dropout households including women and children headed households for a period of 5 months at the rate of 75 USD per beneficiary in Lower Juba. Besides, to build resilience and prevent sudden shocks, this intervention will contribute to household food security through income generating activities while restoring productive communal assets such as Communal water pan and canals.  400 unskilled, but most vulnerable, able-bodied men and women who will work for 80 dollars per months and 8 supervisors/Forman’s @120 for 3 months with benefit from the conditional cash grant. 
The proposed action also targets to provide seasonally appropriate livelihood inputs and tools such as: - nutritionally dense Crop and Vegetable seeds to 500 riverine farmers in Gobweyn, Wirkoy, qamqam, yontoy and Sanguuni locations, this will reduce the dependency syndrome on food aid while contributing to increased agricultural production at the community level. 
To protect key livelihoods assets of IDPs and to preserve future means of livelihoods another 500 vulnerable pastorals from pastoral communities within the district will be supported with livestock treatment drugs and fodder vouchers for their lactating animals to replenish their physical body and enhance their market value. In general, the following will be achieved through this response: 
1. Provide unconditional cash grant to 500 most vulnerable households in Kismayo @75 dollar for 5 round; 
2. Provide seasonally appropriate livelihood inputs (Crop and vegetable) to 500 riverine and small-scale poor farmers along river juba in Kismayo district. 
3.Provide assorted agricultural hand tools to 500 poor farmers to enhance their farming and production ability.
4. 500 pastoral households will be provided with livestock treatment and fodder vouchers 
5. 200HH supported through conditional cash transfer for restoration of communal assets
6. Conduct Good Agricultural Practices (GAP), DRR and Early warnings.

project_name: Provision of integrated management for severely and moderately acute malnutrition among boys, girls and PLWs  including disable group in Lower Juba and Gedo  regions Somalia
project_objective:
According to nutrition cluster and FSNAU recently released nutrition overview in Somalia indicate critical acute malnutrition in Lower Juba and Gedo region this  due to a combination of factors, including food insecurity, high morbidity, low immunization and vitamin-A supplementation and poor care practices. At the national level, the median prevalence of Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) has remained Serious (10–14.9%) over the past three seasons. A Critical (15-29.9%) prevalence of GAM was observed in 10 out of the 33 population groups surveyed, with more areas likely to deteriorate from Serious to Critical between September 2021. A Critical (4-5.6%) prevalence of Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) was observed in the pastoral and agropastoral livelihood of Afmadow and Badhadhe district of Lower Juba region while 14.9% GAM and 2.5% SAM caseload were observed in Gedo region. Morbidity among children was high (≥20%) in 15 out 33 population groups surveyed. However, Crude Death Rate and Under-Five Death Rate were relatively low in most areas. Urgent treatment and nutrition support is required for an estimated
1.2 M children under the age of five years (total acute malnutrition burden), who will likely face acute malnutrition in 2022, including 295,515 who are likely to be severely malnourished while a total of 245,909 pregnant and lactating women will be moderately malnourished hence this require an urgent  Integrated  nutrition interventions to support recovery and prevent deterioration in the nutrition situation.

Gedo and Lower Juba  region were considered hotspot areas with a projected Critical GAM prevalence, indicated by a weight-for-height z-score of 15-29.9% or by a Mid-Upper Arm Circumference below 125 mm of ≥10%, IDP areas of concern  of concern for acute malnutrition and need of urgent nutrition and health support interventions
This project therefore target to reach a total 4,200 vulnerable boys, girls and pregnant and lactating women through an integrated response around Nutrition. It is intended to mitigate the physical and protection consequences of drought on populations and communities directly affected in Lower Juba and Gedo region, in particular, Badhaadhe,Bardheere ,Kismayo and Afmadow  town. The main objective of this project is to provide integrated lifesaving emergency Nutrition services to 4,200 drought affected direct beneﬁciaries and intends to achieve the following, capacity building of nutrition staff on IMAM. Referral of malnourished children with complicated cases will be done to the Outpatient Therapeutic Programme (OTP) centers and directly linked with primary health care services managed by SORDES and other actors in the program areas thus providing more holistic opportunity to the target beneﬁciaries SORDES  will closely coordinate with Local MOH as well as Federal level MOH and social mobilizers, elders all involved in activities on mobilizing communities

project_name: WASH ASSISTANCE TO DISASTER AFFECTED AND DISPLACED PEOPLE
project_objective:
In Qandala District of Bari Region, majority of communities rely on shallow wells, and/or trucked water. TC GATI brought heavy rainfall, which has led to flooding which damaged sewerage systems causing them to overflow, potentially contaminating water supply. Access into the affected areas remains challenging, and it can also be expected that the supply of trucked water may be disrupted. Access to sanitation (latrines) was already inadequate, and open defecation was widespread. These factors combined increase the risk of waterborne diseases such as acute watery diarrhoea. There is likely to be a need to provide safe water through the distribution of water treatment chemicals (aqua tabs) and storage items (buckets, jerry cans). According to preliminary reports, the affected population’s access to basic health services has not been impacted considerably, with emergency mobile teams still able to operate. Somalia remains in a state of protracted crisis which increases the impact of the challenging climatic conditions, amidst inadequate coping strategies and development assistance. 
There is limited expectation that the government and associated other actors support the affected population due to administrative challenges, security and political constraints.

Tentatively 1,900 HHs (11,400 people) will be targeted through this project – specifically those affected in Qandala district of Bari region in Puntland. This equates to 50% of the affected population as per Humanitarian Needs Assessment report 2021 (Qandala rapid interagency assessment led by OCHA and participated by WFP and other partners including our field staff) indicate that close to 5,800 HHs have been affected. Targeting will include drought – affected pastoralists, conflict and drought IDPs living in makeshift shelters and fisherfolk whose livelihoods that need immediate assistance, as well as vulnerable groups including women headed households with many children, the elderly, people with disabilities and critically sick and people injured by Cyclone GATI. This will also include disaggregation of HH data; and actual projections on forecast on HH size. Planning for the Worst case scenario, an estimated 1,539 HHs including IDPs/Refugees vulnerable to the cyclone are affected and exposed to critical Emergency WASH risks due to overwhelmed/collapsed social services in Puntland State of Somalia. 

Moreover, the core problem that the project seeks to address is the extremely weak livelihood, education and health outcomes currently faced by target populations in Qandala district due to inadequate and unsustainable water, sanitation and hygiene facilities and practice. By addressing these WASH issues alongside its work to address other core problems within the sectors of Food, Income and Markets (FIM), Education and Nutrition, Concern intends to make a significant contribution to an overall objective of addressing the high incidences of poverty and vulnerability and the limited quality of life affecting these populations.

project_name: Improved Access to Food and Livelihood Options for Vulnerable Households in Somalia
project_objective:
Ongoing armed conflicts and insecurity, with recurring climate shocks, has resulted in a protracted economic vulnerability and internal displacements across Somalia.Somalis are vulnerable to various shocks such as drought and flood that contribute to poverty and displacement. The Center for Global Development  places Somalia at the top of the list of 167 countries for overall vulnerability to climate change adjusted for coping capacity.
The Cyclical climatic shocks and ongoing conflict are challenging traditional rural livelihoods and causing 
growing number of urban poor and internally displaced people in Somalia. Displacements due to armed 
conflict and political tensions, drought, and lack of livelihoods are expected to continue in 2022, further 
exacerbating food insecurity in many areas.
According to FSNAU,out of the total 3.5 million people in need of urgent food assistance, 640,000 people face significant food consumption gaps. In addition, 3.7 million people are classified in IPC phase 2 (Stressed), engaging in negative coping strategies to meet their food and non-food needs, bringing the total number of Somalis experiencing acute food insecurity to 7.2 million by late 2021.

Furthermore,COVID-19 pandemic and related containment measures seem to have affected the urban poor population more than rural poor population. As a result, the urban poor face moderate to large food consumption gaps, partly due to a slowdown in economic activities in urban areas and the rising costs of food and other essential non-food items.
World Vision proposes a multi pronged interventions  to reverse the current trajectory at which Somalia is going.The interventions would include immediate access to food needs by vulnerable households facing hunger and starvation, improving livelihoods and creating opportunities for diversified livelihoods by protecting key livelihood assets .
The proposed project intends to address the food insecurity situation, loss of livelihood strategies, poor HH and community livelihood assets, as well as minimum interventions integrated to address the environmental degradation on which most livelihoods hinge upon. 
These activities will target IDPs, pastoral and agro-pastoral communities across Somalia, in districts where World Vision operates in.

project_name: Sustainable Livelihood support and strengthening resilience of drought, floods and conflict affected IDPs, returnees and vulnerable communities in Galgadud, Hiraan, Bay, Middle Shabelle and Lower Shabelle Regions, Somalia
project_objective:
Severe food insecurity continues to worsen owing to current depleted livelihoods and diminishing coping mechanisms that has significantly impacted into the lives of the most vulnerable host communities and marginalized IDPs and returnees including the elderly and persons with living with disabilities in  Galgadud, Hiraan, Bay, Middle Shabelle and Lower Shabelle Regions, Somalia. The situation is attributed to combined effects of poor and erratic Gu 2021 rainfall against the  background of previous successive erratic and below average Gu and Deyr 2020 rains compounded by previous successive drought seasons as well as floods along riverine areas of Hiiraan, Middle Shabelle regions hence below-average Gu crop production. The situation is further exacerbated by impacts of desert locust that continue to pose a serious threat to both crop availability and crop production. The project will be implemented through the following activities: Provision of food vouchers for most vulnerable and displaced women and children headed households and those with chronic illnesses and the disabled, rehabilitation of water catchments, farming lands, irrigation canals and feeder roads on CFW scheme, Provision of hay/fodder to the most vulnerable and drought affected, pastoral families, distribution of farm inputs (seed package including seeds and fertilizers) targeted to farming households as well as provision of tractor hours to the targeted farming households.

According to FSNAU-FEWS NET 2021 Post Gu Technical Report of  September 9, 2021, approximately 3.5 million people in Somalia face acute food insecurity Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse outcomes in late 2021 whereas reports of current weather forecasts indicate an increased likelihood of below-average rainfall during the 2021 Deyr (October-December) season across most parts of the country which will seriously affect food security and nutrition outcomes thus food insecurity is expected to deteriorate further to 2022. The project targets 47400 persons (19714 women,18202 men,4740 boys and 4740 girls) and the elderly as well as those with disabilities whose plight is exacerbated by eroded purchasing power and very weak and negative coping strategies.

project_name: Logistics Cluster activities to support the humanitarian response in South Sudan
project_objective: The Logistics Cluster is a service-based cluster and acts, through WFP, as a provider of last resort for common logistics services. The Logistics Cluster aims to augment the capacities of humanitarian organizations and facilitate the timely delivery of humanitarian assistance to vulnerable populations through logistics coordination, information management, preparedness and facilitation of common services to the entire humanitarian community in South Sudan.

project_name: Réponse d'urgence en Education en faveur des enfants  ( filles et garcons)   agés de 6à 17 ans affectés par le déplacement dans les Régions de Maradi et de Tillaberi
project_objective:
La présente réponse éducation du NRC vise à garantir que les enfantsagés de 06 à 17 ans non scolarisés et/ou déscolarisés du fait de la crise dans un contexte marqué par la fermeture de nombreuses écoles aient accès à des opportunités d'apprentissage alternatives et flexibles.  Dans le cadre de notre intervention qui sera menée de façon coordonnée avec les autorités éducatives, un travail de réflexion et de sensibilisation des communautés locales sera effectué pour relancer la demande éducative au profit des enfants affectés par la crise tout en montrant les bénéfices de l’école et plus largement ceux d’une éducation alternative ciblée, flexible et adaptée à leur niveau de maturité cognitive.

 L’objectif est de mobiliser les communautés autour de l’école en y incluant les enfants qui n’ont pas intégré le système éducatif, ou qui l’ont quitté précocement, et en mobilisant la communauté autour des thématiques essentielles en matière de droits à l’éducation. Tout en nous appuyant sur les acquis des pratiques éducatives nous mettrons en place une gamme variée d’offres éducatives non formelles (programme de rattrapage, programme de transition, alphabétisation, PEA …etc.) en vue de lever les obstacles à la scolarisation des enfants et assurer leur enrôlement, maintien et transition vers d’autres opportunités d’éducation ou de formation.  Un accent sera mis sur le développement professionnel des enseignants et des appuis matériels pédagogiques conséquents en vue d’asseoir la qualité des interventions développées et stimuler la rétention des enfants au sein de ces programmes.   Cette intervention contribuera également à une meilleure protection des enfants en veillant à ce qu'ils ne soient pas exposés à des risques de protection (VBG, exploitation sociale…).  Le projet prendra également en compte les besoins des enfants en situation de minorités ( enfants avec handicapes, filles et autres personnes en situation de vulnerabilité)  en veillant à ce que  l'aide humanitaire puisse leur etre fourniei  de manière sûre, accessible, responsable et participative. 4,2% d'enfants en situation de vulnerabilité seront ciblés à cet effet pour leur plus grande inclusion dans les activités du projet.

Notre réponse s’aligne également sur les objectifs de la Stratégie Nationale de Réponse aux Vulnérabilités du Système éducatif 2020 au Niger pour ce qui est de (i) l’amélioration de l’accès pour assurer la continuité de l’éducation ;(ii) de l’amélioration de la qualité de l’éducation ; et enfin (iii) de la gouvernance dans le système éducatif. Les principales interventions sont axées sur les priorités stratégiques du Cluster Education et du Ministère de l’éducation telles et orientés sur l’amélioration de l’environnements d’apprentissage pour le rendre sûrs et protecteurs favorable au bien-être psycho-social des élèves et des enseignants. Par ailleurs, la complémentarité et la synergie développée à travers le secteur protection via la composante ICLA permettra de renforcer l’accès des enfants et des communautés ciblées à la documentation civile et autres documents en lien avec l’accès à la terre, biens et Logements. project_name: Livestock asset protection and restoration (animal health, feed distribution/production, distribution of animals)
project_objective:
The overall estimated Sector PIN for 2022 – of food insecure and those at risk of food insecurity – is estimated at 13.9 million, with 12 million facing acute food insecurity and 1.9 million people at risk of sliding into food insecurity. The acute food insecure figure includes 1.9 million people living in camps and deemed to be 100 percent food insecure. Livestock production is vital in Syria to sustain food availability, food diversity/nutrition and income generation among vulnerable women and men affected by the drought-like conditions and prevailing economic hardships. The sector is facing many challenges that are forcing small-scale vulnerable households to adopt negative copying strategies which includes distress selling-off of their assets, subsequently losing a considerable source of income.
In this context, FAO has designed a project to assist 212,500 vulnerable crisis-affected food insecure farming households (equivalent to 1,275,000 people) in Syria through protecting and restoring their main production assets (livestock).
The objective of the proposed action is to protect the livestock assets of targeted vulnerable herders through the provision of vaccinations and treatment as well as feed for their herds. The expected project outputs are:
Output 1: Livestock productivity for 200,000 vulnerable crisis-affected breeders is maintained and improved. 
This output aims at improving the availability of animal feed for the purpose of asset protection for 50,000 vulnerable households (250 kg of feed per household, in line with sector recommendations) as well as boosting milk availability through enhanced livestock production. Output 1 also seeks to provide veterinary services (vaccines and/or treatment) for 150,000 herders throughout the country.
Output 2. Improving animal reproduction for about 12,500 beneficiaries through artificial insemination and capacity building, contributing to increased livestock production.. This output aims at restoring livestock production through distribution of animals to small scale vulnerable households who lost their animals due to the drought-like conditions and prevailing economic crisis. 
All outputs would include capacity building to enhance the technical skills of herders and technicians and to enable them to resume production in a viable, efficient and productive way and and better cope with the challenging conditions.

project_name: Human rights protection through increasing monitoring, reporting, legal advice, capacity building and advocacy on International Humanitarian Law and International Human Rights Law in the United Nations Syria response
project_objective:
This project is part of an overall program through which OHCHR will strengthen its support to the humanitarian leadership and partners in implementing a robust response based on expanded factual data and legal analysis for the protection of human rights in Syria. This builds on OHCHR’s innovative model of embedding human rights advisors in the humanitarian operation since 2016 enhanced by monitoring and reporting, legal advice and civil society support.
This project builds on work implemented over the last five years by OHCHR since the deployment of Human Rights Advisors to each HC office in the three hubs. It is grounded in the Office's value-added of impartial reporting on the human rights context, robust and responsive legal analysis, and its position as a trusted interlocutor on sensitive issues with key national and international partners, including Humanitarian Coordinators, UN humanitarian agencies and partners across the hubs. The Office also considers work being done by other actors to ensure that its programming contributes to responding to gaps and avoids duplication. 
This project is based on the intersection across all areas of OHCHR's programming, whereby solid monitoring/reporting, legal analysis, support to civil society and technical advice on IHL/IHRL to humanitarian partners mutually reinforce one another. OHCHR shares data reflecting the work in these areas with partners, such as Member States seeking to develop response policies, humanitarian actors focused on addressing urgent concerns, political actors who are working to establish a more stable future for the country, and civil society organisations campaigning on these issues.
The OHCHR Monitoring and Reporting Unit (MRU) monitors, analyses and reports on the human rights situation in the Syrian Arab Republic through the contribution to the Secretary-General's monthly reporting to the Security Council pursuant to Security Council resolutions 2139 (2014), 2165 (2014) and 2191 (2014). MRU continues to be a key source for OHCHR advocacy and data collection. Analysis provided by the Syria Office contributes to numerous speeches and press statements by the High Commissioner, the Deputy High Commissioner and other senior United Nations officials. The information and reports regularly shared by MRU with the Humanitarian leadership and partners support a better protection analysis and informs early warning efforts across the hubs. 
This is complemented by the work of the Rule of Law/Transitional Justice Unit. A series of legal notes on topics including Indiscriminate Attacks and Indiscriminate Weapons in International Humanitarian Law, Attacks on Medical Units in International Humanitarian Law and Human Rights Law, Transfer of the Civilian Population in International Law, International Humanitarian Law and Human Rights Law Relevant to Siege Warfare, Child Recruitment & Use in Hostilities in International Law, Belligerent Occupation: Duties and Obligations of Occupying Powers, Position paper on Syrian Law 10/2018 on HLP rights and a Q&A on Suspected ISIL Fighters & their Families Held in Detention Centres & IDP Camps in Northeast Syria were drafted to support the UN analysis and response in Syria. Legal advice and analysis to humanitarian partners is also provided on an ad hoc basis in response to developments on the ground.
Since 2015, the HRAS work to enhance the integration and mainstreaming of human rights into the work of the UN Country Team and in the region. To this end, HRAs have provided inputs to the Humanitarian Needs Overview and the Humanitarian Response Plans produced by OCHA and humanitarian partners since 2016. 
OHCHR will use HRP funding to expand its reporting, analysis, capacity-building and advocacy on the rights of groups who are most at risk of being discriminated against, including women, girls, young people, adolescents, and persons with disabilities with a particular focus to inform a better protection analysis and advocacy efforts.

project_name: Improve equitable access to preventive and curative nutrition services for under five years children and pregnant and lactating women in Syria
project_objective:
The project aims to address the deteriorating nutrition situation in Syria as depicted by the 2022 HNO. Under the Nutrition Sector framework, this project aims to provide preventive and curative nutrition services for children U5, PLW, and CBA in Syria with a special focus in high severity SD and IDPs camps inside Syria. UNICEF will work in 247 258 sub-districts, out of which 243 256 are with severity scale of 3 and higher  , with the remaining lower severity scale host IDPs who need support to access essential nutrition services.. The project is designed to strengthen nutrition resilience through protecting, promoting, and supporting consumption of optimal diets for children and women, uptake of recommended childcare and feeding practices and improved access to high quality nutrition services.

Good Diets: UNICEF will work closely with the FS Sector to ensure nutrition vulnerabilities and outcomes are mainstreamed and promoted in FSL projects. From an advantage of leading the WASH Sector, UNICEF, through this project will advocate for vulnerable families with children U2 to be prioritized for water and sanitation services to improve food safety and hygiene. To the best extent possible, UNICEF & WFP will continue targeting out of school children with food supplements (HEB and date bars)XXX   to promote education. Also, UNICEF will continue piloting the use of cash to promote nutrition outcomes in NWS.

NGOs and local facilities and Health directorates of the MoH at governorates/sub-districts and community levels. UNICEF will provide IPs with essential lifesaving nutrition supplies to treat and prevent malnutrition and prevent deaths among vulnerable children and women especially during the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic and the devaluation of local and household economy. Nutrition services will focus on raising awareness among vulnerable caregivers on prevention of malnutrition, BF and improving IYCF practices. The project will also provide capacity building for HWs and CHWs to ensure quality service delivery. At national level, support will focus on strengthening the system to provide services through strengthen reporting systems and producing strategic documents (PHC strategy for child, adolescent and women health) and evidence to inform programming and decision making (Nutrition surveillance, Iodine deficiency survey among school children 6-12 years, Nutrition assessment for school-aged children, MICS/SMART). The project will target 3,060,000 beneficiaries.

To strengthen accountability to affected populations and in addition to other UNICEF efforts in monitoring and evaluation mentioned in this proposal, the project will establish face-to-face key informants’ interviews using mentors to assess needs, satisfaction, and gaps in the nutrition services among affected population. Mothers will be trained on MUAC screening and identification of acute malnutrition and how where and when to refer their children to care. project_name: Fostering Resilience through Early Recovery response for the most Crisis impacted Communities in Syria
project_objective:
The Integrated Response for Resilience Programme aims at providing a comprehensive
response through Early Recovery support in 80 communities impacted by the crisis.
Communities, particularly those most dramatically affected – and under additional stress
because of IDPs returns and other displacements - need assistance in reinforcing their
resilience to address these shocks as well as the consequences of the protracted crisis,
and to address their needs on seriously depleted infrastructures and service capacities.
The essence of the Programme is about providing Syrian communities with – still limited -
support to regain control over their basic needs (livelihoods, access to essential services)
and reduce their dependency on humanitarian assistance. Prioritization of locations, is the
outcome of a context analysis and needs assessment conducted on more than 5,000
Syrian communities, based on the following three criteria:
1) Hard to Reach Areas
2) Areas of major IDPs presence and IDPs returns
3) Highest scoring in the Severity Scale
The integrated response consists of the following components: strengthening of social
services-related capacities (access and coverage), livelihoods creation and rural recovery,
PWDs support, social cohesion/community safety, reducing gender inequality and youth
marginality, women empowerment, tensions reduction and rehabilitation of basic
infrastructure and public services.
The program is built in a modular manner both in terms of geographical and
sectoral/thematic interventions and foresees the allotment of average 1 Million US$ per
community. Hence, donors willing to support this approach will be able to pre-select
certain location(s) and/or area(s) of intervention of their preference, within the 200
prioritized communities.
The programme relates directly to the sector objectives:
1. Living conditions
2. Livelihoods
3. Access to social services
4. Access to productive and market infrastructure
5. Social protection
6. Strengthening of local public services delivery capacity
7. Reinforcing opportunities and capacities for civic engagement

project_name: Strengthen provision of PHC across Syria.
project_objective:
WHO will continue supporting primary health care activities in Syria through both mobile teams and fixed primary health care facilities to ensure the delivery of the integrated Essential Health Service Packages to the population of Syria, while ensuring last mile coverage through integrated PHC network and access to healthcare to those in need and leaving no one behind  with focus on the most vulnerable groups.. Estimated number of health facilities to be covered 600 fixed and MMUs along the country.

It is imperative to enhance national health resilience and to reactivate public health partners by supporting the rehabilitation of non-functioning public centers , to repair extensive damage to crucial infrastructure, support ongoing medical training for human resource for health, sustain availability of essential medicines and equipment and to undertake ongoing needs’ assessments to fulfill gaps on the mid- and long term; with focus on advocating and expanding standardized PHC service package along the county. 

WHO will provide the technical expertise to ensure development of essential  PHC essential health service and benefit packages  are upgraded to address humanitarian needs and to improve health system resilient to situations of crisis through the comprehensive integrated health services at static and community-based interventions , with focus on strengthening the capacity  for human resources for health as a key point. This includes prevention of diseases, early detection and standard management for NCDs high risk groups, early essential new-born care services , maternal and childhood care, infection prevention and control at the health facility  and community levels , through the provision of continued education and training, endorsement of standardized clinical guidelines, treatment protocol.

Furthermore, the project aims to support safe health care service through delivery of basic infection prevention and control training, provision of technical support , provision of PPE supplies and the needed resources  to provide IPC standard measures in the context of COVID pandemic to ensure continuity of quality care.

Within the integration approach to essentially service delivery the access to quality care and referral to specialized health services will be introduced through implementation of this project, which includes dialysis, cancer and thalassemia treatment, as well as trauma care and rehabilitation, including provision of life-saving medical supplies and medicine required for the provision of specialized and trauma services.

Moreover, addressing problems related to fragmented and inefficient service delivery is crucial; in addition to inequity to access to basic essential services, lack of minimum standards, linkages with other levels of care/ care continuum, etc, WHO will continue supporting the existing three PHC networks of health facilities across northern Syria (Idleb, Afrin and North Aleppo) serving an estimated 2 million beneficiaries. These networks aim to link and coordinate the operations of participating health facilities of different levels of complexity and capacities to solve health problems, with the overall specific objectives of improving access and efficiency.

Objectives:
Ensuring Access to Integrated Health Service Delivery & Community health 
Support referral system
Capacity building such as infection prevention and control, facility cleanliness and patient safety, pharmacy & warehouse management, facility management, peace building and standardized reporting through DHIS2
Enhance Health Information Systems
Quality monitoring and improvement of service provision
COVID 19 response and continuity of essential health services
NCD integration
TB integration
Nutrition linkage focusing on prevention of malnutrition for Pregnant & Lactating Women and U-5, health promotion acclivities, community-based intervention
GBV first line support is part of the integratory services provided at PHC and community.
