project_name: Améliorer l’accès aux soins de santé primaire et nutritionnels en ambulatoire et en hospitalisation au Tchad
project_objective:
ALIMA et son partenaire Alerte Santé ont pour objectif de contribuer à la réduction de la mortalité des enfants de moins de 5 ans dans les régions sanitaires de N’Djamena et du lac à Liwa et à contribuer à la réduction la morbidité dans la région sanitaire de Liwa à travers des soins de santé primaire adaptés.

Le projet apportera une assistance nutritionnelle à travers la prise en charge médico-nutritionnelle de XXXX enfants de moins de 5 ans dans la province de N’Djamena et XXXX dans la province de Liwa, des activités de sensibilisation à la malnutrition aigüe sévère et le renforcement des capacités de professionnels de santé.

Dans la région sanitaire de N’Djamena, le projet appuiera la prise en charge de la MAS en ambulatoire dans 6 centres de santé appuyés et en hospitalisation à l’UNT HATC. Le projet souhaite également étendre son appui à une autre UNT de la vielle. Dans la région sanitaire de Liwa au Lac, le projet appuiera la prise en charge de la MAS en ambulatoire dans les cliniques mobiles se rendant dans les sites de déplacés ainsi que les postes fixes appuyés par le projet (Djil Kory, Mananara, Kangara, Doudeye, Daboua école, Fadatou, Foul Foul, Kindikou Fodi Oudou, Amma et Diamerom) et en hospitalisation à l'UNT de l'hôpital de district de Liwa.
Le renforcement des soins de santé communautaire sera mis en place avec des activités de porte à porte pour le dépistage précoce de la MAS ainsi que la sensibilisation sur les PFE et le covid-19.

A Liwa, le projet apportera également une assistance de soins de santé primaires aux populations déplacées affectées par les multiples crises de la région du Lac afin de développer l'accès à des soins de santé primaire gratuits et de qualité pour tous, à travers des soins de santé curative et de santé de la reproduction. 

Pour la mise en œuvre de toutes les actions du projet, les capacités des agents de santé seront renforcées en tenant compte du contexte de la pandémie de COVID-19.

project_name: Emergency WASH assistance to Conflict and drought-affected vulnerable IDPs and poor host community members from affected Woredas in Tigray,  Amharic and Somali region of Ethiopia
project_objective:
Ethiopia just like other Horn African countries has been hit by an exceptionally severe drought that was occasioned by the failure of the last three consecutive rains. Poor rains in October-December 2020 and March-May 2021 have been followed by an extremely dry October- December 2021. Current forecasts point to a fourth below-normal rainfall season during March-May 2022, a sequence that was never seen since 1981 in the region, which if it happens as predicted could further exacerbate the current humanitarian challenges in the region. The Somali region of Ethiopia is one of the regions hard–hit by the ongoing drought. The Post- deyr rains assessment and regional drought response plan, prepared in December 2021, confirmed that the whole Somali region is affected by the current drought and 2,279.606 people in the region are reported to be in need of water trucking, at 657 sites across 85 Woredas.  Water resources are increasingly being strained as a result of the drought conditions while most surface water sources have largely dried up in the region. The humanitarian situation in Northern Ethiopia has been worsening since the onset of the war in November 2020 in the region which has affected more than 6 million people, displaced more than 2.2 million people displaced from their homes including almost one million women and girls as the fighting crossed into the Neighboring Amhara and Afar region. In Tigray and Amhara region particularly in the war-affected areas, the conflict has rendered a large number of water points dysfunctional due to damage to water supplies systems, looting of water points, the collapse of water governing structures, disruptions in the Supply chains of Essential WASH equipment in the region. A recent OCHA update reported that there are about 418,000 IDPs in 131 sites in Tigray that require water trucking supports and that about 9300 water points (more than 54%) are not functional in Tigray affecting access of more than 3.5 million people to safe drinking water.
 According to the WASH cluster situation update from the Amhara region (issued 1st march 2022). There are over 256, 491 IDPs in the region, of which the majority are newly displaced. - IDPs are mainly found in North Shewa, North Wollo, Waghemra, and North Gondar zones - There are sheltered in 20 Collective sites across the Amhara region.  In view of the above, Alight proposes emergency WASH Services provisions to the conflict and drought-affected IDPs and vulnerable host communities including Schools and health facilities that are also in need of basic WASH services from affected Woredas in Tigray, Amhara and the Somali region with the aim of saving lives and reducing morbidities associated with WASH-related diseases. In this proposal Alight will:
•	Prioritize emergency Water trucking supports to IDPs and vulnerable host community members for 2 months benefiting approximately 30,000 beneficiaries. 
•	Restore the functionality of 10 strategic boreholes and shallow wells by rehabilitating and providing critical pumping and power systems installations to support durable access to water for the targeted beneficiaries
•	Construct  400 communal emergency latrines and bathing cubicles for IDPs populations
•	Distribute environmental sanitation kits to IDPs especially newly arrived IDPs to help them manage waste.
•	Provide WASH Supports to 14 Institutions (8 schools and 6 Health facilities.
•	Hygiene promotion will remain a key component of the intervention to prevent the spread of Covid 19 and other WASH-related diseases through risk communications and community engagement promoting behaviour changes. 
•	Where feasible, Alight will use Market based programming approach in the delivery of the planned WASH Interventions ( e.g use of commodity and cash vouchers). The project plans to reach a total of 90,000 beneficiaries ( 20700 men, 24300 women,19800 boys and 25200 girls).

project_name: Multi-sectoral support for crisis affected communities in Gedaref State
project_objective:
Gedaref is suffering from multiple shocks which has created a dire humanitarian situation in the state. The sudden influx of Ethiopian refugees from the Tigray region in late 2020, coupled with the ongoing economic crises affecting the country have placed a severe burden on the provision of basic services. Compounding these difficulties has been the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and the devastating floods during the last rainy season. Urgent humanitarian assistance is needed to support local people in Gedaref to meet their basic needs. In response to this crisis, Mercy Corps plans to deliver a multi-sector response comprising of interventions in WASH, FSL, ESNFI, Protection, Health and Nutrition.

The program will strengthen WASH, GBV / protection, shelter provision and health services to enable refugees, host population and vulnerable communities to adapt, withstand, and recover from disasters and emergencies. The project will respond to the needs and priorities of the affected population through an integrated multi-sectoral approach, with gender and protection mainstreamed throughout. Mercy Corps will address WASH needs through rehabilitation of water sources at both community and institutions, formation and training of WASH committees to ensure improved access to clean and safe water. Mercy Corps will then complement the water supply activities through hygiene promotion and train community hygiene promoters who will carry out hygiene promotion awareness raising activities to enhance health and wellbeing of the targeted individuals. During the implementation Mercy Corps will ensure COVID-19 transmission risks are mitigated through behavior change by ensuring adherence preventive practices including social distancing and respiratory hygiene.

MC will deliver a range of nutrition activities targeting children under 5 and pregnant / lactating women (PLW). We will support health facilities with outpatient therapeutic program (OTP) services whilst also training mothers support groups (MSG) to addresses the multi-sectoral causes of malnutrition, such as inadequate diet diversity, poor WASH behaviors, and unsafe food preparation and conservation methods. MC will integrate project activities with respect to nutrition interventions (For example, provision of WASH kits to SAM/MAM children, or referral of SAM/MAM cases to FSL livelihood/GFD response to prevent them from relapsing to malnutrition)

Multiple shocks, including slow and fast onset disasters such as flooding, are continuing to affect a range of vulnerable households in the state. To meet the immediate needs of affected communities, Mercy Corps will provide ES/NFI sectoral interventions including the provision of emergency shelter and NFI kits. A range of vulnerability criteria will be used for inclusion in ES/NFI distributions and the items will be inline with SPHERE standards.  

The protracted humanitarian situation within the state has resulted in multiple protection concern. GBV has been identified as a priority concern and MC will ensure the safety, health and dignity of women and girls by provision of quality multi-sectoral GBV response services with a survivor-centred approach and GBV risk mitigation measures. Activities proposed include support to Women and Girls Safe Spaces, protection monitoring visits and assessments, conducting awareness-raising against GBV and PSEA and the provision of dignity kits for Women and Girls.

project_name: Multi-sectoral Response to Needs of Displaced People in Blue Nile and South Kordofan States
project_objective: The proposed project is to improve the well-being and resilience of people affected by accumulated crises through a one health approach that aims to sustainably improve food and nutrition security, increase access to WASH and FSL  services, strengthen the target communities’, and promote peaceful co-existence in South Kordofan and Blue Nile States. Most of the current interventions in the target states focus on providing humanitarian assistance, even though this is relevant and needed, however there is a pressing need to consider recovery interventions so as to promote dependency reduction and increase resilience of the communities to withstand future shocks. VSFG and partners have established presence in the target areas and (based on their expertise) have been implementing multi-sectoral, multi-actor relief projects addressing FSL, WASH and , Protection needs of the target people. So, this project builds on the assessment results of VSFG and partners on prioritized needs for intervention in the target areas, and lessons learned from previous and ongoing interventions. The security situation has been mostly stable in the localities targeted by the proposed project; which is conducive to introduce development programs, and it also enables VSFG and partners to closely manage implementation of the project activities. Additionally, the political transition is supportive of implementing development programs, as well as the project is in line with the national and state-level strategic objectives. The protracted conflict and the deterioration of the macroeconomic situation in Sudan have negatively affected the capacity of poor households to secure their basic needs such as food, and protection. In addition, the limited access to livelihood opportunities, increased risks of poverty, social exclusion and violent conflict. The local capacities and infrastructure in the target areas are limited, deteriorated and require strengthening and rehabilitation to cope with the high demand on the available services and resources. The proposed project will enhance resilience through a one health approach and contribute to a humanitarian-development-peace nexus in Sudan through performing the following: implementing a multi-sectoral project to provide holistic response to the needs and priorities of the target communities; establishing a strong project management structure; sharing experience and expertise among VSF G and partners to effectively and efficiently address identified needs; and by accounting for the considerable change in the operational context (political and economic) while developing this project (opportunities and challenges).

project_name: Management and Monitoring of Emergency Response, and Enhancing Safety and Security
project_objective:
Management, coordination and monitoring of activities, and deployment of professional staff are essential for UNRWA to deliver timely and effective humanitarian assistance, to ensure efficient coordination with relevant stakeholders and to enhance advocacy on behalf of Palestine refugees.

While the vast majority of posts needed to deliver the mandate of the Agency in Syria will continue to be filled by Palestine refugees and Syrian nationals, UNRWA will maintain some international capacity, particularly specialist staff in the fields of humanitarian response, monitoring and evaluation, and grants management.

UNRWA will continue to conduct safety and security trainings for its staff across Syria,. UNRWA has made significant investments in the safety and security of its staff, assets and facilities despite financial challenges. 

Finally, under this project, UNRWA will also sustain the operational needs of support departments, including HR, Administration, Procurement and Logistics. UNRWA has also included a budget for the minor repair and maintenance of UNRWA facilities to ensure safe and functional delivery of services for both beneficiaries and staff.

project_name: Provision of Non-Food Items (NFIs) and Shelter Assistance to Vulnerable Palestine Refugees in Syria
project_objective:
UNRWA estimates that 420,000 Palestine refugees in Syria will continue to require humanitarian assistance in 2022. Many among them struggle to secure basic shelter and NFI need, and will be supported by UNRWA through this project, as part of the 2022 Humanitarian response plan. This intervention has three components: 
1-Cash assistance for winterization: UNRWA will provide 420,000 PalRefs ( 123,529 families)  with cash assistance for winterization ( one-off distribution of $ 265.37 for each family )  in all locations ( Damascus, Rural Damascus, Homs, Hama, Lattakia, Tartous, Aleppo and Deraa governorates/ urban and rural areas/. This is a direct disbursement of cash transfers through 02 financial service providers. 
2-Cash assistance for minor shelter repair ( small scale): UNRWA will target 700 families (2380 beneficiaries) in three camps ( Ain Al Tal, Yarmouk and Deraa). The transfer value per family is $ 3,500 to be distributed through 02 service providers. 
3-Inkind distribution of NFIs to 2500 families / 8500 beneficiaries (1250 returnee families and 1250 IDP families / 4250 returnee beneficiaries and 4,250 IDPs beneficiaries). At this stage, the locations are not identified and the eligibility of the beneficiaries to this intervention depends on their hardship. The unit cost of NFI kit is $ 61.52/beneficiary  for returnees (blankets, mattresses, kitchen sets, jerry cans and Mats) and $66.92/beneficiary for IDPs (blankets, mattresses, kitchen sets, jerry cans Mats and Tarpaulin)

project_name: Ensuring safe access to emergency education for UNRWA vulnerable refugee students.
project_objective:
The proposed intervention aims at ensuring continuity of learning and safe and equitable access to inclusive and quality education for 20,991 students (9,919 boys and 11,081 girls) and 951 school staff (319 men and 632 women) in a context of increased violence as a result of protracted crisis and continued military occupation, as well as increased vulnerability  due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The project targets 26 schools that are affected by frequent military incursions, clashes and settler violence and are located at risk areas namely East Jerusalem, Hebron H2, Area C, and inside refugee camps.

The first aim of the project is to ensure that students affected by education-related violations or the COVID-19 pandemic benefit from a protective environment and that school-aged children are able to complete  their basic education. This is achieved through the provision of safe transportation to vulnerable children while commuting to and from school, and protective presence in two schools particularly affected by ISF incursions, use of live ammunition and tear gas and settlers' violence.  Emphasis is also given in supporting the psychosocial well-being and enhancing resilience of students and teachers. This is achieved through the deployment of ten school counsellors at high-risk schools; provision of recreational activities through school-based summer camps, enhancement of recreational spaces, and stress management workshops aiming to strengthen teachers’ resilience.  
The second objective of the project is to ensure inclusivity of all vulnerable students. Learning support through catch-up classes will be provided to help children with learning difficulties.  In addition, 1,852 children with disabilities (767 boys and 1,085 girls) and special needs will be supported through assistive devices and referrals. 

In the context of COVID-19, the third aim of the project is to guarantee that schools prevent the spread of COVID-19 and protect the health of the students and teacher.  UNRWA will provide hygiene kits and Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) to all targeted students and teachers. 

Finally, the intervention also aims to improve the confidentiality, safety and accessibility of complaints mechanisms, including complaints of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA). The project intervention provides  multiple child-friendly channels to receive and respond to complaints which are adapted to the target population. UNRWA has developed ad hoc SoPs on the management of cases of SEA which abide to CBCM SoPs.   Complaints of SEA will be handled by PSEA focal points who will ensure a survivor centered approach in how the complaint is handled and support is offered to the survivor. UNRWA West Bank Field Office works closely with the PSEA Network and will undertake compulsory reporting and external referrals. 

This action contributes to the achievement of two of the strategic objectives under the HRP: 

STRATEGIC OBJECTIVE 2: The basic needs of vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation are met through the provision of quality basic services and improved access to resources, in accordance with the rights of protected persons under IHL. 

STRATEGIC OBJECTIVE 3: Safe, accessible mechanisms are in place for reporting complaints and feedback, including complaints of SEA, particularly in high-risk areas.

project_name: Provision of essential primary health care to remote and vulnerable communities of Palestine refugees in the West Bank (Mobile Health Teams)
project_objective: The Mobile Health Teams project seeks to improve accessibility to essential primary health services for remote vulnerable communities in area C and East Jerusalem facing access restrictions to health services due to Israel's restrictive planning system. In providing health services to thirteen selected communities in Area C, the project also aims to raise awareness among beneficiaries on COVID-19 prevention and mitigation measures, as well as on accessibility of SEA complaints mechanisms.  Finally, as long as COVID-19 continues, the project will seek to strengthen the ability of targeted communities to respond to the virus.

project_name: Preventing and Responding to Gender-Based Violence among Palestine Refugees in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem
project_objective:
The West Bank is currently experiencing the fourth wave of the COVID-19 pandemic, with serious socio-economic consequences for Palestinians, including Palestine refugees. The impact of COVID-19 has exacerbated an already complex situation characterised by long-term military occupation, which generated new major humanitarian challenges in 2021, with a significant increase in protection concerns affecting Palestinians, and disproportionally the most vulnerable, including women, children, the elderly, persons with disabilities, Bedouin and herding communities in Area C, and households isolated by the West Bank Barrier. 
COVID-19-related restrictive measures, are likely to remain in place in 2022. Likewise, the protection risks and inherent threats identified will continue to negatively impact the lives of Palestinians, including Palestine refugees, and mutually reinforcing with specific groups such as women, children and persons with disabilities characterised by multiple vulnerabilities across these risks. 
Through the proposed intervention, UNRWA will complement the case management work of its relief and social services programme by providing immediate response to survivors of gender-based violence, and women and girls at risk within the refugee community in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem. The action will contribute to mitigate the negative impact that COVID-19 and conflict-related violence have had in exacerbating the pre-existing vulnerabilities and gender inequalities affecting women and girls. 

In line with Inter-Agency Minimum Standards for GBV in Emergency Programming, UNRWA has a GBV case management framework in place, as well as a solid referral systems, ensuring a multi-sectoral response to GBV survivors. This intervention proposed to complement UNRWA's response by: 
(1) Providing unconditional cash assistance and dignity kits, tailored to the needs of women, girls, the elderly and PwD to 150 GBV survivors living in and outside camps, including in remote and isolated communities (Area C, Bedouin and Herders). 
(2) Localizing the efforts to respond to the needs of 710 GBV survivors and women and girls at risk living in camps and surrounding areas, and enhance the community-led response by providing them with opportunities for socio-empowerment, skills and capacity building; safe spaces, promoting comprehensive, positive and safe physical and psychosocial inclusion.
(3) Improving the safety and accessibility of complaints, including complaints of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA). The project has multiple channels to receive and respond to complaints which are adapted to the target population (including a free hotline, face-to-face reporting via social workers and protection staff) and UNRWA SOPs abide to Community-Based Complaint Mechanism (CBCM) SOPs from different target populations, including vulnerable groups. Complaints of SEA will be handled by PSEA focal points who will ensure a survivor centered approach in the handling of complaints and the provision of support to survivors. UNRWA West Bank Field Office works closely with the PSEA Network and will undertake compulsory reporting and external referrals. 
The intervention is in line with the STRATEGIC OBJECTIVE 2 (The basic needs of vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation are met through the provision of quality basic services and improved access to resources, in accordance with the rights of protected persons under IHL) and 3 (Safe, accessible mechanisms are in place for reporting complaints and feedback, including complaints of SEA, particularly in high-risk areas) of the HRP, as well as with the Palestinian national action plan to implement commitments towards enhancing services to women and girls survivor and victims of violence, as a result of Palestine joining the Gender Equality Forum (GEF)’s Action Coalition on Gender-Based violence and its adoption of Essential Services Package.

project_name: Mécanisme de réponse rapide (RRM) aux mouvements de population au Mali
project_objective:
La présente action vise à répondre aux besoins immédiats et prioritaires des populations du centre, nord et sud du Mali affectées par les déplacements ou une restriction d’accès aux services sociaux de base à la suite de conflits ou de catastrophes naturelles soudaines, à travers le renforcement de la veille humanitaire en zones rurales comme en milieux urbains. Cela se traduira par le maintien et le renforcement d’un système efficace de veille et d’alerte sur les mouvements de population et des évaluations multisectorielles rapides des besoins incluant la protection, l’apport d’une  réponse multisectorielle rapide et coordonnée sous forme de transfert monétaire ou de distribution en nature dans les domaines d’Abris, de Biens Non Alimentaire (BNA), de Sécurité Alimentaire et de l’Eau, l’Hygiène l’Assainissement ainsi  que le monitoring de la qualité des interventions, et la coordination technique et opérationnelle du mécanisme de réponse rapide (RRM) aussi bien au niveau national que régional.
L’action assistera 64 000 personnes (9 000 ménages) dont 60 000 personnes déplacées internes (PDI) et 4 000 personnes affectées par des catastrophes naturelles soudaines. Ces personnes ciblées par cette action seront constituées de 55% des femmes dont 64% de filles et 45% d’hommes dont 64% de garçons. 
Les bénéficiaires de cette action seront sélectionnés selon l’approche de vulnérabilité individuelle (ménage) mixte (matérielle et sociale). Les familles d’accueil des PDI seront pris en compte selon leur vulnérabilité. Chaque assistance sera précédée d’une analyse de risque protection, et suivi d’un monitoring post distribution 21 à 30 jours après intervention par une équipe indépendante à celle de la mise en œuvre. Le cadre de redevabilité : l’implication des parties prenantes et la mise en place du mécanisme de feedback à travers les boites à suggestions, comité des plaintes et le numéro vert seront mis en place, et l’approche Genre et l’application de la politique PSEA de la tolérance zéro de NRC seront placés au cœur de la mise en œuvre de ce projet s’inspirant de la dernière action. 
La coordination avec les autres acteurs humanitaires est une partie intégrante de ce projet. NRC maintiendra ses efforts de coordination avec l’ensemble des acteurs pour renforcer l’efficacité et la cohérence de la réponse via une participation active aux clusters Sécurité Alimentaire, Abris/BNA, EHA, Education et Protection ainsi qu’aux groupes de travail CWG, Genre et Redevabilité.
NRC à travers ce projet, a développé plusieurs approches et outils pour améliorer la qualité de la réponse mais également pour renforcer la coordination sur terrain. NRC continuera de mettre en place la forte dynamique qu’il a poursuivi en 2021 afin d’aboutir à une harmonisation des approches et outils avec les différentes partenaires RRM et des Clusters. 
L’assistance en BNA sera basée sur le standard minimum inspiré des orientations techniques du Sphère et du Cluster Abris/BNA auxquelles se réfèrent également les lignes directrices du RRM Mali, Pour l’efficacité de la réponse, l’assistance en BNA de ce projet sera systématiquement couplée d’assistance alimentaire et en Wash et d’une zone à une autre en santé là où il y aura les acteurs du cadre commun santé.  
Pour besoin d’équité, l’assistance pourrait être adapter à la taille de ménage pour certains items comme la natte, la couverture, la moustiquaire, le bidon et le savon.  
Dans le cadre de transfert monétaire, le montant sera à distribuer par ménage sera calculé en fonction des prix des articles ménagers essentiels du marché local et sur base de taille de chaque ménage. 
La réponse en Abri d’urgence sera basée sur le standard du Cluster lead et elle sera mixte soit en nature, soit en cash ou soit en nature plus du cash, et cela selon les résultats de l’évaluation des besoins et techniques mais également selon le contexte de zone cible. Les détails pour la réponse en Abris seront mis dans la proposition complète.

NRC à travers ce projet, a développé plusieurs approches et outils pour améliorer la qualité de la réponse mais également pour renforcer la coordination sur terrain. Le NRC se concentrera sur la fourniture en temps voulu d'une assistance EHA dans les situations d'urgence aiguës, en mettant particulièrement l'accent sur l’analyse des besoins, la coordination régionale afin de promouvoir des réponses harmonisées et intégrées. Le contenu de l'assistance sera optimisé si nécessaire en fonction de l'évaluation des besoins pour chaque crise et de la coordination avec le cluster EHA (SA) afin d'éviter les lacunes, les doublons et d'assurer la cohérence. Des activités de suivi post-distribution (PDM) seront entreprises pour évaluer l'efficacité, la pertinence et la couverture des réponses.

project_name: Las mujeres y las niñas que han sufrido/están sufriendo la VBG o que corren el riesgo de sufrirla se benefician de la prestación de servicios de calidad y del acceso a los mismos, y están capacitadas para participar cada vez más en la toma de decisiones y en el liderazgo de la respuesta, la mitigación y la prevención de VBG.
project_objective:
El objetivo de este programa multinacional de ONU Mujeres es proporcionar a las supervivientes de la violencia de género y a las personas que corren el riesgo de sufrirla medios de subsistencia y agencia para facilitar su acceso a los servicios humanitarios que salvan vidas y facilitar su voz para promover la responsabilidad de la violencia de género en contextos humanitarios. El impacto del programa será mitigar, prevenir y responder más eficazmente a la violencia de género entre las comunidades afectadas por la crisis. Las intervenciones de ONU Mujeres se centran en tres resultados, dos de los cuales se lograrán conjuntamente con el UNFPA.

Los tres resultados clave del programa se describen a continuación y abarcan aspectos de la programación de las normas sociales que contribuirán a la protección y el empoderamiento de las mujeres y las niñas afectadas por las crisis en los países prioritarios; la ampliación de las asociaciones con las organizaciones de trabajadores locales y las organizaciones de derechos humanos y el fortalecimiento de sus capacidades para participar en la toma de decisiones humanitarias; el aumento del acceso y la mejora de la calidad de los servicios prestados a las mujeres y las niñas afectadas por las crisis (refugiadas, desplazadas internas y en las comunidades de acogida), tanto en relación con la protección como con los medios de vida y la generación de ingresos (incluido el dinero en efectivo para las mujeres). El programa también contribuirá a la protección y abordará las necesidades y prioridades de los grupos en riesgo y marginados, incluyendo las poblaciones LGBTIQ+, las mujeres y las niñas con discapacidad. Los dos primeros resultados se obtendrán en estrecha colaboración con el UNFPA en los 6 países priorizados (resultados comunes: resultados 1 y 2).
Resultado común 1: Las personas destinatarias, a través de las intervenciones del programa, informan de cambios en las percepciones y actitudes hacia las normas y prácticas sociales que perpetúan la violencia de género y las desigualdades de género.
Resultado común 2: Las organizaciones de mujeres y las organizaciones de derechos humanos están capacitadas para participar cada vez más en la toma de decisiones y en el liderazgo de la respuesta, la mitigación y la prevención de la violencia de género.
Resultado 3 (específico de la agencia): Las mujeres y las niñas que han sufrido/están sufriendo la violencia de género o corren el riesgo de sufrirla se benefician de la prestación de servicios multisectoriales de calidad y del acceso a los mismos, incluida la asistencia jurídica.
Resultado 4 (específico de la agencia): Reducción del riesgo de violencia de género a través de la provisión de oportunidades de subsistencia, transferencias de efectivo, incluyendo dinero por trabajo.
El proyecto también invertirá en los organizaciones de mujeres locales para reforzar los conocimientos y las habilidades necesarias para la continuidad de los logros alcanzados en el proyecto. Todas las iniciativas de desarrollo de capacidades se diseñarán con un fuerte enfoque en la impartición de nuevos conocimientos que conduzcan a un cambio positivo en las actitudes y prácticas que promuevan normas de género positivas. Se espera que la programación de las normas sociales y la participación de las mujeres, los miembros de la comunidad y los líderes aumenten la apropiación y la sostenibilidad y mantengan los logros alcanzados. Por último, teniendo en cuenta que los medios de vida y los recursos financieros de las mujeres son una clave y una condición previa para la sostenibilidad, el proyecto tiene un fuerte componente de creación de medios de vida y resiliencia que permitirá a las mujeres, tanto en el entorno de los refugiados como en el de las comunidades de acogida, participar en los procesos de toma de decisiones y en los mecanismos de protección a largo plazo.

project_name: ASISTIR EL FLUJO DE MIGRACIÓN MIXTA TRANSREGIONAL / CONTINENTAL HACIA EL NORTE EN COLOMBIA (DP.0675)
project_objective: El proyecto busca brinda a migrantes transregionales/ continentales en tránsito hacia Norte América servicios de información y orientación con un enfoque de protección, prevención de Violencia Basada en Género (VBG), prevención de la trata y el contrabando para que puedan tomar decisiones y prevenir riesgos de protección. Además, el proyecto responderá con servicios básicos de salud, que incluyen apoyo psicosocial, provisión de equipo médico para mejorar la vigilancia epidemiológica y entrega de kits de higiene diferenciados por sexo y edad.

project_name: Renforcement des mécanismes de prévention et de protection de l'enfance dans les régions de Diffa et de Maradi
project_objective:
Le projet prévoit de répondre à l'ensemble des cas de protection à travers la mise en place efficiente d'une gestion de cas  répondant spécifiquement aux problématiques des violences basées sur le genre (VBG). project_name: Emergency climate-resilient infrastructure rehabilitation and maintenance
project_objective:
South Sudan has one of the world’s most under-developed infrastructures in the world. Out of the estimated 17,000 km of roads, less than two percent are paved. The country’s road density is the lowest in Africa with 15 km of road per 1,000 km of arable land. Building large-scale infrastructure is also challenging due to South Sudan’s increased vulnerability to devastating climate shocks. The average rainy season can last up to nine months. For the last three years, the country has been facing an unprecedented level of flooding which translated into the structural change of the wetlands and increasing its surface.  
The 2022 INFORM Index for risk management assesses South Sudan to be the second highest at-risk country globally after Somalia. South Sudan also ranks the highest of all 189 countries in the lack of coping capacity due to weak infrastructure and institutional capacity. It has extremely high socio-economic vulnerability and high numbers of displacements due to extreme weather events. In 2021, flooding affected 39 of the 78 counties (mainly in northern Jonglei and Unity) and, due to a lack of appropriate preventative or flood management infrastructure, has led to new displacements of over 835,000 people. 
In August 2021, Bentiu town, which has no flood water management system, began experiencing flooding and water levels peaked in October 2021. Despite the highwater levels, most IDPs from Rubkona, Guit and Koch counties sought refuge from the floods in Bentiu town. Following a series of rapid needs assessments across the country, emergency assistance has been provided to 598,957 people in the flood-affected areas. In addition to food distributions, humanitarian organizations have provided health and nutrition supplies and services; water, sanitation and hygiene services; protection services; and fishing kits for livelihood support. Similarly, a nearly catastrophic situation has also been reported in Fangak and Canal/Pigi counties where communities need to choose between physical security and food/ nutrition/ health security.

Through this project, WFP will develop critical infrastructures along main supply routes, primary dykes and community dykes in marginalized areas in Jonglei, Unity, and Upper Nile states. These areas are the most vulnerable to climate change and home to nearly 40 percent of the South Sudanese population, which has been isolated from basic needs and services (food, markets, hospitals, etc.). Other locations in Lakes or Western Equatoria States are also included in the plan due to the poor conditions of the roads and increasing humanitarian needs in the area. 

Another expected result of the project is to reduce isolation and displacement for communities. By repairing key infrastructure, communities will be protected from future shocks and have continuous access to basic necessities. Furthermore, it paves a path for already displaced communities to return to their areas of origin, in time to cultivate and rebuild their livelihoods while contributing to long term disaster risk reduction and climate adaptation.

Improving the transportation network in conjunction with other initiatives aimed at building human capacities (listed within the HRP) and labor force skills and strengthening institutions would provide the basis for a transition to economic growth. Through infrastructure projects, local youth stand better chance to get local employments thus increasing family household incomes. Lastly, in addition to facilitating efficient and cost-effective delivery of food and non-food items to various locations, improved road and river infrastructure will improve rural connectivity, promoting equity and social cohesion and ultimately contributing to peace.

project_name: Provision of primary Health care services for the Vulnerable communities in Balcad and Jowhar Districts of middle shabelle,Garasbaley and Shangani Districts of Banadir Regions, Somalia
project_objective: The population of Somalia consistently experiences some of the worst health outcome indicators in the world; the average life expectancy is estimated to be 51.5 years. Somalia is among the countries with the highest rankings in infant and child mortality rates of, respectively, 76.6 and 121.5 per 1,000 live births. The maternal mortality rate (692 deaths per 100,000 live births) and the fertility rate (average of 6.9 children per woman) are also among the highest in the world, 79 per cent of all births are home delivered without skilled assistance. Overall, 99 per cent of Somali women have undergone female genital mutilation, 64 per cent of these having suffered the Pharaonic type. Overall, only 11 per cent of children aged 12-23 months are fully vaccinated, around 19 per cent of children in urban areas have received all basic vaccinations, while this is the case for less than 1 per cent of children in nomadic areas. The inadequate comprehensive and reliable epidemiological and disease information from all districts makes it difficult to ascertain the extent of gaps in service provision and burden of disease across the country and effectively plan for response among actors. The health status indicators include the coverage of DPT3 and Penta3 vaccinations among children less than 1 year old and the coverage of measles vaccination among children less than 5 years old. The health resources are measured by the presence of functional health facilities per population. For the contextual factors, the overall severe and global malnutrition and the IPC phase were used. For each indicator thresholds were established from severity 1 to 5. During the final analysis, health status was weighted at 40 per cent, health resources at 25 per cent and contextual factors at 3 per cent. Based on this methodology, it is estimated that over 6.56 million Somali people require lifesaving essential healthcare in 2022. Excess mortality in Somalia is driven primary by malnutrition, disease outbreaks (e.g., COVID-19, AWD/cholera, measles, malaria) and violence; as well as non-communicable disease including complications of pregnancy and chronic disease. These are compounded by displacement due to conflict and natural disasters and lack of preventative and curative healthcare. Since the onset of COVID-19 in March 2020 until the 4th of October 2021, a total of 19,980 cases were confirmed in Somalia with a case fatality rate of 5.6 per cent. Vaccine availability is limited, and the vaccine coverage is below 2 per cent by the end of September 2021.People most affected by absence of health care services live in inaccessible districts under control of non-state armed groups. There are no known functional health facilities or services in those districts and health needs remain unaddressed. Key informants in 48 per cent of hard-to-reach settlements assessed reported having no access of any kind of health services. Health services for host communities are scarcer in rural areas than in urban settlements. Young children, girls and women of reproductive age and persons with a disability are most at risk of dying because of a lack of access to health services. In 2022, overall health needs are likely to remain insufficiently addressed. Health services have eroded to bare minimum levels in many locations as health partners face severe funding gaps. Health service delivery in Somalia remains dependent on humanitarian partners who finance and deliver a large proportion of health care to the population. In the absence of sufficient funding there is a danger of erosion of minimum standards of care of primary health care services. Aid vision is already on the ground handling 8 health facilities 4 in middle Shabelle region and 4 in Banadir region. These facilities are providing accessible and quality primary health care services to the vulnerable communities including pregnant and lactating women, children and people living with disabilities

project_name: Offre des services de santé de la reproduction en situation de crise humanitaire
project_objective: Au cours de cette dernière décennie le Niger connait des crises humanitaires liées par l’insécurité avec déplacement des populations mais aussi liées aux aléas climatiques comme la sècheresse où les inondations ou encore des crises sanitaires comme la pandémie de la covid-19 qui sévit actuellement. Force est de constater quelle que soit la forme de la crise les femmes et les filles sont les couches sociales les plus affectées et en payent un lourd tribut quant à leurs droits d’accéder aux services de santé de la reproduction. En effet, la morbidité et la mortalité liées à la SSR sont des problèmes de santé majeurs et les personnes en situations de crise humanitaire sont souvent exposées à des risques élevés et des obstacles supplémentaires en matière d’accès aux services de SSR. L’accès aux soins de SSR est un droit et les personnes touchées par le conflit ou les catastrophes sont habilitées à bénéficier d’une protection et d’une assistance L’offre de services de SSR en temps voulu peut empêcher le décès, les maladies et le handicap liés à la grossesse non planifiée, les complications obstétricales, les violences sexuelles et d’autres formes de violences basées sur le genre, ainsi que le VIH et un large éventail de troubles de la reproduction. La santé sexuelle et reproductive (SSR) est une composante essentielle des interventions humanitaires c’est pour cela que UNFPA prévoit un ensemble d’interventions pour pallier aux conséquences évoquées ci haut d’abord par (i) l’informations des communautés des services disponibles ; (ii) le déploiement des cliniques mobiles pour toucher les zones difficiles d’accès ; (iii) le pré positionnement des kits inter agence (IARH kits) en santé de la reproduction y compris les kits post viol ; (iv) le renforcement des capacités des agents en dispositif minimum en santé de la reproduction en situation de crise et (v) l’appui en personnel qualifié pour l’offre des services de qualité. L’UNFPA se propose de faire toutes ces interventions dans les 5 régions les plus affectées par la crise humanitaire au Niger à savoir Diffa, Tillabéry, Maradi, Tahoua et Agadez.

project_name: Assurer une prise en charge holistique, adaptée et opportune aux survivantes de VGB  pour les déplacées internes, populations hotes des regions de Diffa, Tillaberi, Tahoua, et Maradi et Niamey
project_objective: Le projet vise à assurer dans un cadre bien coordonné, une prise en charge holistique qualitative de proximité adaptée au sexe, à l’âge, au handicap et au statut de déplacement pour les personnes survivant(e)s de VBG et réduire les risques de Violences Sexuelles et Basées sur le Genre, les exploitations et abus sexuels chez les personnes à risque. Il cible les populations, non déplacées /hôtes , les déplacées internes, les  retournées incluant les femmes, les hommes, les filles , y compris  les adolescentes et les personnes handicapées dans les régions de Tillaberi (départements de:  Téra, Torodi, Banibangou, Oullam, Say , Tillaberi , Ayerou, Bankilaré, Abala , Flingué,  Balleyara, Gotheye) ;  Tahoua( départements de : Abalak, Bagaroua, Birnin Koni, Illela, Madaoua , Tahoua, Tchintabaraden, Tillia, Tassara ), Maradi (départements de : Guidan Roundji , Madarounfa, Maradi ville ), et Diffa( départements de Bosso, Diffa, Goudoumaria, Maine-soroa, Ngourti, N'Nguigmi)  et Niamey affectées par les crises sécuritaires et transfrontalières. Le projet mobilisera les autres acteurs humanitaires des secteurs clés, les services déconcentrés de l’Etat, les communautés incluant les femmes, les hommes, les filles, les garçons et les personnes handicapées, pour assurer une participation inclusive dans la mise en œuvre des activités de façon intégrée en veillant au caractère adaptés et opportun pour survivantes de VBG. Ainsi tout en renforçant (formation équipements, suivi) les services de prise en charge, les outils (cartographie, SOP et chemin de référencement ; messages et module de formation à jours et compréhensifs) seront développés et mis à disposition des acteurs. Les acteurs communautaires (para juristes, comités de vigilances, chefs traditionnels, radio communautaires) seront formés et dotés de supports adaptés pour mener les activités de prévention et réduction des risques de VBG et assurer l'orientation des cas selon la stratégie communautaire (information et sensibilisation et orientation vers les services disponibles de qualités sur la base de des cartographie et chemin de référencement). Un mécanisme de gestion de l'information VBG (collecte analyse et partage) basé sur le GBVIMS garantira la qualité des données des cas et des évaluations périodiques renforceront le suivi de la situation pour une réponse adaptée et opportune. Des mécanismes de feed-back et de plaintes à la portée des communautés seront mis en place et opérationnalisés afin de mieux garantir la participation des communautés tout le long du cycle du projet et renforcer la qualité des interventions. Dans ce cadre chaque trimestre des rencontres inter acteurs et bénéficiaires seront organisées au niveau de chaque département où il sera partagé les résultats les insuffisances constatées et dégager les besoins d'amélioration pour la suite. Pour la redevabilité envers les mécanismes de coordination et les partenaires (bailleurs) des réunions mensuelles de coordination au niveau national et sous nationale de l'ensemble des acteurs membres du sous cluster renforcées par des missions de suivi et appui technique de la coordination nationale du sous cluster sur le terrain permettront de faire le suivi de la qualité, la veille de la situation, des rapports et des fac-sheet seront produits et partagés chaque trimestre..

project_name: Provision of Shelter and NFIs to the Conflicts and Climate Shocks affected populations in Lower Shaballe and Middle Shabelle regions, Somalia
project_objective: According to the JMCNA 2021, shelter is one of the top three priority need of more than half of the entire population and of 58 percent of IDPs406. An estimated 3.7 million people need shelter and NFI assistance mainly due to poor shelter conditions, overcrowding and lack of space, poverty, and lack of security of tenure. Those in need of shelter and NFI assistance include displaced and non-displaced populations. However, IDPs, refugee returnees, refugees and asylum seekers are particularly affected as they do not have financial capacity to build adequate shelters. Conflict, drought, flooding, evictions and cyclones are the key drivers of displacement, which in turn exacerbates humanitarian shelter and NFI needs. Natural disasters are one of the main causes of displacement and therefore accelerate migration from rural to urban and peri-urban centers that started decades ago. Lower Shabelle and Middle Shabelle regions are among the most vulnerable parts of Somalia that could face the natural disasters mainly with floods at the districts along the river passing areas, like Marka, Qoryooley, Afgooye, Kurtunwaarey ( Lower Shabelle) and Jowhar and Balcad ( Middle Shabelle) of Somalia. On the droughts and locusts impacts, Baraawe and Wanla Weyn, Marka, Qoryoley ( Lower Shabelle)  and Jowhar and Balcad ( Middle Shabelle). According to the CCCM Cluster, the eviction and Armed conflicts are another factors affecting the Lower & Middle Shabelle communities and therefore an estimated of 1.8 million of IDPs (62 per cent of IDPs) are at high risk of eviction. According to AYUUB assessment on this regard, Wanla Weyn, Marka and Jowhar are the vulnerable locations compared to other parts. However, according to the Detailed Site Assessment 2021, a total of 593,058 IDPs are estimated to reside in high-risk IDP sites due to both conflict and climate related forcing factors. These informal and largely unplanned IDP settlements tend to involve particularly hazardous living conditions. A lack of tenure agreements and housing options for IDPs from minority and marginalized groups leaves them without alternative residence options. Among these population, 42 per cent of the main income-earner of the household are women. Finally, women and girls living in sub-standard and overcrowded shelters such in Km50 IDPs sites in Afgooye and Jiliyaale, Airportka, Sheikh Omar and Tawakal IDPs sites in Jowhar are particularly vulnerable. They tend not to feel safe in makeshift shelters which do not offer privacy and sufficient protection from weather elements and increase the risk of gender based violence. Over a quarter, 27 per cent, of IDPs reported that their bathing facilities are not safe as their main shelter concern. Through this HRP 2022, AYUUB will respond to the conflict and climate impacted 45,000 people with gender disaggregation of (20,000 female, 10,000 male,  7500 Girls and 7500 Boys) in Marka, Afgooye and Baraawe ( Lower Shabelle) and Jowhar and Balcad ( Middle Shabelle)with Shelter and NFIs distribution service. The mode of the distribution will be decided upon the circumstance. AYUUB will further strengthen the community feedback mechanisms through following a proper community complaint mechanisms data collection and enable the IDPs for easily access to AYUUB Hotline to deliver their complaints and their complaints will addressed timely by the respective office.

project_name: Provision of basic and life-saving WASH services in South West, Hirshabelle States, Benadir and Galmudug region of South-Central Somalia
project_objective:
Somalia continued to be under crisis in 2021 with continued conflict, political instability, economic decline, increasing food insecurity, climatic shocks, disease outbreaks including COVID-19, and the worst desert locust infestation in years.. Some 5.9 million people are in need of humanitarian assistance across 74 districts in Somalia in 2021. 
The 2022 Humanitarian Needs Overview states that the high humanitarian needs in Somalia are driven by seasonal floods, severe drought conditions, acute water diarrhea/ cholera outbreaks and protracted crises, exacerbated by the COVID-19 outbreak. Drought remains the main driver of WASH needs in Somalia leading to displacement and communal conflict over water points. 
According to the WHO-UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) 2020, only 39 per cent of people in rural areas have access to water supply. 39 per cent of vulnerable people in Somalia do not have access to sustained, improved and safe water source for drinking and other domestic uses, while 84 per cent still walk for more than 15 minutes to the nearest water source. Due to these constraints, one in five Somalis do not have enough water per day to cover their basic needs for both drinking and domestic use. 92 per cent of the households don’t have water collection and storage containers further impacting their regular access to water. It is estimated that 1.3 million people in 24 drought hotspot locations hugely depend on water trucking during drought due to frequent breakdown or and dry-up of strategic water sources. This is quite unsustainable.
Access to improved sanitation facilities in Somalia is very low. JMCNA 2021 noted that 57 percent of households do not have access to improved sanitation facilities. Additionally, 23 per cent of people across Somalia still defecate in the open, 49 per cent of which are in rural areas. There are 1,507 IDP sites which still have less than 1 latrine per 50 individuals as per the recommended WASH Cluster minimum standards. 
Over half of all IDPs reportedly still faced challenges in terms of access to soap and hand washing facilities according to JMCNA 2021. Only 53 per cent of households across Somalia practise proper hand washing with soap and water while (39 percent) reported that they wash their hands but without soap and only 45 per cent of households have access to Menstrual Hygiene Management (MHM) material at home or can access it through their local market. 
According to the HNO 2022, the population in need of WASH services in 2022 includes approximately 1,619,415 IDPs and 4,818,944 vulnerable host communities. It's estimated that 6,058,603 people (38 per cent) in the 'Severe' category lack access to safe water and proper sanitation services and are highly vulnerable to AWD and cholera and around 379,757 people (2 percent) are in extreme condition as they access water directly from rivers and surface bonds, practice open defecation and lack access to soap and other essential hygiene materials and are susceptible to communicable diseases
Women and girls are exposed to protection risks including gender-based violence (GBV) when collecting water from too distant water sources or using unimproved overcrowded sanitation facilities which lack safety and protection features. 
CPD is targeting 24,900 people and will train gender-balanced management committees in order to avoid over reliance on unsustainable means of accessing clean water by rehabilitating strategic reliable water points. Committees will also be established to maintain clean sanitation facilities, as well as scale up hygiene promotion initiatives to help minimize AWD/cholera outbreaks during the rainy seasons. Marginalized groups will be consulted in all project phases including design and implementation and ensuring that the location, distance and access routes to the water points, latrines and distribution sites are accessible to all members of the community, including the disabled.

project_name: Strengthening food and livelihood security of conflict and disaster affected vulnerable IDPs and host communities through support to agricultural production and cash assistance to meet their immediate basic needs.
project_objective:
In the face of increasing food insecurity and the need to meet other basic urgent needs, initiatives to  address immediate food needs of the most vulnerable and food insecure population are paramount in saving lives and protecting assets of the most vulnerable. The proposed project is in-line with Humanitarian Needs Overview 2022, Food Security Cluster (FSC) priorities and objectives. The project aims at improving the ability of 66,610 vulnerable people including 41,280 IDPs and 9,991 people with disability to meet their food and basic needs and reduce consumption gaps through life-saving cash assistance and agriculture inputs. Of these 52,965 people under FSC CO1 and 13,645 people under FSC CO2. 
These households are affected by multiple shocks – including conflicts and facing wide consumption gaps, due to successive below-average agricultural and pastoral yields, and a lack of casual labour income opportunities in urban and IDP communities. Unconditional cash transfer (UCT) and agriculture input assistance will improve beneficiary household’s access to food and other basic needs, while preventing households from resorting to negative coping mechanisms which erode long-term resilience. Community and stakeholder engagement, gender sensitive vulnerability and eligibility criteria for beneficiary selection and emphasis on participation of men, women, boys and girls of different ages and other at-risk groups will improve gender equality and women’s empowerment and inclusion of marginalized population. Target population will be provided with six months of UCT totaling 3,675,965$ - based on the monthly transfer value recommended by Cash Working Group (CWG). In addition, 2,047 farmers households will be supported with agricultural inputs including seeds and tractor services through in kind and voucher and consumption support of 30$/month for 4 months. Cash for work will generate employment of 22,742 person days to create community assets.
Settlement and beneficiary targeting will follow a participatory and community-based process. To target the settlements, Concern will conduct stakeholder consultations and key informants interview at regional and district level. Village Relief Committees (VRC) with average 8 to 10 members in each comprising both men and women, including representatives from marginalized population groups will be established (or existing ones mobilized) and receive information on the project and the beneficiary selection process. VRCs will lead community based participatory beneficiary selection process, this will also help project to empower participating communities – including women in decision making. A key component in the beneficiary selection criteria will be gender, age and disability considerations. 
In line with Concern’s approach and quality standard for Cash and Voucher based assistance and Accountability to Affected Populations, Concern will disseminate information on its Complaints Response Mechanism (CRM) channels during sensitization to ensure that beneficiaries, target communities and project stakeholders are fully aware of and are able to raise any feedback or issues of concern for timely action. Concern’s independent Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability and Learning (MEAL) unit will regularly monitor the project and will conduct Post Distribution Monitoring (PDM).
Concern with its local NGO partners is implementing both emergency response and longer term programmes in proposed districts in this project. The proposed project will further leverage upon Concern’s efforts and strengthen envisaged resilience outcomes in the target districts, while providing the project with opportunity to ensure convergence and integration while addressing the underlying causes of vulnerability – including gender inequalities and poverty.

project_name: Improving access to quality emergency and essential lifesaving health services for crisis affected populations in Hobyo, Abduwak, Afgooye, Beletwayne and Wadajiir districts
project_objective:
It is estimated that over 6.56 million Somali people require lifesaving essential healthcare in 2022. Excess mortality in Somalia is driven primary by malnutrition, disease outbreaks (e.g., COVID-19, AWD/cholera, measles, malaria) and violence; as well as non-communicable disease including complications of pregnancy and chronic disease. 
In 2022, overall health needs are likely to remain insufficiently addressed. Health services have eroded to bare minimum levels in many locations as health partners face severe funding gaps. Health service delivery in Somalia remains dependent on humanitarian partners who finance and deliver a large proportion of health care to the population. In the absence of sufficient funding there is a danger of erosion of minimum standards of care of primary health care services. Cholera is endemic and seasonal spikes have been identified during rainy seasons, along riverbanks and in locations with high number of IDPs and where access to clean water and sanitation are limited. Oral cholera vaccination (OCV) in hot spot districts to protect vulnerable population against cholera has not been implemented in 2020 and 2021 as public health response efforts focused on COVID-19. As expected with the low measles vaccination coverage rates measles outbreaks continue to occur. There is an urgent need to increase routine vaccination and implement campaigns to ensure vaccination coverage of those children never vaccinated.
CESVI will deliver lifesaving emergency health services including maternal, neonatal and child health through 7 static Health facilities (Elgula, Galbarwaaqo, Abudwaaq, Elasha, Jazeera, Wadajir, Halane) and 4 mobile health clinics (Hobyo, Beletwayne, Elasha and Jazeera). CESVI has a strong presence in all the target locations implementing long term project in different sectors. This action will address endemic diseases like pneumonia, anemia, AWD and ARI which are the leading causes of infant and child mortality in the target villages. The Action will provide primary and referral health care, with special attention to maternal and child health, including basic emergency obstetric care (BEmONC) and EPI Emphasis will be laid on application of standard treatment guidelines as per EPHS at PHC. Health mobile clinics will serve IDP camps and villages in the far villages to deliver quality primary health care services to populations without a static MCH in close proximity. Moreover, Health facilities will be equipped (after minor rehabilitations) with essential drugs, vaccines and post- rape treatment drugs including medical equipment. Further, this intervention will enhance a referral system from primary to secondary health services and TB services and from nutrition to health services and vice versa. Community Health Workers (CHW) will be engaged to actively act as first responders for health and nutrition issues playing a key role in the referral system ensuring better access to health care services for the population to prevent AWD/cholera epidemic outbreak, hygiene promotion campaigns will be organized regularly throughout the action within the target villages. Cesvi will also integrate surveillance and emergency preparedness ensuring adequate stocks for epidemic outbreaks of AWD/Cholera and measles are prepositioned. Moreover, Personal Protective Equipment (PPEs) will be purchased for frontline Health workers as a measure for infection prevention and control (IPC) at service provision points. The project will also undertake confidential identification of GBV survivors for provision of comprehensive care, CMR and psychosocial support in-line with IASC MHPSS standard. The project will provide trainings targeting thematic areas such ANC and BEmONC, drugs consumption and GBV/Protection mainstreaming among others. Joint supportive supervision will also be undertaken with MoH as per of efforts to build their capacity. Health service is integrated with the nutrition being in the same target locations

project_name: Emergency Nutrition Intervention project in El-Afwein of Sanaag Region
project_objective:
The project overall objects is to address the humanitarian challenges of a classified affected hard to reach populations in El-Afwein of Sanaag Region. Sanaag have the highest infant mortality rate, 51 deaths per one thousand live births and U5 mortality rate is 76 per thousand live births. The situation is worse in El-Afwein, Erigavo and Las’anod because of a fewer health facilities, recurrent climate-related shocks and political instability, risks to crop production and food access are key drivers of food insecurity and malnutrition. Lower than expected and delayed Deyr and Gu’ rainfall and desert locust swamps severed crop production and pasture worsened by significant increase of food prices and 10-20 percent decline of remittance all contributed to food insecurity of local people.  A recent assessment carried out by HEAL, shows that most rural health facilities are not with enough staff, supplies and equipment.
Malnutrition is widespread driven by the above multiple factors. GAM prevalence is Alert in El-Afwein and Erigavo (9.9% and 8.6% respectively). Approximately 10,000 U5 children and 3,600 PLW are likely to be moderately malnourished, including 1,400 to be severely malnourished. 
To avoid deterioration, this proposal calls for durable solutions to prevent and treat malnutrition, including focus on gender inequality, addressing of poor hygiene and anti-discriminatory measures, immunisation coverage, accessibility and accountability of services to direct beneficiaries.
This will be achieved through recruiting and training Emergency nutrition teams on standard Somalia IMAM and IYCF tools with the purpose of early detection and treatment of under 5 children with moderate and severe acute malnutrition. Thereafter, the project will help and give integrated services including screening, identifying, and treating and referring children with moderate and severe acute malnutrition. The pregnant/lactating women will receive multiple micro-nutrient supplementation, while benefiting Infant Young Child Feeding (IYCF) counselling services. Breastfeeding promotion is provided throughout the course of the project. Children and mothers by referring to the nearest Health facility. In protection mainstreaming, HEAL fully involves IDPs, including from marginalised communities in the design, implementation, monitoring and evaluation of the projects.
1. The project will support 4 mobile teams in El-Afwein District with linkage to existing health facilities of El-Afwein MCH, Garadag MCH, Huluul MCH. 2. The identification, referral and treatment of 5,605(6-59 months) children suffering from acute malnutrition through OTP/TSFP and community based approaches. 3. The project will strengthen local technical capacity for integration of Integrated Management of Acute Malnutrition (IMAM) into the Primary Health Care system through utilisation of Basic Nutrition Services Package (BNSP). 3. Strengthening supply chain management, well-trained health workers, financing, and use of existing community based nutrition programs in order to scale-up prevention, early identification and treatment of acute malnutrition of children and Pregnant and Lactating (PLW). 4. Service delivered will be Maternal and child nutrition components including IMAM, IYCF, NHHP, referral system, Ready to Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF) supplies, mitigation of COVID-19, nutrition surveillance and as well as mobilising, educating and creating demand for service uptake. 5. Preventive measures are, de-worming, counselling and promotion on infant and young child feeding including Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) in emergencies. Community mobilisation, screening and referral, micro-nutrient supplementation for PLW (multiple micro-nutrients and Iron Folate), Expanded Program on Immunisation (EPI) and U5 (Vitamin A supplements) for children reinforced with Communication for development (C4D). Also Personal protection of staff using PPE. 6. Prevention services will include COVID-19.

project_name: Provision of emergency life-saving essential health care services through static and mobile/outreach to crisis affected populations in Bay, Bakool and Hiran region Somalia
project_objective:
Ongoing   severe drought displacement, armed conflict and insecurity, as well as cyclical climatic shocks, amid compounding political and socioeconomic factors, continue to drive and impact the humanitarian crisis in Somalia. Such factors have resulted in protracted economic vulnerability and the loss of livelihoods, particularly among agro-pastoralists, rural pastoralists and riverine farmers. Violence and limited access to humanitarian assistance and basic social services in rural and hard-to-reach areas has spurred mass population movement toward urban and peri-urban areas, further straining the limited resources and absorption capacity of host communities, this has been worsened by global COVID-19 pandemic and recurrent drought. The combined impact increasingly exposes households to risks of violence, exploitation and abuse. As a result, in 2021  6.5 million Somalis in IDPs, host communities, returnees and refugees are in need of humanitarian assistance across the country of these 51% are female, however, a total of a total of 148,829 displaced and 24,747 non-displaced person in Baidoa, 16,980 displaced and 24,143 non displaced person in Beletweyne as well as 2,572, displaced ,10,119 non-displaced in Ceelbarde and 2,153 and 400 displaced and non-displaced in Rabdhure are in need of physical and mental health as well as in humanitarian crisis.continues in several parts of the country. Confirmed cholera cases from the beginning of the year to epidemiological week 31 (2nd August 2021) recorded 4,134 cases, 31 deaths with a case fatality rate (CFR) of 0.5%, this coupled with COVID-19 pandemic which continues to spread in Somalia with a total of 3,212 COVID-19 cases confirmed; including 193 associated deaths as of second August 2021. The large majority (83 %) of cases are aged between 20 and 60 years, with a Case Fatality Rate (CFR) 3% and 1,827 recoveries. Since the onset of the outbreak in Somalia, 3212 laboratory-confirmed cases of COVID-19 were reported including 93 associated deaths. The large majority (83 %) of cases are aged between 20 and 60 years, with a median age of 32 years (ranging from 1 to 110 years). As in previous weeks, 73% of the laboratory-confirmed cases were amongst male. The number of samples tested during this reporting week is higher than in previous weeks, but the positivity rate is significantly lower than in previous weeks (from 6.7% - 3%)
Therefore, the project intends to support life-saving emergency healthcare to an estimated 17,000 crises affected boys, girls, Women, men including disable beneﬁciaries through 10 static and 8 outreach/mobile clinics in Bay, Bakool and Hiraan regions. Emphasis will be on maternal, neonatal and child health including emergency immunization to the host communities and Internally Displaced People (IDPs). This action will focus on provision of both preventive and curative health services at primary level integrated with nutrition and WASH activities to provide holistic and integrated support. Through deployment of trained health workers including midwives and community health workers in facilities and mobile teams, essential primary care services including treatment of common childhood illnesses, as well as emergency obstetric and neonatal care for pregnant and lactating women will be provided. HIDIG an actor in the target regions will leverage on existing support & activities to ensure the gains made in the post-drought response are not rolled back. Building the capacity of health workers through training on Basic Emergency Obstetric Care (BEmONC) will be done to equip health workers with the required skills to deliver quality health care services to the affected population. The project will ensure to provide mental health and psychosocial service support, clinical case management of rape and inclusion of gender and age appropriate gender mainstreaming to vulnerable boys, girls, women and men including people with disability(PLWD).
