project_name: Provision of nutrition treatment and prevention services to crisis affected populations in Mudug, Hiraan, Banadir and Lower Shebelle Regions
project_objective: 2021 Post Gu FSNAU nutrition analysis shows that at the national level the median prevalence of GAM has still remained at a serious level of 11.1%. Based on the nutrition cluster figures estimation in 2022 around 1.2 million children <5, will be at risk of acute malnutrition. In addition to this, around 245,909 PLWs will be at risk of acute malnutrition. As per the last Somalia 2021 Post Gu Nutrition Map (Projection, Sept-Nov 2021) published by FSNAU, the GAM level for the 5 target districts of this Action is between serious (10-14.9%) and critical (15-29.9%) and IPC level is between 2 and 3 as per the Somalia 2021 Post Gu Nutrition Map (Projection, Oct-Dec 2021). In 2022 food insecurity and nutritional levels are expected to further deteriorate among poor rural, urban, and displaced populations due to the impacts of anticipated, below-average 2021 Deyr season rainfall and a likely reduction in agricultural employment opportunities during the forthcoming Deyr season. It is therefore estimated worse outcomes to be in place between October and December 2021 and along 2022. COVID-19 continues to be another major challenge as it has affected the nutrition service delivery modalities. The nutritional status of children under 5 years of age continues to deteriorate in most parts of Somalia thereby increasing their vulnerabilities and predisposing them to morbidity and mortality. The above factors compounded by the poor health service delivery system, high prevalence of AWDs, poverty and reduced purchasing power further predispose the Somali children to all forms of malnutrition including micronutrient deficiencies and therefore require preventive services. This action will be implemented in Beletweyne, Hobyo, Banadir and Afgooye districts targeting vulnerable populations affected by different cyclic crises. The main purpose of this intervention is to mitigate and prevent malnutrition trends in the aforementioned districts with focus on children < 5 years and PLWs. This will be done through provision of quality curative and preventive nutrition services. In order to achieve the Nutrition cluster objectives, the action will be implemented in the 5 target districts where CESVI has a strong operational presence implementing a broad range of interventions across different sectors: Health, Nutrition, WASH and FSL. This Action targets 6 static Health facilities (Elgula. Galbarwaaqo, Elasha, Jazeera, Wadajiir, Helane) and 4 mobile clinics (Hobyo, Beletweyne, Elasha and Jazeera) delivering both lifesaving curative and preventive nutrition services. Both static health facilities and mobile clinics will provide screening and treatment of children aged between 6-59 months with SAM condition without medical complications. Children with SAM condition with medical complications will be referred to the nearest SC run by different NGOs. Children aged between 6-59 months together with PLWs with MAM condition will be treated in the TSFP centers in both mobile and static Health centers. In order to provide quality services, this action will train Health workers and CHWs on revised IMAM guidelines and nutrition assessments. The trained staff will then conduct screening of children aged below 5 years using MUAC tapes. The trained staff will be also expected to undertake IYCF counselling for PLWs and caretakers. The Action will also train mothers on Mother MUAC Screening. There will also be provision of micronutrient supplements in both static and mobile health facilities. This includes, supplementary nutrition products for children aged 6-23 months, PLWs, Iron folate supplements for pregnant mothers attending ANC clinics, vitamin A supplements for children aged between 6-59 months. Inclusion of beneficiaries with disabilities will be taken into consideration during the design, implementation and reporting phases of the activities. Nutrition service is integrated with the health services implemented in the same target locations

project_name: Emergency Inclusive WASH Program in Galagaduud, Mudug and Hiraan regions, South Central Somalia
project_objective:
Mercy-USA for Aid and Development (Mercy-USA) aims to improve the quality of life and protect vulnerable communities from morbidity and mortality associated with water-related diseases through water, sanitation and hygiene activities. This 12 month WASH project will target vulnerable people affected by drought, floods and conflict in Hiiraan, Galgadud, and Mudug regions by improving access to safe water and sanitation facilities and facilitating the uptake of acceptable hygiene practices. The project activities are in line with relevant strategic plans, including the Somalia National Development Plan, UN Strategic Framework and WASH Cluster priorities and guidance. 
The target populations in Hiraan, Galgadud and Mudug regions have been facing simultaneously multiple barriers and inequalities in accessing WASH services. These barriers include, geographical barriers, where some of the target communities live in rural settings, physical barriers, where persons with disabilities, children, older persons, pregnant women and others vulnerable groups are unable to access WASH services due to inappropriate design, and economic barriers.
Lack of access to safe water and sanitation increases the prevalence of preventable, water-borne diseases such as diarrhoea and dysentery, caused mainly by ingesting unclean water and contaminated food due to poor hygiene and poor human waste disposal. 
Mercy-USA thus seeks to increase access to sustainable and inclusive WASH services for disadvantaged individuals and groups, including IDPs, people living in rural and remote areas, as well as people with disabilities and increase their resilience to emergencies, including current COVID-19 pandemic.
Mercy-USA's proposed inclusive WASH response is immediate and designed to control the spread of water-borne diseases and preserve the health of the target populations, focusing on the severely affected and hard-to-reach. Proposed interventions include the provision of free, safe and sustainable drinking water, routine chlorination of existing water sources, testing of communal water sources for chemical and microbiological hazards by use of a portable water testing kit, construction of gender-segregated VIP latrines for underserved public primary schools and public health facilities and hygiene promotion. Mercy-USA will directly implement project activities. 
Mercy-USA will ensure stakeholder involvement in the implementation of project activities by first carrying out a stakeholder analysis to identify who has an interest or influence over WASH outcomes, at regional level, district level, institutional levels, community level, and private sector level. Mercy-USA will seek to incorporate their needs and ideas to implement inclusive, sustainable and climate-resilient WASH activities. Mercy-USA will ensure synergy with other Clusters to ensure adequate coordination of the activities through regular coordination with Health, Education, Shelter/NFIs, Protection, Nutrition, CWG and FSL Clusters to add value to the overall response through integrated response.

project_name: Increased access to community- and facility-based health services in Banadir, Galgadud, Mudug, Hiran, and Sool regions in Somalia.
project_objective:
Mercy-USA for Aid and Development intends to implement a project to address the urgent health needs in Banadir, Galgadud, Hiran, Mudug and Sool regions of Somalia.  Since the collapse of Somalia's central government in 1991, repeated conflict in conjunction with poor food security, limited healthcare and nutrition service availability and has resulted in Somalia having among the worst health-related indicators in the world.
According to the FSNAU-FEWS NET 2021 Post Gu Technical Release - September 9, 2021, from October to December 2021, food insecurity is expected to further deteriorate among poor rural, urban, and displaced populations due to the impacts of anticipated, below-average 2021 Deyr (October-December) season rainfall, continued insecurity and other food security related risk factors, including rising food prices and cost of living, declining availability of milk for both consumption and sale, and a likely reduction in agricultural employment opportunities during the forthcoming Deyr season. Without sustained humanitarian food assistance, 3.5 million people across Somalia are expected to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse outcomes between October and December 2021. Rural populations are experiencing multiple declines in food and income sources. In pastoral areas, large-scale livestock migration was reported from rain-deficit areas to areas that received relatively better rainfall. 
Mercy-USA will deliver primary health care services through 32 Maternal and Child Health Centers (MCHs). Mercy-USA will be facilitating the provision of medicines, supplies and equipment to the health facilities through UNICEF, while working together with the Ministry of Health (MOH) in each respective region to ensure standard provision of care and to build local capacity. Mercy-USA will train and support healthcare staff and Community Health Workers (CHWs) at each MCH facility to diagnose and treat common illnesses, provide safe pre-natal and post-natal care, and support vaccination and other health services. Mercy-USA will also promote local health, family planning counseling, safe-motherhood and safe-childhood initiatives through community sensitization. 
Mercy-USA will ensure that people with disabilities participate in the implementation of project activities by ensuring that they are represented in all community meetings. During project implementation, segregated focus group discussions will be held with the community to identify gender inequalities, discuss all the genders' needs, and understand the risks faced by people with disabilities in accessing health services. Activities will target to address these needs during program implementation. Access to children with disabilities and their caretakers and/or disabled pregnant and lactating women will be ensured and increased through outreach activities and behavioral change communication campaigns.
During routine and regular program monitoring and evaluation, Mercy-USA staff will collect disaggregated data by disability, age and gender to monitor the impact of programs on vulnerable groups. Mercy-USA, during both monthly and quarterly reviews and analysis of data, will seek to monitor the inclusiveness of programming by comparing achievements versus available population data.

project_name: Provision of lifesaving, sustainable, WASH services to the populations in crisis in; Lower Shebelle, M/Shabelle, Hiraan and Galgadud Regions.
project_objective:
Conflict and insecurity have forced hundreds of thousands of people to flee their homes in 2021 and are expected to remain key drivers of displacement in 2022. Conflict-induced shocks exacerbate the humanitarian situation of both IDP and host communities, with increased numbers of children married earlier as a coping strategy. Children in Somalia continue to face acute humanitarian needs due to conflict and environmental hazards such as drought, conflict and flooding. COVID-19 pandemic has compounded the challenges exacerbating vulnerability of the crisis-affected populations across the country. The crisis in Somalia has negatively impacted the health system and most affected are the vulnerable pregnant and lactating women, girls and boys, including children with disabilities with no access to health and nutrition services. Fear of conflict, insecurity and heightened tensions have triggered massive displacement in Guri Ceel, Galgaduud region over the last few days. Decades of conflict, recurrent climate shocks, disease outbreaks and increasing poverty are devastating the people of Somalia. The country is forecast to experience its third consecutive season of below-average rainfall, which has already resulted in a sharp increase in food insecurity, especially in rural areas. Without humanitarian assistance, nearly 3.5 million are expected to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse outcomes through the end of 2021.

WATER: Provision of emergency safe water to 15600 IDPs through voucher; access of lifesaving water through rehabilitation of 4 shallow wells equipped with solar power complete with water tanks and water kiosks, upgrading 2 boreholes through hybrid system complete, 2 generator and storerooms with construction of 4 elevated water tanks, 4 water kiosks supplied water through piping system;  Construct 2 flood proof shallow wells equipped with solar power pumps complete with 2 elevated water tanks and 2 water kiosks. Chlorinate the rehabilitated water sources on daily basis.
capacity building training to 4 WASH committees and 6 well operators on operation and maintenance an d 100 community members.
SANITATION: To improve the sanitation of the IDP camps and institutions, NWO will construct 4 twin block institutional latrines in 2 school and 100 in the IDP camps. Construct 200 flood proof and gender sensitive latrines with lockable doors and hand washing facilities to IDPs and low income Hhs.
HYGIENE: NWO will train 120 CHWs to carry out comprehensive hygiene promotion campaigns to educate the community on better hygiene promotion practices including hand washing with soap practices through visiting house-to-house, schools, feeding/nutrition centers and health centers; in this project, NWO will provide 1200 HP kits to 1200 households and IDPs who are at risk of AWD/cholera and malnutrition
.
The proposed response took into consideration the impact of the disaster on women, children and people with disabilities in terms of access to WASH services; it proposed specific actions to prevent risk of gender-based violence and hence will contribute to greater gender equality. NWO top management will monitor the quality and quantity of the WASH intervention during the project implementation and its completion.
NWO will conduct DRR and conflict resolution mechanisms workshop to provide valuable insights into the underlying factors of vulnerability to hazards and the features of those hazards to 160 community by:
1.Cultivating a disaster mitigation mindset.
2. Engaging the community in emergency preparedness.
3. Developing mutual aid and assistance agreements.
4. Facilitating rapid response and recovery.

project_name: Vulnerable IDP and Host Communities in Jubaland, Banadir and Galgadud have  Increased Access to WASH Services
project_objective: The project aims to increase WASH services to the over 6.4 M people in need in Somalia targeting districts that are categorized as stressed or severe in the severity scale, those that are hard to reach and those that have reported AWD/cholera cases. The project targets approximately  6,552 vulnerable IDPs  11,448 host communities with a special focus on vulnerable segments of the community including  7 803 women  9,900 children 1,800 PLWD and 875 elderly people. In line with HRP strategic objective 1, specific objective 1.2, this project will contribute to the WASH cluster objective of delivering life-saving WASH assistance to reduce acute needs among most vulnerable settlements and communities through emergency water tracking, water vouchers, provision of hygiene kits and hygiene promotion activities. Lifesaving Wash assistance will target hard to reach communities in Garbaharey and Dolow districts and IDPs households in Banadir and Dolow. This project is also aligned to HRP strategic objective 2, specific objective 2.1, contributing to WASH cluster objective of restoring access to safe and equitable basic WASH services to vulnerable communities and in schools. This will be achieved through rehabilitation of water infrastructures including shallow wells, water pipe network, elevated tanks and water kiosks. Solar pumping systems will be installed in boreholes and shallow wells to reduce the O&M of community water systems. Community mobilizations and capacity building in management of water projects and O&M of solar system will be done to ensure active community participation in the implementation and management of the water facilities. This project will also contribute to the WASH cluster objective of restoring access to basic sanitation and hygiene in schools in Abudwak and Dollow, through rehabilitation of gender segregated latrines with lockable doors from inside with hand washing facilities. All the WASH infrastructures proposed in this project are designed with consideration of the safety, equity and easy accessibility by vulnerable groups such as women, girls, PLWD and the elderly. The target beneficiaries will actively participate in the selection of the sites for water facilities in their locations that will be strategic to serve households within approximately 500m distance that will be in open and clear places to ensure safety of users. Additionally water kiosks will be designed to ensure easy water collection by girls, women, elderly and those with disabilities. For water trucking water collection points will be selected by the beneficiaries and will be at about 500m from the households and in open places for safety purposes. The water collection will be planned such that the elderly and PLWD will have separate times to collect their water. The latrines constructed in schools will be strategically located to ensure safety of users and dignity of users. Hygiene kits will be collected from reasonable distances from the beneficiary households for safety of the beneficiaries as they carry them home. Use of water and hygiene kits vouchers will further enhance safety and equity of vulnerable groups targeted in this project. Mainstreaming of protection and gender in this project will contribute to HRP strategic objective 3, specific objective 3.1 as well as the WASH cluster objective of maintaining safety, equity and accessibility of the vulnerable groups (including women, boys, girls, elderly and people with disabilities) when accessing WASH services. This project will build on WASH and COVID 19 interventions implemented by NAPAD (2019, 2020 and 2021) in Galgadud, Jubaland and Banadir regions that includes rehabilitation of water infrastructures such as water tanks, water pipe networks, installation of solar water pumping systems, installation of handwashing facilities, provision of hygiene kits and mass hygiene promotion using the mass media and door to door promotion by community hygiene

project_name: Reduction of morbidity and mortality related to Acute Malnutrition among PLW and the under five children in Buuhoodle district of Togdheer region
project_objective:
Somalia remains on the frontline of climate change, which continues to induce crises resulting in widespread displacement, rapid urbanization, food insecurity, and increased poverty. Critically, climate change is also increasingly understood as a major driver of conflict in Somalia as the struggle for dwindling resources intensifies clan divisions and inter-clan conflict. The humanitarian situation is deteriorating due to the devastating impact of flooding, desert locust infestation, the COVID-19 pandemic and ongoing conflict A total of 7.7 million Somali women, men and children are estimated to require humanitarian assistance in 2022. nearly 3.5 million are expected to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse outcomes through the end of 2021. With 2.9 million people estimated to be internally displaced throughout the country, Somalia has one of the highest numbers of IDPs in the world. Of these, 2.2 million require urgent humanitarian assistance. IDPs are chronically more food insecure and vulnerable than host communities. Displacements are typically rural-urban in nature, where displaced people moving into urban centres often lack the skills required for urban livelihoods, and IDPs and rural migrants are frequently confined to poor-paying unskilled jobs, if any at all.  NODO is proposing 12-month integrated Health project targeting the most affected populations in Buuhoodle district reaching a total of 15,250 persons including 11,200 women, 1,500 Men, 1,350 girls and 1200 boys)

The proposed nutrition activities will be integrated with the health interventions with the aim of addressing underlying causes of high levels malnutrition as well as to enable early identification of SAM cases for treatment through mobile and fixed in targeted IDPs and host community in the most affected areas in Buuhoodle district. This program will establish a strong community network through competent community nutrition volunteers for early detection/case finding and referral of children and pregnant and lactating mothers with acute malnutrition. In addition to the treatment of acute malnutrition, the project will be promoting positive infant and young child feeding (IYCF) practice by providing IYCF promotion and counselling. NODO is strong partner for the nutrition cluster and therefore, will have close coordination with other partners in the district for identification of vulnerable communities and avoiding overlapping of responses. Through this project, a total 15,250 most affected individuals in Buuhoodle will have access to a package of Emergency lifesaving integrated health and nutrition services for twelve months’ period. The mobile team will provide comprehensive community screening, identification, treatment and referral services from community, IDP areas to the fixed OTP and SC to improve access to the integrated package for the vulnerable community prioritizing rapid referral of the most critical cases (priority will be given to under 5 children and pregnant and lactating women), it shall also capacity building of nutrition staff on IMAM, infant young child feeding best practices, IYCF. Referral of malnourished children with complicated cases will be done to the OTP integrated with PHC services managed by NODO and other actors in the program areas thus providing more holistic opportunity to the target beneficiaries.

project_name: Strengthening protective environment for displacement affected populations In Banadir, Galmudug, Lower Jubba and Gedo Regions through HLP interventions to improve tenure security situation and address post-eviction complications.
project_objective:
The intervention is geared toward preventing and responding to eviction, monitoring of threats to evictions by assessing potential eviction sites, monitoring, documentation and reporting to relevant authorities and relevant clusters to mobilize support for advocacy. The advocacy and campaigns will aim to ensure actors facilitate lawful eviction processes. Capacity development targeting settlement managers, local authorities on Housing, Land and proper protection monitoring through ensuring collection of information based on the methodology of the Somalia Protection Monitoring System (SPMS).
Protection, monitoring and response mechanisms with regards to land, housing and property is lacking in most of protection programming. Most often legal Aid services, land, houses and property rights are not prioritized hence leaving big gaps in the protection response mechanism. There is poor coordination among protection and response service providers especially on land, housing and property rights. Furthermore, the protection response mechanisms have limited or no provision of free legal aid services to IDPs, survivors of GBV and HLP.
Therefore, this project seeks to improve and strengthen coordination among service providers and to enhance legal protection and response mechanism for IDPs on land, housing and property rights. These will be achieved through, improved referral pathways, on spot monitoring and response to assist IDPs reclaim housing, land and properties, awareness raising, free legal aid and innovative and sustainable alternative dispute resolution mechanisms.
NoFYL has presence in Banadir, Galmudug, Lower Jubba and Gedo Regions and has built strong linkages with communities and other actors which will facilitate the access and smooth implementation of project activities. NoFYL has an excellent record in linking with beneficiary communities (returnee, IDPs and host) affected by disasters and conflict, enabling them to cope with life threatening situations and recovery, and have good working relations with the local authorities and camp leaders. The progress of project activities will be monitored by NoFYL field offices in Kismayo and Mogadishu office. NoFYL has developed monitoring tools to monitor the progress. According to the agreed work plan, each activity will be monitored using participatory, results-based feedback mechanisms.

project_name: Life-saving WASH assistance to the most vulnerable displaced and non-displaced disaster affected populations in Somalia.
project_objective:
Project aims to provide live-saving and sustainable WASH assistance to disaster affected displaced (25%) and non- displaced populations(75%). The response targets 109,900 people in severe and extreme WASH needs in order to reduce malnutrition especially among children as result of acute water diarrhea. About 68% of AWD/cholera cases reported between June/May 2021 were <5 children from flood-prone districts whose population depends on unprotected water sources, these districts have also high GAM prevalence rates of >15 per cent. The project will continue to restore access to safe and equitable basic WASH services in targeted locations in a dignified manner. Lack of adequate WASH services to the population is a main cause of spread of Acute Diarrheal Diseases (ADD)/ cholera as well as conflict over water sources and related displaced in distress. 

Access to safe water will be increased through rehabilitation of water sources including 8 boreholes, 10 shallow wells and 15 pipeline extension to reduce distance to water point hence increase protection of women and girls. All water systems will be equipped with distribution infrastructure and hybrid energization systems. Taps stand will be located within a radius of at least 500m to reduce distance and enhance security of women and girls. Project will construct 2 major improved water dams in locations that lack other options. Well heads will be raised at a minimum 0.5m to reduce risk flooding and contamination. Water committees comprising men and women from all community groups including the minority and the marginalized will be trained on management, O&M. Local technicians will be trained and provided with O&M tools to undertake repairs whereas consumers will pay for the technician’s services. For major water supply in urban areas, Private Public Parternship (PPP) management system will be adopted. Where possible NRC will partner with local private investors to establish and manage major water supply systems in a sustainable manner. Project will construct 400 latrines for families reintegrated through the durable solutions. NRC undertakes sanitary surveys periodically to identify contamination risks for timely mitigation. All beneficiaries of latrines will be provided with kettle to promote handwashing and sensitized to use soap for handwashing. Design of infrastructure will take into consideration the needs of special groups in the community including the disabled, old, children to ensure they have equitable access to the services. Life-saving WASH interventions will be implemented in case of sudden disaster to reduce the related mortality and morbidity especially among children. This will be through temporary provision of safe water to 6000 HHs through direct delivery or restricted cash depending on context and market functionality, provision of hygiene kits through voucher (3000 HH), construction of 550 simple design emergency latrines, latrine emptying (450 latrines) and safe fecal sludge disposal and hygiene promotion. Schools and health facilities will be provided with latrines (200 institutional latrines). Latrines will be raised above ground level to reduce the risk of flooding during rains. Women and girls will be involved in identification of sites for facilities to ensure their safety and security is taken into account. Latrines will be gender separated, provided with lockable doors and handwashing equipment. Solar street lights (35 posts) will be provided near water points and latrines to improve the security and safety of women and girls especially in crowded IDP settlements.  The beneficiaries will be provided with adequate information on NRC’s complaints, response and feedback mechanisms.

project_name: Emergency WASH Response for people affected by emergency in Somaliland/Somalia
project_objective:
The humanitarian situation in Somalia remains critical due to the ongoing impacts of drought, conflict, locust infestation, and the COVID 19 pandemic. An estimated 6.61 million people, about 42 per cent of the Somali population are in need of emergency life-saving WASH assistance of which 4.2 million will need safe drinking water, 3.2 million sanitation services, and 5.2 million hygiene supplies. According to FAO/SWALIM draught analysis from 2000 to July 2021, the trend shows that Somalia has been experiencing cyclic drought every five to six years: 2000/2001, 2004/2005, 2010/2011, 2016/2017, and currently in 2020/2021. These drought conditions were triggered by consecutive seasons of below-average rainfall including the below-average Gu rains (April to July 2021) and delay of short Dayr rains (October to December 2021). The Somalia Food Security Cluster as of 18th October 2021 confirms that half of Somalia is still experiencing serious drought conditions (moderate to severe drought with water shortages and livestock losses), with the worst impacts being felt in Jubaland, South West State, Galmudug, and areas of Puntland. The Deyr seasonal rainfall is expected to be below average, with depressed rains not going to be effective in mitigating drought conditions. A devastating drought is likely to continue into 2022 given the 1) La Nina conditions, 2) poor rainfall forecast for October and November and 3) existing drought conditions.
Access to water is mainly dependent on rainfall in the majority of the country. Barkads in nonriverine areas are the major water sources while others depend on shallow/deep groundwater sources. Thus, failure in rains triggers massive shortages as currently being reported from Jubaland, Part of Somaliland, Galmudug, and many other areas. 50 of the 74 districts in Somalia faced severe water shortages and water prices increased by 66 per cent7 in Gedo, Galgadud, Mudug, Sool, and Sanaag regions (JMCNA 2021). The Non-functionality of few strategic boreholes also increases as the operation hours increase. Many shallow-water sources are drying while others are having increased brackish water intrusions. Over 39% of Somalis don’t have access to sustained, improved and safe water. As result, over 84% are walking more than 15minuts to access water while over 92% don’t have water collection and storage facilities. Due to limited access and poor quality of existing water sources, over 1.3 million people in 24 drought-affected locations are dependent on water trucking – the majority of them are private water trucking. Oxfam PDMs and HNO results confirm the majority of Somalis use two jerry cans per day during drought conditions. 39% of people assessed confirm they wash their hands but have reported having no access to soap. 45% of girls assessed have reported having access to Menstruation hygiene management (MHM) materials at or can access from local markets.
Oxfam has been working in Somalia for over 40 years and will continue to provide life-saving humanitarian support and build the capacity of both private and public institutions. Oxfam is working with over 10 national NGOs in a different part of Somalia. In response to the continued emergency, Oxfam will continue supporting efforts to nation/local government in containment and prevention of COVID-19, will monitor and rehabilitate non-function strategic boreholes, will conduct expansion of existing water sources in order to reduce the walking time, will drill boreholes in chronically water insecure areas, will provide cash and voucher assistant for people to access live-saving water, hygiene and MHM kits from local markets or access point established by Oxfam, will work with community health volunteers to increase awareness and handwashing practice during critical times and will construct shared household latrines for communities practicing open defecations.

project_name: Emergency response for nutrition of the crisis affected population in Banadir Region
project_objective:
The report of FSNAU 2021 approximate that 1.2 million children will experience malnutrition and another 3.5 million people will face acute shortage of food.This has been attributed acute food insecurity in Somalia include the combined effects of poor and erratic rainfall distribution, flooding and conflict. 
 A delayed start, early end, and erratic rainfall distribution characterized the April to June 2021 Gu rainfall season. As a result, cumulative rainfall was below the 40-year average across much of the country. However these resources are inadequate to support normal livestock production until the start of Deyr season rainfall in October. Furthermore, floods caused further population displacement and damaged crops and farmland in riverine areas of Hiiraan, Shabelle, and Juba regions. Based on the results of household surveys and field assessments conducted in June and July 2021, more than 2.2 million people face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse outcomes in the presence of planned and likely humanitarian assistance during the July to September 2021 period. An additional 3.4 million people are Stressed (IPC Phase 2), bringing the total number of people experiencing acute food insecurity to 5.6 million.  A majority of the estimated 2.9 million Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) across Somalia are poor with limited livelihood assets, few income-earning opportunities, low communal support and high reliance on external humanitarian assistance. As a result, a significant proportion of IDPs (in both rural and urban settlements) face moderate to large food consumption gaps through late 2021. Some of the urban poor across Somalia also continue to face moderate to large food consumption gaps over the same period, partly due to a slowdown in economic activities in urban areas and the rising costs of food and other essential non-food items.

Physicians Across Continents (PAC) proposes to have interventions on reduction of severe malnutrition in children (under 5yrs) the crisis affected and returnees, vulnerable population of women of reproductive age who face also nutrition deficiencies as a result of food scarcity and other cultural perspectives The project will focus on provision of curative, preventive and promotive approaches in an effort to ensure children and Pregnant and lactating women are provided with nutritious food to thrive.
The interventions for curative will be in case finding, screening, nutrition assessment and provision of treatment for complication and therapeutic feeding. PAC will deploy trained Service providers in a fixed center to receive and care until stable for discharge home. In this intervention also there will be 1 fixed center to accommodate all the sick and malnourished, that will be supported by the 2 mobile teams and 2 outreach services.
The interventions for preventive will be in deploying 20 community health workers after training Infection Control, Focused Antenatal Care,BEMONC, Screening in Malnutrition and referral pathways. On key messaging in the prevention of covid-19 at village level. Of this 20 –two third will be female health promoters, for gender empowerment and increasing facility utilization in skilled birth deliveries. During the training the community health workers will be utilized. PAC will monitor and work closely with local authority to ensure that CHWs have access smoothly to surrounding villages and referral community smoothly to fixed centre.
The interventions for promotive will focus on community engagement and dialogue in promotion of positive culture to enhance that children and PLW are provided with opportunity to seek for healthcare. PAC shall engage the local community regularly for decision making on contact tracing, supporting young girls delay in marriage to enhance future positive maternal health outcomes. PAC will also work closely with partners in protection and WASH as holistic.There will be  2 surveys conducted to inform the trends of nutrition in the community.

project_name: Child Protection response project for drought and conflict affected children living in crisis setiings in Bay and Bakol, Somalia.
project_objective:
The Project proposes protection services that comprises of Child protection case management services through reporting of violations affecting the newly displaced people affected by the ongoing military operations, airstrikes and floods in SWS, and supporting these IDPs with Child friendly spaces, psychosocial support (CP), referral responses for GBV cases affecting individuals to the services and facilities in the areas.
The project will also enhance the activities with community mobilization targeting the various community members, respecting gender equality inclusion, disabled children, adolescent children and other special needs as orphans. READO will provide Family tracing & reunification (CP) to the separated children during the displacement and providing Child friendly spaces service awaiting to reunify with the caregivers and parents. 
The Project targets 2333HHs or 14000 individuals (4200 girls, 2940 boys, 4480 women and 2380 men in Bay- (Baidoa, Bardaale, Dinsoor) and Bakool-(Waajid, Xudur). The project in collaboration with Child Protection sub-cluster will be delivering CP Referral and Response services, Community based CP Awareness activities in the IDP camps and furthering child safeguarding activities by other programs and agencies in the locations targeted.

project_name: Enhancing the resilience and recovery of crises affected persons through the provision of shelter and NFIs in Banadir and Afgooye.
project_objective:
The project is aimed at supporting the most vulnerable IDP families in Afgooye and Banadir to mitigate risks faced through Shelter/NFI interventions. It is expected that a total of 12,000 IDP(Elderly 600 men,1000 women, 4000 boys 1000 girls 3000, disabled 2,200 and non disabled 200) in Afgooye and Banadir will benefit from the distribution of emergency shelter kits and non-food items. Provision of NFI kits and ESKs will target the newly displaced persons and protracted IDPs with shelter structures that barely protect their dignity and privacy. The intervention is aimed at improving the living conditions of the IDPs by speeding up their recovery from damages caused by displacements.
2000 NFI kits and 2000 ESKs will be distributed through voucher and in kind respectively to 2000 IDP households. The ""in kind"" modality is influenced by SSWC's past experience with CBI where beneficiaries did not construct ESKs and channeled the money to other purposes. A market assessment will be conducted prior to the purchase of the items to ascertain their market prices. The beneficiary selection criteria will consider newly displaced persons, female headed households, child-headed households, the elderly in the community and persons with disabilities to ensure the most vulnerable groups are targeted.
To ensure sustainability, the ESKs will be established on lands with relatively long land agreements (three years and above). This will be ascertained through solicitation of written agreements from IDP site leaders and the subsequent confirmation of their validity from respective local authorities. ESK construction will be keen on COVID-19 and basic site planning aspects such as distance between ESKs, roads, fire breaks, drainage and distance from toilets.
Due to COVD-19, SSWC will use hotline numbers for CFRM. The anticipated data to be collected include among others both compliments and complaints: the quality of the ESKs and NFIs, fairness of beneficiary selection processes, shortness of items distributed, delays and other feedback. This will ensure that community participation and AAP is at the center of the project.
Post Distribution Monitoring (PDM) and Post construction monitoring (PCM) will be conducted after every distribution and construction respectively. The monitoring exercises will provide beneficiary feedback on the effectiveness of the distribution. 70% of the beneficiaries will take part of the exercise to ensure proper representation and that exact feelings are recorded about the processes and quality of distribution. The PDM/PCMs will also help to know the beneficiary satisfaction of the items distributed, identify the needs and feelings of the community better and inform on the effectiveness of the activities and achievements of targets while providing guidance towards success.
The activities are geared towards improving the living conditions of the newly displaced IDPs and protracted IDPs living in deplorable conditions hence contributing to the achievement of the shelter cluster’s objectives.

project_name: Essential and Life-saving integrated Health assistance for Vulnerable Populations in Somalia
project_objective:
The proposed project will provide essential and life-saving integrated health assistance to vulnerable communities in Awdal, Bay, Lower Shabelle, Banadir, Bari, Galgaduud, Hiraan, Lower Juba, Mudug, Nugaal, Sanaag, Sool, Toghdeer, and Woqooyi Galbeed. The project aims to reach 928,490IDPs and host communities contributing to 20% of the cluster target of the population affected by conflict and displacement in the targeted geographies using fixed and mobile health facilities. 

The project will seek to contribute to a 5% reduction in excess morbidity and mortality rates from crisis-driven diseases and outbreaks among target vulnerable communities by end of 2022 while scaling up provision of regular health services and providing safe, dignified and meaningful access life-saving assistance (provided directly or through referral) with sensitivity to age, gender and disability status. This will be achieved by supporting the Somalia governments and communities to be able
to delivery free essential package of health services to communities with acute humanitarian needs using development programs as a platform for immediate responses. The proposed project has also been designed with full awareness of the prevailing gender norms and deeply rooted gender inequalities in Somalia that limit women and girls from accessing basic services such as health and nutrition, and expose them to a higher risk of Sexual and Gender Based Violence (SGBV). In order to address
these challenges, Save the Children (SC) will identify and work to remove the physical, cognitive and social barriers by collaborating closely with communities and particularly influencers (community and religious leaders) and gatekeepers. SC will also address the intersectionality of vulnerability factors, such as people with disabilities, minority clans who are likely to face multiple levels of discrimination. SC will also include appropriate child safeguarding measures at every phase and within every programming activity.

Female: 473,529
Male: 454,961
Children (under 18): 129,989
Adult (18-59): 779,932
Elderly (above 59): 18,569
IDPs: 629,859
