project_name: Enhancing the humanitarian health preparedness and response capacity for the most vulnerable populations (IDPs, returnees and other affected migrants) and host communities in rural areas.
project_objective:
The aim of the project is to enhance the capacity of health facilities and health screening at points of entries (PoEs) to  enhance emergency preparedness and response and address the protracted essential health needs for the most vulnerable displaced people and local communities affected by inter-communal conflicts, disease outbreak and natural emergencies. The response plans under the project are in line with Health Cluster Objective 2022: Objective 1- Support essential public health functions with focus strong primary health care, Objective 2- Strengthen emergency preparedness, response, and all hazards emergency risk management. IOM will focus on 17 localities and this includes: Wad Al Mahi (Blue Nile), Yassin (East Darfur), Al Fao, Galabat Ash-Shargiah, Basundah (Gedaref), Reifi Khashm Elgirba (Kassala), Al Fasher, Tawilla (North Darfur), Buram, Gereida, Rehaid Albirdi, Tulus, Um Dafoug (South Darfur), Delami (South Kordofan), Ag Geneina, Jebel Moon, Sirba (West Darfur).  High rates of internal displacement or return have been reported in these localities. The vulnerable people, such as women of reproductive age, pregnant and lactating women (PLW) and children under-five (U5) living inside or outside of IDPs camps as well as their host communities are at high risk of morbidity and mortality due to unavailability and inaccessibility of sustained health services in these localities. IOM will support the health facilities in rural areas to strengthen emergency preparedness and response and address the protracted health needs of the most vulnerable groups of IDPs, returnees and other affected migrants and host communities through enhanced a basic package of primary health services (BPPHS). The BPPHS will include: 1) outpatient consultation and treatment for communicable diseases and non-communicable diseases including support for a prevailing disease surveillance, early warning and response system; 2) supporting reproductive health services; 3) child health services with a focus on immunizations; 4) supporting mental and psychological consultation; 5) environmental health, including waste management and vector control; 6) facilitated referrals and mobile services; 7) health and nutrition promotion services. 

IOM will promote the continuity of BPPHS ensuring a quality of essential and timely life-saving health services on prevention, enhancing risk mitigation means and close monitoring of outbreak disease trend and strengthen community health services. This will be achieved through strengthening capacity of health-care service providers including community health-care workers (CHWs) and Community Midwives (CMs). The COVID-19 mitigation measures will be integrated within the planned capacity building activities with emphasis on strengthening surveillance and reporting systems, infection prevention and control and risk communication and community engagement (RCCE). 

The planned capacity building activities will be extended to support the state Ministry of Health (MoH) and border authorities to enhance disease prevention and response measures at prioritized PoEs. Some of the targeted localities are subject to diverse human mobility patterns including, Sudanese returnees, refugees, and irregular migrants, due to its geographic location at cross-border movements across states and with neighboring countries. IOM will enhance health screening services to mitigate the risk of transmission of communicable diseases including COVID-19 at the prioritized PoEs and this will be made through  building capacity of key stakeholders such as the State MoH, border officials, front-line services workers including health service providers. The support will include IPC measures by installing and updating water and sanitation facilities and provision of other IPC supplies and equipment, and the delivery of hygiene and health promotion campaign enhancing community engagement in the response to disease outbreak including the COVID-19 pandemic.

project_name: Providing Comprehensive Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) Assistance to Crisis Affected Populations in Sudan
project_objective:
This project aims to provide humanitarian WASH assistance to 600,000 beneficiaries (122,400 women, 117,600 men, 183,600 girls, 176,400 boys - 12% of whom are estimated to be either elderly or disabled) to mitigate the suffering of populations affected by natural or man-made disasters and reflect all three Objectives of the 2021 Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene Response Plan. Objective I: 1.87 million crisis-affected population will access basic water services. Objective II: 1.79 million crisis-affected populations will access adequate, protected, and gender-sensitive sanitation services. Objective III: 4.71 million crisis-affected populations will have access to hygiene promotion and other environmental health interventions.  

IOM will aim to assist crisis affected populations (approximately 300,000 individuals) by ensuring dignified and equitable access to basic WASH services. Emergency assistance will be provided to people newly displaced by conflict or natural disasters through the implementation of early recovery approaches where possible, connecting the need for short-term emergency interventions with long-term solutions by working directly with local communities to facilitate ownership and accountability. The objective is to not only focus on WASH emergency interventions but gradually contribute to socio-economic inclusion of forcibly displaced populations and returnees by directly increasing access to basic services for the displaced and host communities and indirectly increasing employment opportunities. 
IOM also seeks to improve and sustain access to safe water in target communities (approximately 250,000 individuals), including returnees, especially in Blue Nile, east Sudan, Abyei, North Darfur and South Darfur as these communities primarily rely on agriculture and livestock, therefore water is critical to their livelihoods. 
As well as improving and sustaining access to safe water and sanitation facilities and services, while hygiene messages will address malnutrition and disease outbreak related risks and increase community resilience to disease outbreaks for approximately 50,000 individuals. IOM will provide emergency water assistance through the establishment and rehabilitation of water points, access to proper sanitation facilities, and hygiene campaigns. This will include environmental impact mitigation such as the provision of solar technology to power water points and monitoring ground water to moderate depletion levels. Exit strategies will be developed to alleviate aid dependency in protracted emergencies by strengthening self-reliance and facilitating community solutions in a more holistic approach.

project_name: Linea de Contacto Inter-Agencial
project_objective:
La Línea de Contacto Interagencial (LdCI) de las Naciones Unidas en Venezuela es un importante mecanismo de comunicación con las comunidades y seguimiento de las retroalimentaciones que funciona de lunes a sábado desde las 8:00 a.m. hasta las 5:45 p.m. a través de un correo institucional, un formulario para aplicación cara a cara y un número telefónico habilitado para recibir llamadas, mensajes de texto y WhatsApp, mediante los cuales las personas pueden:
- Solicitar información sobre las actividades humanitarias de cada una de las organizaciones que participan en la Línea de Contacto.
- Presentar quejas sobre la asistencia humanitaria recibida.
- Dejarnos sugerencias sobre las actividades realizadas por las agencias y/o sus socios implementadores.
- Reportar posibles casos de explotación y abuso sexual, maltrato o uso indebido de servicios y/o actividades humanitarias por parte de personal humanitario.

Después de una fase piloto en los municipios Mara y Maracaibo en el estado Zulia de julio a diciembre de 2021, el Comité Ejecutivo de la LdCI decidió su ampliación a los 4 estados del CCT Maracaibo (Zulia, Lara, Falcón y Trujillo) a partir de enero de 2022, con una ampliación a nivel nacional para recibir posibles casos de explotación y abuso sexual. A partir de julio de 2022, se prevé la expansión a nivel nacional de la LdCI. 

La implementación de la LdCI forma parte de los compromisos incluidos en el Marco Colectivo de AAP en Venezuela, aprobado por el Equipo Humanitario de País en septiembre de 2020. El cuarto compromiso se enfoca en ´crear un mecanismo interagencial de retroalimentación comunitaria seguro y accesible, en complementariedad a los mecanismos establecidos por las agencias y organizaciones socias´.

project_name: Atención básica de salud y nutrición para niños/as y mujeres embarazadas/lactantes en Maracaibo - continuación del proyecto de 2021
project_objective:
Este es un proyecto plurianual ejecutado desde el 01.05.2020 con financiación confirmada hasta el 30.04.2022 y posibilidad de extenderlo hasta mayo del 2024. Todas las cifras presupuestarias, los objetivos y los datos de población meta indicados aquí se aplican únicamente al período de 12 meses del PRH 2022.
Objetivo: Mejorar las capacidades de 3 hospitales y proporcionar atención básica de salud y nutrición a niños/as y mujeres embarazadas/lactantes en Maracaibo.
Contexto y necesidades:
La situación actual de Venezuela es el resultado de una prolongada crisis socioeconómica y política, agravada con la pandemia de COVID-19. Esto ha provocado un colapso de los servicios, el deterioro de las condiciones de vida y desplazamientos masivos. La población es cada vez más pobre y al mismo tiempo la hiperinflación ha provocado un acceso limitado a los alimentos, las medicinas y otros bienes básicos. El resultado es la generalización de las enfermedades, la vulnerabilidad a los brotes epidémicos, la malnutrición y altas tasas de mortalidad.
En Maracaibo, las instituciones sanitarias sufren la falta de personal médico para proporcionar servicios. La infraestructura de salud se está deteriorando; la electricidad y el agua se cortan a menudo durante días. Y conseguir combustible, se vuelve cada vez más difícil y costoso, limitando aún más el acceso de la población a los centros de salud.
Las necesidades de salud y nutrición siguen siendo altas en todo el municipio de Maracaibo y sus alrededores. En segundo lugar, la seguridad alimentaria se está convirtiendo en un problema acuciante para las familias afectadas por un largo período de recesión.  A esto se une la necesidad de proporcionar una ayuda complementaria para la alimentación a la que, sin un ingreso o ayuda de terceros, algunas familias tendrían dificultades para acceder.  Por eso se amplía el programa para intervenir también en las actividades de recuperación de alimentos y en pequeñas iniciativas de producir sus propias verduras, que de otro modo no podrían obtener por falta de ingresos.
Grupo objetivo:
Se ha considerado el marcador de género/edad así como los criterios de vulnerabilidad que están alineados con los datos compartidos por OCHA sobre grupos vulnerables y PIN (personas en necesidad).
- Niños/as hasta 14 años con enfoque en niños/as <5. Sobre todo en asistencia de salud y nutrición.
- A menudo son los niños/as mayores o adolescentes los que cuidan de sus hermanos/as mientras los padres trabajan en el extranjero. Por eso la ampliación del proyecto contempla también a este grupo de edad (adolescentes y jóvenes) que además han quedado sin acceso a oportunidades de vida (estudiar, trabajar). Se les apoya con salud mental y apoyo psicosocial.
- Las mujeres lactantes/embarazadas de la zona de captación de ingresos bajos y medios de los
hospitales, entre ellas un alto porcentaje de madres adolescentes que dependen de los servicios médicos que están cerca y son fácilmente accesibles. Apoyo sobre todo en salud.
- Adultos mayores en las comunidades, a menudo a cargo del cuidado de los niños/as. Apoyo mediante distribución de alimentos y asistencia de salud (asistencia básica y salud mental) a través de visitas del equipo médico que se desplaza a las comunidades.
- Entre estos grupos destinatarios se encuentran aproximadamente el 6% de las personas con discapacidad y el 12,7% de las personas que se reconocen como pertenecientes a la población indígena.
- Teniendo en cuenta la actual pandemia de COVID-19, este proyecto también se dirige al personal sanitario que no tiene acceso a los equipos de protección personal ante contagios, siendo el proyecto la única fuente de provisión de estos elementos.
- Este proyecto también se dirige específicamente a las mujeres como responsables de la toma de decisiones, desarrollando la capacidad de la sociedad civil encabezada por mujeres, incluyendo tres hospitales con una fuerte representación femenina en los puestos de dirección.

project_name: Emergency Water Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) support to population affected by conflict and climate induced crises in Ethiopia
project_objective:
IOM is leading WASH activities in many IDP sites and host communities across Ethiopia, including distribution of hygiene kits, water trucking, construction and rehabilitation of water points, emergency latrines, and handwashing stations, establishment of community-based water or sanitation management committees, and hygiene promotion activities through contextualized campaigns and mobilization of gender-balanced hygiene promoters. 

In Ethiopia currently the internal displacement and humanitarian needs are mainly derived by the ongoing conflicts and droughts in some parts of the country. The displacement level in Ethiopia doubled in 2021, with over 2 million additional people displaced during 2021. According to IOM’s latest Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) National Displacement Report released in December 2021, a total of 4.2 million people were internally displaced across Ethiopia. This includes around 2.11 million IDPs identified in Tigray and neighbouring zones in Afar and Amhara regions as a result of the Northern Ethiopia Crisis. The ongoing displacements continue to pose serious protection concerns for the affected population. The majority of the displaced population live-in collective sites or in spontaneous settlements where they have limited access to essential services, dignified and safe living conditions to sustain their families and communities. A large number of the displaced population are women and children under 18.
 
IOM works under the framework of the 2021 HRP and 2022 draft HRP to enhance understanding of the crisis and assist joint, strategic response planning. This is particularly relevant to address new shocks and the confluence of needs. All interventions occur based on assessed needs, inter-cluster Initial Rapid Needs Assessments (IRNA) and cluster-specific assessments. All assessments integrate specific gender analyses. IOM further considers key protection needs including the risk of exposure to harm, exploitation, harassment, deprivation and abuse, including forms of violence that are gender-based; the ability to meet basic needs; access to basic services; and coping mechanisms. IOM uses both qualitative and quantitative assessment methodologies, including IOM's DTM; questionnaires; household and key informant interviews (including with local authorities and key community leaders); focus group discussions with women and youth; direct observation and review of secondary information. 

IOM has existing WASH programming in Tigray, Amhara, Afar, Oromia (East Hararghe and Borena), Somali (Dawa and Fafan zone), and SNNP regions (Konso zone) covering IDPs, returnees and host communities. Limited access to WASH NFIs, inadequate sources of safe water, inadequate sanitation facilities and prevalence of poor hygiene practices can render the populations living in collective centers/sites at risk of preventable diseases and overcrowded and congested IDP sites also pose a high level of risk to waterborne diseases, such as cholera. Assessments indicated that integrated WASH services are critical to ensure that facilities are maintained at a good standard and can be scaled up in case of population influxes, both in terms of the provision of safe water and increased hygiene promotion to prevent disease outbreaks.

In 2022, IOM appeals for USD 23,5 million to reach 1,6 million individuals through its WASH activities in IDP sites and host communities across Ethiopia. Interventions will comprise water trucking, construction and rehabilitation of water points, emergency latrines including distribution of hygiene kits, and handwashing stations, establishment of community-based water or sanitation management committees, and hygiene promotion activities through contextualized campaigns and mobilization of gender-balanced hygiene promoters. IOM will also support implementing partners, particularly national NGOs to provide access to safe water, WASH NFIs and hygiene promotion.

project_name: Integrated Emergency, Recovery and Resilience Response for Crisis-affected Persons in MMC and Jere
project_objective: The aim of this intervention is: conflict-affected communities in MMC and Jere LGAs are sustainably protected from, and treated for, the main causes of morbidity and mortality; supported to meet immediate and long-term Shelter and Settlement, WASH and Protection needs, while being protected and provided with the legal assistance they need. To achieve this, the proposed project will be implemented by a consortium led by the International Rescue Committee (IRC), in partnership with the Danish Refugee Council (DRC) and Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC). The consortium will leverage the expertise of each partner to deliver a multi-sectoral, area-based response, providing integrated services across the following sectors: Health, WASH, Nutrition, Food Assistance, Multi-purpose Cash Assistance (MPCA), Nutrition, Economic Recovery and Market Systems (ERMS), Protection and Shelter and Settlements. The consortium aims to meet the most immediate and life-saving needs of IDPs, host communities and returnees in MMC and Jere, which will translate into reduced mortality and improved living conditions. The consortium will also address the ongoing, protracted needs, and supporting early recovery through capacity-building, the strengthening of existing health systems and community-based structures, and increasing the ownership of life-saving, life-sustaining, and life-building services by local authorities, service providers, and local communities to ensure sustainability. In order to build the resilience of individuals and communities, the unique humanitarian and development challenges in MMC and Jere LGAs (presence of service delivery actors against an ongoing flux of IDPs in and out of camps and host communities throughout the city) must be addressed simultaneously by increasing access to quality, sustainable basic services, building sustainable livelihoods, and strengthening local systems and structures.

project_name: PRISE EN CHARGE DE LA MALNUTRITION AIGUE MODEREE AU BURUNDI
project_objective:
Le Plan Stratégique Intérimaire du Burundi (2022-2024) prévoit en 2022, la prise en charge de 75,000 enfants de 6-59 mois et 25,000 Femmes enceintes et allaitantes modérément malnutris avec 675 tonnes de Plumpy Sup et 1,125 tonnes de Super céréale Plus (CSB++). Il est en outre bâti sur l'intégration de la Nutrition dans les autres activités dont l’assistance aux populations victimes des catastrophes naturelles afin de contribuer à l'atteinte de l'objectif Malnutrition Zéro au Burundi au regard de l’ampleur de la malnutrition dans ces groupes vulnérables. En effet, le dépistage de masse de la malnutrition aiguë effectué en avril 2021 parmi les populations touchées par les inondations a montré un taux de prévalence de la malnutrition aiguë modérée (MAM) de 4,1% chez les enfants de 6 à 59 mois alors que les cas MAS représentent 1,1%. Il a été constaté que les cas MAM n’étaient pas pris en charge conformément au Protocole National de Prise en Charge de la Malnutrition Aiguë comme les zones touchées n'étaient pas  couvertes par le Programme de Traitement de la MAM alors que les cas de MAS étaient automatiquement référés aux CDS ou hôpitaux les plus proches pour une prise en charge appropriée selon qu’ils étaient avec ou sans complications médicales.  Le Secteur Nutrition a prévu assister 2, 122 enfants  enfants de 6-59 mois  sans aucune femme enceinte et femme allaitante (FEFA)  modérément malnutris victimes des catastrophes naturelles en 2022. Un stock de contingence pour 5,000 enfants de 6-59 mois et 1,100 femmes enceintes et allaitantes avait été introduit dans le Mémorandum d’entente entre PAM et le MSPLS en 2021 mais n’a jamais été disponible pour manque de financement. C’est la raison pour laquelle cette proposition est développée afin de combler ces gaps dans la prise en charge nutritionnelle de la MAM aussi bien parmi les populations générales que celles victimes des catastrophes naturelles. 
Le projet vise  à contribuer à la réhabilitation nutritionnelle des 77,122 enfants de 6-59 mois et 25,000 femmes enceintes et allaitantes modérément malnutris dont 2,122 enfants parmi les populations victimes de catastrophes naturelles au Burundi. De façon spécifique, le projet vise à :  (a) Prévenir la malnutrition aigüe sévère chez 77,122 enfants de 6 à 59 mois et 25,000 femmes enceintes et allaitantes modérément malnutris  dont 2,122 enfants de 6-59 mois parmi les populations victimes de catastrophes naturelles au Burundi ; (b) Réduire le risque de mortalité et morbidité lié à la malnutrition chez 77,122 enfants de 6 à 59 mois et 25,000 femmes enceintes et allaitantes modérément malnutris dont 2,122 enfants de 6-59 mois parmi les populations victimes de catastrophes naturelles au Burundi ; (c)	Accroitre les connaissances sur les produits nutritifs spécialisés et les pratiques d’alimentation du nourrisson et du jeune enfant (ANJE) chez les populations des provinces d'intervention du projet au Burundi.  Les résultats attendus suivant la chaïne des résultats  sont les suivants : Effet : Réduction de la sous nutrition y compris les déficiences en micronutriments chez les enfants âgés de 6-59 mois et les femmes enceintes et allaitantes ; Extrant 1.1 : Distribution des produits nutritionnels et non nutritionnels en quantité et qualité suffisante et au moment opportun aux enfants de 6-59 mois et FEFA ; Extrant 1.2 : Existence de changement  de comportement sur l'utilisatin des produits nutritionnels spécialisés et les pratiques d’alimentation du nourrisson et du jeune Enfant (ANJE). Les activités pertinentes sont réalisées afin d'atteindre les résultats attendus.  La quantité totale de 700 tonnes de Plumpy Sup et 1,040 tonnes de CSB++ sont requises pour la supplémentation nutritionnelle des 77.122 enfants de 6-59 mois pendant 3 mois et 25,000 FEFA pendant 5 mois. Le montant total requis pour la réalisation de toutes ces activités du projet est de 6,005,517USD.

project_name: Improve access to life-saving and life-sustaining coordinated, equitable quality health services for those most vulnerable and in need people in North Syria.
project_objective:
The project aims to provide life-saving and life-sustaining coordinated, equitable health services to address the dire need of health services for all age and sex groups; boys, girls, men, and women, with attention to people with special needs; physical disability, mental disorders, and psychosocial problems, without any sexual discrimination, among IDPs and host communities in northern Syria.
SEMA will prioritize the reduction of morbidity and mortality through improving the access to quality health care (primary and secondary, specialized services, COVID-19 response, community health, and risk communication) in 24 health facilities.
SEMA will provide the following services at the primary healthcare level: RH services (ante-natal care, post-natal care, family planning, normal deliveries, gynecological consultations, and clinical management of rape), Integrated management for child illness, EPI, communicable and non-communicable diseases, Nutrition, MHPSS, health awareness and risk communication for COVID 19, and basic laboratory and radiology services. Services at the secondary healthcare level will include gynecologic surgeries and cesarean sections, trauma management, major surgeries, hospitalization services, blood transfusion, hemodialysis, and ICUs, in addition to COVID-19 response (Case Management for children and adults, Triage, PPE/IPC, RCCE at facility and community level). 
This program also includes MHPSS, MH gap intervention, and focused-non-specialized services by PSWs within SEMA health facilities, also at the community levels. 
In addition, as part of SEMA focus on contributing to its goal of increasing the capacity of the health care professional in NWS through Medical education and training initiatives including the SEMA Vocational Health Education center in Afrin, Academy of Health Sciences, and the Pediatric residency lecture Series in cooperation with The Syrian Board of Medical Specialties (SBOMS).
SEMA's planned activities will meet specific needs to enable access for people with disabilities to health services under their specific situation. 
SEMA will ensure privacy, equity, and easy access to the services as there will be women waiting areas within the hospital, and having available female staff to deal with women and children smoothly.
SEMA will provide quantitative and qualitative reports that include disaggregated information about cases/age, sex, gender, and disability. including reporting to DHIS.

SEMA will participate actively in the COVID-19 Taskforce and will ensure following the protocols and guidelines according to WHO eight pillars. SEMA health facilities will be provided with the required PPEs to keep the frontline staff safe and keep the health facilities running as well.  Additionally, surveillance measures will be enhanced in order to early detection of COVID-19 cases and refer to the respective health facilities. Furthermore, IPC measures and tools will be secured and followed to ensure adherence to the WHO standards and guidelines and prevent the health facility to be a potential source of infection. Moreover, isolation hospitals will be supported by SEMA to provide case management of COVID-19 cases according to WHO and COVID-19 task force protocols.

project_name: Emergency lifesaving WASH assistance for drought and conflict affected locations in Ethiopia
project_objective: The objective of the proposed set of interventions is in line with HRP 2022 WASH cluster objective to protect and sustain access to WASH facilities services for climate and conflict affected Communities and enhance the vulnerable communities’ ability to withstand recurrent and future shocks related with Water supply, sanitation, and hygiene related services. The project targeted 981649 in Afar, Amhara, Oromia, and Tigray regional States of Ethiopia. 75 % of the total case load in each targeted locations were considered in the project. Major activities include, Water system rehabilitation, water trucking, latrine construction/rehabilitation, hygiene promotion and WASH NFI distribution, including Water treatment chemicals.

project_name: Provision of essential lifesaving preventive and curative services to host and IDP communities in Benadir, Galmudug, Nugaal, and Hirshabele regions.
project_objective:
Somalia still faces significant humanitarian challenges with about 5.9 million people in need of humanitarian aid. Currently, over 2.7 million people face emergency levels of food insecurity crisis likely to grow in the year. Compared to the current number of people in need of aid, this number has increased over the years compared to 4.2 million reported.
Further, about 1.2 million people have been displaced as of 2020, and more than 2.6 million people are classified as internally displaced at risk of facing marginalization, and exclusion. The humanitarian needs arise from decades of recurrent impacts of political, armed conflict, climatic shocks, and socio-economic factors driving the needs of most vulnerable including persons with disabilities, children, the elderly, and pregnant and lactating women.

In Somalia, the health sector faces significant challenges with the COVID-19 pandemic and other disease outbreaks stretching the already strained health infrastructure contributing to some of the worst health outcomes, especially in most rural areas. Additionally, the disease outbreaks straining health servicing and access include measles, Acute Watery Diarrhea (AWD) and cholera, and vaccine-derived polio. Without adequate funding, three million people will not have access to essential health care services. The proposed intervention will provide emergency health services in Benadir, Galmudug, Nugaal, and  Hirshabelle regions for internally displaced persons (IDPs) and vulnerable host communities.

The project will support integrated essential lifesaving preventive and curative services in Benadir, Galmudug, Nugaal, and Hirshabelle regions of Somalia improving the utilization of integrated primary healthcare services, including reproductive health and immunization coverage supporting static facilities and use of mobile response to deliver service in areas not currently served by static facilities increasing health care services for marginalized communities.

Under the proposed program, six static facilities (health care clinics) in Benadir and Galmudug regions and  4 Mobile outreaches in Nugaal and Hirshabelle region with facilities equipped to provide basic screening, medical, surgical, laboratory, nutrition, and pharmacy services. Additionally, patients presenting chronic conditions and complications including pregnant women with obstetric complications within the community are to be referred for management in the health facilities. Further, pregnant women in need of Comprehensive Emergency Obstetric Care (CEmONC) will be referred from the facilities to tertiary facilities in the supported regions.

This action will strengthen facility structures through recruitment of support staff, training of healthcare workforce, provision of essential equipment and essential supplies, provision of comprehensive reproductive healthcare services and skilled attended birth, and regular supportive supervision. Community health volunteers will be supported to identify cases and provide referral mechanisms among the marginalized population for instance the pregnant mothers for ANC services and safer births as well as identifying vulnerable community members with non-communicable diseases including persons with mental health needs. Further, GBV survivors receive a survivor-centered approach ensuring survivors’ rights, needs, and wishes are prioritized and always respected. The proposed intervention will address immediate needs i.e., mitigating the spread of COVID-19 and supporting the public health consequences of the pandemic in target locations including Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) including awareness-raising through media and training more community health workers on case definitions as well as to scale up hygiene response in the targeted areas.

project_name: FSA support to the most vulnerable IDPs, host and refugees residing in NES
project_objective:
CARE NES proposed strategy is in line with 2021 Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) and specifically aligns with Strategic Objective 3 (Increase the resilience of affected communities by improving access to livelihood opportunities and basic services, especially among the most vulnerable households and communities). CARE’s proposed intervention will target Hasakah and Deir-ez-Zor (DEZ) governorate in NES, one of the most impoverished areas in the country. CARE proposes to implement the project in this governorates due to the scale of unmet needs. 
The multi sectoral approach integrated with an innovative methodology grounding resilience in socio-economic wellbeing linking increased household economic capacities and opportunities with access to functioning basic infrastructure at community level and inclusive decision making at household and community levels, promoting more inclusive environment and improved ability of copying with stress. Based on that CARE is shifting towards a more integrated cross-cutting approach, allowing for a holistic understanding of the needs of communities and households. CARE has a strong programmatic focus around  value chains since they link producers and buyers from different communities and purposefully integrate women, older persons, people with disabilities, IDPs and/or returnees. CARE’s proposed value chain approach in the short, medium and long term is expected to help Syrian families and communities affected by conflict to achieve a greater level of resilience, mitigate protection risks and participate in economic life.
Under FS & Agriculture, CARE will support the most vulnerable population of NorthEast Syria for economic recovery and the restoration of livelihoods and functioning markets related to wheat and sheep value chains as well as increasing community well-being and social cohesion: more specifically provision of agricultural and livestock inputs (seeds, fertilizers, Drip irrigation systems, sheep, fodder), establishment of veterinary services (vaccinations, trainings of doctors), establishment of vocational training centers. CARE NES team strongly coordinate with NES active clusters including Food Security & Livelihood Cluster, Agriculture working group, Cash Working Group, early Recovery & Livelihood Working Group to avoid any duplication and to be inline with cluster guidelines.

project_name: Delivering Health Assistance for IDPs and Host Communities in NWS
project_objective: The IRC, one of the largest health actors in NWS, will provide integrated primary, secondary, and community health care services inclusive of lifesaving medical supplies and pharmaceuticals through over 15 health care facilities both through direct implementation and jointly working with implementing partners. This includes the provision of reproductive health (RH), non-communicable disease (NCD), communicable disease (CD), and trauma care. The IRC’s health program will ensure full integration of MHPSS programming, COVID-19 response and adaptability as well as continues training for health care workers. The IRC will continue to provide support with partners the Idlib Surgical hospital. The IRC will support the improvement of health service access and will continue its provision of pharmaceutical and medical supplies. In addition, the IRC will work with its health partners to provide and ensure technical and clinical training and supportive supervision initiatives to improve the overall quality of care provided and skills of health care workers. Topics included in these trainings to improve the overall quality of care include, reproductive health, nutrition, NCD, MHPSS, waste management and infection prevention and control (IPC). The IRC will support and follow the Essential Health Service Package (EHSP) for NW Syria and work to align protocols and guidance along with best practices and global standards. The IRC will also ensure accurate and timely data management and tracking through a robust MEAL and health information management system. The IRC is and will remain an active member of the health cluster and sub-working groups.  These services will continue to be provided to IDPs and host communities in Idlib and Aleppo until the end of 2023 with varied scale based on funding availability.

project_name: Lifesaving preventive nutrition services to IDP and Non- IDP populations in Somalia
project_objective:
This project will contribute to the Nutrition Cluster’s strategic objective two, strengthening lifesaving preventive nutrition services, by improving nutritious food acquisition, knowledge, practices, consumption and ultimately nutrition outcomes for rural and IDP populations within IPC 3 and 4.
In Somalia, the high cost of a nutritious diet does not support the creation of an enabling food environment for a healthy population.  In addition to the issue of low affordability, poor and vulnerable people face physical access constraints related to the lack of availability of nutritious diets. These constraints, coupled with poor knowledge and skills in food choices and preparation, contribute significantly to sustained high numbers of malnourished individuals. Children Under-5 and lactating women are consistently the most vulnerable to malnutrition in Somalia. 
FAO plans to support 2,000 rural and IDP households with children between 6 to 59 months with a blended approach prioritizing unconditional cash transfers (UCTs) valued at 80 percent of the Food Minimum Expenditure Basket (MEB) to improve immediate access to nutritious foods. To enhance the impact of cash, this intervention will be complemented by Behavior Change Communication (BCC) and nutrition education adapted to the local context. This activity will engage primary caregivers in cooking demonstrations, role-play and individual counselling to increase the chances of retention and adoption of new healthy habits. The aim is to improve complementary feeding for children 6-59 months to prevent recurrent cases of malnutrition.
 FAO shall also provide 800 pregnant and lactating women (PLW) enrolled in nutrition treatment with conditional cash transfers (CCT), valued at 80 percent of the food MEB by region, on the condition that they attend maternal and child care support groups within their communities. Through these peer support groups, they will receive knowledge and peer support during pregnancy and lactation period. Through the cash assistance, they will have access to nutritious foods to meet their nutritional needs. Under this activity, FAO shall consider approximately 200 PLW to receive UCTs to accommodate participants that would be willing, but are not able to attend trainings. FAO shall work closely with partners to provide flexible ways of receiving the content of trainings for this smaller group.
FAO will also support the creation of mother-to-mother support groups reaching an additional 1,000 women between 15 to 49 years. Each group will be made up of 10-15 mothers from vulnerable households in rural areas. These groups will receive kitchen gardening kits and simple tools to promote the establishment of kitchen gardens that can provide a source of nutritious foods especially during dry seasons.
Nutrition education, awareness and training sessions will be conducted by locally recruited and trained members of the community called Nutrition Champions (one male and one female in every village). These champions will be trained to disseminate information and knowledge on nutrition and services available across their villages.

In total, FAO shall support 4,000 households/ 24,000 individuals with life-saving nutrition assistance. FAO will employ community- led beneficiary selection processes and ensure adequate targeting and representation of extremely vulnerable and minority groups in community committees including women, youth and people living with disabilities (PWD). Interventions proposed will employ a DoNoHarm, a gender lens, and conflict- sensitive approach to reduce protection risks for all individuals, and to reduce the risk of conflict or community tensions.

project_name: Support to Food Security and Nutrition Analysis Unit (FSNAU) of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)
project_objective:
Given the precarious food security, nutrition and livelihood situation across Somalia, conducting assessments and analysis on a regular basis and continuous monitoring of the situation remains vital. At present, the Government of Somalia has limited institutional and technical capacity to generate and provide such data. To fill the gap, the FAO-led Food Security and Nutrition Analysis Unit (FSNAU) provides critical and timely information and analyses on the food security and nutrition situation in Somalia to a broad range of stakeholders.  FSNAU information and analyses facilitate and support effective evidence based decision-making in support of humanitarian, recovery and development interventions. 

FSNAU identifies food insecure populations by livelihood and by district, pinpoints the specific challenges facing vulnerable groups, including women in achieving food security and reports on the population’s nutritional status to support targeted interventions. In addition to its early warning function, FSNAU carries out relevant baseline livelihood studies for an improved understanding of underlying causes of food, nutrition and livelihood insecurity. Gender analysis is an integral part of FSNAU’s data collection analytical process. FSNAU also provides food security and nutrition related technical and institutional capacity development support to Somali institutions and other key actors. The project has two key components:
I.	In 2022, FSNAU will continue to provide information and analysis on current and emerging food security and nutrition situation in Somalia in a manner that supports prioritization and targeting of appropriate food security and nutrition response interventions. FSNAU will also provide additional information through its Early Warning Early Action Dashboard in order to support timely and prioritized response. 
II.	Staff of relevant government institutions at Federal level, Federal Member State level and Somaliland will also be trained and supported to participate in seasonal food security and nutrition assessments and analyses. On 21 September 2021, FAO signed a landmark agreement with the Somali National Bureau of Statistics (SNBS) to commence the gradual transfer of ownership of FSNAU to the Federal Government of Somalia.  Under the agreement, FSNAU will build the  capacity of the SNBS as well as government institutions working in areas such as agriculture, livestock, health, disaster management and statistics. The intended result is to ensure that these institutions gradually acquire adequate institutional capacity to assess, analyse, monitor and report on current as well as emerging food security and nutrition situations in Somalia as well as associated underlying factors that compromise food security, nutrition, markets and livelihoods.  As part of the transition process, core skills training related to food security and nutrition assessment, monitoring, analysis and reporting, equipment and related capacity development support will be provided to government institutions.  

FSNAU products are disseminated through the FSNAU website (www.fsnau.org), mailing list and through regular as well as ad hoc presentations to stakeholders, including the Somalia Humanitarian Country Team.

The main beneficiaries of the information and analysis generated by FSNAU under this project will be government line ministries, UN agencies, local and international NGOs and resource partners. Indirect FSNAU project beneficiaries will be the millions of food insecure people and acutely malnourished children who are expected to benefit from humanitarian assistance and livelihood support provided by the Government, UN agencies, local and international NGOs and resource partners.

FSNAU and REACH provide information and analysis to IASC Clusters in and the HRP/HNO process. FSNAU provides information and analyses that support the Food Security and Nutrition Clusters and REACH provides support to other IASC clusters in Somalia.

project_name: Comprehensive Shelter and Non-Food Item (NFI) Support for Rohingya Refugees and Host Communities in Cox's Bazar
project_objective:
IOM will continue supporting refugees and host communities aiming at reaching 96,946 households living in 18 IOM Areas of Responsibility (AoR) camps with Shelter and Non-Food Items (NFI) including Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) interventions and 300 host community households with shelter upgrades.
Under Objective 1, IOM will implement projects on Transitional Shelter Assistance Phase 3 (TSA 3), new Mid-Term Shelters (MTS) and their maintenance, trainings on shelter reinforcement/disaster risk reduction (DRR) with the inclusion of youth and women, provision of treated borak bamboo poles in all shelter-related activities, replacement of cooking stoves, provision of LPG refills including related trainings, solar lamp distributions, NFI voucher assistance in camps and shelter upgrades through conditional and unrestricted cash transfers combined with Shelter/DRR training in host communities. For TSA 3, Pipeline Partners will be involved, including Caritas (Camp 13 and 19, only borak), NRC (Camp 8E), Save the Children (Camp 8W) and HEKS (Camp 15 and 16), with HEKS also covering NFI voucher assistance.
Activities under Objective 2 include provision of emergency shelter support and NFIs based on the Rapid Damage Verification (RDV), prepositioning of emergency shelter kits (ESK), assisting 30 per cent of households in camps in Ukhia and 100 per cent in camps in Teknaf, provision of tie down kits (TDK) and awareness as part of monsoon preparedness, as well as provision of new LPG packages for those with damaged and new households. IOM will also cover respective camps as camp-level focal points, ensuring camp-level coordination as well as receiving and addressing referred cases from other stakeholders such as Site Management and Protection actors. For Emergency shelter, NFI support and TDK, IOM will work with Caritas (Camp 13 and 19) and HEKS (Camp 15 and 16) as Pipeline Partners.
Under Objective 3, IOM will ensure shelter activities are carried out with the involvement of women, older people, persons with disabilities and gender-diverse populations through cash-for-work activities. IOM will also conduct multiple consultations with communities before and after the implementation to capture the beneficiaries’ feedback in the planning and implementation. Feedback and complaints received will be also utilized for modifying future interventions. 
IOM will maximize the use of voucher and cash for work as implementation modality in all programmes  to ensure beneficiaries have freedom of choice to provide the most needed materials and items. All borak bamboo poles used in shelter-related activities will be treated at IOM’s Bamboo Treatment Facility to provide a longer lifespan and strengthen structures in combination with metal footings. The pilot initiative for care and maintenance of solar lamps will be implemented with trained youth, and basket making initiatives with female cash-for-work beneficiaries.
In all Shelter/NFI and LPG activities, IOM will ensure protection mainstreaming in line with IOM’s Gender-Based Violence (GBV) in Crisis Framework and its concurrent Action. Those identified as households with Extremely Vulnerable Individuals (EVI) will receive porter support. Construction support for shelter-related activities will also be provided to all EVI cases. Distribution points and team composition for the implementations will be arranged to mitigate the risk of GBV. Community feedback mechanisms with complaints desks, community mobilizations, regular project monitoring and post distribution monitoring will be deployed. All data collected during assessment and monitoring activities will be sex and age disaggregated and particular information regarding vulnerabilities will be collected to provide additional support during the implementation. Continuous efforts for the Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) including (refresher) training for all staff and awareness on PSEA for beneficiaries will also be continued.

project_name: Reducing Health-related Vulnerabilities of Rohingya Refugees and Host Communities are through the Provision of Increased Access to Quality and Comprehensive Health Services with Measures in Place for Emergency and Outbreak Preparedness and Response
project_objective:
IOMs’ health interventions aim to provide life-saving assistance and improve the resilience of affected populations, with special attention to gender and age considerations and vulnerable groups. 

This will be achieved through contributing to 
i)	Increased safe, dignified and meaningful access to and utilization of quality comprehensive health services for all crisis-affected populations, with special focus on sexual, reproductive, maternal, neonatal, child and adolescent health; mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS); and non-communicable diseases (NCD);
ii)	Improved health-seeking behaviour, encouragement of healthy living and promotion of the utilization of essential service packages and community engagement, with special attention to vulnerable groups 
iii)	Measures to prevent, control and (timely) respond to health emergencies, during disasters (including monsoon and cyclone) and outbreaks of communicable diseases, including COVID-19 and acute watery diarrhoea (AWD). 
IOM also aims to contribute to the improvement of quality of services through performance monitoring, evaluation, coordination and capacity building.

IOM will directly implement these interventions through eight health posts (HP), 5 primary health care centres (PHCC) and two severe acute respiratory infections treatment centres SARI ITC), as well as work with five implementing partners to support six HP, five PHCC, one comprehensive maternal centre and 383 community health workers (CHW) for Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE). In addition, IOM will support government facilities in host communities through human resource and staff transport as well as supplies and maintenance of infrastructure and equipment, overall supporting two upazila health complexes, four union-level health and family welfare facilities as well as three community clinics.

project_name: Enhancing Conditions for Economic Inclusion, Sustainable Incomes and Livelihoods for the Host Communities and Life-skills and Self-reliance for Refugees in Cox’s Bazar
project_objective:
IOM will undertake a wide range of activities that include transferrable and vocational skills development for Rohingyas to build their resilience and facilitate their sustainable reintegration in Myanmar when conditions become conducive. Such activities will help beneficiaries meet basic needs (food security, income generation). IOM will arrange in-kind asset support for agriculture and other activities to the Rohingya beneficiaries helping them to utilize the skills and gain a modest self-reliance.

The host community support will integrate disaster resilient and green entrepreneurship and livelihoods options into the transferable and vocational skills development activities to improve the resilience of the beneficiaries to external shocks, minimize environmental degradation and increase food security-income. The activities will include provision of trainings on disaster mitigation, disaster resilient crops-seeds, tools & methods for agriculture and other sectors, waste recycling, electronic refurbishment and other vocational and non-vocational skills that are not susceptible to disasters but relevant to markets and economic sectors (e.g. computer skills, tourism, customer service, business skills, plumbing, AC repair, secretary, call center, patient administration, catering).

The targeted vulnerable women beneficiaries who have technical skills but cannot or do not want to work outside their houses will receive Productive Asset Support (PAS) to gain a modest income. The activities include five days of basic business skills training through which beneficiaries prepare basic business plans. Then, the business plan is evaluated by a selection committee which will be comprised of both women and men. The business plans which demonstrate economic feasibility and chance of making a profit will be selected, and productive assets for starting the business may be purchased and delivered to beneficiaries by IOM or implementing partners. 

Beneficiaries will also receive small business grants through Entrepreneurship Program to the existing Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) that can help them adapt and keep their businesses going through the current COVID-19 crisis or other potential shocks. Additionally, it can support to adapt and shift  businesses into potential ecofriendly businesses (solar light production, eco-friendly retailing, organic catering, sustainable items for construction, eco-friendly landscaping, sustainable/eco-friendly event planning, bicycle repairing or refurbishing, handcrafted organic or natural products). 

In addition to PAS and grant support, beneficiaries will receive assistance to develop their institutional capacities through the establishment of women's cooperatives (such as agriculture, livestock and handicrafts) empowering the beneficiaries to take joint business decisions, collective investments and profit sharing. The activity will benefit 2,300 host community beneficiaries.

IOM will help to expand market linkages with the private sector, including labor market, value chain, and unpaid care analysis for the host community that can enable small producers to sell their products to individuals and wholesalers. In addition, IOM will work on empowering young people by helping them find decent work through supporting life and vocational skills and job-matching livelihoods.

project_name: Supporting provision of life saving sexual and reproductive health services in seven Regions in Ethiopia
project_objective:
As a result of the conflicts coupled with the COVID-19 epidemic, the existing health system and social platforms have been further weakened to respond to the Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (SRHR) needs of women and adolescent girls; to provide clinical management of rape survivor’s services. Significant number of health facilities in the northern part of Ethiopia are looted and damaged due to the conflict. 

As a result of the drought in Somali, Oromia and SNNPR, there is high number of  drought induced internally displaced persons as a result of which significant number of the health facilities that are found in the host community are overburdened. The health facilities are depleted of reproductive health commodities, personal protective equipment and medicines and medical equipment that are key for providing life-saving SRH services. There are reports of pregnant mothers delivering in the bush, in IDP camps, and at home due lack of access to health facilities and service providers. The health service referral pathways are not strong enough to enable timely access to appropriate services due to the overwhelming number of IDPs who are living within the host community in the collective IDP sites. 
The interventions will aim to enable health facilities, institutions and health care providers to implement Minimum Initial Service Package (MISP) for SRH that are lifesaving services during emergencies. Moreover, the activities will strengthen the capacity of health offices and health facilities to build a strong health system that is resilient to shocks and capable of responding to the SRHR and GBV needs. These include various capacity building training, equipping the facilities with the necessary equipment and commodities, deployment of midwives, establishing/strengthening mobile health teams, strengthening the referral and linkage between the community and the health facilities, between the host and the refugee/IDP community and their service provision platforms.  
UNFPA is a pipe line manager of inter-agency RH kits for the emergency response, and is expected to important  the emergency RH kits to the health cluster prioritized zones and districts 
Community sensitization, awareness creation and mobilization activities will be undertaken to increase the health seeking behavior in general and SRH in particular; increase referral linkage from the community to health care facilities.

project_name: Enhancing access to health care in NWS
project_objective:
IOM will help to address the critical gaps in healthcare services in NWS by supporting one primary healthcare facility in Barisha, Idlib, through an IP. IOM will cover procurement of the facility’s medical supplies, running costs, salaries of essential staff, and urgent rehabilitation, allowing the health facility to be fully functional and retain its staff. Consultations in the PHC will include a comprehensive range of preventive and curative health services according to the WHO Essential PHC Service Package: basic trauma and injury care, communicable diseases (including compliance with early warning systems for disease outbreaks (EWARN reporting)), sexual and reproductive health, child health, basic nutrition services, basic mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services, and non-communicable disease management.
In addition, IOM, through an IP, will operate one mobile health clinic to provide health care services in two IOM camps that are in remote locations without any current access to services, Kafr Nabi and Mashhad Ruhin. The mobile health team will service each camp 2-3 days per week and will include services such as communicable disease, child health, basic nutrition, MHPSS services, non-communicable disease management, and sexual and reproductive health and hold awareness sessions on various health, hygiene, and nutrition topics. The mobile health clinic will be able to provide basic medications onsite as well as orientate people towards vaccination sites for both routine childhood and COVID-19 vaccinations for adults.
IOM will support hospitals designated to receive COVID-19 patients and those who need hospitalization in the intensive care unit (ICU) with eight lifesaving ventilators with Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) devices. Under WHO’s technical guidance and supervision, these ventilators will be distributed to recently established COVID-19 hospitals in Azaz district, Aleppo. As there is currently only one hospital with an ICU in Azaz district (Mare'a hospital), and the catchment population of Azaz district is 620,671, these hospitals required conversion to COVID-19 case management facilities given the high COVID caseload in Azaz combined with a shortage of health facilities and personnel elsewhere in the district.
IOM will support the Syrian Immunization Group (SIG), which is the only entity authorized by the WHO to implement vaccine activities in NWS Syria, with the procurement of necessary equipment to ensure continuity of services, expand the reach of 200 mobile vaccination teams while maintaining quality data entry and access to the DHIS-2, a health information system. The mobile vaccination teams are vital in the effort to vaccinate the most vulnerable and remote populations in NWS deprived of accessible health care, including those in camps and other hard to reach areas, and to mitigate the effects of infection with the COVID-19 virus.
IOM, through an IP, will aim to support dialysis center in Jarablus to ensure lifesaving and continuity of care to the most vulnerable affected people under severe limitations to access specialized care by supporting the running cost of the dialysis center in Jarablus city (HeRAMS code: B0208014) and collaboration with WHO plans to support dialysis centers with dialysis kits. There are 7 functional dialysis machines in Jarablus dialysis center, and 2 of them had been allocated for patients with Hepatitis B (HBV) and Hepatitis C (HCV).
The IOM, through an IP, will aim to support the Haritan hospital for Women and Children located in Idlib - Harem - Al-Dana - Deir Hassan, which provides free health services to all those in need without discrimination, within the specializations of women's surgery, gynecology, obstetrics, pediatrics, and incubators, by providing incentives to the staff, monthly running cost, and purchasing medical and non-medical equipment, the hospital covers an area that includes 600,000 population, most of them live in camps.

project_name: Programme de cantines scolaires d’urgences au profit des élèves déplacés de 5 régions à haut défi sécuritaire du Burkina Faso
project_objective:
Depuis 2015, le Burkina Faso est en proie à des attaques de groupes armés. Ces actes de violence entrainent des déplacements de populations et la fermeture des établissements scolaires. Ils compromettent l’accès et le maintien des élèves à l’école. A cette situation s’ajoute la crise liée à la pandémie de la Covid-19. Ces crises sécuritaire et sanitaire ont un impact négatif sur le système éducatif. A la date du 31 Octobre 2021, le nombre d’écoles primaires fermées était de 2 266 soit 12,96% des 17 483 écoles que compte le pays. Cette situation affecte 264 424 élèves soit 124 537 filles et 8 646 enseignants dont 2 851 femmes.  S’agissant de la crise sanitaire, la pandémie Covid_19 a entrainé la fermeture des établissements scolaires à compter du 16 Mars 2020 jusqu’à la fin de l’année scolaires 2019_2020. Seules les classes d’examen ont pu réouvrir avant la fin de l’année scolaire. 
En réponse à ces deux crises majeures, le PAM mettra en œuvre en 2022, un programme d’alimentation scolaire en situation d’urgence afin d’assurer la protection des enfants et faciliter leur accès à l’alimentation et à la nutrition. Ce programme d'alimentation scolaire en situation d'urgence, ciblera les élèves déplacés en priorité, qui ont été réinstallés avec leur famille dans des zones sécurisées des régions affectées par l’insécurité. Il vise à sauver des vies tout en contribuant à l’accès et au maintien à l’éducation de base des enfants par la fourniture de repas scolaires nutritifs et la protection des moyens d’existence de leurs parents. Il contribuera à la réduction des obstacles à l'éducation de base des enfants notamment ceux des filles vivant dans les régions du Sahel, du Centre-Nord, de l’Est, du Nord et de la Boucle du Mouhoun et complètera les initiatives sectorielles existantes visant l’amélioration des indicateurs de l’éducation.

project_name: Improve Food Security and Promote a Nutritious Diet for the most Vulnerable population of Blue Nile State.
project_objective:
The proposal was designed in accordance with the multi-sectoral needs highlighted in the 2021 HNO and further described in the section below, and conceived in close coordination between ACTED and WFP. Starting from the School Feeding modality already in place in several schools of Blue Nile, this Action is meant to provide more sustainable solutions to address food and nutritional gaps through the creation of school- and kitchen- gardens and through a strong soft-component of guidance and training sessions on nutrition, agricultural and improved hygiene practices in schools and at HH level. Improved hygiene practices are crucial while handling food and preparing meals, but also to decrease the incidence of water-borne diseases such as cholera and diarrhoea (see the Need paragraph for more details on figures about Sudanese children). The hygiene intervention will also include the construction of handwashing facilities in schools and the provision of hygiene kits to the pupils. Furthermore, hand washing facilities will be set up during the conduction of trainings and distributions. With regard to Education, it is estimated that over three million Sudanese aged 5-13 years are not in classroom. At 43%, Blue Nile is the worst performing state for children who are out of primary school. To tackle the issue, school gardens under this proposal will incentivize school attendance for primary and secondary school-age children, who will be supported through the ready-to-eat rations during the preparation of gardens, in case their school is not already targeted by WFP's School Feeding Program. On food purchase, ACTED will follow a competitive procurement either in Khartoum or Damazine; the ready-to-eat rations will be stored in ACTED's warehouse in Damazine and brought to the final distribution point as per project's workplan; a FS specialist will be recruited to manage the WH and maintain the optimal conditions in terms of ventilation, size, temperature and humidity, for safe storage of food material; quantities of food will be stored as per demand and expiring dates. Furthermore, pupils’ mother will receive cash for the set-up of school-gardens while being trained and guided by ACTED staff allowing them to replicate the garden in their houses. In this way, kitchen garden beneficiaries will get help for sowing and harvesting, and will also have a short-term income available to further invest in their kitchen gardens. Therefore, in terms of population target, the project will operate on multiple levels, engaging primary and secondary school-age children, mothers, women and men at HH level. The selection criteria for FSL activities under this proposal will include but not limited to the following: a) HHs living in areas classified in IPC Phase 3 or above b) Female-headed HHs; c) HHs with chronically ill or disabled family members; d) HHs with acutely malnourished children; d) HHs who do not own productive assets or livestock; e) Daily wage-earning families (i.e., HHs who rely on casual daily labor for income); f) HHs living nearby functioning schools with space and resources for gardening, and whose children are pupils in the school.
Throughout the Action, ACTED will implement COVID-19 prevention measures. ACTED teams will receive trainings on COVID-19 preventive measures and a full set of PPE stock to be used during project activities. During activities, ACTED will ensure the beneficiaries and ACTED staff follow social distancing measures.

project_name: Projet d’accès à une éducation de qualité inclusive et sure des enfants affectés par la crise sécuritaire dans les régions du Nord, de la boucle du Mouhoun et du centre Nord du Burkina Faso
project_objective:
L’impact global de la planification ESU de Educo Pour 2022 est de créer un environnement scolaire sain, pacifique et sécurisé favorable à la continuité des activités d’enseignement/apprentissage au profit des enfants affectés par la crise sécuritaire dans les régions du Nord, de la Boucle du Mouhoun et du centre Nord. En général, le projet vise à l’amélioration de l’accès des filles, des garçons, des adolescents et adolescentes vulnérables de 3 à 17 ans à un format de continuité éducative de qualité dans le respect des normes sécuritaires, sanitaires, organisationnelles, et pédagogiques instituées par le gouvernement.  A cet effet, Le projet renforcera (i) l’accès inclusif à une éducation formelle de qualité, pour les enfants déscolarisés déplacés et ceux des populations hôtes, par le développement des capacités d’accueil des écoles formelles des territoires refuges ( mise en place d’espaces temporaires d’apprentissage (ETA) équipés, dotation en matériel et mobiliers scolaires,…) (ii) le développement d’alternatives d’éducation pour les enfants non scolarisés des populations déplacées et hôtes dans les territoires refuges avec la mise en place de classes SSA/P pour les enfants hors écoles, ;(iii) la qualité de l’éducation par la formation des enseignants et autre personnel éducatif sur des thématiques liées à la gestion de l’ESU (  premiers secours psychologiques, prévention des VBG, détection et référencement des cas de protection,  cohésion sociale, gestion des larges effectifs, etc.), la dotation des écoles en matériel pédagogique et didactique, l’organisation de cours de soutien  pour les élèves ayant des difficultés d'apprentissage, le suivi-supervision des enseignements/apprentissages par les services compétents,(iv) Le renforcement de la résilience des écoles et de la communautés éducative par des activités de formation, de sensibilisation et de plaidoyer sur l’approche Safe School, l’élaboration de plan de sécurité école, (v) le développement d’espaces d’apprentissage sûrs, protecteurs, inclusifs et favorables à la réussite des enfants à travers la réhabilitation des infrastructures et des blocs de latrines différenciés,  la promotion de l'hygiène(séances de sensibilisation, dotations de kits de lavage des mains, kits d'hygiène individuels et collectif, de trousses d’hygiène menstruelle pour les filles vulnérables, la réhabilitation/entretien des forages..,(vi) la protection des enfants à travers la gestion des cas de protection par les services sociaux ou en complémentarité avec d’autres projets, la prise en charge des besoins médicaux et psychologiques, la réalisation d’activités psychosociales au sein de l’école et la mise en œuvre de mécanismes de redevabilité et de remonté des plaintes   ; (vii) des alternatives d’éducation telles que l’éducation à distance par la radio et les espaces d’apprentissage communautaire ouverts pour les enfants résidant dans les zones où les écoles sont fermées ; (viii) des activités pour la promotion de la cohésion sociale en milieu scolaire et communautaire ; (ix) pour les enfants de 3-6 ans des activités de renforcement des Centres d’Eveil et d’Education Préscolaire (CEEP) et des bisongo leur permettront de jouir d’un développement holistique dans un environnement sûr et protecteur.  …
Pour atteindre les objectifs visés, une synergie d’actions et une collaboration étroite avec les services déconcentrés de l’Etat, les ONG et les Organisations à Base Communautaires est necessaire. C’est pourquoi, la mobilisation communautaire et l’implication de toutes les parties prenantes sera au cœur de nos interventions
Les interventions se focaliseront sur les cibles suivantes : 56 192 apprenants des communautés déplacées et hôtes dont 70% d’ élèves déplacés à réinsérer et 60% de filles.
