project_name: Support Acute Mental Health Inpatient and Two Mobile Units in North of Syria
project_objective:
UOSSM seeks to contribute to achieving the following objectives:
Increase access to life-saving and life-sustaining coordinated, equitable humanitarian health services for those most vulnerable and in need 
The proposed project is to keep running the acute mental health unit in Sarmada/Idleb with the two mental health mobile units. The main goal of the project is to promote specialized mental health services to address more severe mental health disorders. 
Upon the need of the affected people to specialized MH services which are not sufficiently available in the area, UOSSM contributed to the response by establishing an acute MH inpatient and outpatient unit where services are provided for the most urgent presentations of severe mental health disorders, like schizophrenia (acute psychotic episodes), bipolar disorder (manic episode), severe depression, suicidal risk, severe substance misuse disorder and severe behavioral disorder related to mental health problems which cannot be managed and addressed in the community, in addition to providing multidisciplinary mental health service in the community (outpatient psychiatric units, psychiatric supervision, follow up and case management, individual, couple and group psychotherapy, and the-mental health supervision), and receiving referrals of more severe and complicated psychiatric beneficiaries from other agencies and health providers.
Also, to cover as many areas as possible, the acute MH unit is linked with two MH mobile clinics, where MH interventions are provided by doctors trained on MHGAP program for beneficiaries of children and adults with signs and symptoms of mild and moderate mental health disorders, in addition to psychosocial support activities for children, which are: self-recovery techniques, coping skills with different situation skills, emotional expression techniques, PFA and PFA for children. Also, to facilitate of awareness campaigns on mental health and protection concerns, such as (detection of signs and symptoms of mental disorders, early marriage, GBV prevention. etc.). Not only the detection and referral of the serious and severe beneficiaries to the acute MH unit in Sarmada, but also the referral of beneficiaries or families to community resources to help in recovery from mental or physical illnesses, and to facilitate access to services provided by other humanitarian actors.
 Objectives of the Project:
•To respond to the most urgent acute and serious mental health problems of the affected populations in the area
•To facilitate access of the affected populations to long-term specialized MH services 
•To enhance and promote the affected communities’ healthy coping mechanisms for both locals and IDPs
•To facilitate access for the affected populations to the available services in the area through an active referral pathway

project_name: Qualified Protection Services for the Conflict-affected Populations, both locals and IDPs, in Northwest Syria.
project_objective:
The proposed project aims at providing comprehensive (S)GBV services in already established Women & Girls Safe Space (WGSS) and Men & Youth Center (MYC) including case management in a safe, accessible, and private rooms which includes the initial/intake assessment for cases of beneficiaries with (S)GBV concerns such as; early marriage, sexual violence, and domestic violence, identifying strengths and assets that support (S)GBV survivors, following up referrals (internal or external) to health, MHPSS, nutrition, livelihood programs, and education services as needed based on a referral pathway developed by the GBV Sub-cluster. In addition to providing PSS activities aim to promote psycho-social wellbeing of (S)GBV survivors and other vulnerable individuals, which include topics such as family and community relationships engagement in meaningful roles and religious or spiritual practices, meeting basic needs, physical security, sense of identity, dignity, and positive self-esteem and physical wellbeing. Primary PSS activities include: Life skills for adolescents, parenting skills for adults, and ""My Safety, My Well-being"" for adolescents provided in line with (S)GBV sub-cluster recommendations. Also, providing group awareness raising sessions for adults, the GBV toolkit by the GBV Sub-cluster including 7 messages. In addition, the project includes vocational trainings for (S)GBV survivors, hairdressing and knitting for women in the WGSS and hairdressing for men in the MYC to empower the survivors to be well-integrated in their communities. The project intends also to support one mobile protection team, considering constraints that women and girls face in accessing services as well as the importance of raising awareness on (S)GBV for women, men, adolescent boys, and girls. The mobile team will contribute to increase the availability of high-quality protection services in the region, ensuring the confidentiality of provided services to avoid stigmatization and encourage beneficiaries to use them. The mobile team will implement awareness-raising activities, which include information-sharing sessions to raise awareness on specific topics depending on the perceived need of the target population. It will also consider topics shared through consultations with stakeholders and other humanitarian actors. Altogether, topics will especially focus on (S)GBV and domestic violence, gender equality, child marriage, and the importance of education, since low education and poverty, alongside the overall stressful and volatile environment, are either root causes or accentuate die risk of (S)GBV. 
The project is estimated to target in total; 5256 beneficiaries

project_name: Amélioration de l’accès à des services de protection pour les filles et les garçons affectés par la crise sécuritaire au Burkina Faso
project_objective:
Le projet s’inscrit dans un contexte marqué une crise sécuritaire sans précédent caractérisée par des attaques des groupes armés non identifiés et des conflits intercommunautaires.  Dans son rapport mensuel du 30 septembre 2021, le Conseil National  de Secours d’Urgence et de réhabilitation(CONASUR)  enregistrait 1 407 685 personnes déplacées internes (DPI) avec 61,13 % d’enfants dont 242 533 ont moins de 5 ans.  Comparativement aux chiffres en décembre 2020, nous constatons une augmentation de 22% des enfants déplacés interne ayant moins de 5 ans.
 La région du Nord est la 4ème région la plus affectée après celles du sahel, du Centre-Nord et de l’Est.  A la même date, elle comptait 128 162 DPI (soit une hausse de 67% par rapport en fin décembre 2020). Les deux provinces les plus affectées restent celles du Yatenga et du Loroum. La province du Yatenga à elle seule comptait 63 460 DPI. Les trois communes qui accueillent le plus de DPI sont Ouahigouya (37 894), Thiou (9 166) et Séguénéga (7 035).  
Les personnes déplacées sont accueillies sur des sites d’accueil et la plupart dans des familles d’accueil. Le contexte sécuritaire a engendré la dégradation des moyens d’existences de PDI et populations hôtes. Cette situation est couplée à une mauvaise récolte liée aux conditions climatiques dans la zone d’intervention mettant plusieurs familles dans les conditions de précarité et de besoins accrus en assistance alimentaire. Les enfants et les femmes sont les plus vulnérables dans ce contexte de crise sécuritaire et de la famine. Ils sont la plupart victimes des risques de protection et de violences basées sur le genre (VBG). Selon le rapport de l’étude base du projet dans la zone d’intervention, on dénombre 43 cas de mariage d’enfants, 67 cas de travail à risque (travaux dégradants pouvant causés des risques de santé, de blessures, atteinte à la vie), 52 cas d’exploitation par le travail (travail non rémunéré,), 49 cas de violences physiques (châtiments corporels,) et 02 cas de viols.
Cette situation augmente la vulnérabilité des ménages, réduisant leurs capacités à répondre aux besoins de base des enfants et poussant même certains parents à commettre des actes de violences sur leurs enfants, à des pratiques préjudiciables comme le mariage précoce des filles et à soumettre les enfants aux pires formes de travail pour faire face aux besoins de la famille.

project_name: Providing Food Security and Livelihoods Support to Vulnerable Households in Jonglei and Upper Nile States
project_objective:
Project Summary
This project aims to provide integrated emergency food security and livelihoods assistance to 60,000 (10,000HHs) vulnerable women, men, boys and girls including IDPs/host communities/ returnees in the IPC crisis and emergency phases in Jonglei and Upper Nile States. This project is in line with the South Sudan Food Security and Livelihoods Cluster Objectives, CO1 Saves lives,CO2. Enhance Protection and CO3 increase resilience and access to services. By providing emergency food security and livelihoods assistance through direct distribution of agricultural inputs, livestock vaccination and treatment services and training on improved agricultural production techniques, this project shall improve access to food, increase vulnerable households food production, strengthen households and community livelihoods and coping capacities, and, consequently, support early recovery and resilience among the targeted households in Jonglei and Upper Nile States. African Leadership Skills Initiative (ALSI) has been operational in the Greater Upper Nile for over a decade with competent and experienced staff that will be rapidly deployed to respond to the needs. The organization currently has implemented FAO-funded food security and livelihoods project (Emergency Livelihood Response Programme-ELRP) in Ayod County for more than seven years. ALSI has built very good rapport and excellent community goodwill, local state ministries linkages, strong local networks and coordination with the FSL Cluster. ALSI shall employ multi-sectoral approach to promote vegetable and crop production, reduction in post-harvest losses and safe guarding animal health, restoration and support of fishing activities, focus on restoring and strengthening livelihoods alongside more multi sector integrated actions (e.g. WASH, Nutrition & Health), advocacy for women’s needs, voice and rights, capacity building and skills transfers, livestock vaccinations and treatments, and increase efficiency and informed assistance through robust assessment and post distribution monitoring. Through inter-cluster synergies, quality programming, cost efficiency in addition to mainstreaming cross-cutting programmatic approaches that include application of Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) principles, protection including Gender Based Violence/ Sexual exploitation mitigation measures, Do No Harm, conflict context analysis, gender equity, Disability inclusion, HIV/AIDS awareness and prevention, environmental conservation and sustainability.

project_name: Essential Health care to Disaster affected populations in Somalia
project_objective:
In Somalia conflict and insecurity have forced hundreds of thousands of people to flee their homes in 2021 and are expected to remain key drivers of displacement in 2022. Conflict-induced shocks exacerbate the humanitarian situation of both IDP and host communities, with increased numbers of children married earlier as a coping strategy. Somalia remains on the frontline of climate change, which continues to induce crises resulting in widespread displacement, rapid urbanization, food insecurity, and increased poverty. 
Critically, climate change is also increasingly understood as a major driver of conflict in Somalia as the struggle for dwindling resources intensifies clan divisions and inter-clan conflict. 
To address these humanitarian crises, CARE  will implement an emergency health services  working with the Ministry of Health, Local partners targeting 30 Health Centres and 5 mobile clinics  in drought and conflicted affected regions  of  Sool, Sanaag, Bari, Nugal, Galgadud, Banadir and Lower Jubba regions. The proposed  intervention will provide services to 120,000 vulnerable persons affected by disasters,  including 58,000 women, 61,200 Men including 11,760  Girls and 12,240  Boys. These will include approximately  20,000 internally displaced populations,13500  individuals with different forms of disability and 200 survivors sexual and gender based violence.
The health interventions  will be aligned to the Health cluster objective  of reducing  excess morbidity and mortality due disease outbreak driven by climatic shocks and conflict among 4.7 million IDPs and non-displaced, contributing  to improvement in physical and mental wellbeing of the population affected by conflict and displacement among 4.7 million IDPs and non-displaced; including 705,000 people with disabilities, Improving equitable access to quality emergency and essential lifesaving health services for the crisis affected population to 1.2 million IDPs and 3.5 million non-displaced population and improving  case management and referral services for 235,000 Survivors of sexual or gender-based violence.
CARE emergency health services will be implemented through   static Health Facilities and  mobile outreach teams that will work closely with the District hospitals in  for referral for safe delivery services, medical cases requiring specialized services. CARE will provide outpatient consultations for both common communicable and non communicable diseases. 
 CARE-supported health facilities will provide Antenatal care, Post natal care and  free BEmONC services. Pregnant women requiring comprehensive emergency obstetric and newborn care will be referred to  District hospitals  providing CEMONC services (including cesarean sections and blood transfusions) to ensure access to timely life-saving services for mothers and neonatal babies. 
Community engagement to create awareness and behavior change will be key in the project.  SGBV (Sexual and Gender-based violence) survivors will be offered confidential CMR (clinical management of rape) services in line with WHO guidelines. CARE will assign specific staff to support person with disability and special needs. Facilities to aid patients' movement will be provided too. In light of the COVID-19 pandemic, CARE health staff will use standard IPC as outlined by WHO. In all health centers and mobile clinics , health workers will be encouraged to exercise a high level of clinical suspicion. Equipped triage stations will be at the entrance to each facility and COVID 19 preventive measures put in place. CARE will train all health workers on diseases surveillance, EPI, IMCI, MHPSS, EWARN, Sexual and reproductive health, Clinical management of rape and health information management system.  CARE will use and build capacity  with MOH Staff at field and regional level while working closely with other Partners for coordination and complementarity.

project_name: WoS Education assistance for vulnerable and out-of-school children and youth in 2022 - 2023
project_objective:
For 2022 and 2023, War Child Holland (WCH) and its consortium of six Syrian implementing partners will provide an education response to 22,000 (11,500 boys and 10,500 girls) highly vulnerable children in North West and North East Syria across a 24-month action. 100% of the sub-districts are severity 3, 4 and 5. A two-year response will support more flexible and sustainable planning.

In Idleb, WCH and its partners will operate in Dana, Harim, Maaret Tamsrin, Qorqeena, Idleb, Ariha & Badama sub-districts. In Aleppo, operations will be in, but not limited to, Al Bab, Afrin, Atareb & Daret Azza  sub-districts. In NES operations are planned, and not limited to, sub-districts of Raqqa, Kisreh, Hajin & Susa.

Recognising the interconnection between protection and education, the action will increase access to non-formal education and strengthen the protection of vulnerable girls and boys who are out of school or at risk of dropping out, to build their resilience and provide a pathway back into a safe and protective environment in school. The action will include non-formal education interventions including Accelerated Learning Program (ALP) for out of school children of the ages 5-17 who have missed more than two years of school. The action will also include guided self-learning for informal settlements with no access to learning spaces to keep children connected to learning, and for youth mainly boys who joined the working force to support their households and girls who are not sent to school and run the risk of early marriage. For schooled children with learning gaps, remedial and homework support will be offered to limit the risk of dropping out.

An effective teacher professional development through a coaching system based on INEE’s TICC and WCH’s Core program to ensure teachers’ and children’s wellbeing, will have coaches build the capacities of 400 teachers receiving incentives under the action. The coaches will be trained and supported by WCH education officer based on INEE’s TICC trainings, to help teachers obtain skills and methodologies for the creation of a safe and quality learning environment for children. For guided self-learning modality, teachers will be trained to support caregivers with guidance and tips to support their children’s learning and provide them with a safe learning environment at home. The action will adopt an integrated approach through developing the capacity of teachers on child protection and enhancing the accessibility and safety of the school environment. Teachers will be trained on safe identification and referral for CP concerns. This prevention and response approach will address immediate and urgent identified risks to access to education while contributing to long-term change.

WCH will pilot social emotional learning as an integrated approach that complements WCH’s evidence-based Deals PSS programs. Teachers will be trained to identify, and work with children to develop their life skill and learning competencies in the safe learning environment of the classroom.

To support in the removal of barriers to education, WCH through its partners will provide transportation to 250 CWD and other vulnerable children such as girls at risk of early marriage, provide cash for education to children who are out of school for economic difficulties based on vulnerability selection criteria, establish temporary learning spaces where none exists to provide a safe travel distance for children. To ensure a safe and quality learning environment, this action will include school rehabilitation with WASH facilities, light repairs, and school kits and stationery.

WCH will be conducting a needs assessment in NWS and NES in 2022 to ensure its response is appropriate to the needs of communities. An inclusion checklist will be applied to assess accessibility, meaningful participation, inclusive development, engagement of marginalised groups, representation in monitoring and evaluation activities.

project_name: MPC in WoS
project_objective:
Through the proposed intervention, World Vision Syria Response (WVSR) will target some of the most vulnerable families in Idleb, Al-Hasakeh and Ar-Raqqa through multi-purpose cash assistance including but not limited to: HHs with PLW and members at high risk of malnutrition, HH with PwD and chronic illness members, GBV, Child labor, Child marriage among others. WV will aim at supporting families to meet their most urgent Survival needs through one-off multi-purpose cash assistance (MPC) of 100 USD based on the harmonized MPC guidance. WVSR follows CWG recommendation in the design and implementation of CVA in the targeted area. The frequency of distribution, targeting, and currency used will be shaped by coordinating and aligning together with other humanitarian actors  active in the targeted area of implementation as well as engaging with the community and in involving them in decision-making around programme design and frequency of MPC distribution.
 
WVSR tends to provide cash and voucher assistance (CVA) as part of its emergency aid for the acute needs of the IDPs and host communities. CVA is intended to reduce the negative impacts created by sudden onset displacement and enable flexibility and adaptability to meet survival needs, especially for IDP populations of high mobility.
As per the recommendation of the lessons learned WV conducted about former CVA intervention in Syria, MPC has been found as the best modality to deliver emergency assistance for people with acute needs. The humanitarian community acknowledges that MPC is the best form of relief assistance where markets are functioning, accessible to beneficiaries and a reliable cash transfer mechanisms exist.
MPC emphasizes crisis-affected households’ ability to prioritize their own needs, upholding their dignity. CVA also has the additional benefit of supporting local markets and boosting the local economy.
In terms of market functionality in NWS, based on the last Syria market monitoring exercise conducted by Reach December 2021, and the regular mentoring activities WV and its implementing partners conduct to mentoring the availability and affordability of the main items. The local markets have been exceptionally resilient, accessible, and responsive throughout the crisis and are expected to remain so in the near future. The primary risks on the economy stems from the high inflation of the Syrian Pound and Turkish Lira but this weakness of local currencies is mitigated via (a) the use of U.S. Dollars in programming and (b) the use of e-value vouchers, which has the further benefit of reducing the pressure on US Dollar liquidity needs. 
Within this operational environment, WV identifies the need to use the hardest currency available in our distributions so that it preserves its purchasing power for beneficiaries. However, following area-based programming, a joint decision between the humanitarian actors on currency to be made based on cost-effectiveness and cost-efficiency and involving the local community at the area level in developing the targeting/prioritization to avoid local tension.
To ensure robust accountability towards recipients and donors, WV cash assistance will rely on its digital platform Last Mile Mobile Solution (LMMS) and LMMS E-cards to ensure accurate management of beneficiaries' data and will contract a trusted financial service provider (hawala) for the hard-cash provision in distribution points accessible and safe for both recipients and staff.
WV MEAL department will monitor local markets pre- and post-project implementation to ensure the functionality of local markets as well as being present during the distribution to ensure regularity of operations and will conduct a post-distribution monitoring PDM exercise to assess the use of cash. For the PDM exercise, WVSR adheres to the usage of the harmonized PDM tool developed by the CWG. A complaint and feedback mechanism will be in place and will allow WV to promptly address recipients feedback.

project_name: GBV & PSEA support for women, girls and individuals at risk in Beirut & North Lebanon
project_objective:
The intervention will focus on strengthening the protection environment for GBV survivors and individuals at risk in Beirut and North Lebanon, through GBV prevention activities and response services as well as the provision of capacity-building to national partners and actors, currently implementing multi-sectoral humanitarian and development programs, across the country.

CARE will work jointly with Abaad and the Lebanese Democratic Women Gathering (RDFL) as best placed national actors with a track record of implementing GBV and PSEA activities. Those two actors were selected thank to a thorough selection process, with three different CARE staff + the Partnership Manager, according to a matrix document.

This project will target women and girls, survivors of GBV and/or at high risk, as well as individuals from the most marginalized communities, including vulnerable Lebanese and refugee populations, in addition to migrant communities, who remain a severely underserved group extensively exposed of violence and exploitation. Particular attention will be given to People with Disabilities, ensuring unhindered, accessible and quality services.

The intervention will build on the existing work conducted by CARE and ABAAD and supported by OCHA in 2020 and 2021 through the first LHF standard allocation, in coordination with the PSEA network, as well as the work conducted by CARE under the Empowered Aid project, in partnership with George Washington University’s Global Women Institute and URDA in Lebanon. Coordination with the PSEA network, along with humanitarian actors in the country will be sustained and further enhanced to ensure unified messaging and proper mainstreaming of PSEA across sectors.

Requests and need for capacity-building and system strengthening are still high and relevant, and this intervention will contribute to fill the gap in a comprehensive and sustainable approach.

project_name: L'amélioration du système d’administration, de la Gestion et de la Coordination pour une réponse effective dans les sites des PDIs dans la province du Lac
project_objective:
Une combinaison de conflits, d'instabilité régionale, de dégradation des ressources naturelles et des effets du changement climatique a entraîné une crise prolongée et une grande fragilité dans plusieurs régions du Tchad.
La région du lac compte 406,573 Personnes Déplacées Internes. Cette province continue d’enregistrer de nouvelles personnes en déplacement forcé à la suite des attaques de GANE.
Les possibilités de retour des PDI sont faibles en raison de l’insécurité, des attaques répétées et des violences dans les zones d’origine. Les perspectives de solutions durables, dont le retour dans la sécurité et la dignité ainsi qu’un accompagnement pour une réintégration, ne semblent pas être envisageables dans un proche avenir et il est urgent d’améliorer le système d’Administration, de Gestion et de la Coordination pour une réponse effective dans les sites des IDPs dans la province du Lac.
La base de la réponse dans le système de cluster au Lac reposerait sur le CCCM qui doit en temps utile s’assurer de la gestion l’information, de faire le Plaidoyer, renforcer le Partenariats et coordination, Participer les acteurs et les bénéficiaires dans la réponse, Surveiller et collecte de données,  Prestation de services techniques, Sécurité et documentation.
Selon DTM Round 16, il y a 166 sites et 57 villages d’hôtes dans la province du Lac. Cependant, il y a seulement 3 administrateurs et 5 gestionnaires dans la province du Lac pour gérer, administrer et coordonner 223 sites et villages 
Pour résoudre les problèmes du manque d’information actuelle et la manque de capacité de collecter l’information et de suivre l’assistance, dans ce projet, nous allons établir les cartographies des sites, enregistrer les bénéficiaires avec les 30 administrateurs, 30 gestionnaires et 01 coordinateur de site.

project_name: Consolidation des sites des déplacés internes dans le cadre CCCM dans la province du Lac
project_objective:
Une combinaison de conflits, d'instabilité régionale, de dégradation des ressources naturelles et des effets du changement climatique a entraîné une crise prolongée et une grande fragilité dans plusieurs régions du Tchad.
La région du lac compte 406,573 Personnes Déplacées Internes. Cette province continue d’enregistrer de nouvelles personnes en déplacement forcé à la suite des attaques de GANE.
Les possibilités de retour des PDI sont faibles en raison de l’insécurité, des attaques répétées et des violences dans les zones d’origine. Les perspectives de solutions durables, dont le retour dans la sécurité et la dignité ainsi qu’un accompagnement pour une réintégration, ne semblent pas être envisageables dans un proche avenir.
Des facteurs d’ordre sécuritaire et opérationnel limitent l’accès des services gouvernementaux et des humanitaires aux personnes affectées pour leur garantir protection et assistance. Les mesures de sécurité prises par le gouvernement, les inondations, l’utilisation des mines et engins explosifs improvisés et le risque que les humanitaires puissent être pris pour cible par les GANE constituent des facteurs limitatifs.
Cet état de fait rend difficile le devoir du HCR d’assurer la centralité de la protection internationale à travers le monitoring, le référencement, l’administration, la gestion et la coordination de l’assistance dans tous les sites.
Ce projet de la consolidation des sites en objet permettra une meilleure sécurité, meilleure accessibilité par la communauté humanitaire et la visibilité de la réponse apportée, en évitant le risque de catastrophes naturelles. Il s’agit d’un projet pilote qui portera sur trois sites de consolidation soit un site par département de la province du Lac et touchera une population totale de 50,000 personnes.
Le projet s’inscrit dans la perspective de la villagisation et du nexus humanitaire-développement.

project_name: Provision of life saving shelter and Non - food items assistance to IDPs and non- displaced drought affected population in Oromia and Somalia Regions.
project_objective:
Natural hazards such as flood and drought remain the main factors impacting people’s lives and livelihoods. The prolonged drought resulting from three consecutive failed rainy reasons since late 2020 has affected the lives of millions people living in Oromia, SNNP, Somali and Southwest regions. Natural hazards such as floods but most notably the drought in the southern part of the country makes the main drivers of needs. UNHCR, through harmonizing  its IDP response with the Cluster system, the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP), the Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO), the Sustainable Development Goals, the Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement (1999) and the Kampala Convention (2009) planes to respond to need of drought affected population in Somali, Oromia and SNNP regions. 
Recognizing that contexts across the region is volatile with unique needs per location, UNHCR Shelter and Non- food item response is planned to address the needs of people in all phases of displacement, with a focus on the emergency phase, care, and maintenance of shelter for people in protracted displacements and supporting sustainable returns and recovery where the context allows. The planned interventions include consideration of shelter preparedness, response, and shelter recovery support to account for both returns and secondary displacement and will be conducted in close coordination with multi-sectoral stakeholders to ensure that approaches are integrated, and that broader needs are addressed. Holding the protection of affected populations at its core: Do no harm principles incl. prioritizing health, privacy, safety, and dignity, accountability, management of expectations, adequate targeting, ensuring meaningful access to affected populations, participation and empowerment of affected people, enhancing resilience, coordination, and context-driven responses will be mainstreamed throughout our responses as per the ESNFI cluster strategy.  Through this interventions, including provision of in-kind assistance and cash when feasible, UNHCR planes to reach 50,048 HH (250,241 Individuals) across the three regions through the below responses.

•	Emergency Shelters (Communal, family shelters or Emergency Shelter kits) provision 
•	Non Food Items and ESNFI provision

In addition, capacity building of staff, authorities, affected populations and advocacy for those with shelter and household needs will also be considered. All the ES/NFIs component will be undertaken in consultation with the IDPs and host communities to ensure it meets their most urgent needs. The IDP hosting communities will also benefit from the responses. As per the cluster guideline 10-15% of the vulnerable communities hosting IDPs will be targeted.

To reduce risk and mitigate Sexual and Gender-Based Violence (SGBV) associated with shelter and NFI responses, UNHCR will conduct awareness-raising sessions to ensure that the communities are made aware of the protection risks in shelter and NFI response and how best to mitigate them. UNHCR will continue to use IASC GBV guidelines & related tools for SEA risk assessment and mitigation, including its newly developed GBV policy guidelines, National Action Plan and victim centered approach for addressing sexual misconduct to ensure accessibility to all women, girls and other at risk group.

As an effort to enhance inclusive humanitarian action principles, UNHCR will also provide awareness-raising and training of those at the forefront of service delivery and from the overall target reserving a minimum 15% of kits (tailor made for disables) to be allocated to households with family members with disabilities

project_name: Protection and response through camp coordination and camp management
project_objective:
UNHCR’s CCCM activities are aimed at enhancing the protection and response of displaced population through camp coordination and camp management activities. UNHCR will target 500,000 including displaced IDPs, vulnerable  host community and returnees living in informal and self-settled sites across 21 districts in Somalia which includes: Kismayu, Afmadow, Dhobley Luuq, Belethawa, Baidoa, Diinsor, Kahda, Daynile, Beletweyn, Jowhar Dhusamareb, Guri’el, Adado, Abudwak, Galkayo, Garowe, Gardo, Bossaso, Hargeisa and Berbera. 

According to Somalia’s Humanitarian Needs Overview, conflicts, recurrent climate shocks, disease outbreaks and increasing poverty are devastating largely the already poor urban and other host community members and also internally displaced populations.  Despite progress made in recent years, the impacts of these shocks continue to affect the living conditions of some 2.2 million displaced people who are already in sub-standard living conditions as they continue to reside in informal settlements or camp-like settings.

As per the detailed site assessment findings (DSA) and site verification assessments conducted by the CCCM cluster, more than 80% of sites are informal settlements established on private land with the majority of sites located in urban areas. The lack of access to land coupled with a weak land tenure system, multiplicity of land ownership, lack of adequate land disputes systems, weak judicial systems to seek redress, and a lack of proper national land policy further exacerbates the vulnerability of IDPs. This has led to frequent incidents of forceful evictions pushing IDPs into worsened situations requiring both emergency and prolonged assistance.  IDP returns are extremely limited as many displaced families have lost livelihoods and are reliant on humanitarian services. 

In addition, (REACH, JMCNA) indicate 11% of all IDPs in Somalia are classified as currently at risk of being evicted from their shelters due to lack of land tenure security therefore UNHCR through inter-cluster efforts of both the Protection and the CCCM clusters will continue to advocate on prevention of evictions and to ensure that displaced populations have access to a dignified relocation where necessary. 
The living conditions in IDP sites across Somalia are challenging due to lack of sufficient services that meet minimum standards and according to joint multisectoral assessment conducted indicate that majority of IDPs cannot receive humanitarian service because of existing service gaps. 
Aligned to the Centrality of Protection strategy, UNHCR will ensure that gender empowerment and meaningful inclusion for minority groups, people with disabilities, age and gender is mainstreamed across all its activities. UNHCR will work closely with leaders from minority and marginalized groups to ensure fair and equal representation in the governance structures at the IDP sites. The project will also ensure women, girls, youths and elderly persons are well represented and are taking part in decision-making process within IDP sites. 

Through enhanced Risk and Community Engagement strategies such as Communication with Communities, UNHCR co-lead CCCM will ensure PoCs have access to information about different humanitarian services available within the site hence closing the gap between the community and service providers. UNHCR will ensure that IDP communities have access to reliable and updated COVID-19 information through applying MoH/WHO RCCE contents alongside ensuring maintenance of other CCCM mechanism including Complaint Feedback and Response Mechanism (CFRM), service monitoring, community participation through camp committees, safety audits and site improvement and maintenance activities among others

project_name: Programme de prévention de la malnutrition chronique
project_objective:
Contexte:
Le Plan stratégique du PAM au Mali pour la période 2020-2024 met un focus très marqué sur le renforcement de la résilience des populations vulnérables sujettes à de multiples chocs. 
Bien que ce plan se concentre principalement sur l'assistance humanitaire et la réponse aux crises, le PAM s’aligne à la stratégie de résilience du Sahel en Partenariat avec le BMZ, l’UNICEF, la FAO et d’autres partenaires pour renforcer, accélérer et intensifier la résilience des ménages et des communautés vulnérables locaux, et déplacés. Pour réaliser un changement transformationnel et renforcer la résilience des individus, des ménages, des communautés et des systèmes, le PAM investit dans les moyens de subsistance, la santé, l'éducation et à la création de revenus. Avec un réseau de 24 ONGs et des structures gouvernementales en charge de ces secteurs, le PAM a commencé la mise en œuvre d'un ensemble intégré d'activités dans 59 sites réparties dans 5 régions du Mali pour toute la période couvrant son plan stratégique pays.
Initié depuis deux ans, beaucoup de réalisations et d’acquis ont été enregistrés durant la mise en œuvre du programme de résilience, il s’agit notamment de :
-	La mise en place d’actifs productifs destinés au renforcement des systèmes de production agricole des communautés, à la restauration des environnements dégradés, à la réhabilitation ou construction des ouvrages de maitrise d’eau, à l’aménagement de périmètre de production etc.
-	Les transferts des ressources (cash et vivres) permettant aux communautés bénéficiaires de participer aux travaux de création d’actifs tout en garantissant leurs besoins immédiats de sécurité alimentaire
-	L’appui à de petits exploitants agricoles en les structurant, en équipements de transformation et de stockage, à réduire leur perte post récolte, à la transformation agroalimentaire et à l’accès au marché qui a permis une production de céréales et légumes de bonne qualité, un développement des chaines de valeur. Ces produits sont plus facilement écoulés sur les marchés 
-	L’investissement dans le développement du capital humain à travers des interventions nutritionnelles pour la prévention et le traitement de la malnutrition chez les enfants mais également l’amélioration des conditions d’apprentissage des élèves dans les écoles situées dans les localités ciblées par le programme.
-	Au renforcement des capacités des ménages et individus à travers les formations, les visites d’échanges d’expérience, la fourniture des articles non alimentaires

Objectif:
- Renforcer la résilience des communautés vulnérables à travers l’amélioration de l’accès à des moyens de subsistance, aux aliments à haute valeur nutritive et l’adoption de pratiques familiales favorables à la santé et la nutrition.
-Améliorer l’accès aux aliments à haute valeur nutritive pour les communautés plus précisément les enfants âgés de 6 à 59 mois et les femmes enceintes et allaitantes vivant dans l’aire des sites de convergence ;
Améliorer l’accès aux services complémentaires tels que la supplémentation en vitamine A, le déparasitage, la vaccination chez les enfants âgés de 6 à 59 mois et les femmes enceintes et allaitantes vivant dans l’aire des sites de convergence ;
-Renforcer les capacités des communautés sur la mise en œuvre des initiatives visant à valoriser des produits locaux à haute valeur nutritive au niveau local et les techniques de transformation et de conservation des produits de l’élevage et du maraichage;

Zones d'intervention: Tombouctou, Gao, Menaka, Mopti, Segou, Kayes et Koulikoro

project_name: Strengthening EPI program in Syria and protect against outbreaks of Deadly Vaccine Preventable diseases
project_objective:
After more than 10 years of conflict in Syria, the Routine Immunization program was affected, subsequently, children suffered outbreaks of Polio and Measles during the course of the years. Strengthening routine vaccination activities is still an essential concern to increase the national coverage rate at national and governorate level, regular routine immunization activities are provided in all governorates, the vaccination activities are continued in coordination with all related partners (including UNICEF and NGOs) to cover the needs of children under 5 and to increase the community immunity especially among all vulnerable groups , WHO has facilitated the delivery of vaccines( by road& Air ) to all governorates in addition to support the operational cost of the filed work including: transportation cost, incentives for mobile teams , operation cost , which will facilitate the field work of the EPI program at national, governorates and district level. Capacity building will be provided to the healthcare workers and managers involved in the reporting, planning, implementation, and monitoring of the immunization activities. MOH is providing vaccination services to all children of Syria (target 2022 is 584282 children under the age of 1 year) in all 14 governorates. Several tactics are used for service delivery through fixed vaccination sites and mobile teams as well in coordination with the local communities to facilitate the access for the families and service providers; WHO and partners support in the coordination, technical and financial support of the activities including the IPC material procurement and cascade training for service providers and supervisors’ capacity building for quality services and gain community trust as well.

In northwest Syria, WHO supported re-establishment of EPI services, and has increased the number of active vaccinations centers from five in March 2017 to 93 in 2021. WHO supports the operational costs of 40 of these centers, covering 62 of a total of 134 vaccination teams. This work has been impeded by security issues leading to huge population movements at the beginning of 2020 and loss of accessibility to some areas. The latter issue necessitated the reallocation of 23 EPI centers to new areas to serve displaced populations inside NWS. 
Within the implementation of this HRP project WHO in cooperation with Syria Immunization group (SIG) and in close collaboration with UNICEF and other NGOs/INGOs actors in the north of Syria is planning to sustain services of the Expanded Program on Immunization EPI in the NWS, including routine re-mapping of communities and new settlements to be able to follow population movements inside the country. The routine Immunization program is targeting children under two years of age with the following antigen: BCG, Hep B 0, OPV, IPV, Penta, MMR. Also, the children in school-age (first & sixth grades) and females in childbearing age CBA (15-49) with Td vaccine especially pregnant women.

project_name: Improving food and nutritional security of vulnerable IDPs and host population in the North West and South West regions of Cameroon.
project_objective:
Cadre Harmonisé” results conducted in Cameroon in October 2021 showed that 1,154,661 people in the North-West and South-West regions are food and nutritionally insecure (crisis to emergency phases) that is, 755,959 and 398,702 people in the North West and South West regions respectively. With 21% increase in food insecure estimates compared to October 2020. 9 Divisions out of 13 are classified as phase 3, Donga Mantung, Bui, Kupé Manenguba and Fako divisions are all classified in phase 2. With continuous humanitarian aid, anticipated peace and next agricultural season running good, it is expected that the number of people suffering from food insecurity would have decreased by March 2022 farming season but remains very worrying. Moreover, the current conflict has plunged the North West and South West regions into a drastic slowdown of economic activities in general, and agro pastoral production in particular

Due to the multiple killings, theft of livestock, destruction of crops and kidnappings perpetrated in rural and urban areas, and with all the trauma associated, many rural workers have left their homelands in search of more peaceful space. The massive shifts in productive workforce has implications not only for the loss of jobs for rural workers, but also on the scarcity of local agro-pastoral products thus an increase in food insecurity and malnutrition of these families. In the current global logic of achieving the sustainable development goals, appropriate humanitarian actions are to be taken into consideration in order to facilitate access to productive assets, preserve livelihoods, combat malnutrition, protect those affected and keep the interest and voice of vulnerable people and to achieve the highest standards of the human rights, especially for women and children.
The unexpected outbreak of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus has spread rapidly across the world, devastating lives and livelihoods. In March 6, 2020 the first case of COVID19 pandemic in Cameroon was declared.  As of November 24, 2021, the number of cases had increased to more than 100 000, with 1795 deaths, indicating an exponential growth in the number of cases. The full impact of the virus on food security is not yet fully known. However, it is clear that the direct and indirect effects of COVID-19 is already having significant negative effects on food supply chains, from producers to processors, marketers, transporters and consumers (FAO, 2020). With the COVID 19 pandemic, it is anticipated that nearly seven million more children across the world will suffer from malnutrition, many in Africa (UNICEF, 2020). This might worsen the situation of communities affected by crisis who are already food insecure.
The proposed one-year intervention will contribute to improving food and nutrition security and reducing the vulnerability of crisis-affected IDPs and host communities in the North West and South West regions of Cameroon, especially women, men and children, through the provision of agricultural support. Specifically, the intervention aimed at (i) increase access and utilization of diverse and nutritious vegetables, (ii) increase access and consumption of eggs, (iii) increase access and utilization of mushrooms, (iv) increase access and utilization of snails.

project_name: Light infrastructure rehabilitation and efficient use of water (irrigation canals, wells and irrigation systems).
project_objective:
Overall, the Food Security Sector (FSS) estimates that 12 million people in Syria are facing acute food insecurity, which is at least 55.3% of Syria population. While the food insecure figures have slightly declined by at least 4% compared to last year’s record increase, the number of people facing acute food insecurity remains extremely high and 51% higher than in 2019, pre-Lebanese financial crisis period and before the COVID-19 outbreak. Moreover, drought-like conditions in Syria are affecting agriculture production capacity, thus affecting farmer’s livelihoods and local food production.  In this context, FAO has designed a project to assist 240, 000 small-scale farming households (equivalent to 1,440,000 people) in Syria, with the objective of protecting and enhancing the livelihoods of vulnerable farmers and IDPs through the restoration of critical irrigation infrastructures and improve water use efficiency to increase household food production and food security. 
. The project outputs include:
•	Output 1: Critical small-scale irrigation infrastructures in the targeted governorates are assessed and light rehabilitation undertaken. 
•	Output 2: Capacity of technical staff and relevant stakeholders including farmers strengthened to increase water use efficiency and establishment of Water Users Associations (WUAs)
A training programme on enhancing irrigation management, water use efficiency in small-scale irrigation, agricultural land management will be based on FAO standards and approaches. It is expected that stakeholders and farmers will participate in the proposed trainings. 
This project is expected to contribute to increasing access to irrigation water for crisis-affected farmers and their families in the targeted areas through the light rehabilitation of critical small scale irrigation infrastructure. Crop cultivation and other agricultural practices, including livestock and animal feed production, will consequently benefit from the improved water supply plans as an emergency response to the prevailing crisis and drought-like conditions. The proposed intervention will strengthen household food production capacities, skills and knowledge and address immediate food security and nutrition needs, through increasing local availability and supply of food. This may in turn promote flourishing of agricultural based livelihoods in the targeted rural communities, which would contribute to social cohesion, peace and stability. The project seeks to utilize intensive labour in order to maximize community participation and inject cash into the local community.

project_name: Increased access to primary healthcare in Akkar
project_objective:
Decades of poor governance, harmful monetary policies, corruption, and political instability have led to the most severe economic and financial crisis in Lebanon's modern history. Poverty rates have soared amongst Lebanese, migrants and members of the refugee community. Imports of goods, including essential goods such as fuel, wheat, and medication are at their lowest levels due to the government’s shortage of USD and the massive spending on subsidies which are set to be stopped at any time. The economic crisis has extended to the health sector in Lebanon leading to decreased access to, and availability of, critical emergency health services, and essential medicines. The situation in Lebanon has also impacted the mental wellbeing of many across the Lebanese territory.
Due to multiple crises, the health institutions in most of the governorates have become unable to provide essential health services to vulnerable people in need. An IRC health feasibility assessment, done in November-December 2020 and still relevant today, identified the imminent need for primary health care and mental health services. This assessment was followed by field assessments and focus discussion groups to design a response. Findings show how the multiple crises affecting Lebanon have impacted routine immunization coverage for children; this was highlighted and confirmed by the Ministry of Public Health (MoPH).  Additionally, the continuity of electricity to PHC centers has been impacted, affecting the vaccine cold chain. 
In the proposed project, the International Rescue Committee (IRC) will contribute significantly to prevention of preventable morbidity and mortality rates which have been on the rise due to the health care system’s collapse. IRC, in coordination with health partners in Lebanon including the MoPH, Primary Health Care Department, National Mental Health Program, UN agencies and NGOs will focus activities on institutional capacity building enabling the MoPH to provide responsive Primary Health Care and Mental Health services. 
Proposed activities will focus on meeting the needs of the vulnerable population groups, specifically Lebanese and migrants, across Lebanon and will include support with essential medicines, cold chain, extended PHC hours, health messaging and protection efforts.  The project will also deploy outreach volunteers from the targeted communities to help with the awareness raising and referral guidance.
Through this project, IRC will support three health facilities with improved access serving beneficiaries with extended hours; provide quality, essential medicines and medical supplies, support three health facilities to ensure cold chain for non-COVID vaccines; reach 9,000 people with integrated and accessible health messaging through outreach volunteers and community health workers; and support 12 outreach workers. Community health workers will be linked to health facilities and will visit the communities where they will supervise the outreach volunteers and ensure proper referrals. 
IRC will select PHCCs that are part of the MoPH PHC network, are not supported by any other INGO, and who serve a vulnerable catchment area with large migrant and Lebanese populations. Contracts with the selected PHCCs and NGO’s will be finalized once the funds are secured. IRC has started looking for international procurement options for the procurement of medicines and the national and regional IRC supply chain staff are working with MOPH to ensure compliance.

project_name: Promote an inclusive and protective humanitarian response in Cameroon
project_objective:
IRC will implement a project that will aim at 1- Reinforce the centrality of Protection in Cameroon through support to the Protection Cluster and Humanitarian actors to mainstream protection, support coordination of specialized protection services, and deliver programs that mitigate and respond to protection risks and incidents in the Far North and 2-responding to GBV priority needs in the Far North region of Cameroon through prevention and response activities. Protection mainstreaming is the first layer needed to achieve the Centrality of Protection, ensuring that a beneficiary in any humanitarian sector can safely access humanitarian assistance without being at risk of harm (outcome 1). In addition to being responsible for placing protection at the center of the humanitarian response in Cameroon, along with the Humanitarian Coordinator, Humanitarian Country Team, and Cluster Coordinators, the Protection Cluster is further responsible to ensure that humanitarian actors develop protection strategies, mainstream protection in their interventions (across sectors), and coordinate specialized protection services for affected populations (outcome 1).
The Centrality of protection is also ensured through the delivery of programs that are based on analysis, identifying who are the most at-need and why, and through joint efforts (and ideally integrated interventions), to respond to those needs while also ensuring the safety and well-being of people (outcome 2).

project_name: INCLUSIVE AND SAFE EDUCATION FOR IDPs AND HOST COMMUNITY CHILDREN IN CAMEROON.
project_objective:
The prevalence of the socio-political crisis within the North West and South West regions of Cameroon has brought the inhabitants of both regions face-to-face with the realities of insecurity, extreme hunger, extreme GBV, destruction of property and sources of livelihood as well as an ever-increasing death toll. In effect, the socio-political crisis has resulted in mass exodus from both regions into the more stable regions of Littoral and the West. According to UNHCR’s locations of persons of concern December 2020 report, both the West and Littoral regions host over 75,000 IDPs each  (a figure that has considerably swelled in 2021 following prolonged instability in both crisis regions). Added to the 711,056 IDPs reported by UNHCR as of January 2021 from both the North West and South West are 321,886 IDP s from the crisis hit Far North region of the country, bringing the total number of displaced persons within the country to a whooping 1,032,942 people within the country. 
This massive displaced population is inclusive of children and other youths of school going age who present as vulnerable education seekers in their host communities, forcing educational institutions to morph into structures that can effectively accommodate this massive influx of students. This has seen the creation and/or upgrade of unilingual French schools into Bilingual schools capable of meeting the needs of the English-speaking immigrants. However, this upgrade is most often not accompanied by relevant structural and human resource upgrade in these facilities, resulting in increased pressure on the available educational resources and poor service delivery to both host community children and IDPs. 
Many IDP children of school going age are unable to access education due to a wide spectrum of hindrances inclusive of financial, social and language barriers. For IDP students who actually make it into schools, language barriers, unresolved trauma, PTSD, insensitivity of both students and instructors, accompanied by adaptation pressures make knowledge acquisition very difficult for these students. This is due to the fact that schools lack the appropriate institutional resources (structural and human) to meet the needs of these IDP students coming in from the crisis zones and living in relatively unstable (both physical and mentally) homes. Little attention is placed on the psychological needs, and even less is made towards easing the adaptation process in view of enhancing language acquisition processes, and allocation of any form financial and material viability. Against this backdrop, effective realization of education for IDP children is next to impossible.  
In view of bettering the position held by IDP children within host communities in the French regions, there is a need to enhance the structures, mechanism and processes put in place to realize the education of IDP children with respect to building capacity and development/implementation of research/evident based approaches for effective realization of IDP children education. In this regard, a cataloguing of all necessary direct stakeholders (inclusive of educational institutions, PTAs , relevant governmental/non-governmental bodies and other community led initiatives) and development of a harmonized approach to the position held by IDP children, as well as capacity enhancement initiatives for local educational institutions are vital. It is for these reasons that the project was developed to realize inclusive and safe academic environments for IDP and host community children within the Littoral and West region.

project_name: Emmergency Food Security and Livelihood Support for Crises-affected and Vulnerable Populations in Sudan.
project_objective:
Sudan  continues to face a number of shocks, complex socio-economic crises and complex transitional political challenges that threaten the lives and livelihoods of the population. A combination of political and economic crisis, conflict, natural disasters and COVID-19 have left millions of people vulnerable, at risk of food insecurity, malnutrition, disease, morbidity and therefore requiring urgent humanitarian support to save lives, protect assets and livelihoods. According to the Humanitarian Needs of Overview (HNO), at least some 9.8 Million people will need food assistance within the coming year. 

This project will respond to critical life sustaining, resilience and early recovery needs by restoring food and livelihood security of over 100,000 most vulnerable populations including IDPs, returnees, vulnerable host community members and impacting other groups of concern including refugees. The overall objective of the project is to restore food and livelihood security of both displaced population and vulnerable host communities across 11 States in Sudan.
It will focus on agricultural support, livestock Support, livelihood cash and voucher support using Cash for Work modality for the restoration of critical community-based and productive assets whilst providing temporary and urgent labor-intensive employment opportunities. It will also support the provision of livelihood and income generation kits as well as vocational, skills and entrepreneurship training.
UNDP will work in close partnership with FAO, using area-based approach to deliver assistance by harnessing the combined collaborative technical advantage and the wide reach of the two organizations across Sudan.

project_name: Mon corps n’est pas un fonds de commerce
project_objective:
Le « Projet - Mon corps n’est pas un fonds de commerce » - Protection des filles et garçons contre l’exploitation sexuelle des enfants à des fins commerciales (ESEC) aves ses axes d’intervention directe et de renforcement du système de Protection a vocation à contribuer à la promotion des droits et la protection des filles et garçons y compris ceux en situation de handicap contre toute forme de Violence, Abus, Exploitation et de négligence (VAEN) dans les milieux familiaux, communautaires et éducatifs "". Prévue pour une durée d'un an renouvelable, l’intervention s’attaque à une des problématiques importantes de protection des enfants au Mali à savoir l’exploitation sexuelle des enfants à des fins commerciales. Le projet sera mis en œuvre dans 20 communes des régions de Ségou et Kayes et le district de Bamako et s’adressera à la protection des enfants les plus vulnérables à savoir les filles travailleuses domestiques, les filles et garçons travaillant dans les sites d’orpaillages, les enfants des quartiers précaires, les scolaires et non scolaires, les enfants en mobilité, les enfants en situation de handicap contre l’exploitation sexuelle. 
Malgré le fait que les filles soient beaucoup plus victimes que les garçons 93,4% contre 6,5% (étude qualitative et quantitative de Ecpact de 2014), la question de l’exploitation sexuelle intéresse tous les deux sexes à ce jour avec une accentuation de la question dû à l’accès démesuré et incontrôlé des adolescentes et adolescents aux réseaux sociaux.   
Ainsi, pour plus d’efficacité, l’intervention fournira une réponse adéquate et adaptée aux besoins des enfants à risque ou victimes d’exploitation sexuelle par la mise en place et/ou le renforcement des dispositifs d’accompagnement protecteur pour la prévention et la réponse.
Avec une implication de l’ensemble des acteurs impliqués dans la protection de l’enfant notamment les titulaires d‘obligation, les titulaires de responsabilités et les détenteurs de droits eux-mêmes, le programme s’exécute à travers 3 axes principaux à savoir :
-	La prévention de l’exploitation sexuelle : elle se fera avec le concours de l’ensemble des acteurs de protection. Les enfants en tant qu’acteurs de leurs propres protections seront les vecteurs de transmissions des messages de sensibilisation. De fortes actions de paires éducations seront développées à ce niveau en milieux scolaires et communautaires pour mieux capaciter les enfants à s’autoprotéger contre l’exploitation sexuelle. Les communautés participeront également à ces actions de sensibilisation.
-	L’accompagnement social personnalisé des enfants à risque ou victimes d’exploitation sexuelle: pour une réponse coordonnée , adaptée aux besoins des enfants à risque ou victimes d’exploitation sexuelle, les enfants, les acteurs institutionnels et les acteurs communautaires travailleront de façon synergique afin que les enfants soient détectés, référés et pris en charge, accompagnés et réintégrés dans la détermination de leur intérêt supérieur et avec leur participation et celle de leur famille.
-	Le plaidoyer et la communication se feront pour le renforcement du cadre juridique, politique et programmatique de protection des enfants contre l’exploitation sexuelle avec une forte implication des enfants.
Ces actions développées avec l’ensemble des titulaires de droits, d’obligations et de responsabilité permettront de renforcer d’une part la réponse communautaire, la réponse nutritionnelle et l’articulation entre ces réponses dans la lutte contre l’exploitation sexuelle au Mali.

project_name: Prevention and Response Interventions to Survivors of Gender Based Violence and Sexual Exploitation and abuse (SEA) in Somalia
project_objective:
Boys and girls continue to endure multiple protection risks such as family separation, sexual and gender-based violence (GBV), child recruitment, mental and psychosocial distress.
Preliminary findings of a UNICEF study on drivers of child recruitment show that Al-Shabaab explicitly targets children through forced recruitment and abduction. Rape and sexual violence remain a threat to children’s survival. Sexual violence increased by 35% when compared to the same period last year.
This project would like to respond first to the problems of sexual exploitation and abuse present in all emergency interventions. UNICEF has carried out an in-country assessment on SEA, and the biggest gap is the establishment of safe complaints mechanisms available to communities.
Secondly the project will address the root causes of GBV in Emergencies through evidence based social norm change programmes; mitigates the risk of GBV occurring in camp and IDP concentration points; and provides multi-sectoral services to survivors of GBV. The three core components of the programme will be implemented in key accessible areas of Somalia in all Federal Member states and engages UNICEF's network of civil society partners who will continue to benefit from capacity building support delivered through UNICEF's local, regional, international team of GBV experts. The purpose of the project is to ensure continued expansion of lifesaving services whilst at the same time undermining the structural causes of GBV. Women, girls and boys accessing GBV risk mitigation, prevention through targeted norm change activities  and response ; Men, women, boys and girls can access a safe complaints mechanism; we will improve the safety of IDP camps and concentration points decreasing the likelihood of SGBV for more than 1 million displaced people;

project_name: renforcement du système de protection de l’enfance et de redevabilité sociale à l’égard des enfants
project_objective:
SC garantira une protection et des soins appropriés aux enfants vulnérables, y compris les enfants victimes de violences basées sur le genre, les enfants séparés / non accompagnés, grâce à l'identification et à la gestion des cas, la prise en charge psychosociale en fonction de leurs besoins spécifiques en respectant le principe de l’intérêt supérieur de l’enfant. Le système de référencement et contre référencement sera renforcé par la mise à jour de la cartographie des services de protection disponibles.  SC s’attèlera également en priorité à une réunification rapide des enfants séparés de leurs parents/tuteurs habituels. Les enfants qui sont dans l’incapacité de se réunir avec leurs familles/ tutrices l’approche communautaire sera privilégiée pour la prise en charge de ces enfants surtout les rapatriés dans des familles d’accueil déjà identifiées qui seront renforcées en compétences parentales positives et devront bénéficier d’un soutien matériel.   

Concernant les survivant des GBV, l’action respectera les principes des survivants : Droit à la sécurité, droit à la confidentialité, droit à la dignité et à l’autodétermination et droit à la non-discrimination. 
 Un modèle multisectoriel, à travers une approche de gestion des cas, sera utilisé pour assurer des interventions holistiques qui impliquent une collaboration et une coordination inter institutions entre les secteurs clés, y compris, les domaines psychosociaux, de la santé, juridique etc. Cette réponse se traduira par un renforcement de la résilience et des mécanismes d'adaptation positifs pour les survivants de la violence sexuelle et sexiste qui doivent se réintégrer dans leur communauté.
 Le projet devra mettre en place des actions/activités qui permettent d’éviter que les actes de violence contre les enfants ne se produisent. Les actions de prévention consistent principalement à la diffusion, par le biais de la communication sociale, de messages de sensibilisation et conscientisation sur les diverses formes de violence à l’égard de l’enfant, sur ses conséquences et sur les comportements à adopter pour la prévenir. Pour répondre aux violations des droits des enfants, les assistants de protection seront renforcés sur la gestion des cas suivant l’approche de Save the Children « Step to Protect » qui comprend une série d'étapes comprenant : l'identification et le screening initial, l'évaluation, la planification de la prise en charge, la mise en œuvre, la revue du dossier et enfin la clôture du dossier
A cote de la gestion des cas les assistants communautaires de protection seront renforcés sur la prise en charge psychosociale qui est un élément fondamental de l’assistance, la prise en charge psychosociale fait référence à l’accompagnement par les travailleurs sociaux de l’enfant et de sa famille dans le but de normaliser son état émotionnel, ses relations familiales et son intégration dans la communauté
En rapport avec la prise en charge l’action renforcera le système de référencement et contre référencement. 
Des réunions de coordination seront organisées pour coordonner les interventions des acteurs clés de protection des enfants. Des réunions régulières sont nécessaires pour que le système local de protection de l’enfant fonctionne.

project_name: Albergues protectores para la atención de la niñez y sus familias en emergencia.
project_objective:
Actualmente El Salvador ha enfrentado múltiples eventos, que han venido provocando daños en los hogares y comunidades debido a desastres naturales a causa del cambio climático, violencia social, y otros tipos crisis humanitarias derivadas por la pandemia dela COVID-19 y por los flujos mixtos (desplazamiento interno o transfronterizo por violencia, caravanas, migrantes extrarregionales en tránsito y retornos). El año 2020, la tormenta tropical Amanda afectó a 10 de los 14 departamentos de El Salvador. Los daños más extendidos fueron en los departamentos de Ahuachapán, La Libertad, San Salvador y Usulután, cientos de personas fueron evacuadas a albergues temporales; en noviembre 2020, con la degradación IOTA, causó constantes lluvias en todo el territorio del país. Como respuesta a estas emergencias, se habilitaron espacios como albergues para brindar a la población resguardo temporales y seguros; en razón de ello es importante, contar con insumos que permitan atender a la población en mención. Debido a que las condiciones de los albergues no siempre cuentan con las condiciones seguras y necesarias para la atención de personas en un momento de emergencia, es necesario proveer y adecuar espacios seguros y con insumos que aseguren a las niñas, niños adolescentes, mujeres y hombres, condiciones con estándares internacionales, para asegurar el bienestar de las personas afectadas por estas emergencias. 

El proyecto Albergues protectores para la atención de la niñez y sus familias en emergencia, contribuirá a fortalecer los mecanismos de coordinación y gestión de albergues que permitan una atención inmediata para contar con albergues que cumplen estándares internacionales de protección, salud, alimentación, educación, seguridad y otros. El proyecto ha sido diseñado para una implementación en 17 meses, y un presupuesto total de $300,000.00. En este registro se documentan las acciones correspondientes a los 12 meses de 2022.

project_name: Livelihood Restoration Support to Youths in Northeast Nigeria
project_objective:
The overall project objective is that vulnerable youth refugees, IDPs, and host community members impacted by displacement crises in urban contexts have access to livelihoods opportunities that safely and sustainably meet their needs and contribute positively to their communities. In order to prepare youth for the world of work, the program will provide a variety of employability support and employment readiness trainings, dependent on the needs and opportunities of each context. The project will deliver activities around three expected results to achieve the project objective; Youth participants acquire market-relevant skills and are prepared for self-employment; New and existing youth-owned businesses are supported to start and grow, Youth participants who are not able or interested in starting a business are prepared for alternative labor market opportunities such as vocational apprenticeships.
IRC will support urban-based host and displaced entrepreneurs to start up or expand home-based
businesses or existing micro and small enterprises (MSEs). Activities will target displacement affected
youth (age 18-35) who are at increased risk of gender-based violence, exploitation, and
negative coping mechanisms. IRC will also specifically target economically vulnerable host and
displaced youth who have the strong interest in entrepreneurship and skills set to generate income
through self-employment. These youth and MSMEs typically face challenges with general
business and financial management, as well as accessing capital to support their businesses. The
program will support new and existing entrepreneurs to access to finance, business development
services, and mentoring needed for their growth, and to ultimately support the growing MSME
market in the northeast region and contribute to increased employment opportunities.
The project will partner with a local community-based organization Learning through Skills Acquisition Initiative (LETSAI) to deliver both the theoretical training as well as practical apprenticeships.
A total of 960 youths (540 in Borno state and 420 in Yobe State) will be targeted in this project to receive livelihood support under this intervention.

project_name: Inclusive Protection Assistance to Crisis-affected Populations in Cox's, Bangladesh
project_objective:
HI began providing services in Cox’s Bazar prior to the 2017 crisis, & has been adapting ever since. Continuing to address complex, acute, & multi-layered needs, HI proposes to foster a safe & protective environment with the provision of specialized & community-based services to Rohingya refugees & host community through a twin modality:
Multi-sectorial (disciplinary) Mobile Units (MU) to address mobility or social barriers. Integrated outreach teams (PSS + Physiotherapist protection officers, sports & recreation officers) deliver home-based services focused on education for beneficiaries & their caregivers on safe, effective identification & safe referral internally & externally for therapeutic exercises & other interventions. Currently, HI has thirteen MU which are teams of trained staff providing direct specialized services (including protection, mental health & psychosocial support, physical/functional rehabilitation, & basic health care/SRH) to vulnerable persons & persons with disabilities in a comprehensive approach.
At HI service centers (static points), teams support beneficiaries with enough mobility to access the facility with rehabilitation, PSS, basic healthcare, safe space. 
HI will continue to provide individual life-saving protection assistance by safely identifying, assessment & referring individuals being most at-risk or survivors of violence, including women & girls with disabilities. Within its ongoing activities, HI has established strong referral pathways (using Inter-agency forms as per Sector recommendation) with specialized camp protection actors in each of its activity sites. HI developed awareness messages to address gaps identified on the following topics: Human Trafficking & Exploitation, PSEA, Inclusion, Children’s Rights & Rights of Persons with Disabilities, Violence (included IPV & GBV), Gender Equality & General Protection. HI also actively participate in the PERU teams, are fundamentally intended for deployment during disasters or emergencies in camp settings. If circumstances dictate, PERU teams can act as an integral component of emergency response teams assigned by other authorities. PSEAH focal in HI are responsible for extensive training of all staff & volunteers using PSEA Network materials & recommendations to ensure adequate level of practice within the organization. Inclusive Feedback & Response Mechanism is in place where feedback is regularly elicited through suggestions boxes, a dedicated hotline for host & refugee communities, community discussions & 1:1 interview. A dedicated Focal Point to receive complaints is assigned in the Cox’s Bazar base to coordinate with camp level team leaders to ensure referral for needed services & ensure survivor advocacy as needed. HI is currently implementing four projects that addresses above mentioned services. HI focused on trainings to humanitarian workers on inclusion of persons with disabilities in services provision, to increase accessibility & inclusiveness of the humanitarian response.
HI created & supports community groups (in form of peer support groups) composed of persons with disabilities, to enforce self-resilience & participation/representation to the community. HI has inbuild capacity to respond to disaster which has been demonstrated in recent fire & flood response. COVID19 protection measures will continue to be adopted & its awareness will be prioritized especially for people with limited access to information.
HI works in partnership with the other actors present at camp level, to ensure the best response to the needs reported. HI coordinates with both NGOs and government bodies, depending on the areas of intervention. HI through his Compliance & Liaison department, is engaging with all relevant authorities (RRRC, DC, UNO, DSS, CiC, NGO AB) to ensure timely coordination & proper communication. HI is part of part of GO & NGO coordination groups at DC & UNO Levels.
