project_name: Integrated Inclusive and Protective Education and Child Protection Services in Bentiu IDP Camp
project_objective:
Given the current state of flooding in Rubkona County and much of Unity State, many families and households have been displaced, instability and fear within communities has settled, and increasingly smaller spaces of dry land are available to accommodate the competing priorities. Under such conditions, Mercy Corps proposes to leverage school infrastructure and institutional standing to enhance quality and inclusive education while expanding child protective factors of schools through intentional interventions and mainstreaming.
Mercy Corps will work to improve the equitable access to safe and protective education and community-based child protection services for 34,427 school-age children (18,049 boys and 16,378 girls), and raise the awareness and capacity of their parents and caregivers, teachers and school personnel, and other frontline and community workers who currently live in the Bentiu IDP Camp (data provided by IOM DTM population count, January 2022). 
Under the Education arm of the proposed project, Mercy Corps will support schools in enrolment of school-age children while continuing to accelerate enrolment and attendance of female pupils and children living with disabilities. To better ensure that this, Mercy Corps will work with school and community leadership to identify key barriers to education and work to remove them through targeted back to learning campaigns and events while also making schools safer and more accessible through rehabilitation of TLS blocks and school-based WASH services. Based on prior activities and community feedback, Mercy Corps will procure and distribute age-appropriate teaching and learning material, ECD kits, and recreational equipment to school locations to benefit learning and wellness outcomes. Mercy Corps will train teachers on pedagogy and inclusive teaching methodologies as well as child wellbeing and child protection mainstreaming. Mercy Corps will work with P8 school leavers through life skills and intermediary vocational development. Finally, Mercy Corps will work with school leadership structures, community partners, and education officials to strengthen emergency response capacity and mitigate the impact of emergencies on learners, teachers and communities. 
Under the Child Protection arm of the proposed project, Mercy Corps will seek to strengthen community-based child protection case management and referral services while continuing to increase engagement and capacity at the school level to identify and direct possible cases and through updated Bentiu IDP Camp referral pathways for child protective—and other protection—services. Mercy Corps will also continue to scale up Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) services in schools to ensure school spaces are protected and child friendly. Mercy Corps will work with school leadership to fit schools for multi-purpose functionality as child friendly and recreational spaces outside of the school day and as centers to enable children to enjoy the fullness of childhood. As such, Mercy Corps will tap into the resources of PTA committee members and community leaders to train them on CPiE and activate awareness campaigns and events to highlight the need for MHPSS and child wellbeing. Mercy Corps will similarly train select teachers and other frontline workers in MHPSS focused and non-focused approaches to enact low-level interventions at the school and community level while referring or elevating more specialized cases to appropriate partners. Working with local community members, Mercy Corps will continue to explore and support the revitalization of traditional games and activities to compliment the organization’s evidence based and tested MHPSS and life skills curriculum for children and adolescents. Mercy Corps will train select staff in case identification and management for children tailored to their specific needs, including the needs of unaccompanied and separated children, or child headed households.

project_name: Upscaling access and utilization of Comprehensive Child Protection services to support children, adolescents and families affected by conflict, hunger, flooding and violence in Pibor, Rumbek Center and East, Rumbek North Cueibet, Yei, Kajokeji, Lainya, Morobo, Magwi, Torit, Kapoeta north &South, Malakal, Counties in South Sudan
project_objective:
The project will be implemented in Central/ Eastern Equatorial, Jonglei, Lakes, Upper Nile and Western Equatorial states in the highlighted counties. This aim to upscale utilization of CP-services including GBV and linkage to multisectoral services to benefit child, adolescents and caregivers. Plan has presence in the proposed locations. 2 counties (Pibor and Kapoeta South) are ranked severity 4 while the rest are under level 3.  81,000 (27,000 girls, 23,000 boys; 16,500 women,14,500men). Out of the 50,000 children targeted, 10,000 (6,000 girls, 4,000 boys) are adolescents while 15% of beneficiaries are persons living with disability.

Beneficiaries profile includes those affected by floods and hunger, living in remote, insecure and hard to reach, IDPs, Returnees, host community, pastoralists, vulnerable adolescents, girl mothers, elderly caregivers, female headed households, UASC, medical concerns etc. 

Key protection risks to be addressed are UASC, school dropout, early/forced marriage and GBV, child labor, family separation and neglect, prevention of recruitments, distress and other MHPSS issues, support for persons living with disability, dangers and injuries, access to justice and access to multisectoral services.

Plan strategies to address the issues includes provision of age- gender responsive comprehensive case management including FTR, alternative family based care, cash assistance (CVA), NFI  and dignity kits to address complex needs, PSS-MHPSS for children/caregivers, positive parenting and life skills education, CP/GBV capacity building for staff, volunteers, community structures and stakeholders, tailored community awareness and dialogues on harmful cultural practices, GBV prevention and CP monitoring and coordination with actors, mainstreaming diverse feedback mechanisms including integrated helpdesks to address CP risk PSEA/safeguarding. Plan will collaborate with Government, community structures, UNICEF, Protection cluster, CPAOR, CPWG, CMTF, UASC, PSS/MHPSS, GBV and CAAFAG WG. Others includes WASH, Education, PSEATF, shelter, Nutrition, FSL for service deliver.

Mixed static and mobile programming approaches including face to face and remote modalities will be integrated to allow adopting to changing needs and context especially deep field locations to support beneficiaries. Key interagency guidelines and Plan manual will be utilized for quality programming which includes revised CPMS standards, IA CM/CP/FTR/ SOPs, IA PSS working group PSS manual, CFS standards among other guidelines. 

Plan will also adopt gender transformative approach, rights based, child/survivor centered approaches to programming to address root causes of child violation and GBV to shift community attitudes and negative behaviors that harm children. Gender/disability inclusion trainings will enhance access for persons with disability. Activities integration will be prioritized in Nutrition, Education, GBV, Food Assistance, WASH to holistically address diverse needs of beneficiaries including elderly. 

COVID-19/EVD integrateration with Ministry of Health/MHPSS guidelines will be prioritized in all activities. AAP and feedback mechanisms will be integrated to address issues affecting boys, girls, men, women and enhance women and girls' access to information through integrated and child friendly desks in CFS, schools, Nutrition sites etc., use of phones, girl's symposiums, community feedback sessions.

Safety audits, safeguarding risk assessment, community risks mapping and safe planning will strengthen centrality of protection/Protection monitoring to mitigate risks for beneficiaries and strengthen protective environment of children. Sustainability strategies includes capacity strengthening of community structures on CPIE creating pool of change agents and linking to development programs for resilience and working with NNGOs IPCS, GREDO, CHADO and MOGCSW (Government) for planning handover and transitioning this project.

project_name: Comprehensive and inclusive community-based protection services for children and adults in 13 communities in Jenin, Tubas, Nablus, Ramallah, Hebron,  and East Jerusalem
project_objective: In the West Bank (WB) and East Jerusalem, Palestinians face ongoing coercion and discrimination due to Israeli policies and practices, including restricted access to basic services and escalating levels of violence. In the WB, 1,021,561 persons are in need of multisectoral services (Protection Cluster Analysis Update August 2022), while the Multi Sector Needs Assessment (MSNA) 2022 identified that 5% of households are using emergency coping strategies, 23% are using crisis coping strategies, and 11% of households are under stress. This situation has deleterious effects on psychosocial well-being, with 12% of households reporting at least one member with psychosocial distress. Girls and women also face GBV risks: 14% of households report risks of verbal harassment affecting girls and 9% of households affecting women, and 6% report risks of sexual harassment or violence for girls and 4% of households for women (MSNA2022). Overall, the oPt PAU identifies 367,000 persons in need of GBV services in the WB. Persons with disabilities (PWD) suffer a range of mental health problems, stigma and lack of accessible infrastructure and services. In WB, 10% of households have at least one member with a disability, of which 4% are children (MSNA 2022). Children with disabilities are vulnerable to protection concerns, with 44% of households reporting safety concerns. The Protection Cluster identifies MHPSS as a key need. The proposed project aligns with Objective 2 of the HRP: “The basic needs of vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation are met through the provision of quality basic services and improved access to resources” and is based on findings of a Needs Assessment conducted by Terre des hommes (Tdh) in September/October 2022. The assessment revealed 13 localities with the highest MHPSS needs as reported by key informants' interviews, and indicated that women and girls were among the most affected, especially those with disabilities. The project aims to ensure Child Protection (CP) and GBV prevention and response mechanisms are accessible to communities in East Jerusalem (Sheikh Jarrah, Old City, Shufat camp), Hebron (H2 area and Dir Samet/Doura), Ramallah (Deir abu Mushal, and KufrNeimeh), Nablus (Burqa and Beita), Tubas (Tamoun and Ein Albeida) and Jenin (Faqoua and Silet Harthieyeh).The action will strengthen community-based protection mechanisms and build the capacities of CBOs to provide quality, inclusive CP, MHPSS and GBV services which are gender and age appropriate. It will equip communities to both establish and sustain community protection mechanisms, which is vital, especially when formal protection mechanisms are lacking. The project demonstrates a holistic approach through a consortium of partners and reflects good complementarity between partners’ areas of strength;   Stars of Hope in disability mainstreaming,  YWCA in vocational training and  WCLAC in legal support alongside Tdh’s proven expertise in MHPSS, GBV and case management, and all organisations will build the skills and professional confidence of partners’ psychologists and CBO Social Workers on MHPSS structured support, the safe identification, case management and referral of CP and GBV cases, disability mainstreaming,  safeguarding and PSEA. GBV survivors will be provided with income generating opportunities, vocational skills and legal counselling and representation as needed. Overall, 7622 persons will directly benefit from the project (1560 girls, 1560 boys, 3906 women, and 596 men). Partners and Tdh will work directly with beneficiaries for activity design and monitoring and they will coordinate with the relevant authorities, child protection actors, the Protection Cluster, GBV-sub-cluster, and CP-AoR

project_name: Integrated psychosocial support and child protection services for the most affected boys and girls in the Gaza Strip Strip
project_objective:
This project will support the delivery of quality, integrated child protection and psychosocial support (PSS) services to the most vulnerable boys and girls aged 6-18 in the Gaza Strip, especially those affected by the 2021/2022 escalations. The escalation has affected all aspects of life in the Gaza Strip, including child protection needs and services.

The project will ensure that 12 family centres and 30 outreach sites in Gaza are fully operational, responding to the pressing mental health and psychosocial and child protection needs of 11,900 children (50% girls) and 4,300 caregivers (20% males). Additionally, 9,900 children and adults will be reached with Explosive Remnants of War (ERW) awareness messages, while 300 non-child protection professionals and community members will benefit from training and coaching opportunities on child protection, detection, identification and referral. 

Service delivery will be directed to the most affected locations and the most vulnerable children through a coordinated continuum of services in Gaza. Each family centre will be connected to a community-based child protection committee that identify the child protection concerns and refer identified children to the family centre within that community. Family centres will operate through established Community-Based Organisations (CBOs) and outreach sites and will assess/screen and refer children for further specialised services through:
1) a case management approach for the most affected;
2) referral of severe and complicated child protection cases to child protection services (managed by relevant stakeholders and Civil Society Organizations (CSOs); and
3) referral of children with further psychosocial support needs to more specialized psychological support services.

Services will also strengthen outreach capacities to detect and link children in need with service providers while providing mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) through the family centres. A total of 11,900 children (50% girls) and 4,300 caregivers (20% males), as well as 300 community members will be reached through the project.

This project aligns with and contributes to the Protection Cluster Objective no. 2, which calls for putting in place protection response mechanisms to prevent and mitigate occupation and conflict-related violence.

Ensuring compliance with the Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) principles and procedures, project beneficiaries will be oriented on prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse. They will receive information on UNICEF and other interagency channels, including SAWA Free toll number, social media platforms, and WhatsApp to report on PSEA.

At least 70% of the project budget will support the two project implementing partners to ensure that timely services are provided to children with protection and MHPSS needs. The funds will be transferred in line with UNICEF Harmonised Approach to Cash Transfer (HACT), which ensures close follow-up on expenditures. Partners are normally micro-assessed and spot checks are regularly conducted to ensure compliance with UNICEF regulations.

project_name: Provision and Management of Education Core Pipeline Supplies for Emergency-affected children, Adolescents, and Youth in South Sudan
project_objective:
The duration of this project will be 12 months staring from 1st January 2022 to 31st December 2022.  The education core pipeline supplies project will contribute to the Education Cluster objectives CLEDU/CO1 and CLEDU/CO2 through the provision and management o teaching and learning materials for emergency-affected boys and girls aged 3-17 years (40% girls) to increase equitable access to safe and protective quality education service in South Sudan.  Essential education supplies play a critical role in effective humanitarian response and the demand for teaching and learning materials will always remain high especially during emergencies.

Through the project, essential education materials will be procured, prepositioned and distributed and efficiently managed to ensure children's right for equitable access to quality education for all children (boys and girls) in South Sudan, particularly the most vulnerable and those affected by conflict and floods are safeguarded. Without education supplies in the hands of the learners, the teaching and learning process at the school level
will be at stake. As most parents cannot afford to provide learning materials to their children, the need for the provision of education supplies remains high in the education system.

UNICEF has adopted the multi-sectoral approach for project implementation.  The provision of supplies will complement integrated WASH and Child Protection interventions in the target schools.  Monitoring of the interventions will be conducted jointly with other sectors and lessons learnt documented for future planning.
 
As the Education Cluster lead and one of the most influential actors with field presence in most of the states, UNICEF will provide support to national NGOs with capacity building in supplies distribution, warehousing, and end-user monitoring.

project_name: Mitigate the worst effects of hunger through provision of emergency assistance in Unity State
project_objective:
According to the IPC released in November 2022, there are over 6.6 million people in South Sudan experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above) between October and November 2022. Food insecurity in the country is highly driven by ongoing conflicts, and climatic shocks, citing from the Humanitarian Needs Overview published in February 2022 states that climate change continues to impact different sectors, particularly agriculture, which is one of the most climate-sensitive economic sectors. Above-normal rainfall for the third consecutive year in 2022 led to prolonged flooding, which impacted areas that had not flooded in previous years constituting a rise in food insecurity countrywide.

Unity state is one of the most food insecure states, that contributes to the estimated 7.8 million people (63% of the population) who likely will face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse acute food insecurity, with 43,000 people likely to be in Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5) in the lean season projection period of April to July 2023. Approximately three-quarters of the state's population is undergoing severe food insecurity, as well as acute malnutrition children attributed to several factors, but primarily because of conflict (including tribal and interclan fighting) and secondarily because of inaccessibility due to poor infrastructure and swampy nature of most of its land that makes it susceptible to floods, resulting to destruction of crops, properties which equates to hunger.

In response to the above problem, Welthungerhilfe (WHH) proposes a project aiming at mitigating the humanitarian crises in Unity State by ensuring the provision of needs-based emergency aid to prevent or decrease morbidities, mortality, and acute malnutrition, especially for vulnerable people in acute humanitarian crises triggered by flight and displacement, droughts, floods, and anticipated periods of hunger. 

The project approach will revolve around addressing issues of climate change through training of 20 DRR committees to develop vulnerability mappings for their specific context on boma (village level) or Payam level (sub-county level), depending on context. The committees will present a cross-section of the population since all ages and genders will be represented. The project will therefore target 56,000 beneficiaries in total in the form of IDPs, returnees and host communities. More specifically, the intervention will target, women and children-headed households, including women of reproductive age and pregnant and lactating women (PLWs), unaccompanied minors, people with disabilities, the elderly and chronically ill with various activities that include the distribution of NFI kits consisting of various household items, cash for work activities to help the most vulnerable households meet the food consumption gap while building household and community assets that reduce the risk of disaster, strengthen livelihoods and build resilience over time. They will also benefit from agriculture crop production training, distribution of ruminants and support to livestock health to help build their resilience to shocks. The project will seek to reduce the deterioration of people’s physical and mental well-being through coping mechanisms.  Target groups will additionally be linked to other ongoing interventions implemented by Welthungerhilfe and other agencies so that they can benefit from the services offered.

project_name: Food assistance to address increasing levels of severe food insecurity in South Sudan
project_objective:
Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity. WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM). WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.
Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (light resilience- building activities, peace/conflict resolution training also called GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness, training, or sensitisation on peaceful resolution of conflicts, mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities which lead to women's economic empowerment and have positive impact on household food security, or other solutions. WFP will also implement resilience building activities including Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) to support communities to improve their food security, restore their livelihoods, strengthen their resilience to shocks and build self-reliance, while contributing to peace. 
Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19, including new variants, and other potential viral outbreaks have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities.

project_objective:
A coherent response that is locally driven is more important than ever in Sudan, not least because funding levels are expected to stay the same during the year. Ensuring an agile and cost-effective humanitarian system, where coordination is seen as an enabler, and the humanitarian programme cycle is lighter, will be priorities during the year.  The office will also continue investing in access and humanitarian negotiations. During 2022 CMCoord forums were set up across several states in Sudan; this will continue in 2023. This is important because of the increasing access and bureaucratic impediments imposed on humanitarian operations following the 25 October 2021 Coup d'état. 

OCHA will maintain a robust field presence in seven states (West, North, Central Darfur and South Darfur – covering also East Darfur; South Kordofan – covering also West Kordofan; Kassala – covering Kassala, Red Sea, and Gedaref; Blue Nile) and the Abyei box, ensuring adequate humanitarian coordination across the country.  As new areas that have been difficult to access over the years open up, OCHA Sudan aims to establish a presence in more remote areas to respond to the increased workload effectively.

The direct beneficiaries of OCHA's coordination services in Sudan include the Humanitarian Coordinator (HC), the Humanitarian Country Team (HCT) and the Inter-Cluster Coordination Group (ICCG) members, implementing partners, i.e., both UN agencies and I/NGOs, donors and government of Sudan counterparts. 

In 2023 OCHA Sudan will continue to support strategic and operational coordination through the HCT, the ICCG, and Area HCT/ICCG at the sub-national level. 

Ensuring humanitarian access and space through monitoring and advocacy efforts will remain a strong focus. OCHA will work on setting up an operating model that is predictable, flexible, and fit for purpose to respond to both sudden and slow-onset crises, including recurring natural disaster events such as floods. 

OCHA Sudan will continue strengthening its leadership role in assessing, planning, coordinating, and monitoring the response in Non-State Armed Group (NSAG) control areas, including Jebel Marra, Blue Nile, and South Kordofan. It will continue to show leadership in humanitarian access and civil-military coordination to ensure the most vulnerable are reached with assistance. 

OCHA managed Sudan Humanitarian Fund (SHF), which allocates funding through the Standard Allocation modality and the Reserve for Emergency modality. With its well-developed Reserve for Emergency (RfE) modality with three instruments available – prepositioning of stock, rapid emergency response, and RfE projects- it is ideally placed to assure humanitarian actors have timely access to funding to respond to new or deteriorating emergency shocks. At the same time, its Standard Allocation is ideal for addressing, through humanitarian interventions, the root causes, the secondary impact of these emergencies and managing chronic needs.

project_name: Mainstreaming Disability in Humanitarian Action in Cameroon in Line with the IASC  Guidelines on Inclusion
project_objective:
Men and women, boys and girls with disabilities are at heightened risk of violence and abuse before and even more during humanitarian crisis. Already, prior to the crisis, they often face disability-based discrimination and rights violation in the different social spheres of life. In the majority of societies, persons with disabilities have started to address those violations and have gained increasingly influence over the decisions affecting their life through for instance representative organizations. As a result, legal and policy frameworks were adapted and/or newly developed to address systemic barriers and promote equal rights enjoyment. This shift towards a rights-based approach to disability-specific discrimination and rights violation has arrived in the humanitarian field only recently, gaining increasing force in 2016 during the humanitarian summit in Istanbul. In the subsequent years, more evidence highlighted the gaps experienced by persons with disabilities during humanitarian crisis. First humanitarian operational policies were developed or adapted to guide and hold humanitarian actors accountable to shift gear and address the gaps in access to and meaningful participation experienced by persons with disabilities during humanitarian emergencies. 
The project will further advance disability-inclusive humanitarian action by supporting the operationalisation of the IASC Guidelines in humanitarian programming and the humanitarian system. To achieve this, CBM intends to train local and international humanitarian actors on the inclusion of persons with disabilities in the humanitarian response in line with the IASC Guidelines on Inclusion of persons with disabilities in humanitarian action.

project_name: Humanitarian coordination and provision of CCCM-integrated responses to displacement-affected populations in Juba and Bor former PoC sites (semi-static) in hard-to-reach areas (mobile)
project_objective:
In line with the CCCM cluster strategy, ACTED will continue to provide humanitarian coordination and CCCM integrated response to displacement affected population in Juba former PoC sites and will provide mobile support in hard-to-reach areas in response to displacement shocks.  Due to natural hazards, localized and state conflicts, displacement waves remain high in South Sudan with 1.64 million people currently being Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) in need of CCCM assistance according to the South Sudan HNO 2022. The trend has been increasing in 2022 following massive natural hazards such as floodings in Jonglei state, leading to the multiplication of displacement sites. 
As South Sudan has been subject to displacement waves since its creation, and particularly following the 2013 civil war, some IDP sites have existed for several years with residents not willing to return to their areas of origin and ongoing humanitarian aid. To address this issue, ACTED aims to provide a more sustainable solution and support these IDP communities to become more empowered and increase their integration into host communities settings. Following a strategy implemented since 2021 in agreement with CCCM cluster, ACTED handed over camp management responsibilities to the community representatives and local authorities, especially Relief and Rehabilitation Commission (RRC) in Bor and Juba former PoC camps in 2022. In 2023, ACTED will strengthen social cohesion between IDPs and host communities in Juba to foster peaceful coexistence and will provide ad-hoc support to community representatives if needed to ensure a smooth transition. 
In parallel, ACTED provides emergency CCCM assistance in response to displacement shocks across the country. Through a well-established coordination system with REACH, the Inter Cluster Coordination Group, the Needs Analysis Working Group and the clusters, ACTED has access to timely information on displacements, allowing for a rapid multi-sectoral intervention whose core is CCCM services. Within its CCCM rapid response, ACTED aims to provide life saving coordination activities among humanitarian actors and build local communities’ capacities to self manage the sites. 
Therefore, ACTED will continue implementing CCCM interventions in line with the following cluster objectives: CO1: Improve living condition of IDPs by facilitating safe, equitable and dignified access to cross-sectoral humanitarian services, including CCCM CO2: Enhance the protective environment, respond to vulnerable population with priority on addressing protection gaps and strengthen the predictability and effectiveness of multi sectorial interventions at site level CO3: Support vulnerable IDPs to recover from the crisis by strengthening community self-management, build resilience to promote solutions for displaced people in sites.

project_name: Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan
project_objective:
As of January 2022, there are some 335,000 refugees and asylum seekers from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, primarily from Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Central African Republic.
At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for longer term stability, hundreds of thousands of South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since the signing of the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan, this spontaneous movement has prompted the development of an area-based approach, to support refugees, returnees and host communities, through enhanced engagement with development actors, to support greater access to services where possible.
Refugees largely reside in conflict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction in basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.
Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will benefit from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Specific protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identified at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with specific protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as verification exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the efficiency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to benefit from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

project_name: Sustainable Agriculture and Livelihoods Empowerment project and Unconditional Cash/Food voucher to the Host and IDPs in Yirol and Awerial Counties.
project_objective: South Sudan underwent series of humans suffering before and after the attainment of Independence all brought by civil wars, communal conflicts and natural calamities such as flooding and COVID-19 pandemic and these hampers people's sources of livelihood and deteriorate the economy. In 2022, the Humanitarian Nee community in South Sudan estimated that two third (2/3) of South Sudan population which is approximately 8.2 million are in need of humanitarian assistance. This includes the 2 million in which 55% of them are women and girls with an additional 2.3 million residing in the countries as refugees. All these negative factors will only aggravate humanitarian conditions in South Sudan. The lands for farming will be limited by flooding and drought and this increases the risk of vulnerability rates and increase in the number of IDPs in the Country. Yirol East recently hosted a huge number of IDPs with 9473 HHs registered and verified by WFP through according to Yirol East Relief and Rehabilitation Commission office in Yirol East County with another 160 HHs that later arrived after the verification, and this will only exacerbate the humanitarian situation Yirol East County as the resources of the host communities are shared and soon will be depleted. In Yirol East County of Lakes State, Help-Hilfe zur Selbsthilfe has been implementing Food security and Livelihood project alongside WASH and nutrition. Major support under this this sector falls under distribution of farm inputs (seeds, tools and implements) and training (Climate Smart Agriculture), conservation agriculture and distribution of fishing gears. Help is scaling up to promote the enterprise farming that will boost other sectors of livelihood such as agribusiness. So far, Help previously supported and trained several groups in Yirol East and West Counties and many of those groups had progressed expectedly. Under the project “Multisector emergency aid for displaced persons and host communities in Eastern Lakes State”, Help is currently implementing a three (3) years project that is targeting 10,000 Households in Lakes and part of Jonglei states to benefit from seeds and tools distribution and agronomic trainings such as kitchen gardening, perm gardening, aerial gardening especially in the flood affected population places. Another 9500 HHs to benefit for unconditional Cash/food voucher where 4000 HHs already distributed food items and other essential things like washing soaps and another 5000 HHs to benefit from fishing gears. The proposed intervention is designed to contribute to Help Interim Country Strategic Plans of 2022-2024. The combination of these interventions will contribute to its work in realizing Sustainable Development Goal 2 to “end hunger, achieve food security and improved nutrition, and promote sustainable agriculture” in South Sudan. As food insecurity problems in Lakes State are complex and interrelated, it requires multifaceted and integrated responses both at household and individual levels in addressing immediate and underlying causes of food insecurity and malnutrition to enhance their capacities and reduce vulnerabilities to disaster risks. The supplementary coping mechanism is acquired through consumption of wild fruits and greens. The IDPs and host community households prepare smaller portion of less nourishing food for survival and the number of meals per a day reduces to one. The project will also incorporate GBV, HIV/AIDS, accountability to affected populations, and gender equality during the implementation. In our intervention, Help implements hand in hand with the community stakeholders Chiefs, Women representatives, church leaders, youth representatives, and government representatives (boma and Payams administrators) during the identification of the most vulnerable households and the distribution of humanitarian assistance and agricultural inputs.  The targeting criteria include women headed HHs, Child headed HHs, destroyed HHs.

project_name: Strengthen the Access to Emergency Heath care to Control, Protect, Detect, Prepared and Respond to Public health Emergency in Sudan
project_objective:
Since 2019, Sudan is in a transition period and despite the recent political efforts from international community and local community lead initiatives to bring the conflicting parties into agreements and to stabilize the situation, the humanitarian health situation remains complicated and fragile. The main drivers of the humanitarian health crisis in Sudan include armed conflict, displacement, disease outbreaks, and floods as much as lack of staff, medicines, medical supplies, equipment, testing capacities and operational costs. Disease outbreaks are mostly water-borne, vector-borne and vaccine preventable. The reporting of recent 18 MPX confirmed cases from 6 states, importation of 2 suspected cases of EVD in Khartoum and identification of invasive vectors for transmission of dengue fever and urban malaria has highlighted low preparedness capacities, weak cross border surveillance mechanisms and added further stress to already strained health system due to risk of importation and further spread of highly fatal zoonotic diseases. The humanitarian health response project aims to address major risk factors, to provide free of-charge essential and life-saving health services to vulnerable populations and to strengthen mitigation, early detection and intersectoral multi-hazard preparedness and response. WHO’s mitigation, detection, preparedness and response to health emergencies is in line with the national health sector and health cluster strategies and follows national and international standards. WHO will provide technical and operational support to strengthen the coordination mechanisms on all levels of the health emergency preparedness and response, will strengthen and support the collection, analysis and dissemination of health related information and data in close collaboration with partners and other stakeholders. WHO will work closely with both Federal and SMoH at subnational levels by providing technical assistance through WHO country office and hubs across the country with the aim to increase the capacities of early detection, verification, risk assessment, confirmation and timely response to public health threats for enhancing the national health security. WHO will focus on all essential primary health care components to achieve universal health covering through providing integrated health services for meeting people’s health needs throughout their lives; addressing broader determinants of health through multisectoral policy and action and empowering individuals, families and communities to take charge of their own health. 
WHO, as provider of last resort, will procure and distribute free of charge medicines, medical supplies, medical equipment, personal protective equipment (PPEs) and laboratory supplies to support the humanitarian health care provided by NGOs and MOH. WHO will also engage in capacity building of health workers on health emergency related subjects such as disease surveillance, rapid response, case management, infection prevention and control and risk communication among others. The project will also include small repair and rehabilitation of health facilities and supporting operational costs for humanitarian health services. Access to health services for all age groups and gender with their specific health needs will be adapted to the local cultural customs, including advocacy and synergic linkages with ongoing recovery-development interventions. 6.4 million people residing in 75 localities with severity ranking level of 4 and 5 for humanitarian health response. As custodian of IHR, the activities related to infectious diseases outbreak control will be extended to address the health security and protection needs of affected population wherever needed. WHO will continue to mobilize all potential resources to address all-hazards emergency risk management including mitigation, detection, preparedness and response measures.

project_name: Improve quality, increase access, and strengthen capacity of primary and secondary healthcare, GBV, and MHPSS services in Bor South, Twic East, and Duk counties in Jonglei State
project_objective:
The project is designed to improve quality, increase access, and strengthen the capacity of primary and secondary health services, integrating MHPSS/GBV and WASH, by reinforcing the national health system at State, County, Boma, and community level. The project will target 30,000 people in need. 
In close collaboration with State Ministry of Health (SMoH) and the County Health Department (CHD), MdM will support both static and medical mobile units (MMU) across Bor South, Twic East, and Duk. MdM partners with Sudan Medical Care as its local implementing partner, who have extensive experience in the aforementioned areas. The project includes provision of technical guidance, support supervision and on-the-job training for health facility staff and community-facilitators/community health workers, emergency referrals for critical cases, repairs of health and WASH infrastructure, provision of essential medicines, consumables and medical equipment, referrals, and linkages to the next level of care and with relevant actors for non-medical services including protection.
MHPSS and GBV will be integrated through counselling at hospital, PHCC, and MMU level, and through awareness raising and a referral system at community level, and will target 3659 adults and 1200 children. WASH will be integrated by rehabilitating essential infrastructure. The project takes a holistic approach in ensuring support is given at all levels, responding to COVID-19 needs, and by integrating the MHPSS, GBV, and WASH components. The main objective is to meet the basic health, MHPSS, and GBV needs of the population in Bor South, Twic East, and Duk counties, focusing on persons with specific needs such as women of reproductive age (project target: ANC4+ 50% and SBA-30%), pregnant and lactating women (project target: 288), at-risk pregnancies (project target: 43 women with high risk pregnancies) and children under 5 (project target: 1200), mental health and psychosocial support cases (project target: 81 consultations) among  displaced people, returnees and host communities.

project_name: Life-saving food assistance in North-East Nigeria
project_objective:
WFP will provide unconditional food assistance to the most food-insecure, crisis-affected populations. Life-saving general food assistance (in-kind food and cash-based transfers) will be delivered to IDPs, returnees, and host populations in North-East Nigeria (Borno, Yobe, and Adamawa States). Early recovery and resilience to shocks will be promoted through asset creation and preservation and increased livelihood opportunities. Joint multi-sectoral assessments and Emergency Food Security Analyses will be conducted regularly to monitor the food security, and market situation in crisis-affected states. 
A gender-transformative approach that meets the needs of women, men, girls, and boys will be adopted. WFP will mainstream protection throughout its work, supported by a solid understanding of the operational context and protection analysis. Training and capacity building of staff and partners in the protection and humanitarian principles will include on-the-job coaching. WFP will ensure that affected populations (women and men) will be consulted throughout the programme cycle; community feedback mechanisms will be tailored to their preferred means of communication. Beneficiaries will continue to be empowered with knowledge of their food assistance entitlements and their rights, including WFP’s zero-tolerance policy on Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA). Protection against Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) will be embedded in M&E tools, community feedback mechanisms, and training of partners and staff.
WFP will continue the collection of key information on beneficiaries and assistance provided as part of its M&E activities. Monthly monitoring will include distribution and activity site management; beneficiary and entitlement verification; and ensuring adequate protection and gender measures. Lessons will be regularly drawn from monthly process and biannual outcome monitoring and reporting, and periodic reviews and evaluation to inform strategic and operational decisions.
WFP will further consolidate partnerships to enhance national and state-level emergency preparedness and response systems, including food security and nutrition assessment and monitoring, early warning, protection, gender analysis, targeting and registration processes, safety nets, cash-based transfer capacities, and supply chain.
Where security and access to land allow, increasing livelihood activities will complement food assistance to support access to productive assets, income-generating activities, and self-reliance in the long term. Assistance will be coordinated with government distributions to ensure food assistance is complimentary with other ongoing assistance from other clusters with no gaps.

project_name: Improving short-term and long-term food security and livelihoods access in Central and Eastern Equatoria and WBeG through investment in food production assets and utilization and strengthening of local capacities.
project_objective:
In line with the FSL cluster strategy for 2022, ACTED will contribute towards improving food security of over 22,754 beneficiaries (excluding beneficiaries reached through WFP funding) to enhance emergency food production and reduce dependency on food and agricultural inputs through resilience building activities such as training and market support functionality. Millions of South Sudanese remain displaced across the country following years of violent conflict that resulted in one of the most devastating humanitarian crises in recent history. Based on the latest IPC analysis and projections, in October 2022, 53.6% of the population living in South Sudan facing high levels of acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above). Specifically, 4.36 million people are facing crisis (IPC Phase 3), 2.22 million people are facing emergency (IPC Phase 4) and 61,000 people are facing catastrophic (IPC Phase 5) food insecurity.  As such, the needs across South Sudan have severely increased, driven by flooding, insecurity, population displacements, declined crop production, diseases and pests, the economic crisis, the effects of COVID-19, limited access to basic services, and the cumulative effects of prolonged years of asset depletion and loss of livelihoods.  The project activity will be in line with the cluster Objectives : 
CO1 : Provide food assistance to prevent famine and improve food consumption, dietary diversity and coping strategies for vulnerable populations (in IPC 5, 4 & some 3)
“CO2: Enhance emergency food production through complementary vegetable and crop seeds and fishing and livestock support (in IPC 3, 4 & 5)”

project_name: Strengthen Health Services Including PHC and STHC Services in NWS
project_objective:
This project aims to achieve the following objectives:
•	Increase access to life-saving and life-sustaining coordinated, equitable humanitarian health services for those most vulnerable and in need

project_name: Protection and Legal Assistance for Displacement affected populations in South Sudan
project_objective:
The NRC seeks to improve the overall protective environment in South Sudan by not only responding to people's most immediate material needs during a crisis, but also by promoting their safety and dignity, as well as preventing, reducing, or mitigating the protection risks they face. It is also to address the root causes of displacement and to contribute to the creation of conditions conducive to long-term solutions for displaced people. To achieve the project objective, NRC will focus on three key components i.e. 1) General Protection; Housing, Land and Property; 3) Gender Based Violence. 

NRC proposes a community-based approach to displaced and conflict-affected populations protection, including static, mobile, and emergency responses.  Protection context assessments will be done in all locations, as well as, where possible, community-based protection monitoring, in which community focal points will be trained to report on protection needs and risks. Protection incidents will be documented and analyzed in order to better understand trends and evolution in the protection context, and the findings will be disseminated to communities and relevant stakeholders. 

NRC will provide at-risk populations with both awareness-raising sessions and individualized assistance in obtaining national identity documentation. Foster improved ability to exercise HLP rights for individuals and groups affected by displacement with priority given to the most vulnerable, including female and child headed households, the elderly, individuals with physical and mental disabilities, and those who are extremely poor. NRC will target conflict-affected areas and areas of potential return.

NRC will also carry out GBV prevention and risk mitigation activities in 6 counties located in hard to reach areas. Activities will include awareness raising, referrals to response services, cash assistance to GBV survivors, distribution of dignity kits and training on GBV basic concepts among others.

To achieve the main objective, the will focus on the below key activities
1) Carrying out of information and awareness raising activities; awareness will focus on GBV (GBV risks, available response services, GBV referral pathways, timely reporting), HLP (social cohesion and collaborative dispute resolution mechanisms, land rights issues) and general protection (protection risks, available services)
2) Provision of cash assistance (individual protection assistance) to persons at GBV survivors and other persons at heightened risks including referral of GBV survivors for response services
3) Training frontline workers and community focal points on basic GBV concepts, GBV guiding principles and responses services.
4) Training of state-level authorities, community leaders and representative on HLP, alternative dispute resolution
5) Facilitating peaceful coexistence and inclusive resolutions of local conflict through training and mentoring the local community in collaborative dispute resolution (CDR) mechanisms
6) Distribute dignity kits to women and adolescent girls.
7) Provision of legal aid and counselling

project_name: Appui à la scolarisation des enfants vulnérables de la région de Tillabéri et de Tahoua affectés par la crise humanitaire
project_objective: Ce projet vise à lever les barrières qui empêchent les filles et garçons d’accéder à une éducation de qualité dans un environnement sûr et protecteur grâce à un programme d'Education en Urgence dans les régions de Tillaberi et Tahoua. Dans ce cadre, 250 écoles primaires seront appuyées dans les Régions de Tahoua et de Tillabéry, venant en aide à  61 943 enfants. 290 infrastructures scolaires seront appuyées à travers des réhabilitations, constructions de classes évolutives et de latrines seront effectuées afin de garantir que les espaces d'apprentissage soient adéquats pour accueillir le nombre croissant d'enfants inscrits. Des formations et un accompagnement pédagogique tout au long de l’action seront proposés aux enseignants en lien avec les services techniques pour améliorer la qualité des enseignements. Les enseignants situés dans des zones difficilement accessibles seront appuyés via l’approche vidéo-coaching. Des dotations de kits scolaires pour les élèves et de ressources pédagogiques pour les enseignants seront effectuées. Le projet travaillera par ailleurs avec les communautés pour les sensibiliser sur l'importance de l'éducation, surtout des filles et des enfants en situation d'handicap et renforcera les structures éducatives communautaires pour qu’elles puissent  élaborer des plans de gestion des risques et la mise en place de codes de conduite dans les écoles. Les enseignants recevront également une formation pour mieux répondre à la détresse des enfants - approche « École sûre », identification de la détresse psychologique et gestion du stress, premiers secours psychologiques et appui psycho-social. Des bibliothèques itinérantes seront créés dans les deux régions afin d’offrir aux enfants un accès facilité à des ouvrages éducatifs mais aussi ludiques.  Afin de favoriser la réintégration de 5400 enfants précocement exclus ou n’ayant jamais intégré le système scolaire, 180 classes passerelles seront mises en place au sein des écoles formelles appuyées. Un programme d’apprentissage par la radio sera mis en place dans les zones où les écoles sont fermées du fait de la situation sécuritaire. La collaboration avec des structures communautaires ainsi que les formations d´enseignants accroitront la durabilité de l´intervention par une mobilisation et un ancrage communautaire. L'accent sera mis aussi sur la responsabilisation des structures communautaires et sur la capacité des enseignants en termes d’encadrement des filles afin d’améliorer la rétention ainsi que le niveau des acquis scolaires des filles.

project_name: Enhancing the Protection of Civilians and Resilience of Communities in South Sudan
project_objective:
The overall objective of the project is to enhance the protection of civilians and resilience of communities in South Sudan. Civilians throughout the country have been severely affected by the existing humanitarian crisis resulting from recurrent violence, insecurity, and natural disasters. To alleviate suffering and increase the protection and security of affected and vulnerable communities, NP will directly implement activities utilizing a participatory model that seeks to further build on local protection capacities, social cohesion, and resilience as well as prevent and respond to pertinent protection concerns. All project activities will be designed to best respond to the immediate security needs of beneficiaries and support the resilience, adaptive capacity, and recovery of communities from violent conflict, insecurity, and environment shocks utilizing NP’s Unarmed Civilian Protection (UCP) methodology. The project’s three programming components which will center upon: 1) General Protection 2) GBV and 3) Child protection.

Nonviolent Peaceforce (NP) will utilize a participatory approach in order to prevent and respond to protection needs, including gender-based violence (GBV) and Child Protection (CP) concerns. All project activities will be designed based on NP’s methodology of Unarmed Civilian Protection (UCP) to respond to the immediate protection needs of affected populations as well as support the resilience, adaptive capacity and recovery of communities from violent conflict and insecurity.

Project activities are implemented in both static locations, as well as through mobile response missions. NP also recognises the specific and unique needs of women, men, boys, girls, elderly and Persons with Disability (PwD). As such, NP has made use of the community feedback/information in the design of the proposed project. During project implementation, concerns of all community members will be captured and disaggregated by age, sex and PwD, and will be constantly reviewed to adapt the project.

project_name: Emergency Food Assistance in Gaza
project_objective:
The unique socio-economic conditions of blockade, with its movement restrictions and destruction of productive capacity, are further compounded by repeated cycles of conflict and political instability, undercutting employment and livelihood opportunities in the Gaza Strip. 

The humanitarian needs of its more than 2 million residents were further exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic, the Ukraine Crisis and the military escalation in August 2022 and May 2021, which negatively impacted livelihoods and access to essential services in Gaza. 

The HRP 2023 Strategic Objective 3 states that the capacity of vulnerable Palestinians to cope with and overcome protracted crisis, including from environmental threats, is supported, while solutions to violations and other root causes of threats and shocks are pursued.  

UNRWA’s emergency food assistance operation provides a critical humanitarian lifeline to Palestine refugees who depend on food aid to meet their most basic food security needs. Under the 2023 HRP, UNRWA targets 864,096 Palestine refugees, that accounts for over 150,000 Palestine refugee families including families with persons with disabilities and female headed households. In quarterly bases, eligible families receive a food basket that is composed of a range of basic food commodities. The project directly contributes to the HRP 2023 FSS Objective 2: Households suffering from limited access to food and to income opportunities are able to meet their basic food needs by providing direct access to food. 
Through its well-established monitoring system, UNRWA will continue to evaluate the food distribution system including the distribution modality that follows strict safety and security measures responding to changing environment around unpredictable situation, while guaranteeing a fair, equal and consistent support to food-insecure Palestine refugees in Gaza.

project_name: PROTECTION AND HUMANITARIAN ASSISTANCE TO VULNERABLE MIGRANTS IN LEBANON
project_objective:
The project aims to provide a range of protection services to migrants in need, strengthen links between targeted community groups and partners, improve the quality of services available, and enhance knowledge on migrant population groups in Lebanon. Based on IOM Migrant Presence Monitoring 2022, services will target both male and female migrants, with a higher caseload of the latter group due to their increased number in country. Beneficiaries will typically be working age, between 18 and 40 years old, however the project will also support families (including one-parent families). In line with IOM’s localization strategy, IOM will work with one or more implementing partners, enhancing capacities of local CSOs to provide protection services for migrants at the local level. Under this project, IOM will continue to promote a holistic approach to protection assistance, with case management as an entry point to support the accurate identification of protection needs (including MHPSS) and to support necessary referrals. Building on the partnerships established in 2022, IOM will build partnerships with existing partners as well as explore new partnerships. The services that IOM will deliver, either directly or through partners, include awareness on legal and protection topics, legal assistance, case management support including mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), individual counselling, safe and temporary shelters for vulnerable migrants and referral to community hosting program, provision of non-food items, financial support and assisted voluntary return and reintegration. These services will be made accessible to migrants by scaling up IOM’s pre-existing case management services, supporting enhanced capacity of partners, and referral to other partners, strengthening culturally appropriate outreach to large migrant groups, including translation and interpretation, and expanding community-level networks to strengthen targeted communities’ awareness of and access to IOM and partner services, as well as wider issues of concern. Provision of or onward referral to multisector assistance such as food or health support will be mainstreamed across the project. 
Additionally, IOM will develop a training curriculum to increase the understanding of cultural sensitivity and migrant inclusivity and build the capacities of service providers. On the data collection and improved understanding level, IOM plans to conduct data collection activities including its third round of the Migrant Presence Monitoring program to update and precise further its baseline assessment on migrants in Lebanon. The MPM informs and builds the sample for the MSNA 2023 which IOM plans also to lead on. Additionally, a nationwide mapping for services available for migrants in Lebanon is planned to take place; IOM piloted this exercise in 2021 in North/Akkar and wish to update findings and expand to the whole country as it would support the Migrant Sector response in assistance to migrants. On another note, IOM plans to support the sector in implementing a protection monitoring /qualitative research with the aim to fill the information gaps from the existing assessments and gaining an in-depth understanding of the migrants’ situation in the country from a protection lens. For instance, topics as children of migrants, migrants in detention, migrants in the workplace, live-in vs. live-out migrants protection concerns, etc. IOM's targets under this proposal include those targeted under preexisting funding, such as the Lebanese Humanitarian Fund (LHF).

project_name: Enhancing access to safe water and basic sanitation and hygiene services for vulnerable conflict-affected populations in and out of camp across Northern Syria
project_objective: The proposed project aims at enhancing access to water, sanitation, and hygiene services for conflict-affected populations across Northern Syria, with emergency, life-saving WASH assistance mostly provided in camp settings, and longer-term, resilience focused assistance mostly provided off camp. ACTED will provide a variety of assistance modalities toward this aim. In-camp, ACTED will provide life-saving water supply (through a mix of trucking and pumping), sanitation services including wastewater and latrine management, and solid waste management services, and water quality monitoring to several camp clusters in Northwest Syria (NWS), as well as Washokani and Areesheh camps and multiple informal settlements in Northeast Syria (NES). Complementary to this assistance, ACTED will provide hygiene promotion and awareness sessions to all targeted camp residents, and distribute WASH NFIs to highly vulnerable displaced persons. Off-camp, ACTED will rehabilitate, through contractors and in coordination with all relevant stakeholders (including WASH Cluster, WASH Working Group, and local councils and technical departments), numerous assets, including water pumping stations, water treatment stations, water towers, etc. ACTED will also install new assets and/or facilities to fit existing assets, in areas where the need for water is highest. ACTED will look to hand over these assets to relevant local stakeholders while providing operation and maintenance support, and capacity-building trainings, in order for WASH-related basic services to remain operational through these assets after the completion of the intervention. In Northwest Syria, ACTED will conduct repairs and rehabilitation of WASH facilities in health centers. ACTED will also provide emergency water trucking out-of-camp in Northeast Syria. Lastly, in the context of the cholera outbreak, ACTED will meet the critical WASH needs of vulnerable individuals in and out of camps, by ensuring the continuation of the provision of WASH services and improving WASH infrastructure to prevent the further spread of cholera in NES. In total, ACTED expects its activities to reach 1,667,924 individuals under the WASH sector in 2023. ACTED will seek synergies with its response in other sectors, primarily Early Recovery activities, notably through activities falling under indicators from both WASH and ERL sectors, such as WASH asset rehabilitation activities. Specifically, ACTED will seek to rehabilitate key water supply assets and systems off-camp in 2023, particularly in NES, in a effort to restore and sustain communities' access to this service, and to hand it over to local stakeholder where possible. This approach is geared for increased sustainability of the WASH response and is expected to increase cost-efficiency in the upcoming years (2023 and beyond) by reducing the need for live-saving assistance off-camp, particularly water trucking. With regards to in-camp interventions, ACTED will work through targeted communities in camp, notably through community-based structures, to build the sustainability of the WASH activities conducted. In NES, this include involving Water Committees from the resident population to participate in water quality monitoring, whilst informing camp residents on how to raise maintenance and water supply issues. In NWS, ACTED is also evaluating the prospects of cost recovery mechanisms. The approach considers social and economic dimensions, including the enabling environment, willingness to pay, and financial considerations such as fixed and variable costs. Active participation in the Cost Recovery in WASH Infrastructure Technical Working Group at the WASH Cluster will further promote informed decisions are taken.
