project_name: Protección a comunidades afectadas por desplazamiento forzado y en riesgo de desplazamiento, personas retornadas con necesidad de protección, personas solicitantes de asilo y refugiadas en El Salvador.
project_objective:
Entre 2006 y 2016, el 1,1% de las familias en El Salvador fueron desplazadas forzadamente, un estimado de 71.500 personas según el ejercicio de caracterización publicado en 2018 por el Ministerio de Justicia y Seguridad Pública. El complejo entorno socioeconómico de El Salvador agrava el impacto de la violencia en las personas desplazadas internamente, refugiadas, solicitantes de asilo y retornadas. Las dinámicas del desplazamiento interno y de los retornos impactan en las comunidades receptoras, donde aumentan las necesidades por la llegada de población en condiciones de vulnerabilidad. Los municipios receptores de población retornada coinciden con aquellos con menor desarrollo económico y social. Las personas retornadas a El Salvador están en mayor riesgo por su condición de vulnerabilidad agudizada debido al proceso de movilidad fallido. El Salvador también acoge un pequeño número de refugiados y solicitantes de asilo. Hasta junio del 2022, había un total de 91 personas refugiadas y 54 solicitantes de asilo.

 ACNUR está comprometido con el apoyo al Gobierno de El Salvador, a través de sus políticas integrales, para identificar y abordar las brechas de protección y soluciones que afectan a las personas refugiadas, desplazadas internamente, retornadas con necesidades de protección y apátridas, con especial énfasis a la protección de la infancia en situación y/o en riesgo de desplazamiento y la prevención de las violencias de género y promover la eficacia de las medidas de recepción a población retornada fortalecer sistemas de información, reforzar la provisión de atención y asesoramiento; así como, para el fortalecimiento de los mecanismos de protección y soluciones.

El empoderamiento comunitario busca mejorar la movilización comunitaria y los canales de comunicación con las comunidades: a través del involucramiento, empoderamiento, la información y la inclusión sistemática y participativa de las opiniones y decisiones de las personas en los programas diseñados por el ACNUR. Así, a través de una serie de procesos consultivos, este proyecto favorecerá el establecimiento de redes de promotores comunitarios y campañas de comunicación en más de 40 comunidades y 17 municipios a nivel nacional. De manera complementaria, el proyecto apoyará las iniciativas de medios de vida y el acceso al empleo, incluyendo la formación y la certificación laboral.
Los diferentes tipos de violencia en las comunidades afectan especialmente a niñas, mujeres y la población LGBTIQ+,. de manera constante sufren diferentes formas de violencia de género (física, psicológica, sexual, patrimonial, económica, etc) . Además, la población LGTBIQ+ experimenta alta vulnerabilidad a las violaciones de derechos humanos en sus comunidades de origen y en las de acogida, lo cual provoca desplazamientos internos. Para ello, ACNUR en estrecha coordinación con las instituciones públicas apoyo psicosocial y asistencia legal, la gestión de casos, los sistemas de remisión, la provisión de espacios seguros para personas LGTBIQ+ y la mejora del acceso a medios de vida de las sobrevivientes (EMIs 5, 6, 7, 8, 10 y 12). 

 ACNUR, impulsará intervenciones para prevenir, responder y mitigar los riesgos de protección más urgentes, incluida la violencia contra los niños, niñas y adolescentes. En este sentido, esfuerzos se orientarán a fortalecer el Sistema Nacional de Protección a la Niñez, mediante el apoyo a Comités Locales de Derechos a nivel municipal y a la implementación nacional de la “Ley Crecer Juntos” al promover la garantía y acceso de derechos a niños y niñas. 

Las acciones de este proyecto se implementarán en coordinación con instituciones públicas a nivel municipal y nacional, socios de las organizaciones de la sociedad civil, para responder a las necesidades de protección de la población refugiada, desplazada internamente, personas solicitantes de asilo, retornadas con necesidades de protección.

project_name: Assistance for Victims of the Lake Chad Crisis in North-East Nigeria and Northern Cameroon
project_objective: The objective of the project is to contribute to reducing the impact of conflict-related food insecurity and improving the protection of the most vulnerable groups of the affected population. Food security will be supported through a mix of cash transfers and in-kind assistance to 1436 households, depending on the local context, sector-specific requirements, and preferences of the affected population and 280 households would be supported with vouchers for seeds and agricultural tools to improve access to/use of land for agricultural self-sufficiency during the lean season, accompanied by training in good agricultural practices. These interventions are complemented by screening 2500 households for malnutrition, treating cases of moderate and acute malnutrition, and training on the use of nutrient-rich foods. In addition, the program will address the protection of those affected by GBV, child abuse, and trauma by identifying and treating up to 300 cases or referring them to specialized services. The project will strengthen community-based Protection Monitoring Systems by training local Protection Monitors and community-based Protection Panels. Accompanying this, 300 victims and survivors of GBV or people at high corresponding risk will be empowered with cash transfers to build income-generating activities. Awareness-raising activities on GBV, child protection, and mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) will also be carried out, targeting the entirety of the project communities and local key actors in the project regions. In addition, the schooling of __ IDP children will be supported through the payment of school fees. Finally, legal assistance in issuing documents will be provided to __ individuals. The project will also strengthen the engagement of local actors in humanitarian coordination processes as well as in the relationship with local civil society actors and contribute to improving the environmental performance of humanitarian assistance.

project_name: Multi-Sector Emergency Assistance for Vulnerable Communities in Central Darfur, South Kordofan, White Nile and Blue Nile
project_objective:
The Overall objective of the project is to improve Food security and Nutrition status of vulnerable people in Central Darfur, South Kordofan, Blue Nile and White Nile states. Geographical locations targeted by the project include 53 health facilities with catchment population found in 11 localities including Tadamon, Ghadeer, Elreef Elshargi, Zalingei, Wadisaleh, Bendasi, Mukjar, Al Diwaim, Guli, Kurmuk and al Tadamon.
The programme will provide integrated and timely assistance to vulnerable populations affected by disasters, conflict, and recurrent shocks/crisis (directly prohibiting recovery) in hard to reach and newly accessible areas. Priority will be given to, returnees, IDPs, nomadic and vulnerable host community members. Children, Adolescent Girls, and Pregnant and Lactating women (PLW) will remain the main target group. Total estimated number of beneficiaries are:  Nutrition: 25,661; Health: 103,304 people WASH: 78,022 (M: 26,130; F: 24,120); FSL: 133,902 (M: 65,612; F: 68,290): and GBV: 39,732.
Food security aims at increasing access to Food and livelihood for 22,317 households in target locations through three major interventions which includes provision of cash assistance for food (Target: 9,960 HH), livelihood cash transfer for IGA/assets (Target: 6,638 HH) and provision of agricultural inputs such as seeds and tools (Target: 5,719). AAH will link Humanitarian response with resilience and development intervention including conducting Value chain assessments, Socio-economic inclusion, Participatory Resilience Analysis Measurement (PRAM), Community action, participatory capacity, and vulnerability analysis (PVCA), Community managed disaster risk reduction (CMDRR), Holistic management and natural resource management. 
In WASH, AAH focus on improving access to Water and Sanitation services and hygiene promotion. Sanitation facilities and Water source construction or rehabilitation, Water quality monitoring, WASH in health, Hygiene promotion distribution, Distribution of hygiene and dignity kit are main interventions. WASH interventions are linked with nutrition and health services and practices.
The goal of Health and Nutrition is to deliver evidence-based quality integrated health and nutrition service and practices for vulnerable people at facility and community level. Major nutrition intervention includes CMAM, IYCF, Micronutrient interventions while health interventions focus on outpatient consultation (IMCI), reproductive health and EPI. Nutrition service will be delivered in 53 OTP/TSFP and Eight stabilization integrated with primary health care and WASH. In CMAM, A total of 25,661 individuals suffering from acute malnutrition are targeted including 3,661 children with SAM and 22,000 children and PLW with MAM (U5 MAM: 19813, PLW: 2188). IYCF counseling will be delivered to 24,611 at facility by skilled counselors and community level though Mother support group. Vitamin A, Iron-folic acid and MNP distribution will be implemented in a coordination to reduce micronutrient deficiency in children and PLWs.
AAH focus on Gender Based Violence (GBV) which is significant protection issue as target areas have recurrent communal conflicts which may increase risk of women for physical or emotional violence. As such, the project targets 39,732 people through capacity building (1,058), support vocational and life skills (370) and community awareness creation (38,304). project_name: Comunidad Activa: transformando comunidades en espacios que promuevan relaciones sanas, seguras y felices.
project_objective: Durante los últimos 3 años, Alight (ARC) ha estado trabajando en El Salvador, junto con las Hermanas Católicas -el Movimiento del Color- implementando actividades en las comunidades promoviendo servicios para la eliminación de las barreras existentes tanto en Popotlán, Apopa y San Luis Portales II, La Chacra . Las comunidades de Popotlán, Apopa and La Chacra en San Salvador, se ven afectados regularmente por desastres naturales y experimentan altos niveles de violencia de género y relacionada con pandillas. Los jóvenes y los niños que crecen en estas comunidades son extremadamente vulnerables a la delincuencia, ya sea como sobrevivientes de un acto violento o incluso forzados a convertirse ellos mismos en perpetradores. Nuestra programación la basamos en un enfoque centrado en la persona identificando en conjunto diferentes actividades de respuesta y prevención. Como mecanismo de intervención para el 2023, Alight (ARC) tiene por objetivo el promover la convivencia comunitaria entre los diferentes sectores, los cuales están sub divididos (como resultado de territorialización de las pandillas, quienes han creado fronteras invisibles). La protección basada en la comunidad (CBP, por sus siglas en inglés) pone las capacidades, los derechos y la dignidad de las personas en el centro de la programación generando resultados de protección más eficaces y sostenibles mediante el fortalecimiento de los recursos y capacidad locales, así como la identificación de las brechas de protección a través de la consulta. La CBP pretende garantizar que todas las personas afectadas disfruten de sus derechos en igualdad de condiciones y puedan participar plenamente en las decisiones que les afectan. En este mecanismo de implementación se enmarcan las actividades del programa denominado “Comunidad Activa”, el cual contiene un enfoque de fortalecimiento de protección comunitario, así como la promoción de la salud emocional en un perímetro de sana convivencia libre de agresiones verbales y abusos contra el libre tránsito, espacios seguros para niñas, adolescentes y mujeres, así como diferentes poblaciones en situación de vulnerabilidad. Los espacios de “Comunidad Activa” son el resultado de un proceso de empoderamiento.Alight (ARC) se asegurará de que todas sus estrategias y actividades den prioridad a los derechos, las necesidades, deseos de las diferentes poblaciones en situación de vulnerabilidad, y que estas estén en concordancia con los estándares internacionales de protección humanitaria. Para garantizar la integración de la protección en todas las estrategias y actividades dirigidas por Alight (ARC), las actividades se basarán en los principios generales de protección, centrándose en garantizar la seguridad y dignidad, acceso significativo de servicios, rendición de cuentas, la participación y empoderamiento, así como el no hacer daño. Alight (ARC) promoverá que todos los servicios disponibles sean accesibles a todos nuestros clientes en colaboración con las hermanas, la comunidad y los actores claves influyentes, se racionalizará, revisará, actualizará y difundirá una vía de derivación para proporcionar servicios de calidad y oportunos de respuesta ante el desplazamiento forzado interno. Así mismo se reforzarán las capacidades de la comunidad a través de sesiones de concientización comunitaria realizando actividades dirigidas en espacios públicos revitalizando su uso por medio de ferias, festivales, torneos, celebraciones comunitarias, conmemoración de fechas representativas. La estrategia de implementación de estas actividades masivas se basará en una coordinación con diferentes proveedores de servicios acercándoles a las comunidades, por igual se distribuirán materiales informativos a las empresas locales, las iglesias, gobierno local, los hospitales, las escuelas y las organizaciones de sociedad civil, tomando en cuenta que los materiales deben incluir información sobre todos los servicios disponibles.

project_name: Respuesta Humanitaria a Grupos Vulnerables Afectados por el Deterioro de sus medios de Vida y la Desnutrición Aguda en Honduras
project_objective:
El proyecto es una respuesta inmediata a las brechas generadas por la convergencia de las tormentas tropicales Eta e Iota, la sequía experimentada en el primer semestre del 2021, y la pandemia del Covid19 en municipios del sur del Corredor Seco de Honduras. Para ello integra de manera complementaria actividades agropecuarias de restauración de medios de vida, y de prevención y promoción de buenas prácticas de alimentación y detección de la malnutrición aguda en grupos vulnerables, especialmente personas discapacitadas, mujeres, niños y niñas.

Las diferentes y concurrentes emergencias humanitarias suscitadas recientemente en Honduras afectaron los medios de vida, la capacidad de recuperación temprana, y la seguridad alimentaria y nutricional de muchas familias. Esta afectación se visibilizó de manera aguda en los municipios del corredor seco y del norte de este país. Dentro de estos municipios, grupos especialmente vulnerables como las mujeres y niñas, personas con discapacidad, jóvenes y personas de la tercera edad, en áreas urbanas y rurales enfrentan mayor pobreza, desempleo, carga de trabajo de cuidados no remunerados, y mayor riesgo de tener niveles de desnutrición aguda.

El proyecto tiene como objetivo contribuir a restablecer los medios de vida de las familias afectadas por la secuencia de fenómenos climáticos adversos y el Covid19, además de asegurar la vigilancia, detección temprana, referencia y prevención del deterioro nutricional de grupos vulnerables. Esto, con un enfoque de equidad de género e inclusión de mujeres, jóvenes, personas de la tercera edad, personas con discapacidad, niños y niñas.

Las actividades propuestas por el proyecto están alineadas con el objetivo sectorial 2 del clúster de Seguridad Alimentaria y Nutricional, y con el objetivo sectorial 1 y 2 del clúster de Nutrición.

project_name: Asistencia humanitaria en Seguridad alimentaria y Nutrición
project_objective:
El proyecto pretende contribuir a aliviar el sufrimiento humano y dignificar la vida de las personas que han sido afectadas por fenómenos naturales o crisis humanitarias. El objetivo del proyecto es ofrecer asistencia humanitaria en seguridad alimentaria y nutrición a los más vulnerables en los departamentos de Yoro, Cortés, Copán, Intibucá, Francisco Morazán, Santa Bárbara y El Paraíso. En estos siete departamentos, se asistirán 23 Municipios a través transferencia multipropósito, distribución de kits agrícolas para la reactivación de medios de vida, asistencia humanitaria en nutrición en coordinación con la Secretaría de Salud y fortaleciendo las estructuras comunitarias para la vigilancia nutricional y referencia de las niñas y niños en desnutrición aguda y moderada a los centros de salud para su recuperación oportuna. A través del proyecto se capacitarán grupos de cuidadores y cuidadores en preparación de alimentos para mejora nutricional de las familias. Adicionalmente se fortalecerán 82 unidades de salud dotando con equipo y formando a su personal, consultores pediatras apoyarán con su formación y con el manejo de desnutrición. El proyecto es inclusivo y promueve la igualdad de género, 69% de la población de los municipios de Intibucá pertenecen al grupo ético lenca, contempla grupos de edad y discapacidad. Entre las metas del proyecto figuran:
*Transferencia multipropósito a 20,700 personas
*Distribución de kits agrícolas y asistencia nutricional a 40,000 personas vulnerables,
*Distribución de silos metálicos para almacenar granos que sustentarán a las familias en épocas de crisis, se beneficiarán a aprox. 5,000 familias.
*24,100 niños y niñas menores de 5 años y 6,300 mujeres embarazadas y lactantes recibirán micronutrientes y estarán en control de las unidades de salud.
* 29,700 cuidadores y cuidadoras recibirán formación en preparación de alimentos para diversificar su alimentación y mejorar la nutrición de la familia.
* 82 unidades de salud fortalecidas
*2,460 voluntarios de salud capacitados
En conclusión el proyecto pretende beneficiar a más de 120,000 personas en acciones relacionadas a la seguridad alimentaria y nutricional. Entre los beneficiarios; el 52% son mujeres, en el departamento de Intibucá y Yoro se incluirán grupos indígenas, estimando un 69% de lencas en Intibucá y un 4% de varias etnias en Morazán, Yoro. Se estima que un 5% de la población beneficiaria son mujeres embarazadas y lactantes, 2.5% tienen algún tipo de discapacidad, 2% de las niñas y niños tienen desnutrición aguda.

Adicionalmente, WVH es una organización con presencia en los 18 departamentos de Honduras. De presentarse una emergencia o crisis, los equipos priorizan la respuestas a la emergencia.

project_name: Increased and sustained equitable access to quality child protection and gender base violence services for children and adolescents affected by conflict in north-east Nigeria.
project_objective:
The UNICEF child protection project will focus on strengthening access to quality preventive and responsive child protection services that address the needs, rights and dignity of children and their caregivers in the conflict affected states of Borno, Adamawa and Yobe (BAY). The emergency response will prioritize the most vulnerable including at-risk children and their families. UNICEF’s efforts to address child protection and gender-based violence in emergencies is part of its over-all strategy on prevention and response to all forms of violence against children (VAC). 
Results will be achieved by providing integrated child protection case management services for children including family tracing and reunification for UASC and delivering quality and sustainable socio-economic reintegration services to children formerly associated with armed groups as well as other vulnerable children and their families. In addition, conflict-affected children will have access to community-based mental health and psychosocial support services (MHPSS) including structured recreational activities and adolescents’ life skills education. The project will also contribute to strengthening capacity of service delivery to GBV survivors. Child and adult survivors of conflict-related sexual violence and GBV will in addition have access to comprehensive minimum lifesaving services including medical, psychosocial, legal and safety. Children and caregivers living in or returning to locations contaminated by unexploded remnant of war (UXO) will be provided with explosive ordnance risk education (EORE) in schools, child friendly spaces, transit and displace camps with the support of the Mine Action sub sector. UNICEF response will target almost 53 percent of the overall child protection sub sector target for 2023. The geographic locations will be prioritized according to the severity of need and access. 

In addition, the project actions will further focus on child protection system strengthening through the roll out of the child protection law in the BAY states, registering under-5 child births, and enhancing the capacity of a professional social service workforce to improve quality service delivery. The UNICEF child protection response will be integrated with other sectors, such as education, WASH, health and nutrition, for increased and comprehensive delivery of services to conflict affected children and caregivers.

Using a nexus-approach, this project will also support the efforts of peaceful coexistence, transitional justice, reinforcing existing local and national capacities including a focus on climate change mitigation where possible.
Grave violations against children affected by conflict will be monitored and reported through the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism (MRM 1612). Data derived from the MRM will be used for high-level advocacy and to inform programming. The signed Handover Protocol (HoP) between the Government of Nigeria and UNICEF will be used to prevent or reduce the detention of children encountered by military and security forces during armed conflict, by identifying and transferring children allegedly associated with armed groups within a limited period to the Ministry of Women Affairs and Social Development (MWASD). 

Finally, UNICEF will use the platform of the Group of Friends (GoF) on children and armed conflict (CAAC) to share information on the impact of conflict on children, raise awareness, support fundraising initiatives, and undertake joint strategic advocacy actions to prevent and end grave violations against children in Nigeria.

project_name: Emergency interventions to improve access to basic WASH services for the most vulnerable unserved and underserved communities in the West Bank.
project_objective:
The proposed project aims to improve the access to safe water and sanitation in the most vulnerable communities in area C (78% of the proposed interventions), area A and B (16%), and H2 (6%) in the West Bank. The interventions will contribute to reducing the targeted communities’ WASH vulnerability with the focus on boys and girls and persons with disabilities (PWD), especially girls as they are considered the most vulnerable and more in need of these critical services. The interventions will target unserved and underserved communities with essential WASH services that will also protect the most vulnerable families under threat of forcible transfer. The interventions will focus on improving the communities’ access to 1) adequate and safely managed water services; 2) sanitation services and 3) WASH facilities in schools and health centres. All interventions will be implemented in parallel with the provision of hygiene materials and hygiene awareness sessions in schools, health centres and communities.

The project interventions were developed based on the WASH Cluster eligible actions for HRP 2023 and targeting the most vulnerable communities according to the Health Care Facilities (HCF) vulnerability assessment conducted by the WASH cluster for the West Bank. Therefore, UNICEF and its implementing partners are proposing to implement:

•	Construction/rehabilitation of water infrastructures (pipes) (10 communities).
•	Construction/rehabilitation of wastewater infrastructures (pipes) (1 community). 
•	Capacity building for two local councils in Hebron Governorate through developing a hydraulic model and supplying maintenance tools and equipment.
•	Construction/rehabilitation of gender sensitive and disability friendly WASH facilities in 20 schools. 
•	Construction/rehabilitation of gender sensitive and disability friendly WASH facilities 16 health centres
•	conducting hygiene awareness sessions in schools, health centres and communities. (20 schools, 16 health centres and 11 communities)

UNICEF and its partners will adopt several implementation methodologies that consider the targeted communities’ locations, proposed response technical standards, and UNICEF's accessibility and partners to these communities. Therefore, UNICEF and the partners will adopt and consider beneficiary/community implementation mechanisms for part of the water interventions in Area C. Implementation through suppliers/contractors will be adopted for WASH facilities in schools, health centers and community water and wastewater infrastructures activity in Area A & B. 

Moreover, the proposed interventions will consider the targeted groups' socioeconomic, protection and COVID-19-related vulnerabilities. UNICEF will target the communities under the risk of demolition and forcible transfer in Area C, vulnerable communities in Area A & B, the families under the poverty line, and the communities highly affected by the COVID-19 outbreak. The proposed interventions will improve the targeted groups' capacities and resilience to deal with the challenges mentioned above.

UNICEF and its partners will carefully consider the special and persistent needs of women, boys and girls , elders and PWDs. Thus, these vulnerable groups will be consulted during the planning, design, and implementation of the interventions. Therefore, UNICEF and its partners will propose the sufficient response of these groups that consider the different social and traditional characteristics in the targeted communities.

project_name: Integrated Protection Response for Conflict-Affected and Displaced Populations in Northeast Syria
project_objective:
IRC will deliver Integrated Protection services directly and through partnerships with LNGOs, reaching 239,257 vulnerable conflict-affected individuals in Raqqa, Hasakeh and Deir ez Zor governorates.
Providing a comprehensive response to the protection needs of all community members who have been harmed or otherwise exposed to violence to recover and/or connect individuals to services that protect them to promote their healing and reduce their vulnerability.
Interventions will include establishing Women and Girls Safe Spaces (WGSS) and Safe Healing and
Learning Spaces (SHLS) combined with outreach teams to provide specialized case management services for GBV survivors and children who have been harmed by abuse, neglect, and exploitation, including supporting CAAFAG children with CPCM and reintegration in the community, providing cash assistance to meet immediate needs, structured and unstructured PSS services, parenting skills training for caregivers, and life skills education for boys and girls.
IRC will regularly monitor the violation of rights and the protection situation in NES to understand the changes over time, to screen and improve access to primary and specialized services and advocate on behalf of vulnerable populations to improve the protection situation in their communities and inform response planning.
Regular assessments and legal analysis on civil housing and property rights will inform legal support, programming, and advocacy. Protection mainstreaming will be within protection activities and other IRC sectors’ activities to ensure safety, access, participation, and accountability. Particular attention
will be given to accessibility and full inclusion for people with disabilities through accessible spaces, inclusive delivery, such as the use of sign language interpreter or having consent forms and other materials in Braille.
IRC additionally delivers capacity building and training about GBV core concept, safe referral, and mainstreaming, CP, PSEA, protection, and humanitarian principles will be delivered to different stakeholders including INGOs staff and LNGOs.
Finally, IRC uses cash for protection in combination with other protection activities especially case management to respond to the most accute and urgent needs.
A Protection Cash program is where: 
•	Cash has been identified as an appropriate modality to address specific protection threats and has been considered alongside or in combination with other modalities (protection services, case management, etc.)
•	The program targets or identifies individuals based on protection-based vulnerability    
•	The use of cash is designed with the purpose of achieving protection outcomes, and the program monitors and reports on protection outcomes 

Cash for protection programming does not include: 
•	Beneficiaries of a protection program who are unable to meet basic needs are referred to economic recovery and development ERD to receive cash to meet their basic needs, or to other livelihoods activities 
•	When meeting basic needs (such as food security) is the primary objective of the program, but the program also includes secondary objectives related to meeting protection outcomes to which the CVA is not explicitly linked
•	Beneficiaries are no longer included in the protection activities or measured on protection outcomes  

While providing our services to people who require hearing aid/sign language support, which is a  dwindling small number, these persons bring along family members or acquaintances who help with the communication to address services and needs.

project_objective: Este proyecto pretende mejorar las condiciones de acceso y permanencia ofrecidas en las escuelas (para 558,000 niños, niñas y adolescentes- NNAs), incluyendo disponibilidad de material educativo para incentivar el acceso y la asistencia regular de los estudiantes (377,000 NNA). Igualmente se ofrecen actividades de apoyo socioemocinal para 377,000 NNA. También se pretende llegar a 60,000 adolescentes con actividades de promoción de habilidades para la vida. Suplementación con hierro y ácido fólico a MEL. Suplementación con micronutrientes a 180,000 niños y niñas de 6 a 59 meses y 80,000 MEL; e. Suplementación para mujeres embarazadas con bajo peso.

Mejorar el acceso a los servicios de salud y nutrición de alta calidad a través de apoyo técnico calificado y provisión de insumos y equipo nutricional. a. 3,500 personal de salud y nutrición capacitados para la prevención y tratamiento de la desnutrición b. 800 centros de atención nuricional fortalecidos con insumos y equipos nutricionales.

project_name: Fortalecer el sistema de protección de NNA con servicios de prevención y respuesta con enfoque en edad, genero y diversidad.
project_objective:
UNICEF mantendrá su enfoque en apoyar a los diferentes integrantes del sistema de Protección para que brinden servicios de prevención y respuestas de calidad con un enfoque en edad, género y diversidad para los NNA y familias más vulnerables y en riesgo. UNICEF mantendrá los esfuerzos en el desarrollo de los objetivos e indicadores sectoriales del Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria 2022-2023, a través de planes de trabajo con socios implementadores nacionales e internacionales. La Protección de la Infancia es la prevención y respuesta a la explotación, abuso, negligencia, prácticas nocivas y la violencia contra los niños, niñas y adolescentes (NNA). Está incorporada en la Convención sobre los Derechos del Niño y las Metas de Desarrollo Sostenible. Con un abordaje socio-ecológico, UNICEF y sus socios trabajaran con un enfoque en los NNA, las familias, las comunidades y el sistema de protección formal e informal para que acciones preventivas y de respuestas para temas de protección de NNA sean implementadas en los estados priorizados del país.  El enfoque principal de esta propuesta es la prevención que se realiza no solamente a través de los socios de protección, pero también con el apoyo de otros sectores como nutrición, salud y educación para cumplir resultados de protección infantil. Los principales temas cubiertos incluyen: VbG y trata, separación familiar/cuidado alternativo, violencia en general incluyendo la de género y crianza positiva. Además de nuestro enfoque central en la prevención, UNICEF Venezuela se enfoca en que ningún NNA se quede atrás: trabajaremos con socios para alcanzar a los NNA con mayor riesgo de protección que incluyen NNA con discapacidades, NNA separados y no acompañados, de poblaciones indígenas y afro-descendientes, en situacion de movilidad y NNA que sufren otras formas de discriminación y exclusión. 
Donde los NNA están sufriendo violaciones, UNICEF trabajará con socios gubernamentales y no-gubernamentales para fortalecer el acceso a los servicios de respuesta para prevenir reincidencia y brindar atención y vinculación segura a otros servicios. Los principales servicios brindados incluyen: apoyo en acceder a registro de nacimiento, salud mental y apoyo psicosocial, gestión de caso incluyendo a NNA sobreviviente de VbG. Una modalidad diferente para alcanzar objetivos de protección será la de las transferencias monetarias/incentivos, otra componente importante de todas las intervenciones es el enfoque en la calidad y en temas transversales como lo de género, AAP, PEAS, adolescencia y inclusión.

project_name: Prevention and Treatment of Acute Malnutrition in South Sudan
project_objective:
The humanitarian situation in South Sudan continues to deteriorate ten years after the country gained its independence in 2011 because of an escalation in armed conflict, subnational violence, devastating climatic shocks, economic instability and high levels of food insecurity. Recurring climatic shocks persist with permanent flooding for the fourth year in a row reaching the largest observed levels in 2022 and at a scale comparable to that of the mid-1960’s. Drought on the other hand continues to affect the South-eastern part of the country which has led to significant delays in the onset of favourable conditions for planting and early crop development, hence reducing cultivated areas and extending the hunger gap.  
 
As of end of October 2022, over 924,000 people4 were reportedly affected by flooding in 31 counties across South Sudan and in the southern part of the Abyei Administrative Area. Humanitarian physical access to flood-affected communities is hampered by flooded roads, rising flood waters, insecurity, and poor road infrastructures whereby less than two percent of the country’s estimated 17,000 km of roads are paved. 
 
The already dire situation in South Sudan is compounded by the significant increase in food, commodity, and fuel prices due to the Ukraine crisis and an economic downfall triggered by US dollar/ South Sudanese Pound exchange rate fluctuations. The prices of staple foods have doubled, and the currency has depreciated by over 30 percent since February 2022, further reducing purchasing power of the most vulnerable and resulting in further deterioration of food security and increased vulnerability. Additionally, the increase in fuel prices triggered a rise in transportation costs in Juba and across other urban counties. Over the first half of 2022, fuel prices increased by 90 percent which is expected to lead to approximately 25 percent rise in the primary transport cost. 
      
The October 2022 Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) results indicated that 7.76 million people – over 63 percent of the population of South Sudan – will likely face high acute food insecurity levels at the peak of the May-July lean season5, with around 43,000 people likely to be in IPC Phase 5. This represents a slight increase over the 7.74 million people in need during the 2022 lean season and is the highest number recorded since independence. 

Additionally, based on the IPC findings, an estimated 1.4 million children under 5 years are malnourished and in need of lifesaving nutrition interventions. Around 738,000 Pregnant and Lactating Women (PLW) and new mothers are acutely malnourished and in need of treatment. This is driven by deteriorating food insecurity, poor diet, high prevalence of diseases, sub-optimal mother and child care practices and limited access to basic health and nutrition services.  
 
In response to the dire nutrition needs in South Sudan, WFP's project will facilitate the provision of nutrition prevention and treatment services to populations affected by conflict, displacement, climate change and insecurity. The project will target residents, IDPs, refugees and returnees (for treatment only) to prevent malnutrition related morbidity and mortality. 

WFP will continue to work with cooperating partners to support an emergency nutrition response through a preventive supplementary feeding programme and treatment services for moderate acute malnutrition targeting children aged 6-24 months (and up to 59 months in IPC 5 locations), pregnant & lactating women, and people living with HIV/TB across all states of South Sudan.
In hard-to-reach areas, WFP will conduct direct delivery of life-saving nutrition services through the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM). The project implementation will be coordinated closely with the Nutrition cluster and use an integrated approach through synergies with activities supported by other clusters (health, education, FSL, WASH).

project_name: Provision of Comprehensive and Integrated Primary and secondary Health Services to Conflict-affected, Displaced and Vulnerable Populations in South Sudan.
project_objective:
IMCs provide comprehensive, integrated primary and secondary health care services through static health facilities complemented by regular mobile outreach to increase and expand fair coverage and access, especially for displaced or hard-to-reach populations with intermittent periods of stability and weather-constrained access. Aligned with the 2022 Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) for South Sudan, IMC's healthcare interventions are designed to (1) Improve equitable access to lifesaving quality healthcare services that includes maternal, child, and adolescent health, sexual and reproductive health, treatment of common illnesses, disability, MHPSS, and GBV health services to approximately 550,000 people in crises in Juba, Malakal, and Wau displacement camps, as well as in Canal/Pigi, Akoka, Balliet, and Panyikang Counties (2) Reduce excess morbidity and mortality by improving the capacity of the country's health system for early detection and response to disease outbreaks, (3) Enhance resilience and promote humanitarian-development linkages to strengthen health system recovery and coping mechanisms. 
IMC will continue to provide Primary and Secondary health care services integrated with Nutrition, SGBV and MHPSS across its 26 supported health facilities located in  Central Equatoria (Juba IDP Camps, Khor Williang PHCC), Western Bahr el Ghazal (Wau IDP camp), Jonglei (Canal/Pigi County), and Upper Nile (Malakal PoC and County, and Akoka, Balliet and Panyikang Counties). These services will include Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI), outpatient consultation for communicable and non-communicable diseases, care for trauma and injuries, community-based health education at the facility and in the community,. Implementation of the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) at static health facilities and outreach sites; Provision of Sexual and Reproductive health services across Juba (IDP and Khor Williang health facilities), Malakal (PoC and Malakal Teaching Hospital), Wau IDP camp, and Canal PIGI sites for vulnerable populations targeting women of reproductive age (15-49 years). IMC will continue to provide community health education and social-behavioral change communication to support disease prevention and health promotion activities and facilitate referrals to nearby health facilities. IMC currently provides advanced emergency obstetric and newborn care, trauma care, surgical interventions, and rehabilitation for injuries.  IMC will focus on supporting static health facilities, mobile outreach teams, and community-based intervention to ensure access, availability, and utilization of appropriate health services. All of IMC's interventions will have a particular focus on vulnerable persons, such as women of reproductive age, pregnant and lactating women, children under 5, and people with specific needs and vulnerabilities, adolescents, people living with disabilities, survivors of sexual abuse, minorities, and marginalized groups, displaced people, and host communities.

project_name: Provision of Integrated Lifesaving Nutrition interventions to conflict affected populations (Children 0-59 months, pregnant and lactating women) in Canal Pigi, Panyjar, Malakal, Fashoda, Panyikang, Manyo and Juba IDP Camps Counties in South Sudan
project_objective:
Through the proposed humanitarian responses, International Medical Corps (IMC UK) will provide integrated lifesaving nutrition service to conflict affected and displaced communities in Juba IDP Camps, Panyijar, Malakal, Fashoda, Panyikang, Manyo and Canal Pigi Counties. With the aim to reduce suffering, morbidity and mortality related to malnutrition among vulnerable populations, IMC will increase equitable access and utilization of quality lifesaving nutrition services for early detection and treatment of acute malnutrition, which are essential for addressing key drivers of acute malnutrition affecting children and women in the aforesaid project locations. IMC UK will also continue to address the prevention of malnutrition in children under two years of age through promotion of appropriate Maternal Infant and Young Child Nutrition Feeding (MIYCN) practices. The service will be delivered through static and outreach sites for remote and hard to reach areas in the targeted project locations. The proposed response will include all components of Community Management of Acute Malnutrition, including Targeted Supplementary Feeding Programme (TSFP), Outpatient Therapeutic Programme (OTP), Stabilization Center (SC) and community mobilization activities. International Medical Corps UK proposes to operate 38 OTPs, 38 Targeted supplementary feeding programs (TSFPs), and 5 SCs across the project sites. IMC UK will work with the Ministry of Health (MoH), UNICEF and WFP to secure timely provision of nutrition supplies, which are necessary for nutrition service delivery. IMC will reach approximately 180,712 individuals, of which 72,285 are IDPs. All project activities will be implemented in line with adapted guidelines for nutrition services delivery in the context of COVID-19 provided by the Nutrition Cluster.
IMC UK will monitor the nutrition status of the population and the nutrition response through routine nutrition program data, quarterly MUAC screening campaigns and population-based SMART Surveys. IMC UK, with its already established Nutrition Surveillance Team, will undertake nutrition assessments in its operational locations and support to undertake in nutrition assessments in Priority counties as well to provide robust information on the nutrition situation of a given population, this information will be key in responding effectively to nutrition needs in the project area. 
This project aims to enhance nutrition-sensitive interventions that will ensure safe, equitable and dignified access to critical cross-sectoral basic services; to further decrease the prevalence of acute malnutrition, and ultimately, to contribute to the prevention and reduction of morbidity and mortality associated to malnutrition in South Sudan. Additionally, IMC UK will reinforce and promote access to integrated nutrition, health, WASH, protection and FSL services provision in the project target areas through geographical integration, activity integration, and integration through common approaches to reduce the burden of malnutrition and improve wholistic impact. IMC will also closely work with Nutrition partners in the target location to prevent overlap of the services and enhance services availability through referral and integration. IMC will also support hygiene interventions to improve nutrition outcomes and reduce risks of hygiene-related morbidities. Nutrition services will be considered as potential entry points for GBV survivors seeking assistance, with nutrition staff trained on GBV referral pathways and other key GBV concepts. The project protection focal points will perform safety audits and assessments of nutrition sites. Safety audits are one of the key approaches used to identify potential GBV related risks at the program sites using a tested tool. The project will conduct safety audit assessments bi-annually at the health and nutrition sites.

project_name: Integrated WASH response to crisis affected population in South Sudan
project_objective:
The project will be implemented in Lainya, Kajo keji, Morobo and Yei counties of Central Equatoria State, Aweil East, Aweil South and Centre of Northern Bahr Ghazal State and Uror, Twic East and Pochalla of Jonglei State. 
Poor food security in all locations, coupled with poor WASH practices, is leading to high rates of global acute malnutrition, over WHO’s critical level of 15%. The strong relationship between poor WASH infrastructure and practices, food insecurity and malnutrition is perpetuating high SAM and MAM rates. Use of unsafe drinking water and poor hygiene and sanitation practices are contributing to the high incidence of diarrhoea and water-borne diseases in vulnerable communities, sustaining the malnutrition-diarrhoea cycle and reducing the nutrient uptake in infants and young children.
The project will target over 141,000 individuals. The project will seek to improve water supply infrastructure to increase access to safe drinking water and facilitate hygiene promotion to encourage behaviour change relating to hygiene and sanitation practices by ensuring access to safe water through rehabilitation/ construction of water points, water quality testing, provision of WASH NFIs, ensuring access to safe sanitation facilities and hygiene promotion.
The project will be in line with WASH Cluster's objective of integrating WASH response with nutrition /food security and Health; addressing live-saving needs in disaster contexts in restoring immediate access to basic WASH services either temporarily or permanently; and building in locations that were affected by flooding in the past three years.
Tearfund will, (1) Improve water supply infrastructure to increase access to safe drinking water and (2) Facilitate hygiene promotion throughout the targeted communities to encourage behaviour change relating to hygiene and sanitation practices, (3) construct and installed hand washing facilities in Health, Nutrition facilities to encourage hand washing hence reducing Covid 19 transmissions. The proposed intervention will enable Tearfund to continue providing critical services addressing access to safe drinking water and increased sanitation facilities, and improved hygiene practices to vulnerable communities in Aweil East & Centre, Uror, Twic East, Pochalla, Kajo keji, Morobo as well expand activities to targeted communities in Yei and Lainya. 
Tearfund has a static presence throughout Jonglei, Northern Bahr El Ghazal, and Central Equatoria. The proposed project is part of Tearfund’s wider programme, which integrates WASH, Nutrition and Food Security and Protection.

project_name: Emergency support to food insecure  communities in South Sudan
project_objective:
This project targets 165,000 beneficiaries (35,000 men, 60,000 women, 35,000 boys and 35,000 girls). The proposed interventions  will be implemented in 10 Counties  of Uror, Twic East, Pochalla, Morobo, Kajo Keji, Yei, Lainya, Aweil East, Aweil Centre, and Aweil South of the 4 states  Jonglei, Greater Pibor Administrative Area and Central Equatoria, Northern Bahr el Ghazal respectively. The needs across all three states continued to escalate throughout 2021, with poor harvests, prolonged floods and conﬂict resulting in depleted stocks. Uror, Twic East and Aweil East, Aweil South are in an In South Sudan, where 95 per cent of livelihoods depend on traditional rain-fed agriculture, crop farming, pastoralism and animal husbandry, climate shocks are likely to lead to an increase in livestock mortality and a decline in the amount and viability of land farmers can cultivate. The project has been designed to address the deteriorating food security in the project locations. The proposed intervention will achieve the HRP Strategic and Cluster objectives in line with the sector objectives:
SO1: Life saving: 
SO2: Centrality of protection: 
SO3: Resilience/ Coping mechanisms vulnerable people withstand & recover from shocks, have their resilience to shocks & stressors built and seek solutions to displacement which respect their rights
CO1: Provide food assistance to prevent famine and improve food consumption, dietary diversity and coping strategies for vulnerable populations (in IPC 5, 4 & some 3) in a way that prevents the spread & transmission of COVID 19 (compulsory use of new SOP & guidelines)
CO2: Enhance and sustain emergency food production through complementary vegetable and crop livelihood inputs, fishing and livestock support in a way that prevents the spread & transmission of COVID 19 (compulsory use of new SOP & guidelines)
CO3: Reduce dependency on food and agricultural inputs to support and strengthen households’ ability to absorb shocks in a way that prevents the spread & transmission of COVID 19 (compulsory use of new SOP & guidelines)
This will be done through the provision of lifesaving assistance to conflict affected communities by providing agricultural inputs and providing training to vulnerable households to increase food production through good agricultural and fisheries practices to improve food security. Emergency livelihood kits distribution, and  increasing access to local markets through seed fairs will  be organised for local farmers and the project will provide direct distribution of food rations to the most vulnerable communities. Tearfund will also look at ways of resilience-building that reduce recipient’s future risk and vulnerability to negative shocks. The project will engage Community Agricultural Extension Trainers to train the groups on community managed disaster risk reduction; organic manure preparation and basic conservation agricultural practices; local production of climate resilient seeds (cereals and tubers); improved agronomic practices for identified crops; post-harvest handling; marketing and record keeping; soil and environment conservation; farming as a business; improved sustainable agronomic practices; early warning systems.
The proposed project activities will enhance and sustain emergency food production through complementary vegetable and crop livelihood inputs, and fishing support in a way that prevents the spread and transmission of COVID 19 with adherence to and compulsory use of new Standard Operating procedures (SOP’s) and guidelines by the Ministry of Health/WHO. The distribution of vegetable seeds will provide the households  with a variety of vegetable food for their consumption in a span of 3-4 months, in addition, surplus harvest will be sold in the market for income or preserved for future consumption during the lean season. The Fishing kit’s will help the households get the much needed proteins almost immediately after they receive them and engage in fishing activities.

project_name: Integrated Nutrition response to crisis affected population in South Sudan
project_objective:
Malnutrition remains a persistent problem in South Sudan that continues to adversely affect the well-being of women and children. In 2023, close to 2.2 children and women will be at risk of acute malnutrition and will need urgent treatment. These include 353, 606 children for severe acute malnutrition (SAM), 1, 084,129 moderate acute malnutrition (MAM) and 737,812 pregnant and lactating women (PLW). High food insecurity, elevated prevalence of diseases, and poor hygiene, health, and environmental sanitation services, along with inadequate maternal and childcare are the main drivers of acute malnutrition in South Sudan. According to the preliminary results from Food Security and Nutrition Monitoring System (FSNMS) Round 28 and the 2022 SMART surveys, the proportion of children 6-59 months suffering from acute malnutrition remains above the emergency threshold of 15 percent (very high acute malnutrition level- WHO classification) was at 16.0% in lean season. The high levels of food insecurity seen among children under five years old in the targeted areas can be partially attributed to the scarcity of food and the consequent lack of variety in diet. This is further compounded by the lack of knowledge of minimum dietary diversity required. Poor Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) practices, low food production and consequently low food reserves are also preventing children from receiving nutritionally dense foods. 
Tearfund has scaled up its nutrition services in flood affected Twic East County with the aim of reaching as many people as possible in hard to reach highlands areas where most of them are currently stationed. It has established five mobile sites to address the nutritional needs when the existing static sites collapsed by the ongoing floods.  Over the past year, Tearfund was able to manage 10,622 SAM, 14,764 MAM children and 5,256 malnourished PLWs newly admitted in 27 Nutrition sites in 3 Counties. Out of these cases, 95% in OTP and 98% U5 children in TSFP were discharged cured. However, there are still notable gaps in terms of scaling up and expansion of services; integration of nutrition with other sectors such as FSL, WASH and Health. In 2023, Tearfund targets to reach 12646 SAM, 31354 MAM U5, 27544 PLW, 48025 Caregivers, 124064 VAS and deworming. Tearfund is the sole organization in supporting nutrition interventions in 27 nutrition sites in three Counties (8-in Twic East; 8-in Pochalla and 11-in Uror) and 4 Stabilization Centers (2-in Uror; 1-in Pochalla and 1-in Twic East). 
The integrated approach will address the high levels of malnutrition by targeting the families of SAM and MAM children for health, FSL and WASH interventions thereby acknowledging that these sectors are a key driver of poor health and malnutrition. Returnees and IDPs will be of special interest to this project because of their high levels of vulnerability.

project_name: Education support for Syria’s children and youth affected by crisis
project_objective:
Syrian children are now affected by a triple crisis: conflict, economic shock and COVID-19. An estimated 2 million children  are out-of-school and face elevated protection risks related to, among others, child marriage and child labour. As per HNO 2022, Ninety per cent of Syrians live poverty. In many governorates poverty is now the biggest reason for children dropping out of school. In addition, the pandemic has had an impact on the continuity of education in classrooms. 

Only 54 per cent of the 17,958 pre-crisis schools were functional as of February 2020, as reported in HNO 2022,  causing overcrowding. Some schools operate in double/triple shifts to accommodate displaced children. In 2021, there were 25 reported attacks on schools  (mostly in NWS), further contributing to the deterioration of access to education. 

Many students are behind in their learning, finding it difficult to return to school or at risk of dropping out. Younger children, adolescents and children with disabilities face further challenges accessing learning services due to limited availability of ECE centres, secondary education services and vocational training opportunities or inclusive education for the estimated 15 per cent of children with disabilities. Key reasons children are not in school include schools not being in their area, schooling not being affordable and children working to support the household, the use of schools for non-educational purposes and other safety concerns—particularly in NWS. 

UNICEF proposes to provide education services for preprimary, primary and secondary school-aged girls and boys to enable them to develop foundational numeracy and literacy skills, as well as life and citizenship skills in schools that are safe and welcoming, in order to strengthen child, family and community resilience.

Through different partnerships with diverse education partners,  UNICEF will contribute to:
A.	Access to inclusive learning
B.	Quality learning in safe and inclusive schools
C.	Resilient Systems

Access will be promoted through Back-to-Learning Campaigns, Vouchers-for-Education, school textbooks and school supplies, support for national exams, rehabilitation of schools (formal and nonformal) and the provision of temporary classrooms. Schools will be furnished, equipped with gender-sensitive WASH facilities, and established in particularly vulnerable areas (Severity Scale 3-5). Rehabilitation is also needed in lower severity areas, where displaced children and returnees as well as large numbers of host community children reside, to contribute to resilience and social cohesion. UNICEF will ensure “safe access” through the clearing of UXO and COVID-19 free physical access will be guaranteed through sanitization of school buildings.

To improve the quality of education services, UNICEF will ensure schools are child-friendly, with teachers trained in child-centered pedagogy, and where children develop academic, cognitive, life and psychosocial skills that empower them to engage, relate, cope and contribute to community and family life. Due to the large number of children at different learning levels within grades, children will be provided with remedial learning support. Corporal punishment and violence in school will be tackled. Nonformal education will give adolescents the chance to find employment or re-integrate into public schools. 

UNICEF will strengthen the resilience of grassroots education systems, facilitating bridges between schools and communities through the establishment of Parent Teacher Associations that cooperate with Headmasters, and by training education staff in monitoring schools, staff performance and children’s learning.

A continued failure to invest in education infrastructure, services and quality will result in squandered opportunities to help children learn and thrive. A substantial number of children will stay out of school, and abandon intentions to ever return.

project_name: Integrated Social Protection Programme for Children with Disabilities – Cash Transfer, Referral and Case Management Services
project_objective:
Syria is witnessing its worst economic crisis in recent history. The economy has shrunk to less than half of its 2011 level. The economic collapse has resulted in increased hardship for many Syrian families, who face price hikes, limited access to basic social services, fuel shortages, increased poverty and unemployment. 79% of the population lives below the poverty line compared to about 25% pre-crisis. It is estimated that over 80% are at risk of food insecurity . Government social spending has decreased significantly. This has led to the breakdown of critical national social protection programmes, including for people living with disabilities.  
Children living with disabilities suffer from social exclusion and live in dire economic conditions. They are socially and economically among the most vulnerable group of children in the country. UNICEF monitoring surveys conducted among families caring for CWD indicate that about 70% of CWD are out of school compared to less than 20% among children without disabilities in the families . They indicate very high level of poverty among families, with their monthly average expenditures being much lower than the minimum income required to meet their basic needs.
UNICEF is implementing the Integrated Social Protection Programme for Children with Disabilities. It provides an integrated response to the needs of CWD through the combination of regular, unconditional cash transfers with case management services. It promotes an integrated social protection model with links to public services, with a view to prepare the ground for a future transition from an emergency response to a nationally owned social protection scheme. Since the programme began in 2016, over 35,000 CWD, 180,000 families in eight governorates have been reached. 
The programme enhances the resilience of the most vulnerable families and strengthens the continuum of humanitarian and early recovery intervention through an integrated response, which combines regular and un-conditional cash transfers with case management services to facilitate the referral of CWD to available social services and increase their social inclusion. For a 24-month period, families of CWD receive a regular quarterly transfer of monthly US$ 40 or quarterly US$ 120. Each child is followed throughout the period by a dedicated and trained case manager. While the cash help families meet the basic needs of children and the households, the case management component facilitates the referral of CWD to available social services, increasing their social inclusion and responding to their specific protection concerns.
During 2021-2022, UNICEF conducted five baseline monitoring surveys for the programme in the governorates of Al Hassakeh, Aleppo, Hama, Homs and Rural Damascus. The surveys provide new evidence about the positive impact of the integrated approach followed by the programme. They also provide a wealth of information about the demographic and socio-economic characteristics of families caring for CWD. All surveys paint a consistent and similar picture of beneficiaries’ socio-economic characteristics and programme impact. Key highlights from Rural Damascus Survey includes:
•	High levels of poverty: The average monthly expenditure of families was SYP 403,000, well below the value of the MEB required by families to meet their basic needs. 
•	High levels of vulnerability among female-headed families. 
•	High levels of education exclusion among children with disabilities: 69% of CWD respectively have never attended school or any other form of education compared to 7 % among children without disabilities in the families.
In 2023, the programme aims to reach 17,000 CWD and their families with regular cash transfer and case management services in nine governorates Dier-ez-Zor; Hassakeh; Aleppo; Hama; Homs; Rural Damascus and as Sweida, Lattakia and Tartous. Accountability to beneficiaries’ is ensured through UNICEF centralized redress & grievance mechanisms &PDMs

project_name: Supporting crisis-affected populations in Far-North region through the provision of multi-sectoral assistance in Cameroon
project_objective:
Following the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus (HDPN) approach that IOM strongly supports and actively promotes in Cameroon, and building on the programmes and activities implemented in the recent years, IOM plans comprehensive emergency interventions for 2023 focusing especially on coordination, shelter, mental health support (health), psychosocial support (protection) and WASH interventions. 
IOM’s multisectoral response aims at contributing to reinforce life-saving assistance and to improve well-being of displaced and the most vulnerable populations affected by the crisis in the Far North region of Cameroon.
Critical data on displacement situation, alerts as well as humanitarian needs following our DTM methodology will be provided to the humanitarian community in the frame of the Coordination Sector. IOM will also distribute shelter and NFI kits using cash-modality solutions when possible (bearing in mind that lack of civil documentation poses a huge challenge) and help the construction for most vulnerable people. In the WASH response, IOM will drill and rehabilitate boreholes, construct water points, latrines and other infrastructures and conduct hygiene sensitization and promotion activities. Finally, IOM multisectoral assistance will also include mental health activities including direct MHPSS assistance using PMTs, reinforcing referral mechanism and capacity building of health actors (Health sector), while also directly providing psychosocial support to populations impacted by crisis by reinforcing safety and social network as well as strengthening community capacity to provide psychosocial support to victims of GBVs (Protection sector). These interventions are complementary to other programmes IOM implements in the region, focusing on DDR or social cohesion and by creating synergies within such initiatives, aim at achieving the HDP collective outcome set by the National HDPN Taskforce of Cameroon : “the most vulnerable populations in the convergence areas or in other regions affected by the crises recover indiscriminately their fundamental rights and improve their physical well-being and social welfare.”
The project will target various localities in the Far North region considering the level of needs and vulnerabilities observed and consulted with coordination with each sector of planned interventions. When feasible and appropriate, participative targeting workshops involving local community members and Humanitarian, Development and Peacebuilding partners in the localities will also be held.  
IOM respects its procedures to handle complaints on SEA starting with a focal person to receive and handle complaints and the building of knowledge of IOM staff and IPs about IOM’s policy and mechanisms to prevent SEA, including training on the proper conduct to handle SEA disclosures. IOM will also make usage of the Far North GBV referral pathway to refer SEA cases.
Through activities, direct feedback from beneficiaries and community members will be gained via IPs and also directly by IOM staff during field visits and visits of the M&E/AAP independent team in accordance with the wider IOM AAP emergencies workplan. AAP focal points will be assigned in Maroua and Yaounde respectively, with clear SOPs to be in place to capture complaints from beneficiaries and to take any appropriate action. Members of IP will be trained on topics such as the proper handling of disclosures of gender-based violence (GBV) incidents, aspects of confidentiality, and respectful communication in high-stress environments.

project_name: Renforcement de la protection pour les personnes en situation de vulnérabilite, en particulier les enfants, les survivants de violence basée sur le genre (VBG) et victimes de traite dans les régions de Diffa, Tillabéri, Maradi et Tahoua
project_objective:
L’objectif vise, d’ici fin 2023, à ce que les risques de violations des droits humains, y compris les risques de traite et de VBG, soient amoindris à travers la promotion d’un environnement protecteur et le renforcement aux services de protection, y compris aux services de Santé mentale et soutien psychosocial, dans les régions de Tillabéri, Diffa, Maradi et Tahoua.
Le projet prévoit 4 axes d’intervention complémentaires :
1. Renforcement des capacités étatiques et des services sociaux de base dans les départements cibles pour une meilleure prise en charge des personnes vulnérables notamment des enfants, y compris des survivant-e-s VBG et des victimes de traite : 
Un cycle de formation sur la protection des victimes de traite sera organisé en coordination avec le cluster protection pour tout acteur de la chaine de protection dans les communes cibles, dont les travailleurs sociaux de la protection de l’enfance et des organisations de la société civile. Il comprendra également des sessions sur la spécificité de la prise en charge des enfants non accompagnés en contexte humanitaire, et les besoins spécifiques des survivantes de VBG. Un appui matériel sera octroyé aux DDPFPE pour pourvoir répondre aux besoins de protection des déplacés.
2. Prévention des violences notamment envers les enfants et les femmes, y compris des VBG et diverses exploitations, à travers le renforcement des mécanismes communautaires de protection, l’appui aux leaders communautaires et la mobilisation des filles et garçons : 
En collaboration avec les DDPFPE, les mairies et les OSC, une cartographie et évaluation des besoins des structures communautaires, y compris les comités de protection, les espaces amis des enfants, les espaces sûrs accueillant des enfants déplacés dans les régions cibles, seront réalisées. Suite à cette analyse, l’OIM appuiera ces structures en matériel, afin que ces dernières puissent jouer leur rôle de protection. Leurs compétences seront renforcées afin qu’ils puissent signaler et référer les cas de protection, mais aussi qu’ils développent des actions de prévention qui encouragent des normes et comportements positifs favorisant des communautés respectueuses, égalitaires, et non violentes à l'égard des femmes et des filles. Des appuis aux initiatives des jeunes pour qu’ils sensibilisent leurs pairs seront réalisés.
3. Atténuation des risques de protection dans les zones ciblées :
En vue de prévenir l’adoption de stratégies de survie négatives des populations et de promouvoir leur dignité, l’OIM poursuivra la distribution des kits de protection adaptés aux besoins, qui seront identifiés avec les populations. Enfin, l'organisation continuera le renforcement de la sécurité sur les sites d'intervention de l'équipe Abris et biens non alimentaires (BNA) & WASH afin de contribuer à la réduction des risques de protection. Les risques seront identifiés au préalable en consultation avec les populations cibles.
4. Offre de services mobiles de SMSPS aux personnes déplacées, notamment les enfants, aux survivants de VBG et aux communautés hôtes : 
La stratégie de services de SMSPS de l’OIM est basée sur son expertise acquise auprès des migrants vulnérables. Des activités de sensibilisation et de formations des leaders communautaires et d’agents de santé seront organisées. Des équipes mobiles se déplaceront pour offrir des activités psychosociales aux populations hôtes et déplacées, là où les structures communautaires sont inexistantes. Une offre de services de santé mentale sera proposée, et les personnes à besoin(s) spécifique(s) seront référées en vertu des mécanismes de référencement mis en place. 
Tout au long du projet, l’OIM s’engagera dans la Protection contre l’exploitation et les abus sexuels et le renforcement de la redevabilité envers les personnes affectées.

project_name: Enhanced  Mental and Psychosocial Health (MHPSS) among women, men, boys and girls at risk of         GBV including  people with disabilities, and  the well-being of service providers through  provision of  specialized MHPSS services in Gaza Strip and West Bank.
project_objective:
This project aims  to support the well-being of  social and health  service providers, and to  provide MHPSS specialized services for women , girls, boys , men  and people             with disabilities, at risk of GBV and referred cases.      
The main outcomes of the project are:
Care for carers (service providers)           by providing MHPSS support  such as stress management  by using WHO  self Help protocol and advanced technical supervision.   
Enhanced capacity of service providers, social and health workers in shelters, safe spaces, Primary Health Care and emergency departments in general hospitals, in WHO mental health gap action programme (mhGAP) intervention guideline v. 2.0 and GBV medical management guideline.
Enhanced Mental and psychosocial health for people in need  through benefiting from specialized mental health services, mainly couples and their families.

The project is built based on the affected community needs and feedbacks, considering the vulnerable groups and women and girls at risk, in addition to UNFPA and WHO partners' experiences and updates from the feld, the established safe spaces, and home visits. Moreover, this project builds by robust experience and evidence the importance of MHPSS mainly after the repeated escalations in Gaza and the unstable political situation in West Bank. Also, both UNFPA and WHO produced many assessments and studies regarding the current MHPSS conditions and status of affected populations in Gaza Strip and West Bank.

project_name: Strengthening the Health Care System in Syria
project_objective:
More than 15.3 million people are in dire need of life-saving health assistance in 2023, a 3.2 million increase from 2022 (N1).
Syria’s shortage of health infrastructure has negatively affected the availability and quality of health services across Syria, including to the most vulnerable populations. In addition, the health care system continues to face chronic challenges to respond to disease outbreaks including COVID-19 and Cholera / Acute Watery Diarrhoea (AWD).
Thus, UNOPS proposes to support the strengthening of the healthcare system in Syria by rehabilitation of hospitals and PHCs, provision of solar energy solutions, delivery of related training, and provision of critical medical equipment and supplies to target health facilities in two governorates (Homs and Hama) in Syria.
The objective of this project is to contribute to enhancing the health sector capacity for a timely response to disaster outbreaks. This project is directly linked with the Strategic Objectives 1 (Save Lives) and 3 (Increase resilience and access to services) of the draft Syria Humanitarian Response Plan 2022 and the immediate response priorities of the Health Sector for 2022 in Syria (N2).
The target locations of this project are Homs and Hama governorates, with possible extensions to other governorates based on the needs. These potential target locations are identified based on the analysis of the needs from the Health Sector and Health sub-sector, taking into account the great barriers, lack of availability and high cost of services, and the ranking on the OCHA severity scale. In addition, the priority needs have been identified in close coordination with the Ministry of Health (MoH) and the humanitarian partners. Once the project is launched, UNOPS will conduct gender-sensitive and technical assessments to finalize the selection of the target locations, the exact scope of work, and the specifications and type of the needed equipment.
Through this intervention, it is expected that five public health facilities (1 hospital and 4 PHCs) will be supported.
To fill the gaps in the shortage of electricity in public health facilities, UNOPS will equip the public health facilities with solar energy solutions through the procurement, installation and commissioning of photovoltaic (PV) hybrid systems and operations and maintenance training will be delivered to the health facilities staff.
It is expected this project will enable targeted public health facilities to offer enhanced pivotal healthcare services to the most vulnerable population in targeted sub-districts of Homs and Hama governorates.
N1:  2023 Syria HNO Health Sector draft
N2: 2022 Syria HNO Health Sector Chapter

project_name: The Access Coordination Unit - Facilitating Access of Humanitarian and Recovery Actors in the oPt
project_objective: Access challenges differ greatly across the oPt, primarily due to the range of political and administrative measures implemented by Israeli and Palestinian authorities. Access and movement restrictions are severe, widespread, costly and difficult to overcome. They increase the impoverishment and vulnerability of Palestinian women, girls, boys, and men within the oPt, and directly impede humanitarian/development operations. They make reaching vulnerable communities difficult and compromise the quality of programming and impact the effectiveness of humanitarian and development interventions. These challenges are particularly severe for local NGO personnel and for communities to reach services. The Access Coordination Unit (ACU) provides a more systematic approach to these challenges and improves access of humanitarian personnel and goods in Israel, Gaza and the WB. Overall, 56% of ACU's UN staff beneficiaries are female (3350 from 6000). Working over all access points, the ACU provides direct engagement and advocacy with relevant authorities as well as direct and timely support, information and advice to international organizations and their personnel. The ACU also facilitates the movement of Palestinian staff serving at duty stations around the world, supporting family reunification and career development of humanitarian personnel. The ACU formulates common policies with a coordinated approach to alleviate constraints to access and to negotiate changes to access policies and procedures with the relevant authorities including Israel, the PA, Gaza authorities, Egypt and Jordan. The ACU currently supports the work of 24 UN agencies, over 200 NGOs, and 65 diplomatic missions whose access to populations in need is impeded by a series of political, physical and bureaucratic restrictions on access and movement imposed by authorities. In addition, an estimated 2.1 M Palestinians in need of assistance throughout the WB and Gaza will indirectly benefit through the more efficient and timely  delivery of humanitarian assistance. One of the primary services of the ACU is a 24/7 access hotline where staff can call the ACU to conduct real-time interventions with relevant authorities to resolve access incidents at checkpoints and crossings for both personnel and goods. The ACU also manages the ACULive mobile app which has 312 active users from 95 organizations, and which enables humanitarian and development personnel and agencies in the oPt to obtain timely and effective access information, guidance and support. The ACU also provides information and advice on procedures for obtaining visas, permits, project approvals and materials coordination as well as conditions and accessibility at checkpoints and crossings via the hotline and beneficiary-specific mailing list which includes 644 individuals working in UN, NGOs, and Diplomatic delegations. During emergencies and contingency situations, the ACU deploys to key field and coordination centres to conduct access and civil-military coordination with the relevant authorities. During the July-August 2014 escalation, the ACU facilitated evacuation of over 1,300 foreign and dual nationals from Gaza to Jordan as well as coordinating other humanitarian activities. ACU coordinated the exit of dual nationals from Gaza during the C19 restrictions, as well as the entry and exit of humanitarian personnel. The humanitarian locations notification system developed by the ACU was launched in 2019 and contains over 900 locations that are regularly shared with the Israeli authorities. During the May 2021 Gaza Escalation the ACU provided support to 1,185 UN, INGO, and diplomatic missions. Finally, information, analysis and messaging on restrictions to humanitarian space are made publicly available to support advocacy efforts undertaken by the humanitarian community and other stakeholders on access.
