project_name: Multi-sectoral emergency response for populations affected by the crisis in the Lake Chad basin in Cameroun
project_objective:
This project started in January 2021. As part of this intervention, AAH provides technical and organizational support to the health centers of the two health districts regularly affected by shocks in order to better equip them to respond to health / nutrition emergencies and to address psychological distress.  Health workers and community volunteers participated in trainings on health / nutrition / mental health and care practices so they can better address the different needs and facilitate referral to activities provided by AAH and other actors in the region. AAH sets up mobile clinics to provide emergency assistance in nutrition / health / mental health for affected and isolated vulnerable populations in the Mayo Sava & Mayo Tsanaga divisions). The package of services and care is delivered free of charge. It targets children under five, pregnant and lactating women, but also disabled people and the elderly among the newly displaced. With regard to the MHCP (mental health and care practices) component, the activities targets children over six and adults with a specific focus on pregnant and lactating women to ensure they follow appropriate care practices and to limit the impact of traumatic stress on pregnancies and infants.
Project Targets: Adults and children Under 5 and above, PLW including IDPs / Refugee, CHWs: including IDPs / Refugee, Health staff and health committee's members, community leaders including IDPs / Refugees, Persons With disabilities including IDPs / Refugees, the elderly : 60 and > including IDPs / Refugee, Host populations.
The project will target 100 people at risk of GBV including 50 GBV survivors (women, men, girls, boys) who will received at least one form of assistance. This may include, but is not limited to, mental health support and case referral. Within this framework, the team will integrate the issue of GBV and psychological first aid training for 200 staff, community relay and local leaders.

project_name: Respuesta integral en seguridad alimentaria y nutricional de emergencia para la población más vulnerable afectada por la crisis en Venezuela.
project_objective: Acción Contra el Hambre (ACH) en Venezuela atiende las necesidades humanitarias de los grupos más vulnerables en riesgo de desnutrición aguda: < de 5 años, 5 – 14 años, mujeres embarazadas y lactantes (MEL), personas con discapacidades o con problemas de salud, en particular adultos mayores. Son agravantes las situaciones de pobreza y necesidades básicas no satisfechas como la falta de acceso a: alimentos, condiciones higiénico-sanitarias adecuadas, servicios de salud, y medios de vida. La desnutrición y el deterioro de la salud repercuten en una mayor exposición a factores agravantes como la violencia de género, embarazos adolescentes y criminalidad. A través del HRP, ACH brindará una respuesta humanitaria para la reducción del sufrimiento y ayudar a salvar vidas, identificando casos de desnutrición aguda y severa en las familias más a riesgo. Se trabajará a nivel comunitario y se coordinará con instituciones locales, en particular con escuelas y centros de salud. ACH trabaja con un enfoque de programa país y dentro de una estrategia regional, con intervenciones complementarias e integrales en: 1) Nutrición: sensibilización y consejerías; detección, tratamiento de la desnutrición aguda, y derivación de los casos con complicaciones médicas; capacitación en el manejo preventivo de la desnutrición aguda; 2) Salud: atención primaria, equipos, insumos, medicamentos, métodos anticonceptivos; 3) Seguridad Alimentaria y medios de vida: distribución de alimentos y apoyo para la producción de alimentos; 4) ASH: acceso a servicios de agua, saneamiento, e higiene, en escuelas y centros comunitarios; distribución de kits de higiene, y rehabilitación/reparación de sistemas de abastecimiento de agua y de saneamiento en comunidades. El sector de Protección y género, de manera transversal, trabajará en prevención de VBG, nuevas masculinidades y DSSR; establecimiento y/o fortalecimiento de espacios seguros para mujeres y niñas; atención psico-social, distribución de kits de higiene menstrual y protección para mujeres en riesgo. La respuesta actual de ACH se concentra en Caracas DC, Guárico, Carabobo, Miranda, Zulia, Bolívar, y próximamente en Falcón, Amazonas y Sucre.

project_name: Enhance food security through the delivery of an Integrated Assistance Package for refugee and host community populations in Cox's Bazar.
project_objective:
GFA: WFP will provide life-saving food assistance to the entire Rohingya refugee population through General Food Assistance. Beneficiaries will receive entitlements that can be redeemed from WFP-contracted local retailers across the camps. E-vouchers provide more flexibility, dignity and greater dietary diversity for the refugees while also creating market linkages with the host community and the wider Bangladeshi economy. To ensure an effective and efficient emergency intervention, WFP will preposition enough food to rapidly respond to the needs of approximately 30,000 households should they be displaced by monsoon, cyclone or conflict. In addition to providing large-scale food assistance, WFP will make sure to address the needs of the most vulnerable households through promoting income generating activities in the camps and host communities. WFP will provide complementary food vouchers to 250,000 extremely vulnerable individuals through Fresh Food Corners. 

DRR: WFP will support vulnerable Bangladeshi communities in Ukhiya and Teknaf by enhancing their capacities to manage natural resources, which are being heavily affected by climate change. Approximately 45,000 beneficiaries (18-59 years old) will be targeted, with a strong emphasis on including women - particularly from female-headed households - and people with disabilities. Participants will engage in activities to support natural resource management and disaster risk reduction (e.g., roadside tree plantation, care, and maintenance; watershed management via channel excavation; improvement of drainage systems).

SR: 30,000 vulnerable individuals from vulnerable households will be provided with agricultural training and inputs to improve diverse food consumption. The Self-Reliance programmes targets the most vulnerable individuals who are often overlooked for other income-generating opportunities (e.g., PWDs & youth)

Livelihood: Through multi-year livelihoods model, the project aims to improve vulnerable women’s food security and nutritional status in the Ukhiya and Teknaf sub-districts of Cox’s Bazar.
The programme provides a combined package of monthly subsistence allowance (MSA) with complementary skills development focused on food production, delivered through Self-Helf Groups (SHGs). The programme works with women as an entry point to transform communities, through empowering them socially and economically and helping them become entrepreneurs. The programme also supports social cohesion and community integration for households who have been impacted directly or indirectly by the Rohingya influx, COVID-19 pandemic, and recent global food crisis.  
•A monthly subsistence allowance of BDT 1,050 (approximately USD 12)
•Technical training to improve production techniques, bring down the cost of production, and increase profit margins
•Additional financial literacy training and negotiation training, social and behavioral change communication sessions, and modules on gender-based-violence (GBV), human rights, disaster risk reduction, hygiene, and health
•Activities related to market linkages, including aggregation centres for on-farm production and ESFN shop for off-farm production.

School Feeding: WFP School Feeding Programme aims to improve children’s learning by addressing the root causes of hunger and micronutrient deficiencies that can have consequences on their cognitive growth. In the camps, WFP will provide a packet of 50gms of micronutrient fortified biscuits to children enrolled in learning centres every school day. In the host community, WFP will provide a packet 75gms of micronutrient fortified biscuits to pre-primary and primary school children in Government schools, approved “madrassas” (Islamic schools) and NGO-run schools every school day. These locally-produced fortified biscuits are fortified with 16 vitamins and minerals, and provide approximately half of the daily micronutrient requirements for a child between 5 and 11 years.

project_name: Improvement of living conditions, social cohesion, enhancement of resilience for Rohingya refugees through the Support and Provision of Shelter, NFI and Contingency stocks
project_objective:
UNHCR will continue shelter interventions to improve the living conditions of refugees considering Age, Gender, Diversity Mainstreaming (AGDM) and individual specific needs to 431, 249 people across all camps in UNHCR's AoR. The project will be based on two sector strategic objectives; 1) to provide life-saving emergency Shelter/NFI support to households affected by disasters and other sudden onset events and 2) to provide safe and decent living conditions to reduce suffering.													
Under specific objective 1) 
Given the temporary nature of shelter material approved for use, coupled with extreme weather conditions in Bangladesh,
refugee shelters require regular maintenance throughout the year. UNHCR and its partners support refugee households to maintain their shelters with bamboo, tarpaulin, rope and wires. In addition, tie-down kits are considered for emergency distribution to reinforce refugee shelters in anticipation of strong winds during monsoon seasons. UNHCR will continue to preposition contingency stocks and conducts distribution based on needs assessments and validation. Regular NFI assistance including soaps and female hygiene kits will be distributed in coordination with WASH sector partners. The distribution and composition of non-food items (NFIs) will be planned and managed in a functional and effective manner in coordination with the Shelter/NFI Sector. To diversify access to NFIs, UNHCR plans to scale-up voucher distribution mechanisms so that refugees can select the items required. Refugees will be informed regarding the NFI distribution schedule with an appointment slip provided in advance. Distributions will be administered through the Global Distribution Tool (GDT) and manual master rolls. Lessons learned through the Joint Multi-Sector Needs Assessment (J-MSNA) and UNHCR's post-distribution monitoring (PDM), will be incorporated into the project and will comprise part of the participatory activity planning.  

Under strategic objective 2, 
UNHCR plans to conduct a detailed shelter needs assessment in it AoR to inform priorities and targeted response. The key interventions will incudes iter-alia; gender and inclusion activities, (inclusion of marganized groups in CFW activities), LGP distribution and refills, energy efficient cookware and support to extremely vulnerable households. Refugees will have access to cleaner fuel with limited exposure to protection incidents through the provision of LPG. UNHCR will expand user training to ensure that all refugees are trained and provided with a more efficient cooking technology and a cookbook outlining how to use and maintain a new more efficient stove and cooking technologies; refugees will benefit from more diversified cooking practices with the distribution of more efficient cooking technologies

Efforts will be in place to facilitate incremental improvement of shelters through reinforcing existing shelters with improved materials including HH level site improvement works. This will include construction of 400 Mid Term Shelters (MTS), and repairs of MTS in camps 4Ext, 21, 4, 2E and 2W.  Shelter repair and maintenance, HLP activities and porter support to EVHHs will also be priortised.

project_name: Provision of lifesaving integrated Gender Based Violence Prevention & Response, & Sexual and Reproductive Health services  for Rohingya refugees & host communities in Cox's Bazar
project_objective:
UNFPA will continue to promote, coordinate & provide accessible, confidential, survivor-centered GBV services in Rohingya Refugee & Bangladeshi host communities within Cox’s Bazar in line with the Inter-Agency standards for GBV in emergency programming. This will be done with special considerations on value for money, accountability of affected populations, & inclusion. 

UNFPA supported 39 Women Friendly Spaces (WFS) & 13 health facilities provide integrated GBV-SRHR services  which include GBV case management, MHPSS services, clinical management of rape (CMR), voluntary family planning, STI testing & treatment, alongside emergency referrals. UNFPA also supports 10 Women Lead Community Centers (WLCC) which promote & advance gender equality & women’s empowerment. WLCCs are open to women, girls, men & boys, to support PSS, life skills development, self-reliance activities, GBV prevention & awareness  programming & referral systems.

UNFPA also provides specific programming for adolescents & youth (A&Y) age 10-24 within the WFSs & WLCCs such as” Girl Shine”, empowering girls to acquire skills & knowledge to identify various forms of GBV & seek services when needed, along with sessions on bodily autonomy, gender equality, MHPSS, SRHR, menstrual health & positive social/emotional skills. This is done in tandem with a boy specific intervention called “Champions of Change” which aims to create a safe space to reflect & redefine masculinity while becoming more supportive, inclusive, and compassionate members of society. 
 
UNFPA works to include particularly vulnerable groups within the camp & host areas (gender diverse populations (GDP), older persons, & persons with disabilities PWDs) by adopting special measures in programming & developing partnership with specialized organizations. UNFPA will also work to capacitate partners on the intersectional needs & vulnerabilities related to GBV to enhance programmatic support and case management services.

The project will ensure community engagement & awareness raising aimed at mobilizing communities alongside enhancing caregiver roles with males & females to challenge gender norms & harmful GBV related practices. This includes the tested SASA! Together methodology to address negative social norms & to prevent & respond to GBV by creating social norm change & cohesion between refugee & host communities through group activities and  joint sessions. This also includes structured, community-level sessions for caregivers to complement awareness building activities for A&Y to challenge existing gender-biased social norms which perpetuate GBV in camps & host communities.

As aid workers and particularly beneficiaries are both at risk of sexual exploitation and abuse, UNFPA will continue to advocate & provide technical guidance alongside capacity development  in accordance to capacity development plans for the year to IPs in coordination with ISCG PSEA network to ensure safeguarding for beneficiaries and that PSEA referral, reporting mechanisms & policies are in place. 

Under the leadership of UNFPA, the GBVSS comprises 67 active partners managing the inter agency response to GBV in Cox’s Bazar. GBVSS will enhance engagement with other sectors & government for integration of GBV prevention, mitigation & response programming for quality services using Inter-Agency Minimum Standards. The sub-sector will expand comprehensive GBV prevention & response programmes for women & girls, focusing on case management & multi-sectoral referral systems. Capacities on the IASC GBV Guidelines  will be enhanced  to sector & sub sector leads, government stakeholders & implementing partners fostering effective coordination in planning, implementing & monitoring essential GBV risk mitigation actions in all humanitarian response & services. This will be supported with regular community based GBV risk monitoring & joint safety/service audits.

project_name: Multi-sectoral services for Refugees in White Nile, Kassala, Gadaref, Khartoum and Gezira.
project_objective:
Due to influx of refugee from different countries, Sudan is hosting more than 1,130,547 refugees and asylum seekers, 61% of the population is out of camp in host communities and urban areas, while 39% is settled in camps primarily in White Nile and East Sudan. South Sudanese make up the majority of refugees along with refuges from other neighbouring countries such as Eritrea, Central African Republic, Ethiopia, and Chad. Sudan also hosts refugees who have fled the wars in Syria and Yemen to seek safety in Sudan. Khartoum hosts the largest number of the refugees living in urban settings. Based on the last update shared by UNHCR, this includes 306,156 individual’s of which 102,052 are part of female-headed House hold, 4302 persons with disabilities, and 1668 Unaccompiand and Separated children (UASC) living in different localities (Elljablian&Elsalam, Jebal Auliya&Omdorum-Naifasha ,Mayo).
Children and adolescent girls and boys experience different child protection risks and concerns: physical and humiliating punishment, neglect, sexual abuse like rape and exploitation for daily work.  These in turn leads to various issues like poor child development outcomes, teenage pregnancy, attempted suicide among girls and boys, and school drop-out.  Agencies and Government departments that are meant to provide crucial support and services face challenges in terms of funding, staffing, logistics and transport capacity.  As a result, there is inadequate protection interventions including lack of appropriate case management and Family Tracing Reunification in camps.

The project is designed around two outcomes - each representing CPiE responses and interventions which build on the  appropriate lifesaving services such as case management interventions to the most vulnerable children, including UASC, children living with disabilities, and out of school children by facilitating access and referral to services, family tracing and reunification, cash or in-kind assistance, and placement in alternative care as needed. This project will also include psychosocial support services (PSS) for individuals and group using the child friendly spaces approaches. Moreover, the project will strength community engagement and participation through establishment of Community-based child Protection networks (CBCPNs) that will monitor and respond to individual cases of children affected by any type of abuse, exploitation or neglect. Referral systems will be improved as part of strengthening local protection systems in the refugee camps. The project will also train relevant staff members and stakeholders. 

This project will also provide full and non-discriminatory essential protection services for Persons with specific needs (PSN), including persons with disability, through proper identification assessment, facilitating access and referral to services. Further, it will support the most vulnerable refugee, asylum seekers, and host community members with multi-purpose cash based on established vulnerability criteria based on UNHCR CBI strategy and SoPs. All this interventions will be based on the Child Protection Minimum Standard (CPMS), Plan International guidelines and Sudan SoPs. 
The project will also address GBV concerns through direct materials support of dignity kit to 500 individuals and awareness campaigns. The project will further support 1000 (750 in White Nile and 250 children in Basundah in Gadaref) with education interventions and 50 teachers in White Nile. The project will further reach out to 25000 refugees in White Nile with WASH and Health interventions through various Health and Nutrition and WASH activities that also include awareness campaigns.

project_name: Continued provision of quality life saving comprehensive and integrated sexual reproductive health and rights services, for Rohingya refugees and host communities targeting women and girls as well as young people and adolescents in Cox's Bazar
project_objective:
To increase Rohingya refugees and host communities equitable access to and utilization of comprehensive and high-quality sexual and reproductive health services (SRH) that save lives UNFPA will continue to strengthen its implementation of integrated SRH and GBV services for women and girls of reproductive age through health systems strengthening and community engagement in 22 health facilities across 11 camps and surrounding host communities. UNFPA will strengthen it's coordination and partnership within a multi-sectoral approach that includes strategic collaboration with the Gender based violence [GBV] Sub-Sector, Community health workers [CHW] Working Group, and government actors, under the direction of the Health Sector and key players. The operationalization and implementation of the recently approved, government-led Cox's Bazar Family Planning Strategic Plan (2022-2025) will be a major focus of UNFPA's strategic, technical, and programmatic guidance pertaining to the provision and delivery of a continuum of care package for essential SRHR services to the last mile. UNFPA will guarantee the continued availability and accessibility of family planning and other SRH-related commodities, supplies, and equipment through enhanced supply chain management in order to satisfy the unmet needs of refugees and surrounding host communities. The project will centralize facilities and community-based family planning, improve and maintain the quality of services through strengthening referrals and transfer of high risk and emergency obstetric cases, availability and accessibility of life-saving SRHR commodities, client-centered quality and respectful midwifery-led antenatal and postnatal care, safe birth, menstrual health, cervical cancer and obstetric fistula screening and treatment, adolescent SRHR services, Maternal and Perinatal Mortality Surveillance and Response, and Evidence based SRHR Information Management and quality assurance through mentorship and support to service providers. The capacity of health practitioners and community health workers to deliver integrated, client-centered, high-quality services, such as family planning and health response to GBV in health facilities and protection spaces such as WFSs, WLCCs, and Youth Centers, will be enhanced. Additionally, these integrated services will reinforce and expand existing behavioral modification strategies.
Through capacity building, stockpiling of supplies, and the design of SRHR policies, UNFPA will enhance its preparedness to fulfill SRHR demands during natural disasters and disease outbreaks. To ensure continuity of comprehensive integrated SRHR service provision, UNFPA will continue its preventative and response interventions, including the operationalization of Isolation Treatment Centers [ITC] and provision of integrated SRHR/GBV services in health facilities, communities, and women, girls, adolescent and youths protected spaces.

project_objective: Debido a secuelas de las restricciones en la movilidad para frenar el contagio del COVID-19 en 2021, así como a los efectos de la temporada de lluvias 2022, donde se refleja en la pérdida de cultivos, la degradación de los medios de vida, la pérdida y/o disminución de empleo tanto para familias del área urbana y rural, el presente proyecto busca fortalecer las principales necesidades alimentarias de las familias más vulnerables, que debido a la situación actual a nivel institucional del país aún no han sido atendidas y que por lo tanto, continúan deteriorando su nivel de vida. En ese contexto, el proyecto promoverá la producción de granos básicos de maíz blanco y frijol negro, fortalecer la producción avícola a nivel familiar, anticiparse a los efectos de las enfermedades avícolas mediante jornadas de vacunación mediante la implementación de botiqunes pecuarios comunitarios, producción familiar de alimentos mediante la implementación de huertos familiares de hortalizas y el establecimiento de estructuras de almacenamiento de agua de lluvia; de forma que mejoren su nivel de vida. Estas actividades se desarrollarán en los departamentos de Alta Verapaz, Izabal, Chiquimula, Quiché y Huehuetenango, lugares donde se cuenta con conocimiento del contexto y alianzas a nivel comunitario, municipal y departamental, así como con instancias de gobierno y organizaciones no gubernamentales.

project_name: Renforcement de l'environnement protecteur des personnes vulnérables affectées par les conflits au Niger
project_objective:
Afin de répondre aux besoins de protection des personnes vulnérables affectées par les conflits et de les renforcer dans leurs droits, DRC identifie des cas de protection et leur apporte une première assistance psychologique (Premiers Secours Psychologiques - PSP). En fonction de leurs besoins de protection (vulnérabilités, risques auxquels ils sont exposés), DRC fournit des assistances de protection d'urgence (API, SNF) et/ou un appui psychosocial, et réfère les cas de protection auxquels ses services ne peuvent pas répondre directement. Ces référencement sont effectués soit vers des structures externes (ex: services techniques déconcentrés, ONG locales, ONG internationales), soit en interne, vers d'autres départements d'intervention de DRC (par exemple, le département Sécurité Alimentaire et Relèvement Économique). En tant que partenaire du RRM, DRC réalise des Évaluations Rapides de Protection (ERP) et adapte ses interventions de protection aux ménages enregistrés suite à des déplacements de populations, sur des cycles de  3 mois d'intervention. DRC contribue par ailleurs aux renforcements des capacités des structures communautaires (conformément à l'approche de protection communautaire), et collabore avec elles afin de mieux connaitre en temps réels les tendances de protection (risques, besoins, etc.),  dans le cadre du monitoring de protection. 

La stratégie d'intervention de DRC dans le secteur de la protection se base sur l'approche vulnérabilité, en ce qu'elle vise à fournir une assistance adaptée à toutes les personnes vulnérables affectées par les conflits (PDI, communautés hôtes, réfugiés),  adaptée à leurs besoins spécifiques  liés à leur âge, leur genre et leurs vulnérabiltités propres (enfants,  personnes âgées, Femmes Enceintes et Femmes Allaitantes - FEFA, personnes en situation de handicap, etc.). DRC s'assure que ses interventions de protection sont réalisées de manière sûre, accessible, redevable et participative pour l'ensemble de ses bénéficiaires.

project_name: Coordination of the Humanitarian Response in Colombia
project_objective: OCHA plays a critical role in monitoring humanitarian developments at territorial level; coordinating the response and providing key analysis to inform decision making. The current coordination architecture includes 12 Local Coordination Teams (LCTs) and 3 Humanitarian local Teams (HLTs) in the border departments of Guanía, Vichada and Amazonas with OCHA leading five of these LCTs, moreover, this will be expanded with the presence of two field information assistants in Bolivar and Vaupes by 2023. OCHA also provides information management support to LCTs in other areas led by other UN agencies. Information gathered from all territories is centralized and analysed regularly to generate information products related to the various emergences taking place in the departments and the status of the response. OCHA leads inter-cluster coordination efforts, the Access Working Group as well as an inter-agency working group to analyse displacement and confinement figures which are published monthly. OCHA also co-leads a working group that analyses conflict dynamics and the classification of armed groups. OCHA also supports the HCT in strategic decision making. It maintains close coordination with the Refugee and Migrants Response coordination mechanism in country to ensure coordinated actions as well as with the RCO and the Peace Mission to facilitate linkages between humanitarian, development and peace building efforts in country. OCHA also maintains close relations with the OCHA office in Venezuela and the focal points in Peru and Equator, particularly in relation to analysis of cross-border dynamics and coordination of some response efforts. Furthermore, OCHA supports the coordination of the response to natural disasters with the state’s National Unit for Disaster Risk Management to complement Governments efforts and fill potential gaps in the response. In 2023 OCHA will expand its presence with coordination staff in 13 departments - those most affected by humanitarian crises.

2- Al Amal PHC (HF-B0204110) with Violet in Azaz,Azaz, Aleppo  
3-Aghtarin PHC (serving as BEMONC) (HF Code- B0204077)  Aghtarin, Azaz, Aleppo with Shafak

project_name: Assistance médico-nutritionnelle pour les personnes déplacées et populations hôtes victimes de choc (déplacements forcés, attaques, etc) dans les régions de Maradi, Tillabéry et Tahoua
project_objective:
ALIMA-BEFEN propose une intervention médico-nutritionnelle afin d'assister les populations déplacées et hôtes des régions de Tillabéry, Tahoua et Maradi en contribuant à la réduction de leur morbi-mortalité, notamment en garantissant un accès aux soins primaires et une prise en charge de la malnutrition gratuits et de qualité avec un focus spécifique sur les femmes enceintes et allaitantes et les enfants de moins de 5 ans. La stratégie d'intervention est à la fois fixe au travers du renforcement de la résilience des structures de santé, et mobile au travers du déploiement des cliniques mobiles afin d'atteindre les populations les plus éloignées des CSI. Le projet assurera le renforcement de la prise en charge des soins de santé primaires dans les structures existantes (CSI et HD) tout en assurant le paquet de soins minimum aux populations ciblées dans les zones plus éloignées des CSI. 
Les cibles principales du projet sont les populations déplacées et les populations hôtes des 3 régions. Les enfants de moins de 5 ans constituent la cible prioritaire de l'action puisqu'ils sont la couche la plus vulnérable de la population. Les femmes enceintes, allaitantes et en âge de procréer seront aussi des cibles prioritaires pour l'action du fait de leur vulnérabilité aux attaques et aux violences basées sur le genre, en plus de leur importance dans la détection de la malnutrition et des maladies chez les enfants. Les personnes blessées victimes de violences sont également visées, afin de combler le manque quant à la prise en charge et la gratuité de leurs soins de santé. Grâce à une stratégie communautaire au travers de la formation de nombreux relais communautaires dans chacune des zones d’intervention, les besoins des populations cibles seront identifiés et pris en charge rapidement. Des sensibilisations à la PCIME, au PB-mère, aux pratiques d’hygiène familiales essentielles, à la SSR, seront effectuées grâce à l’implication de ces relais et matrones formés. L’ensemble du personnel d’ALIMA-BEFEN et leurs partenaires au sein des cliniques mobiles et au travers des CSI seront également formés/recyclés à la détection, à la prise en charge et au suivi des victimes de VBG touchant particulièrement les femmes et les enfants. Un appui psychosocial est apporté grâce à la présence de professionnels dans le domaine en attendant leur référencement vers des structures plus adaptées. ALIMA permet aux populations affectées de jouer un rôle actif tout au long du cycle du projet et veille à ce que les plus marginalisés et affectés soient représentés et puissent faire entendre leur voix, à travers les points notamment l’identification des personnes à besoin spécifique lors de la mise en œuvre des activités ; permettre aux femmes, aux hommes, aux enfants et aux personnes âgées de participer et d'influencer la conception du projet, la mise en œuvre du projet et le suivi et l'évaluation ; veiller à ce que les systèmes de représentation communautaire soient justes et représentatifs, et que les plus marginalisés, vulnérables et affectés aient une voix

project_name: Faciliter l’insertion des enfants et des adolescent(e)s affectés par la crise humanitaire au sein d’un système éducatif sûr et protecteur au Niger
project_objective: COOPI propose une Action d’EiE de 20 mois qui vise à faciliter l’accès et le droit à l'éducation pour les enfants affectéspar la crise humanitaire dans la région de Tahoua, notamment dans le département de Tahoua(frontière malienne)et de Madaoua(frontière Nigeria).Plus particulièrement, l'Action a comme objectif de faciliter l'insertion/réintégration des enfantsles plus vulnérables (refugiés, PDI)dans le système éducatif formel tout en répondant à leurs besoins de protectionpsychosociale et cognitive. Dans 10 écoles primaires d’accueils, il est prévu la mise en place d’un programmed’éducation accélérée(SSA/P), la réhabilitation des salles des classes et la dotation en intrants scolaires (R1).Une attention particulière sera donnée aux enfants les plus vulnérables issus des déplacements et victimes de traumatismes aigues et aux enfants en situation de handicap. Une approche communautaire à plusieurs niveaux sera employée, afin de favoriser une implication forte des communautés ciblées dans l'implémentation de l'Action. Le projet prendra en compte aussi le renforcement des capacités des acteurs clés gravitant autour du système éducatif au niveau communautaire (enseignants et COGES),régionale (Inspections) et humanitaire (R2 et R3).Dans le but de répondre à la demande grandissante de récupération scolaire des enfants victimes de déplacement forcé, le projet prévoit la mise en place de cours de rattrapage à travers l’activation du mécanisme RRM(R4).L'action proposée s'inscrit dans la continuité avec les actions mises en place par COOPI sous financement ECHO depuis 2016 à Diffa et UNICEF depuis 2019 à Tahoua. De plus, elle vise à contribuer aux priorités EiE énoncées dans l’HIP 2022.Enfin, l'action contribuera aux objectifs du Cluster Éducation et du Sous-cluster PE et s'aligne aux politiques du Gouvernement de Niger en matière de protection et éducation formelle.

Some of these sites have potential to provide a solarized alternative of energy to support using hibernate system decreasing the electricity costs of running the systems. In addition to O&M support, there will also be capacity building and feedback consultative meetings arranged to serve as a knowledge sharing with local council, water station management and community focal points on various topics such as cost recovery, maintenance and reporting. Desludging activities are proposed in IDP sites in Azaz (Al-Ryan, Talil sham), and Dana subdistrict. Sewer network rehabilitation and expansions are proposed in the subdistricts of Azaz (6 IDP locations), Dana, and Ras Al Ain. In 2018, WV notably piloted the construction of a wastewater treatment plant (first of its kind) in Sejjo camp with private funds where treated water it acceptable for agricultural purposes. From learnings and ongoing O&M WV. On the institutional setting, WV plans to rehabilitate and construct WASH facilities in 6 schools in Harim, Atareb, & Daret Azza, supporting WASH needs for persons with disability in 3 camps in Azaz. There will be 4 Healthcare facilities in Ras-Alein will be supported with medical waste management services. for hygiene Promotion, and RCCE sessions in various formats (from school messaging, posters in streets, on water tanks, Solid Waste vehicles, social media) with tailored messaging to the appropriate setting and age groups. WV is focusing more on ‘nudges and cues’ such as painted steps to hand washing stations at the school setting to social distancing markers at communal water point to serve as reminders for healthy behaviors. For children, WV will use its existing partnership with Sesame Workshop, in 3 informal learning centers in IDP camps in Azaz, with plans to expand to the formal school setting. The Sesame Workshop program educates and empowers children to healthy lives, through promotion of behavioral changes in sanitation and hygiene through children play-based learning materials, and multimedia content program developed through Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation. project_name: Supporting Health Emergency Preparedness and Response and Protecting the Right to Health for the Most Vulnerable Population in the oPt
project_objective:
This project aims to strengthen the capacity of the Palestinian health system to prepare for and respond to the different emergencies, including those related to communicable diseases, military escalations, and other potential emergency scenarios identified in the Health Cluster contingency plan. The proposed activities will enhance emergency planning and coordination through establishing satellite Public Health Emergency Operation Centers for managing crises at the peripheral level. Interventions will also enable the Ministry of Health (MoH) to adequately manage outbreaks of (re)emerging communicable diseases, through technical guidance, provision of supplies, and capacity building in the areas of diagnostics, case management, surveillance, and infection prevention and control, including supporting International Health Regulations (IHR)  core capacities. The project will contribute to strengthening quality of care at all levels of the trauma pathway (prehospital, hospital, and tertiary care) through technical guidance; adopting unified triage and case management systems and protocols; prepositioning of essential supplies; and building the capacity of health personnel. Additionally, more than 200 partners will benefit from the implementation of the Health Resources and Services Availability Monitoring System (HeRAMS). To advocate for the right of Palestinians to Health, WHO will continue to document and monitor barriers to healthcare services access, including for patients, companions and health workers requiring permits to reach essential healthcare services, as a basis for evidence-based advocacy. 

Around 5,150 health care workers, including more than 2,500 women will benefit from capacity building activities. Approximately, 354,500 people across the oPt, including 173,705 females and 35,450 elderly and people with disabilities (PWD), will directly benefit from planned interventions. 

All project activities have been coordinated at various levels with all relevant partners, counterparts, and Health Cluster working groups.

project_name: Supporting COVID-19 Response and Vaccination coverage in Syria.
project_objective:
COVID-19 in Syria added to the complex emergency, further weakened the fragile health system and increased population vulnerabilitySyria declared the first COVID-19 case on March 22, 20, and at the same time establish COVID-19 Task Force aiming to carry out activities under identified pillars in collaboration with implementing partners. In NWS, the current health system is fragmented and has very limited capacity across the defined pillars of the COVID-19 response: surveillance, laboratory testing, contact tracing, human resources for health and case management and measures at points of entry (PoEs), etc.

A total of 200 776 confirmed cases of COVID-19 were reported in Syria between 22 March 2020 and 31 October 2022, of which 104 160 cases (51.88%) were reported from northwest Syria (NWS), 57 358 cases (28.57%) from government-controlled areas (GoS), and the remaining 39 258 cases (19.55%) were from northeast Syria (NES). 
During the same period, a total of 7 246 related deaths were reported, of which 3 163 (43.65%) were from GoS, 2 505 (34.57%) were from NWS, and 1 578 (21.78%) were from NES. The overall Case Fatality Rate (CFR) is 3.6% (no change in the CFR compared with the previous month). The CFR was highest in GoS (5.5%), NES (4.0%) and in NWS the CFR was 2.4%. 

The overall aim of the project is to reduce morbidity and mortality resulting from COVID-19 among the population of Syria by scaling up the country’s preparedness and response operations, reducing transmission of COVID-19 and protecting all persons within Syria from the disease, and strengthening health systems to attain resilience and respond to emerging and re-emerging public health threats. The project aligns with the Health sector strategy and WHO global strategy and adopts the 11 pillars approach. The main objectives are: 
•	Strengthen existing national multisectoral coordination mechanism to deliver timely and integrated response and to contain the pandemic, by actively engaging Directorates of Health, line-ministries, UN agencies, INGOs and NNGOs.
•	Enhancing Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE) activities aiming to ensure people’s understanding of the situation and their compliance to social and public health measures.
•	Strengthen surveillance for early detection and response of COVID-19 infections to reduce person-to-person transmission.
•	Strengthen the public health laboratory network central and directorate-level public health laboratories for virologic testing of COVID-19 samples and sequencing of SARS-CoV-2.
•	Strengthen and sustain infection prevention and control (IPC) measures to ensure safety of patients, healthcare workers and the caregiving environment.
•	Establish and maintain designated isolation facilities across the country.
•	Maintain stockpile of supplies required for the response. 
•	The continuity of essential health services as to avoid substantial disruptions is secured.

project_name: Improve drinking water quality assurance and healthcare medical waste management systems, prioritizing IDP camps/sites and areas of high returnees
project_objective:
WASH infrastructure requires significant support and substantial investments. Reliability and efficiency of water systems have sharply decreased for the first time since 2016, with nearly 2 million fewer people using water networks as the only household water supply
modality, in comparison to mid-2020. This means up to 47% of the population is relying on often unsafe alternatives to piped water, to meet or complement their water needs (vis-à-vis 38% in mid-2020). Investment in sanitation infrastructure is critical, as at least
70% of sewage is discharged untreated and at least half of the sewerage systems are not functional. In Ar-Raqqa and Deir-ez-Zor, for example, pretty much all the untreated raw sewage is discharged into the Euphrates River, which also serves as the source of drinking
water to a vast majority of the population. In NWS, wastewater from huge camp clusters is openly discharged, forming sewage rivers. Similarly, in NES, no wastewater treatment exists for the IDP sites, resulting in environmental pollution and increased disease
prevalence. Over 30% of garbage is inappropriately disposed or collected with low frequency, while the dumpsites often pose serious health, environmental and protection risks.
Access to sufficient and affordable safe water, adequate sanitation, solid waste management and/or hygiene supplies will remain a challenge for more than 2 million people in IDP sites, highly dependent on continued humanitarian assistance. Up to 96%
of interviewed residents of IDP sites received some WASH humanitarian assistance, but 44% were not fully satisfied with it, mainly due to insufficient quantity or quality of assistance. This is potentially linked with shortage and/or discontinuity of funding. Water
trucking services are the only source of water for 73% of IDP site residents and only 24% households are connected to (simplified) sewer networks, indicating a continued need for medium-term investment in IDP sites infrastructure to provide more sustainable,
affordable, and safer way to supply water and dispose wastewater. Despite the sector assistance, 24% of IDPs in sites couldn’t access one or multiple hygiene items, 23% faced barriers to effective handwashing. Also, 35% of households reported issues with toilet
functionality or wastewater disposal. Disruptions and poor quality of services in IDP sites have also direct negative physical and mental well-being and protection consequences, notably on women and girls.
The 4 Ws indicators are consolidated with WASH sector. The project will also cover the monitoring of safe drinking water quality for 11 camps and 93 IDPs shelters with estimated targeted population of 600,531 individuals in NES GOV.
Currently, WHO has 250,000 USD committed towards WASH programming in 2023. WHO is also actively fundraising with donors and its leadership to support the total WASH needs of 10.2M USD.

project_name: Protection monitoring and  Assistance for Persons of Concern in Kapoeta East county, Eastern Equatoria State
project_objective: The proposed intervention will conduct protection monitoring, referral and provide assistance to the 60% most vulnerable IDPs, 20% returnees (both IDP and refugee returnees,) and 20%Host Community in Kapoeta East County in Eastern Equitoria state. The project will build on the protection work ADRA  previously implemented in Kapoeta East focusing on ensuring that conflict-affected persons have increased access to rights and entitlements. Through the project, ADRA South Sudan will facilitate protection monitoring to determine the threats, needs and concerns of the target population to inform individualized support which will include and not limited to identification and assistance to PSNs, case management, cash based support to PSNS e.g survivors of SGBV, children at risk and referral to the appropriate services. It will be noted SGBV remains one of the critical threats to the protection and wellbeing of women and children  with unclear magnitude because these acts are not culturally recognized as crime and therefore often ignored and not reported by both the community members and the local authorities. This intervention will therefore focus on monitoring these human rights violations, reporting and advocating for mechanisms to mitigate their occurrence. The intervention will also facilitate dialogues on peaceful coexistence since violence is one of the drivers to threats faced by the communities which largely compromise the protective environment of the affected populations. ADRA will facilitate training sessions on human rights, protection and protection mainstreaming targeting the duty bearers such as local leaders, youth, Faith based organizations, teachers and staff of humanitarian partners . The intervention will be implemented to deliver activities under integrated components of protection, GBV and child protection. The integrated protection interventions will seek to address the vulnerability, limited access to services, psychosocial distress, peace building and weak protection structures that continue to characterize the IDPs, returnee’s  and host community context in Kapoeta East county especially among persons of concern including the elderly, persons with disability, pregnant women and lactating mothers, Unaccompanied and separated children, former child soldiers, child-headed households and girls at risk of forced and early marriage. ADRA and partner led assessments reveal that  women and child headed household are at risk of exploitation as they try to cope with the effects of protracted crisis hence they will be a primary target by the proposed intervention. The UNHCR vulnerability criteria will be used during identification of the beneficiaries as it  clearly indicates the categories of individuals to benefit from the proposed intervention. For instance the The proposed project will focus on the persons with specific needs in which category the elderly fall. Households where the elderly are caretakers will be targeted for assistance as well as families that are fostering the elderly, orphans and accompanied/separated children. Additionally, the persons living  with disabilities (PLWD) will be included for assistance. During any activities, deliberate action will be taken to ensure participation of PLWD. The youth who are more often being violet activities like cattle raiding and intercommunal fighting including and not limited to rape, will be targeted with peace conferences, dialogues and quick impact projects like sports for peace. They will be linked to livelihood services that disrupts their minds from criminal activities. The children will not only linked to schools but also engaged through recreational and psychosocial activities to deal with the trauma suffered through witnessing violence in homes and community. Particular focus will be paid to orphans separated and unaccompanied children who will be monitored and provided  assistance which will include family tracing, cash based support, PSS and referral

project_name: Recovery and resilience building to diversify food security options among host, returnees and IDP communities in Upper Nile, Eastern Equatoria and Warrap States
project_objective:
Upper Nile, Eastern Equatoria and Warrap States, like most parts of South Sudan experience perennial food insecurity that is fueled among other things by poor or lack of resilience to impacts of Climate Change on food production and protection of livelihoods and to some extent conflicts.
According to the Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO, 2022), the magnitude and severity of food insecurity are anticipated to increase and worse in 2022/2023 compared to 2021/2022. An estimated 12,374 million people, including refugees, are expected to experience severe food insecurity from December 2022 to July 2023. This represents a 33% increase from the 8.4 million people in need in 2022. The current economic crisis is impacting people’s ability to access markets, while conflict, flooding, drought and seasonal effects are limiting the flow of both commercial and humanitarian goods and services. Continued and increased sub-national violence reported in many states across the country, including Upper Nile and Warrap (particularly Greater Tonj), will continue to disrupt livelihoods and trade. This project will target 15% (39,250 individuals) of the total households under phase 4 (emergency).
The communities of Upper Nile and Warrap have not been spared of these effects. Maiwut, Ulang, Nasir Counties and in Greater Tonj have experienced combinations of year-by-year flooding and inter community conflicts. Eastern Equatoria (Kapoeta East and North) is experiencing drought. This has led to displacement, destruction of crops, livestock, shelters, and disruption of other livelihoods. Livestock die while those that survive are affected by waterborne diseases. Because livestock are the main livelihood for the pastoralist communities, vulnerability to food insecurity increases for them. Factors contributing to the situation include “a combination of shocks; floods, insecurity incidents, the macro-economic crisis, the effects of COVID-19” and the effects of Russia/Ukraine war. These communities have also been affected by continued high food prices due to protracted macro-economic crisis which have heightened poverty & vulnerability brought about by the combination of the above factors.
Intercommunity conflicts have contributed to poor coexistence between communities and among the IDP, returnee and host populations. This has adversely affected women and children as displacements and movement pause direct effect to livelihoods and protection, particularly agricultural and fishing endeavors. Instability is not conducive to sustaining food security as food production activity is disrupted or threatened.
Adventist Development and Relief Agency (ADRA) will design consulted means of creating peace among communities through dialogues and support of community level peace building efforts. Adventist Development and Relief Agency (ADRA) will take the learning from the ‘Peace Infrastructure’ created in the community of Maiwut and Tonj South over the years to advocate for the returnee and IDP communities in the other proposed counties for peaceful core-existence with the host community. ADRA will also deliberately take action in form of supporting the existing government and community level structures in further capacity building them to ensure resilient programming is effective.
In project implementation the project will use a community- based approaches. These will be made up of participatory extension approaches that include the farmer field school; Lead farmer/Farmer/farmer approach innovation platforms, village-based demonstration sites, farmer market school & Exposure and learning visits underpinned by a layering approach. The project will build on previous interventions and experiences, which was successfully implemented by ADRA South Sudan. Farmers, pastoralists, fishermen and traders, have been empowered through various modern agriculture trainings.

project_name: Provision of WASH Assistance to Vulnerable Populations Affected by Conflict and Displacement in Syria
project_objective:
The purpose of NRC’s WASH intervention is to deliver humanitarian WASH supplies and services to the most vulnerable people, and provide support to water, sanitation, and sewage systems to ensure continuous services for affected people in Syria. NRC will respond to the diverse WASH needs faced by vulnerable populations throughout Syria through the delivery of a multi-faceted WASH response. The different components of NRC’s WASH project for 2023 are intended to contribute to the HRP WASH Sector’s Objectives 1, 2, and 4.
NRC will deliver this project through a direct implementation modality: geographic areas will be targeted based on the severity and scale of needs, inter-agency coordination at hub-level, and access. NRC will provide assistance to vulnerable conflict and displacement-affected populations, including IDPs, refugees, members of host communities, and refugee/IDP returnees, and non-displaced households suffering the effects of the conflict. All interventions will seek to prioritize the most vulnerable households and communities. Where appropriate, multi-sectoral vulnerability scoring techniques will be used that integrate vulnerability indicators. The needs of the different genders, elderly, and persons with disabilities (PWDs) will be considered, during design, implementation and monitoring processes.  

This project includes emergency response through the provision of one-off support as part of an integrated, multi-sector response in accordance with the Emergency Preparedness and Response Plans (EPRPs), and comprises of following Result Areas:
-	Temporary WASH services (including water trucking), household assets (Hygiene NFIs), support to Education in Emergencies (WASH services for temporary learning spaces), hygiene promotion activities. 
-	The provision of medium-term WASH support at household- and settlement-level to populations living in and out-of-camps. Comprises of two result areas: provision of WASH infrastructure, and services and hygiene items in camps and communal shelters. 
-	The provision of support for long-term improvements in access to water, hygiene, and sanitation services at the settlement- and household-level. Comprises the following result areas: rehabilitation of community WASH infrastructure (boreholes, including solar energy systems, water and sewage networks, solid waste management); rehabilitation of WASH facilities in institutions (WASH facilities in schools as part of joint interventions with Education, WASH in medical centers, etc.); rehabilitation of household WASH facilities and provision of water storage units (see NRC’s Shelter/NFI project submission).  
The project will also include consultation with communities through FGDs, HHQs, and KIIs, as well as with relevant authorities. Special attention will be given to ensuring that interventions are accessible by all and that there are functional complaint and feedback mechanisms (CFMs) in place. 
NRC will invest in more sustainable, long-term, and cost-efficient WASH service provision in IDP camps, or rehabilitation of WASH infrastructure in in-camp settings, i.e., the rehabilitation and construction of water and sewer networks, reducing WASH needs and costs in 2023 in the targeted locations. NRC will also invest in more sustainable, long-term and cost-effective provision of WASH services, through the rehabilitation of infrastructure and WASH facilities in shelter and community infrastructure. This will minimize the need for short-term emergency solutions, and enable NRC to reduce the needs in covered locations, as well as to focus on other locations that remain in need.

project_name: Child and Youth Education Pathways for Vulnerable Populations Affected by Conflict and Displacement in Syria
project_objective:
NRC’s project will contribute to the HRP Education Sector’s Objectives 1, 2, and 3. NRC will deliver this project through a combination of direct, partner-led, and hybrid modalities.

The Education intervention forms part of NRC’s safe, integrated, and inclusive response in Syria. NRC’s Education team will continue working in close collaboration with NRC’s ICLA/Capacity-building, Shelter, WASH, and Livelihoods and Food Security (LFS) programmes, to enable conflict- and displacement-affected populations to meet their basic needs, enjoy their rights, and benefit from pathways to durable solutions. NRC will deliver pathways back to learning, integration into formal education, acknowledgement of previous learning through supportive policies (accreditation, certification, examinations, and documentation), and expansion of skills for employment. NRC will respond to the diverse problems and needs faced by vulnerable children and youths across Syria through the delivery of its Child Education Pathways (CEP) and Youth Education Pathways (YEP) programmes. Each response modality (Emergency, Transition, and Recovery) is designed to ensure that conflict- and displacement-affected children and youths are provided with age and context-specific educational pathways. All three modalities have been designed to provide equal access and to welcome all out-of-school children and youths, prioritizing those that have been displaced by the conflict and are returning home from both inside and outside Syria. All three modalities include capacity development opportunities for teachers, trainers, facilitators and coaches, and will be implemented in cooperation with NRC’s ICLA/Capacity-building, Shelter, WASH, and LFS programmes and partners. The teacher training package has been adapted from the INEE Teachers in Crisis Context, and includes NRC’s Better Learning Programme (an evidence-based psychosocial support (PSS) intervention developed by NRC and the University of Tromso). Particular focus is paid to safe return to school after periods of COVID-related lockdowns: teacher circles will integrate the guidance included in UNICEF’s “Ready to go back: Teacher preparedness Training Package”.

The target group of NRC’s Education Programme in Syria is defined as conflict and displacement-affected children and youths, including Syrian IDPs, IDPs and refugee returnees, host community members, third country nationals, and Iraqi refugees. Exact target group definitions will vary for the different response options:
-	Emergency response activities will target newly displaced and returnee children and youths;
-	Transitional response will target out-of-school children and youths in contexts of long-term displacement and prolonged absence from school, with activities tailored on their specific context (see more below);
-	Recovery activities will target vulnerable populations living in post-conflict and/or stabilized camp- and non-camp settings (see more below).

Teachers, facilitators, and trainers working in NRC programmes in formal and non-formal education settings, as well as vocational trainers, will also be targeted across the three response options.  Whilst equal access will be provided to both male and female educators, considering the current scarcity of male educators, those present will be actively encouraged to participate, in an effort to provide positive male role models in all activities.
For all NRC Education activities, civil documentation will not be a pre-requisite to receive assistance. Parents’ engagement is fostered through awareness-raising campaigns, and the set-up of Parents and Teachers Associations.

project_name: Providing Information, Counselling and Legal Assistance (ICLA) and Enhancing the Protection of Civilians Affected by Conflict and Displacement in Syria
project_objective:
NRC’s protection response will be two-fold: (1) direct provision of information, counselling and legal assistance (ICLA) to PACD; and (2) increased knowledge and capacity to respond amongst duty-bearers. In addition, ICLA will identify emergency response capacities and multi-sectoral integration with NRC Shelter, WASH, Livelihoods and Food Security (LFS), and Education programmes. NRC will prioritize IDPs, returnees, host community members, as well as Iraqi refugees, Palestinian refugees, stateless individuals, and individuals at risk of statelessness, including third-country nationals (TCNs). Through the delivery of a multi-faceted response, NRC will focus on the protection of rights to legal identity and civil documentation (CD); housing, land and property (HLP) rights; and access to essential services. Geographic areas will be targeted based on the severity and scale of needs, inter-agency coordination at hub-level, and access. 
(1) Provision of Direct Assistance: For 2023, NRC direct services will be aimed at PACD who face legal challenges in relation to civil documentation, HLP rights, and accessing essential services. Key needs include the issuance of basic civil documentation such as birth, marriage, and death certificates, which are necessary in order to access education, health care, and humanitarian assistance. NRC will further prioritize the most vulnerable, taking into account gender, age, disability, ethnicity, and/or religion. This includes a focus on children and youths without proof of legal identity, and female-headed households (FHH) with missing or deceased spouses who require confirmation of their legal status and that of their children. HLP information and counselling will aim to protect security of tenure, and legal assistance will seek to prevent forced evictions. Information and counselling activities may involve home visits to reach beneficiaries who are otherwise inaccessible, to increase inclusivity for differently abled persons. NRC will increase its support to key community stakeholders, including local civil society actors, and continue to carry out HLP due diligence to support Shelter and WASH, Education, and Livelihoods interventions. NRC will launch interventions related to community awareness and training around the rights of children. For all NRC and other humanitarian activities, ICLA will advocate and emphasize that civil documentation should not be considered a prerequisite to receive assistance. 
(2) Increased Knowledge and Capacity to Respond: NRC will continue to undertake legal analysis and research, and will additionally provide technical assistance to community leaders, duty-bearers, and humanitarian partners, through training modules on legal identity, HLP, and employment law. Community leaders who will benefit from capacity building interventions may include formal and traditional authorities, such as Mukhtars, Sheikhs, lawyers/jurists, female leaders, and representatives of vulnerable groups. NRC will continue its support for the resolution of HLP, employment, or labor disputes. Guidance and advice on HLP due diligence procedures will be provided to other NRC programmes, such as Shelter and WASH, as well as the broader humanitarian sector, through continued leadership and coordination in HLP Technical Working Groups. Across interventions, particular emphasis will be placed on the rights of women and girls, as well as the rights of persons with disabilities. NRC will continue to input activities into 4Ws, as often as requested, to ensure accurate Protection service mapping. NRC will further review awareness-raising and training materials on a quarterly basis, to update as needed.

project_name: Protection des personnes affectées et rétablissement de leurs droits (2PARED) Appui aux personnes affectées pour leur résilience (projet APAR)
project_objective:
Le projet a pour objectif général de contribuer à préserver la vie des personnes affectées par la crise sécuritaire et de leur permettre de jouir de leurs droits. A cet effet, le projet aura une approche multisectorielle avec une réponse dans les secteurs spécifiques que sont : la protection (monitoring de protection, protection de l’enfance et éducation, VBG), santé/NUT, Wash. Le monitoring de protection permettra de collecter tous les incidents de protection et violations commises. Il permettra également d’identifier les hommes et femmes, les garçons et les filles, les personnes âgées et en situation de handicap afin que les besoins de chacun soient adressés. Dans le volet protection de l’enfance en situation d’urgence, les enfants à risque seront identifiés et encadrer avec leur participation, à identifier les risques auxquels ils sont exposés et à développer des stratégies palliatives. Parmi les enfants, les survivants de violences, abus ou exploitations (ENAS, EAFGA, associés au travail, etc.) seront pris en charge à travers la gestion de cas qui facilitera l’accès à leurs droits respectifs : santé/NUT, éducation, PSS, bien-être. Le volet VBG fera la promotion du genre avec une forte implication des hommes et des garçons ainsi que des leaders communautaires. Les filles et femmes à risque seront sensibilisées au signalement des violations subies et seront également prises en charge par le système de gestion de cas afin d’accéder à une assistance appropriée selon leur cas. Les interventions en santé/NUT viseront à assurer l’amélioration des conditions de vie et du bien-être des personnes affectées que nous servons. Dans le même sillage des VBG, une sensibilisation sera faite pour la prévention des exploitations et abus sexuelles avec un mécanisme de prise en charge holistique des survivantes identifiées. Notre intervention reposera sur une forte mobilisation communautaire avec la mise en place des comités de protection, les points focaux, la redynamisation des associations de femmes et d’hommes, les associations de jeunes.
Le projet se déroulera sous deux axes : prévention et réponse. A titre de prévention des abus, exploitations et violence contre les enfants, les comités de protection feront des sensibilisations sur les droits, les soins et le bien-être de l’enfant, les bonnes pratiques d’hygiènes (formation FAST et CHAST). Les parents seront accompagnés techniquement et matériellement pour assumer leur rôle de détenteur d’obligation dans la protection et le soin de leurs enfants. Les systèmes de protection seront renforcés (action sociale, agents des formations sanitaire, enseignants, etc.) dans le cadre de la coordination et le monitoring des partenaires communautaires. Les leaders religieux et traditionnels seront eux aussi sensibilisés à prendre part à la lutte contre les différentes formes de violence dans la communauté. Pour le volet santé/NUT la mobilisation communautaire visera le changement de comportement et social pour l’adoption des bonnes pratiques familiales essentielles (hygiène domestique, fréquentation des centres de santé/clinique mobile, lavage des mains, dépistage nutritionnel, etc.)
Le volet réponse aura deux sous volets : la prise en charge des cas de protection de l’enfance et de VBG et les réponses urgentes sur les sites de déplacements. Les assistances comprendront des activités de SPS, de soins de santé primaires et de nutrition, du cash, etc. Dans le cadre de notre engagement pour la redevabilité, les populations affectées auront l’opportunité de nous faire des retours sur nos actions, assistances, attitudes et celles de tous nos partenaires à travers des canaux variés pour garantir l’accès de tous au processus de plaintes, commentaires et suggestions.

project_name: Réponse d'urgence multisectorielle aux populations affectées par l'insécurité alimentaire et le conflit dans les régions de Tillabéri et diffa, et soutien aux services d'information humanitaire au Niger
project_objective:
L'intervention se concentrera sur les zones difficiles d'accès, souffrant d'une très faible couverture humanitaire, notamment le nord de Tillabéri et le nord-est de Diffa. Compte tenu de la continuité de la crise et de l'augmentation des besoins, le programme propose une approche intersectorielle à travers une réponse à 4 niveaux. 
Une assistance alimentaire d'urgence flexible, répondant aux besoins immédiats des communautés touchées par le déplacement et l'insécurité alimentaire, dans les zones difficiles à atteindre. Le programme adaptera l'aide au contexte et aux besoins, en combinant des actions soudaines et des actions en période de soudure. Une approche à deux piliers sera mise en œuvre chaque année en fournissant une assistance alimentaire d'urgence pendant la période de soudure pendant 3 mois et 3 autres mois pendant la période ordinaire. 
Complété par des activités multisectorielles, renforçant la capacité de production alimentaire, les moyens de subsistance et la cohésion sociale, par une intervention dans deux secteurs. Pour soutenir les capacités agricoles et les mécanismes d'adaptation, dans les zones où l'assistance alimentaire sera fournie, le programme soutiendra la production agricole et alimentaire au niveau des ménages, en intégrant les ménages les plus vulnérables dans les systèmes de résilience communautaires. En outre, la diversification des ressources économiques au-delà de l'agriculture est essentielle pour assurer un accès inclusif, en particulier pour les personnes déplacées et les femmes (non-agriculteurs), aux activités économiques et couvrir la sécurité alimentaire et les besoins nutritionnels. Les personnes vulnérables supplémentaires bénéficieront d'un soutien aux AGR et au bétail par le biais i) d'un soutien aux éleveurs, ii) de la vaccination du bétail et des moyens de subsistance, et iii) des AGR.  
Et en tenant compte de la nécessité de mesures de protection au niveau communautaire, en particulier en raison de la crise accrue de la protection et du déplacement ; pour améliorer la qualité, la responsabilité et l'efficacité de la réponse tout en assurant l'accès à la protection de base et aux services WASH pour les personnes les plus vulnérables touchées par le déplacement. A travers des activités de type CCCM en dehors du camp  , la troisième ligne de réponse vise à prendre en compte le lien intersectoriel entre le déplacement et la sécurité alimentaire et à fournir un cadre de protection amélioré pour la population affectée par le déplacement et les communautés d'accueil.

project_name: Provision of lifesaving Health Services for the internally displaced and returnees in Jonglei State and borderline counties of Central Equatoria State.
project_objective:
IMA World Health, a member of the Corus International family, will provide essential primary health care services to 25,635 men, women, boys, and girls in one mobile health facility serving returnees in Morobo, such as in Panyume or Lojulo payams, the Kinyiba PHCU in Kajo-Keji, and the Bori Primary Health Care Center (PHCC) also in Kajo-Keji. Kajo-Keji and Morobo counties contain the second and fourth-highest numbers of people in need of health cluster assistance according to the 2021 Humanitarian Response Plan Health Cluster People in Need (PiN) target sheet, motivating IMA’s selection of these locations for humanitarian intervention within the broader context where the health situation has further worsened throughout 2020 due to intensified conflict, a second year of severe flooding, and the outbreak of COVID-19. IMA’s operates ongoing emergency health projects reaching seven payam-level health facilities and in both Kajo-Keji and Morobo counties which reach over 61,162 people with primary healthcare, reproductive, neonatal, and maternal health, community health, epidemic control, pharmaceutical support in coordination with established pipelines, and SGBV response. The existing presence provides a strong platform from which the proposed project can build in an efficient and cost-effective manner.

The proposed 6-month project aligns with the HNO’s projected health needs improving access to and utilization of essential lifesaving basic health services to reduce excess morbidity and mortality. Disease outbreaks will be investigated within 48 hours’ notice to contribute to the Early Warning Alert System (EWARS) and Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) mechanisms. IMA will adapt healthcare provision in light of the evolving COVID-19 pandemic in the target locations, ensuring appropriate infection prevention and control as well as community health responses. Referral mechanisms from the PHCC, PHCU, and mobile facility will be strengthened and utilized to ensure continuity of secondary care, SGBV, MHPSS, and integrated response for severe acute malnutrition.

IMA World Health, a member of the Corus International family, has worked in South Sudan since 2008, providing primary health care, MNCH, protection, and Visceral Leishmaniasis Control. IMA is the lead for the global $200 million USAID Momentum Integrated Health Resilience project, already operational in South Sudan. IMA is creating, testing, and informing the global conversation around health resilience in fragile settings through this project. Under $57 million in World Bank and South Sudan MOH funding, IMA from 2013-2018 strengthened Upper Nile & Jonglei’s health system, reaching 3.1 million people- over 25% of the country’s population.

Through this proposed project activities, DRC will ensure that all the displaced communities are enabled to partake meaningfully in the governance structures and management of the sites. This project will also encourage camp residents to participate community led care and maintenance activities aimed at improving safety and hygiene in sites, reducing protection and health risks. DRC will work with the camp management committees to facilitate site maintenance through cash-for-work while utilising members of the IDP community by enabling them to earn temporary income. Through this project, DRC will establish or strengthen an inclusive community governance structures and thematic committees at each site level, the engagement of these structures in CCCM coordination mechanisms alongside active humanitarian partners in the respective sites and representatives of relevant local authorities, as well as through continued support for capacity building, mainly through the delivery of trainings adapted to each type of participation (thematic IDP committee members, site governance members, local authority representatives). project_name: Emergency Health Support to Vulnerable Communities in Koch and Rubkona Counties in Unity State and Fangak and Canal Pigi Counties in Jonglei State.
project_objective: A total of 346,119 (Male: 171,705, Female: 174,414) people are in need of health services in Fangak, canal pigi, Koch, and Rubkona counties out of which 69,377(Male 33,461, Female 31,289) are children under five years of age. A fourth consecutive year of flooding has negatively impacted the health status of the populations living in these counties as many of the social facilities; health and nutrition facilities, boreholes, and latrines have been destroyed. Many families have been displaced to higher dry areas and are living without access to safe drinking water and sanitation facilities. They are being exposed to waterborne and vector-borne diseases. Increased snake bites due to an increase in a swampy environment. Lack of essential medicines and medical supplies are the many challenges facing the flood affected populations. Recent flooding and cattle raiding in Koch have worsened the humanitarian situation causing displacements and subsequent loss of livelihood and properties, an estimated 45,777 individuals in (12,472HHs) are said to be in critical need of humanitarian assistance according to the September 2022 IRNA report. Bentiu IDP Camp is currently surrounded by floodwaters and a large scale Malaria outbreak among this population is imminent. HEV transmission continues to persist within the IDP Camp with a surge in the number of cases since the beginning of 2022. In responding to the immediate health needs, this project will ensure the scaling of life-saving essential quality health care services to the population in Fangak, Canal Pigi, Koch, and Rubkona counties through the creation of mobile health outreach units in areas of flood-displaced persons in Fangak and Koch counties. Creation of two PHCUs in Canal Pigi County. Continuation of health services in Sector 1 PHCC Bentiu IDP Camp. Likewise implement Integrated community case management of Malaria, AWD, and Pneumonia will be implemented in Fangak County and Koch County. Activities will also include post-flooding rehabilitation of water damaged facilities, reinforcement of dykes around health facilities in Koch and Fangak counties, and the continued provision of healthcare services through static health facilities. One malaria point will be established in the Bentiu IDP Camp to serve cases during the peak of malaria season to decongest the large numbers of malaria patients going into the health facilities. The project will target a total of 105,000 (Male:53,155, Female:51,845) people as direct beneficiaries, particularly women and children U5 17,850 (7497 M, 10,353 F) and people with disabilities 15,750). Primary services at WRSS-run health facilities will particularly focus on addressing the top three morbidities of malaria, acute watery diarrhea (AWD), and acute respiratory infection (ARI), as well as prevention and control of epidemic-prone diseases like Cholera, measles, EVD, HEV, and other outbreaks. MCH services, EPI, disease surveillance, and infection prevention and control. The response will strengthen local capacity to prevent, detect and respond timely to outbreaks; It will Finally integrate activities with WASH, Nutrition, FSL, and Protection sectors to provide timely and prompt lifesaving interventions to vulnerable populations in the prioritized locations. Referral mechanisms will be established or enhanced for the care of vulnerable people with specific needs like SGBV survivors and SAM children with medical complications. The project will deliver health response to meet health cluster objectives of improving equitable access to life-saving essential quality health care services including maternal, child, and adolescent health, sexual and reproductive health, treatment of common illnesses, disability, MHPSS, and GBV health services to crisis-affected populations; Activities will be monitored through well-coordinated supervision strategies together with the CHD, MOH and UN agencies.
