project_name: Fournir une assistance WASH aux populations déplacées internes et familles d’accueil dans la région de Tillabéry
project_objective:
Dans ce projet, NRC vise de contribuer au renforcement de l’accès aux services d’eau d’hygiène et d’assainissement en vue de réduire le risque et l'exposition aux maladies diarrhéiques auprès de 35 000 personnes déplacées internes et personnes des familles d’accueil touchés par les déplacements, les inondations et les épidémies grâce à un meilleur accès à l'eau potable en qualité et quantité, à des installations sanitaires appropriées et aux bonnes pratiques d'hygiène. Les interventions WASH de NRC se feront dans les villages d’accueil, les sites d’accueil des déplacés et les écoles.  La cible souhaitée est d’atteindre 65% de déplacés internes et 35% de population hôtes. La réponse COVID-19 sera intégrée. Le plan de réponse prévoit de réhabiliter (2) et de construire des nouveaux systèmes d’approvisionnement en eau potable (4)  utilisant les technologies à énergie renouvelable comme le solaire, et là où cela sera nécessaire l’approvisionnement en eau par du water-trucking, le traitement d'eau en situation d’urgence sur les sites temporaires, des infrastructures d’assainissement (500 latrines familiales et 20 latrines scolaires ) et des campagnes de sensibilisation de masse seront organisées pour le changement de comportement (avec 20 relais communautaires ). Pour améliorer la gestion de l’eau, NRC créera et ou renforcera des comités de gestion des points d'eau avec une participation active des femmes visant 50% de participations des femmes dans les comités de gestion. Ces comités comprendront au moins sept membres, hommes et femmes, choisis par une assemblée villageoise.  NRC construira des blocs de latrines et douches dotées chacun d’un dispositif de lavage des mains dans les sites temporaires, dans les familles d’accueil vulnérables et dans les écoles ciblées par ce projet. Des kits d’entretien des latrines seront distribués aux ménages pour le nettoyage et l’entretien des latrines. Les latrines et les douches seront séparées par sexe pour atténuer les problèmes de protection, garantir la dignité des femmes et des jeunes filles et améliorer l'accès gratuit et sûr aux installations.
Pour améliorer l’hygiène en milieu scolaire, NRC mettra en place le paquet minimum d'infrastructures WASH dans les écoles et centres de santé le cas échéant. Des campagnes de sensibilisation pour la promotion de l'hygiène seront organisées afin de promouvoir le changement de comportement et d'encourager les meilleures pratiques d'hygiène personnelle. Pour ce faire, NRC va identifier, former et équiper des relais communautaires d’hygiène en collaboration avec les structures sanitaires avec au moins 50% de femmes. Des kits d'hygiène (5 000) comprenant des articles d'hygiène familiale et des articles de gestion menstruelle pour les femmes seront distribués aux ménages ciblés. NRC métra en place des comités d'hygiène et d’assainissement dans les sites temporaires pour une bonne gestion des structures d’assainissement. Les relais communautaires et les comités d’assainissement vont conduire des campagnes de sensibilisation dans les communautés, les écoles et dans les camps. Les matériels d'IEC et les kits d’hygiène seront conçus par le biais d'une consultation communautaire et après une enquête initiale sur les connaissances, attitudes et pratiques (CAP) menée par le NRC en coordination avec la DRHA, les districts sanitaires afin de se concentrer sur les problèmes les plus pertinents mis en évidence par les communautés et où les résultats de l'enquête montrent les plus grandes faiblesses des pratiques. NRC veillera à ce que les relais d'hygiène communautaires soient formés sur les méthode de communication/sensibilisation au niveau communautaire et équipés avec des matériels IEC. Cela inclura des démonstrations sur les pratiques  afin de conduire vers le changement de comportement parmi les communautés ciblées. NRC conduira une enquête CAP initiale et finale, des post distribution monitoring pour mesurer l’impact des projets et évaluer les indicateurs.

project_name: Education in Emergencies for conflict and disaster affected children and youth
project_objective:
In the First Phase Response the main objective will be to provide immediate access to education for newly displaced children 6-18 to rapidly restore a sense of safety, calming, and provide lifesaving knowledge during emergencies. This intervention will last no longer than 3-6 months with the aim of reducing the out of school period for affected children and the related protection risks. FPR will involve parents, caregivers and community volunteers in PFA and PSS models along with structured recreation in order to create a foundation for future learning, whilst learning outcomes will be limited to basic literacy and numeracy during this phase. A FPR and preparedness SoP will be developed in close coordination with the Emergency Response team. NRC education team will a focus on transition out of FPR in to longer term learning pathways including formal and non-formal education and improved coordination with other EIE actors, (via the Education Cluster and MoE) for the identification newly displaced children of emerging needs.  Preperdenss steps will include DRR and TiCC training along with propositioning of teaching and learning materials such as locally contextualised School-in-Box and hygiene kits. Coordination with the NRC Shelter team will ensure appropriate use of Temporary Learning Spaces for the FPR. 
NRC will establish two Non Formal Education distinct programmes for IDPs/ host community children and youth 10-25 years who are out of school. The main goal of this response area is to assist children and youth in re-entering formal education or embarking on a TVET pathway (See Youth Programming below). First: at the national level NRC intends to pilot an Accelerated Education Programme (AEP). This flexible, age-appropriate programme will run in an accelerated timeframe for overage, out of school children who had their education significantly interrupted. NRC will work in partnership with the MoE to develop and provide a primary level re-enrolment pathway (under national DRR policy), utilising a condensed primary curriculum (curriculum prioritization) along with the external exam mechanism. Through this, long term drop outs will be supported to obtain accredited learning within a condensed timeframe. NRC will collaborate with the MoE and Teacher Training Instititue to train teachers on the condensed curriculum and accelerated teaching methodologies and where appropriate utilise EdTech for follow up training of teachers and facilitators. Second: at the Provincial level, NRC will continue to work with other EiE actors to harmonise a non-accredited provincial level Catch Up Programme for short term out drop-outs. This will be specifically designed for children in Cabo Delgado and will utilise the 20% flexibility. It will incorporate outreach elements to families who have struggled to prioritise education during displacement and financial hardship.
Supporting Transition and Retention in Formal Education will target two groups: Newly enrolled (within the previous 2 academic years) IDP and returnee boys and girls 6-18 and IDP/returnee/ host community boys and girls 6-18 at increased risk of drop out due to the emergency (i.e., children with additional needs such as separated, unaccompanied, children with disabilities etc). Support will build on NRC’s existing strong relationship with provincial level education authorities and primarily employ the SIP model in which PTAs are supported technically, financially and materially to design and implement their own SIPs. Interventions will focus on transition and retention weak spots for affected children; such as transition between different education systems (FPR to Formal or NFE to Formal) and at between grades.
Youth Programming will target female and male IDP, host community, returnee and other vulnerable youth aged 15-25. The TVET start-up response will employ a pathways model, following a placement process, youth will be supported in their chosen carer, business or education pathway.

project_name: Protection and prevention services to the most vulnerable children (boys and girls) and their caregivers in the West Bank including East Jerusalem, and monitoring of protection incidents in Israel and the State of Palestine
project_objective:
This project will ensure 13,607 of the most vulnerable Palestinian children (7,430 boys and 6,177 girls aged 12-17 years old including 204 children with disabilities) exposed to conflict-related violence, and 10,729 caregivers are reached with protection, impact mitigation, rehabilitation and prevention services in the West Bank. It will also foster increased respect for IHL and IHRL and accountability for violations against children through documenting and monitoring violations to inform advocacy and increase accountability. 
This project is in line with and contributes to the Protection Cluster's first and second objectives that aim to increase respect for IHL, IHRL, and accountability for violations as well as ensure that protection response mechanisms are in place to prevent and mitigate the effects of the occupation and conflict-related violence.

The main objective of this child protection project is for children in the West Bank to be safe, protected, and secure from violence, exploitation, and grave violations. The project will: 
- Support initiatives to engage vulnerable and at-risk children positively in structured recreational, educational, awareness-raising, life skills, and resilience-building activities to improve their resilience and coping mechanisms.  
- Support awareness-raising for vulnerable families and communities regarding children’s right to protection; preventing and responding to Violence Against Children (VAC);
- Support vulnerable children affected by conflict-related violence and their families with integration and rehabilitation services especially structured counseling and mental health and psychosocial support including through helpline services. (Level 3),
- Support monitoring, data analysis, and reporting on grave violations trends related to child protection concerns in Israel/Occupied Palestinian Territory (the WB) to provide evidence and inform advocacy.
- Support legal assistance for children affected by conflict-related violence.
- Ensuring compliance with PSEA principles and procedures, implementing partners and project beneficiaries will be oriented on sexual exploitation and abuse and will receive information on UNICEF email, as well as other interagency channels including SAWA Free toll number, social media platforms, and WhatsApp to report on PSEA.

project_name: Support to vulnerable IDPs, returnees and host families to Improve their food security, economic and social well-being in Mayo Sava and Mayo Tsanaga, Logone and Chari
project_objective:
The purpose of the project is to improve food security, economic and social well-being of vulnerable IDPs, returnees and host families in the target areas. 
NRC Cameroon’s Livelihood and Food Security (LFS) programme will target displacement-affected people based on vulnerability criteria and not their displacement status (refugees, IDPs, returnees (former IDPs, and host communities). NRC will apply social and economic vulnerability criteria to identify vulnerable households most at risk to food insecurity. The social vulnerability criteria applied will include female-headed households, child-headed households; households, pregnant and breastfeeding women; elderly people (60 and above); households with a person with physical or mental disability or debilitating chronic disease. For the economic vulnerability criteria, NRC will use as a reference: low income households under the poverty line (28 000/months), poor or limited food consumption score; no food stock, number of meals per day, no productive assets. For agricultural restoration activities, NRC will also include the following criteria: having at least one able-bodied person in the household who can farm land. NRC’s LFS programmes will also target as far as possible vulnerable youth and women for vocational training and economic empowerment. 
To address the intermediate needs of affected populations NRC will use cash, vouchers or in-kind assistance based on the results of market analysis and cash feasibility studies. To maximise the chances of success in this activity, NRC will as far as possible couple livelihoods interventions with food assistance to meet basic food needs. Moreover, NRC will implement complementary activities such as training and awareness raising sessions to support target households. Programme activities will gradually scale down and phase out so that by the end of the projects, communities have the skills and resources needed to be more resilient to shocks and crises in the medium and long term. NRC will work in coordination with local partners such as local technical and administrative structures and will collaborate closely with them so they can provide technical support during programme implementation and continued follow-up after the programme ends. 
The LFS programme will include cash assistance, livelihoods promotion and enhancement applying a market-based approach (MBA) that refers to local traders so to improve access to income and revive/strengthen the local economy. The intervention will be geared towards supporting the most vulnerable displacement-affected households and at the same time building their capacity in food production, food transformation and marketing

project_name: WASH Support for most vulnerable people in the South and Bekaa Region
project_objective:
The objective of the project is that 23,930 most vulnerable individuals in the South and Bekaa regions, are using safely managed drinking water and sanitation services whilst reducing health and environmental risks and improving water quality by increasing the proportion of wastewater that is safely treated. For this purpose, ACF will:
1.	Aim at improving access to water by
a.	conducting water source quality testing in the areas with confirmed or suspected cholera cases as part of the strategy to ensure safe access to clean water to the affected population,
b.	ensuring the access to safe water for at least 14 days via Water Trucking (WT) services or point of use treatment systems, in accordance with the minimum Sphere standards of 35 litres/person/day,
c.	working closely with public institutions to ensure water delivered through the public network is chlorinated and safe to drink.
d.	coordinating with UNICEF to support Water Establishments and municipalities with the provision of chlorine to sterilize water and the reduce risk of waterborne diseases, wherever not already supported by UNICEF,
e.	supporting public institutions, such as schools and primary health care (PHC) facilities to increase water safety delivered to students and patients,
f.	providing solarization and/or other activities that contribute to a lower reliance on fossil fuel for water provision to schools and surrounding communities
g.	providing emergency fuel to pumping stations connected to schools and surrounding communities to maintain water supply via networks.
2.	Aim at improving access to sanitation by:
a.	providing desludging services through already identified and validated suppliers to cholera affected or suspected households and its surrounding areas. The desludging services will only be used for decentralized systems that are not connected to the public wastewater systems, mainly in ITSs and Collective Shelters, but also in Lebanese communities using sceptic tanks (decentralized systems) as their wastewater disposal method,
b.	disinfecting the main areas of the cholera hotspots (latrines, excreta and vomits, garbage dumping sites) and equipped with PPE through our WASH disinfection field teams, which are part of the Rapid Response Teams (RRT).
3.	Enhance access to positive hygiene and WaSH behavior:
a.	carrying out Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE) activities, by providing awareness sessions on the prevention and treatment of Cholera. The sessions will target households with confirmed or suspected cases, as well as surrounding households,
b.	conducting community-based awareness sessions provided by ACF’s field officers will be complemented by the provision of a hygiene kit (HK) with items designed to help prevent and treat Cholera.

project_name: Provision of safe and inclusive quality Education for Children Affected by Conflict in North East Nigeria (Borno and Adamawa States)
project_objective:
The overall objective of this project is to restore and maintain access to safe, inclusive and quality education for children of school going age while supporting those out of school acquire foundational skills and knowledge requisite for learning and integration into formal learning opportunities. Additionally, children who dropped out of school for one reason or the other will be supported to re-enroll back to school. The project will aim at addressing multiple social, cultural, economic, gender, linguistic, status and geographical barriers that limit children from enjoying their right to education across the target states. Guided by a vulnerability criteria, the project will target the most vulnerable children and adolescents aged between six (6) to eighteen (18) years. The focus will mainly be on IDPs, returnees and affected host communities, paying more attention to children from hard to reach areas, including those with disabilities. A total of 37,400 beneficiaries (37,000 children, 200 Teachers and 200 SBMCs) will be targeted in 2023. Education response will be based on identified education needs across Borno and Adamawa states and will be designed around three major outcomes in line with the education sector strategic plan 2021-2023:
•	Increased Access to education for emergency-affected girls and boys
•	Increased continuity of education for emergency-affected girls and boys 
•	Existing learning environments are child-friendly, equitable, and inclusive
•	Improved quality of learning for emergency-affected girls and boys 
Specifically the project will provide of non-formal education for those who have never been to school as well as catch up programs for children who dropped out of school in order to position them to re-enroll back; construct/rehabilitate temporary learning spaces/classrooms; recruitment of non-formal facilitators as well as provision of teaching and learning materials. Additionally the project will facilitate and manage transitions from non-formal to formal education through working with state agency for mass education (SAME) to assess and certify the learners transitioning to formal schools. Learning facilities will be supported to be inclusive, child-friendly, disability- friendly, and gender sensitive through teacher training, PSS integration, and establishment of referral pathways for specialized services beyond the scope of the project. Teaching and learning materials will be provided and teachers will be equipped have sufficient knowledge and skills to deliver quality education. Psychosocial support will also be integrated into the teacher training packages to equip them with skills to integrate PSS into learning activities as this is crucial so social and emotional wellbeing of learners.
The project will target beneficiaries from various LGAs in Borno and Adamawa states, some of which include; MMC, Jere, Monguno, Pulka and Gwoza in Borno state; as well as Yola, Mubi, Madagali and Michika in Adamawa state. Implementation of Education interventions will be done in accordance to the Education sector response plans, the contextualized Nigeria Minimum Standards for EiE, Education sector response plan and HNO 2022 among others. NRC will pay keen attention to the trends and dynamics across various states, bearing in mind that approaches may not uniformly apply across all locations. NRC will work in close collaboration with education authorities and key stakeholders such as SUBEB, SAME as well as other education partners through the EiE working group for ownership and sustainability.

project_name: Improved Food Security and Strengthened Resilience and Livelihoods Opportunities for Vulnerable, Displacement-affected Populations in Syria
project_objective:
NRC's project will contribute to the Food Security Sector’s (FSS) HRP Objectives 1, 2, and 3. 
When relevant and feasible, NRC will seek to have integrated/complementary responses that promote synergies with Multi-purpose Cash Assistance (MPCA) and early recovery and livelihoods assistance, such as linking lifesaving and food assistance interventions with livelihoods/early recovery initiatives and other interventions aimed at creating employment and income generation opportunities, and strengthening target communities’ self-reliance and resilience.
NRC will implement the following interventions: 
FSS Objective 1: 1.1. NRC will provide the assessed food-insecure people with monthly food assistance, to enable them to scale-up and sustain minimum food consumption needs. Depending on needs and available (funding) resources, assistance will be provided for a minimum of 8 and up to 12 consecutive months. 
1.2. In case of mass displacements caused by sudden escalation, NRC will provide emergency response to crisis-affected, vulnerable people, with short- term food assistance. This may be supplemented by MPCA as lifesaving and/or life-sustaining assistance intended for the most vulnerable to enable them to meet general basic needs, ensuring no overlap between the recipients of short-term food assistance and that of MPCA. 
Wherever markets are functional, accessible, and of sufficient capacity, NRC will prioritize unconditional cash as the most appropriate, cost-effective, and most-preferred modality. If needed, NRC will use vouchers or in-kind modalities. Both interventions will contribute to the reduced application of negative coping strategies and, to ensure better utilization of the assistance and increase its impact in promoting FS outcomes, will be accompanied by information campaigns about the importance of dietary diversity and nutritious dietary choices. 
FSS Objective 2: 2.1. Local/home-based food production support will be in-kind and target specific types of agricultural/food production activities, such as horticulture/greenhouse vegetables, dairy farming, poultry, cereals, legumes, etc.  
2.2. Cash for agricultural inputs – NRC will use labelled cash as a modality for this intervention, which will be applied wherever feasible, and for a variety of agricultural/food production activities. 
Regardless of the modality applied, through these interventions the selected small-scale subsistence farmers will benefit from access to and utilization of the inputs they need to rehabilitate or sustain their production, such as fodder, seeds/seedlings, fertilizer, animal vitamins or medicines, equipment (irrigation, greenhouses), and/or tools. Both interventions will be aimed at enabling affected households to protect and build their productive assets, and improve their self-reliance and resilience prospects. To ensure greater impact, effectiveness, and sustainability for beneficiaries, distributions will be preceded by technical training (incl. on climate-smart agriculture), and followed by provision of field advisory assistance.
To facilitate the transition of displacement-affected populations from humanitarian assistance to self-reliance and sustainable livelihoods, NRC will use market-based approaches to support economic recovery of households and facilitate their access to demand-driven Income Generation (IG) and employment through: 
2.3. Small business grants (conditional cash/in-kind) followed-up by coaching/advisory support, to support long-term IG and (self)-employment.
2.4. Cash for Work (CFW) activities as a means to improve access to short-term employment and IG. 
2.5. Vocational, business, and soft skills training, and apprenticeship programmes.
FSS Objective 3: NRC will also use the CFW modality to improve communities' resilience and capacity to sustain households’ livelihoods. Depending on priorities identified, this may include rehabilitation of grain silos, water/irrigation systems, access roads to fields, etc.

project_name: Enhancement of protection of displaced persons, returnees and conflict affected host communities in Syria through integrated, community-based protection activities.
project_objective:
The project aims to strengthen protection and resilience of Syrian IDPs, returnees and vulnerable host communities through advocacy, coordination, provision of community-based protection services and legal services. UNHCR Syria will continue to lead the Protection Sector to ensure coordinated protection interventions programming for IDPs and affected people as well as executing leadership roles in refugee return programmes in collaboration with the Government. UNHCR’s protection interventions will include provision of integrated protection services through a network of 120 centers in all 14 Governorates. The network of Community Centres, paired with some 120 mobile units and around 3,600 outreach volunteers of multifunctional thematic capacities, are fundamental to the implementation of UNHCR’s Protection and Solutions Strategy for Syria through outreach to affected populations, assessment of protection risks and vulnerabilities, consultation, identification and mobilization of community resources, strengthening of community self-help networks, and offering protection services and support to displaced persons, returnees and host communities in response to the priority needs expressed by the communities, while applying a highly participatory age, gender and diversity approach. The protection services extended at the UNHCR Community Centres include, but are not limited to, psycho-social support, GBV prevention, risk mitigation and response and child protection case management, legal awareness and legal aid, non-formal education programmes, services for persons with disabilities and older persons, provision of general and medical in-kind assistance, social and recreational activities, curriculum based awareness activities on various subjects targeting women, men, boys and girls, referrals and information sharing, social protection through livelihoods support to most vulnerable population.
As part of its commitment to Accountability to Affected Population (AAP), UNHCR will ensure meaningful participation of communities based on age, gender and diversity approach, structured focus group discussions and enhancement of the community-based feedback and complaint mechanisms. UNHCR will continue its capacity building efforts to ensure services are delivered according to the standards and that accountability to affected population and do no harm principles are respected.
UNHCR will continue co-leading the AAP Technical Working Group and the Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) In-Country Network and coordinate activities to strengthen AAP and SEA prevention, risk mitigation and response.
Monitoring and evaluation of the planned interventions is based on the reports and observations by the partners and on regular direct observation and ongoing assessment and consultations with the community by UNHCR and partners and the comparison of achievements and related financial expenditures with objectives. Evaluation is conducted through different channels, including post distribution monitoring to determine the effectiveness of/measure the satisfaction of people of concern with the service and the distribution process in addition to multiple satisfaction surveys and tracking tools related to different protection interventions. Monitoring and evaluation activities are carried out at various levels by partners and agencies implementing subprojects, UNHCR Country Office, Sub and Field Offices. Situation reports are submitted by all UNHCR Field Offices to their respective Supervising Office and Country Offices submit a corresponding report to Headquarters.

project_name: Provide immediate access to water services
project_objective: In light of the current economic and fuel crises, the intended intervention will aim to support existing infrastructure for water supply system through procurement and supply of chlorine and other consumables, emergency repair for pumping stations with provision of fuel to maintain minimum operational level and providing the most vulnerable communities with water supply. This approach is deemed to take the most cost-effective pathway to reach a high number of people in need in a short time period. The only way to avoid the complete shutdown of all or part of the water systems in Lebanon is through this intervention and support to pumping stations.

project_name: Provision of lifesaving healthcare and prevention services for IDPs, returnees, and affected community in South Darfur, East Darfur, South Kordofan, Kharotoum, AlGazira, Gedaref, and Kassala states in Sudan.
project_objective: The aim of this Health project is to deliver lifesaving critical health services to IDPs, returnees and host communities through clinics, EMOCs, and mobile clinics to reduce high rates of morbidity and mortality. The total target beneficiaries is 450,000 individuals (88198 men, 91800 women, 137702 girls, 132300 boys). A comprehensive healthcare service package will be delivered through Primary Health Care Centers (PHCC) including support with supplies and equipment such as essential drugs, medical supplies, and furniture to promote and achieve infection protection and control. In collaboration with SMOHs, seconded healthcare staff will be identified and supported with monthly incentives and trainings to better support health care management. EPI campaigns will be supported across target areas, vaccinators will be trained to improve quality and increase coverage. CARE will work closely with community members and Youth Associations to support community health education, outreach, and mobilization, including on protection and GBV. Protection and Youth Committees will provide integrated GBV awareness raising and sensitization in targeted areas using household visits, community leader’s meetings, and public events. CARE will establish and train community Protection Committees to conduct community sensitization on PSEA, GBV risk mitigation and prevention. CARE will also provide SRH services including training service providers/midwives, provision of essential drugs and supplies, clean delivery kits, and EMOC. For strengthening the wider health information and management, CARE will adopt a well-structured health information system (HIS) to capture data and submit weekly Epidemiology reports to SMOH and WHO

project_name: Provision of Integrated Safe, Equitable, Protective and Inclusive Education to Conflict Affected Boys and Girls in South Sudan.
project_objective:
The proposed World Vision International South Sudan's education intervention is aligned to the Humanitarian Strategic Objectives  2 & 3; the sectoral Objectives 1, 2 & 3, and falls directly under the two Strategic Objectives. Given WVI-SS's strong presence and the sector needs identified, World Vision proposes to implement the project in the counties of Baliet, Fashoda, Melut and Renk in Upper Nile; Tonj South, Tonj East, Tonj North in Warrap; Yambio, Nagero, Tambura in Western Equatoria; and Juba in Central Equatoria which are geographical areas affected by conflict displacement or facing acute food insecurity levels.

World Vision has education programs in partnership with ECHO, Education Can't Wait, HPP IrishAid, UNHCR, SSSHF, and Japanese Platform, and CEN. Through this intervention, WVISS will continue to give focus on emergency affected rural and urban areas. This will further consolidate on the efforts on the ground while reaching further and deeper into the areas with dire needs, in hard-to-reach area.

In line with the Education Cluster Response Plan, WVISS will ensure that through this project, 29,357 children will have access to safe and equitable quality education and 645 teachers and 715 PTA’s will be trained and supported with supplies and materials; 1800 youth will be provided life skills and vocational training with starter kits. Out of the 29,357 learners, the project will target about 500 children (200 boys, 300 girls) with disabilities. The learners will also be categorized under social/residential status as internally displaced, host community, or refugees during the actual enrolment in the project. 

WVSS will also prioritize establishment of learning structures with gender-segregated WASH facilities, and other supplies/materials/kits that will be supportive and will enhance motivation of children to go to and remain in school with a particular emphasis on girl’s education. In addition, recreational opportunities will be established and implemented to support the recovery of children and youth and promote their overall wellbeing. All learners will be given equal access to education despite Gender, disability or ethnic background.

project_name: United Nations Humanitarian Air Service
project_objective:
Since 2018, the security situation in Burkina Faso drastically deteriorated with the expansion and intensification of activities of non-state armed groups (NSAGs), exploiting pre-existing inter-communal tensions. A further escalation was observed in 2020 and 2021, with a greater toll on human lives and on vulnerable populations. The non-state armed groups (NSAGs) are fragmented, with multiple internal players; and there are increased external players linked with the regional dynamics (i.e. Central Sahel countries). This has led to massive population displacements and has had a severe impact on already vulnerable populations.

As of October 2021, over 1.4 million persons have been displaced and new displacements are reported daily. The security situation has had repercussions on the overall food and nutritional security of the country. Food security and nutritional situation has been impacted by the growing crisis affecting vulnerable populations. The unprecedented humanitarian emergency left 2.6 million persons in need of humanitarian assistance during the 2022 lean season – according to the last Cadre Harmonisé.

As of 30 November 2022, the number of registered internally displaced persons (IDPs) is 1,810,105 hosted in 299 communes spread over all 13 regions of the country. In addition, according to the Analysis of the Cadre Harmonisé of November 2022, 3,533,220 people, or 16% of the total population, would be food insecure. This includes 572,382 children under 5 years of age (RGPH 2019). These people would be concentrated in the regions of East (19%), Centre-North (18%), Sahel (17%), North and Boucle du Mouhoun (respectively 10%). These areas also correspond to localities with a high security challenge.
Humanitarian access to vulnerable populations in need of assistance is restricted by threats posed by non-state armed groups, counterterrorism operations, the presence of Improvised Explosive Devices (IEDs) planted on roads and the damage or destruction of key road infrastructure (bridges targeted in attacks in the Sahel region for instance). In order to support the planned humanitarian response and enable access to the population in need and project implementation sites, UNHAS aims to provide a safe, effective and efficient passenger air service to the entire humanitarian community and their implementing partners, principally NGOs, UN agencies, red cross/crescent movement, donor organizations and diplomatic missions. UNHAS will be used to deliver assistance to hard-to-reach areas were people are the most vulnerable.

project_name: Water, Sanitation and Hygiene Sector Coordination and Enabling Environment
project_objective:
The Syria crisis is one of the most complex humanitarian crises in recent memory. Humanitarian assistance is provided by a large variety of actors on the ground, operating both from within Syria and from neighbouring countries. Coordination hubs have been established in Damascus, Gaziantep, and NES, with WOS in Amman, which ensures common strategies and the best use of resources from the different hubs.
WASH needs of affected populations will continue to be high across 2023 with sector partners expected to provide quality emergency WASH services and maintain WASH facilities and infrastructure. WASH needs will largely be influenced by:
• Water scarcity and drought-like conditions: The evolution of the situation will depend on winter precipitation and the ability to fill in the dams along the Euphrates River, which will impact hydropower generation and functionality of water systems powered by them.
• Energy supply crisis: If intermittency and further degradation of the electricity supply to WASH systems continue, this will trigger a further increase in the number of people in need of WASH assistance.
• New displacements: New displacements may also be triggered by hostilities or economic or water crises.
• Population living in IDP sites: The population in last resort sites will continue because of the ongoing economic and water crises and the closure of collective centers. Due to the funding decrease, a deterioration of the WASH conditions in IDP sites may be expected.
•Returnee movements: No major change is expected due to political stasis.
As Sector/Cluster Lead agency, UNICEF must ensure that sectoral coordination needs at Hub and WOS levels are met. There is also a growing need to create an enabling environment allowing for the Government of Syria and more specifically the Ministry of Water Resources (MOWR) to be more involved with existing coordination structures. The sector will try to encourage the MOWR management team to engage in leading the sector activities and with data collection processes at different levels. 
This project will fulfill the core coordination functions at WOS and Hub levels to ensure the following objectives: -Increased predictability of geographic coverage and sectoral responsibility -Demonstrated accountability (for sector-wide performance). -Increased field-level capacities to address gaps. -Quality and uninterrupted WASH services. -Maximized coordination and partnership and buy-in from the major humanitarian actors to ensure a more strategic and coherent response. -Advocacy efforts to fund sector needs. -Reinforced sectoral and intersectoral coordination at all levels.
Following the AWD/cholera outbreak declaration in September 2022, UNICEF is playing a key role in the coordination of the response, including in the Incident Management System (IMS) set up in Amman, Jordan for WOS, and in the Cholera Task Forces/IMS in Damascus and Gaziantep. UNICEF leads the pillars for WASH and RCCE, as well as extensively contributing to the case management pillar and co-leading the Operations, Supply, and Logistics pillars. UNICEF, as CLA, continues to coordinate the WASH response at WOS level and across the affected hubs and governorates, through the sector in Damascus, the Cluster in Gaziantep for the cross-border operations, and by collaborating with the WASH Working Group in NES. The WOS WASH Cluster supports the Hub Coordination Teams to ensure inter-Hub coordination, advocacy, and technical support for cholera. The WASH sector/cluster coordinators in Gaziantep and Damascus within the local IMS/Cholera Task forces, co-lead the coordination of the response with the Health Cluster/sector, RCCE, and leads the WASH Pillar, while developing technical SOP and guidance for the response, capacity building of WASH actors.

project_name: Provision of life-saving healthcare services to Palestine Refugees in Syria
project_objective:
The public health system in Syria has been degraded by over a decade of conflict and remains extremely vulnerable as a result of the displacement and migration of qualified professionals and the widespread destruction or damage to health facilities. UNRWA’s health services in Syria are facing growingincreasing pressures due to socio-economic crisis, with an increasing number of Palestine refugees now relying heavily on the Agency for health care. It is expected that at least 790,000 patient visits will be made to UNRWA health centres in 2023. 
The Agency's 25 health facilities in Syria (23 health centres and health points located in Palestine refugee camps and two mobile clinics) provide a range of primary health care services, including out-patient consultations, immunization services, infant and child growth monitoring, dispensing of medications, gynaecology consultations, laboratory services, non-communicable diseases (NCD) care, MCH care, dental care, and mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services. Mobile clinics are deployed to areas that have been the most affected by the conflict and where Agency health facilities have been damaged or destroyed, including Yarmouk and Ein el Tal camps.
UNRWA will continue to subsidise access to secondary and tertiary health care for around 10,000 refugees through a network of partner hospitals and private laboratories. This intervention has become increasingly critical as families’ ability to afford hospitalisation services continues to decrease. Support provided by the Agency will cover between 75 and 95 per cent of the costs, depending on the level of vulnerability and availability of funds.
Dedicated support will be provided to persons with disabilities through the provision of prosthetic devices, including hearing aids for older persons   , while baby kits (including diapers) will be provided to 800 pregnant women for their newborn infants. Persons with long-term disabilities and in need of physiotherapy will be referred to external partners in community-based organizations (CBOs) across Syria. It is estimated that 16,000 physiotherapy sessions will be provided.
In 2023, UNRWA will also conduct minor repairs to 15 of its health facilities that require urgent maintenance (this does not include facilities covered under the Emergency Repair, Rehabilitation and Maintenance of UNRWA Installations section of the present appeal). To promote environmental sustainability, UNRWA will install solar systems at UNRWA health facilities to support an uninterrupted cold chain storage system and internet connectivity for eHealth real-time reporting as well as for lighting. UNRWA aims to establish green spaces around Agency health centres and will phase out the use of plastic bags when dispensing medicines to patients and replace them with paper bags or reusable bags, funding permitting. A review on waste disposal practices in Agency health facilities will be carried out to provide recommendations on how to manage waste to reduce pollution and reduce the risk of infectious diseases spreading.    Partnerships will be sought with other organizations thatwho are supporting environmental conservation measures.
As part of its commitment to AAP, the Agency will familiarise health centre staff on AAP related principles and actions. This will include supporting patients to provide feedback, and act on same. A standardized CFRM will be strengthened for all SFO programmes, including health. 
Under this appeal, UNRWA will continue to respond to COVID-19 by subsidizing COVID-19 testing for 500 Palestine refugees. This assistance is extended to all UNRWA staff to contain the spread of the pandemic and ensure the safety of Agency staff and those they serve. Since 2021, UNRWA has been responsible for administering COVID-19 vaccinations for all UN staff and partner NGOs in Syria as part of the UN vaccination campaign, which has contributed significantly to the inter-agency pandemic response. project_name: Provision of Multipurpose Cash to Vulnerable Palestine Refugees in Syria
project_objective:
UNRWA plans to provide up to 420,000 Palestine refugees with cash assistance to meet their basic needs, including food, non-food items (NFIs), and WASH needs. The Agency will continue to provide this assistance based on a targeted approach introduced in 2019, prioritizing refugees assessed as most vulnerable with a higher cash transfer. In 2022, it is expected that around 149,500 Palestine refugees will be assessed as most vulnerable based on the four vulnerability categories used by UNRWA (female headed households, families with persons with disabilities, families headed by an older person and unaccompanied minors/orphans). The remaining 270,500 vulnerable Palestine refugees will receive a lower cash transfer value as explained below. 

Our cash transfer values were calculated while designing our Emergency Appeal 2023 intervening during the last quarter of 2022. The values were based on discussions with the CWG and in consultation with other humanitarian actors and are aligned with CWG recommendations, and more specifically the suggested MEB transfer values. Based on these discussions and recommendations, our cash transfer values were set to  SYP 495,000 per month for a family of five members belonging to the most vulnerable categories   and SYP 345,000 per month for a family of five members belonging to the remaining caseload of vulnerable Palestine refugees. These transfer values take into consideration the reduction of in-kind food assistance to be provided to the same beneficiaries which is $ 6 per month per individual. 


UNRWA plans to provide its monthly assistance to Palestine refugees covering twelve months over three rounds of assistance in 2023, with each round covering four months of cash assistance. Ideally, the rounds would start on 1 January, 1 May, and 1 September. In reality, UNRWA might adjust the start date and duration of each round depending on fund availability and taking into account cash flow considerations and donor requirements for the different grants. 


UNRWA plans to conduct two post-distribution monitoring exercise in July and December 2023. UNRWA also has a result-based monitoring (RBM) system which tracks a number of indicators for all programmes and interventions including cash assistance. Quarterly management review (QMR) meetings involving relevant staff, including senior management, are held to track and assess the indicators. Mid-year result review (MYRR) and annual result review (ARR) are also conducted with departments at HQ to add another layer of scrutiny and to provide an overall overview of achievements and challenges.

project_objective:
UNRWA estimates that 420,000 Palestine refugees in Syria will continue to require humanitarian assistance in 2023. Many among them struggle to secure basic shelter and NFI need, and will be supported by UNRWA through this project, as part of the 2023 Humanitarian response plan. 
UNRWA estimates that 420,000 Palestine refugees in Syria will continue to require humanitarian assistance in 2023. project_name: Protection Services and Interventions for Palestine Refugees in Syria
project_objective:
UNRWA will continue to provide increasingly needed protection services to Palestine refugees in Syria, especially in light of the current deteriorating economic situation and the additional protection concerns resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic, and in line with its commitment to the humanitarian principles of humanity and impartiality. The Agency will continue to focus on mainstreaming protection in service provision, including through area-based structures and staff capacity building in the identification of intersecting factors affecting individual vulnerability. The Agency will also work towards building a stronger data-driven protection approach to strengthen evidence-based prioritization and programming.
PSS activities for 11,360 refugees, including children, older persons and persons with disabilities, will remain a priority in 2022, to strengthen the response to the increasing psychosocial needs, to foster social cohesion and prevent the adoption of negative coping mechanisms. In light of the risk of COVID-19 exposure, safe practices will be used for in-person PSS activities for particularly vulnerable groups like older persons. 
Legal support will continue to be offered to refugees (mainly women) experiencing GBV, through assistance in obtaining documentation and referrals to external partners. The threat caused by ERW remains a major protection concern in Syria, particularly for children, who are most at risk of being harmed. UNRWA will continue to address this primarily through awareness raising sessions for all UNRWA  students (i.e., 49,500 children) and people from refugee communities (1,500), as well as training for Agency staff (200). Particular focus will be given to areas seeing spontaneous returns of refugee families, especially in Yarmouk, Ein el Tal and Dera’a camps which are potentially heavily contaminated with ERW.
Protection monitoring, reporting and advocacy will remain a priority. UNRWA will continue to participate in global protection mechanisms; engage, as appropriate, with the International Human Rights System (IHRS) in line with the Agency’s IHRS framework; and interact with relevant stakeholders, including the protection coordination structures of the Humanitarian Country Team (HCT) at country and area levels. UNRWA will continue to monitor and advocate for, and respond to, particularly vulnerable groups within the Palestine refugee community, including individuals who remain displaced within Syria and Palestine refugees willing to voluntarily return to their place of habitual residence from within Syria and from abroad, noting that those returning to newly accessible areas with limited services are often amongst the most economically vulnerable.
UNRWA will also strengthen adherence to humanitarian principles, including by conducting installation checks to ensure they are compliant with UN values (including neutrality) and that they are safe, accessible and inclusive spaces.

project_name: Provision of safe, secure, dignified and upgrade shelter and NFI (TDK, solar kit) support to Rohingya refugees and crisis-affected host communities in Ukhiay & Teknaf Upazilla, Cox's Bazar District, Bangladesh
project_objective:
""In 2023 NRC Shelter & Settlement Programme aims to be part of the response to the Sector's two objectives. First, NRC will strive to improve emergency response and provide life-saving emergency Non-food Items (SNFI) support. Secondly, NRC will contribute to the provision of Shelter support, including Energy and HLP, for safe, dignified and improved shelter solutions access to both Rohingya refugees in the camps, and vulnerable crisis-affected populations in the host communities of Ukhiay & Teknaf Upazilla, Cox's Bazar District.

NRC will undertake these activities using a professional training team who has speciality in gender, disability inclusion and PSEA. NRC will conduct all of these interventions following the latest Covid-19 guidelines.

project_name: Provide uninterrupted education for every child affected by humanitarian crisis in Sudan
project_objective:
Despite the enormous benefits to children, societies and entire countries, education is often the first service suspended and the last to be restored during crisis. UNICEF works to provide uninterrupted education for every child affected by humanitarian crisis in Sudan – especially girls, children with disabilities, internally displaced children and adolescents.
The armed conflict which started April 15th resulted in large scale displacement and shattered access to basic services in conflict hotspots including education. Yet far, more than 250,000 people were forced to flee across the boarders and nearly one million people displaced internally. 
This project aims to support 2,821,200 children (1,763,249 girls) to access safe learning spaces, cope with the trauma of crisis, receive psychosocial support, recreational activities, engage with their peers, and to be equipped with learning materials. The project aims to establish learning spaces to enable children and adolescents’ access to learning, and to engage in skills and recreational activities. 
The project is nationwide targeting localities most affected by the humanitarian crisis, displacement, and armed conflict. UNICEF Sudan -as the co-lead of the education sector- will strongly advocate for a child’s right to education and a protective learning environment, forging partnerships at the national and local levels to safeguard learning for every child. UNICEF will explore numerous implementation modalities to engage children in learning and recreational activities through educational material and supplies distribution, as well as, E-learning and digital learning provision. 
UNICEF Sudan is in urgent need for USD 100,033,082 (USD 85,762,245 total programme cost) to support approximately 2,821,200 of the most vulnerable in need girls and boys with inclusive access to learning opportunities across 9,404 safe learning space.
