project_name: Improving access to life-saving Health, Nutrition and WASH services for IDPs and Host Communities in Sudan.
project_objective: The armed clashes between SAF and RSF which occurred on 15 April 2023, in different locations across Sudan, significantly affected the physical safety and security of civilians in the sites where armed conflict erupted including Khartoum state. As a result, many people have been internally displaced to different locations seeking safety and security. Sudan’s health system was under extreme stress prior to the clashed and has been further stretched due to  lack of fuel, electrical outages, insecurity, movement restrictions, looting and closure of drug shop and hospitals, inflations,  lack of access to money which in turn effected on access of patients to a functional health centers within two hours of their home and the situation is getting worse, as many clinics are closing due to lack of medicine of human capacity. This project aims to enhance the life-threatening conditions of the internally displaced population by providing high-quality life-saving humanitarian services to the internally targeted population in therein high-risk states with fifty-four locations through a comprehensive strategy that integrates the sectors of health, nutrition, WASH and that guarantee a decent life for the target groups. This project will continue in the states where highly effected by new war Khartoum WD in addition to the Department of Public Health has intervened in cooperation and coordination with other partners over the previous years. It includes the states mentioned below: West Kordofan, South Kordofan, South Darfur and North Darfur. Kassala (, the White Nile and Abyei. Despite efforts to shelter the IDPs, some health conditions, hygiene, water and environmental sanitation need intervention to reduce diseases related to the respiratory and urinary tract, diarrhea and others, in addition to the importance of nutrition support, Kidney Solutions, mental and reproductive health. Health interventions include providing a package of PHC- SHC, reproductive health (RH) and maternal and child health by supporting health facilities in the targeted states with the necessary and emergency medical supplies and equipment. Interventions will also focus on provide the trauma package in increasing health capacity, health referral support and community health support through the mobile clinic and provide the necessary kidney solution and other necessary medicine. Nutritional interventions include the provision of preventive package and CMAM services to all targeted population groups focusing on sensitive groups (pregnant and lactating women and children) and treatment of severe acute malnutrition, with or without complications for children under five years of age, moderate acute malnutrition of newborns5 and pregnant and lactating women. The project further aims to improve the public health and environmental health of the target communities through the provision of WASH services through hygiene promotion, construction/rehabilitation of community and institutional latrines (in target health facilities, OTPs, SCs, and schools). In addition to improving the target population's access to safe drinking water to reduce the risk of infection. To reach the estimated targets and planned response scale up, GAH will integrated multi-sectoral health sector, WASH by delivery nutrition and WASH services through existing health facilities. and integrated the outreach teams. and use of simplified protocol and explore rapid response mechanisms for timely delivery of nutrition responses in onset emergencies. all activities in health nutrition and Wash are in service activities with response modalities of in kind represent in supplementary, drug and tools that provide from UN agencies (UNICEF, UNFPA, WFP, UNHCR, WHO etc.) the project target 33932 child and 1500 PLWs at nutrition sector in  and (105459 F-73,285M) at WASH sector and (94193.5 F-65,457M) at Health sector. the nutrition activity and  WASH are live saving activity

project_name: provision of emergency lifesaving and resilience WASH, ES/NFI, Education FSL and child protection integrated services for IDPS, returnees and venerable host community of Sudan in CD, WD, BN, Aj Jazirah, Khartoum and SK state.
project_objective:
Starting on 15 April 2023, fighting between the SAF and the RSF, the number of people in need (PiN) of humanitarian assistance has increased from 15.8 million, estimated in November 2022, to 24.7 million in May 2023, representing a 57 per cent increase. 
The primary objective of this project is to safe live through supporting the newly displaced individuals who are the most vulnerable and marginalized people at risk through multi-sectoral lifesaving intervention. This project will prioritize activities that ensure life-saving assistance and protection to people affected by recent crisis primely and also people at risk of epidemics and floods, and other vulnerable residents - in order to reduce mortality and morbidity in the targeted areas. The proposed action will address 350000 (IDPs-175000(F-85750, M-89250), Returnees- 105,000(F-51450, M-53550), Vulnerable community-70,000(F-34300, M-35700)) crisis affected peoples. The WASH component will respond to the most urgent needs through Operationalization of water treatment plants in Khartoum, Water trucking in areas where supply is disrupted including health facilities and the establishment of distribution points, including in gathering and transit points; Essential WASH supplies and NFI emergency sanitation and handwashing facilities will be provided in hotspot locations; Hygiene promotion and household water treatment practices will be promoted as an immediate alternative, especially for those reliant on surface/river water. Following the immediate lifesaving response (stabilization and restoration), Rehabilitate, operate and maintain water supply schemes, replenish supplies and strengthen technical and management capacity for sustained service delivery will continue. This component will be complemented by Education, Child Protection FSL and ES/NFI activities: it will include provision of NFI kits, establishment of rapid-response communal shelters, distribution of tents for swift deployment in mass displacement scenarios. Additionally, upon local market and banking functionality, cash assistance for rent, emergency shelter construction, shelter repair, distribution of Emergency Shelter Kits (ESKs) will be included based on local market availability; Identify acutely vulnerable boys and girls via using outreach methodologies, provided with specialized child protection response services, identification of specific sources of threat and/or vulnerabilities of children, provided with gender & age appropriate (structured) psychosocial support and life skill, and communities are mobilized to support children through activation of child protection networks and community volunteers. 
The FSL project will focus on Cash/Vouchers Based Transfer (Full Ration), Cash/Vouchers Based Transfer (Half Ration) related to food activity while the livelihood part will support on agricultural Support (Seeds, Tools), livestock Support (Distribution, Treatments, Kits), and livelihood Cash/Voucher Support. The Education project will supporting the most vulnerable and marginalized girls and boys at risk of exclusion from education.  TGH will also strategically responding in the hotspot zones (conflict zone – Khartoum, Darfur) through local NGO and CBOs who have strong partnership with TGH, including AORD, & AL Massar. The education response programme aims to prioritize immediate critical life-saving education needs. The response will include awareness session to children age between 5 to 18 years, provision of life skills in emergency training to teachers, ALP Facilitators and PTAs, distribution of Education in Emergency supplies to both schools and safe learning spaces, support for the facilitators in the learning centers, providing psychosocial support through counselling and support to equip children with the skills they need to cope with trauma. By focusing on the same area where the education sector is being targeted, the WASH and child protection response will be delivered and integrated with it.

project_name: Multisectoral lifesaving assistance to newly affected population by conflict in West Darfur, Al Jazeera, Gedaref, Khartoum and Red Sea
project_objective:
SI is proposing to provide multisectoral life-saving assistance (WASH, shelter/NFI and
food) to IDPs and vulenrable host communities.
Firstly, life-saving WASH assistance will be provided to newly displaced people and
affected host-community through emergency water trucking, installation of water
treatment plants and distribution systems and repair of damaged water points to ensure
access to safe water, construction or rehabilitation of emergency/semi-permanent latrines
to mitigate the risk of epidemic outbreak and distribution of hygiene kits coupled with
emergency hygiene promotion.
Access to dignified shelter will then be ensured through the distribution of emergency
shelter kits in areas where local communities cannot host displaced people. Affected
people will also receive NFI kits with basic items such as buckets, mosquito nets, cooking
sets.
Finally, affected populations will receive cash transfers to cover their basic needs. Cash
can be used for vulnerable households to cover their basic needs in places where the
markets are functional. At this point it is expected that most of the MPCA will be used on
food items. In places where the markets are not yet functional the in-kind approach will be
implemented in order to support households in accessing basic food commodities.
The intervention will also look at establishing partnerships with civil society organization
and local NGOs to enhance response capacity based on their areas of expertise and
geographical locations positioning to support affected population.

project_name: Multisector Intervention for South Sudanese Refugees
project_objective: NCA proposes an multisecter intervention for the south sudanese refugees in belail camp in south darfur, the intervention will include, protection, health and nutrition and WASH.

project_name: Multi-Sectoral Assistance to IDPs & Conflict-Affected Communities in South Darfur, central Darfur, North Kordofan, South Kordofan, Gedaref, Khartoum, Kassala, Blue Nile, White Nile and Red Sea States of Sudan
project_objective:
Clashes between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) that erupted on 15 April 2023 are having devastating consequences for people across Sudan. Life-saving responses related to WASH, Food Security, nutrition and agriculture are urgently needed for conflict affected populations. Mercy Corps response plans aims to provide humanitarian assistance to new IDPs and CAPs people during the first 6 month of the crisis.

Goal:
“To provide humanitarian assistance to conflict affected people in Sudan to meet immediate needs for survival and work towards recovery”:

Objectives:
1. Save and protect lives
2. Improve capacity to withstand further shocks (e.g. flooding)
3. Prevent backsliding for vulnerable communities indirectly affected by the conflict

project_name: Basic Package of life-saving health care services to vulnerable Communities in Gedaref, Khartoum, South Kordofan, Blue Nile, White Nile, and Jezira states
project_objective:
The project aims to improve access to life-saving preventive and curative health services in Jezira, White Nile, Gedaref, Khartoum, South Kordofan and Blue Nile states in Sudan. This project will address the priority health needs of target communities leading to reduction in excess morbidity and mortality. The main beneficiaries are persons affected by recent crisis caused by armed conflicts between the Sudan Armed Forces (SAF) and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) including internally displaced communities (IDPs), and vulnerable host communities targeting children under five years of age, adolescent girls, women, boys and men. The project will hotspot areas affected by the current crisis as well as IDP receiving states and will support existing Ministry of Health (MoH) capacity to deliver lifesaving primary health care services, including management of communicable and non-communicable diseases, support reproductive; maternal and child health services including strengthening of expanded program for immunization; mental health and psychosocial support. The IRC will build the capacity of MoH staff, provide essential drugs and medical supplies, including COVID-19 personal protective equipment (PPE), as well as infrastructure improvement and surge teams in the form of mobile medical teams (MMTs) to quickly respond to health emergencies. This is well aligned with the IRC’ Sudan Response Strategy.
Protection services will also be integrated into the IRC’s health programming to achieve greater outcomes for women and girls, including prevention and response to Gender Based Violence (GBV). Through a community-based approach, the project will ensure equity by supporting community health volunteers to provide community health packages to hard to reach and underserved communities. The IRC WASH teams will closely support the HF teams to improve facility WASH infrastructures and practices including medical and non-medical waste management, hand washing stations and hygiene promotion. 
The IRC has strong capacity to deliver health services in Sudan with current support including strengthening the MoH capacity to delivery integrated health services in Gedaref, Khartoum, Jazira and Blue Nile states, and currently expanding to White Nile state. Since 2019, the IRC has supported the delivery of integrated health, nutrition, protection, livelihoods and WASH services providing a one stop center to deliver life-saving interventions to beneficiaries in a safe way. The IRC health technical excellence unit at the headquarter in NY with regional representation in Nairobi provides technical oversight and guidance for adaptation of quality health standards, training and technical supervision including frequent field presence to support country teams. Even in the face of current crisis, the IRC has maintained in country capacity and regional support to continue to deliver essential health services.

project_name: Improve access to quality, sustainable and integrated life-saving health services for IDPs, returnees, and host communities in North Darfur, South Darfur, North Kordofan, South Kordofan, West Kordofan, Kassala, Red Sea, Sinnar, Gedaref and Khartoum States.
project_objective: Kuwaiti Patients Helping Fund (KPHF) proposes to implement integrated and life-saving health interventions to assist vulnerable population affected by displacement, conflict, natural emergencies, malnutrition and disease outbreaks by supporting 156 PHCCs distributed as follows: 32 PHCs in South Darfur State, 17 PHCs in North Darfur State, 10 PHCs in South Kordofan State,  10 PHCs in North Kordofan State, 10 PHCs in West Kordofan State, 25 PHCs in Kassala State, 16 PHCs in Red Sea State, 15 PHCs in Gedaref State, 15 PHCs in Sennar State and 6 PHCs in Khartoum State. The proposed programming will support 998,000 direct beneficiaries including men (298,000), women (400,000), boys (150,000) and girls (150,000), comprising of IDPs, returnees, resident and host communities as well as 350,000 indirect beneficiaries. The project aims are to provide integrated primary health care services, contribute to Strengthen Health Sector capacity to prepare and deliver timely response to populations affected by conflict, natural emergencies, and disease outbreaks as well as strengthen health system capacity to support continuity of care, reinforce community resilience, and enhance risk mitigation measures. This project will be implemented for period of one year. According to SMoH gap analysis reports (health Map), HNO 2021 and HeRAM the current situation in South Darfur , North Darfur, Kassala, Red See, Gedaref, North, South and West Kordofan and Sennar States is very bad due to low coverage of health and nutrition services, food shortage, and malnutrition, lack of clean water, poor hygiene & sanitation as well as epidemic disease. In addition to, covid-19 pandemic also affected on decreasing the uptake of primary health care and disrupted health care services Delivery State. The situation requires urgent intervention to fill this gap. KPHF will intervention through provision of integrated and comprehensive PHCs services packages which include these activities: Provide outpatient consultation, free essential drugs, EPI, disease surveillance focus on covid-19 and other epidemiological diseases, reproductive health services (including ANC, PNC, FP, vaccination against Tetanus and delivery care) and IMCI services. In addition to, provision of basic laboratory investigation, treatment of different injuries and wounds, support referrals of patients to the next level of health care as well as intensive health promotion at clinics and communities level. Response to covid-19 through different activities, which include provide PPE to health cadres, referral of suspected cases, regular disinfection and intensive health education against the pandemic in order to suppress transmission of disease. KPHF will provide support Ministry of Health in epidemic disease surveillance, outbreak response and immunization campaigns. During this proposed project, KPHF will conduct minor rehabilitation on targeted clinics to ensure quality, patient safety, infection prevention and continuity of services. KPHF also intends to continue to provide short-term and on the job training to health facility staff which focus on IMCI , EMoC , IPCs ,family planning ,COVID-19 protocol and other important topic for project staff.

project_name: Improve access to quality, sustainable and integrated life-saving Nutrition services for IDPs, returnees, and host communities in North Darfur, South Darfur, North Kordofan, South Kordofan, West Kordofan, Kassala, Red Sea, Sinnar, Gedaref and Khartoum States.
project_objective: Kuwaiti patients Helping Fund (KPHF) proposes to assist vulnerable population affected by conflict, displaced and malnutrition by supporting 128 OTPs and TSFPs integrated including FBMAM & HF and 3 SCs in the following States: North & South Darfur, North, South and West Kordofan,  Kassala, Red See, Gedaref, Sennar, Gezera, River Nile and Khartoum States. The project is proposed to treat 20,000 children <5 of age from SAM cases at OTPs and 4,000 children <5 of age from SAM with medical complications at SC. In addition, the project will treat 20,000 children <5 of age and 10,000 PLW from MAM cases. Moreover the project will prevent 20,000 children aged from 6-23 months and 10,000 Pregnant and lactating women from MAM by FBMAM. Beside that the project will fortify 15,000 children 6-59 of age who are not acutely malnourished through Home Fortification (HF) intervention service. Finally, the project will provide 90,000 caregiver with IYCF counselling. KPHF will provide health services through SCs and nutrition services through OTPs and TSFPs. Nutrition services to cover SAM and MAM cases for U5 and PLW which include screening at admission, medical treatment of severely acutely malnourished (SAM) children with and without medical complication, dietary management and individual child follow up, among others. It will also cover the administrative (support) cost of case management of moderate acute malnourished (MAM) girls and boys of 6-59 months and pregnant and lactating women (PLW). Furthermore, nutrition education and counseling will be provided for mothers/caregivers in Infant and Young Child feeding (IYCF) practices and hygiene promotion as well as MSGs will built to facilitate of nutrition education and contribution in MUAC screening activities. Selected trainings will be provided on SC case management, CMAM, NiE, identification of medical complications at OTPs and TSFPs level, community screening and follow up. In addition to, women club, women cornea and community awareness session campaigns will be conducted under nutrition program.

project_name: Protection of Rohingya Refugees in Bangladesh and Strengthening of Community Self-Reliance and Cohesion
project_objective:
UNHCR delivers comprehensive protection services throughout Cox’s Bazar and ensures the centrality of protection through protection and gender mainstreaming, inclusive coordination and leadership of the humanitarian response. In 2023, UNHCR will continue to work with the GoB to secure identity and documentation for Rohingya refugees through continuous registration, which will serve as the keystone for protection interventions, assistance delivery and solutions planning. UNHCR will also strengthen its community-based protection approach, which provides the foundation for age, gender and diversity responsive services. UNHCR’s response will deliver integrated protection services including registration and documentation, legal protection, and community-based protection.
UNHCR will conduct protection monitoring in all 33 camps to identify protection incidents/trends to support advocacy and address protection gaps, and identify refugees facing urgent and serious protection concerns, and facilitate multisectoral referrals. UNHCR, in coordination with Government and UN partners, will also promote community safety inititiatives to improve the security environment in the camps, involving refugees and the host community, addressing the broader challenges that undermine protection space while promoting peaceful coexistence and social cohesion. UNHCR will strengthen access to justice through capacity building of law enforcement/justice sector actors, strengthening of legal assistance activities (through its partners) in all 33 camps, including outreach and legal awareness to eliminate barriers for all persons of different ages, genders and specific needs,  legal counselling, legal assistance/representation, and mediation support. 
UNHCR will empower Rohingya refugees by building community capacities for leadership, self-management and engagement with the government and the humanitarian community in 33 camps, including through the elected refugee representatives in four camps. UNHCR will support refugee volunteer networks such as Community Outreach Members (COMs), community groups, and religious networks (including imams and female religious teachers). COMs will identify and support persons with specific needs, and will mobilise communities for protection. Male and female community groups will be supported to deliver community initiatives that foster social change. Communication with communities will be mainstreamed. Community and information centres will also act as essential hubs to disseminate timely, accurate and life-saving information. UNHCR will strengthen disability inclusion in all its protection interventions as well as provide targeted services for persons with disabilities.
Within the current government policy framework, UNHCR will advocate for greater access to age, gender and diversity responsive education and economic inclusion, so that young refugees retain hope and become agents for positive change in the community. UNHCR’s solutions strategy takes into account the government’s policy that voluntary repatriation is the only feasible solution for Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh, and promotes the conditions needed for voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable return in Myanmar, while recognising large scale returns are not likely to take place in 2023. UNHCR will work to improve protection conditions and quality of life for refugees in Bangladesh pending solutions, building upon the framework for responsibility sharing provided by the GCR. Reinforcing accountable government leadership of the response will build a foundation for the inclusion of refugees in the national systems in the future, and UNHCR will continue to support capacity development of both government and humanitarian actors across the operation.

project_name: Improving Skills and Economic Opportunities for the Bangladeshi Community and Rohingya Women Youths in Cox’s Bazar
project_objective:
The project aims to assist refugees in acquiring transferable, and portable skills relevant to the labour market needs in Myanmar and the camp contexts, which would support sustainable return and integration (in Myanmar) when conditions permit; while enabling refugees to maintain hope for the future and have dignified and productive lives in the camps, including through engagement in multi-sectorial camp-based activities, minor livelihood activities, and community works, with the utilisation of acquired competencies. Accordingly, strategies will be geared towards enhancing skills development, economic and social empowerment, and self-reliance of the Rohingya refugees, pending durable solutions. The other initiative will enhance the engagement of refugee women in productive activities inside the camps. These women will produce female hygiene materials for camp consumption. This will be achieved by strengthening the quality of final products, including through improving production processes and upgrading current production centres. The project has a component to create opportunities for the host community women. 
The project will develop occupation-based skills with standard curricula recognisable across the world for 8,000 refugee youths (18-24). Another 1,000 will get non-standardised skills training to enhance their existing skills. The project will also develop 10 standard training curricula packages to implement in the camps. 
The project will create production-based daily wage employment opportunities for 3,000 refugees, 2,000 in different sectors as a volunteer, and 2000 refugee youths will be supported in self-employment. 500 women from the host community will get a chance to earn money by doing artisanal products.

project_name: Enhancing access to comprehensive quality health care services for Rohingya refugees and surrounding host communities in Cox's Bazar District
project_objective:
The project will provide primary and secondary healthcare services to refugees and surrounding host communities in Cox’s Bazar, based on the “Minimum Package of Essential Health Services for Primary Healthcare Facilities in Refugee/FDMN camps, Cox’s Bazar” and the “Standard Operating Procedure for Patient Referrals to Secondary and Tertiary Healthcare Facilities for Refugees/FDMNs, Cox’s Bazar”. The project will be aligned to the Cox’s Bazar Health Sector Strategic plan 2022-2024. 
Services will be delivered through 10 primary healthcare centers (PHC), 5 health posts; 5 drop-in centers for key and gender diverse populations; 1 physiotherapy center and 1 specialized hospital in Ukhiya. The project will include 3 mental health in-patient centers for short term stabilization of clinical mental health cases, two within PHCs in the camps, and one in Ukhiya specialized hospital.
The health facilities will be accessible by older persons and persons with disabilities (PWDs) and accompanied referrals from households supported. Services will be tailored to the needs of PWDs including availability of appropriate equipment. Mental health and psychosocial support services (MHPSS) will be provided integrated into primary healthcare facilities and at community level, with new modalities of Integrated Adaptive Therapy applied. The use of trained refugee community para counselors will bring care closer to the community. Integration of MHPSS with nutrition, WASH, protection, GBV and other sectors will be strengthened.
The project will cater for referral costs and ambulances for its partners, and referral costs for emergency cases in half the camps.
A robust community health system will ensure health promotion, disease surveillance, early identification and response to health hazards e.g., diseases of epidemic potential; and contribute to community resilience. Through coordination of the community health working group, harmonized community-based health interventions by partners in the response will be ensured; and capacity building of CHWs, IEC materials and toolkits for CHWs provided. To support case management of outbreak prone diseases, the project will assure 2 infectious disease treatment centers (IDTCs) in the camp and at Ukhiya specialized hospital, transitioned from the Isolation and Treatment Centers for COVID19.  The IDTCs will be used as health facilities and activated as per need, enabling immediate response as the minimum human resource and equipment will be available. Stockpiling of medicines and medical supplies & support to emergency medical teams will be ensured.
The project will engage refugees in service delivery, through monthly facility-based health forums where the community gives feedback to providers. Camp health focal points will coordinate with various actors at camp level and monitor health services in the camps and health facilities using existing UNHCR and Health Sector monitoring tools.
Monitoring of performance through age and gender disaggregated data collection and analysis systems e.g., the community-based health information system, UNHCR integrated refugee health information system (irHIS), compliance with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare’s (MOHFW) District Health Information Systems -2 and the Health sector’s 4Ws, Early Warning Alert and Response System etc. will be undertaken, and data used to generate evidence to guide interventions.
The project will coordinate with the health sector and all associated working groups including the Sexual and Reproductive Health W, Epidemiology WG, MHPSS WG and Emergency Preparedness and Response committee.
Integration of services with other sectors will continue, aiming at partners implementing integrated health and nutrition services by the end of 2025. Integration will be fostered with WASH, protection, GBV sectors/sub-sectors.
The MOHFW will gradually take over services in the specialized hospital in Ukhiya, assuming full responsibility at the end of 2024.

project_name: Improving Access to WASH Facilities and Services to Rohignya Refugees and Host Community
project_objective:
The project is designed to contribute to a reduction in WASH-related public health risks through improved access for 366,693 people living in 14 UNHCR managed camps and 76,835 affected host communities. 
The WASH response will be based on three sector strategic objectives to; 1) Ensure regular, sufficient, and equitable access to safe water for drinking and domestic needs, 2) Ensure adequate and appropriate sanitation facilities allowing safe management and disposal of excreta and solid waste and 3) Ensure the change of potentially health-compromising behaviours through participatory hygiene promotion and distribution of hygiene items, with particular focus on contagious diseases

In 2023, UNHCR and partners will ensure continuity of essential WASH services through a combination of service provision activities involving the operation and maintenance of existing 54 water supply networks and the development of a large-scale, unified urban-based water systems.  
In addition, UNHCR will continue to support the operation and maintenance of sanitation facilities develop urban scale sustainable sanitation infrastructure. UNHCR will seek approval for integrated household latrines and bathing areas to be adopted as the standard in all new transitional shelter designs covering 3,500 households. Shared household latrine coverage and bathing area, especially for women and children, will be increased and improve coverage rates to UNHCR standards. Faecal sludge treatment capacity will be increased with a mix of large off-site units and increased use of small-bore sewerage and appropriate cost-effective on-site disposal. UNHCR will ensure more effective solid waste management systems and infrastructure and further enhance hygiene promotion activities with community engagement and reduce partner support in favour of refugee ownership.

A particular focus will be given to emergency preparedness and response to disease outbreaks (Acute Watery Diarrhea/Cholera) as well as climate induced disasters such as monsoon and cyclone. UNHCR and partners will explore innovative approaches for community mobilization and engagement for hygiene behaviours.  Other priority interventions will include water quality monitoring, provision of adequate WASH services in learning centers, health and nutrition facilities, child friendly spaces and other public spaces within the camps. In addition, UNHCR will advocate for more durable solutions to be considered and funded for the refugees and hosting communities. In all cases, WASH response will consider gender, environmental, age and disability inclusion and will ensure equal access for persons with special needs

project_name: Population has optimal access to quality education
project_objective: UNHCR will strive to ensure that Rohingya refugee children aged 3 to 24 years have access to equitable quality education opportunities through the continuation of existing programs. This will involve maintaining existing learning facilities, recruiting, training and deploying teachers as well as procuring teaching and learning materials, expanding learning facilities by constructing and maintaining existing classrooms with gender segregated latrines and WASH facilities. Considering the impacts of school closures during COVID-19 on learning, UNHCR and its partners will implement Accelerated Education programs and a range of EdTech interventions to tackle gaps in learning and to support language acquisition needed to access the newly scaled up Myanmar Curriculum (MC).  The continued scale up of the MC, Accelerated Learning and the transition of Learning Competencies Framework and Approach (LCFA) level III students into the MC will be a critical undertaking for 2023. To ensure the provision of quality education, Myanmar language training and continuous Teacher Professional Development will be provided to ensure educators have the required language competencies and expected teaching skills to deliver inclusive quality education. In addition, a two-month basic pedagogy training will be provided to  teachers’ along with refresher training of the on-going mentorship program. The continuation of regular training on cross-cutting issues {such as child protection, gender and disability inclusion, prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA) and mental health, psychosocial support (MHPSS) and gender responsive pedagogy} will also be provided. The project will recruit Rohingya women, trained and deployed to ensure gender parity and also focused on disability inclusion through identifying CWD, ensuring accessibility to the learning facilities, and providing individual support for those most vulnerable. In addition to mainstream education for 41,246 learners, UNHCR will also continue to provide interventions for 9,901 pre-primary children aged 3-4 years with early childhood development (ECD) sessions aligning with the ECD working group standards and guidance. In addition, UNHCR will continue with adolescent clubs, scaling up to reach 20,743 adolescents and youth, whereby basic literacy, numeracy and prevocational activities will be provided. In close collaboration with the livelihood sector, UNHCR will provide upskilling and bridging interventions for 620 adolescents and youth including gender diverse people looking to enhance their problem solving, computer literacy and academic skills. UNHCR will continue ensuring community engagement in the overall project cycle through regular community consultations, monthly parent meetings and Community Education Support Groups (CESG) whilst maintaining Age Gender and Diversity (AGD) principles. It will enhance school community governance and participation mechanisms by including the community in risk reduction activities as well as integrating school community-based participatory planning and conducting community awareness on key areas as they emerge. It will continue its host community support targeting 3,000 students through maintaining and operationalizing of the community technology Access and the satellite teachers training facility, constructing, or renovating classrooms and WASH facilities and provide classroom furniture and supplies.  To engage with the refugee led education activities within the camp such as madrassa education and private schools, it will seek to include refugee teachers from these groups into training opportunities to building a more cohesive relationships between different education provisions existing within the camps. To ensure social cohesion and peacebuilding the project will observe different days such as 16 days activities, literacy days, refugee days and organize annual cultural events and sport competition.

project_name: CCCM Assistance to conflict and disaster-induced displaced persons in South Sudan
project_objective:
According to Round 12 of IOM DTM’s monitoring of displacement and return movement, 2,229,657 people remain displaced in South Sudan, 78% of which are sheltering with already crisis-affected host communities. In a number of displacement sites and collective centers, including current and former PoCs, more than 440,000 individuals continue to live in situations of protracted displacement. Displacement figures have continued to increase despite the signing of the R-ARCSS in 2018 due to an increase of displacement-inducing incidents such as sub-national conflict and unprecedented climate-related disasters.

IOM CCCM aims to target 612,000 people of the total 1.4 million people targeted under the CCCM Cluster Response Plan. IOM will continue to provide displaced communities with basic and emergency camp management services, ensuring that the provision of protection and cross-sectoral humanitarian assistance is equitable, coordinated, monitored and adhering to standards. Of critical relevance to the current displacement environment in the country, IOM CCCM’s interventions will also integrate a robust, community-led disaster-mitigation lens in all care & maintenance interventions and capacity building exercises to enhance protective environments to increase resilience of infrastructure and communities to climate shocks. Further, fully committed to ensuring that AAP is streamlined in any and all activities, IOM will continue to develop and improve AAP mechanisms to ensure that the organization is accountable to the people that it serves and that programmes are informed by the voices of the displaced communities.

IOM intends to contribute to the sectoral objectives through the following interventions:

1)	Continued and adapted provision of critical CCCM activities to IDPs living in Bentiu, Naivasha and Hai Masna IDP Sites as well as critical care & maintenance activities in Malakal PoC.
2)	Deployment of emergency CCCM teams to deliver sustainable mobile responses promoting self-governance, community ownership and resilience in hard-to-reach locations following triggers at the ICCG-level.
3)	Co-lead the CCCM Cluster at national level and continue acting as SFP in WBeG, Jonglei and Upper Nile States in order to support national and state-level partner agencies in accountable CCCM responses and systems.
4)	Continue chairing the CCEWG in order to provide technical CCE support to partner organizations and to operationalize outputs under the 2021 South Sudan AAP Framework.

project_name: Targeted support to persons with specific needs with lifesaving non-food items and emergency shelter to displaced population in hard-to-reach areas and IDP returnee families.
project_objective:
In 2023, Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) continue to face multi-faceted crises which are worsened by conflict and protracted displacement from locations of their habitual residence that is further compounded by flooding. Displaced families often have inadequate shelter and household goods which expose them to heightened protection risks. Increased mobility, continued insecurity and protracted displacement has over the years eroded household coping mechanisms and livelihood options especially considering the poor nature of local markets without stocks for household goods and shelter materials.

UNHCR’s project will focus on responding to the humanitarian needs of IDPs and IDP and refugee returnees with targeted and protection focused core relief items (emergency shelter and non-food items – S/NFIs) prioritizing the most vulnerable households and persons with specific needs especially women and girls.

The project will contribute to the following sectoral objectives:

SO 1 – percentage of the targeted population that is able to access shelter material and non-food items in situations of emergency and transition.
The project will identify the most vulnerable IDPs and returnees through protection monitoring and assessments including through IRNAs and RRMs. The assessments and inter cluster discussions will inform the decisions regarding the specific response modalities between in kind and cash assistance. Unique contextual factors including market conditions will be considered.

SO 2 - Enhance community dignity and engagement in the provision of S/NFI services. The project will deliver timely lifesaving activities while streamlining protection-oriented initiatives including COVID – 19 preventive measures. The project will strengthen community-based protection through the involvement of community-based structures for self-management in response delivery, ensuring that their capacities to cope, recover, contribute to and achieve solutions are enhanced.

SO 3 - Community members’ exposure to environmental hazards is reduced through the construction of disaster-resistant structures.

In 2023, UNHCR will increase its active participation in humanitarian coordination forums, including the ES/NFI cluster, both at national level and in the field, strongly advocating for protection mainstreaming and joint vulnerability assessments, the results of which will be very useful in the optimization of the limited resources. UNHCR will endeavor to provide timely response to the most critical identified needs of vulnerable IDPs and returnees, among other affected populations. Protection risks remain high among women, girls, boys and persons with specific protection needs which may include transitional shelters and other material assistance.

project_name: CCCM services to assist affected populations through static, mobile, and area-based responses in Jonglei, Unity, Upper Nile, Warrap, Western Bahr el Ghazal, Northern Bahr el Ghazal, Western Equatoria and Central Equatoria States.
project_objective:
Targeting 120,000 people in need living in IDP camps, settlements, collective sites and the increasing numbers living in urban areas, this project will focus on the provision of timely, well-coordinated, and integrated Camp Management services. With the aim of improving the well-being of displaced populations, strengthening their resilience and increasing their participation in decision-making processes, in Jonglei, Unity, Upper Nile, Warrap, Western Bahr el Ghazal, Northern Bahr el Ghazal, Western Equatoria and Central Equatoria, all states where UNHCR currently has a static presence through its field office operations, 
UNHCR and partners will put in place mechanisms to strengthen camp coordination and monitoring to enable the effective provision of cross-sectoral services. IDPs’ engagement in the delivery of services in an equal and needs-based manner will be possible through regular feedback and dissemination of information for example through community-based networks. In support of humanitarian interventions aimed at improving the well-being of displaced populations whilst providing some level of dignity and equitability by promoting AAP.
A key component of the project will be to support community-based structures to enhance participation in planning and decision-making, in particular seeking empowerment of communities. This will be done with a focus on vulnerable groups, PSNs and PWDs so that their views are received, and acknowledged and service delivery meets the specific needs of all groups. To this end, protection will be mainstreamed into all CCCM activities to respect and promote the rights of the most vulnerable. Site care and maintenance improvement projects will take place to minimize protection risks and determine the level of assistance required by PSNs.

Supporting the ability of vulnerable IDPs to recover from the external stresses they face, be it floods or conflict, this project will seek to promote capacity building and development of community self-management structures and practices. UNHCR and its partners will also ensure that communication channels with the concerned population are strengthened, diversified, and anchored on the views of the community. This will serve to facilitate timely and accurate information to respond to disasters and mitigate identified risks. CCCM will focus on capacity building, multi-sectoral assessments on a number of displaced persons affected by the flood, and conflict resolution services through CCCM monitoring, coordination meetings at the site level, care and maintenance activities conducted by the safety committee through cash for work initiatives and enhancing feedback and complaint mechanisms.
Finally, as CCCM Cluster Co-lead UNHCR will continue to strengthen and support CCCM partners through strategic guidance, advocacy with donors, and vitally step in as a provider of last resort in areas if partners have a low presence and limited capacity to respond.

project_name: Renforcement de la préparation, de l'alerte et de la réponse en cas de chocs multirisques dans les zones fragiles afin d’assurer une réponse locale la plus rapide possible, au Niger
project_objective: COOPI a prevu une intervention, en consortium avec MC, DP multirisques de, dans 4 communes des departements de Mandourfa, Ayouru et Ouallam, avec un focus spécifique sur la protection, en renforcent les capacités des réponses immédiates des communes pour l’accueil des déplacés, en appuyant aussi la population locale, de façon organisée. L’action prévoie: a)renforcement des capacités de réponse locale immédiate face aux chocs multirisques; b)transfert de compétences techniques et moyens logistiques aux communes; c)appui aux services de base locaux, visant le nexus urgence-développement. Cette intervention a une approche intercommunale, vu que les risques n’ont pas des limites administratives, et que les actions de préparation/réponse doivent être réalisées en coordination/collaboration entre les communes voisines. La redevabilité et le nexus humanitaire–développement seront au coeur aussi de l’intervention : le renforcement de la capacité d’absorption des services de base pour alléger les pressions, et l’accompagnement de la coexistence, en parallèle d’une réponse multisectorielle urgente. Ce projet vise aussi le renforcement de la décentralisation a niveau des communes et profite de l'expérience de COOPI et de Mercy Corps en DRR, leur statut d’organisations de nexus urgence/développement et leur présence de longue date dans ces communes

project_name: Respuesta humanitaria y atención a población en situación de movilidad, tránsito y desplazamiento en contextos de emergencias por desastres en Honduras
project_objective:
Desde 2022, el flujo de personas migrantes en condición irregular y en situación de movilidad que ingresan en Honduras ha incrementado significativamente. Según estadísticas del Instituto Nacional de Migración (INM), entre el 1 enero y el 11 de noviembre del año 2022, han ingresado un total 148.705 personas migrantes, una de las cifras más alta en los últimos años. Esta cifra es ocho veces mayor a la registrada durante el mismo periodo en el año 2021. Adicionalmente, durante la época lluviosa del año 2022 y con el paso de la tormenta tropical Julia y las secuelas dejadas por ésta que solo vienen a evidenciar la fragilidad y vulnerabilidad del país,  se reportaron daños severos en 820 comunidades de 162 municipios de los 298 existentes en el país, con un aproximado de: más de 188.000 personas afectadas, 22 Personas fallecidas, 835 viviendas dañadas o destruidas, 73 centros educativos dañados, 80 sistemas de agua dañados, 100 mil hectáreas de cultivo dañadas, según datos  extraídos del informe de la Oficina de Coordinación de Asuntos Humanitarios (OCHA), en colaboración con las agencias, fondos y programas del Sistema de las Naciones Unidas. 
En este sentido, este proyecto contribuirá a fortalecer los esfuerzos de implementación de las organizaciones que componen el Clúster de Coordinación y Gestión de Albergues (CCCM por sus siglas en inglés), clúster de la arquitectura humanitaria de país coliderado por la OIM, brindando asistencia técnica al Gobierno de Honduras, promoviendo la transferencia de conocimientos e instalación de capacidades a nivel central y local en materia de albergues. Asegurando de esta forma que la población de interés tenga acceso a servicios básicos, asistencia humanitaria, protección y la integración de los enfoques de género, edad, inclusión digna., y la responsabilidad con la respuesta mínima a las sobrevivientes de VBG. 
También desde el proyecto, en coordinación con la Secretaría de Estado en los Despachos de Gestión de Riesgos y Contingencias Nacionales de Honduras (COPECO), Comité de Emergencia Municipal (CODEM), Comité de Emergencia Local (CODEL) y lideres comunitarios se realizarán readecuaciones y mejoras de infraestructuras en espacios definidos como albergues para asegurar estándares mínimos, proveer condiciones dignas de vida de la población desplazada  por desastres, utilizando la guía para instalación de albergues con enfoque de género, garantizando así las normas mínimas a protección, género e inclusión en situaciones de emergencia para mujeres, niños, niñas, adultos mayores, y personas con discapacidad. project_name: Providing Comprehensive Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene Assistance to Crisis-Affected Populations in Sudan
project_objective:
This project will mitigate the suffering of populations affected by man-made crises or disasters related to natural hazards, and reflect the revised 2023 Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) Cluster Response Plan ensuring that the crisis-affected populations have access to gender and climate change-sensitive basic water services, adequate gender- sensitive sanitation and hygiene services, risk communication and community engagement (RCCE), menstrual hygiene management (MHM), vector control, and waste management. The military conflict which broke out on 15 April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has increased the overall WASH needs to 14.9 million people with the cluster targeting 6.1 million people with the priority to support the newly displaced, people stranded, and families at the gathering points including women, children, elderly, people with disabilities, the sick, and caregivers. As well as people affected by epidemics, natural hazards, and climate change implications (mainly water scarcity and floods).
This project aims to provide humanitarian WASH assistance to 900,000 beneficiaries including 183,600 women, 176,400 men, 275,400 girls, and 264,600 boys with approximately 12 per cent of the target population estimated to be either elderly, people with disabilities, or other vulnerabilities. IOM aims to assist approximately 450,000 internally displaced persons (IDPs) newly displaced by conflict or disasters related to natural hazards with WASH services and improve and sustain access to safe water for approximately 400,000 individuals including returnees and crisis-affected communities. The project will focus on crisis impacted communities in various states primarily in areas where water infrastructure is damaged or available capacity is unable to meet the critical needs stretched by the influx of the displaced. IOM will also support communities to improve hygiene through sustaining access to safe water and sanitation facilities and promoting hygiene messages to address and increase community resilience to malnutrition, disease outbreaks, and other public health related risks targeting approximately 50,000 individuals.
IOM will provide emergency water assistance through the establishment and rehabilitation of water points, access to proper sanitation facilities and hygiene items and campaigns. This will include environmental impact mitigation such as the provision of solar technology to power water points and monitoring ground water to moderate depletion levels. Exit strategies will be developed in more secure states of the country to alleviate aid dependency in protracted emergencies by strengthening self-reliance and facilitating community solutions. The project will ensure dignified and equitable access to basic WASH services through the implementation of early recovery approaches where possible, connecting the need for short-term emergency interventions during the ongoing military conflict with long-term solutions by working directly with local communities to facilitate ownership and accountability. The WASH emergency interventions will gradually contribute to socio-economic inclusion of forcibly displaced populations and returnees by directly increasing access to basic services for the displaced and host communities and indirectly increasing employment opportunities.

project_name: Proteger, responder y empoderar para consolidar un ambiente favorable para la protección de las personas desplazadas, retornadas, en movimientos mixtos, refugiadas y solicitantes de asilo.
project_objective:
Honduras es un país de origen, de tránsito y, en menor medida, de destino de personas refugiadas y migrantes. 

Como país de origen Honduras afronta enormes retos asociados a un contexto caracterizado por la multiplicidad de crisis en el ámbito social, económico, político y ambiental, así como al impacto de la violencia generalizada. La población hondureña se enfrenta a riesgos extraordinarios que se constituyen en causas del desplazamiento forzado, así como a múltiples violaciones a sus derechos que ante las limitaciones de la alternativa de huida interna se configura la necesidad de protección internacional.

Durante el 2021 el país ocupó el sexto lugar de nacionalidades con mayor número de solicitudes de asilo a nivel global. Durante ese año, 59.800 hondureños solicitaron asilo, esto representa un incremento del 13% en comparación con el 2020, año en el que se registraron 52.800 solicitudes. Esta cifra que alerta sobre el mayor número de personas que salen en búsqueda de protección internacional se suma a las cifras oficiales sobre personas de nacionalidad hondureña retornadas. Al respecto, el Instituto Nacional de Migración (INM) reporta que entre el 1 de enero y el 31 de diciembre de 2022, 94.339 personas retornaron al país, muchas de ellas en necesidad de protección, considerando el contexto de violencia y la persistencia de las causas de la huida. 

En cuanto al desplazamiento forzado interno, el estudio más reciente, de ámbito nacional, señala que al menos 247.090 personas (el 2.7% de la población hondureña) se vieron forzadas a desplazarse por la violencia de 2004 a 2018. De ellas el 55% eran mujeres, el 45% hombres y el 43% menores de edad. El país no cuenta con cifras actualizadas sobre la magnitud del impacto del desplazamiento; sin embargo, los diagnósticos comunitarios, así como el monitoreo efectuado de manera permanente por el ACNUR dan cuenta de un aumento del número de personas desplazadas internamente. 

Como país de tránsito, Honduras, por su posición geográfica, recibe los movimientos mixtos que se dirigen hacia el norte del continente americano. De acuerdo con cifras oficiales, del 1 de enero al 31 de diciembre de 2022, 188.858 personas ingresaron al país de manera irregular (el 53% de ellas son hombres, el 27%, el 10% niños y el 9% niñas). Por las dinámicas de estos movimientos, un alto porcentaje de estas personas llegan al país en necesidad de protección, de asistencia y servicios especializados. Por esta misma dinámica y la intención de las personas en tránsito, Honduras no es identificado como un país de destino. 

En este contexto, el Proyecto busca responder de manera integral a los impactos generados por la crisis que enfrenta el país, abordar de manera estructural las causas que generan el desplazamiento forzado interno y los vacíos que persisten en los mecanismos y alternativas para la protección para las personas desplazadas por la violencia y en riesgo de desplazamiento; las personas refugiadas y solicitantes de asilo; las personas retornadas con necesidades de protección cuya reintegración se dificulta en la medida en que presentan niveles de riesgo; así como otras personas de interés, como aquellas que integran los movimientos mixtos y requieren protección internacional y/o protección específica. 

La estrategia, en consecuencia, se concentra en tres áreas de impacto consistentes con los tres objetivos generales definidos por el Clúster de Protección: proteger, responder y fortalecer. Bajo estas tres áreas la intervención se enfocará en promover acciones dirigidas a que las personas desplazadas, quienes integran los movimientos mixtos, las personas refugiadas y solicitantes de asilo y aquellas de nacionalidad hondureña que han sido retornadas: (i) se beneficien de un mecanismo de protección integral; (ii)accedan a las necesidades básicas den un entorno seguro; y (iii) cuenten con las herramientas para mitigar sus riesgos y vulnerabilidades, considerando los impactos diferenciados.

project_name: Enhancing Food Security and Livelihoods and Building Resilience of Vulnerable small-scale farmers, Argo pastoralists and pastoralists in Sudan.
project_objective:
The FAO is planning to target under the revised HRP 2023 project to provide emergency agriculture and livestock-based livelihoods interventions to support vulnerable farmers, agro- pastoral and pastoral people from IDPs, returnees, and vulnerable resident host communities in Sudan. The vulnerability of the target populations stems from the protracted crisis, the ongoing economic hardships at the macro and micro-levels, negative impact of long dry spells and floods and recently the ongoing war. 

This project covers all states in Sudan except Khartoum. Targeting 15,000,000 people among the most vulnerable communities including 8,250,000 vulnerable hosting communities’ people, 5,250,000 IDPs and 1,500,000 returnees. The planned interventions will benefit 4,590,000 women, 3,000,000 girls (less than 18 year of age), 4,410,000 men and 3,000,000 boys (less than 18 year of age). The proposed interventions are based on the basic and specific needs of the beneficiaries taking into account the factors of age and gender. The project will target about 1,500,000 venerable people (elderly, chronically ill and people with different types of disabilities.

The project interventions include as a top priority; supporting food insecure people through life-saving and life sustaining through provision of support for agricultural production for 1,700,000 household (8,500,,000 individual), livestock and veterinary inputs and services targeting 1.300,000 household (6,500,000individual). The agricultural production will be improved through provision of climate-smart crop production, livestock and veterinary inputs and support to services. Similarly, small scale farmers will be targeted for reducing food losses and strengthened post-harvest techniques through improved storage of food and crop products and processing facilities.

 

FAO will support coordination with FSL sector partners and harmonises the response to food chain threats including animal and plant pests specially locust and birds; in addition, communities will be involved in protecting and maintaining their productive assets through awareness raising. Accountability to affected populations and environmental concerns will be mainstreamed into the proposed activities, also risk to GBV will be taken into consideration and application of the PSEA measures will be applied in collaboration with sister UN agencies.

project_name: Reduced morbidity, mortality and improved health and wellbeing of Rohingya refugees and host communities through provision of equitable access to and utilization of life-saving health services including mental health and psychosocial support.
project_objective:
""The project seeks to maintain access to essential healthcare that addresses the main causes of mortality and morbidity amongst Rohingya and host community beneficiaries, as aligned to the Health Sector Strategic Objectives and articulated in the strategic plan 2023-2024. Health facilities supported will comprise of 39 facilities (14 PHCCs, 19 Health Post, 3 hospitals and 2 SARI ITC/IDTC), the range of services provided at this facilities will be standardized and aligned to the Minimum Package of Essential Health Services for  primary health care including outpatient curative care, routine immunization, essential non-communicable disease interventions, comprehensive integrated sexual and reproductive health services, GBV prevention and response services (CMR). 
The project will support emergency referral system in line with health sector referral SOP, 14 ambulances will support referrals to secondary hospitals and tertiary hospitals. This referral system will also extend to other health sector partners that may not have adequate referral capacity.   Additionally, the project will support 3 Secondary hospitals (2 Health complexes and Friendship maternity center) to ensure referred patients’ access 24/7 CEMONC services, surgical care for trauma, imaging and diagnostic services and psychiatric services.
All health facilities will be staffed with appropriate human resources. Essential medicines, medical equipment and supplies will be made available. Emergency preparedness and response will be put in place; Surveillance tools including (EWARS) will be adopted in order to detect and investigate diseases with outbreak potential and trigger the necessary response actions for the comprehensive management of communicable diseases (such as AWD, Diphtheria, COVID-19 and Dengue). Additionally, Mobile medical teams will be on standby to support emergency response during cyclone, monsoon and fires.
The project will have special focus on quality integrated comprehensive Sexual and reproductive health services including ANC, PNC, Facility Based Deliveries, Menstrual Regulation and Post Abortion Care, Syndromic Management of STIs, treatment and referral of Obstetric and Gynecological complications across supported facilities. Key emphasis will be placed on Adolescent group with integration of Adolescent Friendly Sexual and Reproductive Health (ASRH) services across supported facilities. In line with the Family Planning (FP) Strategy 2021-2023, the project will provide modern FP Counselling and Services with emphasis on long acting and reversible methods. GBV prevention and response services will be integrated in supported health facilities including Clinical Management of Rape (CMR), Intimate Partner Violence (IPV) and other forms of GBV, referral for psychosocial support and services within established referral pathways. 
IOM will continue to work with existing network of 400 community health workers (CHWs) to improve general health status, health seeking behavior and linking community members to health facilities through promotive preventive outreach health activities. Community engagement sessions will be conducted with key stakeholders including CIC, Madjis, and actively engage men and boys in promoting SRH rights for women and girls.
Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) will be integrated into essential health services including assessment, counselling, support to persons with moderate to severe mental health conditions and referrals to specialized services provided by psychiatrists. At the community level, MHPSS services will be through evidence-based interventions including support groups, socio-relational activities, creative and art activities, ritual and celebration activities, sport and play activities and self-awareness sessions as per the IOM community based MHPSS approach. In mainstreaming MHPSS considerations into humanitarian responses, the team will be supporting MHPSS WG coordination and capacity building of partners

project_name: Improvement of WASH services for the most vulnerable populations in Ukhia and Teknaf Upazila of Cox’s Bazar District, Bangladesh
project_objective:
The project will implement activities to achieve the objective of ensuring all women, men, girls, and boys (including all age groups and persons with disabilities) in the Rohingya refugee camps and targeted host communities have access to WASH services. There will be three main areas of intervention as follows:     

Improved access to water services: two small-scale solar-powered piped water networks will be installed in the newly developed areas for the relocated families to provide safe water to beneficiaries. IOM will continue the operation and maintenance (O&M) and upgrade the existing deep tube wells in IOM AoR Camps and water networks in camps 09, 12, 13, 18, 19, 20 extension and 24.  In newly developed areas, and for the replacement of non-repairable deep tube wells, some deep tube wells will be installed in camps and host communities to ensure better access to the most vulnerable people in need. Six existing fossil fuel-managed water supply systems in camps 09, 12 and 13 will be upgraded to the solarized system along with the biological filter in camp 24 to reduce fuel consumption. IOM will procure, replenish, and replace the emergency stocks for cyclones, fires, floods, or other emergency responses.  

Access to sanitation: to ensure dignified and safe access to the latrine facilities, IOM will continue to upgrade the existing poorly functional latrine facilities with gender-inclusive and disability-related features in consultation with the community. IOM will provide assistive devices (commode chair, commode chair with potty, and urinal bottles for males and females) to people with disabilities or with physical impairments to ensure their specific needs are met based on the assessment. IOM will continue the durable household latrine construction work to cover the sanitation gaps at the targeted host communities in Ukhiya. Decentralized Wastewater Treatment Systems-DEWATS will be built and the upgrade of lime-based fecal sludge treatment plants to the DEWATS system to meet the coverage gaps will be implemented.  In addition, IOM will continue to build six more small-scale Intermediate Sludge Transfer Systems (ISTS) connecting with the FSM units to reduce the sludge transfer cost. To ensure the appropriate waste segregation at the source and engage the community effectively in the chain of Solid Waste Management (SWM), IOM will distribute garbage bins (Red and Green) again to reach each household as the last distribution was in 2020. The complete chain of the SWM monitoring system will be continued and strengthened at all levels. 

Hygiene promotion and community engagement: Critical supplies of hygiene items (soap, water containers, Menstrual Hygiene Management (MHM) materials, etc.) will be provided, with community education and mobilization activities targeting all age groups, genders, and persons with special WASH needs at the community level. IOM will continue the SCOPE distribution system in all IOM camps to better assist with hygiene kits for people in need. MHM kits will be provided to the reproductive age group (10-55 years) based on the field assessment and needs across all the IOM-managed camps. The community will be furthermore engaged in O&M of WASH facilities, waste segregation, and prevention of communicable and waterborne diseases like Acute Watery Diarrhea (AWD), Scabies, COVID-19, etc. Real-time service monitoring and community feedback mechanisms will be continued and strengthened throughout the project period.

Despite the signing of the Juba Peace Agreement (JPA), armed clashes have continued across Sudan, the severe economic crisis continued to negatively impact on the lives of the people in Sudan. These situations have been exacerbated by the recent armed conflict between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF); this fighting has further destabilized the protection mechanisms for children, consequently exposing children and their caregivers to furth violence, abuse, exploitation and neglect. The overall protection needs of the children have increased considerably. According to the updated Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) 2023 for Sudan (May 2023), the revised People in Need (PIN) is 24.7 million, 13.6 of whom are children. UNICEF Sudan plans to reach 11.9 million people, 9.4 million of them are children2. This includes newly displaced people, host communities and those trapped in conflict areas without access to basic services. Given UNICEF’s sector leadership in Education (co-led by Save the Children), Nutrition, WASH and the Child Protection Area of Responsibility, as well as last resort role, UNICEF aims to cover 50-80 per cent of each sector’s need. Actual targets may differ, based on the capacity, specific intervention and other partners’ coverage. International support towards the transitional government has not yet translated into substantive financial and policy support to contribute to a progressive reversal of the situation. As a result, humanitarian needs continued to grow, driven by underlying factors including the economic crisis, food insecurity, flooding, disease outbreaks and intercommunal violence. All these factors have resulted in prolonged displacement in addition to recent fighting in Jebel Marra between different factions of armed groups and intercommunal conflict exacerbated by the deteriorating economic conditions and other political factors. The country has also continued to experience rains and floods emergencies in 2022, affecting people across the 18 states of the country. Moreover, endemic diseases such as Malaria, cholera, dengue fever and chikungunya, other novel diseases are also emerging including some which have not been reported in over ten years.  

 

The people in need in Sudan will be the highest over the past decade. Protection of children from violence, exploitation, abuse, and neglect within such complex emergencies is challenged by many factors that child protection partners are working to address. Children affected by conflict, displacement, disease outbreaks and other emergencies are more prone to all types of violations to their rights including their rights to basic services. Many have been separated from their families due to sudden displacement and become vulnerable to further violations including recruitment and association with armed forces/groups. Others who witnessed violence and atrocities during conflict are psychologically affected and need psychosocial support services to avoid further deterioration to trauma and mental health problems that needs specialized services, which are not available in almost all conflict-affected areas. project_name: Improve equitable access to preventive and curative nutrition services for under five years children and pregnant and lactating women in Syria
project_objective:
The project aims to address the deteriorating nutrition situation in Syria as per the 2023 HNO. Under the Nutrition Sector framework, this project aims to provide preventive and curative nutrition services for children U5 and PLW in Syria with a special focus in high severity SD and IDPs camps inside Syria. UNICEF will work in 257 sub-districts classified with severity scale of 3 and higher. The project is designed to strengthen nutrition resilience through protecting, promoting, and supporting consumption of optimal diets for children and women, uptake of recommended childcare and feeding practices and improved access to high quality nutrition services. 

Healthy Diets: UNICEF will work with the FS Sector to empower communities to access and utilize adequate, safe and diversified, low-cost children's diets. As WASH Sector lead, UNICEF, through this project will advocate for vulnerable families with children U2 to be prioritized for water and sanitation services to improve food safety and hygiene. UNICEF & WFP will continue targeting out-of-school children with food supplements (HEB and date bars) to promote good health and education retention. UNICEF will provide preventative Nutrition supplies (LNS and MMS) to improve the complementary food intake of children, and will continue piloting the use of cash to promote nutrition outcomes.
Nutrition sensitive care Practices: The project will focus on raising awareness and provision of skilled counselling on maternal and young child nutrition/care-practices among primary caretakers of children under 2, including PLW. UNICEF and WFP will pilot the complementary feeding bowl initiative in 2023 as tool for improving children’s feeding practices. UNICEF will work with other sections (Health, FSL, WASH, Protection and Social Policy) to address immediate and underlying determinants of malnutrition-including early marriage and gender based violence.
Increased access and utilization of priority services: A multi-sectorial approach to accelerate stunting reduction, management of child wasting, prevention of micro-nutrient deficiencies and nutrition surveillance will be integral response components. The services will be delivered through fixed and mobile teams run by UNICEF’s IPs which include local and int. NGOs and Health directorates of the MoH at governorates/sub-districts and community levels. UNICEF will provide IPs with lifesaving nutrition supplies to treat and prevent malnutrition and prevent deaths among children and women especially with the current devaluation of Syrian currency and weakened economy. Nutrition services will focus on raising awareness among caregivers on prevention of malnutrition, improving IYCF practices and promotion of exclusive breastfeeding among children 0-6 months. Management of malnourished children 0-6 months will be done in the SC. The project will provide nutrition capacity building for HWs and CHWs to ensure quality service delivery. At national level, UNICEF support will focus on strengthening the health system, to provide services, policy work which include Nutrition strategy, the code, technical guidelines and nutrition information and knowledge management (SMART survey and programme documentation).  The project targets 3,718,977 beneficiaries (2,329,440 HCT including 927,555 under UNICEF Qamishly Field Office, 1,389,537 NWS)
Accountability to affected people: To strengthen accountability to affected populations plus other efforts in monitoring and evaluation mentioned in this proposal, the project will establish face-to-face key informants’ interviews using 3rd party monitors to assess needs, satisfaction, and gaps in the nutrition services among affected population. UNICEF has established a hotline to receive beneficiaries' feedback, suggestions & complaints and UNICEF IPs have established feedback mechanisms in health facilities. All these intervention mentioned above will be implemented in both NWS and HCT hubs, where NES is under HCT hub.
