project_name: Supporting Area C Livelihoods and vulnerable HHs
project_objective:
The project aligns with the HRP's second and third Country Strategic Objectives: “The basic needs of vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation are met through the provision of quality basic services and improved access to resources, in accordance with the rights of protected persons under IHL”, and. Specifically, it is aligned with the FSS SO1: The resilience of vulnerable households is protected, and their livelihoods, food security and productive capacity restored/enhanced; and FSS SO2: “Households suffering from limited access to food and to income opportunities are able to meet their basic food needs.”
This project aims to increase the resilience of vulnerable families, farmers and herders in marginalized communities in the West Bank to restore and protect their livelihoods. Specifically, the project seeks to increase access of vulnerable men and women engaged in agricultural and small livestock activities (855 HHs) living in Area C to employment and income-generating opportunities, agricultural assets and legal aid to support them in meeting their basic needs and protecting their rights (total 4019 individuals, 2037 male, 1982 female). The project will be implemented by Oxfam, in partnership with ESDC and LRC. Oxfam and its partners have a long-standing record and solid experience implementing agricultural activities and providing humanitarian assistance and livelihood support interventions in the West Bank. The project will target localities within the governorates of Jerusalem, Ramallah, Bethlehem and Hebron, particularly Area C, that face various social-economic pressures such as Israeli policies and practices that impede on Palestinian livelihood activities, including demolitions and restriction in access to natural resources.The activities will be implemented in coordination with village councils and Departments of Agriculture (DoA). Initial coordination has taken place with Ministry of Agriculture (MoA) and the design of activities were carried out in consultation municipal and village councils. Activities include Cash for Work (CfW) to support 360 agricultural  workers, multipurpose cash assistance (MPCA) to 100 HHs, rehabilitation support to 100 poultry farms, income-generating activities (IGAs) to support 45 women engaged in agricultural activities, and 250 HHs will  benefit from public awareness on legal protection. The implementation/division of activities will be based on each partner's geographical presence, experience and added value. The project's activities have been designed in consultation with the target groups, through focus group discussions (FGD), the FSS and the Ministry of Agriculture (MoA). The proposed interventions were selected based on the HRP 2023 priority matrix. Oxfam’s leads on integration of cash and voucher assistance in the West Bank, specifically in recent efforts to enhance effectiveness of humanitarian response in coordination and collaboration with cash working group actors and within the cluster specific priorities. Women are at the heart of this response and will be targeted through IGAs and participation in the CfW  and public awareness sessions. Oxfam jointly implements cash assistance and livelihood interventions with local partners by providing technical support, strengthening local leadership through the joint implementation of LRC and ESDC, and sharing learning of humanitarian assistance in the evolving context.Oxfam aligns its programs with safe-programming strategies and guidance that continue to steer its project implementation, across all activities in emergency and non-emergency situations, to ensure communities and beneficiaries are safeguarded against sexual exploitation and abuse. Oxfam will ensure mainstreaming protection throughout the project cycle, starting from assessment through the implementation and monitoring. This will be represented through beneficiaries’ selection through tackling protection-base criteria in addition to the livelihood vulnerability

project_name: Improving agro-food production and income generation for vulnerable communities in the West Bank
project_objective:
This intervention will contribute to enhance access to agricultural and farming livelihoods 
for vulnerable Palestinians in West Bank (WB) to support self-sufficiency agricultural and enhance the potential and sustainability of livelihoods. It aims at addressing the priority 
needs identified by the Food Security Sector Cluster (FSS) committing to the Strategic 
Objective SO3. Within this 
framework, WeWorld-GVC (WW-GVC) and the Applied Research Institute-Jerusalem 
(ARIJ) designed a complementary intervention that capitalizes on each partner expertise 
and resources. Both organizations had different meetings with Ministry of Agriculture to discuss and approve the communities and to the agree on the proposed activities. This was approved by MoA October 2nd, 2022. FSS cluster were updated about this approval. The proposed intervention will contribute to local plans in 
mitigating the risks faced by communities and support resilience building towards 
protracted threats and vulnerabilities. Safe access to resources will be sponsored to 
sustain income generation for households (HHs) with disrupted livelihoods due to 
intensification of demolition and confiscation of agricultural structures and resources, Specifically, the intervention will increase the access to 
natural resources through agricultural land/road/water resources rehabilitation. Also, by 
providing inputs and services, it will increase the productivity of producers both in quantity 
and in quality (hygiene/safer/less-time-consuming processes). Lastly, marginalized 
communities’ contracting power on rights and needs in front of duty-bearers will be 
sustained through advocacy awareness sessions. Priority will be given for females, youth 
and people with special needs. Hence, the action unfolds on 3 pillars: 
1. Restoration of access to natural resources and improving agro-practices: 90 dunum 
agricultural land in 2 communities, 7 km road rehabilitation in 4 communities; 2 wells in 2 communities, 16 cisterns in 2 communities, inputs for dryland farming for 625 dunum in 5 communities; 25 baby greenhouses in 3 communities. 
2. Support to livelihood sustainability: 73 sheep and goat sheds rehabilitation in 6 
communities; 1 automatic milk feeding machine for newborn in one community; 10 hybrid feeders in 1 community; 25 sheep feeders with milking barriers in 2 communities; 30 food processing assets for livestock-breeders in 3 communities; s; 
3. Multi-scale (community, local/national authorities, international actors) advocacy: 
 
group advocacy trainings in 15 communities; elaboration/dissemination of 5 food 
security and livelihood factsheets at governorate level;1 advocacy/dissemination event with relevant stakeholders; elaboration of an advocacy tool-kit. 
The action will benefit 750 HHs in 29 communities mostly in Area C for a total of 3,403 direct beneficiaries (1,016 women, 1,037 men, 659 girls, 656 boys, 86 elders of which 50 
PWD) in 7 governorates: Hebron, Bethlehem, Ramallah, Jerusalem, Jordan Valley (Jericho), Salfit and 
Tulkarem. The action serves beyond mere material needs by addressing broader issues of 
safety and dignity in order to promote gender and age responsive protection, equitable 
participation and access to services while preventing potential harm on different 
population groups. 
The partnership will capitalize on the partners’ experience in such sectorial interventions as well as outreach capacity to communities and relevant stakeholders. WW-GVC is a WASH-expert and is the focal point within the WB Protection Consortium (WBPC) for 169 communities in Area C while ARIJ has an expertise in promoting socioeconomic 
development through enhancing access to food and natural resources by promoting 
innovative and sustainable interventions.

project_name: Enhancing farmers resilience and food security for ‎vulnerable households in Area C.  ‎
project_objective:
The project aims to enhance resilience, livelihood & improve food security of 1778 ‎farmer's HHs with capita of 8712 (2387 women, 2405 men, 3659 children, 261 ‎elderlies) in vulnerable localities that are threatened with confiscation and settlers’ ‎attacks in Bethlehem, Nablus and Salfit governorates.‎
The design of the project relayed heavily on the Food Security Sector “FFS” Hamartian ‎Needs Overview “HNO”, OCHA’s 2022 Multisectoral Needs Assessment “MSNA”, the ‎available data by other national and international NGOs and bodies, and on need ‎assessments conducted by PARC and ACPP. The project was designed based on the ‎Humanitarian Right Based Approach, in which those in the most marginalized situations ‎who face the biggest barriers to realizing their rights were prioritized.‎
The project is directly aligned with the 3rd SO of the HRP strategy in Palestine, and the ‎FSS HRP 2023 objectives, mainly with the 1st and 2nd objective.‎
The project focused on the governorates that are affected by settlements and settlers’ ‎attacks in the WB. For instance, Nablus is surrounded by 13 settlements and 37 ‎settlements outposts, in 2021 and 2022 around 13,193 in Nablus were injured due to ‎settlers’ attacks, Nablus encountered many episodes of confiscation of Agri-lands and ‎heavy expansion of settlements which led to violent escalations harming local ‎communities. While 70% of Salfit’s land was either confiscated or will be confiscated by ‎the occupation to build more settlements, as currently Salfit is surrounded by 25 ‎settlements that are inhabited with nearly 100 k settlers, and residents in Salfit suffer ‎from settlers’ attacks and the occupation’s unhumanitarian measures.‎
Furthermore, Bethlehem has around 18 settlements that are inhabited with 105k ‎settlers, these settlements separate Bethlehem residents from accessing their lands ‎and livelihoods, and during 2021 and 2022 there were around 946 injuries due to ‎settlers’ attacks there.‎
Through the various need assessment and consultation in each governorate; the ‎localities and the needs  in each locality were identified. The proposed ‎project will have two main components
Firstly, agricultural assets and productive capacities of farmers and damaged ‎productive restored.‎
This component focuses on enhancing access of the targeted beneficiaries to ‎productive assets mainly land and water and increasing their productive capacity ‎through provision of inputs and seedlings.‎
Secondly, vulnerably groups in targeted localities increase their economic capacity to ‎meet food security needs. This component invokes the CFW modality and ‎aims at creating a multiplier effect by hiring people who are food insecure and ‎vulnerable in each locality to work on rehabilitation the agriculture roads in return for ‎cash.‎
The project adopts human rights-based, gender mainstreaming and do no harm ‎approaches with respect to core humanitarian standards. To ensure accountability and ‎community engagement project team will announce and formulate Local Committees ‎‎(LC). The project is gender sensitive and takes into consideration the special barriers ‎that face women; in the need assessment workshops women participation was ‎mandatory, and the workshops took place at a time and place that were convenient to ‎women. The needs and fears of women that were stated in the need assessment and ‎in MSNA report were also taken into consideration, and embedded in the project.‎
Furthermore, PARC’s partner ACPP will play a role in documenting the human rights ‎violation and conducts the fast dissemination to international community.‎
Furthermore, while developing the project, MoA was consulted to ensure that no ‎duplication in efforts take place. As indicated in OCHA’s coordination mechanism, the ‎planned activities in addition to targeted locations were send to MoA to ensure no ‎duplication of efforts. While implementing the project MoA will be in LC and the project's steering committee.

project_name: Providing support for the most vulnerable households of the five governorates in the Gaza strip.
project_objective:
This intervention will support 400 of the most vulnerable households (HHs) in the five governorates of the Gaza strip who are impacted by the prolonged economic deterioration caused by more than 15 years of siege. This action aims to ensure the specific basic needs of these 400 HHs are met, notably through the distribution of Multi-Purpose Cash Assistance (MPCA). 
The project is informed by assessments ACTED conducted between September and October 2022, the 2022 Multi-Sectorial Needs Assessments (MSNA), conducted by REACH and OCHA in July 2022, extensive consultations with key stakeholders, and recommendations from the Ministry of Social Development (MoSD) and the Cash Working Group (CWG) in Gaza. Specifically, ACTED and its implementing partners Arab Center for Agricultural Development (ACAD) and the Palestinian Environmental Friends (PEF) will increase beneficiaries resilience and improve coping capacities through the provision of multi-purpose cash assistance (MPCA) to help HHs suffering from limited access to income opportunities meet their basic needs and alleviate the impact of the last escalation in August 2022.
MPCA enables female-headed HHs and HHs with particular needs, such as pregnant and lactating women, families with PwDs and/or chronic diseases, to prioritize their specific needs (i.e. milk, instant formula, medicines, diapers) and to meet their differentiated priorities which are often left unmet through sectoral cash initiatives.
The implementation of this action will be based on past experiences implementing MPCA projects since 2021, funded by the HF pool fund and CDCS, as well as e-voucher projects funded by CDCS and Alliance2015, and implemented in coordination with WFP.
Furthermore, ACTED will rely on its 2 Community Emergency Response Networks’ (CERNs) existing capacity to implement activities throughout the project, to reach beneficiaries, share key PSEA messages, and support ACTED’s Complaint and Response Mechanism (CRM). These 2 CERNs were already established under former HF-funded projects, operate across 3 governorates, and are composed of 3 Community-Based Organizations (CBOs), 4 Community-Based Protection Committees (CBPCs), and 130 volunteers (176 individuals in total). ACTED will also rely on its community representatives in governorates which are not fully covered by the CERNs.
The project will be supported by the mainstreaming of an Integrated Protection Approach (IPA), with specific focus on the most vulnerable groups, including women, girls, boys, PwD and older people. Gender principles will be mainstreamed throughout the entire action and CBPCs will be trained on referral mechanisms of protection cases such as GBV with a particular focus given to women and children. Finally, Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) will be core to the proposed Action.

project_name: Women Aid Women: Humanitarian response in Palestine
project_objective:
Driven and facilitated by community-based, women-led teams in Hebron and Bethlehem governates in previous project by DanChurchAid/Norwegian Church Aid’s (DCA/NCA) and the local organization, the East Jerusalem Young Men’s Christian Association (EJ-YMCA.) The overall project objective is to enhance vulnerable women´s economic coping capacity to overcome the impacts of occupation and socio-economic situation. The implementing partner EJ-YMCA will work closely with established Protection Groups to select and support 96 vulnerable women and their families (451 individual beneficiaries) through unrestricted, multipurpose cash grants that can help beneficiaries in any way they need. While the entry point for identifying target women is their socioeconomic situation, the project’s impact encompasses women with different sensitive and vulnerable living circumstances, of different societal groups and different age groups, and their families including, but not limited to, women headed households, widows, women with disabilities or have disabilities within the family and chronic disease, and elderly women.

The EJ-YMCA will work through a highly participatory approach centered around collaboration with established Protection Groups (PGs) in 14 communities. The project relies on a participatory approach in its design and implementation. Key elements of our project approach are:

A Survivor Community-Led Response (SCLR) method
The SCLR approach puts communities in the driver’s seat when identifying their own needs, deciding on priorities, planning, and implementing actions to respond to needs identified.
Results from previous projects showed that the SCLR approach is effective in enabling communities to identify and address protection and development needs; it contributes to resilience, strengthens cooperation between local community members, and enhances the ownership.
The proposed project will be work with the already established Protection Groups in the two governorates of Hebron and Bethlehem. 

A community Protection Group (PG) is an informal structure that consists of a group of women, young women, men, and young men from the community. PGs were formed through previous projects supported by DCA/NCA. The SCLR approach has equipped the PGs with the necessary skills and preparedness to facilitate, organize, and coordinate any efforts within the community. The proposed project will further empower the PGs as they will play a key role the implementation of the proposed project as they are the connection between communities, DCA/NCA and its partner EJ-YMCA.

The Protection Groups (PGs)
In this project each PG will nominate 3 women and they will act with the EJ-YMCA field teams to reach out to the vulnerable women within their communities. The PG will follow the principles of neutrality and impartiality will nominate three representative women members to map women’s needs in their communities for the vulnerable targeted women, based on their first-hand knowledge of the socioeconomic situation and vulnerability of women in their communities, develop the localized selection criteria, assist the EJ-YMCA project field team collect data, and in documenting the action/process.

Community sensitization With the project relying on nominated PG women, it seeks to promote women as active, capable, resilient participants in their communities. An important element of enhancing community sensitization to the important role of women, is to support the women themselves in making the choice to undertake and commit to responsibilities that go beyond the family sphere and are at community level. The project seeks to enhance their confidence in decision-making and highlight this within their communities. These discussions seek as well to add transparency, accountability, and responsiveness to the PG women’s role and enhance visibility in the communities.

project_name: Increasing and strengthening emergency preparedness and response capacity of the Rafah, Middle Area and Khan Yunis communities in the Gaza strip.
project_objective:
This proposed project will increase the preparedness and response capacity of the Middle Area, Khan Yunis and Rafah governorates in case of future escalation or natural hazards, through prepositioning and replenishing of Emergency NFI kits for Internally Displaced People (IDPs), host families, vulnerable households (HHs) affected/exposed to the risk of harsh weather and by  increasing the response capacity of 300 HHs (historically served as host families in times of emergency). The project will provide tailored NFI assistance to 900 vulnerable HHs with 200 also receiving emergency shelter repair assistance. 1,200 HHs (6,600 individuals) will directly benefit from the project under activities 4 and 6. This project will reinforce the Community-based Emergency Response Networks (CERNs), through trainings and by adding 3 new Community-Based Organisations (CBOs) to improve communication channels with local communities and ensure the CERNs’ sustainability (1 CBO per governorate). This project will be implemented in partnership with Unlimited Friends Association (UFA) and Fares Al-Arab For Development (FAFD). The project leverages on ACTED’s existing network of 4 warehouses in the 3 governorates, pre-positioned with NFIs, under previous HF-funded projects to cover the needs of 17,400 individuals, and which were successfully used following the August 2022 and May 2021 escalations and winter storms/harsh weather in January 2022.
In addition, this project will benefit from the CERNs and the CBPCs established under previous projects, which have a focus on supporting emergency activities.
This project is informed by assessments ACTED conducted in 2022, consultations with key stakeholders, recommendations from the Ministry of Social Development (MoSD) and the Ministry of Public Work and Housing (MoPWH) and the Shelter & NFI in Gaza. This intervention is aligned with the 2023 HNO priorities and supports the achievement of the 2023 HRP for the shelter cluster, most notably by contributing to the Specific Objectives 2 and 3.This involves NFIs stockpiling, improving urban displacement setting to host IDPs, and community capacity building to ensure adequate functionality at time of emergency. The intervention will alleviate unmet needs exposing HHs to harsh weather and provide an emergency assistance (including NFI distribution) to IDPs and Host Communities during escalations of hostilities or natural hazards. 
ACTED, FAFD and UFA will implement a multi-pronged approach, complementary to the HF-funded projects ACTED currently implements, to increase access of vulnerable HHs to safe and secure shelters through the following activities:
A1: Strengthening 2 CERNs through trainings and by adding 3 CBOs
A2: Conducting required maintenance and improvement works of ACTED's 4 warehouses 
A3: Renewing the existing Framework Agreements (FWA) for NFIs supplying and sign new FWA with a contractor for the repair/maintenance works
A4: Providing tailored urgent assistance to affected 900 HHs at risk of manmade or natural hazards (IDPs, Host communities, HHs exposed to harsh weather, damaged HHs during the hostilities)
A5: Replenishing stockpiles with NFIs to prepare for future emergencies.
A6: Increasing 300 host families’ response capacities in the targeted communities
The project will be supported by the mainstreaming of an Integrated Protection Approach (IPA), with a specific focus on the most vulnerable groups (women, girls, boys, PwD and older people). As PwD are sometimes deliberately prevented from expressing their needs, the project team will conduct HH-level visits to assess their specific needs and explain the purpose of the project. PwDs and their caregivers will be consulted throughout the project to better understand their safety and dignity concerns. Gender principles will also be mainstreamed and CBPCs will be trained on referral mechanisms of protection cases such as GBV. AAP will also be core to the proposed Action.

project_name: Rehabilitation of substandard shelters for 150 vulnerable families in Gaza
project_objective:
The Rehabilitation of Substandard Shelters for 150 Vulnerable Families in Gaza program responds to the needs identified by the Shelter Cluster Proposed Objectives and the  Needs and Priorities for HRP 2023 and will renovate substandard shelters (fully or partially) for 150 vulnerable families in Gaza to meet their shelter basic needs and minimum standards. The renovations will include adapting shelters to meet the needs of persons with disabilities (PWDs) and improving the living space of vulnerable groups. The project responds to the Shelter/NFIs Cluster’s Objective n. 2: “Vulnerable households exposed to harsh weather and protection concerns are supported to meet basic needs and enhance their coping capacity.” This is linked to HRP Strategic Objective 2: “The basic needs of vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation are met through the provision of quality basic services and improved access to resources, in accordance with the rights of protected persons under IHL” .
The project’s overall objective is to ensure that 150 of the most vulnerable households (HHs), which Anera identified in current and previous needs assessments, are supported to meet their basic needs and enhance their coping capacity. These HHs live in substandard housing conditions in Gaza without essential protection against the harsh climate and are exposed to humanitarian and protection concerns.
Anera will work with Unlimited Friend Association for Social Development (UFA), which will support the selection of beneficiaries through a detailed technical assessment and supervise rehabilitation works for vulnerable beneficiary HHs. They will assign data collectors to validate the selected beneficiaries based on vulnerability criteria approved by the Shelter Cluster and MoSD.  Anera will finalize and approved the selection of beneficiaries on the standard shelter cluster criteria in coordination with the Ministry of Social Development (MoSD) and the Ministry of Public Works and Housing (MoPWH).
Anera will select contractors to conduct the rehabilitation works through a transparent bidding process according to Anera’s procurement standards. Repair works typically include basic repairs of toilets and kitchens, repairs of roofs and replacement of asbestos ceilings, leakage and isolation works, and basic renovations of children’s bedrooms (lighting, windows, tiles, ventilation, and isolation). Anera will support HHs with members with disabilities with accessible facilities.  In terms of PSEA related activities, Anera will provide a series of targeted PSEA sessions by Anera's PSEA focal point to project personnel, external collaborators (engineers, consulting firms, etc.) ahead of community engagement as well as during the implementation of the project. Anera will also provide PSEA sessions to 150 women/men distributed into 10 groups.
Anera succeeded to secure funding for the rehabilitation of substandard shelters for 50 vulnerable families in southern Gaza to be implemented in 18 months.

project_name: Responding to WASH Needs in Gaza
project_objective:
Responding to WASH Needs in Gaza is a project that Anera and its local partner, Youth Empowerment Center (YEC), will implement in partnership with the Palestinian Water Authority (PWA), the Coastal Municipalities Water Utility (CMWU), and the WASH Cluster. The project responds to the WASH Cluster’s Strategic Objective 2: “The basic needs of vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation are met through the provision of quality basic services and improved access to resources, in accordance with the rights of protected persons under IHL.” The project will also respond to Strategic Objective 3: “The capacity of vulnerable Palestinians to cope with and overcome protracted crises, including from environmental threats, is supported, while solutions to violations and other root causes of threats and shocks are pursued.”
The WASH sector in Gaza is one of the most severely deteriorated sectors. Over two million people face grave challenges and limited accessibility to WASH services at the community and household (HH) level, which creates serious environmental threats including health hazards and pollution.
In response to these challenges, Anera works with local partners to identify gaps in the WASH sector and address needs on the community and HH levels to enhance access to sustainable and clean water and sanitation services to improve overall health and wellbeing. The project will serve 150,660 individuals in different part of Gaza and will include the following interventions:
Installation of wastewater networks in different neighborhoods in Al Karama area - Western Jabalia,
Installation of wastewater networks in different neighborhoods in Eibad Alrahman - Western Jabalia,
Upgrade of water networks in different neighborhoods in Al Karama area - Western Jabalia,
Upgrade of water networks in different neighborhoods in Eibad Alrahman - Western Jabalia,
Installation of stormwater network at Al Attatra area - Western Beit Lahia,
Rehabilitation and upgrading of the pumping stations facilities in Khan Younis,
Rehabilitation and upgrading of two municipal waters in Al Saffa Complex il al _Shijaiah.
Awareness program for 1,000 women from the most vulnerable HHs on hygiene and health standards. 
Anera’s team, through its local partner, YEC, and in cooperation with the relevant stakeholders, will conduct assessments of identified target areas through field visits during the first two months of the project period to identify and approve the exact rehabilitation needs of each area in terms of necessary repair/construction works and materials to support their connection to WASH facilities. Anera and YEC will review and confirm HH beneficiary numbers to identify the cost of HH connections. Anera’s team will review selected project locations and cross-check them with the relevant key players in the WASH interventions to ensure they are not receiving duplicate assistance from other parties.

project_name: Providing Adequate, Sufficient and Affordable Drinking Water in Bethlehem Communities and Adequate Sewerage Services in Jenin Communities
project_objective:
The project was designed and built in reference to the secondary data provided by the Palestinian government, WASH cluster vulnerability mapping that PARC contributed in and according to validation visits and a concrete need assessment that has been conducted by PARC recently where women actively participated in the assessment.

The project can be summarized by two main activities, the first activity is related to drinking water in Bethlehem governorate south WB and the second main activity is related to adequate sewerage in Jenin governorate north WB. The following is a brief summary for each activity:
 
1- The installation of new drinking water distribution networks (6 km) and HH connections (600) in two of Bethlehem communities (Nahhalin and Al Khader). These communities and according to the mapping that was conducted by the WASH cluster in cooperation with the partners showed that those two communities deeply need this kind of intervention. This is due to the low water consumption per capita in these communities. In both communities, Nahhalin and Al Khader, the average drinking water consumption is 30-50 liter per capita per day which is far below the average defined by WHO which is 100 liter per capita per day. Moreover, The high prices of trucked water is an increasing burden on the residents' shoulders especially in summer time when the weather becomes dry and harsh, in such times, one cubic meter of drinking water approximately costs around 20 NIS. Another important activity in this section, is the connection of 600 HHs (400 in Nahhalin and 200 in Al Khader) to the newly installed water network, this will guarantee the provision of high quality, safe and affordable water resource. In this case, it is expected according to PARC experience that the average consumption of liters per capita per day will increase to reach 75 instead of 30-50. In addition the cost per cubic meter will decrease to be around 5 NIS. This is an increase of 100% in consumption and decrease of 75% in cost for the local residents. All these developed elements will be reflected on the livelihood conditions of the targeted communities including health and hygiene.

2- The installation of new sewer pipelines of Anza village south of Jenin, this activity includes the installation of 1km of sewer pipelines including all needed manholes and accessories. This can be considered  as an extension to the existing sewer network that was conducted by PARC 8 years ago. 
According to PARC need assessment, only 70% of Anza's population are connected to the existing sewer network. In this intervention, 50 additional households will be connected to the network. This will reduce the harming environmental impacts of cesspits and increase the amount of treated wastewater of Anza wastewater treatment plant that is being used widely in summer for irrigation and discharged in Wadis safely in winter as treated wastewater up to the Palestinian standards. To conclude, the intervention in Anza will target installation/ extension of 1km of sewer pipelines with all needed accessories and facilities in addition to connecting 50 HHs to the newly installed sewer network. This will provide the sewer services adequately and directly to 50 HHs (approximately 250 capita) and will provide access to sanitation services to future extension projects, expanding landscape and growing population.

PARC believes that the developed and reliable WASH infrastructures (Water and Sanitation), will be reflected on the quality of livelihoods of the local residents in the targeted communities more than anything else. It is highly important to mention that the quality services deeply enhance the resilience of the residents of these communities and decrease the chances of internal migrations to the cities which is directly reflected on a more sustainable, diverse, food secured and  stable community in Palestine.

project_name: Improving WASH and health services in Al-Nasser Medical Compound in Gaza governorate and addressing urgent WASH needs including flood mitigation and prevention at community level in Deir Al Balah and Khan Younis governorates.
project_objective: Strengthening WASH and health services of Healthcare Facilities (HCFs) and underserved communities, are considered extremely urgent needs in Gaza Strip (GS) according to the Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) 2022. Moreover, investing in adequate WASH facilities supports resilience building and strengthens communities’ ability to face protracted threats and chronic vulnerabilities. This project is aligned with HRP 2023 Strategic Objectives 1, 2 and 3 and complements WASH Cluster Objectives 1, 2 and 3, and Health Cluster Objective 2, contributing to SDG6. Improved WASH services in HCFs are essential for achieving all global and national health goals, especially SDG3 (Universal Health Coverage), and specific targets 3.1, 3.2 (reducing maternal and neonatal mortality) and 3.9 (reducing disease burden from unsafe WASH). Moreover, effective WASH and infection prevention and control (IPC) measures are one of the five objectives of the World Health Organization (WHO) Global Action Plan on antimicrobial resistance. The proposed intervention complies with HRP 2023 eligible activities, targeting the most vulnerable communities and HCFs according to the WASH 2022 vulnerability mappings (WASH Cluster). Also, the project complements UNICEF’s Strategy for Health 2016-2030. Finally, the project complies with the Palestinian Water Authority (PWA) Strategic Plan (2017-22) and the Ministry of Health’s (MoH) one (2021-25), and the soon-to-be-published National WASH standards for HCFs (UNICEF/WW-GVC 2022). WeWorld-GVC (WW-GVC), in partnership with Qatar Red Crescent Society (QRCS), aims to enhance the resilience, protection, and dignity of the most vulnerable people in GS. The needs and interventions were coordinated with and endorsed by the MoH, WASH and Health Cluster, Coastal Municipalities Water Utility (CMWU), United Nations Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA) and PWA. The general objective of this proposal is to increase the availability and accessibility of WASH and health services in HCFs and communities including flood mitigation and prevention, contributing to mitigating the impact of COVID-19 and other infectious diseases by (A) improving the access to WASH and Health quality services for Al Nasser medical compound (Al Nasser Pediatric Hospital, Rantissi Specialized Hospital and Ophthalmic Hospital) in Gaza City by implementing sustainable improvement of WASH infrastructure through construction/rehabilitation of handwashing stations, gender-sensitive latrines and sewer system and improving the quality of health services through provision of hygiene material, medical and protective equipment supply, monitoring tools), benefitting annually an average 280,000 people served by the 3 hospitals (data: Health Cluster HeRAMS Dashboard); (B) ensuring access to adequate WASH services at community level in Deir Al Balah, through the installation/rehabilitation of water transmission pipelines and HH connections, and the installation/rehabilitation of sewer collection networks and HH connections, serving 1,535 vulnerable individuals of two unserved communities, Al’Ansar (Al Musaddarc locality) and Block 8 (Al Buriej locality); and in Khan Younis Governorate through the rehabilitation of four wells, increasing the availability of domestic water supply for 13 communities (168,150 beneficiaries); (C) promoting flood mitigation and prevention, through the construction/rehabilitation of stormwater networks and drainage systems in the community of An Nuseirat camp (5,000 beneficiaries) in Deir Al Balah and (D) advocating for the right of the most vulnerable Palestinians to receive adequate access to WASH services through the development of 5 awareness products on access restrictions to WASH, estimating to reach 400,000 beneficiaries. WW-GVC and QRCS will ensure that all proposed interventions trigger positive effects on reducing WASH vulnerabilities and increasing the resilience of communities living under protracted threats in Gaza Strip.

project_name: Enhance accessibility to safe sanitation services in southern governorates at Gaza strip
project_objective: The intervention aims to improve safe and adequate access to sanitation services for the most unserved and underserved vulnerable people in Southern governorates at Gaza strip (Khan Younis and Rafah), which is in line with HRP 2023 strategic objectives, WASH Cluster objectives and comply with HNO 2023 analysis. The communities selected in full coordination with PWA, CMWU, Khan Younis Municipality, WASH cluster coordinator, and Khan Younis WASH area focal point Action Against Hunger (AAH) as the project targeted locations. PEF will contribute in enhancing accessibility to safe and adequate sanitation services for directly 8,300 (6500 in Al Satar, 1800 in Al Furqan) most vulnerable people (1,982 men, 1,969 women, 2,222 boys, 2,127 girls) living in Al Satar and Al Furqan localities in Khan Younis and Rafah respectively, who are currently unserved or not connected to any sewer collection systems and rely on old cesspits/percolation pits, which are not well managed or carefully handled due to peoples’ vulnerable economic situation. Throughout the year, these pits are subjected to frequent flooding and continuous accumulation of wastewater, creating unsafe and unsustainable conditions, and exposing people to dangerous health risks, particularly diarrhea and skin diseases in children. The environment was also subjected to severe deterioration due to the seepage of wastewater into subsurface soil and pollution of the groundwater. In addition, the pests, vectors, and rodents’ outbreaks were frequent phenomena in this area. PEF will formulate gender- balanced communities’ committees to be engaged in the project lifecycle and participate in decision making process. PEF plan to construct sewer collection networks and household connections in targeted locations that are the most efficient, adequate, and affordable solution, according to the Gaza context, to improve people’s access to proper sanitation services and decrease their dependence on expensive or environmentally unfriendly solutions, such as in-open wastewater dumping and cesspits. The installation works of sewer collection networks in the targeted community will include 1) construction of different sized sewer pipelines and manholes, and 2) closing and filling of cesspits and septic tanks and reconnecting the households to the sewer collection system, which will be connected to the public wastewater networks up to the wastewater pumps’ stations to treatment plants as planned by PWA and CMWU through the developed master plans. The installation works will be implemented by highly qualified and expert contractors contracted based on a competitive tendering process to ensure high-quality works are delivered. PEF is an active member in WASH cluster, with broad experience in implementing humanitarian projects in the Gaza Strip. This extensive expertise has gained the communities’ trust and cooperation and resulted in an extensive network of local partners. The action will also address critical safety, health, hygiene, water and wastewater situation, water conservation, protection, safeguarding, GBV, women empowerment and environmental issues and maintain shared responsibilities and total behavioral change practices through awareness community sessions at HHs level including IEC materials. Additionally, PEF will promote community ownership, women empowerment, accountability, and participation throughout the project and community engagement activities, and in-place complaint and feedback mechanism.

project_name: Improving access to adequate WASH services for schools and health clinics in the most vulnerable communities throughout the West Bank
project_objective:
The proposed intervention aims to contribute to the reduction of WASH vulnerability in marginalized communities through improving access to equitable, sustainable, and safely managed WASH services in institutions with a particular focus on vulnerable Schools and Health clinics in the governorates of Hebron, Bethlehem, Jericho, Jerusalem, Ramallah, Nablus, Jenin, and Tubas.
The proposed intervention responds to the 2023 HRP and to WASH Cluster’s Objective 1 and, in particular, Objective 2. It was also designed based on the WASH Cluster’s 2023 Humanitarian Needs Analysis which highlighted access to WASH services in institutions (schools & health care facilities) as a main priority area of intervention. The intervention is also in line with SDG 6 “Ensure access to water and sanitation for all” & SDG 3 “Universal Health Coverage”.
The intervention will achieve its aim through two components: first, its tailored approach to enhancing WASH infrastructure and resources in vulnerable schools and HCFs and second, through enhancing target group’s responsive hygiene practices and awareness. The intervention is designed to ensure equitable and dignified access for most vulnerable community groups with a particular focus on PWDs, children and females across 47 communities in the West Bank.
MA’AN and WeWorld-GVC are proposing to improve WASH facilities and capacities in 47 vulnerable WASH institutions benefiting in total 22,030 direct beneficiaries (7623 boys, 6367 girls, 3746 men, 3578 women, 248 elder men, 310 elder women - of which 392 are PWDs) in the West bank, mainly in Area C (51%), and Area A/B (49%). Through:
i) Rehabilitation of WASH facilities in schools in coordination with & according to MoE standards, targeting 30 schools (1 in Jericho Governorate, 4 in Jerusalem, 3 in Bethlehem, 14 in Hebron, 2 in Nablus, 4 in Jenin, 1 in Ramallah, and 1 in Tubas).
ii) Conducting hygiene awareness campaigns in targeted schools in partnership with MoE health units to promote hygiene and sanitation practices with gender & protection mainstreaming.
iii) The provision of hygiene and cleaning kits for the 30 targeted schools. 
iv) Rehabilitation of WASH facilities in health clinics/HCFs, targeting 17 vulnerable HCFs (2 in Jericho Governorate, 5 in Jerusalem, 2 in Hebron, 2 in Jenin, 5 in Ramallah, and 1 in Tubas).
v) The provision of hygiene and cleaning kits for the 17 targeted HCFs.
vi) Conducting trainings for clinics’ staff on promotion of hygiene practices to patients and protection guidelines including PSEA.
vii) developing awareness raising products (video, factsheets, reports) regarding access restrictions to WASH in Area C
All proposed activities will ensure protection principles on safety, dignity, meaningful access, accountability, participation, empowerment and claiming of rights.
This intervention has been proposed based on coordinated efforts to complement current WASH aid actors’ proposed and ongoing interventions to ensure comprehensive contribution to the reduction in overall WASH vulnerability amongst marginalized and prioritized communities. The proposed intervention also complements another initiative submitted by WW-GVC (with MA’AN as an implementing partner). 
The project has been coordinated and endorsed by the MoH, MoE and the WASH Cluster. It is in line with the MoH Strategic Plan (2021-25). Proposed activities and target locations were selected upon WASH Cluster’s eligible interventions for HRP 2023 and based on the cluster’s community & institutions vulnerability assessments.
MA’AN and WW-GVC will ensure that proposed interventions will trigger a positive effect on the reduction of WASH vulnerability, increasing the resilience of the communities & institutions, especially in Area C, including PSEA promotion and messaging. Moreover, the project will enhance the protection of the communities & institutions, supporting preparedness and promotion of best hygiene practices that would contribute to combating disease outbreaks.

project_name: Emergency Shelter Assistance for Families with Protection Concerns in the Gaza Strip
project_objective: The project provides for the protection and safety of vulnerable families who have poor access to adequate shelter. It includes supporting 145 families living in substandard shelters through rehabilitation and upgrade activities to meet shelter basic needs and minimum standards, focusing on meeting the needs of people with disabilities. The project targets 145 families of people with disabilities who have serious protection concerns due to shelter conditions. This project aligns with the HRP 2023 objective 2 “Vulnerable households exposed to harsh weather and protection concerns are supported to meet basic needs and enhance their coping capacities”. The main activity is to provide cash grants for shelter rehabilitation to address shelter-related vulnerabilities. A cash-based self-help approach for shelter rehabilitation will be implemented according to families' needs. This will maximize the impact on beneficiaries while fostering ownership and resilience of the targeted community. The project complements ongoing activities of MA’AN that support addressing the protection concerns of people with disabilities. The identification of the targeted families will be coordinated with the shelter cluster and the Ministry of social development. MA’AN capitalizes on its community-based emergency response structure to support the implementation process to ensure accountability to the affected population.

project_name: Adequate Shelter Solution for vulnerable households at immediate risk of eviction in Gaza
project_objective:
The project responds to the Shelter/NFIs Cluster’s Objective n. 1 “Displaced populations are provided support that mitigates immediate harm and ensures adequate and safe temporary shelter solutions”, This is linked to HRP 2022 SO.1; “The rights of Palestinians living under occupation, including those living under the blockade, and other restrictions, are protected, respected and promoted in accordance with International Humanitarian Law (IHL), and International Human Rights Law (IHRL), while duty-bearers are increasingly held to account”. 

The overall project objective is to ensure that 150 most vulnerable HHs (855 individuals) from Gaza, North Gaza and middle area Governorates evicted or at immediate risk of eviction from rented shelters or facing imprisonment due to rental debts are protected.  

The proposed response will be tailored on the HHs’ needs and will be including the provision of: 

1) Cash-for-rent and legal support to 150 vulnerable HHs in rented accommodation who according to Ministry of Social Development (MoSD) , Gaza Protection consortium (GPC) and Protection Cluster database are repeatedly exposed to the risk of eviction or already evicted due to their inability to pay the rental costs. This includes provision of cash-for- debt re-payment for cases identified, or at high risk of imminent imprisonment due to being forced to sign promissory note. The cash for rent will cover 4-months’ rent fees including electricity and water bills and will be provided through phased cash payments. 

2) Provision of case-by-case restricted cash assistance for essential household items. The support will be tailored according to needs and may include items such as bedding items, gas stoves, heaters with gas cylinders and fuel, emergency lighting system with batteries. Following the Do No Harm principles in case of heater provision all necessary safety measures will be applied and required items such as fire extinguisher, fire blanket awareness raising, and training will be provided. 

3) Provision of hygiene kits and hygiene awareness material for the targeted families throughout the project cycle. 
This project is designed in consultations and coordination with NRC local partner, the Shelter Cluster, GPC, Protection Cluster and the MoSD, the Ministry of Public Work and Housing (MoPWH) and coordinated with active shelter partners to avoid duplication and ensure fair distribution of the limited humanitarian funds among affected communities across The Gaza Strip.

project_name: Shelter assistance for herders and Bedouins in Area C and vulnerable families in Hebron City's H2 Area.
project_objective:
The intervention will mainly support vulnerable communities affected by the Israeli occupation (Area C) to access standard quality shelters and NFIs. The project will also reinforce the capacities of households and institutions in withstanding crisis caused by different aspects including general context in the West Bank, manmade, and natural crisis in the most affected locations of the West Bank (including H2, Area C as well as Area A and B). Through this project, Action Against Hunger (AAH) will work on three main components in response to the most pressing needs and gaps identified.
 
Firstly, the project will benefit vulnerable herding and Bedouin families in Area C living in inadequate shelters due to the challenging environment – including restrictions on movement, settler violence and lack of building permits. The proposed shelter interventions include the rehabilitation and insulation of substandard shelters and winterization for vulnerable communities. Families with a member that is living with a disability will be prioritized with accessibility arrangements made within and outside the shelter. 
Through these interventions access and accessibility to the shelter will be increased while conditions within the shelter (e.g., insulation) and capacities of the vulnerable families to face adverse weather conditions will be improved thus positively contributing to women, men, boys and girl privacy, safety, and dignity. When implementing this intervention, AAH will adopt it’s newly developed Shelter Model approach. In which, the targeted households will receive support to have a complete residential unit though multi-sectoral interventions. i.e. Not limited to the shelter unit, but also to WASH facilities, Shelter access and fencing, and home garden. This approach aims to Ensuring people’s basic needs are addressed through comprehensive responsive, protective, preventive measures as well as will improve the socio-economic conditions of the people, increase their capacity, and participation through cash-based interventions. AAH has implemented a pilot project based on this approach under the current HF allocation. 
Secondly, AAH will support economically vulnerable families in Areas A, B, C and H2 to improve their capacities in developing preventive and responsive measures while having access to limited financial means by distributing essential Nonfood-items (NFI) and hygiene materials at household level. These interventions will positively contribute to protecting the most vulnerable family members, including elderly and people with chronic diseases, while limiting the pressure on bread winners and the household’s budget. 
Lastly, the project aims at supporting Palestinian community-based organizations (CBOs) and Palestinian local institutions in reinforcing their emergency capacities by providing care centers to have the necessary equipment (NFI/hygiene) to fulfil their mission. The project is estimated to benefit a total of 6,350 individuals, 15 care centers and 20 CBOs and Local Government Units (LGUs). To ensure achieving this component, AAH will adopt the recently developed localization approach. It aims to ensure adopting AAH localization strategy of AAH and it objectives; Local actors rooted in knowledge and experience, National and Local actors cogenerate/co-construct with Action Against Hunger a mutual institutional capacity, leadership and influence aimed at addressing the needs, and support a people-centered approach and the participation of affected communities in addressing humanitarian needs.
 
It matches the Shelter framework, in line with the 2023 HNO, and directly support the Shelter Cluster objectives which are inline also with the HRP 2023 general objective, namely SO2 and SO3.

project_objective:

project_name: Appui au renforcement de la résilience des moyens d’existence des ménages agro pasteurs affectés par les changements climatiques  dans la bande sahélienne du Tchad
project_objective:
La situation pastorale est caractérisée par une bonne disponibilité de pâturages et d’eau d’abreuvement des animaux dans la quasi-totalité des zones sahéliennes et soudaniennes du pays. Cette situation d’abondance de pâturage et de l’eau améliore l’embonpoint des animaux.
La situation zoo sanitaire est relativement calme. On note également une descente précoce des transhumants surtout ceux de la zone de la province du Lac à cause de la remontée des eaux du Lac Tchad. Cela pourrait engendrer des conflits agriculteurs-éleveurs en cette période de récolte.
La production de biomasse moyenne à l’échelle du pays estimée en 2022 à 456.3 Mt de matière sèche est supérieure à la moyenne 1999 à 2022 qui est 418.0 Mt, soit une différence de +9.2%. Cette bonne production est observée sur quasiment l’ensemble du pays exceptés le sud agricole où elle est négative et le nord-nord-est, à la limite de la zone désertique, où les anomalies sont très négatives.
L’analyse produite par ACF dans le rapport de la biomasse laisse apparaître une bonne situation sur l’ensemble du pays avec des anomalie de production de biomasse positives avec des valeurs dépassant +2 σ sur toute la partie centre particulièrement les régions de Barth-El-Gazel, Batha et Ouaddai.

La situation nutritionnelle demeure préoccupante dans la plupart des provinces des zones sahélienne et saharienne. La médiane soudure de la série historique de cinq dernières enquêtes SMART (2017 à 2021), indique des taux de malnutrition aigüe globale (MAG) supérieurs au seuil d’urgence de l’OMS (15%) dans les provinces du Bahr El Ghazal, Batha, Borkou, Ennedi Est, Ennedi Ouest, Kanem, Ouaddaï, Guéra, Hadjer Lamis, Salamat, Sila  et Wadi Fira. Il faut noter que Les résultats de la dernière enquête SMART (DNTA/UNICEF, 2022) révèlent, au plan national, une prévalence de la Malnutrition Aiguë Globale (MAG) de 11% dont 2,1% sous la forme sévère (MAS). Cependant, les prévalences de la MAG sont au-dessus du seuil d’urgence de l’OMS (15%) dans les provinces de l’Ennedi Ouest (18,5%), Ennedi Est (17%), Bahr El Gazal (16,5%), Kanem (16,2%), Wadi-Fira (16,2%), Batha (16%) et du Salamat (15,5%).. De plus le dérèglement généralisé du fonctionnement de l’économie a engendré une situation d’insécurité alimentaire aigüe continue pour un nombre important des ménages les plus vulnérables ce qui pourrait entraîner une utilisation accrue de stratégies d'adaptation néfastes :
• Consommmation des aliments moins appréciés, moins chers ; 
• Réduction du nombre de repas par jour ; 
• Réduction du nombre de repas des adultes au profit des enfants.                                                                  L'adoption de ces stratégies alimentaires néfastes peut avoir un impact négatif sur la nutrition et l’allaitement des enfants.
Cette action permettra à la FAO de préserver ou reconstituer les moyens de subsistance des personnes en situation d’insécurité alimentaire et/ou victime de crises soudaines dans les provinces ciblées.

project_name: Appui à la résilience et à la protection des moyens d’existence des populations en insécurité alimentaire des régions de l’Est, de l’Adamaoua et du Nord.
Développement inclusif des zones d'accueil - Phase 2
project_objective:
L’objectif du nouveau programme DIZA-Est est l’amélioration des conditions de vie et de la résilience des populations autochtones, réfugiées et retournées dans les zones d’accueil, au travers d’appuis à la capacité de préparation et réponse aux chocs, au développement local inclusif, la prévention des conflits par l’amélioration de la cohésion pacifique et l’adaptation durable aux changements climatiques. Le programme vise à minimiser les facteurs contribuant aux tensions entre communautés, à l’instabilité et au risque d’accroissement des migrations forcées, et de renforcer la résilience et la cohabitation pacifique face aux aléas climatiques et aux conflits. Une intégration locale des réfugiés dans les communautés d'accueil sera ainsi rendue possible par le développement des opportunités économiques. Pour ce faire, le nouveau programme s'appuiera sur les apprentissages et les succès du DIZA-Est actuel et sur le renforcement de son approche pilote de l’adaptation face aux changements climatiques. Une mise à l’échelle des activités visera à améliorer les normes et les structures sociales équitables pour les femmes et les hommes.. 
Afin de sortir durablement les populations ciblées déplacées, réfugiés et populations hôtes du Ouaddaï, Wadi Fira et Sila des risques aux chocs et catastrophes et de l’extrême pauvreté, le programme DIZA 2 repose sur trois piliers fondateurs de l’approche Triple-Nexus : 
(i)	Réduction de la vulnérabilité face aux situations de crise et amélioration de la capacité de réponse aux chocs, facilitant l’accès des plus vulnérables à des ressources et à des informations stratégiques;
(ii)	le développement de la résilience économique et environnementale des communautés, 
afin de renforcer leur résilience économique et environnementale ;
(iii)	La sensibilité aux conflits de l’ensemble du programme et la prévention des conflits inter et intra-communautaire autour des ressources naturelles et des enjeux de genre et de VBG.

Cibles: Dans chaque province, entre 20 et 30 villages pourront être bénéficiaires du programme, pour un total de villages allant de 60 à 90 villages bénéficiaires. Il sera possible d’appuyer 6,000 ménages (très pauvres et pauvres) dans le trois provinces d’intervention.

project_name: Child Protection, Education, Health, Nutrition and WASH lifesaving supports to refugee children
project_objective: UNICEF in collaboration with relevant stakeholders is planning to provide lifesaving integrated and multispectral (Child protection, Education, WASH, Health and Nutrition) humanitarian assistance targeting South Sudanese and Ethiopian refugees in White Nile, Kassala, Gedaref, South Kordofan, West Kordofan, North Kordofan, Khartoum, Blue Nile, North Darfur, South Darfur, East Darfur and Central Darfur states. Integrated health and nutrition services under this project will focus on securing essential supplies, and scaling-up the provision of preventative and curative interventions. UNICEF will work with relevant humanitarian actors on the ground to maintain and strengthen the delivery of comprehensive package of primary health care services, community-based management of sever acute malnutrition (CMAM), infant and young child feeding (IYCF) counselling and micro-nutrient supplementation for mothers and children under-five years of age. We aim to reach total of 193,300 children and pregnant lasting women in 33 localities. The WASH interventions aim to reach the most vulnerable refugees’ communities with immediate, life-saving water supply, including water trucking and rehabilitation of existing water facilities, construction of new emergency water facilities, as well as operation and maintenance services. The project will reach approximately 500,000 people. The interventions are based on national WASH strategies with a focus on maximizing inter-agency, multi-sectoral, area-based opportunities, and addressing specific needs, socio-political dynamics and humanitarian presence. As majority of the refugees reside in temporary gathering sites, they are highly vulnerable and face various challenges including trauma, physically abuse, injuries; or loss of family members and personal belongings. Through this project, child protection services will target 50,630 people with focus on supporting case management, referral services for children and family tracing.

project_name: Integrated malnutrition prevention and treatment programme for refugees and local Bangladeshi Communities in Cox's Bazar
project_objective:
""WFP aims to contribute to a reduction in acute and chronic malnutrition rates, and an improvement in nutritional status among refugees and local Bangladeshi communities in Cox’s Bazar through the provision of curative and preventive nutrition services for children below 5 years and pregnant and lactating women (PLW).  WFP will implement its project interventions across 45 integrated nutrition facilities (INFs) in 33 camps, and 130 Community Nutrition Centres (CNCs) in the local Bangladeshi community in partnership with UNICEF, UNHCR and cooperating partners under the coordination of the Cox's Bazar nutrition sector. WFP will provide targeted supplementary feeding program (TSFP) for moderate acutely malnourished children 6-59 months and Pregnant and Lactating Women (PLW) to reduce morbidity and mortality associated with malnutrition in both the refugee camps and in the host community. A 200g daily ration of Super Cereal Plus (Wheat Soya Blend Plus -WSB++) will be provided for children 6-59 months; and 250g of Super Cereal ( Wheat Soya Blend -WSB+) and 16.66g of oil will be provided to PLW under TSFP.
An enhanced prevention of malnutrition package will be put in place to mitigate the increase in prevalence of acute and chronic malnutrition and its associated risks for mortality and morbidity and promote child development. In the camps, this includes provision of the blanket supplementary feeding programme (BSFP) for younger children 6-23 months and PLWs, and a nutrition sensitive e-voucher programme that allows older children (24-59 months) access to fresh fruits and vegetables aimed at enhancing their dietary diversity and promote growth monitoring and uptake of other complementary services at the INF. These children will receive a US$ 3  redeemable voucher. Social Behaviour Change Communication (SBCC) activities and utilization of tools that positively influence behaviour, knowledge, attitudes, and practice around nutrition will be conducted in both the refugee and host communities.
Active case finding through community screening, referral and follow up of malnourished children under five and pregnant and lactating women will be done. Additionally, growth monitoring and promotion for children 6-59 months will be part of the project interventions.
The underlying causes of malnutrition will be addressed through integration of nutrition sensitive approaches in ongoing general food assistance, school feeding, self-reliance, and livelihood interventions. 
WFP will promote the prevention of micronutrient deficiencies particularly anemia through the promotion of dietary diversification. 
WFP will conduct capacity strengthening for partners and stakeholders to improve capacity for implementation of nutrition specific and nutrition sensitive programming. 
WFP will support quantitative and qualitative nutrition assessments to ensure that nutrition programmes are tailormade according to the needs of the targeted populations. 
Project interventions will be adapted to ensure an inclusive approach to promote participation of women, men, older people, adolescent, people who have chronic health conditions and persons with disabilities. Additionally, protection mechanisms will be put in place including complaints and feedback mechanisms and help desks to ensure accountability to affected populations. ""

project_name: WFP Skills Development-Self-Reliance project for Rohingya refugees
project_objective: In 2023, based on the guidance and in line with the suggested curriculum model set by the Skills Development Sector, WFP will transition existing skills development activities into a Combination of foundation and technical trainings. Technical trainings includes TVET (Technical & vocational Education and Training) and upcycling project. WFP will be partner organization under Skills Development Sector and will contribute to the sector by participating in meeting and advocate for portable skills for refugees along with other agencies under its sector. The activities will be conducted in close coordination with the Government of Bangladesh, in particular with RRRC and CiCs for field operation and with other stakeholders in camps (i.e. SWM, FSS). As much as possible, the project also will consider social cohesion between intra-community and refugee and host communities by  i.e. having materials produced at camp to be further add value at host community livelihoods.

project_name: Improved Access to Gender-based Violence Response and Prevention Services for Host Community and Rohingya Refugees in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh
project_objective:
DRC will aim to continue GBV prevention and response programming to reduce the underlying causes and drivers of gender violence and continue providing specialized GBV case management services aimed at providing immediate support to the acute needs of survivors of GBV, including non-specialized psychosocial support, dignity kit distributions and referrals to specialized services. DRC's Response programming will be complemented with interventions aimed at preventing GBV by changing mindsets and harmful attitudes and practices within the community that result in violence against gender.  Wherever appropriate, DRC will seek to strengthen synergies with other protection areas (CP and GP) and between protection and non-protection sectors. This will include building capacities of GBV case workers on CP risks/case management principles, providing training to non-protection staff on GBV mainstreaming, identification and referral of GBV cases. 

Under this project, DRC will address the activities in Camp 6, 8E and Palongkhali, Rajapalong unions from the host community. DRC is committed to ensuring its GBV programming is relevant, appropriate and does not cause harm. DRC will also participate in safety audits for CM conducted from the GBVSS to ensure the services are provided adhering to the GBV guiding principles. Accordingly, protection monitoring activities will be strengthened to ensure more consistent documentation of risks including GBV. DRC also intends to strengthen an AGD approach to data collection to ensure information on risks can be disaggregated by age, gender and diversity profiles including survivors with disabilities and at a later stage hijra and other sexual minorities. DRC GBV team will also extend lifesaving case management services for women and girls, male survivors, gender diverse population, and child survivors in the aforementioned camps and host community. 

DRC will provide outreach sessions and psychosocial support for women and girls in Camp 6 and 2 unions (Rajapalong and Palongkhali union) from host community. Besides, DRC will continue to operate Hizra safe space in Palongkhali. Men and boy engagement activities will also be scaled up in selected areas. DRC will continue to involve the beneficiaries in each stage of planning and implementation for identifying the needs, vulnerabilities, priorities, and coping mechanisms. In all locations, outreach will be designed to make services more inclusive for persons with disabilities and the gender diverse population with specialized outreach and participation modules by focusing on protection mainstreaming in each stage. 

DRC GBV technical expertise will be available to build the capacity of local GBV actors, including local authorities and local NGOs based on tailored needs assessments, and PSEA will also be shared through training. DRC has already an established PSEA mechanism which will be further strengthened by providing training to volunteers and raising awareness on the reporting mechanism. Also, DRC will continue to develop and map a partnership strategy by linking government, local NGOs, and private organizations and aligning the ISCG sector strategies for mainstreaming the activities. DRC will diversify the service accessibility fund in place for contingency needs. A hotline for case management support will be available throughout the year. The selection of locations is based on an analysis of GBV-SS mapping and complements DRC’s other sectoral program. DRC will set up CFRM in the host locations and direct to DRC CoC or CFRM as appropriate in refugee camps for AAP.

project_name: Enhanced Decent and Resilience Livelihoods of Rohingya Refugee and Host communities in Cox’s Bazar
project_objective:
In 2023 DRC will have been integrating both its global strategy and country strategy into this joint response plan to enhances coordination with livelihoods and skill development sector (LSDS), the newly establish sector, in the field. Through this project, DRC will aim to contribute to enhancing the decent and resilient livelihoods to the selected Rohingya and host community people towards the effects of climatic change, environmental degradation, and natural disasters through overall protection services which specifically includes livelihood and skill building on green agriculture, vocational training, cash/grants assistances and climate sensitive innovative interventions for Rohingya men and women under economic recovery. Training will be provided with standard curriculum /module aligned with sector guidance with the support from  hiring experts and government line agencies skilled trainer. The qualified  and interested trained people will receive  relevant inputs and cash grants  by DRC to utilize the gained knowledge for income earnings . DRC will provide  some market development and linkage training to make the enterprise more market healthy and  link them with bigger market actors and financial bodies ,where applicable ( Host only). Backstopping services will also be ensured throug DRC and sectoral support at Camps and host level.During this project targeted both Host and camps communities will be benefited and increase the relationship among them by getting economic benefits.

DRC will aim to address the project in Camp 5, Camp 8E and Jalipalong, Palong Khali and Rajaplong union under host community. Under skill development initiatives, DRC will focus on improving the skill and awareness on livelihoods and emphasis will be given to strengthen the institutional capacity of the community-based organizations/community groups on market systems approach- business plan, entrepreneurship development, women friendly market space identification and improvement through renovation work. At individual level, DRC will ensure inclusive and locally accepted livelihood skills and aim to improve the skills and awareness for adapting climate smart green agriculture and eco system-based adaptation practices, bamboo made handicrafts production, land stabilization through plantation, soil conservation, re/construction of community livelihood assets through mobilizing cash for workers. Under green agriculture a good number of Rohingya women and host community women will increase their skill and knowledge on vertical gardening, compost prepartion and using in their garden. DRC will also initiate technical capacity building of the community volunteers, CBO representatives, implementing partners and relevant field officials of government technical agencies on conservation, green technologies and CBOs sustainability approach for better services. The selected vulnerable Rohingya women through providing skills training and in kind and cash support to start and continue their small-scale business will be another small intervention under livelihood support. 

Apart from Rohingya, vulnerable host community households will also receive unconditional cash grant support as per Cash working group guidance to cope with the recent price hike shocks. The Livelihoods team will continue to support the most vulnerable and marginalized individuals such as FFH,PWD, transgender, survivors of GBV, through cash grants and livelihood inputs such as cattle, poultry, sewing machine, vegetable seeds, nursery plants.  Last but not the least, DRC will establish strong linkage and coordination with government and other actors in camps and host by developing capacity of local volunteers and community-based organizations. Besides, DRC will closely coordinate with the District Commissioner, RRRC, sectors, Food Security Cluster and other agencies to ensure alignment with govt. rules and align the intervention in line with sustainability nexus.

project_name: MHPSS intervention to mitigate self-harm and risky behaviors undertaken by Palestinians in southern communities of the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Gaza Strip.
project_objective:
In line with the strategic objectives, priority needs, and most vulnerable populations established by the Health Cluster and HNO, and considering the regular SWOT analysis conducted as part of our standard project cycle management procedures, as well as the periodic need assessments and risk analysis conducted by our staff and its experience in the area of operation, in addition to the feedback of the beneficiaries of our intervention and our partners, the main outcome of this intervention is to improve access to non-specialised and specialised cross-sectoral prevention and emergency care services at the community and health care level for adults and children experiencing suicidal ideations and behaviours in Palestine, considering two main outputs: 1) Adults and Children presenting suicidal ideation and behaviours are detected and referred at community and medical services levels at an early stage and are provided with an ad hoc support plan that includes access to support services; 2) Suicide, as a major public health concern, is addressed through national and international awareness and advocacy efforts. 
  
Data collected in 2021 showed that 25-38% of households have at least one member reporting self-diagnosed mental distress. In addition, PCBS (2019) reports 29% of Women in oPt had experienced violence (psychological, sexual, economical), 9.1% of these women would need specialized MHPSS services beside protection services. According to last WHO´s fact sheets on adolescents, 13% of children and adolescents experience mental disorders. If untreated, these conditions severely influence children’s development, facing major challenges with stigma, isolation, and discrimination, as well as lack of access to health care and education facilities 43% of the Palestinian population are children and adolescents and there is a need to strengthen mental health services provided to them. A 2019 mixed study conducted by MdM-CH on the risk factors of attempted suicide patients in the WB found that 52% of the total attempted suicide patients were youth, ages 16-25 years old. COVID-19 enlarges this group to include infected patients, as the virus causes various mental and neurological complications. The project proposes activities based on the objectives mentioned above, aiming to: 
 
1. Increase the capacities of medical staff and communities for the proper detection and referral of vulnerable cases to specialized MHPSS services, through specific actions at institutional (hospitals and PHCs/CMHCs) and community level (CBOs and religious leaders) through the implementation of tailored trainings in coordination with the MoH. 
 
2. Integrate MHPSS services at Primary Health Care Centres (PHCs) / Community Mental Health Centres (CMHCs) to better detect, respond, and refer risky behaviours by emphasizing on mhGap intervention, with special attention to the provision of care for youth. 
 
3. Enhance the capacities of Emergency hotlines in detecting, supporting, and referring people presenting self-harm and risky behaviours. 
 
4. Support or update of the mapping of service providers (Health, MHPSS and Protection - PWD & GBV) done by other actors. 
 
5. Promote psycho-education and awareness raising about youth vulnerability (especially girls & PWD) with regards to self-harm, risky behaviours and stigmatization of suicide, involving CBOs, religious leaders, and schools. 
 
The project will coordinate with the MoH, the Health Cluster, the WHO and other partners working on suicide prevention and management, to consolidate efforts and complement the work already done. The project activities will be implemented in the WB (Area A, B, C, H2), EJ and the GS, in an effort to reach people in need of MHPSS interventions geared to the needs of women, adolescents, ex detainees, GBV victims, people presenting suicidal ideations or behaviours and PWDs in the most vulnerable and marginalized communities.
