project_name: Fostering the realization of social cultural and economic rights of vulnerable persons (persons with disabilities, women and older persons) in Syria.
project_objective:
Conflict-affected populations struggle to get access to humanitarian assistance and essential services in an inclusive and equal manner. Vulnerabilities associated with Disability, Gender, and Age (DGA) have been heightened by the conflict. PwDs are highly affected by the crisis and have a right to receive services equally with others. Children, women, and older persons are at a higher risk of exclusion. The project will work removing barriers to provide access to inclusive humanitarian assistance, reduce vulnerability and improve access of persons with disabilities, mainly women with disabilities and older persons. INGO will work to enable persons with disabilities to participate on an equal basis with others, on accessing services through provision of community approach, technical guidance for actors and reasonable accommodation for individuals (individualized support). Specifically, we are building the capacities of humanitarian organizations to be inclusive in their activities as well as building their capacities to better engage with humanitarian structures and organisations. Also, INGO will provide personalised social support and case management to PwDs as well as conducting community awareness sessions on including PwDs. As part of its work, INGO conduct barriers assessments to understand what prevents PwDs from participating on an equal basis with others. Our latest assessments found that humanitarian actors and NGO’s can lack the following: i) understanding of how to identify people with disabilities  ii) clarity regarding the human rights of persons with disabilities; iii) human, operational and financial resources to provide inclusive and accessible services and we also found that people with disabilities themselves are rarely included in the program design, provision and evaluation of service provision and the delivery of the humanitarian assistance. Moreover, there are negative beliefs, attitudes and practices limiting the participation of PwDs in social life at the community and family level. 
Based on this assessment, the INGO action focuses on providing guidance on how to include persons with disabilities mainly women within humanitarian assistance and to overcome risks of increasing vulnerability, as well as working to empower persons with disabilities to know their rights, having the confidence and the right tools needed to actively engage and play a key role within the Humanitarian Programme  Cycle (HPC). As part of this effort there will be activities operationalizing the IASC guidelines on the inclusion of persons with disabilities in humanitarian action  
The INGO acknowledges, among other factors generating inequalities and that need to be considered, that disability, gender and age as socially constructed norms can be observed in any human group, Disability, Gender, and age are key factors to understanding different people’s capacities, needs, and exposure to risks. The impact of inclusion is not only through the direct targets, we rely on increasing the understanding of disability, gender, and age vulnerability risks, within communities, humanitarian actors, clusters, working groups and persons with disabilities themselves which will lead to the inclusion of PWD, older persons and women with disabilities in social, cultural and socio-economic activities. Moreover, empowerment and support persons with disabilities to participate through the project cycle will set an example of good practice for clusters and working groups who will be targeted within this project. Trained persons with disabilities will target wider communities, improving inclusion principles. Another target is the increase of the percentage of persons with disabilities through actor's projects. For example, for partners who will be trained, we are aiming to increase the percentage of PWD they target within their own projects up to 30% (the average percentage of PWD) as some of our partners only target between 10%-15% only.

project_name: Restoring resilience and improving socio-economic well-being of people, local actors and communities in Syria.
project_objective:
This intervention takes a participatory, community-based approach to recovery programming, ensuring market-sensitive livelihoods is provided to vulnerable Syrian households. Increased income, assets and consumption hold the key to promoting an increase in individual economic well-being. Social well-being stems from human capital and positive social relations. The vocational training and on-the-job training or apprenticeships are provided to persons with disabilities, youth and women, who will be offered a selection of enterprise and employment pathways. For those seeking to set up their own small/micro enterprise, a further package of business skills training and business grant will be provided based on their business proposition. Moreover, vocational training graduates are supported to seek employment with small-medium businesses. All skills trainings are identified based on a rigorous assessment of labor market to ensure addressing local sectors of economic growth, gaps in skills, barriers facing persons with disabilities accessing livelihood opportunities and women’s role in the market. Small and micro-business owners whose business has been negatively affected by conflict are supported to relaunch their businesses through a combination of skills, business grants and coaching. Business trainings are provided, particularly for those new to labor market such as youth, women & persons with disabilities. Moreover, Cash for Work schemes are identified to provide benefit to the entire community. Community acceptance for targeted livelihoods activities is ensured through community participation in selection of types of businesses needed in community, beneficiary selection and monitoring project progress. Whether directly or through the potential partnership with other livelihood actors, the Inclusion of persons with disabilities mainly women with disabilities will be ensured through using twin track approach, the logic of intervention will combine a package of activities aimed at empowering persons with disabilities and building more inclusive and accessible working environment at community level. Activities will be based on assessment of barriers faced by persons with disabilities. While the organization will conduct several actions to overcome barriers such as awareness raising on persons with disabilities rights, tailored case management support, and intensive coaching support. Participation of women will be supported through awareness and advocacy with their families, provision of female trainers and skills training for home-based businesses.
Complementary services such as Psychosocial Support (PSS) will be provided based on community needs & vulnerability assessments. The organization provides technical support to other livelihoods agencies to ensure the design and implementation take an inclusive approach and that they provide persons with disabilities with equitable access. This support also includes guidance on the meaningful engagement of older persons and women in activities.

project_name: Improve the Health Status of Conflict-Affected People in Northwest Syria
project_objective:
Our organization aims to improve access to basic preventive and curative health care services for internally displaced and conflict-affected populations in targeted areas in NWS through the provision of life-saving emergency, primary, and secondary health care services including sexual and reproductive healthcare and  cases and those in need of more specialized medical services.  The supported PHCs will provide primary health care services including treatment of common acute and chronic illnesses and injuries; the provision of essential medicines including contraceptives and treatment for chronic diseases; and management of mental health services. Programs will be delivered through support to two maternity and child hospitals and twelve static primary healthcare clinics. four ambulances will also provide transportation for emergency communicable and non-communicable diseases and health education. The PHCs will also provide basic reproductive health services including antenatal care, post-natal care, family planning, and syndromic management of STIs. PHCs will operate a referral system for cases to secondary and tertiary service hospitals. Health activities will maintain and ensure sustaining and expanding essential, quality health services within communities through primary and secondary health care to meet the needs of the most vulnerable groups to both IDPs and host communities. In addition, the community health care workers will provide health education and referrals for a wide range of services, support and assist communities, families, and individuals with preventive health measures, and gain access to appropriate curative health and social services. The maternity and new-born care hospitals will provide Comprehensive Emergency Obstetric and New-bornCare (CEmONC) and outpatient reproductive services including antenatal, postnatal care, and family planning. The organization will support 7 oral rehydration points ORPs to be able to respond to cholera outbreak and treat the suspected cases properly 
Our organization will provide support to twelve static PHCs (Atmeh PHC 1,G0703003), (Atmeh PHC 2, G0703004 ), (Atmeh PHC 3,G0703100 ), (Green Idleb PHC,G0700002  ), (Kafr Yahmol PHC,G0700007  ), (Abi Zar PHC, G0700034),( Souran PHC, B0204038), (Zoghra PHC,B0208011 ),( Bzagha PHC,B0202016 ), (Mhamble PHC, G0705035), Al Zof PHC  and (Al Rayan PHC, B0204044) in addition to tow maternity and newborn hospitals, Al Zahrawi MCH (G0700093) and Afrin MCH (B0203079)

project_name: Integrated Nutrition project in North West Syria
project_objective:
The malnutrition situation continues to deteriorate in NWS, the main drivers include poverty, low socioeconomic status, unsafe living conditions and diseases, suboptimal maternal, infant, and young child feeding (MIYCF) practices, and high rates of maternal malnutrition. The economic downturn and depreciation of the Syrian Pound in addition to the impact of COVID-19 in NWS had an intensifying effect on the staggering results. In response to the identified need, NGO X will implement the following package of activities which will benefit 37,800  individuals 
1.	Provide community-based one-to-one counselling on WHO recommended Infant and Young Child Feeding and maternal nutrition practices.
2.	Provision of specialized nutritious food (LNS) to children 6-59 months 
3.	Early identification and referral of Acute Malnutrition cases in PLW and children 6-59 months 
4.	Provision of supplementary assistance via e-vouchers for households with PLW and/or children under 2 years to access nutritious foods
MIYCF messaging and counselling is a component in varying delivery methods including posters, group sessions and household visits. Family MUAC Approach (FMA) is also included on group and individual levels, providing the caregivers MUAC tapes and the nearest functioning nutrition services for self-referral where needed. Screening and referral by the nutrition staff will be provided at household visits. 
Ongoing activities  blanket distribution of LNS-SQ for children 6-59 months for 6 rounds (months), coupled with MIYCF and FMA activities, to address micronutrient deficiencies and malnutrition. This is implemented in Maaret Tmasrin in Idleb and Azaz, Aghtrin, Suran, and Jandairis in Aleppo. MIYCF messaging and counselling in addition to FMA and screening, through household visits and group sessions will be implemented in Armanaz, Qourqeena, Darkoush in Idleb and Azaz in Aleppo. 
A planned intervention will provide 5 rounds of e-vouchers for households with PLW and/or children under 2 years to access nutritious foods as they are the most vulnerable, have the highest malnutrition rates, and are within the 1,000 days window of opportunity. These HHs will also receive counselling on MIYCF practices to support healthier decisions for nutrition outcomes. This will be implemented in Azaz, Aleppo and Maaret Tmasrin, Idleb.
The project targets the most vulnerable populations living in camps, with a focus on women and children within the following categories: caregivers of children 6-59 months of reproductive age, and pregnant and lactating women. Adolescent and youth (10-24 years) are not targeted directly but included if they fall within the previously mentioned categories. 
All projects will follow SPHERE standards, cluster SOPs, and internal SOPs and regulations. A set of indicators are in place to track progress according to standards and to report on 4W indicators to the cluster on monthly basis. Monitoring is conducted by the M&E team and by third party monitoring, at point of activity/distribution and 3-4 weeks after to assess the quality, usefulness and retention of assistance and information shared. Evaluations includes a base and end line assessment TPM will share reports upon completion of the project. 
NGO X will be implementing this project directly, and 50% of funding has already been secured from multiple different donor sources.

project_name: Multi-disciplinary rehabilitation and mental health-psychosocial support services for conflict affected populations and support to health structures in Syria.
project_objective: The project aims at reducing vulnerability and improving physical and mental well-being of crisis-affected population with particular attention to specific vulnerabilities linked to Disability, Gender, and Age (DGA). The INGO action focuses on providing multidisciplinary rehabilitation services tailored to the needs of people with physical impairment and their caregivers through direct intervention or through the support of local partners in North-West, North-East and GoS-controlled parts of Syria. The intervention includes provision of multidisciplinary rehabilitation services and psychosocial support services to physical rehabilitation beneficiaries and their caregivers. Furthermore, to ensure continuity of the tailored treatment plans, remote follow up services are provided through tele rehabilitation/tele-PSS sessions in case of movement restrictions, due to COVID-19 or existing gender norms. These services help in recovery of physical rehabilitation beneficiaries and support the caregivers through a holistic approach in order to alleviate stress, fatigue and other psychological impacts related to their responsibilities. The project improve access to services through referral, accessibility work in health structures, training of (female) rehabilitation staff and integration of the community through Self-Help Groups, which will increase resilience of beneficiaries and services provided, awareness raising sessions and mobile outreach to increase access for IDPs, underserved communities and persons who are incapable of reaching the service centers. The INGO also mainstreams COVID-19 key messaging in the activities package according to WHO Guidelines. In GoS- controlled areas and NWS the intervention includes the provision of mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services to people suffering from psychological distress without having physical rehabilitation needs. MHPSS services include psychological first aid, psycho education, and individual and/or group session therapy. Across whole of Syria including GoS controlled areas, the INGO focuses on developing rehabilitation services in areas where services are not available. Concerning DGA mainstreaming, all activities and delivered services are prepared based on a rapid assessment to study the sensitivity of the context and ensure inclusion according to DGA. This includes the promotion of equal opportunities for people with different needs and abilities. In North-West conditional cash for transportation is also provided to patients and caregivers according to individual assessed needs based on pre-defined criteria. The INGO closely coordinate with the Cash working group in the targeted hub to align the common standards and guidance. Conditional cash will be provided to patients and/or caregivers based on individual assistance and the INGO criteria taking into account socioeconomic, travel, and clinical factors. The health staff assess the needs case by case based on predefined criteria. The cash is conditioned to the attendance of patient to the treatment sessions aiming to ensure the rationalization of the treatment plan. Acknowledging the dire economic situation in WoS, where possible close linkages with other actors are envisaged to support beneficiaries accessing unconditional cash and support actors to enhance inclusion within CVA programs. The INGO provides support to its local health partners through technical, financial and managerial support, to improve the quality of services and ensure the sustainability of impact of the project. The capacity building support is tailored to the needs of partners. The Inclusion specialist support the health clusters, by guiding through several session on how to implement DGA inclusion principles, how to identify vulnerability risks of persons with disabilities, setting indicators on data for identification of persons with disabilities. In addition to trainings related to understanding needs of PwD including Women.

project_name: Provision of humanitarian WASH assistance and improving basic WASH infrastructure in IDP sites in northwest Syria.
project_objective:
The project aims to support the WASH response of the most vulnerable displaced populations in Northwest Syria through implementing the following set of activities: 
i)	Provision of emergency WASH services to 50 IDP sites (informal camps, planned camps, and reception centres) in 2023, regularly supporting 100,000 individuals in 2023. Activities include the provision of water services, solid waste management, faecal sludge management, , care and maintenance of latrines, provision of water storage tanks, garbage containers, and WASH NFI kits, as well as hygiene promotion, capacity building and community engagement sessions. (Activity 2.1 and 2.2)
ii)	Construction/rehabilitation of sewage networks, including the construction of septic tanks to provide an initial treatment of wastewater produced in informal camps. This specific intervention will target 15 informal IDP sites in 2023, supporting 30,000 individuals in 2023. (Activity 1.3)
iii)	Enhanced water quality assurance, operation, and maintenance of water supply systems through the provision of solar energy in 10 IDP sites in 2023, supporting 22,000 individuals in 2023 (Activity 1.2)
iv)	Provision of WASH services and rehabilitation of WASH facilities in 18 health facilities in 2023, supporting 100,000 individuals in 2023. (Activity 4.2)
Overall, the project will contribute to the following strategic objectives 1,2 and 4 set out by the WASH Cluster.

project_name: Improving Access to WASH Services for Disaster Affected Populations in Upper Nile, Northern Bahr El Ghazal, Warrap and Western and Central Equatoria in South Sudan
project_objective:
In South Sudan, only 36 per cent of households reported having access to an improved water source in under 30 minutes without facing any protection concerns. The remaining 64 per cent of people across the country rely on unimproved or surface water sources (41 per cent), either take more than 30 minutes to reach an improved water source (19 per cent), or are able to reach an improved source in less than 30 minutes but face protection concerns while accessing the water (4 per cent). The highest proportion of households relying on surface water were found in Upper Nile, with 66 per cent, followed by Jonglei with 43 per cent and Central Equatoria with 41 per cent. The quantity of water available per day is also below standards in many locations, with 17 per cent of people unable to collect enough water for drinking, and 39 per cent of people reporting insufficient access to water for hand washing.
Access to sanitation remained low, with only 17 per cent of households reporting owning a latrine in their compound, 4 per cent have access to a shared latrine, and 2 per cent have access to a communal/institutional latrine. This means that 77 per cent of people do not have access to a latrine. In 34 counties, zero to 10 per cent of households reported using latrines. At the country level, open defecation is practiced by 73 per cent of the population.
Regional access to sanitation varied greatly, from 75 per cent in Western Bahr el Ghazal to 8 per cent in Warrap, 9 per cent in Northern Bahr el Ghazal and 10 per cent in Jonglei; 
Poor access to WASH services combined with high levels of food insecurity continue to have a detrimental impact on the health of children, as seen through the high prevalence of malnutrition and water-borne diseases. Counties reporting high GAM rates have also high WASH needs. Mothers and care takers of malnourished children lack basic hygiene knowledge and access to safe water at domicile jeopardizing the benefits again.in nutrition programs, WVISS intends to reach the IPDs and Host community with an integrated WASH intervention which will target the population of Upper Nile (Melut, Renk, Malakal, Kodok, Baliet, Panikang counties), Western Equatoria (Yambio, Nzara, Ezo, Nagero, Tambura), Northern Bahr El Ghazal (Aweil North and East) Warrap ( Twic, Tonj North, Gogrial West and Gogrial East), and Central Equatoria (Juba) states. The proposed project by WVISS is aiming to achieve the following specific objectives: Vulnerable people who experience multi-sectoral severity levels of 4 and 5 have reduced morbidity and mortality through equitable and dignified access to critical cross-sectoral essential services to meet their needs.  Vulnerable people are exposed to fewer protection threats and incidents, and those who are exposed have access to tailored, timely, appropriate services through integrated and inclusive humanitarian action. Vulnerable people withstand and recover from shocks, have their resilience to shocks and stresses built, and seek solutions that respect their rights.
To realize the WASH cluster objectives, WVISS will provide lifesaving WASH emergency interventions in the targeted Counties in  (Melut, Renk, Malakal, Kodok, Baliet, Panikang counties), Western Equatoria (Yambio, Nzara, Ezo, Nagero, Tambura), Northern Bahr El Ghazal (Aweil North and East) Warrap ( Twic, Tonj North, Gogrial West and Gogrial East), and Central Equatoria (Juba) states.  The WASH emergency interventions will improve access to safe water, secured and gender appropriate sanitation facilities and hygiene promotion, which will be integrated in other sectors, among them health, nutrition, Food security and livelihood, and child protection/ GBV.

project_name: Emergency Child Protection, GBV & Mine Action: Prevention, Mitigation & Response to assist IDPs, Returnees and Host Communities in conflict-affected & high risk areas of Warrap, Upper Nile, Western Equatoria and Central Equatoria States, South Sudan
project_objective:
The already high needs of critical child protection services in South Sudan has been exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic, protracted displacement, and limited access to basic services which continues to significantly affect the physical, mental, and social well-being of children, adolescents and caregivers. This situation has been worsened by the limited availability of mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services and the low level of core child protection services, including family tracing and reunification, case management, and reintegration services for children affected by armed forces and groups, leaving many children untreated and unable to access the needed services. Climate shocks, severe drought, massive flooding, and conflicts have contributed to the increase in GBV risks in the country which requires to strengthen GBV case management, psychosocial support, legal service, livelihood, economic support, GBV referral pathways and to integrate GBV into other sectoral responses. The high contamination with landmines and explosive remnants of war (ERW), especially in the Greater Equatoria region, along major supply routes and areas for returnees from Uganda, and the increase in expected returns require to prevent, mitigate and respond to mine risk issues through enhanced preparedness and resilience.
This proposed integrated CP, GBV and EORE project is in line with the Protection Cluster Objectives and will ensure the provision of critical protection-related assistance and specialized services and the prevention and mitigation of Protection risks through enhanced preparedness. The project targets to reach an average of 60,000 (20,000 women, 20,000 men, 10,000 girls, 10,000 men) (CP), 50,000 (20,000 women, 10,000 men, 10,000 girls, 10,000 boys) (GBV) and 20,000 (5000 men, 5000 women, 5000 girls, 5000 boys) (MA) including people with disabilities.
Using the 2023 Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP), World Vision International South Sudan (WVI-SS) aims to reach the most vulnerable populations in 11 counties in Warrap, Upper Nile, Western Equatoria and Central Equatoria States with improved access to quality lifesaving child protection for vulnerable girls, boys, men and women including children with disabilities who are at risk of mortality and morbidity and protection incidents/threats. Through the provision of specialized / lifesaving child protection and multi sectoral services WVI-SS seeks to reduce the suffering of boys, girls, women and men including children with disabilities who are at risk or experience violence, abuse, exploitation and neglect including GBV.
The proposed project will reduce the suffering of GBV survivors including women, men, girls, boys and people with disabilities by providing multi-sectoral specialized GBV response services. Furthermore, WVI-SS seeks to ensure that vulnerable women, men, girls, boys including people with disabilities have improved access to the provision of GBV prevention and risk mitigation interventions. Through protection monitoring, advocacy, awareness-raising and prevention and response services the project aims to reduce the vulnerability of women, men, girls and boys including people with disabilities at increased risk of mortality and morbidity and protection incidents/threats in priority areas.
In line with the Core Humanitarian Standards, WVI-SS will maintain its commitment to engage with affected communities at all phases of the project cycle, through focus group discussions with women, men, boys and girls. Establishing/strengthening local structures such as Project Management Committee is one example of how WVI-SS engages the community in a sustainable and accountable manner to determine and support appropriate need-based responses. WVI's Quality Assurance framework ensures that each project implemented is carried out effectively and continually reviewed in line with community needs and in line with other humanitarian frameworks.

project_name: Improving Access to Lifesaving Integrated Emergency Primary Healthcare Services to IDPs and Host Communities in the States of Warrap, Upper Nile and Western Equatoria, in South Sudan
project_objective: Through the 2023 Humanitarian Response Plan, World Vision International (WVI) South Sudan will provide emergency lifesaving health interventions which will be integrated with nutrition, WASH, protection and FSL activities. The approaches shall revolve around mobile clinics in hard-to-reach areas primary healthcare and secondary healthcare at the static sites and emergency health intervention which will include sexual gender-based violence (SGBV), clinical management of rape (CMR), mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS). Owing to the high mortality rate of under 5 children (90.7/1000), maternal mortality rate (789 deaths/100,000 live births) in South Sudan, World Vision will provide also maternal and child health interventions, mainly skilled birth attendance, prevention of post -partum hemorrhage, ante natal care, post-natal care, basic and comprehensive emergency neonatal and obstetrical care (EMNOC), Sexual and Reproductive Health/ family planning service and Expanded Programme Immunization (EPI) and quality management of Severe Acute Malnutrition with medical complication and community health care through the Boma Health Initiative. The Boma Health Workers (BHWs) shall be trained to provide health promotion, treatment of CU5 for the three common causes of morbity and mortality (malaria, pneumonia, diarrhoea) and identification and referral of severe cases to the nearest health facility for treatment. Additionally, World Vision will ensure that there is continuum of care for under 5 with SAM and MAM so that they have access to OTP and TSFP facilities run by nutrition partners, including World Vision who is a provider of Community Based Management of Acute Malnutrition (CMAM) and Maternal Infant Young Child Nutrition (MIYCN) practice. World Vision will ensure that people with disabilities and mental disorders have priority access to emergency health services and are included as vulnerable groups owing to their high-risk during emergencies. The response plan will be prioritized based on epidemiological status and disease outbreaks, cholera hot spot locations, measles outbreaks, malaria seasonality. The emergency lifesaving response will be done in line with the recommended health cluster emergency clinical services package for primary healthcare units, primary healthcare centers, county hospital, mobile medical team, and Boma Health Initiative. These interventions will be in line with the South Sudan Ministry of Health’s policies and guidelines, named as the basic package of health and nutrition services, Boma Health Initiative, sexual and reproductive health, immunization guidelines and health policy of the Republic of South Sudan. This project plans to reach a total population of 100,000 (51,000F, 49,000 M), 21,000 (10,290M, 10710F) children aged below 5years and 1000 (490M, 510F) persons with disabilities with a budget of approximately USD 2,895,000 over a period of one year.

project_name: Emergency food security and livelihood support in response to food crisis and flooding in Jonglei State and GPAA, 2023
project_objective: This emergency response project aims to serve 55,000 individuals from disaster-affected households in IPC 4/5 in Jonglei state with cash/voucher assistance to meet their immediate food and nutrition needs, and also inputs and training to help them to recover their livelihoods.

project_name: Provision of Life-Saving Health and MHPSS Assistance to displaced populations, returnees and host communities in South Sudan
project_objective:
The protracted conflict in South Sudan coupled with the 3 year unprecedented flooding and intercommunal violence has left left 8.9 million South Sudanese in need of Humanitarian assistance in 2022 (Draft HNO 2022). Additional shocks levied by the COVID-19 pandemic and on-going epidemic disease outbreaks including measles, cholera and Hepatitis E have further stretched existing coping mechanisms and increased vulnerabilities. Inspite of the many challenges, IOM's DTM have reported a mixed population flow reflecting increasing returns of IDPs and refugees in some of the counties including Raja, Morobo and Kajokeji counties.  Health service delivery for vulnerable populations remains heavily reliant on humanitarian assistance. In locations such as Abyei, Unity, Upper Nile, Jonglei, western Equatoria, Warrap, Northern Bar el Ghazal and western Bar el Ghazal where the International Organization for Migration, IOM has been providing life-saving humanitarian assistance to internally displaced persons (IDPs), returnees, and host communities in conflict-affected and hard-to-reach locations across South Sudan, populations remain displaced in IDP camps or far off hard-to-reach locations due to flooding. IOM's life-saving health and MHPSS support to vulnerable IDPs and host community in Abyei, Wau, Rubkhona and Malakal counties and through deployment of 16 Rapid Response Missions in 2022 to crisis affected and IPC4 and IPC5 locations of Fangak, Panyijar, Twic East, Bor South, Abyei, Aweil East, Aweil Center, Aweil West, Aweil South, Gogrial West, terekeka and Juba among others has by epi-week 45 reached a total of over 2,196,659 beneficiaries including 520,726 outpatient consultations, 107,221 routine measles, BCG and DTP3 dozes and 7,372 assisted facility based deliveries in 2022. Through its Rapid Response Teams, IOM conducted 2 rounds of Oral cholera vaccination campaigns in Rubkona county and supported OCV vaccination campaigns in Malakal POC and within Juba town and Munuki Payams of Juba County to reach a total of 502,058 individuals above one year of age whilst supporting the emergency response mechanism to reach a total of 381,536 children with reactive measles vaccination in 11 out of 15 affected counties in the country. In 2023, IOM will target 1,277,947 beneficiaries including 191,692 persons with disabilities so as to continue to provide integrated emergency life-saving primary health care, including outpatient consultations, routine immunization, nutrition screening for children under five years, sexual reproductive health services, clinical case management of sGBV survivors including psychosocial support while increasing surveillance and response to disease outbreaks to underserved and conflict-affected IDPs, returnees, migrants/travelers, and host communities. 

IOM will provide health services through 15 static and 25 mobile clinics, while maintaining its comparative advantage in rapidly deploying rapid response teams to address emerging health needs throughout the country. MHPSS services will be provided through existing recreational and counselling centers and will deploy rapid response teams (RRT) to any areas across South Sudan facing acute man-made or natural disasters with unmet health needs. 
IOM will focus on leveraging existing community systems for sustainable solutions and strengthening both community-based health initiatives and mental health and psychosocial support. Therefore, IOM will provide direct service delivery in partnership with the respective county health departments, while continuing to explore options of partnerships with local NGOs and CBOs towards realizing the localization agenda of the health cluster. MHPSS will utilize static and mobile service in coordination with key humanitarian and developmental partners so as to avoid overlaps and ensure accountability to affected populations.

project_name: Provision of Integrated, quality, life-saving Inpatient nutrition Interventions for Severe Acute Malnutrition with Medical Complication for the most vulnerable in South Sudan
project_objective:
Through the Humanitarian Response Plan Project (HRP) 2023, the World Health Organization aims to contribute towards the reduction of prevalence of acute malnutrition in South Sudan by the end of 2023. South Sudan continues to experience the effects of prolonged conflict, and ongoing subnational violence in most parts of the country, coupled with climatic shocks, these have contributed to increased level of acute food insecurity and malnutrition. About 6.6 Million people are currently food insecure, and the situation is expected to worsen in the lean season (April-July 2023) where an estimated 7.76 Million people will be food insecure with 1.4 Million (345,893 of the children under 5) are expected to suffer from severe acute malnutrition by June 2023. South Sudan suffers from a general deficiency in service level availability across all sectors due to poor performance of the economy characterized by low production and limited access to essential goods and services, hyperinflation, and erratic market prices for essential goods and services contributing to high protection risk and low quality of life (HDI of 0.433) (UNDP 2020) across the country. As a result, Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) rates remains above the emergency threshold of 15 percent (very high acute malnutrition level- WHO classification) at 16.0% (15.4 -16.7) in the lean season. GAM levels have been on the rise since 2019, when the GAM prevalence was 16.2% (13.8-18.5) in lean season. The main drivers of malnutrition in the country are linked to worsening food insecurity, suboptimal infant and young child feeding practices, inadequate availability of safe water and high prevalence of childhood diseases commonly diarrhea, fever, and cough. To address this situation, the WHO strategy will directly target 10% of the children under five who suffer from severe acute malnutrition with medical complications in priority locations with a high burden of acute malnutrition and food insecurity. WHO will ensure that enhanced quality lifesaving medical treatment service is provided for SAM/MC children to reduce the burden of and prevent unnecessary death resulting from medical complications because of acute malnutrition.
WHO will support (a) capacity building of medical doctors, nurses and other health workers responsible for case management of severely malnourished children through trainings and on job mentorship. At least 200 health care workers will be trained on inpatient management of SAM/MC using the SAM/MC package designed by WHO and integrated in the National Protocol (b) treatment of medical complications in children with severe acute malnutrition in stabilization centers through provision of WHO PED-SAM kits 2020 which is especially designed to provide medicines, renewables and equipment suitable for treatment of severe acute malnutrition with medical complications (c) reporting system in stabilization centers through provision of stabilization center reporting tools. d) conduct supportive supervisions to stabilization centers to ensure quality lifesaving service delivery 
In order to maximize the output from the fund WHO will work together with health and nutrition partners to reinforce and promote access to integrated nutrition, health, WASH services provision in the project target areas, through enhanced close coordination and integrated programming with other Clusters (Health, WASH). This project aims to enhance nutrition-sensitive interventions that will ensure safe, equitable and dignified access to critical cross-sectoral basic services; to further decrease the prevalence of acute malnutrition, and ultimately, to contribute to the prevention and reduction of morbidity and mortality associated to malnutrition in South Sudan.

project_name: Emergency response and improved access to essential primary health care across South Sudan
project_objective:
Purpose and overall goal: 
To reduce morbidity and mortality by responding to public health emergencies and providing access to quality essential primary healthcare, including reproductive health, services to survivors of SGBV and mental health services, to girls, boys, men and women in emergency situations, with specific focus on accessibility for persons living with disability and the elderly. To build the resilience of communities and the MoH to prevent, detect and respond to disease outbreaks.

Methodology and target: 
Medair's project focuses on provision of primary health care in areas of high need and where existing services are inadequate, including Leer and Pibor. Activities include provision of curative consultations in primary health facilities; community-based treatment of common illness in children under five; routine vaccination; reproductive and sexual health including provision of ANC, safe delivery, PNC and clinical management of SGBV; management of at-risk infants through MAMI; and mental health treatment. Medair conducts ongoing training and supportive supervision for capacity building staff of Medair, CHD and other partners in order to improve the quality of service provision. Medair primarily targets children under five, women, and people with disability and mental health conditions, due to their unique vulnerability, though not exclusively.
Through the Emergency Response Team, Medair can respond in any area of South Sudan in response to disease outbreaks, acute displacement, reports of increased morbidity and mortality, nutritional emergencies, flooding and other natural disasters. Medair ERT aims to reduce morbidity and mortality of vulnerable populations through outbreak response such as vaccination campaigns or case management, and provision of primary health care services where these are inadequate. Through training and community engagement, Medair aims to increase the capacity of long-term health partners and the local community to be prepared for future shocks. 

All of Medair's health activities are integrated with WASH, Nutrition, Emergency Shelter/NFI and Protection activities to enhance the effectiveness and address underlying causes of morbidity and mortality.

project_name: WASH project for IDPs, returnees, and vulnerable host population to mitigate and prevent malnutrition and gender-based violence in Maiwut, Ulang and Nasir Counties, Upper Nile State, South Sudan
project_objective:
This intervention aims at contributing to the improved health and hygiene status of women, girls, men, boys, the elderly and persons with disabilities (PWDs) through timely and equitable access to safe, potable and adequate water in targeted communities in Maiwut, Nasir and Ulang counties. 
The proposed WASH interventions will be implemented in close coordination with RI’s health , nutrition , protection and FSL programming. Women and girls are the primary users of WASH services, the intervention is designed to be gender-sensitive and prevent GBV. Activities will include provision of safe water supply; upgrading of existing boreholes to solar powered water supply system, pipe line extension from the existing solar powered water supply system and distribution of water purification chemical (PUR), (for those beneficiaries who are depending on river or surface water) , the rehabilitation of water points (boreholes) with secure location and access within the community and nutrition facilities with a focus on construction of flood resilient boreholes for which the apron and flood protective wall will be raised by at least 1m. The designs of the structures will be considered so that people with disabilities (PWDs-both male and female) as well as older people can easily access and collect water. Further, household latrine construction, WASH NFI distribution, and the training of Water Users Committees (WUCs) and pump mechanics will be carried out. RI will encourage selection and participation of female in the WUCs. Each of the WUCs will consist of at least 50% female membership. These WUCs will be responsible for ensuring that sustainable and viable operation and maintenance of these systems are in place at the community level. RI will ensure the quality of water through water quality testing which will be done before and after rehabilitation/construct on of water points.
For the sanitation component, the project plans the implementation of flood resilient communal and institutional ventilated improved pit latrines which will be equipped with hand washing facilities. The design of the structures will be done considering all the segments of the society especially PWDs and older people and ensure that they can access them easily without any barrier. The latrines will be gender inclusive and will have a lock on the doors for protection purposes. The location will also not be far from the beneficiaries’ home and will therefore be easily accessible by women and girls during day and evening time. The construction of latrines will be complemented by the delivery of hygiene promotion messaging on safe excreta disposal to improve the sanitation practices. RI hygiene promoters and trained home health promoters (HHPs) will conduct weekly monitoring visits to at community, nutrition and household level to assess the usage and cleanliness of the latrines and document any challenges or feedback from the household. The HHPs will disseminate information on the five essential hygiene and sanitation practices (fecal–oral route transmission or the ‘F-diagram’), Safe water handling, Safe excreta disposal, Handwashing and personal hygiene, Environmental hygiene and baby WASH messages. RI will continue using its internal hygiene promotion training module as well as the Care Group Manual to train HHPs for the Healthy Practices, Safe Communities Project.
To improve, the WASH condition of the caretakers of SAM/MAM which contributes reduction of malnutrition, WASH NFI kits will be distributed. The integrated approach will address the high levels of malnutrition by targeting the families of SAM and MAM children for WASH interventions and providing access to drinking water, thereby acknowledging that poor WASH services are a key driver of poor health and malnutrition. The WASH intervention in these three counties will be done carefully without creating any conflict among the beneficiaries.
Data will be disaggregated by sex and age wherever possible.

project_name: Integrated Mobile and Static Protection/GBV Response in Upper Nile, South Sudan
project_objective:
Structural gender inequality and unequal power relationships between men and women are the root causes of GBV. Gender equality efforts and women’s empowerment are at the heart of preventing and addressing gender-based violence. Primary GBV prevention programs will be implemented to address harmful social norms and systemic gender inequality and power imbalances. Essential GBV actions will be integrated and undertaken across multiple clusters to save lives and mitigate GBV risks. GBV response interventions will be also implemented in a coordinated manner to ensure the provision lifesaving specialized GBV response services.
This project will provide integrated GBV mobile and static services through an integrated approach with Health in remote and hard to reach locations in Longechuk, Nasir, Ulang and Maiwut Counties of Upper Nile State, where static facilities are not accessible. A target of 22,857 (men 1600, Boys 2286, women 9371,Girls 9600) beneficiaries will be reached. Of this, RI is targeting 15% to be people with disabilities (PWDs).  RI has been providing life-saving services in UNS since 2006 in Health, Nutrition, Food Security and Livelihoods, Water Sanitation and Health and Protection. Since September 2020, RI piloted an integrated model comprising Medical Mobile Units and Mobile Protection Units to deliver life-saving services in Longechuk and Nasir in Health and Protection/GBV response. So far, RI is running a total of 7 MPU teams out of which 2 are in static locations with funding from BHA however, gaps still exist. Both MMUs and MPUs follow the same schedule and rotation. Despite numerous constraints, lesson learned shows that mobile service delivery is the most appropriate approach to deliver services to communities that have been displaced or are unable to access the static services due to a myriad of barriers and risks that hinder safe access to humanitarian services. 

Maiwut is split into two administrative areas, Jekow is IO controlled while Maiwut Centre is controlled by the government. It is important to ensure that both areas receive similar services to manage local political dynamics. A total of 12 MPUs will be formed, 3 in each projection site comprising of 1 static team and 2 mobile teams. GBV prevention priorities will include community engagement, awareness-raising activities on risk factors to GBV, GBV response services, and sensitization on importance of seeking GBV response services within 72 hours of the incidents happening. RI prevention activities will include primary prevention interventions such as Engaging Men in Accountable Practice (EMAP), SASA! and Community Cares programming that transform harmful social norms contributing to gender inequality. The GBV risk mitigation interventions will prioritize integrating GBV risk mitigation and survivor support across different sectors, dignity kit programming, distribution of fuel-efficient stoves, and conducting safety audits. RI’s GBV response priority interventions include providing psychosocial support, GBV case management services, establishing and strengthening GBV referral systems, and implementing Women and Girls safe spaces and providing capacity building training to frontline service providers. RI is committed to providing equal employment opportunities to all qualified people, regardless of race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, age, disability, marital status, national origin, military status, gender identity, pregnancy, or any other basis. Considering the local context, RI will, where possible, recruit female staff to ensure privacy for beneficiaries during service provision, collect sex and age disaggregated data to assess utilization of services, and strive to achieve a gender balance in its capacity building opportunities. Gender appropriate services will be mainstreamed across all RI Sectors.

project_name: Promote lifesaving through malnutrition prevention and improved treatment of acute malnutrition of conflict and flood affected, vulnerable communities in Maiwut, Maban, Nasir, Longechuk counties, Upper Nile State.
project_objective:
RI Nutrition sector primary goal is to promote malnutrition prevention and provision of improved treatment of acute malnutrition to promote good health among conflict affected and vulnerable groups. In 2023, RI’s Nutrition interventions will aim to increase malnutrition prevention activities and provide continuous improved and timely community-based management of acute malnutrition projects in the Greater Upper Nile with Health, WASH, FSL, Protection sectors linkages to address interrelated and under-lying causes of malnutrition, such as food insecurity, suboptimal childcare and feeding practices and lack of safe water and sanitation  

RI’s aim is to support South Sudanese including refugees, internal displaced persons, returnees and vulnerable population including people with disabilities. Our response will prioritize life-saving treatment services targeting children under five years and pregnant and lactating women (PLWs), in compliance with relevant national guidelines. These are the most vulnerable groups to malnutrition due to their increased biological and physiological needs. Geographically, our response will continue to prioritize states in the Upper Nile namely Maiwut, Maban, Nasir, and Longechuk which are characterized by high malnutrition, food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 and 4), conflict and internal displacement. 
The RI nutrition sites will act as hubs for integrated programming. The RI health sector will provide malaria testing and treatment among the severely acute malnourished (SAM) children being treated at the nutrition sites, while the RI WASH sector will provide NFI kits to severely malnourished children’s families and the RI FSL sector will establish kitchen gardens at nutrition sites to demonstrate recommended feeding practices.
Furthermore, the RI nutrition sites will integrate the early childhood development stimulation activities and will be considered as potential entry points for GBV victims looking for assistance, with nutrition staff trained on GBV referral pathways. 
To further localize the RI’s response and to ensure sustainability, RI will strengthen the County Health Department (CHD) responsibilities to oversee the nutrition interventions, to coordinate the response with various stakeholders at the county level and provide stakeholder’s capacity building on the new national guidelines on community based management of malnutrition and maternal, infant, and young child nutrition. 
RI will provide technical support to the CHD to review the county level nutrition intervention’s strategy which includes coming with nutrition county action plan, routine monitoring and supportive supervision of routine nutrition site activities, facilitation of Community-based Management of Acute Malnutrition (CMAM), Maternal, Infant and Young Child Feeding Nutrition (MIYCN) training, VASD campaign, FSNMS surveys, advocacy and focusing Family malnutrition screening for timely cases managements and follow up.
RI will reinforce the nutrition information system and the use of nutrition data at the county and the community level by employing a gender-sensitive approach to mitigate any obstacles compromising women and girls’ ability to receive nutrition support. Women’s participation will be encouraged in programme design and feedback mechanisms. RI will also collaborate with existing and planned development interventions on nutrition, such as those funded by the World Bank in the greater upper Nile. 

RI will pursue four objectives including: 
•	Prevent under-nutrition by increasing access to maternal, infant and young child nutrition interventions and VASD campaign. 
•	Deliver life-saving management of acute malnutrition for the most vulnerable and at-risk U5 children and pregnant and lactating women
•	Enhance nutrition situation monitoring, analysis and utilization of nutrition information for early warning and decision making.
•	Increase access to integrated nutrition, health, WASH, FSL and protection interventions

project_name: Integrated emergency lifesaving primary health care services to the vulnerable communities of Upper Nile, South Sudan.
project_objective:
This intervention aims at provision of equitable access to and utilization  of health  services through  5 static primary health  care facilities including Rirnyang Primary Health Care Unit (PHCU) in Ulang County, Keichkuon Primary Health Care Centre (PHCC) , Makak PHCU, and Wandeng PHCU in Nasir and Jekow PHCU in Maiwut. To reach to the population in hard-to- reach locations in these 4 counties, RI will establish eight Mobile Medical Units (MMUs) and also implement Boma Health Initiative (BHI) targeting 2 bomas per county. The project will target 89,179 (21,119 women, 24,683 girls, 25,228boys, 21,119 men) and 13,377 people with disabilities. RI will recruit and deploy qualified health workers including clinical officers, nurses, midwives, community health workers, and vaccinators to all supported Health facilities and mobile medical units. Boma health workers will be selected at the community level to provide both selected curative services and health promotion as per MoH’s BHI package across the 4 counties.
The intervention will further focus on continuous screening and treatment of communicable and non-communicable diseases through patient consultations. The intervention will also provide the management of injuries, antenatal care, skilled deliveries, postnatal care, and clinical management of rape (CMR) services in the health facilities and mobile medical units. The intervention will also integrate and strengthen mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) and services for people with disabilities. The project will continue streamlining and strengthening the referral pathways for MHPSS, sexual and gender-based violence survivors and, maternal and child health emergencies. RI’s health team, through this response, will conduct routine and outreach immunization services to children under 59 months of age. Throughout the provision of health services, RI will ensure proper infection prevention and control protocol including against COVID -19 and Ebola. All static health facilities, MMUs and BHWs will be equipped with Infection Prevention and Control, Water, sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) materials, Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), and Information, Education and Communication (IEC) materials on prevention epidemic prone diseases such as COVID-19, Ebola, measles etc. Ebola virus disease (EVD) prevention, surveillance, and response readiness will be continued as part of disease outbreak, prevention and response.  The health activities will be coordinated closely with the RI WASH and nutrition teams to ensure integration of interventions for more effective community mobilization and sensitization on health-related messaging including on availability of immunization services, ANC, skilled deliveries, CMR services, and MHPSS services. This project will engage all communities in the targeted counties throughout the implementation stages to enable the sustainability of the program. Additionally, RI will also institute contextualized feedback mechanisms such as regular focus group discussions, meetings, feedback boxes and Accountability to Affected Persons (AAP) groups to continue providing feedback and complaints. RI will involve the communities while selecting the Mobile medical unit (MMUs) sites and the community health workers to ensure acceptability of the project. The selected MMUs and health facilities will be equipped with essential medical equipment, drugs and test kits. RI will ensure the staffing is gender representative and trained on core humanitarian and protection principles including Non maleficence principle.

project_name: Food Security and Livelihood Support to Conflict Prone and Flood Affected Populations in Koch County, Unity State and Pigi/Canal and Fangak Counties in Jonglei State
project_objective:
Integrated Phase Classification (IPC) report (November 2022) indicates that 7.76million South Sudanese (62.7%) of the population will face severe food insecurity (IPC 3+). In Fangak, 178,000 (over 90%) of the people will face severe food insecurity with about 20,000 of these people facing catastrophic food insecurity. In Koch County, 75,000 (over 75%) while in Canal/Pigi 85,000 people (80%) of the people will face IPC 3+ conditions. The main causes of food insecurity are floods and conflicts which have destroyed farms, livelihoods and resulted in displaced populations. Agricultural productivity has been persistently low and coping capacity of these populations has been eroded. At the Macro-economic level, depreciation of the local currency and effects of War in Ukraine have made food more expensive and scarcer. Three consecutive years of flooding have been experienced in these counties. Crops were destroyed before harvesting and in storage. Livestock died through drowning and starvation as grazing grounds were flooded. Coupled with flooding, are intensified sub-national violence arising from political instability, cattle raids and revenge killings. Violence causes instability limiting access to land for cultivation but also results in deaths of productive members of the HH. Coping strategies of affected households have been exhausted and household assets eroded. Without timely humanitarian intervention, this situation could worsen and plunge populations into famine situation.
The goal of this intervention is to support the vulnerable populations in these three counties with livelihood kits and training so as to help these vulnerable communities to restore and sustain their livelihoods. This intervention will be guided by the three cluster objectives (CO). The first CO is to provide food assistance to prevent famine and improve food consumption, dietary diversity and coping strategies for vulnerable populations. The second CO is to enhance and sustain emergency food production through complementary vegetable and crop livelihood inputs, fishing and livestock. The third CO is to reduce dependency on food and agricultural inputs to support and strengthen households’ ability to absorb & adapt to shocks & contextual changes. It is expected that through this intervention, target populations will be able to supplement food provided through general food distribution which had proved to be irregular and therefore unreliable but also increases dependency to external support systems. The intervention will also contribute towards reduction in flood related displacements in the target counties. This will be achieved through disaster risk reduction strategies that will build the community capacity on early warning signs and mitigation measures including construction of dykes to control flow of water. The project will also ensure minimum package for prevention, risk mitigation and response to GBV rolled out in 80% of priority locations, focusing on safe, timely access to quality case management, psychosocial services and capacity building.
A total of 338,000 beneficiaries (56,333 HH) in Koch, Fangak and Canal/Pigi facing IPC 3+ food insecurity will be targeted for this intervention, comprising of 60% women, elderly, youth, disabled and other vulnerable groups will be targeted for crop and vegetable kits. Out of this number, a total of 8,450HHs will be targeted for training on improved agronomic methods, post-harvest handling and utilization. Similarly, 6,500HHs will be targeted with fishing kits, including training on appropriate harvesting methods and fish preservation. This intervention will also target 1,500HHs with Food for Asset intervention to help them build community structures  to mitigate effects of flooding. To help improve sustainable access to quality seeds, the project will work with 500HHs to produce high quality seeds and avail them to other farmers for subsequent use.
The intervention will run from January to December of 2023

project_name: Emergency Nutrition support to vulnerable population in koch, Rubkona Counties in Unity State and Fangak, Canal pigi Counties in Jonglei State, South Sudan
project_objective: The humanitarian nutrition overview for 2022 estimates that 2 million children, pregnant and lactating women (PLW) will require treatment for malnutrition. In the same year, around 1.4 million children under 5 years of age (U5) will need to be provided with nutrition services out of which 302,078 will be admitted for acute malnutrition. 675,578 PLW are expected to be acutely malnourished, which is a significant increment when compared to 2021 needs. The need for humanitarian assistance is increased due to emerging issues related with increased food insecurity, flooding and the continuous impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. The severe flooding in Jonglei State has impacted health and nutrition service provision in Fangak and Canal/Pigi counties. IRNA assessment conducted in August 2021 in the area, indicated that various locations in the counties have been completely submerged in water including nutrition and WASH facilities while the rest remains under the big threat of being flooded. Communities continue to be displaced to relatively dry high lands in Fangak and Cana Pigi counties. In Bentiu IDP, while official counts have shown fluctuation in the population counts over the years, the recent influx of displaced community from surrounding areas due to flooding is likely to continue causing much stress on existing humanitarian services in the IDP camp. Rehabilitation of nutrition and WASH infrastructure is needed to continue providing life-saving services in flood affected counties. A recent SMART survey done at Canal/Pigi and Fangak counties reveals, a GAM rate of 19% for each of the counites. Mass MUAC screenings conducted by WR in New Fangak in February 2020 show a proxy GAM rate of 11.6% and a proxy severe acute malnutrition (SAM) rate of 2% for children U5, and a proxy GAM of 8% for PLW. In Koch County, mass MUAC screenings conducted by WR in 2020 revealed a proxy GAM rate of 10.6% for children U5 and a proxy modern acute malnutrition (MAM) of 11% for PLW. SMART survey done in August 2021 in Bentiu IDP, reveled the prevalence of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) is 2.4%, and GAM prevalence is 9.7. To strengthen life-saving nutrition services, WR will scale up qualitative service and coverage for community-based management of malnutrition (CMAM), extending services hard to reach sites with underserved communities. The project will target 26,064 children U5 and PLW as direct beneficiaries who show signs of SAM and MAM. Care givers of children will be reached through Maternal and Infant Young Child Nutrition (MIYCN) programs in Outpatient Therapeutic Program (OTP) and Therapeutic Supplementary Feeding Program (TSFP) sites. This project will establish four new outreach units in each county to provide outreach nutrition services to communities with limited access to services due to displacement. In Fangak County, WR plans to support 5 new OTP and TSFP sites in Canal/Pigi County. A gender-targeted and nutrition-sensitive service delivery approach will be used and nutrition will be integrated with WASH, health and FSL programming. The aim of the project is to reduce morbidity and mortality among the most vulnerable children and women while promoting and engaging in recovery and resilience activities in the community. The project purpose is in line with Nutrition Cluster Objective and sectoral strategies. Project activities will be monitored through supportive supervision done together with the County Health and Nutrition Department, MOH and UN Agencies. Activities will be monitored by nutrition project staff with support from the WR Juba M&E department and other program team. Relevant reports will be shared to nutrition cluster and other reporting partners. Community based compliant mechanisms will be established within the nutrition sites and at community level to ensure accountability.

project_name: Emergency WASH provision to the Vulnerable populations in Fangak and Canal Pigi, Jonglei State and Koch County in Unity State
project_objective: The main drivers of WASH needs include limited physical infrastructure, sub-national violence and recurring flooding in many parts of the country. Increased displacement also places an extra burden on existing WASH infrastructure in displacement sites. The WASH severity classification conducted in May 2021 showed that all three targeted counties, Koch, Fangak and Canal/Pigi are under WASH severity Phase 4. This situation worsened with the 2022 flooding which reached unprecedented levels. The main drivers of WASH severity included; flooding of WASH infrastructure, destruction of roads and population displacement. As of October 2022, One million South Sudanese had been affected by the flooding (Situation Report 1, October 2022). With most of the WASH facilities destroyed including latrines, boreholes and handwashing facilities which is further compromised by limited access to health services, outbreak of water borne disease is imminent. The World Relief South Sudan (WRSS) WASH interventions and provisions will be integrated alongside other services like health, nutrition, protection, FSL, etc. The main purpose of this WASH intervention is to improve the wellbeing of people affected by disaster or who have been chronically exposed to lack of clean water and basic sanitation services in Koch, Fangak and Canal/Pigi counties. This will be done through reducing water and sanitation related morbidity and mortality; provision of safe, equitable access to clean water and basic sanitation services; mitigating Gender-based violence, supporting recovery and resilience building to achieve durable solutions. This intervention will be done both at community and facility levels (i.e. health & nutrition). Namely, this will be achieved through the rehabilitation of existing water points and drilling of new ones; conducting hygiene promotion campaigns; water quality monitoring; and distribution of WASH NFIs to targeted or blanket populations depending on the context. This WASH assistance will reduce the prevalence of WASH-related diseases and risk of outbreak by transmission contexts upon epidemiological investigations. Secondly, this project will contribute to reducing the high prevalence of malnutrition by creating access to safe water, and promoting hygiene in locations with high malnutrition prevalence and high WASH vulnerability (UNICEF’s normative framework of nutrition 1990). Through this objective, new water points will be drilled, water points will be rehabilitated, water/hygiene committees will be established and trained, hygiene campaigns will be promoted and WASH NFIs will be distributed to target beneficiaries. Thirdly, this project proposes to increase access to basic sanitation services, through the provision of WASH assistance to communities affected by sudden-onset disaster and/or chronically affected by a lack of access to basic WASH services. Fourthly, this project will mitigate gender-based violence (GBV) by carrying out specific activities to mitigate GBV risk for users of WASH facilities and services, especially for women and children. Safety audits will be conducted to identify GBV concerns and implement mitigation measures. The project will ensure construction of water points, latrines and other infrastructure considering the needs of the most vulnerable in society including women, girls, elderly, disabled and children under five years. This will be done with utilization of the WASH Cluster’s Protection Mainstreaming tip-sheet. Community structures including water user management committees (WUC) will be established and trained. They will manage the resources and ensure that no harm is caused by these interventions. Water points will be managed ensuring access to all without causing any conflicts among the intended beneficiaries.

project_name: Fostering Resilience through Early Recovery response for the most Crisis impacted Communities in Syria
project_objective:
The Integrated Response for Resilience Programme aims at providing a comprehensive response through Early Recovery support in 80 communities impacted by the crisis. Communities, particularly  those most dramatically affected – and under additional stress because of IDPs returns and other displacements - need  assistance in reinforcing their resilience to address these shocks as well as the consequences of the protracted crisis, and to address their needs on seriously depleted infrastructures and service capacities.
The essence of the Programme is about providing Syrian communities with – still limited - support to regain  control  over their basic needs (livelihoods, access to essential services) and reduce their dependency on humanitarian assistance. Prioritization of locations, is the outcome of a context analysis and needs assessment conducted on more than  5,000
Syrian communities, based on the following three criteria:
1) Hard to Reach  Areas
2) Areas of major IDPs presence and IDPs returns
3) Highest scoring in the Severity Scale
The integrated response consists of the following components: strengthening of social services-related capacities (access and coverage), livelihoods creation and rural recovery, PWDs support, social cohesion/community safety, reducing gender inequality  and youth marginality, women empowerment, tensions reduction and rehabilitation of basic infrastructure and public services.
The program is built in a modular manner both in terms of geographical and sectoral/thematic interventions and foresees the allotment of average 1 Million US$ per community. Hence, donors willing to support this approach will be able to pre-select certain location(s) and/or area(s) of intervention of their preference, within the 200 prioritized  communities.
The programme relates directly to the sector objectives:
1. Living conditions
2. Livelihoods
3. Access to social services
4. Access to productive and market infrastructure
5.social protection
6. Strengthening of local public services delivery capacity
7. Reinforcing  opportunities and capacities for civic engagement

project_name: Enhanced Access and Utilization of Quality Health Services in South Sudan (Rumbek East, Aweil East, Koch, Mayendit, Panyijar and Rubkona Counties)
project_objective:
Health systems in South Sudan have been impacted by prolonged conflict, natural hazards, epidemics including COVID-19 pandemic. Reliance on humanitarian assistance due to inadequate health financing by the government (<1.9% allocation of the 2021 national budget allocation), inequitable distribution of functional health facility, human resources for health gaps and access constraints due to unprecedented flooding, frequent subnational conflict and runaway inflation contribute to challenges in meeting the health needs of underserved populations in Rumbek East (Lakes State), Aweil East (Northern Bahr El Ghazal State), Koch, Mayendit, Panyijar & Rubkona Counties (Unity State).
The International Rescue Committee (IRC) proposes to respond to the immediate lifesaving health care needs of 340,728 people in need (71,579 Men, 79,095 Women, 93,220 Boys and 96,833 Girls with the inclusion of the elderly and persons living with disability. This project will provide essential outpatient care (communicable and non-communicable diseases), child health care, safe motherhood, Sexual and reproductive health, mental health care, gender-based violence response and emergency preparedness and response. The project will provide support to 12 static health facilities (2 PHCCs each in Aweil East, Rubkona, Panyijar, Koch; 1 PHCC each in Kapoeta South, Aweil South, Rumbek East, & Mayendit), 10 Rapid Response mobile (RRM) outreach posts (2 RRMs each in Panyijar, Mayendit, Koch, and Kapoeta South; 1 RRM each in Aweil South & Aweil East) and strengthen community health services by deploying 80 Boma Health Workers each in the 8 targeted Counties (39% of the BHI gap coverage).
Support to static health facilities will engage communities and County Health Departments (CHD) to map out underserved populations through assessments of intersectoral needs and prioritization of displaced populations without access to health services. The project will support the rehabilitation of structures, qualified staffing, pharmaceuticals supplies and commodities, health management information systems and reporting. Integration of services will be a priority of the project through multi-sector collaboration with food security and livelihoods, nutrition and protection mainstreaming. Providers will have capacity strengthening on provision of mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services, Clinical Management of Rape (CMR) and Infection prevention and control (IPC) measures. The flexible approach deployed by the RRMs including a rapid deployment approach ensures that these teams can provide immediate response within the first 72 hours of an emergency. The IRC will staff, resource, and facilitate early deployment of the RRM teams to locations pre-identified by the community and CHDs factoring the health priorities of affected populations.
Coordination through engagement with local duty bearers and partners, engagement with national and subnational coordination mechanisms will be an integral component of the response. The project will consider the perspective of the affected people through IRC’s Client Responsiveness Measurement Framework using evidence generated during implementation to amplify the voices of the affected people on services provision and decision making. Disability inclusive client responsiveness will be prioritized through engagement of organizations of persons with disability where these already exist and by direct data collection at health service points using the Washington Short Set of questions on disability. Joint support supervision will be an integral part of the intervention to provide mentorship and coaching to health staff. The project will mainstream COVID-19 risk mitigation measures across all service delivery channels to protect clients and the service providers.

project_name: Proteger e Reconstruir II
project_objective: Catholic Relief Services (CRS) proposes an emergency assistance program in Mozambique’s Cabo Delgado province. The Proteger e Reconstruir II (Proteger II) project aims to respond to critical shelter needs among conflict-affected internally displaced persons (IDPs) and host community households supporting IDPs with temporary housing. Proteger II will impart participants with knowledge of resilient shelter techniques and provide household items  to improve overall living conditions and restore dignity to conflict-affected communities. The project will target specific resettlement sites and host communities in Montepuez district. Proteger II will build on the achievements and lessons learned from 15 months of similar program implementation under the initial Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance (BHA)-supported Proteger e Reconstruir (Proteger I) project which also targeted conflict-affected IDPs in Cabo Delgado with emergency shelter assistance. The objective of the program is to improve the living conditions and restore the dignity of displaced people and host communities in the province of Cabo Delgado. CRS, will assist a total of 7,440 participating direct households, in a total of 37,200 individuals. Among those targeted for support, 20,835 will be internally displaced (4,167 households).
