project_name: Provision of access to life-saving and life-sustaining health services for the vulnerable populations in Lebanon
project_objective:
The proposed project aims at improving access to quality, affordable and comprehensive primary health services for vulnerable populations in Lebanon. Given the current deteriorating economic situation in Lebanon – vulnerable populations have become more at risk of being unable to access healthcare in Lebanon. These populations include Lebanese, Palestinian refugees residing in Lebanon, and migrants that are becoming increasingly unable to afford or access healthcare in Lebanon. 
For health activities, IMC will work with 4 PHCCs: Al Moasat PHCC (South), Quabit Medical center (Akkar), Nahda Bedawi (Tripoli) and Nafelaa PHCC (Bekaa). These centers have been selected due to the high density of vulnerable Lebanese as well as a considerable size of migrant populations in the areas. The support to these four PHCCs will include: increasing the hours of operations for PHCCs by four hours a day, five days a week by providing salary support for physicians, nurses, data entry clerks, and other personnel and running costs. Secondly, donating essential acute medications as per the Ministry of Public health (MoPH) essential medication list, and lastly, IMC will be providing PPEs for the healthcare providers at the PHCCs in order to be able to provide high-quality services in a safe manner for both the health staff and the beneficiary. IMC will be recruiting and training Lebanese Health Outreach Volunteers (HOVs) from the target population in order to disseminate and provide health awareness on IMC services to vulnerable Lebanese communities and migrants - as well as identify cases requiring primary healthcare and referring them back to the PHCC. The outreach targeting migrant workers will use specific translated IEC materials and coordination with the migrant sector to identify migrants and reach them.
Lebanon’s multiple crises have contributed to fracturing its already fragile health care system. The medication shortage has exacerbated the situation and health care has become financially inaccessible for most. Vulnerable populations face multiple socio-economic challenges, including unemployment, poor living conditions, and the inability to cover the cost of both transportation and MHPSS services required to treat their mental health conditions. Shortages in skilled health care providers of MHPSS, as well as lack of awareness about where and how to seek services further exacerbate access challenges. This is compounded by the multiple crises, which have seen an increase in people seeking MHPSS services. IMC MH case management teams constituting of case managers, psychotherapists and psychiatrists are based in PHCCs to support provision of MHPSS consultations through an integrated approach and in line with the MH LPSP packages to be finalized following the piloting phase. IMC will work in  two PHCCs, Cedars Medical Association – Cedars Medical Center in Mount Lebanon and Deir El Ahmar PHCC in Bekaa  to support the increase in the number of vulnerable Lebanese and migrants reaching out for MHPSS interventions.  

IMC is planning to procure acute and psychotropic medication which will be donated to the PHCCs. IMC will coordinate with MoPH to complement quantities and try to plug gaps in the MOPH supply chain. IMC will run a detailed assessment, quantities will be shared with MoPH for coordination of numbers and specifying the number of PHCCs to be covered as well as the duration of coverage and timeframe. At the PHCC level, medications will be dispensed free of charge and only upon medical prescriptions.

project_name: Emergency Nutrition Response to mitigate the impact of malnutrition among the most vulnerable under five children and PLW living in, Aweil south, Panyjar , Rumbek east , Rumbek North and Yirol west counties of South Sudan.
project_objective: Malnutrition is one of the top causes of death in children under five years and has a long-term negative impact on the children’s abilities to live to their full potential. South Sudan (SS) has experienced continued crisis including floods, conflict, and food insecurity which have impacted on the key drivers of acute malnutrition and aggravated the nutrition situation within the country. The Food Security and Nutrition Monitoring System (FSNMS) Round 28 and 2022 SMART surveys report GAM prevalence at 16.0% (15.4 -16.7) in lean season.  This indicates no improvement since 2019, when the GAM prevalence was 16.2% (13.8-18.5) in lean season the rate of acute malnutrition remains above the emergency threshold of 15 percent (very high acute malnutrition level- WHO classification). The situation calls for strengthened multisector investment to address the impact of aggravating factors, and to maintain gains in tackling the nutrition situation in South Sudan.The objectives of the action will be; To increase equitable access and utilization of quality preventative nutrition specific service delivery for children, adolescents, and women .To increase equitable access and utilization of quality lifesaving nutrition services for early detection and treatment of acute malnutrition for girls and boys under five years of age and PLW affected by acute malnutrition .To increase equitable access to nutrition sensitive interventions from health, WASH, FSL, Education and Protection sectors through enhanced coordination and joint programming targeting vulnerable groups in Aweil South, Panyijar, Rumbek East, Rumbek North and Yirol West counties by the end of 2023.  The proposed intervention aims to increase coverage and access to the most vulnerable community by providing equitable and accessible nutrition prevention treatment services. The nutrition services will deliver by scaling up the emergency nutrition responses through 62 static OTP/TSFP (10 in Aweil south,10 in Panyijar, 23 in Rumbek east, 7 in Rumbek North, and 12 in Yirol west), 5 Stabilization center (1 in Panyijar, 1 Aweil south, 1 in Rumbek east, 1 in Rumbek north, and 1 in Yirol west) and through 4 RRM mobile tam (2 in Aweil south, 2 in Panyjar,). In addition, the IRC will implement integrated CMAM and MIYCN in all sites. Promotion of optimal nutrition and prevention of malnutrition among young children (0-23 months through the implementation of MIYCN to ensure vulnerable children have optimal growth. IRC will strengthen community participation using existing community structures and active engagements of the affected community. IRC will conduct meetings with MtMSG, regular community sensitization sessions and scaling up of the existing Nutrition response to ensure timely service availability. Scale up family MUAC to ensure early detection of acute malnutrition that contributes to early detection. An estimated 20,085 SAM children,37388 MAM, and 30131 PLW MAM will be reached through this action across all implementation areas in OTP and TSFP, respectively. Continue with the capacity building of CHD, primary health care service providers and nutrition staff. Train health and nutrition staff on CMAM and MIYCN to ensure timely nutrition services. A rapid response team will be deployed to the hard-to-reach area to provide nutrition services that are accessible and vulnerable groups have got timely treatment. Subsequently, the interventions will reduce mortality and morbidity associated with malnutrition. Integration of nutrition activities with other sectors will also be implemented, including integration of health and nutrition education messages, Malaria testing and treatment, promotion of hygiene and sanitation, training on GBV and CP for nutrition staff. Similarly, with food security, establish kitchen garden, cash programs for children discharged cured from SAM treatment, and cooking demonstrations to improve dietary diversification, conduct kitchen garden and cash programs.

To ensure durable and continues access to safe water ; NRC will establish / rehabilitate small scale solar powered water supply schemes , new boreholes through cost effective manual Borehole drilling. project_name: Integrated Food Security and Livelihoods Protection in Rubkona, Mayendit and Panyijiar Counties, Unity State, South Sudan
project_objective:
The project objective(s) is to enhance and sustain emergency food production through complementary vegetable and crop livelihood inputs, fishing, and livestock; reduce dependency on food and agricultural inputs to support and strengthen households’ ability to absorb shocks in floods and conflict-affected communities in Rubkon, Panyijiar and Mayendit counties, Unity state. The IRC proposes to provide a sequence of food production to support to most severe food-insecure and malnourished households in the main season farming of May to July and dry season of Nov to March. To strengthen households’ resilience, the project will mainstream gender, conflict sensitivity, disaster risks reduction to support at-risk households focused on improving vegetable, crop, livestock, and fisheries production and bolstering resilience towards recurrent shocks and stresses. In pursuit of the project objective(s), the following activities will be implemented: 
(a) The IRC together with the complaint and feedback mechanism (CFM/AAP) committee will mobilize, engage community members to inform the needs of the most vulnerable households and selection criteria for registration together with Nutrition partners. 
(b) Preposition and distribute emergency (short-term maturing) agricultural inputs (Cereal & Vegetable seeds, and tools) and fishing kits to 56,400 people. The IRC anticipates FAO will provide complimentary in-kind inputs to support the project.  
(c) To improve nutritional practices for pregnant women and caregivers of children under 5 years with MAM and SAM. Nutrient-dense vegetable seeds will be provided, establish demonstration gardens at nutrition facilities close to water points, provide basic training on vegetable production, harvest, and conservation techniques. The IRC Nutrition team will conduct nutrition-sensitive awareness, food cooking demonstrations showing how to enrich households’ meals with locally available foods.
(d) The IRC will identify 200 potential seed producers, provide foundation seeds, establish seeds multiplication centers and plots. The seed producers will receive at least 200 USD cash grants, training on quality seeds selection, quality seeds production techniques, and crop management practices. Seed producers will be supported to form VSLA to increase access to finance for seeds production and access to markets will be facilitated.  
(e) The IRC with the County Agriculture Department, State Ministry of Agriculture, and FAO will contribute to livestock disease surveillance and monitoring, facilitate vaccination campaigns, mass vaccination exercises and treatments to livestock to be led by CAHW.
(f) Facilitate capacity building to community-based extension agents (CAHWs, AEA’s), crop producers, pastoralists, and fisherfolks on sustainable production skills and provision of proximate extension services on production, post-harvest handling through demonstration gardens. Also, fisherfolks to receive basic training on fish preservation and kit repairs to enhance household nutrition and income.
Overall, the project will reach 5% (188,000 people) (i.e 56,400 people, 9,400 HHs) in emergency or severe (IPC 4 & 5 for 2023) in Rubkona, Mayendit, Panyijiar counties. In Particular, Rubkona (36,000 people, 6,00 HHs), Mayendit (9,600 people, 1,600 HHs) and Panyijiar (10,800 people, 1,800 HHs) equivalent to a total of 56,400 people (5,640 Male children, 8,460 Female children, 13,536 Adult male, 20,304 Adult female, 3,384 elderly Male, 5,076 elder Female) people. By program type: 56,400 livelihoods inputs distribution (Crop, Vegetable, Tools & fishing Kits), 9,400 individuals with production skills (Crop, Vegetables, fisheries skills (Fishing kits repairs, fish preservation etc) training, and 200 seeds growers/producers

project_name: Provision of timely, equitable and integrated food security and livelihood support to emergency affected populations in South Sudan
project_objective:
Protracted crises in South Sudan, including climactic shocks and continued conflict, have resulted in 8.9 million people projected to be in need of humanitarian assistance in 2022. As a result of the shocks, such as flooding, intercommunal violence (ICV) and ongoing armed clashes, the majority of the population are facing increased food insecurity, lack of access to basic services, and protection risks. As per the IPC classification released in November 2022, 7.76 million people (62.7% of the population) are expected to experience severe food insecurity between April to July 2023.

Solidarites International has been operating in South Sudan since 2006, and currently provide assistance in Upper Nile, Jonglei and Unity states. In addition, SI has a fully roving Emergency Response and Preparedness (EPR) team based in Juba that implements frontline responses to new emergencies across the country. SI implements integrated programs in Food Security and Livelihoods (FSL) and Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH). 

In FSL, SI aims at supporting the most vulnerable households, who are suffering from severe food insecurity and/or struggling to restore their livelihoods. In previous years, SI’s FSL activities have included large-scale seed and tool distributions, fishing kit distributions, cash transfers for households affected by malnutrition, and training on agronomic and fishing good practices. In addition, SI provides Income Generating Activities (IGA) for vulnerable population in Greater Upper Nile within a 2 years project. Finally, SI currently provides  flood-adapted responses with, for instance, the development of ""agriculture in sacks"" solution in crowded settlements.

In 2023, SI will focus on providing rapid livelihoods support in emergency affected areas, while developing resilience and reduced dependency. 

SI will support for the most vulnerable emergency affected households (with a focus on households suffering from or at risk of malnutrition) with seeds, tools, and assets for fishing and vegetable production and follow up training. Flood adaptations to regular practices will be developed to reduce the impact of expected future flooding in 2023 (i.e floating garden etc.). Through its roving Emergency Preparedness and Response (EPR) team, SI will deploy to emergency-affected locations identified through the Clusters and Needs Analysis Working Group to provide emergency responses in IPC 4+ locations. SI will expand its EPR programs to include rapid response kits distribution (fishing kits/fast growing seeds) to affected households in new rapid onset emergencies. Activities ensuring access to basic WASH services will be integrated with FSL activities in priority locations to contribute to reductions in malnutrition and food insecurity. In parallel, SI will focus on developing livelihood resilience among communities and reducing dependency on humanitarian aid through programs on seed replication, and value chain addition, while ensuring basic needs for livelihoods inputs are met through main season seed, tool, and fishing kit distributions. Income Generating Activities (IGA) will also be implemented, mainly targeting youths and women, to boost local resilience. All programs will be integrated with nutrition services through beneficiary targeting and support to nutrition centres to develop and maintain kitchen gardens.

CARE is proposing a comprehensive WASH, Health, Nutrition intervention responding to the immediate basic needs of the refugees hosting in Sudan and sustaining access through improving WASH, health & Nutrition and food and livelihoods services. All the proposed services will be delivered in line with the Refugees forum’s and relevant clusters priority of providing basic services to the refugees and asylum seekers from south Sudan and other refugees in three states of Sudan Kassala, East Darfur and South Kordofan.
The project will seek to provide live-saving interventions for WASH, Health & Nutrition through safe, clean water & adequate sanitation facilities, quality primary health care, preventive & curative nutritional intervention. The services will be provided in a holistic & collective manner to enhance peaceful coexistence between refuges & host community & improving the peoples’ wellbeing. Gender, protection &accountability will be mainstreamed throughout the implementation. CARE with national partners will work in coordinated manner to provide the needed support, staff will participate & attend coordination meetings at different levels to provide assistance in coordinated & collaborative manner. The proposed intervention will cover activities of integrated health and Nutrition services,  such as Provision of  mental health consultations to provide essential primary and secondary health care services, Management of moderate acute malnutrition for PLW, Refer cases for specialized treatment (between levels of care across Sudan) to provide essential primary and secondary health care services, Increase access to health services by supporting mobile medical units and referral pathways. Under WASG the project will provide installation, operation, maintenance and provision of water services, provision of sanitation services i.e communal and household latrines, showers and hygiene promotion activities. Under Food security and livelihoods the project will be providing agricultural and livestock support and vocational training and training for youth and women. The project will also conduct PSEA and GBV awareness sessions and dignity kits distribution as cross cutting activities. The primary focus will be the affected women, men, girls, and boys, as well as disabled people in  East Darfur, South Kordofan, Gedaref and Kassala states.

project_name: COL_2022_BHA_ Respuesta humanitaria centrada en la infancia en materia de protección (con WASH integrado) para las víctimas colombianas del conflicto en  Colombia
project_objective:
Proyecto de protección y agua, higiene y saniamiento (wash) para apoyar las familias desplazadas por el conflicto interno en el departamento de Nariño.

Abordar las necesidades humanitarias de las familias vulnerables y de difícil acceso y a los desplazados internos y mejorar los resultados de la protección de los niños colombianos y sus familias afectadas por el conflicto armado en Tumaco, El Charco y Barbacoas de Nariño, proporcionando intervenciones de protección que salvan vidas, construyendo la resiliencia de la comunidad y empoderando a las comunidades para identificar, prevenir y mitigar futuros riesgos de protección.   

RESULTADOS

Al final del proyecto, se reforzará la capacidad de recuperación y los mecanismos de afrontamiento de los niños y las comunidades en las zonas afectadas por el conflicto armado, se abordarán las necesidades urgentes de protección y se mejorarán los mecanismos de protección basados en la comunidad. 
En las zonas de ejecución, los niños y los adultos tendrán un mejor acceso al saneamiento y a buenas prácticas de higiene (incluyendo actividades de promoción de la higiene en las escuelas).

project_name: Provisión de asistencia en el sector de educación para la atención de emergencias humanitarias y contribución a soluciones duraderas para población afectada por el conflicto armado y comunidades anfitrionas vulnerables en Colombia.
project_objective: El objetivo general del programa de Educación de NRC es garantizar que los niño/as, adolescentes y jóvenes afectados por el desplazamiento tengan acceso a servicios de educación relevantes para sus necesidades psicosociales, emocionales y cognitivas. Para abordar las necesidades específicas de los niños y niñas afectados por este tipo de crisis en sus comunidades (conflicto, desastres naturales y cambio climático, COVID) y proveer una oferta educativa adaptada para garantizar continuidad educativa a través de intervenciones de: acceso escolar, nivelación, transición, aceleración del aprendizaje y formación técnica y profesional para jóvenes. También se trabaja el refuerzo de la comunidad y de los padres/cuidadores y de los docentes que también tienen que apoyar a los estudiantes en su proceso académico.

project_name: Renforcement des capacités locales pour la réduction des risques liés aux EEI et mapping d'acteur d'assistance aux victimes.
project_objective:
La menace EEI qui affecte la Région du Sahel et du Bassin du Lac Chad s’étends au Niger et a aggravé crise humanitaire et les déplacements de populations, qui sont les plus exposés à ces engins de nature indiscriminé. MAG propose de soutenir les initiatives Groupe de Travail (Task Force) en développant des activités d’Education aux Risques avec des partenaires locaux, afin de soutenir le Niger dans ses engagements vis-à-vis de la Convention sur l'interdiction des mines antipersonnel. Le choix du partenaire local sera guidé par son expertise dans les activités de base communautaire et son implication au niveau local, pour garantir l’accès et la pérennité des actions.
L’objectif principal de l’intervention est de renforcer les capacités d’organisations locales et la société civile dans les thématiques de liaison communautaire dans le cadre de l’action contre les mines : l’EREE, la collecte de données pour l’analyse de contexte et la cartographie des acteurs.
Les équipes partenaires seront formés à la liaison communautaire et déployées pour la mise en œuvre des activités d’Education aux Risques et de formation de points focaux communautaires pour répliquer les messages de protection. Selon le NILAM 12.10 « L’EREE a pour objectif de réduire le risque à un niveau qui permette à la population de vivre dans de bonnes conditions de sécurité et de recréer un environnement favorable à un développement économique et social libre des contraintes associées à la contamination par des engins explosifs. »
L’analyse de contexte permettra d’acquérir une connaissance précise de l’étendue et des répercussions de la menace posée par les EE, d’identifier les comportements dangereux ainsi que les facteurs qui poussent certains groupes à se mettre en risque. Aussi nous identifierons l’accès à l’information ainsi que les canaux de communications préférés par les communautés cibles de l’initiative. L’analyse de contexte a pour objectif de mieux guider la stratégie d’intervention d’EREE par le biais de l’identification des priorités et des groupes cibles afin d’adapter les messages, méthodologie et moyens de communication aux besoins identifiés. Cette collecte de données permettra aussi d’identifier les mécanismes de réduction des risques déjà existants, afin de les renforcer et de les pérenniser et d’identifier les acteurs d’assistance aux victimes et promouvoir le référencement de ces dernières vers les services adaptés.
MAG apportera son expertise dans les outils et méthodologies de collecte de données, mais aussi dans la création de matériels d’information, d’éducation et de communication adaptés, et de stratégies innovantes pour la compréhension et l’appropriation des messages de prévention et le changement de comportement.
Dans un souci de « Duty of Care », un autre volet aura pour groupe cible les acteurs de la réponse humanitaire, afin de leur permettre de mieux appréhender les risques liés à la présence d’Engins Explosifs (EEI) en adoptant des comportements surs, lors de leurs déploiements sur le terrain. 
Du fait de la durée des initiatives, l’impact sera mesuré avec un échantillon des participants aux activités, via de pré-post test qui permettront de comparer les connaissances initiales et finales, mais aussi de collecter des informations de redevabilité.

project_name: Provision of urgent integrated Gender Based Violence (GBV), Child Protection (CP) and General Protection (GP) services for IDPs and hosting communities in North Darfur,  Central  Darfur , White Nile, River Nile , Northern and Khartoum States
project_objective:
The integrated protection  project aims to meet life-saving acute, urgent, immediate Child protection (CP) , Gender Based Violence (GBV) and protection needs of individual among newly internal displaced persons( IDPs)  and their hosting communities in North Darfur,(ND)  Central Darfur,(CD) White Nile(WN) , Northern ( NS),River Nile (RN) and Khartoum (KRT) states  after the clashes between  Sudan Army force (SAF) and Rapid Support force (RSF)  on April 2023 The project will strengthen community-based prevention mechanisms and improving protection response systems through : provision of  specialized services and enhancing the capacity of the local communities on protections risks, preventions, concerns and needs . The project will provide of mental health and Psychosocial support services (MHPSS)including provision of Psychological first aid, clinical counselling and recreational, social and life skills interventions for vulnerable persons with special needs (PSNs)  with focus on unaccompanied and separated   children (UASC) ,GBV survivors , elderly , and persons with disabilities (PwDs). This will be provided at individual level such as through provision comprehensive case management, FTR or referral services  at group level through provision of structured group sessions,  peer to peer or /and recreation and life skills sessions .To enhance the local technical capacity, the project will  rain  service providers on GBV, in particular, health care providers and social workers and  establishment  and training of 12 community based  protection networks and 12 CB feedback and complaints committees , and support the running and operationalization  of 6 women centers
To ensure dignified response the project will , procure and distribute of dignity kits to vulnerable women and girls of reproductive age  as well as provision of mobility aids, crutches clothes etc to PSNs , The project will  conduct protection monitoring Improving community awareness on protection violations, risks and prevention through conducting public awareness  campaigns protection‐related issues, during emergencies and availability of services.

project_name: Provision of WASH to crisis -affected populations in North Darfur and White Nile States
project_objective:
Based on the Cluster objectives and HNO of the Cluster, the WASH interventions in the 2 States shall focus on improved access to water services ,sanitation and hygiene  which will seek to reduce vulnerability of IDPs and host communities to waterborne and vector-transmitted diseases resulting from deficient environmental health conditions, unsafe disposal of faeces, water-borne diseases, poor personal and household sanitation and hygiene practices. The approaches will seek to address needs related to accessing quality and safe drinking water , access to  basic sanitation and hygiene services and facilities, while also establishing/strengthening community structures for improved self-reliance capacities. The intervention shall also have a focus on building community resilience to WASH-related recurrent shocks with emphasis on community empowerment and engagement of women, girls, and young people as enhanced enablers. On sanitation and hygiene elements, the project will focus on supporting communities through Community Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) interventions to empower women, girls, boys and men to use latrines and live in Open Defecation Free (ODF) communities; rehabilitation/construction of gender segregated and disability-friendly sanitation facilities in schools and primary health centres; conducting of hygiene promotion interventions in the communities and in schools and health centres with focus on handwashing with soap at critical times including menstrual hygiene management in schools. The project will also strengthen community WASH structures through establishment and empowerment of Sanitation and Hygiene Committees to manage sanitation services in all the targeted communities. The interventions shall adopt the following approaches:
Action-oriented rapid survey: This will be the initial step to establish status of critical WASH services, facilities and practices in the target localities. A multi-agency approach will be undertaken to promote wide ownership of the rapid survey. Data from the action survey will also be shared with other sector partners to support in addressing gaps and emerging needs.
Capacity building: This will be through establishment of  and training of Hygiene and Sanitation Committees, Water Committees in target villages and training of  Hygiene Promoters. This approach will seek to enhance community ownership and participation, thus anchoring future support for project activities. Capacity building will also encompass undertaking the communities through the CLTS processes. 
Rehabilitation/Establishment of facilities: These will be through rehabilitation or construction of new sanitation facilities in communities and institutions. The intervention shall also construction and or  rehabilitate Water Yards equipped with solar system and construction of water treatment plants to improve access to clean water including distribution of PUR sachets.  
Awareness campaigns: This is an approach that will seek to change behaviour and attitude of community members on safe personal, households and environmental hygiene practices. 
Provision of WASH NFIs: This will include provision of basic WASH facilities such as soap, water buckets/jerry-cans, mosquito nets and ibriks

project_name: Provision of health and nutrition lifesaving interventions for IDPs, returnees and host community in South and East Darfur, Al Jazeera and Khartoum states
project_objective:
•	The project aims at improving equitable access to quality lifesaving curative and preventive services through the provision of primary health care and nutrition interventions in Al Salam, Belil, Gereida and Dimso localities in South Darfur, Yassin, Adilla, Abukarinka, Abujabra and Aedein localities in East Darfur, Bahri, Khartoum and Omdurman localities in Khartoum, and Wad Madani, Alkamleen,Hasahisa localities in Al Jazeera with focus on vulnerable groups including IDPs and people in hotspots resulting from ongoing clashes between the two armies.  The project target to reach out 535,284 beneficiaries of whom 23% are women, 28% girls, 22% men and 27%boys while 0.02% of total reach are expected to be persons living with disability. 
•	Through this project, Alight will provide primary health care through curative lifesaving services and preventive interventions, and this will be done by supporting 24 health facilities to deliver quality services plus mobile clinics in hotspots and new IPD gathering areas. To achieve this, Alight will improve infrastructure including with light rehabilitation and medical equipment with the aim of improving service provision environment. Alight will ensure supply chain of medicines, medical supplies and nutrition commodities in close coordination with other stakeholders including WHO, WFP, UNICEF and respective SMOHs. Primary health care package will include outpatient consultations, short stay for observation purpose, laboratory services, provision of medicines, reproductive health services including 6 BEmONC  , EPI and minor surgery/dressing services. Referral system will be in place for cases beyond PHCCs levels, where funds allow, referred patients among the most vulnerable will be supported to access secondary care including transport for emergency cases. Alight will also support in management of trauma and through integrated approach will protection sector will provide MHPSS.
•	Nutrition package will include early detection of malnutrition through mass MUAC screening, management of malnutrition cases as per CMAM guidelines including targeted supplementary feeding program, outpatient therapeutic feedings, managing 3 stabilization centers and where there no SC, caregivers are facilitated to access them. 
•	The project will use integrated response modalities between health, nutrition, WASH, protection and other sectors. The selection of areas of focus was based on localities ranked with severity level 4 and 5 as per HNO 2023. Alight plans to prioritize the most vulnerable including IDPs, vulnerable residents in isolated areas where there are no other health and nutrition services. In addition, Alight plans to provide services through existing health and nutrition facilities and where the need arise, use approach of mobile or satellite clinic. Prioritization will be based on vulnerability and available resources; Alight will prioritize the youngest for both health and nutrition while focusing at provision of MISP for reproductive health if any emergency.  Also, the poorest will be prioritized and those at high risk of mortality such as children with acute malnutrition with or without medical complications. 
•	Expected risk include the political situation which is flagile, continued clashes between RSF and SAF, intercommunical conflict which affect access , high inflation rate, inavailability of supplies and rain. Also, targetted areas maybe affected by outbreak, high cases of malnutrition resulting from food insecurity, lack of water, poor sanitation, lack of surveillance,. Alight will continue to monitor the situation, where applicable prepositioning of supplies will be adopted to ensure continuity of services. Alight will participate in different coordination mechanism including health and nutrition cluster to remain updated and ensure coordination efforts in line with sector strategies.

project_name: Enhanced Protection Services for Vulnerable Communities in Sudan
project_objective:
Protection landscape creates urgent humanitarian needs for the physical protection of IDPs, refugees, returnees and other civilian populations in areas of displacement and return including at water and firewood collection points and during cultivation and harvest seasons.
The Protection Cluster’s 2023 HNO PiN is report that 3.2 million, of whom 56 per cent are children, and 22 per cent are women. In Sudan, there are 3.7 million IDPs, of whom 2.1 million need assistance, about 666,000 of the 1.2 million returnees need assistance, and there are also 413,000 vulnerable 
due to the conflict in Sudan Women and girls are further exposed to protection risks due to needs arising from the humanitarian situation and even more with rapid inflation and soaring prices of basic needs. Parents send their children to work, Female IDPs face high protection risks and harassment and are occasionally killed or raped. Women and girls especially face protection risks associated with water, sanitation and hygiene practices. Women and girls remain the primary collectors of water and sometimes must travel more than two kilometers each way for water collection—over four times the Sphere standard of 500 meters. Women also report openly defecating, which exposes them to the elements and gender- based violence. The impact of SGBV is exacerbated and prolonged due to a lack of services and reporting mechanisms. Despite the new government of Sudan making positive strides towards equality with four females holding important cabinet positions, there remains a strong patriarchal culture, especially in areas that have experienced years of conflict.
ADRA’s assessment has shown SGBV is still especially prevalent. Over 78% of respondents affirmed that SGBV is present in their communities, meanwhile almost all respondents (89%) believed that they did not know of any agency or body providing protection services to SGBV survivors and only 61% would report GBV incidences. Women and girls have limited options to access latrines, either going to a distant neighbor or using open field. Further consultations with UNHCR, UNFPA, and HAC indicate that protection services are few while protection needs are expected to be large given increased access to newly freed areas.
ADRA will coordinate and integrate activities within the organization as well as with other agencies. The protection component requires collaboration with other agencies and continuing the efforts made by ADRA to develop a robust and functional referral system and solid case management processes. and also, formation of CBPN and community-based structures to enhance the protection activities in the targeted areas. 
ADRA will update the service directory through a service mapping exercise. A people from community groups will be trained on identification of cases and protection issues within their communities and trained on the referral system in their areas. The same groups will identify prevention measures needed to decrease the current protection risks and identify persons at risk eligible for IPA and cash Assistant. To fortify services to at risk cases, this action will engage in psychosocial counselling to trauma and GBV survivors as well as case management. Case management will ensure that survivors identified through the community structures receive appropriate services, ADRA acknowledges that the needs are high across both communities and continues its efforts to ensure social cohesion and peaceful coexistence.
 ADRA Sudan will Provide protection services, Gender Base Violence, and child protection in Blue Nile, White Nile, West Darfur, Central Darfur and Khartoum,

project_name: Improving living conditions through Shelter/NFI distribution to IDPs and returnees
project_objective:
ADRA will use it's extensive expertise in the area, and in the region to carry out Shelter programing that meets both emergency and protracted needs of vulnerable communities. The main goal is to provide conflict and disaster affected individuals in West Darfur, Blue and White Nile and Khartoum with lifesaving assistance.  Currently, ADRA has projects in 5 states Khartoum, White Nile, Blue Nile, Central Darfur and West Darfur. All of them have faced hazard events such as flooding and intercommunal conflicts in different areas. This crisis directly affects the community, without exception of gender or age, triggering a dangerous and uncertain environment for the affected people, who suddenly loose their houses, jobs and, in some cases, their lives. ADRA looks for recovering their dignity through this project in terms of S/ NFI, complementing other WASH, FLS and Protection projects that have been developing in same areas.
Our purpose is to assist IDPs and returnees improving their currently emergency shelter through Cash Voucher Assistance (CVA). Additionally, we plan to provide shelter kits and NFI kits, for new IDPs, as we have been doing in other opportunities.
ADRA will be working in different localities of White Nile (Kosti, El Jabalian, El Salam, Rabak, and Tendalti), Blue Nile (all localities) and West Darfur (El Geneina, Jebel Moon & Kerinik). The emergency shelter kits will be provided to 5,000 households, benefiting more than 25,000 individuals. With the same number of beneficiaries, we are going to work for the NFI kits, benefiting 5,000 households as well. For those IDPs who needs to improve their emergency shelter, we plan to assist 2,000 households, benefiting around 10,000 individuals. Out of the all beneficiaries, ADRA aims at targeting 2000 HH that need to improve their emergency shelter will be assisted with cash for shelter grants .

project_name: Improving access to health and nutrition services for vulnerable population in Blue Nile and Khartoum States, Sudan
project_objective:
This project aim is to improve equitable access to quality life-saving curative and preventive services through timely provision of Nutrition and Health and protection activities through existing health and nutrition system in Bau locality in Blue Nile State among vulnerable male and female, children under-five, pregnant and lactating women (PLW); and to provide emergency assistance to the people affected by the current ongoing conflict in Sudan - in particular in Jebel Awlia Locality in Khartoum State.  
The project will reach 59,507 beneficiaries in Blue Nile. The key project interventions and activities are integrated primary health care services that include health system support, communicable diseases, child health, sexual and reproductive health, prevention, identification, and treatment of malnutrition through implementation targeted supplementary feeding program (TSFP) for moderate acute malnutrition (MAM), outpatient therapeutic program (OTP) for severe acute malnutrition (SAM), maternal, infant and young-child feeding in emergency (MIYCF-E) and referrals for SAM with complications. 
As part of building resilience, the project will provide IYCF/E counselling for caretakers of children under-five, provide food-based prevention of malnutrition (FBPM) for children under two years, provide food-based prevention of malnutrition (FBPM) for pregnant and lactating women (PLWs), micronutrient supplementation (Vitamin A for under-fives and MNP), provide iron and folic acid supplementation for pregnant women, conduct screening (MUAC/Oedema) of all children 6-59 months and refer to appropriate CMAM sites for OTPs/TSFPs or SCs. Conduct Growth Monitoring to serve as an early detection of deterioration of nutrition situation in children under 5 years, distribute IEC materials for IYCF and nutrition education and maternal and child health (MCH) during anti-natal care, in maternity wards, delivery room, post-natal care, and adolescent as one package of services that will contribute to the surveillance system. Treatment of childhood illnesses (IMCI) will be integrated with CMAM, referral of under-five malnourished children, PLW with breastfeeding difficulties producing milk or children with disabilities or children with difficulties in suckling and swallowing to the nutrition sites/specialist. GBV and PSEA will be mainstreamed during training of nutrition staff, that will include a mandatory signing of code of conduct, provision of key messages on GBV, establishment of feedback and complaints mechanisms. 
To respond to the current conflict that began on 15 April 2023, Medair plans to set up three mobile health teams to provide basic healthcare assistance to the affect population in Jebel Awlia Locality in Khartoum. The response aims to contribute to the reduction of excess mortality and morbidity among the vulnerable population in Khartoum amidst the ongoing conflict. Through the response, Medair aims to improve the access to healthcare services of the people in need and reduce the burden of the open hospitals which are overwhelmed. Medair will aim to provide services to 20,000 beneficiaries during this period through the mobile health teams.

project_name: Multisectoral assistance to children in Syria
project_objective: The objective is to enable children affected by conflict and displacement in Syria to meet their basic needs, increase their protection, human dignity and benefit from community-based initiatives that ensure their inclusion, through an integrated multi-sectoral approach including Shelter, WASH, education and child protection in schools, juvenile centres and within communities, in partnership with local partners. Tdh will contribute to this objective through the direct provision of an integrated package of service-oriented assistance to build the resilience of children and communities, particularly children affected by the conflict across 5 governorates in Syria. Tdh conducted various needs assessments during 2022 in juvenile centres and in schools. The needs remain tremendous! Limited access to non-formal education activities and specialised PSS services, damaged buildings, critical basic living conditions, including lack of food and non-food items, electricity and water. In addition, for children in conflict with the law, there is a clear need for legal support via a lawyer who represents them in court, and reintegration after release into their families and communities. The project is therefore structured around a series of complementary and integrated activities at different levels and crosses several sectors. Firstly, Tdh will address the specific needs of children in juvenile centres, through prevention, protection and reintegration services for children at risk, in contact or in conflict with the law. Through capacity building activities on CP and PSS, the project will address some of the root causes of the problems leading to the detention of children, through awareness raising communities and referrals. The strengthening of non-formal protection systems such as community centres, civil society initiatives and community child protection committees contributes to an overall increase in the accessibility and quality of protection services. The proposed response will also cover food distribution, light rehabilitation of the critical infrastructure damaged in juvenile centers and provision of MHPSS and Non formal education. Protection services will help children in juvenile centers to obtain legal documentation and represent them infront of the courts and advocate for their release from the detention while the protection team will also support the referrals to the different services and work on the restoration of the family links through family visits and phone calls wherever its possible. In addition, recognising the importance of supporting these children after their release, Tdh will also ensure their reintegration into their families and communities. In parallel, Tdh will continue to rehabilitate schools to encourage families to send their children to school or non formal education classes for those who cannot send children to the school. Tdh aims to rehabilitate 4 schools and give children as well as teachers and staff access to functional and safe school facilities through rehabilitation works that will be inclusive for all, gender sensitive and environmentally friendly and sustainable through the use of solar panels. They will have access to clean water, sanitation facilities and hygiene promotion on good practices and behaviours to protect themselves from water-borne diseases, with the distribution of hygiene kits. All schools and classrooms will be rehabilitated and equipped so that users can benefit from a safe and child-friendly learning space. In 2023, Tdh's proposed intervention will target 14,038 children,  120 teachers, 3740 families and 184 child protection workers, including 6,640 girls and 7,398 boys, aged from 0 to 17 and 5,819 women and 4,997 men from 18 and above 50,  with a significant proportion of IDPs and Host communities, using an integrated area-based approach that addresses immediate education and child protection services provided to communities. Tdh has so far secured 20%  of the total budget.

project_name: Displaced children and their families have improved access to safe and affordable drinking water as well as improved access to adequate and equitable sanitation and hygiene in Syria
project_objective:
This project will seek to improve access to lifesaving WASH services to conflict affected children and adults in Syria. Aligned with Objectives 1, 2 and 4 of the Humanitarian Response Plan, this project will address WASH needs in a comprehensive and integrated manner by providing a range of services along-side Child Protection, Education and/or Nutrition activities. The purpose is to provide assistance to vulnerable individuals that are impacted by more than a decade of conflict, COVID-19, and climate change, with the goal of reducing the risk of communicable and water-borne diseases, and improving learning environments for children.  

Implementation will take place in North East Syria and North West Syria, and will in large part be a continuation of existing programming. Community acceptance will be prioritised, and a conflict sensitive approach will be taken to reduce the risk of unintended consequences. Activities will be informed through action plans developed together with the community, and may include rehabilitation of communal infrastructure, including at institutional levels, distribution of hygiene items, hygiene promotion, and basic service provision of WASH services such as water trucking, solid waste management, desludging and operations and maintenance of WASH facilities in camps / settlements.  

The sustainability of the project will be ensured through systems strengthening of the technical departments, or where conditions allow, WASH committees. Children youth, women and people living with disabilities will play important roles in the need identification and design stages.

project_name: Emergency, comprehensive and quality maternal and child healthcare and nutrition in South Kordofan, Sudan
project_objective:
In collaboration with the State Ministry of Health, the project implemented by ALIMA has for objective to reduce the morbidity and mortality for vulnerable host and displaced populations, including women and children, affected by the crisis in South Kordofan. 
It will be achieved through increasing the immediate access to comprehensive health services by vulnerable host and displaced populations affected by the crisis in South Kordofan, including women and children. The project will also increase access to comprehensive quality primary health care, including nutrition, sexual reproductive health and mental health services, through PHCs support and mobile clinics for vulnerable hard to reach populations in Kadugli and Reif Arshargi localities, especially women and children, and increasing access to quality life-saving secondary health care for pregnant and lactating women and survivors of sexual violence at the maternity of Kadugli Teaching Hospital. The project will also aim at strengthening the capacity of SMoH Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) to deliver minimum healthcare services to population affected by disease outbreaks and population displacement due to flooding and armed conflict.
ALIMA aims to improve access to comprehensive primary health care services, including sexual and reproductive health, GBV response, nutrition and MHPSS, through its support of 2 primary health centers whose facilities are still accessible and safe in Moutar and Al-Bardab. To ensure the access of hard-to-reach vulnerable populations to quality care, the project will support the deployment of 6 mobile clinics providing PHC in the remaining areas of Kohliyat, Mashaesh, Miri, Saraf Dai, Hajer Mach and Dara. The team will deliver primary health care for children under 5 and pregnant women, including nutritional screening. They will also ensure the provision of a comprehensive package to ensure the management of sexual violence victims. 
To make the community aware of the services, 50 community health workers (CHW) will be chosen from each community to conduct awareness raising activities about sexual and reproductive health and gender-based violence, essential nutritional practices, health promotion, personal and environmental hygiene, and referrals from the community to the health facility.
Survivor-centered GBV case-management, such as clinical management of rape and MHPSS services will be offered at the ALIMA supported Kadugli Teaching Hospital to the most vulnerable patients. 2 highly skilled midwives will undergo a full capacity building training in mental health issues with ALIMA will ensure MHPSS activities; they will be supervised and their activities coordinated by a sexual and reproductive health manager. Several consulting sessions will be provided to each survivor. 
ALIMA will improve access to quality life-saving secondary health care for pregnant and lactating women and survivors of sexual violence at the maternity in Kadugli Teaching Hospital. ALIMA will support the maternity ward in Kadugli Hospital to deliver comprehensive emergency obstetric and neonatal care.  ALIMA will strengthen the skills of midwives and other auxiliary nurses through on the job-training to improve patient care and global management of the maternity ward.

project_name: Improved Access of Vulnerable Children to Quality Gender Responsive Education
project_objective:
Plan International Sudan will target  50,182 of most vulnerable and marginalized girls and boys at risk of exclusion from education of the newly displaced and vulnerable host communities (27,600 gils and 22,582 boys) in 5 states of Aj Jazirah, Gedaref, White Nile,  South Kordofan,  and Kassala. Those target states areas receiving significant inflows of people fleeing violence, as well state like  South Kordofan  host protracted displaced populations, with current waves of IDP arrivals further straining limited basic services, and exacerbating humanitarian conditions. This response aim to assist the  target children affected by conflict and crisis have access to safe and protective learning environments as well have enhance structured lifesaving learning that promotes personal well-being within a protective environment. The children targeted detailed as follows:
 - Aj Jazirah: 15,000 internally displaced and vulnerable children (8,250 girls and 6,750 boys) in primary schools in 2 localities of Al Hasahisa, and Medani Al Kubra. 
- Gedaref,: 4,000  internally displaced and vulnerable children (2,800 girls and 1,200 boys) in primary schools in 3 localities of Al Fao, and Al Fashaga. 
- White Nile: 15,432 internally displaced and vulnerable children (8,488 girls and 6,944 boys) in primary schools in 4 localities of Aj Jabalain, As Salam / Ar Rawat, Kosti and Tendalti

project_name: Enhance the WOS Nutrition Sector Coordination mechanism for effective, integrated and harmonized nutrition response at scale.
project_objective:
The deteriorating nutrition situation in the Whole of Syria (WOS) depicted a worsening trend in 2022, with the 2023 HNO projecting an even worse trend in 2023. Syria is faced with a triple burden of malnutrition- high chronic malnutrition, increasing levels of acute malnutrition and emergency levels of anaemia among children and women of reproductive age. Aggravating factors promoting malnutrition include food insecurity, elevated food prices, devaluation of the Syrian pound, scarce and unsafe water use, disease spread and loss of household income.  This situation calls for the need for a robust coordination mechanism at all levels that will enhance provision of an equitable, inclusive, harmonized and high-quality response at scale. The nutrition sector estimates that 5.9 million vulnerable people, including 3.7 million and approximately 0.9 million people with disabilities will require life-saving nutrition services in 2023. UNICEF as the cluster lead agency (CLA) for nutrition will undertake the below coordination functions:

Coordination and Information management: CLA will lead the coordination of the collective response planning process to clearly articulate the needs analysis, critical priorities, response strategy and funding requirements. In collaboration with other sector leads, CLA will advocate for availability of required human and financial resources as well as other strategic issues that will provide an enabling environment for a quality response at scale. The sector coordination team will strengthen the reporting systems among nutrition sector partners through use of nutrition information systems and 4Ws to enable generation of information products for an evidence- driven response. To the best extent possible, this project will support the decentralization of coordination mechanisms to lower levels to ensure a harmonized, coordinated, and inclusive response. The coordination from Humanitarian Country Team (HCT) Hub will be undertaken at national and sub-national levels through 6 sub-national sector coordinators covering Government of Syria (GOS) controlled areas. 

Strengthening nutrition resilience: From a vantage point of leading the WASH and Education Sectors as well as child protection Area of Responsibility (AoR), CLA- will provide the required inter-sector support to partners in coordination with Ministry of Health to develop and adopt evidence-based strategies to address the root causes of malnutrition from a multi-sectorial approach. 

Strengthening localization: In line with humanitarian principles and ‘Do No Harm’ approach, CLA will strengthen the technical and operational capacities of local actors to coordinate, plan and implement a high-quality integrated nutrition response as guided by the nutrition sector response plan. CLA, will support the development of standards and guidelines across all hub to empower communities to prevent, detect and refer to treatment all forms of malnutrition. CLA will continue to advocate for improved funding channels directly to local organizations. 

Capacity building and technical support: Through a robust capacity mapping exercise, CLA will work in coordination with the Ministry of Health and sector partners across all hubs to address response capacity and coverage gaps in order to deliver a high quality response.

Contingency planning: In collaboration with other sectors, the nutrition sector will conduct risk  analysis and develop scenario- based contingency plan to strengthen the collective sector’s preparedness capacity. The plan will be updated with on-gong nutrition sensitive surveillance system 
Accountability to affected population (AAP) and considerations of gender and specific groups/children with disability: The sector lead will support and coordinate the mainstreaming of AAP in the nutrition response through ensuring inclusive consultation and engagement of the affected population in the entire project cycle.

project_name: ACCÉLÉRER L'ACTION LOCALE DANS LES CRISES HUMANITAIRES ET SANITAIRES AU TCHAD
project_objective:
Le Partenariat programmatique pilote (PPP) est un partenariat sur 3 ans (36 mois) entre l'IFRC, plusieurs Sociétés nationales membres et la Direction générale de la protection civile et des opérations d’aide humanitaire (DG ECHO). 
Ce programme fait suite à plusieurs constats: 
Le système humanitaire doit constamment s’adapter et répondre aux besoins émergents des personnes touchées par les problématiques mondiales (changement climatique, pandémie de COVID-19) tout en fournissant une assistance ininterrompue aux personnes touchées par les conflits, les déplacements, les catastrophes et autres épidémies. 
Les silos et les contraintes de capacité limitent parfois l’efficacité des efforts de préparation, de réponse et de rétablissement. 
Les communautés et les institutions locales manquent souvent de soutien nécessaire pour anticiper les crises humanitaires et sanitaires (prévention/préparation/réponses). 
Les partenariats sont dans certains cas fragmentés.

Le Programme vise ainsi à promouvoir des approches plus flexibles, efficaces, et axées sur l’anticipation. Il s’agit de mettre en œuvre l’agenda de la localisation, avoir une programmation intégrant des modalités des transferts monétaires, et une plus grande implication de la communauté. 
Cette programmation pluriannuelle renforce la coordination et la collaboration des acteurs humanitaires à travers une approche multirégionale/mondiale. Avec une approche d’interopérabilité, différents acteurs travaillent dans une même logique d’intervention avec des règles d’engagement communes.

project_name: Child Protection response for the most vulnerable and at-risk children and their caregivers in South Sudan
project_objective:
The IRC Child Protection program will continue to provide comprehensive protection response services and create a safe and protective environment for children who are at risk of or have experienced abuse, exploitation, neglect, and violence as a result of recurrent crisis and conflict, assisting them in healing, recovering, and feeling safe again while collaborating with their caregivers and the local government and community-level prevention mechanisms in accordance with the Minimum Standards for CP and national level SOPs, guidelines, and protocols. The IRC CP program will reach 66,201(32,3232M, 33869F) people through an integrated response of static and mobile response approaches in the CP AOR priority locations (severity 3 and 4) of Panyijiar, Mayendit, and Koch Counties in Unity State; Aweil East and Aweil South in Northern Bahr el Ghazal State, and Juba IDPs in Rajaf Counties in Central Equatoria State.
The proposed child protection responses are linked with the strategic objectives of the cluster and three domains of the CP AOR for HRP 2022. Case management services will be provided to children who have concerns about their safety. FTR services, alternative care arrangements for unaccompanied and separated children (UASC), and protection cash aid will also be provided to meet the basic needs of the children. The Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) service will be provided for children and caregivers with psychological distress using a combination of approaches such as Safe Healing and Learning Space (SHLS) and schools for Social and Emotional Learning, Families Make the Difference Curriculum for parenting skills of caregivers, Supporting Adolescents and their Families in Emergencies Curriculum (SAFE) for life skills of adolescents, and IRC’s Brighter Futures Model for malnourished under five years children with protection concerns. Finally, the community-based child protection (CBCP) structures will be established/strengthened to the lower structure of the community, community outreach on CP awareness and COVID-19 prevention messages, and capacity building of the frontline staff and community volunteers.
The CP response will be complementary to the existing IRC’s GBV, general protection, nutrition, health, and livelihood programs to ensure comprehensive care. The existing health and nutrition facilities will serve as screening and awareness-raising spots and IRC will establish CP help desks. IRC’s GBV centers will also serve as a point of referral for rape survivor girls, and the livelihood section will support the cash-based intervention. In addition, the CP team will be part of the integrated mobile team in all locations where IRC is operating.

project_name: Assistance médico-nutritionnelle aux populations affectées par les crises du bassin du Lac Tchad et anglophone dans les districts sanitaires de Makary, Fotokol, Mada, Bali, Batibo et Santa au Cameroun
project_objective:
Depuis 2014, le Cameroun est confronté à deux crises sécuritaires et humanitaires sans précédent à l’Extrême-Nord (EN) et au Nord-Ouest (NO) qui ont entraîné d’importants mouvements de population et continuent de peser sur les moyens de subsistance des populations déplacées, réfugiées et hôtes ainsi que sur les services de base. 

En 2022, le Cameroun a vu les attaques des groupes djihadistes et les conflits intercommunautaires se multiplier à l’EN, notamment pour le contrôle des terres et des points d’eau, et les confrontations entre les groupes séparatistes et le gouvernement s’intensifier au NO. A cela s’ajoute une situation socio-économique fragilisée par la pandémie de la Covid-19 et l’impact du changement climatique sur les moyens de subsistance de la population. 
 
L’action proposée s'inscrit dans la continuité de l’intervention menée par ALIMA en 2022 dans les districts sanitaires de Makary, Fotokol, Mada, Bali, Batibo et Santa situés à l’épicentre des crises du Lac Tchad et anglophone. Elle vise à :
réduire la morbi-mortalité des populations vulnérables déplacées, réfugiées et hôtes à l’EN et au NO en assurant un accès aux soins et une prise en charge médicale, gratuite et de qualité ; et,
garantir une réponse rapide et adaptée aux besoins en cas de choc humanitaire et d’urgence sanitaire.

project_name: Improving access to Justice and specialized services for vulnerable Survivors of Gender Based Violence through integrated GBV/SRHR response in crisis affected communities of Michika and Madagali LGAs of Adamawa state
project_objective:
CDHI will implement 12-month emergency GBV response that improves access to justice and specialized GBV services to affected population in crisis affected communities of Michika and Madagali LGAs targeting IDPs, Returnees and Vulnerable women, men, boys, and girls living in the host communities. The project will provide GBV specialized services and access to legal and justice services to women, men, boys and girls, amongst IDPs, Returnees and Hosting populations. The project will leverage on CDHI’s long standing presence in community-based driven initiatives in GBV, WASH, and Nutrition to deliver quality GBV response that meet the needs of vulnerable people living in the host communities. The GBV project will focus on actions that will increase access to prevention and response services for GBV survivors and individuals at risk of GBV. GBV survivors will receive survivor centered case management services including referrals for special services, including access to justice through formal or informal channels. Through this project formal and informal institutions will be strengthened to facilitate uptake of access and utilization of the justice systems. CDHI will construct Women and girls friendly spaces across communities of Michika and Madagali LGAs.  CDHI will strengthened existing health facilities through training of health workers on clinical management of Rape, provision of supplies including contraceptives', PEP - Kits, delivery kits and facilitation of transportation to survivors for timely uptake of services. The project will establish and/or support existing family support networks to reduce the social isolation of families and increase social support for women and girls. This will increase parent’s ability to provide social.  Similarly, CDHI will facilitate the training of formal institutions including the  NBA, International Federation of Female Lawyers – FIDA, State security architecture, Human Right commission to support facilitation and access to justice for beneficiaries wishing to access justice through the formal system. Additionally, activities to improve resilience and coping mechanisms of women, girls, men, and boys affected by GBV through provision of livelihood support through income generating activities - IGA and fostering social cohesion targeting vulnerable individuals through community-based psychosocial support, provided in newly established safe spaces that will be supported by the project. CDHI through this project targets to provide case management services to identified GBV survivors. 
Similarly, women, men, boys, and girls will benefit from life skills and positive parenting sessions using the adolescent life skill curriculum and positive parenting manual. CDHI will increase local capacity by strengthening community-based mechanisms, through training of community leaders, religious leaders, health workers, security personnel’s on GBV core concept and referral pathway. The project will also increase awareness on the impact of GBV and sexual reproductive health right - SRHR through sensitization during health facility based ante-natal care services and also through outreach to individuals and will work with communities to identify GBV risks in the targeted communities and develop action plans to mitigate these risks. 
Trained facilitators will deliver tailored age, gender, and culture sensitive, appropriate GBV/SRH messages using the provided sensitization guide to members of the communities. Similarly, CDHI will provide and distribute dignity kits accessed from the GBV core pipeline to targeted vulnerable women and girls who meet the vulnerability criteria. Men and boys will also be engaged at the community level through peer discussions to raise awareness and reduce stigma towards women and girls during menstruation. All communication packages will be adopted from the existing key messages and IEC materials developed by the sector.

project_name: Emergency Education and MHPSS in Gaza
project_objective:
The unique socio-economic conditions of blockade, with its movement restrictions and destruction of productive capacity, are further compounded by repeated cycle of conflicts as well as the global emergencies of the Ukraine Crisis followed by the COVID-19 pandemic. For the second consecutive year, UNRWA opened the 2022-2023 academic year with full face-to-face learning, providing quality education to 294,086 students (142,363 girls and 151,723boys, including 5,000 students with disabilities). 

In order to ensure that no child is left behind and that access to education is available to all students regardless of their available resources, UNRWA will provide: (1) additional learning support to enhance children literacy and numeracy skills, (2) material support to assist students’ learning experience,  (3) structured recreational (after-school and summer), (4) cleaning supplies and materials to continue meeting hygiene requirements outlined by the WHO and MoH, (5) support to special education for children with disabilities through Community Based Rehabilitation Centers, (6) mental health and psychosocial support to students and parents.

project_name: Emergency Health and MHPSS in Gaza
project_objective:
The deteriorating socio-economic situation in Gaza combined with recurrent rounds of hostilities and the impact of COVID-19 pandemic are putting further pressure to the health system in the Gaza Strip.
UNRWA continues to provide essential primary health care services to 1.4 million Palestine refugees in Gaza. Expanding the capacity of the UNRWA health services to absorb increasing needs is necessary to support the already over-stretched public health services, ensuring access of Gaza’s vulnerable population to health services. UNRWA’s ability to respond to emergency health needs in Gaza is greatly constrained by the tight funding situation as well as the increasing needs, and ensuring the availability of this intervention is crucial.
In light of these conditions, this proposed intervention aims to support the provision of critical healthcare needs for Palestine refugees in the Gaza Strip, while alleviating the pressure on public health system, through: (1) ensuring access to secondary and tertiary health services for poor refugees in response to MoH’s long-waiting list, (2) providing critical medicines especially for NCD patients, (3) hiring additional staff to cope with increasing needs, (4) enhancing telemedicine services, (5) strengthening the infection prevention control, (6) enhancing health response capabilities in emergency, (7) conducting home visits for vulnerable patients, (8) providing necessary assistive tools to children with special needs, and (9) providing mental health and psychosocial support especially to women, vulnerable groups, people affected by the hostilities and staff.

project_name: Restoring Disrupted Livelihoods and Supporting Early Recovery Efforts for Palestine Refugees in Syria
project_objective:
Over eleven years of crisis in Syria has drastically eroded the living conditions of Palestine refugees and Syrian nationals alike. The rapid depreciation of the Syrian pound accompanied by staggering inflation levels, the impact of Lebanon's financial and banking crisis, and the tightened trade restrictions imposed on the country since June 2020, have all contributed to a worsening of the socio-economic conditions. The COVID-19 pandemic has led to additional stress on basic services that has impacted the livelihoods of Palestine refugees and Syrians. 

To support Palestine refugee youth access to employment opportunities, the UNRWA TVET programme will continue to provide short-term courses to 800 students in Damascus, Dera’a, Homs, Aleppo, Latakia, and Hama offering a variety of specializations that respond to the needs of the local market. Short-term courses (three months on average) are designed to strengthen technical skills, with minimal financial costs to the refugee students, to improve their prospects of accessing the labour market. In addition to the courses offered in the Damascus Training Centre, UNRWA will continue to expand its provision of long-term courses in its vocational training centres (VTCs) in Aleppo, Homs, Latakia and Dera’a and will introduce these in Hama in 2023. This is in response to the increasing demand of refugee youth in these areas for similar courses to those offered in Damascus and to promote equal access for all young Palestine refugees to livelihood opportunities to support their resilience. 

UNRWA will also provide employability and soft skills sessions to TVET students to encourage their confidence and abilities in approaching companies and communicating with potential future employers during job interviews. The Agency will maintain the dormitory at the Damascus Training Centre to provide a limited number of students, who live in remote locations, with accommodation to support the continuation of their TVET training. Transportation of vulnerable students will also be subsidised to mitigate the impact of the fuel crisis and associated rising transportation costs on the ability of students to access VTCs.

The various components of UNRWA's interventions in 2022-2023 will also contribute to supporting refugees who have spontaneously returned to their places of residence either internally or from other countries. Where possible, UNRWA will aim at restarting services in camps that were heavily destroyed during the conflict (Dera’a, Yarmouk and Ein el Tal) through the rehabilitation of the Agency’s installations (including schools and clinics) in these camps.

Finally, depending on the availability of funds, UNRWA will explore the feasibility of conducting small-scale cash-for-work initiatives in 2023 mainly focusing on unskilled job placements supporting UNRWA works in camps and Palestine refugee gatherings.

project_name: Prevention of the forcible transfer of Palestinians in the West Bank and East Jerusalem through humanitarian assistance and evidence-based advocacy
project_objective: This multi-sector Project will support the West Bank Protection Consortium (the Consortium) to deliver assistance to 43783 Palestinians at risk of forcible transfer in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem due to recurrent violations of international law. Building on previous risks and vulnerability analyzes, the Action addresses the protection needs of persons and communities of concern through a multi-sectoral approach that reduces vulnerabilities, builds capacities and responds to threats.Specifically, the Project aims at: (1) preventing and responding to protection incidents  (demolitions, settler-related, military operations) with emergency assistance (cash and in-kind), protective measures, and mental health and psychosocial support interventions; (2) mitigating protection risks for highly vulnerable communities (172) through both legal aid and synergizing community-based protection (CPA)and the provision of basic and social infrastructure, including . the delivery of WASH and health infrastructure, hygiene and RCCE awareness materials, education infrastructure,  as well as livelihood support for women and men; and (3) promoting increased respect for IHL and IHRL and accountability for violations through coalition advocacy and stakeholder mobilization undertaken with Third States, International Organizations, Palestinian authorities and media outlets. The Project provides a mechanism to respond to OCHA triggers for demolitions and settler-related incidents. Shelter, WASH, Education, MHPSS, FSL, legal aid and emergency responses and advocacy will be coordinated through the relevant Clusters/WGs. A protection response plan is updated yearly in each of the 172 community where the consortium implements the CPA approach, which allows the prioritization of activities and monitoring of progress in community members’ safety and access to basic services. Groups traditionally excluded from decision-making (women, children, PWDs) are given particular attention and responses are designed to fit their specific needs. The plans describe what communities need to be better protected from forcible transfer it the 16 sectors (Access, Access to services, Civil Society presence, WASH, Education, Land Status, Protection, Health, Transportation, Livelihood, Gender, Shelter, Energy, Demography, Relation with PA and Settler violence). Legal needs relate to supporting and advising communities and individuals to prevent demolitions and confiscations (including in the cases of demolition orders against schools, such as Ein Samiya and Um Qussa); as well as challenging the increasingly restrictive legal framework underpinning the coercive environment Consequently, the Project is envisaged to contribute to the realization of the following HRP objectives: 1. Increased respect for International Humanitarian Law (IHL) and International Human Rights Law (IHRL) and accountability for violations; 2. Protection response mechanisms are in place to prevent and mitigate the effects of the occupation and conflict related violence. Implementing partners will also submit projects as individual agencies, which will include some of the same activities (including legal aid services; shelter upgrades, WASH and other projects). Some of these projects will complement this Project’s assistance but will respond to a logic of ‘contiguity’ rather than ‘continuity’, since they are informed by different rationales and approaches. For this reason, financial resources will be kept separated. Our planning, monitoring, and reporting systems prevent any duplication.

project_name: Emergency WASH assistance for Palestine refugees in the West Bank

Through these activities, UNRWA aims to ensure that the vulnerable population in the West Bank improve their access to equitable, affordable and sustainable safely-managed WASH services. UNRWA strives to improve the safety and accessibility of complaints, including complaints of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse. The project has multiple channels to receive and respond to complaints which are adapted to the target population (including a local phone line for troubleshooting and complaints, face-to-face reporting via social workers and camp service officers, and hotlines for SEA and serious misconduct complaints) and UNRWA SOPs abide to CBCM SOPs from different target populations, including vulnerable groups. Complaints of SEA will be handled by PSEA focal points who will ensure a survivor centered approach in how the complaint is handled and support is offered to the survivor. UNRWA WBFO works closely with the PSEA Network and will undertake compulsory reporting and external referrals.
