El NRC cuenta con experiencia brindando talleres de manejo de albergues colectivos, actividad que seguirá llevando a cabo mediante este proyecto, teniendo como beneficiarios funcionarios gubernamentales o no gubernamentales cuyo trabajo está vinculado a dar asistencia a población en movilidad.  

 Educativos), asimismo NRC integra elementos transversales tales como: género, edad, movilidad reducida, participación comunitaria y medio ambiente en el diseño y ejecución de sus proyectos.  

A través de estas intervenciones el NRC alcanzará 6500 beneficiarios únicos.

project_name: Emergency Rehabilitation of Shelters for Palestine Refugees in the West Bank
project_objective:
Under this project, UNRWA will seek to provide a safe and dignified standard of living for 200 Palestine refugee households through ‘self-help’ rehabilitation, whereby funds are provided to beneficiaries to carry out the work, with the technical support from the Agency. The most vulnerable segment of refugees that include persons with disabilities and female-headed households are targeted so as to help them meet shelter basic needs and minimum standards. The project will also seek to secure a safe and dignified standard of living for 120 Palestine refugee households who suffer from man-made and natural crisis such as cold, fire, flood, settler violence and winterization by providing cash through checks. These activities service the Cluster HRP Objective of “Vulnerable households exposed to harsh weather and protection concerns are supported to meet basic needs and enhance their coping capacity.”
UNRWA strives to improve the safety and accessibility of complaints, including complaints of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse. The project has multiple channels to receive and respond to complaints which are adapted to the target population (including a local phone line for troubleshooting and complaints, face-to-face reporting via social workers and camp service officers, and hotlines for SEA and serious misconduct complaints) and UNRWA SOPs abide to CBCM SOPs from different target populations, including vulnerable groups. Complaints of SEA will be handled by PSEA focal points who will ensure a survivor centered approach in how the complaint is handled and support is offered to the survivor. UNRWA WBFO works closely with the PSEA Network and will undertake compulsory reporting and external referrals.

project_name: Enable refugees to get cash to meet basic needs
project_objective: The well-being of the refugees is improved and the gap in basic needs is bridged throughuse of cash-based interventions.

project_name: Water, sanitation and hygiene response to the affected population
project_objective: Refugees and asylum-seekers have equitable access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene facilities

project_name: Prevention of under nutrition among children 6- 23 months, in vulnerable districts in the Far North region
project_objective: WFP is implementing a nutrition response frame with a stronger focus on the prevention of malnutrition. The program focuses on preventing malnutrition amongst the most vulnerable populations through strengthening supplementary feeding with a focus on the first 1000 days of life. The program targets all children aged 6-23 months including those children suffering from moderate acute malnutrition-MAM) in the most food insecure departments presenting the highest GAM rates in the Far North, North, Adamawa, and East region, while in the Northwest and southwest region the program targets children aged 6-23 months  in food insecure household. The program activities include 1. Screening for malnutrition and referral of severe cases for treatment; 2.Promotion of infant and young child feeding practices  3.Distribution of specialized nutritious food to children aged 6-23months 4.Social and behavioral change communication in favor of good nutrition and health practices5.Promotion of the use of the blanket feeding platform or provision of complementary services including immunization, micro-nutrient supplementation, deworming, malaria and other childhood illnesses prevention, family planning, etc. WFP in 2023 intends to assist about 44000 nutritionally vulnerable persons in the Far North region

project_name: Strengthening child protection prevention and response mechanism through enhancing community-based child protection and protective environment to protect and safeguard children in the Rohingya community
project_objective:
""IOM’s Child Protection project in 2023 aims to continue to prevent and respond to child protection issues and empower vulnerable girls, boys, parents, and caregivers in camps by strengthening the protective environment through multi-sectoral approach and community-based interventions. 
  
IOM programming incorporates age, gender, and diversity needs of the affected population in line with protective measures and mainstreaming to respond to specific needs, especially to enable girls and boys, children and adolescents, children with disabilities to be instrumental in improving the quality of their life and mitigating risks and dangers in their community and living environment. To achieve these objectives IOM’s prevention and response will focus on enhancing Community-based Child Protection (CBCP) with a participatory approach, allowing to bridge inter-generational gaps to promote social behavioral changes.  IOM will continue to strengthen CBCP at the block level in the camp to enhance the capacity of communities to protect children with the participation and inclusion of children and youth. IOM CP will support these groups and clubs (including adolescents, girls and women led groups) by offering a forum to discuss relevant issues, and to enhance their capacity and awareness to empower the wider community to proactively identify and address child protection issues.  

IOM will also provide specialized child protection services, such as case management, structured static, and mobile PSS block-level to reach out to boys and girls, including adolescents, with dignified and safe access to services and facilities, with special focus on children with disabilities, children caring for family members and child mothers. IOM PSS support will build on cultural education to nurture Rohingya roots and identity and promoting intergenerational discourse. Aiming to increase engagement with boys, IOM plans to engage more through inter-generational discussions and training on traditional livelihood skills.   Parents and caregivers will be provided PSS and positive parenting support, including facilitated group discussions based on the evidence-based curriculum between adults and children / adolescents. IOM will continue to support child survivors of GBV and trafficking in the camps through direct implementation and our IPs on legal interventions. 

IOM will closely work with the Government especially the Camp in Charge (CiC) and other relevant government officials in the camp area. IOM will also provide relevant training to law enforcement agencies, like the Armed Police Battalion (APBN) as part of their child protection mainstreaming. 
Services will be provided through IOM direct implementation in camp 9 and 20 with a cross-cutting approach IOM closely cooperates with other sectors and IOM Units such as Health/MHPSS, Shelter, WASH, Site Management/ Communication with Communities and Social Cohesion to mainstream child protection, child safeguarding, age, gender and disability throughout programming; to coordinate disaster preparedness and emergency response; to strengthen PSEA awareness and to respond effectively to the Community 
Feedback Mechanisms to ensure accountability for the affected population. 
IOM is committed to child protection inter-agency efforts and contributes to the CP Sub-Sector, CP Case Management Technical Working Group, MHPSS Working Group and PSEA Network as well as field level coordination.""

project_name: IMPROVING SKILLS AND ECONOMIC OPPORTUNITIES FOR THE BANGLADESHI COMMUNITY AND ROHINGYA WOMEN & YOUTHS IN COX'S BAZAR
project_objective:
""IOM will undertake wide variety of activities to create an enabling environment for the Rohingya refugees towards eventual sustainable voluntary return and reintegration in Myanmar in the future when conditions may permit. Such activities will help Rohingya beneficiaries increase self-reliance skills. The livelihoods activities will also focus on the host communities affected by the influx by integrating income-generating livelihoods through support to agricultue and other sectors.
IOM will implement skills development projects to promote the economic resilience of Rohingya refugees in the camps. This training will enhance their capacity and help them utilize their skills in the camps in Bangladesh as self-reliance opportunities and can be used as transferrable skills by them upon return to Myanmar. Rohingya beneficiaries will receive skills training related and applicable to the humanitarian sector (e.g. health, wash, sanitation, site development-construction, etc.) to enable them earning income in the camps. After the end of the training IOM will facilitate in-kind asset support materials to  Rohingya beneficiaries working outside the agricultural sector who are willing to gain basic skills or competencies but lack the physical assets to do so.
IOM will provide host communities with transferable and life skills training (e.g., computer skills, communication, negotiation, psychosocial) and vocational skills training including skills related to green businesses and green financing such as plumbing, ac repair, secretary, patient administration, catering to disaster resilient off-farming tools and methods, waste recycling, electronic refurbishment, financial literacy related to resilient investments and planning, etc. The trades will be identified by thorough skills and needs assessment exercises. This training will give scope to beneficiaries in the host community for income generation. Productive asset support will be given to women beneficiaries who have technical skills but lack inputs/opportunities/assets but are willing to earn a modest income. IOM will provide small business grants through Entrepreneurship Program to the existing Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) to help beneficiaries expand and strengthen their businesses. Support will be given for the establishment of women's cooperatives (such as livestock, handicrafts, etc.,). Cash for work activities will also be included as an income-generation activity in the host community.
To enhance the private sector engagement and promote market linkages, wage subsidy opportunities for beneficiaries will be implemented. To ensure sustainable income generation, emphasis will be given to activities like product fairs for/by the beneficiaries in the host community to sell and promote their products to individuals and wholesalers.  A labour market assessment will be conducted to identify the needs of the beneficiaries based on which suitable activities will be selected. All these activities in both host, as well as refugee community, will be carried out by either implementing partners or implemented directly by IOM. IOM will ensure integration of various cross-cutting issues in the project design by identifying and including the most vulnerable beneficiaries through gender and disability-sensitive beneficiary selection criteria. The selection criteria of vulnerable women will be based on eligibility criteria such as  female-headed households, income below the poverty line, widow, etc.  IOM will also focus on disability throughout the beneficiary selection criteria and assist livelihoods and self-reliance opportunities. Women empowerment, leadership, and decision-making will be promoted by incorporating income opportunities and entrepreneurship opportunities, business development training, financial literacy, etc., for women in the Host Community and self-reliance opportunities for women in the camps to ensure sustainable development and integration into the society.

project_name: Gender-Based Violence (GBV) Risk Mitigation, Prevention and Survivor-Centered Support for Rohingya and Host Communities
project_objective:
""IOM will adapt and strengthen its GBV program, established in 2017, targeting Rohingya refugees and host communities centered on three pillars: 1) survivor-centered support, 2) risk mitigation, and 3) addressing root causes that perpetuate GBV in line with IOM´s GBV in Crises Institutional Framework. 
IOM directly implements case management providing a multisectoral package of support via nine Women and Girls Safe Space (WGSS) across eight sites and through an emergency safe shelter. To mitigate risks, prevent GBV and empower women and girls, the WGSS provides information, age-appropriate and structured psychosocial support (PSS), roll out  Ma Boinor Rosom and Girl Shine Curriculum, awareness and educational activities, life-skills and opportunities, forums for two-way information-sharing and learning, including peer-led curriculum on GBV, sexual and reproductive health, menstrual hygiene and disaster preparedness.   
Ensuring sustainability and localization, IOM and PULSE   Bangladesh Society, IOM’s IP, will scale up capacity building and support with community groups, advocates, imams, majhis, volunteers and women´s committee members, to transition key WGSS awareness and outreach activities through regular meeting, capacity building sessions and regular supervision as appropriate. This will enhance community ownership and accountability by working holistically with communities to address the root causes of gender inequality.  IOM will implement structured and evidence-based GBV prevention activities such as EMAP in the proposed areas.  IOM will work closely with the Protection Research Unit to develop peer led evidence-based curriculum working with men, boys, women, girls and persons with diverse Sexual Orientations, Gender Identities and Expressions, and Sex Characteristics’ (SOGIESC) to ensure inclusive approaches. Such strategies will ensure safe and non-stigmatizing entry points to GBV services for male survivors and survivors with diverse SOGIESC.   
IOM´s program will feature a greater focus on GBV risk mitigation in the WASH sector through enhancing the participation of women and girls in the design and maintenance of WASH infrastructure. IOM´s primary focus will be on menstrual health education through peer-based models building on the findings of IOM´s summary report Ma Boinor Rosom or “Mother and Sister´s Ways” and its related curriculum, piloted and rolled out as a model of best practice. The curriculum, among other complementary outreach tools (MBR-1, MBR-2) focused on life skills and male engagement, will be further developed using participatory approaches for both Rohingya and host communities. 
Empowerment and skills development activities including tailoring and handicraft training for Rohingya and Host community, IT and Arts training (not certification courses) for host community women and girls will become more participatory, structured and diversified. IOM will scale up the production of re-usable sanitary pads working with volunteers. Participants who have graduated from skills-building classes and groups will be engaged as peer trainers and supported with coaching and capacity building. IOM will support  Rohingya women to identify opportunities for strengthened women’s participation and engagement through multi-stakeholder approaches and plans to scale up and replicate its Women´s Participation Project, piloted in 2020 and 2019 as a best practice model for fostering social cohesion and ensuring disability inclusion. 
IOM is an active member of the GBV Subsector Working Group, GBV Case Management and Dignity Kit Task Teams and Co-chair of the PSEA Network. IOM GBV staff serve as interagency GBV Camp Level Focal Points and as part of interagency emergency and response structures such as the Mobile Medical Teams and the PERUs. IOM will continue work with the DC, UNO, RRRC Office and CiC Offices at the camp level by coordinating regularly and providing capacity building on GBV.""

project_name: Protecting Rohingya and Host Communities by Facilitating Meaningful Access to Humanitarian Assistance, Dignity and Human Rights
project_objective:
""IOM’s Protection project for the 2023 JRP connects two strategic objectives with activities that aim to benefit the most vulnerable Rohingya and host community persons, specifically to reach older persons, widows, single-headed households, persons with disabilities and persons with diverse sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and to target authorities and partners in a way that does no harm, assists based on needs, and prioritizes respect for human rights, safety and dignity.  
IOM will continue serving as the Protection focal point lead in seven camps, directly implementing most activities. IOM’s protection monitoring activities will facilitate beneficiaries’ meaningful access to all humanitarian assistance, dignity, and human rights. IOM will strengthen community-based protection through community engagement, awareness raising, sensitization, case management and specialized Protection services for individuals in need. IOM’s core counter-trafficking activities will be prevention, protection, and capacity building, which will be implemented in 17 camps and 10 Union of host communities in Cox’s Bazar district. These activities aim to reduce trafficking incidents and risks in the camps and host communities through the comprehensive activities that follow the governmental National Plan of Action. The Counter Trafficking activities will foster collaboration among stakeholders who respond to human trafficking cases. The aforementioned integrated approach to Protection strives to have sustainable impact and improve peaceful coexistence between various communities. 
The research component that is now embedded in the IOM protection team will help tailor activities, institutionalize, and analyze the impact of IOM Protection and IOM’s general programming. The information that is gathered through the research team serves as a basis for monitoring and evaluation to ensure that IOM does no harm, and activities remain relevant and culturally appropriate. As well as being aware of the constantly changing dynamics that need to be considered.
For disaster risk reduction, IOM will work with a range of partners, including other Sectors, community-based protection networks in the camps and relevant authorities to identify extremely vulnerable individuals or households needing specialized assistance and preparation before a disaster. IOM will verify the needs of EVIs, coordinate services, and support other partners to mitigate harm during disaster response. IOM will continue leading the Protection Emergency Response Units (PERU).   
IOM’s protection mainstreaming activities will promote a holistic lens, incorporating the age, gender, and diversity needs of the affected population in Cox’s Bazar into programming through capacity building, training, as well as activity monitoring and modification. Finally, IOM will continue to co-chair the Sector’s Anti-Trafficking Working Group (ATWG) and be a proactive member of the Protection Working Group (PWG), the Protection Task Team and other related working groups.""

project_name: Shafak Nutrition Program for Conflict Affected Population in North West Syria
project_objective:
In 2023, Shafak will continue to deliver nutrition lifesaving services in northwest Syria. It plans to support 106639 individuals including 71481children,35867 F,35614 M under five, and 35153 pregnant and lactating women including people with disabilities. 
The project targeted locations and intended activities are outlined as follows:
- Aleppo,Jebel Saman, Atareb:Activities will be implemented through six Rapid Response Teams (RRTs), one Outpatient Therapeutic Program Center(OTP),and Targeted Supplementary Feeding Program through WFP supplies-TSFP).
- Idleb, Idleb, Maaret Tamsrin: Activities will be implemented through one Stabilization Center(SC) with capacity of 10 beds to admit theSAMcases with medical complications as it is the only referral center in the subdistrict also admitSAM cases withCholera referred fromCTCs, oneOTPCenter,7 RRTs, and SFP.
- Aleppo,Afrin, Jandairis: activities will be implemented through one RRTs. - Aleppo, Azaz, Aghtrin: activities will be implemented through one RRT.Aleppo, Azaz, Suran: activities will be implemented through one RRT. - Aleppo,Azaz,Mare: activities will be implemented through one RRT. - Idleb,Harim,Dana:  activities will be implemented through 3 RRTs. - Idleb,Harim,Armanaz:activities will be implemented through twoRRTs.Shafak selected the locations of this proposal according to its current existing supported health facilities and nutrition teams funded by other donors. Through the proposed intervention, Shafak intends to achieve the following objective, which aligns with nutrition Strategic Goals to ensure continuity and increased coverage of nutrition services for prevention and treatment of acute malnutrition (SAM and MAM) among children aged 6-59 months and among pregnant and lactating women (PLW) in the supported Shafak health facilities and through RRTs.Shafak's Nutrition response is being implemented under operational guidance that stipulates adaptations in the context of Cholera Outbreak and COVID-19 to mitigate the risk of infection while ensuring continuity of life-saving nutrition services, mainly services for treatment and prevention of acute malnutrition, micro-nutrient supplementation, and IYCF-E. Also Shafak will implement CVA activities Under the NC's last recommendations and guidelinesThe RRTs’ activities require the list of supplies on a monthly basis which Shafak receives from UNICEF regularly through PAC warehouses in northwest Syria. The supply monthly needs will be calculated and submitted to UNICEF and the nutrition cluster through the established channels.WFP will secure supplementary feeding supplies (plumpy sup.) to Shafak nutrition teams and centers. WFP will support 3 Rapid response teams in the same areas of Shafak FSL project funded by WFP (General Food Assistant-GFA). This partnership with WFP will complement Shafak's intervention by applying 2 approaches of the CMAM program: Blanket supplementary feeding program and targeted supplementary feeding program in the same areas of proposed RRTs.
In 2023, Shafak is planning to apply most of the recommendations shared by Nutrition Cluster depending on the last results of SMART Survey conducted in 2022: -Scale up the provision of CMAM services including SAM and MAM treatment.-Accelerate Scale up the mother MUAC approach to strengthening early identification and referral of acute malnutrition among children and PLWS -Develop and implement an agreed IYCF package at different levels of care (facility, community, and individual levels) among all sector partners -Work with FSL, WASH, and Health to harmonize an integrated malnutrition preventive package focusing on the first 1,000 days with clear referral pathways and criteria -Scale up cash for nutrition in hotspots and underserved areas  -Strengthening capacity of health and nutrition staff for anemia detection and treatment as well as investment in equipment for testing anemia and ensuring adequate supplies andsupplements for appropriate treatment and prevention

project_name: Enhance the protection environment of the most vulnerable women, men, girls and boys in NWS through provision of integrated protection services.
project_objective:
In 2023, Shafak Organization proposes to mitigate and respond to the protection risks faced by the conflict-affected people in Jabal Samaan, Jarablus, Al-Bab, and Azaz districts in Aleppo governorate, as well as in Harim, Ariha, and Idleb districts in Idleb governorate.

The project aims to empower local communities and conflict-affected individuals in Northwest Syria and support their role in building society and in determining their future by the provision of protection services and emergency protection services to 130,750 IDPs and host community members, through five community centers, and 28 mobile outreach teams. The provided protection services will comprise both mitigation and response services as well as specialized and non-specialized protection services.

The proposed project will offer gender and age-appropriate general protection services including, structured and recreational PSS, recreational and MHPSS activities, case management involving life-saving assistance to vulnerable people in ensuring their access to existing services, referral to specialized and non-specialized services, awareness raising on protection-related topics, life skills and vocational training to enhance the community resilience and livelihoods opportunities, legal assistance and legal awareness raising session of HLP and CSD through qualified and well-trained legal teams, protection monitoring, as well as supporting community committees. Moreover, Shafak will establish community committees from the same communities and train them on protection topics such as; CPMS, Safe identification, and referral and communication skills to enable them to identify and refer people in need to the case management team. 

Shafak will maintain a gender-balanced team in all its projects in order to facilitate the access of all gender groups to services in line with humanitarian principles. Moreover, training on HLP and CSD will be delivered to partners’ legal staff and community actors in Syria and Turkey by specialized legal staff in accordance with the protection cluster and HLP TWG guidance and SOPs.

These services will be offered to vulnerable IDPs and host community members with particular emphasis on quality services to the following groups:
• Women-headed households
• Children-headed households
• PWDs
• Elderly women and men
• Family has children at risk of child labor
• UASC and orphans who are being cared for by another family.
• New IDPs who fled their home and have no financial means

In case of emergencies, the project activities will be shifted to respond to the emergency protection needs of newly displaced people delivering the protection emergency package like PFA, referrals, and emergency case fund support to respond to the urgent needs of IDPs.

The activities will emphasize equity and non-discrimination, reinforcing the basic social and human rights of participants while taking into consideration the cultural, historical, and social specificities of targeted populations. All static centers will be rehabilitated and well-equipped to be disabled-friendly spaces.
COVID-19 precautionary measures will be taken in line with WHO, Global Protection Cluster and the Protection Cluster’s Guidance, including strict enforcement of physical distancing, minimizing of participants per activity to a maximum 12 people and maintaining the social distancing between BNFs and staff, the use of personal protective equipment (PPE) by staff/beneficiaries.

project_name: Strengthen Protection Services to Nigerian refugees and Host Communities of the Far North Region Cameroon
project_objective:
International Medical Corps (IMC) will work alongside the International Rescue Committee to implement a three-year integrated protection intervention focusing on mitigating and responding to child protection and gender-based violence risks in the Far North region. The project will aim at providing a safe and secure environment for women and children among Nigerian refugees and vulnerable households from host communities to both reinforce the community protective environment and strengthen access to basic services for the most vulnerable and at-risk individuals. Building on IMC & IRC’s child protection experience, the two organizations will focus on two components. The first component will aim at strengthening the protective environment for children, through building local capacities of key actors including government actors, community members and caregivers on protection including mental and psychosocial impact, to facilitate behaviour change in communities and with caregivers. Considering that behaviour change can only be achieved through a sustained intervention, these activities will be implemented over a three-year period and the strategy for Y2 and Y3 will be adapted according to the progress reached in Y1 and Y2, respectively. Capacity building will be scaled up throughout the three years of the project with increased support in Y2 and Y3 of local structures (government and community-based actors) to lead and coordinate activities. Youth empowerment activities for vulnerable youth will be integrated into the protection response aiming to strengthen their resilience and facilitate the development of life skills. The second component will focus on emergency response to child protection risks faced by vulnerable and at-risk children affected by the conflict and will be implemented through case management, development of safe learning and healing spaces and support for civil documentation. 
The proposed project will target communities affected by the Lake Chad Crisis in Logone and Chari Divisions of the Far North. The project will target in 10,695 refugees (32% of the total refugee population). While the project is intended to target locations with high numbers of refugees, child protection and GBV services will be provided to all vulnerable women and children with identified needs including refugees, returnees, and host community members. GBV activities will primarily target survivors of GBV and vulnerable women and adolescent girls, while child protection activities will primarily target vulnerable children, including unaccompanied and separated children, and children without birth certificates. The selection of members of community-based structures, where they do not exist, will prioritize women and trusted members of the community and will strive to achieve a diverse balance of ages, ethnicity, and refugee status.

project_name: Medico-nutritional response and emergency preparedness for refugees, internally displaced persons and host communities affected by the Lake Chad Basin crisis in the Far North region, Cameroon
Integrated response to multisectoral emergency and post-emergency needs of conflict-affected communities in Southwest Cameroon
project_objective:
In light of the protracted nature of the crisis, the proposed intervention aims to respond to both emergency and post-emergency needs of conflict-affected communities in the Southwest and support long-term solutions to protracted displacement over a period of 36 months. Through a combination of protection, shelter/NFI and livelihoods interventions, DRC will provide a comprehensive response at all phases of the displacement cycle, transitioning from emergency to early recovery. DRC will build on its access strategy to design this two-pronged approach programme, focusing on the emergency needs in both hard-to-hard and peri-urban communities; and on post-emergency needs of populations living in less sensitive peri-urban areas. 
To ensure that the most at risk are targeted and can benefit from DRC’s expertise based on needs and vulnerability, DRC’s approach will identify all beneficiaries of all sectoral interventions of this programme via the protection team, using protection criteria, and in order to reach protection outcomes. Once the identification of individuals’ needs will be done, DRC will internally refer the most vulnerable individuals to the different sectors. The integrated approach of this programme could be further enhanced by using multi-purpose cash assistance (MPCA) to cover the multi-faceted needs of extremely vulnerable households, which DRC ambitions to pilot in peri-urban areas. For the shelter/NFI component of the action, DRC used a combination of socio-economic vulnerability and sector specific vulnerability criteria to identify not only those without an adequate access to shelter and NFI items but also those suffering the greatest financial barriers to meeting their basic needs. The socio-economic vulnerability ranking prioritised households with disabled or chronically ill family members, pregnant and lactating women, single and female headed households as well as those supporting unaccompanied minors. Distribution sites are chosen together with the community with the safety and accessibility of beneficiaries in mind. Special attention is given to the needs of vulnerable groups such as elderly, people with disabilities, pregnant and lactating women, and children headed households to make sure they are able to access the distribution site and are given priority during distribution. Distribution days are previously agreed upon so as not to interfere with activities such as market days.
The proposed approach is based on the “Do No Harm” principle and is conflict-sensitive, with activities tailored to the specific context of Southwest Cameroon. One of the pillars of this principle is to ensure local ownership. DRC will build the capacities of Community-Based Protection Committees (CBPC) and Protection Focal Points (PFP) already formed during previous actions and identify members in new communities of intervention. In addition, Community-based Targeting Committees (CTC), respecting a status, gender and age balance will promote local acceptance and transparency in the beneficiary selection process. 
DRC’s engagement with civil society is at the heart of its programming and part of the “Go local” initiative promoted by DRC 2025 Global Strategy. In the Southwest region, DRC has been partnering with the NGO LUKMEF since 2021 and initiated a partnership with Grace Chin in 2022. DRC seeks to expand and strengthen equitable, long-term, and strategic partnerships with local NGOs to provide humanitarian assistance in the most effective manner and to foster local capacities. To realise this ambition, DRC is to launch a Call for Expression of Interest.
The programmatic strategy’s key objective centres around providing continuous support to the conflict-affected populations in DRC’s current intervention areas (Fako and Meme divisions) while also expanding to the Kupe-Manenguba division.

project_name: Assistance for Victims of the Lake Chad Crisis in North-East Nigeria and Northern Cameroon
project_objective: L'objectif global du projet est de contribuer à réduire l'impact de l'insécurité alimentaire liée aux conflits et à améliorer la protection des groupes les plus vulnérables de la population concernée. La sécurité alimentaire sera soutenue par un mélange de transferts en espèces et d'aides en nature pour 19 300 ménages, en fonction du contexte local, des contraintes sectorielles et des préférences des populations concernées. Ces mesures sont complétées par le dépistage de la malnutrition chez 6 000 ménages, le traitement des cas de malnutrition modérée et aiguë et la formation à l'utilisation d'aliments riches en nutriments. En outre, 5 100 ménages recevront une aide en espèces et une formation aux pratiques agricoles durables sur les sites du projet, où les bénéficiaires peuvent avoir accès à la terre. En outre, le programme s'occupera de la protection des personnes touchées par la VBG, la maltraitance des enfants et les traumatismes en identifiant et en traitant jusqu'à 2.000 cas ou en les orientant vers des services spécialisés. Le projet renforcera les systèmes de surveillance de la protection à base communautaire en formant des moniteurs de protection locaux et des comités de protection à base communautaire. Parallèlement, 2 000 victimes de la VBG ou personnes à haut risque seront habilitées à mettre en place des activités génératrices de revenus grâce à des transferts d'argent. De plus, des activités de sensibilisation sur la VBG, la protection de l'enfant, la santé mentale et le soutien psychosocial (MHPSS) seront menées auprès de l'ensemble des communautés du projet et des acteurs clés locaux dans les régions du projet. De plus, l'éducation de 15.000 enfants IDP est soutenue par le paiement de frais de scolarité. Enfin, 15.000 personnes bénéficieront d'une assistance juridique pour l'établissement de documents. Le projet renforcera également l'engagement des acteurs locaux dans les processus de coordination humanitaire ainsi que dans les relations avec les acteurs locaux de la société civile et contribuera à améliorer la performance environnementale de l'aide humanitaire.

project_name: Supporting crisis-affected populations in North-West, South-West, Littoral, and West regions through the provision of multi-sectoral assistance in Cameroon
project_objective:
In the North-West, South-West, Littoral and West regions, following the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus (HDPN) approach that IOM strongly supports and actively promotes in Cameroon, IOM plans interventions for 2023 to respond to the most urgent needs of displaced populations through a multisectoral approach focusing on coordination, shelter and NFI, mental health support (health), psychosocial support (protection) and WASH interventions. 
The last Multi-Sectoral Needs Assessment (MSNA) exercise conducted in the North-West and South-West regions of Cameroon, undertaken in August 2022, showed needs in most of the sectors, including access to water, food, health, education, etc. In the West and Littoral regions, the last Mobility Tracking assessment showed that the North-West (NW)-South-West (SW) crisis impact continue to spill over to these neighbouring regions with the number of IDPs coming from NW-SW increasing from the previous year, while the last MSNA, undertaken at the same time, showed again severe needs in most of the sectors. In view of such needs identified, IOM plans to expand its programmes accordingly and in line with each mandate and capacity, with a multisectoral response aiming at contributing to reinforce life-saving assistance and to improve well-being of displaced and the most vulnerable populations affected by the crisis. IOM will mainstream protection and recovery through the development of local capacities, in all its proposed activities to support displaced populations in preparing and achieving durable solutions. 
IOM will support the work of the Coordination sector through the collection and production of critical data on displacement situation, alerts as well as humanitarian Multi-sectoral humanitarian needs following its DTM methodology, that will be provided to the humanitarian community to inform its humanitarian programming. In the frame of the Shelter Sector response, IOM will distribute emergency shelter and NFI kits, both in-kind and using cash-modality solutions when possible (bearing in mind that lack of civil documentation and concerns of diversion of cash to non-licit uses poses very important challenges) and help the construction for most vulnerable people. In the WASH response, IOM will drill and rehabilitate boreholes, construct water points, latrines and other infrastructures and conduct hygiene sensitization and promotion activities combined with distribution of WASH kits. Finally, IOM multisectoral assistance will also include mental health activities including direct MHPSS assistance using PMTs, reinforcing referral mechanism and capacity building of health actors (Health sector), while also directly providing psychosocial support to populations impacted by crisis by reinforcing safety and social network as well as strengthening community capacity to provide psychosocial support to victims of GBVs (Protection sector).
Through activities, direct feedback from beneficiaries and community members will be gained via IPs and also directly by IOM staff during field visits and visits of the M&E/AAP independent team in accordance with the wider IOM AAP emergencies workplan. AAP focal points will be assigned in Buea and Yaounde respectively, with clear SOPs to be in place to capture complaints from beneficiaries and to take any appropriate action. Members of IP will be trained on topics such as the proper handling of disclosures of gender-based violence (GBV) incidents, aspects of confidentiality, and respectful communication in high-stress environments. Targeting of beneficiaries will be done according to a vulnerability criterion including  persons living with disabilities assessed through RRM household level assessments conducted by IOM. Also, IOM will integrate measures to ensure gender-specific needs and to mitigate risks of GBV in all activities (e.g., including through training of IPs on GBV core concepts, guiding principles as well as on how to respond to disclosures of GBV).

project_name: Improved living conditions, dignity and protection of vulnerable displacement affected population of the Littoral, West, South West and North West Regions of Cameroon
project_objective:
In the North West and South West regions, approximately 32,000 people are self-settled in the bushes and in immediate and acute need of shelter and household items. The rest of displaced population is reported to have self-settled (52 percent) in shelter or to stay with host families. Most accommodations across all displaced population (including the ones hosted) are reported to be critically below standards also lacking basic sanitary services. The locations where the IDPs have fled for safety include areas where they are living with relatives and friends in homes whose space is insufficient to provide the needed separation and privacy between the different ages and sex while some IDPs rent houses which are mostly substandard and very small to meet the space and other requirements for and adequate housing. Their vulnerability is further compounded by the lack of adequate household items. This situation makes the longer- term prospects for recovery more difficult. Common shelter models of this populations include makeshift and inadequate shelter in bush settlements, overcrowded hosting family regions, and renting.

Target group
The NRC programme will target IDPs, returnees and vulnerable host communities’ households who need shelter assistance to improve their living conditions. Particular attention will be given to households that meet the following vulnerability criteria:
•	IDPs living in makeshift shelters exposing them to bad weather;
•	IDPs living in host communities where they scramble for the very limited space available and share sleeping spaces;
•	IDPs in rental accommodation who are at risks of eviction as a result of inability to pay rents,
•	Returnees (former IDPs), where houses have been vandalised, destroyed or dilapidated due to the crisis;
•	Schools in conflict affected areas with increase in number of students as a result of influx of IDPs and those that are used as collective centres by IDPs. 
NRC’s Shelter interventions in the North West and South West aims to reach a total of 15,500 displacement affected individuals (7,904 females and 7,596 males) targeting 2,584 households.
NRC will integrate safe programming principles for people with disabilities and the elderly to ensure meaningful access and equal participation of people with disabilities and special needs. NRC will ensure the participation of beneficiaries so that shelter designs are culturally appropriate and meet the special needs of women and girls.
In 2023 NRC will adapt the strategy of working with partners to implement Shelter activities in target communities. Currently, we are identifying potential partners who will be trained and engaged.

project_name: Enhancing the ability of displacement affected people in the Far North Region to exercise and enjoy HLP rights and achieve durable solutions
project_objective:
This project aims to improve access to housing, land and property for returnees, displaced persons, refugees and host communities in Mayo-Sava, Mayo-Tsanaga and Logone-et-Chari divisions in Far North region of Cameroon. This will be achieved through the provision of information, counselling and legal services to the beneficiaries and capacity building of stakeholders for collaborative resolution of HLP disputes.
NRC’s mobile teams will be deployed in target communities to provide counselling and legal services to the target populations in displacement and return areas, including IDP sites and refugee camps. Through information sessions, affected populations will be adequately informed of the HLP rights and obligations as well as available remedies in cases of rights abuse.
Additionally, NRC will provide legal assistance to conflict-affected population (IDPs, refugees) in need of securing their HLP rights. This consist of assisting the vulnerable individuals to obtain signed agreements from local authorities and traditional leaders (chief of villages) for beneficiaries at risk of forced eviction , and representation of beneficiaries before disputes resolution structures for mediated and negotiated settlements of disputes. Priority will be given to female heads of household, widows, displaced persons, and vulnerable or affected host community members. This process will contribute to the prevention of forced eviction for the target population. 
Furthermore, NRC will build the capacity of local and traditional authorities on HLP issues through the provision of training and coaching on HLP rights and CDR (Collaborative Dispute Resolution) and provision of materials and equipment to strengthen their HLP response. NRC will also train humanitarian actors operating in sectors such as shelter, WASH, education, and food security. This will help ensure that these sectors prioritize land tenure agreements instead of the direct and customary land transfer in their interventions and prevent or solve land-related conflicts. For due diligence approach, NRC will work with beneficiaries of Livelihoods and Food Security (LFS), Shelter, Wash and Education programmes to secure access to land for them. In order to avoid or reduce forced evictions, NRC will assist people benefiting from shelter, Wash and LFS support to access land with increased security of tenure. 
In order to strengthen the coordination and give further visibility to the needs of affected populations with regard to access to land, housing and property, NRC will provide leadership in the coordination of HLP response through the HLP Area of Responsibility. This will also contribute to an integrated and multi-sectoral response to HLP from national and local authorities, as well as humanitarian actors.  
NRC will advocate for the HLP rights of conflict-affected populations to be respected. Round tables with relevant government officials and humanitarian actors at national and regional levels will be held with the objective of developing a plan of action to follow-up on the challenges and recommendations identified in NRC’s studies and needs assessments.
Finally, NRC Cameroon will continue to collaborate with other stakeholders to facilitate access to HLP rights and ease the restitution processes.

project_name: Support to vulnerable IDPs, returnees and host families to Improve their food security, economic and social well-being in Northwest South West (NWSW) regions
project_objective:
The purpose of the project is to improve food security, economic and social well-being of vulnerable IDPs, returnees and host families in the target area. 
NRC Cameroon’s Livelihood and Food Security (LFS) programme will target displacement-affected people based on vulnerability criteria and not their displacement status only (IDPs, returnees (former IDPs) and host communities) will be targeted. NRC will apply social and economic vulnerability criteria to identify vulnerable households most at risk to food insecurity. Priority will be given to female-headed households, child-headed households; pregnant and breastfeeding women; elderly people (60 and above); households with a person with physical or mental disability or debilitating chronic disease. For the economic vulnerability criteria, NRC will use as a reference: poor or limited food consumption score; no food stock, number of meals per day, no productive assets, and loss of income. For agricultural restoration activities, NRC will also include the following criteria: having at least one able-bodied person in the household who can farm land. NRC’s LFS programmes will also target as far as possible vulnerable youth and women for vocational training and economic empowerment. 
To address the intermediate needs of affected populations NRC will use cash, e-vouchers or in-kind assistance based on the results of market analysis and cash feasibility studies. To maximise the chances of success in this activity, NRC will as far as possible couple livelihoods interventions with food assistance to meet basic food needs. Moreover, NRC will implement complementary activities such as training and awareness raising sessions to support target households. Programme activities will gradually scale down and phase out so that by the end of the projects, communities have the skills and resources needed to be more resilient to shocks and crises in the medium and long term. NRC will work in coordination with local partners such as local technical and administrative structures and will collaborate closely with them so they can provide technical support during programme implementation and continued follow-up after the programme ends. 
The LFS programme will include Cash/voucher assistance, livelihoods promotion and enhancement applying a market-based approach (MBA) that refers to local traders so to improve access to income and revive/strengthen the local economy. The intervention will be geared towards supporting the most vulnerable displacement-affected households and at the same time building their capacity in food production, Livestock production and Income generating activities.

project_name: « Projet de veille, coordination et réponse intégrée visant à couvrir les besoins de base des populations vulnérables (hôtes et déplacées) affectées par la crise du NOSO dans la région de l’Ouest (Cameroun) »
project_objective:
Les régions du Nord-Ouest et du Sud-Ouest subissent une crise de protection majeure se traduisant par une atteinte grave aux droits des populations civiles entrainant des déplacements massifs. Dans ces deux régions, le nombre de personnes déplacées internes est estimé à plus de 788 540 dont 114 111 à l’Ouest (OCHA, Aout 2022). La situation sécuritaire dans ces régions est extrêmement volatile et de nombreuses attaques sont perpétrées contre des écoles, des enseignants, des étudiants, etc. Les besoins prioritaires pour les populations déplacées sont la nourriture et l’accès à l’eau, alors même que peu d’acteurs humanitaires sont présents dans la zone. Ce projet fait donc suite à l’évaluation de mars 2021 qui a révélé des besoins en EHA, Food, Abri/AME et Protection. Ainsi, PUI propose de mettre en œuvre un projet de veille et de coordination avec les acteurs locaux afin de déployer une réponse rapide pour couvrir les besoins de base des populations. 

ASSISTANCE
En ce qui concerne l'assistance, notons que l'accent est mis sur le respect des standard minimum émis par les différents secteurs.
Abris : Des recommandations du Shelter cluster  sont prises en compte pour l'octroi des kits en inkind au déplacés mais en cas de besoin, une évaluation pourrait pousser PUI à opter pour du TMMU pour aider ceux des déplacés qui se sont vu offrir par les populations hôtes un abri nécessitant des travaux de réparation.

POLITIQUE PEAS.
L’exploitation et l’abus sexuels constituent un échec catastrophique pour ce qui est de la protection. Ils sont préjudiciables à ceux que les organisations humanitaires et leurs partenaires ont le mandat de protéger et compromettent la réputation de ces organisations. Ils violent également les normes et standards juridiques internationaux universellement reconnus. Des allégations d’exploitation et d’abus sexuels généralisés concernant les femmes et enfants réfugiés et déplacés par les travailleurs humanitaires et leurs partenaires ont poussé les organisations humanitaires à mettre sur pied des politiques strictes en matière de PEAS. Celle de PUI  qui date de plus de 12 ans condamne fermement toute violation  de cette politique par l’un de ses staffs, prestataire, partenaire ou fournisseur. Cette politique conforte la bonne  tenue et le bon suivi  du système de collecte et  remontée de plaintes. Cette politique est une des politiques pour laquelle PUI mettra  des mesures coercitives en cas de son non respect.

project_name: Renforcement des services de prévention et de réponse à la violence basée sur le genre pour les populations affectées par le conflit dans les départements du Mayo-Sava, Mayo-Tsanaga et Logone et Chari ; Région de l’Extrême-Nord, Cameroun
project_objective:
La situation sécuritaire dans la région de l'Extrême-Nord du Cameroun reste toujours extrêmement volatile en raison de l'insurrection de Boko Haram dans le bassin du lac Tchad. Bien que leur fréquence ait diminué, les raids de Boko Haram continuent de pénétrer dans les départements du Logone et du Chari, du Mayo Sava et du Mayo Tsanaga, entraînant des meurtres, des pillages et des vols de bétail, des enlèvements et des incendies de villages. Les enlèvements se poursuivent dans les zones frontalières, provoquant un traumatisme au sein des familles et des communautés. Au 31 Aout 2022, OIM à travers le DTM Round 25 a enregistré e 573 184 personnes en situation de déplacement dans la région de l’Extrême-Nord. Parmi ces personnes, 385 372 sont des PDIs, 138 152 retournés et 49 660 réfugiés vivant hors du camp de Minawao.  Ces personnes sont déplacées par le conflit lié au GANE, au conflit intercommunautaire et aux inondations. Cet afflux des populations crée des besoins de base à satisfaire, mais aussi une pression énorme sur les populations hôtes. Les femmes, en particulier les jeunes femmes et les enfants, sont très affectés par les conflits et sont exposés à la violence, aux abus et à l'exploitation, séparation des familles et ont des besoins importants en matière de santé reproductive et besoins psychosociaux.
Dans ces situations d'instabilité, les femmes et les enfants représentent toujours plus de 75 % des personnes enregistrées et sont les plus vulnérables. Les violences sexuelles et sexistes, notamment les viols, les agressions sexuelles, les violences physiques, économiques ou psychologiques, sont fréquemment perpétrées, avec peu ou pas d'obligation de rendre des comptes, ce qui constitue une violation des droits humains et une atteinte supplémentaire à la dignité des femmes et des filles. De janvier à octobre 2022, 1,665 incidents de VBG ont été rapportés aux services spécialisés. La violence sexuelle est signalée à 11%. Elle comprend le viol, l'agression sexuelle et les mariages forcés. 74% des cas des IPV sont également signalés au sein du couple, et 5% des cas d'abus sexuels sur des enfants. Le déni de ressources/opportunités est signalé à 45%, les abus physiques à 25% et la violence phycologique à 19%. 
Les services disponibles en matière de VBG restent un grand défi pour certains départements affectés par la crise, y compris par les inondations, avec de nombreux cas de viols enregistrés par certaines associations locales. La plupart des partenaires de la GBV AoR offrent une PSP à tous les survivant(e)s, et environ 84% des survivant(e)s ont reçu un soutien psychosocial, 11% des services liés aux moyens de subsistance, 3,8% des services de refuge, 0,8% des services médicaux et 0,1% une assistance juridique. Le circuit de référencement montre une absence de services essentiels de santé, de santé mentale et de soutien psychosocial dans de nombreuses localités. Il est très important d'étendre la couverture géographique des activités de lutte contre la VBG en cours afin d'atteindre davantage de personnes dans les zones difficiles à atteindre. L'UNFPA, en tant que agence lead de la GBV AoR, vise à garantir que les personnes dans le besoin dans ces localités soient atteintes. Il doit également renforcer les services là où ils sont déjà disponibles. Étendre les services à un plus grand nombre d'établissements offrant des services aux personnes vivant avec un handicap, qui sont plus vulnérables et affectées, et qui sont des survivants de la violence sexuelle et du viol.

project_name: réponse en abris aux inondations à Ndjamena
project_objective:
En 2022, les inondations fluviales et pluviales qui affectent le Tchad ont atteint des niveaux extraordinaires, si l’on tient compte les dix dernières années. Du bassin des fleuves Logone et Chari, particulièrement vulnérables aux inondations, en passant par les provinces frontalières du sud avec la RCA et celles de la frontière orientale avec le Soudan, ainsi que N'Djamena et enfin la province du Lac, toute la moitié centrale et méridionale du pays a été touchée par des inondations. 
Les inondations pluviales qui ont débuté fin juin ont touché un peu plus d’un million de personnes dans 19 des 23 provinces du pays jusqu'à fin octobre. À N'Djamena, des pluies torrentielles, ainsi que la crue sans précèdent du fleuve Chari, dont le pic a été enregistré fin novembre, ont laissé des quartiers entiers submergés par les eaux, et ont provoqué le déplacement de dizaines de milliers de personnes, dont 182 000 regroupées dans 20 sites (y compris 5 situés dans la province de Hadjer- Lamis, frontalière avec la capitale). Bien que la communauté humanitaire ait apporté une réponse multisectorielle en appui aux efforts des autorités, d’importants besoins humanitaires des sinistrés des sites restent non couverts, particulièrement en abris.

project_name: Cooperation on Migration and Partnerships to Achieve Sustainable Solutions (COMPASS)
project_objective: The International Organization for Migration (IOM) in Chad has been tracking and monitoring complex mobility dimensions since 2014. IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) was first activated in 2014 to respond to the influx of Chadian returnees in the southern part of the country as a result of the Central African crisis. In 2015, the DTM was further activated in the Lac region to respond to the displacement crisis resulting from the Boko Haram insurgency. In 2017, another component of the DTM was deployed in Northern Chad to track and monitor migration flows, whether these were intra-regional or towards Europe. Since the beginning of 2018, IOM Chad has observed steady and increasing economically motivated migration flows through the north of Chad bordering Libya, presumably resulting from limited economic opportunities, on ongoing food security crisis, and imposed austerity measures. In order to continue providing crucial information on displacement and migration dimensions, IOM’s intervention will focus on three pillars: i) mobility tracking and stability index; ii) emergency tracking and iii) flow monitoring.

project_name: Shelter, NFI and MHPSS support to populations affected by flooding in N’Djamena Chad
project_objective:
Since 2014, the crisis unfolding in Lac Province has been characterized by numerous challenging factors, such as insecurity, flooding, large-scale and continuous population movements (Internally Displaced Persons, returnees) as well as community clashes and socioeconomic-related tensions. While Chad habitually faces seasonal flooding due to severe rains, the flooding in 2022 has been the worst flooding since 1961, with the Chari River rising to 8.11m to date, causing massive displacement within the city of N’Djamena. During the initial months of July – August 2022, flooding as a result of excessive rainfall led to over 440,000 individuals being affected across the country, while in N’Djamena itself, 5,678 houses were completely or partially destroyed.  While the displacement had subsided temporarily, a secondary flooding due to an rising water levels of the Chari and Logone rivers since October, has led to 118,700 people displaced in N’Djamena. These individuals are currently residing in 8 official displacement sites, with an unconfirmed 34,824 more displaced in 5 other sites based on recent estimations of UN OCHA. To provide lifesaving assistance, IOM suggests the implementation of a three-fold response: 
1)	Strengthening of displacement data management to support decision-making, planification and direct assistance, through the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM)’s neighborhood flooding assessment and rapid kobo registration in displacement sites. 
2)	Shelters and Non-Food Items (NFI) procurement and distribution for most vulnerable displaced people.
3)	Supporting affected population with psychosocial support in the displaced sites in N’Djamena.

project_name: Cash for WASH addressing Incontinence and Hygiene
project_objective:
To increase capacity of SRCS in Cash for WASH, PGI and CEA through field practice in the refugee camps of 
Gedaref state. 
Specific Objectives: 
By increasing capacity in these 3 cross cutting sectors SRCS will be able, to:
1. Run targeted, quality and sustained WASH activities specifically linked to the context of Gedaref; 
2. Gather learn lessons to be used as a baseline for scaling the activities for future implementations, capitalize field experience and build track records. 
3. Focusing on the needs of the most at-risk groups the project will focus on an integrated approach 
that will enhance dignity and access to WASH services. Through a CEA and PSEA approach, the 
participation and safety of affected population will be mainstreamed in the whole response. This will 
be done by coordinating closely with relevant NGOs, INGOs, PNs and other humanitarian actors currently promoting CEA, PGI, Cash for WASH components in the Gedaref camps.

project_name: Multi-sectoral response to vulnerable individuals and refugees in Khartoum, Gadaref , and Blue Nile States, Sudan
project_objective:
The IRC’s Integrated Protection program in Gedaref and Blue Nile, will provide lifesaving specialized gender-based violence prevention and response services to support the old and new returning refugees and other most vulnerable women and girls at risk, such as elderly women, pregnant women, breastfeeding women, women and girls with disabilities, and female-headed households (HHs). The project will support the integration of reproductive health and GBV services to ensure gender-based violence (GBV) survivors can access safe, confidential, and timely clinical care for the harmful health consequences both physical and emotional. The project will also focus on delivering lifesaving Child Protection (CP) services including specialized case management and PSS, prevention and response to child separation from family, and promoting family-based -care in the child’s best interest to ensure that children are safe in their homes and receive support when they experience harm. The IRC will implement this intervention through existing Safe Healing and Learning Spaces (SHLS) in Tunaydbah refugee camp where the IRC's Social and Emotional Learning (SEL) curriculum will be implemented as well as integrate/set up temporary SHLS within the health facility in Blue State. The IRC will also promote community participation in all stages of the project and engage community members to further mitigate potential risks for children and adolescents. 

Additionally, the IRC will introduce activities to assist in reducing the risk of water-borne diseases and vector control within the catchment areas of the supported Health Facilities through risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) activities by involving IRC Integrated protection. The IRC will target the refugees in both Blue Nile and Gedaref states, affected by WASH-related diseases and outbreaks as well as flooding and malnutrition, to address their dire needs in terms of WASH support. The IRC prioritizes gender and protection as cross-cutting themes across all areas of intervention to ensure that services are equally accessible and safe for clients and that the unique needs of individuals are addressed. especially children under 5 and pregnant, lactating women (PLW), and people with disabilities. WASH activities will be bolstered by life-saving, integrated health and nutrition services to reduce excess morbidity and mortality for the refugee population. This will be done through primary health care facilities and referral of complicated cases to secondary facilities. The health package will include reproductive, maternal and child health services, treatment of communicable and non-communicable diseases, mental health and psychosocial support, emergency preparedness and response including response to COVID-19 pandemic and other outbreaks. The IRC will provide life-saving treatment for severe acute malnutrition (SAM) and moderate acute malnutrition (MAM), referrals to stabilization centers and counseling of pregnant and lactating women (PLW) on infant and young child feeding (IYCF). The IRC will work directly in the camps to provide services, and through established Ministry of Health (MoH) facilities to scale up services to refugees in urban areas including capacity building to healthcare providers and basic health infrastructure improvements to deliver quality health and nutrition services for the refugees.

project_name: Asset creation project to strengthen food and nutrition security, early recovery and resilience of 116,000 vulnerable people affected by shocks in the Far North, North, Adamawa, East, North West and South West regions of Cameroon
project_objective:
The project aims to improve access to food and contribute to improving social cohesion and supporting early recovery and building resilience of vulnerable and food-insecure communities affected by the Boko Haram crisis and violence in the Far North region, the influx of refugees in the eastern regions, Adamawa and the North linked to the Central African crisis, the internal socio-political crisis in the North-West and South-West regions.   This project will address the immediate food needs of 116,000 vulnerable people, including refugees, internally displaced persons, returnees, and local populations who are severely affected by the 03 crises mentioned above, disrupting economic, agricultural, and pastoral activities in these regions. The 116,000 beneficiaries will be distributed as follows: 86,000 people to be assisted under the FFA for early recovery and 30,000 people by the FFA for Resilience. The Resilience FFA will be implemented only in the regions (04) affected by the Boko-Haram crisis and the CAR crisis while the Early Recovery FFA covers all regions (06) affected by the three crises. The implementation of livelihood activities, community participatory planning (CBPP) sessions are conducted in collaboration with local community members (women and men) to identify the real needs and priorities of local communities that will help affected populations develop their own response strategies and build resilience. This community-centred approach ensures the provision of effective solutions with beneficiaries and reduces reliance on relief. 
Assistance through for FFA, will be implemented using cash modality and in-kind Food for four months under the FFA-early recovery, and eight months for the FFA-Resilience. Therefore, the cash transfer value is aligned with the in-kind food ration. It considers beneficiaries' food preferences for the commodities and prices on the local market. The transfer value is calculated based on the identified food gap and is designed to assist beneficiaries to reach the recommended minimum calories intake of 2,100 Kcal per person per day. The use of cash-based transfers is expected to improve the cost-effectiveness of WFP's operations, while seizing the economic opportunities of local markets, with particular consideration for the beneficiaries’ choice and dignity.
WFP will collaborate closely with Government technical ministries, cooperating partners and communities to ensure project implementation and sustainability. Nutrition, Gender and protection issues are taken into consideration at all the stages of the project elaboration, implementation, monitoring and evaluation. Gender and protection risk analysis will be carried out and the most vulnerable will be targeted, including female-headed households, pregnant and lactating women, persons with disabilities.
Project sites will be in secure areas and at convenient distance from the homes of the beneficiaries.
To support smooth project implementation and ensure sustainability, capacity strengthening sessions will be organized for all stakeholders on gender and protection policy, project management, monitoring and nutrition.

project_name: Emergency support to ensure access to essential health Services in Ayod and Fangak Counties
project_objective: CRS and local implementing partner Healthcare Foundation Organization (HFO) will scale their current activities in Fangak and Ayod to ensure that children under five years and pregnant women use more equitable and better quality essential maternal, newborn and child health services. CRS and HFO will target a population of 392,124, focusing on girls and boys under five years of age, adolescent girls and women to increase equitable access to quality health services and adoption of appropriate health behaviors. CRS and HFO will collaborate with county health departments (CHDs) to improve consistent delivery of low-cost, high-impact, people-centered, equitable primary health care services to the most vulnerable populations through an agile mix of essential front-line health services, regular outreach to hard-to-reach populations, community-based health services through the Boma Health Initiative (BHI), safe motherhood initiatives, and emergency preparedness and response to bolster community resilience and continuity of basic services provision during times of shock and inaccessibility. Interventions will align with the South Sudan National Health Policy (2016-2026) objectives, Boma Health Initiative (BHI), the 2023 South Sudan HRP, and the UNICEF South Sudan 2023- 2025 Health programme. CRS and HFO will coordinate with UNICEF-funded nutrition cluster partners, conduct malnutrition screening for children under-five and pregnant and lactating women and refer cases to the nearest nutrition facility. Health and nutrition services will be co-located in health and UNICEF funded nutrition facilities to maximize efficiency and strengthen coordination at the lowest level of health service delivery.

project_name: Emergency and Relief Intervention - Nutrition Activities in South Sudan by Medair
project_objective:
Medair will continue multi-sectoral intervention in its proposed catchment areas and ERT interventions across South Sudan. The total targets for 2023 are based on Medair’s mapped catchment populations and at least 60% coverage in all areas will be 3545 SAM admissions, 8787 U5 MAM, and 8213 PLWs.  Medair will continue to integrate MIYCN at both community and health and nutrition site levels and will support VAS in Medair’s catchment areas when no other actors are conducting. The proposed interventions in the plan align with the strategic and sector objectives and contribute to increasing equitable access and utilization of quality preventative, lifesaving, early detection and treatment of malnutrition and program monitoring, analysis, and utilization of nutrition information.
The 2022 FSNMS+ estimates GAM rate in Leer County as 19.2% (SAM 6.1%). But, in the mass MUAC screening conducted in August 2021, the proxy GAM rate was 7.9% (SAM 0.6%).  Medair is the major nutrition actor currently covering a catchment population of 41,200 in Leer County (6) and 1 site Luol in Mayendit County. Medair plans to expand its nutrition program to cover the whole county by increasing its sites to 19, starting January from 2023. Medair is continuing multisectoral programming—community health, nutrition—CMAM and MIYCN via Care Groups (CG) WASH, and MHPSS to address some of the underlying factors.
In the recent IPC classification (HNO 2022) Pibor was classified as IPC 4 with pockets of IPC level 5, “famine likely” with extremely critical levels of acute malnutrition. In 2023  projections nutrition cluster prioritized Pibor as one of the neediest areas with no significant improvement from last year’s situation. Medair continues to run the SC and set up multisectoral programming in Gumuruk and Lekuangole (est. population of 55,126 (Feb 2021 OCV Campaign). OTP and TSFP services will are projected to continue to be covered by Plan and JAM. As part of Medair’s health and WASH programming Medair will set up a community Care Group (CG) network which will cover MIYCN and other public health topics as well as ensure Mother’s MUAC is established and well linked to JAM’s services through referrals. Health facilities will also conduct nutritional screening and referral of U5 and PLWs as part of BPHNS. As no actor is addressing at risk infants <6 mo, Medair will continue exploring integrating MAMI with the health services in 2 PHCUs. To avoid duplication, Medair will continue to coordinate activities with JAM/PLAN to manage all the coexisting illness referrals. Medair will continue supporting minimum WASH packages and child friendly spaces and early child development activities will be promoted.
ERT continues to respond to emergency levels of acute malnutrition by establishing CMAM services to address the most lifesaving needs, in areas with high GAM and low program coverage. The RRTF in collaboration with the NC gives input on priority areas and intervention modalities in scenarios characterized by agreed triggers where other actors are absent or unable to fully intervene. The team will work with the partner on the ground to identify areas for capacity building for quality service delivery. The team will provide nutrition emergency services for up to 3 months and thereafter handover services to an identified partner before exiting.

project_name: Protection of civilians against explosive weapons in Syria
project_objective:
Throughout 2021 Norwegian People’s Aid (NPA) established a humanitarian Mine Action and Disarmament (MAD) programme in Syria. NPA’s newly established programme will operate in territories currently under the control of the Government of Syria (GoS) with the primary objectives of protecting civilians from the impact of explosive ordnance (EO) and ensure safe access to livelihood opportunities and basic infrastructures for Syrian civilian population.
In 2022, NPA commenced its operational phase focusing on the recruitment and training of national teams conducting survey and clearance of EO contaminated areas as identified under the Syrian Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO), the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) and in coordination with the UN Mine Action Area of Responsibility (AoR) and UNMAS for the implementation period. In 2023, NPA will continue deployment, and expansion, of its operational capacity.
Currently approximately 70% of all people in need of mine action and EO intervention, are living within Government controlled areas, according to the recent 2022 Mine Action analysis of need. More than a decade of civil conflict in Syria has left the country heavily contaminated. Improvised landmines, Improvised Explosive Devices (IEDs), cluster munitions and wide variation of other EO affect all 14 governorates of the country. The contamination is particularly dense in areas previously held by the Islamic State, with both rural and urban areas impacted. Reports from Aleppo, Hama and Homs indicate a significant amount of contamination left by all sides of the conflict, as do reports from Daraa in the southern parts of the country, as well as from Rural Damascus. Moreover, these extremely high needs are not matched with the presence on the ground of qualified, professional humanitarian mine action actors that can address the problem in an efficient and timely manner. NPA's intervention aims at responding to these needs by ensuring the mapping, marking and safety removal of landmines, IEDs and other EO in full compliance with international standards and best practices.
Throughout the project period NPA will develop and deploy a total of up to twenty multi-skilled operational teams in conflict affected areas in order to protect the Syrian civilian population from the threats posed by landmines, cluster munitions, improvised explosive devices (IEDs), and other EO. During 2023, NPA will recruit, train and deploy an additional ten teams to be deployed in Damascus and Rural Damascus governorates and according to the needs and priorities identified throughout 2022. Each NPA team will consists of seven team members and will be capable of performing non-technical survey, technical survey, mine clearance, battle area clearance, high risk search, Explosives Ordinance Disposal and Improvised Explosives Device Disposal. The work of the teams' will be guided by strict prioritizations criteria in order to target those people most in need of mine action and EOD/IEDD interventions. In line with these principles, NPA will primarily allocate its limited financial and operational resources in communities reporting explosive contamination in severity scales 3, 4, and 5.
Since the beginning of the programme NPA established a sound quality management system to ensure high quality and safety of clearance operations on the ground. In addition, NPA's work in Syria is guided by a robust conflict sensitive and “do no harm” approach which takes into account relevant risks and identifies corresponding mitigating measures. Finally, NPA Syria ensures a diverse work environment with staff of different gender, ethnic and religious backgrounds from a wide range of age groups.

project_name: Food Security and Livelihoods Programme Cabo Delgado
project_objective: NPA is supporting its implementing partner União Provincial de Camponeses de Cabo-Delgado (UPC CD) in the implementation of Foods Security and Livelihoods Programme in northern province of Cabo-Delgado. The Programme aims to provide life-sustaining emergency livelihood support to crisis affected persons in Metuge district in the Cabo Delgado province, in line with the response priorities in the 2023 Humanitarian Response Plan.The programme also aims to restore and strengthen people’s livelihoods to improve their sustainability and thus their resilience. The programme’s main objective is to provide access to quality agricultural inputs (seed and tools) for increased household food productivity, increased access to sufficient food in quantity and quality to meet dietary needs and enable livelihoods access to food through production (agriculture) or income. The agriculture inputs assistance will enable target households to meet their immediate needs in initiating life sustaining food production (6 weeks cycle for horticulture inputs and 3 to 6 months for cereals), diversify and improve their nutrition.
