project_name: Espacios educativos seguros y dignos para niños, niñas y adolescentes vulnerables en Guatemala
project_objective:
Partiendo del principio de que la educación es un derecho fundamental de todos los NNA, particularmente en situaciones de emergencia. Es necesario asegurar que sus necesidades básicas de aprendizaje de calidad estén cubiertas. Las emergencias suelen crear necesidades adicionales y urgentes de aprendizaje que el plan de respuesta humanitaria debe abordar.
Para Guatemala, los centros educativos, representan un factor determinante para la seguridad, la igualdad, la participación, la integración y la mejora de las condiciones de vida de la comunidad educativa, principalmente de los NNA pertenecientes a los sectores más vulnerables, que son testigos silenciosos de cómo sus centros escolares se convierten en albergues o son destruidos de forma parcial o total ante un desastre. 
La mayoría de los deterioros a escuelas, incluyen daños de infraestructura (techos, muros, accesos, drenajes, filtraciones, cocinas en mal estado, colapso de baterías sanitarias y falta de agua potable mejorada). Muchas escuelas se inundan; se destruye el mobiliario y material escolar y didáctico. 
En Guatemala, los huracanes ETA e IOTA y Julia dejaron daños sin precedentes, con cerca de 600 escuelas afectadas a nivel nacional, principalmente en las regiones Noroccidental, Central y Petén, dónde existe un número creciente de estudiantes sin acceso a la educación formal o no formal, retrasando la reapertura de las escuelas que en los últimos 2 años han permanecido cerradas por efecto del confinamiento de la pandemia por Covid-19. 
Con la reapertura de las escuelas, las reparaciones son urgentes, especialmente en lo que respecta a las instalaciones de agua potable y saneamiento, que son obligatorias para la reapertura. 
Un retorno seguro a los centros educativos requiere de acceso a agua y saneamiento para garantizar las condiciones básicas para recibir a los estudiantes. En este contexto, el Acuerdo Ministerial número 33-2022, que contiene las normas sanitarias para la prevención y control de infecciones por Covid-19, establece la necesidad de la constante higiene de manos y la disponibilidad de estaciones con agua y jabón para los alumnos y el personal docente, además, después de cada jornada habrá que desinfectar el aula.
UNICEF incluirá el suministro de agua, saneamiento e higiene en las escuelas para garantizar un ""regreso seguro a la escuela"". UNICEF trabajará para reintegrar a los niños que han estado fuera de la escuela y evitar la deserción escolar una vez que se abran las escuelas.
A través de esta acción, UNICEF creará oportunidades para los niños expuestos a altos niveles de violencia en comunidades que incluyen a familias retornadas o desplazadas, mediante la provisión de múltiples vías de educación, acceso a materiales de aprendizaje de calidad y apoyo psicosocial que faciliten la permanencia en el hogar.
Por medio de esta propuesta, el apoyo de UNICEF al Ministerio de Educación aumentará el número de estudiantes que se benefician de una infraestructura escolar restaurada, segura y digna con instalaciones de agua, saneamiento e higiene, asegurando oportunidades para la continuidad de la educación y el bienestar de los NNA.

project_name: Responding to GBV across the country and creating safer communities for women and girls
project_objective:
In recent years, the protection context in Lebanon has drastically deteriorated. Lebanon has witnessed a series of compounded crises, placing the country on the brink. On top of the ongoing refugee crisis, Lebanon now faces the most severe economic and financial collapse in its recent history, further compounded by COVID-19, political turmoil, and the Beirut Port explosion. These conditions have deepened pre-existing vulnerabilities and compounded underlying issues of gender inequality and discrimination in Lebanon, resulting in heightened risk of gender-based violence (GBV), and in households being forced to adopt negative coping mechanisms. These problems have also increased tensions among communities and placed burdens on women and girls. Recent assessments  point to increased safety risks for women and girls, who describe a general environment of fear and security deterioration in the places where they live. 

According to the data collected through the Gender-Based Violence Information Management System (GBVIMS), Intimate Partner Violence (IPV) reporting continued to increase in 2022, with 5% increase in third quarter of 2022 accounting for 62% of reported GBV cases compared to the second quarter. Physical and emotional abuse were the most commonly reported type of violence against women and girls, accounting for 36% and 34% of the incidents respectively;  Sexual abuse remains underreported due to the stigma associated with it  and incidents of rape and sexual assault constitute 17% of all reported incidents. 

When it comes to adolescent girls, they are often excluded, marginalized and at risk of GBV and negative health outcomes; they are disproportionately affected by the multi-layered crises and their access to education and other essential services have been disrupted, increasing their exposure to certain harmful practices, such as child marriage, representing a direct manifestation of gender inequality; recent data  shows an increase in percentage of this harmful practice among Syrian refugee girls with 21.9% in 2022 compared to 20.4% in 2021. 

Responding quickly and effectively to GBV can save lives and is a critical first step toward starting the healing process for survivors. UNICEF, through this project, will deliver urgent care and referrals for 4,400 GBV survivors and works with communities and institutions to challenge social norms that tolerate violence and abuse. 

UNICEF, in partnership with local women-led organizations and international non-governmental organizations (NGOs), will provide safe spaces for 4,400 women and girls to come together for support. Through supporting women and girls to enhance their psychosocial well-being, gain better economic independence and play a meaningful role in the decision-making that affects their lives, UNICEF will foster conditions in which women and girls not only survive and heal the effects of violence but also ultimately thrive. On the other hand, UNICEF GBV program will also engage around 6,700 women, girls,  men and boys through the GBV risk mitigation activities to contribute to a more secure environment, through sensitizing them to GBV in collaboration with UNICEF partners.

project_name: PRISE EN CHARGE DE LA MALNUTRITION AIGUE MODEREE AU BURUNDI
project_objective:
Le taux de Malnutrition Aiguë Globale (MAG) au Burundi est estimé à 4,8% dont 1.4% de malnutrition aiguë sévère (MAS) selon les résultats de l’Enquête sur la Situation Nutritionnelle et la Mortalité (ENSNMB2022) ; ce qui place la situation nutritionnelle dans la catégorie ""acceptable"" selon les seuils de l’OMS 2018. Ce taux atteste d’une amélioration de la situation nutritionnelle puisqu’il était de 6,1% dont 1,1% de MAS en 2020 selon l’Enquête Nationale sur la Situation Nutritionnelle et la Mortalité (ENSNMB2020). Le secteur Nutrition a choisi de mettre en oeuvre le projet de traitement MAM dans 6 provinces (Cankuzo, Kirundo, Makamba, Ngozi, Rutana, Ruyigi), identifiés comme prioritaires en raison de la prévalence élevée de la malnutrition aiguë globale (MAG) et des facteurs de vulnérabilité comme la prévalence de la malnutrition chronique , l’alimentation minimale acceptable chez les enfants de 6 à 23 mois, ainsi que des mouvements de population susceptibles de détériorer la situation nutritionnelle des personnes concernées. 
Il a ciblé environ 50 pour cent des cas attendus de malnutrition aiguë modérée (MAM), soit 75,384 enfants de moins de 5 ans (37,363 filles et 38,021garçons) et 25,011 femmes enceintes et allaitantes (FEFA) pour une prise en charge de la MAM. Cependant, vue la sitution de la malnutrition aiguë au Burundi jugée acceptable avec ses conséquences sur la mobilisation des financements face aux sollicitations de divers pays en situation d'urgence à cause de la sécheresse et d'autres aléas climatiques dans la Corne de l'Afrique et ailleurs, 55,000 enfants de 6-59 mois et 20,500 FEFA ont été retenus afin de rester dans l'enveloppe initialement prévue avant l'accroissement des prix des produits nutritifs spécialisés (PNS).
L'objectif principal du traitement de la malnutrition aiguë  modérée est de contribuer à la réhabilitation nutritionnelle de 55,000 enfants de 6-59 mois et 20,500 FEFA modérément malnutris au Burundi.    
 De l'objectif général découle trois objectifs spécifiques suivants :  
  (i) Prévenir la malnutrition aigüe sévère chez 55,000 enfants de 6 à 59 mois et 20,500 FEFA modérément malnutris y compris les personnes vivant avec handicap, les déplacés internes et rapatriés au Burundi ; (ii)	Réduire le risque de mortalité et morbidité lié à la malnutrition aiguë modérée chez 55,000 enfants de 6 à 59 mois et 20,500  FEFA y compris les personnes vivant avec handicap, les déplacés internes et rapatriés au Burundi ; (iii) Accroitre les connaissances sur les produits nutritifs spécialisés et les pratiques d’alimentation du nourrisson et du jeune enfant (ANJE) chez les populations bénéficiaires y compris  les personnes vivant avec handicap, les déplacés internes et rapatriés au Burundi. 
Avec un budget total de 6,000,442 USD, ces objectifs seront atteints avec la réalisation des activités suivantes :  
i. Acheter, stocker et livrer 495 tonnes de LNS/LQ et 923 tonnes de Super cereal Plus pour la prise en charge des cas de malnutrition aiguë modérée ; ii. Organiser la prise en charge de 20,500 FEFA et 55,000 enfants de 6 à 59 mois modérément malnutris.  Les enfants seront pris en charge avec LNS/LQ à raison de 100g/ jour pendant 3 mois et les FEFA seront prises en charge par le CSB++ à raison de 250g/ jour pendant 6 mois ; iii. Animer les séances de communication pour le changement social et de comportement ; iv. Organiser des missions de supervision en respectant les niveaux du système sanitaire ;  v. Assurer le suivi de la chaîne d’approvisionnement et de l’utilisation des intrants nutritionnels jusqu’au dernier kilomètre (End User Monitoring) ; vi. Renforcer les capacités des prestataires de services de supplémentation nutritionnelle afin d’améliorer la qualité de la prise en charge de la malnutrition aiguë modéréé ;  vii. Assurer le rapportage des données de qualité, la coordination, le suivi des activités et l'évaluation du projet pour permettre d’agir en temps réel et tirer des leçons.

project_name: Provision of enhanced protective environment through prevention, risk-mitigation and response services for vulnerable individuals and communities affected by conflict and displacement in Akobo and Wau Counties of Jonglei and Western Bahr el Ghazal States of South Sudan.
project_objective:
This project will target a total of 13,400 persons (2,680 men, 3,752 women, 3,350 boys and 3,618 girls), which is further broken down into 6,700 IDPs, 4,020 host communities and 2,680 returnees, with a main focus on protection analysis and advocacy and reducing the sufferings of gender-based violence (GBV) survivors. For the purposes of ensuring an in-depth understanding of protection environment, allowing for appropriate prevention and response activities, Nile Hope (NH) will focus on protection data collection and analysis. This is to say that, NH will ensure that protection concerns are captured and highlighted in toolkits such as assessment reports, monitoring reports and protection snapshots, therefore, allowing for appropriate and relevant advocacy with the national cluster, humanitarian partners and other relevant stakeholders. 

In order to ensure that appropriate and principled actions are taken to prevent and respond to protection risks or concerns, NH will ensure that this project is centered on both individual and community level by ensuring evidence-based interventions. During the implementation of this project, NH will promote partnership with the affected communities through already established and function community structures including vulnerable groups and individuals, with the aim of identifying protection risks and coping strategies, community and individual intentions and resilience amongst the affected population. Notably, these activities will enhance communities’ and at risk individuals’ preparedness and resilience. Moreover, NH will work closely with communities’ protection watch groups/committees, facilitate focus group discussions, awareness raising and training on basic human rights and protection mainstreaming, with an aim of preventing and mitigating identified protection risks. 

Needless to say, NH will provide timely, coordinated, and complimentary protection responses based on the identified protection needs. Most important to realize, is that protection will be central to all interventions which will include service mapping, safe referrals, individual protection assistance for at-risk individuals, information sharing, awareness raising on fundamental human rights and protection mainstreaming. To ensure that this objective is achieved, the project will integrate with other sectors including S/NFIs, FSL, WASH, Education, Nutrition, Health and Peace Building Programs. Furthermore, the project will primarily focus on ensure that the safety and dignity persons and communities affected by displacement are prioritized and a do-no-harm approach is mainstreamed during all aspects of the implementation. Out of the 6,600 persons that this intervention seeks, 1000 persons will be people with disabilities. 

Accountability to the targeted beneficiaries will be adhered to through appropriate information dissemination alongside beneficiary feedback sought during post-intervention monitoring. In addition to this, ad-hoc assessments in the proposed locations will be conducted, with priority being given to the highly affected regions and persons with special needs. Special attention will be given to people with disability to make sure that they are not left out, we shall ensure we mainstream protection principles throughout the implementation of this project to ensure that we are not exposing the beneficiaries to harm with our interventions. We have ongoing partnership with UNFPA in Akobo and Wau Counties, however, the protection risks remain enormous in these locations and the proposed ones as well.

project_name: Education is a priority: An Integrated Approach to Enhance Access and Quality of Education in vulnerable and Underserved Communities Within Syria.
project_objective:
As part of its education response, PUI is targeting vulnerable and underserved communities with a bundle of activities, with the overall objective of enhancing the access to quality education provided in protective and suitable learning environment for affected children, to ensure that they don’t become a lost generation. Indeed, with the protracted crisis approaching its twelfth year in Syria, an entire generation of children and youth is being subject to persistent lack of opportunities to access quality education. This situation could have long-term negative consequences, affecting children’s mental health and wellbeing and preventing them from developing in good and safe conditions, as well as gaining essential life skills and knowledge.
The proposed project in brief:
- Will target locations where high education needs are documented by Education Sector.
- The cost per beneficiary is 40$ for remedial classes, 40-50$ for Self-Learning Program, 60$ for Early Childhood education (which covers incentives for teachers, stationery for the ECE cycle, children kits and furniture for the ECE space), 10$ for awareness sessions, 10$ for back to learning campaigns, 170$ for teachers’ capacity building and 100,000$ for the school rehabilitation activity as the works will vary to address all the needs including addressing protection, safety, WASH and electricity issues and might include installing a solar power system. The cost per beneficiary is around 104.455$ (Calculated by dividing the total budget by the total number of people the project will target.)
- It is estimated that around 679 individuals of targeted beneficiaries may have disabilities where all concerned teachers and educational staff members will attend specialized sessions related to child protection inclusive education and how to deal with CwDs, PUI will ensure to include at least 1 CwD in  each established children club. Furthermore,  these children will be referred to relevant stakeholders based on their needs.
This project aims at encouraging out of school students and dropped-out students to resume their education through tailored back to learning campaigns and empowering those children with self-learning program conceived as transition programs to enable them to catch-up and reintegrate the formal education system after this transition period. In addition, PUI will assist children in their education by providing them with kits,
education supplies and remedial classes to cover for any gaps and ensure every child’s educational needs are met and to prevent them from dropping out of school. Furthermore, PUI will contribute to enhancing the quality of education by providing capacity building activities to teachers and MoE staff, training them on active learning, PSS, and life skills. PUI will also initiate parenting awareness campaigns for parents and caregivers in order to provide guidance on parenting best practices and how to deal with different situations and age groups, in addition to raising their awareness regarding children’s rights and their importance for the children’s future. Lastly, in parallel to the abovementioned activities, PUI will ensure that children have access to safe and protective learning environment where they can access quality education by rehabilitating damaged schools in targeted locations.

project_name: Apoyo al acceso a una educación inclusiva, equitativa y de calidad, en el estado Trujillo.
project_objective:
Durante los años 2020, 2021 y 2022, RET implementó varios proyectos relacionados directamente con educación. El proyecto “Asistencia directa en salud y educación, en las poblaciones más vulnerables especialmente Niños, Niñas, Adolescentes (NNA) y Mujeres afectadas por la crisis en Venezuela, Colombia y Ecuador, financiado por ECHO, en el marco del consorcio “Rutas por la Igualdad "" el cual mejoró el acceso a 1938 NNA a una educación inclusiva y de calidad, incluyendo a maestros y docentes con la permanencia en el sistema de educación formal implementando estrategias de educación digital frente al COVID-19 y fortaleciendo el acceso a escuelas seguras. En el estado Trujillo el proyecto “Respuesta de Asistencia Humanitaria en las áreas de Agricultura y seguridad Alimentaria, Salud y WASH, a las poblaciones afectadas por la profundización de la crisis socioeconómica y el colapso de los servicios básicos en 05 estados de Venezuela” que se desarrolló en los municipios La Ceiba y Rafael Rangel en las comunidades de Santa Apolonia, La Gira y la Ceiba, beneficiando a 4.562 personas capacitados a través de cursos y planes de formación para el desarrollo de habilidades y capacidades con la implementación de 80 huertos orgánicos familiares con doce variedades de cultivos, la intervención en 04 centros educativos  en el sector WASH con la conformación de Clubes de promoción de higiene, rehabilitaciones a la infraestructura para mejorar el acceso al agua, capacitaciones y dotaciones para reforzar las buenas prácticas de higiene. 
A finales de año 2021 RET amplio su cobertura en el programa de comidas escolares como Socio Implementador de PMA en 06 municipios más del estado Trujillo atendiendo a 62 centros de educación inicial y escuelas de educación especial permitiendo tener acceso a la zona baja del estado e identificando las necesidades y el contexto de la zona.
Según los datos e investigaciones recogidas por diferentes organizaciones que conforman el clúster de educación, se destacan los siguientes elementos sobre la situación de los grupos vulnerables en relación a los temas de educación, salud y protección: 
•	El 59% de los hogares venezolanos afirmaron en un estudio realizado no disponer de ingresos suficientes para comprar alimentos.
•	Las razones para no asistencia de los NNA a las instituciones educativas predominan principalmente con la falta de alimentación en el hogar con un 45% y el no tener acceso a la adquisición de implemento escolares con un 30%.
•	En relación con los servicios básicos en las escuelas el 56%, tienen problemas para el acceso al agua potable y el 69% fallas en el sistema eléctrico. 
•	La precarización de las condiciones laborales del personal educativo, entendidas como el alza en las brechas salariales, acceso a la alimentación, a materiales para la enseñanza, a insumos básicos de bioseguridad, aumentando la deserción laboral, deteriorando aún más las condiciones de las escuelas para atender la demanda escolar. 
En otras publicaciones se destaca:
•	La cobertura educativa en el contexto de post-pandemia ha ido descendiendo progresivamente entre las edades de 3 a 24 años a nivel nacional, siendo en la actualidad un 63%. Se estima que 1.500.000 NNA permanecieron fuera del sistema escolar. La responsabilidad de apoyar a los niños sigue recayendo en un 71% sobre la mujer como jefa de familia (ENCOVI, 2022)
•	Los resultados expresados en el clúster de WASH, afirma que se debe reforzar en las instituciones educativas la disponibilidad de insumos para jornadas de mantenimiento y limpieza (jabón, cloro), el funcionamiento de los baños y la gestión de los residuos.
•	En 2021 se aplicó en la prueba EGRA (Early Grades Reading Assessment) La prueba EGRA se aplicó a 1.028 estudiantes de tercer grado de todo el país. A ese nivel, explicó el profesor Eduardo Cantera, el niño ya debería saber leer y comprender lo que lee. Los resultados evidenciaron que, si bien la comprensión oral y la comprensión lectora son altas.

project_name: School Feeding Project
project_objective:
Provision of school meals to 970,000 number of children in 80 localities for 180 days, ensuring that children coming from poor and vulnerable households are able to access education. The project will incentivize learning for children who often have to walk long distances and learn on empty stomachs, gravely affecting their health and cognition abilities. School meals programmes are designed to support children coming from poor and vulnerable households, often facing critical household food insecurity and malnutrition. This leads in many parts to poor attention in class, ill-health and subsequent absenteeism and drop out. 
Emerging evidence is seeing nutritious school meals as a necessary component of health for school children. In UK, the medical sector is calling for an expanded Free School Meals to all children in households that live on Universal Credit, arguing that it is a first step to improve children's nutrition and protect their health.
In Sudan, the HNO notes that, 4.5 million school-aged children (ages 6-18) are experiencing crisis, emergency, or catastrophic levels of food insecurity. Most of these children are not attending school; those who are, are at a high risk of dropping out or having their educational attainment curtailed if they are not adequately supported through a full package of educational interventions, including school feeding. Food insecurity, driven by many factors including a protracted conflict and disasters is expected to increase in 2023. This is against a background of two years of the Covid 19 pandemic whose impacts are still felt in many sectors, the Ukraine-Russian war which has affected food and oil supply chains driving up the cost of food. The additional factors of teachers' strikes, floods, closures of schools all greatly affect the children's ability to catch up with their counterparts in other countries. 
The school meals will address both hunger at school and enable consistent class attendance for the children which will positively contribute to their academic performance. In addition, nutrition awareness will be carried out to both PTAs and children on the benefits of healthy diets.

project_name: Improved access to safe water and vector control activities for the crisis affected population in Sudan
project_objective: The current situation in Sudan will have implications on vector borne diseases prevention and control. Most of Khartoum people (figures changing) has displaced to 7 states where malaria and other mosquito borne arboviruses are reported. The existing control programs are poor and will demand additional financial and logistical resources. The displaced population as well as the host communities in Gazera and Sinnar require immediate coverage by core vector control interventions to ensure their protection from the upcoming malaria season that will be affected by the low immunity of the people coming from low transmission to highly endemic areas. The expansion of the conflict from Khartoum to other states increasing the demand for vector control. The current situation in Sudan will have implications on communicable diseases prevention and control. Most of Khartoum people (figures unknown and influx is continue) has displaced to 7 states where malaria and other mosquito borne arboviruses are reported. The displaced population and the host communities in Gazera and Sinnar require immediate coverage by core vector control interventions to ensure their protection from the upcoming malaria season. The armed clashes that erupted on 15th April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have had a devastating impact on people and infrastructure throughout Sudan. Vector borne diseases continued to spread in Sudan, Sudan support to basic WASH programs remains neglected, and malaria and other vector borne diseases continued to take a great toll on human health. WASH services  require urgent scale up of surveillance and control measures to prevent communicable diseases outbreaks among vulnerable population. Arboviral diseases, including dengue, chikungunya, yellow fever, are persistently increasing. The invasion of Aedes Albopictus to Sudan will impact the surveillance and vector control measures due to it is elasticity and ability to establish itself in diverse environments. 84 localities from 12 states reported 8,673 cases with attack rate of  4.2/10,000 in late 2022 up to the mid of April 2023 before the war breaks out. Access to safe water and sanitation, as well as the ability to maintain good personal and hand hygiene and universal health coverage and improving the house keeping in healthcare settings especially infection prevention among reported causalities, are critical to prevent more injuries, wounds contamination and infectious diseases and individual’s dignity, safety, and privacy. With the low coverage of WASH services identified by different surveys including the MICS, S3M l ; access to improved WASH services at community and facility levels are vital. A recent WHO assessment of WASH at 335 heath care facilities revealed that only 34.3% have Piped water supply into premises, 43% have improved sanitation, 30 % of HCF have a functional hand hygiene facility at the point of care, and 6.6 % segregating  medical waste at generation point. WHO will ensure the protection of crisis affected population from exposure to WASH hazards through managing all risk factors by supporting entomological surveillance, Water quality monitoring, vector control Interventions, and community mobilization to apply effective measures for their own protection against WASH related diseases. A Chemical control of aquatic and adult vectors, active surveys will also be conducted to update/map risks of vector borne diseases in affected areas and IDPs settlements with focus on the invasive vectors. Training of 1000 environmental health officers, CHW workers from MOH and partners, community volunteers on multiple environmental health (WASH) packages with total cost of ??????M USD. WHO will work closely with partners to improve water quality activities. project_name: Emergency school feeding for at risk children affected by war in Sudan
project_objective:
Since the conflict between the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Army Forces (SAF) broke out on 15th April 2023, over 1,042,1114 individuals have been internally displaced. Of this number, it is estimated that 404,028 children of school age have equally been displaced. The situation is fast evolving, and the numbers are expected to change.  319,194 people are estimated to have fled the country to neighboring countries. The Revised HRP 2023 indicates that 8.6 million children have been affected by the conflict. This war has compounded the challenges facing the education sector in Sudan. Prior, schools had remained closed in January and February, adding further to the entrenched loss of learning for Sudanese children. Through this proposal, WFP attempts to contribute towards mitigation of the impact of the conflict on school children by integrating school feeding into a comprehensive package of support falling under access and protection by ensuring that at risk boys and girls are protected from completely falling out of education. WFP proposes provision of emergency school meals to support both formal and informal learning. WFP will work with other core partners such as UNICEF to create conducive child friendly spaces for children affected by war as part of a comprehensive education sector response to the crisis which has affected millions of Sudanese with over a million people being internally displaced and hundreds of thousands others fleeing the country. While efforts are being made for internally displaced children to access education, it is still not clear how those that have fled the country will be integrated into those countries’ education systems. 
Inter-communal conflicts between the Masalit and the Arabs in West Darfur have also broken out, a possible indication that the regular tribal conflicts may resume, which may further increase insecurity and place extra burden on communities hosting the IDPs.
The education sector like other sectors, has been hit by the ongoing war. School infrastructure has been damaged, or classes occupied by either forces or indeed IDPs.  Schools in Darfurs, Khartoum, Northern, North Kordofan and West Kordofan were forced shut six weeks before end of the school calendar. Teachers and students alike have fled schools and are displaced. Ongoing assessments indicate deaths of children who have been caught in the cross-fire.
There are real concerns that children will be more affected and an increase in drop-out rates is expected. Children from affected states and poor families, girls and those in hard-to-reach areas are the most vulnerable. Further, children due to write grade six examinations are at real risk of failing to do so, whilst those that have fled to other countries may not have the opportunity to access learning. Stakeholders are worried about access to basic services for children such as education, nutrition and health. Sudan has among the highest number of food insecure people in the world. Looting, lack of access to communication, the impending rainy season which may result in floods will further affect both access and quality of education. Further, the traumatic experiences that children and teachers have been exposed to since the conflict started will remain a scar in their minds, unless stakeholders mobilise a comprehensive support package to help children refocus their minds away from the war.
The provision of complementary feeding will support all other activities as both an enabler of access and retention through provision of meals for children. The meals will attract children to safer spaces to be created by UNICEF and protect them from further mental and physical harm.
This project targets the eastern part of the country that have had minimal disruption from the war, in particular, Blue Nile, Kassala, Gedaref, Red Sea and South Kordofan targeting 365,717 children (296,321 vulnerable residents and 69,396 IDPs) in the first phase of the project.
