project_name: Enhancing IDP and Returnees Protection Services in South Sudan
project_objective:
South Sudan continues to undergo complex and multidimensional protection risks in  2023. Prior to the outbreak of violence in Sudan on 15 April 2023, the country grappled with displacement caused by inter-communal violence catalyzed by competition over scarce resources, politically instigated violence, cattle raiding, revenge killings and the impact of climate change epitomized by drought and floods.	

This year, the macroeconomic conditions continued to deteriorate with the increase of global interest rates sending the currency into free fall with little hope for recovery and causing inflation. The increased cost of living simultaneously coincided with  reduced donor funding across the entire humanitarian sector, as the needs of displaced populations continued to increase. 

The prevailing context persisted and was worsened by an influx of the returnees and refugees in April from Sudan which stand at 84,400 HH/ 367,800 individuals. 82% being South Sudanese returnees; a larger population being concentrated in Upper Nile and CES. Additionally, Jonglei has received returnees from Gambella in Ethiopia

Heightened protection risks ranged from: Gender Based Violence including Intimate Partner Violence, sexual violence, psychological trauma, to: lack of access to documentation to support housing land and property reclamation, illegal occupation, theft, destruction of personal property. Child  protection challenges such as child marriage and family separation are also present. 

Within this context, population movements have been influenced by this intricate web of pull and push factors and increased vulnerabilities among displaced populations as they seek safety, humanitarian assistance and attempt to rebuild their lives. The 2024, UNHCR HRP will focus on life saving humanitarian interventions linked to: i() General protection - monitoring and analysis to identify needs and provide tailored protection response; (ii) GBV - provision of case management, cash based assistance, psychosocial support and awareness to support prevention; (iii) Child protection - identification of children at risk, cash based assistance, physical support and training for individuals working with children through the community based protection networks and referral pathways; and (v) HLP - through legal aid and counseling, cash assistance, strengthening and establishing alternative dispute mechanisms.

Lifesaving humanitarian assistance will be provided to women, men, boys and girls based on need. Profiling will be conducted to identify the most vulnerable. Identification will be guided by the age, gender and diversity policy which ensures inclusion for all groups including persons with disabilities, youth, women, elderly and LGBTQ+. Activities will consider accountability to affect people and seek to ensure communication and transparency, participation and inclusion, feedback and response as well as adaptations and learning. Needs  will be addressed through: direct implementation, implementation with partners, mobile teams to ensure access to hard-to-reach areas where there is need, cash and in-kind support. Response will further consider interventions intended for durable solutions such as legal aid, access to documentation, reintegration and cash-based assistance.

To address these needs, ACTED will continue to play a role of a strong FSL partner and conduct activities in line with the following cluster objectives:

project_name: Strengthen the Health System Through the Sustainability of PHC and STHC Services In NS
project_objective:
In 2024, 4.5 million people reside in an area outside the control of the Syrian regime, with the population in NWs estimated to be 5.1 million according to another OCHA report. These individuals face severe deprivation, worsened by the recent earthquake. Recent assessments reveal the top five priority needs: Medicines and other commodities (60%), Paediatric consultations (48%), Treatment for chronic diseases (45%), First aid/emergency care (41%), and General/specialized surgical services (29%). The main barriers to accessing health services include the high cost of transportation (88%), lack of medicines/medical equipment (65%), inability to afford health services (64%), lack of transportation (61%), difficulty accessing facilities for those with mobility impairments (46%), and overcrowded health facilities (44%).
The project aims to reduce mortality and morbidity rates among IDPs and hosts in conflict-affected communities in NWS by improving access to lifesaving and life-sustaining coordinated, equitable humanitarian health services for those in need, especially the vulnerable people, including women, children, and the elderly as well as the people with disabilities

To accomplish these objectives, UOSSM seeks to support 17 HFs, including 5 hospitals,5 specialized centers, and 7 PHCs in Idleb, Aleppo and Ar-Raqqa. The mentioned HFs are well-equipped but have a gap in salaries, medical supplies, and operational costs. The HFs are located in areas with high priority, according to the health cluster and the TWGs, and distributed in densely populated and accessible locations, most of the people are IDPs with a low level of medical care and a dire economic situation. Notably, 4 of these HFs are recognized by the Syrian Board of Medical Specialties as training centers for specialized physicians.
Supporting and upgrading the capacity of these HFs is very important in light of their strategic locations in addition to the size and variety of health services provided that include:
- PHC services: IMCI, management of NCDs and CDs, providing RH and dental services, applying IPC measures, lab tests, vaccination and bandage services.
- Hospital services: 3 general hospitals (Al-Andalus, Jisr-Ash-Shugur and Quenya) provide delivery services, maternal and child health care as well as general surgeries and related health services; in addition, 2 specialized hospitals offer ophthalmic health care, audiogram services, pronunciation rehabilitation, orthopedic and reconstructive surgeries, and associated services.
- Specialized centers services: diagnostic, treatment, and blood transfusion services for thalassemia patients, specialized radiography services, dialysis services, and providing patients with blood products for them as well as providing the surrounding hospitals with blood units through the blood bank

To ensure the integration and continuity of health services, UOSSM also seeks to sustain the functionality of the referral system through support ambulance vehicles within the central referral system in Idlib, which coordinate referrals (3500 patients per month) through 60 ambulances between HFs in Idleb and Aleppo western rural. Also, as a CRS, it is interested in raising staff capacity in other referral and ambulance systems so that technical training will be conducted for 100 paramedics on ACLS. Those paramedics are staff from the CRS and other functioning ambulance systems in the field

It's important to note that all UOSSM staff will undergo training on PSEA, sign a TOR, and be familiar with the organization's internal PSEA policy. Monitoring of this policy is carried out by both the HR and MEAL teams. Additionally, all UOSSM staff will sign a code of conduct that includes a commitment to PSEA. The team is equipped to identify any cases of concern regarding PSEA and refer them to UOSSM's designated PSEA focal point for management and follow-up. Furthermore, beneficiaries will be provided with the PSEA hotline for lodging complaints.

project_name: Programme transfrontalier de promotion des solutions durables aux situations de déplacement au Cameroun et en République Centrafricaine (RCA)
project_objective:
Le consortium DRC-ACF-CARE-NRC propose un programme transfrontalier intégré contribuant directement à apporter des solutions durables, diversifiées et localisées aux situations de déplacements au Cameroun et en République Centrafricaine (RCA). Cette action permettra :
●	De répondre aux besoins de base des réfugiés/retournés et communautés hôtes dans les zones d'accueil et de retour (OS1) ;
●	Le renforcement de l’autonomisation économique des populations en situation de déplacement face aux chocs et au changement climatique (OS2) ;
●	Un plus grand respect des droits des populations affectées par les situations de déplacements entre le Cameroun et la RCA (OS3).
Ces axes contribuent aux objectifs du Pacte mondial sur les réfugiés et du Cadre d’action global pour les réfugiés. L’action propose une approche régionale cohérente avec les engagements pris par les Etats dans la Déclaration de Yaoundé en avril 2022, en contribuant à la mise en œuvre des axes III (soutien au cadre institutionnel), IV (promotion de l’inclusion, la résilience et l’autonomisation économique des réfugiés et populations hôtes), V (soutien aux conditions propices au retour durable) et VI (mise en place d’un mécanisme régional de coordination). Le consortium se propose de participer au suivi de ces engagements aux côtés du HCR dans les mécanismes de coordination régionaux et/ou nationaux qui seront mis en place. 
En cohérence avec les programmations multi-annuelles 2021-2027 entre l’Union européenne (UE) et le Cameroun d’une part, l’UE et la RCA d’autre part , l’action sera basée sur l’amélioration du bien-être socio-économique des populations et sur la protection et la promotion des droits humains, avec un accent particulier sur les victimes de violations de droits, notamment parmi les femmes, les jeunes, les réfugié-e-s, les retourné-e-s et les déplacé-e-s. Leur soutien se fera à travers le renforcement de capacités communautaires et étatiques de prise en charge, le renforcement des opportunités économiques, la sensibilisation sur l’accès aux droits et le plaidoyer aux niveaux local et national/transfrontalier. Le programme renforcera le processus de décentralisation impulsé par l’Etat depuis 2019 à travers un appui aux Collectivités Territoriales Décentralisées (CTD) qui sont au premier plan de la réponse aux mouvements de populations. Les acteurs locaux tels que les OSC seront des partenaires privilégiés de l‘action afin de favoriser le transfert de compétences et à terme la localisation de l’assistance et la durabilité des actions initiées. En ligne avec le GAP III de l’UE et la résolution 1325 de l'ONU sur la participation des femmes aux processus de paix, l’égalité des genres, l’autonomisation économique et le leadership des femmes et des filles seront promus à travers des activités ciblées et leur participation dans l’action et dans les processus décisionnels.
Le programme proposé est également en ligne avec le Pacte Vert de l’UE. Du fait de la pression exercée par la démographie croissante sur des ressources naturelles menacées, le programme fera de la protection de l’environnement l’une de ses priorités, à travers la promotion de pratiques agricoles agroécologiques, la définition de plans de développement territoriaux durables, ainsi que l’appui à la gestion durable de l’eau et des espaces agro-sylvopastoraux.

project_name: Rights Restored: Bridging Legal and Civil Documentation Gaps in Crisis Affected Populations in Cabo Delgado
project_objective:
Displaced and vulnerable populations, uprooted by conflict, natural disasters, or other calamities, grapple with the loss of identity and rights due to the absence of essential documents. In these critical moments, the inability to prove one's identity, secure property rights, or access basic services amplifies the challenges faced by individuals and communities. This project emerges as a beacon of hope in this chaos, seeking to weave together a comprehensive and sustainable framework to bridge the gaping legal and civil documentation gaps haunting crisis-affected populations.
The significance of legal and civil documentation in times of crisis cannot be overstated. It forms the bedrock of an individual's identity, underpinning access to education, healthcare, and legal protection. However, as communities are shattered and lives are disrupted, the very fabric of these identities is torn apart, leaving individuals in a precarious state of limbo. This project steps into this void, recognizing that the ability to assert one's existence and rights is not just a bureaucratic necessity but a lifeline for those grappling with the aftermath of calamity.
As the global community faces an increasing frequency of humanitarian crises, the imperative to address this documentation crisis becomes ever more pressing. The project endeavours to be not merely a project but a catalyst for systemic change—a conduit through which individuals can reclaim their identities and rebuild shattered lives and more importantly fully exercise their rights. It is a call to action, rooted in the belief that a comprehensive and innovative approach can mend the frayed bonds of legal recognition, offering solace and empowerment to those navigating the tumultuous aftermath of crisis

project_name: Les populations affectées par la crise au Niger bénéficient d'une assistance adaptée à leurs besoins en matière de la documentation civile dans les régions de Tillabéri (Tillabéri, Téra et Abala), Tahoua (Madaoua) et Maradi (Guidan Roumdji et Madarounfa).
project_objective:
Dans le souci de promouvoir les droits à la documentation civile et d'identité juridique des PDI, des communautés d'accueil touchées par le déplacement et des autres groupes vulnérables dans les régions de Maradi, Tahoua et Tillabery NRC à travers son programme d'information, de conseil et d'assistance juridique (ICLA), entreprendra des activités facilitant l'accès à la documentation civile et d'identité juridique et garantissant la protection des droits fondamentaux. 
Les solutions proposées s’alignent à la fois aux objectifs stratégiques du secteur protection. 
ICLA organisera des campagnes / Caravane  de sensibilisations sur l'importance de la documentation civile et d'identité juridique ;  fournira des conseils juridiques aux PDI en vue de les aider à surmonter les obstacles les empêchant d’exercer leur droit à la documentation civile et d'identité juridique, apportera une assistance juridique pour l'obtention des actes de naissance et cartes nationales d'identité, et renforcera les mécanismes communautaires et les services techniques en charge de l'établissement des actes de naissance. De même, le programme ICLA apportera son assistance sur sollicitation d’autres acteurs humanitaires intervenant dans la même région et suivant l’analyse de la situation sécuritaire par NRC. ICLA portera une attention particulière aux femmes et filles dont le taux d'enregistrement reste faible dans ces zones précitées. ICLA favorisera l'approche inclusive et participative pour les communautés cibles en facilitant les dialogues communautaires contribuant à identifier les obstacles à l'exercice de ces droits. En outre, les acteurs humanitaires et les décideurs seront ciblés pour le renforcement des questions de plaidoyer. 
Le projet contribuera de manière significative à la protection des personnes déplacées interne, refugiés et communauté hôte vulnérables à travers la promotion et la facilitation de l'accès à la documentation civile et légale. Ceci se fera à travers les actions d'information, conseil et assistance juridique. Un accent sera mis sur le renforcement des capacités des acteurs d'état civil et des appuis matériel apporté afin de faciliter la délivrance du service.  Les aspects de plaidoyer seront développés pour faciliter l’accès aux plus grands nombres. On s'assurera de prendre en compte 3% de personnes handicapés.
Dans le cadre de la mise en œuvre de ce projet les acteurs locaux auront un rôle participatif et inclusif. Il s'agira à titre purement illustratif de la participation et l'implication des autorités et leaders communautaires (maires, les chefs de quartiers et villages ainsi que les responsables des sites) lors des activités de caravane de sensibilisation, de dialogue communautaire pour l'identification des défis liés à l'exercice du droit à l'identité juridique ainsi que les pistes de solution voire la stratégie et plan d'action pour adresser ce défi, le renforcement des capacités de ces acteurs sur les innovations apportées par la loi de 2019 régissant l'état civil.
Pour la stratégie de prise en compte du genre, il convient de souligner que le projet étant exclusivement inclusif et participatif, il sera question de mettre en valeur le SIP qui est la programmation sûre et inclusive afin de mieux prendre en compte les exigences liées à leurs besoins spécifiques.

project_name: Soutien à la réponse d'urgence en éducation  dans la région Diffa (SURE)
project_objective:
Le projet contribuera au HRP 2024 par le ciblage de 25 320 bénéficiaires directs. Il répondra aux besoins éducatifs urgents dans 65 écoles suivant les objectifs sectoriels du Cluster Education à travers une approche basée sur trois axes : accès à l’éducation de qualité, la protection et la résilience des communautés scolaires.
1. Les filles et les garçons ont accès à des offres d’éducation inclusive continue et de qualité dans les écoles primaires formelles et non formelles.
Le projet sera en phase avec la campagne Back to school pour l’inscription/réinscription des filles/garçons en âge scolaire y compris ceux vulnérables. L’éducation à distance à travers les clubs d’écoute radio, des cours de rattrapade et la Stratégie de Scolarisation Accélérée pour Passerelle (SSA/P) seront développés pour répondre aux besoins d’accès et de continuité de l’éducation. L’approche d’éducation à distance de Concern développée dans la région de Tillabéri sera étendue à la région de Diffa. Pour améliorer la qualité des apprentissages, les élèves seront dotés en kits scolaires d’urgence selon les standards du Cluster Education. Les enseignants recevront du matériel pédagogique d’urgence ; ils seront formés et suivis sur la pédagogie inclusive au handicap et au genre. Ils seront également formés puis encadrés sur les didactiques de français et mathématiques. Les filles les plus vulnérables et les enfants handicapés bénéficieront de suivis pour leur maintien scolaire. Les filles vulnérables y compris celles handicapées recevront du cash transfert non conditionnel mensuel pour les besoins alimentaires et d’hygiène menstruelle.
2. Les filles et les garçons y compris ceux qui sont handicapés des communautés déplacées et hôtes touchés par les crises humanitaires bénéficient d’un environnement d’apprentissage sûr et protecteur.
L’accès à l’éducation sera soutenue par la réhabilitation d’urgence de salles de classes et de latrines, la mise en place d’espaces temporaire d’apprentissage (TLS) accessibles aux personnes handicapées, Ces infrastructures seront équipées et munies d’un dispositif de lavage de mains. Les enseignants seront formés sur les thématiques clés liées à la problématique des crises pour un environnement protecteur : soutien psychosocial, violences basées sur le genre en milieu scolaire (VBGMS), éducation en situation d’urgence. Ces enseignants formés seront encadrés pour la fourniture de soutien psychosocial et la mise en place des comités de protection scolaire. Les écoles bénéficieront de matériels ludiques pour le développement des activités créatives et récréatives. Un mécanisme de référencement pour la prise en charge psychosociale des enfants en détresse psychologique sera mis en place et piloté par un point focal au niveau des écoles. Concern participera au plaidoyer auprès des autorités nationales et locale en faveur la protection des écoles contre les attaques pour la mise en œuvre de la déclaration Safe school.
3. Les filles et les garçons y compris ceux qui sont handicapés des communautés déplacées et hôtes et le personnel scolaire ainsi que les membres de la communauté sont soutenus dans la préparation et la réponse aux urgences.
A la suite d’une formation des enseignants et des structures communautaires (APE/AME/CGDES), un plan de préparation et de réponse aux risques et aux urgences sera mis en place afin d’identifier les mesures de prévention et de protection pour la sécurité des enfants et des enseignants. Pour favoriser la gestion de l’école en mode décentralisé les APE, AME, CGDES seront redynamisées ou établies et leurs compétences renforcées/ Avec les enseignants, ils seront impliqués dans la lutte contre les violences basées sur le genre en milieu scolaire (VBGMS), la cohésion sociale et la protection de l’enfant. Dans chaque école, un mécanisme de gestion de plaintes sera mis en place aux côtés du comité de protection scolaire avec l’implication des Comités Villageois de Protection de l'Enfant.

project_name: Enhancing access to Health services for vulnerable populations in Aleppo, Hama, Lattakia, Rural Damascus, Deir ez-Zor and Quneitra
project_objective:
Needs: 
The severity of humanitarian needs has continued to increase, with an estimated 14.9M people in need of health assistance. The health sector severity scale revealed catastrophic need in areas like Aleppo, Ar-Raqqa and Rural Damascus in 2024. In 2023, these governorates faced outbreaks of AWDs, measles and meningitis. In Aleppo, Hama and Lattakia, health services have been severely impacted by the Feb 2023 earthquake. HFs have insufficient consumables and equipment. Lack of essential medicines and inadequate HWs were key barriers to health care access, particularly for NCDs, which account for 49.8% of mortality. Patients are facing reduced access due to sharp increases in medication prices. According to HNO 2024, 65% of HFs do not provide services to NCDs and mental health. 
Intervention, Implementation of activities: 
Medair integrates activities to ensure delivery of quality services and supports rehabilitation works, medical equipment and furniture for PHCs to restore functionality. Medair works closely with DoH and provides oversight to engineering firms to ensure that rehabilitation work complies with standards. HWs will receive training on NCDs, IPC, SGBV, RH & PFA. EWARS notifiable cases will be identified and reported. CHWs will share health messages and identify PLWMI for AD. Through CVA, Medair will support referral for obstetric cases, SAM with complications and acute events to nearest SHC services and provide a voucher for the vulnerable NCD patients to access medications at pre-identified pharmacies. Protection Risk Analysis: 
Medair’s approach to protection mainstreaming and integration seeks to provide the most vulnerable clients with access to tailored services that adhere to the principle of Do No Harm. Medair conducts regular context analysis, monitoring, and communication with local authorities, and participation of affected populations. 
GBV related risks: mitigation measures to reduce this include training HWs on how to deal with survivors of GBV, confidentiality, survivor-center approach, and referrals. 
Service provision: low quality services might expose beneficiaries to further harm and deterioration of their health conditions. Mitigation measures include regular monitoring of service provision, capacity building, effective feedback and complaints mechanisms. 
Protection monitoring allows Medair to track whether clients are able to access services, as well as their degree of satisfaction or any concerns associated with the services received.  
PSEA (Protection from Sexual Exploitation & Abuse) strategy: 
Abuse and exploitation both towards staff and beneficiaries seeking services, either in exchange for services/assistance or not. All acts falling under the definition of SEA are prohibited and considered a gross violation of Medair Code of Conduct, which all Medair employees must sign and commit to adhere to. Medair makes available immediate and confidential mechanisms to report SEA for Medair staff members or any other person who may have been a victim of SEA or may have witnessed or otherwise been informed of a case of SEA involving Medair. 
Risks, Assumptions & Mitigating measures: 
Risks: the existence of many checkpoints may limit access to the project area. Medair will coordinate with local government. All required documentation will accompany shipments of goods along with staff who are familiar with the situation.
Risk: HWs may leave workstations due to deteriorating social and economic conditions. Medair considers covering their night shift compensation and transportation costs & will collaborate with DoH to have adequately trained staff. 
Risks: Delays in procurement. Mitigation: a procurement plan will be completed at the start of the project to ensure sufficient lead time.  
Risk: Planned activities are not approved by relevant Ministries or SARC or approved with but with significant delays or adjusted procedures. Maintain engagement with each Line Ministry to facilitate approvals.

project_name: Providing Adequate Water Supply (Quantity, Quality, Access) with capacity building and awareness raising to Vulnerable Communities in Specific Locations
project_objective:
The economic situation compounds the protracted crisis and recent natural disasters means that finances for and access to clean, safe water is a daily struggle for 13.6M Syrians in need of WASH assistance and waterborne diseases remain a concern across Syria. WASH infrastructure in Syria requires substantial repair and operational support, including O&M training for rehabilitated sites. The proposed project will provide life-saving WASH interventions at both the community and HH levels to increase water supply. Fuel/electrical supplies for infrastructure have become untenable. Medair proposes specific activities/per need in each operating location, such as rehabilitation and/or solarization of Water Pump Stations, boreholes, and elevated water tanks; fixing damaged sections of water distribution networks; Water trucking; and rehabilitating WASH facilities in clinics where Medair also conducts health activities. Complementing Medair’s health messaging via community health workers, hygiene awareness training is included. The health and hygiene messages will be delivered through house-to-house visits to ensure widespread coverage. Capacity building of Water Establishment staff in O&M will occur wherever water supply work is completed.
	Protection Risk Analysis: RISK: Increased water supply is inequitably distributed in the network. MITIGATION: Community consultation and extensive, systematic mapping with various populations to ensure that no households are missed; consultation should include vulnerable populations and be done by appropriate facilitators (gender, age), MoWR staff O&M training. Kept incident log, shows incidents or results of incident investigations RISK: Resulting system creates hazards for community, including vulnerable persons MITIGATION: Build to accessibility standards within Sphere/local sector standards. Ensure trained technicians and engineers are the implementers, Consult community, inclusive of vulnerable populations about perceived risks, existing mitigations. Quality assurance validation according to standards. Post-project monitoring for safety incidents
	PSEA strategy: RISK: Risk of exploitation to and by Medair employees, prospective employees, contracted workers MITIGATION: Organization-wide PSEA awareness regularly trained and discussed; relevant PSEA mitigations in HR, accountability for prevention to managers, established staff feedback/reporting mechanisms. 	Risks, Assumptions and Mitigating measures: RISK: Delays in planned procurement and/or importation MITIGATION: A procurement plan will be completed at start of project cycle to ensure sufficient lead-time for normal operations. project_name: Early recovery support to conflict-affected communities across Northern Syria
project_objective:
Needs : In Syria, 15,4 million persons are expected to need early recovery and livelihoods assistance in 2024, as per the 2024 HNO. Across Syria, a general deterioration in access to livelihoods, ability to meet basic needs, availability and affordability of infrastructure and services is observed, threatening the resilience and social cohesion of households. Inflationary trends on key goods and services, widespread low productivity of inputs, low wages, and lack of employment, among other factors, continue to impact households’ priority needs and exacerbate the income-expenditure gapacross the country. According to REACH, early recovery livelihoods is regularly reported within the top (3) priority needs of households across the country.  The economic crisis has significantly worsened in certain areas, leading to a substantial increase in the cost of the Survival Minimum Expenditure Basket (SMEB) by 86% over 12 months. With 99% of the population in Northeast Syria (NES) living below the extreme poverty line of USD 1.90 per person per day, urgent investments in economic recovery are crucial.  Ongoing drought in NES has led to a loss of daily work opportunities, particularly in agriculture, the main source of livelihood in the region. Agricultural value chains, particularly wheat and barley production, have been severely affected, causing a decline in employment opportunities. 

 

Activities : The proposed project by ACTED focuses on the Early Recovery Livelihoods (ERL) sector with the objective of restoring urban livelihoods in conflict and earthquake-affected communities across Northern Syria. The plan involves a multifaceted approach, incorporating short-term income opportunities through Cash-for-Work schemes, sustainable restoration of basic services, and value chain improvement. This includes the repair, installation, and rehabilitation of key assets like water infrastructure and schools. Also, livelihoods support and market recovery efforts will be done through grants and training for small-to-mid-scale businesses.

ACTED will continue its Area-Based Approach, providing multi-sectoral assistance and building the capacity of local stakeholders for community-driven response plans. The organization aims to reach 254,677 individuals in 2024 and contribute to limiting the migration of affected populations to Internally Displaced Persons (IDP) camps. 

In terms of business support, ACTED plans to implement Cash for Work schemes in specific areas, targeting vulnerable households to provide temporary income opportunities. These schemes will focus on unskilled or low-skilled work, determined through a participatory process involving community input. Activities may include tasks like compost industry, poly tunnel construction support, school repairs, public garden rehabilitation, and fencing. The goal is to ensure community acceptance and accessibility for various population groups, including women, the elderly, and individuals with disabilities. Participants are expected to work for three months, receiving a daily wage of approximately 4.5 USD. 

In the context of the ERL sector, ACTED is actively contributing to household and community resilience by offering increased opportunities for sustainable livelihoods, inclusive access to basic public services, and enhancing the capacity of local institutions and civil society to support early recovery efforts. Additionally, the organization has provided solar systems to strengthen resilience and improve access to services.  

PSEA : All ACTED staff receive induction and regular refresher trainings on the Code of conduct, PSEA, and Child Safeguarding policies. Contractors have the obligation to sign an ethical declaration and respect ACTED Code of Conduct. Contractors are briefed on PSEA before the implementation of the project.

project_name: Provision of life-saving WASH services in Northern Syria
project_objective:
The 2024 Humanitarian Needs Overview estimates that 16.6 million of people will be in need of WASH services in Syria. Nearly two-thirds of water treatment plants, half of all pumping stations, and one-third of water towers have been damaged due to the conflict as per the August 2022 Water Crisis response plan. In camps across Syria, the drinking water is still mainly provided by trucks with only 21% of all camps connected to water networks, leaving the majority of IDPs in camps dependent on costly and unsustainable supplies of safe drinking water. The proposed project aims at enhancing access to water, sanitation, and hygiene services for conflict-affected populations across Northern Syria, with emergency, life-saving WASH assistance mostly provided in camp settings, and longer-term, resilience focused assistance mostly provided off camp. Acted will provide a variety of assistance modalities toward this aim. Off-camp, Acted will rehabilitate, through contractors and in coordination with all relevant stakeholders (including WASH Cluster, WASH Working Group, and local councils and technical departments), numerous assets, including water pumping stations, water treatment stations, water towers, etc. Acted will also install new assets and/or facilities to fit existing assets, in areas where the need for water is highest. Acted will look to hand over these assets to relevant local stakeholders while providing operation and maintenance support, and capacity-building trainings, in order for WASH-related basic services to remain operational through these assets after the completion of the intervention. In Northwest Syria, Acted will conduct repairs and rehabilitation of WASH facilities in health centers. Acted will also provide emergency water trucking out-of-camp in Northeast Syria. In-camp, Acted will provide life-saving water supply, sanitation services including wastewater and latrine management, and solid waste management services, and water quality monitoring to several camp clusters in Northwest Syria (NWS), as well as Washokani and Areesheh camps and multiple informal settlements in Northeast Syria (NES). Additionally, to further enhance sanitation conditions and in effort to increase access to water Acted plans on piloting household-level grey wastewater treatment and recycling systems to support wastewater management on camp. Complementary to this assistance, Acted will provide hygiene promotion and awareness sessions to all targeted camp residents, and distribute WASH NFIs to highly vulnerable displaced persons. In total, Acted expects its activities to reach 875,348 individuals under the WASH sector in 2024. Acted will seek synergies with its -saving assistance off-camp, particularly water trucking. With regards to in-camp interventions, Acted will work through targeted communities in camp, notably through community-based structures, to build the sustainability of the WASH activities conducted. In NES, this include involving Water Committees from the resident population to participate in water quality monitoring, whilst informing camp residents on how to raise maintenance and water supply issues. In NWS, Acted is also evaluating the prospects of cost recovery mechanisms. The approach considers social and economic dimensions, including the enabling environment, willingness to pay, and financial considerations such as fixed and variable costs. Active participation in the Cost Recovery in WASH Infrastructure Technical Working Group at the WASH Cluster will further promote informed decisions are taken. All Acted staff are trained on the Code of Conduct and its 8 policies, including the PSEA and Child Protection Policy. As part of every training, the staff is trained on recognizing sexual exploitation and abuse situations and concrete steps to follow for reporting any concerns or suspicions.
This project will target 875,348 beneficiaries.

project_name: Improving uninterrupted access to quality lifesaving Sexual and Reproductive Health Services for the displaced and vulnerable women, girls and adolescents from IDP camps and returnees in the Northeast States of Borno, Adamawa and Yobe in Nigeria
project_objective:
The project will focus to improve and uninterrupted access to life-saving Sexual and Reproductive Health (SRH) care services to the IDPs and vulnerable women and adolescent girls, including the returnees and those from the host community in Borno, Adamawa and Yobe States (BAY States). The minimum initial service, and comprehensive SRH services covering but not limited to antenatal care, postnatal care, support for delivery services, clinical management of rape and family planning services to women and girls in need will be strengthened through the supported health facilities and partners. In addition, the project will also strengthen the integration of MHPSS in SRH service provision and make sure that clear referral channels are available for those with the severe psychosis. The survivors of sexual violence and women with obstetric emergencies who need tertiary-level care will also benefit from the specialized referral support services of the project. UNFPA will also procure inter-agency emergency reproductive health kits, including clinical management of rape kits and other essential medical items to support uninterrupted SRH service delivery, as well as for the prepositioning. UNFPA will ensure the last mile distribution of the kits and medical commodities to all agreed Health facilities and mobile outreaches. 
The unpredictable situations of cholera outbreaks will also be considered in the response while also ensuring the continued provision of vital SRH services. In order to do so, UNFPA will provide capacity building trainings to different service providers and partners.  The efforts of advocacy and leadership of the SRH sub-working group under the health sector will be strengthened to maximize the momentum of SRH response, including the preparedness for any emergency across BAY States. In addition, the clinical management of the rape task force (CMR TF) under SRH SWG will be strengthened and ensure the integration of SRH and GBV, to ensure the GBV survivors receive appropriate, timely health care services and mental health and psychosocial support services (MHPSS). The ultimate aim of the project is to ensure the continuation and strengthening of SRH services through the provision of reproductive health supplies, capacity building and enhancing coordination across the BAY States.

project_name: Strengthening social cohesion in Syria
project_objective: The program’s overall objective is to strengthen social cohesion amongst conflict affected communities in North Syria and contribute to long-term peace and stability of Syria. Strengthening cohesive communities is vital to supporting the stability that is finally emerging in North Syria, and reinforcing post-conflict economic recovery. The combination of improving inter-communal relationships and reducing resource-based tensions will serve to prevent the escalation of some economic-based disputes into violence – for example between host and IDP communities over livelihood opportunities or social service provision – and reduce the ability of political actors to manipulate ethno-religious divisions and mobilise violence. To this end, and in close collaboration with local and neighborhood councils, Mercy Corps will implement community service projects to support local economic development and address resource-based tensions. Mercy Corps social cohesion approach is grounded on a sound context, conflict and conflict sensitivity analysis that supports the identification of viable entry points for strengthening social cohesion within and between communities on different sides of the conflict divide. Mercy Corps supports community members with the knowledge, skills and confidence they need to analyze opportunities and impediments to strengthening social cohesion; and to formulate and implement options for strengthening social cohesion at the community level. Through participatory methodology including community mobilization, dialogue, interest based negotiation and the use of sports and creative arts; Mercy Corps will encourage positive interactions between and among community members from across the conflict divide. Mercy Corps will also support conflicting communities to address drivers of conflict through the joint implementation of projects that address resource based conflict drivers. Mercy Corps community mobilization methodology multi-pronged approach to social cohesion Conflict sensitivity is at the heart of all social cohesion activities. The project will develop a conflict sensitivity strategy, guided by various conflict sensitivity analysis tools including the do no harm matrix and stakeholder analysis matrix, building off the findings of context and conflict analysis in the areas of implementation. Mercy Corps social cohesion project will ensure the meaningful participation of all sections of the community with an emphasis on women and youth (male and female).

project_name: Reviewed Refugee Response Plan for Sudanese 2024
project_objective:
Chad hosts the largest number of people fleeing violence in Sudan, including 496,834 newly arrived Sudanese refugees as of December 2023, and 93,700 Chadian migrant returnees according to the International Organisation for Migration (IOM), in Ouaddaï, Wadi Firas, Sila and Ennedi Est provinces. 
New arrivals – mostly women and children – often arrive in poor health, malnourished, traumatized and wounded. New arrivals first settle in overcrowded, spontaneous sites along the border, where they sleep in makeshift shelters. They need protection and assistance, including psychosocial support, food, shelter, water and sanitation services, and core relief items such as mattresses, soap and cooking utensils. Given the high proportion of those who have been physically assaulted, survivors of gender-based violence (GBV) and women and children among new arrivals, mental health and psychosocial support and child protection are critical concerns. Due to insecurity in areas along the borders, relocating newly arriving refugees to settlements remains a top priority. 
The new arrivals come mostly from Darfur, one of Sudan’s regions most affected by violence and where the escalation of conflict, including attacks, indiscriminate violence, lootings, and intense fighting, continues to force thousands of people to flee. Some 500,000 people were displaced to Chad by the end of 2023.    An additional 250,000 refugees and 60,000    Chadian migrant returnees could arrive in Chad in 2024.
New refugees continue to arrive in an area that was already hosting 407,000 Sudanese refugees. In this region, where natural resources are scarce, infrastructure, essential services, and livelihood activities are limited, the most vulnerable host, refugee and returnee families already face incredible hardship, with refugee families hit the hardest.
The latest food security and nutrition surveys conducted in 2023 showed high food insecurity and malnutrition rates. More than 577,990 people are severely food insecure and cannot meet their most basic food needs without external assistance. Food insecurity affected an additional 536,852 persons during the lean season, the period between harvest when food is most difficult to access. Food stocks were depleted, and people did not have enough money to buy food. 
Refugee families are hit the hardest. More than 80 per cent of refugees have a poor or borderline consumption level, with food insecurity impacting almost 83 per cent of new arrivals compared to 73 per cent of the existing refugee population. Refugee families with specific needs are among the most food insecure. In these regions, 10 per cent to 16 per cent of families resort to negative coping strategies to survive. These include selling household assets, reducing the quantity and nutritional quality of meals, begging, survival sex, borrowing from traders, and taking children out of school for daily work to be able to buy food. Levels of malnutrition are also extremely concerning, with the prevalence of global acute malnutrition exceeding 10 per cent in all three provinces.

project_name: Food and agricultural Assistance to the Crisis-Affected Families through the Appropriate Modality.
project_objective:
The food security situation in Syria has drastically deteriorated since last year. In 2024, 16.7 million people (8.4 million female, 8.3 million male) are assessed to need humanitarian assistance across Syria, up from 15.3 million in 2023. Of the 16.7 million people in need, 5.5 million are displaced, including over 2 million who live in last resort sites. After 12 years of hostilities and persistent economic crisis, people in Syria saw their situation worsen when a series of earthquakes hit northern Syria and Türkiye on 6 and 20 February 2023. The earthquakes uprooted hundreds of thousands of families, resulted in almost 5,900 deaths and more than 12,800 people injured in Syria, and severely damaged infrastructures already weakened by the conflict. Many families lost their main breadwinner due to death or injury, at a time when the economic situation was already dire, increasing the vulnerability of millions of people previously unable to meet their basic needs.
The impact of Syria’s crisis continues to hinder people’s ability to meet their immediate food needs and livelihoods, in a context marked by very complex drivers and contributing factors. This includes economic worsening and weakened local currency, soaring food and non-food prices, as well as drought-like conditions and severe agro-climatic fluctuations, water scarcity, and limited energy supply. In addition, food and agriculture commodities prices increase, inflation, lack of purchasing power due to limited livelihood and lack of income sources, population movements that show no sign of abating, and the Ukraine crisis have had an important economic impact on markets and commodities cost. Oxfam assessments also confirm the above-mentioned information and the findings show the high need for rehabilitation of basic infrastructure ( bakeries, Mill, Market-related agriculture activities), and support local community in agriculture inputs, and appropriate training Oxfam has very experienced and competent staff to implement the rehabilitation of basic infrastructure, increase their skills, and provide needed capacity building for the target group to enable an increase in their food security in additional distribution of agricultural inputs, and linking between target beneficiaries and the Market, based on market assessment and value chain assessment for agriculture goods. risk assessment will be done before the start of the project to understand the beneficiary's preferences, modality, delivery mechanism, and potential risk and mitigation measures.
The planned activities will include: Farmer field schools and pastural field schools, distribution of agricultural inputs and climate smart inputs, in-kind modality or cash, and the rehabilitation of irrigation infrastructure with traditional equipment and renewable energy based on technical assessments, and the rehabilitation of irrigation canals in addition to providing communal mobile solar systems. Moreover, Oxfam will rehabilitate market infrastructure related to agricultural value chain and will provide trainings will all these interventions to the relevant stakeholders.
It will further adopt a participatory community engagement approach to ensure the active participation of the target people enhance inclusion and reduce exclusion errors. 
A total of 49,552 HH  households will be benefited from this intervention and 25% of them are female-headed households.
 
The action will conduct price monitoring of the basic items in the critical market , and climate change impact to understand the changes of price trends and adjust the aid , and type of intervention accordingly. DDP, Post distribution monitoring , and evaluate the applicaants practice will be conducted to measure the impact and beneficiaries' satisfaction. (continued in extended project summary)

project_name: Food assistance to vulnerable conflict affected populations in Northern Syria
project_objective:
As the Syria crisis moves into its twelfth year its impact continues to blight the present, and the future prospects of its population, with the impacts felt most negatively on the lives of vulnerable civilians across the country. In response to these needs, People in Need's (PIN's) project proposes to contribute towards saving and sustaining lives of targeted conflict-affected communities in Northern Syria through the provision of food assistance (multiple modalities). Responses between immediate needs and resiliencebuilding will be adapted according to continuous assessments and analysis of the local contexts within a flexible and responsive framework. 

Activities will be underpinned by emergency preparedness and response plans developed in coordination with relevant clusters, working groups, and partners – to promote timely, efficient and joined-up responses that seek to maximize geographic and sectoral coverage and minimize gaps. PIN will also focus upon assisting vulnerable, conflict-affected to meet basic food needs. Activities will target the most vulnerable households in communities chronically affected by the adverse impacts of the conflict, using common assistance modalities and selection criteria, per the recommendation of the working groups. 

PIN will plan to reach beneficiaries with monthly food assistance (food baskets, food vouchers, MPCA), agriculture vouchers, agriculture business grants, and bakery support hrough reduced-price bread on a community level through providing contracted bakeries with 50% of flour and 50% of yeast to reduce the price of the bread price up to 37% in comparison with the free market bread price. Beneficiaries are targeted from both IDPs and host community members, meeting eligibility and vulnerability criteria to avoid creating tensions within and across communities. Selection criteria was elaborated in consultation with the affected communities, as well as based on evidence from previous project monitoring and community feedback obtained through the Community Feedback and Response Mechanism (CFRM), and include low-income families from the following groups: Femaleheaded households (FHH); Child-headed HH; Elderly-headed HH; HH with disabled and chronically ill members; HH with high dependency ratio; Unemployed male and female youth; Poor farming HH. PIN is aware that needs are different amongst gender and age groups, and other vulnerable groups such as people with disabilities. PIN aims to provide the most needed assistance by employing a wide spectrum of different activities to meet the distinct needs, establishing beneficiary selection criteria to prioritise the inclusion of those most vulnerable, and adapting its assistance delivery to promote access for the most vulnerable people. PINs programmes are coordinated with local authorities at various levels – from cross-border to hubs to district and village levels. PIN engages in regular dialogue with authorities to ensure transparency, accountability, and protection mainstreaming; including consultations and briefings on needs, humanitarian principles, PIN procedures, and beneficiary selection at projects' planning, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation stages.

project_name: Provisión de servicios especializados de protección para individuos y comunidades a través de respuesta integral
project_objective:
A través de la provisión de asistencia especializada y del fortalecimiento de las capacidades de las comunidades e instituciones del Estado, la programación de NRC busca prevenir y mitigar riesgos de protección a nivel individual y comunitario. La respuesta individual tiene como objetivo de reestablecer el bienestar físico, mental y psicosocial bien como los derechos de las personas afectadas por violencia una vez que haya ocurrido. Se pretende alcanzar este objetivo a través de mecanismo de remisiones internas y externas que garanticen acceso a los servicios pertinentes y la provisión de apoyo psicosocial, cuando relevante. El acceso se facilita inclusive a través del fortalecimiento de capacidades de instituciones publicas identificadas en el marco del mapeo, cuyo involucramiento es esencial para garantizar una respuesta de protección integral y sostenible. Al mismo tiempo, el proyecto pretende también fortalecer las capacidades de las comunidades para prevenir riesgos de protección y mejorar sus propios mecanismos de respuesta, mitigando así los impactos de la violencia. Se pretende alcanzar este resultado a través de la metodología de NRC de autoprotección civil, y de sensibilizaciones sobre participación comunitaria, coexistencia pacífica, no discriminación y resolución de conflictos. 

Los siguientes riesgos identificados se podrán prevenir, mitigar y/o responder a través de las acciones propuestas como parte de la programación del NRC: ataques a civiles y a bienes civiles se manejarán mediante la gestión de casos y la protección comunitaria, en función de la naturaleza específica de la amenaza. La separación forzosa de familias se aborda mediante la gestión de casos y la reunificación siempre que sea posible, teniendo en cuenta el mandato de la organización; siempre que se trate de la separación de un niño, se remitirá a actores especializados en protección de la niñez. La denegación de recursos, oportunidades, servicios y/o acceso humanitario se mitigará a través de la gestión de casos y las remisiones internas siempre que sea pertinente, así como a través de la protección basada en la comunidad mediante el desarrollo de sus capacidades para negociar con actores armados a fin de garantizar el acceso para la prestación de asistencia humanitaria. Asimismo, mediante sesiones informativas tanto sobre derechos como sobre acceso a servicios se contribuirá a mitigar la desinformación y la denegación de acceso a la información dentro de las comunidades, que repercuten en su seguridad y bienestar. Se responderá al reclutamiento forzoso mediante la gestión de casos o la asistencia de protección individual, basándose en un enfoque centrado en la persona y dependiendo de la urgencia de las circunstancias; cuando se trate de niños asociados en grupos armados, éstos serán remitidos a actores especializados de protección de la niñez. Los abusos psicológicos y emocionales se mitigarán mediante intervenciones de apoyo psicosocial tanto a nivel individual como comunitario. El robo y el saqueo, así como el desalojo forzoso o la destrucción de bienes personales, se tratarán y mitigarán mediante la gestión de casos, la asistencia para la protección individual y la remisión interna, según las necesidades. La tortura o los tratos crueles, inhumanos o degradantes se tratarán y mitigarán mediante la gestión de casos, el apoyo psicosocial y la protección comunitaria, según la naturaleza de cada caso. Las restricciones a la libertad de movimiento se mitigarán principalmente a través de acciones de protección basadas en la comunidad, y el desplazamiento forzoso con una respusta específica dependiendo de si se trata de una amenaza individual, familiar o comunitaria. Se reforzarán las capacidades de insituciones publicas en brindar respuesta a derivaciones de estos tipos de casos, según relevante, a través de acciones mencionadas en cima y talleres dirigidos a estos actores al fin de contribuir a resultados de protección.

project_name: Mejora de los servicios esenciales de Agua, Saneamiento e Higiene de las personas en situación de desplazamiento afectadas por la crisis de proteccion en Venezuela.
project_objective:
NRC tiene como objetivo brindar protección a los desplazados internos y a las personas en movimiento que enfrentan altos riesgos de protección. El programa WASH en Venezuela persigue beneficiar de soluciones de salud pública dignas y duraderas a las personas afectadas por el desplazamiento, pero también minimizar los riesgos de protección a las que están expuestas. En Venezuela, la limitación de servicios como el suministro de agua o la contaminación de esta, la ausencia de sistemas que aseguren el tratamiento de aguas negras de manera segura, la presencia de residuos en el entorno y la proliferación de vectores en las comunidades priorizadas crean un entorno insalubre con altas probabilidades de enfermedades. El bajo conocimiento en prácticas higiénicas y las instituciones de salud debilitadas por la falta de suministros energéticos, instalaciones en mal estado, falta de insumos o personal, aumentan el riesgo médico, especialmente de NNA. Niñas y mujeres se exponen a enfermedades derivadas de una gestión de la higiene menstrual en malas condiciones. Por el rol de cuidadoras que terminan por ejercer, las mujeres limitan sus actividades productivas. Las economías de las familias disminuyen al invertir en medicamentos, servicios médicos o desplazamientos a los centros de salud. Este hecho, aumenta otros riesgos de protección de distinta índole. Escuelas en malas condiciones aumentan la probabilidad de abandono, generando riesgos adicionales para los niños. Finalmente, la falta de puntos de agua a nivel domiciliar y la inexistencia de baños operativos que obligan a salir de casa, exponen a NNA y mujeres a riesgos de violencia sexual. 
Dadas las necesidades y riesgos de protección identificados, se propone una intervención integral WASH con un enfoque H2R que incluya el nivel comunitario, de hogar e institucional. A nivel institucional se incluirán escuelas y ambulatorios de las zonas priorizadas. Los objetivos de las intervenciones consistirán en:
1.	Provisión de servicios: instalación, mantenimiento o rehabilitación de infraestructura ASH a nivel institucional. 
a.	Se mejorarán sistemas de almacenamiento, manejo, tratamiento, provisión y protección del AGUA
b.	Se incrementará el acceso a SANEAMIENTO seguro, enfocándose en reducir la contaminación de fuentes de agua y del entorno por aguas negras, residuos y vectores. Mejoramiento de sistemas de pretratamiento de aguas negras y de gestión de residuos sólidos.
c.	Se intervendrán los baños, incluyendo diseños adaptados según edad, género y necesidades especiales.
2.	Provisión de insumos: Para asegurar la puesta en marcha o continuidad de políticas de Prevención y Control de Infecciones (PCI) en los centros de salud incluso escuelas, se entregarán kits institucionales (tratamiento y monitoreo de agua, limpieza y desinfección, gestión de residuos, control vectorial y EPP). A nivel hogar se entregarán kits TANDAS, de higiene e higiene menstrual.
3.	Mejorar las prácticas de HIGIENE. Las intervenciones se orientarán no sólo a aumentar el conocimiento sino a cambiar de comportamiento en prácticas higiénicas y tratamiento de agua como línea de acción clave para reducir enfermedades. Se incluirá el trabajo con familias, comunidades y personal de escuelas y centros de salud, garantizando en estos la aplicación de unas correctas políticas de Prevención y Control de Infecciones (PCI).

project_name: Emergency Agriculture-based Livelihood assistance to vulnerable and conflict affected households in North East Nigeria
project_objective:
Nigeria is among the top 10 largest food crises in the World and the largest food crisis in West Africa, south of the Sahara, despite its remarkable potential for food production. According to the preliminary result of October 2023 Cadre Harmonise (CH), approximately 4.4 million people in BAY states are projected to experience high acute food insecurity (CH Phase 3 or worse) during the peak of the lean season (June to August 2024), a period that coincides with the rainy season. The situation could have been worse due to the lack of dedicated funding for livelihood interventions. The main drivers of the prevailing food insecurity in Nigeria are largely conflict and insecurity, i.e., the protracted armed insurgency in the northeast led by Boko Haram, banditry, kidnappings, and natural resource-based conflicts in the northwest and north-central. The situation has been exacerbated by the continued increase in food prices as a consequence of the ongoing Russia-Ukraine conflict and new government economic measures, including the removal of fuel subsidies and the continued devaluation of the country's currency (Naira). This has worsened rural households' capacity to access food and agricultural inputs. The most affected are vulnerable groups such as internally displaced persons (IDPs), returnees, and host communities, and within those groups, more especially, children, women, and persons with disabilities. Without sustained and scaled-up food availability, facilitation of food access, and livelihood support, it is estimated that a significant proportion of the population in BAY states will continue to endure food insecurity and economic hardship. In addition, negative impacts of climate change and variabilities such as floods and frequent dry spells, pests, and diseases potentially cause severe crop losses. 
This year, the northeast states of Borno, Adamawa and Yobe (BAY) have experienced a prolonged dry spell (June- July 2023), affecting food production and food insecurity.  Climate variability negatively impacts people living in conflict areas, further compounding the vulnerability of the food production system, which results in poor crop yields and livestock productivity loss with a direct negative impact on households’ livelihood, income, and food security and nutrition. 

The greatest burden of food insecurity is in the northeast, in BAY states which are being affected by protracted conflict. The armed insurgency in the northeast BAY states has been ongoing for over a decade and is responsible for severe hardship in most communities. Insecurity led to massive displacement across the BAY states with over 2.2 million people IDPs, of whom 82 percent in Borno, 10 percent in Adamawa, and 7 percent in Yobe (IOM DTM Nigeria Displacement Report 43, February 2023) . A significant number of IDPs (58 percent) are hosted in communities, while approximately 42 percent live in camps or camp-like settlements. 

Also, the continued risk of child mortality due to acute malnutrition is alarming, as the number of children suffering from acute malnutrition has increased from 1.74 million in 2022 to over 2 million in 2023. According to the latest IPC Acute Malnutrition Report for May 2023-April 2024, over 1.53 million children under the age of 5 years are acutely malnourished (GAM), with over half a million severely malnourished (SAM). In addition, more than 200,000 pregnant and lactating mothers across BAY are acutely malnourished . 
The attacks on civilians have gradually decreased, and in line with the Government’s policy of closing IDP camps and facilitating resettlement in their place of origin, approximately 2 million people have returned to communities of origin, according to IOM.

project_name: Building the resilience of crisis-affected Syrian women, men, boys, and girls through adequate WASH
project_objective:
Needs: In 2024, there are 16.7 million people in Syria requiring humanitarian aid, up from 15.3 million in 2023. Of these, 5.5 million are displaced, with over 2 million living in precarious conditions. The situation worsened due to earthquakes in February 2023, which uprooted hundreds of thousands, caused nearly 5,900 deaths, and over 12,800 injuries. The earthquakes further damaged already weakened infrastructure and left many families without their main breadwinner, exacerbating an already dire economic crisis and increasing the vulnerability of millions.
Interventions: Oxfam, drawing on its experience in Syria since 2013, continues to collaborate with local authorities and communities to address water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) needs in vulnerable populations across several districts and subdistricts, including Aleppo, Hama, Idlib, Latakia, Rural Damascus, Dar’a, and Deir Ezzor. This involves assessing needs, prioritizing based on severity, and adapting to emerging needs. Through integrated assessments conducted from January 2022 onwards, covering approximately 50 communities, Oxfam consulted with local and international NGOs, utilized secondary data, and considered the Humanitarian Needs Overview. The targeted areas face significant WASH challenges, categorized under severity scales 3, 4, and 5. In 2024, the project will emphasize life-saving WASH interventions, bolstering existing systems, such as water supply and sewage networks, wastewater treatment, and solid waste management. Additionally, it will integrate public health and hygiene promotion activities, including providing hygiene NFIs. Gender sensitivity is prioritized throughout the project, with a response strategy guided by community engagement and safe programming approaches, tailored to access and security concerns.
Protection Risk Analysis
Risk: Due to access restrictions& limited funds, Oxfam cannot always adopt a blanket distribution, and at the same time is unable to directly identify beneficiaries eligible to NFI in alignment with its vulnerability/selection criteria, which generates a risk of selection bias, inclusion/exclusion errors and community perceptions of unfair eligibility criteria or discriminatory practices. Likelihood: Medium. Impact: High MM: community-based targeting and selection; Risk-informed selection criteria; multi-layer verification of the list of selected beneficiaries; Programme data is disaggregated per gender, disability, and status i.e., displaced, returnee, host, so red flags are identified if any. Oxfam, in 2024, will also review its conflict-sensitive framework to ensure building on the connectors and not exacerbating dividers throughout the project cycle. Risk: limited options of sites for distributions & bureaucratic/admin impediments that further condense the timeframe for implementation, could lead to compromising on essential safe& inclusive requirements e.g., access ramps for PWD or elderly, proximate distance from ben. residences, limited number of beneficiaries approaching the site per day (crowded setting can increase the risk of GBV and tensions). Likelihood: Medium. Impact: High MM: operational CFM, planning more in advance with considering external barriers, consider CVA modalities to improve dignified outcomes. project_name: Integrated Approach to Treatment and Prevention of Acute Malnutrition for Affected Communities, Especially Girls and Boys Under Five and Pregnant and Lactating Women, in Duk and Fangak (Jonglei State), Gogrial West (Warrap State), Aweil East and Aweil Centre (NBeG state) counties and Kessengor in Greater Pibor Administrative Area.
project_objective:
Action Against Hunger strategy is designed to address the main causes of malnutrition through an integrated approach linking nutrition with health, FSL and WASH interventions to foster a meaningful impact upon communities' resilience and prevent childhood morbidity and mortality. Under this project, the proposed activities include prevention, treatment of severe and moderate acute malnutrition in children U5 and PLW using the national guidelines; provision of basic health services at our Stabilization Centers (SC) and community-based healthcare using ICCM approach through the outreach clinics; provision of minimum WASH services to beneficiaries at nutrition sites and at community level. Additionally, Action Against Hunger will provide nutrition preventive services through early screening at the community level using the Family MUAC approach and referrals, increasing access to MIYCN services, deworming and Vitamin A supplementation as well as improving the access to integrated nutrition, health, WASH and FSL services. Innovative activities for malnutrition prevention will be implemented in the project areas in collaboration with UNICEF and WFP. The project will be implemented in line with the transition strategy by the Ministry of Health and the nutrition cluster. Action Against Hunger will work closely with the Ministry of Health and other stakeholders at all levels to ensure effective coordination and service delivery.
Disaster Risk Reduction is a key element of the proposed project given the locations and both natural and man-made disasters experienced frequently in these areas. South Sudan continues to face extremely high prevalence of Gender-Based Violence (GBV) and we will use the findings from the GBV RM research to plan our interventions. Action Against Hunger proposes to a) continue its efforts to mainstream GBV and gender considerations in its Nutrition, WASH and health programs, and b) support the humanitarian community in South Sudan to remain accountable for GBV and gender-sensitivity. Action Against Hunger will strengthen nutrition surveillance mechanisms through accurate and timely reporting, conducting SMART surveys and monitoring and analysis of data for early and objective decision-making.
We will hold regular community meetings at project site including local leaders during planning and implementation of the project activities; to discuss about the types of services available; feedback mechanism in place and how they can approach our teams on ground to provide their feedback on the services on regular basis. All the modalities of the feedback mechanism implemented will be introduced to the community members to enable them to choose the modality. All feedback from beneficiaries will be analyzed and used to improve the relevant intervention/project. Safety Audits will serve as an additional Feedback and Complaints Mechanism (FCM) modality in our nutrition program and will be conducted using the tool provided by the nutrition cluster. As part of the MEAL system surrounding Men Group Discussions, participants will be specially asked to share their concerns with the program and suggest improvements.
To mitigate risk of SEA and GBV committed by and/or against staff and our beneficiaries, Action Against Hunger staff are bound to our Policy on Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA), which prohibits sexual exploitation and abuse by employees and its representatives and affirms its zero-tolerance approach to such cases.

project_name: Targeted Food Assistant in all over Syria in 2024
project_objective:
As highlighted in the FSA 2024 HNO, the food security crisis in Syria remains characterized by very complex drivers and contributing factors, the food security situation of Syrian families continues deteriorating. According to recent HNO figures, around 15.5 million people, which accounts for 65% of the population, require food or livelihood support. This is an increase compared to last year's figure of 15.3 million people. The number includes around 2.1 million people living in camps and 2.6 million at risk of insecurity. WFP’s TFA covers critical food needs of Syrian families across 14 governorates. Subject to availability of funds, WFP’s TFA will ensure that food needs are being met through a food basket planned to have a minimum basic caloric value .In total, WFP ICSP aims to target 4.5 million food-insecure people each month in 2024.   
Needs: After 12 years of hostilities and persistent economic crisis, people in Syria saw their situation worsen when a series of earthquakes hit northern Syria and Türkiye on 6 and 20 February 2023. The earthquakes uprooted hundreds of thousands of families, resulted in almost 5,900 deaths and more than 12,800 people injured in Syria, and severely damaged infrastructures already weakened by the conflict. Many families lost their main breadwinner due to death or injury, at a time when the economic situation was already dire, increasing the vulnerability of millions of people previously unable to meet their basic needs. 
Implementation of activities: WFP will cover critical food needs of Syrian families across 14 governorates (almost all districts and sub-districts) based on 2024 Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) data based on the FSA/FSLA (Food Security Assessments) results and latest SMART results to select the sub-district/s with highest prevalence of food and nutrition insecurity. Additional layer of analysis was implemented reflecting on the conflict sensitivity, urban vs rural context, access, and food security sector coverage. Subject to availability of funding, WFP will ensure that basic food needs are met through a minimum planned food basket.
WFP aims to target 4.5 million food-insecure people each month in 2024, including those assessed as severely food-insecure. WFPs aims to target these people through four interventions:
1)Intervention 1: Emergency Response would be implemented where an onset emergency happens. It would be timebound for a maximum 6-month period. 
2)Intervention 2: selected Closed camps will be targeted for a duration of 12 months with food baskets of 2,100 kcals per person per day.
3)Intervention 3: implemented through nutrition entry point: to narrow down to targeting specific sub-districts, WFP applied additional criteria to prioritize areas of high prevalence of Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) rates (5% and above) that is used to identify the nutrition status of family members of PBWGs and children as main criteria.
4)Intervention 4: WFP will implement a guided community-based targeting approach engaging communities and partners through consultations and focus group discussions and KIIs that will take place between December 2023 and January 2024. The discussions will be facilitated by WFP partners and WFP with the communities and stakeholders to come up together with a ranked list of verifiable and clear criteria suitable for the relevant context. Analysis will be conducted afterwards by WFP FOs and CPs to estimate number of households that meet the criteria versus the available resources (allocations at sub-district level) and a combination of criteria may be adopted as a result. 
WFP aims to provide this assistance through either in-kind food basket or cash-based transfer modality. Transfer modality will be based on beneficiary preferences (based on monitoring tools and feedback mechanisms), cost effectiveness and efficiency, and feasibility analysis including local macroeconomic conditions and market functionality.
