project_name: Preventing and responding to protection concerns of affected boys, girls and their families in Cox's Bazar
project_objective:
"Save the Children (SC) is committed to strengthening protective factors and reducing risk factors in Cox's Bazar through its Integrated and Holistic Child Protection program. This program will operate at every level of the socio-ecological framework, aiming to reach 277,532 people of concerns including 1,87,159 children in 12 camps and 04 unions in Ukhiya and Teknaf Upazila. SC's Child Protection Program will encompass both preventive and responsive measures to ensure a protective environment for children. It will focus on critical interventions and services tailored to the needs of children of varying ages, genders, and diverse groups. Special attention will be given to Unaccompanied and Separated Children (UASC), child-headed households, child marriage and pregnancy, children with disabilities, domestic violence, and child labor.
The program will promote the overall well-being of children and establish a protective environment through a range of services, including case management for at-risk children, structured and semi-structured psychosocial support (PSS), life skill-based sessions, adolescent-led initiatives, parenting training, community-based activities, and System Strengthening. SC operates 98 Child Protection Multipurpose facilities in the camps to provide these services, strengthening community mechanisms as a core project intervention to build resilient communities.
To ensure inclusivity, SC will conduct surveys using Washington Set questionnaires to identify people, especially children with disabilities, for inclusion as project participants. Multi-Purpose Child and Adolescent Centers (MPCAC) will accommodate children of different ages in various time slots and shifts, and materials will be procured and distributed with age-sensitive specifications and sizes. MPCAC also will be act as a child protection hub where will be organize capacity-building training, awareness-raising sessions, workshops, and meeting on child protection.
Capacity-building activities will be scaled up for various stakeholders, including government authorities (CIC, police, LEA agencies), service providers, community-based groups, and community volunteers, including Para social workers (PSWs), parents, and caregivers as part of System Strengthening. SC will also take the initiative to make the Child-Friendly Police Desk operational by providing technical and logistic support.
To address the Early Childhood Development (ECD) needs of children, a dedicated ECD corner will be established in existing MPCACs. Trained facilitators will conduct home-based ECD sessions, and caregivers will receive training and awareness focusing on ECD. SC will maintain regular coordination with Child Protection Sub-Sector (CPSS) and operate the program in alignment with the sector's strategy. Coordination with CPSS, PWG, and relevant working groups will continue, and SC will contribute to various initiatives, including dedicating staff for CP focal points and submitting different reports, including 5W reports.
Periodical training and awareness sessions on policies, including child safeguarding and the Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA), will be conducted for staff, volunteers, and related stakeholders. SC will prioritize these policies to ensure protection against sexual harassment, exploitation, and abuse throughout the project cycle. By targeting equality in access to services, SC will strengthen social cohesion.
Multiple accountability mechanisms in line with the Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) principles will be applied to actively collect feedback while ensuring the safety and dignity of program participants. By fostering partnerships through localization, SC can enhance its technical capabilities and address areas of improvement proactively."

project_name: Supported integrated basic life-saving services to vulnerable populations in Darfur, Sudan
project_objective:
The Darfur states remain one of the areas worst-affected  by the ongoing conflict which erupted in April 2023 between the Sudan Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which is heavily impacting civilians and has triggered in Sudan the world's largest displacement crisis. The project's overall objective is to provide emergency health, nutrition, and pss services to crisis-affected populations in Central and West Darfur, IDPs, and host communities, by ensuring i) basic lifesaving integrated health services are supported and provided to IDPs and host communities; ii) significant access to essential integrated prevention and management of acute malnutrition for the targeted population at HF and community level and iii) communities are involved in the improvement of their health, nutrition and psychosocial status, selecting and training community volunteers, providing health, nutrition and pss awareness to targeted communities and providing protection training and service mapping.
PUI will continue to support the already supported Mother and Child Centre (MCC) in Geneina as the main primary care service for mothers, conducting maternity care, such as ante-natal care (ANC), post-natal care (PNC) and Family Planning. Given the context evolutions in the whole Darfur states, with increasing health, nutrition and MHPSS needs while access is improved, PUI will also start supporting one additional HF in Zalingei, Central Darfur. Zalingei’s PHC will provide free primary healthcare, including Sexual and Reproductive Health (SRH) services, to its catchment population area, while Geneina MCC will more specifically target women of reproductive age, PLWs and children under 5, providing SRH minimum essential package and integrated management of childhood illness (IMCI).
PUI will ensure the provision of  essential pharmaceutical commodities following standard quality process for purchase, storage, distribution and management, and non-medical equipment and supplies to health facilities, their financial support and necessary rehabilitation. PUI will continue to coordinate with UNFPA and WHO for the provision of SRH and IEH kits. PUI will provide support on outbreak preparedness and routine immunization program, ensure the training and capacity building of health staff, support access to quality healthcare services, including (SRH), and referral systems, provide PSS services. As per MISP recommendation, Clean Delivery Kits will be distributed to PLWs in communities where access to HF and skilled birth attendants is not ensured to reduce risk of maternal and neonatal mortality. As per SOPs and safe and dignified programming principles, menstrual hygiene kits will be provided to displaced teenagers (14 – 25) and women under 25 coming to the HFs seeking care. 
2 OTPs will be set inside the supported HFs to provide treatment to children under 5 suffering from SAM without complications, and will be accessible by both IDPs and host communities. PUI will liaise with UNICEF and WFP for nutrition commodities provision. SAM with complications cases will be referred to Geneina’s Stabilization Centre (SC), set in Geneina Hospital and supported by MSF, and to Zalingei SC, set in Zalingei’s hospital, which World relief is planning to support. PUI will support SAM with complications referral to higher level of care with cash for transportation, as well as health and SRH referrals. Two Mother Support Groups of 10 mothers each will be established. Under the supervision of PUI health and nutrition officer, they will be provided with sensitization on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) best practices, including exclusive breastfeeding, and cooking demonstrations on how to prepare nutritious food from locally available ingredients.
PUI will provide Psychosocial Support Services, at HF and community levels.

project_name: Distribution d'Enov' Nutributter et d'Enov' Mum pour améliorer la qualité des soins de santé maternelle et infantile dans le district sanitaire de Liwa, Tchad
project_objective:
Selon l'enquête SMART 2022, la province du Lac est l'une des 15 provinces du Tchad où la situation nutritionnelle est très alarmante. Avec une prévalence de la malnutrition aiguë globale (MAG) de 11%, la province du Lac se situe au-dessus du seuil d'alerte élevé de 10%. En janvier 2023, une enquête nutritionnelle rapide a été menée par un consultant externe dans les sites de déplacés internes d'ALIMA/AS à Liwa. L'objectif de cette enquête était d'évaluer la prévalence de la malnutrition aiguë globale (modérée et sévère) chez les enfants âgés de 6 à 59 mois parmi les personnes déplacées dans le district sanitaire de Liwa dans la province du Lac. Les principaux résultats de cette enquête sont les suivants : 
- La prévalence de la malnutrition aiguë chez les enfants âgés de 6 à 59 mois dans les sites de déplacés de Liwa est élevée selon les normes de l'OMS. Elle se situe en phase 3, ce qui constitue une situation grave selon la classification MNA de l'IPC (10 %-14,9 %). La malnutrition aiguë sévère (MAS) dépasse les 2%, ce qui constitue une urgence humanitaire. La MAG est encore plus élevée, à 23,5 %, et la MASc (MAS avec complications) est de 6,9 %.
- La prévalence du retard de croissance est très élevée selon les seuils de classification de l'OMS fixés à 30%. Une attention particulière doit être portée sur cet indicateur nutritionnel également.
- La prévalence des enfants en surpoids est faible, cependant, il reste important de maintenir cet indicateur à ce bas niveau.

Dans le district de Liwa, ALIMA/AS travaille actuellement dans 9 sites de déplacés internes par le biais de la clinique mobile, dans 4 postes de santé, dans 7 sites de déplacés internes supplémentaires pour le traitement à base communautaire des maladies infantiles courantes, à l'ITFC du district de Liwa et dans 1 centre de stabilisation, par le biais d'un projet de 12 mois financé par la BHA. Le projet vise à réduire la morbidité et la mortalité parmi les populations déplacées et hôtes dans le district de Liwa, dans la province des lacs du Tchad, en fournissant un ensemble complet de services préventifs, curatifs, de promotion de la santé et de la nutrition, ainsi que de protection. L'action proposée est complémentaire à ces activités et renforcera la composante prévention du programme nutritionnel mis en œuvre par ALIMA sous le financement de la BHA. L'action proposée fournira :
- Une supplémentation préventive systématique en Enov' Nutributter pour les enfants âgés de 6 à 24 mois dans les 20 établissements de santé soutenus par ALIMA/AS. ALIMA/AS sera en mesure d'offrir un ensemble complet de soins de santé pédiatriques combinant des soins préventifs et curatifs. La distribution aura lieu sur une base mensuelle dans les établissements de santé soutenus. Elle sera complétée par des initiatives SAM supplémentaires menées dans le cadre du projet pluriannuel financé par la BHA, notamment la détection précoce de la malnutrition par la formation des mères à l'utilisation du MUAC (programme MUAC for Mothers) et des activités de sensibilisation au sein des communautés locales (telles que des démonstrations culinaires).  
- Supplémentation préventive systématique d'Enov' Mum aux femmes enceintes et allaitantes (PLW) après chaque consultation prénatale tout au long de la grossesse, en plus des nouvelles mères et des femmes allaitantes jusqu'à 3 mois après l'accouchement. La distribution aura lieu dans les établissements de santé soutenus et devrait contribuer à augmenter la fréquence des consultations prénatales et postnatales des bénéficiaires cibles.

project_name: Cost-efficient, safe, dignified and flood-resilient WASH services to IDPs, host communities, and returnees in South Sudan
project_objective:
The project aims to provide cost-efficient, safe, dignified and flood-resilient access to water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services to IDPs, host communities, and returnees living in extreme and catastrophic conditions in South Sudan.

For that, IOM’s interventions will focus on locations identified by the WASH Cluster as key priorities:  intersectoral priority 1 counties (Rubkona), priority 2 counties (Malakal) and priority 4 counties (Wau, Abyei Region). Through its Static and Rapid Response Teams, IOM will extend its support to acute and protracted needs to Unity State and Upper Nile. IOM will remain the main water service provider in Wau’s Naivasha IDP Camp during 2024. 

IOM’s HRP project contributes to the 5 WASH Cluster Strategic Objectives, focusing on integrating WASH programming with Nutrition, providing access to basic WASH services in PoC/Camps, whilst mitigating WASH GBV and reducing community’s exposure to environmental hazards. In total, IOM plans to reach 300,000 individuals (67,158 women, 64,305 men, 81,094 girls, 87,443 boys) by deploying a range of activity packages that combine hardware and software interventions, adapted to the context at play and to the needs of the most affected population. To support nutrition gains, IOM will rehabilitate/install WASH infrastructure within nutrition sites and/or at community level, while in locations where WASH services need to be rapidly restored due to sudden emergencies, IOM will rehabilitate/drill new boreholes, rehabilitate/set up/operate surface water treatment systems (SWATs) and affordable filters at household level. IOM will also ensure the sustainability of WASH infrastructure through the formation and training of community-based operation and maintenance groups. These hardware interventions will be complemented with hygiene promotion, as well as distribution and demonstration on usage of WASH NFIs and/or Menstrual Hygiene Management (MHM) to help communities sustain the learnt practices. All activities will contribute towards mitigating GBV risks and to improve accessibility to people with special needs, as demonstrated by IOM’s commitment to allocate 2.9 % of the project budget to GBV risk mitigation mainstreaming Where needed, activities will be adjusted to be climate resilient and/or to build the capacity of communities to respond quicker to natural disasters. Where possible, IOM will also prioritise market-based programming approaches, using local markets to support WASH responses. As the largest direct WASH service provider in camp settings, IOM will also continue servicing conflict-affected populations in Malakal Protection of Civilians (PoCs), Bentiu and Wau’s Naivasha Internal Displacement Camp (IDP), and Bentiu’s IDP sites (A, B and C). IOM will provide WASH services through the operation and maintenance of safe and accessible water supply systems, care and maintenance of accessible and secure sanitation and handwashing facilities, as well as management of solid and liquid waste. IOM will also continue investing in cost-effective and climate-resilient means of ensuring adequate service provision within these settings by setting up, maintaining, and scaling up water supply solar systems. IOM will support the transition process at these sites working to transfer WASH service provision towards community-based ownership where possible, through a participatory approach, with a focus on women’s empowerment. Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA), Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP), and COVID-19 prevention measures will also be mainstreamed throughout the project cycle.

project_objective:
Due to the protracted and complex humanitarian crises facing communities in the NW SW regions and the protection needs and gaps identified by IRC and partners, IRC is proposing a 12-month holistic project to respond to humanitarian needs in 3 protection domains : child protection, women’s protection and general protection (rule of law).

Focusing on hard-to-reach areas within both the NW and SW, IRC will support survivors of human rights violations (adults, women and children ) and survivors of gender-based violence (GBV) through protection monitoring and advocacy activities, tailored case management services for adults, women and children including survivors of GBV, IGA for GBV survivors to support to promote resilience, specialised and non-specialised PSS services, capacity-building and awareness-raising targeting different audiences (community and government actors) on protection issues to improve the protection environment and also to enhance sustainability of the intervention.

IRC expects a deterioration in the security and access environment during the run-up to the 2025 presidential election – something we’ve already started to see in the hardening of positions from both NSAGs and the military and civil authorities in the NWSW in the last six months1. This will require flexibility and adaptations to service delivery to meet new needs as the crisis evolves.

Building on the experience gained through IRC’s implementation and community acceptance in the NW and SW regions IRC/Cameroun has the tools and the experience to work with affected communities and partners on reviewing and adapting activities to to the changing contexts.

project_name: Empowering Education: Ensuring Safe and Inclusive Access for Conflict-Affected Children and Adolescents in Northwest Syria
project_objective:
In 2024, 16.7 million people (8.4 million female, 8.3 million male) are assessed to need humanitarian assistance across Syria, up from 15.3 million in 2023. After 12 years of hostilities and persistent economic crisis, people in Syria saw their situation worsen when a series of earthquakes hit northern Syria and Türkiye on 6 and 20 February 2023. The earthquakes uprooted hundreds of thousands of families, resulted in almost 5,900 deaths and more than 12,800 people injured in Syria, and severely damaged infrastructures already weakened by the conflict. Many families lost their main breadwinner due to death or injury, at a time when the economic situation was already dire, increasing the vulnerability of millions of people previously unable to meet their basic needs. (HNO, Summary, 2024). Within the education sector, numbers indicate an increase in the number of PiN in 2024 to 917,778 in Idleb, and 1,312,862 in Aleppo who are in dire need for education services.
In alignment with the education cluster’s strategic objectives for 2024-5, Shafak aims to expand access to high-quality formal and non-formal education for a total of 115,594 individuals, comprising 113,823 (3-17 yrs. old) children (52,997boys; 60,826 girls, including 8,091 children with disabilities) and 1,771 education personnel (909 males, 862 females).
a) Formal education initiatives in 32 schools will target approximately 23,040 students (b/g and age disaggregated), basic education and high schooling, with monthly incentives provided to teachers and education personnel, alongside educational materials for students and teachers, and operational costs coverage such, as water trucking printing costs…etc. Renovation of damaged schools and creating safe temporary learning spaces, ensuring gender and disability sensitivity, will be prioritized. Transportation services will be provided for children with disabilities through cash modality, while professional development sessions on child-centered pedagogy and classroom management will be conducted monthly, addressing overcrowding and inclusivity. ECCE (Early Childhood Care and Education) intervention includes provision of ECD kits, daily school feeding programs, play activities, and psychosocial support for children aged 3-6.
b) Non-formal education efforts, facilitated through BTL campaigns, will reintegrate children aged 8-12 into inclusive education. Support will be extended to 48 Non-Formal Education centers, benefiting approximately 34,560 children (b/g and age disaggregated), offering modalities aligned with the NFE matrix and supplemented with psychosocial support sessions, to support transition to formal education.
c) Winterization support by supplying heating fuel to 208 schools for 113,823 students (b/g and age disaggregated) in severely affected sub-districts, alongside heaters, fuel tanks, and winter clothing for students. The project design will incorporate stakeholder input, including children, adolescents, older individuals, and persons with disabilities, ensuring tailored access to humanitarian services and information.

project_name: Projet d'assistance d'urgence multisectorielle au profit des populations (Hôtes, déplacées, retournées) agricoles et pastorales affectées par les chocs climatiques, sécuritaires et sanitaires dans la région de Diffa et dans la région de Tahoua dans le département de Abalak.
project_objective:
L’action présente s'inscrit dans une logique de continuité (MR) et a pour objectif de contribuer à la réduction des impacts négatifs des chocs sécuritaires, climatiques et sanitaires sur les conditions de vie des populations vulnérables hôtes et déplacées au Niger dans la région de Diffa (Diffa, Maine-Soroa,  N’guigmi et Bosso)  à travers une approche multisectorielle adaptée aux pics de vulnérabilités. Afin de réduire d'une manière drastique et holistique ces impacts, Action contre la faim (ci-après ACF) propose un projet qui vise l'amélioration de l'accessibilité aux services de santé par la mise en oeuvre d'un mécanisme de réponse rapide (ci-après RRM santé) du paquet santé et nutrition et l'appui aux structures de santé fragilisées par les conflits, le renforcement de la sécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle notamment en période de soudure pour les populations vulnérables y compris les populations pastorales, l'amélioration de l'accès à l'eau potable et des conditions d'assainissement et des bonnes
pratiques d'hygiène et de changement de comportement au niveau communautaire en prévention des épidémies dans ces zones sensibles.
ACF agira en synergie avec les acteurs humanitaires dans les deux zones en complémentarité à la mise en oeuvre du mécanisme de RRM santé. Ce projet sera renforcé en garantissant l’environnement protecteur des communautés à travers une réponse à leurs besoins et une coordination efficace pour un accès libre et durable aux services sociaux de base dans le respect des principes humanitaires. Action Contre la Faim propose donc une approche fondée sur un mécanisme de réponse rapide (RRM) pour assurer l'accès aux services de santé et de nutrition auprès des populations affectées par la crise du bassin du Lac Tchad dans la région de Diffa au Niger. Cette réponse viendra compléter et intégrer les interventions actuelles des autres mécanismes de RRM en cours par d’autres acteurs RRM dans la région. Le mécanisme proposé sera basé sur un système de surveillance et d'alerte construit sur des réseaux communautaires et les informations régulières recueillies directement auprès des centres de santé. Les structures sanitaires ciblées seront appuyées pour intégrer une surveillance de qualité des maladies à potentiel épidémique. Cet aspect sera assuré par l’amélioration des bases de données et métadonnées et de la promptitude de remontée des données épidémiques au Ministère de la Santé Publique, de la population et affaires sociales. Selon la nature de l'alerte, une évaluation rapide sera réalisée pour identifier la nature des obstacles à l'accès local aux services de santé et une réponse appropriée. Les évaluations rapides se feront selon les modalités d’évaluation mises en œuvre dans le RRM Santé et seront couplées dans la mesure du possible à celle d’autres secteurs dans les Zones affectées. Lors de l’évaluation, Action Contre la Faim fournira déjà dans la mesure du possible une première réponse en santé et nutrition avant la réponse multisectorielle conduite après l’analyse des besoins. 
Le paquet minimum d’activités Santé nutrition du RRM Santé reposera sur deux principales modalités de réponse (flexibles) : 
- L’implantation des Cliniques mobiles : des équipes mobiles capables de fournir le soutien nécessaire aux structures de santé affectées et / ou si nécessaire directement aux communautés par le biais de services mobiles équipes. La stratégie mobile sera composée de soins curatifs gratuits pour toute la population (soins de santé primaires, santé de la reproduction, prise en charge de la MAS), des soins préventifs (vaccination, CPN). L’appui psychosocial à base communautaire et une détection précoce des cas de protection des enfants et des femmes (composante GBV) suivi d’un référencement vers les autres acteurs pour une prise en charge plus globale. ACF accordera aussi , une attention particulière aux groupes spécifiques vulnérables et à besoin spécifiques pour les personnes âgées , les handicapées et tous

project_name: Strengthening Child Protection interventions for girls and boys most at risk of violence, abuse, neglect and exploitation across whole of Syria
project_objective:
In light of the devastating and long-term effects of earthquakes, ongoing armed conflict, limited livelihood opportunities, as well as new and old layers of explosive contamination in Syria, the ongoing hostilities, protracted displacement, and economic crisis highlighted
in the HNO 2024 have further weakened the protective environment and resilience of communities. This situation exposes children to greater risks of violence, abuse, exploitation, and neglect. Explosive hazard contamination not only poses severe socioeconomic implications for families and communities by depriving them of livelihoods and sources of income but also increases vulnerabilities. Insecurity and economic hardship persist, exacerbating child protection concerns and leading to harmful coping mechanisms such as the worst forms of labor and child marriage. Additionally, high levels of psychosocial distress prevail among children and caregivers due to multiple stresses, including the continued escalation of conflict, poverty, earthquakes, and restrictions on movement that limit access to social services.

In line with the CP AOR Strategy, UNICEF will enhance equitable access to quality CP services with a resilience focus, for prevention and response to CP risks, including for survivors of abuse, violence, neglect and exploitation, CWD, unaccompanied and separated children, targeting high severity sub-districts.

UNICEF will focus the intervention under this proposal on the following activities:
• The provision of structured MHPSS activities for 234,500 girls and boys through child-friendly spaces, mobile teams, and community structures.
• Engagement of 50,000 parents and caregivers in structured and sustained parenting programmes to facilitate the creation of a safe and enabling environment in families and communities free from violence against children.
• Implement EORE sessions for 653,600 children and parents/caregivers in communities including through using mobile teams.
• Provide integrated specialized child protection services, through case management, to 16,920 children, including family tracing and reunification for separated and unaccompanied children, children in contact with the law, violence against children, child marriage, child labour, and children with disabilities.
• Build technical capacity of 3,000 implementing partners' social workers on child protection/GBV services delivery and ensure regular monitoring of activities. In coordination with the GBV AoR UNICEF will build capacities on GBV risk mitigation.
• Elimination of VAC, including GBV prevention and empowerment for 120,550 girls, boys, and women, and prevention of violence in schools, homes, and communities through awareness-raising sessions.
• Awareness-raising on CP risks and SBC interventions on child protection issues for 200,000 girls, boys, women and men.

UNICEF will generate evidence to inform the humanitarian response and advocacy, including setting up an information management system for case management. UNICEF will also continue to support the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism on grave violations against children.

Violence prevention is a key priority. UNICEF will work to protect children from violence and abuse through prevention activities in schools, homes, and communities and by providing survivors of violence with child-friendly and gender-sensitive services. Support will be provided for PSEA mechanisms to protect beneficiaries and build the capacity of humanitarian actors.

PSEA by humanitarian workers and service providers is high on the UNICEF agenda to ensure that no violations and abuse happen during implementation. UNICEF, as co-lead for the ICN on PSEA, will continue to support and work closely with other agencies to enhance the PSEA portfolio by building continuous capacity for humanitarian workers with zero tolerance for SEA. As a pre-condition for contracting implementing partners, PSEA assurance and capacity-building plans are guaranteed.

project_name: Education support for Syria’s children and youth affected by crisis
project_objective:
As per HNO 2024, the sector PIN indicates a 4% increase from the previous year for children and teachers in need of education assistance. Access to education remains a challenge for many children, as the numbers of Out of School Children remain high. The main barriers are related to the deteriorating economic situation and the ongoing protracted crisis. Even for children in school, learning spaces continue to be unconducive with overcrowded classrooms, limited number of teachers and limited availability of teaching and learning materials.
UNICEF proposes to provide 3,182,074 children and teachers with education services in areas of severity 3-5. This includes children from preprimary, primary and secondary school-aged girls and boys to enable them to develop foundational numeracy and literacy skills, as well as life and citizenship skills, in order to strengthen child, family and community resilience. Additionally, support to enhance the physical learning spaces as well as provision of psychosocial support for children and teachers. 
UNICEF will contribute to: 
A. Providing equitable access to education 
B. Supporting quality education in protective environment
C. Strengthening education systems 
Access will be promoted through Back-to-Learning Campaigns, Vouchers-for-Education, provision of non-formal education programs, school textbooks and school supplies, support to national exams to enhance access to accredited education as part of a multi-sector approach, rehabilitation of schools (formal and nonformal) and provision of temporary classrooms. Rehabilitation is also needed in lower severity areas, where displaced children and returnees as well as large numbers of host community children reside, to contribute to resilience and social cohesion. 
For school rehabilitation UNICEF coordinates with relevant authorities to identify schools in need. UNICEF conducts an assessment to confirm needs and works through vetted independent contractors to commence rehabilitation, including the improvement of WASH facilities, enhancing accessibility for children with disabilities. This is complemented by the provision of school furniture and supplies.
UNICEF will support the Self-learning program to ensure that OOSC have an opportunity to learn, this includes provision of materials, establishment of learning spaces, provision of supplies and support to teacher training. To improve the quality of education services, UNICEF will ensure schools are child-friendly, with teachers trained in child-centered pedagogy, and where children develop academic, cognitive, life and psychosocial skills that empower them to engage, relate, cope and contribute to community and family life. Due to the large number of children at different learning levels within grades, children will be provided with remedial learning support. To support system resilience, UNICEF will establish Parent Teacher Associations that cooperate with Headmasters, and train education staff on monitoring schools, staff performance and children’s learning. UNICEF monitors ongoing activities through staff and implementing partner visits, Third Partner Monitoring and through established feedback mechanisms. In NWS, TPMs provide on-site verification and beneficiary interviews.

Risk of sexual exploitation by Teacher education personnel, NGO staff (risk of harassment) of boys and girls 5. Teachers or other education personnel participate in physical punishment or bullying of students Or Students participate in bullying of students
PSEA policy will be respected as per UNICEF rules and mandate.

project_name: Renforcement de la préparation, de l'alerte et de la réponse en cas de chocs multirisques dans les zones fragiles afin d’assurer une réponse locale la plus rapide possible, au Niger
project_objective:
"COOPI a planifié, en consortium avec Mercy Corps, une nouvelle phase d'intervention sur la thématique de la RRC dans 6 communes des régions de Tillaberi et Maradai, départements de Tillaberi, Ayouru, Ouallam, Madarounfa, Gabi et Guidan-Roumdji. project_name: Improve shelter and living conditions in the affected areas in NWS
project_objective:
In the midst of dire humanitarian conditions in northwestern Syria, the lack of adequate shelter remains a significant issue due to insufficient support and ongoing conflicts, exacerbated by the earthquake in 2023. The region continues to be ravaged by these crises, leaving many vulnerable individuals and families without proper shelter or protection. In 2023, the inadequacy of shelter has increased by 12% in Idleb and 32% in Aleppo governorates, according to MSNA data.
Primary data collected by CARE in November 2023 in 26 sub-districts in Aleppo and Idleb governorates revealed that 24% of people in communities are in need of high/moderate rehabilitation and 73% are in need of light rehabilitation. In IDP sites, 46% of IDP households reported that their shelter required major rehabilitation, while 44% reported a need for light rehabilitation.48% of the access roads were reported as in need of improvement. 11% of respondents indicated that the access roads were so poor that trucks and lifesaving activities were unable to reach the sites. 60% of the drainage systems were rated as bad or very bad, and 57% reported experiencing flood conditions at their site in the past year. Regarding NFIs, the top items identified as urgently required by IDPs are fuel for heating and cooking (96%), winter clothing (80%), blankets (68%), stoves (64%), kitchen utensils, shoes, and hygiene items. 42% of respondents at IDP sites said there were no available services for women and girls.

project_name: Food Security for IDPs and Host communities in NWS
project_objective:
Needs: 
Twelve years of unrelenting conflict in Northwest Syria have inflicted a devastating toll on its people, displacing over 2 million residents, with 1.8 million confined to congested and often unsanitary IDP camps. This vulnerable population faces a multitude of hardships, including a rapidly deteriorating humanitarian situation in 2023. The recent earthquake, coupled with worsening food shortages and the most significant escalation of hostilities in four years, has pushed them towards the brink. Food insecurity runs rampant, with many households struggling to access essential and nutritious food due to limited income, disrupted livelihoods, and skyrocketing prices. These dire living conditions, coupled with the recent rabies outbreak, pose serious health risks. Traditional coping mechanisms have been disrupted, leaving families with limited options to meet their basic needs, often resorting to risky strategies to survive. This project aims to address these critical and urgent needs by providing targeted food security assistance and emergency rations, empowering vulnerable households to prioritize their immediate needs and rebuild their lives with dignity and resilience.

Implementation of Activity:
- Objective: Reducing food insecurity and inability to meet basic immediate needs, through monthly food security assistance, emergency ready-to-eat rations
The objective will be achieved through providing food security assistance, and emergency food assistance. The program will achieve its purpose by improving food security, reducing reliance on risky coping mechanisms, and enabling current and newly displaced HHs and vulnerable communities to simultaneously meet their immediate multifaceted food needs with dignity and flexibility. This will further support the overall program goal by addressing lifesaving needs and promoting self-resilience leading toward early recovery.
- Targeted BNFs: The project aims to target 30K HHs with monthly cash for food distribution.
Locations: in Aleppo (Azaz, Al-Bab, Jarablus, Jabel Saman) and Idleb (Idleb, Ariha, Harim, Jisr-Ash-Shugur).
- Modality: E-card, where each beneficiary will get 65 USD per round for 8 rounds
- The selection criteria are:
1- Families with no regular income / limited income
2- Two or more family members unless one elderly living alone (above 60)
3- Families living in the targeted area/community/camp
4- Targeted families are not from the contracted vendors (for vouchers)

project_name: Providing Protection and GBV services to populations at heightened protection risks in Northwest Syria
project_objective:
Needs: In 2023, CARE delivered GBV case management services through integrated approach with SRH, supporting a total of 891 survivors across NWS. The breakdown of CARE's GBV case management caseload shed light on various types of GBV incidents. Specifically, 42% of cases reported physical assault, 19% indicated psychological/emotional abuse,20% reported denial of resources, while sexual assault cases comprised 7% of the total reached, which align with VOICES from Syria 2023 report when findings indicated that women and girls across Syria experienced a range of abuses, including physical violence, psychological and emotional violence. They faced sexual violence, including assault, exploitation, harassment, and rape, as well as technology-facilitated violence and social violence, such as stigma and discrimination. Adolescent girls subjected to early marriage, and denied rights, resources, opportunities, and services specifically education. Furthermore, 64% of perpetrators were identified as intimate partners according to CARE GBV CM tracker, while 24% were identified as family members, which suggests the presence of entrenched patterns of violence within domestic relationships. CARE efforts to address GBV will continue to include tailored support services addressing the specific needs of survivors and interventions aimed at GBV prevention and changing harmful gender norms and promoting healthy, respectful relationships. 
Intervention, Implementation of activities: CARE will continue providing protection and GBV services within 3 static community centers,5 WGSSs, GBV teams included in 5health facilities, 2 helpdesks, and one mobile WGSS and 14 outreach units. CARE utilizes different approaches through static and mobile services to reach to the most vulnerable people including GBV survivors, women and girls at risks, PWDs, and people living in camps including windows camps. CARE will ensure integration between the GBV and SRH services in addition to the MHPSS and legal counselling.  Additionally, services will include individual and group PSS counselling, legal counselling, GBV response services (GBV Case Management/CVA and referrals, PSS for GBV survivors), GBV risk mitigation and prevention services including safety audits, training for Non GBV actors on GBV, structured awareness raising on GBV, , skills development trainings, life skills targeting women and adolescents, engaging men and boys through information sharing and tailored PSS and recreational activities. 

Protection Risk Analysis: CARE is committed to establishing internal referral system between health and GBV teams, accompanied by training and supervision for both teams to ensure that GBV survivors accessing services within health facilities encounter no risks of stigmatization. CARE will engage with local authorities and introduce project services and selection criteria to ensure community acceptance and avoid any backlash from local communities towards the project. Moreover, some of the project GBV activities will engage different groups such as community leaders, men, and adolescent boys to ensure strong allies for girls and women rights. CARE will ensure a solid and comprehensive cash risk assessment before deciding the CVA modality in GBV CM, and increase collaboration with other sectors including cash, shelter, basic needs, and livelihood to avoid additional harm to the GBV survivor from the community and family members upon CVA distribution.

PSEA strategy: CARE is actively working to prevent sexual harassment, exploitation, abuse, and child abuse. Any reports or allegations are handled with the utmost gravity, as CARE adopts a survivor-centered approach that places paramount importance on the needs and dignity of survivors. Ongoing staff training, community-level awareness campaigns on PSEA and safeguarding, as well as maintaining accessible channels for feedback and complaints, are among the measures to be consistently upheld through implementation.

project_name: Improving access to safe and sufficient water supplies, sanitation and hygiene infrastructure and services for 850,000 people in NW Syria
project_objective:
The latest HNO report available, from February 2023, highlighted the dire circumstances in NW Syria. Among the 1.9 million individuals residing across 1,437 IDP sites, two earthquakes led to an additional 108,906 displacements, intensifying the urgent need for WASH and Shelter support. It highlighted   a critical water crisis, exacerbated by drought, damaged, unreliable and inequal access to water infrastructure. 
Recent findings from CARE’s assessment in Nov, 2023, in 31 sub districts in Aleppo and Idleb Governorate, show that 48% of respondents in communities, and 47% in IDP camps reported lack of water to meet their needs. a vast majority (91%) of households in these regions are dependent on secondary water sources. In communities, 30% of respondents reported not having adequate water storage available. While 87% of respondents reporting having a water network in their community. In IDP camps, 57% of IDP households reported that their household  water storage was shared with other families. The main water source for households living in IDP sites is water trucking (85%) which is primarily provided by humanitarian actors.

Through this project, CARE will focus on providing the following services:
Activity1: Water trucking services and distribution of water tanks
Activity2: Rehabilitation and operational support to water systems
Activity3: Repair, rehabilitation and operational support to sanitation system 
Activity4: Installation of latrines and desludging services
Activity5: Wastewater Treatment Plant Rehabilitation 
Activity6: SWM
Activity7: HP sessions and HKs distribution.
CARE is targeting a total of 350,000 beneficiaries through rehabilitation and operation of WASH infrastructure (SO 3) as well as 450,000 beneficiaries through the provision of emergency WASH services (SO1).

Protection Risk Analysis:
-Quality and/or quantity not adequate as per humanitarian standards
-Not enough water distribution points available
-Water distribution not safe to access or not accessible
-Support to wastewater systems

Assumptions/risks and Contingency measures:
1-Conflict and deterioration of security conditions: Undertake a context and security analysis, with regular updates and information-sharing between the project partners; dedicated security personnel and harmonized operational standards to establish safe and secure routines with the teams and counterparts; establish risk mitigation plans for the project; establish a workflow for the reporting of incidents; training staff on security measures; developing protection/self-protection measures/protocols.
2-Negative impact of COVID-19 and cholera: CARE has developed COVID-19 SOPs for all programming areas as well as for its operations. Ensure application of COVID-19 protocols in planning and implementation; monitor health trends alongside duty-bearers and health/WASH agencies, taking pre-emptive measures where necessary to mitigate identified increases in case rates. Mitigation measures are regularly updated according to changes in context and coordination with relevant actors. CARE has developed Risk Communication and Community Engagement Plan on cholera to work with and inform women, girls, men and boys on cholera preparedness and response.
3-Coercion into ways of working that contravene humanitarian principles: centrality of protection embedded in operational SOPs, strong internal communication mechanisms that flag issues for decision-making, clear definition of red lines amongst SMT Supply chain is interrupted and procurement delayed– markets will be actively monitored so that potential alternatives can be identified for procurement. 
4-Extreme weather patterns/natural disaster: regular monitoring of weather events and early warning indicators, use of environmental and social assessments, engage with DRR actors to assist in community action plans.

project_name: Strengthening and provision of sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services for conflict-affected populations in Syria.
project_objective:
An estimated 16.7 million people are in need of humanitarian assistance (HA)  in 2024, an increase of 1.3 million compared to 2023. This includes 8.4 million women and girls, with 4.1 million of reproductive age. Over 500,000 women are expected to become pregnant and give birth in 2024, of which 380,000 are in need of HA including ANC, safe delivery, PNC, and FP services. Among them, 56,000 are likely to face complications and will require EmONC. Additionally, there are 2 million adolescent girls across Syria in need of HA. An estimated 7.2 million people are internally displaced and approximately 90% of the population live below the poverty line. These structural and economic realities reduce women’s access to SRH services, as does the partial or complete damage of 40% of health facilities and severe HRH shortages.  

UNFPA will continue to reduce maternal and newborn morbidity and mortality; support the EPHS; provide FP commodities, and provide medical assistance and care to GBV survivors. This will be achieved by 1) ensuring the availability of and access to integrated quality SRH services and information; 2) building health worker capacity; 3) increase access to services where no SRH services exist; 4) ensuring availability of essential medicines and supplies; 5) delivery of complementary services, including MHPSS and NCDs; and 6) strengthening referral mechanisms and improving SRH coordination.

UNFPA will follow the Whole of Syria approach, implementing in all governorates from Damascus (including to NES), and cross-border from Türkiye. Vulnerable populations prioritized include WRA, IDPs, host communities, returnees, adolescents, and PwDs. Through December 2023, UNFPA reached 1,147,345 people with SRH services through 77 static SRH clinics, 19 EmONCs, and 108 mobile clinics and 4 satellite points in government-controlled areas and 175,443 people with SRH services through 11 facilities  including 9 EmONC facilities and 2 mobile clinics.

Key 2024 objectives include:
Increasing access to: (1) lifesaving health services for the most vulnerable and in need persons, including >57,000 deliveries and >6,000 C-Sections; (2) to secondary and tertiary (in SCO) healthcare for high risk pregnancy, malnourished PLW, EmONC cases, and complex cases which cannot access treatment in their area, including > 95,000 referrals for delivery, including referrals out of Al-Hol and Areesah camps; (3) to primary healthcare by providing EPHS to cover RMNH needs; (4) to vulnerable rural areas and camps with service gaps through mobile teams and the community midwifery networks throughout NWS, NES and GoS.

Supporting  (1) SRH and GBV integration to ensure access for GBV survivors to SRH services, 117 health facility under integration initiative, in addition to 1500 health staff to be trained; (2) essential infrastructure maintenance, equipment repair and supply to health facilities, including expansion of maternity clinic in Al-Hol camp; (3) health sector coordination and HIS, emphasizing enhancing protection, access to health services, and coordination within and across hubs, and joint contingency and preparedness planning; (4) continuity of care, strengthening community resilience, responding to IDP movements and shifts in control, and beneficiaries’ participation in programming; (5) resilience and early recovery through one midwifery school in NWS and 2 in GOS/NES; (6) leadership of women to be able to lead the SRH program in NW Syria (7) voucher assistance to enhance access to FP and PNC, including transportation and value vouchers. 

Strengthening and consolidating medical supply chains, ensuring availability of quality supplies and medicines for SRH services. Pre-positioning emergency stocks of RH kits, in line with contingency scenarios for reduced access and increased hostilities.
Adapting, updating, and adopting national RH guidelines, including on CMR and Health and Nutrition of PLW in 2024, with MoH, and developing training packages.

project_name: Addressing GBV in Syria
project_objective:
According to the 2024 GBV HNO, Voices from Syria 2024, and the GBVIMs 2023 trends reports, GBV continues to be a dominant feature in Syria, affecting the lives of millions of women and girls.
The project aims to ensure the provision of quality GBV response services to GBV survivors and women and girls at risk and that measures are put in place to prevent and mitigate the risks of GBV.
UNFPA works with local IPs to support the delivery of GBV services and will build on its achievements, promising practices and lessons learned to reach the following objectives:
Service Delivery: Increase the availability of and access to specialized GBV services, through different service delivery points (Women and Girls Safe Space and mobile teams). UNFPA will continue providing essential lifesaving GBV services and will provide CVA, specifically in the framework of GBV case management and to ensure that women and girls, including persons with disabilities, can access the care they need in some of the most vulnerable areas in Syria. Furthermore, UNFPA seeks to continue procuring and supporting GBV AoR partners to distribute dignity kits as this has proved a strategic entry point for provision of GBV response services while meeting the hygiene and protection needs of women and girls through the provision of context specific items. 

Capacity Building: Improve capacity of service providers and implementing partners to provide high-quality, inclusive, and comprehensive GBV services. UNFPA Syria and Turkey XB will continue to build the capacity of UNFPA partners and, through the GBV AoR, of other GBV actors, including women led-organizations.

GBV Prevention and Social Norms: Challenge negative social norms that prevent the empowerment of women and girls and develop accountable models of engagement of men and boys. Through the Turkey XB hub, UNFPA will continue implementing the full scope of the GBV SC prevention program based on the awareness raising toolkit. UNFPA’s IPs will also carry out the full scope of activities under the “Adolescent Mothers Against All Odds” (AMAL) initiative, which has been designed to meet the immediate needs of adolescent girls who are pregnant or first-time mothers, while simultaneously addressing community awareness and engagement. UNFPA Syria’s four-year social norms pilot project in Aleppo will continue. At the same time, UNFPA will continue GBV information dissemination efforts at the community level, about GBV risks,consequences and available services. 

Coordination: UNFPA effectively leads the Whole of Syria GBV coordination structure, supporting GBV coordination in Syria, NW Syria and NE Syria hubs. UNFPA Syria will continue to coordinate the GBV sub-sector, while UNFPA Turkey XB will continue to lead the GBV SC including the GBVIMs technical working group


Protection Risk Analysis
Providing GBV services is critical to ensure survivors are able to recover and heal, if these are not confidential, they may put survivors at further risk of stigmatization or even death. If services are not survivor centered, this will have a negative impact on help-seeking behavior with dramatic consequences on survivor's health. Communities may be resistant to engaging around topics of GBV and ultimately prevent women and girls from attending. To mitigate these risks, UNFPA carries out thorough risk analysis of its interventions and works with communities to reduce risks of GBV. All services will aim to be confidential and survivor centered by building the capacity of partners. UNFPA continuously conducts assessments on barriers to access services including safety audits to identify GBV risk. Women and girls are at the centre of the decision making at every phase of the project implementation.
PSEA
UNFPA assessed and score partners capacity based on a set of eight core standards of PSEA organizational policies and procedures. UNFPA assessed all IPs and they now have full capacity to safeguard, identify report, investigate cases.

project_name: REACH: Responsive Emergency Assistance for Crisis-ridden Humanity in Syria—Prioritizing Integrated Health, Nutrition, WASH & Protection, including Essential Life-saving and Sustaining Support.
project_objective:
The MSNA conducted by IMC in 5 governorates in Syria highlighted urgent humanitarian needs in sectors including Health, Nutrition, Mental Health and Psychosocial Support, Gender-Based Violence, Child Protection, livelihood and WASH. The assessment revealed a dire situation with limited access to essential healthcare services, high malnutrition, psychological distress among population, increased incidents of GBV, and growing concerns related to child protection risks. People faced lack of affordable healthcare, transportation difficulties, limited access to nutrition services, availability of GBV services and awareness gaps on health and protection risks and services.  In response, IMC implemented a comprehensive intervention plan to address identified needs. IMC deployed MMTs to provide Primary Health Care services, referrals, nutrition screenings and integrated MHPSS support. IMC also supported both MOH operated and IMC-operated PHCs by providing capacity building, essential trainings, medical supplies, equipment, WASH structure repairs, and solar panels. Specialized GBV and CP programming including comprehensive case management, tailored structured and unstructured Psychosocial Support Services and prevention activities through dedicated facilities. WASH interventions focused on developing user-friendly facilities in PHCs and MMTs locations, with a focus on ensuring accessibility for people with disabilities and gender-sensitive infrastructure. IMC will continue implementing integrated health and nutrition interventions, addressing urgent healthcare and nutritional needs of affected population in targeted areas. These interventions include providing essential primary and secondary health care services, including referrals, mental health consultations, and treatment, nutrition screenings and integrated mental health and psychosocial support. Child protection intervention will be provided using facility-based approach in three centers (in a CFS, community center and family center). These interventions include CP case management, structured PSS using child resilience curriculum, positive parenting, disability & inclusion activities, awareness raising & sensitization, establishment of community-based groups and training for staff and communities. GBV interventions will be provided in three existing facilities (WGSS, community center & family center) and a mobile team. These interventions include GBV case management, structured PSS for women using women rise curriculum, GBV prevention activities using curriculums such as girl shine & EMAP, women empowerment through vocational & life skills, and GBV mitigation through safety audits and dignity kits provision. Also, providing capacity building for GBV and non-GBV staff to maintain a two-way strong internal referral system for specialized SRH services and mental health consultations upholding GBV guiding principles.
A Protection Risk Analysis was conducted by IMC to identify risks to beneficiaries and project implementation. Key risks included loss of access to services due to security concerns, financial losses due to fraud and corruption, disease outbreaks, disruptions in supply chain, and staffing challenges. IMC implemented mitigating measures to address identified risk, including security assessments, anti-fraud mechanisms, health education for disease prevention, procurement contingency planning, and recruitment capacity building. IMC developed a robust (PSEA) strategy to ensure safeguarding of beneficiaries and confidentiality of their data. This strategy included protocols for collecting informed consent from patients, secure data management procedures, and a Community-Based Feedback and Response Mechanism to address complaints and feedback from beneficiaries. IMC committed to providing transparent information about project services, consulting with and engaging beneficiaries throughout the project cycle and maintaining high standards of data protection and privacy.

project_objective: AccED contribuera à la réinsertion et la continuité de l'accès à une éducation inclusive, sûre et de qualité des filles, garçons et adolescent/es les plus vulnérables affectés par la crise humanitaire dans la région de Tillabéri en réduisant les obstacles à l'éducation. project_name: Strengthening the resilience of out-of-camp refugees, displaced populations and local populations affected by food insecurity, malnutrition, and the effects of climate change in the Logone et Chari, Mayo Sava, and Mayo Tsanaga divisions of the Far North Region of Cameroon.
project_objective:
The Far North region is facing exogenous and complex shocks resulting from the precarious security situation caused by Non-State Armed Groups (NSAG), security situation remains unstable in the Far  North Region. Multiple attacks by non-state army groups were registered during the year 2023. Most attacks were concentrated around the Nigeria border with three divisions typically affected (Mayo-Sava, Logone-et-Chari, and Mayo-Tsanaga). Continuous displacement of population is reported. The Displacement Tracking Matrix Round 27 (DTM, October 2023) shows a total of 700 766 people in displacement with 453 661 IDPs, with 6% in transit? than the last report, 198 940 returnees and 48 165 out-of-camp refugees. The high number of mobile people displays the seriousness of the security situation in various areas, and that it is not safe enough yet for people to feel comfortable returning to their homes. The latest alert by the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) on 28 October 2023 was in Mayo-Tsanaga division where 542 households and 4696 people fled from their homes to have secure places around Mokolo town. 90% of interviewers confirmed that the main cause of displacement is permanent attacks from NSAGs followed by climate change impacts (7%) and community conflict (3%). About inter-communal conflictsin the  Mayo Sava division, the displacement of 4,574 people was observed recently.  This situation confirms the extent of the food insecurity in these divisions.
The impacts of climate change have contributed to decreased food production  worsening the food security condition. Hazards and vulnerability constitute key drivers that directly affect availability, accessibility, utilization, and stability. Climate change has induced unusual disasters and shocks which reduce coping strategy capacity for people especially the vulnerable. As a fragile agro-ecological zone, the Far North Region has experienced 3 weeks of continuous drought at the reproductive phase of crops. This has caused the appearance of caterpillars in most divisions impacting cereals production which is the staple food. Data in the Mayo-Sava division reported a loss of 31.4% of cultivated cereals by drought associated with caterpillars (ENSAN, October 2023). 

The region has also faced challenges such as reduced production of foods especially for staple foods.. For agricultural households, access to food (for direct consumption and income generation) was drastically reduced and affected their livelihood and nutritional status. More than 50% of households experienced soaring prices of staple food. Maize and sorghum have increased in price by  about 85% over the past five years (ENSAN, October 2023). 
FAO and IMC will work in integrating food security and livelihood interventions with nutrition-sensitive and nutrition-specific interventions to improve the nutritional status of the crisis affected populations and build their resilience. Integrating the nutrition interventions with FSL interventions will enhance the resilience of the crisis-affected populations. Nutrition is recognised to be both an input to and outcome of strengthened resilience. In emergency situations, households that are least resilient are at the greatest risk for malnutrition. Well-nourished individuals and households that are nutritionally secure can better withstand, endure and recover more quickly from external shocks   
The project will focus on crisis affected vulnerable households such as IDPs, refugees out of the camp and returnees with focus on gender, age, socio-economic status, and location according to the food security analysis and the availability of persons with disabilities and out-off camp refugees that are not considered during food distributions analysis. Vulnerable host population will also be involved after the targeting process. Community activity such as nutrition education, community management of acute malnutrition will be carried out at the village level.

project_name: Scaling up the accelerated education programme for out-of-school children affected by Lake Chad basin crisis and protection response to vulnerable communities affected by displacement and conflict in the Northwest Southwest region of Cameroon.
project_objective:
In the Logone et Chari, Mayo-Sava and Mayo-Tsanaga divisions, 62 schools are still closed, and 50 others have been destroyed affecting over 35,000 students. Among the key factors impeding access to school are limited and poorly maintained infrastructures (including water and sanitation), shortage of qualified teachers as many have been displaced by the security situation, shortage of learning materials and unaffordable school fees. The number of girls and children with disabilities that are out of school in those divisions shows that the situation is disproportionally affecting them.  

To respond to those needs, NRC and Plan International will scale up their ongoing education programme,  in four subdivisions (Makary, logone Birni Kolofata and Mora) in the two most affected divisions (Logone et Chari, Mayo Sava) of the Far North region. The programme aims to meet the immediate needs of out-of-school children to access basic quality education, while building the capacity of duty-bearers and the communities to respond to the needs of both out-of-school children and those in formal school in the longer term. In coordination with MINEDUB, the programme will provide alternative education activities aligned with the ten key principles developed by the Global Accelerated Education Working Group (AEWG) as well as the recommendations included in the framework document for the implementation of the AEP in Cameroon, as defined by the MINEDUB. The action will mainly support out-of-school children’s return to learning through implementing accelerated education and catch-up classes, following up with support to ensure successful integration into the formal school systems.

project_name: Improving access to legal and civil documentation and scaling up protection for people affected by the crisis in the Lake Chad Basin and armed conflict in the North West and South West Cameroon.
project_objective:
Cameroon is currently grappling with a triple humanitarian crisis. a) Insurgency in the Lake Chad Basin, which has rendered Far North Cameroon as the second most affected after Nigeria (Northeast) by the Boko Haram activities. b) Escalating violence in the two English-speaking regions of North-west and South-west. c) Presence of over 325,000 refugees from the Central African Republic (CAR) residing in the East, Adamawa, and North regions of Cameroon with grave humanitarian consequences. This has created enormous humanitarian needs which are further compounded by structural development deficits and chronic vulnerabilities that further challenge the long-term recovery of affected people. Lack of legal and civil documentation (LCD) among crises-affected populations in the Far North (48%) and NWSW (38%) has been identified as a key protection concern.  Main reasons advanced for the lack of LCD reported by the MSNA are: lack of supporting documentation, limited information, difficult access to civil registration and identification centres and limited access to legal assistance.
This project seeks to improve protection and enable enjoyment of legal identity rights for people affected by crises in the Far North, North West and South West regions. Through the provision of legal protection services including information, counselling, legal assistance and capacity building on legal identity, NRC will enable more people to exercise their rights and take steps to possess LCD. The project will increase the number of children in possession of birth certificates while more young people will be supported to obtain national identity cards to ensure freedom of movement, prevent arbitrary arrests and detention and enjoy other rights and general protection. NRC’s Legal Mobile teams will target IDPs, returnees, refugees and vulnerable host communities with general information on LCD while people identified with specific needs will be provided legal counselling and legal assistance. Capacity building will target municipal, judiciary, health and administrative authorities concerned with civil status registration to improve their knowledge of the legal framework so that they can provide quality and timely services. The project will also build the capacity of humanitarian actors and civil society leaders in charge of promoting and protecting legal identity and other human rights. NRC will work with her local implementing partners to effect this change.

project_name: Providing adequate shelter within safe and healthy settlements for vulnerable population affected by displacement in the Southwest and Northwest regions in Cameroon.
project_objective:
This project aims to provide adequate and safe shelter solutions and improve the living conditions of vulnerable households affected by displacements in the Southwest and Northwest regions of Cameroon. This will be achieved through the provision of shelters, the rehabilitation of community and public infrastructures and the distribution of essential households items to 36,000 individuals. 

The latest multisectoral needs assessment (IOM, 2023) highlighted that approximately 464,146 individuals are self-settled in the bushes and in acute need of shelter and household items in the Northwest and Southwest regions. Furthermore, most accommodations across all displaced populations are critically below standards in terms of location (official, informal/bush, and collective shelter); type of shelter; square meter per person; structural damages, land tenure, etc. 

To respond to this need, and ensure the project reaches the most vulnerable groups, NRC will mainstream gender, age, and disability into its programming, ensuring groups with specific needs and challenges have meaningful access and can actively participate in the project. Consultations with communities will ensure the designs of the shelter are culturally appropriate and meet the specific needs of groups with specific needs. Lastly, NRC will actively communicate with targeted communities, ensuring their feedbacks are captured and contribute to the adaptation of its programming.
