project_name: Provision of Lifesaving Child Protection and GBV Protection Assistance to Populations Affected by Conflict, Displacement, and Natural Hazards.
project_objective: The intervention strives to fortify response and prevention services in target communities for a total of 241,915 individuals, with 198,255 individuals for CP and 43,660 for GBV, by strengthen the protection system, through conducting 10 CP and 5 GBV monitoring, assessments, and safety audits, these efforts intend to illuminate grave violations against children in humanitarian contexts, emphasizing the protection of children in conflicts. The assessments will specify sources of threat and vulnerabilities, particularly for children at high risk of abuse, neglect, exploitation, or violence. Additionally, the development and enhancement of safe and ethical CP and GBV referral pathways, ensuring that the most vulnerable children have access to health, psychosocial, legal aid, and other essential services. Moreover, the initiative plans to capacitate 650 protection and humanitarian actors, and other duty bearers, aiming at empowering them to prevent and respond to grave violations, CP, and GBV concerns, and further enhance their protection skills, integration, and coordination by in cooperating Centrality of Protection, PFA, and Safe Referral and Identification. In addition to, the training of 200 non-GBV service providers in GBV prevention, risk mitigation, and response strategies. Enhancing the protection of Children at Risk including UASC, CAFFAGs, and GBV survivors through specialized Case Management and FTR services is prioritized. Where comprehensive individual assessments are planned to be conducted for a total of 3,690 children (3,350 CP and 340 GBV) based on their BIAs. The result includes providing appropriate interim or long-term alternative care for 300 registered vulnerable children, including UASC, while actively tracing their biological families. Furthermore, direct cash support will be offered to extremely vulnerable children and their families based on a best interest assessment. The initiative also plans to identify and train 2,997 alternative caregivers and foster parents, focusing on positive parenting using SCIs' common approach to Safe Families, child safeguarding, CP reporting, and referral mechanisms. Monthly Parental and Children's sessions will be conducted with foster children and alternative caregivers. Additionally, to ensure the quality of the provided Case Management service the case officers, assistants, case workers, and facilitators will undergo training on case management, FTR, alternative care, the CPIMS+, and Caring for Child Survivors (CCS). Also, the response will provide MHPSS specialized services to 2,150 children. The response will enhance the protection status of the most vulnerable children by reinforcing monitoring, reporting, and follow-up through community-based protection mechanisms in the affected area. By the establishment of 55 CBCPNs each comprising 15 members and representing various groups within the community. These networks will be supported with necessary equipment and capacitated on CR, CP, and GBV relevant aspects, as well as monitoring and reporting according to CBCPN's TOR. The strategy will also include capacity-building for 825 community members on GBV prevention, risk mitigation, and/or response. Also, community outreach sessions and campaigns will be conducted in the target communities, reaching 72,240 individuals, with a specific focus on preventing and responding to CP and SGBV risks. Additionally, the plan involves organizing 70 awareness campaigns on GBV. In addition to, enhancing the protection status and psychosocial well-being of affected children through a multi-faceted approach. Through the establishment and/or rehabilitation of permanent/semi-permanent safe spaces, MPCs, and CFSs dedicated to delivering unstructured play activities and basic PSS to the most vulnerable boys and girls, targeting 65,000 children, and providing PSS dignity kits and hygiene items to 12,360 children. Finally, supporting 850 girls and women through the distribution of dignity kits

project_name: Provision of Emergency integrated Nutrition and Health interventions to vulnerable population in Borno and Yobe states, NE Nigeria.
project_objective:
The overall aim is to reduce mortality, morbidity and undernutrition by providing life-saving nutrition and health services in health facilities and communities.
1.	Affected populations have improved access to quality primary healthcare services in the targeted areas for reduction of morbidity and mortality
2.	Affected populations have access to quality nutrition treatment and preventive services through strengthening the capacity of health facilities
The program will be focusing on; 
-	Provision of quality primary health care services that includes basic management and prevention of communicable diseases for all age groups from children to adults, 
-	Providing medical equipment, supplies and pharmaceuticals and nutritional supplies to the health facilities through the award and in coordination with SMOH and LGA authorities.
-	Sexual and Reproductive health services; antenatal and postnatal care services, support to uncomplicated vaginal delivery services and minor perinatal complications, 
-	Support to referral services for specialized care.
-	 Support to Routine Childhood Immunization in collaboration with SMOH and WHO.
-	 Support to provision of clinical management of minor physical injury
-	 Prepositioning of treatment kits and supplies for Cholera and Measles outbreak in the targeted LGAs 
-	Provision of nutrition services through IMAM approach in targeted communities.
-	Supplementary Nutrition assistant program through CVA modality for PBW (Porridge MOM)
-	Reinforcement of technical capacity through sector/sub-sector specific technical trainings for quality service delivery. 
-	Building institutional and community capacity for promotion and provision of appropriate IYCF-E integrated with priority health and hygiene practices.
Target:
1.	Children 0-59 months of age for malnutrition treatment and other children for provision of primary health services. 
2.	Women: key target of the project, both in its direct activities (e.g. Care Groups) and preventive and curative health services, as well as with the women empowerment agenda applied across the project.
3.	Men: men in the targeted communities will be provided with primary health care services for the management of non-communicable diseases (NCD) and communicable diseases. 
4.           Health workers and community-based structures e.g CHIPS, CV etc
5.           People with Disability and Special Needs.

project_name: Respuesta integral para atender las necesidades de los migrantes y sus comunidades de acogida en los estados Bolívar y Delta Amacuro
project_objective: HelpAge International (HAI) como socio principal en la implementación y sus socios locales, brindarán apoyo vital a las personas mayores (PM), personas con discapacidad (PcD), sus familias y migrantes no acompañados en tránsito hacia Brasil, Colombia y Trinidad & Tobago con un enfoque diferencial basado en género y edad. El proyecto se dirige a áreas clave y/o comunidades que actualmente no son suficientemente atendidas por ayuda gubernamental o humanitaria. En el interior del país, la atención se centra en los puntos clave, en gran medida descubiertos, en las rutas por el Orinoco desde el estado Delta Amacuro, siendo localidades con necesidades de atención general. Siguiendo un enfoque holístico de inclusión, se implementarán intervenciones adaptadas a la edad, el género, la discapacidad inclusiva, así como adaptadas a la identidad cultural de los pueblos indígenas (Warao, Amorua, Pemón), teniendo en cuenta las medidas de prevención de enfermedades, en línea con el enfoque de triple nexo, construyendo un puente hacia soluciones a largo plazo y fortaleciendo la coexistencia pacífica de los migrantes en tránsito y las comunidades de acogida. El proyecto beneficiará directamente a un total de 110,166 personas vulnerables, al apoyar las necesidades más críticas en las áreas WASH (acceso a agua potable, potabilización y dotación de instalaciones de saneamiento, así como kits de higiene, kits de dignidad y capacitación para la prevención de enfermedades endémicas, con especial énfasis en el lavado de manos), seguridad alimentaria (kits de alimentos o platos servidos) y salud (actividades de fortalecimiento y dotación de insumos básicos a establecimientos de salud cercanos a las comunidades seleccionadas y el entrenamiento y sensibilización a trabajadores del área, así como atención con consultas médicas básicas y medicación a los beneficiarios). En consecuencia, la protección se constituye en un eje transversal (apoyo psicosocial, a cargo de una Oficial, la entrega de dispositivos de asistencia, acceso a TICs y concientización en materia de riesgos). El enfoque inclusivo de poblaciones en los más altos niveles o riesgo de vulnerabilidad (personas mayores, personas con discapacidades, mujeres víctimas o en riesgo de violencia basada en género, mujeres gestantes o lactantes, con hijos menores de 5 años, cabezas de familia, otros grupos minoritarios incluyendo población LGBTIQ+, pero especialmente la población indígena) implica requerimientos de atención y protección diferencial, basada en las necesidades identificadas en terreno y la adaptación del contenido de la intervención. Esto es particularmente visible en los temas alimentarios, en las inversiones en infraestructura para agua y saneamiento básico y en la aplicación del enfoque de género intercultural con comunidades indígenas. La asistencia en áreas remotas requiriendo transporte fluvial y largos trayectos en carretera, elevan los costos de atención ligeramente sobre los estándares. Por ello, se realiza la cobertura de un número menos amplio de beneficiarios de la atención integral. Por último, el objetivo es cubrir una gran brecha humanitaria existente en áreas específicas, en 2 de los 8 estados priorizados del país. Basado en datos sólidos recopilados directamente durante los últimos dos años y alineado con las necesidades del HRP, los objetivos del Clúster de Protección y el Grupo de Trabajo de Edad y Discapacidad, así como también la sinergia generada con el sub-clúster de protección CCT Guayana y el Foro ONGI. Hemos desarrollado intervenciones exitosas en el área de protección junto a Convite y Kapé-Kapé, ambas reconocidas como especialistas en poblaciones indígenas, garantizando el respeto a la interculturalidad y una comunicación efectiva en idiomas autóctonos. El componente de género, a cargo de una Oficial, contempla no solo la sensibilización individual, comunitaria y a trabajadores del sector salud sino también la asistencia material y la orientación psicosocial

project_name: Provide dignified, inclusive, and improved access to WASH services by ensuring clean, safe, and functional water supply, sanitation, and waste management facilities in Rohingya refugee camps and adjacent host communities.
project_objective: The strategic focus of Save the Children (SC) is to promote quality and durable solutions to essential WASH services. SC will continue the existing WASH services in camps 17, 20, 25, and 27 that will be safe, inclusive, and resilient services by latrines, bathing, tube wells, water supply, and waste management facilities functional by adequate repair, maintenance, improvement, and renovation. Water quality in households will be prioritized as the critical stage of the safe water chain, and provisions made for gender-specific safe WASH spaces. SC will enhance the quality of services by ensuring quality benchmarks and bi-weekly functional monitoring to ensure the safety, privacy, and specific needs of vulnerable members of the community. It will ensure dignified and improved access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene management and practice. WASH program focuses on a cost-efficient participatory program delivery to boost emergent community ownership and open new avenues of program sustainability. The program will ensure conflict-sensitive, sustainable, and gender-segregated WASH facilities for the Rohingya camps and adjacent host communities. Environment-friendly fecal sludge and solid waste management will also be considered a priority issue. SC will manage solid waste and fecal sludge to prevent negative environmental impacts through robust planning, risk mitigation, and monitoring that will prevent any health hazards and outbreaks. SC will operate green fecal sludge treatment plants to manage the sludge of latrine pits and septic tanks. As a part of an innovative approach and to make the solution environment-friendly, instead of using any chemicals SCI applies biological conversion, physical filtration, and absorption with anaerobic processes and converts wastewater as safer for vegetable cultivation. In addition, garbage disposed of in communal waste pits will regularly be collected to produce composting fertilizer from organic waste. Moreover, the project will prioritize to use of solar power rather than fuel power for operating WASH facilities. SC will be rationing safer water and compost fertilizer for vegetable gardening after the greenish treatment of the community human sludge and solid waste that will be a part of a 360-degree circular economy which will contribute to three zero theories i.e., zero unemployment, zero carbon emission, and zero poverty. SC will conduct regular hygiene promotion sessions for all. However special sessions will conduct for children and adolescent girls. SC provided menstrual hygiene management sessions to train them on how to make reusable sanitary pads. SCI continues hygiene promotion awareness sessions for children through demonstration, role play, storytelling, singing songs, etc. Furthermore, a bi-weekly cleaning campaign will be conducted led by the WASH committees, hygiene promotion volunteers, and nonpaid youth volunteers who will mainly work with local resident groups.Different groups like children, adolescent girls, WASH committees, and non-paid youth volunteers will engage in new roles for bringing positive changes in the community such as cleaning campaigns, WASH facilities cleaning, garbage pickup, and drain cleaning, which are mainly conducted by hygiene promotion volunteers. The program will cover hygiene promotional activities for host communities inside the camp and adjacent to the camp, especially in schools. Save the Children strictly follows the unified design and climate-resilient infrastructures and keeps a contingency plan and stockpiling to respond immediately to any disasters. We reflect on gender, age, disability, and accountability, with emphasis on preparedness and response for natural disasters, public health risks, and disease outbreaks. SC gives special attention to the person with disabilities by making inclusive WASH facilities. All the activities will be implemented in close coordination with WASH sector and government agencies.

project_name: WASH intervention to Vulnerable IDPs and Host Affected children/caregivers by Conflict in BAY states.
project_objective:
In 2024, the SCI will expand its multi-sector integrated approach to better prioritize the WASH-related acute vulnerabilities from a risk reduction perspective, through risk mitigation and case area targeted interventions, such as before the rainy season in the flood-prone areas and cholera hotspots. Considering the population movements and lessons learned regarding the cholera outbreak and historic floods, SCI will also reinforce the local capacities and prepositioning of the most cost-efficient common pipeline supplies. SCI will continue to mainstream protection and mitigate gender-based violence (GBV) to ensure that access to WASH services is framed after systematic consultations with women and girls from accountability for affected population (AAP) perspective at the top level beyond the feedback mechanisms, in particular women and children can do so in a safe manner. SCI will prioritize the following activities under the various categories and strategic objectives of the HRP:
• WATER: Support life-saving assistance through the provision of safe water at the household level by ensuring emergency and sustainable water sources are available for the affected population. In camps and hosting communities, support for health and nutrition centres that will present acute water shortages will be prioritized. The partners will increase responses in water quality through routine monitoring and chlorination (household and communal level). Additionally, the safety of beneficiaries to access water points will be increased by ensuring the functionality of water points, and improved ownership by the community and technical designs to reduce incidences of theft and vandalism of submissible pumps and equipment as reported in 2023.
• SANITATION: Improve access to sanitation, by ensuring the availability of gender-segregated sanitation facilities to the affected population, desludging to compliant dumping site, and by the introduction of eco-friendly sanitation solutions for fecal sludge management (FSM). Additional support will be prioritized to Health, Nutrition centres and Temporary Learning Spaces which will be closely coordinated with respective sectors. Before the rainy season, the sector will prioritize vector control campaigns in camps and scale up preparedness plans, including dislodging capacity support.
• HYGIENE: Promote in local languages culturally appropriate hygiene messages for social behaviour change, all along the key WASH NFIs distribution and monitoring by the WASH partners to all target populations, namely the households with SAM children and/or cholera cases. Prevention and awareness messages will be aimed at breaking the transmission cycle of communicable diseases (especially cholera) which will improve food intake and health of children especially those under 5, significantly contributing to health and nutrition objectives. Priority will be given in Borno State to Bama, Damboa, Dikwa, Gwoza, Jere, Kala/Balge, Konduga, Mafa, Magumeri, Maiduguri, Mobbar, Monguno and Ngala LGAs, in Yobe State to Fika, Geidam, Gujba, Gulani and Jakusko, and in Adamawa State to (Girei, Madagali, Michika, Mubi North, Mubi South, Shelleng, Yola North, Yola South. Further, the sector will target women and girls with menstrual hygiene awareness items and messaging including improving the capacity to locally prepare produced menstrual hygiene items.
In addition, SC will tailor the program through its active local partners to ensure Integration into its existing nutrition program to address issues of malnutrition, the outbreak of communicable diseases and improved access to schools by ensuring water and sanitation access for TLSs (temporary learning spaces), in line with the centrality of protection with guidance from Protection Sector. 
Localization will be prioritized and improved capacity of response for national organizations through capacity building and promoting partnerships.

project_name: Emergency sanitation provision to displaced households (HHs) in Kodok, Upper Nile State, South Sudan.
project_objective:
Food insecurity in the Upper Nile region is driven by climatic shocks, insecurity, population displacements, crop deficits and limited access to basic services with the cumulative effects of years of asset depletion eroding households coping capacities and loss of livelihoods. 
The area was already at IPC 4 levels of food insecurity, when in November fresh fighting erupted between armed forces in Fashoda County, resulting in close to 40,000 people being displaced. An inter-agency mission (OCHA and UNMISS) has estimated 21,000 people have gathered in Kodok and near the local UNMISS compound. The people managed to escape with livestock, however 2600 animals have recently died leaving them with no alternative source of food or income. The affected population, including the elderly, disabled and large numbers of unaccompanied children. It is estimated that 75% of the IDP’s are women and children.  Newly displaced persons continue to arrive.  They have no access to food or cash, are traumatized and have lost most of their assets. They come from an already compromised food security and nutrition position. The markets in the area are however operational and food items are available. A lack of sanitation facilities is resulting in widespread open defecation with women reportedly walking long distances to relieve themselves.    
This project intends to complement a START funded emergency response, coordinated by CA and launched by multiple partners. (The project has recently concluded). CA and ADA provided cash assistance for food security and 3 agencies provided safe water (World Vision, Solidarite and Cord-Aid). This met the Sphere standards. Health care and SGBV services was provided by Mercy Corps, while UNICEF supported child protection and reunification of children with their families. Bearing in mind the resource level available under the HEF fund and in line with the needs assessment and community consultation the immediate priority needs are cash/food security and sanitation facilities.    
Outcome 1: To address the food access crisis for the new arrivals, the project will provide multipurpose cash to 681HH (4,086people). Targeting mainly women, the elderly and child headed HHs. 20% of the cash assistance will target the host community who are equally vulnerable. This is to promote inclusion and apply conflict sensitivity to the project design. The cash value of £82 per household has been set by the National Cash Working Group. 
Outcome 2: The project will provide 6 pit latrines of 5 holes using temporary materials. In this instance corrugated iron sheets will be used and plastic slabs. This design is proposed to ensure privacy and safety for users. Hygiene awareness will be conducted through the 15 hygiene promoters identified and trained from both the displaced population and host community. IEC materials will be developed to disseminate health and hygiene information, feedback mechanisms and safeguarding and accountability messages. This outcome is being proposed to prevent disease outbreaks and provide dignified sanitation facilities for the displaced population especially women and girls. These latrines will not meet Sphere standards of 1:20 but will compliment ongoing sanitation provision efforts while CA and other partners fundraise to scale up the response.

project_name: Anticipatory actions to save lives and agricultural livelihoods affected by El Niño 2023-2024 phenomenon in El Salvador
project_objective:
The objective of this intervention is to save lives and agricultural livelihoods of 25,000 families residing in the Dry Corridor, who were affected by the effects of El Niño in 2023 and who face the threat again in 2024. 
In 2023, not only the lag at the beginning of the rains was observed but also the erratic distribution and intense (concentrated) rains, which caused losses in the Primera 2023 harvest and damage to the Postrera because the water did not arrive at the time the plant needed it. As a result of this, household food reserves have been compromised, which could become a nationwide critical situation given that the next Primera 2024 harvest would not be ready until August 2024. This means an extra extended lean season.
The above is supported by data generated by FAO-DIEM in 2023. It has been possible to analyze the results of the survey carried out between April-May 2023 and November-December 2023, that means, before and after the rainy season. The DIEM data show that 48% of those surveyed stated that they had had difficulties planting corn in Primera due to insufficient water for their crops (irrigation or rain). Farmers who planted in May lost the sowing seed or the corn in its first stages. The vast majority had to move the planting date to June when the rains returned, however, 61% of those who planted reported having had losses in corn and 53% in beans.
The above suggests that households were not able to produce enough to save reserves, sell and pay loans. 83% of households report not having sufficient corn reserves for 2023 and that what they have could last 1-3 months. Only 21% of households say they have reserves for 6 months or more.
Regarding crops funding, 86% report that they did it with their own resources and with the result of loss of the harvest they have been left without those resources; 11% reported that they took out a loan (with banks, cooperatives, savings associations) that they are paying, while 2% had credit and have managed to pay recently.
The FAO - FIES indicator (Food Insecurity Experience Scale) as of December 2023 is reported at 24.5% at the national level, having had an increase of 1.6% between the beginning and the end of the rainy season influenced by the El Niño Phenomenon. However, when observing the FIES data at the departmental level, the attention is taken to the department of Usulután reports 39.3% of the population in moderate to severe hunger, the department of Morazán with 36.6% and San Vicente with 32.1%. At least six departments exceed the FIES national average. Curiously, in three FAO - DIEM surveys carried out in El Salvador, the four departments in the east of the country, which are part of the Dry Corridor, reports higher FIES data compared to the other areas of the country.
The data cited allows us to identify some actions that must be strengthened or implemented by the government, producers, cooperation, humanitarian and development organizations, to counteract the impacts on families, for example, under the scheme of anticipatory actions they can be promoted and implemented drought-tolerant seed banks, the use of renewable energy, switching to an early harvest and good post-harvest management, making more efficient use of water by avoiding compromising water for consumption, improving the monitoring and management of pests and diseases, and others adaptive practices. It is clear that all of the above must be done being duly informed and aware of the conditions of the phenomena, threats and possible impacts for which the monitoring carried out by the DOA-MARN is key.

project_name: Réponse en Abris et articles ménagers essentiels pour les personnes déplacées et retournées de la région de l'Extrême Nord du Cameroun.
project_objective:
La crise sécuritaire du bassin du Lac Tchad continue à impacter négativement les populations civiles, leurs biens ainsi que les infrastructures sociales de base dans les zones frontalières avec le Nigeria et le Tchad. La persistance de la violence est la cause principale des déplacements ce qui aggrave le niveau de vulnérabilité préexistante issu de la pauvreté. Selon le mécanisme de réponse rapide (RRM) 30 000 personnes sont nouvellement déplacées à cause de l’insécurité. Trois attaques sur les formations sanitaires notamment à Oudjila (Mayo-Sava), Goldavi et Ouzal (Mayo-Tsanaga) ont été rapportés. L’impact direct de ces attaques sur les civils, les biens et infrastructures sanitaires demeure importante avec des cas de décès, d’enlèvements et des pillages. La montée des eaux, consécutive aux pluies abondantes dans la région conduit au débordement du fleuve Logone et entrainant dans la plupart des inondations sur des vastes étendues de culture dans le Logone et chari et Mayo Danay exposant les deplaces dans une précarité exacerbée. Les risques d’inondations sont toujours redoutés. 
Avec les efforts menés par le gouvernement camerounais le long des frontières ainsi que le rétablissement de paix dans les localités victimes des conflits intercommunautaire ainsi que le retrait des eaux du fleuve Logone après les pluies favorisent le retour des certains déplacés vers les localités d’origine. Ces personnes retournées peu qu’ils soient, sont soumises aux conditions de vie très difficile et précaire du fait de la dégradation et inexistence de leurs habitats après plusieurs années d’abandons. Ce qui les conduits à loger dans les espaces communautaires ou dans les familles d’accueil en attendant des solutions meilleures pour leur habitat.
Au vu de ce besoin et sévérité élevée, il demeure nécessaire d’apporter une assistance à ces personnes en situation de déplacement et ceux retournées et les retournés ainsi qu’a famille d’accueil des communautés hôtes vulnérables en soutien pour soutenir l’Etat camerounais.L’objectif principal étant de restaurer la protection physique dans la dignité en améliorant le cadre de vie des personnes en situation de déplacement et retours.

project_name: Protección de la seguridad alimentaria y nutricional de la población migrante irregular en tránsito por Honduras.
project_objective:
Honduras se ha convertido en territorio de tránsito de migrantes que provienen de otros continentes y/o de Sudamérica y el Caribe, que deciden tomar una ruta migratoria que los expone a numerosos riesgos a lo largo de su ruta hacia Estados Unidos. Entre el 1 de enero de 2023 y 1 de enero de 2024, 550,752 personas han transitado por territorio hondureño, luego de ingresar de manera irregular. Estas cifras incluyen 224,507 venezolanos, 81,791 cubanos, 80,988 haitianos, 44,759 ecuatorianos, 12,596 colombianos y 11,402 chinos entre más de 140 nacionalidades, esto según datos del INM-Honduras. La situación demandó de una respuesta humanitaria para proporcionar alimentos, refugio, atención médica y nutricional, así como transporte a personas en movilidad en extrema vulnerabilidad. 

La oferta actual de atención requiere de ampliación o fortalecimiento en alojamiento temporal con condiciones dignas, acceso a agua de consumo, alimentación, elementos de higiene, en todos los puntos fronterizos.  Es por esto que la FAO, ha diseñado la intervención en fortalecimiento y proporción de suplementos nutricionales a 12,500 personas migrantes en condiciones de tránsito mixto, especialmente a mujeres embarazadas y lactantes. Así cómo también la elaboración de una Normativa alimentaria Nacional para Honduras con un enfoque de respuesta humanitaria que sirva como documento técnico base a nivel de país y un documento técnico, para la integración de la productos agrícolas y pecuarios locales a las raciones de alimentos (fresca, seca y caliente) en apego con los requerimientos nutricionales según la OMS.

project_name: Building and strengthening the agrifood systems in vulnerable IDPS, host communities and returnees' communities in Northern Mozambique
project_objective:
Northern Mozambique, especially Cabo Delgado province has been affected by armed conflict, violence and insecurity caused by non-state armed groups (NSAG) from October 2017, resulting in the destruction of civilian infrastructure, disruption of local economies and agriculture-based livelihoods. The conflict is complex and multi-dimensional, with several endogenous and exogenous factors and dynamics contributing to its persistence. Whilst the NSAGs have driven violence, the conflict is rooted, amongst other causes, in poverty and inequality.  In the endogenous dimension, the main factors identified include phenomena of socioeconomic inequalities and expectations related to the exploitation of natural resources, especially among local youth. This adds to factors of perceived political exclusion, limited participation, and few economic opportunities, affecting young people. Northern Mozambique is in fact one of the country's areas with higher poverty indicators, levels of unemployment, illiteracy, and limited access to basic services such as healthcare and education. The provinces of Niassa, Cabo Delgado and Nampula host 36% of the Mozambican population, with a significantly higher levels of poverty than the central and southern regions. Cabo Delgado has a poverty prevalence rates of around 50%. One-third of children and youth aged 5 to 24 are not enrolled in school; the average secondary school enrollment rate is 13.3% in Cabo Delgado, while the national level is 23.9%. Gender parity in primary education is also below the national average.
In Cabo Delgado Province, the armed conflict has disrupted the lives and livelihoods of 1.28 million Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs). Many IDPs have fled conflict multiple times — forcing them to abandon their personal belongings, assets, livelihoods and means of survival with each displacement. Despite continued fighting, according to the DTM data of August 20237, there were a total of 627,846 IDPs still leaving in resettlement sites or in host communities, while 540,958 IDPs have returned to their home district and the number of IDPs have reduced from over a million, prompted by the pursuit for better livelihood opportunities.8 Returning IDPs require both humanitarian assistance and resilience building interventions to meet their basic needs and to successfully rebuild their livelihoods for self-reliance. Mozambique is also prone to extreme climatic shocks (cyclone, floods, drought) which further decapitalize already vulnerable households.
Currently, FAO assists IDPs, host communities and returnees to produce their own food and build resilience, actions that guarantee the livelihood of the population as well as improve their self-sufficiency. In line with the current human mobility tendency, FAO intends to expand its emergency and resilience assistance to returnees and will work to restore the agricultural capacity of returnee families, while continuing to assist IDPs and host community families in displacement sites. This approach is shared by the government, which has requested urgent livelihoods support for returnees.  
With a total ask of USD 17 207 008.00 FAO can support 430 175 IDPs, host community members and returnees in 22 districts of Cabo Delgado (17), Niassa (3) and Nampula (2) to rebuild and restore agriculture-based livelihoods (crops, livestock and, fisheries) and improve households' food and nutrition security, laying the foundation for resilient and people-centered agrifood systems. These interventions will be combined with FAO’s technical assistance and training on good agricultural and fisheries practices, animal husbandry and health and crop post-harvest and post-catch losses management/reduction to maximize production and food availability.

project_name: Multisectoral approach to food security and resilience for IDPs and host communities in Ar-Raqqa and Deir ez-Zor in Northeast Syria
project_objective:
Since September 2021, arche noVa implements a multisector food security project in rural Ar-Raqqa and Deir ez-Zor governorate. Low rainfall and drought like events during the last years are major reasons for reduced availability of water at households as well as in agriculture sector. Lack of clean drinking water represents the greatest and most comprehensive threat to the population. Restoring the function of water networks and pumping stations is essential for building structural resilience. Agriculture and thus the resilience of the majority of the inhabitants in NES are also significantly dependent on the water and irrigation infrastructure. The restoration of the irrigation facilities is therefore planned for the beginning of the project. The availability of arable irrigated land is a precondition to improve food security in the frame of the project activities. The project will facilitate landless IDP and vulnerable host communities to access land, seeds, livestock and knowledge. Higher crop yields also mean better availability of food in the market and higher incomes and purchasing power. Without increased purchasing power, the economy cannot develop either and young people remain unemployed. Many of the young adults have had little opportunity to attend school in recent years. The establishment of vocational training centres in rural areas will provide opportunity to create a solid basis for self-employment in relevant sectors. Ideally, this will also have a direct impact on the agricultural sector,
The project will benefit from synergies of overlapping location and beneficiaries as well as complementary activities of education and the multisector humanitarian aid project under the HDP NEXUS approach.
Overall objective is it to strengthening the resilience of vulnerable IDP households and host communities through increased food security, income generation activities in relevant sectors, and improved and safe access to safe drinking water and sanitation.
(1)	Food security in 8 communities in the project region has increased due to improved access to land, agricultural inputs, crop diversification and improved practices.
(2)	The incomes of vulnerable households in the project region have increased as a result of vocational training and self-employment.
(3)	Inhabitants of the communities in the project region have improved access to clean water and sanitation and the number of waterborne diseases is reduced.

The project summary illustrates the targets of the whole 4-year's project, while the submission is isolating the results remaining in budget year three of the the project. As such, each sectorial activity for 2024 is part of the whole framework. For 2024, FSL activities focus on cleaning of sub-irrigation channels (Cash for Work), fodder support to existing livestock keepers, food processing trainings and provision of  equipment, seed and input support for growing vegetables.
ERL activities focus on two main activties: vocational training of youths in two centers on four vocations per training round (sewing, beautification, house electrics and solar panel installation/maintenance, plumbing, AC and cooling equipment repair and maintenance). The youth will receive a start-up kit after graduation. Additionally, existing small businesses in rural communities are supported by business management trainings and in-kind support to enhance their businesses.
WASH activties are only focusing with minimal remaining budget on rehabilitation of one water stations and water networks, depending on regional priorities, while other activties had been completed in the previous years.

project_name: Promoting resilience through access to quality education and psycho-social support for conflict-affected children in Northern Syria
project_objective:
The proposed action seeks to increase the access to quality education and PSS services in target areas by implementing a combination of high quality formal and non-formal education activities along with a comprehensive package of support that complement each other where possible. PIN takes an integrated and holistic approach to address Education in Emergencies (EiE) and Child Protection needs. PIN employs a dual approach to supporting education through establishing temporary learning centres (TLCs) for provision of PSS and non-formal education using different modalities such as  the Self-Learning Programme (SLP) curriculum and accelerated learning programme (ALP) in areas with acute concentrations of OOSC – including in IDP camps and informal settlements; and assistance to formal schools where education has been disrupted through providing construction and repair works, school furniture and equipment, teaching and learning materials, support for running costs, PSS sessions are provided to all enrolled students and teachers as its been integrated to schools regular timetables. 

 Additionally, provision of after-school catch-up and remedial classes to support pathways into education and reduce drop-out. The successful transition of children to formal schools, emphasizing the importance of providing Psychosocial Support Services (PSS) to aid in this process. This support is not only crucial for children who have faced significant challenges in recent years but also essential for helping them adjust to their new circumstances. Additionally, our focus extends to caregivers, who play a central role in the well-being and resilience of the children under their care. PIN takes an evidence-based approach to programming based on rigorous feedback loops to promote accountability and enhance impact. All activities will be implemented in line with relevant Education cluster tools, materials, and approaches, in addition to core INEE and Sphere standards, with a focus upon promoting safe learning spaces and essential WASH facilities and maximizing accessibility for those at risk of education disruption, including girls and children living with disabilities. All our NFE activities  are aligned with the NFE matrix developed by developed by the Non-Formal Education Task Force and thoroughly reviewed by the Technical Working Group. Also , involvement of PIN in assessment led by cluster to ensure evidence based approaches. Teaching and student kits will be provided to facilitate quality learning opportunities and minimize education barriers for children from low-income HH.  

Additionally, in efforts to support community cohesion and raise awareness PIN will be supporting schools and the surrounding communities through caregiver awareness sessions, training for teachers, school management and cleaners. The process will ensure the participation of relevant stakeholders to consider local priorities while also ensuring that transparency is at the forefront and that PIN is accountable to the populations in its areas of intervention. Assessments will be conducted by PIN staff and engineers in collaboration with local authorities, where relevant. PIN will target communities where education services have been disrupted due to conflict, where there is no, or limited, access to education. Experience highlights that significant gaps also exist in such areas to meet teachers’ and students’ needs for safe and quality learning. There will be a strong focus on community outreach and engagement throughout the entire cycle, including caregivers. All activities have the final aim of reintegrating children into education through formal and non-formal accelerated learning programmes and the creation of child protection safety nets. PIN is providing a holistic approach by providing access to Education the learning enters and providing numeracy and literacy condensed courses.

project_name: Nutrition Assistance for food-insecure populations in Sudan.
project_objective:
The nutrition assistance in Sudan seeks to improve the nutritional status of food-insecure residents in 
targeted localities affected by very high malnutrition prevalence and food insecurity. This is achieved through the provision of preventive and curative nutrition activities to children aged 6–59 months and pregnant and breastfeeding women or girls (PBW/G). In Sudan, WFP plays a leading role in defining nutrition responses for treating and preventing Moderate Acute Malnutrition (MAM), in collaboration with the nutrition and food security clusters and other key agencies that contribute to better nutrition prevention and treatment programmes. As the lead United Nations agency responsible for addressing and preventing moderate acute malnutrition, WFP continues to maintain and build excellence in emergency and fragile settings, ensuring the direct delivery of programmes to treat and prevent malnutrition through WFP’s focus on humanitarian response. WFP works with government and partners, including the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), World Health Organization (WHO) and the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), to treat moderate acute malnutrition where needed and to maintain the continuum of care. WFP has a special role in procuring, delivering and distributing specialized nutritious foods, which are an essential component of acute malnutrition treatment programmes. Following a shock and until relevant indicators stabilize, WFP conducts emergency blanket supplementary feeding for all PBW/G and children aged 6-59 months in affected populations, complementing general food assistance. 
WFP also uses community-based nutrition centres as platforms for treating moderate acute malnutrition using a targeted supplementary feeding programme and food-based prevention of acute and chronic malnutrition. The food-based prevention programme targets the first 1,000 days of life to prevent stunting and wasting and will provide for nutrition rations for at-risk PLW/G and children under the age of five years. accompanied by context-specific nutrition-sensitive interventions targeting both women and men, such as inter-active nutrition training, community and household gardens, cooking demonstrations and 
indigenous food preservation and processing. WFP provides technical and financial support towards the generation of food and nutrition evidence to inform programme designing and advocating for resources for scale up. 
Throughout its operations, WFP will remain mindful of the critical importance of leaving no one behind, especially the most vulnerable demographics. WFP ensures that the specific needs of women and girls are sufficiently monitored and addressed, with protection and accountability staff receiving gender-specific training on issues including PSEA and GBV following the conflict. 
In conclusion, WFP continues partnering closely with the government in strengthening the country’s capacity to develop strategies and implement  programmes while scaling up high-quality nutrition interventions.

project_name: Improving WASH services in Unity State
project_objective:
The project aims to improve access to WASH services in six counties of Unity State i.e. Rubkona, Guit, Leer, Mayendit, and Koch. The project will target Returnees, IDPs, and host communities who have insufficient WASH services to meet their needs. This will reduce the risk of WASH-related morbidity and mortality among women, men, boys, and girls. This will be achieved through the repair and rehabilitation of water systems, boreholes, etc; upgradation of existing boreholes to solar water yards; drilling and equipping new boreholes; formation/revitalization of water management committees; construction/rehabilitation of sanitation facilities; health and Hygiene information dissemination; and Environmental Hygiene campaigns. 

The project will serve a total of 51,000 individuals (Female 39,617 Male 11,383).

In Rubkona / Bentiu, the project will upgrade 1 existing water point to a solar power system; repair 62 handpumps/boreholes (Koch 14, Bentiu/ Rubkona 18, Mayendit 15, Leer 15); Formation/revitalization of 77 WASH committees; Train 134 Pump Mechanics (Koch 32, Bentiu/ Rubkona 38, Mayendit 30, Leer 34); Re/training of 86 hygiene promoters; distribution of 12 standard tool kits (Koch 3, Bentiu/ Rubkona 3, Mayendit 3, Leer 3); Construction of 5 permanent institutional latrines blocks (each with 4 stances) (Koch 1, Bentiu/ Rubkona 2, Leer 2); Construction of 10 blocks of durable solution family shared-Latrines in IDP Sites A-E; Construction of 150 Household Latrines through subsidy approach, -(Koch 40, Bentiu/ Rubkona 30, Mayendit 40, Leer 40); Form and strengthen 6 school hygiene and sanitation clubs in schools; and facilitate the collection and disposal of solid waste in Sites. 

Water supply in different areas will benefit a total of 51,000 individuals. Mercy Corps will engage with the state ministry and target community at the beginning of the project to ensure that the local authority and community take the responsibility of managing the new boreholes. The Water Management Committees (WMCs) will be formed and trained to ensure routine operation and maintenance (O&M) of the hand-operated/ solar water systems. User feel will be introduced in all the water facilities to ensure constant maintenance. Water quality will be constantly monitored.

The sanitation facilities will serve a total of 7,220 individuals in different counties. The family shared latrine blocks where 5 families will share one stance will be constructed and locked. It will be the responsibility of these family members to clean and maintain the latrine block. Institutional latrines will be constructed in schools/ health facilities as per the need. The management of these institutions will also be responsible for cleaning and maintaining the sanitation facilities in their respective institutions. Household latrines will target the most needy families. A selection criterion will be developed for the beneficiaries. It will be the responsibility of the family to dig the pit while Mercy Corps will provide the slab, 4 iron sheets for lining purposes, and technical guidance in the construction of the latrine. 

Hygiene promoters will be trained to disseminate health and hygiene messages among the community members. Schools’ hygiene clubs will be formed/ Revitalized and trained on positive behavior changes. It is known that children are very good agents of behavior change and at this point they will be used to influence both at the school level and in their respective homes.

Environmental hygiene will be achieved through public campaigns which will be done through the local leaders.  Community members will be mobilized for the clean-up campaigns on a weekly basis. Tools and equipment (Brooms, Rakes, Wheelbarrows, waste collection papers (For IDPs) etc.) will be distributed to the communities to facilitate them in the collection of garbage.

project_name: Provision of Life-Saving Health and MHPSS Assistance to displaced populations, returnees and host communities in South  Sudan
project_objective:
According to the Health cluster inputs for the South Sudan Humanitarian response plan, about 8.9 million people in the country need one or more forms of humanitarian assistance, especially in the counties most affected by floods, conflicts, IDPs (Internally Displaced Persons), returnees and disease outbreaks.   Additional shocks levied by the COVID-19 pandemic and on-going epidemic disease outbreaks including measles, cholera and Hepatitis E have further stretched existing coping mechanisms and increased vulnerabilities. IOM's DTM have reported a mixed population movement owing to increasing returns of IDPs and refugees in some of the counties including Raja, Morobo and Kajokeji counties. Health service delivery for vulnerable populations remains heavily reliant on humanitarian assistance where populations remain displaced in IDP camps or far off in hard-to-reach locations due to flooding.  In 2023, IOM provided life-saving health and MHPSS support to vulnerable IDPs and host community in Abyei, Wau, Rubkhona and Malakal counties and through deployment of 9 Rapid Response Missions to crisis affected locations of Abyei, Twic, Ezo, Nagero,Raja, Renk, Yei, Morobo, Kajokeji. IOM specifically responded to the Sudan crisis by reinforcing its existing operations at the points of entries in Wau (Wau Airport), Juba (Juba International Airport), Rubkona (Panakuach PoE and Roriak PHCU), Renk( Wunthou PoE, Wunthou PHCU and Abayok PHCU) and in Malakal (Bulkat and Malakal Airport) to support South Sudanese returneses with emergency medical care, pre-departure medical screening and to provide referral services to available health facilities for patients requiring secondary level medical care. IOM specifically stepped-up vaccination at PoEs in response to on-going measles outbreaks in Sudan and continued to support health cluster efforts to prevent, detect and respond to various public health threats and emergencies at the respective PoEs. 
IOM’s HRP health project for 2024 aligns with the 3 health cluster strategic objectives to Improve equitable access to life-saving essential quality health care services, reduce excess morbidity and mortality by timely detection and coordinated response to epidemic prone diseases and Enhance resilience and promote humanitarian-development linkages to strengthen health system recovery and coping mechanisms targeting a total of  865,237 beneficiaries including 129,786 persons with disabilities so as  to continue to provide integrated emergency life-saving primary health care, including outpatient consultations, routine immunization, nutrition screening for children  under   five years, sexual reproductive health  services, clinical case management of sGBV survivors including psychosocial support while increasing surveillance and response to disease outbreaks to underserved and conflict-affected IDPs, returnees, migrants/travelers, and host communities.
IOM will provide health services through 17 static and 7 mobile clinics and 12 additional health facilities through 6 Rapid Response mission deployments ensuring to maintain its comparative advantage in rapidly deploying rapid response teams to address emerging health needs throughout the country.  MHPSS services will be provided through existing recreational and counselling centers.
IOM will focus on leveraging existing community systems for sustainable solutions and strengthening both community-based health initiatives and mental health and psychosocial support. Therefore, IOM will provide direct service delivery in partnership with the respective county health departments, while continuing to explore options of partnerships with local NGOs and CBOs towards realizing the localization agenda of the health cluster.

project_name: Provision of actionable information on population movement and evolving needs to inform evidence-based humanitarian and early recovery programming
project_objective:
The complex and dynamic humanitarian context in South Sudan requires accurate, triangulated, timely and readily accessible information. This project aims to provide the humanitarian community with well analysed and actionable data to fill existing and anticipated information gaps on displacement, returns, and general population movement across South Sudan and inform a fair and evidence-based humanitarian response delivery and early recovery programming. The main deliverables will include:
- A regularly updated IDPs and returnees baseline at location and area level. Information will include population presence, movement reasons, and needs of IDPs and returnees.
- Providing regular information on sudden displacement and return movements requiring humanitarian assistance through IOM Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) event tracking mechanism.
- Biometric data management for accountable, effective, and targeted delivery of humanitarian assistance.
- Representative Inter-Sectoral Needs Assessment (ISNA) on the household level to provide information on needs, vulnerabilities, and intentions to feed into South Sudan’s Humanitarian Response Planning (HRP) and Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO).
- Regular updates on population mobility at border points and key internal transit hubs, including displacement sites, through DTM’s flow monitoring mechanism.
- Data for Solutions to Internal Displacement (DSID) to measure progress towards durable solutions

project_name: Provision of air services to the humanitarian workers implementing projects
project_objective:
The United Nations Humanitarian Air Service (UNHAS), managed by the World Food Programme (WFP), offers safe, reliable, cost-efficient and effective passenger and light cargo transport for the wider humanitarian community to and from areas of crisis and intervention. It is the only humanitarian air service that gives access to all humanitarian entities. UNHAS responds to the need for access to the South Sudan’s most remote and challenging locations, often under precarious security conditions, where no safe surface transport or viable commercial aviation options are available.
In 2024, UNHAS is targeting to provide air transport services to 74,000 passengers and 1080 metric tons (MT) light humanitarian cargo for 234 registered humanitarian organizations to approximately 54 regularly scheduled locations in South Sudan.
The main objective of UNHAS is to continue supporting Humanitarian community with a safe, effective, cost-efficient and reliable air services. In addition to serving destinations on the fixed regular schedule, UNHAS will support 100 percent of non-scheduled location booking requests for emergencies response (security relocations, medical evacuations and Inter-Cluster Working Group Rapid Response Missions).
UNHAS requires $52,637,000 to sustain its operations across the year and continue supporting the entire humanitarian community.

Beneficiaries will receive entitlements that can be redeemed from WFP-contracted local retailers across the camps. E-vouchers provide more flexibility, dignity and greater dietary diversity for the refugees while also creating market linkages with the host community and the wider Bangladeshi economy. project_objective: La intervención está dirigida a apoyar la respuesta a emergencias a las familias mas vulnerables cuya seguridad alimentaria y nutricional se ha deteriorado debido a los efectos de diferentes choques climáticos y el efecto del fenomeno del niño que actualmente está afectando a nuestra region. project_name: Asistencia alimentaria de emergencia para personas afectadas por la inseguridad alimentaria severa en Honduras.
project_objective: El proyecto tiene como objetivo apoyar los esfuerzos del Gobierno de Honduras en el proceso de restaurar el estado de seguridad alimentaria de los territorios más afectados por eventos climáticos y disrupciones en general Mediante la ayuda alimentaria, el PMA busca promover acciones inmediatas para preservar la vida de 50,000 familias (aproximadamente 250,000 personas de 72 municipios). Son familias que ya han agotado sus reservas de alimentos y se han involucrado en mecanismos de afrontamiento negativos que representan una gran amenaza para sus vidas. Se propone una intervención integral a través de la atención complementaria de asistencia alimentaria en los municipios donde las agencias socias del clúster de Seguridad Alimentaria y Nutricional han priorizado acciones para la reactivación de medios de vida. Esto se ha logrado gracias a la coordinación del equipo humanitario de país. Las intervenciones planteadas consisten en la asistencia alimentaria a través de transferencias de efectivo en las distintas modalidades, según la capacidad de cada territorio. Así mismo se emprenderán acciones de fortalecimiento de las capacidades y de la igualdad de género para la prevención-preparación y respuesta a las emergencias. Los hogares se seleccionarán de acuerdo a los siguientes criterios: a) hogares que han perdido sus bienes, su principal fuente de ingresos, carecen de ahorros, acceso al crédito ya empleo, haciendo uso negativo de estrategias de sobrevivencia; b) hogares a cargo de mujeres o con un solo sostén familiar; c) hogares con poca o ninguna experiencia en autogestión y con una estructura organizativa deteriorada o limitada y la focalización de mujeres embarazadas y lactantes, hogares con presencia de niños menores de 2 años, ancianos y personas con condiciones de salud preexistentes y comunidades indígenas y afrodescendientes. La focalización la realizarán conjuntamente WFP, la ONG asociada para la implementación, los Comités de Emergencia Municipales (CODEM) y representantes de las comunidades.

project_name: Approvisionnement en Eau et aux services d'assainissement et Hygiène  en urgence pour les populations affectées par les conflits dans les Provinces du Logone Oriental, Mandoul et Moyen-Chari, le Mayo Kebbi Ouest et Est au Tchad
project_objective:
L’objectif principal de ce  projet et de  contribuer efficacement à améliorer de conditions de vie des personnes retournées de la RCA, les personnes déplacées (IDP's) et les communautés hots à travers l'approvisionnement en eau potable, assainissement de base et promotion des bonnes pratiques d'hygiène dans les Provinces affectées par la crise des conflits armés en République Centrafricaine, conflits intercommunautaires  et l'inondation.
En 2021, 2022 et 2023, le Tchad a continué des mouvements migratoires observés notamment au niveau des points de suivi des flux installés par l’OIM au Sud (Logone Occidental, Logone Oriental, Mandoul et Moyen-Chari, Mayo Kebbi Est, Mayo Kebbi Ouest). Selon le Cadre des résultats 2024 du Cluster WASH, 606,634 personnes déplacées seront dans le besoin d’une assistance au Sud dans les provinces prioritaires. Les personnes déplacées viennent pour la plupart de la RCA à cause des conflits armés entre les rebelles centrafricains et les conflits intercommunautaires. Les inondations de l’année 2022-2023 dans les provinces du Sud ont affecté une grande partie de la population du Mayo Kebi Ouest qui se sont retrouvées sans abris. Ces personnes étaient principalement des ressortissants tchadiens et centrafricains.
Le projet va répondre aux besoins identifiés par le Cluster WASH pour une population cible de   90 995 personnes qui représentent 15 % de la cible du cluster en assurant l'accès à un paquet d'interventions WASH pour les nouveaux déplacés, les retournés et les populations hôtes dans les 5 Provinces prioritaires au Sud.

project_name: WASH Humanitarian Response 2024
project_objective:
The overall objective of the 2024 Humanitarian program is to provide emergency response and develop resilience of affected communities, including children and women, by improving their access to quality water services as well as their capacities to withstand water borne diseases through proper sanitation and good hygiene practices.
According to the HNO 2024 an estimated 6.5 million people require humanitarian assistance in the country, including 3.2 million children. Of these, more than 3.7 million people need adequate WASH services, including 1.8 million lacking access to safe water. The program targets for 2024 are the following: - 800,000 people accessing a sufficient quantity and quality of water for drinking and domestic needs - 800,000 people accessing appropriate sanitation services - 1,000,000 people reached with handwashing and behavior change programmes.
