project_name: United Nations Humanitarian Air Service
project_objective:
As of 2023, the security situation in Burkina Faso remains a significant challenge. Since 2018, there has been a drastic deterioration, marked by the expansion and intensification of activities by non-state armed groups (NSAGs). These groups exploit pre-existing inter-communal tensions, and the situation escalated further in 2020 and 2021, resulting in a higher toll on human lives and vulnerable populations. The NSAGs are fragmented with multiple internal players, and external players linked to regional dynamics, particularly in the Central Sahel countries.
The consequences of this insecurity include massive population displacements and severe impacts on already vulnerable populations. As of October 2021, over 1.4 million people have been displaced, with new displacements reported daily. The security situation has had repercussions on the overall food and nutritional security of the country. The food security and nutritional situation have been adversely affected by the growing crisis affecting vulnerable populations.
During the 2022 lean season, an unprecedented humanitarian emergency left 2.6 million people in need of assistance, according to the Cadre Harmonisé. As of November 30, 2022, the number of registered internally displaced persons (IDPs) is 1,810,105, hosted in 299 communes spread across all 13 regions of the country. Additionally, the Analysis of the Cadre Harmonisé of November 2022 indicates that 3,533,220 people, or 16% of the total population, would be food insecure. This includes 572,382 children under 5 years of age, concentrated in regions such as East (19%), Centre-North (18%), Sahel (17%), North, and Boucle du Mouhoun (10%). These areas also correspond to localities with high security challenges.
Humanitarian access to vulnerable populations is severely restricted due to threats posed by NSAGs, counterterrorism operations, the presence of Improvised Explosive Devices (IEDs) planted on roads, and the damage or destruction of key road infrastructure, especially bridges targeted in attacks in the Sahel region. In response to these challenges, UNHAS aims to provide a safe, effective, and efficient passenger air service to the entire humanitarian community and their implementing partners, including NGOs, UN agencies, the Red Cross/Red Crescent movement, donor organizations, and diplomatic missions. UNHAS plays a crucial role in delivering assistance to hard-to-reach areas where people are the most vulnerable. UNHAS aims to provide a safe, effective, and efficient passenger and cargo air service to the entire humanitarian community and their implementing partners, principally NGOs, UN agencies, the Red Cross/Crescent movement, donor organizations, and diplomatic missions. The Logistics Cluster and UNHAS will coordinate all necessary efforts to deliver assistance to these areas where people are the most vulnerable.

project_name: Strengthening food security, nutrition and resilience of the host and Rohingya community
project_objective:
Food Security Sector (FSS) helps to strengthen the Nutrition and Health of the Rohingya refugees and the host communities of the Teknaf and Ukhiya Upazila of Cox’s Bazar district. Under the ongoing global climate crisis and rapidly changing local climate, an effective FS programme reduces climate vulnerabilities and protection risks and enhances peace and stability.
BRAC's Food Security Sector in Cox's Bazar will undertake a holistic humanitarian approach, incorporating development nexuses as the crisis has entered a protracted mode. As per sectoral objective 2, BRAC FS sector will provide support to develop the food security resilience of 20,967 Rohingya refugees in 25 camps through climate-sensitive food production in the camps. Moreover, to promote sectoral objective number 3, BRAC will work on the adjacent host communities to strengthen the food security of the 6,152 individuals in 6 unions of Ukhia and Teknaf Upazila through climate-smart agricultural production, agro-processing, creating market linkages, resilient income opportunities and disaster response preparedness with early actions. BRAC has piloted and developed a “Resilience Framework” considering its impact on host communities in Ukhiya. While developing this matrix, BRAC ensured the participation of all age and gender groups and persons with disabilities from the targeted communities. 
From the learning of responding to this crisis since 2017, BRAC will focus on sectoral integration and prioritise localisation by developing the capacity of local NGOs, CBOs, youth clubs, and government stakeholders through training and supporting them in implementation activities. BRAC will also work for land stabilisation, environmental restoration, and local awareness raising to protect the climate, natural resources and local ecology. BRAC aims to emphasise building resilience against environmental risks and hazards. The FS programme will have a contingency plan to protect and replenish agricultural products so that the affected households and individuals most adversely affected by the influx can recover and rebuild their food security and livelihoods.
25% of the project resources will be allocated for cash transfer interventions, including conditional cash transfer and cash-for-work (e.g., plantation, nursery preparation) in the host community. BRAC will aim to cover 85% of project participants to be adult females from both communities, prioritizing widows, female-headed families, transgender, LGB communities, people with long-term illnesses, GBV/SGBV victims and persons with disabilities across all age groups.

project_name: WASH Intervention for IDPs Camps and Settlements in Aleppo Governorate
project_objective:
The project aims to achieve the main goals:
Vulnerabilities of IDPs and recently war-affected populations in the Al-Bab and Jarablus districts of Aleppo are reduced through improved access to safe water and equitable access to wash facilities with the provision of personal hygiene items in emergency settings to the targeted population/IDPs, conforming to the sphere standards and local customs, taking into consideration the special needs of men, women, boys, and girls, and paying special attention to the needs of the disabled persons in the camps and informal settlements. QRC will mainstream protection for all aspects of this intervention during the project cycle.

The proposed intervention will provide life-saving integrated WASH services (safe and adequate water supply, provision and maintenance of gender-appropriate water distribution points, water quality monitoring, solid waste collection, and management, as well as the periodic distribution of hygiene items accompanied by hygiene promotion based on training for community hygiene promoters) in camps and informal settlements for IDPs displaced from Idleb, in addition to long-term IDPs living in settlements. This intervention supports the main strategic priority and matches with WASH sector objective 2 "Deliver humanitarian WASH supplies and services to the most vulnerable people." This intervention is directly supporting WASH cluster strategic objective 1 "Provide life-saving humanitarian assistance to the most vulnerable people, with emphasis on areas with high severity of needs, including those in UN-declared besieged and hard-to-reach areas."


QRC’s WASH field team intervention will provide basic WASH support to internally displaced populations who have settled in 55 camps and settlements in the Al-Bab and Jarablus districts of Aleppo. QRC’s framework for response builds on 12 months of intervention and seeks to ensure that the households residing in these settlements continue to survive in a way that respects their right to water and safety. Humanitarian actors in Syria have struggled to secure funding for informal camps and self-settlements, where conditions have continued to deteriorate as influxes continue to arrive in what remains of a haven in Syria. QRC will provide chlorinated water to 40,600 individuals in 55 camps and settlements in Al-Bab and Jarablus districts. The trucks used to transfer this water will be cleaned and chlorinated by QRC staff to prevent waterborne diseases. The water will be delivered to steel tanks (QRC will provide 1587 tanks during this intervention), which will provide a ‘water point’ in the settlement where beneficiaries will be able to access water at their convenience, decided on through discussions with the community. Each water tank can provide water to four people simultaneously, and the placement of the water tanks will reduce the waiting time and distance that people have to travel to access water. QRC will test this water (at the source, tankers, and in tanks) on an ad hoc basis to ensure it is potable.
Based on QRC's observations in camps, much-needed de-sludging will be undertaken in 50 of the camps; the total quantities will be 711 trucks (with 4500 liters as capacity), to ensure their ongoing operationality and to prevent overflow and the dangerous risk of spreading disease.
QRC will remove solid waste from 55 camps and remove the waste to landfills; this is a crucial step since much of the waste is currently dumped within proximity to the camps. QRC will distribute rubbish bins to prevent littering. QRC will distribute 9,022 Hygiene Kits in 55 camps. Important hygiene promotion will take place in gender-segregated groups, accompanied by the distribution of hygiene kits. This component contributes to the mobilization of the community, as the hygiene promoters will come from the communities themselves.

project_name: Una mirada noble al Autismo y sus fronteras, desde la practica de la risoterapia y el acompañamiento de actividades de aprendizaje socioemocionales.
project_objective:
Todo influyen significativamente en el desarrollo social e intelectual de NNA. Dentro de esta relación, es sumamente lógico que los NNA influencien a sus respectivas familias y se puede notar como ésta influencia adquiere un carácter mucho más significativo cuando el NNA tiene discapacidades y aunque el nivel de dicha influencia se relacione con factores tales como la severidad y la naturaleza del problema, cualquier discapacidad de un miembro de la familia afecta inmediatamente a la misma. La mayoría de las familias de NNA con autismo, declaran que aunque la situación les causa muchísima angustia, dolor, confusión, llanto, risa, trauma emocional, requieren de una dosis inmensa de paciencia, pero que al mismo tiempo les proporciona recompensas. A través de este proyecto se tiene como objetivo principal brindar técnicas y recursos pedagógicos  a padres, madres, responsables y docente, para lograr el bienestar socioemocional de las familias que están inmersas en el autismo o cualquier otro trastorno que afecta la salud mental.

Se pretende abarcar una población total de 2200 NNA, en edades comprendidas de 7 a 17 años, de diversos planteles educativos y/o comunidades del municipio Sucre, específicamente de las parroquias Valentín Valiente, Santa Inés y Parroquia Raúl Leoni y del municipio Cruz Salmerón Acosta, las parroquias Chacopata y Araya, siendo estos municipios priorizados desde la Autoridad Única de Salud del estado con quien ya nos hemos reunido para evaluar las necesidades.
 
En cooperación con el Observatorio Acción Educativa y Salud de Caritas Cumaná logremos integrar salud y educación para dar respuesta al proyecto, que desde las evaluaciones realizadas en las jornadas y atenciones dadas hemos obtenido como resultado que la población de NNA con necesidades especiales requiere de acompañamiento desde la salud y educación, teniendo en el estado una población de 578 NNA con autismos y 456 NNA con otras condiciones diagnosticadas desde nuestro centro observatorio y que esta ha sido confirmada desde el Centro de Atención Integral a las Personas con Autismo. El proyecto comprende tres fases, una primera fase de Evaluar y Diagnosticar  a NNA que son considerado como población flotante dentro del sistema educativo por no tener un diagnostico claro de sus necesidades intelectuales, psicológica y emocionales. Una segunda fase de intervención que basado en la evaluación y el diagnostico se establecerá un plan de actividades de ASE, tareas, estrategias y capacitaciones que desde la acción curricular de las instituciones educativas a intervenir, podamos lograr resultados favorables en el bienestar de los NNA, madres, padres, representante y docentes. Llegando a la ultima fase de acompañamiento a la familia y la concientización comunitaria para reforzar los avances logrados en las intervenciones  y descartar la estimatización de las personas por su condición. Al mismo tiempo dotar de insumos y materiales a espacio de Centros de salud y Centros educativos cercanos entre sí en los municipios ya mencionados, con el fin de fortalecer la atención integral a las enfermedades no trasmisible, como el autismo, la depresión, la ansiedad y el suicidio como trastornos mentales, buscando dar respuesta  al acceso a los servicios de salud de calidad a nivel ambulatorio y comunitario para la atención de las personas con necesidades priorizadas como son la ENT. Todo en completa comunicación con las autoridades del estado desde las distintas mesas técnicas de salud y educación.

project_name: Lifesaving Wash Emergency Response and restoration of basic WASH services to enhance resilience and to ensure equitable and sustainable access to Water and Sanitation in Syria
project_objective:
In 2024, 13.6 million people are still in need for WASH assistant all around the country according to HNO 2024, 5.5 million are displaced, including 2 million who live in last resort site.

Twelve years of crisis coupled with fragile environment (droughts) followed by the earthquake in February 2023 and its consequences, WASH needs remain critical and vital.

UNICEF through this project will support repair and rehabilitation of critical parts of water supply and sewerage systems, that witnessed destruction and deteriorated dramatically during the past 12 years, several criteria will be used for the project identification and selection, including cost per participant, level of project complexity, neutrality, accessibility, severity scale, number of returnees, number of IDPs, quality and quantity of water, and sanitation services currently available. At the same time UNICEF is supporting the usage of alternative power sources such as solar power for rehabilitated WASH systems to ensure longer term sustainable restoration for water services, power supply sector is at its worst since 2011. so, WASH interventions must consider power component to ensure systems functionality. UNICEF will also support the procurement of Sodium Hypochlorite countrywide as a preventive measure against AWD including cholera.
UNICEF will continue providing life-saving WASH interventions, as well as distributing supplies of non-food items related to WASH to the most vulnerable population in Syria. in lights of continuous internal displacement, also plans and preparation actions and contingency planning will also be maintained at a high level, together with stocks of necessary materials for responding rapidly to changing needs if access becomes more difficult or mass displacements occur in the northwest and/or northeast Syria.

Also, UNICEF will continue to ensure high level of coordination with major humanitarian actors and relevant stakeholders and advocacy efforts to respond to sector needs and reinforced sectoral and intersectoral coordination.  

Humanitarian assistance is provided and coordinated between large variety of actors on the ground, operating from within Syria, Gaziantep, and NES with WoS, ensuring compliant strategies and responses are applied.
UNICEF as the sector lead agency, is working to ensure that sectoral coordination is practiced and applied at hubs levels and WoS. 

PSEA strategy: 
As part of the core commitment to children in humanitarian actions, UNICEF will continue strengthen the internal system, partners’ capacity, and networking with other actors to ensure the effectiveness of our PSEA programming. in 2024 PSEA strategic priorities are: safe and accessible reporting, accountability and investigation, quality and accessible survivor assistance and capacity building to humanitarian community members. 

Protection Risk Analysis: 
 -Water distribution is not safe or accessible, especially for women, girls, children, the elderly, and people with disabilities (likelihood: low) mitigation in place: Consult separately girls, boys, women and men, including older people and those with disabilities in the assessment, design, and implementation phases to ensure that the distance of water collection points remains at a minimum distance. 
Ensure the accessibility of collective and low GBV risks WASH facilities to people with disabilities and promote gender-sensitive hygiene
messages/actions. Train partners and contractors on the Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse. Also, UNICEF includes the standard mitigation measures in all design for the water tank, filling points and sanitation blocks by engaging women with the process of selecting the location, pavement of the roads, increase lighting and visibility in locations where females will approach.

project_name: Integrated Social Protection Programme for Children with Disabilities – Cash Transfer, Referral and Case Management Services.
project_objective:
Families and children across Syria are sliding deeper into poverty and finding it overwhelmingly difficult to make ends meet. Over 13 years of conflict have plagued Syria into deeper poverty, stemming from multiple crises: armed conflict; the loss of human capital; the economic and financial downturn; the severe water crisis; continued food insecurity; the consequences of the Ukraine- Russian war; health emergencies such as Covid-19 and cholera; and the devastating February earthquake. 
The humanitarian situation in Syria continues to deteriorate, with an estimate 16.7 million people in need of humanitarian assistance in 2024. The economy is back at the level where it was in the mid-1990s, and some child development indicators have fallen back to the level they were over three decades ago. 
Poverty is invading the country, with basic services and other critical infrastructure are on the brink of collapse. UNICEF’s State Budget Brief 2023 showed that public expenditures continue to fall in real terms. Compared to the pre-conflict level, the budget is less than one-quarter of its 2011 level. Foreign aid is becoming increasingly important in Syria, with aid in the health sector is now slightly higher than the government allocations and is now four times larger than government allocations to the water and sanitation sector. 
These multiple crises are affecting overly the most vulnerable people, including families of children with severe disabilities. The MSNA conducted in 2022 showed that households headed by a member with a disability were more likely to report being unable to meet their basic needs compared with other households, this applies to all population groups in all governorates in Syria. In addition to insufficient income, households with members with disabilities reported spending 50 per cent more on health care and medical expenses compared to other households. More importantly, and because of barriers and subsequent inequalities, households with members with disabilities resort to more negative coping mechanisms than others. Children living with severe disabilities are now the most socially and economically vulnerable group in Syria. UNICEF is implementing the Integrated Social Protection Programme for Children with Disabilities. It provides an integrated response to the needs of children with disabilities through the combination of regular and unconditional cash transfers with case management services. It is the largest social protection intervention in Syria. The intervention promotes an integrated social protection model with links to public services, with a view to prepare the ground for a future transition from an emergency response to a nationally owned social protection scheme. Since 2016, over 40,000 CWD in eight governorates have been reached.it enhances the resilience of the most vulnerable families and strengthens the continuum of humanitarian and early recovery intervention through an integrated response, to facilitate the referral of CWD to available social services and increase their social inclusion. For a 24-month period, families of CWD receive a regular quarterly transfer of US$ 40 per month or US$ 120 per quarter. Each child is followed throughout the period by a dedicated and trained case manager. While the cash help families meet the basic needs of children and the households, the case management component facilitate the referral of CWD to available social services, increase their social inclusion and respond to their specific protection concerns. In 2024, UNICEF aims to reach 25,000 CWD and their families with regular cash transfer and case management services in ten governorates Dier-ez-Zor; Hassakeh; Aleppo; Hama; Homs; Rural Damascus, as Sweida, Qunaitera Lattakia and Tartous. Accountability to beneficiaries’ is ensure through 2 main channels: centralized redress and grievance mechanisms; and regular post-distribution monitoring surveys.

project_name: Enhancing Employability and Humanitarian Micro-Enterprises (HME)
project_objective: As HNO 2024,16.7 million people(50% female)are in need for assistance across Syria,up from 15.3 million in 2023. the 12 years of crisis have led to negative impacts on all aspectst of life,such as,high inflation,currency depreciation,and increase in commodity prices.This continued to exacerbate the level of vulnerability of millions of people, and lack of access to services.The Aga Khan Foundation in Syria(AKF) community-based Humanitarian Micro-Enterprises(HME) approach has been proven as a sustainable model of establishing and developing local micro-enterprises,and an effective tool to build resilient livelihoods,that is achieved through the blended-finance modality(grants with micro-loans).AKF aims to adopt this approach to support entrepreneurs in Salamieh and Mesyaf districts,Hama governorate by supporting them with financial grants and micro-loans from the First Micro-Finance Bank (FMFB), a sister agency of AKF, so they can purchase enterprise-related assets, or solar-energy systems that will promote green solutions.This is accomplished by the standard rubric for implementing activities:1)Form Local Consultation Group(LCG) representatives of local community to review criteria, develop  registration application, and engage in decision-making.2)Conduct a Rapid Needs Assessment(RNA) for the market’s of professions.3)Conduct training courses for 300 business owners on topics about entrepreneurship, business management, market analysis.4)Assess the business plans of the candidates with the Grants Review Committee(GRC) 5)Support 150 final beneficiaries with blended-financing and mentorship services.Protection Risk Analysis:•Collaps of social cohesion Likelihood:Low. Impact: Medium. AKF will ensure diversity by targeting various groups in coordination with CBOs and stakeholders.•Gender-related norms may limit women's participation in some works. Likelihood: Medium. Impact: Medium. AKF will ensure the participation of all community groups in awareness sessions on gender, social roles. AKF will ensure that female beneficiaries are comfortable by choosing what they prefer. AKF will maintain regular monitoring of women working environment and activate feedback and complaint mechanism which provide updates on the implementation and reduce barriers.•LNGOs accused of bias in selecting beneficiaries, Likelihood: High, Impact: Medium. AKF will manage the selection process to ensure precise implementation based on the selection criteria. PSEA:AKF is committed to safeguarding including Prevention from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) and has its Global Safeguarding Manual. HME will develop a specific Risk’ Register (RR) to identify SEA risks and develop relevant mitigation measures to reduce the likelihoods and the impact of the risks on the beneficiaries, especially children and vulnerable adults. RR will be reviewed and examined frequently to evaluate the residual risks and modify the procedures accordingly. AKF has responding measures in place to address SEA cases including speak-up channels, reporting mechanisms, case management, investigation procedures, and disciplinary process that adopt the approach of “Zero Tolerance’’. AKF has developed specific methods and procedures to mainstream Safeguarding, including PSEA, into its all processes and operations including, but not limited to, Recruitment, Contracting, Procurement and Partnerships in order to decrease the risks of SEA incidents and enhance the culture of PSEA during dealing and contracting with partners, individuals, and community groups and members. A mandatory Safeguarding/PSEA training and refresh sessions will be provided to staff, service providers, volunteers and associated members.All staff, volunteers, vendors, contractors and service providers will sign Code of Conduct which outlining the expected behaviors. AKF adopts the Survivor-Focused Approach to consider the survivor’s wishes, safety, and well-being to be a priority in all matters and procedures.

project_name: Provision of life saving assistance and environment to survivors and/or victims of GBV through prevention, risk mitigation and response services in Akobo, Juba and Wau Counties of Jonglei, Central Equatoria and Western Bahr el Ghazal States of South Sudan.
project_objective:
This project will target 14,000 persons (2,800 men, 3,920 women, 3,500 boys and 3,780 girls), which is further broken down into 7,000 IDPs, 2,800 host communities and 4,200 returnees, with a main focus on protection analysis and advocacy and reducing the sufferings of gender-based violence (GBV) survivors. For the purposes of ensuring an in-depth understanding of protection environment, allowing for appropriate prevention and response activities, Nile Hope (NH) will focus on protection data collection and analysis. This is to say that, NH will ensure that protection concerns are captured and highlighted in toolkits such as assessment reports, monitoring reports and protection snapshots, therefore, allowing for appropriate and relevant advocacy with the national cluster, humanitarian partners and other relevant stakeholders. 

In order to ensure that appropriate and principled actions are taken to prevent and respond to protection risks or concerns, NH will ensure that this project is centered on both individual and community level by ensuring evidence-based interventions. During the implementation of this project, NH will promote partnership with the affected communities through already established and function community structures including vulnerable groups and individuals, with the aim of identifying protection risks and coping strategies, community and individual intentions and resilience amongst the affected population. Notably, these activities will enhance communities’ and at risk individuals’ preparedness and resilience. Moreover, NH will work closely with communities’ protection watch groups/committees, facilitate focus group discussions, awareness raising and training on basic human rights and protection mainstreaming, with an aim of preventing and mitigating identified protection risks. 

Needless to say, NH will provide timely, coordinated, and complimentary protection responses based on the identified protection needs. Most important to realize, is that protection will be central to all interventions which will include service mapping, safe referrals, individual protection assistance for at-risk individuals, information sharing, awareness raising on fundamental human rights and protection mainstreaming. To ensure that this objective is achieved, the project will integrate with other sectors including S/NFIs, FSL, WASH, Education, Nutrition, Health and Peace Building Programs. Furthermore, the project will primarily focus on ensure that the safety and dignity persons and communities affected by displacement are prioritized and a do-no-harm approach is mainstreamed during all aspects of the implementation. 

Out of the 14,000 persons that this intervention seeks, 1000 persons will be people with disabilities. The project will target most vulnerable Households which includes old people and persons with disabilities. An overall percentage of 10% is allocated to catering for persons living with disabilities. Older persons and persons with disabilities (PWD) will be considered at the decision-making level to ensure their needs and issues affecting them are brought forward. The registration and distribution sites will be chosen considering the challenges affecting PWD and older people. They will be near, safe, and accessible for all. Localized methods and approaches will be developed to ensure that the old and disabled people are considered not to miss out on any topic. The PDM tools, other data collection tools and sample size will also consider the inclusion of the marginalized groups and 3% out of the 10% sample size will be allocated to them when collecting data. This will also ensure their feedback and or complaint is included.

project_name: Providing Mental Health and Psycho Social Support to Conflict Affected Children in the North West and South West regions of Cameroon.
project_objective: The outbreak of the anglophone crisis on the 6th of October 2016 has led to the massive displacement of over 700000 people from rural areas (UN News.org 2021) mostly women and children. This continues crisis has led to multiple deaths, witnessed by children exposing them to risks such as Mental Health and Psycho Social distress, and other protection risks hindering the successful transition of these children from childhood to adulthood. It is due to this emergency situation that the Martin Luther King Jr Memorial Foundation seeks to implement a project titled “Providing Mental Health and Psychosocial Support to Conflict Affected Children in the North West and South West regions of Cameroon by establishing 2 Child Friendly Spaces per communities in 20 project communities in the divisions of Manyu, Meme, Boyo, Ngoktunja, Fako and Lebialem where by the project will be owned and implemented by community.  Therefore selected community based agents will be trained on how to provide adequate MHPSS through and provide other services. This project will thus be geared towards building the resilience of these affected children and facilitating their successful transition to adulthood, targeting a total 5600 children for a period of 12 months that is 35 children (5-17 years old) per child friendly space (CFS), with 2 CFS for 20 project communities, renewable every 3 months.

project_name: Conflict-affected households in North Syria provided with access to sufficient and safe WASH services and improved hygiene conditions
project_objective:
Mercy Corps (MC) will respond to priority needs with life-saving and life-sustaining WASH assistance across the governorates of Al-Hasakeh, Aleppo, Ar-Raqqa, Deir-ez-Zor and Idleb - Across both Northeast and Northwest Syria. 

Informed by a multi-sectoral needs assessment conducted in September in 2023 on WASH needs at WoS level, MC will work on improving access to basic Water and sanitation services through the delivery of water trucking, SWM, Desludging and the rehabilitation of water supply infrastructure in IDP locations and areas with a high number of IDPs and returnees, and areas we anticipate significant inward displacement (Ar-Raqqa and DEZ, Dana, Daret Azza and Atareb in Idleb and north Aleppo). In NW, MC will continue providing a full WASH package camps and IDP sites, which includes Cholera related interventions, Water Quality monitoring and treatment and hygiene education. Hygiene education, using carefully tailored messages, and the distribution of hygiene kits will complement the other WASH interventions. Through ongoing Coordination with WASH cluster, working groups, local councils and other agencies, MC will be coordinating its response in relation to the gaps identified and associated needs. In 2024, a special focus will be given by MC to seek solutions for operation and maintenance (O&M), through support to local committees and water authorities directly after the completion of water supply rehabilitation. MC will work actively to identify and implement water trucking sustainable solutions and cost efficient sanitation management in the targeted IDP locations. Internal water supply networks, water tanks and toilets will complement more comprehensive HH shelter activities, providing safe and dignified accommodation standards for displaced  and for those who have chosen to return. MC will also distribute multi-purpose cash assistance to conflict-affected households based on regional SMEB values, which include hygiene items.

project_name: Mejora del acceso a la salud, nutrición y protección en comunidades vulnerables de Bolívar, Miranda y Amazonas
project_objective:
El objetivo del proyecto es mejorar el acceso a la salud, WASH en comunidades vulnerables y de difícil acceso en el estado Bolívar, Miranda y Amazonas, priorizando la atención de población indígena, mujeres embarazadas y lactantes, y niños. El proyecto se presenta como una intervención multisectorial en la cual el centro de salud es el elemento vertebrador en el que se realizan actividades (atenciones en salud primara , SMI y SSR) y desde el que parten  actividades hacia la comunidad (intervenciones en atención primaria principalmente).

La selección de centros de salud y comunidades se hará en base a 4 criterios principales: refuerzo de capacidades en atención primaria; trabajo en centros de salud que, independientemente de su tamaño, sean de referencia para varias comunidades y tengan una gran área de cobertura; trabajo en centros que hayan sido seleccionados por las autoridades sanitarias como lugares priorizados y la intervención en infraestructura (ASH incluyendo gestión de residuos, AEE) debe representar un cambio notable en la capacidad de atención en salud del centro.  Para esta identificación se han empleado herramientas del sector como el WASH Fit y entrevistas semiestructuras a informantes clave (representantes de los centros, de las comunidades y representantes del Ministerio de Salud).

De esta manera, el proyecto apoyará a 30 centros de salud y beneficiará a 30 comunidades, con personal, insumos, equipos y rehabilitaciones, brindará servicios como atención primaria, salud reproductiva, manejo clínico de la violación (CMR) e inmunización. El proyecto también capacitará a promotores de salud comunitarios para que realicen sesiones de concientización y derivaciones sobre diversos temas de salud, como enfermedades transmisibles (EC), enfermedades no transmisibles (ENT), infecciones de transmisión sexual (ITS), planificación familiar. Acceso a agua potable, buenas prácticas de higiene, alimentación de lactantes y niños pequeños (IYCF), nutrición materna y de personas mayores.

Se realizarán intervenciones integrales en los centros de salud con la instalación/rehabilitación de sistemas de agua, la rehabilitación de salas de baño (pocetas, lavamanos y duchas) y fosos sépticos existentes o la construcción de sistemas sépticos biodigestores, la rehabilitación de sistemas eléctricos o la instalación de sistemas FV en los lugares con graves dificultades de acceso a la energía, además del desarrollo de planes de gestión de residuos y la construcción de áreas para el almacenamiento y tratamiento de los mismos (incluye incinerador, fosos para cenizas y punzocortantes, triturador de vidrios, área de lavado de contenedores y otros); promoción y la prevención de infecciones a través de la creación/reactivación de comités ASH/PCI el  tratamiento, desinfección y almacenamiento seguro del agua además de las prácticas de higiene adecuadas a nivel hospitalario y comunitario.

project_name: Providing access to quality education for children in Syria.
project_objective:
PUI targets children and youth in vulnerable and underserved communities to enhance their access to quality education in a protective and suitable learning environment. The educational intervention of PUI provides non-formal education programs to help children and youth in Syria integrate/return to formal education and continue their academic attainment.  This proposed intervention aims at encouraging out-of-school children and dropped-out students to resume their education through tailored Back to Learning Campaigns, in addition to empowering those children with Self-Learning Program to enable them to catch-up and reintegrate in the formal education system. PUI will also assist children by providing them with kits, education supplies and Remedial Classes to cover for any gaps and ensure every child’s educational needs are met. Quality of education will further be enhanced by providing capacity building activities to teachers and school staff, training them on Active Learning, psycho-Social Support, and Life Skills. Moreover, PUI will ensure that children have access to safe and protective learning environment by rehabilitating damaged schools in the targeted locations and by initiating Parenting Awareness Campaign for parents and caregivers. The light rehabilitation of the schools will provide pupils with education facilities, promoting the safety and well-being of students, teachers and administration, while the Awareness campaign will contribute to a safer and more inclusive environment for students. The comprehensive strategy developed by PUI will have a direct impact on both access and quality of education, contributing to enable children’s full potential. More specifically, access will be increased by rehabilitating schools and by targeting OOSC and CwD while quality will be improved by teacher trainings and remedial classes.  PUI formulates its intervention at the local level, in close collaboration with local authorities such as the Directorate of Education, as well as the local communities. 

PUI policies and operational guidelines align with IASC's Commitments to Accountability to Affected Populations. PUI ensures accountability by placing affected populations at the center of all decisions and actions that affect their lives. Thus, targeted populations will be involved throughout all phases of the project to feed into the design of the interventions and guide the identification of both activities and beneficiaries based on PUI’s selection criteria.  PUI’s field team will inform the community and beneficiaries about the Beneficiary Feedback Mechanism (BFM) to address any issues related to PUI’s intervention. PUI’s MEAL department will ensure timely management of all feedback received and that an accurate response of what has been done by PUI is provided to the people who shared them within a suitable time frame. In addition, PUI’s MEAL department will independently monitor all activities and will conduct post-implementation/distribution monitoring when needed.  Finally, PUI aims to build a program to meet the needs of girls, boys, women and men living in targeted locations, taking into consideration vulnerabilities, to enhance their access to basic services, foster their self-sufficiency, but also promote social cohesion while ensuring that the program would have no negative side effects and that the risk for girls, boys, women and men to be exposed to any kind of risk when accessing assistance would be mitigated. All PUI staff are regularly trained on the organization’s strategy for Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA), Child Protection Policy, and Code of Conduct. Awareness sessions will be conducted for the community (including parents, teachers and children) to educate them about PSEA and Child Protection. Gender and Protection will be mainstreamed within this intervention, with gender, disability and age-sensitive school rehabilitations and a focus on equal access to education.

project_name: Construyendo Resiliencia: empoderamiento local para la gestión del riesgo en Sucre
project_objective:
En Venezuela, 80% de la población reside en zonas de alto riesgo sísmico, enfrentando el edo. Sucre particularmente una alta microsismicidad, que afecta a Cumaná y Cariaco debido a la falla de El Pilar. Las condiciones físicas, socioeconómicas y geológicas, junto con la falta de personal y recursos, agravan la situación. Los servicios esenciales y la agricultura, principal fuente económica, se concentran en las zonas más afectadas, siendo Sucre, Ribero y Güiria los municipios más amenazados (con severidad N°3 según el Clúster AEE); y Ribero, Andrés Mata y Montes los más vulnerables en acceso a servicios esenciales seguros y dignos. La respuesta a emergencias carece de enfoque de género, edad y protección; lo que se suma a: falta de capacitación, replicación limitada de acciones de Cariaco, debilidad en la aplicación de herramientas de identificación y evaluación de amenazas y resiliencia comunitaria, y falta de infraestructura sísmica resistente. RET.
A partir del conocimiento de la realidad de la zona en la cual operamos desde 2021 (con proyectos multisectorial dirigidos a atender necesidades básicas de las familias en situación de vulnerabilidad), y la sólida experiencia de RET a nivel Regional en la mitigación de riesgos y gestión de desastres, se plantea una intervención en el marco del triple nexo con el objetivo de establecer directrices para la implementación de planes de prevención, mitigación y respuesta a emergencias, atendiendo las diversas necesidades, capacidades, vulnerabilidades, prioridades y riesgos presentes en la comunidad, para ofrecer una respuesta efectiva e inclusiva. Se promoverá prácticas de mayor calidad y pertinencia, mejorando la eficacia de la respuesta en su conjunto, mediante el trabajo conjunto entre RET y las autoridades locales de protección y prevención para la identificación y evaluación de riesgo, con enfoque diferenciado de género, edad y diversidad; centradas en los planes de prevención, mitigación y respuesta a emergencia; involucrando a jóvenes de las comunidades priorizadas a través de la conformación de brigadas juveniles; y creando una red de voluntarios con conocimiento, entrenamiento y práctica en primeros auxilios, evacuación y control de incendios. Se evaluará la resiliencia comunitaria ante desastres y se establecerá planes de acción específicos para fortalecer esa resiliencia. Se desarrollará herramientas didácticas, mesas técnicas, mapas de riesgo comunitarios y Sistemas de Alerta Temprana; dotando, además, de lámparas solares en calles y portátiles comunitarios, y rehabilitando espacios seguros comunitarios y educativos con enfoque diferenciado de género, edad y diversidad.
La población meta del proyecto son 3.351 beneficiarios (559 niñas, 526 niños, 1.225 mujeres, 1.041 hombres): Ribero 1.751, Montes 865, Andrés Mata 485 y Sucre 250. De ellos, 335 NNA y adultos con discapacidad y 670 del pueblo Kariña, contribuyendo en 70,7 % al valor meta de los indicadores planteados en el Clúster de AEE.
Teoría del Cambio: Si los miembros del Cuerpo de Bomberos y de Protección Civil y Administración de Desastres son capacitados en normas de convivencia, código de conducta y resiliencia comunitaria, y son dotados de equipos, insumos y materiales didácticos, se puede generar un impacto que se extienda a comunidades y escuelas. Si estas cuentan con espacios seguros para eventos socio naturales y se organizan en Brigadas de Riesgo con acceso a equipos tecnológicos de comunicación, iluminación y kits de energías alternativas, se logra un nivel adicional de preparación. Como resultado, se espera que estas comunidades y escuelas se vuelvan más resilientes, se fortalezca sus capacidades en la prevención y gestión de riesgos, se minimice la desproporción en la afectación a niñas, mujeres y personas genero- diversas durante las crisis, y se incremente el empoderamiento mediante la Rendición de Cuentas y mecanismos de retroalimentación.

project_name: Food and Livelihoods in Crisis For Affected Communities in Unity and Warrap State
project_objective:
Mercy Corps’ Food Security and Livelihoods in Crisis For Affected Communities in Unity and Warrap State intends to impact the most vulnerable internally displaced persons (IDPs), returnees, and host individuals by alleviating stressed populations of hunger and enabling resilient opportunities for communities facing extreme climate and economic crises. The project aligns with Objectives 1, 2 and 3 of enhancing and sustaining emergency food production while reducing dependency and increasing households’ resilience to shocks, according to the HRP and Cluster’s focuses.

The project aims to complement traditional food assistance and livelihoods through resilience using Mercy Corps’ Market Systems Development (MSD) in Crisis approach, a framework used to enable proper food production, inclusive market access, and equitable livelihood opportunities. Food Security and Livelihoods in Crisis for Affected Communities will focus and impact communities in Unity and Warrap State which are classified as Priority 1, 2, and 3, aligning with the Humanitarian Response Plan’s (HRP) intersectional coordination of response and needs. Among the communities most affected include Rubkona, Koch, Leer, Guit, Mayendit, Panyijiar and Tonj South which are the targeted areas of Mercy Corps’ HRP plan that will enhance the food security and livelihoods of extremely vulnerable persons.

Mercy Corps’ approach to Food Security and Livelihoods using an MSD in Crisis framework is tried and tested in South Sudan with programs like Mercy Corps’ Strengthening Resilience in Agriculture, Livelihoods and Markets Through Local Institutions (STREAM) which enhanced the food security of over 6,350 households through increased market access, agricultural production, and off- and non-farm livelihood opportunities. By STREAM’s first phase endline report, households feeling the impact of hunger reduced while the percentages of increased access to income-generating opportunities increased across all sites in Greater Mundri, Western Equatoria, and Koch, Unity State; the outcomes greatly improved when compared to the baseline assessments which saw high-stress levels of hunger, extreme losses of crops, and unprecedented rates of unemployment in vulnerable communities.

By using MSD in Crisis and lessons learned through STREAM, among other programs, Mercy Corps expects to reach IPC- 3 and 4 rated communities in Unity and Warrap State, using modalities involving Cash, Economic Recovery in Markets through linkages, livelihood growth, agriculture production, seed system security, and value-chain development. Ultimately, the purpose of Food Security and Livelihoods in Crisis for Displaced Communities is to decrease hunger, diversify and develop income-generating opportunities, and enable resilience to occur in environments of crisis in Unity and Warrap State.

project_name: Optimizing legal protection and enjoyment of HLP rights for crisis-affected populations in the Far North, North West and South West regions of Cameroon.
project_objective:
The project seeks to increase the capacity of conflict-affected populations in the North West, South West and Far North regions to prevent and resolve HLP disputes. This will be achieved through the provision of legal protection services to 20,000 individuals to improve knowledge on HLP rights and procedures and increase the ability to advocate and protect rights of displacement-affected individuals.  
In the Far North, the project will target IDPs, returnees, out-of-camp refugees and vulnerable host community members whereas in the NWSW, same groups of people will be targeted except for refugees. In all activities, NRC will prioritize women and girls, elderly persons and persons living with disabilities as they are disproportionally facing protection risks linked to their HLP rights. 
Information on HLP rights, responsibilities and remedies will be provided to all crisis-affected persons in the project locations irrespective of sex, religion, ethnicity, and displacement status. Persons having difficulty in accessing housing, land, and property, and especially those at risk of forced eviction will receive individual legal assistance to ensure they can exercise the HLP rights and secure their assets. Geographic location for information sessions will be defined based on data collected through multisectoral needs assessments, HNO, partners and local authorities. 
Returnees will be accompanied in re-accessing land through close collaboration with administrative and local authorities. Local partners, community and traditional leaders will play a key role in contributing to social cohesion among displaced and host populations. Local authorities and traditional leaders with a special emphasis on women leaders will be at the forefront of conflict resolution using collaborative dispute resolution methods (e.g. mediation). The regional and divisional delegations of the Ministries of both State Property and Land Affairs, and Social Affairs, Ministry of Agriculture, will provide technical support to these structures and ensure that they respect existing laws and policies.
Workshops will be organized to enhance the capacities of local and traditional authorities, women and youth leaders, and humanitarian actors  participating in existing conflict prevention/resolution mechanisms based on the Collaborative Dispute Resolution (CDR) approach and associated tools. 
As co-lead of the HLP AoR, NRC will leverage this project to enhance the coordination of HLP interventions with partners and other clusters, including in the organization of monthly meetings, sharing of updates and joint advocacy with partners.   
The ultimate outcome of the project is a greater enjoyment of HLP rights and increased security of tenure for the affected populations.

project_name: Child and Youth Education Pathways for Vulnerable Populations Affected by Conflict and Displacement in Syria
project_objective:
The education sector in Syria faces severe challenges exacerbated by an earthquake in February 2023, leading to a 4% increase in the education sector's PIN. This crisis has left 2.4 million children out of school, with 1.6 million at risk of dropping out. The earthquake's aftermath poses additional risks, including increased child early marriage, child labor, and psychological distress among children. Women-headed households, already struggling, report an inability to meet basic needs. 
The Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) presents a comprehensive Education Intervention as part of our integrated response in Syria. In collaboration with NRC’s Information Counselling and Legal Assistance (ICLA)/Capacity building, Shelter, WASH, and Livelihoods and Food Security (LFS) programs, this initiative aims to address the urgent needs of conflict- and displacement-affected populations, providing pathways to durable solutions. The proposed interventions align with the HRP strategic objectives 1 and 3.
Expected outcomes of NRC’s interventions include Increased enrollment and retention of conflict-affected children and youths in formal and non-formal education settings, enhanced skills and knowledge for teachers, facilitators, and trainers, Improved learning environments through rehabilitation works and greater community involvement and awareness. These interventions will target conflict and displacement-affected children and youths, including persons with disabilities, Syrian IDPs, IDPs and refugee returnees, host community members, third country nationals, and Iraqi refugees. Teachers, facilitators, and trainers across formal and non-formal education settings. Equal access to male and female educators, promoting positive male role models will be put into consideration. 
NRC’s Child and Youth education interventions aim to. 
• Deliver pathways back to learning, integration into formal education, and skills expansion for employment. 
• Implement Child Education Pathways (CEP) and Youth Education Pathways (YEP) programs with a focus on Emergency, Transition, and Recovery modalities. 
• Target newly displaced and returnee children and youths in emergency response. 
• Address long-term displacement challenges for out-of-school children and youths in transitional response.
• Target vulnerable populations in post-conflict and stabilized settings during recovery activities. 
The proposed interventions are broadly categorized as follows;
a. Education Programs:
- Child Education Pathways (CEP): Transition, Remedial, Basic Literacy, and Numeracy. 
- Youth Education Pathways (YEP): Transition, Employability, Basic Literacy, and Numeracy.
- Creating Welcoming Schools program with soft and hard components. 
b. Teacher Training:
- Adapted from INEE Teachers in Crisis Context. 
- NRC’s Better Learning Program for psychosocial support. 
- Integration of UNICEF’s “Ready to go back: Teacher preparedness Training Package.” 
c. Rehabilitation Works:
- Rehabilitation of WASH facilities, learning spaces, and provision of basic furniture.
- Adherence to protection standards, ensuring gender separation.
- Installation of solar systems to address energy challenges. 
d. Parental Engagement:
- Civil documentation not required for assistance. 
- Parental engagement through awareness campaigns.
- Establishment of Parents and Teachers Associations. 
NRC’s Education Intervention in Syria addresses the immediate and long-term challenges in the education sector, providing holistic support to conflict-affected children and youths. Through integrated programs, teacher training, and infrastructure rehabilitation, this initiative aims to rebuild educational pathways and contribute to the overall resilience and recovery of the affected population.
Education programming is primarily implemented by NRC. In exceptional circumstances, select Education activities may involve partner implementation for anonymity reasons.

project_name: Provision of WASH assistance to vulnerable populations affected by conflict and displacement in Syria
project_objective:
The crisis in Syria remains a complex humanitarian and protection emergency. According to the Global Peace Index (GPI, 2023), Syria remains the third least peaceful country in the world with 16.7 million people, including 5.5 million displaced and 2 million in last resort sites (HNO, 2024). The earthquake in February 2023 resulted in widespread damage, further impacting already vulnerable populations. It also worsened infrastructure challenges including limited access to basic services, damaged water treatment plants, pumping stations, elevated tanks, and electricity shortages affecting critical services.
The Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC)'s Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) intervention in Syria aims to deliver humanitarian supplies and services to the most vulnerable population by ensuring continuous water supply and restoration, sanitation, solid waste management and sewage systems support. The project contributes to HRP Objectives 1 and 3 and to sector objectives 1, 3 and 4.
Targeting: The project will target vulnerable conflict and displacement-affected populations, including IDPs, refugees, host communities, and returnees, with a focus on prioritizing the most vulnerable households. Prioritization will be based on vulnerability indexes shared by OCHA and the WASH sector, with detailed needs assessments conducted. 
NRC will undertake direct implementation, with geographical targeting based on needs severity, inter-agency coordination, and access considerations. The WASH Project components will include:
Emergency Response: Provision of temporary WASH services (including water trucking), household assets (Hygiene NFIs), support to Education in Emergencies i.e WASH services for temporary learning spaces) and Hygiene promotion activities. NRC has prepositioned hygiene kits to ensure a quick response in case of emergency. This stock is part of the internal emergency response plan NRC has, which aims to ensure the required surge capacity in case of an onset emergency.
Medium-term Support: Provision of WASH infrastructure and services in camps and communal shelters. Distribution of hygiene items in camps and settlements. Long-term Improvements: Rehabilitation of community WASH infrastructure (boreholes, solar energy systems, water and sewage networks, solid waste management). Rehabilitation of WASH facilities in institutions (schools, medical centers). Rehabilitation of household WASH facilities and provision of water storage units. Community Engagement: Consultation through FGDs, HHQs, KIIs, with a focus on accessibility for all and functional complaint and feedback mechanisms (CFMs). 
Sustainability Approach: Investment in sustainable, long-term WASH service provision, reducing reliance on short-term emergency solutions. 
The main focus of activities implemented by NRC will be around sustainable water and sanitation system rehabilitations, prioritizing coordination with local authorities, installing solar systems to address energy challenges and reduce running costs and Hygiene Kit Provision.
