project_name: Common Transport Services for Humanitarian Partners in South Sudan
project_objective:
The Common Transport Services (CTS) is a free-for-user service that transports key
humanitarian supplies on behalf of humanitarian actors. CTS serves as a critical link in
the supply chain, enabling products and materials that arrive from regional and
international suppliers to move onwards to partners located deep in the field rapidly. IOM
has been managing the CTS on behalf of the Logistics Cluster since 2011. During this
time, the project has significantly grown from delivering 2,000 MT of humanitarian cargo
in 2011 to a total of 18000 MT by the end of 2022, making a yearly average of 25000 MT
since the beginning, highlighting the increase in the use of road transport as the most
cost-efficient mode of transportation as access improves. IOM has continued to maintain
flexibility and adaptability to the operating environment in South Sudan. Through CTS,
IOM works with more than 100 unique agencies in key operational locations in Jonglei,
Unity, and Greater Upper Nile Region, in Humanitarian Logistics Hubs (Malakal, Bentiu),
and Bor, Juba, and Wau. IOM will maintain heavy vehicles and transport cargo
from the main ports of dispatch via air, road, and river including LC beyond responses and
will continue support for common warehouse management in key operational locations.
Through the effective management of the CTS, IOM aims to support organizations'
preparedness measures to mitigate risks associated with increased insecurity,
looting/theft of humanitarian supplies, critical access impediments to vulnerable people,
and reduce expensive air and road transport costs, which ultimately supports the timely
response to the needs of the affected populations. With this funding, IOM will directly
work with 100 plus humanitarian organizations located in different areas, enabling them
to deliver critical life-saving humanitarian services and assistance items.

project_name: Addressing Protection and GBV Risks and Mitigating and Resolving HLP disputes in Crisis-Affected Areas of South Sudan
project_objective:
This IOM project contributes to the achievement of all three Protection Cluster Objectives and the core GBV AoR and HLP AoR priorities. IOM’s Protection, Gender Equality and Inclusion Unit will implement protection, disability inclusion and GBV programs across South Sudan to address the needs of South Sudanese individuals (including returnees, IDPs and host communities) who have experienced or are at risk of experiencing protection violations, including GBV. The project seeks to build resilience among the most vulnerable, including women, children, persons with disabilities and the elderly, among others, to reduce their vulnerabilities. IOM will work to achieve these aims by implementing GBV prevention programs, mitigating protection and GBV risks across multisectoral interventions and addressing the violations experienced by vulnerable members of the community through protection and GBV response services. The project will include provision of individual protection cash assistance (IPA) to those facing protection risks or those who have survived protection violations. The project will also continue raising awareness on protection and conducting protection monitoring in hotspots of both conflict and climatic shocks. Building on longstanding relations with South Sudan OPDs, and in line with the IASC Guidelines for Inclusion of Persons with Disabilities in Humanitarian Action and the Must Do Actions defined therein, IOM will implement robust disability inclusion programming, including OPD capacity building and direct assistance to persons with disabilities. IOM DTM products will improve availability of quantitative data on IDPs and returnees, disaggregated by disability via the Washington Group Questions, while findings from barriers and facilitators assessments and KIIs with persons with disabilities will further inform inclusion efforts. IOM will contribute to strengthening the humanitarian response to GBV through building humanitarian staff capacity to implement GBV prevention, risk mitigation and response programming based on the Interagency GBV minimum standards. IOM will also join interagency service mapping and development of referral pathways.   In all, IOM aims to support more than 240,000 individuals (44,000 girls; 44,000 boys; 80,000 women; 76,000 men) with core protection and GBV awareness and support services. These interventions will target IDPs, host communities and returnees, including those who have fled the conflict in Sudan.
Committed to full implementation of the PSEA National Action Plan, IOM will have a range of dedicated PSEA activities, including, inter alia, SEA risk assessments and implementation of mitigation measures, review of high-risk areas and processes, orientation and training of staff, dialogues with staff aimed at addressing attitudes, and community engagement and awareness raising, as well as the operationalization of field-level PSEA taskforces and community-based complaints mechanisms.
The IOM HLP component will implement due diligence processes for any activities that are linked to land and property in order to safeguard the communities’ and the agencies’ rights and mitigate and prevent HLP issues. Since HLP is one of the core grassroots issues in South Sudan and one of the main drivers of conflict country wide, working with the government, traditional authorities and the communities is key. IOM will focus on building the technical capacity of government officials and traditional authorities on HLP best practices and alternative dispute resolution (ADR) mechanisms. IOM will also raise awareness in communities on HLP rights and ADR, in addition to identifying HLP needs and providing needed support services, such as tailored counselling, legal assistance, legal drafting of agreements and accompaniment for concerned entities and other related HLP assistance.

project_name: Empowering vulnerable communities with safe shelter and NFI support to foster resilience, dignity, and self-reliance
project_objective:
South Sudan faces a critical humanitarian crisis, with conflict, floods, and natural disasters displacing thousands of people. These displaced individuals are in urgent need of shelter and non-food items (NFIs) to secure their basic needs and improve their living conditions. Upper Nile, Unity, and Jonglei are the most severely affected regions.

IOM will continue to provide comprehensive and timely response to the 238,639 conflict and flood-affected displaced and returnee populations from the SNFI Cluster prioritized locations. This response will include:

Maintaining a mobile team for emergency response: IOM will continue to maintain a dedicated team of over 25 staff members for Shelter and NFI mobile and static response in the country. This team will ensure that they can be swiftly deployed to any location within 72 hours in the event of an emergency, particularly in situations where no other partners are available to respond to S-NFI needs.

Conducting needs assessments: IOM will conduct comprehensive needs assessments to understand the specific needs and vulnerabilities of each displaced group. The need assessment will ensure that assistance is tailored to the specific needs of each community and that potential negative impacts of the response are mitigated.
Distributing shelter and NFIs: IOM will provide a range of shelter and NFI assistance, including in-kind items such as plastic sheeting, ropes, cooking pots, kangas, solar lamps, and blankets. IOM will also provide cash and voucher assistance to enable households to purchase essential items.
Providing durable shelter solutions: In 2024, IOM seeks to implement innovative and sustainable shelter solutions that are culturally appropriate and adapted to the local climate. This will include the use of local materials and techniques, as well as promoting disaster risk reduction (DRR) measures.
Improving conditions in camps and camp-like settings: IOM will work to enhance the living conditions of displaced people residing in camps and camp-like settings. This includes shelter maintenance and shelter repair.
Coordinating with partners: IOM will continue to collaborate closely with other humanitarian organizations to ensure a coordinated and effective response to the crisis. The collaboration will include sharing information, coordinating distributions, and advocating for joint integrated multisectoral responses.
Support to Sout Sudan returnees: IOM will continue to provide shelter, in kind and cash support to returnees affected by the Sudan conflict. This includes constructing transitional shelters for returnees and providing them with in kind support.
Ensuring robust monitoring and evaluation: IOM will ensure robust monitoring and evaluation of its ongoing programs to improve program quality and accountability to affected people. This monitoring will include rapid, post, and continuous remote monitoring using the latest tools. IOM will continue to shares lessons learned and challenges with partners and updates its Activity Info dashboard.

Integrating HLP principles: IOM will continue to integrating HLP principles into its programming, conducting thorough risk assessments, and advocating for joint integrated multisectoral responses. Recognizing the sensitive nature of S-NFI activities, IOM will undertake gender-sensitive, protection-sensitive, and conflict-sensitive risk assessments and analyses prior to any activities to ensure adherence to the Do No Harm principles.
IOM's comprehensive approach to addressing shelter and NFI needs in South Sudan is guided by a commitment to providing timely, equitable, and effective assistance to the country's displaced and returnee populations. Through its strong presence, expertise, and partnerships, IOM will continue to play a crucial role in improving the lives of thousands of people affected by conflict and displacement.

project_name: Provision of life saving child protection services to children and families affected by the conflict in Sudan
project_objective: Sudan is faced with one of the worst humanitarian disasters in human history, with multiple protection issues driven by disease, epidemic and violation of human rights by state and non-state actors. Children and women are the most affected. OCHA estimates that 4.85 million people are internally displaced in Sudan. The country has the highest number of child displacements, with a total of 3.2 million children living in IDP camps and host communities.  Children have not been spared from grave child rights violations. At least 79 per cent of grave child rights violations verified since the conflict began involved the killing and maiming of children, while 8 per cent of grave child rights violations verified since the conflict began involved sexual violence against children. This is recorded from accessible communities, and the overall situation could be worse than what is reported.  A breakdown in social service delivery due to unpaid social workers and government officials has left vulnerable children, especially unaccompanied and separated children, exposed to abuse and exploitation. Lack of livelihoods and the weathering away of the traditional social support network triggered recourse to negative coping mechanisms, deepening the suffering faced by children. UNICEF and its partners aim to stop the suffering of 368,000 children by providing child protection services and preventing recourse to negative coping mechanisms. The deteriorating mental health and psychosocial support needs will be met through structured and semi-structured psychosocial support interventions in fixed and mobile safe spaces. Identification of unaccompanied and separated children and provision of alternative care such as placement in foster care, group homes and family reunification will be the core of the programme. Risks of killing and maiming by remnants of war and unexploded ordinances will be reduced by delivering child-friendly messages that build children's and caregivers' knowledge of prevention techniques. Child survivors of rape and sexual violence will receive medical care, livelihood support, safe housing, and mental health support through direct support and referral to specialised services. To ensure accountability to affected communities, reporting mechanisms will be set up in the communities. Communities will receive PSEA training on reporting to ensure an end to the misuse of power by humanitarian workers.

project_name: To provide for every child uninterrupted and sustainable learning and skills development opportunities in safe and accessible environment
project_objective:
The conflict created massive displacement, with over 6.1 million people forced to leave their homes in search of safety elsewhere. To date, 3 million children are displaced making Sudan the country with the highest number of displaced children globally. In addition, 19 million are not in school. To date, only one state (River Nile state) managed to reopen schools for the academic year (2023 – 2024), with eight other non-conflict states struggling to announce a date for schools reopening. Leading factors to the ministry of education inability to reopen schools includes the use of school grounds by displaced population, and the government inability to pay teachers’ salaries consistently since April 2023. Nearly 9% of schools countrywide are either used to shelter displaced populations in receiving states or occupied by armed groups in conflict affected states. 
UNICEF humanitarian response project for 2024 aims to enable 1,681,627 (1,008,976 girls, 672,651 boys) children to access formal and non-formal education opportunities, including early learning. A cornerstone of the response is the establishment of safe learning spaces (MAKANNA), to enable girls and boys, especially the displaced to access lifesaving and life-sustaining learning, skills, and education opportunities. Access to formal and non-formal learning spaces activities aims to be inclusive and targets 168,163 (100,898 girls) children. Furthermore, the project will aim to equip 1,177,139 (706,283 girls, 470,856 boys) children with essential education supplies, including 117,714 children (70,628 girls) with disabilities. The interventions will include supporting local partners and the Ministries of education in safe states where schools are reopened for the remaining of the 2023 – 2024 & and the next academic years. Another element of the project is the provision of technical assistance, coordination, and capacity building to local partners, MoEs, education personnel, and communities to open schools and learning centers, where is safe to do so, and to sustain their operation.
In line with the strategic objectives of the HRP 2024 (SO2 & SO3), UNICEF project will aim to provide 1,681,627 (1,008,976 girls, 672,651 boys) children with Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) training through their learning programmes in schools and safe learning spaces. As well as engage 134,530 (80,718 girls) young people in adolescents led activities on skills development, recreational and learning activities. 
The purpose of the UNICEF education HRP project is to provide for every child uninterrupted and sustainable learning and education opportunities in safe and accessible environment. UNICEF education response will build of engagement of children, caregivers and communities in the design and preparedness of all interventions. The project will integrate protection activities, accountability to the affected populations and reporting mechanisms for protection and sexual exploitation and abuse.

project_name: UNICEF: Lifesaving nutrition preventive and curative interventions targeting most vulnerable population across Sudan
project_objective:
The malnutrition situation in Sudan remains dire with an expected increase in the number of children with acute malnutrition due to the deteriorating nutrition determinants as result of the ongoing catastrophic humanitarian crisis. The nutrition sector estimates that 4.7 million children under five and pregnant and lactating women are acutely malnourished and in need humanitarian assistance in 2024.

Through this project, UNICEF aims to (1) increase equitable access to an integrated lifesaving and preventive nutrition services focusing more on the “1000- day window”- as a critical opportunity to prevent child wasting and stunting among under five children, (2) improve early detection of acute malnutrition (3) improve access to quality lifesaving nutrition services to treat severe acute malnutrition among under-five children. UNICEF will target all states in the country with more focus on hotspots and IDP hosting states through scaling up integrated lifesaving nutrition preventive and curative services.

The preventive package includes iron-folate supplementation for pregnant and lactating women, maternal, infant and young child feeding nutrition (MIYCN) counseling and support for pregnant and lactating women. The package for under five children includes the provision of micronutrient supplements, Growth Monitoring and Promotion, as well as deworming. Overall, 1.4 million pregnant and lactating women, and over 4.9 million under five will be targeted with the preventive package. Additionally, UNICEF will support the provision of cash transfers to 150,000 of the poorest pregnant women and caregivers of children under-two to help eliminate the financial barriers that women and children may experience in accessing nutritious diets and essential nutrition services. UNICEF will ensure more focus on IYCF-E interventions as part of emergency preparedness and response, with intensive advocacy and orientations to mobilize humanitarian partners to protect and support infant feeding in the emergency context.

UNICEF will strengthen early detection and referral of children suffering from wasting. The key strategy will be large-scale integrated nutrition campaigns through house-to-house modality to significantly scale up the early identification, referral, and management of acutely malnourished children, in addition to integrating it with other preventive services such as micronutrient supplementation for children and women. Through this, 4.9 million children under five will be targeted with early detection of wasting and referral activities. 

UNICEF will work toward the expansion of the geographical coverage of the treatment programme for severe acute malnutrition through the establishment of fixed and mobile sites to reach the planned target of 539,858 children under five suffering from SAM, representing 75 per cent of children under five with SAM in 2024. As part of this, UNICEF will continue working closely with WFP and WHO to ensure the complementarity and continuum of care among the three levels of management for acute malnutrition program. Different strategies will be implemented including (i) maintaining functionality and expanding coverage of OTPs to deliver lifesaving nutrition services and (ii) supporting mobile clinics to reach displaced, hard-to-reach communities with lifesaving nutrition services, and (iii) Expanding active case finding.  Additionally, UNICEF will support evidence generation through implementing SMART surveys.  

To support the implementation of integrated preventive and curative nutrition services UNICEF will:
•Secure the pipeline of all essential preventive and curative nutrition supplies to prevent and treat children with malnutrition. 
•Expand the partnerships with various stakeholders across the country.   
•Strengthen the health system through efforts to strengthen supply chain management, nutrition information systems, monitoring, frontline nutrition workers payment and capacity building.

project_name: Intervención humanitaria de WASH para reducir la desnutrición aguda en Huehuetenango
project_objective:
El proyecto se centra en brindar asistencia humanitaria para abordar las necesidades urgentes de WASH (Agua, Saneamiento e Higiene) en los municipios de Santa Cruz Barillas, Santa Eulalia, San Juan Ixcoy, Aguacatán y Huehuetenango del departamento de Huehuetenango. Estos municipios se enfrentan a una grave situación de desnutrición aguda en donde la falta y deficiencia de servicios de Agua, Saneamiento e Higiene son factores claves que contribuyen a la desnutrición de niños y niñas de la primera infancia. El proyecto atenderá a 88,355 personas pertenecientes a los grupos más vulnerables, incluyendo mujeres, niñas y niños. La información de base del HNO, INFORM (2022) y otras fuentes como la línea de base de la Gran Cruzada Nacional por la Nutrición, se utilizaron para evidenciar la severidad de la situación y tomar estas medidas de urgencia en esta área. 
 
Global Communitties y UNICEF enfocará la respuesta de manera urgente en 5 municipios de Huehuetenango en donde las intervenciones estarán enfocadas en: Rehabilitar sistemas de agua, implementar sistemas de tratamiento del agua a nivel comunitario y de hogar, desarrollar procesos de entrenamiento rápido para la práctica de hábitos higiénicos y sistemas de saneamiento para bloquear las rutas de contaminación feco-oral para contribuir en la reducción de casos de desnutrición aguda. 

Además, se rehabilitará los módulos de WASH en establecimientos de salud para facilitar la atención a la población afectada en la región de cobertura. Se coordinará y complementará esfuerzos y actividades a nivel departamental y municipal con diferentes instancias como la Coordinadora Nacional para la Reducción de Desastres (CONRED), Ministerio de Salud Pública y Asistencia Social (MSPAS) y otras instancias representadas en Huehuetenango y así fortalecer sus capacidades en la respuesta a emergencias.

project_name: Renforcement de la prevention et la prise en charge de la malnutrition aiguë sévère chez les enfants âgés de moins de 5 ans au Niger
project_objective:
L'UNICEF s'engage à intensifier ses interventions humanitaires en 2024, en mettant l'accent sur plusieurs objectifs stratégiques. Ces actions visent à renforcer la réponse aux urgences, en accordant une attention particulière à la coordination aux niveaux central et décentralisé. En parallèle, elles cherchent à accroître les capacités des acteurs aux  niveaux opérationnels, en se concentrant sur le dépistage précoce, le référencement, la prise en charge des enfants souffrant de malnutrition aiguë sévère, et la promotion de l'alimentation du nourrisson et du jeune enfant (ANJE) dans les contextes d'urgence, la préparation et la réponse aux urgences.
Un axe crucial sera le renforcement de la chaîne d'approvisionnement en intrants nutritionnels, comprenant les aliments thérapeutiques prêts à l'emploi (ATPE), les laits thérapeutiques, les médicaments du traitement systématiques de la malnutrition aigue sévère, les équipements et les matériels anthropométriques. En parallèle, l'organisation s'engage à soutenir le fonctionnement du système d'information sanitaire (DHIS 2), l’analyse, l’exploitation des données et à superviser étroitement la mise en œuvre des interventions.
Dans une approche multisectorielle, l'UNICEF collaborera étroitement avec la Santé, la Sécurité Alimentaire/Moyens d'Existence, la Protection, et l'Eau/l'Hygiène/l'Assainissement. L'objectif est d'optimiser la synergie des interventions, assurant ainsi un impact plus significatif sur les bénéficiaires. Cette collaboration multisectorielle vise spécifiquement à réduire l'incidence des cas de malnutrition aiguë sévère au sein des communautés, en mettant l'accent sur la prévention et une prise en charge précoce et adéquate des cas de malnutrition.
Au cœur de cette stratégie préventive réside l'engagement communautaire. L'UNICEF reconnaît que la participation active des communautés dans la préparation, la mise en œuvre et le suivi des interventions est essentielle pour garantir leur succès à long terme. Dans cette perspective, les ménages joueront un rôle central dans la détection précoce des enfants malnutris grâce à l'approche PB/Famille. De plus, ils seront sensibilisés sur les mesures à prendre en cas d'identification d'enfants souffrant de malnutrition aiguë. Les Agents de Santé Communautaire, en tant que relais locaux, seront également activement impliqués dans la mise en œuvre des activités de prévention du changement de comportement au sein des communautés.
Pour garantir la transparence l'UNICEF adoptera des mécanismes de partage d'informations robustes. Les réponses aux feedbacks communautaires seront communiquées de manière ouverte  lors de réunions communautaires régulières.                                                                                                                                   La collaboration avec d'autres acteurs sera facilitée par l'établissement de plateformes de coordination formelles. Des réunions régulières, des échanges d'informations et des protocoles d'échange de données garantiront une coordination fluide entre les organisations, tout en respectant les normes de confidentialité et de protection des données.
Les nouvelles informations et la mises en œuvre de nouvelles strategies seront également partagés à travers une variété de canaux.

project_name: Renforcer la gestion des sites et collecte de données pour comprendre les besoins des retournés tchadiens déplacés par la crise du Soudan
project_objective: Ce projet vise à soutenir les activités d'enregistrement en cours ainsi que les évaluations des sites et des villages et les enquêtes sur les intentions de retour, afin de fournir à la communauté humanitaire et aux décideurs des informations actualisées sur les besoins et les vulnérabilités des rapatriés à Ouaddai et Sila. Sur la base de ces informations, et conformément à l'un des principaux besoins signalés par les rapatriés, l'OIM apportera son soutien en fournissant aux rapatriés nouvellement arrivés des abris transitoires et en soutenant les mécanismes de gestion des sites.

project_name: Prosperamos, Fortalecimiento de la resiliencia de las familias vulnerables en Honduras
project_objective:
Sobre la base de casi 60 años de brindar asistencia humanitaria y de desarrollo en Honduras, incluidas las iniciativas actuales apoyadas por BHA, CRS ha diseñado "Prosperamos, Fortalecimiento de la resiliencia de las familias vulnerables en Honduras", una intervención de 36 meses con el objetivo de apoyar a los hogares vulnerables afectados por desastres en la Zona Norte (Cortés y Santa Bárbara) y el Corredor Seco (La Paz e Intibucá) para recuperarse de los impactos de los desastres recientes, vivir con seguridad y dignidad, y mejorar su resiliencia a los riesgos relacionados con el clima.
Prosperamos pretende beneficiar un total de 5,000 familias y 22,500 individuos con transferencias monetarias y WASH.

project_name: -	Respuesta alimentaria y nutricional a necesidades urgentes de familias vulnerables afectadas por eventos climáticos en parte de región de corredor seco y Gracias a Dios
project_objective: Este proyecto tiene como objetivo articular una respuesta humanitaria que contribuya a mejorar las condiciones de seguridad alimentaria y el estado nutricional de familias afectas por la sequía en los departamentos de La Paz y Lempira. Esto se perseguirá a través de tres estrategias principales, a saber: 1) Para región de corredor seco: transferencias monetarias multipropósito y no condicionadas: se realizarán transferencias de efectivo, siguiendo criterios de necesidad, y observando estricto respeto de las elecciones y la dignidad de las familias en situación de vulnerabilidad, promoviendo sus capacidades y autonomía  para que sean agentes de cambio en su propia recuperación, promoviendo con ello la restauración y sostenibilidad de los medios de vida bajo los enfoques de género, edad y diversidad. ; 2) Para región corredor seco y Gracias a Dios: capacitaciones sobre temas nutricionales: se proveerá información y entrenamiento a las familias vulnerables para promover cambios de comportamiento y decisiones adecuadas en materia de nutrición y manejo de recursos alimenticios; 3)    actividades de fortalecimiento de la gobernanza local para corredor seco y Gracias a Dios: se dinamizarán los sistemas de retroalimentación comunitario, promoviendo la rendición de cuentas a las comunidades afectadas e integrando participantes del gobierno local, cooperantes y población de la comunidad bajo un enfoque de género, edad y diversidad,   y apoyando a los grupos comunitarios y gobiernos locales en la adopción, uso efectivo y mantenimiento de Sistemas de Alerta Temprana (SAT). 4. Asistencia alimentaria y medios de vida apoyados para poblaciones de Gracias a Dios afectadas por los eventos climáticos.

project_name: Assistance  agricole d'urgence pour soutenir les moyens d'existence des populations vulnérables dans les 7 régions du Niger.
project_objective:
Le projet vise à contribuer à l'amélioration des moyens d'existence des populations affectées par les chocs  naturelles et anthropiques dans 7 régions du Niger notamment les  régionss de Diffa, Tillabéri, Tahoua, Maradi, Zindier, Dosso et Agadez. Le projet touchera 84 009 ménages  en semence pluviale et outils agricoles, la  réhabilitaion de 4500 ha, l'appui en semence de contre saison de 30 ménages et l'appui en AGR pour transformation agro alimentaire des 4000 femmes.  D'après les analyses de la campagne pluviale 2023, la production  céréalière 2023 est  en baisse de 14% par rapport à l’année 2022 et de 4% par rapport à la moyenne des cinq dernières années. Selon les données d'analyse du cadre harmonisé de novembre 2023, pendant la période d'octobre à décembre 2023, 2.318.639 personnes, soit 8,87% de la population du Niger (contre 1.044.331 personnes en  Novembre 2022) seront en insécurité alimentaire sévère (crise et plus) dont 42 921 personnes en urgence alimentaire. Cette situation se déteriorerait en période de soudure 2024 pour atteindre 3 231 825 personnes qui seraient en insécurité alimentaire sévère soit 12,36% de la population totale (crise et plus) contre 2 872 278 personnes pour la soudure 2023 . 
Les ménages seront appuyés en semences de mil et niébé pour la saison pluviale, et en semences irriguées pour la contresaison. Chaque ménage recevra en cultures pluviales 10 kg de mil et 5 kg de niébé  et en cultures irriguées 40 g de semences potagères (tomate, chou, laitue, carotte) et 5 kg de maïs. Pour la contre-saison des appuis en intrants agricoles  pour les cultures irriguées seront distribués à 30 000 ménages. Au moins 10 % des bénéficiaires d’intrants agricoles pour la campagne hivernale seront les femmes cheffes de ménages. Les  femmes seront concernées par les activités génératrices des revenus.

project_name: Mozambique logistics cluster
project_objective: The Northern provinces of Mozambique continue to be confronted with insecurity leading to continued displacements of men, women and children. Logistical access within Cabo Delgado, the epicenter of the insecurity is expected to remain a challenge. The advent of the rainy & drought   season will exacerbate the tenuous situation in some of the more remote locations. Logistical support also requires to be expended to other provinces of displacement including Niassa and Nampula provinces in northern Mozambique to where of the displacement has taken place.

project_name: Quality equitable and inclusive education for crisis affected Rohingya and host community children, adolescents and youth in Cox’s Bazar District.
project_objective:
UNICEF will provide access to and deliver quality, inclusive and equitable early childhood development, pre-primary, primary and secondary education, and skills development opportunities for 283,500 children (50% girls) refugee crisis-affected children and adolescents aged 3-18 years in the camps and 2,160 in Teknaf and Ukhyia upazilas of Cox’s Bazar District. 

UNICEF will implement Myanmar formal education curriculum for kindergarten to grade 10 as well as ALP for the over-aged learners, when appropriate, by working with implementing partners (IPs) on learners’ enrolment, attendance, transition of learners to the next grade, and teachers capacity development as well as community engagement. 4,096 learning facilities (LFs) will provide access to the necessary teaching and learning materials. 

For inclusive education, UNICEF, in partnership with Humanity Inclusion, will ensure inclusive practices are mainstreamed by providing services directly to children, capacitating partners, teachers and the community, Rohingya disability volunteers will be assigned per camp, teachers will receive pedagogy training for working with children with disabilities, model LCs will be established to serve as examples as well as a policy for children with moderate disabilities will be developed. 
For equitable education, UNICEF will mainstream gender-responsive education activities through capacity development of key stakeholders, teacher training on gender-responsive pedagogy, and strategies for improving the attendance of adolescent female learners (AFL). Access to education for AFL will be facilitated by providing gender-segregated classes for which female Rohingya volunteers will be assigned; they will walk with the AFLs to and from the LCs and attend classes with them. 

For quality education, teacher professional development (TPD) programs will be implemented for teachers and master trainers (MTs) to teach the Myanmar curriculum for KG to grade 10. Teachers from KG to grade 10 will receive grade and subject-specific TPD to improve pedagogical skills and content knowledge. Teachers will also be enrolled in language courses and general pedagogy training and receive PSEA, Child Safeguarding, and DRR training. Mentor teachers and master trainers will be available to guide and support teachers further. For learning assessment, teachers will receive training to conduct formative assessments during the year, and children in grade 3 and higher will be given summative exams for transition to the next grade. A record of learning will be provided for enrolled children upon completion of the school year. The use of technology for education (T4E) will support taking attendance and recording learning assessment data, TPD and support teachers with interactive audio lessons based on the Myanmar curriculum.

Community engagement will continue with Rohingya caregivers and the community education support groups (CESGs), who will be established per cluster per sector guidance to meet monthly. The Rohingya caregivers, the CEGSs, and implementing partners (IP) staff will receive training on PSEA, Child Safeguarding, gender and girls’ education, disability and inclusive education, and DRR. Capacity development of IP staff will also include training on data management to meet the Data Quality Assessment standards for reliability and integrity. 

UNICEF will implement skill programmes for out-of-school (OOS) adolescents through cross-sectoral interventions in Multi-Purpose Centres; those aged 15 to 18 years will have access to Lifeskills as well as literacy and numeracy courses. 

In the host communities of Teknaf and Ukhyia, UNICEF will support 2160 adolescents, including those with disabilities, in accessing vocational skills.

project_name: Sustainable and quality WASH services for Rohingya Refugees and most  vulnerable populations in Ukhia and Teknaf Upazila of Cox’s Bazar District, Bangladesh
project_objective:
The overall aim of this project is to contribute to improving the overall health, well-being, gender equality and resilience of Rohingya Refugees and vulnerable people in host communities of Cox’s Bazar District.  In the Rohingya camps, the project will continue to support routine repair, operation, and maintenance of existing piped water supply systems and hand pump wells.  In addition, new water network supply systems will be constructed and upgraded to cover gaps and enhance the resilience of the facilities against extreme weather events.  The capacity and performance of water networks and handpumps will be assessed and improved. UNICEF will transit from supporting quarterly water quality  monitoring/surveillance through DPHE to engage its partners  testing  water-networks more frequently than tube-wells.
 The project will support operations, maintenance and improvement of existing latrine and bathing spaces to ensure functionality, quality, safety, and privacy and address the needs of women, girls, Persons with Disabilities (PwD), older adults and other vulnerable people in the camps.  The project will upgrade latrines and bathing facilities to ensure inclusive access for women, girls, older adults, children, and persons with disability.  New latrines, solid waste, and (Fecal Sludge Management ( FSM) sites will be constructed to fill critical gaps, while efforts will be made to improve FSM effluent quality in all camps.  In line with the approved FSM strategy, UNICEF will endeavour to review and reduce the number of  FSTP in few camps to minimize the operational cost. The operation and maintenance of Solid waste management sites will be supported, while the project will strengthen integration with nutrition and livelihood for the use of compost.  House-to-house waste collection will be scaled up in all eight camps. UNICEF will assess the cost and efficiency of plastic recycling plants for continuation.    With the funding cuts, this project will focus on community engagement for behaviour change and sustainability of WASH services.: The participatory approaches such as CCCPLTH (Clean Camp Campaign-People Let Total Hygiene) and RANAS (Risk, Attitudes, Norms, Abilities and Self-Regulation) will be supported for changing identified high-risk behaviours.  The project will continue working and engaging community WASH structures/groups to maintain WASH services.  The project will work with other sectors for the harmonization and rationalization of the engagement of volunteers.  UNICEF will support participatory community monitoring and feedback mechanisms to contribute to AAP (Accountability to Affected Populations).  Gender, GVB and Disability inclusion will be mainstreamed in all interventions.  The project will support the provision of WASH supplies such as soap, Aquatab and MHM materials and emergency stock of WASH supplies.  
 
UNICEF will implement WASH services for host community people to strengthen humanitarian, development and peace nexus.  Actions include community approach for total sanitation (CATS) and Sanitation Marketing (SanMark) for creating open defecation free (ODF) and water safe communities as well as private sector development.  Facilitating hygiene promotion for improving personal behaviour and environmental health is an integral action in the project.  The project supports WASH in Institutes (school & health) following a 3-star approach and WASH Fit.  As Cox’s Bazar is historically climate threatened, the project will support emergency coordination, assessment, planning, and responses as an integral part of the overall districtwide WASH programme.  The project will also support WASH emergency preparedness and response, mainly targeting extremely poor adjacent host communities.  As part of system strengthening, the project will support government counterparts and local government on evidence generation, WASH planning, demonstration of good practices, monitoring, reporting and capacity building.

project_name: Provision of preventive and curative nutrition interventions for Rohingya children, women, adolescents, and vulnerable host populations in Bangladesh
project_objective:
Rohingya camp: In 2024, UNICEF will continue effective treatment of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) and preventive nutrition services to reduce the risk of mortality and morbidity among children under five, pregnant and lactating women (PLW) across 26 integrated nutrition facilities (INFs) in 19 camps. UNICEF will also be responsible for nutrition supply chain management including procurement, distribution, and monitoring of supplies such as RUTF for SAM treatment in 14 UNHCR-supported camps. A total of 12,175 children with SAM (745,3 in UNICEF and 4,722 in UNHCR supported camps) will therefore be admitted and treated. Children identified with medical complications will be treated in stabilization centers, that will be integrated into primary healthcare centers in 2024. Nutrition interventions are also implemented at the community, and household level using trained community nutrition volunteers who conduct house visits for active case identification of children with SAM.  
UNICEF’s nutrition universal premise is that prevention comes first, in all contexts. When efforts to prevent fall short, early detection and treatment of children with acute malnutrition is a must. UNICEF is strengthening preventive services especially to protect and promote appropriate maternal nutrition and infant and young child feeding (IYCF) and caring practices. The caregivers of children under two years of age are screened to identify needs for counseling and support by trained IYCF counselors. 
Moreover, UNICEF supports community-based nutrition activities such as nutrition awareness sessions with mother-to-mother support groups, sensitizations, cooking demonstrations, and Mukhe Bhat sessions.  Monthly growth monitoring and promotion (GMP) sessions are conducted in all the INFs. Community mobilization activities are conducted by trained volunteers including follow-up visits with an emphasis on absentees, defaulters, and non-responders from treatment. To further promote early stimulation and positive parenting, early childhood care and development (ECCD) activities are integrated targeting children 0-3 years old are integrated into the INFs.  Iron folic supplementation (IFA) and nutrition education are provided to pregnant women and the adolescent for the prevention of anemia. Furthermore, homestead gardening is promoted to increase access to diversified and nutritious diets. 
 The existing Emergency Preparedness Response Plan (EPRP) will be revised to reflect the current needs, and partners trained to tackle any unanticipated weather incidents including fire outbreaks. All nutrition centers will be equipped with disability-friendly facilities including access during monsoon.  The service providers will be trained on disability inclusion, child safeguarding, the prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse and messages displayed in the INFs. Furthermore, the existing comprehensive complaint and feedback mechanism and referral linkage will continue to be strengthened by the agency as per approved mapping in the camps.
Host Community:  To ensure quality nutrition services, Upazila nutrition supervisors, counselors deployed in Upazila health complexes and the union health and family welfare centers as well as frontline service providers will be trained, and essential nutrition supplies provided for the prevention and treatment of malnutrition. Community engagement activities include support for mother/caregivers on improving the quality of complementary foods through cooking demonstrations and Mukhe bhaat ceremonies. Furthermore, UNICEF will continue collaborating with the Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE), the Department of Livestock Services (DLS), and local NGOs to build the capacities of households on homestead gardening and poultry rearing for improved access to diversified diets.

project_name: Quality,  integrated and equitable health service delivery and effective coverage  to support the health and well-being of children under 5 years and their mothers, including those infected and affected by HIV through strengthening the district and upazila health systems, in Rohingya Refugee Camps and Host Communities affected by the Rohingya Crisis
project_objective: UNICEF will provide support to ensure equitable quality and gender sensitive maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health and immunization services as well as provision of sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services including counselling and referral for GBV and support to pregnant and lactating women (inclusive of children with HIV) with inclusion of people with disabilities. The project will focus and ensure adherence with the Minimum Package of Essential Health services for primary health care in PHCs in Rohingya camps, and comprehensive newborn care support. UNICEF work with other partners both in health sector and other sectors to ensure integrated health services are provided. The project will target 555,820 direct beneficiaries (493,186 refugees and 62,634 people in host communities). The project will be implemented in 6  health facilities in the camps (6 PHCs ) and strengthen newborn health care in the camp through newborn technical sub-committee coordination,  government health system and the health facilities in adjacent host communities in Ukhiya and Teknaf (2 union sub centres and 16 community clinics). Following the 2022 Rationalization exercise in the health sector, and further agreements with the SAG, UNICEF will work in 6 PHCs, in camps 5, 8W, 10, 16, 17 and 18. Health posts in Camp 3 and 18 will be closed by December 2023, while Health Post in Camp 16 is almost ready to be upgraded to PHC as per plan, and will be operational in January 2024  to provide 24/7 maternal and newborn care. A special focus will continue to support well functional Newborn Stabilization Unit (NSU) with Kangaroo Mother care, across all the Upazila health complexes, Special Newborn Care unit (SCANU) at the district hospital. UNICEF will continue to play her leading role in supporting vaccine logistic and supply and ensure vaccine availability in all service provision sites in all the camps and host communities in Cox's bazar district. UNICEF will continue to provide technical support, supply and transportation of vaccines and logistic and enhance cold chain capacity and advocacy and social mobilization for strengthening immunization services across all the camps. UNICEF will continue to strengthen the Health Management Information System (HMIS/DHIS2/OpenSRP/OpenMRS) through deployment of technical staff to the office of the Civil Surgeon and build the capacity of service providers on HMIS and support the government in rolling out the e-tracker for improve data collection and monitoring on immunization and maternal health services and reduce zero dose. UNICEF has developed emergency response plan to ensure better preparedness and respond to emergency and disasters including strengthening Infection Prevention and Control measures in all the supported health facilities and support the scale up of outbreak related vaccinations including COVID 19 vaccination program in the camps and host communities. UNICEF will ensure risk communication and community engagement for the promotion of preventive behaviour for disease prevention and mobilize communities to increase uptake of routine immunization, capacity building of front-line workers on communication skills for the strengthening of continuum of care for health services (MNCAH) and managing disinformation related to disease outbreaks through engagement with communities and key social influencers

project_name: Fourniture d’assistance  Humanitaire de Protection aux populations affectées par la crise dans les régions de la Boucle du Mouhoun, des Cascades, Centre Nord, Centre-Est,de l’Est,  Nord et du Sahel
project_objective: L’UNICEF continue de contribuer à la réponse à la crise humanitaire que connait le Burkina Faso. Dans le secteur de la Protection de l’Enfant Unicef est à la fois Agence lead et acteur de dernier recours, son rôle est important tant dans la réponse que dans la coordination. Ce projet vise à renforcer le système de protection et de prise en charge y compris la promotion des droits des filles et garçons (incluant les enfants en situation de handicap) victimes et susceptibles d’être victimes d’actes de violences, d’abus, d’exploitations et de négligences dans les zones affectées par la crise humanitaire ainsi que l’intégration de la protection de l’enfant dans les autres secteurs humanitaires au niveau national et local. Le projet se penchera principalement sur la sensibilisation sur la protection de l’enfance en urgence ainsi que la mise en place et/ou le renforcement des mécanismes communautaires de protection de l’enfant. L’UNICEF va former des personnes (parents, personnes des autorités etc.), membres des organisations partenaires sur différentes thématiques de protection de l’enfance. Ce projet suggère également donner accès aux enfants séparés ou non accompagnes au processus de identification, documentation, recherche et réunification (IDTR) ; aux des espaces amis des enfants (fixes et mobiles) où il y aura un service d’appui psychosocial; à l’identification et référence aux services d’appui, soit des cas de traumatise ou d’abus sexuels tels que des enfants associes aux forces et groupes armes (garçons combattant et filles ou garçons pour l’esclavage sexuel ou des services d’appui). Le projet va continuer à vulgariser la cartographie des services de prise en charge des enfants et ce, à tous les niveaux administratifs. Ceci c’est pour informer les enfants et les autres membres des communautés ainsi que les autres acteurs sur les services existants au sein de leurs communautés et les modalités d’accès. UNICEF et ses partenaires vont organiser la formation des prestataires des services sur la protection de l’enfant en urgence, la sureté et les principes de référencement. Ce projet propose la mise en place ou le renforcement de cellules communautaires en protection de l’enfance comme (CCPE). Les membres de ces cellules vont identifier les enfants en besoin de protection et les référer vers les services de prise en charge; ils vont faire des sensibilisations au niveau communautaire et aussi des plaidoyers. Le projet est conçu avec une attention particulière sur l’intégration de la protection de l’enfant dans les autres secteurs humanitaires.Au niveau national, 2 clusters bénéficieront d’une formation sur la protection de l’Enfant en urgence et seront accompagnés par le staff dans le développement d’un check liste intégrant certains standards minimums pour la protection de l’enfant. UNICEF collaborera avec la coordination du sous cluster protection de l’enfant dans la tenue de formations et la mise en place de check lists, les outils disponibles seront utilisés ou adaptés et en cas d’absence d’outils

project_name: Psychosocial Support, care and protection from violence, exploitation and abuse for children affected by the North-West and South-West crisis in Cameroon
project_objective: The Anglophone Crisis continues to have devastating effects on the people of the North West and South Regions of Cameroon. Girls and boys are the primary victims of the current crisis. This translates into serious violations of their fundamental rights and constant insecurity, causing both visible and invisible trauma in the short and long-term, separation from their families and limited access to basic social services such as education, for the past four years. Being direct or indirect witnesses of violence linked to the conflict, their wellbeing, both physical and psychological, is fundamentally at stake. Through this project, UNICEF and its partners will work to protect children affected by armed conflict from violence, abuse, and exploitation through a series of interventions. These will include mental health and psychosocial support targeting children and caregivers; case management for unaccompanied and separated children and other vulnerable children; birth registration for conflict-affected children; sensitization campaigns, with specific attention to parents to pass on messages on child protection in emergencies, trauma early warning signs for children affected by armed conflict, effects of family separation, GBV in emergencies and other types of violence children are at risk of at the community level so that parents and community members can play an active role in child protection in emergencies.

project_name: Contribution a la protection des enfants retournes et de la communaute hote affectes par la crise soudanaise.
project_objective: L'action proposée vise à renforcer la protection des enfants affectés par la crise soudanaise.  A cet effet, le projet mettra l’accent sur la prise en charge holistique des enfants victimes de violences (y compris la violence sexuelle) et ceux à risques de protection entre autres les enfants non accompagnés, les enfants séparés et les enfants ex associes aux forces et groupes armes, les enfants vivant avec un handicap. Pour ce faire, le projet contribuera à renforcer les capacités des communautés à travers les mécanismes communautaires de protection de l’enfant pour prévenir les violences et référer les enfants victimes vers les services de prise en charge adéquats.

project_name: Assistance d'urgence en articles ménagers essentiels (AME) aux personnes déplacées au Tchad
project_objective:
La situation humanitaire au Tchad peut être décrite comme une combinaison de crises multidimensionnelles prolongées exacerbées par le changement climatique. En 2024, plus de 5,8 millions de personnes au Tchad auront besoin d’une aide humanitaire. Depuis avril 2023, le Tchad reçoit un afflux important de réfugiés soudanais et de rapatriés tchadiens. Le Tchad accueille environ la moitié des réfugiés d’Afrique de l’Ouest et centrale (1 million sur 2,2 millions). Le Tchad reste très vulnérable aux épidémies et aux événements climatiques, notamment les inondations et les sécheresses. Le Tchad est également confronté à une crise alimentaire et nutritionnelle prolongée. L'accès aux services essentiels reste limité. L'UNICEF continuera de faciliter l'accès aux interventions vitales telles que la distribution d'articles ménagers essentiels (AME) aux personnes déplacées. L'UNICEF veillera à ce que les articles non alimentaires soient disponibles et distribués en temps opportun aux personnes déplacées les plus vulnérables.

L'objectif du projet est de fournir des kits d'AME à 146 000 personnes déplacées à travers le pays. Le budget total du projet est de 6 300 000 $.

project_name: Provision of Lifesaving Emergency Shelter and Non-Food Items Assistance in Sudan
project_objective: This project will ensure that the newly displaced and most vulnerable populations affected by conflict or disasters related to natural hazards with specific needs have timely access to Emergency Shelter (ES) and Non-Food Items (NFIs), Communal Shelter, Tents, and Cash or Cash for Rent assistance. This project contributes to the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) Strategic Objectives 1 (provide timely multi-cluster lifesaving assistance to crisis affected people to reduce mortality and morbidity). IOM proposes to purchase, preposition, and distribute 40,000 NFI kits to reach 200,000 individuals, and 10,000 ES to reach 50,000 individuals. IOM will also provide 10m x 24m communal shelters for 1,000 households (HH) reaching approximately 5,000 individuals, distribute 5,000 tents reaching 25,000 individuals, and provide cash support or cash for rent to 2,000 HH reaching approximately 10,000 individuals as a preparedness and response measure for addressing the needs of newly displaced and vulnerable people with special needs and from protracted displaced populations in different states. Each NFI kit will have seven items: (1) two (5 by 6) meters plastic sheets, (2) two jerrycans, (3) one kitchen set containing 36 pieces including items such as pots and utensils; (4) three blankets, (5) three sleeping mats, (6) two mosquito nets and (7) one solar lamp. Each ES will have materials inclusive of bamboo sticks (30mm / 50mm), grass mats, wooden poles (Y poles), rope (1kg), tarpaulins/ plastic sheet (4m x 6m). The communal shelters will measure 10 meters by 24 meters and tents will be family size measuring 23 square meters inclusive of materials and necessary tools for installation. IOM will distribute cash for rent for approximately 2,000 vulnerable HH for a duration of six months as part of rental subsidy support. The assistance will reach approximately 10,000 beneficiaries considering a HH has an average of 6 people, based on Cash Working Group (CWG) standard calculation of an average number of people per household. Currently the most effective modality is cash in hand or using mobile money and IOM will continue to explore other options depending on the security situation and bank capacities such cash transfers using bank applications. To mitigate potential housing, land, and property (HLP) issues, IOM will facilitate a rental agreement between landlord and beneficiaries only and will hand over the monthly rental amount to the landlord in presence of the beneficiary. ES/NFI needs, market as well as feasibility assessment missions will utilize data from IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), ES/NFI cluster, and the CWG to select the most vulnerable households to be assisted. IOM will transport the ES/NFIs, communal shelter materials, and tents to the distribution locations and will also make arrangements for cash support or cash for rent to be distributed to the most vulnerable populations in selected states. The distributions will be conducted in close coordination with ES/NFI sector lead, cash working group and partners and relevant stakeholders to ensure consistency in provision of assistance and to reduce possible duplications. As a final stage, IOM will undertake post-distribution monitoring (PDM) missions to monitor usage and relevance of the assistance two to four weeks after the distributions. IOM will adapt its interventions to the current context, ensuring it maintains safe access to services for beneficiaries and supporting staff to be able to deliver in-kind goods to locations that are secure especially with regards to cash distribution where added security measure will need to be in place. IOM will mostly target newly displaced persons but also vulnerable members of the host community eligible for assistance to mitigate risks of community tensions.

project_name: Providing Humanitarian Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene Assistance to Crisis-Affected Populations in Sudan
project_objective: In line with the 2024 Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) Cluster Response Plan, this project will seek to mitigate the suffering of crisis-affected populations ensuring that they have access to basic water services that are climate change-sensitive, adequate gender-sensitive sanitation facilities, and hygiene services (including vector control, waste management, hygiene kits inclusive of menstrual hygiene management (MHM) items, and risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) for hygiene awareness). The armed conflict that began on 15 April 2023, between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) led to an overall increase in WASH needs, affecting approximately 18.9 million individuals, with the cluster targeting 8.9 million people. The primary focus of the relief effort is to assist those who are recently displaced, individuals stranded in certain areas, and families congregating at designated points. Assistance is particularly aimed at vulnerable groups such as women, children, the elderly, persons with disabilities or other vulnerabilities. Additionally, efforts are being made to address the needs of individuals affected by epidemics, natural disasters, and the consequences of climate change, notably water scarcity and floods. This project aims to provide humanitarian WASH assistance to 900,000 beneficiaries including 183,600 women, 176,400 men, 275,400 girls, and 264,600 boys with approximately 12 per cent of the target population estimated to be either elderly, people with disabilities, or individuals with other vulnerabilities. IOM aims to assist approximately 450,000 internally displaced persons (IDPs) newly displaced by conflict or disasters related to natural hazards with WASH services and improve and sustain access to safe water for approximately 400,000 individuals including returnees and crisis-affected communities. The project will focus on crisis impacted communities in various states primarily in areas where water infrastructure is damaged or available capacity is unable to meet the critical needs stretched by the influx of the displaced. IOM will also support communities to improve hygiene through sustaining access to safe water and sanitation facilities and promoting hygiene messages to address and increase community resilience to malnutrition, disease outbreaks, and other public health related risks targeting approximately 50,000 individuals. IOM will provide emergency water assistance through the establishment and rehabilitation of water points, access to proper sanitation facilities and hygiene items and campaigns. This will include environmental impact mitigation such as the provision of solar technology to power water points and monitoring ground water to moderate depletion levels. IOM will also participate in the Cholera Taskforce; ensuring access to WASH facilities while supporting management of cholera cases in cholera treatment centres and units through provision of safe drinking water, water chlorination, and water quality monitoring and hygiene promotion/cleaning campaigns. Exit strategies will be developed in more secure states of the country to alleviate aid dependency in protracted emergencies by strengthening self-reliance and facilitating community solutions. WASH committees shall be established, and maintenance tools/spare parts supplied. The project will ensure dignified and equitable access to basic WASH services through the implementation of early recovery approaches where possible, connecting the need for short-term emergency interventions during the ongoing military conflict with long-term solutions by working directly with local communities to facilitate ownership and accountability. The WASH emergency interventions will gradually contribute to socio-economic inclusion of forcibly displaced populations and returnees by directly increasing access to basic services for displaced and host communities and indirectly increasing employment opportunities.

project_name: Strengthening GBV prevention mechanisms and providing comprehensive life-saving interventions for populations in need in Sudan
project_objective:
Sudanese civilians have endured more than eight months of violent conflict since clashes erupted between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF)  and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in April 2023. The conflict initially started in Khartoum but quickly spread to Darfur and the Kordofans, followed by an extension of fighting into central and eastern regions of Sudan in December 2023. This ongoing conflict has affected every state in the country.
Gender-based violence (GBV) remains a life-threatening concern across Sudan in 2024. The situation has been worsened by various factors, including armed conflict, tribal clashes, forced displacement, and recurring natural disasters such as floods. The fighting that began on April 15, 2023 between the SAF and RSF has resulted in hundreds of casualties and, according to figures from the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), 7.4 million people have been displaced, seeking refuge both inside and outside Sudan. Consequently, 6.7 million people require GBV prevention and response services, with the GBV Sub Sector aiming to provide prevention, mitigation, and response measures to 1.8 million individuals, prioritizing women and girls in conflict- and disaster-affected areas, and areas hosting refugees. A significant number of households in these areas have resorted to negative coping mechanisms. The severity of protection needs is categorized as critical (4-5) in 143 localities across the 18 states of Sudan.
UNFPA aims to fully address the GBV sub-sector target for individuals in severity ranking 5, achieve 50% of the target for severity ranking 4, and approximately 30% of the target for severity ranking 3 .
This project has three main objectives. First, the project will provide life-saving GBV services of high quality for the next 11 months. These services include comprehensive support for survivors, case management, psychosocial support, and reinforcement of referral pathways. The project will particularly focus on women and girls with disabilities and adolescent girls and is aligned with the Humanitarian Response Plan's Strategic Objective 1. The services provided will encompass case management, psychosocial support, referrals, assessments, community awareness-raising, distribution of dignity kits, and capacity building for frontline GBV actors.
Second, the project will integrate GBV risk mitigation measures into all aspects of the humanitarian response. This objective, aligned with the Humanitarian Response Plan's Strategic Objective 3, involves training non-GBV humanitarian actors on GBV-related issues. Third, the project will strengthen the national and sub-national coordination mechanisms for GBV, while aiming to enhance data collection and information management related to GBV.
Overall, the project seeks to deliver essential GBV prevention and response services, promote GBV risk mitigation, and enhance coordination and data management to address the urgent needs of vulnerable women and girls affected by the conflict and other crises in Sudan.

project_name: Provision of live-saving and live-sustaining support for conflict affected vulnerable farmers, agro pastoralists, pastoralists and fishery communities in Sudan
project_objective:
FAO under HRP 2024, is planning to provide emergency agriculture and livestock-based livelihoods interventions to support vulnerable farmers, agro- pastoral and pastoral people from IDPs, host communities and venerable non-displaced population in Sudan. The vulnerability of the target populations stems from the protracted crisis, the ongoing economic hardships at the macro and micro-levels, negative impact of long dry spells and floods and recently the ongoing conflict. 

This project covers all states in Sudan targeting 9,023.696 people among the most vulnerable communities including 3,429,004 IDPs, 2,255,924 host communities, and 3,338,768 non -displaced people. The planned interventions will benefit 4,602085 females, 4,421,611 males and 3,609,478 children of which 1,804,769 girls (less than 18 year of age), and 1,804,769 boys. (less than 18 year of age). The project will also support 902,370 elderly (above 60) and 451,185 male and female people with disabilities. The proposed interventions are based on the basic and specific needs of the beneficiaries considering the factors of age and gender. FAO will coordinate with sector partners, government, and UN agencies to get actual information on numbers and locations of the people with disabilities to support them with suitable livelihoods interventions.

The project interventions under FSL SO1 (Improve the food security status of assessed severely food insecure people through emergency live-saving agriculture, livestock, emergency livelihood and social protection support through cash and in-kind transfers for 8,250,000 person (1,650,000 households). And 773,696 persons (154,739 households) under FSL SO2 (Strengthen affected food insecure households through live-sustaining and restoring food, agriculture, and livelihoods) to ensure that people have regular access to enough high-quality food from their own production to meet their family needs and sell the surplus in the local markets to generate income and avail diversified foods for others at their locations and at a reasonable price. During that process they will receive extension support to intensify their production and build their resilience to overcome natural or manmade risks and hazards. They will be encouraged to protect their natural resources to sustain their livelihoods base.
The FAO will collect information, conduct assessments, studies to better inform the decisions on the implementation of this project. Crop and Food Supply Assessment Mission (CFSAM) will be conducted during 2024/ 2025 to enhance the country planning and ensure that all Sudanese are food secure otherwise suitable interventions will be developed.
FAO will support coordination with FSL sector partners and harmonises the response to food chain threats including animal and plant pests specially locust and birds; in addition, communities will be involved in protecting and maintaining their productive assets through awareness raising. Accountability to affected populations and environmental concerns will be mainstreamed into the proposed activities, also risk to GBV will be taken into consideration and application of the PSEA measures will be applied in collaboration with sister UN agencies.

project_name: Protection Support for Internally Displaced and Returnees in Sudan
project_objective:

project_name: Resilient livelihoods for the most vulnerable IDPs and host populations in the crisis-affected communities in the North West South West regions of Cameroon.
project_objective:
According to OCHA’s “Situational Baseline, 31 November 2023” there are more than 1, 306, 768 IDPs, 658, 544 returnees a as well as an increasing number of victims on the military side, non-state actors and civil level as well. The current context in the NWSW regions remains dynamic and is characterized by continued displacement of families leading to food and nutrition insecurity.
About 508, 480 food insecure people have lost their access to farmlands, assets and livelihoods in the NWSW regions. The result of this is presented in the October 2023 Cadre Harmonisé analysis that shows an average of about 22% of the population in NW/SW applying negative livelihood coping mechanisms. Food insecurity is worsening because of the war between Ukraine and Russia Crisis that has led to drastically increased input prices especially seeds and fertilizer. For the first time ever all 13 divisions are classified as under “pressior” phase”. 
According to the recent Multi Sectoral Needs Assessment (MSNA) of Septembre 2023, food security represents represented the highest need. Due to lockdowns and ghost towns access to markets and services become more and more challenging for the population and for humanitarian partners. About 80 % of farms in remote locations remain inaccessible and sometimes crops are abandoned. Due to insecurity, most people have moved from rural areas (where there is land) to cities where even space for home gardens is very limited. There are some functioning local markets with partial access to regional markets
According to the IOM Labor Market Survey 2022 , there is therefore a need to scale up agricultural production and further build up the local capacity to transform and process raw material that could eventually contribute to local economic development.
The outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic restricted usual execution of agricultural extension services and feeding the markets with agricultural products. Direct access to extension services for farmers was limited due to travel restrictions and banning of public gatherings. Both lead to an increase in food prices and agricultural resource prices. The war between Ukraine and Russia has worsen food supply chain like the supply with fertilizer. This in turn has a major impact on food demand and consequently leads to food insecurity with a great effect on the most vulnerable people. The combination of the war in Ukraine, the COVID 19 pandemic and the crisis in the North-West and South-West regions has a tremendous economic impact on agricultural activities on IDPs, Persons living with Disabilities (PwD) and host communities. 

The proposed one-year intervention will contribute to strengthening livelihoods and reducing the vulnerability of crisis-affected IDPs and host communities in the North-West and South-West regions of Cameroon, especially women, men, children and PwD, through the provision of agricultural support. Specifically, the intervention aims (i) to increase access and utilization of diverse and nutritious vegetables, (ii) to increase access and consumption of eggs, (iii) to increase access and utilization of mushrooms, (iv) to increase access and utilization of snails. Furthermore, 75 % of the beneficiaries selected will be reached by FAO and WFP. Implementing partners organizations will take care of the remaining 25% of the beneficiaries.

project_name: Appui à la qualité et à l'inclusion de l’éducation dans un environnement sûr pour les enfants filles et garçons impactés par les crises humanitaires  dans les régions de Tillabéry, Tahoua , Maradi et Diffa,
project_objective:
La présente réponse éducation de l’Unicef contribuera à la  la prise en charge d'une proportion d'enfants et adolescents non scolarisés et/ou déscolarisés  dans le contexte d'EiE. La vision est d’assurer la continuité educative perturbée par la fermeture de nombreuses écoles, le mariage des enfants et la paupérisation des communautés, qui constituent des privations d' accès à des opportunités d'apprentissage alternatives et flexibles   
L’intervention sera menée de façon coordonnée avec les autorités éducatives et les communautés. L’objectif est de mobiliser les communautés autour de l’école en y incluant les enfants qui n’ont pas intégré le système éducatif, ou qui l’ont quitté précocement, et en mobilisant la communauté autour des thématiques essentielles en matière de droits à l’éducation. Capitalisant sur les acquis des pratiques éducatives le projet mettra en place une gamme variée d’offres éducatives non formelles en vue de lever les obstacles à la scolarisation des enfants et assurer leur enrôlement, maintien et transition vers d’autres opportunités d’éducation ou de formation. Le segment formel sera soutenu et appuyé pour accroitre les capacités d’accueil, en équipement, matériels et fournitures scolaires pour répondre au reversement des formules SSAP et CEA et à la demande. Un accent sera mis sur le développement professionnel des enseignants et des appuis matériels pédagogiques conséquents en vue d’asseoir la qualité des interventions développées et stimuler la rétention des enfants au sein de ces programmes.  Cette intervention contribuera également à une meilleure protection des enfants en veillant à ce qu'ils ne soient pas exposés à des risques de protection (VBG, exploitation sociale…). Un accent particulier sera mis sur la protection des écoles dans une approche contextualisée à travers la mise à jour et ou la mise en place des plans de préparation et réponses aux urgences dans les écoles de concert avec les communautés.
Il sera fait usage du transfert monétaire conditionnel pour briser la barrière économique au retour et ou inscription des populations les plus vulnérables ou encore pour le maintien des filles et enfants handicapés.
Le projet s’aligne sur les objectifs ci-dessous du Cluster.
1. OSS 2.1.1 : Accès à des offres éducatives inclusives et de qualité pour les enfants déplacés, les réfugiés et la communauté d'accueil  pour les  enfants de 6 à 17 ans touchés par les crises humanitaires,                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      2. OSS 2.1.2 : Assurer un environnement d'apprentissage sûr pour les enfants déplacés, réfugiés et de la communauté d'accueil,                                                                
3. OSS 3.3.1 : Les enfants et le personnel scolaire des écoles vulnérables sont soutenus dans la préparation et la réponse aux urgences
