project_name: Provision of primary health care services for vulnerable children and women in Syria
project_objective:
As per the HNO, more than 14.9 million people are in need for life-saving primary & secondary care health assistance in 2024.The February earthquake damaged 67 health facilities in Northwest Syria, of which 6 were destroyed. In contrast, 6 health centers in Latakia and Tartous suffered significant damage and went out of service. In addition, 133 primary health care centers and 18 hospitals in Aleppo, Hama, Latakia, and Tartous were partially damaged. Emerging and re-emerging infectious, vaccine-preventable, and neglected tropical diseases, such as influenza-like illnesses, measles, meningitis, and waterborne diseases including cholera, hepatitis A, and leishmaniasis; continued to pose a significant threat to affected communities across Syria accounting for more than 16% of the total consultations reported from the health system through the surveillance system
The cholera outbreak declared in September 2022 is expected to persist in 2024, with seasonal variations in caseloads. As of 21 October 2023 (epi-week 42), 217,512 suspected acute watery diarrhea/cholera cases reported from all 14 governorates of Syria, with 106 associated deaths at a case fatality rate of 0.05 percent. While the outbreak initially overstretched the already-weak health system, and had direct consequences on vulnerable communities and patients, increasing morbidities and mortalities, the latest reports showed a gradual decline and partners have started considering integrating response operations into existing primary health services.
Access to and functionality of basic health services remain a huge challenge; almost 40 percent of primary and secondary care health facilities - serving over 4.8 million people in need of life-saving health services - are either partially functioning or not functional. In addition, non-functioning primary health care and specialized facilities increased from 16 percent and 18 percent in 2022 to 24 percent and 31 percent in 2023 respectively. 
Children and women are the most vulnerable groups especially in NES and IDP camps, coverage with vaccines is still below 80% which is the minimum level to achieve the heard immunity, and it is more critical in camps due to hardship living conditions. Women in childbearing age needs more support for antenatal and postnatal care in addition to safe deliveries in camps or in high-risk areas. 
Primary and secondary health care are constrained due to the high percentage of health centers who are damaged due to the war or the earthquake, and referral to hospitals in NES is restricted to very few private hospitals due to the unfunctional public hospitals or very limited specialized services in those hospitals and shortage of specialized doctors.
Delivery of supplies to the NES governorates is also constrained due to security issues and long leading time to reach the destination after many liars of approvals.
This proposal aims to support the provision of basic lifesaving curative, preventive and promotional health services (including vaccination services)  and health seeking and care practices, while enhancing early recovery and resilience of the sector by contributing to: strengthening service delivery to vulnerable population who cannot afford paying for health services, specifically children (through providing free-of-charge medical services by NGOs, rehabilitating damaged public health facilities, and installing prefab clinics in areas with no health centers), supporting community health delivery platforms through capacity building for those NGO, with major focus on community engagement through volunteers to include and integrate them within the health facilities and be part of the community health system to ensure sustainability of those voluntary services. 
To overcome the problem of delays in getting approvals for transporting health supplies to NES, UNICEF is engaging the state planning commission in approving a list of planned supplies and getting a blank approval for the planned list.

project_name: Improve equitable access to preventive and curative nutrition services for children under five years, adolescents, and pregnant and lactating women in Syria.
project_objective:
The nutrition needs of children and women of Syria continue to rise, year after year. The socioeconomic status has deteriorated further, in addition to the February earthquake that exacerbated the needs and amplified vulnerabilities. The erosion of service capacity continues, with water and sanitation systems, health systems, and social protection systems under immense strain. According to Humanitarian Needs Overview 2024, Syria faces a concerning escalation in the prevalence of wasting, stunting, and anemia affecting children under the age of five. Elevated levels of anemia for women of reproductive age, particularly among adolescent girls (15–19 years). The prevalence of Global Acute Malnutrition has witnessed a substantial threefold increase over the past five years, surging from 1.7% in 2019 to 4.7% in 2023 with a total of 508,892 children urgently requiring life-saving treatment for Acute Malnutrition, out of which 109,642 children suffer from severe acute malnutrition (SAM), a 44% increase from 2023. Stunting rates have consistently risen across Syria, increasing from 12.6% in 2019 to 16.1% in 2023, with an estimated 650,000 children under the age of five in Syria being stunted. 6-23 months of age children’s access to nutritious food is concerning, with only 6% of them meeting their minimal adequate diet. Consequently, 1 in 2 children suffers from anemia, posing additional risk for child growth and cognitive abilities.
Iron deficiency anemia and poor maternal nutrition during pregnancy and sub-optimal breastfeeding practices contribute to an increased risk of preterm delivery or low birth weight, leading to stunted children later in life. 1 in 10 women is wasted, and one in four women aged 15–49 years suffers from anemia, with an even higher prevalence observed among teenage girls, where 1 in 2 girls is anemic.

UNICEF through its implementing partners (IPs), both through fixed and mobile clinics, will provide a minimum package of preventive and curative nutrition services for children 6-59 months of age and pregnant and lactating women based on the area’s severity, with a special focus on the first 1,000 days of life. UNICEF and its IPs will scale up the early detection of acute malnutrition and the provision of treatment for SAM. In addition, UNICEF will provide children and their mothers with preventive nutrition supplies for the prevention of all forms of malnutrition, including multiple micronutrient supplementation (MMS) and small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS). UNICEF will continue its support to optimize the infant and young child feeding practices. In addition, UNICEF in Syria will introduce MMS for adolescent girls 15-19 years to tackle anemia and break the vicious cycle of maternal and child anemia. Furthermore, UNICEF will improve children’s and mothers’ access to safe and nutritious food through strong integration of social protection activities into the nutrition program.
In addition to those activities, UNICEF will work with its implementing partners to set up a national nutrition information system that enables timely and quality data, increases the efficiency of activities, and prevents duplication. UNICEF will also prepare a national nutrition strategy and update the national CMAM guidance in alignment with the new global WHO guidance, and consequently, UNICEF will build the capacity of its national partners on the CMAM program as well as IYCF.



UNICEF works closely with its sister agencies for complementarity on the ground. UNICEF coordinates with WFP for provision of lipid-based nutrient supplement for children 6-23 months of age to ensure continuation of services and prevent duplication of efforts. Under the  CMAM program, UNICEF works with WFP and WHO to provide treatment for all types of acute malnutrition, including MAM and SAM with complications, which are the responsibility of WFP and WHO respectively.

project_name: Expanding Social, Civic and Economic Engagement and Social Cohesion Interventions for Conﬂict-Affected Adolescents and Youth in the Syrian Arab Republic
project_objective:
Needs: Young people in Syria face a myriad of interrelated barriers that prevent their meaningful economic, social, and civic participation and engagement. They face stigma and discrimination regarding their capacities to lead positive change in their communities. Limited opportunities for economic, social, and civic engagement, particularly for the most marginalized adolescents and youth, contribute to their systematic exclusion and exacerbate feelings of isolation and disenfranchisement. However, experiences from other contexts of protracted crisis have shown that supporting young people’s social and civic engagement can have positive social outcomes and be conducive to increased community resilience and social cohesion.
Intervention: In support of the ERL Sector, UNICEF will further its support for the Generation Unlimited initiative and No Lost Generation Agenda by empowering vulnerable adolescents and youth, both female and male, as well as those with disabilities, to access social, civic, and economic opportunities for skill development and engagement (including participation in social cohesion initiatives) with the objective of contributing to enhancing resilience and social cohesion. UNICEF will build on strategic partnerships, integration, and at-scale programming focusing on the most vulnerable adolescents to strengthen skills development, employability, and meaningful engagement through friendly spaces and mobile teams. The proposed project will support 342,883 young women and men per year to have better access to civic, social, and economic opportunities for skill development and engagement, and to unleash their potentials and increase their learning, leadership, and employability opportunities. UNICEF will work in the following two pillars and related interventions: (1) Strengthen social, civic, and economic engagement of adolescents and youth and foster volunteerism and social cohesion-building. (2) Support young entrepreneurs to start their own projects through seed funding. UNICEF will continue strengthening the capacity of local partners, including services providers, youth workers, and young volunteers, to improve the quality of provided services and enhance evidence generation.
Protection Risk Analysis: After enduring 12 years of conflict and ongoing economic turmoil, young Syrians have faced devastating hardships that have eroded their resilience. This has particularly affected girls, who have resorted to harmful coping mechanisms such as dropping out of school, engaging in addictive behaviors, entering child labor, and marrying early. Social norms in many communities also hinder girls' and people with disabilities' participation in sports, cultural activities, and community engagement. The compounding effects of COVID-19, earthquakes, and economic challenges have exacerbated these risks. UNICEF will continue to mainstream the principles of safety, dignity, and do no harm, as well as the inclusive and meaningful access of the most marginalized boys and girls, especially those who live with disabilities, to ensure that no one is left behind. UNICEF will increase safe access to skills development, social cohesion, awareness-raising, and engagement opportunities. UNICEF will prioritize developing the capacity of the implementing partners through providing technical support in the fields of Child Safeguarding, Code of Conduct, and PSEA.
Risks: Economic deterioration and transportation barriers, along with potential conflicts between IDPs and host communities, as well as risks of exploitation or abuse. To address these risks, there will be capacity building for staff and volunteers, awareness campaigns on risks, mandatory screening during recruitment, establishing complaint mechanisms with adequate staff for follow-up, and ensuring data protection and confidentiality.

Assumptions: The project assumes support for integrated and joint approaches and the promotion of youth participation nationwide.

project_name: MPC-Basic Needs Support Programme for vulnerable families in Syria
project_objective:
Families and children in Syria are sinking deeper into poverty, facing immense challenges in making ends meet. Over 13 years of conflict have worsened the situation, marked by armed conflict, loss of human capital, economic downturn, water crisis, food insecurity, impacts of the Ukraine-Russia war, and health emergencies like Covid-19 and cholera. The aftermath of the February earthquake adds to the devastation
The humanitarian crisis continues to worsen, with an estimated 16.7 million people needing aid in 2024. Syria has plummeted 42 places on the Human Development Index, its economy regressing to mid-1990s levels, and child development indicators falling back over three decades. Poverty is rampant, with critical infrastructure on the brink of collapse. UNICEF's State Budget Brief 2023 highlights the decline in public expenditures, now less than one-quarter of pre-conflict levels. The 2023 budget is a mere USD 5.88 billion or USD 256 per capita, significantly lower than before. Foreign aid, especially in the health sector, surpasses government allocations, four times higher than those for water and sanitation. In urban and peri-urban slums of Syria, especially those headed by females or caring for orphaned children or internally displaced persons (IDPs), cash assistance is crucial for meeting basic needs. Seasonal peaks like winter and the start of the school year escalate financial strain. UNICEF survey underscores the socio-economic vulnerability of female-headed households, often relying on charity or remittances. To address this, UNICEF will implement targeted cash assistance and protection measures, aiming to improve well-being and resilience while enhancing stakeholder participation
The program outputs include 1) Targeted Cash Assistance: A Structured schedule and selection criteria for cash assistance to families affected by the earthquake, female-headed households with children, and families of children facing heightened health-related financial burdens, in NES/DEZ, Aleppo, Hama, Homs, Lattakia, AS Swidaa, AL Qunitera, and Rural Damascus. 2) Strengthened Community Empowerment: The response will utilize a categorical-geographical targeting strategy, focuses on impoverished urban and peri-urban areas, particularly those severely affected by the crisis, natural disasters and climate change impact, e,i droughts, floods, and fire accidents
Targeted Beneficiaries for 2024: A total of 235,000 individuals will be assisted. Of this group, 32,341 families extremely affected by earthquake in Hama, Lattakia and Aleppo will receive their second cash installment. Additionally, UNICEF will provide MPC assistance to 21,595 individuals/ 4,319HHs in Homs and Rural Damascus, each receiving three rounds of cash totaling $180 during the winter season spanning 2023-2024. The remaining 51,700 individuals / 10340 HHs will benefit from a humanitarian cash transfer program designed to meet their basic needs. These families will receive four Qs payments of $90 each, along with supplementary top-us for children’s additional expenses for each school-aged child and/or children with chronic illnesses
Efforts will be amplified to enhance stakeholder engagement in pinpointing the specific communities in need. This will involve empowering civil society organizations to effectively convey the eligibility criteria and selection procedures to the target audience
Coordination and Accountability The Prog aligns with MPC interventions in Syria. UNICEF coordinates with CWG for targeting and TV harmonization.Also, beneficiary accountability will be considered via redress, PDMS, and onsite monitoring
Risk Analysis and Mitigation: Cash assistance programs pose various risks, like social tensions, abuse by implementing partners, and protection risks during distribution. UNICEF's PSEA strategy combats sexual exploitation and abuse among aid workers, co-chairing the inter-agency network to enhance networking, identify risks, and preserve affected people's dignity

project_name: Integrated malnutrition prevention and treatment programme for refugees and local Bangladeshi Communities in Cox's Bazar.
project_objective:
WFP aims to contribute to a reduction in acute and chronic malnutrition rates, and an improvement in nutritional status among refugees and local Bangladeshi communities in Cox’s Bazar through the provision of curative and preventive nutrition services for children below 5 years and pregnant and breastfeeding women (PBW).  WFP will implement its project interventions across 45 integrated nutrition facilities (INFs) in 33 camps, and 55 nutrition sites in the local Bangladeshi community in partnership with UNICEF, UNHCR and cooperating partners under the coordination of the Cox's Bazar nutrition sector. WFP will provide targeted supplementary feeding program (TSFP) for moderate acutely malnourished children 6-59 months and Pregnant and Breastfeeding Women (PLW) to reduce morbidity and mortality associated with malnutrition in both the refugee camps and in the host community. A 200g daily ration of Super Cereal Plus (Wheat Soya Blend Plus -WSB++) & 100g daily ration of Ready to Use Supplementary Food (RUSF) will be provided for children 6-59 months in the host community and camps respectively; and 250g of Super Cereal (Wheat Soya Blend -WSB+) and 16.66g of oil will be provided to PBW under TSFP.
An enhanced prevention of malnutrition package will be put in place to mitigate the increase in prevalence of acute and chronic malnutrition and its associated risks for mortality and morbidity and promote child development. In the camps, this includes provision of the blanket supplementary feeding programme (BSFP) for younger children 6-23 months and PBWs, and a nutrition sensitive e-voucher programme that allows older children (24-59 months) access to fresh fruits and vegetables aimed at enhancing their dietary diversity and promote growth monitoring and uptake of other complementary services at the INF. These children will receive a US$ 3 redeemable voucher. Social Behaviour Change Communication (SBCC) activities and utilization of tools that positively influence behaviour, knowledge, attitudes, and practice around nutrition will be conducted in both the refugee and host communities.
Active case finding through community screening, referral and follow up of malnourished children under five and pregnant and breastfeeding women will be done. Additionally, growth monitoring and promotion for children 6-59 months will be part of the project interventions.
The underlying causes of malnutrition will be addressed through integration of nutrition sensitive approaches in ongoing general food assistance, school feeding, self-reliance, and livelihood interventions. 
WFP will promote the prevention of micronutrient deficiencies particularly anaemia through the promotion of dietary diversification. 
WFP will conduct capacity strengthening for partners and stakeholders to improve capacity for implementation of nutrition specific and nutrition sensitive programming. WFP will actively engaged at nutrition sector and support programme intervention as member of SAG, Assessment, IYCF & CMAM technical working group.
WFP will support quantitative and qualitative nutrition assessments to ensure that nutrition programmes are tailormade according to the needs of the targeted populations. In addition, WFP will also conduct a study in Ukhiya & Teknaf local community on alternative feeding options for acute malnutrition treatment in collaboration with icddr,b .
Project interventions will be adapted to ensure an inclusive approach to promote participation of women, men, older people, adolescent, people who have chronic health conditions and persons with disabilities. Additionally, protection mechanisms will be put in place including complaints and feedback mechanisms and help desks to ensure accountability to affected populations.

project_name: Support Provision of integrated quality lifesaving health emergency and essential health care activities for IDPs and vulnerable communities in response to different health emergencies in Sudan
project_objective:
The escalation of  conflict in Sudan between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) added a new dimension to an already deteriorating humanitarian situation in the country as, ten months on, the violence continues to make healthcare delivery increasingly difficult. , Sudan HNRP launched in November 2023 identified Over 14.7 million people are facing critical challenges in accessing essential life-saving primary health care as the health sector is collapsing due to the reduction of functioning health facilities along with an acute shortage of medical supplies, water and fuel, and the increase of attacks on health facilities, as result of these, devastated health situation across the country has been reported either directly due to above reasons or due to access challenges that hindering  humanitarian actors to respond to the growing needs. Since the eruption of conflict in Sudan, Humanitarian needs are reported high in all times, according to HRP the Health cluster aims to assist 4.9 million people, representing 33 per cent of the total people in need. WHO in coordination with Health cluster (HC) partners will focus on disease outbreak preparedness, detection and response in line with the three HC strategies for 2024 HRP, these are (1) Support essential public health functions (including emergency trauma response) with a focus on strong primary health care services, (2) emergency preparedness, response, and all-hazards emergency risk management, and (3) Address the needs of vulnerable groups who are disproportionally affected by health emergencies.
Disease outbreaks are increasing in the face of disruptions of basic public health services, including disease surveillance, functioning public health laboratories and rapid response teams. In addition, insecurity, displacement, limited access to medicines, medical supplies, electricity, and water continue to pose enormous challenges to delivering health care across the country. About 65 per cent of the population lack access to healthcare and between 70 - 80 per cent of hospitals in conflict-affected areas are no longer functional. Almost 9,000 suspected cases of cholera, including 245 associated deaths, were reported as of 6 January 2024 from 46 localities of nine states, according to the Federal Ministry of Health (FMoH) and the World Health Organization (WHO) Sudan Outbreaks Dashboard. This is an increase of about 43 per cent compared to the number of cases reported on 6 December 2023. However, this indicates a downward trend and a much lower increase compared to previous months. Between 6 November – 6 December the number of cases increased by 143 per cent, and between 6 October and 6 November the increase was 175 per cent. During December 2023, oral cholera vaccination campaigns have been organized in Gedaref and Aj Jazirah states, with about 2.2 million people vaccinated. There are 2,746 suspected cases and 95 associated deaths in Red Sea; 2,036 suspected cases of cholera and 50 associated deaths in Gedaref; 1,860 suspected cases and 26 associated deaths in Aj Jazirah; 1,246 suspected cases and 32 associated deaths in White Nile; 525 suspected cases and 26 associated deaths in Khartoum; 346 suspected cases and eight associated deaths in South Kordofan; 121 suspected cases and four associated deaths in Sennar; 99 suspected cases and four associated deaths in Kassala; and three suspected case in Blue Nile State (OCHA).  INGO forum reported   17 humanitarian colleagues who were at the frontline providing humanitarian assistance in Khartoum and Darfur before they lost their life.
Its estimated that Over 8,000 civilians have been killed and about 10,000 individuals have
been injured and about 4.2 million people at risk of gender-based violence.

project_name: Humanitarian Assistance for Rohingya and Host Community in Bangladesh
project_objective:
This Shelter and Camp Coordination and Camp Management (S-CCCM) project will cover a comprehensive target of 107,462 individuals or 22,156 households across Rohingya and host communities. The geographical coverage includes Camp 1E, 1W, 2E, 2W, 21, 3, 4 Ext, 5, 6, 7, 17, 21 and Kutupalong RC, and the host community in Rajapalong, Palongkhali, Haldia Palong and Jalia Palong. The targeted activities are derived from the J-MSNA 2023, Shelter minimum standard assessment report, BRAC’s database, and internal need assessment conducted in 2023. 
The Shelter support activity involves the reuse and recycling of used shelter materials, and new shelter construction for 800 (650 in camps and 150 in Host community) households. Regular shelter support will be provided to 2,500 households where treated bamboo processed in BRAC bamboo treatment plants will be used. Among them, 700 Extremely Vulnerable Individuals (EVI) households will receive labour and porter support. Household-level site improvement activities extend to 3,023 populations across multiple camps, encompassing various constructions, repairs, and improvements such as bamboo drain (1,164 meters), bamboo-geotex retaining wall (1,940 meters), geo-bag pathway (800 meters), ramp (50 meters), stair (700 meters), and bamboo wooden bridge (500 meters). 
BRAC will mainstream Disaster Risk Management (DRM) with multisectoral engagement in both the camp and host community. It will provide support for reforestation activities and restore and conserve natural ecosystems. Moreover, a pilot initiative will be conducted to develop a resilience matrix, which will further help in decision-making in terms of disaster preparedness, response, and mitigation of the camp. In addition, BRAC will operate 4 Mobile Firefighting Units (MFU), and 7 cyclone preparedness units, and engage 120 well-trained volunteers for multi-hazard response. BRAC also focuses on empowering community representatives for resilience and utilizing local resources to mitigate risks. To enhance preparedness, BRAC has prepositioned Emergency Preparedness and Response (EPR) equipment, including search and rescue gear, first aid equipment, Cyclone Preparedness Programme (CPP) gear, and Mobile Firefighting Unit (MFU) gear. BRAC also will provide capacity building in EPR, communication, and overall community engagement techniques. Moreover, the distribution of Tie Down Kits and emergency shelter support for cyclone preparation, tailored for 1,500 households. 
The overall camp management includes stakeholder coordination in the camp, service monitoring, and reporting gaps. BRAC will lead coordination meetings and advocate for identified gaps. To involve affected people in decision-making, BRAC will maintain community engagement structures through thematic groups formed through inclusive consultations.
BRAC will ensure a swift response to community concerns through the Complaints Feedback and Response Mechanism (CFRM) in each of the targeted camps. This system, which will be working with site management and community-based protection teams, allows for quick project adjustments based on community feedback. Monthly monitoring reports enhance project effectiveness and empower the community through a dynamic feedback loop. Besides, the 4Ws, camp profile, service monitoring, volunteer management tool, and central inventory for all the previously completed and updated assessments of service monitoring in an interactive information management system, will enable humanitarian aid providers to conduct accurate and meaningful need assessments.
For oversight, a dedicated monitoring team employed by BRAC will utilize a real-time online tool to assess progress and quality regularly. The project's success will be gauged through the frequency of evaluations and adjustments made based on valuable feedback.

project_name: Provision of basic lifesaving WASH services among Rohingya refugees and Host Communities in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh
project_objective:
The BRAC WASH project for 2024 is designed to align with the WASH sector objectives, aiming to provide adequate and equitable access to inclusive and culturally acceptable WASH facilities. This is achieved through regular repair and maintenance of the facilities and the improvement of WASH behaviour practices among the targeted people. Following the WASH sector mega rationalization process, BRAC's geographical coverage includes 8 camps (1E, 2W, 3, 4 extensions, 5, 10, 13, and 20 Ext) as well as the host community.
The BRAC project design includes comprehensive WASH services in camps with an emphasis on the operation and maintenance of the WASH facilities, Solid Waste Management (SWM), faecal sludge management, new construction and upgradation of latrines, bathing cubicles, and tap stands to address the needs of age segregated diverse groups including men, women, persons with disabilities, , children and others. BRAC will ensure community engagement in repairing and maintaining the WASH facilities through capacity building of the user groups and WASH committees while providing necessary repair and maintenance materials to the community. Additionally, women's leadership will be promoted in each WASH user group.
In the host communities, BRAC will install water points, latrines, and bathing cubicles, as well as address menstrual hygiene management in schools and solid waste management. Additionally, BRAC will work on new initiatives, such as the installation of rainwater harvesting systems and wastewater recycling. Water quality will be monitored in both host communities and camps.
BRAC will involve local and national NGOs in different camps where the WASH gaps are significant, aiming to develop the capacity of the local NGOs in terms of WASH humanitarian response under the pooled fund. Furthermore, BRAC will exclusively work on plastic waste management in camps to mitigate physical and long-term environmental impacts. The overall objective of the project is to contribute to the reduction of plastic waste pollution in camps by developing a comprehensive and human-centric waste management system that involves all relevant stakeholders in the waste management value chain. BRAC will also work through partner NGOs for the improvement of the solid waste situation in camps 1E, 1W, 2E, 2W, and camp 3. 
The BRAC WASH project design also includes integration with different sectors within BRAC, especially Health and Nutrition, Livelihoods and Skills Development, Education, and Protection, to deliver integrated services in an efficient and cost-effective manner. BRAC will address the solid waste problem at the marketplace and adjacent host community with the involvement of CBOs. To manage non-valuable waste and dispose of it environmentally, BRAC will take the initiative of joint advocacy along with the WASH sector and fundraising to construct a new sanitary landfill and will be continuing the regular operation of existing sanitary landfill sites. BRAC will make a contingency plan 2024 to address outbreaks of Acute Watery Diarrhoea (AWD), Scabies, Dengue, and other hazardsincluding heavy rain, cyclones, etc. in host and camps.
In terms of budget allocation for 2024, BRAC plans to allocate 24% in host communities and 76% in camps. BRAC has project implementation quality (PIQ) indicators based on which a project monitoring plan will be developed in alignment with the Joint Response Plan (JRP) monitoring framework and will be periodically monitored by the BRAC MEAL team for improvement and necessary adjustments to the WASH program. During the implementation of the project, BRAC will ensure proper coordination and collaboration with different stakeholders, such as RRRC, CiC, DPHE, UNO offices, UN agencies, NGOs, and the WASH sector. BRAC will follow WASH sector strategies and guidelines in all stages of the implementation, avoiding any overlapping while considering Core Humanitarian Standards and Accountability to Affected Population principles.

project_name: Emergency Assistance and Rapid Response to improve the access to Health, Nutrition and Mental Health services in the Logone-et-Chari department, Far North region, in Cameroon
project_objective:
The goal of this project is to improve access to basic social services in health, nutrition and WASH for vulnerable communities affected by population displacements in the Goulfey health district. 
ACF has implemented projects in the area of Goulfey and Kousseri, under ECHO, French Embassy and SIDA funding since 2017 and enjoys a great acceptance in the area. 
This current project aims to meet the urgent health needs in the Logone et Chari division of Cameroon, through the provision of emergency and quality primary and secondary health care services integrating MHPSS to populations affected by the crisis and particularly children under five and pregnant and lactating women (PLW). A mobile clinic will be deployed in the supported areas providing primary health care to beneficiaries, with a focus on children under 5, PLW, but also delivering services to adults for most common pathologies. ACF integrates into its intervention support for health centers and one district hospital and the implementation of a community approach through identification and training of CHWs. The CHWs will be trained and supervised to provide community management of acute malnutrition without complications. This project will support the rapid response mechanism in the Far North region by deploying its mobile clinic and supporting the health center to preposition stocks, prepare SOPs, train staff and deploying evaluations after the displacements and/ or flooding and rapid health, nutrition and mental health responses, including supplemental vaccination campaigns and distribution of hygienic kits and NFIs.
At the MC site, all children aged 0 to 5 years, PLW and adults will be offered free medical and preventive consultations by qualified medical staff and sensitization awareness sessions will be held by the CHWs and ACF staff.  The staff will provide treatment for common childhood illnesses using national guidelines / and standardized IMCI protocols. The immunization status will be assessed and linkage to the EPI program. People living with disabilities will have access to the services by dissemination messages adaptable to their conditions and linkage to specialized services.
Additionally, as preventive consultations, children will be growth monitored, screened for malnutrition using MUAC (6-59 months), weight, size and oedemas, dewormed (12-59 months) and provided with vitamin A supplementation (6-59 months). Children (0-23 months of age) will also benefit from IYCF counselling provided to their mothers and caregivers.
The package of care will also include medical and MHPSS care for GBV victims (including rape clinical case management), especially women and children, and referral to appropriate facilities for those whose post-rape condition requires further in-depth care, including, for example, social reintegration.
A map of GBV actors and services in the various intervention areas will be created or updated based on the map produced by the GBV sub-working group. A referral system will then be set up or integrated in areas where it already exists to facilitate the referral of survivors to other GBV service providers. This referral pathway will be formalized through  SOPs.This map of GBV stakeholders and services will be disseminated to project teams in addition to the capacity-building they will receive on GBV, the clinical management of GBV cases and the referencing of GBV cases.Through an active participation in working groups and sub-working groups at the regional and local levels, collaboration with other GBV service providers will be strengthened in order to ensure that the referral mechanisms put in place are properly coordinated.
This project will target all people affected by the crisis: men, women, PLWs, children aged 0-5 and above, adolescents, IDPs, host populations, people living with a disability, the elderly, health staff from supported health centers and district hospital and community actors.

project_name: Multisectoral emergency assistance to returnees and host communities in Eastern Chad
project_objective:
The multisectoral emergency assistance to returnees and host communities in Eastern Chad aims at providing protection to the most vulnerable returnees and host communities population through the provision of life-saving assistance and essential services. The response strategy is designed based on NRC expertise in delivering large-scale emergency assistance and on the added value of a complementary, integrated and protection-driven approach centred on relevant NRC’s emergency flagship core competencies of Education, camp management, shelter & NFI, food security & livelihoods and protection services.

The local communities in eastern Chad live in extreme poverty. The load posed over the years by the displaced populations has depleted natural ressources and excacerbated the conditions. The new wave of refugees is further deteriorating the situation. Prices of food are soaring in towns near the Sudan border with markets disrupted by conflict and rising demand. As a direct consequence, the number of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) among children is 60% higer than previously preducted. As refugees, returnees and host communities have nearly the same vulnerabilities, to avoid escalating tensions humanitarian support must also adress the essential needs of the most vulnerable host communities

project_name: Les populations déplacées et les communautés d'accueil affectées par la crise au Niger bénéficient d'une assistance adaptée à leurs besoins d’accès aux droits au Logement, à la Terre et aux Biens pour des solutions durables dans les régions de Tillabéri (Ayérou, Tillabéri, Ouallam, Téra et Abala), Tahoua (Madaoua) et Maradi (Guidan Roumdji et Madarounfa).
project_objective: Le projet contribuera de manière significative à la protection des personnes déplacées interne, refugiés et communauté hôte vulnérables à travers la promotion et la facilitation de l'accès au droit au Logement à la terre et aux biens. Ceci se ferra à travers les actions d'information, conseil et assistance juridique. Un accent sera mis sur le renforcement des capacités des acteurs humanitaire et autorités locale et administrative. Des appuis matériels seront apportés afin de faciliter la délivrance du service. NRC Mettra un accent sur la coordination autour des acteurs LTB afin d'harmoniser les interventions et mener les actions de plaidoyer. Aussi, dans le souci de promouvoir le droit d’accès au Logement, à la Terre, au Bien  et aux Ressources Naturelles (LTB) aux PDIs, aux communautés d'accueil touchées par le déplacement et aux autres groupes vulnérables dans les régions de Maradi  et Tillabery, et Madaoua  NRC à travers son programme d'information, de conseil et d'assistance juridique (ICLA), entreprendra des activités facilitant l'accès à la terre et garantissant la sécurité d’occupation à ces populations, incluant des solutions durables à leurs conflits. ICLA organisera des campagnes de sensibilisations sur  la protection des droits LTB;  fournira des conseils juridiques aux PDIs en vue de les aider à surmonter les obstacles les empêchant d’exercer et de jouir de leurs droits LTB, mènera des plaidoyers pour leur faciliter l’accès temporaire ou durable aux droits LTB, apportera une assistance juridique pour l'obtention des documents fonciers, et renforcera les acteurs locaux et les services techniques impliquées dans la prévention et la résolution des conflits fonciers, et la délivrance des documents fonciers . De même, le programme ICLA apportera son assistance à travers la fourniture de services de diligence raisonnables, sur sollicitation d’autres acteurs humanitaires intervenant dans les mêmes régions et suivant l’analyse de la situation sécuritaire par NRC. ICLA portera une attention particulière à l'accès des femmes à la terre et favorisera l'approche inclusive et participative pour les communautés cibles en facilitant les dialogues communautaires contribuant à identifier les obstacles à l'exercice de ces droits. NRC travaillera en collaboration avec les différentes commissions foncières au niveau centrale régional départementale et communale afin de faciliter la sécurisation et l’accès aux des personnes vulnérables. La stratégie de solution durable étant dans sa phase d’opérationnalisation, NRC veillera à la prise en compte des questions LTB dans ce processus afin de garantir son succès et le respect des droits quelques soit la solution envisagé et ceux dans toutes les phases.

project_name: Providing Lifesaving WASH intevention in North East Nigeria (Pro-life WASH project Phase 2)
project_objective:
The lingering crisis in the BAY States, coupled with  destruction of water and sanitation facilities, vandalization and theft , climate change, have increased the gaps existing already and have increased the vulnerability of the people in the region. These challenges and population increase have also increased thereby throwing people deeper into vulnerability.Inadequate supply of safe and clean water, poor sanitation and hygiene condition of the populace have further compounded their problems increasing chances of disease outbreak including acute watery diseases like cholera. If these are not urgently address will lead to death especially of children under 5.
 Caritas Nigeria will provide provide safe and clean water , improved sanitation and deliver  comprehensive Hygiene promotion  to the proposed locations i the BAY States. This is based on needs identified by our project team over the past 10 years in the BAY States from our needs assessment.
Caritas Nigeria have identified wide gaps in these thematic areas which are corroborated by reports from the sectors' dash boards.
Our provision of water is Eco-friendly as we will be upgrading/converting high yielding hand pumps to solar powered boreholes with full reticulations. These facilities will be designed with rams and rails at water fetching points for inclusivity of people with disabilities. The reticulation of water close to the beneficiaries is meant to reduce vulnerability of girls and women who are often exposed in their quest to search for water. We will also providing dignified sanitation facilities by construction and rehabilitation of VIP latrines and regular de-sludging for safe use by the public. Young girls and women within reproductive ages will be trained on production of dignity kits (re-usable sanitary kits) and will be given starter packs. Others include regular hygiene promotion in the IDP camps and Host communities, so that the chain of diseases transmission will be broken.

project_name: Providing Protection and Housing, Land, and Property Rights support for displacement affected communities in South Sudan.
project_objective:
The overall object of this project is to support affected communities in addressing protection risks and strengthen the Housing, Land, and Property rights of the displaced affected communities including internally displaced persons, returnees, and vulnerable communities in South Sudan through preventative and remedial mechanisms. The proposed interventions aim to provide timely, effective, and quality lifesaving protection responses and service provision to promote enjoyment of Land, and Property rights.
The proposed project will target refugees, returnees, IDPs, and vulnerable host community members in South Sudan for integrated General Protection and HLP assistance.
To achieve the project objective, NRC will focus on two key components i.e. 1. ) General Protection; 2) Housing, Land and Property.
General Protection will be through awareness raising, Protection Monitoring, and Protection Case Management, persons with specific protection risks will receive individualized assistance (Individual Protection Assistance – IPA), including psychosocial support and, as necessary, material assistance. Following the initial rounds of community engagement and awareness raising, NRC staff will work with volunteers in affected communities, training them on peer-to-peer psychosocial support techniques, guiding community-level PSS efforts, and creation of peer support networks.  Community-based Protection Community-based protection structures are established or enhanced, and activities implemented.  
NRC teams will continue to assess the protective environment for shifts in risks and negative coping mechanisms and adjust awareness-raising messages to better suit the needs of targeted populations. Initially, messages and broader activities will emphasize responding to acute protection needs; eventually, greater primacy will be placed on mitigating new risks and establishing some resiliency at the community level.
Prevention of HLP rights violations will be approached using community structures in dispute settlement, advocacy and through information, counselling and legal assistance The project will assist displaced persons in claiming and exercising their HLP rights and attain durable solutions through the prevention of further displacement by supporting them to overcome legal obstacles related to accessing and controlling housing, land, and property rights. The project will strengthen dispute resolution for community structures through collaborative Dispute Resolution (CDR) training to ensure alternative dispute resolution mechanisms are used to resolve HLP-specific cases in the first instance and litigation and advocacy. To further enhance collaboration and multisector responses to forced evictions, the project will work closely with the protection and shelter cluster and other humanitarian actors. Land tenure secured through communal land agreements will be implemented before construction of any humanitarian infrastructure and alternative land will be negotiated and secured for populations at risk of HLP violations.
As the community-based protection systems are often male-dominated and often discriminate against women, NRC will prioritize female beneficiaries during information sessions and legal assistance considering their vulnerability levels. Community participation processes will be used to identify beneficiaries and ensure interventions are both inclusive and community driven. Field level Community engagement through consultations with the affected communities before and after the implementation of project activities. This approach will be used to strengthen community networks while gender will be mainstreamed within all the initiatives.
NRC proposes to target 43,000 beneficiaries (refugees, Internally Displaced Population, Returnees, and Host Communities through HLP and General Population and Housing, Land, and Property Rights Assistance.

project_name: Conflict and displacement-affected communities receive Shelter and Settlements assistance enabling them to capitalize onset their resources and achieve higher self-reliance throughout ongoing conflict and recurring hazards.
project_objective:
Intense hostilities and fighting since the escalation in violence across Sudan on April 15, 2023, have left 24.7 million people in need of humanitarian assistance. Fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has caused significant human suffering and exacerbated pre-existing humanitarian needs among the civilian population in Sudan.

There are 5.7 million people in need of shelter assistance, but the Shelter & Non-Food Items (NFI) Cluster in Sudan faces multiple challenges as it strives to provide critical assistance to vulnerable populations. Before April 15, 2023, shelter and NFI needs were already acute, worsened by the significant underfunding of the cluster’s work.

The intensity of the new clashes and their seemingly indiscriminate nature is causing widespread damage and devastation to housing, household assets, and public infrastructure, prompting many to flee their homes. 6.5 million people have been forced to flee their homes, continuing the same upward trend. Out of those, the estimated number of internally displaced persons (IDPs) across Sudan is 5.1 million.

Countless people fleeing for their lives urgently need shelter and NFI assistance, as many, including children, women, the elderly, and others with specific needs, find themselves crammed into overcrowded public buildings or forced to sleep outdoors exposed to severe weather and threats. Immediate provision of shelter will be critical to ensure privacy and safety, mitigate gender-based violence (GBV) risks, and safeguard displaced populations from harsh environmental conditions to preserve their health amid the upcoming rainy season. Provision of essential household items will be crucial for restoring basic daily activities, such as bedding, cooking utensils, solar lamps for safety and security after dark, and solar chargers for maintaining connectivity, as well as mosquito nets to combat the upcoming malaria season.

The fallout of the escalation in violence includes soaring inflation, scarcity of essential commodities, diminishing cash liquidity and purchasing power, and shortages of energy and fuel for transportation, telecommunications, life-saving medical equipment, and cold chain storage, among others. Finding solutions amidst this incredibly constrained environment becomes increasingly challenging.

The Shelter & NFI Cluster will primarily target Eastern Sudan while simultaneously intensifying efforts to reach displaced populations in Darfur, Kordofan, and Khartoum. Attention will also be given to transit locations within the country and along the borders with Egypt, Chad, South Sudan, Central African Republic, and Ethiopia.

The primary objective is to support newly displaced people in open spaces, public buildings, and camps, as well as those residing with friends or relatives, including populations in transit at border points or within the country. The focus extends to supporting vulnerable residents in hotspot areas, utilizing community-based structures, and those returning to areas where safety has been restored. Flood-impacted communities and those enduring prolonged displacement will receive targeted aid for shelter repair and replenishment of damaged or stolen items.

project_name: Prevention and Treatment of Acute Malnutrition in South Sudan
project_objective:
The humanitarian situation in South Sudan continues to deteriorate since the country gained its independence from Sudan over a decade ago in 2011. The multidimensional crisis in the country is defined by insecurity from unresolved sub-national conflict and communal violence, economic downfall triggered by exchange rate fluctuations and currency depreciation, climatic shocks, volatile political dynamics, and lack of basic services.  

This already challenging humanitarian situation is further exacerbated by an economic downfall trigged by exchange rate fluctuations (US dollar/South Sudanese Pound) and a significant rise in food, commodity and fuel prices due to the Sudan conflict. Trade and supply chains have been disrupted, driving up food prices and constraining food access for the returnees and the host communities. A comparison of the cost of the standard food basket before and after the outbreak of the conflict in Sudan found a 28 percent increase in the cost of standard food basket across monitored markets. Additionally, fuel prices continue to be elevated contributing to increased transport costs and food prices.  

The IPC results from November 2023 indicate that between July 2023 and June 2024, an estimated 1.65 million children between 6-59 months are expected to suffer acute malnutrition including 480,000 million children expected to suffer Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) and 1.17 million expected to suffer Moderate Acute Malnutrition (MAM). Approximately 870,000 pregnant or breastfeeding women (PBW) are also expected to suffer acute malnutrition in this period. An estimated 72 percent of the acute malnutrition burden is concentrated in the five states of Jonglei, Northern Bahr el Ghazal, Upper Nile, Unity and Warrap. Almost 58% of the counties are classified as IPC Phase 4 (critical) and 19% as IPC 3 (serious). 
This is a significant deterioration from last year, with contributing factors of high disease prevalence (55% of children reported to have been ill two weeks prior). Poor access to improved drinking water and sanitation compromises hygiene practices. Only 58.4 % of the population reported having access to improved sources of water leaving close to half the population depending on unsafe sources. Inadequate feeding practices of infants and young children is another high-risk contributing factor to acute malnutrition. Only 5 children out of 100 are getting the recommended quality and frequency of food required for optimal growth. 34.6% achieved the Minimum Meal frequency while only 21% achieved the Minimum dietary diversity. 
In response to the dire nutrition needs in South Sudan, WFP's project will facilitate the provision of nutrition prevention and treatment services to populations affected by conflict, displacement, climate change and insecurity. The project will target residents, IDPs, refugees and returnees to treat and prevent malnutrition related morbidity and mortality. 
WFP will continue to work in close collaboration with the Ministry of Health, the Nutrition Cluster, sister agencies and with implementing partners to support an emergency nutrition response in two key ways: First, through a preventive supplementary feeding programme targeting children aged 6-24 months (and up to 59 months in IPC 5 locations), pregnant & breastfeeding women, and people living with HIV/TB in highly food insecure locations of South Sudan. Second, WFP will implement a treatment of acute malnutrition programme in 61 out of 80 counties in the country, targeting children under 5 years of age, PBWs, elderly and PLHIV/TB/Kalazar. 
In hard-to-reach areas, WFP will conduct direct delivery of life-saving nutrition services through the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM). The project implementation will be coordinated closely with the Nutrition cluster, UNICEF, MOH and use an integrated approach through synergies with activities supported by other clusters (health, education, FSL, WASH).

project_name: Mejorando la seguridad alimentaria de las familias del corredor seco
project_objective:
La seguridad alimentaria y nutricional en el corredor seco de Guatemala, durante la última década ha sido afectada por diferentes factores. Guatemala es un país en donde los niveles de vulnerabilidad de la población son elevados y el riesgo a sufrir fenómenos multiamenaza como la sequía y las inundaciones son muy altos. En la última década la sequía está causando fuertes estragos en una población que depende de la agricultura de subsistencia para vivir. 
Para este proyecto los municipios priorizados presentan altos índices de inseguridad alimentaria, lo cual se refleja en el incremento de la desnutrición aguda en los niños y las niñas de cero a 5 años. Es por ello que se realizarán acciones integrales de entrega de raciones de alimentos y transferencias monetarias no condicionadas, para que las familias puedan contar con alimentos y suplir necesidades básicas; así también se contempla la entrega de insumos agropecuarios para el increment0 de la producción y de esta forma se promueva la reactivación económica de las comunidades afectadas. Estas acciones incluyen elementos para la adaptación al cambio climático y el empoderamiento de mujeres y jóvenes.
El proyecto responde a los siguientes objetivos:
• Restablecer la seguridad alimentaria de las familias en situación de inseguridad alimentaria a través de transferencias monetarias y/o bolsas de alimentos
• Recuperar los medios de vida y la capacidad productiva de las familias en situación de inseguridad alimentaria

project_name: “Atención Psicosocial a Personas en Movilidad Humana: Abordando Necesidades Emocionales y Sociales”
project_objective:
Continúa la vigilancia constante de flujos de personas en tránsito en las áreas
fronterizas del país, registrando un aumento sostenido en la movilidad entre los
municipios de Esquipulas y Ayutla. Durante septiembre, se observó un promedio
diario de 2.322 personas en tránsito por Guatemala, marcando un incremento del
28% en comparación con las 1.815 personas registradas en agosto. Las
necesidades fundamentales identificadas entre estas personas incluyen alimentos,
agua, saneamiento e higiene, albergues, atención médica y protección.
Los grupos más vulnerables en este trayecto son los niños, niñas y adolescentes
(NNA) acompañados y no acompañados, mujeres embarazadas y lactantes, así
como las personas de la tercera edad. Esta propuesta surge como respuesta a la
recomendación formulada en el informe SITREP 2 de flujos mixtos/OCHA, que
aboga por ampliar las acciones de atención en el municipio de Ayutla,
específicamente fortaleciendo a los actores locales en la provisión de servicios;
Asimismo, proveer información a las familias sobre rutas y servicios locales y los
factores de riesgo del trayecto, compartiendo con ellos materiales prácticos de
bolsillo; se activará el asocio con la casa del migrante ubicada en Ayutla;
acompañando en los procesos de atención a los niñas, niños y adolescentes ,
mediante actividades lúdicas de ocupación constructiva de su tiempo y mitigación
emocional; para los niños de primera infancia se realizarán actividades de
estimulación temprana y a los padres de familia se trabajará la salud mental
familiar y atención psicosocial para afrontar con mayor resiliencia sus destinos.
Como parte de estos procesos de información se orientará en la familia con
información Jurídica, representaciones legales, opciones de refugio, asilo, abrigo,
derechos a servicios públicos, ayudas humanitarias, retorno voluntario etc.

project_objective:

En el departamento de Gracias a Dios 556  familias, 3,475 participantes para ayuda humanitaria  bajo la modalidad de raciones de alimentación y medios de vida,población que  abarca los  grupos étnicos:Misquitos, Garífunas,Pech.
Se brindará asistencia humanitaria con el fin de mejorar el consumo inmediato de alimentos. Sobre la base de la experiencia de CASM en un departamento vecino, se espera que haya 100 hogares encabezados por mujeres y 850 hogares encabezados por hombres.
La región de La Moskitia es el hogar de un número particularmente grande de 4 pueblos originarios que principalmente cultivan sus propios alimentos, ya que comprar alimentos es caro y las opciones son limitadas debido a desafíos logísticos. Como resultado del cambio climático, las condiciones se han vuelto extremadamente difíciles para el cultivo de alto
rendimiento y las pérdidas de cosechas son frecuentes, esto deja a la población rural miskita vulnerable y afectando el sector agrícola y como consecuencia de ellos un a crisis de seguridad alimentaria de los poblados e incrementado la crisis de migración de la población.Con la llegada de las pasadas tormentas tropicales  más de  3000 hogares resultaron damnificados como producto de las lluvias e inundaciones.Se registran pérdidas de aproximadamente 7,282 Mz de las tierras usadas para el cultivo de yuca,banano, plátano, arroz y frijol.
