project_name: Respuesta integral en salud,  seguridad alimentaria y nutricional de emergencia para la población más vulnerable afectada por la crisis en Venezuela.
project_objective:
ACH realiza un análisis de contexto previo al inicio del proyecto, y un análisis de necesidades de fuentes secundarias, el cual se complementa con información  de primera mano al inicio de la implementación. El análisis de riesgos de protección, incluidos los de VBG y de protección de NNA es un estudio que se prevé realizar en la primera fase de implementación del proyecto.

En el sector de salud, ACH proporcionará consultas integrales de atención primaria de salud, la cual se centrará en la detección, diagnóstico y tratamiento de anemias nutricionales, diagnóstico y tratamiento oportuno de enfermedades prevalentes en la infancia, así como desparasitación preventiva y curativa. También se ofrecerán servicios de SSR. Desde el sector de nutrición, se realizará tamizaje nutricional con identificación y tratamiento de casos de desnutrición aguda con la provisión de alimentos terapéuticos, al tiempo, estas personas se beneficiarán con la entrega de asistencia alimentaria y kits de higiene familiar y de higiene menstrual, así como un tanque o filtro para el almacenamiento seguro de agua. Los casos identificados recibirán seguimiento hasta su recuperación. ACH reforzará las capacidades técnicas del personal médico y actores comunitarios. Asimismo, se llevarán a cabo sensibilizaciones a los beneficiarios. Además, ACH va a capacitar a trabajadores de salud y líderes comunitarios en APS, nutrición e igualdad de género, reparto equitativo de las tareas del hogar, prevención de la VG y la violencia sexual. La distribución por cada estado y/o comunidad será definida una vez se aplique la línea de base. ACH proporcionará consultas de Salud Mental y Apoyo Psicosocial a través de asesoramiento individual y familiar incluyendo la integración del enfoque de protección.

Seguridad Alimentaria: ACH prevé la distribución de cestas de alimentos a familias con miembros identificados en situación de riesgo nutricional. Esta acción está completamente entrelazada con los sectores WASH, NUT, y género y protección para garantizar un apoyo intersectorial. ACH reconoce que las diferentes culturas tienen diversos valores, creencias y prácticas relacionadas con los alimentos, por lo que se ACH se centra en respetar y adecuar la asistencia de acuerdo a las comunidades seleccionadas. 

Desde el sector de WASH, ACH hará distribución de kits de higiene familiar y filtros y tanques para el tratamiento y almacenamiento de agua segura. Las mujeres recibirán un kit con productos para la gestión de la higiene menstrual tras la asistencia a unos talleres de promoción de la salud y la higiene menstrual desde un enfoque de empoderamiento femenino. Además, ACH rehabilitará sistemas de abastecimiento de agua a nivel comunitario y centros de salud, acompañado de la creación y/o reactivación de comités de agua y saneamiento, o mesas de agua. Las actividades del sector WASH son sensibles a la nutrición, por lo que son complementarias. Las distribuciones irán acompañadas de sesiones de formación sobre el uso y mantenimiento de los artículos entregados y buenas prácticas de higiene; además, se llevará a cabo un análisis de las barreras para el uso de los productos HWTS y se adaptará la estrategia de comunicación.

Desde protección, se prevén actividades de sensibilización para prevenir los riesgos de protección (VBG, abuso infantil  y trata). Formación del personal sanitario y promotores en el enfoque transformador de género, así como formaciones en protección humanitaria y en igualdad de género.

La prevención de la VBG está integrada transversalmente en todas las actividades para abordar de manera integral las dinámicas de género y proteger a las poblaciones vulnerables. En nutrición, por ejemplo, se implementan programas de sensibilización que abordan las desigualdades de género en el acceso a alimentos y promueven prácticas alimentarias equitativas.

project_name: Respuesta para restablecer los servicios de agua, saneamiento e higiene de las poblaciones vulnerables en la zona norte de Honduras
project_objective:
Basic Info
Project Name	Start Date End Date
01/05/2024   31/12/2024
Respuesta para restablecer los servicios de agua, saneamiento e higiene de las poblaciones vulnerables en la zona norte de Honduras

Project Summary
Acción contra el Hambre (ACH) cuenta con experiencia en la implementación de proyectos en diversas áreas rurales en el ámbito de acceso al agua potable, el saneamiento y la higiene; salud, nutrición, seguridad alimentaria, gestión de riesgos y atención y respuesta a la emergencia. Centra su trabajo en mejorar las condiciones de vida de familias vulnerables afectadas por la situación de crisis humanitaria como consecuencia de los diferentes fenómenos climáticos (sequía, desastres naturales, el cambio climático) y la situación de violencia generalizada, entre múltiples amenazas y, en consecuencia, el hambre.
La propuesta “Respuesta para restablecer los servicios de agua, saneamiento e higiene de las poblaciones vulnerables en la zona norte de Honduras” tiene como objetivo restablecer los servicios tanto domésticos como comunitarios esenciales para las personas más vulnerables de la zona norte de Honduras, zona afectada por desastres naturales como los ocurridos desde en noviembre de 2020 con los huracanes Eta & Iota y octubre de 2022 con las inundaciones producidas por el huracán Julia y ejes de vaguada, así como los efectos del cambio climático , que obligan a la población a desplazarse. Además de intervenciones comunitarias en restablecimiento de sistemas de agua, promoción y acceso digno a instalaciones de saneamiento diferenciadas, inclusivas y seguras, gestión de drenajes y excretas, y sensibilizaciones, se prevé, alineados con el Objetivo Sectorial 2, fomentar la sostenibilidad de los servicios WASH en centros educativos y establecimientos de salud. Estas dos tipologías de establecimientos se han visto muy afectadas, en primer lugar, por la crisis sanitaria de la COVID-19 y, por otro lado, por la transformación de los centros escolares en albergues durante los eventos naturales extremos.
Se enmarca en la zona priorizada por el clúster WASH, poniendo su foco en tres municipios de los departamentos de Cortés. Se realizará un diagnóstico detallado en los mismos para poder proporcionar una mejor respuesta adaptada a las necesidades específicas de cada grupo con enfoque de edad, género, diversidad y protección.
Cabe destacar que la perspectiva climática del último trimestre predice 
 
posibilidades de algún fenómeno natural peligroso. Por lo que, desde ACH, se va a trabajar paralelamente el fortalecimiento de las capacidades de las estructuras sociales comunitarias (Juntas de Agua, CODEL, CODEM).

project_name: Prevención y Respuesta Especializada a la VbG San Marcos y Huehuetenango 2024
project_objective:
La violencia de género es una violación de los derechos humanos, un problema de salud pública y un obstáculo para la participación cívica, social, política y económica. Además de degradar la dignidad y la salud de quienes la sufren. La violencia de género en Guatemala sigue siendo prevalente, según la Organización Panamericana de la Salud (OPS), en su reporte de ABORDAR LA VIOLENCIA CONTRA LAS MUJERES EN LAS POLÍTICAS Y PROTOCOLOS DE SALUD DE LA REGIÓN DE LAS AMÉRICAS, Un informe de la situación regional, el 21% de las mujeres guatemaltecas sufren violencia a lo largo de su vida. Las condiciones económicas y sociales tensas, además de las normas tradicionales perjudiciales son factores que contribuyen a la violencia de género en el país.
En 2020, según el Ministerio Público, Observatorio de la Mujer. Informe Guatemala 2020 se presentaron 58.060 denuncias por violencia contra la mujer en el Ministerio Público a nivel nacional, lo que lo convierte en el primer delito más denunciado en Guatemala. La tasa de homicidios de mujeres en Guatemala es 2,3 veces superior a la media de América Latina y 4,7 veces superior a la media mundial.
El Sub-clúster de Violencia basada en Género en Guatemala determinó como objetivos prioritarios el Fortalecer el acceso a servicios integrales de atención y acciones de prevención,  basados en los mínimos estándares interagenciales de VBG de calidad, seguros, pertinentes centrados en las personas sobrevivientes de VBG en contextos de movilidad humana y poblaciones afectadas por la inseguridad alimentaria, y Promover espacios seguros de base comunitaria para la prevención, la atención y mitigación de riesgos de VBG y la prestación de servicios integrales a población afectada por la inseguridad alimentaria y nutrición.
Dado el contexto guatemalteco de violencia basada en género, el fuerte y constante flujo migratorio, los objetivos del Sub-clúster de Violencia basada en Género, y la lógica de implementación para la protección y el empoderamiento de la mujer (WPE por sus siglas en inglés), el IRC propone la siguiente intervención para llegar con el apoyo de sus socios a un total de 10 mil clientes:
1-           La provisión de servicios de gestoría de casos, tanto tradicional como de emergencia.
La gestión de los casos de violencia de género es una parte integral de la respuesta de WPE. La gestión de casos de violencia de género es un método estructurado para proporcionar ayuda a una superviviente mediante el cual se informa a la superviviente de todas las opciones disponibles y se identifican y se hacen un seguimiento coordinado de las cuestiones y problemas a los que se enfrenta, y se le proporciona apoyo emocional durante todo el proceso. La gestión de casos de violencia de género también se ha convertido en el principal punto de entrada para que las supervivientes reciban apoyo psicosocial y de crisis a largo plazo, dada la falta de proveedores de servicios de salud y apoyo social más establecidos en entornos humanitarios.
2-           La entrega de kits de dignidad
La entregade kits de dignidad que permiten el apoyo no solo económico a las mujeres, pero más allá promueve su participación en espacios públicos, espacios de educación, toma de decisión, espacios laborales, todo a la vez que les permite sentirse vistas e incluidas en la programación humanitaria.
En este caso se propone la entrega como servicio complementario a la gestoría de casos y a los ESMN.
3-           La implementación de un espacio seguro para mujeres y niñas móvil.
Una de las principales modalidades de servicio comprobadas de WPE para mujeres y niñas, tanto en emergencias como en otras situaciones, para la gestión de casos de violencia de género centrada en las mujeres y las niñas, la programación para adolescentes, el APS y las sesiones de reducción de riesgos dirigidas por mujeres. El IRC propone la implementación mediante su metodología móvil en los departamentos de Huehuetenango y San Marcos.

project_name: Delivery of Life-saving Healthcare Services to Conflict-affected Communities in Gedaref, Khartoum, South Kordofan, Blue Nile, White Nile, Red Sea, and Jazira states
project_objective:
The project aims to reduce excess morbidity and mortality through improving access to life-saving preventive and curative health services in Jezira, White Nile, Red Sea, Gedaref, Khartoum, South Kordofan, and Blue Nile states in Sudan. The main beneficiaries are persons affected by the recent crisis caused by armed conflicts between the Sudan Armed Forces (SAF) and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) including internally displaced communities (IDPs), and vulnerable host communities targeting children under five years of age, adolescent girls, women, boys and men. The project will hotspot areas affected by the current crisis as well as IDP-receiving states and will support the existing Ministry of Health (MoH) capacity to deliver lifesaving primary health care services, including management of communicable and non-communicable diseases, support reproductive; maternal, and child health services including strengthening of expanded program for immunization; mental health and psychosocial support. The IRC will build the capacity of MoH staff, and provide essential drugs and medical supplies, including supplies for infection prevention and control, as well as infrastructure improvement and surge teams in the form of mobile medical teams (MMTs) to quickly respond to health emergencies. This is well aligned with the IRC’s Sudan Response Strategy. 
Protection services will also be integrated into the IRC’s health programming to achieve greater outcomes for women and girls, including prevention and response to Gender Based Violence (GBV). Through a community-based approach, the project will ensure equity by supporting community health volunteers to provide community health packages to hard-to-reach and underserved communities. The IRC WASH teams will closely support the HF teams to improve facility WASH infrastructures and practices including medical and non-medical waste management, hand washing stations, and hygiene promotion. 
The IRC has a strong capacity to deliver health services in Sudan with current support including strengthening the MoH capacity to deliver integrated health services in Gedaref, Khartoum, Jazira, and Blue Nile states, and currently expanding to White Nile and Red Sea states. Since 2019, the IRC has supported the delivery of integrated health, nutrition, protection, livelihoods, and WASH services providing a one-stop center to deliver life-saving interventions to beneficiaries in a safe way. The IRC health technical excellence unit at the headquarter in NY with regional representation in Nairobi provides technical oversight and guidance for the adaptation of quality health standards, training, and technical supervision including frequent field presence to support country teams. Even in the face of the current crisis, the IRC has maintained in-country capacity and regional support to continue to deliver essential health services.

project_name: Livelihoods support to food insecure and vulnerable populations in Upper Nile, Warrap and Central Equatoria states of South Sudan
project_objective: GOAL proposes livelihoods support to 72,500 vulnerable individuals in Twic county (Warrap State), Ulang and Renk counties (Upper Nile State) and Kajo Keji County (Central Equatoria state). This intervention will leverage GOAL’s previous interventions and continue to provide sustainable and innovative early responses as well as durable solutions. In the three states, GOAL works with the FSL cluster through active participation in the bi-weekly meetings and supporting food security assessments. GOAL also leads Inter-Agency Rapid Needs Assessments (IRNA) in the event of disasters and when called upon by deep field OCHA coordination. Nationally, GOAL participates actively in FSL meetings, HRP workshops and meetings and any food security related events. GOAL is also an active member of the Cash Working Group (CWG) and is a cooperating partner of both WFP and FAO. In these partnerships, GOAL updates its programming based on Humanitarian Response Plans and food and nutrition security assessments. GOAL also complements the efforts of UN agencies and humanitarian actors implementing cluster objective 1 to avoid duplication and to transition beneficiaries from emergency to resilience support. In all the three states proposed for response, health and nutrition will be integrated with FSL through inclusion of market-based and livelihoods interventions in the treatment and prevention of malnutrition and disease prevention. Mother to mother support groups (MTMSGs) and Male Peer Educators (MPE) will be supported to produce crops and vegetables for home consumption and for sale of surplus to improve household food and nutrition security and to generate income for meeting other household needs. This will contribute to prevention of the root causes of malnutrition and to reduce relapse of malnutrition. GOAL also proposes rehabilitation of livelihoods infrastructure and systems through conditional cash distribution. This will provide relief to households affected by floods, drought, the Sudan Crisis and other disasters in South Sudan  while ensuring access to critical facilities. In Counties where fish is a major source of livelihood, GOAL will support fish production and value addition while ensuring that beneficiaries are aware of nutrition benefits of fish as well as post-harvest practices. In the event of floods and drought, access to fuel wood for cooking is not only limited but also a risk to women and girls as they travel long distances to fetch it. To reduce reliance community’s reliance on fuelwood, GOAL will pilot production and distribution of locally made energy saving stoves through capacity building of community structures to ensure durable solutions. For sustainability, GOAL will train the community members to make energy saving stoves and utilize or sell for income generation.  All livelihood interventions will be done in close collaboration with state and county government especially State and County Agriculture, Environment and Forestry department.

project_name: Provision of Integrated Safe, Equitable, Protective and Inclusive Education to Conflict Affected Boys and Girls in South Sudan.
project_objective:
In 2023 an estimated 9.4 million people, more than two thirds of the country’s population, are in need of humanitarian assistance – 53% of people in need are children. In this context, education plays a crucial role for South Sudan’s children. Education provides safety, keeping children and youth from physical harm, whilst also contributing to psychosocial wellbeing and health, when complemented by WASH and school feeding interventions. Schools provide safe spaces that also function as a platform to deliver lifesaving interventions, such as food, water, sanitation, mental and physical health services. Education programmes mitigate the impact of humanitarian crises by building resilience among children, young people and their communities. Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) programmes in education curricula and preparedness plans equip and strengthen children’s ability to deal with emergencies and mitigate the impact of future disasters. WV will implement EiE projects in the counties where it has a strong operational presence, characterized with very high needs, especially in education and other related sectors: CES (Juba) Upper Nile (Malakal, Melut, Renk), WES (Yambio, Nzara, Tambura), Warrap (Tonj North, Twic, Gogrial East, Gogrial West, Tonj South and Tonj East), Northern Bahr El Ghazal (Aweil North, Aweil South) targeting populations affected by conflict or disaster in 2023.

WV is currently implementing education programs in partnership with ECHO, Education Can't Wait, EMPOWER Irish Aid, UNHCR and GPE. To consolidate on current efforts while reaching further and deeper into the areas with dire needs, in hard-to-reach areas WV will continue to focus on emergency affected rural and urban areas. 

In line with the Education Cluster Response Plan, WV will ensure that through this project, 28,200 children will have access to safe and equitable quality education; 600 teachers, and 650 PTA’s will be trained and supported with supplies and materials; 1500 youth will be provided life skills and vocational training with starter kits. Out of the identified learners, the project will target about 400 children (200 boys, 200 girls) with disabilities. The learners will also be categorized under social/residential status as internally displaced, host community, or refugees during the actual enrolment in the project.

WV will also prioritize establishment of learning structures with gender-segregated WASH facilities, and other supplies/materials/kits that are supportive and enhance motivation of children to go to and remain in school with a particular emphasis on girl’s education. In addition, recreational opportunities will be established and implemented to support the recovery of children and youth and promote their overall wellbeing. All learners will be given equal access to education despite Gender, disability or ethnic background.

project_objective:
Islamic Relief Worldwide is a humanitarian organization has been working in South Sudan since 2004 and providing humanitarian support for the flood, drought and conflict affected people in need including provision of WASH services at Warrap state (Tonj north county) Central equatoria (Kajokeji and Yei counties) Eastern equatoria (Kapoeta East and Kapoeta north counties) Islamic Relief South Sudan (IRSS) has developed “Enhancing resilience for equitable WASH services for IDPs, returnees and host
communities project to respond and increase resilience capacity of the food, drought and conflict affected communities to achieve the following objectives:
i.	Contribute to reducing WASH-related morbidity and mortality in priority counties through WASH integrated programming with Nutrition
ii.	Provide access to basic WASH services in emergencies and/or WSC 4 and 5
iii.	WASH specific activities for GBV mitigation
iv.	Community members’ exposure to environmental hazards is reduced through the construction of disaster-resistant structures.
The proposed action intended to provide lifesaving inclusive WASH services to 44;556 (Men 11,139, women 12,476, Boys 10,248, Girls 10,693 & PWD 6,683). people in need in Warrap state (Tonj north counties) Central Equatoria (Kajokeji and Yei counties) Eastern equatoria (Kapoeta East and Kapoeta north counties). This project is anticipated to positively impact on the lives of people through increasing access to improved water supplies systems/facilities, restoring dignity in women and girls through provision of gender sensitive sanitation infrastructure and hygiene services/products for women and girls, boys and men, elderly people, people with disability including people suffering chronic illnesses.
To achieve the project objectives, Islamic Relief South Sudan will be focusing on the Right Based Approach linked with the Accountability to the Affected Population (AAP) approach to address the pressing WASH needs and gender/protection related concerns in order to minimize or mitigate the common causes of vulnerabilities.
This project strives to provide timely and equitable access to clean and safe water supply, gender and vulnerability sensitive water supply and sanitation infrastructure and hygiene services/products through construction of new water facilities/sources (Hand pump boreholes, solarized water yards. Conduct rehabilitation activities for the nonfunctional/defunct water sources/schemes, and sanitation facilities such as institutional latrines, incinerators, hand washing facilities. The project shall as well integrate the aspect community capacity building strategy through awareness campaigns, formation and training of Community based WASH structures such as; Hygiene promoters, leaders, Water Management Committees (WMC) and Hand Pump Mechanics to improve on operation and maintenance for sustainability purposes.

project_name: Développement d'un modèle d'approvisionnement durable en eau potable dans des contextes fragiles affectés par les conflits et le changement climatique au Tchad
project_objective:
Le Lac Tchad est décrit comme l'urgence la plus complexe au monde. Dans tout le bassin du lac Tchad, 11 millions de personnes ont besoin d'aide humanitaire. Le plan de réponse humanitaire Tchad 2022 estime que 4,1 millions de personnes sont en situation d'insécurité alimentaire, 3,7 millions de personnes sous-alimentées, 1,5 million de personnes déplacées et 1,3 million nécessitant un soutien ciblé en WASH. Ceci est une conséquence du changement climatique, de l'extrémisme violent (lié à la présence de Boko Haram), de la croissance démographique, de l'insécurité alimentaire, de la forte prévalence des maladies infectieuses, de l'affaiblissement de l'État et de la corruption. 
Cette crise a aggravé des conditions de vie déjà précaires d’une grande majorité des populations de cette province en accentuant le manque d´accès aux services de base notamment à l’eau potable. Les communautés dépendent de l'eau provenant de puits et de forages et bien que les eaux souterraines soient largement disponibles à faible profondeur (10-30 mètres) à partir de pompes manuelles, l’accès à l’eau de bonne qualité est problématique. Le contexte géologique et hydrogéologique particulier de la province du lac Tchad est à l'origine des problèmes de salinité. Pour mieux comprendre ce problème, en 2017 Oxfam en collaboration avec les partenaires du secteur WASH a réalisé une cartographie de la qualité de l'eau pour mieux comprendre les ressources en eau dans cette zone. Cette étude a mis en évidence l'existence d'un gradient hydraulique du Sud au Nord où la salinité augmente au fur et à mesure qu'on s'éloigne du Lac jusqu'à un maximum de 7000 μS/cm où 79% des ouvrages de la Cuvette Nord du Lac Tchad sont caractérisés par des conductivités supérieures à la norme de 2500 μS/cm contre 16% dans la partie Sud. La salinité plus faible dans la zone sud du Lac s'explique par les eaux douces du Lac qui alimentent l'aquifère. Mais plus on s'éloigne du Lac, plus le temps de résidence des eaux souterraines est long et le contact au sein des roches évaporitiques provoque une minéralisation (augmentation de la salinité). 
C’est ainsi qu’avec le financement de fonds innovation Wash Oxfam  2021-2022, la mission d’Oxfam au Tchad a conduit une étude de faisabilité sur une technologie de dessalement de l’eau dénommé « l’OSMOSE INVERSE » dans la sous-préfecture de Daboua.  L’étude de faisabilité a ciblé Daboua Centre (chef-lieu de la sous-préfecture de Daboua) et Tataverom (chef-lieu de canton). Les deux lieux accueillent des personnes déplacées/IPD et des populations hôtes. Dans ces zones, certaines personnes s’approvisionnent au niveau de puits traditionnelle ou bien ceux qui en ont les moyens paient l'eau potable qui est acheminée par camion à plus de 25 km, l'eau salée locale n'étant utilisée que pour d'autres besoins comme la cuisine, la lessive et les animaux.
 Au cours de la réalisation de l'étude de faisabilité, les personnes interrogées ont constamment confirmé que la qualité de l'eau était un problème majeur dans toutes les zones visitées. Même à Bagasola, qui est située dans la zone de faible salinité, les gens indiquaient qu'il y avait quelques points d'eau que les gens préfèrent parce que l'eau a meilleur goût. A Daboua Centre, différents entretiens ont confirmé que la source d'eau douce la plus proche se trouve au Niger (Blablime) ou à Bélégue (à 25 kilomètres).
D’après les résultats de l’étude de faisabilité, techniquement, économiquement et écologiquement, le dessalement via l’OSOMOSE INVERSE est une meilleure solution pour répondre aux besoins en eau de boisson dans la zone de Daboua que les interventions actuelles à court terme sur lesquelles les partenaires humanitaires et de développement se concentrent encore principalement. C’est ainsi qu’Oxfam se propose de développer un projet de dessalement de l’eau  de boisson pour les population de la zone de Daboua.

project_name: Réponse humanitaire en matière de protection et d'éducation pour les enfants affectés par la crise multidimensionnelle à Mopti
project_objective:
Au Mali, l'insécurité, les conflits et les catastrophes naturelles ont empêché plus de 582
600 enfants d'accéder à l'éducation en toute sécurité en 2023. L’aversion des groupes
armés luttant contre le modèle d’éducation occidental dans les régions du centre et au
nord du Mali reste une constance depuis le déclenchement de la crise en 2012. A cela
s’ajoutent les conflits communautaires et les catastrophes naturelles telles que les
inondations qui réduisent les opportunités d’accès à l’éducation et la qualité des services
de supervision des apprentissages.
Selon les données collectées par le Cluster Education et le gouvernement du Mali, 1 762
écoles demeurent fermées en février 2023. Cela révèle que, malgré les efforts déployés
pour ouvrir des écoles, le nombre d'écoles touches par le conflit continue d'augmenter
chaque année. Par exemple, en 2020, le nombre d'écoles fermées était estimé à 1 344,
puis à 1 664 en 2021, pour arriver à un pic de 1 776 en 2022. Les régions de Mopti,
Tombouctou, Ménaka, Ségou et Gao, sont celles qui comptent avec le plus grand nombre
d'écoles non fonctionnelles en raison de l'insécurité.
De plus, 419 incidents de protection (dont le 16% concerne des enfants) ont été signalés
entre depuis le début de 2023 dans la seule région de Mopti (Rapport de Monitoring de
Protection, Cluster Protection). Une analyse rapide de besoins d’éducation et protection
des enfants dans communes urbaines de Mopti et communes rurales de Fatoma et
Bassirou réalisée en février 2023. Sur la base des informations collectées, les enfants
sont particulièrement affectés par les violations graves de leurs droits, notamment le
recrutement et utilisation des enfants par des groupes armés, les enlèvements, les
attaques contre les structures sanitaires et éducatives. La fermeture des écoles constitue
davantage un facteur de risque et d’exposition des enfants à la violence et aux abus. De
plus des signes de détresse psychologique, inclus un sentiment d’insécurité (Rapport
d’évaluation rapide : NRC, SCI, SLDSES de juillet 2022), ont été remarqués. Le besoin de
services de soutien psychosocial et de santé mentale se manifeste pour les enfants
affectés par le conflit, déplacés et de la communauté hôte, inclus les élèves des écoles
fermés et leurs enseignants. Les filles restent particulièrement exposées aux violences

project_name: Restoring Access to Safe, Dignified, and Functional WASH Services in Daraa, Rural Damascus, Idleb, Aleppo, and Homs
project_objective:
To strengthen community resilience to the water crisis and associated shocks, DRC plans to rehabilitate three damaged water networks in Aleppo, Dar'a, and Idleb, expected to benefit approximately 13,500 individuals through a regular and safe supply of water for drinking and other domestic purposes, including a foreseen increased daily water availability. Based on pre-defined criteria, DRC will prioritize water infrastructure with the most appropriate surface or underground water sources that are critically underserving basic needs. Upon selection, DRC engineers will undertake environmental assessments using NEAT+ to determine environmental risks, mitigation strategies, and opportunities for regenerative practices prior to implementation, especially related to water sources and risks of depletion and sustainable use/disposal of water.  A damage assessment will also be conducted using appropriate methods and tools, such as visual inspection, leak detection, pressure testing, and water quality analysis, and will assess the impacts of water infrastructure failure (e.g., water scarcity, environmental and health risks). Based on the findings, a rehabilitation plan will be developed to refine the scope of works and technical BoQs, taking into consideration groundwater depletion and opportunities to improve water delivery targeting and reduce water use wastage. To restore access to safe, dignified, and functional excreta disposal facilities and reduce environmental impacts and health risks, DRC will also rehabilitate three damaged sewage networks in Rural Damascus, Aleppo, and Homs, benefiting approximately 16,000 individuals. DRC will prioritize sewage networks where contamination of drinking water sources has been identified and present serious public health risks. In-depth technical assessments of each infrastructure will be conducted to collect the baseline capacity and identify the extent and causes of damage/dysfunction, as well as unmet sanitation needs. 

Across both water and sanitation interventions, rehabilitation works will be delivered through local contractors, selected through a competitive and transparent tendering process, with technical supervision and oversight of DRC engineers. Daily monitoring visits will be conducted by DRC technical teams to ensure that the contractors are implementing activities as per the approved BoQs, to verify that safety measures are in place, and to identify and rectify any challenges that may arise. Once the rehabilitation works are completed, DRC will initiate a structured handover to ensure the seamless transfer of ownership and responsibility for the rehabilitated WASH infrastructure to DoWR. DRC teams will also share technical knowledge and guidance with relevant staff from the DoWR, who will be the responsible unit for the management of the infrastructure after the handover, including the renewable energy systems, and will work with them to locate water points and establish maintenance strategies with clear responsibilities and future needs for sustainable access to water and sanitation services.

project_name: Provide Integrated Lifesaving Gender Responsive Health, Nutrition, WASH, Food Security & Livelihoods and Protection Support to Reduce Risks and Improve the well-being of IDPs, returnees, and host communities in Khartoum, South Darfur, East Darfur, Kassala, Gedaref, Al-Gezira and South Kordofan.
project_objective:

The overall objective of this project is to contribute to “Decreased morbidity, mortality, and Gender Based Violence risks through provision of improved and sustained access to Cash, food assistance, livelihood support, water supply, sanitation, hygiene promotion, health, nutrition, protection and GBV services. This objective is developed in line with the 2024 Sudan humanitarian response plan and the FSL, WASH, health, nutrition, protection, and GBV clusters priorities in addressing the growing needs for the affected population across Sudan after the 15th of April conflict through construction and rehabilitation of facilities, operation and maintenance and capacity building of communities. The total number of individuals targeted by this project is 1,327,738
affected population over all sectors. 
CARE’s HRP project for 2024 is targeting to reach 10% of the Sectors’ targets in all CARE’s operating localities.

In addition, supporting the Early detection of the malnutrition among under 5 yrs old and PLW through MUAC screening and early referral for treatment (2) CARE will support the Blanket Supplementary Feeding Program in its operating areas to reach a target of 1% of children from 6-59 months and PLW to prevent the risk of developing acute malnutrition. In addition, (4) CARE will be supporting providing evidence and monitoring, through SMART surveys and supporting the monitoring and reporting at CARE’s supported sites to monitor admissions trends and to monitoring of supplies. 
CARE Health HRP project for 2024, will focus on (1) Supporting essential public health functions with focus on PHC. CARE will continue supporting the continue of essential PHC service, to prevent and control communicable diseases, provision of SRH services and supporting the provision of EPI activities.  In addition, CARE will address the gaps in Secondary health care services, supporting the operation of hospitals in overstretched areas. (2) Strengthen emergency preparedness, response, and all-hazards emergency risk management: through supporting the early alerts identification, reporting and investigation in all the supported localities and health facilities, through strengthening the surveillance systems and EWARS, and addressing the gaps for supporting the (RRT) where is needed in CARE’ operating localities.
CARE ensures that H&N supported facilities are integrated with WASH essential services insides the facilities, and communities are oriented about Hygiene promotion messages. 
CARE projects for Health, Nutrition, WASH, FSL and protection will ensure interventions integrate PSHEA from planning up to reporting in addition to projects’ FAMs, PSHEA will be budgeted.  All CARE staff, MoH Staff and community workers and volunteers in all projects will be oriented and trained in PSHEA
To overcome the ongoing challenges of access, availability of health staff and supplies, CARE will continue to ensure good coordination with all clusters including the logistics cluster, authorities and SMoH, and humanitarian actors at State and National level.  CARE management team at national and state level will ensure adaption of projects and having agile and flexible implementation modalities according to the context to ensure continue of activities.

project_name: Improved Access to basic services through Provision of Integrated WASH, Education, FSL, Health and Nutrition services mainstreamed by Protection interventions for Ethiopian, South Sudanese refugees and war affected populations in Gadaref, Blue Nile and West Kordofan
project_objective:
IR-Sudan is planning to implement this integrated project which aims to enhance access to basic services education, food security and livelihood, WASH, Health & Nutrition, and protection for vulnerable communities including IDPs, Refugees, and host communities and war affected populations in three States, West Kordofan in El Nuhud, Wad Banda and Babanousa Localities with a total target group 47,498 South Sudan Refugees, 4,727 IDPs war affected and 13,738 vulnerable host communities, Blue Nile with total target 26,240 IDPs affected by recent inter-communal conflict in Rosaires & Wadelmahi localities (10,496 & 15,477) respectively, in addition to around 3,788 IDPs from recent war and Gadaref State Babikri refugee camp and Basundah locality with a total target of 30,000 Ethiopian Refugees and host-communities, as well as war affected populations displaced from KHT, estimated around 7,410 individuals. In Education sector and in line with strategic objectives 1&2 of revised HRP, the project will focus on improving access to quality education through increasing access and improving the school environment for target groups, to ensure increasing additional learning spaces to accommodate the new war affected IDPs students whom displaced with their parents from war hotspot areas, in addition to the Eritrean and South Sudan refugees and resident host communities. The proposed activities under this sector will include enrolment of children in child-friendly learning spaces, provision of recreational (kits), and hygiene/Dignity kits, hand washing stations, safe drinking water, rehabilitate gender responsive latrines, rehabilitate temporary learning spaces, and provision psychosocial support.
In WASH, the project will support refugees, war affected IDPs and host communities to improve their access to WASH services that will include sanitation and hygiene promotion services aligned with strategic objectives 1&2 of revised HRP 2023. 
Health sector interventions will focus on increasing access to health services by rehabilitating and refurbishing nonfunctioning health facilities, as well as provision of medical equipment, strengthening the capacity of health care providers and community health care workers to provide essential health services in targeted areas.
In FSL and livelihood, the project will aim to enhance the beneficiaries’ resilience and self-reliance through diversifying their livelihoods options, improving access to employment opportunities and income generating activities, especially for those fleeing from war hotspot areas and lost their work opportunities. This will be achieved through provision of simple agricultural tools, provision of seeds, deliver extension trainings to farmers and conduct vocational trainings for youths and support them with income means. The project will support women households in particular with provision of goats restocking to help in promoting their income, and train them on food processing.
The protection interventions will focus on delivering services to acutely vulnerable boys and girls, girls and boys will be provided with specialized child protection response services. Specific sources of threat challenging vulnerabilities of children will be identified and addressed particularly high risk of abuse, neglect, exploitation, or violence. Vulnerable and at-risk children will be provided with gender & age appropriate (structured) psychosocial support and life skills including literacy and numeracy. Communities will be mobilized to support children through activation of child protection networks. Finally the project will enhance and build human resource capacity through targeted groups to respond to child protection concerns at all levels.

project_name: ​​Proyecto de acción anticipatoria para reforzar o implementar capacidades de vigilancia y control de la calidad del agua en cinco municipios afectados por la sequía ocasionada por el fenómeno natural El Niño/Oscilación del Sur (ENOS).​
project_objective:
El proyecto tiene como objetivo reforzar o instalar capacidades técnicas y operativas de las instituciones a nivel local y regional encargadas de la vigilancia y control de la calidad del agua, estableciendo una estructura sólida y coordinada para mitigar el impacto de la sequía. Enfocando la implementación de medidas tempranas, incluyendo la provisión de equipamiento y la capacitación de los técnicos de salud ambiental, las juntas administradoras de agua, y los gobiernos locales. Facilitando la vigilancia comunitaria y el monitoreo continuo de la calidad del agua, abarcando también los sistemas de almacenamiento de agua en las instalaciones sanitarias. 

El proyecto aborda la mejora de la salud mediante la dotación de equipamiento y capacitación a los Equipos de Salud Familiar (ESFAM) y Brigadas de Salud. Se enfoca en la vigilancia, prevención y control de enfermedades relacionadas con la escasez de agua o su consumo inadecuado. Además, incluye acciones como el diseño, impresión y distribución de materiales para la comunicación de riesgos, la participación comunitaria con un enfoque inclusivo, y la implementación de sesiones formativas y campañas de promoción de la salud. 

El proyecto mejorará la vigilancia y manejo de los sistemas de agua en cinco municipios prioritarios. Esto se logrará a través de actividades de vigilancia de la calidad del agua, beneficiando al menos al 20% de la población total. Además, se busca fortalecer la capacidad de los servicios de atención primaria para llevar a cabo acciones de vigilancia epidemiológica de enfermedades transmisibles. 

El proyecto y sus actividades están directamente relacionados con los impactos del fenómeno de El Niño (ENOS) en el corredor seco de Honduras. Este fenómeno ha ocasionado pérdidas en cultivos y ganado, inseguridad alimentaria, déficit de agua para consumo humano y un riesgo potencial de aumento en enfermedades diarreicas, desnutrición aguda y arbovirosis. 

La situación crítica en la zona sur, donde solo uno de los 20 sistemas de abastecimiento de agua cumplió con los estándares nacionales de calidad, no es un hecho aislado. Más bien, destaca los desafíos en la calidad del agua y la capacidad del sistema de salud para desempeñar su rol como entidad rectora en la vigilancia, según lo establecido en el Código de Salud.

project_name: Access to learning opportunities and Protective Learning Environment for 90,000 crisis-affected children in the NWSW regions of Cameroon.
project_objective:
Data from the NWSW regional delegations of basic and secondary education for 2022/2023 revealed that a total of 4,195 schools are operational, out of the expected 6,557 schools, leaving a total 2,365 schools (36 per cent) still not operational. This is an improvement over 18 per cent compared to the preceding school year where 54 per cent of schools were still non-functional.  However, this situation continues to deprive around 298,000 children of access to education.  
This increase in the number of formal schools open confirms the gradual improvement in the security situation in certain areas, the interest of communities in sending their children to school and the growing needs. A total of 632,457 pupils (54 per cent girls) are enrolled out of the 930,335 expected, and only 2 per cent of the pupils enrolled for the 2022/2023 school year were children living with a disability. At least one inclusive primary school has been opened in each division, but there is still a lack of material, financial and technical resources available to school communities and education actors. Other children are left behind simply because they live with a disability and either their parents do not want to send them to school, or the available schools are not prepared to receive them.
Despite continued attacks, there has been a comparative improvement from the previous years in terms of access to formal education within the Northwest and Southwest regions. However, the risks for children, youth and education personnel remains high, especially in rural areas and zones under full control of the NSAG. The only possible opportunity for these children remains the non-formal education. 
To address this, UNICEF has been supporting 60 communities in eleven divisions where schools are closed to implement a non-formal radio education program easily accessible in rural areas that have poor internet and cellular connectivity and has provided learning continuity while reducing the risk of attacks in communities. 
The overall objective of the project is to facilitate access to learning opportunities as well as the protective learning environment for crises-affected children in and out of schools including IDPs children in the Northwest and Southwest regions. 
The aim of the project is to meet the educational needs of 120,000 out-of-school children who are unable to attend school because of the risks involved, but also because schools in their area have been closed for several years due to the crisis.  The project will have the advantage of taking a longer-term view, to ensure the link between non-formal and formal education, so that when the security situation allows, children who have participated in the radio education program can enroll in formal schools in the higher grades. 600 teachers will equally benefit from the training in Psychosocial Support (PSS) and Conflict/Disaster Risk Reduction (CDRR) to supervise 36.000 children from targeted schools.
This project will help provide a child-friendly and child-led space, offering a variety of activities for children and youth.  The learning spaces will be gender-sensitive and inclusive, where children and young people will feel they can learn and express their opinions. This will help to strengthen links with their community and improve their self-confidence and the development of their cognitive skills. The aim is for children to develop a better sense of self-esteem and self-confidence to improve their social and emotional well-being.

project_name: SMSD - Strengthening the equitable provision of humanitarian services and Disaster Risk Reduction through Coordination, Site Care and Maintenance, Community Participation and Engagement Ensuring Minimum Standards in Areas of Response.  Shelter/NFI -Comprehensive Shelter and NFI Support for Rohingya Refugee Response
project_objective:
"This project aims to enhance the equitable provision of humanitarian assistance in refugee camps and host communities, with a central focus on coordination, community participation, capacity building, Complaints and Feedback Mechanism, Accountability to Affected Population (AAP), disaster risk reduction (DRR), Shelter and Non-Food Items (NFI) including Liquefied petroleum-related (LPG) interventions as part of the SAFE Plus 2 initiative consisting of LPG activities and refills, a collaboration with FAO, WFP, and UNHCR, aimed at enhancing climate resilience, food security, and safety for affected community.
SMSD will focus on site management support coordination, information management, advocacy for minimum standards, CFP Mechanism, representation, and refugee population engagement through AAP. Communication with Communities is prioritized to inform residents of their entitlements and will be promoted through capacity-building programs, and the establishment of platforms for meaningful dialogue with camp stakeholders to reinforce community capacity and ownership.
To mitigate multi-hazard risks, the project will implement cash-based site development, Shelter/NFI and DRR interventions, including infrastructure maintenance, environmental restoration, Shelter construction, repair and maintenance, porter support and solar streetlight installation. Strengthening community-based disaster response volunteer capacity and coordination systems at the camp level.
IOM is leading the effort to provide cleaner cooking energy to refugees through LPG activities and refills. This helps ensure food, nutrition security, reduce health risks, gender-based violence exposure, and environmental impacts. IOM shall collaborate with UNHCR in streamlining and harmonizing the LPG supply chain to leverage the combined volume of the LPG requirement against the overall purchasing price.  Furthermore, efforts will be maintained in replacing damaged cooking stoves with new ones. Simultaneously, IOM shall empower the Rohingya community by providing training and spare parts to facilitate stove repairs. Continuous training for all beneficiaries on the safe use of cooking fuels and efficient cooking methods will be a priority during LPG distribution and refilling.
IOM plans to implement gender and inclusion activities (17 camps), Second phase of Shelter Upgrade and Maintenance (SUM) (13 camps), construction of new MTS and repairing works. NFI distribution (5 camps), and solar lamp distribution (10 camps), and distribution of emergency shelter kits and NFI to affected refugee households in the aftermath of disasters based on Rapid Damage Verification (RDV), while continuing to be the Shelter Focal Point and directly assist as per the verification in Camp 8E, 8W, 9, 10, 18, 20, 20 Extension, 22, 24, 25 and through its pipeline partners in Camps 13 and 19 (Caritas), 14, 15, and 16 (HEKS) and 11,12  (BDRCS).  
For the implementation of SUM, Camp 8E, and 8W will be covered by NRC and DRC, and Camp 15 will be covered by HEKS utilizing the materials provided by IOM through Pipeline. The remaining SUM caseload will be covered by IOM directly. For the NFI voucher programme, Camp 24, 25, 18, 8W, and 10 will be covered by IOM and through Pipeline Partners. Emergency shelter kits and NFI will be prepositioned (i.e., up to 30% for Ukhiya camps and 100% for Teknaf camps) to respond to disasters in IOM AoR. 
Needs and Population Monitoring (NPM) will continue to support informed humanitarian and development decision-making through the identification of needs, conditions, and service provision for the refugee and host communities, enabling strong evidence-based response planning by administering thematic assessments, joint multi-sectoral needs assessment, assisting the inter-sectoral coordination group (ISCG) on the post-disaster and preparedness through daily incident reporting, shelter addressing system, facility mapping and joint needs assessment framework.

project_name: Enhancing health and wellbeing of Rohingya refugees and host communities in Cox’s Bazar through equitable access to and utilization of live saving health services.
project_objective:
The project seeks to enhance access to essential healthcare addressing the main causes of mortality and morbidity amongst the Rohingya refugees and host communities in line with the Health Sector Strategic Plan 2023-2024. IOM will provide services at 38 health facilities (14 PHCs, 18 health posts, 3 hospitals and 2 infectious disease treatment centers) standardized and aligned to the Minimum Package of Essential Health Services including emergency care, outpatient care, routine immunization, communicable disease control, non-communicable disease interventions, palliative care, laboratory services and sexual and reproductive health services. The health facilities will be deployed with adequate number of healthcare workers and supplied with essential medicines and equipment placing quality improvement measures. 

The project will continue to support an emergency referral system comprising of a medical referral unit, 14 ambulances and provision of referral cost support for acute life-saving conditions. The project will support 3 secondary hospitals (2 Health complexes and Friendship maternity center) as well as upgrade the services at PHCs. 

IOM will operate two integrated infectious disease treatment centers for management of outbreak potential diseases. Disease surveillance and case management services, including EWARS, sentinel sample collection/testing, and early diagnosis, isolation, and treatment, will remain integrated in IOM health facilities. IOM will continue to coordinate and build capacity of 33 mobile medical teams (10 run by IOM) of health sector partners leading the MMT TWG, to respond to emergencies.  

Comprehensive Sexual Reproductive Health (SRH) services including antenatal care (ANC), postnatal care (PNC), facility-based deliveries including caesarian sections (C/S), menstrual regulation and post abortion care(MR&PAC) and syndromic management of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) including HIV/AIDS, family planning (FP) counselling and services with a focus on long acting and reversible contraceptives (LARC) and adolescent sexual reproductive health services  (ASRH)  will integrated into supported health facilities. Quality basic (BEmONC) and comprehensive (CEmONC) emergency obstetric and newborn care services with emergency obstetric referral pathways will be strengthened to mitigate maternal and perinatal morbidities and mortalities. Gender based violence (GBV) prevention and response services will be strengthened including clinical management of rape (CMR), Intimate Partner Violence (IPV) with safe and confidential referrals along established referral pathways.

IOM will continue to work with the existing network of 400 community health workers (CHWs) for health promotion, improve preventive and health seeking behavior, community-based surveillance. CHW will be the frontline workers for household visits, community engagement sessions and engagement with community opinion leaders. They will also actively engage men and boys in promoting SRH rights for women and girls and conduct community referrals including pregnant mothers for facility-based deliveries, immunization and address high rate of home deliveries in the camp.

Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) will be integrated into health services including assessment, counselling, support to persons with moderate to severe mental health conditions and referrals to specialized services provided by psychiatrists. At the community level, MHPSS services will be through evidence-based interventions including support groups, socio-relational activities, creative and art activities, ritual and celebration activities, sport and play activities and self-awareness sessions as per the IOM community based MHPSS approach. IOM will support MHPSS WG coordination and capacity building of partners. Through the Rohingya Cultural Memory Centre IOM will continue to document and preserve the Rohingya cultural heritage while promoting psychosocial well-being.

project_name: Protecting Rohingya and Host Communities by Facilitating Meaningful Access to Humanitarian Assistance, Dignity and Human Rights
project_objective:
IOM’s Protection Project for the 2024 JRP connects two strategic objectives with activities that aim to benefit the most vulnerable Rohingya and host community persons, specifically to reach older persons, widows, single-headed households, persons with disabilities, and persons with diverse sexual orientations and gender identity/expressions, and to target authorities and partners in a way that does no harm, assists based on needs, and prioritizes respect for human rights, safety, and dignity. 
IOM will continue serving as the Protection Focal Point in seven camps (9,18,19,20,20 extension,24, and 25), directly implementing the activities. IOM’s protection monitoring activities will facilitate beneficiaries’ meaningful access to all humanitarian assistance, dignity, and human rights. IOM will strengthen community-based protection through community engagement, awareness raising, sensitization, case management, and specialized Protection services for individuals in need. IOM’s core counter-trafficking activities will be prevention, protection, capacity building and partnership, which will be implemented in 17 camps and 10 Union of host communities under Cox’s Bazar district. These activities are intended to reduce the trafficking incidents and risks in the camps and host communities through comprehensive activities that follow the governmental National Plan of Action. The Counter Trafficking activities will foster collaboration and increased capacity among stakeholders who respond to human trafficking cases. The aforementioned integrated approach to Protection strives to have sustainable impact and improve peaceful coexistence between various communities.
The research component within the IOM protection team is to help tailor our activities, institutionalize, and analyze the impact of our work and IOM’s general programming as a whole. The information that is gathered through the research team serves as a basis for our monitoring and evaluation to ensure that we do no harm, and our work remains relevant and culturally appropriate. As well as being aware of the constantly changing dynamics that need to be considered.
For disaster risk reduction, IOM will work with a range of partners, including other Sectors, community-based protection networks in the camps, and relevant authorities to identify Extremely Vulnerable Individuals (EVIs) or households needing specialized assistance and preparation before a disaster. IOM will verify the needs of EVIs, coordinate services, and support other partners to mitigate harm during disaster response. IOM will continue leading the Protection Emergency Response Units (PERU) in five IOM Protection-led camps (19,20,20extension, 24, and 25). 
IOM’s protection mainstreaming activities will promote a holistic lens, incorporating the age, gender, and diversity needs of the affected population in Cox’s Bazar into programming through capacity building, training, as well as activity monitoring and modification. Finally, IOM will continue to co-chair the Sector’s Anti-Trafficking Working Group (ATWG) and be a proactive member of the Protection sector, the Protection Task Team, and other related working groups.

project_name: Coordination Cox's Bazar
project_objective:
Under the leadership of the Government of Bangladesh, and in close coordination with the RRRC and DC, the ISCG Secretariat will support the overall humanitarian coordination structure and lead streamlining and rationalization efforts to ensure the coherence and cohesiveness of the response. 
The ISCG Secretariat will strengthen the work of the Sectors and provide clear and strategic linkages between the Inter-Sector Meeting, Refugee Operations and Coordination Team (ROCT), and the Strategic Executive Group (SEG), under the leadership of the SEG Co-Chairs in Dhaka. The Sector Coordinators will be staffed by the Sector Lead Agency and will play a neutral coordination role. The ISCG Secretariat will manage the joint response planning cycle, from assessment and strategic planning, to supporting resource mobilization, monitoring, and effective reporting. Supported assessments include a Joint Multi-Sector Needs Assessment (J-MSNA), the Refugee Vulnerability Assessment (REVA), and the Resilience Index Measurement and Analysis (RIMA), which will be undertaken in coordination with the Office of the RRRC. The ISCG Secretariat will deliver information management, external relations, and communication services. ISCG is also engaging with development partners to promote complementarity between development efforts in the District and the humanitarian response. 
The coordination system will also assist in mainstreaming cross-cutting issues across the work of all Sectors and humanitarian partners. This includes ensuring the Centrality of Protection as outlined in the Protection Framework. Protection mainstreaming is a way of designing and implementing all programmes, considering protection risks and potential violations and ensuring that the protective impact of aid programming is maximized. Through the mainstreaming of Age, Gender, and Diversity (AGD), the humanitarian community seeks to ensure that all individuals in affected communities have equal access to their rights. Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) is a commitment by humanitarian partners to take account of, give account to, and be held to account by the Rohingya refugees and host communities. Disaster risk reduction and management as well as Energy & Environment will also be integrated across the response for a coordinated approach to emergency preparedness and response, as well as energy solutions, natural resource management, and environmental protection. Finally, efforts are ongoing to ensure Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA), which is a form of gender-based violence that constitutes an abuse of power by humanitarian aid workers against the affected population. All JRP partners, i.e., the UN and NGOs, are required to be members of the PSEA Network and comply with PSEA standards, including through the PSEA Standard Operating Procedures, which are in line with global standards.

project_name: Improving access to safe, equitable, inclusive, competency-based  and age-appropriate learning opportunities for girls and boys in Rohingya camps and host communities
project_objective:
Save the Children (SC) is committed to sustaining educational services for children and adolescents by providing secure, fair, inclusive, skill-focused, and developmentally suitable learning opportunities for the children of age group 3-18 years. This commitment extends to fostering a child-friendly and protective environment within the camps and host communities in Ukhiya and Teknaf of Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh.

The initiatives will focus on maintaining, enhancing, and increasing additional Learning Centres (LCs) to accommodate learners in the Myanmar Curriculum (MC) under two shifts along with establishment of new Community-Based Learning Facilities (CBLF). Additionally, efforts will include the implementation of Peer Education Programs (PEP), Distance Education (DE), Learning Management System (LMS), Mobile Library and the capacity development of the Master Trainer of the Education Sector Partner on the Accelerated Learning Program (ALP).

Focused efforts are underway to empower Rohingya women, enhancing their skills to serve as proficient teachers. Save the Children (SC) is implementing targeted interventions, encompassing Early Childhood Development (ECD), the Myanmar Curriculum (MC), and Community-Based Learning Facilities (CBLF), catering to children aged 3-18 in both Rohingya and host communities. These interventions extend across multiple camps, featuring 147 Learning Centres in Refugee Camps (RR) and 418 CBLF-RR across various locations. Key camps include Camp 01E, 04, 7, 8W, 10, 13, C, E, F, G, 14, 15, 16, 18, 19 , 25 , 26 . Additionally, 3 Learning Centers in host communities, is in Jaliapolong Union, Ukhiya Upazila.

SC will continue to extend support to 20 Government Primary Schools in Ukhiya. The interventions also encompass empowering parents and caregivers with the knowledge and skills to actively contribute to their children's learning, development, and social well-being. There is a focus on enhancing teaching quality through continuous professional development support for all partners in the education sector of ALP. The training will cover inclusive elements such the integration of Mental-Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS), gender-responsive approaches, child-sensitive psychosocial support, and considerations for disability and gender-friendly practices.

Efforts will be continue to promote integration across sectors, including livelihood, child protection and health, ensuring that activities are customized to address the diverse needs of girls and boys, thereby ensuring equitable benefits from the interventions including specialized training initiative spanning 8-10 months will be initiated within selected camps to equip targeted Rohingya women to become skill teacher.

Particular emphasis will be placed on enhancing the skills of relevant staff members in crucial teaching-learning methodologies aligned with the new Myanmar Curriculum (MC) and Accelerated Learning Program (ALP), as well as addressing Social and Emotional Learning (SEL) issues. Gender-segregated WASH points, including Menstrual Health Management (MHM) services, will be incorporated into all learning facilities. In the capacity of a sector co-lead, SC will maintain a pivotal role in advocating for, improving the quality of, and ensuring the sustainability of education services for displaced Rohingya and the neighboring host communities. Besides advocating for the continuation of education as an essential service and the permission of technology-based interventions in the camps, SC will also support lower-performing government primary schools to ensure quality education among learners.
The project and programmatic initiatives are and will be enhancing social cohesion within the host and Rohingya communities. 

The project will reach a total of 38,095 learners out of which 46% are girls and 54% are boys.

project_name: Supporting Host and FDMN communities by promoting Gender Sensitive Livelihood intervention
project_objective: The program aims to promote eco-friendly micro-entrepreneurship & alternative livelihood opportunities for the targeted marginalized population, especially women and other excluded people, in Ukhiya and Teknaf Upzaila of Cox’s Bazar district. This will be done by creating increased and sustainable income opportunities through different on-farm activities such as Raising nursery, Fisheries and Aquaculture, Crop Farming and Gardening, Poultry Farming, livestock farming and any other on-farm IGA as per choice of participants , which will ultimately contribute to peaceful conflict resolution. ACF will provide support to 975 beneficiaries in particular women and youth for Eco friendly and alternative livelihoods opportunities. Among the 975 beneficiary, at least 70% of the beneficiaries will be women and 7% will be the PWD and or other disadvantaged groups with a special focus on female-headed households and beneficiaries with age between18-35. The project participants will be selected from the most vulnerable households, including those headed by females, households with persons with disabilities, orphan-hosted households, and households with elderly individuals. ACF has a beneficiary targeting tool which generate vulnerability score for each of the households (HH). PRA techniques such as transact walk, wealth ranking and community consultation will be done to get initial list of the beneficiaries. The higher the score indicated the higher level of vulnerability. ACF will ensure training, input and market linkage support on Raising nursery, Fisheries and Aquaculture, Crop Farming and Gardening, Poultry Farming, livestock farming for the targeted host community as per their choice.  ACF will adopt Climate smart agricultural technology to cope with multi hazards like tidal surges, floods, salinity, drought and others. Workshops on market linkage and income generating activity opportunities will also be facilitated for the host communities. Finally, awareness will be raised among the project participants for social cohesion between the host and refugees' communities as tensions between these communities appear as an obstacle to stability and maximization of opportunities. These activities will allow the participants to acquire marketable skills that will create opportunities for them to engage in self-sustaining and life-enhancing activities, notably through income generation. The new skills of on-farm IGA and income-earning opportunities created by the proposed project will enable the beneficiaries to build-up on the support they receive from aid agencies and government, and at the same time improve their well-being and regain of self-esteem. ACF's MEAL team will develop tools based on the project's output and outcome. The MEAL unit will conduct periodic surveys, focus group discussions, and participatory development meetings with the targeted population. In the project implementation area, an effective complaints and feedback mechanism will be established to ensure community participation, transparency, and accountability. Additionally, a contingency plan will be included in the project to address any disasters that may occur during the project period, and all staff will be equipped with the necessary tools and protective gear to respond to emergencies within 72 hours. ACF planned for the most vulnerable affected population by the Cyclone or any disaster in host community of Ukhiya and Teknaf Upazila and two refugee at camp (Camp 1w & camp 11) through Emergency Support Program (ESP) of SIDA RRM. This program targeted for emergency support for 3400 refugee households and 5880 host communities. The proposed project will adhere to the Food Security Sector (FSS) policy and guidance.
