project_name: Salvando vidas: respuesta multisectorial a las necesidades de las poblaciones en alto riesgo en Venezuela.
project_objective:
Para el año 2024 World Vision Venezuela ha desarrollado una estrategia basada en la información compartida por las agencias de la ONU presentes en el país, por las ONG y socios locales, universidades e información propia levantada en terreno por el staff de WV, logrando contextualizar la situación de emergencia humanitaria y socioeconómica de la Venezuela actual y los diferentes ámbitos de la vida nacional.



La misión exploratoria iniciada en 2021 y su rápida evaluación de necesidades mostró que 70% de hogares del país experimentaban pobreza y hambre moderadas a severas y que cerca de 30% de niños menores de 5 años sufrían desnutrición crónica. Tras un análisis cuantitativo llevado por el equipo de operaciones y MEAL, podemos constatar que esta situación se mantuvo durante 2023 y en estados como Amazonas o Delta Amacuro estos valores sobrepasaron al 90% de los hogares. Es importante destacar que la falta de acceso a agua segura suele ser una de las principales causas de enfermedades infecciosas que afectan el estado nutricional, mientras que la lactancia materna es una medida para hacer frente a la falta de alimentos. En términos de protección, sigue evidenciándose la falta de servicios y planes de atención a la niñez, generando brechas en las medidas de protección efectiva en todo el sistema; un dato importante en este sentido es la identificación de niñez con rezago pedagógico producto de la diáspora migratoria o víctimas de explotación por trabajo infantil, especialmente en zonas de minería, sin medidas de atención ni protección por parte del Estado.



Estos y otros aspectos han sido confirmados por los resultados de la ejecución de los proyectos en 2021, 2022 y 2023, evidenciando que la situación generalizada de emergencia humanitaria se mantiene en Venezuela. Por lo que para 2024, WV continuará con presencia en Distrito Capital, Anzoátegui, Barinas, Bolívar, Delta Amacuro, Falcón, Miranda, Monagas, Táchira y Zulia; a los cuáles sumará el Estado Amazonas, con especial enfoque en comunidades rurales, indígenas y personas con discapacidad, a la par de su misión dedicada a la niñez y la educación con ternura. WV considera que para lograr una sociedad justa y segura, los principios y sectores humanitarios juegan roles fundamentales en el trabajo con la niñez, por lo cual se mantendrá el trabajo en los sectores de nutrición, salud, seguridad alimentaria, protección, ASH y educación (con enfoque en la educación en emergencias y reintegración de NNA fuera del sistema educativo), reconociendo las variaciones culturales y étnicas de cada territorio y del contexto, para el trabajo con comunidades urbanas, rurales e indígenas.. Además, renueva su compromiso con el ambiente, tomando cada vez más medidas de bajo impacto ambiental en sus procesos de asistencia.



En el sector de nutrición, se contará con la adopción de actividades centradas en la innovación, y el cambio de comportamiento para la inclusión de herramientas tecnológicas de prevención, detección y rehabilitación de casos de desnutrición, así como de la geolocalización, sistematización y estandarización de metodologías para soporte y cumplimiento de sus proyectos a nivel nacional para fortalecer a las instituciones de la red pública sanitaria, activar la referencia y contrarreferencia de casos de desnutrición a través de la Ruta Nutricional y las actividades de vigilancia nutricional a través del manejo de información de NutriVision

Las operaciones orientadas al logro garantizan la seguridad y operatividad en cada uno de los Estados, a través del enlace directo con las organizaciones basadas en la fe insertadas en las comunidades, que gozan del reconocimiento necesario para reproducir un ecosistema de agentes llamados a ayudar bajo el respeto de los principios humanitarios y bajo los más altos estándares ESFERA.

project_name: Multi-sector Humanitarian response for conflict and protracted crises affected People in Central Darfur, South Kordofan, White Nile and Blue Nile State, Sudan
project_objective:
Adapting to major changes in Sudan socio-economic and security context, in 2024, ACF will focus on responding to the humanitarian need of conflict affected people, particularly IDPs and refugees, through multi-sector approach while scaling up its operation area in additional localities and cities within the four states to reach IDPs and refugee where they are largely resided. Adopting balanced approaches of prioritization and feasibility, with consideration of the current realities of access and operational capacity, ACF intend to scale-up Lifesaving and protection assistance through critical basic services and livelihood opportunities. 
The overall project objective for 2024 is “To provide safe, dignified and gender-responsive life-saving humanitarian assistance to the most vulnerable groups’’. The objective aims to tackle life-threatening conditions, address protection needs and provide livelihood opportunities. ACF will endeavor to ensure a more equitable, equal and participatory approach throughout the project cycle. 
ACF will continue to operate in and expand to hard-to-reach areas as well as scale up to IDP and Refugee camps in Central Darfur, South Kordofan, White Nile and Blue Nile states. Expansion to Khartoum and Port Sudan is under review. The project will cover 19 Localities/cities, 75 Health facilities and their catchment area and Seven Hospitals (stabilization Center). The geographical targeting is based on the inter-sectorial highest severity of needs (especially nutrition and food insecurity) and ACF's access, operational capacity, multi-sector needs assessments, as well as limited to no presence of other major INGOs in those areas.
ACF’s 2024 programme will focus on four core sectors, by promoting synergies and complementarities, to ensure a holistic approach, Nutrition & Health Water Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH), Food Security and Livelihoods (FSL), and GBV (Protection). In Nutrition and Health, in line with HRP 2024 and both sectors’ objectives, ACF will scale up treatment and preventive nutrition interventions integrated with Primary Health Care (PHC). Main interventions include CMAM, Emergency IYCF, Micronutrient powder distribution, food-based prevention of malnutrition, prevention and treatment of communicable diseases (cholera, dengue. Etc.), Mental Health and Psycho-Social Support (MHPSS), outpatient consultation, reproductive health, vaccination, and health education. In WASH, aligned to cluster objective and SDG 6, ACF will maintain WASH assistance for vulnerable populations to ensure their access to safe water, dignified sanitation services and increased good hygiene practices through hygiene promotion sessions and Baby WASH. ACF will increase access to safe water and sanitation through rehabilitation and construction of water points and Latrines, water trucking, water treatment, distribution of WASH kits and waste disposal. In FSL, in line with HRP 2024 and sector’s objectives, ACF will focus on responding to the immediate food and livelihood needs of internally displaced people and protracted crisis victims through multi-purpose cash assistance, Agri-input distribution and income generating activities.  ACF will mainstream gender and protection throughout all activities prioritizing safety and dignity of vulnerable groups, Do No Harm for all for an effective and impactful programming. Considering the added value of local partners in terms of access and acceptability, especially during active conflict, ACF will collaborate with grass root level Community Based Organizations (CBOs) and women led organization to implement activities. 
The programme will give priority to the immediate need of conflict affected IDPs, refugees, returnees, nomadic and vulnerable host community members. Children, Adolescent Girls, and PLW will remain the main target group. Total estimated number of beneficiaries is Nutrition and Health: 392,765, NUT:58,314,WASH: 959,611, FSL: 46,923, and Protection-GBV: 39,485

project_name: DRC (Danish Refugee Council) 2024 Protection Response for Sudan
project_objective:
DRC works alongside affected communities and local authorities to address protection issues and meet basic needs in food security and livelihoods (FSL), shelter and non-food items (SNFI), and humanitarian mine action (HMA) in Sudan. DRC has also started implementing activities within water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), site management support (SMS), and multi-purpose cash assistance (MPCA) sectors to address the growing emergency needs and widening gaps in support to affected communities impacted by the war.

DRC will continue to target Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs), host communities and returnees in Central Darfur, Khartoum, and South Kordofan as well as refugees in Gedaref along with other vulnerable groups in the state. Since the war broke out, DRC has also added two more operational bases: White Nile State and Al Jeziera, and will be expanding programmatic operations to Port Sudan within the coming months. In South Kordofan, DRC operates a non-technical Mine Action programme through two activities:  (1) providing EORE to vulnerable persons and (2) conducting non-technical surveys

DRC has grown its emergency response through several interventions such as intersectoral mobile response teams and cross border programming. For the former, these teams will be based in Port Sudan and Gedaref but able to be deployed throughout Red Sea State, Northern State, Gedaref, River Nile, Sennar and Kassala. Regarding the latter, DRC will work with its counterparts in South Sudan and Chad to support cross border populations. From Sudan, this programming will particularly focus on those located in Darfur and White Nile State with possible support in South Kordofan. Furthermore, DRC has been providing technical and financial support to a local partner in Khartoum. The partner has been providing emergency support since the start of the war in Khartoum to support life-saving self-relocations of highly vulnerable individuals.

In addition to direct and immediate assistance and despite the challenges due to the outbreak of the conflict in April 2023, DRC continues to engage in and implement programming to build resilience and support for vulnerable populations, particularly with displaced and returnee communities; to address their priority needs, reducing aid dependency, supporting early recovery and paving pathways to durable solutions. One key dimension to this work is through ensuring that all stakeholder groups’ needs and vulnerabilities are considered and accounted for in the project’s implementation; community engagement, mobilization, and feedback are also key to the approach, ensuring participation of all relevant stakeholder groups. DRC also focuses on partnership building to ensure complimentary and integrated response and programming.

Throughout its interventions, DRC works to secure government buy-in and ensure that coordination with relevant federal, state, and local authorities is continuous throughout all projects such as HAC and line ministries. DRC will also collaborate with local NGOs and representative community structures that already have an operational presence in the areas of intervention. This approach aims to increase the efficiency of community engagement while improving the ownership of the local community and actors in the response. The engagement of local actors will improve local acceptance and understanding of the activities and serve to ease the delivery of activities vis-à-vis communities and authorities, given that these stakeholders are already part of the community and are familiar with the social context and its internal dynamics.

project_name: Protéger les enfants touchés par les conflits armés au Mali
project_objective:
Les enfants comptent parmi les premières victimes de l’insécurité et des conflits armés au Mali. Ils sont exposés à des risques élevés de violences, abus, exploitation et violations graves de leurs droits. L’objectif général de ce projet est d’assurer la protection des enfants dans les zones les plus touchées par le conflit au Mali notamment dans le centre et le Nord du pays, en fournissant aux enfants les services d’appui médical, psychosocial et de réintégration nécessaire pour atténuer les effets négatifs à long terme.
Le projet vise à offrir des services de protection en faveur de 300 enfants survivant.e.s de VBG, 800 enfants sortis des forces et groupes armés et 2800 enfants non accompagnés et séparés, pour la prise en charge transitoire holistique (médicale, psychosociale, alimentaire, vestimentaire) et l’appui à la réintégration socioéconomique. En outre,  283 295 enfants affectés par les conflits  recevront un soutien psychosocial, individuel ou à base communautaire dans des espaces sécurisés. Finalement, 38 268 enfants beneficieront des activités d'éducation aux risques d'engins explosifs. Le total de 572 500 personnes auront acces aux mécanismes  de signalement surs et accessibles  pour reporter les cas d'exploitation et d'abus sexuel. 
L’UNICEF collaborera étroitement avec les partenaires gouvernementaux ainsi que les agents de l’état civil pour assurer que leurs capacités soient développées. En répondant aux besoins des enfants les plus vulnérables, ce projet garantira que les enfants seront protégés et pourront ainsi contribuer à la paix et au développement durable du pays, en assurant leur dignité et leur accès aux services nécessaires.
La redevabilité vis-à-vis des communautés ciblées sera intégrée aux activités, y compris via un mécanisme de plainte. Outre les activités spécifiques visant à traiter directement la réponse et la prévention de l'exploitation et l'abus sexuelle (EAS), tous les partenaires d’exécution recevront une formation sur la PSEA conformément à la stratégie de l’UNICEF concernant l’évaluation des partenaires récemment introduite.

project_name: Providing Access to Life-Saving and Essential Primary Health Care Services for Conflict Affected and Vulnerable People in Akobo, Nyirol and Uror counties-Jonglei, Wetwil Refugee Camp in Awiel West and Abyei Administrative Area
project_objective:
Save the Children (SC) proposes to implement health activities in Akobo, Nyirol and Uror counties in Jonglei State, Aweil West and Abyei county in Abyei State Administration Area through static, mobile and outreach services. The 2023 Integrated Food Security phase classification reports high levels of acute food insecurity with Jonglei and Abyei states requiring priority attention in meeting the humanitarian needs of people in the states. Additionally, returnees and asylum seekers from the Sudan conflict settled within Abyei, Akobo and Wedweil Refugee camp in Aweil West. The proposed health project seeks to reduce morbidity and mortality particularly amongst under-five children, adolescent girls, pregnant and lactating women and other vulnerable populations by increasing access and utilization of quality basic primary health care services for communicable and non-communicable diseases including, reproductive health, emergency clinical management for survivors of SGBV, injury and first aid care, mental health, nutrition and community health activities, for women, girls, boys and men as well as surveillance and control of epidemic prone diseases and response to public health emergencies.  Save the Children has presence in these locations that need to be strengthened to ensure life-saving healthcare services are provided to target populations and people in great need of health services. This will be achieved by supporting the State Ministry of Health (SMoH) and County Health Department (CHD) and in coordination with the health cluster through static and mobile health facilities and community outreach supporting the Boma Health Initiative. SC will coordinate the response with the RRC as well as with the health clusters and other actors in the areas to consider the need for initial assessments. The project will implement activities aimed at achieving the following strategic objectives; 1.	Vulnerable crises-affected people have reduced morbidity and mortality through equitable, safe and dignified access to life-saving assistance to meet their needs; 2.	Vulnerable crises-affected people’s protection risks are mitigated as humanitarians uphold a commitment to the centrality of protection in humanitarian action through AAP, protection mainstreaming and monitoring and; 3.	Vulnerable people’s capacity to withstand or cope with the impact of new and protracted crises is increased, and durable solutions to root causes of their vulnerability and shocks are enabled by humanitarian action.
Methodology and target: The project will target a total population in need (Residents, IDPs, and Returnees) of 120,016 (Abyei Administrative Area: 36,886, Awiel West: 3,943, Akobo: 27,155, Nyirol: 25,660 and Uror: 26,372).  SC will support MOH in delivering quality and cost-effective healthcare services, health system strengthening, capacity building of staff at national level, state level including the CHD as well as coordination activities. Supported activities will include provision of curative consultations for adults and under-five children in targeted health facilities, mobile and outreach clinics, provision of routine immunization, ante-natal care for pregnant women, safe delivery through skilled birth attendants, post-natal care for newborns and lactating women, family planning counselling and service provision, nutrition screening for under-five children and PLWs, community based service delivery through BHWs as well as clinical management of rape survivors. In collaboration with the CHD, supportive supervision and on-job coaching of health providers will be done to build skills and competencies of health staff in managing health emergencies. Communities will be engaged through consultative meetings, focus group discussions with men, women, boys and girls as well as client exit interviews at facilities in order to receive feedback from communities aimed at improving the quality of care provided to patients and clients.

project_name: Emergency life-saving  health response to Crisis-affected and displaced population in South Sudan
project_objective:
The WHO’s commitments during the year 2024 is outlined in this HRP project   “Emergency life-saving health response to Crisis-affected and displaced population in South Sudan” that will significantly contribute to the reduction of excess morbidity and mortality due to health emergencies orchestrated by the ongoing effects of acute food insecurity, localized violence within communities, flooding, and the consequences of the Sudan crisis along with related population displacement into South Sudan which together exacerbates the public health situation in the country. 
WHO envisions an integrated and seamless health response where all sources of health insecurities are addressed for maximum impact. As such, the project will support timely, independent, and rigorous risk assessment and situation analysis to provide health partners with information to facilitate prompt response decision making. In addition, WHO will deploy technical officers to support partners and improve coordination of health responses. 
In addition to the above, the project will provide Inter-agency Emergency Health Kits (IHEK) to responding partners, capacitate the implementing partners and counties to provide quality essential health services through training of frontline health workers and provision of guidelines and SoPs on case management of common communicable and non- communicable diseases, and provision of safe maternal and child services, Mental and Psychosocial care. Moreover, WHO will deploy a multidisciplinary teams; the emergency Mobile Medical Teams (eMMTs), to provide integrated health services in deep field locations through mobile outreaches to bridge service delivery gaps in areas with critical unmet health needs.
The project will also strengthen the country’s capacities to prevent, prepare for, detect, and respond to emergencies at all levels through investments in the public health surveillance, and reporting system (IDSR/EWARN) while facilitating integration into DHIS2; the mobile phone based EWARS reporting by the static and mobile clinics will be supported through capacities to implementing partners in counties. This will enhance weekly reporting and ensure early detection of and response to disease outbreaks. Besides, the national and state Rapid Response Teams (RRTs) and the Emergency Mobile Medical Teams will be deployed to conduct risk assessments, alert, and outbreak investigation, and to provide initial public health response during emergencies to reduce excess morbidity and mortality. As part of outbreak prevention and response, WHO will lead the implementation of preventive and reactive vaccination campaigns for vaccine-preventable diseases such as measles and cholera.
Further, WHO will conduct regular water quality testing and surveillance, IPC/WASH assessments in health facilities and implement IPC measures as a component of risk identification and mitigation efforts to healthcare-related infections. Lastly, the project will contribute to enhancing the capacities for diagnosis and management of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) and associated medical complications with a view of reducing avoidable mortality in collaboration with the Nutrition Cluster.
The project will also support prevention and response to GBV, MHPSS delivery to affected people by mainstreaming the needs of affected people into ongoing programming, and work with organizations of persons living with disability to assess and address their needs. Finally, interventions will prioritize reproductive health providing EmONC (emergency newborn and obstetric care) and Clinical Management of Rape.
Overall, the above strategy and interventions will contribute to the three health cluster objectives of (1) Improving equitable access to life-saving essential quality health care services, (2) Reduce excess morbidity and mortality by timely detection and coordinated response to epidemic prone diseases and (3) Enhancing resilience and promoting humanitarian-development linkages

project_objective:
L'OIM prévoit d'apporter une réponse sous forme d'abris et d'articles ménagers essentiels pour couvrir les besoins immédiats, mais aussi de soutenir la mise en œuvre de solutions durables au déplacement par la distribution de 2 000 kits complets d'articles ménagers essentiels (NFI) et la distribution et la construction de 3 000 abris transitoires, en utilisant une approche basée sur la communauté. L'OIM soutiendra également la construction de 30 trous de sonde afin de garantir un approvisionnement en eau de bonne qualité et efficace.

project_name: Respuesta multisectorial humanitaria en Venezuela
project_objective:
DRC en Venezuela busca proporcionar asistencia humanitaria a poblaciones vulnerables afectadas por la intensa crisis socio económica que vive el país y que originan flujos migratorios mixtos hacia fuera de Venezuela, desplazamientos internos hacia lugares con contextos de riesgos de protección altos, en los que vemos problemáticas relacionadas a actividades ilícitas y conflictos por grupos armados. Al mismo tiempo DRC busca espacios en los cuales se puedan integrar componentes con soluciones más duraderas construyendo y fortaleciendo estructuras comunitarias adecuadas.
Por medio de una intervención multisectorial, DRC brindará asistencia de humanitaria con un enfoque de protección tanto para personas desplazadas internas, personas con intención o en proceso de migrar, comunidades de acogida, retornados, refugiados aplicando de manera transversal un enfoque sensible a la edad, el género y la discapacidad. Los perfiles priorizados por DRC serán aquellos que presenten altos niveles de vulnerabilidad como lo son las personas con necesidades específicas de protección (NNA, mujeres, LGBTIQ+, ancianos, etc.), personas con discapacidad, sobrevivientes o personas en riesgo de violencia basada en género, víctimas de desplazamiento masivo o confinamiento, grupos indígenas entre otros. 
Este proyecto será implementado en todas las regiones en las cuales DRC trabaja en Venezuela, que, al mismo tiempo, son zonas de mayor proporción de necesidades humanitarias severas de acuerdo con el HRP aprobado para el próximo periodo: Zulia, Sucre, Apure y Amazonas. Esta acción tiene como objetivo ofrecer una intervención de protección integrada que combina la protección y asistencia humanitaria para mejorar las condiciones de las poblaciones vulnerables antes mencionadas. 
La acción propuesta incluye los siguientes sectores/actividades:  Protección, Seguridad Alimentaria y medios de vida, Salud, Agua, saneamiento e higiene y Educación. El presente proyecto tendrá como línea de intervención principal, el abordaje de las necesidades de protección encontradas en una evaluación de campo actualizada  en Diciembre del 2023 en los estados de Sucre (municipios de Arismendi, Cajigal, Mariño y Valdés, Bermudez, Benitez), Zulia (municipios de Maracaibo, Catatumbo y Jesus Maria Semprun), Apure (municipio Páez, romulo gallegos y Pedro Camejo) y Amazonas (Atures y Autana) y como líneas complementarias a los sectores de WASH, educación y seguridad alimentaria y medios de vida. Es por ello que DRC plantea una respuesta integral no solo a necesidades de  protección como son, el acceso a información, asistencia legal y acceso a documentación para población vulnerable, incluidas las personas sobrevivientes y en riesgo de VbG,  el acceso a asistencia individualizada  y especifica de protección y protección basada en comunidad sino también a cubrir necesidades básicas de seguridad alimentaria y medios de vida;  mediante distribuciones mensuales de kits familiares alimenticios en las zonas de intervención y capacitaciones en empleabilidad y emprendimiento, salud; como asistencia individualizada de protección educación; proveyendo suministros escolares y de higiene personal y familiar, y huertos escolares a través de una intervención multisectorial y previamente coordinada con autoridades y comunidades locales. También vemos que es necesario seguir generando informacion sobre problemáticas de protección, para esto DRC implementa un programa de monitoreo de protección con el fin de crear evidencia para la incidencia y la adecuada dirección de nuestras intervenciones.

project_name: Provide access to quality education services to IDPs, host communities, returnee children and adolescents affected by conflict, hunger and climatic conditions in Awerial, Pibor, Yei, Lainya, Kajokeji, Renk, Malakal, Mayendit, Rubkona, Leer, Yirol East counties of Jonglei, Lakes, Unity, Upper Nile and Central Equatoria states.
project_objective: This project is for twelve-month and will be implemented in Awerial, Pibor, Yei, Lainya, Kajokeji, Renk, Malakal, Mayendit, Rubkona, Leer and Yirol East counties designed to provide quality education to children especially adolescent girls and young women including those living with disabilities, affected by floods, food insecurity and conflict. The interventions will target 20585 as direct beneficiaries (1000F,1020M and 9282G, 9283B). The men and women targeted by this project will be within the age range of 18-60 years while the school age going learners targeted are those between 3-17 years and out of this target, at least 15% of adults, youth and children will be People Living with Disabilities (based on the cluster recommendation). The intervention will mainly focus on ECD, Primary and Alternative Education Program and secondary school levels of learning in all targeted locations. The project is mainly designed to create access of learners to schools and inclusive learning centers while ensuring that barriers like poor access to schools, lack of scholastic materials, school retention for girls and WASH facilities for children's education are addressed. This project will also improve the quality of education by building the capacity of teachers through continuous professional development tailored to increase their teaching skills. In addition, the capacity of local education authorities such as County and Payam Education Supervisors and Inspectors will be strengthened by training them on better skills of school supervision, report writing and how to develop strategic plans alongside equipping their offices. This will improve the already ravaged system of education in the counties and Payams and ensure delivery of quality education services to schools is attained. Also the project shall distribute teaching and age-appropriate learning materials to both teachers and learners targeted since a lack of school supplies have been identified as one of the factors causing poor attendance and learning outcomes in schools. Moreover, the project intends to create better learning environments in schools through construction of temporary inclusive learning spaces to cater for all learners including CWDs. Additionally, the program plans to renovate those schools that have been destroyed by conflict and floods to enable learners access education in targeted locations and also ensure that gender segregated latrines and WASH facilities are established in schools lacking such facilities to address issues of girl’s hygiene while attending classes. Also distribution of sanitary materials to adolescent girls alongside training them on MHM and SRHR issues will be targeted by this intervention such that girl’s attendance and retention in schools is improved. The project will further establish Roll Models in the community who shall engage community members on importance of education of children especially the girl child. This will be done in close coordination with the PTAs/SMC who will be trained on school development as well as community outreach activities to engage parents and guardians of school children and youth on education related issues

project_name: Nutrition Service  provision for children  and PLWs of Rumbek Center, Wulu and Cueibet counties, Lakes State
project_objective:
This project aims to promote optimal nutrition practices, prevent and treat acute malnutrition in the most vulnerable population groups like children under five years, pregnant and lactating mothers. These aims will be fulfilled through implementation of community management of acute malnutrition (CMAM) and maternal infant and young child nutrition (MIYCN) interventions in Rumbek Centre, Wulu, Cueibet counties of Lakes state. The project implementation period will be from January 1, 2024 - December 31, 2024. PI will ensure that most marginalized groups like those with disability, minority ethnic groups and other groups due to economic, political, social and cultural factors are reached and participated throughout the project cycle. Furthermore, preventive activities like MIYCN counselling, health, nutrition and WASH education /promotion, setting up demonstration gardens, complementary food cooking demonstration and distribution of WASH and other preventive NFIs (like soap, aqua tab, mosquito net etc.) will be done at nutrition sites and at community level. As part of treatment protocol, all children with MAM and SAM will be screened and treated for malaria according to the national protocol / or referred to nearby health facilities. Furthermore, preventive kits (jerrycans, Mosquito nets, and soaps) shall be provided to mothers /caregivers of children who are enrolled for treatment in OTP or TSFP or SC sites as these children are at higher risk of being infected and to promote proper personal hygiene and sanitation practice. All children who will be discharged cured from OTPs will be enrolled to TSFP programs for full nutritional recovery and those deteriorated while in OTP will be referred to SC. Besides, if a child in TSFP is nutritionally deteriorated, he/she will be enrolled/referred to OTP/SC program. Those who recovered shall be given protection ration for two weeks and referred to other (FSL, BSFP) services after providing counselling. When there is deworming and Vitamin A supplementation campaign, PI will support the project counties to ensure children under five years old in the counties get the services in collaboration with SMOH/CHD, UNICEF, WFP and the health partner in the county. Furthermore, PI will participate in FSNMS, SMART and other joint assessments that may happen in the counties of operation. PI will implement OTP and TSFP programme together in Cueibet (14) county and shall implement OTP in Rumbek Centre (21 nutrition sites) and Wulu (14) counties. Besides, Plan International will provide service in 2 stabilization centres; one in Rumbek Centre and one Cueibet county. In addition to the aforementioned interventions, PI will implement BSFP in Cueibet county of Lake State. In total, this project will benefit 146,386 populations (boys, girls, men, women, people with disability) in different services. Of the total beneficiaries, 126,19 are children under five and   the rest 20,191 are adults.
To ensure the efficient project implementation, enhance community and local government support and ensure sustainability of the project, Plan will prioritise in local capacity building activities throughout the project cycle. The community volunteers (MSGs, CNVs and community representatives) and local government staffs in CHD and health facilities will be capacitated in different ways including training, involving them in support supervisions, feedback and complaint meetings and review meetings so as to ensure effectiveness, sustainability and ownership of this project. Besides, majority of project staff and all volunteers will be recruited locally. Existing nutrition sites were selected through participation of CHD and the community, and future expansion, be it static or outreach sites, will be established in the same way. Furthermore, the CHD and communities will be notified that it is a temporary measure that PI is doing the nutrition program and they should prepare to take over the program step by step.

project_name: Strengthening Health Sector Coordination Towards Improving Access to Health Care Services and Promoting Ealy Recovery Across BAY States
project_objective:
As the crisis in northeast Nigeria continues to persist, the operational environment remains complex. Despite significant counter-terrorism efforts by the Nigerian military and its partners, access to affected areas remains challenging due to insecurity. The humanitarian community continues to struggle to respond to urgent humanitarian needs with the already overstretched available capacity. The response capacity to a crisis of this scale is not commensurate to the needs of the affected population, especially the new influx, forced displacement of communities, and state returning IDPs back to their LGAs of origin. Overcrowding in camps continues to be prevalent with over 40 percent of camps in Borno State remaining over-congested and some closed. As military operations are expected to intensify in the coming months across Borno State, further evacuation and displacements of civilians are expected. This situation will likely worsen the overcrowding situation and have a direct impact on the health situation of the population, especially in light of the ongoing measles and cholera outbreaks in the region. The onset of the rainy season coupled with a weak sanitation infrastructure further increases the risk of a cholera outbreak further exacerbating the situation, especially in IDP camps. The Aftermath of the flooding in the year 2023 (Adamawa state) will tell a lot in the coming months which has its effects on food security. In addition, Lack of shelter and food has a direct impact on people’s health especially children, pregnant women, the elderly, and other vulnerable groups exposed to harsh weather conditions.
The health sector, in collaboration with development partners including the State MoHs and Ministries/Committees of Reconstruction, Rehabilitation, and Resettlement (MoRRR), will support a comprehensive recovery strategy for the reconstruction and rehabilitation of health facilities with the overall objective of health system restoration and with the underlying principle of “building back better.”. Moving away from geographically and thematically fragmented interventions. The program is designed with the flexibility to respond and adjust to situational changes and to address the health needs of each community. The provision of well-measured training and incentive packages to health professionals to offer essential uninterrupted healthcare services in communities is an additional priority of the health sector. Training of state M&E and partners to improve data collection and inform better decisions also needs to be prioritized.

project_name: Empowering women and girls to prevent and mitigate their protection risks through an integrated protection and mine action response in Adamawa and Borno State
project_objective:
Through an integrated mine action and gender-transformative protection response, the project will enhance the protective environment of vulnerable communities, especially vulnerable women and girls, affected by mine-related incidents. Based on the assumption that strengthening the female protective environment passes both by enhancing their inclusion in key community initiatives and addressing their specific protection risks, DRC and its implementing partner will pull together their specific expertise to 1) strengthen female leadership in key prevention initiatives related to mine incidents and Gender-Based Violence (GBV), and 2) provide a community-based protection response that directly prevents and mitigates mine action and Gender-Based Violence (GBV) risks, to which women and girls are particularly exposed.  

The innovative approach that consists of integrating mine action and gender-specific concerns into the protection response will particularly materialize through the implementation of HMA and GBV-sensitive protection monitoring tools, specific capacity-building for female community members on mine action and GBV prevention, and the strong interaction between Psychosocial Support (PSS) and prevention activities on mine incidents and GBV

project_name: Decent Job Creation through Community Infrastructure Works
project_objective:
Unemployment rate has continued to deteriorate over the past several years and remains high at 21.9% according to the latest official statistics. Even if a worker has a job, majority of economic activities are estimated to take place in the informal sector, where workers are exposed to decent work deficits such as in terms of lack of access to appropriate wages, social protection coverage, OSH, career development opportunities and prospects, to name but a few. 
Accordingly, ILO proposes to implement two-year employment-intensive infrastructure recovery works with the dual objective of decent job creation and community infrastructure rehabilitation. This approach maximizes the wages rate as percentage of the total expenditures for infrastructure works through alternative engineering solutions. It also promotes decent work principles throughout project lifecycle. The project although it will support the people to meet their immediate needs however, as ILO we do encourage our target groups to be productive, self-reliance and experience good exposure to the labour market especially for youth and women through providing decent employment.
This can be achieved through short-term jobs (3 months) through the community works, roads rehabilitation, and cultural heritage site maintenance. In addition, formal apprenticeship programmes will be implemented with the aim of increase the long-term employability by supporting skills development through on the job training in partnership with local enterprises. The estimated budget is USD 11,614,498 for two years implementation with the aim of creating 4,498 decent short term decent jobs with 323,820 workdays, and 900 beneficiaries enrolled in the apprenticeship programme, generating 93,600 workdays. The proposed interventions will be implemented in Aleppo, Homs, Hama, Lattakia, and Rural Damascus governorates based on the following criteria: number of people in need and target as set by ERL sector; high severity of needs; actual needs for infrastructure improvement for accessibility to basic services; and the presence of ILO and its partners in the targeted areas.
Protection risk 1: There is a risk of biased selection of community members (workers) who engage in the proposed infrastructure works and apprenticeship programmes, at the exclusion of others. Such a skewed selection does more harm than good in terms of social cohesion.(Likelihood: low, Impact: high).
Mitigation plan 1: The project will establish a local steering committee for each area with the equal representation of female, male, youth, people with disability, internally displaced persons, and other concerned parties, to give voices to all in an inclusive manner. Recruitment advertisement will be publicly announced, with an established and agreed upon quota for the particularly vulnerable categories, based on vulnerability assessment. 
Protection risk 2: Occupational injuries of workers at worksites due to exposure to biological, chemical and physical occupational hazards without control measures put in place.(Likelihood: High, Impact: High)
Mitigation plan 2: Occupational safety and health (OSH) training will be conducted prior to start of any worksite activities for infrastructure works, for both workers and employers. Safety managers will be recruited to ensure the safety of the works, while all workers will be covered by injury and health insurance. Targeted training and labour inspection will be conducted at factories for apprenticeship programmes to ensure the compliance of OSH measures by employers.
GBV Risk – Female workers may be exposed to worksite harassment by co-workers or employers during the activities’ execution.(Likelihood: medium, Impact: high).
Mitigation plan – GBV training will be conducted for each worksite to raise awareness in prevention of violence and harassment at work. Assign Female team leaders as a focal point. A help line will be established to receive complaints and provide necessary measures.

project_name: Provision of integrated, equitable, and Timely FSL services to emergency affected populations in South Sudan.
project_objective:
Protracted crisis in South Sudan, including climactic shocks and continued conflict, have resulted in 9 million people projected to be in need of humanitarian assistance in 2024.On top of these multilayered shocks, the Sudan crisis has adversely impacted South Sudan with more than 375,000 people having crossed the countries northern borders, predominantly from Renk. As a result of the shocks, such as flooding, inter-communal violence (ICV) and ongoing armed clashes, the majority of the population are facing increased food insecurity, lack of access to basic services, protection risks and mass displacement. As per the Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) 2023, lack of or inadequate access to clean water and improved sanitation and hygiene practices, lack of shelter and survival means, will negatively impact the most vulnerable South Sudanese.

Since 2006, Solidarités International has become a key humanitarian actor in South Sudan, implementing emergency lifesaving responses across the country and providing integrated WASH services to crisis-affected populations in areas of static presence in Upper Nile and Unity States. Since 2012, SI has played a key role in the Emergency Preparedness and Response (EPR) strategy in South Sudan, implementing multi-sectoral assessments and delivering emergency responses to crisis-affected populations all over the country. In 2023, SI became member of the ERRM country response and was able to deploy emergency response team in Upper Nile following new conflict and or displacement alerts.

In 2024, SI will continue to provide emergency live-saving WASH, FSL and Shelter responses across South Sudan to restore basic access to safe water, hygiene, and sanitation while ensuring equitable access, safety, and accountability to supported populations. Through its Emergency Rapid Response Mechanism team, SI will deploy to emergency-affected locations to provide first phase and second phase responses. It will include WaSH, Shelter and as well FSL quick response under cash or in-kind distribution to tackle emergency food insecurity situations. Fishing and agricultural support will be as well provided in second phase response to improve coping mechanism as well as livelihood economic opportunities for long term recovery for the population.

At the same time, SI will expand its presence in Upper Nile, and Unity to provide basic WASH, FSL and Shelter services that target the most vulnerable, including those suffering malnutrition, food insecurity and protection threats (including GBV survivors). 

Static programs will focus on providing community-based solutions for second phase response with the assistance of the population in agricultural and fishing sector with specific designed kits and trainings to allow durable response and economic activities that can be maintained independently by communities. Engagement and joint programming with Protection and Nutrition actors will ensure a multisectoral response of SI that can be accessed by the most vulnerable and will have a tangible impact on reducing overall priority humanitarian needs. The increased integration of protection, inclusion, and conflict sensitivity analysis in all programming will ensure that WASH services and resources can be safely accessed by all in the community. Greater engagement of communities and local markets will support the design of long term and flood designed solutions starting from the supply chains to implement the activities to ensure that interventions produce durable results for communities.

project_name: Provision of emergency food and livelihood assistance to conflict and flood affected food insecure IDPs, returnees and host communities in South Sudan
project_objective:
Save the Children proposes an emergency food and livelihood assistance intervention in response to the protracted humanitarian crisis resulting from inter communal violence, effects of climate change, the ongoing Sudan crisis and economic shocks that have exacerbated acute food insecurity and access to basic services. The targeted states include Eastern Equatoria, Jonglei, and Upper Nile including Abyei administrative area. These locations are severely food insecure, have high malnutrition rates, continue to receive returnees and internal displaced people worsening the humanitarian situation. The proposed interventions seek to save lives by addressing the immediate needs, meet the food security needs, restore and protect livelihoods to enhance capacities of the communities to absorb shocks. The project targets the conflict and flood affected households including children and youths of the food insecure displaced (IDPs), returnees and host communities.

In response to the escalating food insecurity and limited access to other basic needs, Save the Children proposes an emergency food security and livelihood based project to improve food security and access to livelihood opportunities. The proposed intervention will strengthen the household’s capacities to access food, income including agricultural inputs and productive assets to improve emergency food production and livelihoods. In addition, key messaging on nutrition, early warning systems will be done to enable communities to anticipate and respond to shocks. 

The project geographical targets include the conflict and flood affected food insecure locations that are categorized under the IPC 3, 4 and 5 locations. The targeted households will be inclusive of internally displaced people (IDPs), returnees and host communities' households meeting the defined vulnerable criteria. The most vulnerable youths at risks, female headed households, widows, elderly, people with disability, low-income households, food insecure households, households taking care of chronical ill members, orphans, separated children, households with high dependency ratio will be considered.  The interventions proposed include, unconditional cash assistance (MPCA), conditional cash assistance, emergency agricultural and fishing inputs provisions, emergency livelihood support coupled with post-harvest handling, business management, agronomic, nutrition sensitive and climate smart agricultural trainings. Key messaging on gender, protection, early warning systems, environmental management, climate change, conflict sensitivity, hygiene, nutrition and disaster risk management will be cascaded, and efforts done to ensure they are incorporated into project activities working with the community structures. The accountability to the affected population mechanisms will be strengthened to ensure beneficiaries are aware of the project activities, aware of complaint feedback mechanisms, can safely access distribution sites with dignity to enable safe programming. 

The design of the proposed project is informed by findings from the need assessments, multi-sectoral assessments, IPC analysis, other partner reports, humanitarian updates and project evaluations.
The proposed response is in line with the Food Cluster Objectives (CO1, CO2 and CO3) that contributes to the HRP 2024 Strategic Objectives (SO1, SO2 and SO3). The project will reach out to 136,236 people (at least 60% female, 15% people with disability), which fall under IPC 5, 4 and 3 in three States of South Sudan, Jonglei (Akobo), and Eastern Equatoria (Budi, Torit and Magwi), Upper Nile (Renk) and Abyei Administrative Area. Save the children will coordinate with other actors in the areas of location to avoid duplication and ensure harmonization of cash transfer values, targeting and strengthen complementary.

project_name: 2024 Multi-Sector Needs Assessment to Inform the Humanitarian Needs Overview and Humanitarian Response Plan Process in Sudan
project_objective:
Previously, and until 2020, there had been no nationwide Multi-Sector Needs Assessment (MSNA) conducted in Sudan. Primary data collection has historically been challenging, limited in scope, and often focused in areas where there is a significant humanitarian presence. Coinciding with the changes in Sudan’s political landscape and the needs and gaps identified by the humanitarian community, the first nationwide MSNA in Sudan was led by OCHA and IOM and supported by the REACH Initiative. It provided updated information and analysis on the country’s humanitarian situation to feed into the Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) and to inform response planning under the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP). In 2022, the nationwide assessment was completed for the third consecutive year under IOM implementation. Its results were one of the main sources of inter-cluster primary data and were used to complement data from inter-cluster and cluster-specific assessments. The MSNA is the central component of providing a sound evidence base for the HRP and is coordinated to support cross-sector strategic decision making in Sudan. The specific needs, vulnerabilities and human rights concerns of IDPs and other vulnerable groups do not automatically disappear when a conflict or natural disaster ends. Nor do they fade away when people initially find safety from ongoing conflict or disaster. Rather, the displaced, whether they return to their homes, settle elsewhere in the country, or try to integrate locally, usually face continuing problems, requiring support until they achieve a durable solution to their displacement. Given the current volatile security situation in Sudan, humanitarian actors face serious challenges in collecting data in a systematic and comprehensive way, often resulting in significant gaps in the information required to design, plan, and evaluate their programming. Despite the limitations to DTM's logistical operations (given the deteriorating security and economic environments) and telecommunication challenges, DTM has been able to maintain key data collection operations and has provided the humanitarian community with preliminary estimates of displacement and return. These estimates provide baseline information for inter-agency coordination on future humanitarian intervention and support DTM's partners to identify hotspots of vulnerability.	
In 2024, IOM DTM will aim to implement the MSNA across all 18 states, covering remote and hard to reach locations, where accessibility is made possible, to provide critical information to partners for addressing urgent information gaps on priority needs and vulnerabilities. The information collected will be critical for addressing urgent information gaps on priority humanitarian needs and vulnerabilities outside of areas where humanitarian partners are currently operating. However, amidst the current armed conflict escalating across Sudan, a nationwide, field based MSNA may not be possible unless security and tele connectivity improve. However, DTM is prepared to enact alternative methods to collect vital multisector data including but not limited to a remote, "phone bank" style MSNA, or, collecting fewer indicators, selected in conjunction with sector leads, on a monthly or bi-monthly basis through our Mobility Tracking methodology to provide up-to-date information on multisector needs in an innovative method which accounts for security and mobility restrictions. DTM is committed to ensuring that necessary data is collected and disseminated, regardless of conflict, in ways that center high-quality data collection and the protection and rights of beneficiaries and field teams in all activities. DTM is best placed to provide evidence-based information about the humanitarian context which IOM and other organisations rely on for their programming due to its extensive experience and coverage.

project_name: Provision of integrated, equitable, and timely WASH, Shelter services to emergency affected populations in South Sudan
project_objective:
Protracted crises in South Sudan, including climactic shocks and continued conflict, have resulted in 9.4 million people projected to be in need of humanitarian assistance in 2023. On top of these multilayered shock the Sudan crisis has adversely impacted South Sudan with more that 320,000 people having crossed the countries northern borders, predominantly from Renk. As a result of the shocks, such as flooding, inter-communal violence (ICV) and ongoing armed clashes, the majority of the population are facing increased food insecurity, lack of access to basic services, and protection risks and mass displacement. As per the Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) 2023, lack of or inadequate access to clean water and improved sanitation and hygiene practices, lack of shelter and survival means,  will negatively impact the most vulnerable South Sudanese.

Since 2006, Solidarites International has become a key humanitarian actor in South Sudan, implementing emergency lifesaving responses across the country and providing integrated WASH services to crisis-affected populations in areas of static presence in Upper Nile, Jonglei, and Western Bahr el Ghazal. Since 2012 SI has played a key role in the Emergency Preparedness and Response (EPR) strategy in South Sudan, implementing multi-sectoral assessments and delivering emergency responses to crisis-affected populations all over the country.

In 2024, SI will continue to provide emergency live-saving WASH and Shelter responses across the South Sudan to restore basic access to safe water, hygiene, and sanitation while ensuring equitable access, safety, and accountability to supported populations. Through its  Emergency Rapid Response Mechanism team, SI will deploy to emergency-affected locations to provide first phase and second phase responses including distribution of household water treatment items and soap, emergency provision of safe water, shelter kits, and rapid repair of emergency-affected infrastructure.

At the same time, SI will expand its presence in Upper Nile, and Unity to provide basic integrated WASH,  and Shelter services that target the most vulnerable, including those suffering malnutrition, food insecurity and protection threats (including GBV survivors). Static programs will focus on providing community-based solutions for sustainable WASH services that ensure that improvements in access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene are durable and can be maintained independently by communities. Engagement and joint
 
programming with Protection and Nutrition actors will ensure that WASH services can be accessed by the most vulnerable and will have a tangible impact on reducing overall priority humanitarian needs. The increased integration of protection, inclusion, and conflict sensitivity analysis in all programming will ensure that WASH services and resources can be safely accessed by all in the community. Greater engagement of communities and local markets will support the design of long term and flood resistant WASH infrastructure and supply chains to ensure that interventions produce durable results for communities.

project_name: Integrated Nutrition response to crisis affected population in South Sudan.
project_objective:
South Sudan is still going through some of the worst humanitarian crises driven by a number of factors, which includes, extreme weather conditions fueled by climate change, a deepening economic crisis, as well as sub-national violence among others. Considerable internal and cross-border displacement has further strained scarce resources, livelihoods, and basic services, increased protection risks, and inter-communal tensions, with the biggest impacts felt by children and women. In 2022, 8.9 million people, including 4.7 million children, and 1.3 million people with disabilities required humanitarian assistance. All these factors are contributing to malnutrition.

Malnutrition, in particular under-nutrition, continues to pose as one of the major challenges affecting the health sector across the Republic of South Sudan and in particular Jonglei State. According to the 2022 FSNMS surveys, the prevalence of GAM rate at national level was at 16.0% which is above the WHO estimated emergency threshold of >15%. More so, during the IPC report of 2022, the most food insecure states where more than 50% of their populations were facing crisis (IPC 3) or worse acute food insecurity were Jonglei (68.0%) on top followed by Unity (66.7%) and last by Lakes (56.9%). 

Due to recent shocks, the country will continue to face one of the world’s worst food security emergencies as these recurrent shocks have driven a reduction in food availability, regularly cut off household access to food, and limited households’ capacity to recover from past shocks. Continued conflict and displacement are contributing to high levels of food insecurity and poor WASH infrastructure and practices, and increasing rates of global acute malnutrition (GAM) and morbidity in Uror, Twic East and Pochalla Counties. The floods make the roads impassable, destroy critical infrastructure, washing away acres of cropland and increasing the risk of contamination of water sources and post-flooding disease outbreaks. The recent needs assessment in these Counties have shown that the livelihoods of community members have suffered greatly, leaving thousands of people in need of humanitarian assistance. The recent surge violence in Pochalla had eroded the gains in the management of acute malnutrition and this will take another time to improve the nutritional status of under-five children, pregnant and lactating women.

Poor Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) practices, low food production and consequently low food reserves are also preventing children from receiving nutritionally dense foods. Therefore, this project will provide a multi-sectoral response to effectively address malnutrition, through addressing gaps in WASH infrastructure and poor hygiene practices, food security and emergency nutrition needs. Tearfund is the sole organization supporting nutrition interventions in Uror, Twic East and Pochalla, in 27 Feeding Centres and 4 Stabilization Centres.

In the first 9 month of this year across the three locations of Uror, Twic East and Pochalla, 33,170 under-five children were reached through Nutrition specific intervention such as Maternal, Infant, and Young Child Nutrition (MIYCN) key massages, health and hygiene massages, Vitamin A supplementation and Deworming, 10,948 pregnant women were reached through Nutrition specific interventions such as the screening and referrals of pregnant women at the community to TSFP sites. 41,299 admitted and managed with acute malnutrition. Out of these cases, 94.9% in OTP and 95.4% U5 children in TSFP were discharged cured.

project_objective:

project_name: Prévention, dépistage précoce et prise en charge de la malnutrition aiguë sévère chez les enfants de 6 – 59 mois et les femmes enceintes et allaitantes vivant dans les zones d’urgence du Burkina Faso
project_objective:
Le Burkina Faso fait face depuis quelques années à une crise humanitaire multifactorielle marquée par l’insécurité, le changement climatique, la fragilité socio-politique ainsi que des problèmes économiques et sanitaires. L’escalade de l’insécurité en 2023 s’est traduit par la poursuite des déplacements massifs de populations, le dysfonctionnement des services sociaux de base (formations sanitaires, marchés…) et la réduction de l’accès humanitaire avec augmentation du nombre de zones enclavées, passant de 23 en novembre 2022 à 37 en novembre 2023. 
Au 31 mars 2023, le CONASUR dénombrait plus de 2 millions de PDIs dont 50% d’enfants de moins de 14 ans. Au 31 août, d’après le CORUS, c’est 778/2117 formations sanitaires qui étaient fermées ou fonctionnaient à minima privant de soins médicaux et nutritionnels plus de 3,5 millions de personnes. 
Du fait des contraintes d’accès, l’enquête nutritionnelle nationale selon la méthodologie SMART n’a pu être réalisée que dans 11/13 régions et n’a pu couvrir que 37/45 provinces, ne permettant pas d’avoir une prévalence nationale de la malnutrition aiguë globale (MAG). Une enquête SMART Rapide a été réalisée au mois de juillet dans 25 communes et localités difficiles d’accès et abritant un grand nombre de PDIs dans les 6 régions les plus affecté par l’insécurité. Cette dernière a révélé des prévalences de MAG allant de 5.5% à dans la commune de Ouargaye à 21.6% dans la localité de Diapaga et 22.6% dans la commune de Tougouri ; avec une MAS de plus de 2% dans 17 des communes et localités enquêtées, traduisant la situation alarmante qui prévaut dans les zones difficiles d’accès.
L’analyse IPC-AMN réalisé en novembre fait état de 07 provinces en situation sérieuse (IPC 3), 27 provinces en situation d’alerte (IPC 2) et 03 provinces en situation acceptable (IPC 1) pour la période d’août 2023 à janvier 2024. L’analyse de la situation selon le cadre harmonisée quant à elle fait état de près de 2,3 millions de personnes en phase 3 et 4 d’insécurité alimentaire, traduisant une situation de crise et d’urgence.
Au Burkina Faso Les principaux facteurs associés à la malnutrition sont principalement les maladies, l’apport alimentaire inadéquat, les pratiques inappropriées d’alimentation du nourrisson et du jeune enfant, l’insécurité alimentaire, le faible accès à l’eau potable et les conditions inadéquates d’hygiène. Tous ces facteurs sont aggravés par les différents chocs évoqués plus haut.

Ainsi, dans le cadre du plan de réponse humanitaire de 2024, l’UNICEF poursuivra l’appui au Gouvernement dans la mise en œuvre d’un paquet intégré de services de prévention et de prise en charge de la malnutrition aiguë en mettant l’accent sur les zones à défis sécuritaires à travers les interventions suivantes : (i) la promotion et le conseil sur les pratiques optimales d’alimentation du nourrisson et du jeune enfant en situation d’urgence ciblant 384 567 femmes enceintes et allaitante ; (ii) le renforcement du dépistage précoce de la malnutrition à travers les GASPA et l’approche PB à domicile visant 576 850 enfants de 6-59 mois ; (iii) l’appui à la référence des enfants dépistés malnutris aiguë; (iv) l’acquisition et l’appui au transport d’aliments thérapeutiques pour assurer le traitement de 101 999 enfants malnutris aiguës sévères; (v) le renforcement des capacités (plateau technique, formation, RH) aux niveaux institutionnel et communautaire pour une prise en charge de qualité des enfants MAS; (vi) l’appui à la mise en œuvre d’approches alternatives de prise en charge de la malnutrition aiguë sévère dans les zones à fort défis sécuritaire ; (vii) et l’appui à la surveillance nutritionnelle intégrant le renforcement du système d’information de routine et la réalisation des enquêtes nutritionnelles
L’UNICEF continuera également à jouer le rôle de Chef de file en Nutrition en assurant la coordination du cluster aux niveaux national et régional

project_name: Proteger, responder y empoderar para consolidar un ambiente favorable para la protección de las personas desplazadas, retornadas, en movimientos mixtos, refugiadas y solicitantes de asilo.
project_objective:
Honduras es un país de origen, de tránsito y, en menor medida, de destino de personas refugiadas y migrantes.

Como país de origen Honduras afronta enormes retos asociados a un contexto caracterizado por una multiplicidad de crisis. La población hondureña se enfrenta a riesgos extraordinarios que se constituyen en causas del desplazamiento forzado, así como a múltiples violaciones a sus derechos que ante las limitaciones de la alternativa de huida interna se configura la necesidad de protección internacional.

Durante el 2022, Honduras fue la octava nacionalidad con mayor cantidad de solicitudes de asilo presentadas globalmente, registrando un incremento del 33% entre el 2021 y el 2022. A finales de diciembre de 2022 había casi 200,000 solicitudes de asilo presentadas por personas hondureñas pendientes de resolver, principalmente en Estado Unidos (66%), México (29%) y España (3%). Entre enero y octubre de 2023, solo en México se registraron más de 36,000 nuevas solicitudes de asilo de personas hondureñas lo cual representa un aumento del 39% en comparación con el mismo periodo en 2022.

En cuanto al desplazamiento forzado interno, el estudio más reciente, de ámbito nacional, señala que al menos 247.090 personas (el 2.7% de la población hondureña) se vieron forzadas a desplazarse por la violencia de 2004 a 2018. De ellas el 55% eran mujeres, el 45% hombres y el 43% menores de edad. El país no cuenta con cifras actualizadas sobre la magnitud del impacto del desplazamiento; sin embargo, los diagnósticos comunitarios, así como el monitoreo efectuado de manera permanente por el ACNUR dan cuenta de un aumento del número de personas desplazadas internamente.

En este contexto, el Proyecto busca responder de manera integral a los impactos generados por la crisis que enfrenta el país, abordar de manera estructural las causas que generan el desplazamiento forzado interno y los vacíos que persisten en los mecanismos y alternativas para la protección de las personas desplazadas por la violencia y en riesgo de desplazamiento; las personas refugiadas y solicitantes de asilo; las personas retornadas con necesidades de protección cuya reintegración se dificulta en la medida en que presentan niveles de riesgo; así como otras personas de interés, como aquellas que integran los movimientos mixtos y requieren protección internacional y/o protección específica.

La estrategia, en consecuencia, se concentra en tres áreas de impacto consistentes con los tres objetivos generales definidos por el Clúster de Protección: proteger, responder y fortalecer. Bajo estas tres áreas la intervención se enfocará en promover acciones dirigidas a que las personas desplazadas, quienes integran los movimientos mixtos, las personas refugiadas y solicitantes de asilo y aquellas de nacionalidad hondureña que han sido retornadas: (i) se beneficien de un mecanismo de protección integral; (ii) accedan a las necesidades básicas en un entorno seguro; y (iii) cuenten con las herramientas para mitigar sus riesgos y vulnerabilidades, considerando los impactos diferenciados.

project_name: Provision of Shelter and NFI assistance to vulnerable populations affected by conflict and displacement in Syria
project_objective:
HNO 2024 estimates 16.7 million people in need in Syria, with 6.8 million requiring shelter assistance and 6.2 million in need of NFI support. The economic crisis in Syria hampers the population's ability to improve shelters and access essential NFIs and limits access to basic services, protection, and physical safety. The Shelter/NFI intervention in Syria aims to provide lifesaving and life-sustaining shelter and non-food item (NFI) support, enhancing community resilience and cohesion by addressing housing and related infrastructure needs. 
The project aligns with HRP Objective 1. NRC interventions will target vulnerable conflict and displacement-affected populations, including IDPs, refugees, host community members, returnees, and non-displaced households impacted by the conflict. The target locations are determined by severity, inter-agency coordination, and accessibility. Implementing multi-sectoral vulnerability scoring techniques where applicable. The key project Components will include: 
Shelter: 
•	Rehabilitation of collective shelters in Hasakeh city to enhance living conditions for displaced families. 
•	Structural rehabilitation of housing buildings in Aleppo to reinforce protection and community cohesion.
•	Camp infrastructure maintenance and repair.
•	Dignified transitional shelter solutions in specific regions. 
•	Installation of new/ replacement of existing tents
•	Supply and installation of HH level solar energy systems.
NFI Assistance: Winter assistance through blanket distributions in preidentified vulnerable areas, providing winter clothes to affected communities. 
Winterization assistance (cash or in-kind) for affected populations. 
Distribution of NFI kits. 
NRC will implement the interventions through an integrated approach with joint program for Shelter and NFI activities, with modalities (emergency, transitional, and recovery) based on access constraints and capacity. Gender, elderly, and Persons with Disabilities (PWDs) considerations integrated into design, implementation, and monitoring processes. NRC’s future Focus (2024/2025) will be exploration of housing and infrastructure projects linked with solar energy; pilot projects planned. Rehabilitation of community infrastructure such as markets, schools, and medical centers in coordination with relevant sectors.

project_name: Provision of multipurpose cash assistance to vulnerable Palestine refugees in Syria
project_objective:
The political, economic and humanitarian crisis in Syria continue to exert significant pressure on the Palestine refugees remaining in the country with high poverty levels. The results of a PDM survey conducted by UNRWA in October 2023 show that 92 % of households had to borrow food or rely on help from friends and 64% reduced the number and quantity of meals per day to cope with being unable to purchase enough food   In addition, 40 % of assessed households showed to resort to emergency livelihoods coping strategies  characterized by begging (4 %) and selling productive assets (such as sewing machines, wheelbarrows and bicycles) that are difficult to recover (36 %), indicative of refugee households’ diminishing ability to cope with the increasing poverty. 
This PDM has also assessesd the household perceptions on ability to meet basic: About 45 % of assessed households reported that they are able to meet at least half of their basic needs, a slight reduction from 48 % at the same time last year. When disagregating against broader household vulnerability categories, 46 % of the most vulnerable households reported ability to meet at least half of their basic needs compared to 43 % in the other vulnerable category. About 7 % reported being unable to meet any of their basic needs, about the same percentage for both vulnerability categories. Lastly, 48 % of households reported being able to meet a few of their basic needs, 47 %i n the most vulnerable category and 51 % in the other vulnerable category. The main reason for inability to access basic services was lack of money to buy basic services, reported by 99 % of households while 1 % reported lack of basic items in the market. This finding generally reflect the worsening economic situation in the country marked by persistent increase in prices of basic goods and services.

UNRWA plans to provide up to 420,000 Palestine refugees with MPC to meet their basic needs. The Agency will provide this assistance based on a targeted approach introduced in 2019, prioritizing refugees assessed as most vulnerable with a higher cash transfer.
In 2024, it is expected that around 155,500 Palestine refugees will be assessed as most vulnerable based on the four vulnerability categories used by UNRWA (female headed households, families with persons with disabilities, families headed by an older person and unaccompanied minors/orphans). The remaining 264,500 vulnerable Palestine refugees will receive a lower cash transfer value as explained below.
 The transfer values were based on discussions with the CWG and aligned with CWG recommendations. The cash transfer values were set to:
•	 SYP 2,194,209 / month for a family of 5 members belonging to the most vulnerable categories. This transfer value takes into consideration the reduction of the in-kind food assistance to be provided to the most vulnerable beneficiaries which is $ 7.133 /month / individual.
•	 SYP 1,716,000 /month for a family of 5 members belonging to the remaining caseload of vulnerable Palestine refugees who are not eligible to the in-kind food assistance. UNRWA distributes cash through BBSF Bank and Al Haram Company in addition to its own cash distribution centre in Damascus.
Risks, Assumptions and Mitigating measures:
Assumptions: 
1 Humanitarian needs of PRs in Syria remain relatively stable
 2. Sustained commitment of donors to support UNRWA financially
 3. Security situation and active violence do not deteriorate any further. 
Risks linked to CVA implementation e.g. further inflation, liquidity issues, economic deterioration, impact on the market, etc. 
Mitigation: UNRWA is engaged very closely with the UN Country Team in its negotiations with the Central Bank of Syria CBS to address the spread between the informal and formal exchange rate and the liquidity risk is discussed with CBS.
