project_name: Preventing Child Abuse and Supporting Sustainable Reintegration of Conflict-Affected Children in Northeast Nigeria
project_objective:
Now in its fourteenth year, the conflict in northeast Nigeria continues to disrupt the lives and livelihoods of millions of people across Borno, Adamawa and Yobe (BAY) states. Violent attacks by non-state armed groups (NSAGs) and military counter-operations have displaced men, women, and children, disrupted farming and other livelihoods, and limited the functionality of markets and other basic services.
The UNICEF Child Protection project will continue to focus on strengthening access to quality preventive and responsive child protection services that address the needs, rights and dignity of children and their caregivers in the conflict affected states of Borno, Adamawa and Yobe (BAY). The emergency response will prioritize the most vulnerable including at-risk children and their families. UNICEF’s efforts to address child protection  and gender-based violence in emergencies is part of its over-all strategy on prevention and response to all forms of violence against children (VAC) through adopting a nexus approach that addresses the urgent protection concerns facing children affected by crises; reinforce existing local and national capacities and systems for children’s protection; transitional justice and promoting peaceful coexistence  including a focus on climate change mitigation where possible. 
The present project module is part of ongoing efforts to provide a comprehensive, multi-year child protection and gender-based violence programme that aims to support the psychosocial wellbeing of conflict affected children and caregivers, quality case management services for unaccompanied and separated children (UASC) and survivors GBV violence and community-based reintegration of children and adolescents formerly associated with Non-State Armed Groups (NSAGs) within their communities. Girls, boys and women survivors of gender-based violence (GBV), including conflict-related sexual violence (CRSV) will also have access to safe spaces and benefit from case management, information and referral systems to specialized services. 
In addition, project actions will further focus on child protection system strengthening through the roll out of the child protection law in the BAY states, registering under-5 child births, and enhancing the capacity of a professional social service workforce to improve the quality, coordination and sustaining the response. The UNICEF child protection response will be integrated with the work of other sectors, such as education, WASH, health and nutrition, for increased and comprehensive delivery of services to conflict affected children and caregivers. 
Results will be achieved by providing integrated child protection case management services for children including family tracing and reunification for UASC; delivering quality and sustainable socio-economic reintegration services to children formerly associated with armed groups as well as other vulnerable children and their families. In addition, conflict-affected children will have access to community-based mental health and psychosocial support services (MHPSS) including structured recreational activities and adolescents’ life skills education. The project will also contribute to strengthening capacity of service delivery to GBV survivors. Child and adult survivors of GBV will in addition have access to comprehensive minimum lifesaving services including medical, psychosocial, legal and safety. Children and caregivers living in or returning to locations contaminated by unexploded remnant of war (UXO) will be provided with explosive ordnance risk education (EORE) in schools, child friendly spaces, transit and displace camps s with the support of Mine Action sub sector. Grave violations against children affected by conflict will be monitored and reporting through the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism (MRM).

project_name: Safe and Uninterrupted Access to Quality, Equitable and Inclusive Education for displacement affected children and youth in South Sudan
project_objective: The proposed intervention seeks to ensure that emergency affected 35,929 children and youth (19,042 girls and 16,887 boys) have access to continuous, quality driven, equitable learning opportunities in safe and inclusive environments.  Of these at least 3,594 children (50% girls) will be children with disabilities. Target locations will be those prioritized by the cluster and where NRC has existing physical presence in the CES (Juba, Kajokeji), Unity (Mayom, Panyijiar, Leer and Koch), Jonglei (Akobo, Bor South, Duk, Twic East), WBeG (Wau, Raja), NBeG (Aweil East, Aweil West, Aweil North), Warrap (Gogrial West and Twic) and Upper Nile (Renk) States.  In addition, NRC will activate the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) education response in identified locations as per the education cluster agreed triggers for emergency education response.  Both the static and mobile response mechanism will target children and youth (aged 6 – 17) from returnee, IDP and host community families with education services in both formal schools and non-formal learning centres. Proposed education interventions will align with cluster strategic objectives of improving access to quality education and educational systems strengthening.  NRC will conduct enrolment social mobilisation through back to learning campaigns, construct/rehabilitate classrooms and provide desks to reduce congestion which has recently been aggravated by the influx of returnees from Sudan because of the conflict that erupted and displaced hundreds of people with 302,838 [at least 50% being school aged children] having crossed to South Sudan at various border crossing. (OCHA, 6 Oct, 2023), For improved physical safety, NRC will construct gender segregated WASH facilities and conduct hygiene promotion activities in school communities, distribute IEC materials with disease prevention messaging, promote child participation through supporting child-led activities in school clubs, distribute recreational kits for structured recreational activities.  Activities aimed at improving the quality of education will include teacher training, distribution of teaching and learning materials, provision of textbooks, and supplementary reading materials, supporting catch-up classes for returnee and children previously out of school to facilitate reintegration and transition. The intervention will support continuous teacher professional development through teacher learning cycles and other short trainings. To retain female teachers in hard-to-reach locations, NRC will avail incentives and other non-monetary forms of motivation. In addition to pedagogical training educators will undergo capacity building in conflict sensitive education, PSS, life-skills training, code of conduct, referral pathways, PSEA and safeguarding.  The proposed intervention will link up quality issues with education systems strengthening and conduct trainings for PTA/SMCs on school governance, deliver school management training for county education staff on school supervision and teacher mentorship.  Trainings will cover cross-cutting issues i.e., gender mainstreaming, peacebuilding, environment, and disaster risk reduction.

project_name: TREAT ME RIGHT - Health Care and Protection for the Displaced, Host and Vulnerable Population in Wabane Subdivision, Lebialem Division
project_objective:
The armed repression of the 2016’s protests in the North West and South West regions of Cameroon against the linguistical and cultural marginalisation of the Anglophone population exacerbated in an armed conflict between government military forces and organised armed groups that continues to this day. The ongoing socio-political crisis impacts the civilian population of the two regions caught between the two parties armed clashes. Among the impacts for the civilian population, we register the destruction of medical health centres and consequent issues of access to medical care as well as a number of protection issues affecting the most vulnerable segments of the population (SGVB, stigmatisation and violence against people with disabilities) without any adequate systems of prevention and mitigation and any responsive psychosocial services to support the survivors.  
Treat Me Right is a multisectoral (health/protection) one year emergency project targeting 3 health areas in the health district of Wabane within the Lebialem division of the South West region of Cameroon where due to the ongoing conflict the most vulnerable segments of the population (women, children under 5 years old and people with disabilities (PwD)) are lacking appropriate medical care and protection systems catered to both their specific and circumstantial (conflict induced) psychosocial needs. 
The overall objective of the project is improving the physical, mental and social health conditions of host and displaced populations in the Lebialem department in the South West region. The specific objective of the intervention is Improving the quality of and access to health care and protection services for displaced and host populations and vulnerable groups in the 3 health areas of Wabane district (Bamumbu, Bechati and Fotang). This objective is pursued with the following targets: 
-	16 141 patients (8629F, 7512M, 12 636 <18 y/o, 131 PwD) access medical care in the 3 targeted health areas.
-	10 000 people (5.100 F e 4.900; 1.900 <18 y/o; 650 PwD) are supported by protection monitoring activities. 
The expected result from the health sector’s activities is that of improving the access to primary health and psychosocial support services thanks to an increase in the safety, accessibility, and supply of integrated health centres in Bambumbu, Bechati, Fotang and Nkong. Specifically, the targets are: 
-	4 integrated health centres (Bamumbu, Bechati, Fotang and Nkong) are equipped with basic hygienic services in line with protection and sustainability standards.
-	23 medical professionals (10 F; 13M) are adequately trained on medical and mental health care.
-	5584 consultations in general medical care and 8694 consultations in paediatrics are provided.
-	720 ANC1 (ante-natal care1) are provided, and 386 assisted deliveries are performed.
-	1200 people (650 F, 550 M, 500 minors, 100 PwD) access psychological support.
The expected result from the protection sector’s activities is that of guaranteeing access to protection and support services at the personal, family and community level for the most vulnerable groups such as women at risk or survivors of SGBV, children under 5 years of age and PwD. Specifically, the targets are: 
-	100 people (90 F, 10 M; 19 <di 18 y/o; 6 PwD) benefit of community social support networks to prevent, mitigate and respond to SGVB cases.
-	24 families and 140 PwD (79 F, 61 M, 68 <18 y/o) access to the Peer Counseling service.
-	10 000 (5.100 F, 4.900; 1.900 <18 y/o; 650 PwD) are reached by the raising awareness and outreach activities.  
-	At least 30 social workers in the health sector (15 F, 15 M) and members of Community Based Organizations (CBO) are trained on inclusivity of PwD.
Beneficiaries will be selected on the basis of medical criteria, vulnerability and humanitarian needs, without any discrimination on the basis of gender, place of residence, ethnicity, religion and political affiliation.

project_name: RRM-Frontline
project_objective:
Mis en place en mars 2019, le RRM-Frontline est une initiative de quatre ONG internationales (ACF, SI, DRC et HI) pour apporter une réponse rapide aux besoins urgents des populations déplacées dans un contexte de détérioration rapide de la situation sécuritaire et humanitaire au Burkina Faso qui va se poursuivre en 2024.  S’appuyant sur leurs expériences et expertises, ces organisations ont développé un mécanisme de réponse rapide contextualisé permettant d'assurer une veille humanitaire des déplacements de population dans ses zones prioritaires d'intervention ainsi qu'une réponse multisectorielle, informée et modulable afin de fournir un accès amélioré à la sécurité alimentaire, l'eau, l’hygiène et l’assainissement, aux articles non alimentaires, à un abri, à la protection et aux premiers secours psychologiques. En tant qu'acteur "frontline", le RRM-Frontline priorise les zones difficiles et très difficiles d'accès, y compris les zones IPC4+ et zones d’urgence malnutrition. 

Les personnes déplacées internes de moins de trois mois, sont la cible du projet. Lorsque les capacités ne permettent pas de couvrir les besoins de la totalité des PDI ou dès lors que l’intervention sera considérée hors période, sauf dans le cadre d’interventions dans les zones dites difficiles d’accès ou en IPC 4+, des critères socio-économiques cumulés à des critères de protection seront appliqués et pondérés pour cibler les ménages les plus vulnérables, y compris les familles d’accueil. Dans le cadre de la protection, les évaluations rapides de protection permettent de déceler les besoins de protection ainsi que les individus ou les groupes spécifiquement vulnérables qui ont été exposés à des situations de choc psychologique ou émotionnel. Les bénéficiaires de services de soutien psychosocial seront identifiés à travers les activités de SMSPS (PSP, sensibilisations) mais aussi lors des ERP et du ciblage.

project_name: Anglophone Crisis Emergency Response IV (ACER IV)
project_objective:
In response to the immense needs resulting from the conflict in the Northwest (NW) and Southwest (SW) regions in Cameroon, CRS is implementing fourteen-month project - Anglophone Crisis Emergency Response (ACER IV). ACER IV builds on the success and learning of the previous phases of the response. Changes and adaptations are based on community consultations and input, needs assessments, coordination and harmonization with other humanitarian actors, and changes in the security context and accessibility.
The goal of the ACER IV project is to improve food security and alleviate suffering of displaced and host households in the Northwest Region of Cameroon. The project seeks to achieve this goal through two purposes: (1) vulnerable displaced and host households in the Northwest meet their basic food and NFI needs, and (2) vulnerable displaced and host households in the Northwest improve poultry production. In partnership with the Archdiocese of Bamenda, CRS is delivering an integrated package of assistance, providing vulnerable displaced and host households with poultry production training and support, as well as emergency food and NFIs. The project is using market-based approaches to support 10,800 people in 1,800 households over 14 months.
The Project's Theory of Change is,  Assuming that markets and vendors’ supply chains remain accessible and functional and the security situation remains stable, if households have improved access to sufficient quantity, quality and diversity of food; and if they purchase essential non-food items (NFIs); and if they raise poultry to improve their livelihoods and generate income; then they will improve their food security and experience reduced suffering; because the first three phases of the ACER project have demonstrated that market access to food reduces household hunger scores, broader humanitarian evidence shows that food assistance leads to improved food security, and poultry interventions in Cameroon’s ACER III program have  demonstrated the potential to improve income and facilitate more sustainable access to food
ACER IV responds directly to the normative and felt needs of the affected population. In the International Organization for Migration (IOM)’s multisector needs assessment (MSNA) conducted in August 2022, food and non-food items (NFIs) continue to be priority needs. IDPs, people with disabilities, older people, and female-headed households are disproportionately impacted by the crisis. In the NW, nearly one million people are food insecure and cannot meet basic household needs.  In response, ACER IV will provide food assistance and NFIs using an e-voucher modality that leverages local markets and stimulates the local economy. In CRS community consultations, affected populations have expressed interest in receiving support to restart their livelihoods and generate income so that they do not continue relying on humanitarian assistance. Poultry production was among the most cited and viable livelihoods options considering the context – difficult access to agricultural land and a tradition of a booming livestock sector including egg production. In ACER IV, CRS will scale up the poultry assistance to reach more participants and locations -a subset of the food assistance participants. The poultry pilot intervention includes training, input distribution and strengthening collaboration and engagement with the Ministry of Livestock, Fisheries and Animal Industries (MINEPIA) and Livelihood Field Agents (LFAs).
ACER IV will cover 5 Divisions -Momo and Mezam from previous phases and Ngoketunjia, Boyo and Bui (newly added) in the Northwest, where there is demonstrated need and major gaps in humanitarian assistance. ACER IV will continue to work in Bamenda I, II and III, Santa, Bafut and Batibo sub-divisions (old locations) and will expand to Bali and Tubah in Mezam,  Mbengwi in Momo, Belo in Boyo, Balikumbat in Ngoketunjia and Oku in Bui.

project_name: Supporting crisis-affected populations in North-West and South-West regions through the provision of multi-sectoral assistance in Cameroon
project_objective:
In the North-West, South-West regions, IOM plans interventions for 2024 to respond to the most urgent needs of displaced populations through a multisectoral approach focusing on coordination, Shelter and NFI, Mental health support (health), psychosocial support (protection) and WASH interventions. The last Multi-Sectoral Needs Assessment (MSNA) exercise conducted in the North-West and South-West regions of Cameroon, undertaken in September 2023, showed needs in most of the sectors, including access to water, food, health, education, etc. The last Mobility Tracking assessment showed that the North-West (NW)-South-West (SW) crisis impact continues also to spill over to the neighbouring regions with the number of IDPs coming from NW-SW increasing from the previous year, while the last MSNA, undertaken at the same time, showed again severe needs in most of the sectors. In view of such needs identified, IOM plans to expand its programmes accordingly and in line with each mandate and capacity, with a multisectoral response aiming at contributing to reinforce life-saving assistance and to improve well-being of displaced and the most vulnerable populations affected by the crisis. IOM will mainstream protection and recovery through the development of local capacities, in all its proposed activities to support displaced populations in preparing and achieving durable solutions. 
IOM will support the work of the Coordination sector through the collection and production of critical data on displacement situation, alerts as well as humanitarian Multi-sectoral humanitarian needs following its DTM methodology, that will be provided to the humanitarian community to inform its humanitarian programming. In the frame of the Shelter Sector response, IOM will distribute emergency shelter and NFI kits, both in-kind and using cash-modality solutions when possible (bearing in mind that lack of civil documentation and concerns of diversion of cash to non-licit uses poses very important challenges) and help the construction for most vulnerable people. In the WASH response, IOM will drill and rehabilitate boreholes, construct water points, latrines and other infrastructures and conduct hygiene sensitization and promotion activities combined with distribution of WASH kits. Finally, IOM multisectoral assistance will also include mental health activities including direct MHPSS assistance using PMTs, reinforcing referral mechanism and capacity building of health actors (Health sector), while also directly providing psychosocial support to populations impacted by crisis by reinforcing safety and social network as well as strengthening community capacity to provide psychosocial support to victims of GBVs (Protection sector).
Through activities, direct feedback from beneficiaries and community members will be gained via IPs and also directly by IOM staff during field visits and visits of the M&E/AAP independent team in accordance with the wider IOM AAP emergencies workplan. AAP focal points will be assigned in Buea and Yaounde respectively, with clear SOPs to be in place to capture complaints from beneficiaries and to take any appropriate action. Members of IP will be trained on topics such as the proper handling of disclosures of gender-based violence (GBV) incidents, aspects of confidentiality, and respectful communication in high-stress environments. Targeting of beneficiaries will be done according to a vulnerability criterion including  persons living with disabilities assessed through RRM household level assessments conducted by IOM. Also, IOM will integrate measures to ensure gender-specific needs when conducting needs assessment and to mitigate risks of GBV in all activities (e.g., including through training of IPs on GBV core concepts, guiding principles as well as on how to respond to disclosures of GBV). IOM will also ensure the effective participation of these communities in  decision-making processes and in establishing community based mechanisms.

project_name: Projet integré de renforcement à la nutrition au Tchad
project_objective:
Le Programme Alimentaire Mondial de par ces interventions en nutrition compte apporter un appui aux efforts nationaux à la réduction de la prévalence de la malnutrition chronique de 40 %. Le PAM cherche à mettre en place grâce à un ensemble intégré de services combinant des interventions spécifiques et sensibles à la nutrition une approche communautaire afin d’améliorer la situation nutritionnelle des enfants et des femmes enceintes et allaitantes dans les provinces du centre, de l'ouest dans la population locale. Ce projet permettra d'augmenter la couverture des interventions de nutrition et la qualité des soins pour les enfants souffrant de malnutrition aiguë avec l'approche communautaire; d'améliorer l'accès aux soins prénataux pour les mères, y compris l'accès à une nutrition adéquate, pendant la grossesse; d'assurer un suivi postnatal approprié des femmes enceintes, y compris l'accès à une nutrition adéquate pour les mères allaitantes, l'allaitement maternel exclusif pendant les 6 premiers mois de la vie de l'enfant, la vaccination, la supplémentation en micronutriments, le suivi de la croissance et des conseils diététiques pour les enfants ; de renforcer les connaissances et les pratiques des mères et des soignants en matière d'alimentation du nourrisson et du jeune enfant et les pratiques familiales essentielles en matière de santé, d'hygiène et de nutrition; d'améliorer l'accès à une alimentation de qualité à travers la mise en œuvre d'initiatives communautaires de diversification alimentaire; diversifier les approches de prévention de la malnutrition aiguë grâce à l'introduction d'approches intégrées de CCSC et basées sur les transferts monétaires visant des options localisées pour la nutrition maternelle et infantile ; de renforcer la synergie avec d'autres interventions sensibles à la nutrition telles que les activités de soutien à la résilience communautaire, l'eau, l'hygiène et l'assainissement, afin de s'attaquer aux causes sous-jacentes et profondes de la malnutrition.
La cible primaire du projet sera les enfants âgés de 6 à 59 mois ainsi que les femmes enceintes et femmes allaitantes souffrant de malnutrition. Tandis que les interventions de prévention de la malnutrition cibleront les enfants de 6 à 23 mois et les femmes enceintes et femmes allaitantes.

project_name: Respuesta Humanitaria a familias altamente vulnerables a la INSAN en el departamento de Chiquimula, Guatemala.
project_objective:
El Análisis de INSAN aguda de la CIF (mar 2023- feb 2024), indica que 3.1 millones de personas continuarán en Crisis (Fase 3) o Emergencia (Fase 4) para el período sept 2023-feb 2024.  Se prevé que 10 departamentos se clasifiquen en Crisis (Fase 3) entre los cuales se encuentran Chiquimula y Huehuetenango. Entre los supuestos: impacto negativo del fenómeno de El Niño en las cosechas de granos básicos del ciclo de Primera y en las siembras del ciclo productivo de Postrera y del Altiplano; así como en la demanda de mano de obra para los trabajos agrícolas, en el acceso al agua e incremento de las enfermedades transmitidas por alimentos en la población menor de cinco años. 
De acuerdo con el informe del Instituto Nacional de Estadística (INE), el costo de la canasta básica al mes de noviembre 2023 es de GTQ 3899.67 la que es GTQ 281.09 más alto que en noviembre 2022. Los meteorólogos predicen que el actual fenómeno de El Niño, que comenzó en junio, será intenso, quizá tanto como el que terminó en 2016, que contribuyó a que ese año fuera el más caluroso jamás registrado hasta esa fecha, algo que es probable que se supere con creces en 2023-2024. En consecuencia, y de acuerdo con patrones anteriores, se espera que amplias zonas de Centroamérica y el noreste de América del Sur experimenten condiciones más secas y cálidas que la habitual. 
 
Para responder a la crisis alimentaria causada por el fenómeno de El Niño, el proyecto propone brindar asistencia alimentaria a familias priorizadas por alta vulnerabilidad a la seguridad alimentaria en Chiquimula (municipios de Jocotán y Camotán) a través de transferencias monetarias no condicionadas durante el periodo de hambre estacional en 2024. La producción y difusión de información sobre la inseguridad alimentaria de las comunidades serán abordadas utilizando metodologías estandarizadas CARI e IPC. Se implementará un Sistema de Preguntas Quejas y Retroalimentaciones (PQR) para conocer el nivel de satisfacción de personas beneficiarias y otros actores de la asistencia del proyecto.

project_name: Garantizar la supervivencia de niñas niños con desnutrición aguda a través de identificación y tratamientos oportunos y cuidado nutricional y de salud integral materno infantil en Huehuetenango, Alta Verapaz, Escuintla y Chiquimula, Guatemala
project_objective:
La situación de inseguridad alimentaria en Guatemala se ha acentuado, derivado de las consecuencias de eventos relacionados al cambio climático y la pandemia, que han tenido consecuencias de mediano y largo plazo, ya que no han permitido la recuperación de las poblaciones afectadas en el área de Huehuetenango, Alta Verapaz, Escuintla y Chiquimula. En 2023, se ha registrado un incremento de la desnutrición aguda en la niñez menor de cinco años comparado con el año 2022, situación derivada de la inseguridad alimentaria en las familias. A la semana epidemiológica 50 (16 de diciembre) se registraron 25,237 casos de desnutrición aguda; un 26% más que el mismo período de 2022 (20,085 casos); así mismo, se ha registrado un incremento del 14% en el número de casos de desnutrición aguda severa y se reporta que 54 niños y niñas han muerto por desnutrición aguda.
El porcentaje de desnutrición aguda ha aumentado considerablemente hasta 43% de los casos de desnutrición en Alta Verapaz, 28% en Escuintla, 25% en Chiquimula respectivamente; en el departamento de Huehuetenango se observó un incremento del 40% de casos de desnutrición aguda severa identificados por medio de signos clínicos.  Esta situación es sumamente preocupante porque aumenta asimismo el riesgo de muerte por esta causa; estos cuatro departamentos reportan el 56% (30/54) de los casos de mortalidad por desnutrición aguda. 

En el proyecto se implementarán acciones integrales de atención nutricional y salud a través de “brigadas integrales” que llegan hasta las comunidades más lejanas y donde la presencia de salud es muy limitada.  La pertinencia de esta Estrategia ha sido validada y ha probado ser efectiva desde 2018 en contexto de emergencias.  La Estrategia ha sido tan efectiva que ha logrado identificar y tratar oportunamente a niñas y niños afectados por desnutrición aguda que no habían sido detectados previamente por los servicios de salud (hasta un 68%). Es un abordaje estandarizado y monitoreado que ha sido mejorado y complementado hasta que el día de hoy brindan atención integral a la niñez  (evaluación nutricional, tratamiento oportuno, suplementación con micronutrientes múltiples en polvo, zinc y vitamina A, desparasitación, consejería alrededor de los temas de la Ventana de los 1,000 días, vacunación) y a las mujeres en edad fértil incluyendo adolescentes, embarazadas y en período de lactancia (evaluación nutricional, suplementación con hierro y ácido fólico, vacunación y consejería). Adicionalmente, para complementar las acciones, estas brigadas adicionalmente dejan formados “agentes de cambio” (líderes y lideresas formados en aspectos básicos para identificación oportuna de desnutrición aguda, signos de peligro, y alimentación infantil e higiene) para orientar a su comunidad.

El proyecto responde a los siguientes objetivos:
• Identificar la población afectada por desnutrición aguda y brindar tratamiento inmediato para salvar sus vidas.
• Mejorar las competencias del personal de salud y otros actores locales para la atención nutricional en emergencias
• Brindar insumos necesarios para el cuidado nutricional
• Fortalecer capacidades de líderes y lideresas comunitarias en la preparación y respuesta para la atención nutricional en emergencias
• Activar sistemas de alerta temprana nutricional en la comunidad

project_name: Atención Nutricional para población vulnerable en situación de movilidad en Esquipulas, Chiquimula
project_objective:
La situación humanitaria en la frontera Agua Caliente ubicada en el municipio de Esquipulas, Chiquimula, se ha agravado debido al flujo de población en situación de movilidad, alcanzando picos históricos en el mes septiembre de 2023. El promedio diario de personas en tránsito por Guatemala monitoreadas por la Organización Internacional para las Migraciones (OIM) durante septiembre fue de 2,213 personas. Esto representa un incremento del 22 % comparado con agosto de 2023 donde se monitorearon 1,815 personas. Los grupos de personas en movilidad que transitan por este territorio son integrados por una proporción significativa de niñas y niños menores de 5 años, adolescentes, mujeres embarazadas y en periodo de lactancia materna. Las condiciones del viaje como el difícil acceso y disponibilidad a alimentos, condiciones inadecuadas de agua, saneamiento e higiene y el difícil o nulo acceso a servicios de salud y nutrición ponen en riesgo el estado nutricional de la población, especialmente de los más vulnerables; es por esto por lo que, es necesario conocer el estado nutricional de la población y brindar atención de nutrición, para la prevención de deterioro del estado nutricional. La estrategia anteriormente utilizada para nutrición en emergencias ha sido Brigadas de Nutrición, la cual ha sido implementada desde 2018 desde el Clúster de Nutrición, dando respuesta a diferentes situaciones de emergencia (erupción de Volcán de fuego, aumento de la mortalidad por desnutrición aguda, aumento de la inseguridad alimentaria y nutricional por sequía, COVID-19 o fenómenos climáticos como tormentas tropicales).
El proyecto tiene como objetivo brindar atención nutricional a grupos vulnerables en movilidad por territorio guatemalteco, para la prevención de la malnutrición. Para la atención a esta población en situación de vulnerabilidad se adaptará la estrategia de Brigadas de Nutrición a equipos móviles de nutrición, la cual consistirá en la entrega de servicios de nutrición a niños y niñas menores de 5 años, y mujeres en edad fértil con énfasis en adolescentes, mujeres embarazadas y en periodo de lactancia materna. Además, se apoyará la mejora de las capacidades y la calidad de la atención en los servicios de alimentación que se encuentran en el territorio, por medio del fortalecimiento de las capacidades de las personas encargadas. Como parte del proyecto se incluye la rendición de cuentas a la población afectada, el proyecto incluye un proceso de escucha y diálogo con personas en situación de movilidad para identificar las necesidades de comunicación e información en materia de nutrición.

project_name: Clean water for all
project_objective:
Since the conflict began in 2011, Syria has faced the worst humanitarian crisis. Our project addresses one of the most pressing needs for people affected by the war: access to safe and clean water. 
In 2024, ADRA is planning to intervene in several types of activities, such as water system rehabilitation, borehole rehabilitation and solar systems installation (in locations where household-level access to water is limited due to electricity outages), High water tank rehabilitation to ensure proper pressure in the water network, implementation of reverse osmosis unit to provide clean drinking water in the eastern Ghouta where there is high contamination with nitrate due to the damages in sewage network and the absence of sewage water treatment plants also the usage of fertilization in agriculture.
This project will improve access to safe water and sewage services for approximately 1,879,117 beneficiaries (375,823 households). The targeted category includes newly returned returnees, IDPs and vulnerable host communities across the governorates of Lattakia, Aleppo, Rural Damascus, and Deir-Ez-Zor. The beneficiaries will be selected on a detailed needs assessment, and those with the highest need and underserved by the humanitarian community will be prioritized for assistance.
The project will use a participatory and integrated approach to ensure that the needs of men, women, boys and girls are taken into account from the project design stage, throughout the implementation and during the post-implementation monitoring of the work. Children, adolescents, young adults, middle-aged adults and older adults will be solicited during the initial needs assessment for the project and in the post-implementation stage. In addition, each age and gender group will be able to provide timely feedback to ADRA on the intervention through regular contact with ADRA monitoring staff.
The needs of young children, children, adolescents, young adults, middle-aged adults and older adults will also be considered, as children, adolescents, and middle-aged and older adults may require more water for cleaning and cooking.
ADRA has already secured 25% of the estimated budget for planned 2024 WASH activities.

project_name: Provision of essential health care services and psychosocial support to conflict-affected populations in NES
project_objective:
In Syria, where 14.9 million people require healthcare aid, approximately 2.2 million reside in NES, facing weak, disrupted health systems compounded by public health emergencies. According to HNO2024, various emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases, along with vaccine-preventable and neglected tropical diseases, such as influenza-like illnesses, measles, meningitis, and waterborne diseases like AWD/cholera, hepatitis A, and leishmaniasis, continue to pose a significant threat to affected communities throughout Syria. These diseases account for more than 16% of the total consultations reported from the health system through the surveillance system. The cholera outbreak, declared by the Syrian Ministry of Health in September 2022, is expected to persist in 2024, particularly in NES, with seasonal variations in caseloads. Socio-economic challenges, poor infrastructure, and inadequate WASH conditions hinder access to quality healthcare, particularly in Al-Hasakeh, Ar-Raqqa, and Deir-ez-Zor. NES camps lack sanitation, exacerbating health risks and gender-based violence. Challenges there include severe shortages of medicines and medical supplies, inadequate availability of healthcare personnel, and insufficient referral capacities, with over 1,000 patients classified as "cold cases" unable to obtain life-sustaining specialized services due to a lack of resources and services within the camps.
In 2024 and 2025, the IRC will maintain its focus on three response priorities determined through health system assessments, monitoring, and community feedback. The IRC will deliver comprehensive primary healthcare services and provide support to secondary-level health facilities through direct implementation and partnerships. In 2024, these health services will benefit 299,794 vulnerable individuals affected by conflict in Raqqa, Al-Hasakeh, and Deir ez-Zor governorates through 20 healthcare interventions, including 7 static primary healthcare clinics and the pediatric unit, 10 mobile medical units, 2 Basic Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care (BEmONC) facility, and 1 field hospital. Primary healthcare delivery, including malnutrition screening and treatment referrals, will integrate primary, reproductive, MHPSS, and community health across service delivery points to ensure comprehensive curative and preventive services. The IRC will contribute to disease surveillance through systematic data collection, analysis, and reporting of health data, utilizing the Early Warning and Alert Reporting System (EWARS). BEmONC services will be supported 24/7, and CCSAS services for GBV survivors will be linked with existing protection programs. Life-saving pharmaceuticals, PPE, and medical supplies will be provided to all supported facilitie
Given the high risk of GBV in the Syrian context, IRC and its partners staff facilitate safe referrals for GBV through inter-agency referral pathways. Additionally, efforts are made to enhance coordination on protection responses and capacity building within the Protection Cluster and sub-clusters. Ensuring gender sensitivity and privacy in service delivery is paramount. Health facilities are equipped with private rooms to ensure confidentiality during examinations and counseling, and a secure data recording system is in place. Orientation sessions on GBV are conducted for staff, and specialized training on the Clinical Management of Rape is provided to selected personnel. A comprehensive strategy is implemented to mitigate the risk of sexual exploitation and abuse. Information, Education, and Communication (IEC) materials are provided to beneficiaries, outlining reporting channels for incidents of PSEA. Referral mechanisms and disease surveillance systems are in place, along with protection measures to address risks like service disruption, stigmatization, and access barriers.

project_name: Multi-Sectoral Humanitarian Response Through the Provision of MPCA to Conflict-Affected Communities in Northeast Syria, Enhancing Economic Wellbeing, Addressing Urgent Needs, Mitigating Protection Risks, and Reducing Negative Coping Strategies
project_objective:
In 2024, 16.7 million people in Syria are expected to require assistance, the largest number since 2011. Approximately 7.2 million Syrians remain displaced, many residing in overcrowded camps. The presence of unexploded ordnance poses significant risks to livelihoods and mobility, hindering long-term solutions for those in need. Additionally, the loss of civil documentation and property documents further compounds the challenges faced by hundreds of thousands of IDPs, exacerbating physical and psychological hardships and increasing the risk of statelessness. October’s JMMI factsheet noted a 4% increase in the SYP-USD exchange rate, leading to price spikes, especially for water, bread, eggs, and vegetables. Despite economic challenges, support for livelihoods and SMEs is limited, with insufficient mechanisms for loans or credit. Syrians are getting poorer as the economy continues its freefall. Since Feb 2023, the Syrian pound (SYP) has lost about half of its value against the US dollar, averaging, in Nov 2023, around SYP14,200/US$1 in the parallel foreign exchange market. From February to Sept 2023, inflation, as proxied by the WFP minimum food basket price index, rose by 88 per cent, driven by reduced access to goods, disrupted supply chains, and heightened logistics costs, all of which exerted significant upward pressure on prices.
The MPCT program includes 3 rounds to 3,488 HHs and 6 rounds to 1,048 HHs of cash distributions with a transfer value of $120 according to the CWG guidance, prioritizing vulnerable groups like PWDs, blast wound survivors, and GBV survivors. Beneficiaries receive financial literacy training, covering needs vs. wants, living costs, and start-up business skills. Cash distribution facilitated through Hawalas, chosen for environmental friendliness. In 2024, IRC will support 4,536 beneficiaries (3 rounds to 20,377 individuals and 6 rounds to 6,151 individuals), totaling 26,528 and including 18,835 IDPs and 3,183 PWDs. IRC employs WGQs to identify PWD. Barriers faced by PWDs and individuals with serious health issues are addressed through adaptive and inclusive measures. This includes incorporating ramps at IRC distribution sites and implementing door-to-door distributions as necessary. Criteria cover income, housing, family size, disabilities, and food security, with referrals from IRC’s Protection and Health Departments. IRC prevents duplication by coordinating with all partners and similar service providers in NES. This involves sharing monthly 4Ws with CWG, detailing planned locations and the number of targeted households. Furthermore, IRC utilizes a unique beneficiary identification platform to minimize any potential duplication.
IRC ensures marginalized groups review selection criteria, conducts FGDs, and engages authorities for clarity. Pre-project security assessments address conflict risks. Protection Risk Analysis identifies tension, mitigated through robust selection criteria and ongoing community engagement. Medium likelihood risks are addressed through collaborative plans, project plan amendments, and awareness of complaint mechanisms among clients. IRC's cash team, with IP team support, promotes "Do No Harm" principles and PSEA. Awareness is raised among stakeholders, and clients are informed about entitlements and support procedures. Stakeholders and staff are sensitized to uphold humanitarian principles. Confidential reporting mechanisms are available, and program activities are integrated with the protection sector to aid survivors and ensure referral pathways during beneficiary selection, data sharing, and follow-up. Community tension poses risks for project staff, mitigated through area-based coordination, robust selection criteria, harmonized targeting, engagement with leaders, adherence to standards, accountability, and staff PSEA training. Medium likelihood and high-impact risks are addressed through collaborative plans, coordination, and beneficiary awareness of complaint mechanisms

project_name: Asistencia humanitaria Agua,Saneamiento e Higiene para población vulnerable a los efectos adversos del cambio climático.
project_objective:
Hacia Mayo 2021 y tras el paso de ETA / IOTA, de 3426 comunidades reportando daños en sistemas de agua potable y saneamiento (APS) al Clúster de WASH bajo la coordinación de UNICEF, solo 1459 habían recibido asistencia humanitaria; y de 535 sistemas registrados con daños según el gobierno, con un costo de $14millones, solo 8 habían sido priorizados para financiamiento por $4millones. La fase de primera respuesta continúa siendo una necesidad para comunidades que requieren obras APS de infraestructura mayor. Las reparaciones realizadas a sistemas APS por las comunidades y municipalidades, son en su mayoría temporales, no aplican criterios de resiliencia climática, y no garantizan los criterios mínimos para calidad del agua. Solo un 8% de los centros educativos reportados fueron atendidos con mejoras de Agua, Saneamiento e Higiene (ASH).
El proyecto se enfocará en proporcionar asistencia humanitaria ASH con enfoque en la niñez para comunidades afectadas cuyos sistemas APS continúan colapsados, según brechas de atención identificadas a través del Clúster de ASH, y en fortalecer la resiliencia climática de los sistemas que han sido temporalmente restaurados, así como el acceso seguro a servicios de ASH en centros educativos, integrando un enfoque de género a través del manejo de higiene menstrual, en coordinación con actores relevantes.
El proyecto se alinea con los objetivos del Cluster a través del acceso sostenible a servicios de ASH, integrando enfoques de género y edad para la población más vulnerable en situación de primera respuesta ante sistemas colapsados de APS, y en situación de acceso precario ante sistemas APS sin criterios de resiliencia climática.
La población afectada consiste en familias vulnerables ubicadas en albergues y/o comunidades afectadas por las inundaciones y deslaves en zonas geográficas de la zona norte, occidente, sur y el litoral atlántico, a ser identificadas específicamente a través de declaratorias nacionales de emergencia y/o solicitudes especificas de apoyo a través de la Red Humanitaria/ Solicitudes especificas de CODELs
y CODEMs, y con base en los Informes vigentes de Situación de COPECO, a ser documentadas a través de Evaluaciones rápidas de Necesidades (EDANs). Las actividades de respuesta humanitaria ASH se implementarán según los Compromisos Básicos para la niñez en emergencias, estándares del clúster de WAASH y normas esfera, con el propósito de mejorar el acceso al agua potable para el consumo humano, el saneamiento y la higiene, así como el control de vectores y la gestión de residuos sólidos. También se trabajará en soluciones sostenibles que contribuyan a las respuestas intersectoriales y en campañas que promuevan prácticas seguras de WASH. (HRP2021-2022, WASH).

project_name: Proteger y fortalecer con acciones anticipatorias ante la sequía, la seguridad alimentaria y los medios de subsistencia de los hogares de pequeños agricultores en el corredor seco hondureño
project_objective:
Según  HNO se proyecta al menos 2.4 millones de personas en necesidades humanitarias, que viven en 162 (54 por ciento) de los 298 municipios, muchos de ellos ubicados en zonas rurales del corredor seco hondureño dispersas de difícil acceso. La secretaria de estado en el Despacho de Gestión de Riesgos y Contingencias Nacionales de Honduras declaro alerta roja en 160 de los 298 municipios por la sequía que causara el fenómeno del Niño. Es por esto que FAO abogando por la producción local de alimentos que respondan a las necesidades de las poblaciones afectadas a enfrentar la sequía y mitigar sus efectos en sus sistemas de producción agrícolas y pecuarios ha diseñado la presente propuesta que constará de las siguientes intervenciones:

1. 22,500 hogares donde el 30% favorezca a mujeres jefas de hogar, reciben insumos agrícolas para proteger y reactivar la producción y el establecimiento de huertos familiares y siembra de granos básicos resistentes a sequía. 

2. 7,400 hogares con enfoque de interculturalidad e interseccionalidad   instalan sistemas de riego, filtros de agua gris y estructuras para almacenamiento de agua. 

3. 4,500 hogares bajo el enfoque de interculturalidad e interseccionalidad  con acceso a insumos pecuarios para la elaboración y almacenamiento de forraje. 

4. 2 campañas de vacunación donde mujeres participan y se potencien su conocimientos y capacidades para la protección de animales domésticos.

5. 22,5000 hogares reciben entrenamiento en agricultura sostenible y protección de la sanidad animal, con un enfoque de Acciones Anticipatorias (AA) ante sequía, interculturalidad e interseccionalidad.

6. 80 estructuras comunitarias, reservas de granos/bancos de granos son fortalecidas con el abastecimiento de granos básicos en época de escases de alimentos.
 
7. 80 ECA’s agrícolas y pecuarias que incluyan un enfoque de género son fortalecidas en el territorio influencia del proyecto

project_name: Mainstreaming disability inclusion in the shelter, settlements, camp coordination and camp management programme cycle.
project_objective:
This project solely targets people with disabilities, including individuals with physical, visual, hearing, and psychosocial impairments. Individuals with disabilities will receive assistive devices, home, and shelter modifications, and benefit from accessible service centers in the community.

CBM and CDD’s current project takes place in the same geographical locations as the proposed project locations: camps 8W, 8E, 11, 13, 18, and 19 and Rajapalong, Ratanapalong, and Holdiapalong Unions in the host community. No other agencies provide the same/similar services in the proposed project locations.

Capacity building of Site Management and Site Development:  CBMG and CDD provided technical support to IOM and its implementing partners CARE and DRC on capacity building on inclusive Camp Coordination and Camp Management. The capacity-building support will extend in the proposed six camps. 

Home and community accessibility modifications:  The project will provide assistive devices and home/shelter modifications for 1,000 people with disabilities and will promote service center accessibility in the community. Providing this support will improve health for people living in already difficult conditions, in makeshift shelters, on rough terrain, and with limited healthcare services. Without these services, people with disabilities are unable to participate in their community and are a burden on family members who have become carers. These services will improve their functional abilities and allow for greater independence.     

Accessibility at the public and communal Facilities: To create access to different services for people with different types of disabilities, the project aims to conduct accessibility audits and install accessibility features (e.g., ramps with handrails, accessible WASH facility modifications) in three public offices, two health centers, six primary and secondary schools in the host community, and 12 communal facilities in the Rohingya Camps. 

Assistive Devices: A rehabilitation team will assess the clients to determine the types of assistive devices required. The project then will procure height-adjustable devices (e.g., crutches, walkers, toilet chairs) available in the local market and produce customized assistive devices (e.g., wheelchair, special seat chair, tricycle, prosthetic limbs) at CDD’s workshop and distribute to the clients. The materials of the assistive devices will consider the durability, cultural context, availability in the community, and appropriateness for the terrain. 

Ultimately, this project will facilitate clients' ability to move, see, and communicate, help reduce the risk of secondary complications, and provide require support to clients for overcome environmental barriers in certain situations to better engage in community life. Through the proposed interventions, people with disabilities in the camps and host community will have greater access to humanitarian and social protection services, improved quality of life, better functional independence in their daily regular and productive activities, and increased participation in the community.

Documentation: The project will develop some knowledge management documentation along with a video documentation of the accessibility modifications that will be produced to showcase the work and to be used in training and advocacy to present examples of good practice to other actors, who will improve facilities and services for more people with disabilities across the camps.

The project will be managed within CBMG and CDD’s current Inclusive Rohingya Response Program providing interventions in five camps and three Union Parishad in the host community. CDD’s office in Ukhia will monitor operations.

project_name: Improve access to inclusive, gender-responsive, safe, and child-friendly quality learning interventions for Rohingya refugee and host community children and adolescents in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh.
