project_name: Provision of standard Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) services for the most vulnerable populations in Ukhiya and Teknaf Upazila of Cox’s Bazar District, Bangladesh.
project_objective:
The project will implement activities as per the following description to achieve the targeted objectives for all women, men, girls, and boys (including all age groups and persons with disabilities) in the targeted Rohingya refugee camps and host communities. Access to WASH services will be achieved through the three sub-sectors of intervention that are presented below:
Improved water services: IOM will continue the Operation & Maintenance (O&M) and upgrade the existing deep tube wells and water networks in camps 09, 10, 11, 12, 18, 20, and 20 extensions.
In the targeted area, non-repairable deep tube wells will be decommissioned, and new deep tube wells will be installed where necessary to ensure improved access to the most vulnerable people in need and meet humanitarian standards.
5 small-scale solar-powered piped water networks will be newly installed in camp 9, 13, and 20Extn. to provide safe water to the targeted beneficiaries. Moreover, the existing solarized water supply systems in camps 09, 12, and 13 will be upgraded or rehabilitated where necessary.
Access to Sanitation: To ensure dignified and safe access to the latrine facilities, IOM will continue to upgrade the existing poorly functional latrine and bathing facilities with gender-inclusive and disability-related features in consultation with the community. IOM will provide assistive devices (i.e., commode chairs, commode chairs with potty, urinal bottles for males and females, etc.) to people with disabilities or physical impairments to ensure their specific needs are met based on the assessment. Moreover, IOM action will continue the construction of durable household latrines to cover the sanitation gaps at the targeted host community villages in Ukhiya.
Decentralized Wastewater Treatment Systems (DEWATS) will be built, and lime-based faecal sludge treatment plants will be upgraded to the DEWATS system to meet the coverage gaps. In addition, IOM will continue to build 14 Intermediate Sludge Transfer Systems (ISTS) connecting with the FSM units to ensure cost-effective sludge transfer mechanisms in targeted areas. In addition, IOM will collaborate with UNHCR and DPHE to link the existing faecal sludge treatment approach to the mega FSTP built by UNHCR and DPHE for easy operation to address recommendations of WASH Sector FSM Strategy and mega rationalization.  
To ensure appropriate waste segregation at the source and engage the community effectively in the chain of solid waste management (SWM), IOM will ensure garbage bins (red and green) in each household. Existing material recovery facilities (MRF) operation and maintenance will be ensured, and a new MRF will be installed. The complete chain of the SWM monitoring system will be continued and strengthened at all levels.
Hygiene Promotion and Community Engagement: Critical supplies of hygiene items (soap, water containers, Menstrual Hygiene Management (MHM) materials, etc.) will be provided through community mobilization activities targeting all age groups, genders, and persons with special WASH needs. IOM will continue the utilization of the SCOPE distribution system in all camps to ensure duplication is avoided and a systematic distribution is ensured for people in need. Sector-standard MHM kits will be distributed to the reproductive age group (10–55 years) based on the field assessment and needs across all the IOM-managed camps every six months. The community will be further engaged in O&M of WASH facilities, waste segregation, prevention of mass transmission, and waterborne diseases like Acute Water Diseases (AWD), scabies, COVID-19, etc.
Notably, IOM will procure, replenish, and replace the emergency stocks for cyclones, fires, floods, or other emergency responses, and real-time service monitoring with community feedback mechanisms will be continued and strengthened throughout the project period.

project_name: IMPROVING SKILLS AND ECONOMIC OPPORTUNITIES FOR THE BANGLADESHI COMMUNITY AND ROHINGYA WOMEN & YOUTHS IN COX'S BAZAR
project_objective:
IOM will undertake a wide variety of activities to create an enabling environment for the Rohingya refugees towards eventual sustainable voluntary return and reintegration in Myanmar in the future when conditions permit. Such activities will help Rohingya beneficiaries increase self-reliance skills. The livelihoods activities will also focus on the host communities affected by the influx by integrating income-generating livelihoods through support outside the agricultural sector Off-farm activities.
IOM will implement skills development projects to promote the economic resilience of Rohingya refugees in IOM AOR camps. This technical (1,500 individuals)/ vocational (600 individuals) training on Community Health Worker, Plumbing, Small Engine Mechanic, jute-bag products, shoe making, etc will enhance their capacity and help them utilize their skills in the camps in Bangladesh as self-reliance opportunities and can be used as transferrable skills by them upon return to Myanmar. Rohingya beneficiaries will receive skills training related outside the agricultural sector Off-farm activities that are applicable to the humanitarian sector (e.g. health, wash, site development-construction, etc.) in the camps. IOM will facilitate in-kind asset support materials to Rohingya beneficiaries working outside the agricultural sector “Off farm activities” who are willing to gain basic skills or competencies but lack the physical assets to do so. 200 beneficiaries receiving  formal vocational training will be referred to the relevant sectors for volunteer engagement. Besides livelihood opportunities will be created for 1,000 beneficiaries.
IOM will provide host communities with transferable and life skills training (e.g. communication, negotiation, psychosocial) and vocational skills training including skills related to green businesses and green financing such as plumbing, catering to disaster resilient outside the agricultural sector, Off-farming tools and methods, waste recycling, electronic refurbishment, related to resilient investments and planning, etc. The trades will be identified by skills and needs assessment. The productive asset support will be given to beneficiaries who have technical skills but lack inputs/opportunities/assets and are willing to earn a modest income. IOM will provide small business grants through the Self-help groups (SHG) to help beneficiaries expand and strengthen their businesses for outside the agricultural sector “Off Farm activities”.
To enhance the private sector engagement and promote market linkages, wage subsidy opportunities for beneficiaries will be implemented and to ensure sustainable income generation, IOM will organise activities like product fairs in the host community to sell and promote their products to individuals and wholesalers.
The selection criteria of beneficiaries will be based on eligibility criteria such as female-headed households, income below the poverty line, widow, etc. IOM will also focus on disability throughout the selection criteria and assist livelihoods and self-reliance opportunities. One of the major challenges for vocational training is the literacy and numeracy level of the communities. IOM will address the challenge by incorporating Accelerated adult learning (3,500 individuals) into the program to improve the literacy and numeracy level of the beneficiaries. Women empowerment, leadership, and decision-making will be promoted by incorporating income opportunities and entrepreneurship opportunities, business development training, financial literacy, etc., for women in the host community and self-reliance opportunities for women in the camps to ensure sustainable development and integration into the society. The budget for vocational training has been calculated as the standard cost per beneficiary shared by the sector. All activity costs include non-operational costs and are presented as a total of operational and non-operational costs.

project_objective:
Avec un budget total d’environ $3,080,000.00  , SCI compte appuyer les populations touchées par l’insécurité alimentaire et permettre le renforcement des moyens d’existences en faveur de 230,313 bénéficiaires dont 60% enfants dans les régions de la Boucle du Mouhoun, du Sahel ,du Nord et du Centre Nord. project_name: Contribuer à la réduction de la mortalité liée à la malnutrition par la prévention et le traitement de la malnutrition aiguë et le renforcement des capacités gouvernementales afin d'améliorer l'accès et la qualité des services de nutrition.
project_objective:
Selon l'enquête rapide SMART menée dans 19 communes, la situation est alarmante dans 16 localités où la malnutrition aiguë globale (MAG) est supérieure à 10%. De plus, la prévalence est élevée ou très élevée dans de nombreuses localités. Parmi les 11 localités où la prévalence de la MAG est comprise entre 10% et 15%, la situation est considérée comme élevée à Bani (10,4%), Djibo (10,2%), Ouahigouya (10,5%), Pissila (11,2%), Kaya (13%), Dori (13,4%), Gorgadji (13,6%), Séguénéga (13,9%), Bourzanga (14,5%), et Gorom-Gorom (14%). La prévalence de la malnutrition est encore plus sévère dans cinq localités où elle a dépassé le seuil de 15%, à savoir Tougouri (22,6%), Matiacoali (17,3%), Dédougou (16,3%), Gayéri (15,4%), et Nouna (15,4%). Ces résultats indiquent la nécessité d'interventions urgentes pour éviter une détérioration de la situation et améliorer l'état nutritionnel des populations affectées.
La situation nutritionnelle des enfants de moins de cinq ans est très préoccupante, et il en va de même pour la FEFA. Selon la mesure PB, la malnutrition est un problème important dans certaines zones, avec une prévalence modérée de MAG à Gorgadji (6,5%), Dori (8,9%), Gayéri (6%), Gorom-Gorom (9,5%), Kompienga (9,9%), Matiacoali (7%), Ouahigouya (5,6%), et Séguénéga (6%). La malnutrition sévère est particulièrement répandue parmi les FEFA à Bourzanga (1%), Gayéri (1,8%), Kompienga (2,1%), et Pama (1,2%).  Selon une évaluation récente menée par le Conseil danois pour les réfugiés (DRC), après le déplacement de Seytenga, 40 % des ménages de la commune de Dori étaient hébergés dans des familles d'accueil, 34 % étaient en location et 33 % n'avaient pas d'abri ou un abri précaire. En outre, la guerre en Ukraine a eu un impact significatif sur les prix des produits de traitement nutritionnel. Le coût des aliments thérapeutiques prêts à l'emploi, essentiels pour traiter la malnutrition aiguë sévère, a augmenté de 20 %. De même, les prix des CSB+ et CSB++, utilisés pour traiter la malnutrition aiguë modérée, ont augmenté respectivement de 290 % et 159 %.
SCI vise à atteindre les résultats suivants dans le cadre de son plan d'intervention pour 2024 pour 100 000 personnes :
•	Les femmes enceintes et allaitantes améliorent leurs pratiques d'alimentation des nourrissons et des jeunes enfants. 
•	Les enfants malnutris de moins de 5 ans reçoivent un traitement contre la malnutrition aiguë avec le soutien du SCI et de ses partenaires.
•	Les agents de santé communautaires et les prestataires de soins de santé sont formés, avec le soutien de SCI ou de ses partenaires, à des approches fondées sur des données probantes (par exemple, la gestion intégrée des cas au niveau communautaire, la gestion de la malnutrition au niveau communautaire, l'alimentation des nourrissons et des jeunes enfants, etc.

project_name: Renforcer la réponse rapide et intégrée en matière de protection et de santé mentale et de soutien psychosocial aux besoins des populations touchées par la crise sécuritaire, en particulier les enfants dans les zones d'urgence.
project_objective:
La protection et le soutien psychosocial sont de la plus haute importance pour les communautés touchées par l'insécurité dans tout le pays, en particulier dans les six régions d'urgence où les attaques violentes et les engins explosifs improvisés contre les civils sont en augmentation. Avec des écoles fermées et une crise alimentaire croissante, les garçons et les filles sont confrontés à un risque accru de recrutement dans des groupes armés, d'exploitation, d'abus, de violence sexuelle, de viol et de mariage d'enfants. Cette situation d'urgence a exacerbé les inégalités et les vulnérabilités existantes, en particulier pour les filles et les femmes. En substance, la crise a profondément aggravé la situation des enfants, les exposant plus que jamais aux six graves violations commises à l'encontre des enfants dans les conflits.
Save the Children Burkina Faso fournira une assistance à 90 000 personnes affectées par le biais des activités suivantes :
1. Les enfants vulnérables sont protégés contre toutes les formes de violence et leur bien-être psychosocial est amélioré.
2. Amélioration des systèmes et services de protection au niveau communal et provincial
3. Les garçons et les filles vulnérables touchés par les conflits et l'insécurité améliorent leur sécurité et leur bien-être grâce à un accès meilleur, plus équitable et inclusif à des services de protection de l'enfance complets et sensibles aux conflits.

project_name: Projet de veille, coordination et réponse multisectorielle de premier recours pour soutenir les personnes en situation de vulnérabilité aigüe à l’Extrême Nord du Cameroun (Mayo Sava, Mayo Tsanaga, Mayo Kani, Mayo Danay) affectées par les chocs liés aux conflits armés et aux aléas climatiques, tout en préservant leur sûreté et leur dignité  (RRM)
project_objective:
L’action vise à répondre aux besoins vitaux des populations déplacées, en situation de vulnérabilité aiguë suite aux conflits armés et aux catastrophes naturelles à travers le déploiement d’une réponse multisectorielle rapide, en complémentarité avec le mécanisme national de Réponse Rapide aux Mouvements (RRM) dont Action Contre la Faim est un acteur. Les alertes reçues par les points focaux sont triangulées. Améliorer le mécanisme de veille, alerte et réponse rapide en AME/ Abris, Eau Hygiène et Assainissement, et Sécurité alimentaire, ainsi que la coordination et le plaidoyer au profit des personnes nouvellement déplacées ou nouvellement accessibles dans les départements de Mayo Tsanaga, Mayo Kani, Mayo Sava, Mayo Danay, Extrême Nord du Cameroun.

project_name: Integrated Response for the Conflict and natural disaster Affected Population of South Kordofan and North Darfur States, Sudan
project_objective:
The conflict between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has caused tremendous displacement and exacerbated pre-existing humanitarian needs across Sudan. As of end 2023, over 7 million Sudanese families are displaced. In response to identified needs within the Sudan HRP 2024,  GOAL proposes to undertake an integrated multi-sector project targeting 337642individuals, including:66178 men, 68879 women,  99267 boys and 103318 girls in North Darfur and South Kor
from Abu Jubayhah, Ar Rashad, Gadeer, Habila & Talawdi localities in South Kordofan State:

The overall goal of the program is to provide timely multi-sectoral life-saving assistance to crisis affected people to reduce mortality & morbidity by providing life-sustaining basic services while mitigating protection risks and responding to protection needs. This program will; provide safe, equitable and dignified access to critical Health (with strong emphasis and integration of reproductive health (RH) services), Nutrition, food security and WASH as well as GBV to people in need of humanitarian assistance in the targeted areas. GOAL has  an operational presence, expertise, and experience across the 13 localities in SK and ND targeted and will leverage these in addition to their existing programing to complement and maximize overall program impact. GOAL  will provide integrated health and nutrition services with outpatient therapeutic program (OTP) services including the Nutrition Impact and Positive Practice (NIPP) intervention which will directly address the multi-sectoral causes of malnutrition, such as inadequate diet diversity, poor WASH behaviors, and unsafe food preparation and conservation methods from 54 health facilities and 4 stabilization centers. 
. This will involve an assessment in all target localities, establishing and maintaining community-based protection networks, and strengthening case identification, referral, and management.
GOAL will continue to support the provision of comprenhensive health & nutrition services in 27 Primary health facilities across South Kordofan (Habila, Abukarshola, Rashad, Dilling, Abujebeha, Gadeer and Talodi localities including support for Stabilization Center in Talodi, Rashad and Habila) and 27 clinics in North Darfur (Kutum, Al Waha, Umbaru, Seref Omra, Kekabiya and El Sireaf localities including support for Stabilization Center in Kutum Hospital), The targeted areas have high numbers of confict-affected households (including newly displaced persons, long-term IDPs, vulnerable host communities, and some returnees) GOAL will conitnue support to rural and hard-to-reach facilities in these Localities.
Services include Reproductive Health, EPI, early warning and outbreak response, support and training for health staff, clinic running costs, provision of drugs, medical supplies and equipment, and support for the Locality Health Department, including the Health Information System, supportive supervision and training and deployment of Rapid Response Teams. GOAL also provides community health through Care Groups, community health promotion, defaulter tracing for RH and OTP services, and the Nutrition Impact and Positive Practice (NIPP) approach to prevent and treat Moderate Acute malnutrition. GOAL will ensure comprehensive care in supported facilities, and GOAL will continue to
closely coordinate through the Ministry of Health and Health and Nutrition Sectors in El Fashir and Kadugli and will also engage in ongoing coordination with other partners in each locality to ensure no overlap. GOAL provides a package of lifesaving primary healthcare services in all supported facilities. PHC services include curative consultation, provision and dispensing of essential drugs, managing injuries, EPI to increase the immunization rates in children and pregnant mothers, nutrition screening for children under 5, OTP for management of SAM children

project_name: Apoyo a niñas, niños, adolescentes y mujeres, especialmente a aquellos en condiciones de mayor vulnerabilidad, para incrementar su acceso a servicios de salud de calidad, más pertinentes, oportunos, incluyentes y eficaces, incluso en contextos de emergencia en 54 municipios.
project_objective:
UNICEF will contribute to the inter-agency humanitarian response in 2024 and will also complement UNICEF's development work under its 2023-2026 country programme.

Objective: UNICEF is committed to continuing to focus on critical unmet needs and remaining inequalities related to maternal, neonatal and under-five child survival.

Project Description: The project focuses on improving access and quality of basic services to address the multiple health deprivations faced by children, adolescents and pregnant women. UNICEF's response incorporates a child-centred approach and is built around community settings, including health centers and surrounding communities. Priority will be given to supporting health systems that reliably provide integrated service packages for children, adolescents and women, focusing on health, nutrition and WASH, also facilitating child protection services and linked to social protection and social well-being initiatives, as well as as well as the educational sector. , particularly for health promotion and prevention, improving health literacy, screening and promoting early childhood development and the mental health and well-being of children and their caregivers.

Strategies and implementation: UNICEF will promote three approaches to achieve the goals:
1. Address inequalities in health outcomes;
2. Strengthen health systems, including emergency preparedness, response and resilience; and
3. Promotion of integrated and multisectoral policies and programs.

The strategy also includes:
Strengthen service delivery, empower communities for health promotion, prevention and social behavior change, build capacity of health service providers, strengthen supply chain systems (essential products and equipment ), generate demand and strengthen accountability.

Monitoring and evaluation: To ensure the effectiveness of the project, UNICEF will implement a robust monitoring and evaluation system. This will involve periodic monitoring of health interventions, evaluations of health professionals after training and monitoring of the distribution and use of supplies, as well as evaluation of the quality of case management based on compliance with standardized protocols and regulations.

These actions will be implemented in selected urban, peri-urban and remote rural areas of 10 nationally prioritized states, with the exception of HIV interventions and immunization coverage is national, and will reach 750,303 people, including 559,291 children and 125,000 pregnant women .

project_name: Provision of seasonal cash assistance during the winter season for the most vulnerable HHs in NW Syria
project_objective:
Syria continues to be one of the most complex protracted conflict humanitarian crises globally, exposed to high levels of ongoing conflict, and prone to natural disasters and epidemic outbreaks. These factors have forced an increase of 1.4M of people in need (PIN) since 2023, totaling 16.7M (HNO, 2024) people in need in Syria. Given the myriad needs and vulnerabilities, Concern proposed this action across Northwest Syria (NWS). Concern has proposed intervention areas in line with the severity of the needs identified by Humanitarian Needs Overview where there continues to be lack of, or challenges for NGOs to provide assistance in Afrin and Azaz Districts. Concern will work with local partners to comprehensively address gaps in the response, ensuring the inclusion of diverse beneficiaries, including girls, children with disabilities, and marginalized communities.
The intervention will involve implementing cash for winterization for the crises affected population in NW Syria. the cash will be distributed during the last two months of the year prior to the coldest winter months and locations be selected in coordination with the SNFI Cluster.
Cash Value: Concern will comply with the SNFI Cluster recommendations currently fixed at $150 and the transfer currency will be primarily USD to preserve the value of the assistance and protect the purchasing power of recipient HHs, as long as 100 USD / 50 USD bills remain available. An alternative would be TRY if local/current context justifies; and provided decision is consulted with the SNFI Cluster, Donor, and other NGOs in the same area.
Distribution point selection: All distribution sites will be agreed upon with the local authorities for security and coordination purposes. The selected distribution point should be meeting the minimum requirement of safety and security including:
•	Safe for both staff and Beneficiaries, with a minimum of one entrance and one exit
•	Located in a central location from all beneficiaries’ residence
•	Accessible for all beneficiaries including PWDs, and should have enough space for two separate lines
•	Shaded from weather conditions, equipped with a water resource for drink, and separate latrines for males and females
Beneficiary Selection Criteria: the below criteria serve as a guideline to identify and prioritize households in need of assistance during the winter period:
1.	Disability.
2.	Chronic Diseases.
3.	Pregnant/Lactating Women.
4.	Children Attending School.
5.	No access to Non-Food Items (NFI) in the last 6 months.
6.	Living in a temporary settlement.
7.	Household with no source of income.
8.	Household headed by a person with a disability.
9.	Household hosting orphaned, unaccompanied children or homeless relatives due to the conflict.
10.	No access to fuel or other heating resources in the last 1 to 3 months.
11.	Households affected by recent floods/last winter floods.
Beneficiary Invitation: each of the selected beneficiaries will receive a coupon from the local council agent specifying the date, time and location of the distribution. 
Voucher Distribution: The beneficiaries will collect their vouchers from the distribution table in the distribution point after verifying the beneficiary ID against the approved beneficiary list. The program staff responsible for voucher distribution will stamp the voucher “verified” once the verification is completed and collect beneficiary’s signature on the Voucher Distribution Form, then guide the beneficiary to the redemption table.

project_name: Actions Educatives Urgentes pour les Enfants Affectés par les Crises humanitaires au Niger
project_objective:
Le Projet « Actions Éducatives Urgentes  pour les Enfants affectés par les crises humanitaires au Niger »  dans les régions de Diffa et Tillaberi se veut une contribution au cadre des résultats du Cluster Éducation HRP 2024 en réponse aux défis auxquels les enfants du Niger sont confrontés en termes d’accès et de continuité éducative du fait  des effets conjugués de l'instabilité et la dégradation de la situation sécuritaire, des  défis climatiques  et  des sanctions et restrictions de la CEDEAO et de l'UEMOA prises à la   suite du changement de régime politique  depuis le 26 Juillet 2023 .
Le projet vise à assurer l’accès à une éducation de qualité, continue et pertinente dans des environnements sûrs et protecteurs pour 70532    enfants dont 34416  filles  de 7 à 17 ans déplacées et ceux des communautés hôtes, y compris les enfants en situation de handicap affectés par les conflits dans les  régions de  Diffa , département de Bosso , Diffa ,Maine Soroa et Tillaberi, Département de  Ayerou, Filingue , Gothèye ,Tera ,Tillaberi et Torodi
Pour ce faire, les interventions du projet se focaliseront autour des trois résultats ci-dessous
1. Améliorer l’accès à des offres éducatives inclusives, diversifiées  et de qualité pour les enfants déplacés et  ceux des communautés hôtes  d âgés de 7 à 17 ans touchés par les crises humanitaires. Il s’agira de travailler à la sensibilisation communautaire sur l’importance de l’éducation des enfants, l’ identification et le placement des enfants déplacés filles et  garçons   et ceux  des communautés hôtes  dans les offres éducatives formelles et non formelles dont les infrastructures réhabilitées sont adaptées aux personnes vivant avec handicap et au genre , le renforcement des capacités des enseignants sur des thématiques de la pédagogie et le suivi pédagogique par les Inspecteurs pédagogiques .Il est envisagé la dotation de kits scolaires aux élèves et des kits pédagogiques pour les enseignants et animateurs des centres SSA/P. project_name: Multi Sectoral assistance for IDPs and conflict affected households in Sudan
project_objective:
Clashes between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
that erupted on 15 April 2023 are having devastating consequences for people across
Sudan. Life-saving responses related to WASH, Food Security, nutrition and agriculture
are urgently needed for conflict affected populations. Mercy Corps response plans aims
to provide humanitarian assistance to new IDPs and CAPs people..
Goal:
“To provide humanitarian assistance to conflict affected people in Sudan to meet
immediate needs for survival and work towards recovery”:
Objectives:
1. Save and protect lives
2. Improve capacity to withstand further shocks (e.g. flooding)
3. Prevent backsliding for vulnerable communities indirectly affected by the conflict

Mercy Corps will distribute seeds through a restricted value voucher system to conflict
households. Project participants will then be able to redeem their value voucher for their
choice of seeds at selected certified seed suppliers. Mercy Corps will provide basic and
refresher trainings on the CMAM guidelines and the Essential Nutrition Package to the
existing MoH staff and community volunteers. The training sessions will focus on the
four main components of CMAM, including community outreach, OTP, targeted
supplementary feeding program (TSFP), and inpatient care by the MoH. To ensure a
continuous high standard of care, Mercy Corps will provide biannual refresher training
sessions for the nutrition center staff. Mercy Corps will also conduct SAM treatment for
children 6-59m (without complication) in OTPs (first 6 months) as well as SAM treatment
for children 6-59m (without complication) in OTPs (Second 6 months).Through the
nutrition interventions about about 76% of the nutrition sector’s lifesaving response
activities will contribute to nutrition resilience. IYCF (MYCN), OTP and TSFP activities will also be included in the nutrition response along with AAP and GBV in nutrition context. The nutrition programming will also be integrated with WASH, monitoring and reporting, Mercy Corps will also support capacity building for nutrition staff. 
Mercy Corps through implementing partners will provide GBV, Child protection training and as cross cutting activities across all other thematic areas. As part of the GBV strategy, Mercy Corps will promote
prevention of gender-based violence and will provide support to survivors and their
families as well as promoting responsive legal and justice systems. Mercy Corps will
ensure that children protection and GBV is an integral part of the programs in order to
ensure that women and girls are protected and given the opportunity to participate in the
project implementation. In the target locations, water collection is typically the
responsibility of women and girls. Limited access to water sources forces women and
girls to walk long distances in search of water, often exposing them to additional
protection risks. This intervention will help to reduce these risks through rehabilitating
infrastructure which will increase the availability of water and reduce the distance women
and girls are forced to walk to collect water. In addition, Mercy Corps will ensure that
women and girls are represented in the community-level WASH committees – minimum
50 percent of WASH committee members are women. Mercy Corps also plans to
encourage the involvement of women and girls in all elements of the community-based
operation and maintenance of the water sources. In terms of child protection Mercy
Corps will conduct awareness campaigns on children’s rights and protection concerns,
plus establishing community-based child protection committees trained on child
protection standards and referral mechanisms. Mercy Corps will address WASH needs
through rehabilitation of water sources for both community and institutions, and
formation and training of WASH committees to ensure improved access to clean and
safe water is sustained.

project_name: Provide Life-saving Food and Nutrition Assistance to Refugees in Sudan
project_objective:
The recent and ongoing conflict in Sudan has exacerbated already high levels of food insecurity, acute malnutrition, and stunting. Over 16.2 million individuals, amounting to over a third of the Sudanese population, were already acutely food insecure prior to the conflict, according to WFP’s Comprehensive Food Security and Vulnerability Assessment. According to the most recent Integrated Phase Classification released in August 2023, the number of acutely food insecure in Sudan (IPC Phase 3 and above) has increased to 20.3 million, amounting to over 42 percent of the country’s population. Driven by a protracted conflict, insecurity, and displacement, this is the highest number of acutely food insecure in recent history in Sudan. Over 5.6 million people have been newly displaced, of which nearly 4.5 million are newly displaced and over 1.1 million have sought refuge.
Among the refugees, the food security situation remains particularly dire. 56 percent of refugee households in Sudan were food insecure during the first quarter of 2023 according to the Food Security Monitoring System (FSMS), of which 11 percent are severely food insecure. This was an increase of 11 percent compared to 2022. The levels and severity of food insecurity has likely increased further due to the ongoing conflict, decreased access, and deteriorating macroeconomic situation. The refugees in Kharasana and Elmairam in West Kordofan are the most food insecure at over 95 percent. 31 percent of refugees rely on non-agricultural wage labour while 20 percent rely on informal transfers. 62 percent of refugees adopt negative food-based coping strategies, of which 29 percent are adopting a high level of coping mechanisms. The most commonly adopted food-based coping strategies includes relying on less preferred and less expensive food, limiting portion sizes and reducing the number of meals consumed per day. In addition, 45 percent of refugee households adopt negative livelihood-based coping strategies, of which 9 percent adopted emergency-level coping strategies. The most commonly adopted livelihood-based coping strategies include reducing non-food expenses on health, withdrawing children from school, and spending savings. Finally, economic vulnerability remains high among refugees, with 60 percent unable to afford one local food basket, and 92 percent spending more than 65 percent of their expenditure on food. 
This project aims to support settlement-based refugees in Blue Nile, Central Darfur, East Darfur, Gadarif, Kassala, North Darfur, North Kordofan, South Darfur, South Kordofan, West Kordofan, and White Nile in Sudan to meet their basic food and nutrition needs through an integrated unconditional food assistance.
Amid a lack of availability of resources and access constraints, WFP Sudan is targeting with unconditional General Food Assistance (GFA) 705,260 refugees of whom 343,169 will receive life-saving nutritional support. GFA at Full ration of the in-kind food basked depending on resource availability, each recipient will receive 475g of sorghum per person per day, 60g pulses, 30g oil and 10g salt per person per day, meeting the daily minimum dietary requirements . Concerning nutritional support, both children under the age of five years and pregnant and breastfeeding women and girls will receive 100g per day of Plumpy Sup and 50 g per day of Plumpy Doz for treatment of moderate acute malnutrition and prevention of malnutrition respectively. In addition, children aged 6-59 months will receive 0.5g/day of micronutrient powders (MNPs) to prevent micronutrient deficiencies. 
This shall be complemented by thorough engagement with Sudan's Commissioner for Refugees (COR), UNHCR, cooperating partners, community and customary leadership, and targeted locations to identify and sensitize beneficiaries to the anticipated assistance, with process and output monitoring undertaken at scheduled frequencies to assess the implementation of interventions on-ground.

project_name: Support to primary health care in WoS, including EPI and other immunizations
project_objective:
According to HNO 2024, over 14.9 million of the Syrian population are estimated to be in need of life-saving primary care health assistance, including 5.33 million IDPs, 3.3 million children <5 years including 532,595 live births expected, 6.6 million women of reproductive age, 1.2 elderly people and 2.6 million persons with disabilities.  A key concern is the limited access to PHC services, mainly antenatal & child  health services, as well as care for NCDs. Less than 65% of PHCs are fully functional. In 2023, DPT3 immunization coverage increased from 65% to 71%, but 47 districts remain below the 80% threshold. In 2024, the EPI will focus on catch-up campaigns for zero-dose children, outreach in high-risk districts, and broader development initiatives supported by GAVI and BHA funding, including the BCU campaign.
In 2024, WHO SYRIA will: 
-Procure of lifesaving supplies & equipment
-Standardize guidelines developed
-Building HCW capacity 
-Conduct assessments & surveys 
-Support integrated outreach and referral services 
-Enhance & expand IMCI & newborn care at home coverage 
-Strengthen HIS
-Monitor quality and promote improvement of service delivery
-Support printing of IEC materials 
-Conduct basic restoration of priority PHCs 

In NWS, out of the 5.1M of population 3.4M are IDPs, and close to 2M people, are living in camps while an estimated 3.9M people living is subdistricts of severity 4 or 5 are in need of health care services and dependent on XB operations. The current crisis is devastating: disease outbreaks were compounded by the earthquake (Feb 2023), leading to >15K deaths & injuries, increasing the demand on an already fragmented and under-resourced health system. WHO’s Health Needs Assessment for NWS points to a critical need for medical equipment, essential medications, and infrastructure support, as well as improved HIS and coordination. 
Through a coordinated plan involving NGOs/donors, WHO will gradually reduce its direct service delivery contracts moving towards a last-resort approach, while aiming to mitigate potential consequences of reduced direct operational presence in NWS. In 2024 WHO will:
-Lead TWGs, including mapping services & conducting prioritization
-Monitor the implementation of the EHSP, including integration of vertical programs (e.g EPI)
-Coordinate with UNICEF within the SIG mechanism to achieve & maintain at least 77% vax coverage for all antigens at all national/SD level, with a drop-out rate of <10%
-Develop a capacity-building plan that includes a needs assessment, supportive supervision & mentoring
-Generate public health evidence through assessments
-Provide essential medicines & medical supplies
-Support all hazards preparedness & response 
-Advocate for/provide support to facilitate handover of last-resort support to iNGOs while addressing critical gaps
WHO utilizes the health sector PRA to ensure protection of the most vulnerable within the delivery of its services, including health care workers themselves. Additionally, both hubs have a dedicated PSEA focal point and have instituted a pillar-based approach to PSEA to ensure awareness AND response capacity within WHO and its implementing partners. These activities are further overseen by regional focal points. WHO also pursues and integrated approach by aligning GBV, PSEA and MHPSS to enable comprehensive response capacity. Finally, both hubs have developed and regularly update a risk matrix with specified mitigation measures. Business continuity plans are updated quarterly and WHO global has also rolled out readiness checklists to ensure offices are ready to respond to emergencies.

project_name: Provision of Lifesaving Emergency Nutrition and Recovery Response to IDPs and Host Communities in North Darfur, Sennar, RiverNile, RedSea, Al Jazirah and Blue Nile states
project_objective:
According to the 2024 humanitarian needs and response overview, the current conflict in Sudan has created massive displacement, with over 6.1 million people forced to leave their homes in search of safety. Of the 4.85 million people displaced internally, 54 percent are women and over half are children under 18 years of age .Sudan is among the top four countries in the world with the highest prevalence of global acute malnutrition (GAM), with an estimated 13.6 percent. The nutrition outlook is expected to deteriorate in 2024 due to ongoing conflict, food security decline, and compromised health and WASH services, and prolonged displacement.
Sudan is one of the top four hunger hotspots of highest concern globally with a third of the population soon becoming food insecure. Malnutrition rates among under-five children are among the highest in the world and are an increasing concern in all states for children and pregnant or lactating women, raising the risks of compromised immune systems, vulnerability to disease, and associated mortality.
A household survey conducted in El Fasher locality in North Darfur state in July 2023 revealed that 72% of the households struggled to access nutritious food for their consumption mainly due to lack of money and not having income sources and 93% of the households did not have diverse food intake (less than 4 food groups). Reasons given to explain difficulty in accessing food or difficulty in getting adequate and diverse diet included: lack of money (56%), insecurity due to the current conflict (28%), unavailable of food in the market (9%), and high food prices (7%). 69% of the households did not seek nutritional support or assistance for specific health conditions or deficiencies and 24% of household heads were not aware of the recommended breastfeeding practices for infants and young children. Malnutrition-related diagnosis mainly OTP/TSFP/SC accounted for only 6% among the different of diagnosis people sought at the health facilities.
RI will target and prioritize the 2024 nutrition response based on six areas: (i) Prioritizing the youngest and most vulnerable children with the highest mortality risk, (ii) Providing life-saving preventive and protective nutrition package, (iii) Treating SAM cases with medical complications, (iv) Treating SAM cases without medical complications among children under-five years, (v) Implementing non-food and food-based malnutrition prevention programs, and (iv) Generating evidence for planning, advocating for resources and decision-making. RI will improve access to nutrition care and services in 81 primary healthcare facilities (47 in ND, 12 in BN, 4 in Sennar, 4 in River Nile, 4 in Red Sea, and 10 in Al Jazirah). Through the proposed nutrition services, RI will build the capacity of 324 (M: 156 and F: 168) nutrition workers through formal and on-the-job training that will strengthen service delivery at both facility and community levels. Furthermore, RI will strengthen the referral mechanism and will ensure that complicated SAM have access to stabilization centers.
Through the proposed project, RI intends to reach 207,664 (M: 67,648 and F: 140,016) 7) and will provide quality nutrition lifesaving and recovery services to conflict- and natural disaster-affected IDPs and host communities in six localities in North Darfur (El Fasher - 52,539, Mellit - 19,225, El Tawisha – 7,886, Kalemindo– 3,094, Dar Al Salam – 5,757 and Al Malha – 27,575); four localities in Blue Nile (Al Rosaries - 5,620, Damazine - 4,794, Geissan – 5,720, Wad Almahi – 1,148); two localities in Al Jazirah (Wad Madani – 10,833 and South Al Jazirah – 11,176); two localities in Sennar (Sennar – 10,746 and Singa – 8,597), two localities in River Nile (Atbara – 5,970 and Shendi – 7,642) and two localities in Red Sea (Port Sudan – 10,985 and Suakin – 8,358).

project_name: Provision of  Emergency water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH)  assistance to conflict affected IDPs and host communities in North Darfur (ND), Blue Nile(BLN), Sennar(SN), Aj jazirah (AJ) ,River Nile and Red Sea States in Sudan.
project_objective:
According to the 2024 Humanitarian Needs and Response plan (HNRP), the humanitarian needs in Sudan are widespread and severe. As indicated by the  IMMAP situational analysis (2024), currently there are a total of 5.3 million people displaced inside Sudan. The current crisis is an addition of already existing inadequate WASH coverage, low investment in new facilities, high rate of non-functionality (25%), non-affordable water points, high level of open defecation and low hygiene awareness and practices. 
As per the WASH cluster severity scale most of the RI target localities in Blue Nile state (BLNS) are within severity 4 and above, while for ND, Sennar and Red sea states the target localities are within severity 3 and 4.   The IMMAP report, indicated that an estimated 7.4 million children lacked access to safe drinking water, putting them at risk of contracting waterborne diseases, which, alongside poor nutrition, can result in serious illness or death. As per the National MoH cholera report, the total number of cholera cases have surpassed 9,500 with a total of 264 deaths as of 13 Jan2024. The National Cholera Taskforce that was established in September assessed a number of WASH-related risk factors present in the affected areas, identifying the need for emergency WASH interventions and hygiene awareness campaigns (OCHA, 2023). 
This project aims to provide emergency WASH assistance   to 434,000beneficiaries (88,536women, 85,064 men, 132,804 girls, 127,596 boys) to address the scarcity of water supply, sanitation services and hygiene promotion for populations affected by armed conflicts and to contribute to the 2024 - WASH humanitarian Response Plan contributing to the revised 2024 strategic objective:SO1:  Provide safe, timely, principled and gender-responsive life-saving humanitarian assistance to the most vulnerable groups to reduce mortality and morbidity in areas with high severity of need or at risk of a further deterioration of critical humanitarian needs. The proposed RI’s  emergency response will be in line the 2024 HNRP strategic objectives  and  with the cluster priority, which focus on life saving  and will ensure restoration of WASH services through time. Essential WASH services will also be provided for the health and nutrition facilities. 

RI will aim at rehabilitating mal-functioning rather than constructing  new water facilities for utilizing the available resources effectively and reaching the targeted  IDPs and host  communities in a timely manner at the target locations. Renewable energy sources, like solarization of water yards, will be given priority during the phases, of project implementation in order to avail durable solutions and ensure continuous availability of safe water supply and reduction of  the operation/maintenance costs. Strengthening and capacity building of WASH staff and  the Water user committees (WUCs)will be part of the proposed interventions. 
By the end of the phase of project implementation, RI will provide operation and maintenance/rehabilitation support for 57water points (10 water yard rehabilitation including solarization, 21handpump rehabilitations and 26 water yards operation and maintenance support) for the targeted localities of ND, BLN, SN, AJ, River Nile and Red sea states. In addition, water provision through water trucking will be provided for a number of health and nutrition facilities based on needs and in the absence of other options. Overall a total of 165,500individuals will benefit from the water supply service,  21,720 people with the Sanitation activities, and 434,000 people (88,536women, 85,064 men, 132,804 girls, 127,596 boys) will be reached through hygiene promotion activities in the target localities of North Darfur,Blue nile, Sennar, AjJazirah, River nile and Red Sea states.

project_name: Enhancing Access to life saving Protection Services for At-Risk Women, Girls, Boys, and Men in Sudan
project_objective:
According to the 2024 HNRP, the protection environment in Sudan has grown increasingly dire,marked by a stark disregard of civilians’ safety and civilian infrastructure.This deterioration is linked to urban warfare in Khartoum,the spreading conflict in Darfur, complex fighting in South Kordofan, and ongoing strife in Blue Nile.Multiple joint assessments highlight pressing child protection needs, family separation, GBV, child exploitation and abuse and child recruitment;emotional trauma and psychological distress.Over 3,150 child rights violations and 165 cases of sexual violence against women and girls have been reported.The GBV AoR and service providers have received surging GBV cases including sexual violence against IDPs on transit and during looting of homes.The number of domestic violence cases is rising and sexual violence/exploitation as women and girls are displaced, in transit, in temporary shelters, or at border crossings waiting for visas and economic hardship due to increasing prices of basic goods including food, water, and fuel . RI will provide the following services to address identified needs:
General Protection:
RI will provide protection assistance, mental health and psychosocial support(MHPSS) including referrals and raise awareness on general protection issues targeting 11,094 individuals.294 project participants (100 girls,100 boys,50 women and 44 men) will be targeted with protection assistance; 400 adults (200 women and 200 men) with MHPSS through health facilities and 300(150 women and 150 men) referrals.Awareness raising will benefit 10,000 individuals (1500 girls,1500 boys,3500 men and 3500 women) while 100(50 men and 50 women) will be trained on protection and safe service delivery.1 community based network will be established to strengthen community linkages;protection monitoring through 5 focus groups and 5 protection needs assessments conducted.
Child Protection:
To address prevailing child protection issues,9660 children and caregivers will be targeted.Case management services including referrals will target  390(195 girls,195 boys) at-risk children,including unaccompanied and separated children,at-risk of or experiencing psychosocial distress,violence etc and those in need of alternative care.To address psychological needs of distressed children,structured and sustained MHPSS including mental health counseling will target 1945 children (973 girls and 972 boys).325 parents/caregivers (163 women,162 men) will access positive parenting skills.6900 individuals (1725 girls,1725 boys,1725 women and 1725 men) will receive Child Protection Awareness raising & Information Dissemination while 9 adults and children groups/committees supported to encourage active community participation.To strengthen and ensure a more predictable,accountable, and effective CP response,50 women and 50 men frontline staff will be trained on CPIE and case management.  
Gender Based Violence:
This intervention will target 7230 individuals with GBV services.1 Women & Girls safe space/ center  will provide psychosocial support, awareness raising and information sharing and adolescent girl’s sessions.10 women and 10 girls’ capacity will be strengthened through vocational skills and start-up capital;500 adolescent girls and 500 women reached with life skills and recreational activities.Specialized GBV response services will target 1000 women and girls (500 women and 500 girls) while 1800 dignity kits (900 adolescent girls,900 women) are distributed.To improve community knowledge on GBV,available services,referral pathways etc. awareness sessions will target 5,000 individuals (1000 girls,500 boys,3000 women and 500 men) including 4 public campaigns.To enhance community linkages and referrals,3 CBPNs will be supported.Capacity building will target 75 men and 75 women involved in GBV prevention;GBV mainstreaming (5 men and 5 women); and specialized GBV trainings for frontline staff (25 women and 25 men).1 GBV assessment conducted.

project_name: Integrated WASH preparedness and responses for reinforcement of resilience building across nutrition, health, food security-livelihood, and protection to both natural and manmade disaster affected communities through both rapid mobile and static presence across priority locations South Sudan and Abyei.
project_objective:
The recurrent instabilities in most parts of South Sudan both political and inter-communal conflicts, coupled with migration of refugees and returnees in addition to the effect of floods including the limited food security and livelihood opportunities result in the displacement of communities and the economic regression exerting much stress on already limited WASH services across South Sudan.
PAH experience in successfully implementing both static and rapid responses various sectors will use its strong WASH expertise to robustly respond with emergency lifesaving-assistance to vulnerable communities across South Sudan by improving access to portable water, sanitation services and the knowledge and capacity for the affected communities for a better wellbeing. 
PAH will prioritize the vulnerable people affected by high level of WASH vulnerability especially in locations faced with IPC levels 3, 4 and 5, displaced people due to a variety of factors,  returnees and host communities with over-stretched resources due to migration of IDPs, in locations with outbreaks waterborne disease such as cholera, HEV,  and where refugees and returnee refugees have settled or in transit to their resettlement destinations. To improve the access to clean and safe water for drinking, cooking and personal hygiene plus other domestic uses, PAH will conduct repair/rehabilitation and construction of water points mainly boreholes, water yards, shallow wells, rain water harvesting systems etc in the affected communities as well as in institutions especially nutrition and health facilities for integration of the response. PAH will prioritize sanitation at the institutional level, while at community level, PAH will encourage community participatory approach at community and household levels for sustainability as well as exit strategy. To enable a positive behaviour change of the affected population and the sustainability of the operation and maintenance of the WASH infrastructure, PAH will design a community led hygiene and health promotion messaging, combined with protection, health, nutrition and other cross-sectoral topics are integrated in the messaging. PAH will chose  from the affected population people who will be trained as hygiene promoters, water management committees, sanitation committees, pump mechanics etc and engage them within the community. 
PAH will ensure accountability to affected population  (AAP) is key in its programming by ensuring that the beneficiaries are aware of the services at all stages and can report complaints through established complaints and feedback committees established within their community. Recognizing the cross-cutting nature of WASH, PAH will integrate the WASH with  other sectors by providing dignity kits and NFIs, Protection mainstreaming etc to ensure that exploitation of the beneficiates especially the women and girls is minimized. 
PAH, were feasible, will implement flood resilient infrastructure construction, such as elevated platform boreholes, community latrines and will encourage construction of flood resilient household level latrines, with use of local materials.

project_name: MPC response for IDPs in NW Syria
project_objective:
Based on HNO 2024, now in its 13th year of crisis, Syria is grappling with a catastrophe of unprecedented magnitude, with new emergencies adding to existing crises and taking a heavy toll on the people living in Syria. Protracted displacement, economic decline, global inflation, escalation of hostilities, and the aftermath of the earthquakes that struck south-eastern Türkiye and northern Syria in February 2023 are some of the biggest challenges Syrians currently face.
The number of people in need of humanitarian response in Syria has increased from 15.3 million to 16.7 million since 2023. Overall, 268 out of 270 sub-districts are now classified as being under severe or extreme conditions. 
The main goal of the project is to deliver flexible humanitarian assistance (regular multi-purpose cash MPC) to the most vulnerable IDP people in the subdistricts Azaz and Afrin in Aleppo and Maarat Tamsrin in Idleb. It is planned to assist nearly 1500 HH (7500 Men, Women, Boys, and Girls) through multi-purpose cash assistance to cover their minimum survival needs. The cash value is planned to be $100 per Household (HH) per month for 6 rounds. 
The beneficiaries will be selected according to the need and vulnerability in coordination with civil authorities to reach the most vulnerable HHs and 100% verified by the MEAL team in the targeted areas based on the vulnerability and eligibility criteria, including displacement duration criteria, since the new IDPs are the most vulnerable groups to the shocks. Also, the project will prioritize the women-headed households and the households with children, disabilities, and pregnant and lactating women.
The financial service providers in the targeted area will be assessed and contracted for the redemption process. Market assessments will be conducted in the target areas. Considering the price of basic food commodities remains volatile. It is subject to speculation and disruptive events, specifically displacement; COVID-19 and Cholera have harmful and immediate consequences on the households’ economy and may result in reduced consumption and exclusion, requiring the delivery of unconditional/unrestricted cash assistance that gives households the agency to prioritize their most immediate needs. Therefore, the activity will help them to increase their food security, and their most urgent NFI and WASH needs while reducing negative coping strategies.
Market assessment will be conducted using tools approved by the Cash Working Group, where the capabilities and capacities of the market will be assessed in terms of material availability, accessibility, storage, price stability, quality of goods, cash availability, support for local products, and prevention of damage or inflation and to make sure the local markets are functioning and able to replenish stocks without causing a shortage in supply and to ensure all beneficiaries have good and equal accessibility to the different goods and services.
Accountability to beneficiaries’ is ensured through three main channels: (i) redress and grievance mechanisms; (ii) Post Distribution Monitoring Surveys (PDMS) and focused group discussions (FGDs) as needed; (iii) on-site monitoring activities. 
The SDI’s plan for the year 2025 is similar to the year 2024, as the activities will be similar to the general budget for 2024, with a focus on continuing the same activities and services provided.

project_name: Enhancing self-sufficiency of IDP households in several major crops in an organic and sustainable manner.
project_objective:
This project aims to enhance the food security of the affected men, women, boys and girls, with particular attention to PWDs, in Northwest Syria (NWS), as a part of and aligned with the objectives outlined in the Syrian Arab Republic Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) of 2024.

The humanitarian project, slated for implementation in 2024, aims to address the escalating food insecurity crisis in Syria, which, as outlined in FSA Sector HNO Chapter 2024, continues to affect an estimated 15.5 million people, representing 65% of the population. This dire situation is underscored by a comprehensive needs assessment encompassing over 42,000 households, revealing an alarming increase in food insecurity compared to previous years. Key findings highlight significant food needs, particularly in regions such as Idleb (73% estimated in need of food assistance) and Aleppo (58%). Throughout 2023, limited funding and resources led to a reduction in food assistance levels, exacerbating the plight of vulnerable households. The repercussions were evident in household consumption trends, with approximately 67% of the population experiencing insufficient consumption, as reported by the WFP Remote Monitoring System. Furthermore, soaring food prices placed immense strain on households' purchasing power, and trade and financial constraints have hindered agricultural productivity, perpetuating food insecurity. Agricultural production, particularly of staple crops like wheat, remains well below national needs due to various factors, including economic downturns, weather anomalies, and disruptions to supply chains. Natural disasters such as earthquakes and wildfires have exacerbated these challenges, further compromising food access and livelihoods, particularly in affected regions.

This humanitarian project will contribute to addressing those needs by prioritising the distribution of life-saving food assistance to vulnerable households, particularly those newly displaced in Jandairis, Afrin and Maarat Tamsrin subdistricts, which are of extreme severity of needs (score 4) and high PiN according to FSA PiN Severity - HNO 2024. 

SDI will aim to provide life-saving emergency food assistance to the newly displaced individuals, mostly women and children, with special attention to PWDs, including food baskets and Ready-to-Eat Rations (RTER)

The proposed activities include:

1- Provision of Food Baskets:
SDI aims to distribute food baskets to 2,000 households. The baskets will be meticulously designed in accordance with cluster recommendations. Each food basket, weighing 60 kilograms and providing about 1,600 kilocalories per person per day, is tailored to meet the nutritional needs of a family for one month.

2- Distribution of Ready-to-Eat Rations (RTER):
Additionally, SDI plans to distribute 3,000 Ready-to-Eat Rations (RTER) to households newly displaced in open areas or residing in vulnerable camps. Each RTER package, weighing 23.32 kilograms and offering 2,128 kilocalories, is intended to sustain a family of five members for five days.
SDI will directly execute these activities through its proficient field team stationed in Syria. The procurement and distribution of food baskets will be conducted with utmost efficiency to ensure a swift response to the urgent needs of the newly displaced population.

Regarding beneficiary selection, SDI will prioritize the most vulnerable households, irrespective of gender, based on eligibility criteria tailored for both food baskets and RTER distributions. These criteria encompass factors such as income level, household composition, and specific vulnerabilities such as pregnancy or lactation. SDI will continuously assess security conditions before and during project implementation to safeguard the well-being of field personnel, beneficiaries, suppliers, and all stakeholders involved. Mitigation strategies will include ongoing security evaluations and proactive risk avoidance measures.

This approach is informed by an analysis of the severity of needs using assessments and key indicators. The Food Security program by Bahar prioritizes time-sensitive interventions that not only address immediate needs but also lay the groundwork for sustainable recovery and a swift transition to long-term development.

Modality: In-kind assistance with ready-to-eat meals.

Indicative Value: Varied based on the type and quantity of agricultural inputs provided.

8. Coordination with Stokholders: Coordination with other humanitarian organizations involved in emergency response to ensure efficient targeting and avoid duplication of efforts.
Collaboration with the FSL Cluster and other humanitarian actors to ensure comprehensive coverage and avoid gaps in assistance.
 Coordination with local markets and vendors to ensure availability of essential food items and fair pricing.
Collaboration with agricultural extension services, farmer cooperatives, and other stakeholders involved in agricultural development to maximize impact and sustainability.

project_name: Provision of comprehensive food and agricultural support to the most vulnerable and affected population in NW Syria.
project_objective:
The project aims to support the resilience of communities through food security and agriculture Response in NW Syria to address the identified needs of the most vulnerable population of IDPs and Host Communities in NW Syria Aleppo The intervention will be designed in line with FSL Cluster guidelines, and the strategic objectives of the sector in HRP 2024 with considering the lessons learnt from similar projects that have been implemented by Bonyan.

Syria's humanitarian landscape in 2024 presents a grim picture, with 16.7 million individuals requiring assistance amidst ongoing crises. The devastating earthquake further compounded the situation, displacing hundreds of thousands, causing nearly 5,900 deaths, and injuring over 12,800 people. The crisis has spawned a relentless cycle of vulnerability, with a disproportionate effect on the most needy, including people with disabilities. The escalating cost of living, exemplified by the quadrupling price of food baskets over two years, underscores the acute need for food assistance and agricultural services, affecting 15.4 million people across the nation.

To address these needs, the project establishes a comprehensive assistance intervention targeting 24,500 individuals (11,000 men and 13,500 women). This multifaceted approach includes:

[1] daily distribution of bread bundles to ensure basic nutritional needs are met.
[2] Provision of food vouchers to offer flexibility in food choices and support local markets for 8 distribution rounds.
[3] Distributing of agricultural inputs for farmers 
[4] Establishment of income-generating activities, with a focus on vocational training for youth and women. This initiative aims to empower them to create sustainable businesses, contributing to economic resilience.
[5] Rehabilitation of critical infrastructure, related to bread supply chain and irrigation systems, to improve food production and distribution efficiencies.

Community engagement forms the backbone of the project's strategy. By establishing committees comprised of IDPs, host community members, agricultural association representatives, and local council members, the project ensures an inclusive and participatory approach to beneficiary selection and verification. The needs assessment conducted by SI in November 2023 in Tabqa and Markada provided a comprehensive understanding of the challenges faced by vulnerable communities in these areas.
In Tabqa, a strategic economic location in NES due to its hydroelectric dam, the assessment highlighted significant infrastructure damage resulting from past conflict, including destruction of public services such as electricity, water, sewage networks, schools, health facilities, and roads. Despite some improvements following market rehabilitation efforts, Tabqa still faces critical gaps, particularly in basic services. Furthermore, the assessment identified key economic challenges, including low income levels, lack of employment opportunities, and barriers to accessing financial resources for livelihood activities. The need for support in various sectors, such as dairy and cheese processing, corn drying, and silo rehabilitation, was emphasized by local authorities and stakeholders.
Similarly, in Markada, located in the south of Al-Hassake Governorate, economically, the assessment revealed the decline of poultry farming, a previously common practice in the area, due to the economic crisis and violence. While egg production could be a viable investment to address food security, limited resources hinder households from engaging in poultry farming. Furthermore, the assessment revealed decreased access to economic opportunities.
Overall, the needs assessment underscored the urgent need for infrastructure development, improved access to basic services, and support for livelihood activities to address the challenges faced by vulnerable communities in Tabqa and Markada.

project_name: Rehabilitation of educational and health facilities affected by the earthquake of February 2023 in Syria.
project_objective:
The action plan is based on recent needs assessments conducted by the organization with external consultants, other stakeholders, and cluster gap analysis reports. Primary data collection methods, including key informant interviews and household surveys, were triangulated with secondary data sources and field observations. Vulnerable groups such as children, the elderly, and people with disabilities were given special attention. The earthquake exacerbated challenges in education and health facilities across Northwest Syria. Pre-earthquake, attendance rates were 88%, but seismic damage has rendered 452 schools non-functional. Over 1 million school-aged children need education support, and more than 25,000 individuals require school rehabilitation. Health facilities also suffered, with 55 damaged, leading to a 28% increase in morbidity. Women, girls, and people with disabilities face barriers in accessing health services. the organization technical report highlights structural damages in preselected schools and health facilities, indicating compromised safety and functionality during seismic events. The action plan aims to address these urgent needs, focusing on rehabilitation and strategic planning to rebuild education and health infrastructure with a resilient approach.

The organization will support the restoration of the education and health systems in NWS, focusing primarily on facilities located in the districts of Harim, Idlib and Jisr Elshogur, in Idlib governorate as well as Jebel Saman in Aleppo governorate. the organization has pre-selected the areas of implementation based on critical needs of rehabilitation for educational and health facilities, for host communities and IDPs.
This project invests in rehabilitation and construction, and consequently has a large budget dedicated to rehabilitation of schools and health facilities as well as water supply and sanitation infrastructures. The Shelter Team will undertake the responsibility of preparing all pertinent documents, encompassing Bill of Quantities (BoQs), design drawings, and other essential paperwork. This team is already trained to develop designs suitable to a post-earthquake response. the organization would also engage an external consultant to conduct technical assessment of the EQ damaged buildings (moderate to heavy damage) and use the data generated to carry out the structural analysis of the buildings to assess the gaps in the existing structural system and produce a retrofitting design to address those gaps in accordance with the organization "Build Back Better" approach. The project will use contractors to carry out the construction/rehabilitation work, which will be supervised by the organization teams. The budget also includes provision of various protection mainstreaming equipments and furniture for the facilities
The risk analysis and contingency plan for the project involve identifying various risks and outlining mitigation measures. Risks include restricted physical access, technical limitations due to remote management, violence escalation, natural disasters, political influences, economic challenges such as increased material prices, and social issues like assistance duplication. the organization, confident in its regional experience, plans to monitor and adapt to the security situation, maintain transparent decision-making, and address economic fluctuations through existing agreements with suppliers. The contingency plan involves temporary closures or activity reductions in response to escalated violence, constant security monitoring, and engagement with local authorities. Assumptions for successful implementation include stable security conditions, unimpeded physical access, cooperation from local authorities, sustainable material prices, availability of construction materials, contractor compliance with recommended construction methods, absence of major natural disasters, and effective coordination to avoid aid duplication.

project_name: Réponse alimentaire et nutritionnelle aux populations affectées par la crise sécuritaire et alimentaire dans les régions de l’Est, du Nord, des Cascades et des Hauts Bassins.
project_objective: L’intervention a pour objectif de réduire l’insécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle des populations déplacées et résidentes affectées par la crise sécuritaire et alimentaire dans un contexte humanitaire dégradé. En effet, le contexte humanitaire du Burkina Faso connait une forte dégradation depuis la fin de l’année 2021 notamment avec l’apparition de nouvelles zones de conflit, l’augmentation des zones à accès difficile et la multiplication des attaques des Groupes d’Opposition Armés (GOA), obligeant le déplacement de 2,06 millions de personnes à l'intérieur du pays (CONASUR, mars 2023). Cette situation a accentué la vulnérabilité structurelle des ménages déjà très fragiles, caractérisée par la pauvreté et la récurrence des chocs et risques de catastrophes. Cela renforce la hausse des prix liée à la déstabilisation des marchés et à la baisse de la production agricole aboutissant à une inflation sans précédent. La perturbation de la conduite normale des activités génératrices de revenus, les difficultés d’approvisionnement des marchés et d’acheminement de l’assistance demeurent par endroit et limitent l’accès des ménages vulnérables aux services sociaux de base.  Les prix des céréales ont connu une baisse généralisée par rapport à l’année 2022 à la même période, mais restent en hausse par rapport à la moyenne quinquennale. A titre illustratif les prix du maïs et du sorgho ont respectivement connu une baisse d’au moins 13% et 15.19% par rapport à l’année passée. Comparés aux prix moyens des cinq dernières années, les prix sont en hausse d’au moins 27.94% pour le maïs et 35.78% pour le sorgho.   Sur le plan alimentaire, le disponible céréalier prévisionnel couvre les besoins de consommation de la population pour l’année 2023-2024 à hauteur de 99,6% et dégage un déficit brut de 81 099 tonnes. En considérant le solde import-export, l’excédent net se situe à 611 696 tonnes, soit un disponible prévisionnel apparent de 226 kg/habitant. Cependant, des disparités existent entre les régions et entre les ménages agricoles. Tous ces facteurs affectent la capacité des personnes à répondre à leurs besoins de base surtout alimentaire qui est identifié comme un besoin prioritaire par la majorité des ménages lors des déplacements ou pendant la période de soudure agricole. Ce projet vise à (i) atténuer les effets immédiats de l’insécurité alimentaire aiguë au sein des ménages les plus vulnérables des régions du Nord, de l’Est, des Hauts-Bassins et des Cascades à travers une assistance alimentaire, et (ii) reconstituer ou renforcer les moyens de subsistance des personnes affectées par le développement d’activité génératrice de revenus pour leur permettre un relèvement précoce et renforcer leur résilience à moyen et long terme. En parallèle, cette assistance sera optimisée avec la distribution de farine infantile aux enfants de 6-23 mois et de compléments alimentaires aux femmes enceintes et femmes allaitantes (FEFA) afin de maximiser l’impact positif du projet sur la situation nutritionnelle des ménages bénéficiaires. La modalité de l’assistance alimentaire privilégiée est le transfert monétaire et non restrictif via un système e-cash. L’assistance nutritionnelle sera assurée par une distribution en nature d’intrants nutritionnels qui seront acquis auprès de fournisseurs locaux. Par ailleurs, les appuis à la mise en œuvre d'activités génératrices de revenu (AGR) seront fournis soit en espèces ou en coupons aux ménages bénéficiaires de l'assistance alimentaire afin de leur offrir la flexibilité de faire un choix optimal des types d'actifs productifs qu’ils souhaiteraient acquérir.

project_name: Multi-purpose cash support to meet life basic needs among conflict-affected households (HHs) living in Northwest and North-central Syria
project_objective:
The initiative aims to fulfil its objectives by providing both multi-round and one-off emergency cash support to the most vulnerable households (HHs) in North Central Syria (NCS) and Northwest Syria (NWS). This approach is designed to assist displaced households and vulnerable communities, allowing them to address their immediate basic needs for food and non-food with dignity and flexibility. This support is critical in contributing to the overarching goal of the intervention, which focuses on saving lives by meeting urgent needs.

Syria Relief (SR) will assist 30,000 displaced individuals (5,000 HHs) across NWS and NCS by offering them a regular MPCA of $100 for eight rounds. Additionally, 60,000 individuals (or 10,000 HHs) will receive a one-off emergency MPCA of $150. This dual approach of regular and emergency MPCA grants beneficiaries the freedom to purchase necessary items from local markets, thereby addressing their basic needs for food and other essentials in a dignified manner. The allocation of funds for both types of assistance is based on the latest recommendations from the CWG, with the amounts and program design subject to adjustments according to monthly updates and price monitoring reports from REACH.

To ensure assistance reaches the most vulnerable HHs in NWS, the distribution process will incorporate registration and verification steps, utilizing a scoring system to identify and prioritize those in greatest need. The selection criteria will be set according to the harmonized vulnerability and eligibility criteria issued by the CWG.
