project_name: Garantizar supervivencia de niñas y niños con desnutrición aguda a través de identificación y tratamientos oportunos y cuidado nutricional y de salud integral materno infantil en Huehuetenango, Quiché,Alta Verapaz, Izabal en Guatemala
project_objective:
En los departamentos de Huehuetenango, Quiché, Alta Verapaz, Izabal convergen problemas nutricionales como el aumento de casos por desnutrición aguda pero también son departamentos golpeados por los fenomenos naturales. Para el 2024, el PMA prevé que Guatemala atraviese una situación de inseguridad alimentaria y malnutrición muy alarmante, como parte de los efectos del fenómeno del niño. Para principios de año, la población más vulnerable no habrá superado los efectos negativos residuales de 2023. El precio de una canasta básica de alimentos aumentó un 17% de noviembre de 2021 a noviembre de 2022, y los precios de los fertilizantes han aumentado en promedio, de noviembre de 2021 a noviembre de 2022, un 56%, afectando así fuertemente la economía de los hogares y la generación de ingresos de los pequeños productores.
A pesar de que el total de niñas y niños con desnutrición aguda reportados ha disminuido en 2022 comparado a 2021 (probablemente por la falta de identificación), el porcentaje de desnutrición aguda severa ha aumentado en Izabal 46.5% y Chiquimula 35.5%.  Esta situación es sumamente preocupante porque aumenta asimismo el riesgo de muerte por esta causa. El último análisis de la CIF estima que, debido a la tormenta tropical Julia y a anteriores perturbaciones climáticas, se espera que 3,2 millones de personas experimenten inseguridad alimentaria aguda (CIF 3+), incluidas 128.000 personas en fase de emergencia (CIF 4), durante el periodo comprendido entre octubre de 2022 y febrero de 2023,19 lo que supone un aumento sustancial respecto a los 2,5 millones de personas estimadas en el mismo periodo de 2021-2022. Se espera una tendencia similar para 2023 y 2024. Las previsiones muestran un aumento de la exposición a huracanes en la zona del Atlántico Norte, con un 60% de probabilidad de que la temporada de este año vuelva a ser superior a la media. En respuesta, se propone implementar acciones integrales de atención nutricional y salud oportuna a través de “brigadas integrales” que llegan hasta las comunidades más lejanas y donde la presencia de salud es muy limitada.  La pertinencia de esta Estrategia ha sido validada y ha probado ser efectiva desde 2018 en contexto de emergencias.  La Estrategia ha sido tan efectiva que ha logrado identificar y tratar oportunamente a niñas y niños afectados por desnutrición aguda que no habían sido detectados previamente por salud (hasta un 68%). Es un abordaje estandarizado y monitoreado que ha sido mejorado y complementado hasta que el día de hoy brindan atención integral a la niñez  (evaluación nutricional, tratamiento oportuno, suplementación con micronutrientes múltiples en polvo, zinc y vitamina A, desparasitación, consejería alrededor de los temas de la Ventana de los 1,000 días, vacunación) y a las mujeres en edad fértil incluyendo adolescentes, embarazadas y en período de lactancia (evaluación nutricional, suplementación con hierro y ácido fólico, vacunación y consejería).  Estas brigadas adicionalmente dejan formados “agentes de cambio” (líderes y lideresas formados en aspectos básicos para identificación oportuna de desnutrición aguda, signos de peligro, y alimentación infantil e higiene) para orientar a su comunidad.
El proyecto responde a los siguientes objetivos:

•	Identificar la población afectada por desnutrición aguda y brindar tratamiento inmediato
para salvar sus vidas.
•	Mejorar las competencias del personal de salud y otros actores locales para la atención
nutricional en emergencias
•	Brindar insumos necesarios para el cuidado nutricional
•	Fortalecer capacidades de líderes y lideresas comunitarias en la preparación y respuesta para la atención nutricional en emergencias
•	Activar sistemas de alerta temprana nutricional en la comunidad

project_name: Support for Humanitarian Logistics Services and Operations
project_objective:
Support the humanitarian community in implementing the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) 2024 in Burkina Faso and the clusters in implementing their actions, programs, and interventions throughout the year. A further escalation was observed in 2023, with a more significant toll on human lives and vulnerable populations with a massive increase in Hard-to-reach Areas (Sahel, North, Centre Nord, East, West, Cascades, Haut Bassin, and Southwest). The Logistics Cluster will coordinate all necessary efforts to deliver assistance to these areas where people are the most vulnerable. In 2024, humanitarian logistics actors (grouped in the Logistics Cluster and supported by UNHAS and The Logistics Cluster Lead Agency WFP) will aim to support humanitarian actors in implementing their actions, programs, and interventions. 
In terms of Coordination, the cluster will undertake, in collaboration with key partners, the following coordination activities: 
- At the national level, the cluster will maintain representation in decision-making forums, including the Intercluster Coordination Group, CMCoord, Access Working Group, etc., and conduct bi-monthly coordination meetings.
- At the regional level, the Logistics Cluster will participate in the meetings of the regional ICCGs and will be in the main hubs of Ouahigouya, Kaya, Dori, and Fada. Information Management The logistics cluster will continue to ensure the provision of information on operational issues for storage and transport) and (ii) access issues (provision of access constraint maps and ad hoc recommendations if necessary). Other tools will be provided, such as SitReps, contact lists, infrastructure, and logistics services assessments. The logistics cluster has begun to establish five operational hubs in Ouagadougou, Ouahigouya, Kaya, Dori, and Fada. In addition, it will prioritize its resources in 2023 and 2024 to support the efforts of partners who target the most affected populations. 
- Temporary storage: the logistics cluster offers a temporary storage service in the capital and the regions, open to all humanitarian organizations in Ouagadougou, Ouahigouya, Kaya, Dori, and Fada. In the regions and remote areas, the Logistics Cluster will facilitate the deployment of Mobile Storage Units (MSUs) or smaller units to benefit partners who request and manage them.
- Road transport Subject to physical and safe accessibility, the logistics cluster will also be able to coordinate/consolidate partners' requests for humanitarian cargo and facilitate access to a dedicated fleet of trucks operationalized by WFP and the private sector to support partners' projects’ implementation. 
- Inter-agency humanitarian cargo to Hard-to-Reach Areas. A system for providing logistics services will be set up between the Logistics Cluster and the humanitarian actors who will use the service, which will include a cost-recovery procedure. 
–The Logistics Cluster coordinates the delivery – by air – of humanitarian aid to areas that are difficult to access for certain items/sectors identified as priorities: Water, Hygiene and Sanitation, Food Security, Shelter, Health, and Nutrition. Helicopters, operated by UNHAS, carry out rotations to priority geographical areas. The defined areas served and the goods that can be chartered are established based on priorities defined by the Humanitarian Country Team and the Intercluster Coordination Group.
Training The Logistics Cluster will facilitate access to training aimed at developing the capacities of logisticians present in Burkina Faso in various fields of humanitarian logistics (supply, warehouse and inventory management, transport, integrated management of humanitarian corridors, etc.). In addition, it is essential to increase the number of logisticians experienced in emergency response and humanitarian coordination mechanisms.

project_name: Línea de Contacto Inter-Agencial
project_objective:
La operación de Venezuela ha avanzado en el enfoque colectivo de AAP, con la incorporación de un Marco Colectivo de AAP aprobado por el Equipo Humanitario de País (HCT) en septiembre de 2020 y revisado en julio de 2023, para orientar a los actores humanitarios y de desarrollo sobre la adopción del enfoque de AAP en las intervenciones realizadas, que busca poner a las personas al centro. 

Como parte de los compromisos de AAP adoptados en Venezuela, en 2021 se estableció una Línea de Contacto Interagencial, como parte una iniciativa conjunta de varias Agencias del Sistema de Naciones Unidas en Veneuzela, con la finalidad de establecer un mecanismo colectivo de retroalimentación comunitaria seguro, accesible, y confidencial, que ha sido reconocida como una de las pocas respuestas  

Basados en los resultados de la prueba piloto, se amplió el proyecto a una cobertura nacional para contribuir a la mejora de la respuesta humanitaria basada en una mejor comprensión de las necesidades de la población vulnerable (personas con discapacidad, comunidades indígenas, niños y adolescentes, personas mayores, comunidad LGBTIQ+ y mujeres). Asimismo, en estrecha colaboración con la Coordinadora de la Red de Prevención contra la Explotación y Abusos sexuales (PEAS), la Línea de Contacto ha permitido a la comunidad humanitaria en Venezuela cumplir con sus responsabilidades y compromisos hacia PEAS, garantizando la promoción en las comunidades y el acceso a un mecanismo de reporte para la atención prioritaria de estos casos, contando con el respaldo del Equipo Humanitario de País, el Grupo de Trabajo de AAP, el Grupo-Interclúster, la Red PEAS y la Red de Igualdad de Género. 

Actualmente, la LDC funciona de lunes a sábado de 8:00 a 17:45 a través de varios canales (llamadas telefónicas gratuitas, WhatsApp, mensajes de texto, correo electrónico y la atención personalizada a través de un formulario) donde las personas pueden: expresar sus opiniones, sugerencias y contar su experiencia con la asistencia; aclarar dudas o solicitar más información sobre la asistencia humanitaria y reportar o alertar sobre comportamientos inapropiados de los y las trabajadoras humanitarias; con la finalidad de garantizar una respuesta más efectiva y eficiente, basada en las necesidades y experiencia de las personas afectadas.

project_name: Livelihoods, Resilience and Social Protection in Syria, 2024-2025
project_objective:
A decade-long crisis in Syria has reversed human development, impoverished the lives and livelihoods of Syrian families, and eroded the resilience of vulnerable communities. Syria has also been experiencing an unprecedented economic downturn since 2019, with soaring inflation and a devaluation in the value of the Syrian pound.

The Syrian crisis is estimated to have resulted in physical capital destruction, including productive assets and communal infrastructure. The result has been a near-total collapse of food systems in many rural and urban areas, leading to food insecurity and food assistance dependency. The HNO estimates that more than 16.7 million people are in need. Due to earthquake 170,000 workers lost their jobs directly affecting the livelihoods of 154,000 HH and over 725,000 individuals.

In response and to reduce the high levels of dependency from food assistance, WFP implements a range of projects designed to create livelihoods and reconstitute the resilience of households, communities, and food systems. These efforts contribute to Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 2 (Zero Hunger), in addition to having significant positive multiplier effects towards SDGs 1 (no poverty), 4 (quality education), and 5 (gender equality).

In line with the HRP Strategic Outcomes 1, 2 and 3 and in coordination with the FSA and ERL sectors, WFP identifies the need of enhancing resilience and early recovery to play a significant role in addressing the protracted crisis and food insecurity situation in Syria. In 2024-25 WFP will be scaling up the activities in SO 03 of the HRP. In fact resilience-building become a crucial aspect to enable vulnerable smallholder farmers and livestock keepers become self-reliant through the improvement of livelihood assets, rehabilitation of irrigation systems and other community assets, restoration and enhancement of the national bread value chain.

The WFP Livelihoods Strategy focuses on early recovery interventions as necessary tools to relieve the pressure from emergency food interventions and prevent households and communities currently at risk to fall further into food insecurity. The WFP Strategy has 4 pillars: 1: Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) through, a) Provision of household and group-based productive assets; and b) Rehabilitation of agrarian community assets. 2: Food Assistance for Training (FFT) through human capital development. 3: Market Access Support via Retail Sector Rehabilitation, with a specific focus on the wheat-to-bread value chain. 4: Social Transfer/Basic Income via Financial Inclusion and social transfers.

WFP plans to support 200,000 beneficiaries (40,000 HHs) in 2024-25, with livelihoods and resilience activities. 80% of the beneficiaries are expected to be the users of the rehabilitated assets, while the remaining caseload will be assisted with households’ level complementary activities, including Food Assistance for Assets (FFA), Food Assistance for Training (FFT), both done through food vouchers and vouchers, as well as other livelihoods and income-generating activities.

The long-term overarching goal is to enhance the food security of Syrian communities and enable planning a long-term reduction of food assistance needs in the country. In the rollout of this approach, WFP will closely coordinate with other UN agencies such as FAO and UNDP, as well as with the FAS and ERL sectors. In particular, despite directly reporting to FAS, WFP will foster complementarities with ERL.

WFP plans its activities using the Three-Pronged Approach (3PA) to define appropriate interventions, accurate targeting, and geographical coherence. The tools are also important to minimize exclusion errors and to reduce the risk of exacerbating existing conflicts, by ensuring extensive dialogue with communities and other stakeholders.

The present project is expected to contribute to the reduction of food insecurity by restoring the community resilience and by rehabilitating disrupted value chains.

project_name: Empowering Adolescent girls, women and vulnerable communities to prevent and responds to Gender Based Violence
project_objective:
This is for twelve months’ project and will be implemented in Awerial, Pibor, Yei, Lainya, Kajokeji, Renk, Malakal, Mayiandit, Rubkona, Leer and Yirol East counties designed to empower Adolescent girls, young women, women, men and vulnerable community groups in preventing and responding to GBV risks.
The intervention will specifically target to empower adolescent girls, young women, Adolescent women and groups with special needs to have knowledge, information, skills and enhance their resilience capacity to GBV risks and improve GBV support-seeking behavior for survivors. The intervention will also target community supportive structures power holders: community leaders, religious leaders, parents, community social workers, health workers, police officers, government leaders, and teachers to take active measures to prevent GBV. The project will implement both prevention and response actions through capacity building of rights holders and groups at risk mainly: Adolescent girls, Young women, UASC, children and adolescents with disabilities who are disproportionally more impacted and at high risks of facing violence, neglect and exploitation including family-separation. 

The project will use gender transformative approaches to provide gender and age-appropriate and tailored support for adolescent girls, vulnerable women, UASC, child mothers, survivors of GBV among the returnees and arriving returnees and work with men and boys through community dialogues, social behavior changes Communication and advocacy approaches and community-driven harm prevention approaches. 
The project will use participatory approaches to create awareness in the community on the GBV effect and prevention of harmful practices targeting 24000 people in 10 Counties (8000 girls, 7000 boys,5000 females and 4000 men, disabilities inclusive). The awareness sessions aim to address the root causes of abuse including GBV risks such as inequality in the distribution of power and resources, harmful practices and under-representation of women and girls' decision-making and leadership opportunities. The community mobilization and engagement approach will integrate social behavior change models to empower girls, boys, men, and women for gender socialization and positive masculinity and community actions renouncing harmful practices and GBV risks to adolescent girls, women, and persons with disabilities using the SASA approach.
 Conduct mapping and update the GBV referrals and disseminate the information on the referral for the community to be aware of GBV services in the area. Conduct mapping and dissemination of GBV referral pathways in collaboration with adolescents groups,  community women groups/women-led organizations and youth groups , safeguarding risks mitigation, and referral pathways including in partnership with adolescents and young people (6 youth groups): The project will engage young people in safety audits and support them to conduct community mappings to identify community-based GBV risks and vulnerabilities also working together to identify ways to prevent and mitigate GBV risks at the community level, updating of existing referral pathways and disseminate them in schools, communities and community spaces. The intervention will facilitate a functional GBV referral pathway with stakeholders, youth and women-led organizations to upscale access to GBV case management, MHPS and capacity building of social workers. 
Provide Capacity building on life skills training for adolescent girls and boys at risk of, and survivors of GBV, in school and out-of-school adolescents (10-19 years) 16000 adolescent girls and 14000 boys on life skills and GBV prevention using PALS and Champion of change models for empowering adolescent girls and boys on gender equality, prevention of GBV, Child marriage, MHM support them to stay safe and adopt healthy behavior, the Champion of Change approach will promote positive masculinity and meaningful engagement of men and boys.

project_name: Strengthening child protection prevention and response mechanism through enhancing community-based child protection and protective environment to protect and safeguard children in the Rohingya population.
project_objective:
In 2024, IOM's Child Protection (CP) programming is dedicated to proactively addressing and preventing child protection issues while empowering vulnerable children, parents, and caregivers in Camps 9 and 20. This aligns with resolutions from the 2022 and 2023 CP Sub-Sector rationalization processes. Objectives include enhancing Community-based CP (CBCP), cultivating inter-generational connections, and promoting positive behavioral changes. To achieve this, IOM aims to fortify CBCP at the camp block level, empowering the community to safeguard children. IOM supports adolescent groups, fostering skills and awareness for effective child protection.

Importantly, IOM provides specialized child protection services, including case management, structured activities in child-friendly spaces, and outreach at the block level, with a focus on the needs of children with disabilities, as well as those caring for family members, and young mothers. IOM’s case management prioritizes the needs of each child and their family, ensuring that issues are systematically tackled with a focus on the child's best interest, to mitigate and respond to interconnected risks and vulnerabilities leading to protection violations. IOM’s Psycho-Social Support (PSS) emphasizes education that aims to preserve Rohingya heritage and encourage inter-generational dialogue. Parents and caregivers receive PSS and positive parenting support through facilitated group discussions based on evidence-based curricula involving both adults and children/adolescents. IOM maintains its commitment to supporting child survivors of gender-based violence (GBV) and trafficking in the camps through both direct implementation and through partner organizations that work with other IOM units specializing in legal interventions.

IOM works with the government, including the Office of the Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commissioner (RRRC) and Camp in Charge (CiC), and offers training to law enforcement agencies like the Armed Police Battalion (APBN) to mainstream child protection. IOM’s programming also adopts a comprehensive multi-sectoral approach and leverages community-based initiatives that prioritize inclusivity across age, gender, disability, and other dimensions of diversity. IOM’s CP team works closely with involving other IOM units, such as Health/Mental Health, Shelter, WASH, Site Management/Communication with Communities (CwC), and Social Cohesion to ensure the incorporation of child protection, child safeguarding, and considerations of age, gender, and disability throughout the programming, along with disaster preparedness and emergency response coordination.  By intertwining strategic objectives with community engagement, IOM strives to create a robust and sustainable framework for child protection in the specified camps.

Discussed more below, to ensure accountability to the affected population, IOM establishes feedback mechanisms, regularly consults with beneficiaries, and has dedicated officers and champions focused on preventing and addressing Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA) issues among beneficiaries.

IOM coordinates all activities with the CPSS, of which it is an active member.  IOM is also an active member of the Protection Sector.  We co-chair the Anti-Trafficking Working Group and have actively worked to ensure that trafficking issues affecting children are properly being understood and addressed. We are a technical member of the Age and Disability TWG, where again we will be working to ensure that CP issues are addressed and supported for the full response.  We are also an active member of the Gender Diverse Population Working Group and are committed to supporting children of diverse SOGIGESC.

project_name: Assistance to Refugees
project_objective:
The deteriorating socio-economic, political and security situation witnessed in Sudan since 15 April 2023 has resulted in unprecedented levels of humanitarian needs, including those of refugees. In response, UNHCR aims to support refugees, asylum-seekers, and other persons of concern across Sudan in several different sectors including general protection, child protection, GBV, education, health and nutrition, shelter/NFI, energy and environment, food security and livelihoods, as well as WASH. UNHCR will work with a wide range of implementing partners, including government ministries and agencies, UN agencies, national NGOs and international NGOs. 

UNHCR’s interventions are aimed at realizing rights-based and equal access to services and sustainable solutions for PoC to ensure they have an improved quality of life and security regardless of their nationality or where they live. Through its interventions UNHCR will continue to maintain focus on coordination and collaboration with other entities to deliver quality, AGD sensitive and evidence-based programming informed by monitoring and needs assessments, aimed at addressing priority needs, mitigating protection risks and reducing vulnerabilities. UNHCR will also strengthen efforts to achieve the inclusion of PoCs in national systems and development programs through advocacy, capacity building of national institutions, coordination, inclusive partnerships, and joint and/or complementary programming.

Further, UNHCR’s interventions aim to improve the protection environment for refugees and asylum-seekers in key areas that contribute to an environment where duty bearers are empowered to effectively fulfil their obligations and, refugees, asylum seekers and stateless persons enjoy their rights without discrimination. Sustaining a strong protection environment with effective responses to protection risks, including through empowerment of communities to mitigate protection risks, can strengthen their resilience and engagement in peaceful coexistence with host populations.

GoS capacity to effectively conduct continuous registration and documentation of refugees, including the provision of refugee identity cards will continue to be supported. UNHCR support to the GoS to strengthen civil documentation and legal identity for PoCs will be enhanced to prevent and reduce the risks of statelessness. In furtherance of the global CBI policy, UNHCR will continue to explore and expand the use of CBI as a programmatic response modality for delivering assistance to populations of concern.

project_name: Insulin and Renal Dialysis Kits For Sudan
project_objective:
The aim of this project is to sustain continues supply of Insulin and Adult Heamodialysis kits to avoid preventable mortality among diabetics and renal failure patients. 
UNDP has been procuring those two life saving items for Sudan National Medical Supplies Fund since 2017 through funds provided by the government. Since war erupted in Sudan, funding from the government was irregular resulting in interrupted supply and frequent stock outs of the two items. This was associated with plenty of preventable mortality. 
NMSF annual expenditure on insulin is around USD5.01 million and Adult dialysis kits is USD13.1Million. Both items are subsidized by the government to patients. 
Through this project, UNDP request partial funding to support procuring Insulin and Adult Heamodialysis kits so as to assure continues supply and prevent deaths related to stock out.

project_name: Emmergency Food Security and Livelihood Support for Crises-affected and Vulnerable Populations in Sudan.
project_objective:
The deadly conflict between Sudan Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) which erupted on April 15, has further exacerbated the already precarious situation in Sudan, putting millions of lives and livelihoods in danger. According to the 2024 Humanitarian Response Plan, 24.8 million people – or every second person in Sudan – will need humanitarian assistance. While this overall figure remains equivalent to that estimated in 2023, the severity of needs has increased. A “catastrophic” severity of needs has now been observed in 17 localities (in comparison to 14 localities estimated in May 2023). – almost half of which are in the Darfur region. 
As a result, some 20.3 million Sudanese (ie 42% of Sudan’s population) are now experiencing high levels of food insecurity of IPC Phase 3+ (crisis and above), driven by conflict and displacement across several states particularly in Khartoum, and the Darfur and the Kordofan regions. The conflict is also affecting the relatively stable eastern and northern states as communities are hosting high numbers of IDPs. The most severe impacts on household livelihoods and acute food insecurity continue to prevail in conflict hotspot urban areas experiencing heavy fighting, as well as in areas hosting high numbers of IDPs. In most rural areas, the impact of the conflict continues to be more indirect as insecurity along trade routes is reducing trade flows, input supplies and causing prices to rise above seasonal levels, thereby negatively affecting household access to staple foods and related commodities at a time when reliance on market purchases is typically high. 

The situation is also compounded by climate shocks and hazards and economic down-turns/crises manifested due to subsidy withdrawals, devaluation, and inflation. The conflict has triggered a large-scale displacement of 7.6 million people across the country, according to OCHA. 
The situation has compromised the food and livelihood security of the most vulnerable and threaten to worsen the conflict dynamics. Apart from growing criminality and insecurity in conflict-affected areas, unprecedented spike in acute food insecurity has been induced by previous dry spells and erratic rains, high price inflation for food, fuel and other commodities, floods, and persistent disease outbreaks. 
According to the HRP 20024, available evidence suggests a correlation between conflict intensity and the levels of severity and prevalence of food insecurity. The highest levels of severity and prevalence of food insecurity are reported where the conflict is more intense, namely in the Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan regions and Khartoum State. The large-scale displacement and extensive disruption to agricultural production are likely to significantly hamper the seasonal improvement in the food security outlook period between November 2023 and April 2024.

This project will provide critical life saving and life sustaining food security and livelihoods assistance to over   469,900.00 (of which 30% women, 30% men, 20% girls 20% 2,850 boys). These include 40% vulnerable host community members: 40% IDPs and 20% refugees and impacting other groups of concern including returnees. The overall objective of the project is to save lives by protecting the food and livelihood security of both displaced population and vulnerable host community member across 13 States in Sudan. It will focus on emergency agricultural support, livestock Support, livelihood cash. Skills development and income generation, support using Cash for Work modality.

project_name: Assistance multisectorielle d’urgence aux personnes déplacées internes et aux communautés hôtes dans les région du centre et du nord du Mali.
project_objective:
En décembre 2022, la ville de Ménaka comptait 30,928 personnes déplacées internes (PDI) réparties sur 23 sites. Selon les autorités locales, 36,752 personnes sont arrivées à Ménaka entre janvier et fin mars 2023 et près de 1,969 ménages sont arrivés en avril 2023 après la prise de contrôle du Cercle de Tindermène (région de Ménaka) par l'EIGS. Pour répondre aux besoins urgents et vitaux des populations déplacées et des communautés hôtes de Ménaka, IRC propose une réponse multisectorielle en assistance alimentaire, eau, hygiène et assainissement (EHA), éducation, protection et violences basées sur le genre (VBG). 
Pour renforcer la résilience communautaire, IRC soutiendra le développement d´activités maraichères et de petit élevage au profit de 500 personnes en situation de vulnérabilité. L´amélioration des conditions d´accès à l´eau et à l´hygiène sur les sites de déplacés sera couverte au travers de la réalisation de latrines semi-durables, point d´eau et la distribution d´articles ménagers essentiels (AME/NFI). Le projet prendra aussi en compte les besoins en éducation en urgence au profit des enfants déplacés et ceux des communautés hôtes au travers de la mise en place d´espaces temporaires d ´apprentissage (EAT), la fourniture de kits scolaires et la dispense de formations aux enseignants sur les thématiques transversales, y compris l´appui psychosocial, essentiel pour mitiger les effets dévastateurs du conflit armé sur la santé mentale des enfants. La couverture des besoins en protection sera assurée au travers du volet prévention, de l ´identification des survivantes de VBG y compris d’autres cas de protection au référencement. IRC propose la mise en œuvre de l’approche ‘’Girl Shine’’, approche innovante visant à l´empowerment féminin et la réduction des VBG envers les femmes et les adolescentes. 
Cette réponse sera complétée et renforcée par 3 projets multisectoriels, couvrant la commune de Ménaka, en cours de mise en œuvre par IRC (1 projet BHA et 2 projets ECHO), permettant une couverture des besoins plus large et complète. Ceci permettra une complémentarité géographique et programmatique. La réponse en éducation en urgence sera faite en complémentarité avec le projet ECHO, ce qui permettra d´optimiser l´utilisation des ressources et d´augmenter les capacités de réponse. Le volet assistance d ´urgence en réponse aux besoins alimentaires immédiats des populations déplacées (RRM et post RRM) présents sur le projet BHA, complètera le soutien aux moyens d’existence proposés sur le projet OCHA ici présenté. De même, sur le volet protection, les cas de protection détectés sur le projet OCHA seront référés sur le projet BHA qui dispose d´un volet réponse (le référencement sera aussi fait des cas de VBG du projet BHA au projet OCHA. Toujours dans un souci de complémentarité, la couverture des besoins urgents en santé sera assurée sur le projet ECHO. La proposition ici présentée sera mise en œuvre en partenariat avec l´ONG Cabinet de Recherches Actions pour le Développement Endogène (Crade), structure ayant un très bon ancrage communautaire dans la région de Ménaka et bénéficiant de la confiance des communautés. Présent à Ménaka depuis 2013, et bénéficiant d´une bonne expertise technique programmatique, CRADE interviendra dans l´ensemble des secteurs proposés.

project_name: Appui intégré en sécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle, EHA et protection pour l'amélioration de l'accès sécurisé à l'assistance humanitaire, pour les femmes, les hommes, les filles et les garçons des sites de déplacés, dans les quartiers de retour et hôtes d’Ansongo et Gao au Mali
